judges: Amal Ranaraja, J. | B. Sasi Mahendran, J.
offence_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The appellant was indicted in the High Court of Anuradhapura for murdering Wedhahenalage Premadasage on or about 30 May 2013 at Anuradhapura. A neighbour (PW02) observed the appellant assaulting the deceased with his hands and heard him utter words suggesting an intention to kill gradually, and later another witness (PW04) saw the deceased injured in the appellant’s house before transporting him to hospital with the appellant and a third person. The deceased died the next day while receiving in-patient treatment, and the post-mortem revealed multiple blunt-force injuries to the head and chest, including fractures and intracranial haemorrhages. The High Court convicted the appellant of murder and sentenced him to death, leading to this appeal.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court of Anuradhapura convicted the appellant of murder under section 296 of the Penal Code based on the evidence of assault, surrounding circumstances, and medical findings. The court inferred that the appellant was responsible for the fatal injuries sustained by the deceased. It accordingly imposed the mandatory sentence of death.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: On appeal, the defence argued that the conviction was based on inadequate circumstantial evidence which did not justify the inference that the appellant was the killer. It was contended that the trial judge failed to recognise and properly apply the principles governing circumstantial evidence, particularly by not excluding the reasonable possibility of a third party committing the offence. The appellant also contended that the prosecution did not establish a murderous intention beyond reasonable doubt. These alleged errors were characterised as errors in law and evaluation of evidence.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Prosecution case is based on circumstantial evidence and the items of circumstantial evidence are insufficient to draw an adverse inference that the appellant committed the murder. | The learned High Court Judge failed to identify and treat the case as one of circumstantial evidence and misapplied the legal principles applicable to such cases. | The prosecution failed to exclude the possibility that a third party, particularly the third individual seen with the appellant and the deceased, may have committed the offence, thereby creating reasonable doubt. | The prosecution failed to prove murderous intention beyond reasonable doubt, so the appellant should not have been convicted of murder.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analysed PW02’s eyewitness account, noting that she saw only limited assaults by hand on the face and arm but did not see blows to the head or chest or stamping while the deceased was on the ground. Medical evidence from the Judicial Medical Officer described extensive injuries, including fractures of ribs, hyoid and thyroid cartilage, and intracranial haemorrhages, likely caused by blunt-force assault with hands and feet, which the court found could not be attributed to the limited acts described by PW02. PW04’s evidence about a third individual at the scene and the absence of evidence excluding that person as the assailant led the court to conclude that the chain of circumstantial evidence was incomplete and compatible with the appellant’s innocence.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal held that the proven facts did not exclude the reasonable possibility that a third person inflicted the fatal injuries, and that the circumstantial evidence was consistent with both guilt and innocence. Applying established principles, it found that suspicious circumstances and incomplete inferences could not sustain a conviction and that any doubt must operate in favour of the appellant.
defence_version_summary: The appellant’s position was that he had no connection with the circumstances surrounding the deceased’s death and denied responsibility for the fatal injuries. There is no indication that he relied on an alibi or called defence witnesses; his stance appears to have been a general denial. The Court of Appeal found that this denial could not be rejected in light of the prosecution’s failure to exclude a reasonable hypothesis of innocence, particularly the potential role of the third individual seen with the deceased.
legal_errors_description: The Court of Appeal found that the High Court had erred in treating the case as if it were based on direct proof rather than circumstantial evidence and failed to apply the strict legal tests governing convictions based solely on circumstantial evidence. It held that the trial judge did not adequately consider the possibility of a third party committing the offence and effectively convicted the appellant on suspicion rather than proof beyond reasonable doubt.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal emphasised that this was a purely circumstantial case and carefully scrutinised whether the proven facts were consistent only with the appellant’s guilt and inconsistent with any reasonable hypothesis of innocence. It highlighted that PW02’s account of the assaults did not explain the severe internal injuries described by the JMO and that the presence of a third individual with the appellant and the injured deceased raised a reasonable possibility that someone else inflicted the fatal injuries. Relying on established precedent, the court held that suspicion, however strong, cannot substitute for proof and that the prosecution had not discharged its burden to exclude other reasonable explanations. Considering the long lapse of time since the offence and the unreliability of proceeding further, it declined to order a retrial, set aside the conviction and sentence, and acquitted the appellant.
brief_judgment_file_summary: This Court of Appeal judgment concerns an appeal against a High Court conviction and death sentence for murder under section 296 of the Penal Code arising from the death of Wedhahenalage Premadasage in May 2013 at Anuradhapura. The appellate court re-analysed the circumstantial evidence, including a neighbour’s limited eyewitness account, the presence of a third person, and detailed medical findings of multiple blunt-force injuries, and concluded that the evidence did not exclude the reasonable possibility that someone other than the appellant inflicted the fatal injuries. Applying well-established principles on circumstantial evidence, it held that the conviction was based on suspicion and that the prosecution had failed to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt. Given the twelve-year lapse since the offence and the evidential deficiencies, the Court set aside the conviction and death sentence, refused to order a retrial, and acquitted the appellant.
defence_counsel: Amila Palliyage with Sandeepani Wijesooriya, Savani Udugampola, Subaj De Silva, Lakitha Wakishta Arachchi
cause_of_death_exact_text: Death was due to multiple injuries sustained to the head and chest, likely resulting from an assault with blunt objects, most probably involving hands and feet.
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court treated the available evidence as sufficient to attribute all relevant injuries and the resulting death to the appellant and convicted him of murder. The Court of Appeal criticised this approach for failing to recognise the case as one based purely on circumstantial evidence and for not applying the rigorous standards required in such cases. It held that the High Court had overlooked the significance of the third person’s presence and the mismatch between PW02’s observations and the extensive internal injuries, thereby arriving at a conviction unsupported by proof beyond reasonable doubt.
precedents_cited_list: Munirathne And Others vs. The State – 2001 2 SLR 382 | The Queen vs. M. G. Sumanasena – (citation referred via Munirathne, exact page not fully specified) | Bandara Deegahawathura vs. Attorney General – CA No. 61/2001 decided on 02.08.2005 | King vs. Abeywickrama – 44 NLR 254 | King vs. Appuhamy – 46 NLR 128 | Podisingho vs. King – 53 NLR 49 | Emperor vs. Browning – (1917) 18 Cr. L.J. 482 | Queen vs. G. K. Jayasinghe – 69 NLR 314
standard_of_review_applied: Review for misapplication of principles governing circumstantial evidence, failure to exclude reasonable hypotheses of innocence, and conviction based on suspicion rather than proof beyond reasonable doubt.
final_charge_after_appeal: Murder under section 296 of the Penal Code (charge quashed on acquittal)

judges: B. Sasi Mahendran | Amal Ranaraja
offence_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The accused, known as Manju, was charged with murdering Jawahir Mohamed Amir on 09.09.2014 by inflicting multiple cut injuries with a manna knife. The seriously injured deceased was transported in a three-wheeler and made statements to PW1 and PW8 identifying Manju as his assailant before being taken first to Marawila Hospital and then to the Colombo General Hospital, where he later died. Police later arrested the accused the same day while he was attempting to flee with a blood-stained manna knife, which the Government Analyst confirmed was stained with human blood.
evidence_type_primary: Dying declarations conveyed through eyewitness testimony (PW1 and PW8)
evidence_type_secondary: Medical evidence, expert opinion, and recovery of a blood-stained manna knife with human blood
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court of Chilaw convicted the accused of murder under Section 296 of the Penal Code for causing fatal cut injuries to the deceased. Relying primarily on the deceased's dying declarations and corroborative medical and circumstantial evidence, the court found that the prosecution had proved the charge beyond reasonable doubt and imposed the mandatory death sentence.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant contended that the High Court failed properly to evaluate the evidence, particularly by treating PW8 as a credible witness despite inconsistencies and by accepting PW1's identification based on the deceased's statement. He argued that the trial judge misapplied established legal principles governing dying declarations and circumstantial evidence, and erred in concluding that the prosecution had proved its case beyond reasonable doubt. It was also alleged that the judgment was merely a recital of the evidence without a proper analysis.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: PW8's evidence was inconsistent and he should not have been treated as a credible witness. | PW1's evidence regarding how he identified the appellant from the deceased's statement was inconsistent. | The High Court failed to apply accepted legal principles relating to dying declarations. | The High Court failed to apply accepted legal principles relating to circumstantial evidence. | The High Court erred in law in holding that the prosecution had proved its case beyond reasonable doubt. | The High Court judgment was a mere recital of evidence and lacked proper evaluation.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found PW1 and PW8 to be credible and consistent, noting that both independently attributed the injuries to the accused through the deceased's dying declarations. The court observed that PW2 corroborated PW1 by seeing the deceased talking to him in the three-wheeler, and that PW8's evidence was strengthened by his prompt attendance at the scene, arrest of the accused with a blood-stained knife, and subsequent recording of the deceased's statement in hospital. The medical evidence given by the Judicial Medical Officer corroborated the seriousness and nature of the injuries and confirmed that the deceased was conscious and capable of speech when the declarations were made.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal held that the prosecution evidence, particularly the two dying declarations and recovery of the blood-stained weapon from the accused, established guilt beyond reasonable doubt and that no reasonable basis existed to give the accused the benefit of the doubt.
defence_version_summary: In a dock statement, the accused denied any involvement in the incident, stating that he was at work doing daily wage labour on the day of the crime and had no dispute or enmity with the deceased. He claimed that the police, without justification, arrested him and linked him to the case. No alibi witnesses or other defence witnesses were called, and the High Court rejected his bare denial as insufficient to create a reasonable doubt.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal carefully reviewed the law on dying declarations, citing several precedents, and held that the High Court had correctly applied these principles in accepting the statements attributed to the deceased by PW1 and PW8. It emphasised that the deceased was medically proven to be conscious and capable of coherent speech when he named the accused as the assailant, and that both witnesses were credible, consistent, and had no motive to implicate the accused falsely. The court also relied on the arrest of the accused shortly after the incident while attempting to flee with a blood-stained manna knife bearing human blood, together with the pattern and severity of the injuries which demonstrated the necessary mens rea for murder. The accused's bare dock denial, in the face of strong incriminating evidence, was found inadequate, and adverse inferences were drawn from his failure to explain the incriminating circumstances.
coa_sentence_type: Death
brief_judgment_file_summary: This Court of Appeal judgment concerns an appeal against a conviction for murder by the High Court of Chilaw, where the accused was found guilty of killing the deceased by inflicting multiple deep cut injuries with a manna knife on 09.09.2014 and sentenced to death. The appeal challenged the credibility of key witnesses, the treatment of two alleged dying declarations, and the application of legal principles on dying declarations and circumstantial evidence, as well as the adequacy of the High Court’s evaluation of evidence. After reviewing the testimony of PW1, PW2, PW4, and PW8, the medical and analyst reports, and the authorities on dying declarations and adverse inferences from failure to explain incriminating circumstances, the Court of Appeal concluded that the prosecution had proved the case beyond reasonable doubt. It therefore affirmed both conviction and sentence and dismissed the appeal.
defence_counsel: Rashmini Indatissa
cause_of_death_exact_text: Death was due to multiple deep cut injuries to the head, face, and neck causing heavy blood loss, several of which were life-threatening.
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court relied primarily on the deceased's dying declarations to PW1 and PW8, corroborated by medical evidence and the recovery of a blood-stained manna knife from the accused, to find that the prosecution had proved murder under Section 296 beyond reasonable doubt. The Court of Appeal held that the High Court had properly evaluated the credibility of PW1 and PW8, correctly applied the stringent legal tests governing dying declarations, and justifiably inferred intention to kill from the nature and severity of the injuries. It therefore found no error in the High Court’s reasoning or conclusion.

Queen – 66 NLR 409 | Ranasinghe v. Attorney-General – [2007] 1 S.L.R. 218 | Korinvige Anura Lakshman Silva alias Pechchei alias Chooti v. The Attorney General – CA No. 288/2013 (04.05.2018) | King v. Thajudeen – 6 NLR 16 | R v. Lord Cochrane and others – (1814) Gurney's Report 479 | Sumanasena v. Attorney General – (1999) 3 SLR 137 | Baddewithana v. The Attorney General – (1990) 1 SLR 275 | Aruna Alias Podi Raja v. Attorney General – 2011 2 SLR 44
standard_of_review_applied: Re-evaluation of evidence and application of legal principles on dying declarations and inferences from unexplained incriminating circumstances.
final_charge_after_appeal: Murder under Section 296 of the Penal Code

judges: P. Kumararatnam J. | K. M. G. H. Kulatunga J.
offence_sections: Sections 54A(d) and 54A(b) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance as amended by Act No. 13 of 1984
location_of_offence: Near De Lasalle Junction, close to Muthuwella playground, Colombo 01 (Dematagoda area)
brief_facts_summary: The Police Narcotics Bureau received specific information that a person known as Anton from the Dematagoda area was transporting heroin in a three-wheeler towards a watta near De Lasalle Junction, Colombo 01. A police team led by PW1 went to the location, stopped the identified three-wheeler and, upon searching the driver (the appellant), recovered a small parcel containing a brown substance that tested positive for heroin. The appellant was arrested at the scene after allegedly panicking and attempting to escape when handcuffed, and the substance was later weighed at the Bureau and found to be about 70.400 grams, though the indictment referred to 33.25 grams. At trial, the prosecution relied mainly on the police officers involved in the raid, while the appellant gave only a dock statement asserting that a passenger in the back seat escaped when the police intervened.
evidence_type_primary: Eyewitness testimony of police officers regarding the raid, search, and recovery of heroin
evidence_type_secondary: Documentary and forensic evidence including the production chain and Government Analyst-related material
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Sections 54A(d) and 54A(b) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance as amended
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court of Colombo accepted the evidence of the Police Narcotics Bureau officers regarding the receipt of information, the raid, the search of the appellant and the recovery of heroin from his person. The court rejected the appellant’s dock statement, found him guilty on both counts of possession and trafficking of heroin, and sentenced him to life imprisonment on 2022-12-08.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant contended that the prosecution case did not satisfy the test of probability and therefore failed to establish guilt beyond reasonable doubt. It was further argued that the High Court had wrongly rejected the defence evidence by misappreciating the defence version and mixing it up with the prosecution evidence. The defence also highlighted suspicious alterations in the police information book and later allegations against the raiding officers, which were said to undermine the integrity of the investigation.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Prosecution case does not satisfy the legal test of probability and thus does not prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt. | The High Court wrongly rejected the defence evidence by misdirecting itself and mixing up the prosecution and defence versions. | Alterations in the time entry of the police information book create doubt about the reliability and integrity of the investigation. | Later arrest of the raiding officers on allegations of carrying heroin raises a possibility of misconduct and manipulation of the quantity produced in court.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The prosecution called four witnesses, mainly officers of the Police Narcotics Bureau who participated in the raid, transport of the suspect, weighing, sealing and handing over of the production. Their evidence was criticised by the Court of Appeal due to unexplained alterations in the time of receipt of information and delays that undermined the claimed urgency, as well as the later arrest of these officers on heroin-related allegations. The appellant did not call any defence witnesses and relied only on a dock statement asserting that another person in the three-wheeler escaped, which the High Court had rejected but the Court of Appeal found had not been properly and fairly evaluated.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal stressed that criminal guilt must be established to a high degree of probability equivalent to proof beyond reasonable doubt and that mere fanciful possibilities cannot convict. It found that unexplained alterations in the time entries, delays despite an urgent request to rush to the scene, and the misreading of defence evidence rendered the prosecution version improbable and required giving the appellant the benefit of the doubt.
defence_version_summary: When called for his defence, the appellant made only a dock statement, stating in essence that there was another person seated at the back of the three-wheeler who escaped upon seeing the police officer signal the vehicle to stop, implying that the contraband did not belong to him. He did not adduce any independent defence witnesses or documentary evidence. The High Court rejected this version by mixing it up with the prosecution evidence, but the Court of Appeal held that this rejection was based on a misdirection and that the defence version and its probabilities should have been considered alongside the highlighted irregularities in the police evidence.
legal_errors_description: The Court of Appeal identified that the High Court judge misdirected himself by mixing up the prosecution and defence evidence regarding how and when a person in the three-wheeler allegedly escaped, and by rejecting the defence evidence without a proper analysis of probability. The failure to address the alteration of the time of receipt of information and its implications for the integrity of the investigation was also treated as a serious error causing prejudice to the appellant.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal reiterated that the prosecution bears the burden to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt and that a criminal case must satisfy a high degree of probability, relying on authorities such as Mohamed Nimnaz v. Attorney General, Attorney-General v. Rawther, Miller v. Minister of Pensions and R v. Hepworth. It found that the altered time entry for receipt of information, the delay in leaving the Bureau despite an urgent call, the misreading of the defence version about who escaped from the three-wheeler, and the later arrest of the raiding officers on heroin allegations collectively undermined the reliability of the prosecution case. The Court criticised the High Court for rejecting the defence evidence without proper analysis and for failing to consider the probability factors and investigative irregularities that caused serious prejudice to the appellant. Concluding that the prosecution had failed to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt, it set aside the conviction and life sentence and acquitted the appellant.
brief_judgment_file_summary: This appeal arose from a conviction in the High Court of Colombo where the appellant was found guilty of possession and trafficking of heroin under Sections 54A(d) and 54A(b) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance and sentenced to life imprisonment. The Court of Appeal examined the two grounds that the prosecution case did not satisfy the test of probability and that the defence evidence had been rejected on a wrong premise, scrutinising in particular the altered time entries in the police information book, the delay in acting on allegedly urgent information, and the way the trial judge conflated the prosecution and defence versions of an alleged escapee in the three-wheeler. It relied on established case law concerning the burden and standard of proof and emphasized that investigative integrity and probability assessments are central to determining guilt in criminal cases. Finding that these irregularities and misdirections caused great prejudice and that the prosecution failed to prove the case beyond reasonable doubt, the Court of Appeal allowed the appeal, set aside the conviction and sentence, and acquitted the appellant.
prosecution_counsel: Hiranjan Peiris, SDSG for the Respondent
defence_counsel: Neranjan Jayasinghe for the Appellant
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court had accepted the prosecution version of events, found that heroin was recovered from the appellant in the three-wheeler and rejected his dock statement as improbable, thereby convicting and sentencing him on both counts. The Court of Appeal held that the High Court failed to give equal and fair consideration to the defence evidence and did not properly analyse the probabilities in light of the altered police notes and the circumstances of the raid. It concluded that the rejection of the defence on an incorrect factual premise and the disregard of highlighted irregularities amounted to serious error and prejudice to the appellant.
precedents_cited_list: Mohamed Nimnaz v. Attorney General – CA/95/94 | Attorney-General v. Rawther – 25 NLR 385; 1987 1 SLR 155 | Miller v. Minister of Pensions – (1947) 2 All E.R. 372 | R v. Hepworth – 1928 AD 265
standard_of_review_applied: Failure to evaluate evidence and probabilities properly, misdirection on facts, and assessment of whether the finding of guilt was consistent with proof beyond reasonable doubt.

defence_version_summary: When called for his defence, the appellant made only a dock statement, stating in essence that there was another person seated at the back of the three-wheeler who escaped upon seeing the police officer signal the vehicle to stop, implying that the contraband did not belong to him. He did not adduce any independent defence witnesses or documentary evidence. The High Court rejected this version by mixing it up with the prosecution evidence, but the Court of Appeal held that this rejection was based on a misdirection and that the defence version and its probabilities should have been considered alongside the highlighted irregularities in the police evidence.
legal_errors_description: The Court of Appeal identified that the High Court judge misdirected himself by mixing up the prosecution and defence evidence regarding how and when a person in the three-wheeler allegedly escaped, and by rejecting the defence evidence without a proper analysis of probability. The failure to address the alteration of the time of receipt of information and its implications for the integrity of the investigation was also treated as a serious error causing prejudice to the appellant.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal reiterated that the prosecution bears the burden to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt and that a criminal case must satisfy a high degree of probability, relying on authorities such as Mohamed Nimnaz v. Attorney General, Attorney-General v. Rawther, Miller v. Minister of Pensions and R v. Hepworth. It found that the altered time entry for receipt of information, the delay in leaving the Bureau despite an urgent call, the misreading of the defence version about who escaped from the three-wheeler, and the later arrest of the raiding officers on heroin allegations collectively undermined the reliability of the prosecution case. The Court criticised the High Court for rejecting the defence evidence without proper analysis and for failing to consider the probability factors and investigative irregularities that caused serious prejudice to the appellant. Concluding that the prosecution had failed to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt, it set aside the conviction and life sentence and acquitted the appellant.
brief_judgment_file_summary: This appeal arose from a conviction in the High Court of Colombo where the appellant was found guilty of possession and trafficking of heroin under Sections 54A(d) and 54A(b) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance and sentenced to life imprisonment. The Court of Appeal examined the two grounds that the prosecution case did not satisfy the test of probability and that the defence evidence had been rejected on a wrong premise, scrutinising in particular the altered time entries in the police information book, the delay in acting on allegedly urgent information, and the way the trial judge conflated the prosecution and defence versions of an alleged escapee in the three-wheeler. It relied on established case law concerning the burden and standard of proof and emphasized that investigative integrity and probability assessments are central to determining guilt in criminal cases. Finding that these irregularities and misdirections caused great prejudice and that the prosecution failed to prove the case beyond reasonable doubt, the Court of Appeal allowed the appeal, set aside the conviction and sentence, and acquitted the appellant.
prosecution_counsel: Hiranjan Peiris, SDSG for the Respondent
defence_counsel: Neranjan Jayasinghe for the Appellant
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court had accepted the prosecution version of events, found that heroin was recovered from the appellant in the three-wheeler and rejected his dock statement as improbable, thereby convicting and sentencing him on both counts. The Court of Appeal held that the High Court failed to give equal and fair consideration to the defence evidence and did not properly analyse the probabilities in light of the altered police notes and the circumstances of the raid. It concluded that the rejection of the defence on an incorrect factual premise and the disregard of highlighted irregularities amounted to serious error and prejudice to the appellant.
precedents_cited_list: Mohamed Nimnaz v. Attorney General – CA/95/94 | Attorney-General v. Rawther – 25 NLR 385; 1987 1 SLR 155 | Miller v. Minister of Pensions – (1947) 2 All E.R. 372 | R v. Hepworth – 1928 AD 265
standard_of_review_applied: Failure to evaluate evidence and probabilities properly, misdirection on facts, and assessment of whether the finding of guilt was consistent with proof beyond reasonable doubt.

judges: P. Kumararatnam, J. | K. M. G. H. Kulatunga, J.
offence_sections: Sections 54(A)(b) and 54(A)(d) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance as amended by Act No. 13 of 1984
location_of_offence: Near the petrol shed on Ramakrishna Road, Wellawatta, Colombo
brief_facts_summary: Officers of the Police Narcotics Bureau, acting on information from private informants, initially conducted an unsuccessful stake-out at Bambalapitiya Railway Station and then received fresh information that a person known as Badowita Chaminda would be bringing heroin to Ramakrishna Road, Wellawatta. At the indicated location, the officers stopped the appellant, searched him, and recovered a parcel containing a substance believed to be heroin from his trouser pocket, later weighed and sealed at the Police Narcotics Bureau. The Government Analyst reported that the substance contained 3.83 grams of pure heroin (diacetylmorphine). The High Court acquitted the appellant of trafficking but convicted him of possession and imposed a life sentence, which he appealed on grounds relating to probabilities of the prosecution version, failure to consider the defence, and defects in the inward journey of the productions.
evidence_type_primary: Police eyewitness testimony and recovery of heroin from the person of the appellant
evidence_type_secondary: Forensic analysis by the Government Analyst and documentary production and chain-of-custody records
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 54(A)(d) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance as amended
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court of Colombo tried the appellant on two counts under Sections 54(A)(b) and 54(A)(d) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance for trafficking and possession of heroin. After trial, the court acquitted him of the trafficking count but found him guilty of the possession count relating to 3.83 grams of heroin. On 25 April 2019, the learned High Court Judge imposed a sentence of life imprisonment for the possession conviction.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant contended that the learned High Court Judge failed to consider the probability of the prosecution version in light of the surrounding circumstances and inconsistencies. He further argued that the defence version was not properly evaluated or given due weight. A third ground of appeal was that the prosecution failed to satisfactorily prove the inward journey of the productions and thereby the integrity of the production evidence. Collectively, these grounds were advanced as creating reasonable doubt sufficient to vitiate the conviction.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Alleged failure by the High Court to consider the probability and improbability of the prosecution narrative. | Complaint that the learned High Court Judge failed to adequately consider and evaluate the defence version. | Allegation that the prosecution failed to properly prove the inward journey and chain of custody of the productions in this drug-related case.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal scrutinised the testimony of the police witnesses, noting improbabilities such as the suggestion that the appellant walked on a flyover where pedestrians are not permitted and the lack of clarity on whether he was also known as Badowita Chaminda. It also highlighted serious discrepancies in the handling of productions, including the unusual retention of the production in PW1's personal locker, errors in the Magistrate’s case number, and inconsistencies in the recorded dates of dispatch to the Government Analyst. These contradictions and irregularities led the Court to conclude that the prosecution witnesses failed the test of probability and that the production evidence was not satisfactorily proved.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal expressly applied the test of probability and improbability, guided by case law and academic commentary, to assess the competing versions. It found that key aspects of the prosecution story, including the alleged route taken by the appellant and the manner of handling productions, were highly improbable, whereas the defence version appeared more consistent with ordinary human conduct. These improbabilities and contradictions generated reasonable doubt, which the court resolved in favour of the appellant.
defence_version_summary: The appellant gave evidence from the witness box and categorically denied possessing heroin at the time of his arrest. He maintained that he had arrived in the area by three-wheeler rather than on foot, which contradicted the prosecution claim that he walked via a flyover where pedestrians are not allowed. The defence highlighted the improbabilities in the prosecution narrative and the irregularities in handling the productions. The Court of Appeal considered the defence version more probable in light of the weaknesses and contradictions in the prosecution case.
legal_errors_description: The Court of Appeal held that the learned High Court Judge failed to properly apply the test of probability to the prosecution and defence versions and convicted the appellant despite substantial contradictions and irregularities in the production evidence. This misappreciation of evidence and failure to give the benefit of doubt to the accused rendered the conviction unsafe in law.
procedural_defects_description: There were significant irregularities in the handling of the productions: the heroin was kept in PW1's personal locker instead of being handed to the reserve officer after entry in the production register; PW7 incorrectly referred to the Magistrate's case number; and the Information Book recorded an inconsistent date for handing over the production to the Government Analyst, none of which were satisfactorily explained.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal examined the evidence in light of established principles on assessing probabilities and the requirement to strictly prove the chain of custody in drug-related cases. It found that the police evidence contained serious improbabilities regarding the appellant’s movements and that the chain of production was compromised by unexplained discrepancies, such as the use of a personal locker for storage and inconsistent dates and case numbers. The court concluded that these defects undermined the credibility of the prosecution and that the High Court had erred in preferring that version over the defence without properly addressing the reasonable doubt arising therefrom. Consequently, the Court of Appeal set aside the conviction and sentence and acquitted the appellant.
brief_judgment_file_summary: This appeal concerned a conviction from the High Court of Colombo where the appellant had been charged with trafficking and possession of heroin under Sections 54(A)(b) and 54(A)(d) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance. Although acquitted of trafficking, he was convicted of possession of 3.83 grams of heroin and sentenced to life imprisonment. On appeal, the Court of Appeal considered grounds alleging failure to assess the probabilities of the prosecution and defence versions, as well as failure to prove the inward journey of the productions. After reviewing the police testimony, precedents on probability and chain of custody, and the irregularities in handling productions, the Court held that the prosecution case was riddled with improbabilities and contradictions that created reasonable doubt. It therefore set aside the conviction and life sentence and ordered that the appellant be acquitted of the charge.
defence_counsel: Ershan Ariaratnam
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court accepted the evidence of the police officers as sufficient to establish possession of heroin by the appellant and did not give decisive weight to the alleged improbabilities or to defects in the production chain. It proceeded to convict the appellant on the possession count and impose a life sentence. The Court of Appeal held that this approach was flawed because the High Court had overlooked or minimised material contradictions and irregularities, failed to properly evaluate probabilities, and thereby reached a conviction that could not be sustained beyond reasonable doubt.
precedents_cited_list: Wickremasuriya v. Dedoleena and others – 1996 (2) SLR 95 | Iswari Prasad v. Mohamed Isa – 1963 AIR (SC) 1728 at 1734 | Perera v. Attorney General – [1998] 1 Sri L.R. 378 | Witharana Doli Nona v. The Republic of Sri Lanka – CA/19/99 | Mohamed Nimnaz v. Attorney General – CA/95/94
standard_of_review_applied: Failure to properly evaluate evidence and apply the test of probability; deficiencies in proving the chain of custody of productions rendering the conviction unsafe and contrary to proof beyond reasonable doubt.
final_charge_after_appeal: Section 54(A)(d) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance – Possession of heroin (charge unchanged but conviction set aside and appellant acquitted)

judges: B. Sasi Mahendran, J. | Amal Ranaraja, J.
offence_sections: Section 54A(b) and Section 54A(d) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance as amended by Act No. 13 of 1984
brief_facts_summary: On 13.08.2013, PW1, a Sub-Inspector attached to the Special Task Force, received a tip from an informant regarding an individual trafficking narcotics in the Sedawatha area and informed his superiors. Acting on the information, he and a team of officers set up a roadblock on Wellampitiya road at Katupelalla, stopped a three-wheeler and searched its driver, the appellant. They recovered a pink plastic bag from the appellant containing eight small packets of brown-coloured powder, which PW1 identified as heroin mixed with other materials, and arrested him. The Government Analyst later determined the weight of the substance, but a discrepancy emerged between the gross weight recorded at seizure and the weight found in analysis, which became central at the appeal.
evidence_type_primary: Police eyewitness testimony of raid and recovery
evidence_type_secondary: Government Analyst’s report and forensic analysis of the seized substance
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 54A(b) and Section 54A(d) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance as amended by Act No. 13 of 1984
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court of Colombo convicted the appellant on both counts of trafficking and possessing 2.39 grams of heroin under section 54A(b) and 54A(d), accepting the prosecution account of the raid and recovery. It treated the recovery by PW1 and the Government Analyst’s findings as sufficient to prove the charges beyond reasonable doubt. The court imposed a sentence of life imprisonment on the appellant.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant challenged the conviction and sentence on several grounds. He argued that the prosecution story was inherently improbable and not tenable. He further contended that there had been no proper adoption of evidence under section 48 of the Judicature Act by the succeeding High Court Judge and that the judge had altered the proceedings on 16.02.2018 and 20.02.2018 without the consent of either party. Finally, he complained that the High Court failed to consider the significance of the discrepancy between the weight of the substance recovered at the scene and the quantity analysed by the Government Analyst.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The prosecution’s story is not tenable and is inherently improbable. | A proper adoption of evidence under section 48 of the Judicature Act No. 02 of 1978 (as amended) was not carried out by the succeeding High Court Judge. | The Learned High Court Judge altered the proceedings on 16.02.2018 and 20.02.2018 without the consent of the prosecution and/or the defence. | The Learned High Court Judge failed to consider the significance of the discrepancy between the weight of the substance purportedly recovered by PW1 and that sent to the Government Analyst for analysis.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal noted that the prosecution case centered on the testimony of PW1, a Special Task Force officer who led the raid and claimed to have recovered heroin from the appellant. While it accepted that PW1 could legitimately engage in raids in addition to his security duties and that his decisions about taking the appellant to the Narcotics Bureau and not tracing the original supplier were within his prerogative, the court found a serious unexplained discrepancy between the gross weight of the substance recorded at seizure (09.09 grams) and the quantity determined by the Government Analyst (07.12 grams). This discrepancy, together with the High Court’s reliance on presumptions to explain it, was held to undermine the overall credibility of the prosecution evidence.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal considered the unexplained weight discrepancy to be fundamental, concluding that it seriously eroded the reliability of the prosecution case and justified drawing an adverse inference against the prosecution. It held that, in the absence of a satisfactory explanation, the appellant was entitled to the benefit of the doubt, and that a retrial would be unjust given the long lapse of time since the incident.
defence_version_summary: The appellant categorically denied the prosecution narrative and asserted that he had been wrongfully implicated by the police. He claimed that the evidence presented against him was inaccurate and fabricated. There is no indication in the judgment of an alibi or of defence witnesses being called, and the Court of Appeal treats his position as a denial of the prosecution account whose plausibility must be assessed against the prosecution evidence.
procedural_defects_description: The Court of Appeal observed that the High Court Judge did not follow the established process for correcting proceedings, particularly regarding changes to markings of productions and the recorded gross quantity of the powdered substance. Although these were described as rectifications of clerical or transcription errors intended to align the record with earlier proceedings, the judge failed to adopt the usual motion-and-hearing procedure when making such corrections.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal first addressed the complaint about adopting evidence under section 48 of the Judicature Act, relying on recent Supreme Court authority to hold that, in the absence of an application by the accused, the successor judge was not obliged to recommence the trial or resummon witnesses. It then considered the corrections made to the record by the High Court Judge, noting that although proper procedure for correcting clerical errors had not been strictly followed, the corrections merely aligned the record with previously recorded facts and did not cause a failure of justice. The court’s decisive concern was the substantial unexplained discrepancy between the gross weight of the substance allegedly recovered at the scene (09.09 grams) and the weight determined by the Government Analyst (07.12 grams), which it held ran through the prosecution case and seriously affected credibility. Applying appellate precedents on unexplained discrepancies and the prejudice caused by long delays, the court concluded that the conviction was unsafe, declined to order a retrial more than a decade after the incident, and acquitted the appellant.
brief_judgment_file_summary: This appeal arose from the conviction of the appellant by the High Court of Colombo for trafficking and possession of heroin under section 54A(b) and 54A(d) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance and the imposition of a life sentence. The Court of Appeal considered grounds relating to the alleged improbability of the prosecution story, the adoption of evidence under section 48 of the Judicature Act, corrections made to the proceedings by the High Court Judge, and a major discrepancy between the weight of the seized substance and the quantity analysed by the Government Analyst. While it found no merit in the complaint about section 48 and regarded the corrections as clerical in nature that did not cause a failure of justice, it held that the unexplained weight discrepancy was significant, permeated the prosecution case and undermined its reliability. In light of this evidentiary defect and the lapse of about twelve years since the alleged offence, the Court of Appeal set aside the conviction and life sentence and acquitted the appellant without ordering a retrial.
defence_counsel: Rienzie Arsecularatne, P.C. with Namal Karunaratne
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court relied on the testimony of PW1 and the Government Analyst’s findings to convict the appellant and imposed a life sentence. In dealing with the discrepancy between the gross weight of the seized substance and the weight analysed, the High Court made generalized comments and attributed the difference to defective weighing by an inadequately trained officer, without specific evidentiary support. The Court of Appeal regarded this as a misdirection based on presumptions and assumptions, though it treated the corrections to the record as clerical and not causing a failure of justice, and ultimately held that the High Court had failed properly to address a critical evidentiary discrepancy that undermined the conviction.
precedents_cited_list: SC Appeal 139/2019; SC Appeal 02/2022; SC/SPL/LA/267/2018 (Samayawardhena J., 05.04.2024) | Kumaravel Yoganadan alias Yoga v. The Hon. Attorney General – CA HCC 0468/2017 | P. M. Peter Singho v. M. B. Werapitiya – 55 NLR 155 | The Queen v. G. K. Jayasinghe – 69 NLR 314
standard_of_review_applied: Failure to evaluate and explain a material evidentiary discrepancy, misdirection in correcting proceedings, and consideration of whether a retrial would be just after a long lapse of time.
final_charge_after_appeal: Trafficking and possession of heroin under sections 54A(b) and 54A(d) (original charges; conviction set aside on appeal)

judges: P. Kumararatnam | K. M. G. H. Kulatunga
offence_sections: Section 365B(2)(b) of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The appellant, the biological father of the victim, was charged with committing grave sexual abuse on his 12-year-old daughter during the night while she was asleep. She woke to find her father naked on her body, her undergarment lowered, and a sticky substance on her thighs, and was threatened not to disclose the incident. At the time, the victim’s mother was receiving in-house treatment at Badulla General Hospital for a mental condition, and the child initially kept silent due to fear and respect, later disclosing the incident to her grandmother. A police investigation commenced following a call to the emergency line, and the JMO who examined the victim did not exclude the possibility of sexual abuse.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 365B(2)(b) of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court, after hearing the prosecution and the defence, accepted the testimony of the child victim as credible and convincing. The court held that the ingredients of grave sexual abuse under Section 365B(2)(b) were proven beyond reasonable doubt. Consequently, the appellant was convicted as charged and sentenced to 12 years rigorous imprisonment, a fine, and compensation to the victim.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The main ground of appeal was that the learned High Court Judge misdirected himself in concluding that all the ingredients of the offence were proved beyond reasonable doubt. Counsel argued that there was no evidence that the appellant used his penis, any other part of his body, or any instrument on any orifice or part of the victim’s body for his sexual gratification. The challenge was essentially to the sufficiency and quality of the evidence, particularly the victim’s testimony, to sustain a conviction for grave sexual abuse.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Alleged misdirection by the High Court Judge in holding that all ingredients of Section 365B(2)(b) were proved beyond reasonable doubt. | Argument that prosecution failed to adduce evidence of any act using the appellant’s penis, any other part of his body, or any instrument on any orifice or part of the victim’s body for sexual gratification. | Implied contention that the victim’s testimony and available evidence were insufficient to sustain a conviction for grave sexual abuse.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal emphasised the need for careful assessment of the credibility and testimonial trustworthiness of the child victim, whose evidence was consistent with the history given to the doctor. The court held that contradictions and omissions highlighted in her evidence were not material or forceful enough to undermine her credibility or the core issues of the case. The JMO’s evidence that sexual abuse could not be excluded was treated as consistent with the victim’s account, while the appellant’s denial from the witness box was not sufficient to create reasonable doubt.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court found the victim’s account inherently credible and consistent with the medical evidence, concluding that her testimony alone, treated with caution, was sufficient to prove the charge. It held that the alleged contradictions did not affect the probability of her version or the core of the prosecution case, and thus the prosecution had discharged its burden beyond reasonable doubt.
defence_version_summary: After the prosecution closed its case, the appellant gave evidence from the witness box and denied the allegations of grave sexual abuse. There is no indication of an alibi or other specific alternative version being put forward, nor of any additional defence witnesses being called. The courts rejected his bare denial, finding it insufficient to displace the credible evidence of the child victim.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal focused on the credibility of the child victim, stressing that her evidence must be approached with care but may suffice to ground a conviction if found reliable. Relying on authorities concerning child witnesses and the treatment of contradictions, the court held that the minor inconsistencies did not undermine her trustworthiness or the substance of her complaint. It accepted the High Court’s evaluation of the evidence, noted that the JMO’s findings did not contradict the victim’s account, and reaffirmed that the prosecution had proved the ingredients of grave sexual abuse beyond reasonable doubt. Finding no basis to interfere, the court dismissed the appeal and affirmed the conviction and sentence.
coa_sentence_type: Rigorous Imprisonment 12 years plus fine and compensation (unchanged)
brief_judgment_file_summary: This appeal concerned a conviction from the High Court of Monaragala where the appellant, the biological father, was found guilty of grave sexual abuse of his 12-year-old daughter under Section 365B(2)(b) of the Penal Code and sentenced to 12 years rigorous imprisonment, a fine, and compensation. On appeal, it was contended that the trial judge misdirected himself in holding that the ingredients of the charge were proved beyond reasonable doubt and that there was no adequate evidence of an act of sexual abuse. The Court of Appeal analysed the evidence of the child victim, the corroborative medical evidence, and the alleged contradictions, applying authorities on child witnesses and inconsistencies, and concluded that her testimony was cogent and convincing. Holding that the prosecution had proved its case and that the High Court’s judgment of 28.04.2023 disclosed no basis for appellate interference, the Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal and ordered that the sentence operate from the original date of sentence.
defence_counsel: Niroshan Mihindukulasuriya
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court had accepted the child victim’s testimony as credible and sufficient, supported by the JMO’s evidence that sexual abuse could not be excluded, and convicted the appellant accordingly. In reviewing this reasoning, the Court of Appeal noted that the trial judge had properly assessed the competence and credibility of the child witness, treated her evidence with appropriate caution, and dealt with contradictions and omissions correctly. The appellate court agreed with the High Court’s evaluation and held that its findings on the facts and law were sound and did not warrant interference.
precedents_cited_list: Ranjeet Kumar Ram v. State of Bihar [2015] SCC Online SC 500 | The Attorney General v. Sandanam Pitchai Mary Theresa [2011] 2 SLR 292
standard_of_review_applied: Assessment of whether the High Court properly evaluated the credibility of the child witness, the impact of contradictions, and whether the conviction was supported by evidence proving the ingredients of the offence beyond reasonable doubt.
final_charge_after_appeal: Grave sexual abuse under Section 365B(2)(b) of the Penal Code (unchanged)

judges: B. Sasi Mahendran, J. | Amal Ranaraja, J.
offence_sections: Section 54A(b) and Section 54A(d) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance as amended by Act No. 13 of 1984
offence_category: Drug trafficking and possession of heroin
location_of_offence: Mattakkuliya, near a childrens’ park adjacent to Eliyas Road close to the main Mattakkuliya road
brief_facts_summary: On 23.08.2013 Sub-Inspector Amarasinghe (PW1) received information that the appellant was involved in narcotics trafficking in the Mattakkuliya area and organised a police raid. At a childrens’ park near Eliyas Road, PW1 and PW4 apprehended the appellant carrying a plastic bag marked “Sale House” which contained a parcel with 13 smaller green plastic packets of powdered substance suspected to be heroin. The appellant was arrested and the substance was sent to the Government Analyst, who reported a gross weight of 1293.56 grams containing 480.92 grams of pure heroin. The High Court of Colombo thereafter convicted the appellant on both counts of trafficking and possession based on this evidence.
evidence_type_primary: Police eyewitness testimony of the detection, search and recovery of the heroin from the appellant
evidence_type_secondary: Forensic/chemical analysis by the Government Analyst and documentary productions relating to the seized substance
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 54A(b) and Section 54A(d) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance as amended by Act No. 13 of 1984
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court of Colombo conducted the trial in absentia in respect of the appellant. At the conclusion of the trial, the learned High Court Judge found the appellant guilty on both counts in the indictment for trafficking and possession of heroin. The court imposed a sentence of life imprisonment for each of the two charges.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: On appeal, counsel for the appellant argued that the evidence of PW1 and PW4 contained significant inconsistencies and inter se contradictions which undermined their credibility. He highlighted divergences concerning where the police vehicle stopped, the timing and conduct of the informant, the side of the road used by the appellant, the appellant’s initial reaction when approached, the manner in which the powder was examined at the scene and how the appellant was handcuffed. It was contended that the learned trial judge failed properly to consider these contradictions and the resulting improbabilities in the prosecution narrative. On that basis, the appellant sought to have the conviction and sentencing order set aside.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Alleged inconsistency between PW1 and PW4 regarding the location at which the police vehicle was brought to a halt upon reaching the destination. | Alleged inconsistency regarding the time at which the informant arrived and how he interacted with the officers at the location. | Alleged inconsistency as to the side of the road on which the appellant walked while in possession of the powdered substance. | Alleged inconsistency concerning the appellant’s initial reaction when he was accosted by PW1 and PW4. | Complaint about the manner in which the powdered substance purportedly recovered from the appellant was examined at the scene prior to the arrest. | Complaint about the manner in which the appellant was handcuffed upon his arrest. | Ground that the learned trial judge failed to consider the inconsistencies per se and inter se in and between the testimonies of PW1 and PW4. | Ground that the learned trial judge failed to consider the improbabilities in the prosecution’s case.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal evaluated each of the discrepancies highlighted between the testimonies of PW1 and PW4 and concluded that they were minor and arose from differences in perspective and roles during the raid. It held that matters such as where the vehicle stopped, whether a security guard was present, what each officer observed of the informant, and whether PW4 saw PW1 open a packet did not affect the core narrative of the detection. Both witnesses were consistent on essential aspects including the identity and arrest of the appellant, his approach to the scene, the recovery of the parcels and the involvement of other officers, and therefore their evidence remained credible.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal held that the highlighted discrepancies were non-material and did not undermine the essential facts of the detection, arrest and recovery of the heroin. It concluded that the trial judge’s acceptance of the prosecution evidence was reasonable, that no reasonable doubt arose in favour of the appellant, and that there was no justification to disturb the conviction.
defence_version_summary: The trial was conducted in the absence of the appellant and there is no indication that any defence witnesses or alibi evidence were led on his behalf at the High Court. At the appellate stage the defence case consisted of submissions attacking the credibility of PW1 and PW4 and asserting improbabilities in the prosecution narrative and handling of the production. The Court of Appeal rejected these arguments, finding the alleged inconsistencies to be immaterial and holding that the defence had failed to demonstrate any reasonable doubt regarding the prosecution case.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal focused on whether the alleged inconsistencies in the testimonies of PW1 and PW4 were material enough to undermine the prosecution case. Referring to authority on the treatment of discrepancies in witness evidence, it held that only contradictions going to the root of the matter and assailing the basic version require intervention and that the divergences here did not concern the identity of the appellant, his arrest, the recovery of the parcels or the safe custody of the productions. The Government Analyst’s report was accepted as reliably establishing the nature and quantity of heroin, and the court found that the trial judge had reasonably evaluated the evidence and correctly applied the law. As no misdirection, procedural error or sentencing error was found, the court declined to interfere with either conviction or sentence and dismissed the appeal.
coa_sentence_type: Life Imprisonment
brief_judgment_file_summary: This appeal arose from a conviction in the High Court of Colombo where the appellant, tried in absentia, was found guilty and sentenced to life imprisonment on two counts of trafficking and possessing 480.92 grams of heroin recovered from him during a police raid in Mattakkuliya in August 2013. On appeal, the defence challenged the conviction by pointing to alleged inconsistencies between the police witnesses and supposed improbabilities in the prosecution narrative, including details of the vehicle position, the informant’s actions, the appellant’s movements and the handling of the production. The Court of Appeal carefully analysed each alleged discrepancy, held that they were minor, explained by differing vantage points and roles, and did not affect key issues such as the identity of the appellant, his arrest, the recovery of the heroin or the safe custody of the productions. Applying established principles on the materiality of contradictions, the court affirmed the findings and sentence of the High Court and dismissed the appeal, directing that its judgment be communicated to the High Court for compliance.
defence_counsel: Kasun Liyanage
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court’s reasoning, as reflected in the Court of Appeal judgment, was to accept the evidence of the police officers and the Government Analyst as proving that the appellant was in possession of and trafficking a substantial quantity of heroin. The trial judge treated the core aspects of the detection, arrest and recovery as reliable and was not persuaded that minor discrepancies undermined the prosecution case. The Court of Appeal expressly stated that it was not inclined to interfere with either the judgment or the sentencing order, thereby endorsing the High Court’s evaluation of the evidence and application of the law.
precedents_cited_list: The Attorney General v. Sandanam Pitchi Mary Theresa – [2011] 2 SLR 292 | Boghi Bhai Hirji Bhai v. State of Gujarat – AIR 1983 SC 753
standard_of_review_applied: Assessment of whether alleged inconsistencies in the prosecution evidence were material and whether the trial judge’s evaluation of credibility and findings on the facts were reasonable or perverse.
final_charge_after_appeal: Trafficking and possession of 480.92 grams of heroin under sections 54A(b) and 54A(d) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance (unchanged).

judges: B. Sasi Mahendran, J. | Amal Ranaraja, J.
offence_sections: Section 54A(b) and (d) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance No. 13 of 1984 as amended
offence_category: Drug trafficking and possession of heroin
brief_facts_summary: The accused was indicted in the High Court of Colombo for having been in possession of and trafficking 1.58 grams of heroin on 23.08.2016 at Stasepura. According to the prosecution, a police team encountered the accused near a littered area; when he behaved suspiciously and attempted to walk away towards a housing scheme, officers stopped him, searched his pockets, and found a pink cellophane parcel containing heroin. The heroin was weighed and sealed, and the accused was arrested and taken to the Grandpass Police Station. Following trial, he was convicted on the first count under the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance.
evidence_type_primary: Police eyewitness testimony and recovery of heroin from the person of the accused
evidence_type_secondary: Physical production evidence including the heroin parcel and marked productions
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: First count under the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance relating to possession/trafficking of heroin
hc_sentence_type: 7 years of rigorous imprisonment and a fine with 1 year rigorous imprisonment in default
hc_judgment_summary: After the accused pleaded not guilty, the High Court heard evidence from 13 prosecution witnesses and admitted 7 productions before finding the accused guilty on the first count relating to heroin. The court acquitted him on the second count and, considering the statutory framework for quantities of heroin of 2 grams or below, imposed the minimum mandatory sentence of 7 years rigorous imprisonment plus a fine of 100000 with 1 year RI in default. The High Court noted factors such as his youth, lack of prior convictions, and family circumstances but nonetheless applied the statutory minimum sentence.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The accused challenged the High Court judgment on the basis that the trial judge failed to properly consider contradictions in the prosecution evidence, failed to evaluate the defence case, and overlooked weaknesses in the credibility of prosecution witnesses, resulting in a judgment contrary to the evidence. In addition, at the hearing of the appeal, counsel focused on the severity of the sentence, urging mitigation due to the accused’s youth, absence of previous convictions, and responsibility for several minor children, including an infant. The appeal thus combined both evidentiary and sentencing challenges.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Alleged failure of the High Court to consider contradictions in the prosecution witnesses. | Complaint that the High Court failed to take into account the defence evidence and version. | Allegation that the High Court did not consider weaknesses and incredibility of prosecution witnesses. | Contention that the judgment was delivered in contravention of the evidence placed before court. | At the argument stage, counsel challenged the sentence as harsh given no previous convictions, the young age of the accused, and his minor children.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal briefly recounted the testimony of PW7, a police officer, who described observing the accused behaving suspiciously, stopping him, and recovering a pink cellophane parcel containing heroin from his pocket before arresting him and transporting him to the police station where the drugs were weighed and sealed. The judgment records that the prosecution called 13 witnesses and marked 7 productions but does not engage in a detailed re-evaluation of their credibility or alleged contradictions. Instead, the appellate court focused primarily on sentencing issues and accepted the High Court’s assessment of the evidence.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal did not undertake a fresh assessment of probabilities on guilt; it implicitly accepted the High Court’s findings and confined itself to reviewing whether the minimum statutory sentence imposed, after consideration of mitigating factors, was appropriate, ultimately deciding there was no reason to disturb the sentence.
defence_version_summary: The accused pleaded not guilty and gave evidence under oath, but the judgment does not reproduce or analyze his substantive version of events. On appeal, his counsel did not press detailed factual defences but instead relied on mitigating circumstances, stressing his lack of previous convictions, his young age, and that he had several minor children including a six-month-old infant. The Court of Appeal treated these factors as having already been considered by the High Court and did not identify any credibility issue in the defence that warranted altering the conviction or sentence.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal observed that counsel for the accused ultimately challenged the sentence, arguing for mitigation on the basis of youth, absence of prior convictions, and family responsibilities. The court reviewed sentencing principles, citing Archbold and leading Sri Lankan authorities, emphasizing that judges must balance aggravating and mitigating factors, the gravity and incidence of the offence, deterrence, and the public interest alongside the offender’s personal circumstances. It noted that for heroin quantities of 2 grams or below, the statute prescribes imprisonment of not less than seven years and a fine of not less than 100000 and not more than 500000, giving the trial judge discretion only within that range. Finding that the High Court had imposed the minimum mandatory sentence after considering the mitigating factors and that the offence remained serious in light of public interest and deterrence, the Court of Appeal declined to interfere with the sentence or conviction.
coa_sentence_type: 7 years of rigorous imprisonment and a fine of 100000 with 1 year rigorous imprisonment in default (unchanged)
brief_judgment_file_summary: This appeal concerned a High Court conviction of the accused for possession and trafficking of 1.58 grams of heroin at Stasepura under the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance, following a police detection in which heroin was recovered from his pocket and later weighed and sealed. The High Court, after hearing 13 prosecution witnesses and the sworn testimony of the accused, convicted him on the first count, acquitted him on the second, and imposed the statutory minimum sentence of seven years’ rigorous imprisonment plus a fine of 100000, with one year rigorous imprisonment in default. On appeal, although the formal grounds alleged failures to consider contradictions, weaknesses in prosecution evidence, and the defence case, counsel primarily pursued mitigation based on the accused’s youth, lack of prior convictions, and responsibilities toward several minor children. The Court of Appeal, applying established sentencing principles and noting the mandatory minimum regime for heroin quantities at or below 2 grams, held that the High Court had properly balanced mitigating factors against public interest and deterrence in imposing the minimum sentence and therefore dismissed the appeal.
defence_counsel: Nuwam D. Alwis
hc_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal recognized that the High Court had sentenced the accused under the statutory scheme applicable to heroin quantities of 2 grams or below, which mandates imprisonment of between seven and twenty years together with a fine. It noted that the High Court had expressly considered mitigating matters such as the accused’s youth, his role as a father to minor children, and the absence of previous convictions, yet nonetheless imposed the minimum term in view of the seriousness and societal impact of drug offences. The appellate court agreed that this approach properly balanced individual circumstances with public interest and deterrence, and thus found no misdirection or misuse of sentencing discretion.
precedents_cited_list: The Attorney General v. H.N. De Silva – 57 NLR 121 | Rex v. Boyd – (1908) 1 Cr. App. Rep. 64 | The Attorney General v. Mendis – 1995 1 SLR 138
standard_of_review_applied: Review of sentencing discretion and compliance with statutory minimum penalties to determine whether the High Court misdirected itself or failed to consider relevant aggravating and mitigating factors.
sentencing_principles_applied: The Court applied principles that sentencing must reflect the gravity of the offence, statutory ranges, deterrence, incidence and difficulty of detection of such crimes, and the public interest, while also taking into account mitigating factors such as age, antecedents, and family circumstances; it emphasized that reformation is subordinate when public interest and state welfare require a robust response to serious drug offences.
final_charge_after_appeal: Same as High Court conviction on the first count under the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance for possession/trafficking of heroin

judges: B. Sasi Mahendran J | Amal Ranaraja J
offence_sections: Section 20(1)(g) and Section 40(1)(b) of the Forest Conservation Ordinance No. 30 of 1945
offence_category: Forest offence – illegal sand extraction in violation of permit conditions
location_of_offence: Land named Ura Oya in the Monaragala District
brief_facts_summary: The appellant is the registered owner of a tractor and trailer bearing registration numbers UPRS 4264 and UPRW 3860, which he routinely rented to third parties. On 2015-10-20 he rented the vehicles to a third party to transport sand extracted from a land known as Ura Oya in the Monaragala District under a permit. Forest officers seized the tractor and trailer after discovering that sand had been extracted and loaded in breach of the permit conditions, and the persons involved were prosecuted and convicted under sections 20(1)(g) and 40(1)(b) of the Forest Conservation Ordinance. Following their conviction, the Magistrate ordered confiscation of the tractor and trailer, which order was affirmed by the High Court on revision and then challenged before the Court of Appeal by the vehicle owner.
evidence_type_primary: Oral testimony of the registered owner at the confiscation inquiry
evidence_type_secondary: Documentary evidence including the sand extraction permit marked වී-1
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 20(1)(g) and Section 40(1)(b) of the Forest Conservation Ordinance No. 30 of 1945
hc_sentence_type: Confiscation of the tractor and trailer used to commit the forest offence
hc_judgment_summary: In the High Court revision application, the appellant sought to set aside the Magistrate’s order confiscating the tractor and trailer on the basis that he, as a third-party owner, had taken all necessary precautions to prevent the vehicles being used for an offence. The High Court, by order dated 2020-05-26, dismissed the revision and affirmed the Magistrate’s confiscation order, in effect upholding the view that the appellant had not satisfied the proviso to section 40(1)(b) of the Forest Conservation Ordinance.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant contended that as a registered owner who was not an accused in the main case, he had taken all reasonable and necessary precautions to prevent the tractor and trailer from being used to commit any offence. He argued that he had specifically instructed the driver not to use the vehicles unlawfully and had verified the validity of the sand permit before renting them out. He further claimed that the Magistrate and the High Court failed to properly evaluate his unchallenged evidence and misdirected themselves in law when ordering and affirming confiscation under section 40(1)(b). The appeal therefore sought to set aside the confiscation orders and to have the vehicles released to him.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Appellant, as a third-party registered owner, had taken all reasonable precautions to prevent the tractor and trailer from being used to commit an offence. | He instructed the driver not to use the vehicles for any illegal activity and checked the sand extraction permit (marked වී-1) before renting the vehicles. | The Magistrate and High Court failed to properly assess and give weight to his unchallenged evidence at the confiscation inquiry. | The lower courts misdirected themselves on the proper application of the proviso to section 40(1)(b) of the Forest Conservation Ordinance when ordering and affirming confiscation. | The confiscation of the tractor and trailer was therefore unlawful and should be set aside, with the vehicles released to the appellant.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: At the confiscation inquiry, the appellant, as the registered owner of the tractor and trailer, gave evidence and was the only witness called on behalf of the owner. He testified that he had instructed the driver not to use the vehicles unlawfully and had personally checked the sand permit before renting them out. The Court of Appeal noted that his evidence was clear, implicit and not impeached under cross-examination, and held that it amounted to irrefutable proof that he took necessary precautions to prevent the commission of an offence using the vehicles.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal, relying on the principle that a third-party owner must satisfy the court on a balance of probabilities, accepted the appellant’s unchallenged testimony and treated it as irrefutable evidence of having taken necessary precautions. It held that in such circumstances corroboration was not necessary and that the benefit of the proviso to section 40(1)(b) should accrue to the appellant.
defence_version_summary: The appellant’s version was that he simply rented the tractor and trailer in the ordinary course of business, having expressly instructed the driver not to use them for any unlawful purposes. Before renting them for the sand transport, he checked the permit marked වී-1 to ensure that the third party had a valid authorization for sand extraction and dispatch. He was not involved in, nor aware of, any violation of the permit conditions by those who actually extracted and loaded the sand. The Court of Appeal found his evidence credible and unchallenged, concluding that he had acted as a reasonable owner and taken all necessary precautionary measures.
legal_errors_description: The Court of Appeal held that the High Court Judge failed to adequately consider the appellant’s clear and unchallenged evidence demonstrating the precautions taken as a third-party owner and thereby misdirected himself in affirming the Magistrate’s confiscation order. It also implied that the Magistrate erred in law in ordering confiscation despite the appellant having satisfied the proviso to section 40(1)(b) on a balance of probabilities.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analysed section 40(1)(b) of the Forest Conservation Ordinance and emphasised that, while vehicles used in a forest offence are generally liable to confiscation, the proviso protects third-party owners who prove that they took all necessary precautions to prevent such use. Evaluating the evidence, the Court noted that the appellant’s testimony that he instructed the driver not to commit any offence and verified the sand permit was unchallenged and implicitly credible, amounting to irrefutable proof of reasonable precautions. Referring to Adambarage Kelum Thushantha Alwis v. Attorney General, it confirmed that corroboration is not essential where the owner’s evidence satisfies the court on a balance of probabilities. The Court concluded that the High Court had misdirected itself by not appreciating these facts and principles, set aside both the Magistrate’s and High Court’s orders, and directed release of the tractor and trailer to the appellant.
coa_sentence_type: Confiscation orders of the Magistrate and High Court set aside; tractor and trailer ordered to be released to the appellant
brief_judgment_file_summary: This appeal under section 331 of the Code of Criminal Procedure arose from a High Court revision order affirming the Magistrate’s confiscation of a tractor and trailer used in a forest-related sand extraction offence.
