The appellant, the registered owner and a non-accused in the main case, had rented the vehicles to a third party and claimed to have taken all reasonable precautions, including instructing the driver not to commit any offence and checking the sand extraction permit. The Court of Appeal found his evidence at the confiscation inquiry to be implicit, unchallenged and irrefutable, and applied the legal test that a third-party owner need only satisfy the court on a balance of probabilities that precautions were taken. Holding that the High Court had misdirected itself by not properly considering these facts and the protective proviso to section 40(1)(b), the Court of Appeal set aside the confiscation orders and directed that the tractor and trailer be released to the appellant.
prosecution_counsel: Padmal Weerasinghe De Silva, S.S.C for the 3rd and 4th Respondents
defence_counsel: Udaya Sri Keerthiwardena for the Appellant
appeal_type: Other (Appeal from High Court revision order against confiscation order)
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court, in HCRA 9/2017, dismissed the appellant’s revision application and affirmed the Magistrate’s order of 2018-07-19 confiscating the tractor and trailer, effectively accepting that the appellant had not proved the necessary precautions under section 40(1)(b). The Court of Appeal criticised this approach, observing that the High Court Judge failed to give due consideration to the appellant’s credible and unchallenged testimony about the instructions given to the driver and the verification of the permit. It held that by overlooking these material facts and the correct legal standard under the proviso, the High Court had misdirected itself, warranting interference by the appellate court.
precedents_cited_list: Adambarage Kelum Thushantha Alwis vs. The Attorney General – CA (PHC) 211/2019, decided on 07.02.2023
standard_of_review_applied: Misdirection on law and failure to properly evaluate unchallenged evidence in a confiscation inquiry under section 40(1)(b) of the Forest Conservation Ordinance
sentencing_principles_applied: The Court applied the principle that confiscation is a penal measure which should not be imposed on a third-party owner who, on a balance of probabilities, proves that he took all reasonable precautions to prevent his vehicle being used in the commission of an offence, and that in such a case corroboration of the owner’s credible evidence is not essential.
final_charge_after_appeal: No change to the underlying forest offence convictions under sections 20(1)(g) and 40(1)(b); only the confiscation order against the vehicle owner was set aside

judges: B. Sasi Mahendran, J. | Amal Ranaraja, J.
offence_sections: Section 364(2)(e) of the Penal Code
offence_category: Rape of a girl under eighteen
location_of_offence: At the accused's house where the victim stayed overnight, within the jurisdiction of the High Court of Anuradhapura
brief_facts_summary: The accused, known to the victim's family through a neighbour named Jayaratne, was introduced as the owner of a fancy shop where the victim, who had just finished her O/Ls, was to work. On 31.12.2013 the victim and her parents went to the accused's house, where she was left to stay overnight and given a room with a broken door lock. In the early hours of the morning the accused came into the room, lay on the same bed, hugged her, removed her clothes and had sexual intercourse with her against her will, amounting to rape of a girl under eighteen. Thereafter she was taken back to her mother's workplace, disclosed the incident to her parents, was examined at the hospital where her father worked, and a police complaint was lodged.
evidence_type_secondary: Medical evidence and surrounding circumstantial evidence
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 364(2)(e) of the Penal Code
hc_sentence_type: Rigorous Imprisonment 15 years plus fine and compensation
hc_judgment_summary: After a full trial in which 15 prosecution witnesses and one defence witness testified, the High Court of Anuradhapura found the accused guilty of committing rape on a girl under eighteen contrary to Section 364(2)(e) of the Penal Code. The court sentenced him to 15 years of rigorous imprisonment, a fine of 10000 with 6 months rigorous imprisonment in default, and ordered compensation of 300000 to the victim with a default term of 2 years simple imprisonment. The High Court thereby applied a custodial sentence within the statutory range to reflect the gravity of the offence.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: In his petition of appeal the accused initially contended that the prosecution version failed the test of probability and that the learned High Court Judge misdirected himself by failing to judicially evaluate the evidence. However, when the matter was supported, counsel for the accused informed the Court of Appeal that he was only challenging the sentence and sought mitigation based on the accused's medical condition. Thus, the appeal effectively proceeded only on the ground that the sentence was excessive or should be reduced in light of personal circumstances.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Allegation that the prosecution version failed the test of probability. | Allegation that the High Court Judge failed to judicially evaluate the evidence. | At the hearing, counsel limited the challenge to the sentence and sought mitigation based on the accused's medical condition. | No specific complaint was ultimately pursued regarding evidentiary contradictions or procedural irregularities.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The prosecution relied primarily on the detailed testimony of the victim, who described the events at the accused's house and the non-consensual sexual intercourse, supported by her prompt complaint to her parents and subsequent medical examination at the hospital where her father worked. The defence consisted of an unsworn dock statement by the accused and one defence witness, but no alternative coherent account or alibi was established. The courts accepted the victim's evidence as credible, emphasising her vulnerability and the mental and social impact described in her statement, and found no basis to disturb the High Court's assessment.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal treated the victim's account, corroborated by her immediate complaint and medical examination, as sufficiently probable and compelling, focusing instead on sentencing. It emphasised the gravity of rape of a minor and the public interest in deterrent punishment, and rejected the notion that the accused's medical condition or other factors created any basis to doubt the conviction or significantly reduce the sentence.
defence_version_summary: The accused pleaded not guilty at the High Court and later gave an unsworn dock statement while calling one defence witness, but the contents of that version are not detailed in the judgment. No alibi or alternative innocent explanation was accepted by the court, and the defence failed to present persuasive reasons to disbelieve the victim. Both the High Court and the Court of Appeal implicitly treated the defence version as lacking credibility and insufficient to displace the prosecution case.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal limited its analysis to sentencing after counsel abandoned the evidentiary grounds and sought a mitigated sentence based on the accused's medical condition. It examined the statutory framework under Section 364(2)(e) of the Penal Code and Section 13 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, noting the legislature's intention that rape of a minor be punished with a term of rigorous imprisonment between ten and twenty years, together with fine and compensation. Relying on authorities such as The Attorney General v. H.N. De Silva, The Attorney General v. Mendis, and The Attorney General v. Ranasinghe and Others, and an English case (Roberts), the court stressed public interest, deterrence, protection of women, and the need for immediate custodial sentences for rape. It found no mitigating factors in the accused's favour, highlighted the victim's vulnerability and powerful statement about the injustice she suffered, and concluded that the 15-year rigorous imprisonment, fine and compensation imposed by the High Court were appropriate and required no appellate interference.
coa_sentence_type: Rigorous Imprisonment 15 years plus fine and compensation (unchanged)
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused, Fawool Hameed Muhuthar, was tried before the High Court of Anuradhapura for rape of a girl under eighteen years of age, contrary to Section 364(2)(e) of the Penal Code, based on the victim's account of being lured to work at a fancy shop and sexually assaulted while staying overnight at the accused's house. After hearing 15 prosecution witnesses and one defence witness, the High Court convicted him and imposed 15 years rigorous imprisonment, a fine and default term, and ordered compensation to the victim. On appeal, although the petition initially questioned the probability of the prosecution case and the High Court's evaluation of evidence, counsel ultimately challenged only the severity of the sentence, seeking mitigation on medical grounds. The Court of Appeal, stressing the seriousness of rape, legislative sentencing policy, deterrence and the victim's vulnerability and emotional statement, held that no mitigating factors justified reduction and dismissed the appeal, affirming the conviction and sentence.
defence_counsel: Shanaka Ranasinghe, PC with Sandamali Peiris
cause_of_death_exact_text: Not applicable; the case concerns rape and no death occurred
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court reasoned that the victim's testimony, her immediate complaint to her parents, and the subsequent medical examination were sufficient to establish rape of a girl under eighteen by the accused, warranting a substantial custodial term within the statutory limits and financial sanctions in the form of fine and compensation. The Court of Appeal did not identify any misdirection or misappreciation of evidence by the High Court, particularly as the evidentiary grounds were not pursued at the hearing, and focused solely on whether the sentence was appropriate. It concluded that the High Court had properly exercised its sentencing discretion in view of the seriousness of the offence and the victim's vulnerability.
precedents_cited_list: The Attorney General v. H.N. De Silva 57 NLR 121 | The Attorney General v. Mendis 1995 1 SLR 138 | The Attorney General v. Ranasinghe and Others 1992 2 SLR 81 | Rex v. Boyd (1908) 1 Cr. App. Rep. 64 | Roberts (Court of Appeal of England, rape sentencing case)
standard_of_review_applied: Review of sentencing discretion for rape, considering whether the sentence within the statutory range was inadequate or inappropriate in light of gravity, public interest, deterrence, and mitigating factors, with no misdirection on law found.
sentencing_principles_applied: The court applied principles that rape is inherently serious and ordinarily calls for an immediate custodial sentence, that public interest and protection of women may outweigh the offender's personal circumstances, and that gravity, deterrence, prevalence of the crime, and the victim's age, relationship to the offender, repetition of acts, and mental impact are key factors in fixing sentence; it found no mitigating factors to reduce the 15-year term.
final_charge_after_appeal: Rape of a girl under eighteen under Section 364(2)(e) of the Penal Code (unchanged)

judges: B. Sasi Mahendran, J. | Amal Ranaraja, J.
offence_sections: Section 365B (2)(b) of the Penal Code
location_of_offence: Accused’s son’s house, Ketawalamula Patumaga, Colombo 09
brief_facts_summary: The accused was indicted for committing grave sexual abuse on minor victim Gladwin Roshani by inserting his fingers into her vagina while she was at his son's house watching TV. The victim reported the incident the next day to her friend, who informed teachers, leading to police involvement and medical examination. The prosecution relied primarily on the victim's testimony, which the High Court accepted, convicting the accused.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 365B (2)(b)
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the accused of grave sexual abuse on the testimony of the prosecutrix, finding it corroborated. He was sentenced to 8 years rigorous imprisonment, fined Rs. 20,000 with 4 months default, and ordered to pay Rs. 50,000 compensation to the victim with 10 months default.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The accused appealed on grounds of no specific date in indictment, inter se and per se contradictions in prosecution case, PW1 not credible, High Court misdirection on corroboration by JMO statement, and failure to consider prosecution's P4 letter where the recent incident was omitted.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Failure to mention a specific date on the indictment. | Failure to recognize inter se and per se contradictions of the prosecution’s case. | PW1 is not a credible witness. | Learned High Court Judge misdirected himself on corroboration by JMO. | Failure to consider document marked P4.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court found the prosecutrix's testimony unreliable due to omission of the specific incident in her letter P4 written two days after, mentioning only prior abuses. No independent corroboration existed, and the scenario at the accused's son's house with an unattended infant for 20 minutes raised probability doubts. Medical evidence did not strongly support the claim.
probability_assessment_by_court: Low probability due to implausible 20-minute act with imminent return of mother to infant, and inconsistencies in P4 letter; benefit of doubt to accused.
defence_version_summary: Accused gave dock statement and called one witness denying the incident. Defence emphasized contradictions, especially P4 omission and improbability. Court assessed defence credibility higher, finding prosecution evidence unconvincing and unreliable.
legal_errors_description: High Court misdirected on corroboration and failed to consider P4 letter
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: Appeal allowed as victim's uncorroborated testimony failed consistency and probability tests due to P4 omission. High Court erred in not evaluating P4 and misdirecting on JMO corroboration. Prosecution credibility undermined by inconsistencies; defence successful. Precedents emphasized caution in sexual cases without corroboration.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The Court of Appeal allowed the appeal against conviction and sentence for grave sexual abuse under Section 365B(2)(b), setting aside the High Court's 8-year rigorous imprisonment, fine, and compensation due to unreliable uncorroborated victim testimony inconsistent with P4 letter and improbable circumstances.
defence_counsel: Darshana Kuruppu with Anjana Adhikramge
hc_analysis_summary: High Court relied solely on prosecutrix's testimony, deeming it corroborated by JMO without considering P4's omission of the incident. COA held this a misdirection, as evidence lacked consistency and probability, failing to prove case beyond reasonable doubt.
precedents_cited_list: Glanville Williams, The Proof of Guilt, Third Edition | CA/129/2002 | Dingiribandage Sumanadasa v. The Republic of Sri Lanka CA No’147/2005 | Bhoginbhai Hirjibhai Vs. State of Gujarat (1983) AIR S.C. 753 | Gurcharan Singh vs. State of Haryana AIR 1972 S.C. 2661 | King vs. Athukorale 50 NLR 256 | Premasiri vs. Queen 77 NLR 86
standard_of_review_applied: Misdirection on evidence evaluation and failure to consider key document

high_court_location: Provincial High Court of Western Province holden in Negombo
judges: B. Sasi Mahendran J | Amal Ranaraja J
offence_sections: Section 25(2) read with Section 9(1) and Section 40(1) of the Forest Ordinance as amended by Act No. 65 of 2009
offence_category: Forest offence – illegal transportation of timber without permit
brief_facts_summary: The accused driver was arrested on 30.07.2022 for transporting timber in lorry WP LC 0162 without a valid permit and was charged in the Magistrate Court of Negombo under the Forest Ordinance. After the accused pleaded guilty and was sentenced, the Magistrate, acting under Section 40, ordered the confiscation of the lorry, despite the registered owner asserting she had taken precautions and had no knowledge of the offence. The Provincial High Court of Western Province, Negombo, affirmed the Magistrate’s confiscation order and also held that the appellant was not the registered owner at the time of the offence. The registered owner appealed to the Court of Appeal challenging both the factual findings and the application of the legal test under Section 40.
evidence_type_primary: Testimony of the registered owner at the confiscation inquiry regarding precautions taken and lack of knowledge of the offence
evidence_type_secondary: Documentary evidence including the certificate of registration of the motor vehicle and background facts about the driver’s employment history and absence of prior illegal use
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 40 of the Forest Ordinance as amended by Act No. 65 of 2009 (confiscation of vehicle following forest offence conviction)
hc_sentence_type: Confiscation of vehicle (lorry bearing No. WP LC 0162)
hc_judgment_summary: The Provincial High Court of Western Province, Negombo, affirmed the Magistrate’s order dated 25.10.2022 confiscating the lorry used to transport timber without a permit. The High Court further concluded that the appellant was not the registered owner of the vehicle at the time of the commission of the offence based on its reading of the registration certificate. Consequently, the High Court dismissed the appellant’s challenge to the confiscation order.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant contended that as the registered owner she had taken all reasonable precautions to prevent the use of the lorry for illegal activities and had no knowledge of the commission of the offence. She argued that the Magistrate misdirected herself in law by considering irrelevant facts, including an unsubstantiated assumption that the driver’s father had a prior conviction under the Forest Ordinance, and by failing to properly apply the legal test under Section 40. The appellant also challenged the High Court’s conclusion that she was not the registered owner at the time of the offence, pointing to the registration certificate showing ownership from 20.07.2022. She maintained that the evidence on a balance of probabilities established due precautions and lack of knowledge, rendering the confiscation unjustified.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Appellant asserted she was the registered owner of lorry WP LC 0162 at the time of the offence as evidenced by the certificate of registration showing transfer on 20.07.2022. | She claimed to have taken all necessary precautions to prevent the vehicle being used for illegal purposes and to have been unaware of the timber transportation on 30.07.2022. | She alleged that the Magistrate misapplied Section 40 of the Forest Ordinance by focusing on irrelevant considerations, including an unsupported belief that the driver’s father had a prior conviction for a similar offence. | She argued that the High Court erred in law and fact by affirming the confiscation order and by incorrectly holding that she was not the registered owner at the time of the commission of the offence.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal focused on the evidence of the appellant, who testified that the driver had worked with her and her father for more than three years, during which period there had been no prior use of the lorry for illegal activities. The Court noted that the record contained no indication that the driver’s father had previously been convicted of a similar offence, contrary to the Magistrate’s assumption. Relying on the appellant’s testimony and the absence of evidence of prior illegal use, the Court concluded that she had taken reasonable precautions and that the vehicle had been used without her knowledge, satisfying the balance of probabilities standard.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal held that under Section 40 the owner bears the burden of proving on a balance of probabilities that she took all precautions to prevent the use of the vehicle for the offence and that it was used without her knowledge, and found that this standard was met on the evidence led.
defence_version_summary: In the confiscation inquiry, the appellant as registered owner maintained that the lorry was lawfully operated in connection with her family’s business, that the driver had been a trusted employee for over three years, and that there had been no prior incidents of illegal use of the vehicle. She stated that she had taken precautions by entrusting the lorry only to this known driver and that she had no knowledge that he would transport timber without a permit. The Court of Appeal accepted her version as credible and sufficient to establish due precautions and lack of knowledge on a balance of probabilities.
legal_errors_description: The Court of Appeal found that the Magistrate erred in law by considering irrelevant matters, including an unsupported assertion that the driver’s father had a prior conviction, and by failing to properly apply the legal principles governing confiscation under Section 40(1) of the Forest Ordinance. It also held that the Provincial High Court Judge erred in concluding that the appellant was not the registered owner at the time of the offence, contrary to the certificate of registration showing ownership from 20.07.2022.
procedural_defects_description: No specific procedural defects in the conduct of the inquiry or appeal process were identified; the errors were in the legal analysis and evaluation of evidence rather than procedure.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal examined Section 40 of the Forest Ordinance and relevant case law, emphasizing that a third-party owner can avoid confiscation by proving on a balance of probabilities that all precautions were taken and that the vehicle was used without his or her knowledge. It held that the Magistrate had misdirected herself by relying on irrelevant and unsubstantiated facts and by failing to focus on whether the appellant had discharged this burden. The Court also rejected the High Court’s finding that the appellant was not the registered owner at the time of the offence, pointing to the registration certificate indicating transfer on 20.07.2022 and noting the State Counsel’s acceptance of this position. Concluding that the appellant had taken necessary precautionary measures and that the lorry was used without her knowledge, the Court set aside both the Magistrate’s and High Court’s confiscation orders and directed the release of the vehicle.
coa_sentence_type: Confiscation orders set aside and vehicle directed to be released to the appellant
brief_judgment_file_summary: This judgment concerns an appeal by the registered owner of lorry WP LC 0162 against the confiscation of the vehicle ordered by the Magistrate of Negombo and affirmed by the Provincial High Court of Western Province, Negombo, following the driver’s conviction for transporting timber without a permit under the Forest Ordinance. The Court of Appeal reviewed Section 40 and key precedents, reiterating that a third-party owner avoids confiscation by proving on a balance of probabilities that all precautions were taken and that the vehicle was used without the owner’s knowledge. It found that the Magistrate relied on irrelevant and unsupported facts, particularly an assumption about a prior conviction of the driver’s father, and that the High Court erred in holding that the appellant was not the registered owner at the time of the offence despite the registration certificate showing ownership from 20.07.2022. Holding that the appellant had in fact taken reasonable precautions and that the lorry was used without her knowledge, the Court allowed the appeal, quashed the confiscation orders, and directed that the vehicle be released to the appellant.
prosecution_counsel: Jayalakshi de Silva SSC for the Respondent
defence_counsel: Anura Seneviratne with Gayal Kalatuwawa for the Registered Owner-Petitioner-Appellant
hc_analysis_summary: The Provincial High Court Judge had upheld the Magistrate’s order of confiscation and concluded that the appellant was not the registered owner of the vehicle at the time of the offence. The Court of Appeal held that this conclusion was erroneous in light of the certificate of registration, which showed that the transfer of ownership to the appellant occurred on 20.07.2022, prior to the offence on 30.07.2022. It therefore found that the High Court failed to correctly interpret the documentary evidence and, by affirming the confiscation order founded on an incorrect legal approach, had perpetuated the Magistrate’s errors.
precedents_cited_list: The Finance Company PLC v. Agampodi Mahapedige Priyantha Chandana and 5 others – SC Appeal 105A/2008 | Umma Habeeba v. OIC, Dehiattakandiya & Other – (1999) 3 SLR 89 | Officer In Charge of Police Station Dummalasuriya v. The Attorney General – CA(PHC) 152/2018, decided on 07.02.2020 | Matilda Silva v. Inspector of Police, Habrana and Another – (2020) 2 Sri LR 265
standard_of_review_applied: Review of whether the Magistrate and High Court misdirected themselves in law and misappreciated the evidence, particularly in applying Section 40 of the Forest Ordinance and assessing whether the owner had proved on a balance of probabilities that she took all precautions and lacked knowledge of the offence.
sentencing_principles_applied: The Court applied the principle that confiscation of a vehicle as an additional punishment should not be imposed on an innocent third-party owner who proves on a balance of probabilities that reasonable precautions were taken to prevent illegal use and that the vehicle was used without the owner’s knowledge.
final_charge_after_appeal: Underlying forest offence under Section 25(2) read with Section 9(1) of the Forest Ordinance against the driver remains unchanged; only the confiscation order under Section 40(1) relating to the vehicle is set aside.

judges: B. Sasi Mahendran, J. | Amal Ranaraja, J
offence_sections: Section 25(2) read with Section 9(1)
offence_category: Illegal transportation of timber without permit
brief_facts_summary: The accused was arrested on 30 July 2022 for transporting timber without a valid permit using a lorry owned by the appellant. The accused pleaded guilty and was sentenced by the Magistrate who also confiscated the lorry after an inquiry. The High Court affirmed the confiscation order. The appellant, as the registered owner, appealed claiming she had taken precautions to prevent the offence and was unaware of it.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 25(2) read with Section 9(1) of the Forest Ordinance
hc_judgment_summary: The Provincial High Court affirmed the Magistrate's order confiscating the lorry. It concluded that the appellant was not the registered owner at the time of the offence based on the registration document. This decision was made on 10 January 2024.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant challenged the Magistrate's order on the grounds that irrelevant facts were considered, such as the alleged prior conviction of the driver's father, and that the legal principles under Section 40 were not properly applied. The High Court's affirmation was contested for erroneously concluding that the appellant was not the owner at the time of the offence. The appellant asserted she had taken all precautions and was unaware of the offence.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Magistrate considered irrelevant facts including unproven prior conviction of driver's father | Magistrate failed to apply the correct test under Section 40 of the Forest Ordinance | High Court erred in interpreting the vehicle registration document and determining ownership date
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The appellant testified that she took due precautions to prevent the offence and was unaware of it. The Court noted no evidence supported the Magistrate's finding of the driver's father's prior conviction. The Court accepted the appellant's evidence on a balance of probability, considering the driver's long employment without prior issues.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court evaluated that the appellant established on a balance of probability that she took all precautions and the offence was committed without her knowledge.
defence_version_summary: The appellant claimed she took all necessary precautions, was unaware of the offence, and the driver had worked for over 3 years without prior issues or use of the vehicle for illegal activities. No defence witnesses were specified beyond the appellant's testimony. The Court found her version credible on balance of probability. There was no alibi or dock statement as this was an inquiry into confiscation.
legal_errors_description: The Magistrate misapplied Section 40 by considering irrelevant facts and not focusing on whether precautions were taken and lack of knowledge. The High Court erred in concluding the appellant was not the registered owner at the time of the offence based on misinterpretation of the registration document.
procedural_defects_description: Improper conduct of the confiscation inquiry by considering unproven and irrelevant facts.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court allowed the appeal, finding the Magistrate erred in law and facts by considering irrelevant matters and not applying the correct test under Section 40. It held the appellant proved on balance of probability she took precautions and was unaware. The High Court's error on ownership was corrected, noting transfer occurred before the offence. Precedents on confiscation provisions were applied. The confiscation was set aside, and the vehicle ordered released. Prosecution credibility not directly at issue; defence credible. No contradictions, chain of custody, circumstantial evidence, or dying declaration involved. No sentence considerations for the appellant.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The judgment involves an appeal by the registered owner of a lorry against its confiscation following the accused driver's conviction for illegal timber transport under the Forest Ordinance. The Court of Appeal found errors in the Magistrate's and High Court's decisions, held the owner proved she took precautions and was unaware, set aside the confiscation orders dated 25 October 2022 and 10 January 2024, and directed the release of the lorry to the appellant.
defence_counsel: Anura Seneviratne with Gayal Kalatuwawa
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court affirmed the confiscation, reasoning the appellant was not the registered owner at the offence date based on the registration certificate. The Court of Appeal found this conclusion erroneous, as the document showed transfer on 20 July 2022, before the 30 July 2022 offence. The position was accepted by the State Counsel.
precedents_cited_list: The Finance Company PLC. V. Agampodi Mahapedige Priyantha Chandana and 5 others (SC Appeal 105A/2008) | Umma Habeeba v. OIC, Dehiattakandiya & Other, (1999) (3) SLR 89 | Officer In Charge of Police Station Dummalasuriya v. The Attorney General CA(PHC)/152/2018 | Matilda Silva Vs. Inspector of Police, Habrana and Another (2020) 2 Sri LR 265
standard_of_review_applied: Error in application of law under Section 40 and factual findings on ownership and precautions

judges: P. Kumararatnam J | R. P. Hettiarachchi J
offence_sections: Section 354, Section 365B(b)(2)(b) and Section 345 of the Penal Code
offence_category: Kidnapping from lawful guardianship and grave sexual abuse of a child
location_of_offence: A forested and hilly area en route from Oluvil Harbour to Ampara
brief_facts_summary: The Appellant, a police officer and relative of the eight-year-old victim, took her from home with the mother’s permission to visit Oluvil Harbour and then to his house in Ampara. On the way he stopped in a forested area, made her sit on his motorbike and kissed her, and after being warned away by a villager, took her to a nearby hilly area, laid her on a rock, removed her undergarment and kissed her again. Villagers accompanied by a police officer apprehended the Appellant at the scene and handed him over to the Buddhangala Police Post, after which both he and the child were taken to the Ampara Police Station for investigation. The prosecution charged him with kidnapping from lawful guardianship and grave sexual abuse, and he was later also convicted of an offence under section 345 of the Penal Code.
evidence_type_secondary: Circumstantial evidence arising from the conduct of the Appellant and his apprehension by villagers and a police officer
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 354 and Section 365B(b)(2)(b) (first and second counts) and Section 345 (third count) of the Penal Code
hc_sentence_type: Rigorous imprisonment terms on each count with fines and compensation to the victim
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court of Ampara, after trial, accepted the evidence led by the prosecution on all three counts and rejected the Appellant’s version. The court convicted the Appellant for kidnapping from lawful guardianship, grave sexual abuse and an offence under section 345 of the Penal Code. It imposed 4 years rigorous imprisonment on counts 1 and 3 and 15 years rigorous imprisonment on count 2 together with fines and substantial compensation to the victim, with default sentences of simple imprisonment.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: On appeal the Appellant contended that the trial judge failed properly to apply the test of probability and improbability to the testimony of the child victim, and that the prosecution had not proved its case beyond reasonable doubt. He argued that the trial judge failed to evaluate the inter se and per se contradictions in the evidence of the prosecution witnesses and to consider the defence evidence and material favourable to the Appellant. As a preliminary ground, counsel challenged the conviction under section 345 of the Penal Code when the Appellant had not been indicted for that offence and complained that counts 2 and 3 arose from a single sexual act, so that dual convictions and sentences were improper and prejudicial. After the DSG indicated that she would not contest the sentence on the second count, the defence ultimately focused on the sentences imposed on the remaining counts.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Alleged failure of the trial judge to consider the test of probability and improbability in assessing the testimony of PW1, the child victim. | Assertion that the prosecution failed to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt. | Alleged failure by the trial judge to evaluate inter se and per se contradictions in the evidence of prosecution witnesses. | Complaint that the trial judge failed to consider the defence evidence led on behalf of the Appellant. | Complaint that the trial judge failed to consider evidence favourable to the Appellant. | Preliminary objection that the Appellant was convicted under section 345 of the Penal Code without being indicted for that offence and that counts 2 and 3 improperly arose from a single sexual act, causing prejudice through dual convictions and sentences.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The conviction was founded primarily on the testimony of the eight-year-old victim regarding the sexual acts and on the observations and intervention of villagers and a police officer who apprehended the Appellant at the scene. The Appellant gave evidence from the witness box in his own defence, but the High Court preferred the prosecution version and convicted him on all three counts. The Court of Appeal, while intervening on the second count as a matter of law, otherwise accepted the High Court’s assessment of the evidence.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal was satisfied that the overall prosecution narrative, including the victim’s account and the circumstances of the Appellant’s apprehension by villagers and a police officer, was sufficiently probable and cogent to sustain the convictions on counts 1 and 3. It did not find any material improbability or inconsistency warranting interference with those convictions and rejected the contention that the prosecution had failed to establish a reasonable and coherent case.
defence_version_summary: The Appellant entered a plea of not guilty and gave evidence from the witness box in his own defence, seeking to cast doubt on the credibility and reliability of the child victim and the prosecution witnesses. No other defence witnesses were called. The High Court rejected his evidence as less credible than the consistent account of the victim and the surrounding circumstances of his arrest, and the Court of Appeal saw no basis to disturb that assessment in respect of counts 1 and 3.
legal_errors_description: The Court of Appeal held that it was improper for the Appellant to stand convicted on both the second and third counts when they arose out of a single sexual act. It therefore set aside the conviction and sentence on count 2 and acquitted the Appellant on that count, while affirming the remaining convictions.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal considered the evidence and the submissions of both counsel and accepted that the High Court had been entitled to rely on the victim’s evidence and the corroborative circumstances to convict on the kidnapping and section 345 counts. It agreed with the complaint that counts 2 and 3 related to a single sexual act and that maintaining both convictions would result in improper duplication, especially in light of the stance taken by the DSG. Accordingly, it quashed the conviction and sentence on the grave sexual abuse count, affirmed the convictions and sentences on counts 1 and 3, and ordered those sentences to run concurrently from the original date of sentence.
coa_sentence_type: 4 years rigorous imprisonment on count 1 and 4 years rigorous imprisonment on count 3 to run concurrently from 2023-08-11, together with the fines and compensation ordered by the High Court on those counts
brief_judgment_file_summary: This appeal concerned a police officer convicted by the High Court of Ampara of kidnapping an eight-year-old girl from her lawful guardianship, grave sexual abuse and an associated offence under section 345 of the Penal Code, and sentenced to rigorous imprisonment, fines and compensation. On appeal he challenged the assessment of the evidence, alleged failures to consider contradictions and the defence case, and raised a preliminary objection to being convicted under section 345 when not indicted, as well as to dual convictions based on a single sexual act. The Court of Appeal, having noted that the second and third counts arose from one sexual transaction and in light of the concession of the Deputy Solicitor General, set aside the conviction and sentence on the grave sexual abuse count and acquitted the Appellant on that count. It affirmed the convictions and sentences on the kidnapping and section 345 counts but ordered those sentences to run concurrently from the original date of sentence, thereby partially varying the outcome while otherwise dismissing the appeal.
defence_counsel: Amila Palliyage with Sandeepani Wijesooriya, Savani Udugampola, Lakitha Wakishta Arachchi and Subaj De Silva
hc_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal recognized that the High Court had largely evaluated the evidence correctly in accepting the child victim’s account and supporting testimony and in rejecting the Appellant’s evidence. However, it found that the High Court erred in maintaining separate convictions on the second and third counts where both were founded on a single sexual act, thereby exposing the Appellant to double punishment. The appellate court therefore corrected this error by setting aside the conviction and sentence on count 2 while affirming the remainder of the High Court’s reasoning and orders.
standard_of_review_applied: Review of the sufficiency of evidence and correction of a misapplication of law in permitting dual convictions for a single sexual act and the resulting sentencing error
sentencing_principles_applied: The Court applied the principle that an offender should not suffer multiple punishments for the same transaction and directed that only one conviction should stand for the single sexual act while ordering the remaining custodial sentences to run concurrently in light of all the circumstances.
final_charge_after_appeal: Count 1 under Section 354 of the Penal Code for kidnapping from lawful guardianship and Count 3 under Section 345 of the Penal Code for sexual misconduct, with Count 2 under Section 365B(b)(2)(b) set aside

judges: B. Sasi Mahendran J | Amal Ranaraja J
offence_sections: Section 20(b) read with Section 20(a)(vi) of the Bribery Act No.11 of 1954 (as amended)
location_of_offence: Narahenpita and Maharagama, within the jurisdiction of the High Court of Colombo
brief_facts_summary: The complainant and PW02, who was operating bus CP GO 2274, sought to obtain a passenger transport permit in PW02's name and were directed by an intermediary (PW03) to the accused at the Ceylon Transport Board office. The accused allegedly agreed to assist in obtaining a fresh route permit for a payment of Rs.300,000 and thereafter received Rs.200,000 in cash and a further Rs.100,000 via bank deposit. Despite receiving these sums, the accused failed to secure the permit and later denied having taken money for that purpose, leading PW01 to complain to the Commission to Investigate Allegations of Bribery or Corruption. The prosecution case centred on these alleged solicitations and acceptances of gratification, while the accused maintained that, as a wealthy businessman, he had no need to solicit money.
evidence_type_primary: Eyewitness testimony of complainant and associated witnesses
evidence_type_secondary: Documentary evidence including power of attorney and bank deposit slip, and official records relating to bus ownership and route permits
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 20(b) read with Section 20(a)(vi) of the Bribery Act No.11 of 1954 (as amended)
hc_sentence_type: Rigorous Imprisonment 5 years on each of the three charges, plus fines and compensation with consecutive default terms
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court of Colombo found that the prosecution had proved beyond reasonable doubt that the accused had solicited and accepted gratification from PW02 to assist in obtaining a passenger transport permit. The court convicted the accused on all three charges and imposed five years rigorous imprisonment on each charge, fines on each count, and ordered payment of compensation with consecutive default terms of imprisonment. The High Court reasoned that the elements of the bribery offences were established on the evidence led.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: On appeal, the defence challenged the conviction and sentences, arguing among other things that there was a discrepancy between the journal entry and the written judgment as to whether the appellant was convicted on all three charges. The appellant also complained that the charges improperly combined conduct under sections 20(a) and 20(b) of the Bribery Act and that any errors in the particulars were not material to mislead him. Further, it was contended that the prosecution had failed to prove that PW02 was the registered owner of the bus or that the appellant was in a position to influence the National Transport Commission to issue the route permit. The defence maintained that, given these deficiencies, the prosecution case was not proved beyond reasonable doubt and that the appellant should receive the benefit of the doubt.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Alleged discrepancy between the journal entry, which recorded conviction on all three charges, and the written judgment, which appeared to convict only on the first two charges. | Complaint that the indictment improperly combined distinct conduct described in section 20(a) and section 20(b) of the Bribery Act into single charges, allegedly causing prejudice to the appellant. | Argument that the prosecution failed to prove that PW02 was the registered owner of bus CP GO 2274 at the relevant time, which was said to be essential to substantiate the charges. | Argument that the prosecution failed to establish that the appellant was in a position to influence the National Transport Commission in issuing the route permit, an essential element for the offences as charged. | Reliance on the appellant's dock statement asserting his inherited wealth and lack of financial need, to deny any motive to solicit or accept gratification.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The prosecution relied mainly on the testimonies of PW01 and PW02 regarding their dealings with the appellant, supported by PW03 who introduced them to the appellant and PW04 who spoke only to the appellant's association with a regional office of the Central Transport Board. The Court of Appeal noted that, while these witnesses described payments and discussions about a route permit, the prosecution failed to adduce cogent evidence proving PW02's status as registered owner or that the appellant could in fact influence the issuance of the permit. The court found that the discrepancies and omissions in the prosecution case materially weakened its cogency so that the standard of proof beyond reasonable doubt was not met.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal held that, in light of the failure to prove key elements such as the appellant's capacity to secure the route permit and PW02's registered ownership, the prosecution had not established the charges beyond reasonable doubt and the benefit of the doubt had to be given to the appellant.
defence_version_summary: In his dock statement, the appellant categorically denied soliciting or accepting any gratification from PW02 and asserted that, as the son of a successful businessman with inherited wealth, he had no financial need to engage in such conduct. He maintained that he was not pressed for money and thus had no motive to act as alleged. The Court of Appeal considered that these assertions did not show that he had been misled by any alleged errors in the particulars of the charges but focused instead on whether the prosecution proved the essential elements of the offences.
legal_errors_description: The Court of Appeal found the High Court's reasoning erroneous in concluding that the prosecution had established the appellant's guilt, despite the absence of substantial evidence linking the appellant to the authority of the National Transport Commission and the failure to prove PW02's registered ownership of the bus. It held that the learned High Court Judge's conclusion, reached in the face of these evidential deficiencies, was based on flawed reasoning that materially affected the outcome.
procedural_defects_description: There was a discrepancy between the journal entry, which recorded that the judgment convicted the appellant on all three charges, and the written judgment, which appeared to convict him only on the first two charges, though the Court of Appeal treated this as a typographical error that did not cause a failure of justice.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal carefully examined the indictment, the evidence of the prosecution witnesses, and the High Court's reasoning. It held that, notwithstanding the typographical error in the judgment about the number of charges of conviction, the core issue was whether the prosecution had proved beyond reasonable doubt that the appellant both solicited and accepted gratification in circumstances where he could influence the National Transport Commission to issue a route permit. The court concluded that the prosecution had failed to establish that PW02 was the registered owner of the bus or that the appellant was in a position to procure the permit under the National Transport Commission Act, and that PW04's evidence went only to his association with a regional office of the Central Transport Board. Finding that these evidential deficiencies and discrepancies materially undermined the prosecution case, the Court of Appeal set aside the conviction, judgment and sentence and acquitted the appellant, also declining to order a retrial due to the lapse of 17 years since the offences.
coa_sentence_type: No sentence imposed as the appellant was acquitted of all charges
brief_judgment_file_summary: This appeal arose from a High Court of Colombo conviction of the appellant on three counts of soliciting and accepting gratification under section 20(b) read with section 20(a)(vi) of the Bribery Act, based on allegations that he took Rs.300,000 in total to assist PW02 in obtaining a passenger transport permit for bus CP GO 2274. The High Court sentenced him to five years rigorous imprisonment on each count, fines, and compensation with consecutive default terms. On appeal, the Court of Appeal considered challenges to the form of the charges, the discrepancy between the journal entry and the written judgment, and, crucially, the sufficiency of the evidence regarding PW02's status as registered owner and the appellant's capacity to influence the National Transport Commission under the National Transport Commission Act. Finding that the prosecution had failed to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt and that the High Court's reasoning was flawed, the Court of Appeal set aside the conviction, judgment and sentencing order, acquitted the appellant of all charges, and refused to order a retrial due to the 17-year lapse since the offences.
prosecution_counsel: Anuradha Siriwardhana, Assistant Director General for the Respondent
defence_counsel: Priyantha Nawana P.C. with Ravihansa Wijesinghe for the Accused-Appellant
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court had concluded that the prosecution had proved all three charges of solicitation and acceptance of gratification, reasoning that the appellant's conduct met the elements of the bribery offences. However, as noted by the Court of Appeal, the High Court accepted the prosecution case despite the lack of cogent proof that PW02 was the registered owner of the bus and the absence of evidence that the appellant could influence the National Transport Commission to issue a route permit. The Court of Appeal held that this amounted to flawed and erroneous reasoning, and that the High Court should have entertained reasonable doubt about the appellant's guilt on all three charges.
precedents_cited_list: Queen v. G. K. Jayasinghe – 69 NLR 314
standard_of_review_applied: Assessment of whether the prosecution had established the offences beyond reasonable doubt, including scrutiny of the High Court's evaluation of evidence and its reasoning for finding guilt in the face of evidential deficiencies.

judges: P. Kumararatnam, J. | R. P. Hettiarachchi, J.
offence_sections: Section 140, Section 296 read with Section 146, Section 296 read with Section 32, Section 317 read with Section 146, Section 317 read with Section 32, Section 315
brief_facts_summary: On or about 22.06.1990 at Bogahakumbura, the accused, together with others, went to the house of PW2 and PW3, where their mother, sister and two brothers were present. Armed with a long knife, the 1st Appellant attacked PW2 and then, inside the house, the deceased family members were brutally cut to death while PW2 and PW3 escaped. The prosecution relied mainly on the evidence of PW2 and PW3, whose father PW1's prior testimony was admitted under Section 33 of the Evidence Ordinance, supported by medical evidence and recovery of the knife upon a statement of an Appellant. The case centred on whether the appellants shared a common murderous intention under Section 32 of the Penal Code.
evidence_type_secondary: Medical and post-mortem evidence, and recovery of the weapon
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 296 read with Section 32 (four counts of murder) and Section 315 (causing hurt)
hc_sentence_type: Death sentence on four counts of murder and two years rigorous imprisonment plus fine for causing hurt
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court of Badulla, after a non-jury trial, convicted the three appellants on counts 7 to 10 for murder under Section 296 read with Section 32 and on count 11 for causing hurt under Section 315. The court sentenced them to death for the four murder counts and to two years rigorous imprisonment, with a fine of 5000 and a default sentence of six months simple imprisonment, on the hurt count. The High Court found the eyewitnesses credible and held that the appellants acted with common murderous intention.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The 1st Appellant argued that he was deprived of a fair trial because he was not afforded an opportunity to cross-examine witnesses after being produced under Section 241(3), that the High Court Judge improperly examined witness statements, that the judgment was merely a narration of evidence without analysis, and that the burden of proof was misdirected and wrongly cast on the defence. The 2nd Appellant contended that the prosecution evidence lacked credibility and that the judge erred in law in concluding that he shared a common murderous intention. The 3rd Appellant maintained that the judge failed properly to assess whether his presence was merely presence or participatory presence and similarly complained of improper use of witness statements. Collectively, the appellants challenged both the factual findings on credibility and common intention and the legal and procedural correctness of the trial.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: 1st Appellant: Alleged deprivation of fair trial due to failure to allow cross-examination of witnesses after his appearance under Section 241(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure. | 1st Appellant: Complaint that the High Court Judge examined or relied on police statements of witnesses when writing the judgment. | 1st Appellant: Allegation that the High Court judgment was merely a narration of testimony and lacked proper analysis and reasons. | 1st Appellant: Ground that the High Court Judge misdirected himself on the burden of proof and effectively shifted the burden onto the appellants. | 2nd Appellant: Challenge to the credibility of the prosecution witnesses, arguing that their evidence does not meet the test of credibility. | 2nd Appellant: Allegation that the judge erred in law in concluding that the 2nd Appellant entertained common murderous intention. | 3rd Appellant: Complaint that the judge failed to appreciate whether the 3rd Appellant’s presence was participatory or merely passive. | 3rd Appellant: Ground that the High Court Judge improperly examined or referred to witness statements in the judgment.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal noted that PW2 and PW3, who were 15 and 13 years old at the time of the incident, gave consistent and cogent evidence identifying the appellants and describing the attack, with any discrepancies being minor and not affecting the core of the prosecution case. PW1’s earlier deposition, admitted under Section 33, corroborated their account, as did the medical evidence of the JMO that all deceased sustained cut injuries to vital parts of their bodies. The court accepted that the appellants were together inside the house throughout the incident and that their conduct, including restraining PW2 and the recovery of the knife on an appellant’s statement, demonstrated common murderous intention.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal, relying inter alia on Bandara v The State, held that minor discrepancies which do not go to the root of the prosecution case should be disregarded, particularly where all probability factors favour the witnesses' version. It concluded that the appellants' evidence did not generate a reasonable doubt and that the probabilities clearly supported the prosecution narrative.
defence_version_summary: The appellants denied liability and sought to undermine the prosecution case by challenging the fairness of the trial, the use of prior statements, the credibility of PW2 and PW3, and the finding of common murderous intention. The 1st and 2nd Appellants gave sworn evidence from the witness box, while the 3rd Appellant made a dock statement, but the judgment does not set out a detailed alternative factual version such as an alibi. The High Court, as affirmed by the Court of Appeal, found that the defence evidence failed to create any reasonable doubt in the prosecution case or to displace the strong eyewitness and medical evidence.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal held that the High Court had afforded a fair trial to all appellants, correctly applied Section 241(3), and was entitled to refuse a de novo trial or recall of witnesses because the 1st Appellant’s absence was mala fide. It rejected the complaint that the judge improperly examined police statements, finding instead that the decision was based on trial evidence, and it concluded that the judgment did contain adequate analysis and reasons. On the merits, the court held that the evidence of PW2 and PW3, corroborated by PW1’s prior testimony, the medical evidence and the recovery of the knife, firmly established the appellants' participation and common murderous intention, and that alleged contradictions did not affect the core of the case. Consequently, the Court of Appeal found no misdirection on the burden of proof or other legal error and affirmed both conviction and sentence.
coa_sentence_type: Death sentence on four counts of murder and two years rigorous imprisonment plus fine for causing hurt, affirmed
brief_judgment_file_summary: This appeal arose from the conviction of three appellants by the High Court of Badulla for four counts of murder under Section 296 read with Section 32 of the Penal Code and one count of causing hurt under Section 315, relating to a 1990 incident at Bogahakumbura in which a mother, daughter and two sons of the main eyewitness were brutally killed. After a complex procedural history, including an earlier appeal and retrial, the appellants challenged their convictions on grounds of denial of fair trial, alleged improper use of witness statements, lack of analysis in the High Court judgment, misdirection on the burden of proof, lack of credibility of the eyewitnesses and failure to establish common murderous intention. The Court of Appeal, emphasising the right to a fair trial and principles on use of prior statements and common intention, held that the High Court had properly conducted the trial, adequately analysed the evidence and correctly applied the law, and that the eyewitness and medical evidence, together with recovery of the weapon, proved the charges beyond reasonable doubt. It dismissed all grounds of appeal and affirmed the convictions and sentences, including the death penalty on the murder counts and the custodial sentence and fine on the hurt count.
prosecution_counsel: Shanil Kularatne, PC, ASG for the Respondent
defence_counsel: Saliya Peiris, PC with Thanuka Nandasiri and Dhimarsha Marso for the 1st Appellant; Shantha Jayawardena with Hiranya Damunupola, Wihangi Tissera and Tharuka Ranatunga for the 2nd Appellant; Neranjan Jayasinghe with Randunu Heelage and Imangsi Senarath for the 3rd Appellant
cause_of_death_exact_text: All deceased had sustained cut injuries to the vital parts of the body resulting in death.
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court analysed the testimony of PW2 and PW3, corroborated by PW1’s prior evidence and the medical and physical evidence, and concluded that their accounts were credible and that the appellants were present together inside the house throughout the attack. It inferred from their conduct, including the 1st Appellant’s use of the knife, the restraining of PW2 by the 2nd and 3rd Appellants, and their collective presence until departure, that they shared a common murderous intention under Section 32 of the Penal Code. The Court of Appeal agreed with this reasoning, finding that the High Court correctly applied the principles on common intention and evaluated the alleged contradictions as minor.
