judges: B. Sasi Mahendran J. | Amal Ranaraja J.
offence_sections: Section 140, Section 146 read with Section 296, Section 32 read with Section 296, Section 394 of the Penal Code
location_of_offence: Location adjacent to the kitchen of the deceased's house
brief_facts_summary: The deceased, who ran a bakery, was at home having dinner when the first appellant jumped over his parapet wall, called him out in abusive terms and assaulted him, after which other accused, including the second appellant, joined in. The second appellant went back to his house, returned with a knife, declared he would finish the deceased and inflicted multiple knife injuries while the first appellant encouraged him. The deceased sustained 19 external injuries, including 13 cut injuries, which the doctor opined were the cause of death. The prosecution case rested mainly on eyewitness testimony and medical evidence, while the first appellant remained silent and the second appellant gave a dock statement denying involvement and referring to a land dispute.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 32 read with Section 296 of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the first and second accused of the third charge, namely causing the murder of the deceased under section 32 read with section 296 of the Penal Code, and sentenced them to death. The trial judge evaluated the prosecution and defence evidence holistically, testing credibility and corroboration, and found the prosecution witnesses convincing and logical. The judge rejected the second appellant's dock statement as lacking credibility and concluded that the prosecution had proved the third charge beyond reasonable doubt.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: On behalf of the first appellant, it was argued that the evidence warranted consideration of the exception of sudden fight under Exception 4 to section 294 of the Penal Code, which would reduce the offence from murder to culpable homicide. On behalf of the second appellant, it was contended that the High Court judgment was legally and factually flawed and violated section 283 of the Code of Criminal Procedure Act. In particular, non-compliance with section 283(2) was alleged, suggesting that the judgment did not adequately specify the conviction and punishment in terms of the statute. The appellants sought to have the conviction and sentence set aside or reduced on these grounds.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: First appellant: the evidence at trial required consideration of the exception of sudden fight within Exception 4 to section 294 of the Penal Code, so the conviction for murder should be mitigated to culpable homicide. | Second appellant: the High Court judgment is legally and factually flawed and untenable. | Second appellant: the judgment violates section 283 of the Code of Criminal Procedure Act No. 15 of 1979. | Second appellant: specific complaint of non-compliance with section 283(2) regarding specification of the offence, section of law and punishment.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal noted that the High Court judge had listed and considered the witnesses, assessing their testimony in a holistic manner rather than in isolation. The trial judge applied tests of credibility and corroboration, cross-referencing oral testimony with physical and documentary evidence, and found the prosecution evidence convincing and logical. The evidence of the second appellant given from the dock was expressly rejected, while the prosecution eyewitness and medical evidence were accepted as sufficient to prove the charge.
probability_assessment_by_court: Both the High Court and Court of Appeal considered the totality of evidence and concluded that the prosecution version was credible and consistent, while the defence version was improbable, so that a reasonable and prudent person would believe the accused to be guilty beyond reasonable doubt.
defence_version_summary: The first appellant chose to remain silent and did not call any witnesses in his defence. The second appellant did not call witnesses but made a dock statement, denying any involvement in the incident and stating that there had been a dispute over a block of land the deceased had given him and later sought to buy back, leading to threats through third parties. The High Court judge gave reasons for rejecting the second appellant's statement as unconvincing and not raising a reasonable doubt, and the Court of Appeal agreed with this assessment.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: On the sudden fight argument, the Court of Appeal analysed the sequence of events and held that the incident was pre-arranged and premeditated rather than a sudden, unplanned fight; the first appellant aggressively summoned the deceased out of his house, multiple accused gathered, and the second appellant had time to go home, arm himself with a knife and return to stab the unarmed deceased. These findings showed undue advantage and cruelty, disqualifying the appellants from the benefit of Exception 4 to section 294. Regarding the section 283 complaint, the court reviewed the structure and reasoning of the High Court judgment, noting that it clearly set out the charges, identified witnesses, evaluated evidence holistically with proper credibility assessments, and specified the conviction and sentence, thus complying with section 283. The Court of Appeal endorsed the High Court's view that the prosecution evidence was convincing and that the defence dock statement lacked merit, and it found that the conviction on the third charge and the death sentence were neither perverse nor unlawful.
coa_sentence_type: Death
brief_judgment_file_summary: This Court of Appeal judgment concerns an appeal by the first and second accused, who, together with others, were indicted in the Colombo High Court for unlawful assembly, murder and related offences arising from the fatal stabbing of a bakery owner on 25 August 2009. The High Court convicted the two appellants on the third charge of causing murder under section 32 read with section 296 of the Penal Code and sentenced them to death, while acquitting the remaining accused. On appeal, the first appellant relied on the sudden fight exception under section 294, and the second appellant challenged the legality and sufficiency of the High Court judgment under section 283 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The Court of Appeal examined the facts, emphasised the pre-arranged nature of the attack and the use of a deadly weapon against an unarmed victim, and concluded that the requirements of Exception 4 were not satisfied. It further held that the High Court judgment complied with statutory requirements, properly evaluated the evidence, and that the conviction and sentence were supported by credible prosecution evidence, thereby dismissing the appeal.
defence_counsel: I.B.S. Harshana for the 1st Accused-Appellant; Indika Mallawaratchy for the 2nd Accused-Appellant
cause_of_death_exact_text: Death was due to multiple cut injuries; the doctor observed 19 external injuries, 13 of which were cut injuries and opined that the cut injuries were the cause of death.
hc_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal observed that the High Court judge began by clearly setting out the charges and listing the witnesses, thereby framing the issues for decision. The judge evaluated the evidence in a holistic manner, applying tests of credibility and corroboration and cross-referencing oral testimony with physical and documentary material. The High Court found the prosecution evidence compelling, rejected the second appellant's dock statement with reasons, and held that the elements of the third charge were proved beyond reasonable doubt; the Court of Appeal endorsed this approach and found no fault with the reasoning or sentence.
precedents_cited_list: Amaranath Singh – AIR 1928 OUD 282 | Chandrasena and Others v. Munaweera – [1998] 3 SLR 94 | Ibrahim v. Inspector of Police – 59 NLR 235 | Thusaiya v. Pathihamy – 15 CLW 119 | James Silva v. The Republic of Sri Lanka – [1980] 2 SLR 167 | Jayasena v. The Queen – 72 NLR 313
standard_of_review_applied: Review for misapplication of Exception 4 to section 294 and for compliance with section 283 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, assessing whether the High Court properly evaluated evidence and whether its findings were perverse or unsupported.
sentencing_principles_applied: The Court of Appeal affirmed that the death sentence imposed upon conviction for murder under section 296 was not perverse and left it undisturbed, without elaborating further sentencing principles.
final_charge_after_appeal: Murder under section 32 read with section 296 of the Penal Code (third charge)

judges: P. Kumararatnam, J. | R.P. Hettiarachchi, J.
offence_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The Accused-Appellant, Gamage Don Ajantha Kumara, was indicted for two counts of murder of Meegahawattage Don Rathnawathi and Wanduraba Dewage Jinadasa alleged to have been committed on or about 30/05/2005, punishable under Section 296 of the Penal Code. Following a non-jury trial in the High Court of Kalutara, he was convicted on both counts and sentenced to death on 26/10/2017. On appeal, material was placed before the Court of Appeal indicating that the Appellant suffered from a major mental illness, Schizophrenia with cognitive impairment, and there was evidence suggesting he was of unsound mind at the time of the offence. The Court of Appeal considered a detailed forensic psychiatric report and proceeded to deal with the case under Section 338 of the Code of Criminal Procedure.
evidence_type_primary: Medical and psychiatric evidence regarding the Appellant's mental condition
evidence_type_secondary: Documentary evidence such as the Diagnosis Ticket and Consultant Forensic Psychiatrist's report
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code (two counts of murder)
hc_judgment_summary: After a non-jury trial, the High Court of Kalutara convicted the Appellant on two counts of murder under Section 296 of the Penal Code. The court imposed the death sentence on both counts. The trial judge rejected the defence of insanity on the basis that the Appellant failed to establish it on a balance of probabilities, despite a Diagnosis Ticket being produced subject to proof.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The Appellant appealed against the conviction and sentence seeking to have both set aside. During the appellate proceedings, counsel for the Appellant brought to the Court's attention materials indicating that the Appellant was suffering from a mental disorder and had a record of unsoundness of mind. A subsequent forensic psychiatric assessment concluded that the Appellant suffered from Schizophrenia with cognitive impairment and was likely of unsound mind at the time of the alleged offence. The appeal thus effectively focused on the Appellant's mental incapacity at the time of the commission of the acts and the consequent inappropriateness of the death sentence.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Challenge to the conviction and sentence for two counts of murder imposed by the High Court. | Reliance on materials indicating that the Appellant had been suffering from a mental disorder and had a record of unsoundness of mind. | Submission of a Consultant Forensic Psychiatrist's report stating that the Appellant suffered from Schizophrenia with cognitive impairment and was incapable of understanding the nature and wrongfulness of his acts at the time of the offence. | Request to consider the case under Section 338 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, quashing the death sentence and dealing with the Appellant as a person of unsound mind.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The judgment of the Court of Appeal does not analyse in detail the prosecution or defence witnesses regarding the facts of the murder itself. Instead, the focus is on the Appellant's mental state, including his prior admission to Ward No.59 of the National Hospital in 2003 and the subsequent forensic psychiatric evaluation. The Consultant Forensic Psychiatrist concluded that the Appellant suffered from a major mental illness, Schizophrenia with cognitive impairment, and was incapable of understanding the nature and wrongfulness of his acts at the time of the alleged offence.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal, relying on the Consultant Forensic Psychiatrist's report, held that it was most probable that the Appellant was of unsound mind when he committed the acts in question, and that he was incapable of knowing the nature of his actions or that they were wrong or contrary to law. The court therefore treated him as a person who, although guilty of the act, was legally insane at the time within the meaning of Section 338 of the Code of Criminal Procedure.
defence_version_summary: At the High Court trial, the Appellant raised a defence of insanity supported by a Diagnosis Ticket showing his admission to Ward No.59 of the National Hospital from 30.03.2003 to 10.08.2003, but the trial judge rejected this defence as not proved on a balance of probabilities. On appeal, additional psychiatric material was obtained, and a Consultant Forensic Psychiatrist opined that the Appellant suffered from Schizophrenia with cognitive impairment and was unable to understand the nature or wrongfulness of his actions at the time of the offence. The Court of Appeal accepted this opinion for the purposes of Section 338 CPC and treated the Appellant as having been of unsound mind, though still responsible for the physical acts.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal focused on the Appellant's mental condition, noting that both parties accepted there was a record of unsound mind and that the court had obtained a report from a Consultant Forensic Psychiatrist. The Psychiatrist opined that the Appellant suffered from Schizophrenia with cognitive impairment and was incapable of understanding the nature and wrongfulness of his acts at the time of the alleged offence, and that he would have been of unsound mind then. Applying Section 338 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, the Court held that although the Appellant was guilty of the acts charged, he was legally insane at the time and therefore quashed the death sentence. The court ordered that he be kept in safe custody at the National Institute of Mental Health, Mulleriyawa New Town, and directed that the matter be reported to the Minister of Justice and National Integration for further orders.
coa_sentence_type: Sentence of death quashed; order for safe custody in a mental health institution under Section 338 of the Code of Criminal Procedure
brief_judgment_file_summary: This is a Court of Appeal judgment arising from an appeal by Gamage Don Ajantha Kumara, who had been convicted by the High Court of Kalutara of two counts of murder under Section 296 of the Penal Code and sentenced to death. On appeal, his counsel produced material indicating that he had a history of mental illness, and the court obtained a detailed report from a Consultant Forensic Psychiatrist at the National Institute of Mental Health. The Psychiatrist concluded that the Appellant suffered from Schizophrenia with cognitive impairment and was incapable of understanding the nature and wrongfulness of his acts at the time of the offence, and that he would have been of unsound mind then. The Court of Appeal, acting under Section 338 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, quashed the sentence of death, ordered that the Appellant be kept in safe custody at the National Institute of Mental Health, and directed that the case be reported to the Minister of Justice and National Integration, while leaving the conviction for the acts undisturbed.
defence_counsel: Indica Mallawarachchi
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court of Kalutara conducted a non-jury trial and convicted the Appellant of two counts of murder, sentencing him to death. At trial, the Appellant raised a defence of insanity, relying on a Diagnosis Ticket from his prior admission to the National Hospital in 2003, but the High Court rejected this defence as not proved on a balance of probabilities. The Court of Appeal did not expressly characterise the High Court's reasoning as erroneous but, in light of the later forensic psychiatric report and Section 338 CPC, took the view that the Appellant was most probably of unsound mind at the time of the offences and therefore intervened only in relation to the sentence.
standard_of_review_applied: Application of Section 338 of the Code of Criminal Procedure based on unsoundness of mind and reconsideration of sentence in light of psychiatric evidence
sentencing_principles_applied: Application of Section 338 of the Code of Criminal Procedure to quash the death sentence and order safe custody for an offender who was of unsound mind at the time of the offence
final_charge_after_appeal: Same as original: two counts of murder under Section 296 of the Penal Code, with sentence modified under Section 338 CPC

judges: B. Sasi Mahendran J | Amal Ranaraja J
offence_sections: Section 364(2)(e) of the Penal Code as amended by Act No. 22 of 1995
brief_facts_summary: The accused was indicted in the High Court of Puttalam for committing rape on Rajapakshe Arachchilage Nirmala Manel Kumari, who was around 14 years old at the time of the incident. The accused was a close relative of the victim, with a social responsibility to care for her. As a result of the sexual abuse, the victim suffered trauma and was unable to continue her schooling as usual. The High Court convicted the accused under Section 364(2)(e) and imposed a substantial custodial sentence, fine, and compensation.
evidence_type_primary: Victim's testimony and eyewitness testimony (oral evidence)
evidence_type_secondary: Other prosecution witness testimony; no scientific or forensic evidence is discussed in the judgment excerpt
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 364(2)(e) of the Penal Code as amended by Act No. 22 of 1995
hc_sentence_type: Rigorous Imprisonment 12 years plus fine and compensation with default terms of simple imprisonment
hc_judgment_summary: By judgment dated 16.07.2024 the High Court of Puttalam found the accused guilty of rape under Section 364(2)(e) of the Penal Code. The court imposed a sentence of 12 years rigorous imprisonment, a fine of 20000 with 3 months simple imprisonment in default, and ordered payment of 200000 as compensation to the victim with 1 year simple imprisonment in default. In determining sentence, the High Court considered the statutory range of 10 to 20 years, the circumstances of the offence, and imposed a sentence above the statutory minimum.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: In his petition of appeal the accused initially challenged the conviction, alleging that the prosecution case was inherently improbable and contradictory, that there were glaring contradictions and omissions in the evidence of the alleged eyewitness, and that the evidence of the victim lacked independent corroboration and did not inspire confidence. He also complained of contradictions among material prosecution witnesses. However, when the matter was supported before the Court of Appeal, counsel for the accused expressly confined the appeal to the sentence and sought mitigation rather than a challenge to the finding of guilt.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Alleged failure of the High Court Judge to consider the inherently improbable and contradictory nature of the prosecution case. | Alleged failure to consider glaring contradictions and omissions in the evidence of PW03, the alleged eyewitness, affecting the authenticity of the prosecution case. | Alleged failure to consider inter se and per se contradictions between material prosecution witnesses. | Alleged lack of independent corroboration for the evidence of PW01 (the victim) and that her evidence did not inspire confidence. | At the hearing before the Court of Appeal, counsel limited the challenge to the severity of the sentence and sought mitigation rather than contesting the conviction.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The prosecution led evidence from 8 witnesses, including the victim (PW01) and an alleged eyewitness, PW03, and closed its case after marking productions P1 to P3. The defence consisted solely of a dock statement by the accused with no defence witnesses being called. In the appeal as finally argued, the Court of Appeal did not re-evaluate the entirety of the evidence but proceeded on the basis that the conviction stood and focused on whether the sentencing discretion of the High Court was properly exercised.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal proceeded on the basis that the trial judge had properly evaluated the credibility of the prosecution witnesses and found the prosecution case proved beyond reasonable doubt. As the appeal was confined to sentence, the Court did not disturb findings on probability or credibility and held there was no basis to interfere with the trial judge's evaluation. The benefit of doubt was not extended to the accused as no misappreciation of evidence was demonstrated.
defence_version_summary: After the close of the prosecution case the accused opted to make a dock statement and did not call any defence witnesses. The content of this dock statement is not set out in the judgment excerpt, and there is no indication that any alibi or alternative version was supported by independent evidence. Both the High Court and the Court of Appeal treated the defence as insufficient to create a reasonable doubt in the face of the prosecution evidence, and in the Court of Appeal the defence ultimately concentrated on mitigation of sentence.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal noted that the statutory punishment for rape of a girl under eighteen under Section 364(2)(e) is rigorous imprisonment between 10 and 20 years, together with a fine and compensation, and treated 10 years as the base sentence. Relying on authorities including Badde Liyanage Wasantha Kumara v. Attorney General, Attorney General v. Ranasinghe and Others, and English sentencing guidance, the Court emphasized deterrent sentencing for sexual offences against children and the need to weigh aggravating and mitigating factors. It accepted that the High Court had carefully considered the mitigating circumstances advanced on behalf of the accused (age, lack of previous convictions, family responsibilities, long attendance at court) as well as aggravating features (victim's young age and the accused's familial relationship), and concluded that a sentence of 12 years rigorous imprisonment appropriately reflected a balanced and reasoned assessment. Finding no error in principle or disproportion, the Court declined to interfere with the sentence but backdated it to the date of conviction.
coa_sentence_type: Rigorous Imprisonment 12 years with fine of 20000 and compensation of 200000, backdated to date of conviction
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused, Wijjapathi Muththalage Ariyadasa, was indicted in the High Court of Puttalam for rape of a girl of about 14 years, a close relative, contrary to Section 364(2)(e) of the Penal Code. After hearing evidence from 8 prosecution witnesses and a dock statement from the accused, the High Court convicted him and sentenced him to 12 years rigorous imprisonment, a fine of 20000 with 3 months simple imprisonment in default, and compensation of 200000 to the victim with 1 year simple imprisonment in default. On appeal, although the petition initially questioned the conviction on the basis of contradictions and lack of corroboration, counsel ultimately confined the challenge to the severity of the sentence and sought mitigation based on the accused's age, lack of previous convictions, family responsibilities, and long period of litigation. The Court of Appeal, having considered relevant sentencing authorities and the aggravating factors of the victim's young age and the accused's familial position, held that the High Court had properly exercised its sentencing discretion and declined to reduce the sentence, merely backdating it to the date of conviction.
prosecution_counsel: Wasantha Perera DSG for the Respondent
defence_counsel: Darshana Kuruppu with Tharushi Gamage and Anjana Adhikaramge for the Accused-Appellant
cause_of_death_exact_text: Not applicable; this is a rape case and no death is in issue.
hc_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal recorded that the High Court had considered both the statutory range of punishment under Section 364(2)(e) and the competing aggravating and mitigating circumstances when fixing sentence at 12 years. The High Court treated 10 years as the base sentence and moved upward in light of the gravity of the offence, the victim's tender age, and the breach of trust by a close relative, while also recognizing the accused's personal circumstances such as age, lack of prior convictions, family responsibilities, and prolonged involvement in court proceedings. The Court of Appeal endorsed this reasoning as a careful, balanced evaluation warranting no appellate interference.
precedents_cited_list: Badde Liyanage Wasantha Kumara v. Attorney General – SC Appeal 70/2018 | Attorney General v. Ranasinghe and Others – (1993) 2 SLR 81 | Kieth Billiam – 82 Criminal Appeal Reports 347 | Archbold: Sentencing Guidelines (2019) – Thomson Reuters
standard_of_review_applied: Appellate review of sentencing discretion, assessing whether the trial judge properly evaluated aggravating and mitigating factors, applied the statutory framework, and imposed a sentence within the permissible range without error in principle or manifest inadequacy or excess.
sentencing_principles_applied: Deterrent sentencing for sexual offences against children; use of a statutory minimum as a starting point within a prescribed range; upward adjustment where aggravating factors such as the youth of the victim and breach of trust are present; consideration of mitigating factors including age, lack of previous convictions, family responsibilities, and delay, guided by Supreme Court and comparative sentencing authorities.
final_charge_after_appeal: Rape under Section 364(2)(e) of the Penal Code

judges: B. Sasi Mahendran, J. | Amal Ranaraja, J.
offence_sections: Section 364(2)(e) of the Penal Code as amended by Act No.22 of 1995
brief_facts_summary: The appellant, a 21-year-old male and relative of PW01, was charged with raping an 8-year-old girl on or about 8 April 2006, an offence punishable under section 364(2)(e) of the Penal Code. PW01 had been in the temporary custody of the appellant at the time of the incident, which the Court treated as a serious breach of trust. After the incident, the appellant attempted to communicate with PW01 while she was in the custody of probation officers, which the prosecution characterised as showing a continuing inclination to reoffend. A medico-legal report was produced, which noted an absence of external injuries on the victim.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 364(2)(e) of the Penal Code as amended by Act No.22 of 1995
hc_sentence_type: Rigorous Imprisonment 20 years plus fine and compensation with default sentences
hc_judgment_summary: At the conclusion of the High Court trial at Galle, the appellant was found guilty of raping PW01 contrary to section 364(2)(e) of the Penal Code. The High Court imposed the maximum term of 20 years rigorous imprisonment together with a fine of 25,000 and compensation of 500,000 payable to PW01, with terms of simple imprisonment in default ordered to run consecutively.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: Although the notice of appeal challenged both conviction and sentence, at the hearing counsel for the appellant confined the appeal to the sentence, arguing that it was disproportionate and excessive and contrary to sentencing policy. He submitted that the 20-year term was the statutory maximum and that in the circumstances of the appellant and the case a lesser term was warranted. In mitigation, he relied on the appellant's age at the time of the offence and conviction, absence of external injuries on the victim according to the medico-legal report, lack of previous convictions or pending cases, first-offender status, family responsibilities as a married father of two, and the delay of 14 years between incident and sentence. On that basis he sought a variation of the custodial term in favour of the appellant.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Ground confined at argument to challenge only the sentence as disproportionate and excessive. | Sentence of 20 years rigorous imprisonment identified as the statutory maximum under section 364(2)(e). | Appellant was 21 years old at the time of the offence and 33 years old at the time of conviction. | Medico-legal report indicated no external injuries on PW01. | Appellant had no previous convictions or pending cases and was a first offender. | Appellant was married and a father of two children. | There was a 14-year delay between the incident and the imposition of sentence, urged as a mitigating factor.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The judgment notes that PW01, who was 8 years old at the time of the incident, was under the temporary care of the appellant, a relative, highlighting a grave breach of trust. The Court refers to a medico-legal report that recorded no external injuries on the victim, but this absence of injuries was not treated as undermining the conviction. The prosecution further relied on the appellant's attempts to contact PW01 while she was in probationary custody as indicative of a continuing propensity, which the Court regarded as aggravating in assessing sentence.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal did not revisit the factual findings of guilt but proceeded on the basis that the conviction was sound and that the offence was proved beyond reasonable doubt. Its analysis focused on the gravity of the proven offence, the breach of trust and the vulnerability of the victim, balanced against mitigating circumstances, for the limited purpose of recalibrating sentence.
defence_version_summary: On appeal, the defence did not advance a substantive alternative version of events but instead focused exclusively on mitigation of sentence. Counsel emphasised the appellant's youth at the time of the offence, his lack of previous convictions, first-offender status, family responsibilities and the long delay between the offence and conviction. The Court accepted some of these factors as mitigating for sentencing purposes but did not treat them as undermining the credibility of the prosecution case or the correctness of the conviction.
legal_errors_description: The Court of Appeal did not identify any legal errors or misdirections in the High Court judgment and addressed only the question of whether the sentence required adjustment in light of applicable sentencing principles and mitigating factors.
procedural_defects_description: No procedural defects in the conduct of the High Court trial or appeal were noted in the judgment.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal considered the statutory sentencing framework under section 364(2) of the Penal Code, emphasising that rape, especially of a very young child, is a grave offence with serious consequences for both the victim and society. It highlighted aggravating features such as the victim's age (8 years), her being under the temporary care of the appellant, and the appellant's attempts to contact her while she was in probationary custody, underscoring a serious breach of trust and risk to the younger generation. At the same time, the Court took into account mitigating factors including the appellant's youth at the time of the offence, absence of previous convictions, first-offender status, non-repetition of the offence, family responsibilities, and the delay between incident and conviction. Applying the principles in Attorney General vs. H. N. de Silva and Attorney General vs. Ranasinghe, and drawing on English sentencing guidance in rape cases, the Court concluded that while a substantial custodial term was necessary for deterrence and public protection, the maximum term of 20 years was not required and reduced it to 15 years while leaving the fine and compensation intact.
coa_sentence_type: Rigorous Imprisonment 15 years plus fine and compensation unchanged
brief_judgment_file_summary: The appellant, Udageiyalage Sarath Kumar, was indicted in the High Court of Galle for committing rape on PW01, an 8-year-old girl under his temporary care, contrary to section 364(2)(e) of the Penal Code as amended. After trial, he was convicted and sentenced to 20 years rigorous imprisonment, a fine of 25,000 and compensation of 500,000 to the victim, with default terms of simple imprisonment ordered to run consecutively. On appeal, counsel ultimately confined the challenge to the sentence, arguing that the imposition of the statutory maximum was excessive in light of the appellant's youth at the time of the offence, first-offender status, absence of previous convictions, family circumstances and the long delay between the incident and conviction, while the State stressed the gravity of the offence, the victim's age, the breach of trust and the appellant's later attempts to contact the victim. The Court of Appeal, after reviewing the statutory framework and relevant authorities including Attorney General vs. H. N. de Silva and Attorney General vs. Ranasinghe, held that a substantial custodial term was warranted for deterrence and protection of the public but that the ends of justice would be met by reducing the sentence from 20 to 15 years rigorous imprisonment, with the fine, compensation and default terms left unchanged and the conviction otherwise affirmed, resulting in the appeal being dismissed subject to this variation.
prosecution_counsel: Maheshika Silva, D.S.G. for the Respondent
defence_counsel: Selvaraja Dushyanthan with Dhanushka Thilini instructed by Rohitha Deshapriya for the Accused-Appellant
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court of Galle convicted the appellant of rape under section 364(2)(e) and imposed the maximum term of 20 years rigorous imprisonment together with a fine and substantial compensation to the victim, with default terms of simple imprisonment ordered to run consecutively. The Court of Appeal did not criticise the High Court's reasoning on guilt or identify any misdirection, and proceeded on the basis that the conviction was proper. Its intervention was limited to reassessing the appropriateness of the quantum of sentence in light of aggravating and mitigating factors.
precedents_cited_list: Attorney General vs. H. N. de Silva – 57 NLR 121 | Attorney General vs. Ranasinghe – [1993] 2 SLR 81 | Roberts (4) – observation of the Lord Chief Justice in the English Court of Appeal on sentencing for rape | Keith Billiam [5] – English Court of Appeal guidance on starting points and aggravating factors in rape sentencing
standard_of_review_applied: Review of sentence for proportionality and conformity with statutory limits and sentencing principles, including consideration of aggravating and mitigating factors and the need for deterrence and public protection.
sentencing_principles_applied: The Court applied principles that sentencing must reflect the gravity of the offence, its impact on the victim and society, the need for deterrence, and the breach of trust, while also considering the offender's age, previous good character, and mitigating circumstances, drawing expressly on Attorney General vs. H. N. de Silva, Attorney General vs. Ranasinghe, and English appellate guidance on rape sentencing.
final_charge_after_appeal: Rape of a minor under section 364(2)(e) of the Penal Code as amended

judges: P. Kumararathnam J. | Pradeep Hettiarachchi J.
offence_sections: Section 364(2)(e) of the Penal Code
location_of_offence: Within the jurisdiction of the High Court of Vavuniya
brief_facts_summary: The accused-appellant was indicted in 2015 in the High Court of Vavuniya for committing rape on a female under the age of 18, an offence punishable under section 364(2)(e) of the Penal Code. Following the first trial, he was convicted on 30.11.2016, but the Court of Appeal later set aside that judgment and ordered a trial de novo. The retrial commenced on 19.07.2019 and on 09.10.2020 the High Court again convicted the appellant and imposed a sentence of 12 years rigorous imprisonment, together with a fine and compensation to the prosecutrix. The present appeal to the Court of Appeal is confined solely to the question of sentence, particularly the treatment of the lengthy period the appellant spent in remand custody and the absence of an opportunity to make mitigation submissions.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 364(2)(e) of the Penal Code
hc_sentence_type: Rigorous Imprisonment 12 years plus fine and compensation
hc_judgment_summary: After the trial de novo, the High Court of Vavuniya convicted the appellant of rape of a female under 18 under section 364(2)(e) of the Penal Code. The court imposed a sentence of 12 years rigorous imprisonment, a fine of 10000 with a default term of 3 months simple imprisonment, and ordered compensation of 300000 to the prosecutrix with a default term of 18 months simple imprisonment. The sentence was imposed immediately upon conviction and the appellant was not afforded an opportunity to tender mitigating factors, nor was the period spent on remand expressly credited.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: Although several grounds of appeal were initially urged, at the hearing counsel for the appellant confined submissions solely to the question of sentence. The appellant sought relief under section 333 of the Code of Criminal Procedure as amended by Act No. 25 of 2024, requesting that the time he had spent in remand custody be treated as part of his sentence. He also effectively complained that he had not been given an opportunity to make submissions in mitigation at the time of sentencing by the High Court. The appeal therefore focused on whether the existing sentence was excessive and unjust in light of the lengthy pre-conviction custody and the procedural omission regarding mitigation.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Appeal confined at the hearing to challenging only the sentence and not the conviction. | Reliance on section 333 of the Code of Criminal Procedure Act as amended by Act No. 25 of 2024 to seek credit for time spent in remand custody as part of the sentence. | Complaint that the High Court imposed sentence immediately after conviction without affording the appellant an opportunity to make submissions in mitigation. | Assertion that failure to credit lengthy pre-conviction detention and the absence of mitigation made the effective sentence manifestly excessive and unjust.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal judgment does not revisit or analyse the trial evidence in detail, as the appeal was expressly confined to the issue of sentence. There is no discussion of the nature or credibility of eyewitness, medical, or forensic testimony. The court proceeds on the basis of the existing conviction and focuses solely on sentencing factors such as the period spent in remand custody and the lack of an opportunity to present mitigation.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal does not reassess the probabilities relating to guilt or innocence, but accepts the conviction as it stands and limits its analysis to whether the sentence should be adjusted in light of pre-conviction custody and procedural fairness at sentencing.
defence_version_summary: In this appeal, the defence does not advance an alternative factual version of events or challenge the conviction itself. Instead, the appellant’s case is confined to seeking a reduction or adjustment of sentence based on the long period spent in remand custody and the absence of an opportunity to tender mitigation before sentence. There is no mention of an alibi, dock statement, or defence witnesses in the Court of Appeal judgment, and the court notes only that the appellant has no previous convictions, which it treats as a mitigating factor.
legal_errors_description: The Court of Appeal observes that the appellant was not accorded an opportunity to make submissions in mitigation before the High Court imposed sentence, thereby denying him his right to place mitigatory facts before the sentencing judge. It also notes that the remand period was not considered in fixing the sentence, an omission that the Court of Appeal corrects by exercising its power under section 333 as amended.
procedural_defects_description: The High Court imposed sentence immediately after conviction without inviting or hearing mitigation submissions from the appellant, depriving him of a procedural opportunity to present personal and other mitigating circumstances. As a result, the remand period and his lack of previous convictions were not taken into account at the time of sentencing.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyses section 333 of the Code of Criminal Procedure Act as amended by Act No. 25 of 2024, emphasising that time spent in custody before conviction or pending appeal should be credited as part of an accused’s sentence to avoid double punishment. It notes that the appellant was in remand custody from 23.11.2016 to 02.04.2020 and again from the date of conviction on 09.10.2020, amounting to roughly eight years, and that the High Court did not consider this period because no mitigation was submitted and the appellant was not afforded an opportunity to do so. Taking into account the lengthy remand period and the absence of previous convictions, the Court of Appeal finds it just and appropriate to deduct eight years from the original 12-year sentence, effectively reducing it to four years rigorous imprisonment from the date of conviction. The conviction itself is left undisturbed, and the orders on fine, compensation and default sentences are affirmed.
coa_sentence_type: Rigorous Imprisonment 4 years (effective from date of conviction), with fine and compensation unchanged
brief_judgment_file_summary: This Court of Appeal judgment in CA/HCC/0077/2023 concerns an appeal by Rathnapalake Hemashiri Subasinghe against the sentence imposed by the High Court of Vavuniya for rape of a female under 18 under section 364(2)(e) of the Penal Code. After a first conviction in 2016 was set aside and a trial de novo was held, the High Court again convicted him on 09.10.2020 and imposed 12 years rigorous imprisonment, a fine, and compensation, without affording him an opportunity to tender mitigation or crediting his lengthy period in remand custody. Applying the newly amended section 333 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, the Court of Appeal stresses that pre-conviction detention is a curtailment of liberty that should be treated as part of the sentence to prevent double punishment and manifestly excessive outcomes. It notes that the appellant has spent approximately eight years in remand custody and has no previous convictions, and therefore orders that eight years be deducted from the 12-year term, reducing the operative sentence to four years rigorous imprisonment from the date of conviction, while leaving the conviction, fine, compensation and default sentences intact; the appeal is thus partly allowed.
defence_counsel: Indika Mallwarachchi
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court of Vavuniya, after the trial de novo, convicted the appellant of rape under section 364(2)(e) and imposed a sentence of 12 years rigorous imprisonment together with a fine and compensation, without expressly discussing remand custody or mitigation. The Court of Appeal notes that the High Court did not consider the substantial period spent on remand, partly because no mitigation submissions were made and the appellant was not afforded an opportunity to present them. While not disturbing the conviction, the Court of Appeal implicitly treats this omission at sentencing as a defect and rectifies it by recalibrating the sentence to account for the remand period and the appellant’s lack of previous convictions.
standard_of_review_applied: Sentence review under section 333 of the Code of Criminal Procedure Act, focusing on fairness, credit for time spent in custody, and prevention of manifestly excessive punishment.
sentencing_principles_applied: Credit for pre-conviction and pre-appeal remand custody as part of the ultimate sentence; recognition that pre-trial detention is a deprivation of liberty equivalent in hardship to post-conviction imprisonment; avoidance of double punishment and manifestly excessive sentences; consideration of absence of previous convictions and the interests of justice in determining the effective custodial term.
final_charge_after_appeal: Rape of a female under 18 punishable under section 364(2)(e) of the Penal Code

judges: B. Sasi Mahendran, J. | Amal Ranaraja, J.
offence_sections: Section 296
brief_facts_summary: The accused and the deceased were childhood friends living in the same area. On or around 13.08.2014 at about 9:30–10:00 p.m., the deceased allegedly came to his house at Grandpass bleeding and stated that 'Safreen brother stabbed me', and was thereafter taken to hospital where he died. The prosecution case rested on this alleged dying declaration relayed by PW01 (the deceased's father), certain surrounding circumstances, and a knife said to have been recovered under a Section 27 statement. The Court of Appeal ultimately found serious doubts about whether the deceased in fact made the alleged statement at his residence, about the surrounding circumstances, and about the evidential value of the purported recovery.
evidence_type_secondary: Section 27 statement and alleged recovery of knife
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 296
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court of Colombo convicted the accused of murder under Section 296 of the Penal Code and imposed the death sentence. The conviction appears to have been based on accepting the alleged dying declaration, the circumstantial evidence, and the Section 27 recovery as sufficient to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt. The High Court rejected the accused's dock statement as not worthy of credence.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The accused appealed against both conviction and sentence, contending that the learned High Court Judge erred in treating the circumstantial evidence led by the prosecution as sufficient to infer guilt as the only reasonable inference. It was further argued that the trial judge unreasonably rejected the dock statement of the accused. The appeal therefore challenged both the sufficiency of the prosecution evidence and the evaluation of the defence version.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Alleged erroneous finding that the circumstantial evidence was sufficient to lead to the one and only inference that the accused committed the offence. | Complaint that the learned High Court Judge rejected the dock statement of the accused on unreasonable grounds.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The prosecution called seven witnesses, with PW01 (the deceased's father) giving the only direct account of the alleged dying declaration, but his testimony contained significant inconsistencies regarding the presence of bloodstains, who took the deceased to hospital, and the clothes worn by the deceased. PW02, a neighbour, testified instead that he saw the deceased with another child and took him to hospital, and that no family member accompanied the deceased, thereby cutting across PW01's version. The doctor who performed the post-mortem noted different clothing, and the alleged Section 27 recovery of a knife from a hardware shop could not be linked to the accused, leading the Court of Appeal to hold that there was no evidential value in that recovery and that the prosecution's case was not proved beyond reasonable doubt.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal held that the circumstantial evidence, including the uncorroborated and doubtful dying declaration and the unsupported Section 27 recovery, did not exclude reasonable hypotheses consistent with the accused's innocence. Therefore, the prosecution had failed to establish guilt beyond a reasonable doubt, and the benefit of the doubt had to be given to the accused.
defence_version_summary: In his defence the accused gave only an unsworn dock statement and did not call any defence witnesses. The High Court rejected this dock statement as unreasonable or not credible, a rejection which the accused specifically challenged on appeal. The Court of Appeal focused primarily on the insufficiency of the prosecution evidence rather than on the positive strength of the dock statement, holding that the conviction could not stand because the prosecution case itself was not proved beyond reasonable doubt.
legal_errors_description: The Court of Appeal found that the High Court erred in treating the alleged dying declaration and other circumstantial items as sufficient to prove guilt and in relying on a Section 27 recovery that was not linked to the accused. The appellate court held that the trial judge failed to properly evaluate the weaknesses and inconsistencies in the prosecution evidence in a circumstantial case before convicting.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal reviewed the legal principles on dying declarations and circumstantial evidence, stressing that such evidence must be carefully scrutinised and must be totally inconsistent with the innocence of the accused. Applying these principles, it found the alleged dying declaration doubtful, since PW01's testimony was inconsistent, unsupported by other witnesses, and contradicted by objective features such as the absence of bloodstains and differing accounts of clothing and hospital arrangements. The court also held that the Section 27 knife recovery from a hardware shop had no evidential value because the prosecution failed to connect the place of recovery with the accused. Concluding that the prosecution had not proved the case beyond reasonable doubt, the Court of Appeal allowed the appeal, quashed the conviction and sentence, and declined to treat the circumstantial evidence as sufficient for guilt.
coa_sentence_type: None (sentence quashed)
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused, Mohamed Saleem Mohamed Safreen, was tried in the High Court of Colombo for the murder of his childhood friend, alleged to have been stabbed near the latter's residence at Grandpass on or around 13.08.2014. The prosecution's case relied primarily on an alleged dying declaration communicated through the deceased's father (PW01), surrounding circumstantial evidence, and an alleged recovery of a knife on information given by the accused under Section 27 of the Evidence Ordinance. The Court of Appeal undertook a detailed survey of Sri Lankan case law on dying declarations and circumstantial evidence, and on examining the testimony, found PW01's version doubtful and uncorroborated, with contradictions regarding bloodstains, clothing, and who accompanied the deceased to hospital, while PW02's evidence cut across PW01's account and the Section 27 recovery of the knife was not linked to the accused. Holding that the prosecution had failed to prove the charge beyond reasonable doubt, the Court of Appeal allowed the appeal, quashed the conviction and the death sentence, and effectively acquitted the accused.
prosecution_counsel: Shanaka Wijesinghe, PC, ASG for the Respondent
defence_counsel: Neranjana Jayasinghe with Randuna Heellage and Imangsi Senarath for the Accused-Appellant
cause_of_death_exact_text: The judgment does not set out a precise medical formulation of cause of death but indicates that the deceased died following a stabbing incident and subsequent bleeding.
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court had accepted the alleged dying declaration, circumstantial features, and the Section 27 knife recovery as sufficient to convict for murder under Section 296 and imposed the death sentence. The Court of Appeal held that this approach was erroneous because the dying declaration, as narrated solely by PW01, was inherently weak and uncorroborated, his testimony contained important inconsistencies, and no other evidence supported his account. It also ruled that the High Court should not have placed weight on the knife recovery, as the prosecution failed to connect the place of recovery with the accused, leaving the conviction unsafe.
precedents_cited_list: Queen v. Anthonypillai – 69 NLR 34; 68 CLW 57 | King v. Asirivadan Nadar – 51 NLR 322 | Justin Pala v. Queen – 66 NLR 409 | Gamini Mahaarachchi v. The Attorney General – CA 106/2002, decided on 22.08.2007 | Ranasinghe v. Attorney-General – [2007] 1 S.L.R. 218 | Sigera v. Attorney General – 2011 (1) SLR 201 | B.R.R.A. Jagath Pramawansha v. The Attorney General – CA Appeal No. 173/2005, decided on 19.03.2009 | King v. Abeywicrama – 44 NLR 254 | King v. Appuhamy – 46 NLR 128 | Podisingho v. King – 53 NLR 49
standard_of_review_applied: The Court of Appeal re-evaluated the evidence to determine whether the circumstantial evidence and dying declaration proved guilt beyond reasonable doubt, focusing on whether the trial judge failed to properly assess the inherent weaknesses of a dying declaration and to apply the strict test that circumstantial evidence must be inconsistent with innocence and only consistent with guilt.

judges: P. Kumararatnam | R.P. Hettiarachchi
offence_sections: Section 364(1) of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The Appellant was accused of raping a 17-year-old prosecutrix on or before July 9, 2011. The prosecutrix stated that the Appellant entered her house at night, proposed marriage, and had sexual intercourse without her consent. She did not raise cries or inform her father immediately, and the complaint was lodged only after her mother returned from abroad three months later. The Appellant was residing in the same house at the time.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 364(1) of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the Appellant in absentia for rape under Section 364(1) of the Penal Code. He was sentenced to 12 years rigorous imprisonment, a fine of Rs. 10,000, and compensation of Rs. 200,000 with default imprisonment terms.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The Appellant argued that there were fatal procedural irregularities denying him a fair trial, including lack of counsel and improper record-keeping. He also contended that the prosecution failed to prove the charge beyond reasonable doubt, particularly regarding the absence of consent.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Fatal procedural irregularity denying fair trial | Charge not proved beyond reasonable doubt
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The prosecutrix's testimony had inconsistencies, such as not informing her father immediately and varying accounts of the incident. Key witnesses like her mother and grandmother were not called, weakening the prosecution case. The Court found the evidence tainted with shortcomings.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court found prosecution evidence tainted with shortcomings and ambiguity, leading to benefit of doubt for the Appellant.
defence_version_summary: The Appellant absconded during trial, so no defence was presented. In appeal, he argued procedural errors and insufficient evidence. The Court noted the absence of defence witnesses and lack of opportunity to present a case.
legal_errors_description: Procedural errors included failure to read indictment, assign counsel, and maintain proper records, denying fair trial.
procedural_defects_description: Trial conducted in absentia without proper procedures, no record of indictment reading or counsel assignment, and no opportunity to prove absence bona fide.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found serious procedural irregularities denied a fair trial, including lack of counsel and incomplete records. It held that prosecution evidence was unreliable due to inconsistencies and failure to call key witnesses, leading to acquittal based on benefit of doubt.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The Court of Appeal allowed the appeal, acquitting the Appellant of rape charges due to procedural irregularities and insufficient evidence. The Court highlighted failures in fair trial procedures, including lack of counsel and unreliable prosecution evidence, and set aside the High Court's conviction and sentence.
defence_counsel: Kavithri Hirusha Ubeysekera
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted based solely on the prosecutrix's testimony without considering inconsistencies or procedural flaws. The Court of Appeal found this approach erroneous due to lack of corroboration and failure to address fair trial issues.

judges: P. Kumararatnam | R.P. Hettiarachchi
offence_sections: Section 365(B)(2)(b) and Section 364(2) of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The appellant, a mason, allegedly committed grave sexual abuse on a 9-year-old victim while working at her house. He sent her brother to buy cigarettes, then inserted his finger into her vagina. The brother witnessed the appellant leaving the room and informed the mother, who lodged a police complaint.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 365(B)(2)(b) of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the appellant for grave sexual abuse under Section 365(B)(2)(b), sentenced to 8 years rigorous imprisonment, a fine of Rs.7500, and compensation of Rs.300,000. The appellant was acquitted on the charge of statutory rape.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant raised grounds including inconsistencies in the victim's testimony, denial of fair trial due to evidence taken in the judge's chambers, failure to call the victim's brother as a witness, lack of medical corroboration, and that the evidence did not prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Victim initially denied abuse but later testimony matched police statement, raising doubt of tutoring. | Denial of fair trial as part of evidence was taken in judge's chamber and victim's mother was summoned. | Prosecution failed to summon victim's elder brother, an eye witness, warranting Section 114(F) application. | Evidence not corroborated by medical evidence. | Evidence of PW1 not corroborated and does not inspire confidence.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The victim's testimony was inconsistent, initially denying abuse but later confirming. The brother was an essential eye witness but not called. Medical evidence did not confirm vaginal penetration but did not exclude inter labia penetration.
probability_assessment_by_court: The court found that the evidence was not credible and lacked corroboration, creating reasonable doubt.
defence_version_summary: The appellant made a dock statement but no details are provided. No defence witnesses were called. The court found the prosecution evidence insufficient to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt.
legal_errors_description: Procedural errors in taking evidence in chambers without proper basis, failure to call essential witness, and not properly assessing child witness credibility.
procedural_defects_description: Judge took evidence in his chambers and summoned PW2 without medical report, and adjourned trial for 11 months without plausible reason, causing prejudice.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The COA allowed the appeal due to inconsistencies in victim's testimony, failure to call the brother as a witness, lack of medical corroboration, and procedural errors. The prosecution failed to prove the case beyond reasonable doubt. Precedents on child witness and corroboration were applied.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The Court of Appeal set aside the conviction and sentence, acquitting the appellant. Key reasons included inconsistencies in the victim's testimony, the prosecution's failure to call an essential witness (the brother), lack of medical corroboration, and procedural errors during the trial.
defence_counsel: Darshana Kuruppu with Tharushi Gamage, Anjana Adhikaramge, Sahan Weerasinghe and Pramuditha Senevirathne
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted based on the victim's testimony without sufficient corroboration and failed to consider the absence of the brother's testimony. The COA found that the HC did not properly assess the credibility of the child witness and procedural errors occurred.
precedents_cited_list: Ranjeet Kumar Ram v. State of Bihar [2015] SCC Online SC 500 | King v. Seneviratne 38 NLR 208 | Sunil and others v. Attorney General [1986] 1 S. L. R 230 | Premasiri v. Attorney General [2006] 3 Sri.L.R | State of Andra Pradesh v. Garigula Satya Vani Murty AIR 1997 SC 1588

judges: P Kumararathnam, J. | Pradeep Hettiarachchi, J.
offence_sections: Section 364(2)(e) of the Penal Code as amended by Act No 22 of 1995
brief_facts_summary: The appellant was accused of raping a girl under 16 years of age who lived with her maternal grandmother in a single room where all occupants slept on a mat on the floor. The prosecutrix alleged multiple incidents of rape, but her testimony contained inconsistencies regarding the number of times and the circumstances, such as the lights being on and others present. Medical evidence showed old hymenal tears indicating repeated penetration, which contradicted the prosecutrix's account of the timing.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 364(2)(e) of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court found the appellant guilty of rape based on the prosecutrix's testimony and sentenced him to 12 years rigorous imprisonment, a fine of Rs. 20,000, and compensation of Rs. 500,000. The judge convicted without a jury, relying on the evidence presented.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant appealed on grounds that the prosecutrix's story was improbable, suspicious, and contradictory, and not corroborated by other witnesses. The prosecution failed to call a vital witness, PW2, the grandmother, and the High Court judge failed to properly evaluate contradictions and omissions in the evidence.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The story of the prosecutrix is highly improbable, suspicious and contradictory and it was not corroborated by other witnesses | The prosecution has failed to place before the court a vital witness Senanayake Arachchige Mily Charlet PW2 | The learned High Court Judge has failed to properly evaluate the contradictions and omissions marked on behalf of the appellant
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the prosecutrix's testimony inconsistent and improbable due to contradictions with medical evidence and the scenario of the alleged rape. The failure to call PW2, who could have corroborated or contradicted the testimony, weakened the prosecution case. The medical evidence indicated repeated penetration over time, which did not align with the prosecutrix's account.
probability_assessment_by_court: The court assessed the probability of the events and found it improbable that rape occurred with lights on and others present on the same mat, given the prosecutrix's cries and assaults did not awaken them.
defence_version_summary: The defence challenged the credibility of the prosecutrix through cross-examination, highlighting contradictions and omissions in her testimony. The appellant did not present a separate defence version or alibi, but relied on undermining the prosecution's case and the failure to call a key witness.
legal_errors_description: The High Court judge failed to adequately analyze and evaluate the improbabilities and inconsistencies in the prosecutrix's testimony and the medical evidence, leading to an unsafe conviction.
procedural_defects_description: The prosecution failed to summon PW2, the grandmother, who was a vital witness capable of corroborating or contradicting the prosecutrix's testimony, violating the principle of unfolding the narrative.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal allowed the appeal, finding the prosecutrix's testimony inconsistent and improbable due to contradictions with medical evidence and the failure to call PW2. The prosecution did not prove the case beyond reasonable doubt, as the evidence lacked credibility and corroboration. Precedents on reasonable doubt and witness credibility were applied to quash the conviction.
coa_sentence_type: Acquitted
brief_judgment_file_summary: The Court of Appeal allowed the appeal, quashing the conviction and sentence imposed by the High Court. It found the prosecutrix's testimony inconsistent and improbable, especially given the medical evidence of old injuries and the failure to call a key witness. The prosecution failed to prove the case beyond reasonable doubt, leading to the appellant's acquittal.
defence_counsel: Isuru Somadasa
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted the appellant based on the prosecutrix's testimony without adequately considering its improbabilities and inconsistencies with medical evidence. The Court of Appeal found that the High Court judge failed to properly evaluate these aspects, leading to an erroneous conviction.

judges: Amal Ranaraja J. | B. Sasi Mahendran J.
offence_sections: Section 70 of the Bribery Act No. 11 of 1954 (as amended); Section 102 of the Penal Code read with Section 70 of the Bribery Act
brief_facts_summary: The Commission to Investigate Allegations of Bribery or Corruption received a complaint and, after investigation, directed the Director-General to institute criminal proceedings against the accused in the Magistrates Court in 2017 on corruption-related charges. During that trial, after one witness had completed evidence and another had begun, the defence raised an objection that the Commission had not collectively directed the institution of proceedings, relying on the Anoma Polwatta decision, and the Director-General then withdrew the case, leading the Magistrate to acquit the accused under section 189 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. In 2022 the Director-General filed an indictment in the High Court on the same charges, but the High Court Judge in 2024 upheld a preliminary objection based on autrefois acquit and section 314 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and discharged the accused. The Director-General sought revision in the Court of Appeal to set aside that order and to have the indictment restored.
evidence_type_primary: Procedural and documentary evidence (prior court records and orders)
evidence_type_secondary: Limited prior witness testimony from PW01 and PW02 in the Magistrates Court proceedings
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court of Colombo held that the accused had already been acquitted by the Magistrates Court on the same charges and that this acquittal had not been set aside by a competent court. Treating the Magistrate's order as a bar under section 314 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, the High Court concluded that the indictment could not be sustained. The High Court accordingly rejected the indictment and discharged the accused on the preliminary objection.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The petitioner contended that the High Court Judge erred in law by treating the Magistrate’s acquittal following withdrawal under section 189 of the Code of Criminal Procedure as a bar to a fresh indictment under section 314. It was argued that the accused had not been 'tried' in the sense required by section 314 because there had been no full opportunity for both sides to lead evidence and the acquittal lacked the evidential foundation presupposed by that provision. The petitioner relied on Supreme Court authority, including SC Appeal No. 12A/2009, to clarify the meaning of 'tried' and on the Anoma Polwatta decision to explain the procedural background. On that basis, the petitioner sought revision to set aside the High Court order and to allow the indictment to proceed.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The High Court misapplied section 314 of the Code of Criminal Procedure by treating the Magistrate's order after withdrawal under section 189 as a bar to further prosecution. | The accused had not been 'tried' within the meaning of section 314 because there was no full opportunity for both prosecution and defence to lead evidence. | An acquittal given in the context of withdrawal without a completed trial does not constitute an autrefois acquit situation under section 314. | Supreme Court precedent, including SC Appeal No. 12A/2009, supports a narrower interpretation of 'tried' which the High Court failed to apply.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal focused primarily on the procedural history rather than a detailed evaluation of substantive evidence. It noted that in the Magistrates Court proceedings PW01 had completed testimony and PW02 had begun, but the case was withdrawn before either party had a full opportunity to present evidence supporting their positions. This lack of a complete evidentiary process was central to the Court of Appeal’s conclusion that the accused had not been 'tried' for the purposes of section 314.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal did not undertake a factual probability analysis, instead resolving the application entirely on the legal interpretation of section 314 and whether the earlier acquittal constituted a bar to further proceedings.
defence_version_summary: The defence position, as reflected in the order, was that the accused had already been acquitted by the Magistrates Court on the same charges and that this acquittal, not having been set aside, was final and barred further prosecution under section 314 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. They argued that the indictment in the High Court could not proceed while that acquittal remained in force. No alternative factual narrative, alibi, or independent defence witnesses are described in the Court of Appeal order, which records only this legal objection.
legal_errors_description: The Court of Appeal held that the High Court misdirected itself in law by treating the Magistrate's acquittal following withdrawal as an acquittal within the meaning of section 314, and by concluding that the accused had been 'tried' so as to attract the bar on a second trial. It found that, because there had been no full opportunity for both sides to lead evidence, the requirements of section 314 were not met and the High Court’s discharge order was erroneous.
procedural_defects_description: The primary procedural defect identified was the High Court’s decision to reject the indictment and discharge the accused on a preliminary objection based on an incorrect application of section 314, thereby prematurely terminating the High Court proceedings.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analysed section 314 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, stressing that a person is considered 'tried' only where there has been an opportunity for both the prosecution and the defence to lead evidence in support of their respective positions. Referring to Supreme Court authority, it held that an acquittal rendered in the context of a withdrawal without such an evidentiary foundation, as occurred in the Magistrates Court proceedings, does not fall within section 314 and therefore does not bar further prosecution. The Court concluded that the High Court Judge erred in treating the Magistrate’s order as a final acquittal giving rise to autrefois acquit and in using that to reject the indictment. It therefore set aside the High Court’s order, dismissed the objection, and directed that the High Court case be restored to the roll and proceeded with to conclusion.
brief_judgment_file_summary: This revision application was filed by the Director-General of the Commission to Investigate Allegations of Bribery or Corruption challenging a High Court order that had rejected an indictment and discharged two accused on corruption charges under the Bribery Act and Penal Code. The High Court held that an earlier Magistrates Court acquittal following withdrawal of a complaint on the same charges barred further proceedings under section 314 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The Court of Appeal, analysing the meaning of 'tried' in section 314 with reference to case law and legal commentary, concluded that the Magistrates Court proceedings had not reached the stage of a completed trial with full opportunity to lead evidence, so the acquittal did not attract the double jeopardy bar. It therefore set aside the High Court order, dismissed the preliminary objection, and directed the High Court to restore the case to the roll and proceed with the indictment to its conclusion.
prosecution_counsel: Anusha Sammandapperuma, Assistant Director Legal with Kajalakshi Sivasasramaniam and Gaya Rajapaksha for the Petitioner
defence_counsel: Senarath Jayasundara with Sheshan Rathnayake and Chathurangi Wadege for the 1st and 2nd Accused-Respondents
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court reasoned that because the accused had been acquitted by the Magistrates Court on the same charges and that acquittal remained in force, section 314 of the Code of Criminal Procedure prohibited a second trial on those facts. It therefore rejected the indictment and discharged the accused on a preliminary objection. The Court of Appeal held that this analysis was flawed because the earlier proceedings did not amount to a 'trial' within section 314, and thus the High Court’s reliance on that provision to terminate the case was a misdirection.
precedents_cited_list: Anoma Polwatta vs. The Commission to Investigate Allegations of Bribery or Corruption – SC Writ Application No. 01/2011 | SC Appeal No. 12A/2009 – Supreme Court of Sri Lanka (decided 2011-05-05)
standard_of_review_applied: Misdirection on law and erroneous application of section 314 of the Code of Criminal Procedure to the effect of a prior acquittal after withdrawal
final_charge_after_appeal: Corruption charges under Section 70 of the Bribery Act against the 1st accused and abetment under Section 102 of the Penal Code read with Section 70 of the Bribery Act against the 2nd accused remain to be tried in the High Court

judges: Pradeep Hettiarachchi J | P Kumararatnam J
offence_sections: Section 54A(b) and Section 54A(d) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance (as amended)
offence_category: Drug trafficking and possession of heroin
brief_facts_summary: The appellant was charged in the High Court of Colombo with trafficking and possessing 2.16 grams of heroin at Ratmalana on or about 13-08-2013. STF officers, acting on information from an informant, conducted a raid near Sumangala Mawatha and intercepted the appellant arriving on a motorcycle. During a search, they recovered a parcel hidden in the appellant's groin area containing a brown substance that field-tested positive for heroin, weighing 20.430 grams gross. The prosecution sought to prove the charges mainly through the testimony of the police officers involved in the raid, supported by field testing, weighing and subsequent handling of the production.
evidence_type_primary: Police officer eyewitness testimony regarding the raid and seizure
evidence_type_secondary: Forensic/chemical testing procedures and documentary records of the raid and productions
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 54A(b) and Section 54A(d) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance (as amended)
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court of Colombo accepted the testimonies of the STF officers as credible and mutually corroborative regarding the raid, the search of the appellant and the recovery of heroin. The trial judge held that the prosecution had proved both counts of trafficking and possession beyond a reasonable doubt and convicted the appellant on both counts. The judge imposed a sentence of life imprisonment, treating it as appropriate under the dangerous drugs legislation.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: On appeal, the appellant contended that the High Court Judge failed to consider vital contradictions among the prosecution witnesses and thereby wrongly concluded that their evidence was fully consistent. The appellant argued that inconsistencies, particularly about where and how the informant met the officers and the handling of crime notebooks, undermined the reliability of the prosecution case. He also argued that the sentence of life imprisonment was excessive in light of Act No. 41 of 2022, which amended the dangerous drugs law. The appeal therefore challenged both the conviction and the sentence.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Failure by the High Court Judge to consider vital contradictions between the evidence of PW1, PW2 and PW5 regarding the informant, the location of Keells Super and the raid procedure. | Error in concluding that the prosecution witnesses fully corroborated each other despite material inconsistencies. | Complaint that the sentence of life imprisonment is excessive in view of Act No. 41 of 2022 amending the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: Five police witnesses testified for the prosecution, and no witnesses were called for the defence. The Court of Appeal closely examined the testimonies of PW1, PW2 and PW5 and found significant inconsistencies, particularly regarding the location of Keells Super, where the informant met the officers, the parking place of the jeep and the issuing and use of crime notebooks. These contradictions were held to go to the root of the prosecution version of how the raid was initiated and conducted, creating reasonable doubt about the reliability of the alleged recovery of heroin.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal emphasised that the prosecution must prove its case beyond reasonable doubt and that material contradictions in the accounts of the officers reduced the overall credibility of the raid narrative. In the presence of such doubts, and without being able to rely on any weakness in the defence case, the court concluded that the appellant was entitled to the benefit of the doubt.
defence_version_summary: The defence did not call any witnesses and did not lead a dock statement; instead, the case for the accused was conducted by way of cross-examination aimed at highlighting contradictions and weaknesses in the prosecution evidence. The High Court judge had criticised the defence for failing to offer even a simple explanation, but the Court of Appeal held that the accused was under no obligation to explain anything until the prosecution had proved its case beyond reasonable doubt. The appellate court found that the trial judge had wrongly used perceived weaknesses in the defence to bolster an already weak prosecution case.
legal_errors_description: The Court of Appeal found that the High Court Judge failed to consider material contradictions between PW1, PW2 and PW5 regarding core aspects of the raid, thereby mis-evaluating the evidence. It also held that the judge misdirected himself on the law by treating the absence or weakness of a defence explanation as strengthening the prosecution, contrary to the presumption of innocence and the rule that the prosecution must stand or fall on its own evidence.
procedural_defects_description: No specific procedural defects in the trial process were identified; the primary issues related to evidential evaluation and legal directions on burden of proof.
