coa_sentence_type: 6 years rigorous imprisonment and a fine of 7500 with 6 months simple imprisonment in default (affirmed)
brief_judgment_file_summary: This Court of Appeal judgment concerns an appeal by an accused convicted in the High Court of Badulla for unlawful possession of a live hand grenade under section 2(1)(d) of the Offensive Weapons Act. The appellant challenged his conviction mainly on the basis that exclusive possession was not proved and that the main police witness’s evidence on recovery lacked corroboration. The Court of Appeal, applying principles on appellate deference to credibility findings and the sufficiency of a single trustworthy witness in police detection cases, accepted the prosecution narrative that the grenade was recovered from the appellant’s locked room and locker on information given by him, with PW9 corroborating the recovery and the chain of custody proved. Finding no misdirection or procedural error and considering the defence version to be an afterthought riddled with contradictions, the Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal and affirmed both conviction and sentence.
defence_counsel: Sri Lal Dandeniya
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court had accepted the evidence of PW1 regarding the appellant’s statement, the location of the keys and the recovery of the hand grenade from the appellant’s locker, treating this evidence as credible and sufficient to prove possession. It also relied on the supporting testimony, including that of another police officer and chain of custody witnesses, to conclude that the prosecution had proved the charge beyond reasonable doubt. The Court of Appeal held that the High Court’s evaluation of credibility and facts was sound, not manifestly wrong and fully justified by the evidence, and therefore saw no reason to interfere with its conviction or sentence.
precedents_cited_list: Kumar De Silva and two others v. Attorney General – [2010] 2 Sri LR 169 | Dharmasiri v. Republic – [2010] 2 Sri LR 241 | Attorney General v. Devundarage Nihal – SC/Appeal 154/2010, decided on 03.01.2019 | Vadivelu Thevar v. State of Madras – SIR S C 614
standard_of_review_applied: Appellate deference to the trial judge’s findings of fact and credibility, assessment of sufficiency of evidence and application of principles permitting conviction on a single credible witness in police detection cases absent manifest error.
final_charge_after_appeal: Possession of an offensive weapon, namely a live hand grenade, punishable under section 2(1)(d) of the Offensive Weapons Act No. 18 of 1966 (unchanged)

judges: B. Sasi Mahendran, J. | Amal Ranaraja, J.
offence_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code
location_of_offence: near the residence of the deceased
brief_facts_summary: The accused, who was the son-in-law of the deceased, went to the deceased's house on 14.09.2012 looking for his wife and spoke with the deceased for about half an hour. According to PW 01, the deceased's wife, the accused then abused the deceased, called him closer under the pretext of telling a secret, and suddenly attacked his neck with a cleaver, inflicting multiple injuries while PW 01 watched in fear. PW 01 locked the house and fled, later contacting her daughter, and the accused was arrested the same day. The post-mortem by the JMO revealed multiple incised injuries to the head, neck and chest consistent with repeated blows from a curved weapon, corroborating PW 01's account.
evidence_type_secondary: Medical/post-mortem evidence and recovery of weapon
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court of Kegalle accepted the testimony of PW 01 as a credible and reliable eyewitness account of the stabbing of the deceased by the accused. Although there was conflicting evidence about how the cleaver was recovered, the Judge excluded that aspect and relied primarily on PW 01's evidence, supported by the medical findings of multiple incised injuries inflicted with a curved weapon. The court held that the prosecution had proved the charge of murder beyond reasonable doubt and convicted the accused under Section 296, imposing the death sentence.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The accused appealed against the conviction and sentence, contending that the learned High Court Judge failed to extend the benefit of the doubts arising in the case to the accused. Another stated ground concerned the evaluation of the accused's previous and post-incident behaviour. At the hearing, counsel further argued that on the evidence the accused should, at most, have been convicted of culpable homicide not amounting to murder on the basis of grave and sudden provocation. The Court of Appeal considered these arguments and the evidentiary record in rejecting the appeal.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Alleged failure of the High Court Judge to give the benefit of arising doubts to the accused-appellant. | Complaint regarding the assessment of the accused's previous and post-incident behaviour. | Argument that the facts established only culpable homicide not amounting to murder due to alleged grave and sudden provocation, and that the conviction should be reduced accordingly.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The prosecution called 12 witnesses and marked productions P1 to P7, with PW 01 providing the sole direct eyewitness account of the stabbing, which the courts found consistent and credible even under cross-examination. The JMO, PW 11, gave detailed medical evidence of 13 incised injuries on the head, neck and chest caused by a curved weapon, corroborating PW 01's narrative. Evidence about the recovery of the cleaver was inconsistent between PW 10 and PW 01, leading the High Court Judge, as noted by the Court of Appeal, to exclude PW 10's testimony on that specific point, while still finding the remaining prosecution evidence sufficient to sustain the conviction.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal held that PW 01's direct evidence, corroborated by medical findings, established the prosecution case beyond reasonable doubt, leaving no room for reasonable doubt or for a reduction of the offence based on provocation.
defence_version_summary: After the close of the prosecution case the accused did not call any witnesses but made only a dock statement, the detailed contents of which are not set out in the judgment. The defence also sought to cast doubt on PW 01's opportunity to witness the stabbing during cross-examination and later argued provocation as a mitigatory basis to reduce the offence to culpable homicide. Both the High Court and the Court of Appeal found that the defence version did not undermine the credibility of the eyewitness or create a reasonable doubt as to guilt, and that the requirements of grave and sudden provocation were not met.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal carefully examined PW 01's testimony, including cross-examination passages in Sinhala, and concluded that she consistently and firmly maintained that she saw the accused stab the deceased and that nothing appeared suspicious before the attack. The Court placed significant weight on the JMO's post-mortem evidence of multiple incised injuries consistent with repeated blows from a curved weapon, which strongly corroborated PW 01 and supported an intentional and brutal attack. It rejected the appellant's attempt to rely on grave and sudden provocation, emphasising that there was no evidence of abusive or provocative conduct by the deceased or PW 01, nor any loss of self-control by the accused, and that the weapon had been brought by the accused to the scene. Applying the legal tests for Exception 1 to Section 294, the Court found no basis to reduce the offence, no misdirection or evidentiary misappreciation by the High Court, and therefore affirmed the conviction and death sentence.
coa_sentence_type: Death
brief_judgment_file_summary: This Court of Appeal judgment concerns an appeal by an accused convicted by the High Court of Kegalle for the murder of his father-in-law, whom he attacked with a cleaver at the latter's residence on 14.09.2012. The prosecution case rested primarily on the evidence of PW 01, the deceased's wife and the accused's mother-in-law, whose eyewitness account of the stabbing was found to be credible and was strongly supported by the post-mortem findings of multiple incised injuries from a curved weapon. On appeal, the accused challenged the High Court's failure to give him the benefit of doubt and argued that he should only be convicted of culpable homicide not amounting to murder on the basis of grave and sudden provocation, but the Court of Appeal held that there was no evidence of such provocation or loss of self-control. Finding no misdirection or error in the High Court's appreciation of the evidence or application of the law, the Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal and affirmed both the conviction for murder under Section 296 and the death sentence.
prosecution_counsel: Maheshika Silva DSG for the Complainant-Respondent
defence_counsel: Jagath Nanayakkawa for the Accused-Appellant
cause_of_death_exact_text: Death was due to multiple incised injuries to the head, neck and chest caused by repeated blows from a curved weapon resulting in extensive bodily harm.
hc_analysis_summary: As recounted by the Court of Appeal, the High Court relied on PW 01 as the sole eyewitness who directly observed the accused stabbing the deceased and found her evidence cogent and consistent. The High Court accepted the JMO's medical findings of numerous incised injuries inflicted with a curved weapon as corroboration of PW 01's account. While it disregarded the contested portion of PW 10's testimony regarding recovery of the cleaver, it nonetheless concluded that the remaining evidence proved an intentional killing amounting to murder under Section 296 and imposed the death sentence.
precedents_cited_list: K.D.J. Perera v. The King – 53 NLR 193
standard_of_review_applied: The Court of Appeal examined whether there was any misdirection in law or improper evaluation of evidence by the High Court and whether the conviction was supported by credible evidence, ultimately finding no basis for appellate intervention.
final_charge_after_appeal: Murder under Section 296 of the Penal Code

judges: B. Sasi Mahendran, J. | Amal Ranaraja, J.
offence_sections: Section 5(2) of the Offences Against Public Property Act No.12 of 1982; Section 398 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: Durga Agencies, owned by the appellant, imported goods into Sri Lanka through a bank transaction handled by the manager of the People’s Bank Ginthupitiya branch (PW01). On 22 May 2000, relying on the appellant’s assurance that the international division of the bank would be paid before clearance, PW01 released the bills of lading and invoices to the appellant with a covering letter to the bank’s international branch. The goods were later cleared, but documents relating to payment to the importer’s bank were discovered to be forged. The prosecution alleged that the appellant thereby deceived PW01 and dishonestly induced delivery of the documents, causing wrongful gain to the importing business entity.
evidence_type_primary: Eyewitness testimony of bank manager regarding the transaction
evidence_type_secondary: Documentary banking records including bills of lading, invoices and related correspondence
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 5(2) of the Offences Against Public Property Act No.12 of 1982
hc_sentence_type: 26 months simple imprisonment and a fine with 3 years simple imprisonment in default
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the appellant on the first charge of cheating in relation to public property, based primarily on the testimony of PW01 and the documentary banking records. It found that the appellant’s dishonest assurance induced the release of the bills of lading and invoices, thereby satisfying the elements of the offence. The court then imposed a custodial sentence and a fine calculated in line with the statutory regime under section 5(2) of the Offences Against Public Property Act.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant contended that the indictment was defective as it did not properly contain the necessary ingredients of cheating and that the prosecution had failed to prove damage or loss to the Government. He further argued that PW01 was not a credible witness and that the High Court judge failed to properly evaluate his credibility and the defence evidence. It was also alleged that the judge drew erroneous or irrelevant conclusions amounting to misdirection in law and that the overall judgment was bad in law. Finally, the appellant challenged the sentence as being excessive in light of his personal circumstances.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Alleged defect in the indictment for not setting out all essential ingredients of the offence of cheating. | Alleged failure of the prosecution to prove damage or loss caused to the Government as part of the offence. | Challenge to the credibility of PW01 and complaint that the High Court failed to treat him as an unreliable witness. | Alleged failure of the High Court to properly consider and evaluate the defence evidence. | Allegation that the High Court judge misdirected himself by reaching erroneous or irrelevant findings, rendering the judgment bad in law. | Complaint that the sentence imposed is excessive having regard to the appellant’s circumstances.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal emphasised that PW01 was a long-standing bank manager who knew the appellant well and had no demonstrated animosity towards him, making his testimony intrinsically credible. It noted that the defence failed to point to any material contradictions in PW01’s evidence or to provide convincing reasons to doubt his account. The court also observed that the High Court judge had evaluated the totality of the evidence holistically and given clear reasons for rejecting aspects of the defence case.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal found the prosecution version inherently probable given the existing relationship of trust between PW01 and the appellant, and the appellant’s undertaking to pay which was not honoured. In the absence of material contradictions or evidence of bias, the court declined to extend the benefit of the doubt to the appellant.
defence_version_summary: The appellant maintained his innocence, asserting that he had been misled and manipulated by the second accused into engaging in what he believed were legitimate transactions with the bank. He portrayed himself as acting in good faith and not intending to cheat or cause wrongful gain. The High Court, and subsequently the Court of Appeal, found this version unconvincing when weighed against the consistent testimony of PW01 and the surrounding documentary evidence, and accordingly rejected the defence.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal held that the appellant’s conduct fell within the second limb of section 398 of the Penal Code, concerning inducement to deliver property, and thus it was unnecessary to prove actual damage or loss as a separate ingredient. It affirmed the credibility of PW01, noting the absence of animosity and material contradictions, and endorsed the High Court’s holistic evaluation of both prosecution and defence evidence. The court rejected the arguments on defective indictment and misdirection in law, finding that the essential ingredients of cheating and the offence under section 5(2) of the Offences Against Public Property Act were correctly appreciated and applied. It further held that the sentence, including the fine equal to three times the amount related to the offence, was consistent with the statutory provisions and not excessive.
coa_sentence_type: 26 months simple imprisonment and a fine of 2550000 with 3 years simple imprisonment in default
brief_judgment_file_summary: This appeal by the first accused-appellant from a conviction of cheating, punishable under section 5(2) of the Offences Against Public Property Act, concerned the release of bills of lading and invoices by a bank manager on the appellant’s assurance that payment would be made to the bank’s international division. The Court of Appeal analysed the legal concept of cheating under section 398 of the Penal Code and concluded that the case fell under the limb relating to inducement to deliver property, making proof of actual damage or loss unnecessary. It upheld the credibility of the bank manager, rejected complaints about defective indictment, misdirection, and failure to consider the defence, and affirmed that the High Court had properly evaluated the evidence. The appeal was dismissed and the original conviction and sentence, including a fine three times the amount involved, were left undisturbed.
prosecution_counsel: Maheshika Silva, D.S.G. for the Respondent
defence_counsel: Kaneel Maddumage with Praveen Premathilaka for the 1st Accused-Appellant
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court had accepted the evidence of PW01 and the banking documents as proving that the appellant dishonestly induced the bank to release the bills of lading and invoices on a false assurance of payment. It treated the established relationship of trust between PW01 and the appellant as explaining why the manager acted on the appellant’s undertaking. The Court of Appeal endorsed this reasoning, finding that the High Court judge evaluated the evidence in a comprehensive, holistic manner and gave cogent reasons for rejecting parts of the defence evidence, with no misdirection in law or assessment of facts warranting interference.
precedents_cited_list: AG vs. Wijerama [1937] 17 CLR 160
standard_of_review_applied: The Court of Appeal reviewed the case for misdirection on the law relating to cheating, correctness of the indictment, and reasonableness of the High Court’s evaluation of evidence, and found no perversity or failure to consider material evidence.
sentencing_principles_applied: Sentencing was examined with reference to section 5(2) of the Offences Against Public Property Act, applying the statutory requirement that the fine be three times the amount related to the offence, and the Court of Appeal held that the sentence so fixed was appropriate.
final_charge_after_appeal: Cheating punishable under section 5(2) of the Offences Against Public Property Act No.12 of 1982

judges: B. Sasi Mahendran | Amal Ranaraja
offence_sections: 365B (2)(b) of the Penal Code as amended by Act No.22 of 1995
brief_facts_summary: The appellant, a neighbor of the 11-year-old victim PW01, went with her and his son to repair a blocked water pipe at a nearby stream. After repairing the pipe and sending his son home to check the water flow, the appellant made PW01 sit on his lap, caressed her vagina, and made her caress his penis. PW01 called out to the son, who returned, after which the appellant released her, leading to a police complaint and medical examination.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: 365B (2)(b) of the Penal Code as amended by Act No.22 of 1995
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the appellant on both charges of grave sexual abuse. He was sentenced to 10 years rigorous imprisonment on each charge, with fines of Rs.10,000 per charge and additional payments to the Victims and Witness Protection Fund. The sentences were to run consecutively.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant argued that the High Court failed to follow mandatory procedures when amending the indictment. The judge was prejudiced from the outset, denying a fair trial through an unjustified remand order after PW01's testimony. The conviction was against the weight of evidence, material witnesses were excluded, and the sentence was unfair.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The Learned High Court Judge has failed to ensure that the mandatory provisions of the Code of Criminal Procedure Act have been followed when the indictment was amended. | The Learned High Court Judge erred in law and has been prejudice towards the appellant from the very outset of the trial and thereby denied the appellant of his right to a fair trial. | The conviction of the appellant was contrary to law and against the weight of the evidence presented at the trial. | The Learned High Court Judge has failed to consider that the prosecution has excluded material witnesses. | The sentence imposed on the appellant was unfair and unreasonable.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: PW01, the child victim, provided direct testimony of the abuse. PW02's testimony was recorded after an adjournment, but details are not analyzed in depth. The medico-legal report by Dr. S. Kodikara was marked but not detailed.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal did not delve into probabilities or benefit of doubt on evidence, focusing instead on procedural fairness.
defence_version_summary: The appellant denied the allegations, admitting to going to the water source with PW01 and his son to fix the pipe, but claiming they all returned together and PW01 stayed to play with his son. No alibi or defence witnesses were mentioned. The court noted inconsistencies in defence due to change in counsel affected by the remand order.
procedural_defects_description: Unjustified remand order without reasons, leading to prejudice and denial of fair trial.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the High Court Judge's remand order after PW01's testimony was unjustified and punitive, undermining the appellant's confidence in counsel and leading to inconsistencies in defence. This denied a fair trial. Prosecution credibility was not questioned on evidence, but procedural bias was key. No detailed assessment of contradictions or evidence, as the bias ground sufficed. Retrial ordered due to seriousness of charges. Precedent CA/CPA/132/2023 applied on remand reasons.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The Court of Appeal set aside the High Court conviction and sentence for grave sexual abuse due to procedural unfairness from an unjustified remand order that prejudiced the appellant's defence. A retrial was ordered given the seriousness of the charges involving a minor victim. The judgment emphasizes the need for judges to justify remand decisions to ensure fair trials.
defence_counsel: Akila Amunugama
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted based on PW01's testimony and medical evidence, imposing sentences without noted errors in evidence evaluation. The COA criticized the HC for issuing an unjustified remand order after PW01's evidence, delaying PW02's testimony without reason, which appeared punitive and prejudiced the defence. This led to the appellant changing counsel amid Covid-19 challenges, resulting in defence inconsistencies.
standard_of_review_applied: Failure to provide reasons for remand order, leading to denial of fair trial

judges: P. Kumararatnam, J. | R. P. Hettiarachchi, J.
offence_sections: Sections 54(A)(b) and 54(A)(d) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance as amended by Act No.13 of 1984
offence_category: Trafficking and possession of dangerous drugs (Heroin)
brief_facts_summary: Upon information from a personal informant, PW1, an Inspector of Police attached to the Special Task Force, and other officers went to Thoppuwa Junction on 16.08.2013 and observed the Appellant. Acting on a phone call from the informant, PW1 and PW2 approached the Appellant at a bus stop on Dankotuwa Road, introduced themselves, and recovered a cellophane bag containing nine packets with a substance suspected to be heroin from his trouser pocket. The Appellant was taken to the Police Narcotics Bureau, where the substance was weighed on an electronic scale and the productions were sealed and sent for analysis, leading to a Government Analyst’s report indicating a different weight. At the High Court trial, the police officers’ evidence was accepted and the Appellant, who in his dock statement denied ever possessing drugs, was convicted and sentenced to life imprisonment on both counts.
evidence_type_primary: Police eyewitness testimony and recovery of heroin from the Appellant
evidence_type_secondary: Government Analyst report and chain of custody documentation relating to the seized drugs
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Sections 54(A)(b) and 54(A)(d) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance as amended by Act No.13 of 1984
hc_judgment_summary: After trial before the High Court of Chilaw, the court accepted the evidence of the police officers that the Appellant was found in possession of heroin and that the productions were properly handled. The Appellant’s dock statement denying possession was rejected, and he was found guilty on both counts of trafficking in and possession of heroin under Sections 54(A)(b) and 54(A)(d). The learned High Court Judge imposed a sentence of life imprisonment on each count.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The Appellant contended that the prosecution failed to prove the inward journey and identity of the productions beyond reasonable doubt due to a substantial discrepancy between the weight of the substance recorded by the police and that indicated in the Government Analyst’s report. He further argued that the learned High Court Judge failed to consider material inter se contradictions among the main prosecution witnesses. It was submitted that these defects undermined the reliability of the prosecution case and disturbed the chain of custody of the drugs. On this basis, the Appellant sought to have his conviction and sentence set aside.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Prosecution failed to prove the chain of inward journey of the production beyond reasonable doubt due to a discrepancy between the weight recorded by the Police Narcotics Bureau and the weight in the Government Analyst’s report. | The learned High Court Judge failed to consider material inter se contradictions in the evidence of the main prosecution witnesses who conducted the inquiry. | The weight discrepancy and evidential contradictions created serious doubt as to the integrity of the production and the fairness of the conviction.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The prosecution relied primarily on the testimony of PW1 and PW2, who described the detection, search and recovery of nine packets of suspected heroin from the Appellant and the subsequent weighing and sealing of the productions, supported by PW4 and the Government Analyst’s report. However, the Court of Appeal noted a significant discrepancy between the weight recorded at the Police Narcotics Bureau and the weight recorded by the Government Analyst, as well as contradictions and improbabilities in the prosecution evidence. The court found that the chain of custody regarding the inward journey of the productions was not satisfactorily established, and that these weaknesses created serious doubt about the integrity of the exhibits.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal held that the substantial discrepancy in the recorded weights of the heroin, coupled with gaps and contradictions in the chain of custody and sealing of productions, created a reasonable doubt which had to be resolved in favour of the Appellant, thereby undermining the prosecution case.
defence_version_summary: The Appellant gave a dock statement in which he categorically denied ever having been in possession of any dangerous drugs, challenging the prosecution’s version of events. He did not call any defence witnesses and relied solely on his dock statement and the weaknesses in the prosecution evidence. The Court of Appeal found that the doubts arising from the chain of custody and weight discrepancy supported the stance taken by the Appellant and contributed to the decision to acquit him.
legal_errors_description: The Court of Appeal found that the High Court failed to address and analyse the significant discrepancy between the weight of the heroin at the Police Narcotics Bureau and the weight at the Government Analyst’s Department, thereby neglecting a vital aspect of the chain of custody. The High Court also misdirected itself in concluding that the productions were properly sealed in the presence of the Appellant despite evidence that one of his signatures was absent on the sealed envelope. These omissions and misdirections were held to have caused substantial prejudice and denied the Appellant a fair trial.
procedural_defects_description: There were procedural lapses in documenting and preserving the productions, including the unexplained reduction in the recorded weight of the heroin between police custody and the Government Analyst’s examination and the absence of one of the Appellant’s signatures on the sealed envelope. These defects undermined the reliability of the chain of custody and the integrity of the exhibits.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal reaffirmed the principle that the prosecution bears the burden of proving guilt beyond reasonable doubt and must establish an unbroken and reliable chain of custody in drug-related offences. It held that the large and unexplained discrepancy between the weight recorded at the Police Narcotics Bureau and that recorded in the Government Analyst’s report, together with deficiencies in the sealing and documentation of the exhibits, seriously compromised the identity and integrity of the productions. The court also observed that the High Court failed to evaluate these defects and contradictions, thereby depriving the Appellant of a fair trial, and concluded that the benefit of the resulting doubt must accrue to the Appellant, warranting the setting aside of the conviction and sentence.
coa_sentence_type: None (conviction and life imprisonment sentence set aside)
brief_judgment_file_summary: This appeal from the High Court of Chilaw concerned a conviction for trafficking in and possession of heroin under Sections 54(A)(b) and 54(A)(d) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance, arising from a detection at Thoppuwa Junction in August 2013. The prosecution relied on the evidence of police officers who claimed to have recovered nine packets of heroin from the Appellant and on a Government Analyst’s report confirming the substance to be heroin, resulting in a High Court conviction and life imprisonment on both counts. On appeal, the Court of Appeal scrutinized the chain of custody and found a substantial and unexplained discrepancy between the weight of the substance recorded by the police and the weight recorded by the Government Analyst, as well as deficiencies in sealing and documentation, including a missing signature of the Appellant on the production envelope. Holding that these defects created reasonable doubt and that the High Court had failed to address them, thereby denying the Appellant a fair trial, the Court of Appeal set aside the conviction and sentence and acquitted the Appellant from all charges.
defence_counsel: Isuru Somadasa
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court of Chilaw accepted the police evidence of detection, recovery and weighing of heroin, treated the productions as properly sealed and handled, and convicted the Appellant, imposing life imprisonment on both counts. However, the Court of Appeal later observed that the High Court had not commented on or resolved the serious weight discrepancy between the police weighing and the Government Analyst’s measurement, nor had it addressed contradictions and shortcomings relating to sealing and signatures on the production envelope. The Court of Appeal held that these omissions and misdirections by the High Court affected the root of the case and contributed to an unsafe conviction.
precedents_cited_list: Woolmington v. DPP – [1935] A.C.462 | Mohamed Nimnaz v. Attorney General – CA/95/94 | Perera v. Attorney General – [1998] 1 Sri.L.R | Koushappis v. The State of WA – [2007] WASCA 26; (2007) 168 A Crim R 51
standard_of_review_applied: Failure to prove chain of custody and identity of productions beyond reasonable doubt; inadequate evaluation of material evidence and contradictions; misdirection leading to denial of a fair trial
final_charge_after_appeal: Same as original charges under Sections 54(A)(b) and 54(A)(d), but conviction set aside and accused acquitted

judges: Hon. P Kumararathnam, J. | Hon. Pradeep Hettiarachchi, J.
offence_sections: Section 296 Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The appellant was indicted in the High Court of Kalutara for murdering his partner, Thanuja Lewke Bandara, allegedly by striking her with a plastic torch and pushing her during a dispute over her refusal to take meals. Following the assault, he sponged her bruises with hot water and took her to hospital, where she later died on 2015-02-21. The postmortem revealed an acute-on-chronic right-sided subdural hemorrhage over a pre-existing chronic subdural hematoma, with only minor external injuries and no skull or other fractures. The High Court nevertheless convicted him of murder under Section 296 and imposed the death sentence, leading to this appeal.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 296 Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court of Kalutara, after a judge-alone trial, found the appellant guilty of murder under Section 296 of the Penal Code. It appears to have proceeded on the basis that the assault caused skull fractures and internal hemorrhage and that the appellant had assaulted the deceased with a broom until it broke, treating the conduct as evincing murderous intent. On that footing, the court imposed the mandatory sentence of death.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant challenged both conviction and sentence, contending that the High Court failed to consider inter-se contradictions and weaknesses in the prosecution evidence and did not properly evaluate the defence submissions. He argued that, in light of the postmortem findings and his subsequent conduct in assisting the deceased, the prosecution had not proved the requisite mens rea for murder. It was further maintained that the judgment was contrary to the evidence led at trial and that the injuries described in the autopsy report did not support a conviction for murder. The appellant sought a reassessment of the legal classification of the homicide and the evidential basis of the conviction.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Failure by the High Court Judge to consider inter-se contradictions in the prosecution evidence. | Failure to pay due attention to the submissions made by the defence. | Failure to evaluate the weaknesses and lack of credibility in the prosecution evidence. | The judgment being contrary to the evidence led at the trial. | Mischaracterisation of the medical evidence and failure to address the issue of mens rea and the appellant's knowledge, particularly in light of the autopsy report and the appellant's subsequent conduct.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: Prosecution eyewitnesses described an assault in which the appellant struck the deceased once with a plastic torch and pushed her, causing her to fall, but they did not see him repeatedly beating her with a broom. The Judicial Medical Officer gave detailed expert evidence that the external injuries were minor, with no skull or bone fractures, and that death was due to an acute-on-chronic right-sided subdural hemorrhage over a pre-existing chronic condition. The Court of Appeal preferred the medical and eyewitness evidence over the High Court's findings, holding that the trial judge had drawn conclusions about skull fractures and broom assaults that were not supported by testimony.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal emphasized that where death results through a supervening condition, the prosecution must prove a very high probability that the condition arose from the original injury and that the injury was sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death. Applying authorities such as Mendis v Queen and Farook v A.G., the court held that the medical evidence did not establish that the single blow and push, by themselves, were sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death.
defence_version_summary: The defence did not put forward an alibi but argued that the appellant lacked murderous intent, relying heavily on the medical evidence and his subsequent conduct in sponging the deceased's bruises and taking her to hospital. There is no indication of defence witnesses being called, and the record primarily reflects legal submissions that the autopsy did not support a finding of murder and that the death occurred three days after the assault. The Court of Appeal accepted that the evidence was consistent with knowledge of risk rather than an intention to kill, while still holding the appellant criminally liable for culpable homicide.
legal_errors_description: The Court of Appeal found that the High Court Judge misinterpreted the medical evidence by assuming skull fractures and extensive internal hemorrhage where the JMO had found none, and by relying on an alleged broom assault that no eyewitness had seen. The trial judge also failed to explain under which limb of Section 294 the act amounted to murder and to set out proper reasons for classifying the homicide as murder when the evidence did not show injuries sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal carefully analysed Section 294 of the Penal Code and relevant case law, distinguishing between murderous intention and the third limb, which focuses on whether the intended bodily injury is sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death. It held that the medical evidence showed only minor external injuries and no fractures, and that death was due to an acute-on-chronic subdural hemorrhage supervening on a pre-existing chronic condition, so the appellant's act alone could not be treated as sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death. The court criticised the High Court for basing its findings on facts not supported by the evidence and for failing to articulate under which limb of Section 294 murder was made out. While rejecting a murder conviction, it concluded that the appellant acted with knowledge that his conduct risked causing serious harm, and therefore substituted a conviction for culpable homicide not amounting to murder under Section 297 with a reduced custodial sentence and fine.
coa_sentence_type: Rigorous Imprisonment 10 years plus fine of 50000 with 3 years' default imprisonment
brief_judgment_file_summary: The appellant, convicted of murder and sentenced to death by the High Court of Kalutara for causing the death of his partner, appealed on the basis of evidential contradictions and the absence of murderous intent. The Court of Appeal reviewed the eyewitness and expert medical evidence, which showed only minor external injuries and an acute-on-chronic subdural hemorrhage over a pre-existing chronic hematoma, with no skull fractures or severe trauma. It held that the High Court had misread the medical evidence, relied on unsupported findings such as a broom assault and skull fractures, and failed to identify the proper limb of Section 294 justifying a murder conviction. Reclassifying the offence as culpable homicide not amounting to murder on the basis of knowledge under Section 297, the Court of Appeal set aside the death sentence, imposed 10 years' rigorous imprisonment and a fine, backdated the term to the original conviction date, and partly allowed the appeal.
prosecution_counsel: Malik Azeez, SC for the State
defence_counsel: Ershan Ariaraynam for the Accused–Appellant
cause_of_death_exact_text: Acute-on-chronic right-sided subdural hemorrhage resulting from blunt force trauma to the head
hc_analysis_summary: According to the Court of Appeal, the High Court concluded that the deceased suffered skull fractures and internal hemorrhage due to the appellant's assault and that he had repeatedly beaten her with a broom until it broke. These findings were not supported by the evidence, since the JMO found no fractures and the eyewitness PW1 explicitly denied seeing a broom assault, instead describing a single blow with a torch and a push. The appellate court held that the High Court had convicted for murder on a flawed factual basis and without explaining how the ingredients of murder under Section 294 were satisfied.
precedents_cited_list: Withana and Another v The Republic [2007] 1 SLR 169 | Gunasiri & Two Others v Republic of Sri Lanka [2009] SLR 39 | Virsa Singh v State of Punjab AIR 1958 SC 465 | State of Maharashtra v Arun Savalaram 1989 CR LJ 191 | Mendis v Queen 54 NLR 177 | Farook v A.G. [2006] 3 SLR 174 | Vithana & Another v The Republic of Sri Lanka [2007] 1 SLR 169
standard_of_review_applied: Review for misdirection and misapplication of the law on murder versus culpable homicide, and for perverse or unsupported factual findings contrary to medical and eyewitness evidence, including failure to properly evaluate causation and the sufficiency of injuries under the third limb of Section 294.
sentencing_principles_applied: In re-sentencing, the Court of Appeal considered the appellant's age, absence of previous convictions, and the fact that he had been incarcerated from the date of conviction, backdating the custodial term accordingly and imposing a finite term of 10 years' rigorous imprisonment with a moderate fine and default term instead of the death penalty.
final_charge_after_appeal: Culpable homicide not amounting to murder on the basis of knowledge under Section 297 Penal Code

judges: S. U. B. Karalliyadde, J. | Dr. D. F. H. Gunawardhana, J.
offence_sections: Section 6, 7 of Termination of Employment Workmen (Special Provision) Act, No. 45 of 1971
brief_facts_summary: The Appellant closed its garment factory in Gampaha in 1990, resulting in retrenchment of employees. The 1st Respondent initiated proceedings under the Termination of Employment Workmen Act for compensation. The Magistrate convicted the Appellant and ordered payment of Rs. 100,727,203.27, but the Appellant disputed the amount, claiming liability only for Rs. 10,680,611.66.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 7 of Termination of Employment Workmen (Special Provision) Act, No. 45 of 1971
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court dismissed the revision application, acknowledging that the Appellant is liable only for Rs. 10,680,611, but found no misconstruction of law to interfere with the Magistrate's orders. It held that the Appellant's conduct did not warrant revisionary jurisdiction.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The Appellant argued that the institution of proceedings in the Magistrate's Court was flawed as no certificate or determination under Section 6 of the Act was filed. Additionally, the entire Magistrate Court proceedings were flawed due to improper admission by the Attorney-at-Law, not a responsible officer. The Appellant contended that the High Court erred in dismissing the revision application despite accepting the lower liability.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Institution of proceedings flawed due to lack of certificate under Section 6 | Admission by Attorney-at-Law not equivalent to plea by responsible officer | Magistrate's order based on erroneous admission | High Court erred in dismissing revision application
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The case primarily involved documentary evidence and legal admissions, with no detailed witness testimony analysis. The Court emphasized procedural flaws over witness evidence.
probability_assessment_by_court: The court applied strict liability but emphasized that penal statutes should be construed strictly, with benefit of doubt to the subject.
defence_version_summary: The Appellant defended that it was only liable to pay Rs. 10,680,611.66 and argued procedural flaws in the proceedings. There was no alibi or dock statement; the defence relied on legal arguments. The court found the admission by counsel improper and not a valid plea.
legal_errors_description: The institution of proceedings was flawed as no certificate under Section 6 was filed; the admission by Attorney-at-Law did not constitute a proper plea; strict liability was misapplied.
procedural_defects_description: Failure to file required certificate under Section 6; improper plea by counsel instead of responsible officer; Magistrate's order based on invalid admission.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The COA allowed the appeal in part, finding that the proceedings were flawed from inception due to lack of proper certificate under Section 6 and invalid admission by counsel. It cited precedents on strict construction of penal statutes and benefit of doubt. The COA set aside the High Court's dismissal of the revision and upheld the finding on lower liability.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The Court of Appeal partly allowed the appeal, setting aside the High Court's dismissal of the revision application. It found the Magistrate Court proceedings flawed due to lack of proper certificate under Section 6 and improper admission by counsel. The COA held that the Appellant is liable only for Rs. 10,680,611 and that employees can seek remedies under other laws.
prosecution_counsel: Sudharshana De Silva, S. D. S. G.
defence_counsel: Shavindra Fernando, P. C. with NimeshaWanaguru, M. T. M. Ahamed, Amanda Imbulana, and R. Fernando
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court dismissed the revision application, acknowledging the lower liability but finding no misconstruction of law to interfere with the Magistrate's orders. The COA found this erroneous as the proceedings were fundamentally flawed.
precedents_cited_list: Eastern Bus Company v Inspector of Labour – [1951] 53 NLR 372 | Harding v Price – [1948] 1 KB 695
standard_of_review_applied: Misdirection on law and procedural errors

judges: P. Kumararatnam, J. | R. P. Hettiarachchi, J.
offence_sections: Sections 54(A)(d) and 54(A)(b) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance as amended by Act No.13 of 1984
brief_facts_summary: Acting on information about an impending drug deal, CI Randeniya and a police team raided Room No. 23 of Hotel Sancharina in the Wattala police area on 2013-06-10 and found the two appellants allegedly packaging heroin. The officers recovered 13 polythene parcels containing 520 small packets of a substance suspected to be heroin and arrested both appellants. At Wattala Police Station the packets were emptied onto paper and weighed on an electronic scale, with a gross weight recorded as about 16.100 grams, and the productions were sealed and handed over for safe custody. The Government Analyst later reported a weight of 8.64 grams of heroin, giving rise to a significant discrepancy compared with the police-recorded gross weight.
evidence_type_primary: Police eyewitness testimony regarding the recovery and possession of heroin
evidence_type_secondary: Government Analyst report and documentary evidence relating to sealing, custody, and quantity of the heroin exhibits
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Sections 54(A)(d) and 54(A)(b) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance as amended by Act No.13 of 1984
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court of Negombo accepted the prosecution version that the appellants were in possession of and trafficking heroin in Room No. 23 and convicted them on both counts under Sections 54(A)(d) and 54(A)(b). Relying primarily on the testimony of the police officers and the Government Analyst report, the learned High Court Judge imposed life imprisonment on each count. The judgment did not address the substantial discrepancy between the weight recorded by the police and that in the Analyst's report, nor the absence of one appellant's signature on the sealed production envelope.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: Both appellants jointly contended that the learned High Court Judge erred in law by failing to consider a vital discrepancy in the quantity of heroin said to have been recovered from them. They argued that the difference between the police-recorded weight of 16.100 grams and the Government Analyst's figure of 8.64 grams undermined the integrity of the production and the chain of custody. The appellants maintained that this failure to analyse the discrepancy, together with issues about sealing of productions including a missing signature, deprived them of a fair trial. They relied on principles concerning the prosecution's burden of proof and the need to establish an unbroken and reliable inward journey of productions in drug cases.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Failure by the High Court to consider and analyse the significant discrepancy between the gross weight of heroin recorded by the police (16.100 grams) and the weight in the Government Analyst report (8.64 grams). | Challenge to the integrity and chain of custody of the heroin exhibits, including whether the productions analysed were the same as those allegedly seized from the appellants. | Complaint that the learned High Court Judge misdirected himself by treating the productions as properly sealed despite the absence of one appellant's signature on the sealed envelope. | Allegation that these evidentiary and chain of custody deficiencies created reasonable doubt and resulted in an unfair trial contrary to the proper burden of proof in criminal cases.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The prosecution case at trial rested mainly on the evidence of PW1 CI Randeniya and PW4 PC Sisira Kumara, who described receiving information, conducting the raid, seizing 13 parcels containing 520 packets, and weighing the substance at Wattala Police Station. The Court of Appeal found that, although these officers spoke to seizure and weighing, their evidence did not satisfactorily explain the substantial reduction in weight between the police weighing and the Government Analyst report or the absence of one appellant's signature on the sealed envelope. The Court held that these deficiencies, together with contradictions and improbabilities in the prosecution evidence about the inward journey of the productions, created serious doubt about the reliability of the exhibits relied on to convict.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal held that the unexplained and substantial discrepancy in weight and the irregularity in sealing the productions raised a reasonable doubt as to whether the heroin analysed was the same as that allegedly seized from the appellants, and therefore extended the benefit of that doubt to them.
defence_version_summary: In their dock statements the appellants denied ever being in possession of dangerous drugs as alleged by the prosecution. They said they were merely staying at a hotel in Wattala and that narcotics recovered from persons in Room No. 22 were wrongfully introduced against them by the police. No defence witnesses were called, and the defence rested on these dock statements and the alleged weaknesses in the prosecution's chain of custody and evidence. The Court of Appeal considered that, in light of the serious doubts about the productions, the defence position could not be rejected beyond reasonable doubt.
legal_errors_description: The Court of Appeal identified misdirection and error in the High Court's failure to consider and evaluate the large discrepancy between the police-recorded weight of the heroin and the Government Analyst's weight, and in treating the productions as properly sealed despite the absence of one appellant's signature. The appellate court held that these matters went to the root of the case and that the High Court's omission to address them deprived the appellants of a fair trial.
procedural_defects_description: The handling of the productions revealed an unexplained reduction in weight between seizure and analysis and an irregular sealing process in which one appellant's signature was missing from the sealed envelope. Additionally, the prosecution failed to present clear, specific evidence covering all stages of the inward journey of the exhibits to prove safe custody and identity of the drugs beyond reasonable doubt.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal reiterated the principle that the burden of proof lies on the prosecution and that in drug cases the chain of custody of productions must be proved beyond reasonable doubt, with particular emphasis on the inward journey. Citing authorities such as Woolmington v. DPP, Mohamed Nimnaz v. Attorney General, Perera v. Attorney General, and Koushappis v. The State of WA, the court emphasised that the weight discrepancy of 8.46 grams between the police weighing and the Government Analyst report and the missing signature on the sealed envelope seriously undermined the reliability of the exhibits. It held that the High Court's failure to address these issues constituted misdirection, created serious doubt about whether the drugs analysed were those allegedly seized, and resulted in prejudice to the appellants' right to a fair trial. Consequently, the Court of Appeal set aside the convictions and sentences and acquitted the appellants.
coa_sentence_type: None (acquitted)
brief_judgment_file_summary: The appellants were tried in the High Court of Negombo for possessing and trafficking heroin under Sections 54(A)(d) and 54(A)(b) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance, arising from a police raid on Room No. 23 at Hotel Sancharina in the Wattala police area on 2013-06-10. Police witnesses testified to seizing 13 parcels containing 520 packets of suspected heroin, weighing 16.100 grams at the police station, sealing the productions, and sending them to the Government Analyst, who later reported 8.64 grams of heroin. The High Court convicted both appellants on both counts and imposed life imprisonment without adequately addressing the substantial difference in weight or a sealing irregularity involving the absence of one appellant's signature. On appeal, the Court of Appeal held that the unexplained discrepancy and defects in the chain of custody, together with contradictions and improbabilities in the prosecution evidence, created serious doubt about the identity and integrity of the exhibits and deprived the appellants of a fair trial. It therefore set aside the convictions and sentences and acquitted the appellants of all charges.
prosecution_counsel: Lakmini Girihagama, Deputy Solicitor General, for the Respondent
defence_counsel: Kamal Suneth Perera for the 1st Appellant; Saliya Peiris, PC with Susil Wanigapura for the 2nd Appellant
cause_of_death_exact_text: Not applicable – no death; the case concerns possession and trafficking of heroin.
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court relied on the evidence of the police officers and the Government Analyst report to conclude that the appellants were in possession of and trafficking heroin, treating the productions as properly sealed and the chain of custody as intact. However, the Court of Appeal noted that the High Court failed to consider the large discrepancy between the gross weight recorded at the police station and the weight in the Analyst's report and ignored the absence of one appellant's signature on the sealed envelope. The appellate court found that this omission amounted to misdirection and resulted in an unsafe conviction.
precedents_cited_list: Woolmington v. DPP – [1935] A.C. 462 | Mohamed Nimnaz v. Attorney General – CA/95/94 | Perera v. Attorney General – [1998] 1 Sri L.R. | Koushappis v. The State of WA – [2007] WASCA 26; (2007) 168 A Crim R 51
standard_of_review_applied: Failure to properly evaluate critical evidence on chain of custody and quantity of drugs, and misdirection in law leading to an unsafe and unfair conviction.
final_charge_after_appeal: Original charges under Sections 54(A)(d) and 54(A)(b) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance – appellants acquitted of all charges

judges: B. Sasi Mahendran | Amal Ranaraja
offence_sections: 303 read with 490, 102 read with 303, 323
offence_category: Causing miscarriage, Aiding and abetting, Causing hurt to public servant
brief_facts_summary: Police received information about illegal abortions at Randeniya Medical Center and conducted a decoy operation with WPS Renuka posing as a pregnant woman. The accused provided her with medication to induce miscarriage, but when she revealed her police identity, the first accused bit her hand and the second snatched her phone. Tablets and marked money were recovered during the raid.
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court acquitted the accused on charges of causing miscarriage and aiding but convicted them on causing hurt to a public servant. Each was fined Rs. 25,000 with a default sentence of six months simple imprisonment. The judge found the decoy's evidence convincing and that the accused intended to harm the public servant.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The accused argued that the prosecution failed to establish that the hurt was caused to a public servant. They also contended failure to prove the decoy was acting under a specific search warrant. Additionally, they claimed reaction out of fear due to absence of warrant and impersonation concerns.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Prosecution failed to establish person hurt was a public servant | Prosecution failed to establish WPC 4035 Renuka was performing as decoy on search warrant MC 1831/2/2009
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The decoy's (PW 04) testimony was central and examined with caution as per legal precedents on decoy evidence. It was corroborated by PW 06 and physical evidence like injuries and recovered tablets. The court found her evidence convincing despite lack of corroboration requirement for decoys.
probability_assessment_by_court: Prosecution established beyond reasonable doubt on third count; benefit of doubt not given as evidence convincing
defence_version_summary: The first accused gave evidence from the witness box admitting the decoy identified as police, while the second made a dock statement denying seeing the identity card. They claimed reaction out of fear of impersonators, no alibi presented. The court found their versions conflicting and unconvincing compared to prosecution evidence.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The COA affirmed the HC conviction on the third count, finding the decoy's evidence convincing after careful examination. Prosecution credible, defence not; no contradictions warranting reversal; search warrant not necessary for decoy role; precedents on decoy evidence applied including Beddewela v. Albert. Sentence appropriate.
coa_sentence_type: Fine
brief_judgment_file_summary: The judgment dismisses the appeal against conviction and sentence for causing hurt to a public servant during a decoy operation for illegal abortion. It details the facts, evidence, grounds of appeal, and legal analysis on decoy testimony, affirming the High Court's decision.
defence_counsel: Dulindra Weerasooriya, PC with Ranjith Caldera and Pasan Malinda
hc_analysis_summary: The HC convicted based on the decoy's evidence of intentional hurt after identity reveal, acquitting on abortion charges. The COA found the HC correctly examined the evidence with care and no reason to disagree with findings. HC ruled warrant not necessary as decoy acting in duty.
precedents_cited_list: Beddewela v. Albert, 42 NLR 136 | Coldera v. Pedrick | Almeida v. Adiriya | Ariyarantne v. Food and Price Control Inspector, Galle, 74 NLR 19 | Wickremadasa v. The Food Price Controller, 78 NLR 3

judges: Hon. P. Kumararatnam, J. | Hon. Pradeep Hettiarachchi, J.
offence_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The accused-appellant was indicted for the murder of his wife, Usliyanage Piyaseeli, by cutting her neck on or about 15.04.2008. The prosecution led five witnesses including the Judicial Medical Officer, while the accused made a dock statement and called the deceased's daughter as a defence witness. The Judicial Medical Officer described a single deep cut injury around the neck, almost severing the head, caused by a heavy sharp weapon such as an axe. The accused claimed he acted under grave and sudden provocation after allegedly seeing his wife with a paramour, but the courts found no supporting evidence and rejected this version.
evidence_type_secondary: Circumstantial evidence including timing of the incident and recovery of the weapon
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court of Gampaha, after trial, found the accused guilty of murder under section 296 of the Penal Code. The court rejected the contention that the offence was committed under grave and sudden provocation and imposed the mandatory death sentence. In its judgment dated 02.02.2018, the High Court explained why the dock statement was not worthy of belief and why the evidence did not establish an exception reducing the offence.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: Although several grounds were initially raised, at the hearing counsel for the appellant confined the appeal to challenging the conviction for murder, contending that the offence should be reduced to culpable homicide not amounting to murder on the basis of grave and sudden provocation. It was argued that the accused lost self-control upon seeing his wife with her paramour and used a bread knife found on the table to cut her neck. Counsel also contended that the High Court failed to properly evaluate and wrongly rejected the appellant's dock statement in assessing the defence of grave and sudden provocation. The appeal thus focused on the classification of the offence rather than on the sentence itself.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Conviction for murder under section 296 should be reduced to culpable homicide not amounting to murder on the basis of grave and sudden provocation. | The accused allegedly lost self-control upon seeing the deceased with her paramour and used a bread knife found on the table to cut her neck. | The learned High Court Judge failed to properly evaluate the accused's dock statement and erred in rejecting it. | The High Court failed to appreciate that the facts brought the case within the exception of grave and sudden provocation.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The prosecution led five witnesses, including the Judicial Medical Officer, whose evidence established a single deep cut injury around the neck, almost severing the head, caused by a heavy sharp weapon such as an axe, and not by a bread knife. Prosecution witnesses confirmed that the incident occurred around 10.30 p.m., and this timing was not challenged in cross-examination, leading the Court of Appeal to treat it as an accepted fact. The defence called the deceased's daughter, whose evidence only showed that the accused suspected an illicit affair but did not support the presence of a paramour at the time of the killing, while the accused's dock statement was found to be false and inconsistent with the medical and other evidence.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal held that the prosecution had proved the charge of murder beyond reasonable doubt and that the accused had failed to establish any exception. The court considered the unchallenged evidence on the time of the incident and the medical evidence on the nature of the injury as compelling, while finding the dock statement false and incapable of raising a reasonable doubt. The defence theory of grave and sudden provocation was rejected as improbable and inconsistent with the evidence.
defence_version_summary: The accused in his dock statement claimed that he returned home at about 3.30 p.m., found his wife talking with a man named Dayananda with whom he suspected she had an illicit affair, lost self-control and used a bread knife lying on the table to cut her neck under grave and sudden provocation. The defence also called the deceased's daughter, who spoke to prior suspicions and an inquiry at the deceased's workplace but did not corroborate the presence of a paramour at the time of the incident. The Court of Appeal held that the alleged time of the attack and the use of a bread knife were contradicted by the prosecution and medical evidence, and concluded that the dock statement was untrue and did not establish grave and sudden provocation.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analysed whether the offence of murder could be reduced to culpable homicide not amounting to murder on the basis of grave and sudden provocation and concluded that it could not. It relied heavily on the Judicial Medical Officer's evidence that the neck injury, which almost severed the head, must have been caused by a heavy sharp weapon such as an axe and could not have been inflicted by a bread knife, and on the unchallenged testimony of prosecution witnesses that the incident occurred around 10.30 p.m., providing a long cooling-off period even if the accused had seen the deceased with a man earlier. The court found no evidence of grave and sudden provocation at the time of the killing, considered the accused's dock statement to be false and unworthy of belief, and held that the High Court had correctly rejected it and properly applied the law on provocation. Applying authorities on murder, provocation, and the effect of failure to cross-examine, the Court of Appeal affirmed both conviction and death sentence.
coa_sentence_type: Death
brief_judgment_file_summary: This appeal arose from the conviction and death sentence imposed by the High Court of Gampaha on the accused-appellant for murdering his wife by cutting her neck on or about 15.04.2008. At the hearing, the appeal was confined to the question whether the conviction for murder should be reduced to culpable homicide not amounting to murder on the basis of grave and sudden provocation, grounded mainly on the appellant's dock statement. The Court of Appeal, after reviewing the evidence of the Judicial Medical Officer and the prosecution witnesses, held that the fatal injury could only have been caused by a heavy sharp weapon such as an axe, that the incident occurred at about 10.30 p.m., and that there was no credible evidence that the deceased was with a paramour at the time of the killing or that the appellant acted under grave and sudden provocation. Finding the dock statement demonstrably false and the High Court's evaluation of evidence and rejection of the provocation defence correct, the Court of Appeal affirmed the conviction under section 296 and the death sentence and dismissed the appeal.
prosecution_counsel: Sudharshana de Silva, S.D.S.G. for the Respondent.
defence_counsel: Chathura Amaratunga, Assigned Counsel for the Accused – Appellant.
cause_of_death_exact_text: Death was due to a single deep cut injury around the neck, almost severing the head and cutting vital neck structures, caused by a heavy sharp cutting weapon such as an axe.
hc_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal noted that in the judgment dated 02.02.2018 the learned High Court Judge had considered the accused's dock statement, found it devoid of truth, and concluded that the offence was not committed under grave and sudden provocation. The High Court had relied on the medical evidence regarding the nature of the fatal injury and the other prosecution evidence to find that the ingredients of murder under section 296 were proved. The Court of Appeal found no misdirection or error in that reasoning and held that the High Court's findings on the facts and law were justified.
precedents_cited_list: Bakhtawar v State of Haryana AIR 1979 SC 1006 | Dadimuni Indrasena & Dadimuni Wimalasena v AG (2008) | Pilippu Mandige Nalaka Krishantha Kumara Tissera v AG (2007) | Sarwan Singh v State of Punjab AIR 2002 SC 111 | Motilal v State of Madhya Pradesh 1990 CLJ NOC 125 MP | Mancini v Director of Public Prosecutions [1941] UKHL J1016-1 | K.M. Nanavati v State of Maharashtra AIR 1962 SC 605
standard_of_review_applied: Evaluation of the evidence and application of the legal exception of grave and sudden provocation to determine whether the High Court's findings and conviction for murder were justified.
final_charge_after_appeal: Murder under section 296 of the Penal Code

judges: P. Kumararatnam, J. | R.P. Hettiarachchi, J.
offence_sections: Section 140; Section 296 read with Section 146; Section 300 read with Section 146; Section 296 read with Section 32; Section 300 read with Section 32; conviction under Section 297 and Section 300 of the Penal Code
offence_category: Culpable homicide not amounting to murder and Attempted murder
location_of_offence: Ambalantota, at the house of PW1
brief_facts_summary: The dispute arose in Ambalantota on 08-08-2005 when cattle belonging to the 2nd Accused allegedly damaged the crop of PW1, leading to a confrontation and assault between PW1 and the 2nd Accused. Later, a group of about 15 persons, including the accused, entered PW1's house and a fight ensued. The Appellant entered the house armed with a gun, and during a struggle between PW1 and the Appellant to take control of the weapon, it discharged, causing serious injury to PW1's hand and fatal gunshot injuries to the chest of the deceased who had come with the group. Evidence indicated that the gun was brought to the scene by the deceased, and the incident occurred in the course of a sudden fight without premeditation.
evidence_type_secondary: Background and circumstantial evidence relating to the prior dispute and group assault
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 297 and Section 300 of the Penal Code
hc_sentence_type: Rigorous Imprisonment 10 years on each of counts 4 and 5 (concurrent), plus fines and compensation
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court, after a non-jury trial where the prosecution led eight witnesses, convicted only the Appellant under Section 297 on the 4th count and under Section 300 on the 5th count, acquitting him on the 1st, 2nd and 3rd charges and acquitting all the other accused of all charges. The court imposed 10 years rigorous imprisonment on each of the 4th and 5th counts to run concurrently, with fines of 50000 on each count and compensation of 500000 to the deceased's side, with default terms of imprisonment. The conviction reflects the court's acceptance of the prosecution version that the Appellant bore criminal responsibility for the fatal and injurious gunshot discharge during the incident.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: In his written submissions the Appellant initially raised ten grounds of appeal but, at the hearing, restricted the challenge to a single ground. The principal contention was that the learned High Court Judge had failed to consider and properly evaluate the evidence of a sudden fight when determining the conviction and sentence. It was argued that the circumstances fell within the sudden fight situation, thereby warranting a lesser degree of culpability and a reduced sentence under the relevant Penal Code provisions. The appeal was essentially directed against the severity of the sentence imposed rather than the factual basis of the conviction.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Although ten grounds were raised in the written submissions, only one ground was pursued at the oral hearing. | The Appellant contended that the learned High Court Judge failed to consider the evidence of a sudden fight in the judgment. | It was argued that the incident occurred without premeditation, in the heat of passion upon a sudden quarrel, which should attract the application of the sudden fight exception and justify a lesser sentence. | The appeal was primarily against the sentence as being unduly severe in light of the circumstances of the sudden fight.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The prosecution led eight witnesses, including PW1 and PW2, the husband and wife who directly experienced the events, and whose testimony described the initial dispute over cattle, the subsequent group intrusion into their home, and the struggle over the gun leading to the injuries and death. Their evidence established that the deceased had brought the gun and that the weapon discharged during a struggle, supporting the conclusion that the incident arose from a sudden fight rather than a premeditated attack. The defence consisted only of dock statements by the accused, which did not displace the consistent and coherent account given by the prosecution witnesses, and the courts accepted the prosecution version as credible.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal accepted that the probabilities supported a sudden, unpremeditated fight in which the gun, brought by the deceased, discharged during a struggle, reducing the degree of moral blameworthiness though not exonerating the Appellant. The court balanced the need for punishment with mitigating factors such as sudden fight, youth of the offender, and long delay, and adjusted the sentence rather than disturbing the conviction.
defence_version_summary: After the prosecution closed its case, the Appellant and the other accused opted to give dock statements and closed their defence without calling any witnesses. Their dock statements amounted to denials of liability but did not present a coherent alternative narrative or an alibi, nor were they supported by independent evidence. Both the High Court and the Court of Appeal found that these unsworn statements could not outweigh the consistent eyewitness testimony of PW1 and PW2 and the surrounding circumstances.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal noted that while the High Court had convicted the Appellant under Section 297 and Section 300, it was not clearly articulated under which exception to Section 294 the decision was grounded, and therefore it was necessary to identify the appropriate exception. Accepting the submissions of President's Counsel, and with the Senior Deputy Solicitor General's concession, the Court of Appeal held that the incident clearly arose out of a sudden fight, thus bringing it within exception 4 to Section 294, which reduces culpability from murder to culpable homicide not amounting to murder. The court further considered mitigating factors, including that the Appellant was only 19 years old at the time of the incident and that the matter had taken about 19 years to conclude, and found the original sentences of 10 years RI on each count to be excessive in the circumstances. Without disturbing the conviction, the Court of Appeal reduced the terms of imprisonment on each of the relevant counts while allowing the fines and compensation to stand, thereby partly varying the sentence.
coa_sentence_type: Rigorous Imprisonment 5 years on each of counts 4 and 5 (to run concurrently) plus fines and compensation as imposed by the High Court
brief_judgment_file_summary: The Appellant, together with four others, was indicted in the High Court of Hambantota for offences relating to an unlawful assembly at Ambalantota on 08-08-2005, resulting in the death of one person and injuries to PW1. Following a non-jury trial, only the Appellant was convicted under Section 297 on the 4th count and Section 300 on the 5th count, and was sentenced to 10 years rigorous imprisonment on each count (concurrent), with fines and compensation, while the other accused were acquitted. On appeal, though ten grounds were initially raised, counsel restricted the argument to the single ground that the High Court failed to consider the incident as a sudden fight, engaging exception 4 to Section 294. The Court of Appeal agreed that the evidence showed a sudden, unpremeditated fight in which the deceased brought the gun and it discharged during a struggle, took into account the Appellant's youth and the long delay in concluding the case, and accordingly reduced the sentences on counts 4 and 5 to 5 years rigorous imprisonment each, concurrent, leaving the fines and compensation intact, and otherwise dismissed the appeal.
prosecution_counsel: Hiranjan Peiris, Senior Deputy Solicitor General (SDSG)
defence_counsel: Saliya Peiris, PC with Amila Egodamahawatta and Nisal Hennadige
cause_of_death_exact_text: The deceased sustained serious gunshot injuries on his chest and was pronounced dead on admission to hospital.
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court accepted the prosecution evidence that a group, including the accused, came to PW1's house after an earlier quarrel over cattle and that, during a struggle over a gun, PW1 was injured and the deceased was fatally shot. While the indictment included charges involving unlawful assembly and murder read with common object provisions, the High Court ultimately limited its findings to convicting the Appellant alone for culpable homicide not amounting to murder under Section 297 and attempted murder under Section 300, acquitting him on the other counts and acquitting all co-accused entirely. The Court of Appeal did not find fault with this evaluative process but questioned the lack of clarity regarding the precise exception under Section 294 and used that analysis mainly to recalibrate the sentence.
standard_of_review_applied: Review of sentence for failure to give full effect to the sudden fight exception and for manifest excessiveness in light of the offender's youth and the long delay
sentencing_principles_applied: Mitigation based on exception 4 to Section 294 (sudden fight without premeditation), youth of the offender at the time of the offence, and the inordinate delay of about 19 years in concluding the case, with concurrent sentences and sentence commencement from the date of conviction.
final_charge_after_appeal: Culpable homicide not amounting to murder under Section 297 and attempted murder under Section 300 of the Penal Code (unchanged)

judges: P. Kumararatnam | R. P. Hettiarachchi
offence_sections: Section 296 read with Section 32; Section 297 (second limb)
offence_category: Murder (reduced to culpable homicide not amounting to murder)
brief_facts_summary: The deceased, his employee PW1, and others attended a coming-of-age ceremony at the house of Wimalaratne, where the appellants were also present. A quarrel arose when the deceased repeatedly switched off a cassette player so he could deliver a speech while the 1st appellant wanted the music to continue, leading to a sudden physical fight outside the house. PW1 claimed the 1st appellant stabbed the deceased several times with a knife while the 2nd and 3rd appellants held the deceased, and the victim was taken to Horana Base Hospital where he was pronounced dead. Medical evidence recorded a fatal deep cut to the chest and two skin-level injuries, and PW1 later identified all three appellants at an identification parade.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 296 read with Section 32 of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court of Kalutara convicted all three appellants of murder on the basis that they acted with common intention to stab and kill the deceased at the ceremony. The court accepted the prosecution eyewitness version, found their participation proved beyond reasonable doubt, and sentenced each appellant to death as charged.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellants contended that the prosecution had failed to prove the case beyond reasonable doubt and that the High Court neglected to analyze contradictions between PW1 and PW2 and between eyewitness and medical evidence. They argued that the trial judge failed to properly consider and apply the law on common intention under section 32 and did not evaluate the dock statements of the 2nd and 3rd appellants or the defence evidence generally.
