AG (2007) | Sarwan Singh v State of Punjab (2002) AIR SC III | Motilal v. State of Madhya Pradesh (1990) CLJ NOC 125 MP | Mancini and Director of Public Prosecutions [1941] UKHL J1016-1 | K.M. Nanavati v. State of Maharashtra, AIR 1962 SC 605
standard_of_review_applied: Evaluation of evidence and application of legal principles on provocation
final_charge_after_appeal: Murder under Section 296

judges: Amal Ranaraja J | B. Sasi Mahendran J
offence_sections: Section 300
brief_facts_summary: On 26 December 2018, neighbours of the appellant heard commotion from his house and called the police, who learned of a domestic dispute between the appellant and his wife. Shortly after the officers withdrew to their vehicle, the appellant's wife ran towards it with the appellant pursuing and physically assaulting her while armed with a knife, causing a bleeding injury to her back. She was admitted to hospital where a medico-legal report recorded a single non-grievous stab or cut injury. The appellant was arrested and later indicted in the High Court for attempted murder under section 300 of the Penal Code.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 300
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court of Hambantota convicted the appellant of attempted murder under section 300 of the Penal Code on the basis that he stabbed his wife with a knife during a domestic dispute. The court treated the conduct as an attempt to commit murder and imposed a sentence of 13 years rigorous imprisonment together with a fine of 10000 and one year rigorous imprisonment in default. No compensation order is recorded in the judgment.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: On appeal, counsel for the appellant argued that the trial judge had totally failed to properly consider the facts of the case. It was contended that the nature of the injury and the nature of the weapon had not been correctly appreciated and that the essential ingredients of the offence of attempted murder had not been adequately considered. Counsel further submitted that even accepting the prosecution evidence, the appellant could only be convicted of simple hurt and that, in light of these matters, the appellant had not received a fair trial.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Alleged total inadequacy in the trial judge's consideration of the facts of the case. | Complaint that the nature and seriousness of the injury sustained by the complainant were not adequately considered by the trial judge. | Allegation that the nature of the weapon was completely misunderstood by the trial judge. | Contention that the ingredients of the offence of attempted murder under section 300 were not properly analysed or applied. | Submission that, even on the prosecution version, the appellant could at most be convicted of simple hurt rather than attempted murder. | Allegation that, due to one or more of the above issues, the appellant did not have a fair trial.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal noted that when the police first came to the house no complaint was made about any attempt to cause injury or kill the appellant's wife and no threats to her life were reported by neighbours. The medical evidence was limited to a medico-legal report tendered through a court officer, describing a single non-grievous stab or cut injury to the back without further explanation of the sensitivity of the area or possible internal damage. In the absence of fuller medical testimony and any evidence of threats or conduct pointing to a lethal intent, the court held that the prosecution had not established an attempt to commit murder, although the evidence was sufficient to prove voluntarily causing hurt with a dangerous weapon.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal held that the prosecution had not proven beyond reasonable doubt that the appellant attempted to cause his wife's death, as there was no evidence of threats, lethal intent or imminently dangerous acts and only a single non-grievous injury was proved. It therefore rejected the probability of an attempted murder but accepted that the proven facts established an offence of voluntarily causing hurt with a dangerous weapon.
defence_version_summary: The appellant maintained that he had been falsely implicated and insisted that he had committed no offence. The judgment does not record any alibi or the calling of defence witnesses, nor does it describe a detailed positive version of events beyond his assertion of innocence. The Court of Appeal does not expressly assess the credibility of his denial but instead focuses on whether the prosecution evidence met the requirements of attempted murder.
legal_errors_description: The Court of Appeal found that the High Court had erred in treating the incident as an attempt to commit murder under section 300 in the absence of evidence of lethal intent or circumstances indicating a likelihood of death. It held that the trial court failed to properly analyse the nature of the injury, the role of the weapon, and the statutory ingredients of attempted murder, and that the evidence supported only an offence of voluntarily causing hurt with a dangerous weapon under section 315.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal carefully examined the factual matrix, noting that no threats to the complainant's life were made or reported when the police first attended and that the neighbours did not hear any such threats. It highlighted deficiencies in the medical evidence, including the presentation of only a medico-legal report through a court officer, the classification of the single back injury as non-grievous, and the unexplained discrepancy between a stab wound and a cut injury, as well as the absence of evidence regarding possible internal organ damage. On this basis, the court concluded that the essential elements of attempted murder under section 300, particularly intention or knowledge that death was likely, had not been established, though the facts proved an offence of voluntarily causing hurt with a dangerous weapon under section 315. The court therefore substituted the conviction and sentence accordingly while otherwise dismissing the appeal.
coa_sentence_type: Rigorous Imprisonment 3 years and fine
brief_judgment_file_summary: The appellant, originally convicted by the High Court of Hambantota of attempted murder under section 300 of the Penal Code for stabbing his wife during a domestic dispute, appealed against both conviction and sentence. The Court of Appeal reviewed the eyewitness and limited medical evidence and found no proof of threats or conduct indicating an intention or knowledge to cause death, while the medico-legal report recorded only a single non-grievous stab or cut injury to the back and no internal damage. Holding that the ingredients of attempted murder were not established, the court set aside the conviction under section 300 and instead convicted the appellant of voluntarily causing hurt with a dangerous weapon under section 315, imposing a sentence of three years rigorous imprisonment and a fine of 10000 with six months simple imprisonment in default. Subject to this variation of charge and sentence, the appeal was otherwise dismissed.
defence_counsel: Palitha Fernando P.C. with Iranga Wijegunawardena
cause_of_death_exact_text: Not applicable; the medico-legal report recorded a single non-grievous stab or cut injury to the back.
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court had accepted the prosecution evidence and convicted the appellant of attempted murder under section 300, treating the stabbing during the domestic dispute as an attempt to cause death and imposing a lengthy term of rigorous imprisonment. The Court of Appeal held that the High Court failed to adequately consider the actual nature and seriousness of the injury, the limited medical material, and the absence of threats or circumstances suggestive of lethal intent. It concluded that these deficiencies led the High Court to misapply the law on attempted murder and that, on a proper evaluation of the evidence, only an offence of voluntarily causing hurt with a dangerous weapon was made out.
standard_of_review_applied: Re-evaluation of evidence and application of the legal ingredients of attempted murder, finding a misapplication of section 300 and a failure to properly assess intention and the nature of the injury.
final_charge_after_appeal: Section 315 – voluntarily causing hurt with a dangerous weapon

judges: P. Kumararatnam, J. | R.P.Hettiarachchi, J.
offence_sections: Section 364(2) of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The appellant was indicted in the High Court of Hambantota on three counts of statutory rape of a 15-year-old girl, committed between 01/02/2008 and 19/03/2008. The victim later gave birth to a child and a DNA report obtained on the application of the State, with defence concurrence, established that the appellant was the biological father. In light of this report, the appellant, who was 47 years old at the time of the offences, pleaded guilty unconditionally on 16/02/2023. The High Court sentenced him to 12 years rigorous imprisonment on each count to run consecutively, with fines and compensation to the victim.
evidence_type_primary: DNA report and plea of guilty
evidence_type_secondary: Victim's pregnancy and background circumstances including her young age, living arrangements and threats by the appellant
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 364(2) of the Penal Code
hc_sentence_type: Rigorous Imprisonment 12 years per count (three counts) to run consecutively, plus fine and compensation
hc_judgment_summary: Upon the appellant's unconditional plea of guilty to three counts of statutory rape, the High Court of Hambantota convicted him under Section 364(2) of the Penal Code. The court imposed 12 years rigorous imprisonment on each count ordered to run consecutively, amounting to a total of 36 years. In addition, it imposed a fine of 5000 on each count and ordered payment of 600000 as compensation to the victim with default custodial terms.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant appealed against the High Court judgment, being aggrieved by the conviction and sentence. At the hearing, counsel expressly confined the challenge to the manner in which the sentences were ordered to run consecutively. It was argued that, in light of the plea of guilty and other mitigating circumstances, the total of 36 years rigorous imprisonment was excessive. The appellant sought an order for the sentences on the three counts to run concurrently rather than consecutively.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Appeal confined to the sentence and not to the finding of guilt. | Challenge to the order that the three terms of 12 years rigorous imprisonment run consecutively, resulting in a total of 36 years. | Contention that the sentence is excessive and disproportionate given the plea of guilty and mitigating circumstances. | Request that the sentences for the three counts be ordered to run concurrently.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The case ultimately turned not on a contested trial but on an unconditional plea of guilty following the production of a DNA report. The Court of Appeal noted that the DNA analysis confirmed that the appellant was the biological father of the child born to the underage victim as a result of the incidents. The court recounted the factual background, including the victim's age, her living situation with her sister, and the threats made by the appellant, but did not undertake a detailed assessment of oral witness testimony as the conviction rested on the plea.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal accepted the conviction based on the DNA evidence and the appellant's plea of guilty and did not revisit factual probabilities or extend the benefit of the doubt. Its analysis was confined to assessing the proportionality and appropriateness of the sentence rather than the sufficiency of proof of guilt.
defence_version_summary: The appellant did not advance an alternative factual version at trial and instead, following the DNA report, entered an unconditional plea of guilty to all three counts of statutory rape. On appeal, his counsel informed the Court of Appeal that the appellant was only contesting the consecutive operation of the sentences and argued that the total of 36 years was excessive. The defence relied on mitigating factors such as the plea of guilty, the appellant's current age and family circumstances, and the fact that the victim was now settled with her own family life. The Court of Appeal treated the plea as a significant mitigating factor but did not question the credibility of the admitted facts.
legal_errors_description: The Court of Appeal held that ordering three terms of 12 years rigorous imprisonment for statutory rape to run consecutively, resulting in a total of 36 years, was not appropriate and was disproportionate to the offence in the circumstances. It treated the High Court's exercise of sentencing discretion as erroneous in failing to give adequate weight to the plea of guilty and other mitigating factors and corrected this by directing that the sentences run concurrently.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal focused on sentencing principles, emphasising that punishment must be proportionate to the seriousness of the offence and guided by statutory maxima, deterrence, and fairness. Referring to Attorney General v H.N. Silva, it reiterated that courts must consider the gravity of the offence, the need for deterrence, the offender's position of trust, incidence and detectability of such crimes, and public interest in sentencing. It noted that while the maximum sentence for statutory rape is 20 years, imposing three consecutive terms of 12 years each, totalling 36 years, was inappropriate, especially where the appellant had pleaded guilty, thereby saving judicial time, and was now 58 years old with a family, and the victim too was settled with her own family life. The court thus found the original sentence manifestly excessive in its cumulative effect and ordered that the three terms of 12 years rigorous imprisonment run concurrently while maintaining fines, compensation and default terms.
coa_sentence_type: Rigorous Imprisonment 12 years per count (three counts) to run concurrently, with fine and compensation unchanged
brief_judgment_file_summary: This Court of Appeal judgment concerns an appeal from the High Court of Hambantota where the appellant was convicted on his own plea of guilty of three counts of statutory rape of a 15-year-old girl under Section 364(2) of the Penal Code. The prosecution obtained a DNA report, with the concurrence of the defence, which established that the appellant was the biological father of the child born to the victim as a result of the incidents, after which the appellant pleaded guilty unconditionally. The High Court imposed 12 years rigorous imprisonment on each count to run consecutively (36 years in total), as well as fines on each count and compensation to the victim. On appeal, the appellant challenged only the consecutive nature of the sentences, and the Court of Appeal, applying general sentencing principles and the precedent Attorney General v H.N. Silva, held that a total of 36 years was inappropriate and varied the sentence by directing that the three terms of 12 years rigorous imprisonment run concurrently, while affirming the conviction and leaving fines, compensation and default terms untouched.
defence_counsel: Harshana Ananda
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court, after recording the appellant's unconditional plea of guilty, convicted him on three counts of statutory rape and imposed 12 years rigorous imprisonment on each count to run consecutively, along with fines and substantial compensation to the victim. Its reasoning, as reflected in the Court of Appeal judgment, appears to have centred on the serious nature of statutory rape and the statutory maximum of 20 years. The Court of Appeal, however, considered that in imposing consecutive sentences totalling 36 years, the High Court had not appropriately balanced the gravity of the offence against mitigating factors such as the plea of guilty and the current circumstances of both the appellant and the victim, and therefore adjusted the cumulative effect of the sentence.
precedents_cited_list: Attorney General v H.N. Silva – 57 NLR 121
standard_of_review_applied: Reassessment of sentencing discretion for manifestly inappropriate and disproportionate cumulative sentence
sentencing_principles_applied: The Court applied principles of proportionality and fairness in sentencing, considering the statutory maximum, deterrent effect, gravity of the offence, incidence and difficulty of detection of similar crimes, the offender's circumstances and position, and public interest as articulated in Attorney General v H.N. Silva.
final_charge_after_appeal: Statutory rape under Section 364(2) of the Penal Code

judges: B. Sasi Mahendran, J. | Amal Ranaraja, J.
offence_sections: Sections 54(A)(b) and 54(A)(d) of the Poisons, Opium, and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance as amended by Act No. 13 of 1984
offence_category: Drug trafficking and possession of heroin
brief_facts_summary: The Attorney General indicted the accused in the High Court of Colombo for possession and trafficking of 14.28 grams of heroin (diacetylmorphine) under Sections 54(A)(b) and 54(A)(d) of the Poisons, Opium, and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance, with the offence relating to conduct on or about 20 December 2019 and detection noted as on 21 May 2021. The indictment was served on 06.10.2021 and the trial commenced on 10.08.2023, when PW01, a police officer involved in the raid and arrest, began giving evidence but was not fully examined. On the next trial date, 17.11.2023, PW01 was absent due to training at the National Police Training College, and the State sought an adjournment and reissue of summons. The High Court Judge refused the adjournment, held the explanation insufficient, concluded the trial, and acquitted the accused at that stage.
evidence_type_primary: Police witness testimony regarding the raid, arrest, and production of heroin
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court of Colombo, on 17.11.2023, refused the State Counsel's application for an adjournment when PW01 failed to attend, despite having earlier warned the witness to appear. The Judge emphasized that police witnesses must comply with court orders and suggested that only matters involving national security or special presidential operations could justify absence from court. Treating the failure of PW01 to attend as fatal, the Judge concluded the proceedings, treated the case as having reached its technical end, and acquitted the accused of the charges.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The Attorney General, as petitioner, challenged the High Court order of 17.11.2023 on the basis that the Judge had no authority under the Code of Criminal Procedure to acquit the accused during the trial merely because the prosecution was temporarily unready owing to the absence of a witness. It was argued that Section 263(1) empowered the High Court to adjourn the trial where a witness was absent for reasonable cause and that provisions on acquittal, such as Sections 200 and 220, apply only at the close of the prosecution case. The petitioner further contended that the Judge misdirected himself in law by relying on principles applicable in Magistrates' Courts (Section 188) and by prematurely terminating the prosecution when PW01 had not completed his evidence. The Attorney General therefore sought to set aside the order of acquittal and have the case restored to the trial roll.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: High Court Judge erred in law by acquitting the accused at the trial stage when the prosecution was not ready to proceed solely due to the absence of PW01. | The Judge failed to apply Section 263(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, which allows adjournment where a witness is absent for reasonable cause. | The High Court misapplied or relied on provisions that apply to Magistrates' Courts (Section 188) and ignored that acquittal in the High Court is permissible only at the close of the prosecution case under Sections 200 and 220. | The order prematurely terminated the prosecution despite PW01 not having completed testimony, thereby constituting a procedural misdirection and error warranting appellate intervention.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: Only PW01, a police officer involved in the detection and raid, had partly given evidence when the High Court prematurely terminated the trial. The Court of Appeal noted that PW01 had not concluded his testimony and that there was no indication of prior absences, while the State explained that the witness was in training on the second date fixed for trial. The appellate court emphasized that the prosecution process was ongoing, that the Judge could and should have adjourned the trial under Section 263(1), and that there was no evidential basis to conclude that the prosecution case had failed so as to justify an acquittal.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal did not evaluate probabilities or competing versions of events but focused instead on whether the High Court had lawfully exercised its powers in terminating the trial and acquitting the accused before the close of the prosecution case.
defence_version_summary: No defence evidence or dock statement was led because the trial was stopped at an early stage, after only partial testimony from PW01. The High Court acquitted the accused without calling for a defence, and the Court of Appeal therefore had no defence version to assess. The appellate court treated the accused's acquittal as a consequence of procedural misdirection rather than any evaluation of defence credibility and directed that the matter proceed to trial so that a proper defence, if any, could be presented.
legal_errors_description: The Court of Appeal held that the High Court Judge misdirected himself in law by assuming a power to acquit during the trial stage in the absence of a witness, contrary to the scheme of the Code of Criminal Procedure which permits acquittal only at the close of the prosecution case, and by failing to use the adjournment power under Section 263(1) despite a reasonable explanation for the witness's absence.
procedural_defects_description: The High Court refused an adjournment requested by the State when PW01 was absent due to training, ignored that this was only the second trial date and that the witness had partially testified, and then prematurely concluded the trial and acquitted the accused, thereby improperly terminating the prosecution process.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed the relevant provisions of the Code of Criminal Procedure, holding that Sections 200 and 220 allow acquittal in the High Court only after the close of the prosecution case and that Section 263(1) authorizes adjournment where a witness is absent for reasonable cause. Relying on authorities such as Attorney General v. Gunawardhena, The Attorney General v. Baranage and R. v. Galbraith, the court held that a trial may be stopped early only where all material prosecution evidence has effectively been led and further evidence would be merely formal, which was not the situation here. The court found that PW01 had only partly testified, the prosecution case remained incomplete, and there was no basis to conclude that continuing the trial would be a waste of time. It therefore held that the High Court had no authority to acquit at that stage, set aside the order of acquittal as untenable, and directed that the case be restored to the roll and proceeded with according to law.
brief_judgment_file_summary: This judgment concerns an appeal by the Attorney General under Section 15(a) of the Judicature Act read with Section 331 of the Code of Criminal Procedure against an order of the High Court of Colombo dated 17.11.2023 acquitting an accused charged with possession and trafficking of heroin. The Court of Appeal reviews the statutory framework on adjournments and acquittals (Sections 188, 200, 220 and 263 of the Code) and observes that the High Court Judge wrongly treated the non-appearance of PW01 on the second trial date as sufficient to conclude the trial, instead of adjourning the case. Referring to leading authorities, the court reiterates that acquittal at the High Court can follow only at the close of the prosecution case or its virtual end when all material evidence has been led, which had not occurred because PW01 had only partially testified. The Court of Appeal therefore finds that the High Court lacked authority to acquit at that stage, sets aside the acquittal order, and directs that the case be restored to the trial roll and proceeded with in accordance with the law.
prosecution_counsel: Jayalakshi de Silva, SSC for the Complainant-Petitioner
defence_counsel: Randunu Heellage for the Accused-Respondent
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court reasoned that police witnesses are obliged to attend court when warned and suggested that only matters concerning national security or special presidential operations could excuse non-appearance. Treating the absence of PW01 on the second trial date, despite earlier warning, as unjustified and not accepting the explanation that he was undergoing training, the Judge refused to adjourn, declared the trial effectively concluded, and acquitted the accused. The Court of Appeal criticized this approach as contrary to the Code of Criminal Procedure, holding that the High Court had no statutory power to acquit at that mid-trial stage, should have exercised its adjournment power under Section 263(1), and thereby committed an error requiring the order to be set aside and the case restored to the roll.
precedents_cited_list: Attorney General v. Gunawardhena – 1996 (2) SLR 149 | Pauline de Croos v. The Queen – Court of Criminal Appeal (citation not fully specified) | The Attorney General v. Baranage – 2003 (1) SLR 340 | R. v. Galbraith – 1981 (2) All ER 1060 | Attorney General and Others v. Sumathipala – 2006 (2) SLR 126
standard_of_review_applied: Misdirection on law and acting without statutory authority in acquitting at the trial stage; failure to properly apply provisions governing adjournment and the stage at which acquittal is permissible; order characterized as untenable and tainted by legal error.
final_charge_after_appeal: Charges for possession and trafficking of heroin under Sections 54(A)(b) and 54(A)(d) of the Poisons, Opium, and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance remain unchanged and are to proceed to trial.

judges: B. Sasi Mahendran | Amal Ranaraja
offence_sections: Section 365 B (2) (b)
brief_facts_summary: The appellant, an adult male, befriended PW01, a 15-year-old boy who frequented a nearby hardware store. On one occasion, the appellant invited PW01 to his house, offered him a drink that made him dizzy, and committed an act of grave sexual abuse by placing his penis between PW01's thighs. On a subsequent occasion, the appellant committed another act of grave sexual abuse by inserting his penis into PW01's anus.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 365 B (2) (b)
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the appellant on two charges of grave sexual abuse under Section 365 B (2) (b) of the Penal Code. The court sentenced him to 7 years simple imprisonment on each charge, along with a fine of Rs. 10,000 per charge and Rs. 100,000 in compensation to PW01. The sentences were to run consecutively as imposed.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant limited the appeal to the ground that the sentence is excessive. Counsel argued for application of principles from SC Reference 3/2008 to vary the sentence. Mitigatory circumstances include the appellant's stage four kidney disease, which requires special diet and care that may not be feasible in prison, placing him at a disadvantage.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Sentence is excessive | Apply principles from SC Reference 3/2008 | Mitigatory circumstances: stage four kidney disease and health management challenges in prison
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The judgment relies on PW01's account of the incidents as the primary evidence. No detailed analysis of credibility or contradictions is provided in the appeal judgment, as the appeal focused solely on sentencing. The appellant remained silent in his defence at trial.
defence_version_summary: The appellant kept silent when called upon for his defence. There was no alibi presented, no defence witnesses called, and the court noted this in the context of the offences.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal upheld the conviction, finding aggravating factors such as the victim's young age, pre-planning, and repeated offences, which outweigh the new mitigatory health evidence not presented to the High Court. The court emphasized public interest, deterrence, and the seriousness of grave sexual abuse, citing precedents like SC Reference 03/2008 and Attorney General vs. H. N. de Silva. While not interfering with the conviction or sentence length, the terms were ordered to run concurrently.
coa_sentence_type: Simple Imprisonment 7 years concurrent
brief_judgment_file_summary: The judgment details the appeal against conviction and sentence for two counts of grave sexual abuse on a minor under Section 365B(2)(b) of the Penal Code. The Court of Appeal reviews the facts, charges, and High Court sentence, discusses mandatory sentencing and judicial discretion per SC Reference 03/2008, considers mitigatory health factors, upholds the conviction and sentence but orders concurrent terms, emphasizing deterrence and public interest.
defence_counsel: Sarath Jayamanne P.C, with Vineshka Mendis, Prashan Wickramaratne, Sajeewa Meegahawaththa, Dakshin Abeykoon and Chathushi Vidushika
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted the appellant based on the evidence presented and imposed the mandatory minimum sentences under the Penal Code. The Court of Appeal noted that the High Court was not aware of the mitigatory health factors now raised and found the sentences not excessive. The COA affirmed the High Court's approach but varied the sentences to run concurrently.
precedents_cited_list: SC Reference No. 03/2008 | Warnakulasooriya Mudiyanselage Jayanth Warnasuriya vs. Attorney General CA/HCC/169/2022 | Attorney General vs. H. N. de Silva 57 NLR 121
standard_of_review_applied: Review of sentencing for excessiveness and application of judicial discretion despite mandatory minimum
sentencing_principles_applied: Balance between public interest, deterrence, offender's circumstances; discretion to go below mandatory minimum with adequate reasons per SC Reference 03/2008
final_charge_after_appeal: Section 365 B (2) (b)

judges: P. Kumararatnam J | K.M.G.H. Kulatunga J
offence_sections: Section 296 read with Section 32 of the Penal Code
location_of_offence: Kirulapone, Rasikwatta canal near Ilma International School
brief_facts_summary: The appellant, a 17-year-old relative of the 6-year-old victim Krishna Kumar Dushanthini, lived with her family along a canal-side road in Kirulapone. On the night of 30.06.2012, after a church procession, the victim disappeared from the appellant's house and was later found dead in a garbage canal near Ilma International School with one slipper nearby. The prosecution relied on evidence that the appellant was last seen taking the child by the hand and riding a bicycle with her near the canal, that witnesses heard a child fall into the water crying for her mother, and that the appellant had long nails matching nail imprints on the child's neck. Medical evidence established asphyxia due to drowning with signs of sexual interference, and the High Court convicted the appellant of murder while acquitting the co-accused.
evidence_type_primary: Circumstantial evidence and eyewitness testimony (last seen evidence)
evidence_type_secondary: Medical and expert forensic evidence including post-mortem findings and nail mark comparison
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 296 read with Section 32 of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court of Colombo acquitted the 2nd and 3rd accused but found the 1st accused, the present appellant, guilty of the murder of the 6-year-old victim as charged. It relied on a chain of circumstantial evidence, including last seen testimony, nail marks corresponding to the appellant's long fingernails, and medical evidence of drowning and sexual interference, to conclude that the prosecution had proved the charge beyond reasonable doubt. The court imposed the mandatory sentence of death for murder.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: In his petition and written submissions, the appellant alleged that he was convicted without being given the benefit of doubts arising from prosecution witnesses, that the evidence was analysed contrary to law, and that the prosecution case was not proved beyond reasonable doubt. He further complained that the trial judge failed to appreciate that the prosecution evidence lacked uniformity and probability and did not properly consider the defence evidence and his dock statement. At the hearing, counsel effectively confined the appeal to arguing that the trial judge should have considered culpability only for the lesser offence of culpable homicide on the basis of knowledge under Section 297, and that the death sentence was unlawful because the appellant was under 18 at the time of the offence in view of the amended Section 53 of the Penal Code read with Article 6(5) of the ICCPR.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Failure to grant benefit of doubt arising from prosecution evidence. | Improper and unlawful analysis of prosecution evidence. | Prosecution case not proved beyond reasonable doubt. | Failure to give due weight to inconsistencies and improbabilities in prosecution testimony. | Failure to properly consider the defence evidence and dock statement. | Trial judge's failure to consider culpability for a lesser offence under Section 297 based on knowledge rather than murderous intention. | Illegality of imposing the death sentence because the appellant was under 18 at the time of the offence in light of amended Section 53 of the Penal Code and Article 6(5) of the ICCPR.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal treated the case as one based on circumstantial evidence, emphasising that the deceased was last seen alive in the appellant's company, that independent witnesses saw him riding a bicycle with her near the canal, and that others heard a child fall into the water calling for her mother. It noted that PW-04 and PW-07 were not cross-examined, treating their unchallenged testimony as proved facts, and regarded the appellant's false denial on returning home as corroborative of guilt. Expert medical evidence linking nail imprints on the victim's neck to the appellant's unusually long fingernails, together with the timing of the last meal and death, was found to complete an unbroken chain of circumstances inconsistent with innocence.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court held that when all the circumstances were cumulatively considered, the only reasonable and irresistible inference was that the appellant caused the victim's death, and that any other hypothesis consistent with innocence was highly improbable. It also applied the 'last seen' doctrine, finding that the narrow time window between the appellant being last seen with the child and the medically established time of death left no realistic possibility of another perpetrator and therefore did not entitle the appellant to the benefit of the doubt.
defence_version_summary: The appellant did not give sworn evidence but made a dock statement and called his father as a defence witness, seeking to distance himself from responsibility for the child's death and to cast doubt on the prosecution version. The High Court judge carefully summarised and evaluated this evidence, ultimately finding that the appellant had deliberately uttered falsehoods indicative of a guilty mind and that his father's testimony was also false. The Court of Appeal agreed that the defence evidence failed to introduce any reasonable doubt in the prosecution case, and no credible alibi or alternative explanation for the events was established.
legal_errors_description: The Court of Appeal found no legal errors in the High Court's approach to evaluating the circumstantial evidence, applying the last seen theory, or directing itself on intention versus knowledge, and rejected the argument that the amended Section 53 of the Penal Code applied retrospectively to invalidate the death sentence.
procedural_defects_description: No procedural defects or irregularities affecting the fairness of the trial were identified.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal upheld the High Court's reliance on circumstantial evidence, especially the last seen circumstances, the medical finding of asphyxia due to drowning, and the expert opinion that nail marks on the victim's neck matched the appellant's long fingernails, together with witnesses hearing someone struggling in the water. It stressed that the appellant's unexplained return without the child and his false denial of knowledge were strongly incriminating and corroborated the prosecution's theory. The court rejected the contention that the facts supported only culpable homicide based on knowledge, holding that throwing or causing a 6-year-old girl to be in a canal with 90 cm of water showed murderous intention because death by drowning was the natural and probable consequence. It also dismissed the sentencing argument, ruling that the 2021 amendment to Section 53 of the Penal Code operated only prospectively and did not affect a death sentence imposed in 2016.
coa_sentence_type: Death
brief_judgment_file_summary: The appellant, a 17-year-old at the time of the offence, was convicted of murdering his 6-year-old relative, whose body was found in a canal near Ilma International School at Kirulapone after she disappeared from his house following a church procession on 30.06.2012. The prosecution led 12 witnesses, including the victim's mother and brother who described the child's last movements, independent witnesses who saw the appellant with the child on a bicycle near the canal and heard a child falling into the water, the investigating officer who recovered the body and a slipper near the canal, and expert medical evidence establishing asphyxia due to drowning with nail imprints on the neck consistent with the appellant's unusually long fingernails. The High Court acquitted the 2nd and 3rd accused but convicted the appellant of murder under Section 296 read with Section 32 and imposed the death sentence. On appeal, arguments that the conviction should be reduced to culpable homicide under Section 297 based on knowledge and that the death sentence was invalid under amended Section 53 of the Penal Code and Article 6(5) of the ICCPR were rejected, the Court of Appeal affirming that the circumstantial evidence formed an unbroken chain proving murderous intention and holding that the 2021 amendment to Section 53 applied only prospectively, thereby dismissing the appeal and affirming the conviction and sentence.
prosecution_counsel: Anoopa De Silva, DSG for the Respondent
defence_counsel: Rajinda Kandegedara with Akila Ranawaka for the Accused-Appellant
cause_of_death_exact_text: The pathologist gave the cause of death as asphyxia due to drowning.
hc_analysis_summary: According to the Court of Appeal, the High Court judge correctly identified the case as one resting on circumstantial evidence and applied the principles that such evidence must irresistibly point to guilt, relying on the last seen evidence, the timing of death vis-à-vis the last meal, the nail imprints matching the appellant's fingernails, and the appellant's false denial. The High Court considered and rejected the defence evidence and dock statement as false and incapable of creating reasonable doubt. The Court of Appeal endorsed these findings as reasonable and lawful and saw no basis to interfere with the High Court's assessment of facts or its conclusion that the charge of murder had been proved beyond reasonable doubt.

standard_of_review_applied: The Court of Appeal reviewed whether the inferences drawn by the trial judge from the circumstantial evidence were reasonable, whether the last seen doctrine was properly applied, and whether there was any misdirection on law regarding intention versus knowledge or retrospective application of the amended Section 53 of the Penal Code.
sentencing_principles_applied: The court held that before the 2021 amendment to Section 53 the sentencing court was bound to impose the mandatory death sentence for murder on an accused who was not under 18 at the date of conviction, and that the amendment shifting the relevant age to the time of the offence was a substantive change operating prospectively only, so it did not alter sentences lawfully imposed before it came into force.

judges: B. Sasi Mahendran | Amal Ranaraja
offence_sections: Section 296 read with Section 32 of the Penal Code
location_of_offence: On an estate road in the Bulathsinhala area
brief_facts_summary: The four accused were alleged to have attacked the deceased, Hettige Premajiwa alias Ranji, on 23.06.2007 while he was working in an estate, following prior incidents of tyre-cutting and a death threat by the 4th accused. The deceased was found injured on a road, taken first to Bulathsinhala Hospital and then to Horana and another hospital, where he later died. On the way and at the hospital he made three dying declarations to his wife, his brother and a relative, naming all four accused as the assailants. The prosecution relied mainly on these dying declarations and medical evidence of multiple head injuries to prove the case.
evidence_type_secondary: Medical/post-mortem evidence and surrounding circumstances including prior complaints and threats
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 296 read with Section 32 of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court of Kalutara convicted all four accused of the murder of the deceased on the basis of three consistent dying declarations and corroborative medical evidence of homicidal violence to the head. The court rejected the defence theory that the injuries were caused by a fall from a moving vehicle and accepted that the deceased was in a position to speak and identify his assailants. Accordingly, the High Court imposed the mandatory sentence of death.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The accused appealed contending that the High Court failed to consider contradictions in the prosecution case and did not properly consider the defence case. They argued that the trial judge did not adequately assess the weaknesses and non-credibility of the prosecution witnesses. It was further claimed that the order was made in contradiction to the evidence, including the contention that the injuries could have resulted from a fall from a vehicle and that the dying declarations lacked corroboration.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: High Court failed to consider contradictions in the prosecution case. | High Court did not properly consider the defence case. | High Court failed to consider weaknesses and non-credibility of prosecution witnesses. | The order was given in contradiction to the evidence, including the defence version of accidental injury and alleged lack of corroboration for dying declarations.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal noted that the prosecution led eleven witnesses, including the deceased's wife, brother and a relative who each testified to separate dying declarations consistently naming the four accused. The court observed that the defence did not dispute that the declarations were made or that the deceased could speak and identify his assailants, but mainly attacked the absence of corroboration. The medical officer described multiple external injuries, including skull fractures and brain bleeding, and identified head injuries as the cause of death, which the court found consistent with an assault rather than a mere fall. The defence dock statements and one defence witness suggesting accidental injury were rejected as inconsistent with the medical evidence and the pattern of injuries, including defensive wounds.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal considered the three consistent dying declarations, the lack of challenge to their making or to the deceased's ability to speak, and the medical evidence of assault-type injuries and defence wounds, and concluded that the prosecution version was proved beyond reasonable doubt. The alternative explanation of a fall from a moving vehicle was regarded as inconsistent with the injuries and inherently improbable, so no reasonable doubt arose in favour of the accused.
defence_version_summary: The accused gave evidence from the dock and called one defence witness, putting forward the position that the deceased sustained his injuries by falling from a moving vehicle rather than by an assault by the accused. They also argued that there were weaknesses in the prosecution case and that the dying declarations should not be acted upon without corroboration. The High Court and the Court of Appeal found this defence version incredible in light of the medical evidence showing multiple blows, including defence injuries, and the consistent dying declarations naming all four accused. The courts therefore rejected the defence story and preferred the prosecution narrative.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal undertook a detailed review of the law on dying declarations, citing local and Indian authorities to emphasise that while such statements have inherent weaknesses, they may, if found truthful and accurate, form the sole basis for conviction without corroboration. Applying these principles, the court held that the three dying declarations were consistently made, the deceased was capable of speaking and identifying the assailants, and the defence never challenged the fact of the declarations or the witnesses' credibility on that point. The court found the prosecution evidence, particularly the medical testimony of severe head injuries and defence wounds, to be cogent and consistent with an intentional assault, and considered the defence explanation of a fall from a vehicle to be inconsistent and improbable. Concluding that the High Court had correctly evaluated the evidence and applied the law, the Court of Appeal affirmed both the conviction and sentence.
coa_sentence_type: Death
brief_judgment_file_summary: This Court of Appeal judgment concerns an appeal by four accused convicted by the High Court of Kalutara for the murder of Hettige Premajiwa alias Ranji on 23.06.2007 under Section 296 read with Section 32 of the Penal Code. The case against them rested primarily on three separate dying declarations made by the deceased to his wife, his brother and a relative while being transported to and treated in hospital, consistently naming all four accused, together with medical evidence of multiple head injuries and defence wounds. On appeal, the accused argued that the High Court failed to consider contradictions, weaknesses in prosecution witnesses, and the defence claim that the injuries were due to a fall from a moving vehicle, and they challenged reliance on uncorroborated dying declarations. The Court of Appeal, after an extensive survey of the law on dying declarations and their evidential weight, held that corroboration was not legally required where the declarations were found to be true and accurate, accepted the medical evidence as confirming an assault, rejected the defence version as improbable, and ultimately affirmed the High Court's conviction and the death sentence, dismissing the appeal.
defence_counsel: Charith Calhena for the 1st to 4th Accused-Appellants
cause_of_death_exact_text: The judicial medical officer stated that the deceased had skull fractures and internal bleeding in the brain, and that the injuries inflicted on the head and their effect on the brain were the cause of death.
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court accepted the three dying declarations as reliable, observing that the deceased consistently named the four accused and that there was no serious challenge to the witnesses who recounted these statements. It relied on the post-mortem findings of multiple head injuries and defence wounds to conclude that the death was homicidal and not accidental. The Court of Appeal held that the High Court had correctly applied the principles on dying declarations and reasonably rejected the defence theory of a fall, and therefore found no error warranting interference.
