Inspector of Police – 59 NLR 235 | Thusaiya v. Pathaimany – 15 CLW 119 | Verupadian v. Sollamuttu – 1901 1 Brown's Reports 384 | James Silva Vs. The Republic of Sri Lanka – (1980) 2 SLR 167 | Jaya sena Vs. The Queen – 72 NLR 313 | Mukhtiar v. State of Punjab – 1995 Supreme Court Cases (Cri) 296 | State of Andhra Pradhesh v. Gowthu Ranghunayakulu & Others – 1995 Supreme Court Cases (Cri) 540
standard_of_review_applied: The Court of Appeal examined whether there was misdirection in law and non-compliance with Section 283 CPC, whether the trial judge failed to evaluate the totality of the evidence including the defence, and whether the conviction was perverse or unsafe in light of contradictions, implausible explanations for delay, and the requirement that reasonable doubts based on reason and common sense be resolved in favour of the accused.
sentencing_principles_applied: The Court observed that the distinction between Section 364(1) and Section 364(2)(e) of the Penal Code is material primarily at the stage of sentencing and that mislabelling the subsection, though erroneous, does not by itself vitiate the conviction, but ultimately the conviction itself was found unsafe and set aside.
final_charge_after_appeal: None; the appellant was acquitted of the rape charge under Section 364 of the Penal Code

judges: P. Kumararatnam, J. | R. P. Hettiarachchi, J.
offence_sections: Section 4(2) of the Offensive Weapons Act read with Section 32 of the Penal Code; Section 300 read with Section 32 of the Penal Code
location_of_offence: In or around Galle while the victim was returning home
brief_facts_summary: The appellant and two co-accused were indicted for attempted murder of Kirimadura Upali Mendis, a security officer at the Galle Municipal Council, allegedly by ambushing him, throwing a hand grenade and firing shots as he returned home. The victim sustained injuries and was hospitalized, and his non-summary deposition was later marked in evidence after he went missing before completing his testimony at trial. The High Court of Balapitiya convicted the appellant on both counts and acquitted the second accused. On appeal, the Court of Appeal examined whether the incomplete non-summary deposition of the missing victim and the remaining evidence were sufficient to sustain the conviction beyond a reasonable doubt.
evidence_type_primary: Eyewitness testimony of the victim recorded at the non-summary inquiry
evidence_type_secondary: Medical expert evidence and other witness testimony
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Convicted on Count 1 under Section 4(2) of the Offensive Weapons Act read with Section 32 of the Penal Code and on Count 2 for attempted murder punishable under Section 300 read with Section 32 of the Penal Code
hc_sentence_type: Rigorous Imprisonment 12 years on Count 1 and 2 years on Count 2 (concurrent) with fines and compensation
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court Judge of Balapitiya, after a non-jury trial in which six prosecution witnesses testified and the appellant and the second accused gave evidence under oath, convicted the appellant on both attempted murder counts and acquitted the second accused. The judge relied inter alia on the victim's non-summary deposition, which was marked under Section 33 of the Evidence Ordinance after the victim went missing, together with other prosecution evidence. The appellant was sentenced to 12 years rigorous imprisonment and a fine on the first count, 2 years rigorous imprisonment and a fine on the second count, and ordered to pay compensation to the victim's wife, with the custodial sentences to run concurrently.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant contended that the learned High Court Judge failed to apply her judicial mind to whether the prosecution had proved the case beyond reasonable doubt and misdirected herself by not properly evaluating contradictions and omissions in the evidence. It was argued that the judge failed to legally consider and evaluate the evidence of PW1 elicited at the non-summary trial under Section 33 of the Evidence Ordinance and the incomplete testimony of PW1 at the High Court trial. The appellant further claimed that the conviction was contrary to law and against the weight of the evidence and that the judge failed to properly consider the totality of the evidence, depriving the appellant of a fair trial.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Failure by the High Court Judge to apply her judicial mind to whether the prosecution had proved the case beyond reasonable doubt. | Misdirection by failing to judicially evaluate inter se and per se contradictions and omissions affecting the credibility of prosecution witnesses. | Failure to legally consider and evaluate the evidence of PW1 at the non-summary inquiry marked under Section 33 of the Evidence Ordinance and the incomplete testimony of PW1 at trial. | Conviction alleged to be contrary to law and against the weight of the evidence, including an erroneous determination of the culpability of each accused. | Failure to properly and legally consider the totality of the evidence, thereby depriving the appellant of a fair trial.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The prosecution led six witnesses and marked productions P1–P4, relying heavily on PW1, the victim, whose non-summary deposition was later marked under Section 33 of the Evidence Ordinance after he went missing before completing his evidence at trial. The Court of Appeal held that this deposition was incomplete and could not be lawfully used to found a conviction, and that the High Court Judge misdirected herself by relying on it while simultaneously acknowledging its incompleteness. The remaining prosecution evidence, including the JMO's testimony describing non-grievous injuries and indicating that PW1 had attributed the attack to an unidentified person in the history given to the doctor, was found insufficient to establish the charges against the appellant beyond reasonable doubt.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal held that once the incomplete non-summary deposition of PW1 was excluded, the remaining evidence did not prove the appellant's guilt beyond reasonable doubt and that the benefit of the doubt should therefore go to the appellant.
defence_version_summary: The appellant and the second accused gave evidence under oath in their defence, but the judgment does not set out the details of their versions. The High Court rejected the defence and convicted the appellant, whereas the Court of Appeal focused on the prosecution's failure to adduce complete and legally admissible evidence rather than on accepting any particular defence narrative.
legal_errors_description: The Court of Appeal found a serious misdirection by the High Court Judge in relying on an incomplete non-summary deposition of PW1 marked under Section 33 of the Evidence Ordinance to convict the appellant, despite acknowledging its incompleteness. It held that this irregular adoption of evidence caused great prejudice to the appellant and that the remaining evidence was inadequate to sustain the conviction.
procedural_defects_description: The main procedural defect was the marking and use of PW1's non-summary deposition under Section 33 of the Evidence Ordinance when his evidence at trial was incomplete and he had gone missing, and then relying on that incomplete deposition to convict the appellant. This was treated as a significant irregularity that undermined the fairness of the trial.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal concluded that the High Court had misdirected itself by using an incomplete non-summary deposition of PW1 as substantive evidence under Section 33 of the Evidence Ordinance to find the appellant guilty. It emphasized that PW1's absence and incomplete testimony meant his non-summary evidence could not be relied upon, and it further noted that in the history given to the doctor, PW1 had referred to an unidentified assailant, which weakened the prosecution's case on identification. The Court held that other prosecution witnesses did not bridge the evidential gap and that the charges were not proved beyond reasonable doubt, so the appellant was entitled to an acquittal. In doing so, it accepted the concession of the Additional Solicitor General and underscored the importance of properly evaluating admissible evidence and safeguarding fair trial rights.
coa_sentence_type: No sentence (conviction set aside and appellant acquitted)
brief_judgment_file_summary: The Attorney General indicted three accused in the High Court of Balapitiya for attempted murder of Kirimadura Upali Mendis, alleging an ambush involving a hand grenade and gunfire, with the appellant as the third accused. After a non-jury trial in which six prosecution witnesses and two defence witnesses testified, the High Court convicted the appellant on both counts, acquitted the second accused, and imposed concurrent terms of rigorous imprisonment, fines, and compensation. On appeal, the appellant challenged the conviction on grounds including misdirection, improper evaluation of contradictions, and wrongful use of PW1's non-summary deposition under Section 33 of the Evidence Ordinance after PW1 went missing. The Court of Appeal held that the High Court had seriously misdirected itself by acting on an incomplete deposition, found the remaining evidence insufficient to prove the charges beyond reasonable doubt, and accordingly set aside the conviction and sentence and acquitted the appellant, allowing the appeal.
defence_counsel: Akkila Jayasundara with Akhila Mathishi
cause_of_death_exact_text: No death occurred; the JMO described four non-grievous injuries that were not sufficient to cause death in the ordinary course of nature.
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court of Balapitiya treated PW1's non-summary deposition as admissible under Section 33 of the Evidence Ordinance and relied on it, along with other evidence, to convict the appellant on both counts of attempted murder, despite acknowledging that PW1's trial testimony was incomplete due to his disappearance. The Court of Appeal criticized this approach as a serious misdirection and an irregular adoption of incomplete evidence, holding that the High Court had thereby erred in law and fact. It also concluded that, apart from the inadmissible or incomplete evidence of PW1, the other prosecution evidence did not sufficiently prove the appellant's guilt beyond reasonable doubt.
standard_of_review_applied: Misdirection on law and procedure in adopting incomplete non-summary evidence and failure to properly evaluate whether the admissible evidence proved the case beyond reasonable doubt.
final_charge_after_appeal: Attempted murder under Section 4(2) of the Offensive Weapons Act read with Section 32 of the Penal Code and attempted murder punishable under Section 300 read with Section 32 of the Penal Code, of which the appellant was acquitted on appeal.

judges: P. Kumararatnam, J. | R. P. Hettiarachchi, J.
offence_sections: Section 296 read with Section 32 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The three Appellants and the deceased consumed liquor together at the house of PW4, where the 1st Appellant assaulted the deceased after attempting to take something from the bag on his bicycle. The deceased complained to PW4 that the 1st Appellant had hit him once and was not seen alive thereafter. Later that evening, the 1st and 2nd Appellants threatened PW9 and PW10 and the 1st Appellant confessed to killing the deceased, while the investigation recovered clubs and a knife linked by expert evidence to a cotton tree. Medical evidence established that death resulted from a hard blow to the right side of the head causing severe brain damage.
evidence_type_secondary: Eyewitness testimony, dying declaration, medical and forensic evidence, and extra-judicial confession
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 296 read with Section 32 of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court of Chilaw, after a non-jury trial in which the Appellants made dock statements and led no defence witnesses, convicted all three Appellants of murder under Section 296 read with Section 32 of the Penal Code. Relying on circumstantial evidence, the utterance of the deceased treated as a dying declaration, and supporting medical and forensic material, the court held that the prosecution had proved the charge beyond reasonable doubt. All three Appellants were sentenced to death on 2019-04-05.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The 1st Appellant challenged whether the prosecution had proved the ingredients of murder beyond reasonable doubt, the acceptance of prosecution witnesses as trustworthy, the treatment of the deceased's utterance as a valid dying declaration, and the failure to consider material contradictions. The 2nd Appellant argued that the High Court had failed to apply settled principles on circumstantial evidence, had not properly appreciated the probabilities in the prosecution version, and had overlooked contradictions among witnesses. The 3rd Appellant contended that the prosecution had not proved the charge beyond reasonable doubt and that the High Court erred in treating prosecution witnesses as trustworthy. All Appellants thus attacked the sufficiency and evaluation of circumstantial, testimonial, and dying declaration evidence.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Prosecution failed to establish the ingredients of the murder charge beyond reasonable doubt. | High Court erred in law by concluding that prosecution witnesses were trustworthy and credible. | High Court erred by treating the deceased's statement as a dying declaration under Section 32 of the Evidence Ordinance and basing the judgment on it. | High Court failed to consider or properly evaluate material contradictions and omissions in the prosecution evidence. | High Court failed to consider well-settled principles of law applicable to a case entirely based on circumstantial evidence. | High Court failed to appreciate probability factors bearing on the credibility of the prosecution witnesses. | For the 3rd Appellant, the evidence did not prove his involvement beyond reasonable doubt, particularly regarding identification and movement near the deceased's house.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal reviewed the circumstantial mosaic built from several prosecution witnesses, including PW4, PW6, PW5, PW7, PW8, PW9 (adopted under Section 33 of the Evidence Ordinance), PW10, the investigating officers, the Government Analyst, and the JMO. PW4 and PW6 testified to the initial assault and the deceased's utterance naming the 1st Appellant, while PW9 and PW10 spoke to extra-judicial confessions and threats by the 1st and 2nd Appellants. PW5 linked the 1st Appellant to the cutting of a club, and the Government Analyst and JMO provided forensic and medical evidence confirming the cause of death and linking recovered weapons to a cotton tree; however, the evidence placing the 3rd Appellant near the deceased's house contained a material omission in PW7's prior statement, leading to reasonable doubt as to his involvement.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court held that the cumulative circumstantial evidence, including the initial assault, extra-judicial confessions, threats, and weapon recovery, eliminated any reasonable hypothesis of innocence for the 1st and 2nd Appellants. In contrast, a material omission in PW7's prior statement and the lack of positive identification in proximity to the deceased's house created reasonable doubt regarding the 3rd Appellant, who was given the benefit of that doubt.
defence_version_summary: After the prosecution closed its case and the High Court Judge found a case to answer, all Appellants elected to make dock statements and called no defence witnesses, offering only unsworn explanations. No specific alibi or alternative narrative corroborated by independent evidence was presented. Both the High Court and the Court of Appeal found that these dock statements did not cast sufficient doubt on the prosecution case against the 1st and 2nd Appellants, though the Court of Appeal considered that the evidential gaps and omissions required acquittal of the 3rd Appellant.
legal_errors_description: The Court of Appeal held that the learned High Court Judge erred in failing to treat the omission in PW7's police statement regarding the presence of the 3rd Appellant as a material omission going to the root of the case against him. This failure led to an unsafe conviction of the 3rd Appellant in the absence of positive identification near the deceased's house and in circumstances where other witnesses only clearly identified the 1st and 2nd Appellants.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal reaffirmed that this was a case resting entirely on circumstantial evidence and applied established principles that guilt must be inferred from the cumulative weight of circumstances, eliminating any reasonable hypothesis consistent with innocence. It found the circumstantial evidence, dying declaration, extra-judicial confessions, threats, and expert testimony to be cogent and incriminating against the 1st and 2nd Appellants, and rejected criticisms of the prosecution witnesses' credibility in relation to them. However, the Court held that the omission in PW7's police statement about seeing the 3rd Appellant, combined with the absence of other positive identification of him near the deceased's house, created reasonable doubt and should have been considered in his favour. While upholding the High Court's treatment of the dying declaration and circumstantial evidence generally, the Court partially interfered with the conviction by acquitting the 3rd Appellant.
coa_sentence_type: Death sentence affirmed for the 1st and 2nd Appellants; 3rd Appellant acquitted and released
brief_judgment_file_summary: Three Accused were tried in the High Court of Chilaw for the murder of Warnakulasuriya Antony Nevil Orbis, arising from an incident in 1998 following a drinking session at PW4's house, where the 1st Appellant assaulted the deceased and later allegedly confessed to killing him. The prosecution case was entirely circumstantial and relied on testimony about the assault and subsequent movements, a statement by the deceased to PW4 treated as a dying declaration, threats and confessions made by the 1st and 2nd Appellants to PW9 and PW10, recovery of clubs and a knife linked to a cotton tree, and medical and forensic evidence that the deceased died from a hard blow to the head. The High Court convicted all three Accused of murder under Section 296 read with Section 32 of the Penal Code and sentenced them to death. On appeal, the Court of Appeal upheld the convictions and death sentences of the 1st and 2nd Appellants, finding the circumstantial chain against them strong, but held that a material omission in PW7's police statement and lack of positive identification created reasonable doubt concerning the 3rd Appellant, whose conviction was quashed and who was acquitted.
prosecution_counsel: Maheshika Silva, DSG for the Respondent
defence_counsel: Jagath Nanayakkara for the 1st Appellant; Nihara Randeniya for the 2nd Appellant; K.A. Upul Anuradha Wickramaratne for the 3rd Appellant
weapon_type: Clubs made from cotton tree wood and a knife (katty)
cause_of_death_exact_text: Death resulted from a hard blow to the right side of the head which caused severe brain damage.
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court analyzed the circumstantial evidence, including the initial blow inflicted by the 1st Appellant, the deceased's subsequent statement implicating him, the movements and conduct of the Appellants, the recovery of weapons, and the medical and forensic findings, and concluded that all three Accused were liable for murder under Section 296 read with Section 32. The Court of Appeal agreed that the High Court correctly applied the law on circumstantial evidence and dying declarations in relation to the 1st and 2nd Appellants. However, it held that the High Court erred in failing to appreciate the materiality of PW7's omission about seeing the 3rd Appellant and in treating the evidence as sufficient to sustain his conviction, leading the appellate court to acquit him.
precedents_cited_list: R v Waters – [2023] QCA 243 | Shepherd v The Queen – (1990) 170 CLR 573 | Dharmawansa Silva and Another v. The Republic of Sri Lanka – [1981] 2 Sri L.R. 439 | The Attorney General v. Sandanam Pitchi Mary Theresa – (2011) 2 Sri L.R. 292
standard_of_review_applied: Assessment of circumstantial evidence and whether it excludes reasonable hypotheses of innocence, evaluation of material contradictions and omissions affecting credibility and identification, and scrutiny of the High Court's application of principles on dying declarations.
final_charge_after_appeal: Murder under Section 296 read with Section 32 of the Penal Code maintained against the 1st and 2nd Appellants; 3rd Appellant acquitted of the charge.

judges: P. Kumararatnam, J. | R. P. Hettiarachchi, J.
offence_sections: Section 296, Section 297
offence_category: Murder / Culpable homicide not amounting to murder
location_of_offence: Dikkanda Estate, within the jurisdiction of the High Court of Gampaha
brief_facts_summary: The appellant and the deceased were both employed as security officers at Dikkanda Estate, where a long-standing dispute arose after the deceased spread rumours about the appellant's extra-marital affair. In the early hours of 30.07.2003 the appellant stabbed the deceased inside the estate and then informed his superior (PW1) by telephone that he had done so, explaining that he could not face society due to the rumours. He also went to PW2, again admitting that he had stabbed the deceased, and thereafter accompanied PW1 to the police station where he was arrested and the knife used in the incident was produced. The prosecution relied on these admissions together with surrounding circumstances and medical evidence to establish that the deceased died as a result of stab injuries inflicted by the appellant.
evidence_type_primary: Extra-judicial confessions and oral testimony of co-workers
evidence_type_secondary: Medical and other documentary evidence relating to injuries and death
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 297 of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court, after a judge-alone trial, accepted the prosecution evidence including the appellant's admissions to PW1 and PW2 and found that he had unlawfully caused the death of the deceased in circumstances amounting to culpable homicide not amounting to murder under Section 297 of the Penal Code. Having so convicted him, the court imposed a sentence of 14 years rigorous imprisonment together with a fine of 30000 and a default sentence of 12 months rigorous imprisonment.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: In the Court of Appeal the appellant, through President's Counsel, expressly limited the challenge to the sentence and did not contest the conviction under Section 297. It was argued that the High Court had failed to consider the grave and cumulative provocation arising from the deceased's conduct, as well as the appellant's post-offence conduct, age, remorse and the inordinate delay of about 21 years between the offence and conviction. Counsel contended that these factors required a substantially lesser custodial term and that the sentence imposed was disproportionate to the gravity of the offence and the appellant's personal circumstances. Reliance was placed on authorities dealing with cumulative provocation and sentencing principles to support a reduction of sentence.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Appeal confined to the severity of the sentence imposed under Section 297 and not to the conviction itself. | Alleged failure by the High Court to properly evaluate grave and cumulative provocation arising from the deceased repeatedly spreading rumours about the appellant's extra-marital affair. | Complaint that the High Court did not give adequate weight to mitigatory factors such as the appellant's immediate confessions to PW1 and PW2, lack of pre-planning, surrender to police, and production of the weapon. | Reliance on the long lapse of approximately 21 years between the offence and conviction, without fault on the part of the appellant, as a significant ground for reducing the custodial term. | Submission that the appellant's advanced age (72 years at sentencing), status as a first offender and expressed remorse required a more lenient and proportionate sentence. | Invocation of case law on cumulative provocation and proportionality in sentencing to argue that the 14-year term was manifestly excessive.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The prosecution led eight witnesses at the High Court trial, including PW1 the chief security officer and PW2, both of whom testified that the appellant voluntarily admitted to stabbing the deceased and explained his motive linked to rumours about his illicit affair. No eyewitness saw the actual stabbing, but the appellant's confessions, his subsequent conduct in going to the police with PW1 and producing the knife, together with medical and related evidence of injuries, were treated as strong proof of his involvement. The defence consisted only of a dock statement in which the appellant claimed he stabbed the deceased after being struck from behind, a version which did not materially undermine the prosecution case or the finding of culpable homicide under Section 297.
probability_assessment_by_court: Both the High Court and Court of Appeal treated the appellant's consistent admissions, motive arising from the deceased's rumours and his prompt surrender and production of the weapon as making his involvement highly probable, while recognising that the circumstances pointed to culpable homicide with provocation rather than murder.
defence_version_summary: The appellant did not call any defence witnesses and gave only a dock statement, asserting that he stabbed the deceased when he was struck from behind and acted in sudden anger due to the deceased spreading rumours about his extramarital affair. He did not dispute that he inflicted the stab injuries but sought to place the incident in the context of ongoing provocation affecting his family life and reputation. The courts considered that this version was consistent with the prosecution narrative of a sudden, provocation-induced attack but did not negate liability for culpable homicide. His credibility was enhanced to some extent by his immediate admissions and cooperation with the police, which were later treated as mitigating factors in sentencing rather than as a defence to guilt.
legal_errors_description: The Court of Appeal found that the High Court had failed to sufficiently apply the legal framework on grave and cumulative provocation and to properly factor in key mitigating elements such as long delay, remorse, age and first-offender status when fixing sentence under Section 297, and therefore corrected the sentence to bring it in line with principles of proportionality and relevant precedent.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal endorsed the High Court's finding that the appellant was correctly convicted under Section 297, noting ample evidence of provocation arising from the deceased's persistent rumours but holding that this did not exonerate him from culpable homicide. It analysed Section 294 Exception 1 and Section 105 of the Evidence Ordinance, drawing on authorities such as Nandana Senarathbandara and Premalal to emphasise that cumulative provocation can reduce murder to culpable homicide. Turning to sentence, the Court stressed the appellant's immediate confessions, lack of pre-planning, cooperation with law enforcement, the 21-year lapse between the offence and conviction, his advanced age and first-offender status, as well as sentencing principles of proportionality, deterrence and correction discussed in Illakotulena Thilakerathna and Alister Anthoney Pereira. On this basis it held that a 14-year custodial term was excessive and reduced the sentence to four years rigorous imprisonment while maintaining the fine and imposing compensation to the deceased's family.
coa_sentence_type: Rigorous Imprisonment 4 years plus fine and compensation
brief_judgment_file_summary: This appeal arose from the conviction of the appellant, a security officer at Dikkanda Estate, for culpable homicide under Section 297 of the Penal Code following the stabbing death of a co-worker who had been spreading rumours about the appellant's extra-marital affair. The High Court conducted a judge-alone trial, accepted the appellant's confessions to colleagues and his conduct in surrendering to police and producing the knife, and sentenced him to 14 years rigorous imprisonment and a fine. In the Court of Appeal the appellant challenged only the sentence, arguing that the High Court failed to sufficiently consider cumulative provocation, his remorse, age, first-offender status and the 21-year delay between offence and conviction. While affirming the conviction and recognising that the appellant acted under grave and cumulative provocation, the Court applied sentencing jurisprudence and proportionality principles to reduce the custodial term to four years rigorous imprisonment from the original sentencing date, maintaining the fine and adding compensation of 200000 payable to the deceased's family.
defence_counsel: Sarath Jayamanne, PC with Asith Siriwardana, Vineshka Mendis, Prashan Wickramaratne, Dakshin Abeykoon, Dinindu Ratnayake and C. Widushika
cause_of_death_exact_text: death caused by injuries inflicted by stabbing the deceased with a knife
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court accepted the prosecution evidence, including the appellant's admissions and the background of provocation, and convicted him under Section 297 while imposing a lengthy custodial sentence of 14 years rigorous imprisonment and a fine. The Court of Appeal acknowledged that the High Court had correctly categorised the offence as culpable homicide in light of provocation but criticised its approach to sentencing for failing to adequately consider cumulative provocation, delay, remorse, age and other mitigating circumstances. The appellate court therefore intervened only in relation to sentence, holding that a lesser term would sufficiently meet the ends of justice.
precedents_cited_list: R. W. M. Nandana Senarathbandara v Attorney General, SC Appeal 32/2015, SC minute dated 17.07.2020 | Premalal v AG [2000] 2 SLR 403 | Chandrakant Ganpat Sovitkar v State of Maharastra (1975) 3 SCC 16 | Anura Herath v CIABOC CA-HCC 0089-090/18 dated 05.07.2023 | AG v Devapriya Walgamage and Others [1990] 2 SLR 212 | Illakotulena Gamaralalage Thilakerathna v The Attorney General SC Appeal No. 173/2017 | Alister Anthoney Pereira v State of Maharashta [2012] AIR 3820 (SC)
standard_of_review_applied: Review of sentence for proportionality and failure to consider mitigating circumstances and long delay, while accepting the factual findings and conviction under Section 297.
sentencing_principles_applied: The Court applied principles of proportionality between crime and punishment, the twin objectives of deterrence and correction, the relevance of aggravating and mitigating factors, the impact of long delay without fault of the accused, the offender's age and first-offender status and the need to balance societal interests with individual circumstances when fixing sentence.
final_charge_after_appeal: Section 297 of the Penal Code (culpable homicide not amounting to murder)

judges: Menaka Wijesundera J | Wickum A. Kaluarachchi J
offence_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The accused, a police officer, was married to the deceased, who was pregnant and living with him and her grandmother at Ranasinghewatte, Meetiyagoda. On 2005-04-23, after a quarrel where the accused abused and threatened the deceased and chased away PW-1 and the grandmother, PW-1 returned and saw the accused putting the deceased into a well in front of the house and then running away. Neighbours pulled the deceased out and she was taken to hospital where she was found dead. At trial the accused suggested that the deceased had committed suicide by jumping into the well.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court of Balapitiya tried the accused on a charge of murdering his pregnant wife by putting her into a well. Accepting the evidence of PW-1 as to how the accused pushed or dropped the deceased into the well and rejecting the defence that she committed suicide, the court found that the prosecution had proved murder beyond reasonable doubt. The accused was convicted under Section 296 of the Penal Code and sentenced to death.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: In the written submissions, the defence initially raised several grounds including that the High Court failed to consider the improbability of the prosecution case, did not properly evaluate medical and police evidence about the absence of signs of struggle, and failed to address contradictions and inconsistencies in the testimony of the sole eyewitness and the interestedness of witnesses. A further ground alleged grave prejudice from the High Court Judge not adequately informing the accused of his rights in presenting his defence. At the oral hearing, counsel confined the argument to three main grounds: the alleged improbability of the prosecution story, the absence of injuries or signs of resistance on the deceased, and the failure to consider inconsistencies in PW-1's evidence. The Court of Appeal treated these as aspects of a single contention that the prosecution version was inherently improbable.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Alleged improbability of the prosecution case, including the claim that no human being could lift the deceased by her waist while facing her and put her into the well in the manner described by PW-1. | Failure to consider medical evidence that there were no injuries on the deceased's body suggestive of resistance, which the defence argued supported suicide rather than homicide. | Failure to consider the evidence of police officers who inspected the scene and found no signs of a fight or resistance. | Failure to consider and properly evaluate inter-se contradictions and inconsistencies in the prosecution evidence and in the testimony of the sole eyewitness PW-1. | Failure to consider the interestedness or bias of prosecution witnesses. | Alleged grave prejudice to the accused because the High Court Judge failed to fully notify the accused-appellant of his rights in presenting his defence. | At the hearing, these were effectively reduced to three grounds focused on improbability of the prosecution story, absence of injuries or signs of resistance, and inconsistencies in the eyewitness evidence.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: PW-1, a close relative living nearby, gave an eyewitness account of the quarrel, threats, and of actually seeing the accused putting the deceased into the well and running away, and the Court of Appeal found her account clear, consistent and credible. Her evidence that the deceased was heavily pregnant, had no suicidal intention, and had just asked the grandmother to go to the police was treated as inconsistent with suicide and consistent with homicide. The medical officer who performed the post-mortem explained that the absence of external injuries was compatible with the deceased being firmly held and released into the well, and the defence witnesses were found to support only an afterthought suicide story which had not been told to the police and did not raise a reasonable doubt.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal held that there was no impossibility in the manner described by PW-1 of the accused putting the deceased into the well, that the absence of external injuries was reasonably explained by the medical evidence, and that the deceased's late-stage pregnancy and request to involve the police made suicide highly unlikely. It concluded that the prosecution had excluded suicide beyond reasonable doubt and that no reasonable doubt arose on the probabilities of the case.
defence_version_summary: The defence case was that the deceased committed suicide by jumping into the well, a theory suggested to PW-1 and PW-2 and supported by two defence witnesses, one of whom claimed the accused told her this version. The accused himself did not even make a dock statement explaining that the deceased had committed suicide, despite evidence that he had chased and threatened her and then ran away after she was put into the well. The Court noted that the defence witness had not told the police about the alleged suicide statement and treated the suicide version as an afterthought which did not create a reasonable doubt. Overall, the defence evidence was rejected as not credible.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analysed the eyewitness, medical and defence evidence together and held that the prosecution had proved beyond reasonable doubt that the accused put his pregnant wife into the well with murderous intention. It accepted PW-1 as a credible witness, finding no improbability in her description of the incident and noting that she never said the deceased resisted, which tallied with the medical evidence of no external injuries. The court considered the possibility of suicide, as argued by the defence, but found it excluded by the deceased's imminent delivery, her lack of suicidal intent, and her request to inform the police. Finding that the High Court had properly evaluated the evidence and that the defence suicide version was an afterthought, it declined to interfere with the conviction or the death sentence.
coa_sentence_type: Death
brief_judgment_file_summary: This appeal from the High Court of Balapitiya concerned the conviction of a police officer for the murder of his pregnant wife by putting her into a well at Ranasinghewatte, Meetiyagoda on 2005-04-23. The prosecution relied chiefly on the eyewitness testimony of PW-1, a relative who saw the accused quarrelling with and threatening the deceased, and later saw him putting her into the well, together with medical evidence explaining the absence of external injuries and supporting the prosecution version. On appeal the defence argued that the incident was a suicide, that the prosecution story was improbable, that the medical and scene-of-crime evidence suggested no struggle, and that the sole eyewitness was inconsistent and interested, and further complained of procedural prejudice in the conduct of the trial. The Court of Appeal rejected these contentions, held that the prosecution had excluded suicide and proved murder beyond reasonable doubt, found no error in the High Court's evaluation of evidence or procedure, and accordingly affirmed the conviction under Section 296 and the sentence of death, dismissing the appeal.
defence_counsel: Anuja Premaratna P.C. with Imasha Senadeera and Ramith Dunusinghe
cause_of_death_exact_text: Death due to drowning after being put into a well.
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court reasoned that PW-1's eyewitness account of the accused putting the deceased into the well, coupled with the surrounding circumstances of threats and quarrelling and the deceased's pregnancy, established intentional homicide rather than suicide. It rejected the suicide theory and defence evidence, accepted the medical explanation for the lack of external injuries, and concluded that murder under Section 296 was proved beyond reasonable doubt. The Court of Appeal held that this assessment of credibility and probabilities was correct, that the defence version was an afterthought, and that there was no misdirection or misappreciation requiring appellate intervention.
precedents_cited_list: CA – HCC – 0289/2014, Kosgoda Durayalage Premachandra v. The Honourable Attorney General – decided 26.07.2022 | CA – HCC – 44/2015, Don Chandana Priyantha Rupasinghe v. Hon. Attorney General – decided 26.11.2019 | King v. Seneviratne – 38 NLR 208
standard_of_review_applied: Assessment of whether the prosecution had excluded suicide and proved murder beyond reasonable doubt and whether the High Court's findings on credibility and probabilities were unreasonable or perverse.
final_charge_after_appeal: Murder under Section 296 of the Penal Code

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance as amended by Act No. 13 of 1984
offence_category: Possession and trafficking of dangerous drugs (heroin)
location_of_offence: Pearl City Hotel, Bambalapitiya, within the jurisdiction of the High Court of Colombo
brief_facts_summary: The appellant and a co-accused, both Maldivian nationals, were under investigation by the Police Narcotic Bureau based on information that they were involved in drug trafficking. After surveillance, officers led by PW-01 conducted a raid at Pearl City Hotel, Bambalapitiya, where the appellant was arrested in the hotel lobby allegedly carrying a duty-free tulip bag containing a Bata shoe box with two parcels of heroin, and further parcels were recovered from a travelling bag in room 710 attributed to the second accused. The pure quantity attributable to the appellant was 265.31 grams of heroin, while 69.08 grams were linked to the second accused. The High Court convicted the appellant on possession and trafficking counts but acquitted the second accused due to insufficient proof of his conscious possession and knowledge of the heroin.
evidence_type_primary: Police officer testimony and physical drug productions
evidence_type_secondary: Government Analyst report and documentary records such as PNB instruction letters and admissions under section 420 of the Code of Criminal Procedure Act
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Possession and trafficking of 265.31 grams of heroin under the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance as amended by Act No. 13 of 1984
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court of Colombo found the appellant guilty on the counts of possession and trafficking of 265.31 grams of heroin, accepting the evidence of the raiding Police Narcotic Bureau officers as proving exclusive possession. It held that the pure quantity of heroin was far above a user quantity and therefore indicative of trafficking, justifying a life sentence on both counts. The second accused was acquitted because the court found the prosecution had not proved beyond reasonable doubt that he had knowledge of or conscious possession over the heroin recovered from the room.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: On appeal, the appellant contended that the trial judge failed to consider the dock statement of the second accused, which allegedly corroborated the appellant’s dock statement that no bag containing heroin was with him at the time of arrest, thereby causing grave prejudice. He argued that in light of this omission, and the rejection of his own dock statement, he was denied a fair trial guaranteed under the Constitution. The defence also criticised the prosecution’s failure to follow the written instructions in P-01 and P-02 to arrest the suspects at the airport, the failure to obtain and produce CCTV footage from the hotel and casino, and the failure to call hotel staff as witnesses, suggesting that these amounted to withholding the best evidence and undermining the prosecution case.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Alleged failure of the High Court Judge to consider the dock statement of the second accused, which purportedly corroborated the first accused-appellant’s claim that no bag was recovered from his possession at the time of arrest. | Allegation that the appellant did not receive a fair trial as guaranteed under the Constitution because the exculpatory dock statement of the acquitted co-accused was ignored. | Complaint that the appellant’s own dock statement was unfairly rejected by the trial judge. | Criticism of the investigating officer’s decision not to follow the written instructions in P-01 and P-02 to arrest the suspects at the airport, implying a doubtful or irregular investigation. | Allegation that the prosecution failed to obtain and produce the best evidence, namely CCTV footage from the hotel and casino, and failed to call any hotel witnesses, inviting an adverse inference under section 114(f) of the Evidence Ordinance.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The prosecution relied mainly on the testimony of PW-01, the experienced PNB officer who led the raid, and Police Inspector Subodha, whose evidence corroborated her account of surveillance, the raid at Pearl City Hotel, and the recovery of heroin from the appellant’s tulip bag and the room. Their evidence withstood extensive cross-examination, including suggestions that the heroin was actually detected at Pearl Garden Hotel near the airport and later introduced, and that the prosecution was hiding CCTV footage; both witnesses denied these suggestions and explained the confusion between Pearl City and Pearl Garden hotels. The defence admitted the chain of custody, the sealed condition of productions, and the Government Analyst findings, while seeking to cast doubt through dock statements and a defence witness (the Registrar) about attempts to obtain CCTV recordings.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal viewed the defence theory that heroin had been found at a different hotel and falsely attributed to the appellant as a speculative and fanciful doubt, emphasising that reasonable doubt must arise from evidence and common sense. It accepted PW-01’s professional judgment in choosing surveillance over immediate airport arrest and treated the admitted facts of arrest at the hotel, occupancy of room 710, and possession of the bag and productions as rendering the prosecution version highly probable and the defence version improbable.
defence_version_summary: In his dock statement, the appellant admitted being arrested with the second accused in the lobby of Pearl City Hotel after returning from Bally’s Casino, but denied carrying a tulip bag or a Bata shoe box containing heroin and claimed he was merely questioned about heroin brought the previous day. He asserted that nothing belonging to the second accused was in his room and that he later realised heroin had been detected at Pearl Garden Hotel near the airport, leading him to believe the PNB officers mistakenly thought he had brought that heroin to Sri Lanka. The second accused, later acquitted, gave a dock statement saying he lived in Dehiwala, that the appellant stayed at Pearl City Hotel, that they went together to Bally’s Casino and returned, and that although the appellant’s travelling bag was taken by PNB officials, nothing was found with them and his own purse remained with him. A defence witness, the Registrar of the Negombo Magistrate’s Court, was called to show applications and orders regarding CCTV footage; however, the High Court and Court of Appeal found the dock statements unconvincing in light of the consistent prosecution evidence and the lack of any credible innocent explanation for the large quantity of heroin.
legal_errors_description: The Court of Appeal held that the trial judge correctly treated dock statements as evidence subject to their inherent infirmities, rightly declined to use the second accused’s dock statement in favour of the appellant, and properly applied the law on burden of proof and reasonable doubt, finding no misdirection or legal error warranting appellate intervention.
procedural_defects_description: The Court of Appeal rejected arguments that the failure to arrest the appellant at the airport, the absence of CCTV footage, or the non-calling of hotel staff amounted to procedural defects, holding that the investigation strategy was reasonable, that the prosecution was entitled to rely on the testimony of the raiding officers without CCTV, and that the admitted facts made additional hotel witnesses unnecessary.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal reappraised the evidence and concluded that PW-01’s decision not to arrest the appellant at the airport but to conduct surveillance was a rational investigative choice and did not cast doubt on her credibility. It held that the prosecution had led the best available evidence through the raiding officers, that the admitted chain of custody and Government Analyst reports firmly established the presence and quantity of heroin, and that the absence of CCTV footage—explained by automatic deletion at the hotel—did not justify an adverse inference under section 114(f) of the Evidence Ordinance. The court reaffirmed that dock statements are evidence but cannot be used for or against a co-accused, rejected the attempt to rely on the second accused’s dock statement in favour of the appellant, and found that the trial judge had properly evaluated and ultimately rejected the appellant’s dock statement as improbable when viewed against the totality of the evidence. It also relied on established authorities on reasonable doubt and dock statements, concluding that the prosecution case was proven beyond reasonable doubt and that this was not a case of fanciful doubts or investigative unfairness.
coa_sentence_type: Life imprisonment on both counts (affirmed)
brief_judgment_file_summary: This appeal concerned a conviction of a Maldivian national by the High Court of Colombo for possession and trafficking of 265.31 grams of heroin, following a Police Narcotic Bureau raid at Pearl City Hotel in Bambalapitiya. The appellant argued that the trial judge erred in failing to consider the dock statement of his acquitted co-accused, unfairly rejected his own dock statement, and that investigative deficiencies such as the lack of CCTV footage and the decision not to arrest him at the airport undermined the prosecution case and his right to a fair trial. The Court of Appeal, after reviewing the evidence and relevant case law on burden of proof, reasonable doubt, and dock statements, held that the prosecution had proved exclusive possession and trafficking beyond reasonable doubt, that dock statements cannot be used in favour of or against a co-accused, and that the investigative choices and absence of CCTV did not create a reasonable doubt. The appeal was dismissed and the life sentences on both counts were affirmed.
prosecution_counsel: Sudharshana de Silva, S.D.S.G. for the Respondent
defence_counsel: Shavindra Fernando, P.C. with Mirthula Skandarajah for the Accused-Appellant
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court accepted the testimony of the PNB officers as truthful and found that the appellant was in exclusive possession of the bag containing heroin when arrested in the hotel lobby and that the heroin quantity attributable to him was proven by the admitted Government Analyst reports. It reasoned that the pure quantity of heroin, 265.31 grams, was well beyond a user quantity and must necessarily be for trafficking, thereby supporting both possession and trafficking counts and warranting a life sentence. As to the second accused, the High Court found that the prosecution had not proved his knowledge or conscious possession of the heroin found in the room and accordingly acquitted him, a conclusion with which the Court of Appeal expressly agreed.
precedents_cited_list: Pantis v. The Attorney General (1998) 2 SLR 148 | Narender Kumar v. State of Delhi (NCT of Delhi) AIR 2012 SC 2281 | Karunadasa v.
