He also effectively complained that he had not been afforded an opportunity to present mitigating factors at the time of sentencing in the High Court. The appeal thus centred on whether the sentence was excessive when viewed in light of the long remand period and the absence of mitigation being taken into account.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Appeal ultimately confined to a challenge to the sentence imposed by the High Court rather than to the conviction itself. | Relief sought under section 333 of the Code of Criminal Procedure Act as amended, requesting that time spent in custody prior to conviction and pending appeal be treated as part of the sentence and that the prison term take effect from the date of conviction. | Complaint that the High Court imposed sentence immediately upon delivering judgment after the trial de novo without affording the appellant an opportunity to make submissions in mitigation. | Argument that in light of the prolonged remand custody and absence of prior convictions, the 12-year term without credit for remand was manifestly excessive and should be reduced.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: This judgment is confined to sentencing issues and does not analyse the evidence led at trial in any detail. There is no discussion of the testimony of the prosecutrix, other witnesses, or expert or forensic evidence. The Court of Appeal proceeds on the basis of the existing conviction and focuses solely on the fairness and proportionality of the sentence in light of the appellant's remand history and lack of prior convictions.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court assessed the overall justice of the sentence in light of the probabilities and circumstances, emphasising that ignoring approximately eight years of remand custody would result in a manifestly excessive and unjust punishment. It reasoned that pre-conviction detention is a real loss of liberty equivalent in effect to post-conviction imprisonment and should therefore be credited towards the ultimate sentence.
defence_version_summary: The judgment does not set out an alternative factual narrative of the offence by the defence; rather, the appellant had already been convicted at a retrial and the conviction was not challenged at this stage. On appeal, the defence confined itself to sentencing issues, arguing that the appellant had spent around eight years in remand custody, that he had no previous convictions, and that he had been denied the chance to present mitigatory factors before the High Court imposed sentence. The Court of Appeal records these mitigation-related submissions and uses them, together with the new statutory proviso, to reassess the appropriate term of imprisonment.
legal_errors_description: The Court of Appeal identified that the High Court imposed sentence immediately after delivering judgment at the trial de novo without giving the appellant an opportunity to make submissions in mitigation. It also noted that the remand period was not taken into account at sentencing and applied the new proviso to section 333(5) to correct this omission and avoid a sentence that would be manifestly excessive.
procedural_defects_description: The principal procedural defect was that, after the trial de novo, the learned High Court Judge straightaway imposed sentence on the appellant without affording him an opportunity to present mitigatory facts. This deprived the appellant of his right to address the court in mitigation and contributed to the failure to consider the lengthy period he had spent on remand when determining the sentence.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal examined the amendment to section 333 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, particularly the new proviso allowing time spent in custody before conviction and pending appeal to be treated as part of the sentence. It articulated the principle that pre-conviction detention is a genuine curtailment of liberty and that failure to credit such time can lead to sentences that are manifestly excessive and unjust, especially where delays are beyond the control of the accused. In light of journal entries showing the appellant had been in remand from 23.11.2016 to 02.04.2020 and again after conviction, and noting that he had no previous convictions, the court considered it just to deduct eight years from the 12-year sentence. It therefore reduced the operative term of imprisonment to four years effective from the date of conviction while leaving the orders on fine, compensation and default sentences intact, and characterised the appeal as partly allowed.
coa_sentence_type: Rigorous Imprisonment 4 years; fine and compensation unchanged
brief_judgment_file_summary: This Court of Appeal judgment concerns an appeal from the High Court of Vavuniya in which the appellant, convicted of rape of a girl under 18 under section 364(2)(e) of the Penal Code, challenged only the sentence imposed. Applying the 2024 amendment to section 333(5) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, the court held that pre-conviction and pre-appeal remand custody is a real deprivation of liberty that must be credited to avoid double punishment and manifestly excessive sentences. It found that the High Court had imposed 12 years rigorous imprisonment, a fine and compensation without affording the appellant a chance to present mitigation and without accounting for roughly eight years spent in remand. The Court of Appeal accordingly deducted eight years from the sentence, ordered that the four-year term take effect from the date of conviction, left the monetary orders unchanged, and partly allowed the appeal.
defence_counsel: Indika Mallwarachchi
cause_of_death_exact_text: Not applicable; the case concerns rape and no death is in issue.
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court, after the retrial, convicted the appellant for rape and imposed a sentence of 12 years rigorous imprisonment together with a fine of 10000 and compensation of 300000 plus default sentences. It did so immediately upon delivering judgment, without inviting mitigation, and without explicitly considering the substantial period the appellant had already spent in remand custody. The Court of Appeal observed these omissions, inferred that the remand period had not been factored into sentencing, and treated this as warranting intervention under the amended section 333 to adjust the effective term of imprisonment.
standard_of_review_applied: Review of sentence under section 333(5) of the Code of Criminal Procedure with emphasis on fairness, proportionality, and proper crediting of time spent in remand custody.
sentencing_principles_applied: The court applied principles that pre-conviction detention is a real deprivation of liberty equivalent in effect to post-conviction imprisonment, that an accused should not be punished twice by both lengthy remand and the full custodial term, and that sentences ignoring such detention can become manifestly excessive and unjust; it also considered the absence of prior convictions in calibrating a just sentence.
final_charge_after_appeal: Rape of a female under 18 punishable under section 364(2)(e) of the Penal Code (unchanged)

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code
location_of_offence: Sampathgama, Sudharshanagama, within the jurisdiction of the High Court of Anuradhapura
brief_facts_summary: The deceased, a three-year-old girl named Sandunika Upeksha Lakmali, had been handed over by her grandmother to the accused-appellant and his wife for care. Evidence from villagers indicated that the child was ill-treated, assaulted and subjected to cruelty while living with them, and that the appellant and his wife attempted to place her in an institution due to their inability to care for her. On the day of the incident, the appellant was seen walking with the child and repeatedly assaulting her with a stick, and shortly thereafter the child was found unconscious and later pronounced dead. The post-mortem revealed multiple external and internal injuries inconsistent with a simple fall and indicative of intentional assault, including fatal head injuries and signs of prior torture.
evidence_type_primary: Circumstantial evidence and medical expert evidence
evidence_type_secondary: Eyewitness testimony of a villager and background evidence of prior ill-treatment by fellow villagers
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code (Murder)
hc_judgment_summary: After a judge-alone trial, the High Court of Anuradhapura found the appellant guilty of murdering the three-year-old child under his care, relying on circumstantial evidence including eyewitness observations of assault and detailed medical findings showing intentional injuries. The court rejected any suggestion of accidental causation and sentenced the appellant to death. The conviction and sentence were based on the conclusion that the appellant intentionally inflicted the fatal injuries.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: On appeal, the defence contended that there was no direct evidence against the appellant and that the conviction rested on circumstantial evidence which raised only suspicious circumstances. It was argued that the High Court compartmentalized the evidence instead of viewing it as a whole, and wrongly applied section 105 of the Evidence Ordinance by treating the case as one involving general exceptions. The appellant further claimed that the trial judge relied entirely or excessively on expert medical evidence in reaching the conviction.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: No direct evidence against the appellant; conviction based solely on circumstantial evidence allegedly amounting only to suspicious circumstances. | Allegation that the learned High Court Judge compartmentalized the evidence instead of considering its totality. | Complaint that the provisions of section 105 of the Evidence Ordinance were wrongly applied to the facts, misplacing the burden regarding general exceptions. | Allegation that the trial judge relied entirely or excessively on expert (JMO) evidence to convict the appellant.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal noted that there was no eyewitness to the specific incident causing the fatal injuries, but accepted the testimony of a villager (PW-10) who saw the appellant shortly before the death repeatedly assaulting the child with a stick. Evidence from fellow villagers corroborated that the child had been subjected to ongoing cruelty while under the appellant’s care, and the JMO’s detailed medical findings showed multiple injuries inconsistent with a mere fall or attempts at resuscitation. The court held that, taken cumulatively, these pieces of circumstantial and expert evidence formed a strong, coherent chain pointing only to the appellant’s guilt.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal applied the standard principles on circumstantial evidence, holding that the proved circumstances must be consistent only with the appellant’s guilt and inconsistent with any reasonable hypothesis of innocence. It found that the appellant’s explanation of an accidental fall and attempts to revive the child was incompatible with the medical evidence and surrounding facts, so that the only reasonable inference was that he intentionally inflicted the fatal injuries.
defence_version_summary: The appellant, in a dock statement, accepted that the child had been entrusted to him and his wife but claimed that she accidentally fell off a bank while running near a bridge after he lightly hit her with a small stick to stop her. He stated that she became unconscious and that he squeezed her cheeks and tried to clear phlegm from her mouth before taking her home and then to hospital, asserting that he did not commit any crime. The courts found this version inconsistent with the pattern, location and severity of injuries described by the JMO and rejected it as an inadequate and false explanation, concluding that no reasonable doubt arose from the defence.
legal_errors_description: The Court of Appeal identified a misdirection in the High Court’s application of section 105 of the Evidence Ordinance and the general exceptions in the Penal Code, noting that this was not truly a case where the appellant relied on a general exception such as accident. However, the court held that this misdirection on law did not prejudice the appellant’s substantial rights or occasion a failure of justice.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal carefully reviewed the circumstantial evidence, emphasizing established principles that such evidence, taken cumulatively, must exclude any reasonable hypothesis of innocence. It held that the High Court had not compartmentalized the evidence but had properly considered the child’s living conditions, the appellant’s custody and conduct, the eyewitness account of assault with a stick shortly before death, and the JMO’s detailed findings, which were inconsistent with a simple fall or resuscitative efforts. While the court acknowledged a misdirection in the use of section 105 regarding general exceptions, it concluded that this error caused no prejudice and that the chain of circumstantial and medical evidence irresistibly pointed to the appellant’s guilt. Accordingly, it affirmed the credibility of the prosecution case, rejected the defence dock statement as false, and upheld both conviction and sentence.
coa_sentence_type: Death
brief_judgment_file_summary: The appellant was indicted in the High Court of Anuradhapura for murdering a three-year-old girl, Sandunika Upeksha Lakmali, entrusted to his care, at Sampathgama, Sudharshanagama in June 2005. Villagers testified that the child was ill-treated and a villager (PW-10) saw the appellant shortly before the death repeatedly assaulting her with a stick, while the JMO documented numerous external and internal injuries, including a fatal contusion to the forehead and subdural haemorrhage, incompatible with a mere fall or resuscitative attempts. After a judge-alone trial, the High Court convicted the appellant under section 296 of the Penal Code and imposed the death sentence. On appeal, the Court of Appeal discussed the law on circumstantial evidence, found that the totality of circumstances and medical evidence conclusively pointed to intentional assault by the appellant, held that a misdirection on section 105 of the Evidence Ordinance was non-prejudicial, and dismissed the appeal, affirming both conviction and death sentence.
prosecution_counsel: Lishan Ratnayake, S.C. for the Respondent
defence_counsel: Rizwan Uwais for the Accused-Appellant
cause_of_death_exact_text: Death was due to a forcefully inflicted head injury causing subdural haemorrhage associated with an oval contusion on the left forehead, which the JMO opined could not have resulted from a simple fall.
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court evaluated the circumstantial and medical evidence, including the appellant’s custody of the child, her prior ill-treatment, the eyewitness account of assault, and the JMO’s findings, and concluded that the appellant intentionally caused the fatal injuries, convicting him of murder and sentencing him to death. The Court of Appeal recognized that the High Court had treated the appellant’s explanation as invoking general exceptions and applied section 105 of the Evidence Ordinance, which it considered a misdirection in law. Nonetheless, it held that the trial judge had in substance properly assessed the totality of the evidence and that the misdirection had no vitiating effect on the otherwise sound reasoning and conclusion.
precedents_cited_list: The King v. Abeywickrama – 44 NLR 254 | Don Sunny v. The Attorney General – (1998) 2 SLR 01 | King v. Gunaratne – 47 NLR 145 | Regina v. Exall – 176 English Reports, Nisi Prius 853 | Karunaratne v. Attorney-General – (2005) 2 SLR 233
standard_of_review_applied: Review of whether the circumstantial evidence was properly evaluated so that it was consistent only with guilt and inconsistent with any reasonable hypothesis of innocence, coupled with scrutiny of a misdirection on law regarding section 105 of the Evidence Ordinance under the Article 138 proviso requiring prejudice or failure of justice for interference.
final_charge_after_appeal: Murder under Section 296 of the Penal Code

judges: Wickum A. Kaluarachchi J | Menaka Wijesundera J
offence_sections: Section 22(3) read with Section 22(1) of the Firearms Ordinance as amended by Act No. 22 of 1996; Section 27(1)(b) of the Explosives Act as amended by Act No. 18 of 2005 for violating Section 9(2)
offence_category: Illegal possession of firearm and ammunition
location_of_offence: Near Kottukatchchiya temple in Kottukatchchiya area on the Anamaduwa–Puttlam road
brief_facts_summary: Police officers on traffic duty near Kottukatchchiya temple stopped a fast-moving Dolphin van and, on searching under the driving seat carpet, found an automatic rifle and two magazines, one loaded with 30 live ammunitions. The 1st accused was driving the van and the 2nd accused was seated in the front passenger seat. Both were arrested and taken to the police station along with the van. At trial the prosecution relied mainly on the police officers who recovered the weapon, while the 1st accused in his dock statement denied that any firearm, magazines or ammunitions were found in the van.
evidence_type_primary: Eyewitness testimony of police officers who recovered the firearm and ammunition from the van
evidence_type_secondary: Physical evidence of an automatic rifle and magazines with live ammunitions found under the driving seat carpet
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 22(3) read with Section 22(1) of the Firearms Ordinance; Section 27(1)(b) of the Explosives Act read with Section 9(2)
hc_sentence_type: Life imprisonment for the first count and a fine with default simple imprisonment for the second count
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court of Puttalam convicted the 1st accused for possessing an automatic rifle and 30 live ammunitions without a valid license and acquitted the 2nd accused on both counts. The court imposed life imprisonment on the 1st accused for the firearms offence and a fine of 2500 with a default sentence of three months simple imprisonment for the ammunition offence.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: On appeal the 1st accused argued that the High Court erred in law by rejecting the defence evidence and effectively reversing the presumption of innocence. It was contended that the findings of the trial judge were based on surmises and conjectures and were unsupported by the evidence. The appellant further argued that the prosecution failed to eliminate the possible involvement of a third party and that exclusive possession of the firearm by the 1st accused was not established, particularly in light of the 2nd accused’s acquittal.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Alleged error in law by the High Court in rejecting the defence dock statement and reversing the presumption of innocence when evaluating the evidence. | Complaint that the High Court judgment was based on surmises and conjectures rather than evidence properly led at the trial. | Argument that the prosecution failed to exclude the involvement of a third party, particularly given that the vehicle did not belong to the 1st accused. | Argument that exclusive possession of the firearm and ammunitions by the 1st accused was not established, especially when the 2nd accused was acquitted on the basis of lack of knowledge.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal considered the evidence of the police officers, particularly PW-1, who discovered the firearm and ammunition under the driving seat carpet and found their evidence cogent and reliable. The court rejected the dock statement of the 1st accused, holding that it did not create a reasonable doubt about the prosecution case and noting that the physical circumstances (a 99 cm firearm under the driver’s carpet) made it highly probable that the driver knew of its presence. The absence of any animosity or motive for the police officers to falsely implicate the appellant further strengthened the prosecution evidence.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal accepted the High Court’s reasoning that a long firearm hidden under the driver’s seat carpet would almost certainly have been noticed by the 1st accused while driving, making it highly probable that he had custody and knowledge of the weapon, and that the police had no reason or opportunity to falsely plant the firearm.
defence_version_summary: The 1st accused gave a dock statement asserting that no firearm, magazines or ammunitions were found in the van he was driving and effectively denied possession altogether. He did not suggest any animosity or motive for the police to falsely implicate him, nor did he call any defence witnesses or put forward an alibi. Both the High Court and the Court of Appeal held that this dock statement was not believable and did not create a reasonable doubt in the prosecution case.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal re-evaluated the evidence and held that the High Court had correctly accepted the prosecution version that a firearm and ammunition were recovered from under the driver’s seat where the appellant was seated. It emphasized that, given the size and position of the firearm, the appellant as the driver must have been aware of its presence and that his denial in the dock statement did not raise a reasonable doubt. The court rejected the contention that the judgment was based on surmises, treating the trial judge’s observations about the protruding carpet and ease of driving as legitimate inferences from the evidence, and found no reason for the police to fabricate a case against the appellant. It also held that the acquittal of the 2nd accused, based on doubt as to his knowledge, did not affect the clear evidence of possession and knowledge on the part of the 1st accused, and affirmed both conviction and sentence.
coa_sentence_type: Life imprisonment for possession of an automatic rifle and a fine of 2500 with a default sentence of three months simple imprisonment for the ammunition offence (affirmed)
brief_judgment_file_summary: This appeal from the High Court of Puttalam concerned the 1st accused’s conviction for possession of an automatic rifle and 30 live ammunitions found under the driver’s seat carpet of a van stopped at a traffic roadblock near Kottukatchchiya. The appellant argued that the trial judge erred in rejecting his dock statement, relied on surmises, failed to exclude third-party involvement and did not establish exclusive possession. The Court of Appeal held that the evidence of the police officers was credible, that the physical circumstances made it highly probable that the driver knew of the weapon, and that there was no plausible reason for the police to falsely implicate him. It therefore affirmed the High Court’s judgment, convictions and sentences and dismissed the appeal.
prosecution_counsel: Jayalakshi De Silva, Senior State Counsel for the Respondents
defence_counsel: Amila Palliyage with Sandeepani Wijesooriya, Savani Udugampola, Lakitha Wakishta Arachchi and Subaj De Silva for the 1st Accused-Appellant
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court had accepted the testimony of the police officers who recovered the firearm and ammunition from under the driving seat and rejected the 1st accused’s denial as failing to raise a reasonable doubt. It reasoned that, given the size and placement of the weapon, the driver must have been aware of its presence and that there was no credible basis to believe the firearm was planted by the police. The Court of Appeal endorsed this reasoning as correct in law and fact, concluding that the High Court had properly weighed the evidence and applied the law on possession and knowledge.
standard_of_review_applied: Reappraisal of the evidence to determine whether the High Court misdirected itself on the presumption of innocence, relied on surmises and conjectures, or made findings unsupported by the evidence, and whether its conclusions on possession and knowledge were perverse.
final_charge_after_appeal: Possession of an automatic rifle and ammunition without a valid license under Section 22(3) read with Section 22(1) of the Firearms Ordinance and Section 27(1)(b) of the Explosives Act read with Section 9(2)

judges: P. Kumararatnam J. | Sampath B. Abayakoon J.
offence_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The deceased, an elderly woman living alone, was found lying in a pool of blood near a Buddha statue in her ransacked house after her children became concerned when she failed to answer telephone calls. Police arrived around 10.15 a.m., secured the scene, and called fingerprint experts, who examined the scene for several hours and uplifted latent prints, including one from an almirah handle. The appellant was arrested the same day, and his fingerprint samples were taken and later matched by the Registrar of Fingerprints to the latent print on the almirah handle. Medical evidence revealed multiple stab and cut injuries, with fatal wounds to the chest and neck, and the cause of death was shock and hemorrhage due to deep penetrating wounds to the liver and a main artery.
evidence_type_primary: Circumstantial evidence based on fingerprint identification
evidence_type_secondary: Medical evidence and testimony of family members and investigating officers
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court of Gampaha, after a non-jury trial, found the appellant guilty of the murder of the deceased under Section 296 of the Penal Code. The conviction was based primarily on strong circumstantial evidence, particularly the fingerprint found on the deceased's almirah handle that matched the appellant, together with the medical and scene-of-crime evidence. The appellant was accordingly sentenced to death on 2019-10-04.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant argued that the High Court failed to properly apply the legal principles governing cases based entirely on circumstantial evidence. He further contended that the conviction was based solely on a single fingerprint found on the almirah handle, that the trial judge improperly used weaknesses in the defence to bolster the prosecution case, and that the defence evidence was not analysed in its correct perspective and was rejected on an incorrect premise. These grounds collectively challenged both the evaluation of circumstantial and expert evidence and the treatment of the defence version.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Alleged failure of the High Court Judge to apply the well-settled principles of law relating to a case entirely based on circumstantial evidence. | Complaint that the conviction was based only on the fingerprint found on the handle of the almirah. | Allegation that the trial judge used the weakness of the defence evidence to strengthen the prosecution case. | Allegation that the trial judge failed to analyse the defence evidence in the correct perspective and rejected it on a wrong premise.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal noted that the prosecution led evidence from family members who discovered the deceased, police officers who secured and examined the crime scene, the fingerprint experts who uplifted and analysed latent prints, and the JMO who gave comprehensive medical evidence. The fingerprint uplifted from the deceased's almirah handle was positively matched to the appellant's sample prints, with no effective challenge by the defence to the process or result. The court observed that the appellant, who gave only a dock statement, failed to offer any explanation as to how his fingerprint came to be on the almirah handle, and his evidence did not create any reasonable doubt in the face of the strong prosecution case.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal held that the circumstantial evidence, particularly the fingerprint on the almirah handle, formed a complete and unbroken chain pointing irresistibly to the appellant's guilt and excluding any reasonable hypothesis consistent with innocence, thereby leaving no room for reasonable doubt.
defence_version_summary: After the close of the prosecution case, the appellant did not call any witnesses and only made a dock statement. In that statement he did not provide any explanation as to how his fingerprint came to be on the almirah handle inside the deceased's house. The High Court, and subsequently the Court of Appeal, found that his bare dock statement was insufficient to undermine the strong circumstantial and expert evidence led by the prosecution and did not create a reasonable doubt.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal carefully reviewed the circumstantial evidence and concluded that all proved circumstances, taken together, pointed solely to the appellant as the perpetrator of the murder, consistent with established authorities on circumstantial evidence. It held that the High Court Judge, though not expressly reciting the principles, had in substance applied the correct tests and correctly appreciated the evidence, including the medical and scene-of-crime evidence. The court found the fingerprint evidence reliable and decisive, noting the secure crime scene, the timing of the upliftment, expert comparison, and the appellant's failure to give any innocent explanation for the presence of his fingerprint. It rejected the contention that the trial judge relied on defence weaknesses to bolster the prosecution, instead holding that the defence dock statement had been properly considered but was incapable of raising a reasonable doubt, and accordingly affirmed both conviction and sentence.
coa_sentence_type: Death
brief_judgment_file_summary: This appeal arose from the conviction of the appellant by the High Court of Gampaha for the murder of an elderly woman who lived alone, whose body was discovered in her ransacked home with multiple stab and cut injuries. The prosecution case was purely circumstantial and relied heavily on a latent fingerprint uplifted from the handle of an almirah in the deceased's house, which was subsequently matched by the Registrar of Fingerprints to the appellant's sample prints taken after his arrest, alongside strong medical and investigative evidence. On appeal, the appellant challenged the evaluation of circumstantial evidence, the reliance on the fingerprint as the sole basis for conviction, and the treatment of the defence dock statement, alleging misapplication of legal principles and unfair use of defence weaknesses. The Court of Appeal, applying established case law on circumstantial and expert evidence, held that the chain of circumstances was complete and consistent only with the appellant's guilt, found no legal or procedural errors in the High Court's approach, and dismissed the appeal, affirming the conviction for murder under Section 296 and the sentence of death.
defence_counsel: Nihara Randeniya
cause_of_death_exact_text: Shock and hemorrhage due to deep penetrating wounds to the liver and main artery caused by multiple stab injuries to the chest and neck.
hc_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal observed that the High Court Judge had considered all the relevant evidence, including the testimony of the witnesses, the medical findings, and the fingerprint analysis, in reaching the conviction. Although the judgment did not expressly set out the legal principles governing circumstantial evidence, the Court of Appeal held that the High Court had in substance applied those principles by evaluating the totality of circumstances and finding that they pointed to the appellant's guilt. The Court also noted that the High Court rightly rejected the purported recovery of the knife under Section 27(1) of the Evidence Ordinance but correctly relied on the fingerprint and other evidence, and that it properly considered and rejected the appellant's dock statement as insufficient to create reasonable doubt.
precedents_cited_list: C. Chenga Reddy and others v. State of A.P. – (1996) 10 SCC 193 | McGreevy v. Director of Public Prosecution – [1973] 1 WLR 276 | Attorney General v. Potta Naufer & others – [2007] 2 SLR 144 | Kusumadasa v. State – [2011] 1 SLR 240 | Premawansha v. Attorney General – [2009] 2 SLR 205 | The Queen v. Wijehamy – 62 NLR 425 | The King v. Jayasena – [1933] 2 CLW | King v. Logus – 34 NLR 255 | Singo Appu v. The King – 46 NLR 49
standard_of_review_applied: Assessment of sufficiency of circumstantial evidence, proper application of legal principles on circumstantial and expert fingerprint evidence, and evaluation of whether the High Court's findings were consistent with the evidence and free of misdirection.
final_charge_after_appeal: Murder under Section 296 of the Penal Code

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 98(1)(a) and 101(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure Act; Sections 23A, 23P, 23Q and 23R of the Central Environmental Authority Act
location_of_offence: Neighbourhood around the Church at No. 11, Wijaya Mawatha, Chilaw
brief_facts_summary: The Officer-in-Charge of Chilaw Police Station filed an application under section 98(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure Act before the Chilaw Magistrate’s Court complaining of noise pollution caused by Church services conducted by the respondent using loud sound equipment. After receiving the police report and evidence, the Magistrate issued a conditional order on 07-07-2017 and later, on 17-10-2017, made that order permanent under section 101(3), prohibiting the use of loudspeakers in the Church. The respondent challenged the Magistrate’s order by appeal and revision before the Provincial High Court of the North Western Province holden in Chilaw, which on 21-05-2021 vacated the Magistrate’s order on the basis that the Church was not a public place under section 98 and that religious institutions may use loudspeakers. The virtual complainant then invoked the revisionary jurisdiction of the Court of Appeal, which re-examined the legality of the High Court’s decision and the scope of section 98 in relation to noise pollution from religious institutions.
evidence_type_primary: Police report and witness testimony on noise pollution from the Church
evidence_type_secondary: Written and oral legal submissions and reliance on reported case law and statutory provisions
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Not applicable; the High Court vacated a conditional order made under section 98(1)(a) and 101(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure Act
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court held that the Church or prayer centre maintained by the respondent could not be regarded as a public place for the purposes of section 98 of the Code of Criminal Procedure Act. It further reasoned that religious institutions such as temples and churches, by virtue of cultural and historical practices, could use loudspeakers and sound-emitting devices even if some public nuisance resulted. On that basis, the High Court vacated the Magistrate’s order of 17-10-2017 and granted relief to the respondent in both his appeal and revision applications.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The petitioner contended before the Court of Appeal that the Magistrate had correctly exercised jurisdiction under section 98 of the Code of Criminal Procedure Act in treating the noise pollution as a public nuisance emanating from a public place. It was argued that the High Court misdirected itself in holding that the Church was not a public place and that noise pollution from religious institutions falls outside section 98. The petitioner also emphasized that the respondent failed to follow the statutory procedure under section 98(2) to seek modification of the conditional order and instead tried to have it wholly set aside. Further, the petitioner complained that the High Court failed to appreciate that the complainants did not seek closure of the Church but only control over excessive noise, and that the High Court’s interpretation conflicted with established jurisprudence on public nuisance and noise pollution.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: High Court erred in law in holding that a Church or prayer centre cannot be considered a public place under section 98 of the Code of Criminal Procedure Act. | High Court erred in concluding that noise pollution from religious institutions does not fall within section 98(1)(a) and in disregarding case law on noise pollution and public nuisance. | Respondent failed to make an application under section 98(2) to set aside or modify the conditional order and chose not to call evidence, so the Magistrate correctly made the conditional order absolute. | High Court misappreciated that the complainants sought only to control loud noise and not to shut down religious activities, thereby failing to balance the rights of residents and the respondent. | High Court failed to consider that the respondent’s activities also violated statutory noise control provisions under the Central Environmental Authority Act.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: Before the Magistrate, the court received a police report and took evidence regarding the impact of noise from the Church on residents in the surrounding area, and the Magistrate relied on this material together with legal authorities to issue a conditional order and later make it absolute. The respondent deliberately chose not to lead evidence and instead relied solely on legal submissions challenging the jurisdiction of the Magistrate and the applicability of section 98, which limited the factual basis upon which his challenge could rest. The Court of Appeal considered that the Magistrate had appropriately evaluated the available evidence and legal principles, whereas the High Court mischaracterized the nature of the place and the nuisance despite the material before it.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal focused on whether the legal thresholds for public nuisance and the concept of a public place were met, noting that the evidence of noise affecting nearby residents and the respondent’s refusal to seek modification of the order justified making the conditional order absolute. It treated the respondent’s purely legal challenge as insufficient to outweigh the proven nuisance and emphasized that religious freedom cannot justify persistent noise that infringes on the rights of neighbouring residents.
defence_version_summary: The respondent’s position was that he was conducting religious activities in a duly registered Church and that the sound emitted did not fall within section 98(1)(a) of the Code of Criminal Procedure Act because a Church is not a public place under that provision. He asserted that loudspeakers were not used and that only baffles were employed on occasions with large congregations, such as Sundays, weddings and funerals, contending that the Magistrate lacked jurisdiction and had acted without sufficient evidence and without properly considering both sides. The respondent chose not to call any evidence in the Magistrate’s Court and sought entirely to set aside, rather than modify, the conditional order. The Court of Appeal found his legal arguments unsustainable, held that the Church and its noise could constitute a public nuisance affecting the surrounding public, and considered that his failure to invoke section 98(2) or to seek reasonable modification undermined his position.
legal_errors_description: The Court of Appeal held that the High Court misinterpreted section 98(1)(a) of the Code of Criminal Procedure Act by treating it as applicable only to ways and waterways and by excluding religious institutions from the concept of a public place. It also considered erroneous the High Court’s view that cultural or religious practices permit the use of loudspeakers despite the resulting nuisance and that noise pollution from the Church did not constitute a public nuisance under section 98. In addition, the Court of Appeal held that the High Court failed to appreciate that the Magistrate had followed the correct statutory procedure and that the respondent had not invoked section 98(2) to seek modification of the order.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal carefully analyzed section 98(1)(a) and section 98(4) of the Code of Criminal Procedure Act, concluding that the provision has two limbs and that public nuisance can be addressed not only in relation to ways and waterways but also in relation to any public place, which can include a Church when its activities affect the surrounding public. Relying on the Supreme Court decision in Ashik Vs. Bandula And Others and the older case of Marshall Vs. Gunaratne Unnanse, the Court reaffirmed the secular approach to public nuisance and rejected the notion that religious practices can justify causing annoyance to neighbouring residents through excessive noise. It held that the Magistrate had acted within jurisdiction, had considered evidence and relevant legal principles, and had properly made the conditional order absolute when the respondent declined to lead evidence or seek modification. The Court also drew support from statutory provisions of the Central Environmental Authority Act regulating noise pollution, emphasizing that the respondent could not lawfully use loudspeakers or similar equipment to create excessive noise without an appropriate permit, and therefore restored the Magistrate’s order while setting aside the High Court judgment.
coa_sentence_type: Not applicable; restoration of a conditional order prohibiting use of loudspeakers and loud sound equipment without a valid environmental permit
brief_judgment_file_summary: This revision application was filed by the virtual complainant challenging a judgment of the Provincial High Court of the North Western Province, Chilaw, which had vacated an order of the Chilaw Magistrate made under section 98(1)(a) and 101(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure Act regarding noise pollution from a Church. The Court of Appeal reviewed the background that the Officer-in-Charge of Chilaw Police had sought a conditional order to remove a public nuisance caused by loud religious services, which the Magistrate had first issued and later made absolute after the respondent declined to lead evidence and only made legal submissions. The High Court had held that a Church was not a public place within section 98 and that, given cultural and historical practices, religious institutions could use loudspeakers even if some nuisance resulted, and accordingly vacated the Magistrate’s order. Disagreeing, the Court of Appeal held that section 98 covers public nuisances from any public place including religious institutions, that religious freedom does not shield noise that annoys nearby residents, and that the Magistrate had properly exercised his powers and followed due process, especially in light of noise control provisions under the Central Environmental Authority Act. The Court therefore set aside the High Court judgment dated 21-05-2021, affirmed the Magistrate’s order of 17-10-2017 making the conditional order permanent, and clarified that the respondent remains free to conduct religious activities provided he does not emit loud noise to the open air without obtaining the requisite environmental permit.
prosecution_counsel: Tenney Fernando with Terin Marasinghe for the Petitioner; Lishan Ratnayake, S.C. for the Respondents
defence_counsel: Ranjan Mendis for the Respondent-Appellant-Respondent
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court had reasoned that section 98(1)(a) applies only to public ways and waterways and that religious institutions such as Buddhist temples, churches and Hindu temples are not public places for the purposes of that section, thus finding that the Magistrate lacked jurisdiction to treat noise from the respondent’s Church as a public nuisance. It further distinguished the Supreme Court decision in Ashik Vs. Bandula And Others on the basis of factual differences and relied on cultural and historical practices to justify the use of loudspeakers by religious institutions despite potential annoyance. The Court of Appeal rejected this reasoning, holding that the High Court had misunderstood the structure of section 98, had unduly narrowed the meaning of public place, and had failed to appreciate both the jurisprudence and statutory framework on noise pollution and public nuisance.
precedents_cited_list: Ashik Vs. Bandula And Others (Noise Pollution Case) (2007) 1 SLR 191 | Marshall Vs. Gunaratne Unnanse 1 NLR 179 | In Re Noise Pollution – AIR 205 – SC 3136
standard_of_review_applied: Revisionary review for misdirection on law and erroneous interpretation of section 98 of the Code of Criminal Procedure Act and misappreciation of public nuisance jurisprudence
final_charge_after_appeal: Same as original: public nuisance / noise pollution dealt with by a conditional order under section 98(1)(a) of the Code of Criminal Procedure Act

judges: Menaka Wijesundera J. | Wickum A. Kaluarachchi J.
brief_facts_summary: The accused-appellant, Samarawickrama Liyanage Nandasena, was indicted in the High Court of Matara for the murder of his brother allegedly committed on 2010-04-13 at their home where they shared a well. On the day before the Sinhala New Year, the deceased’s wife (PW-01) heard a shout that the accused had assaulted the deceased, and when she came out she saw the deceased fallen, the accused running away with a mammoty, and another man, Sarath, standing nearby. The deceased was rushed to hospital and died on 2010-04-23 from his injuries. The prosecution relied mainly on the evidence of PW-01, police witnesses, the doctor, and an alleged recovery of a mammoty under Section 27(1) of the Evidence Ordinance, while the accused gave a dock statement and called two defence witnesses.
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court of Matara tried the appellant on a charge of murdering his brother and, after hearing the testimony of PW-01, police officers, and the doctor, found him guilty as charged. The trial judge treated the case as one based on circumstantial evidence, relied on PW-01’s narrative linking the accused to the incident, and gave weight to an alleged discovery of the mammoty under Section 27(1) of the Evidence Ordinance. The judge rejected the dock statement and defence evidence and entered conviction and sentence against the appellant.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant challenged the conviction and sentence on several grounds, including the failure of the prosecution to call a vital witness named Sarath and to disclose the true first statement of PW-01, thereby denying a fair trial. It was argued that the prosecution case, though presented as circumstantial, was not proved beyond reasonable doubt because Sarath’s possible involvement was not excluded and key omissions and contradictions in PW-01’s statements were ignored. The appellant also contended that the trial judge misdirected himself on the law relating to Section 27(1) recoveries and improperly treated the accused as having to prove his innocence. These issues were said to amount to serious procedural and legal errors warranting the setting aside of the conviction.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Prosecution failed to call the vital witness Sarath, whose presence at the scene was spoken to by PW-01, leaving a serious gap in the narrative and an unexcluded alternative hypothesis regarding culpability. | The prosecution failed to disclose and tender the earlier statement of PW-01 made before 2010-04-16, despite PW-01 admitting its existence, thereby depriving the defence of the true first information and undermining the right to a fair trial. | PW-01’s statement of 2010-04-16 contained a fundamental omission about Sarath shouting that the accused assaulted the deceased and a contradiction regarding a dispute over the well, which were not properly appreciated by the trial judge. | The trial judge misdirected himself on Section 27(1) of the Evidence Ordinance by treating the alleged recovery as supporting exclusive possession by the accused, despite serious doubts about the timing and reliability of the alleged discovery of the mammoty. | The trial judge placed an unreasonable burden on the accused by holding that the mere denial in the dock statement did not create a reasonable doubt, thereby undermining the presumption of innocence and the correct burden of proof. | Overall, the prosecution’s circumstantial case was said to be insufficient, with key links missing and vital legal principles on circumstantial evidence, fair disclosure, and evidential evaluation ignored.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal noted that PW-01 was the sole lay prosecution witness and that her testimony contained critical omissions and a contradiction regarding the presence of Sarath and a dispute over the shared well, which the trial judge failed to treat as material. The absence of any statement or testimony from Sarath, who was said to be with the deceased at the time and at the scene when PW-01 arrived, created a serious lacuna in the prosecution case. The court also found that the evidence surrounding the alleged recovery of the mammoty under Section 27(1) was doubtful, particularly in light of PW-01’s evidence that it had already been recovered on an earlier date than that claimed by the police, undermining reliance on that recovery.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal held that, given the non-availability of Sarath’s evidence, the serious omission in PW-01’s first statement about the incriminating shout, and the doubts concerning the weapon recovery, the prosecution had failed to exclude reasonable doubt as to whether someone other than the accused could have committed the offence. It concluded that the circumstantial evidence did not meet the standard of proof beyond reasonable doubt, and therefore the appellant was entitled to the benefit of that doubt.
defence_version_summary: The accused-appellant made a dock statement denying involvement in the incident and called two defence witnesses in support of his position. The High Court treated this dock statement as a mere denial and found that it did not create a reasonable doubt in the prosecution case, effectively placing a burden on the accused to prove his innocence. The Court of Appeal criticized this approach as a misdirection that undermined the presumption of innocence and the correct allocation of the burden of proof.
legal_errors_description: The Court of Appeal identified multiple legal errors, including the trial judge’s misdirection on the proper approach to circumstantial evidence and Section 27(1) recoveries, treating the discovery as establishing exclusive possession rather than merely knowledge of the location. It also held that the trial judge wrongly shifted the burden of proof by expecting the accused’s dock statement to create reasonable doubt, and failed to apply the correct principles regarding the prosecution’s obligation to disclose first information and to call or explain the absence of a vital witness, thereby infringing the appellant’s right to a fair trial.
procedural_defects_description: Procedurally, the prosecution failed to disclose to the defence and the court the earlier statement of PW-01, which constituted the true first information, and did not question police witnesses about it. They also failed to record or tender a statement from Sarath or to explain his absence as a witness, despite his central role in the narrative as described by PW-01. The Court of Appeal regarded these omissions as serious prosecutorial lapses that caused a miscarriage of justice and denied the appellant a fair trial.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal scrutinized the prosecution’s circumstantial case and found that the omission to provide the first statement of PW-01 and to call Sarath, a vital witness present at the scene, created an irreparable gap in the evidence and raised a reasonable doubt about the appellant’s culpability. It emphasized that the trial judge failed to appreciate the material omission concerning the incriminating shout, and the contradiction about a dispute over the well, and that he misapplied Section 114(f) of the Evidence Ordinance by not drawing an adverse inference from the failure to call Sarath. The court also held that the approach to the Section 27(1) recovery of the mammoty was legally flawed and that the judge wrongly burdened the accused by discounting his dock statement merely as a denial. Considering these cumulative defects, the Court of Appeal concluded that the appellant had been denied a fair trial and that the conviction could not safely stand.
coa_sentence_type: None (acquitted)
brief_judgment_file_summary: This appeal from the High Court of Matara concerned a conviction for the murder of the appellant’s brother, based primarily on PW-01’s testimony, police evidence, the doctor’s evidence, and an alleged Section 27(1) recovery of a mammoty said to be the weapon. The Court of Appeal found that the prosecution and the trial judge failed to address critical omissions and contradictions in PW-01’s statements, and that the non-calling of Sarath, a key eyewitness in the narrative, created a serious lacuna in the case which the prosecution did not explain, engaging Section 114(f) of the Evidence Ordinance. It further held that the trial judge misdirected himself on the law relating to Section 27(1) by treating the recovery as confirming exclusive possession of the weapon, and improperly shifted the burden of proof by dismissing the dock statement as a mere denial. Concluding that these errors and lapses denied the appellant a fair trial and that the circumstantial case did not exclude reasonable doubt, the Court of Appeal allowed the appeal and acquitted the accused-appellant.
prosecution_counsel: Anoopa De Silva, DSG for the Respondent
defence_counsel: Sarath Jayamanne P.C., with Vineshka Mendis, Prashan Wickramaratne, Sajeewa Meegahawaththa, Dakshin Abeykoon and Dinidu Rathnayake for the Accused-Appellant
cause_of_death_exact_text: The deceased was rushed to hospital and succumbed to his injuries on 2010-04-23 following the incident.
hc_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal held that the High Court had failed to apply the basic principles governing circumstantial evidence, including the need to rule out any reasonable possibility that someone other than the accused committed the crime. It found that the trial judge had not given due weight to the omission of the incriminating shout from the first recorded statement, the contradiction about a dispute over the well, or the prosecution’s failure to call Sarath or explain his absence. The Court of Appeal also criticized the High Court’s treatment of the Section 27(1) recovery and its approach to the accused’s dock statement, concluding that these misdirections vitiated the conviction.
precedents_cited_list: Wijepala v The Attorney General (2000) 1 Sri L.R. 46 | Walimunige John and another v The State 76 NLR 488 | Etin Singho and another v The Queen 69 NLR 353 | Veerasamy Sivathasan v Honourable Attorney General SC Appeal 208/2012
standard_of_review_applied: Failure to evaluate circumstantial evidence and omissions properly, misdirection on Section 27(1) recovery, and denial of fair trial and constitutional safeguards
final_charge_after_appeal: Murder (original charge; conviction set aside on appeal)

judges: P. Kumararatnam J. | R. P. Hettiarachchi J.
offence_sections: Section 365B(2)(b) and Section 364(2) of the Penal Code as amended by Acts No.29 of 1998 and No.16 of 2016
offence_category: Grave sexual abuse and statutory rape
location_of_offence: At the victim's house within the jurisdiction of the High Court of Monaragala
brief_facts_summary: The appellant, a mason, was engaged in masonry work at the victim's house when the alleged incident occurred. The prosecution alleged that when the victim's parents were absent, the appellant sent the victim's elder brother to buy cigarettes and then inserted his finger into the vagina of the 9 year old victim. The brother allegedly witnessed the appellant leaving the room and informed their mother, who lodged a police complaint the same day. The Judicial Medical Officer later opined that there was no vaginal penetration but did not exclude inter labia penetration.
evidence_type_primary: Child eyewitness testimony of the victim and testimonial evidence regarding the brother's observation
evidence_type_secondary: Evidence of the victim's mother about the complaint and medical evidence from the Judicial Medical Officer
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 365B(2)(b) of the Penal Code as amended
hc_sentence_type: Rigorous Imprisonment 8 years plus fine and compensation
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court Judge convicted the appellant on the first charge of grave sexual abuse under Section 365B(2)(b), primarily relying on the testimony of the child victim. After receiving submissions on sentencing, the court imposed 8 years rigorous imprisonment, a fine, and compensation to the victim, while acquitting the appellant on the second charge of statutory rape. The High Court thus accepted the prosecution version as having proved the first charge beyond reasonable doubt.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant contended that the victim's initial testimony clearly denying any abuse and her later changed evidence, which matched her police statement after almost a year, created a reasonable doubt and suggested tutoring. He argued that his right to a fair trial was violated when part of the victim's evidence was taken in the judge's chambers and the victim's mother was summoned there. The appellant further complained that the prosecution failed to call the victim's elder brother, an alleged eyewitness, that the victim's evidence was not corroborated by medical evidence, and that PW1's evidence lacked independent corroboration and did not inspire confidence. Collectively, these grounds challenged both the reliability of the child's testimony and the fairness and completeness of the trial process.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Victim initially denied any abuse but nearly a year later gave evidence consistent with her police statement, suggesting possible tutoring or influence and creating reasonable doubt. | Part of the victim's testimony was taken in the judge's chambers and the mother (PW2) was summoned there, allegedly denying the appellant a fair and public trial. | Prosecution failed to summon the victim's elder brother, described as an eyewitness, thereby warranting an adverse inference under Section 114(f) of the Evidence Ordinance. | The victim's evidence was not corroborated by any medical evidence, particularly in light of the JMO's opinion on lack of vaginal penetration. | PW1's evidence was not corroborated from any independent source and did not inspire confidence, so the prosecution failed to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The key prosecution witness was the child victim, whose initial reluctance and testimony indicated only an attempt and later, after an 11 month adjournment, changed to align with her police statement. PW2, the mother, gave hearsay evidence that her son informed her of the incident and that she then complained to the police, but the son himself, identified as an eyewitness, was never called. The Judicial Medical Officer stated there was no vaginal penetration though inter labia penetration could not be excluded, which did not strongly corroborate the prosecution version of abuse. The Court of Appeal found that the uncorroborated and ambiguous testimony of the child, coupled with the absence of the brother's evidence, rendered the prosecution case unreliable.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal held that the probabilities did not favour the prosecution because the victim's evidence was unclear and changed over time, and because an essential eyewitness, her brother, was not called to corroborate the incident. In these circumstances, the court found that the prosecution failed to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt and that the appellant was entitled to the benefit of the doubt.
defence_version_summary: The appellant did not call any defence witnesses and relied solely on a dock statement made at the close of the prosecution case. The judgment does not set out the detailed contents of this dock statement, and there is no indication that any alibi or specific alternative narrative was advanced through other evidence. The High Court effectively rejected the defence by convicting, but the Court of Appeal allowed the appeal not because it accepted a positive defence version, but because it found the prosecution evidence insufficient and unreliable.
legal_errors_description: The Court of Appeal held that the High Court erred in convicting the appellant on the uncorroborated and ambiguous evidence of the child victim without properly evaluating her credibility, particularly in light of her changed testimony after a long adjournment. It also found fault in the failure to call the victim's brother, an essential eyewitness, thereby ignoring a serious evidentiary gap. These errors rendered the conviction unsafe as the prosecution had not discharged its burden of proof beyond reasonable doubt.
procedural_defects_description: Part of the victim's evidence was taken in the judge's chambers and the victim's mother was summoned there, rather than conducting the proceedings fully in open court or formally in camera as contemplated by Article 106. The trial was adjourned for approximately 11 months based on an informal observation of the child's supposed psychological condition without obtaining any medical report, causing prejudice to the appellant and creating an opportunity for tutoring.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal scrutinised the victim's testimony and noted that on the first day she spoke only of an attempt and did not describe a completed sexual act, and that after an 11 month delay her evidence shifted to match her police statement, suggesting possible influence. It emphasised that the victim's brother, who allegedly witnessed the appellant leaving the room and recounted the incident to the mother, was an essential witness whose absence deprived the court of crucial corroborative evidence. Relying on authorities concerning the assessment of child witnesses and the need for corroboration in sexual offence cases, the court concluded that the evidence of PW1 lacked clarity, consistency, and probability and was further undermined by the failure to call the brother. Accordingly, the court held that the prosecution had failed to prove the charge beyond reasonable doubt, set aside the conviction and sentence, and acquitted the appellant.
coa_sentence_type: No sentence, conviction set aside upon acquittal
brief_judgment_file_summary: This Court of Appeal judgment concerns an appeal from a conviction in the High Court of Monaragala where the appellant was found guilty of grave sexual abuse of a 9 year old girl under Section 365B(2)(b) of the Penal Code and sentenced to 8 years rigorous imprisonment, a fine, and compensation. The appellant challenged the conviction on the basis of the victim's inconsistent and delayed testimony, the conduct of part of the proceedings in chambers, the failure to call the victim's elder brother as an eyewitness, and lack of medical and independent corroboration. The Court of Appeal analysed the legal framework for in camera proceedings, the duties of a trial judge in assessing child witness credibility, and the importance of calling essential witnesses, citing several precedents on corroboration and the prudence required in sexual offence trials. Concluding that the victim's evidence was ambiguous and uncorroborated and that the absence of the brother's testimony created a serious evidentiary gap, the court held that the prosecution had not proved the case beyond reasonable doubt, allowed the appeal, and acquitted the appellant, setting aside the High Court conviction and sentence.
defence_counsel: Darshana Kuruppu with Tharushi Gamage, Anjana Adhikaramge, Sahan Weerasinghe and Pramuditha Senevirathne
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court appears to have accepted the victim's later version of events and convicted on the basis of her testimony without adequately addressing the earlier denial of abuse or the long intervening delay. It treated the child's evidence as sufficient despite the JMO's opinion that there was no vaginal penetration and despite not having the alleged eyewitness brother testify. The Court of Appeal criticised this approach, finding that the High Court failed to properly assess the credibility and reliability of the child witness and to recognise the evidentiary significance of the missing eyewitness, rendering the conviction unsafe.
precedents_cited_list: Ranjeet Kumar Ram v. State of Bihar [2015] SCC Online SC 500 | King v. Seneviratne 38 NLR 208 | Sunil and others v. Attorney General [1986] 1 S.L.R 230 | Premasiri v. Attorney General [2006] 3 Sri L.R | State of Andra Pradesh v. Garigula Satya Vani Murty AIR 1997 SC 1588
standard_of_review_applied: Failure to properly evaluate and corroborate the evidence of a child witness, failure to call an essential eyewitness, and conviction being unsafe as the prosecution had not proved the case beyond reasonable doubt.
final_charge_after_appeal: Grave sexual abuse under Section 365B(2)(b) of the Penal Code, with the conviction set aside on appeal and the appellant acquitted

judges: Amal Ranaraja J | B. Sasi Mahendran J
offence_sections: Section 70 of the Bribery Act No. 11 of 1954 (as amended); Section 102 of the Penal Code read together with Section 70 of the Bribery Act No. 11 of 1954 (as amended)
brief_facts_summary: The Commission to Investigate Allegations of Bribery or Corruption directed the Director-General to institute proceedings in the Magistrates Court of Colombo in 2017 against the first accused, then Director-General of the National Rupavahini Corporation, for corruption under section 70 of the Bribery Act, and against the second accused for abetment under section 102 of the Penal Code read with section 70. During the Magistrates Court trial, after PW1 had testified and PW2 had begun giving evidence, the defence objected on the basis that the Commission had not collectively authorized the institution of proceedings, relying on the Supreme Court decision in Anoma Polwatta. The Director-General then withdrew the Magistrates Court case, and the Magistrate treated this as a withdrawal under section 189 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and acquitted the accused in July 2021. A subsequent indictment on the same charges was filed in the High Court of Colombo in August 2022, but the High Court Judge rejected the indictment and discharged the accused on the footing that the prior acquittal barred further proceedings, leading to this revision application.
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court of Colombo held that the accused had already been acquitted by the Magistrates Court on charges identical to those in the High Court indictment. Relying on section 314 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and the principle that a person should not be tried twice for the same offence, the Judge concluded that the indictment could not be maintained while the earlier acquittal subsisted. Accordingly, the indictment was rejected and the accused were discharged.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The petitioner contended that the High Court erred in law in treating the Magistrates Court order as an acquittal attracting the protection of section 314 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. It was argued that the accused had not been 'tried' within the meaning of section 314, as there had been no full opportunity for both sides to lead evidence, and that the Magistrates Court order made upon withdrawal under section 189 did not preclude a subsequent indictment. The petitioner further relied on Supreme Court authority, including SC Appeal No. 12A/2009, to clarify the meaning of 'tried' and the scope of autrefois acquit in the Sri Lankan context. On this basis, the petitioner sought revision of the High Court order and restoration of the indictment.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: High Court misapplied section 314 of the Code of Criminal Procedure in holding that the Magistrates Court order constituted an acquittal that barred a subsequent indictment. | Accused were not 'tried' for purposes of section 314 because there was no full evidentiary proceeding affording both prosecution and defence the opportunity to lead evidence. | An acquittal upon withdrawal under section 189 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, in circumstances where evidence has not been fully led, does not attract the plea of autrefois acquit. | High Court failed to correctly interpret and apply Supreme Court authority, including SC Appeal No. 12A/2009, on the meaning of 'tried' in section 314.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal noted that in the Magistrates Court proceedings PW1 had completed his testimony and PW2 was in the process of giving evidence when the defence raised an objection as to the maintainability of the case. The Director-General then withdrew the case and the Magistrate acquitted the accused under section 189, meaning that neither side had a full opportunity to lead all their evidence. The Court emphasized that this lack of a complete evidentiary process meant that the accused had not been 'tried' within the meaning of section 314.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal did not assess factual probabilities or weigh guilt versus innocence, as the case turned entirely on a point of law about double jeopardy and the meaning of 'tried' under section 314. Its analysis focused on whether the earlier acquittal legally barred the High Court indictment rather than on the strength of the underlying evidence.
defence_version_summary: At the preliminary stage the accused, through counsel, argued that they had already been acquitted by the Magistrates Court on the same charges and that this acquittal, not having been overturned, constituted a final verdict. They claimed that section 314 of the Code of Criminal Procedure therefore prohibited any further trial on the same facts, and on this basis sought to have the High Court indictment rejected and themselves discharged. No separate alibi, dock statement, or defence witnesses were discussed in the Court of Appeal judgment, which dealt solely with this legal objection.
legal_errors_description: The Court of Appeal found that the High Court Judge misdirected himself in law by treating the Magistrates Court order made upon withdrawal as an acquittal falling within section 314, and by concluding that the accused had been 'tried' so as to attract the pleas of autrefois acquit or double jeopardy. It held that, given the absence of a full opportunity for both prosecution and defence to lead evidence, the statutory requirements of section 314 had not been satisfied and the High Court’s rejection of the indictment was erroneous.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed section 314 of the Code of Criminal Procedure in light of the maxim 'nemo debet bis vexari pro una et eadem causa' and the pleas of autrefois acquit and autrefois convict. Drawing on Supreme Court authority, particularly SC Appeal No. 12A/2009, it held that a person is 'tried' for purposes of section 314 only where there has been an evidentiary proceeding in which both sides had an opportunity to adduce some evidence. Because the Magistrates Court case had been withdrawn after only partial prosecution evidence and without a full evidentiary trial, the resulting acquittal did not fall within section 314 and did not bar a subsequent indictment on the same facts. Accordingly, the Court concluded that the High Court had misapplied the law and set aside the order discharging the accused, directing that the High Court restore the case and proceed to conclusion.
brief_judgment_file_summary: This revision application by the Director-General of the Commission to Investigate Allegations of Bribery or Corruption challenged an order of the High Court of Colombo rejecting an indictment and discharging two accused on bribery and abetment charges under section 70 of the Bribery Act and section 102 of the Penal Code. The High Court had accepted the defence contention that an earlier Magistrates Court acquittal, following withdrawal of proceedings under section 189 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, barred the indictment under section 314. The Court of Appeal examined the legal principles of double jeopardy and the meaning of 'tried' in section 314, relying on case law and academic commentary to conclude that an acquittal without a full evidentiary trial does not attract the protection of that provision. It therefore held that the High Court Judge had misdirected himself, set aside the order of 05 January 2024, dismissed the objection to the indictment, and directed the High Court to restore the case to the roll and proceed with the trial.
prosecution_counsel: Anusha Sammandapperuma, Assistant Director Legal with Kajalakshi Sivasasramaniam and Gaya Rajapaksha for the Petitioner
defence_counsel: Senarath Jayasundara with Sheshan Rathnayake and Chathurangi Wadege for the 1st and 2nd Accused-Respondents
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court of Colombo accepted the defence objection that the accused had already been acquitted by the Magistrates Court on identical charges and that this prior acquittal, not having been set aside, barred further proceedings under section 314 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. On that basis the High Court rejected the indictment and discharged the accused. The Court of Appeal held that this reasoning was flawed because the Magistrates Court acquittal, made following a withdrawal under section 189 in the absence of a full evidentiary trial, did not satisfy the statutory concept of having been 'tried' for purposes of section 314 and thus could not operate as a bar to a new indictment.
precedents_cited_list: Anoma Polwatta v. The Commission to Investigate Allegations of Bribery or Corruption – SC/Writ Application No. 01/2011 | SC Appeal No. 12A/2009 – Supreme Court of Sri Lanka, decided on 2011-05-05
standard_of_review_applied: Misdirection on law and erroneous application of section 314 of the Code of Criminal Procedure regarding double jeopardy and autrefois acquit
final_charge_after_appeal: Same as original indictment: corruption under section 70 of the Bribery Act No. 11 of 1954 (as amended) against the 1st accused and abetment under section 102 of the Penal Code read with section 70 of the Bribery Act against the 2nd accused

judges: Pradeep Hettiarachchi | P Kumararatnam
offence_sections: Section 54A(b) and Section 54A(d) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance (as amended)
offence_category: Heroin trafficking and possession of dangerous drugs
location_of_offence: Ratmalana, in and around Sumangala Mawatha and Aththidiya Road area
brief_facts_summary: The STF received information from an informant that a person known as 'Ratmalane Ratnapala' would arrive on a motorcycle at Sumangala Mawatha carrying heroin. Acting on this tip, a team of STF officers went to the Aththidiya/Maliban Junction area, positioned themselves near a Keells supermarket and Sumangala Mawatha, and stopped the appellant when he arrived on his motorcycle. On searching him, PW1 recovered a newspaper-wrapped parcel concealed in the appellant's groin area, which contained a cellophane bag of brown substance that a field test indicated was heroin weighing 20.430 grams. The High Court accepted the STF officers' evidence, convicted the appellant for trafficking and possession of heroin, and imposed life imprisonment, which led to this appeal.
evidence_type_primary: Police eyewitness testimony of STF officers regarding the raid, search, and recovery of heroin
evidence_type_secondary: Forensic/chemical testing of the substance and documentary/police notebook evidence relating to the raid and handling of productions
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 54A(b) and Section 54A(d) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance (as amended)
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court of Colombo convicted the appellant on both counts of trafficking and possessing 2.16 g of heroin, accepting the evidence of the STF officers as credible and sufficient to prove the charges beyond reasonable doubt. The court imposed a sentence of life imprisonment on the appellant. It also noted the absence of any plausible explanation from the defence and treated that as supporting the prosecution case.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant challenged the High Court judgment primarily on the basis that the learned High Court Judge failed to consider vital contradictions and inconsistencies in the evidence of the key prosecution witnesses (particularly PW1, PW2, and PW5), and wrongly concluded that they fully corroborated each other. It was argued that these contradictions, especially regarding the place where the informant was met and how the crime notebooks were issued and used, went to the root of the prosecution case and created reasonable doubt. The appellant further contended that the sentence of life imprisonment was excessive and ought to be revisited in light of Act No. 41 of 2022.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The High Court failed to properly consider vital contradictions between the testimonies of PW1, PW2, and PW5 regarding the location of the Keells supermarket, where the informant was met, and where the jeep was parked. | The prosecution evidence on the process of issuing and using crime notebooks and on the officers' note-taking was contradictory and not adequately scrutinized by the trial judge. | The learned High Court Judge wrongly concluded that the prosecution witnesses fully corroborated each other and that their credibility with respect to material facts was never challenged. | The sentence of life imprisonment imposed on the appellant was excessive in view of the amendments introduced by Act No. 41 of 2022.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: Five prosecution witnesses testified, including STF officers involved in the raid, while the defence called no witnesses. The Court of Appeal closely examined the evidence of PW1, PW2 and PW5 and found material inter se contradictions as to where the Keells supermarket was located (Aththidiya Road vs. Galle Road), where the jeep was parked, and where and how the informant met the officers. There were further inconsistencies about the issuance and possession of crime notebooks and whether PW1 had recorded key information, which the Court of Appeal held undermined the credibility of the prosecution case and created reasonable doubt.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal held that the material contradictions among the key STF witnesses, particularly concerning the receipt of crucial information and the handling and documentation of the raid, created a reasonable doubt that must enure to the benefit of the accused. It reiterated that the prosecution must stand or fall on its own evidence and cannot rely on weaknesses in the defence to cure gaps in its case.
