Concluding that the prosecution had failed to prove the case beyond reasonable doubt and that the Appellant had been denied a fair trial, the Court of Appeal set aside the conviction and sentence and acquitted the Appellant.
prosecution_counsel: Maheshika Silva, DSG, for the Respondent
defence_counsel: Neranjan Jayasinghe with Harshana Ananda and Imansi Senarath for the Appellant
cause_of_death_exact_text: Not applicable; this case concerns drug trafficking and possession, not a homicide.
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court had convicted the Appellant by accepting the police account of the raid and recovery of heroin and by rejecting the defence version without adequately engaging with the defence evidence. The Court of Appeal held that the High Court misdirected itself in finding that PW1 and PW6 had not denied, or had admitted, the prior arrest of Rizwan, and in ignoring contradictions between their evidence as to the manner of recovery of heroin from the Appellant. It concluded that the High Court failed in its duty to weigh prosecution and defence evidence on an equal footing and that its approach to the defence witnesses and factual findings seriously compromised the fairness and reliability of the verdict.
precedents_cited_list: Mohamed Nimnaz v Attorney General CA/95/94 | Attorney-General v Rawther 25 NLR 385 | Miller v Minister of Pensions (1947) 2 All E.R. 372 | R v Hepworth 1928 (AD) 265 | Sisilinona v Balasuriya [2002] 1 SLR 404 | The Queen v David Perera 66 NLR 553 | Gamage v Attorney General and Others [2020] 1 SLR 44
standard_of_review_applied: Assessment of whether the prosecution case was proved beyond reasonable doubt, scrutiny for misdirection in evaluating evidence, failure to consider material contradictions, and denial of a fair trial through improper judicial intervention.
final_charge_after_appeal: Same as original: trafficking and possession of heroin under Sections 54 (A) (b) and 54 (A) (d) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance, but charges not proved and Appellant acquitted.

judges: Amal Ranaraja, J. | Sampath B. Abayakoon, J.
offence_sections: Section 54A(b) and Section 54A(d) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance as amended by Act No. 13 of 1984
offence_category: Trafficking and possession of heroin (dangerous drugs)
location_of_offence: W. A. De Silva Mawatha, Wellawatta, Colombo
brief_facts_summary: Two accused were indicted in the High Court of Colombo for trafficking and possessing 9.77 grams of diacetyl morphine (heroin) at Wellawatta on 14 February 2015, based on a tip-off received by narcotics bureau officers. A police team with an informant conducted surveillance near a bookshop at W. A. De Silva Mawatha, stopped a threewheel scooter, and seized a parcel of heroin mixed powder from the 1st accused, later confirmed by the Government Analyst. After trial, the High Court convicted the 1st accused on both counts and sentenced him to life imprisonment on each count, while acquitting the 2nd accused.
evidence_type_secondary: Forensic evidence (Government Analyst report on heroin mixed powder)
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 54A(b) and Section 54A(d) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance as amended by Act No. 13 of 1984
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court of Colombo found the 1st accused guilty of trafficking and possessing 9.77 grams of diacetyl morphine under Section 54A(b) and 54A(d), relying primarily on the testimony of narcotics bureau officers and the analyst report. It sentenced him to life imprisonment on each charge and acquitted the 2nd accused of all charges.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant contended that the High Court misdirected itself in law by shifting a burden onto him to rebut the prosecution case and by failing to apply the test of probability to the prosecution version. He argued that the judge ignored a vital contradiction in PW1's description of the heroin parcel and failed to appreciate that the prosecution's narrative was inherently improbable. He further complained that the High Court did not properly evaluate his dock statement in line with appellate guidelines.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Alleged misdirection in law by casting a burden on the accused-appellant to rebut the prosecution case. | Failure by the High Court Judge to consider a vital self-contradiction in PW1's evidence regarding the description of the parcel containing heroin. | Failure to assess the prosecution case using the test of probability and improbability, leading to acceptance of an inherently improbable police narrative. | Failure to reach a proper conclusion regarding the appellant's dock statement in accordance with guidelines laid down by the Court of Appeal.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal closely scrutinised the testimony of PW1 and PW2, both narcotics bureau officers, and found their narrative about taking the informant to the location and exposing his identity to be unusual and improbable. It held that the High Court failed to apply the test of probability and improbability when assessing these trained police witnesses, contrary to established authorities. The Court also treated PW1's inconsistent descriptions of the parcel (regarding the colour and arrangement of the plastic bags) as a material self-contradiction undermining his credibility, which the High Court had wrongly dismissed as a mere typographical error.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal held that the prosecution version was bizarre and improbable, particularly the conduct of the officers in exposing the informant and not stopping the threewheel at the earliest opportunity. Applying the test of probability and improbability to the evidence of trained police officers, it concluded that serious doubt arose as to the certainty and trustworthiness of their testimony, so the prosecution had not proved the case beyond reasonable doubt.
defence_version_summary: The defence rested primarily on a dock statement by the appellant, the contents of which are not detailed in the judgment summary. One of the grounds of appeal was that the High Court failed to evaluate this dock statement in line with appellate guidance; however, the Court of Appeal ultimately allowed the appeal on the basis of the improbability and contradictions in the prosecution evidence and therefore did not find it necessary to analyse the dock statement in detail. There is no indication of any defence witnesses being called.
legal_errors_description: The Court of Appeal found that the High Court misdirected itself by failing to apply the test of probability and improbability to the evidence of PW1 and PW2, both trained police officers, and by accepting an improbable narrative without adequate scrutiny. It also held that the High Court erred in dismissing PW1's material self-contradiction about the parcel as a typographical error despite the correction of proceedings and lack of prosecutorial clarification, thereby wrongly assessing witness credibility.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal examined the surveillance and arrest narrative and found the conduct of PW1 and PW2 in taking the informant to the vicinity of the transaction and exposing him to the suspects to be contrary to normal precautions, rendering their account improbable. Relying on authorities cautioning against uncritical acceptance of trained police officers' testimony, it held that the High Court failed to apply the test of probability and improbability and should have viewed their evidence with greater scepticism. The Court further considered PW1's inconsistency about the colour and configuration of the parcel as a material contradiction affecting credibility, rejecting the High Court's characterisation of it as a typographical error. Concluding that the prosecution evidence did not prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt and that the credibility of key witnesses was in serious doubt, it declined to order a retrial and acquitted the appellant.
coa_sentence_type: Acquitted - no sentence imposed
brief_judgment_file_summary: This appeal concerned the conviction of the 1st accused by the High Court of Colombo for trafficking and possessing 9.77 grams of diacetyl morphine at Wellawatta, based solely on a narcotics bureau raid and the testimony of police officers corroborated by an analyst report. The Court of Appeal analysed the factual narrative, especially the unusual decision to take the informant to the scene and expose him to the suspects, and found the officers' conduct and account of events to be bizarre and improbable. It also treated PW1's inconsistent descriptions of the parcel containing heroin as a material contradiction that the High Court had improperly discounted as a typographical error. Applying the test of probability and caution towards trained police witnesses, the Court held that the prosecution had failed to establish guilt beyond reasonable doubt, refused to order a retrial, allowed the appeal, and acquitted the appellant.
prosecution_counsel: Anoopa De Silva, Deputy Solicitor General, for the State
defence_counsel: Shanaka Ranasinghe, President's Counsel, with Niroshan Mihindukulasuriya for the Accused-Appellant
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court accepted the police officers' version of the raid and seizure at face value, relying on their testimony and the analyst report to convict the 1st accused and impose life sentences on each count while acquitting the 2nd accused. In reviewing this reasoning, the Court of Appeal held that the High Court had failed to evaluate the probability of the officers' conduct and to apply the test of probability and improbability to their evidence. It further faulted the High Court for treating PW1's clear self-contradiction about the description of the parcel as a mere typographical error, thereby misdirecting itself in its assessment of credibility and contributing to an unsafe conviction.
precedents_cited_list: Anthony Michael Morril v. Attorney General – CA 26/06, decided on 25.05.2010 | Wickremasuriya v. Dedoleena and Others – [1996] 2 SLR 95 | Nallaperuma Danuka Roshan v. Attorney General – CA 216/15, decided on 12.10.2017 | Sinnaiya Kalidasa v. Attorney General – CA 128/2005, decided on 07.09.2010 | K. Padmatillake alias Sergeant Elpitiya v. The Director General, Commission to Investigate Allegations of Bribery or Corruption – SC Appeal 99/2007, S.C. Minute dated 30.07.2009
standard_of_review_applied: Failure to properly evaluate evidence and credibility, particularly by not applying the test of probability and improbability to trained police witnesses and by basing the conviction on an improbable and contradicted narrative.
final_charge_after_appeal: Same as original charges under Section 54A(b) and Section 54A(d) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance, but the appellant was acquitted.

judges: K.M.G.H. Kulatunga, J | Menaka Wijesundera, J
offence_sections: Section 383 read with Section 32 of the Penal Code; Section 44(a) of the Firearms Ordinance
brief_facts_summary: The 2nd and 4th accused, together with others, robbed cash and gold necklaces from employees and bystanders at the Kandy Sweet boutique in Sedawatta on 27.11.1997, using a pistol and a knife. The premises included a shop, sweet factory, and house, and the robbery occurred in the late afternoon while the victims were at work. Several witnesses identified the accused as part of the group that entered the business, threatened staff, and removed money and jewellery. Police investigations, Section 27 statements, and an identification parade led to the indictment and eventual conviction of the appellants for robbery.
evidence_type_secondary: Police testimony, Section 27 discovery statements, physical exhibits, and identification parade notes
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 383 read with Section 32 of the Penal Code (robbery) on counts 6 and 8, though initially framed with Section 44(a) of the Firearms Ordinance
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court of Colombo tried the accused on charges of robbery associated with firearms and ultimately convicted the 2nd and 4th accused on counts 6 and 8 as lesser offences of robbery under the Penal Code. The trial judge had earlier held that the use of a firearm was not proved, declined to proceed under the Firearms Ordinance, but imposed life imprisonment and a fine of 20,000 on each count for each appellant. The judgment did not clearly record that the convictions were for Penal Code robbery, leading to confusion later corrected by the Court of Appeal.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellants initially filed appeals against both conviction and sentence but, at the hearing, expressly abandoned the challenge to conviction and pursued only sentence. Counsel argued that life imprisonment could not be maintained where the operative conviction was for robbery under Section 383 of the Penal Code and that an appropriate lesser custodial term should be imposed. It was also contended, and conceded by the State, that the High Court had misdescribed the convictions with reference to Firearms Ordinance counts despite having found no prima facie case under that law. The long delay between offence, indictment, conviction, and appeal was relied on as a factor warranting reduction of sentence.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Appeals originally lodged against both conviction and sentence, but at argument limited to challenging only the sentences. | Contention that the operative conviction was for robbery under Section 383 of the Penal Code and that a sentence of life imprisonment was legally inappropriate and excessive. | Complaint that the High Court judgment misdescribed the convictions by referring to Firearms Ordinance counts despite the trial judge having excluded those charges earlier. | Reliance on prolonged delay between the 1997 offence, 2004 indictment, 2023 conviction, and pending appeals as mitigation for sentence reduction.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The prosecution relied primarily on the testimonies of employees and bystanders at the Kandy Sweet premises, who described how a group of men loitered, then entered armed with a pistol and knife, threatened staff, and robbed cash and necklaces. Their evidence was supported by police officers who spoke to the investigation, discovery under Section 27, and an identification parade at which the appellants were identified. The defence consisted only of dock statements alleging improper exposure to witnesses before the identification parade, but these matters had not been put to the police witnesses in cross-examination, and the courts treated the prosecution evidence as credible and consistent.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal accepted that the robbery was a pre-planned, armed crime against vulnerable shop employees, and emphasised the seriousness and societal impact of such conduct while still recognising the lengthy passage of time and the appellants ongoing remand as mitigating factors. The court did not entertain any reasonable doubt about the appellants involvement but focused on calibrating sentence proportionately to the offence and surrounding circumstances.
defence_version_summary: Both the 2nd and 4th accused gave dock statements, with the 2nd accused claiming he had been arrested near Grandpass in December 1997, brought to the sweet factory, and shown to witnesses before being produced at the identification parade. No defence witnesses were called and these allegations were not challenged through cross-examination of the police witnesses or objections at trial. The courts therefore accorded little weight to the dock statements, treating them as uncorroborated and inconsistent with the prosecution case.
legal_errors_description: The Court of Appeal identified that, although the trial judge had found no prima facie case under the Firearms Ordinance and called for the defence only on Penal Code robbery counts, the final High Court judgment erroneously recorded convictions under Firearms Ordinance counts. The appellate court corrected this by varying the judgment to specify convictions for the lesser offence of robbery under Section 383 read with Section 32 of the Penal Code. It also held that life imprisonment was not an appropriate or lawful sentence for those lesser offences and substituted a determinate term of rigorous imprisonment.
procedural_defects_description: There was a misdescription in the High Court judgment where the appellants were shown as convicted under Firearms Ordinance counts despite the defence having been called only on Penal Code robbery counts and no prima facie case found for firearm use. This created ambiguity in the recorded basis of conviction, which the Court of Appeal rectified by expressly varying the conviction to Penal Code robbery. No other significant procedural defects in the conduct of the trial were identified.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal first clarified that, on a proper reading of the High Court record and reasoning, the appellants had been found guilty of robbery under Section 383 of the Penal Code, not of firearm offences, and formally varied the judgment to reflect convictions for the lesser offences. It then considered sentencing in light of the statutory maximum of 20 years for robbery committed while armed with knives, the pre-planned nature of the crime, the vulnerability of the victims, and the broader societal impact of armed robberies on commercial activity. Balancing these aggravating factors against the 17 to 18 year delay in finalising the case, the appellants middle age, lack of previous convictions, and time already spent in remand, the court reduced the sentence from life imprisonment to four years rigorous imprisonment on each relevant count, ordered compensation to the victims, and directed that two years already in custody be credited under Section 333(5), resulting in a final aggregate sentence of two years rigorous imprisonment.
coa_sentence_type: Four years rigorous imprisonment on each of two robbery counts to run concurrently, with two years credited as time served and compensation ordered in default recoverable as a fine
brief_judgment_file_summary: This Court of Appeal judgment concerns sentence-only appeals by the 2nd and 4th accused who had been convicted by the High Court of Colombo for an armed robbery committed at the Kandy Sweet boutique in Sedawatta in November 1997. The appellate court recounted the facts of the robbery, the eyewitness and police evidence, and the High Court finding that firearm use was not proved, before noting that the trial judge had nevertheless misdescribed the convictions by reference to Firearms Ordinance counts. Correcting the record, the Court of Appeal held that the appellants were in law convicted of robbery under Section 383 read with Section 32 of the Penal Code and that life imprisonment imposed for those offences was unduly severe. Taking into account the seriousness of the pre-planned robbery, the long delay, the appellants personal circumstances, and the time spent in remand, the court substituted concurrent terms of four years rigorous imprisonment on each count, ordered compensation to two victims, gave credit for two years custodial time already served, and thereby fixed the final aggregate sentence at two years rigorous imprisonment while partially allowing the appeals.
prosecution_counsel: Udara Karunathilaka, Senior State Counsel for the Attorney General
defence_counsel: Nihara Randeniya for the 2nd Accused-Appellant; Sachithra Harshana for the 4th Accused-Appellant
cause_of_death_exact_text: Not applicable, as this case concerns robbery and no death or medical cause of death was in issue.
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court concluded that there was no prima facie case under the Firearms Ordinance, declined to proceed with those counts, and called for the defence only on Penal Code robbery counts, yet its written judgment ambiguously referenced Firearms Ordinance provisions when recording the convictions. It nonetheless accepted the eyewitness and police evidence, rejected the dock statements as unsubstantiated, and convicted the 2nd and 4th accused for the robbery counts. The Court of Appeal noted these features, accepted that the High Court had in substance treated the case as one of armed robbery under Section 383, but corrected the misdescription of the offences and reassessed the appropriateness of the life sentences imposed.
standard_of_review_applied: Appellate review of sentencing discretion and correction of a misdescribed conviction, examining whether the sentence of life imprisonment was lawful and proportionate to a robbery offence under Section 383 and whether the High Court properly recorded the legal basis of conviction.
sentencing_principles_applied: The Court applied principles of proportionality between offence and punishment, the need for deterrent sentences for serious armed robberies affecting commercial activity, and the relevance of mitigation such as inordinate delay, middle age of the offenders, absence of previous convictions, and time already spent in custody, including credit for remand periods under Section 333(5) of the Criminal Procedure Code.
final_charge_after_appeal: Robbery under Section 383 read with Section 32 of the Penal Code

judges: Menaka Wijesundera J | K.M.G.H. Kulatunga J
offence_sections: Section 296
brief_facts_summary: The appellant and the deceased were neighbours living in congested tenements at Weligoda in the Grandpass area, and there had been prior disputes involving the appellant, his mother, and the deceased's daughter-in-law. On the night of 13 May 2008, after an earlier altercation and hospital treatment for the daughter-in-law, PW1 (the widow) saw the appellant run towards their house armed with a club and warned her husband to run. She testified that she then saw the appellant pursue the deceased towards a tea boutique and deliver a single blow with the club to the deceased's head, after which nobody else assaulted him. Police later recovered a club from the appellant's house on a statement made by him, and the High Court convicted him of murder and sentenced him to death mainly on the strength of PW1's testimony.
evidence_type_secondary: Police testimony and recovery of alleged weapon
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 296
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court of Colombo accepted the evidence of PW1, the widow of the deceased, as credible and trustworthy and treated her as a reliable sole eyewitness to the fatal assault. It found that the appellant, armed with a club, chased and struck the deceased on the head causing his death, and rejected the defence version given in the dock statement. Accordingly, the court convicted the appellant of murder under section 296 of the Penal Code and imposed the death penalty.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant challenged the High Court judgment primarily on the basis that PW1's evidence contained material contradictions and omissions and that it was unsafe to convict on her sole testimony. He argued that the High Court had failed to treat PW1 as an unreliable or interested witness, failed to appreciate that key prosecution witnesses were not called, and failed to address the non-identification of the alleged weapon. The appellant further contended that the High Court did not properly consider or give due weight to his dock statement. One ground relating to the failure to call key witnesses was later abandoned.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Alleged failure of the High Court to consider material contradictions and omissions in PW1's evidence regarding the time of the prior brawl, the weapon used on the daughter-in-law, and the exact location from which PW1 observed the incident. | Assertion that PW1 was not a credible witness and that it was unsafe to base a conviction for murder solely on her testimony. | Complaint (later abandoned) that the prosecution failed to call key witnesses. | Alleged failure to properly identify the alleged murder weapon marked as P-2 and to evaluate that deficiency. | Alleged failure of the High Court to adequately consider and give due weight to the appellant's dock statement. | Argument that PW1, being the widow of the deceased, was an interested witness whose evidence required special scrutiny.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal noted that the case rested almost entirely on PW1 Seelawathie, the widow of the deceased, who was the sole eyewitness to the assault. It held that although her evidence contained discrepancies about the time of the earlier incident, the precise weapon used on the daughter-in-law, and exact locations, these related to a prior fracas and minor details and did not undermine her core account of seeing the appellant chase and strike the deceased with a club. The court emphasized that the defence failed to properly prove contradictions under section 145 of the Evidence Ordinance and that PW1's hesitation about identifying the weapon at the High Court demonstrated truthfulness rather than fabrication.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal held that minor discrepancies in PW1's narrative were attributable to human frailty and lapse of time and did not shake the basic version of the prosecution case. It accepted the trial judge's view that PW1 was a truthful and reliable witness, concluded that no reasonable doubt arose on the core events she described, and therefore refused to extend the benefit of the doubt to the appellant.
defence_version_summary: In his dock statement, the appellant denied killing the deceased and claimed that the deceased was a known drug dealer whose two sons had been killed due to their association with an underworld leader. He asserted that there was an ongoing feud between the deceased's family and a man named Anil, and that because the appellant associated with Anil, he was falsely implicated in this murder. The Court of Appeal noted that the appellant failed to explain his absconding for about two years after the incident, that the alleged enmity was with Anil rather than the appellant, and that the reference to Nimal or Anil appeared for the first time only in the dock statement and was not suggested in cross-examination. The court therefore agreed with the trial judge that the dock statement was incomplete, improbable, and deficient when viewed alongside the totality of the evidence.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal carefully reviewed the High Court's evaluation of PW1's evidence, emphasizing that credibility is primarily a matter of fact for the trial judge. It held that the defence had failed to properly prove alleged contradictions and omissions under section 145 of the Evidence Ordinance and that the discrepancies highlighted were minor, related mainly to a prior incident, and did not affect the core account of the fatal assault. The court found PW1's testimony cogent and unimpeached, considered the recovery of the alleged weapon but noted that the trial judge had not relied on it due to identification issues, and agreed that the dock statement was deficient given the unexplained absconding and the lateness and improbability of the suggested false implication. It rejected arguments that PW1 was an 'interested' witness in the legal sense, applied authorities on appreciation of sole eyewitness testimony and minor discrepancies, and concluded that the conviction and death sentence were justified and lawful with no misdirection or non-direction warranting interference.
coa_sentence_type: Death
brief_judgment_file_summary: This appeal from the High Court of Colombo concerned a conviction for murder under section 296 of the Penal Code arising from the fatal clubbing of the deceased at Grandpass in May 2008. The prosecution case depended almost entirely on PW1, the widow of the deceased, who described prior disputes between the appellant and her family, an assault on her daughter-in-law, and later seeing the appellant armed with a club chase and strike the deceased. The defence sought to rely on alleged contradictions in PW1's evidence, failure to call further witnesses, non-identification of the weapon, and a dock statement suggesting false implication due to underworld-related enmities. The Court of Appeal held that the defence had not properly proved contradictions, treated the discrepancies as minor and natural, upheld the trial judge's acceptance of PW1 as a truthful sole eyewitness, and regarded the dock statement as incomplete and improbable. It further rejected the notion that PW1 was an 'interested' witness in law, affirmed that there was sufficient evidence for conviction with no material misdirection or procedural defect, and accordingly dismissed the appeal, affirming the conviction for murder and the sentence of death.
prosecution_counsel: Disna Warnakula DSG for the Respondent
defence_counsel: Kaneel Maddumage with Praveen Premathilake and Narthana Wevita for the Accused-Appellant
cause_of_death_exact_text: Fatal head injury caused by a single blow with a club to the deceased's head.
hc_analysis_summary: From the perspective of the Court of Appeal, the High Court judge evaluated PW1's evidence using appropriate legal tests, treated discrepancies relating to the prior incident as minor, and accepted her as a credible and reliable sole eyewitness to the fatal assault. The High Court did not rely on the section 27 weapon recovery because the club was not properly identified, and it considered but rejected the appellant's dock statement due to his unexplained absconding and the improbability of the alleged false implication. The Court of Appeal found no misdirection or misappreciation of evidence in this reasoning and therefore saw no error warranting interference.
precedents_cited_list: Kumara De Silva v Attorney General – 2010 (2) Sri LR 169 | Gamini Sugathsena v The State – 1998 1 Sri LLR 405 | Appabhai v State of Gujarat – 1998 Supp SCC 241 | Queen v Buddharakkita Thero – 63 NLR 442 | King v Vallayan – citation not specified | Ajit Samarakoon v The Republic (Kobaigane Murder Case) – 2004 2 Sri LR 209 | Sarath v Attorney General – 2006 3 Sri LR 96 | Myladimmal Surendran v State of Kerala – AIR 2010 SC 3281; 2010 AIR SCW 5248 | State of Rajasthan v Smt Kalki and Another – (1981) 2 SCC 752 | K v Endoris – 46 NLR 498 | Ebert Silva v K – 52 NLR 505
standard_of_review_applied: The Court of Appeal applied the standard that it does not retry the case on facts but examines whether there was evidence on which the trial judge could reasonably reach the verdict and whether there was any misdirection or non-direction in the evaluation of evidence or law.
final_charge_after_appeal: Murder under Section 296 of the Penal Code

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 296 read with section 32 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The 2nd accused in High Court of Kalutara case HC 454/17 applied in revision to the Court of Appeal challenging three interlocutory orders made during the evidence of PW-01 in a murder trial. PW-01, an eyewitness, deviated from her police statement and claimed poor memory due to ill health, leading the prosecuting State Counsel to seek to have her refresh her memory and to question her using her prior police statement. The defence objected, alleging intimidation of the witness and misuse of the police statement contrary to the Evidence Ordinance and fair trial guarantees. The High Court nevertheless permitted leading questioning and allowed PW-01 to read her police statement while giving evidence, prompting the present revision application.
evidence_type_secondary: Previous police statement and prior inconsistent statement of witness
hc_judgment_summary: There was no final High Court judgment on conviction or sentence; the High Court only made interlocutory orders permitting the prosecuting State Counsel to question PW-01 using her police statement, including allowing leading questions and allowing the witness to refresh her memory by reading that statement.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The petitioner contended that the High Court orders allowing the use of PW-01's police statement to refresh memory and to ask leading questions amounted to an unjust and illegal procedure. It was argued that the prosecution intimidated its own witness by threatening prosecution for giving false evidence and that a police statement can only be used to contradict a witness, not as substantive evidence. The petitioner further claimed that these rulings violated his constitutional right to a fair trial and safeguards under the ICCPR Act. Accordingly he sought to have the impugned orders set aside and a proper trial ensured.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Challenge to orders permitting PW-01 to refresh memory and give evidence by reference to her police statement under sections 159 and 160 of the Evidence Ordinance. | Complaint that prosecuting State Counsel intimidated PW-01 by warning her of possible prosecution and imprisonment if she departed from her police statement. | Argument that a police statement under section 110 of the Code of Criminal Procedure can only be used to contradict or discredit a witness, not as substantive evidence in chief. | Allegation that the impugned orders and questioning pattern violated the petitioner's right to a fair trial under Article 13(3) of the Constitution and ICCPR Act No. 56 of 2007.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The only witness discussed in detail is PW-01, who was expected to give eyewitness evidence but deviated from her police statement and repeatedly stated that she could not remember events due to ill health. The prosecuting State Counsel attempted to confront her with and effectively read out portions of her police statement, using leading questions and threats of future prosecution to elicit testimony implicating the accused. The Court of Appeal held that allowing PW-01 to refresh her memory by reading her police statement and to testify on that basis was illegal, rendered her evidence of no legal value, and undermined the fairness of the trial.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal did not assess the probabilities of guilt or innocence but focused on whether the manner of leading PW-01's evidence and using her police statement was legally permissible and compatible with a fair trial; it concluded that the irregularities were so serious that her evidence must be expunged and the trial recommenced.
defence_version_summary: The defence had not yet presented a substantive factual version of events; instead, counsel for the petitioner concentrated on objecting to the prosecution's methods of examining PW-01 and the High Court's rulings on those objections. No alibi or defence witnesses are discussed, and the proceedings were still in the prosecution case. The Court of Appeal accepted that defence counsel's objections correctly highlighted violations of the accused's fair trial rights and misapplication of the law on prior statements.
legal_errors_description: The Court of Appeal found that the High Court misdirected itself on the scope of sections 159 and 160 of the Evidence Ordinance and section 110 of the Code of Criminal Procedure by allowing a lay witness in a criminal trial to refresh her memory and give evidence by reading her police statement. It also held that permitting extensive leading questions in chief, combined with threats of future prosecution for false evidence, was illegal, unconstitutional, and contrary to fair trial principles.
procedural_defects_description: Procedural defects included the prosecuting State Counsel intimidating her own witness by warning of future prosecutions, using leading questions in chief to suggest answers drawn from the police statement, and relying on that prior statement as if it were substantive evidence. The High Court compounded these errors by formally authorising the procedure through orders P-02, P-03, and P-04 and by allowing PW-01 to read her police statement in the witness box, thereby undermining the fairness of the proceedings.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analysed the impugned orders against Article 13(3) of the Constitution and the statutory framework governing prior statements and memory refreshing, notably sections 154, 159 and 160 of the Evidence Ordinance and section 110 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, with reference to Indian precedents such as Simon v. State of Kerala, Chinnammal v. State of Tamil Nadu and Varkey Joseph v. State of Kerala. It concluded that a police statement in a criminal case cannot be used by a lay witness to refresh memory or as substantive evidence and that leading questions suggesting answers drawn from such statements in examination-in-chief are impermissible, especially when accompanied by threats of prosecution. The Court found that the cumulative effect of the prosecuting State Counsel's conduct and the High Court's orders was a serious violation of the accused's right to a fair trial, shocking the conscience of the court. As a remedy it set aside the impugned orders, expunged PW-01's evidence, and directed that the trial be recommenced in accordance with proper legal principles.
brief_judgment_file_summary: This revision application by the 2nd accused in a murder case challenged three interlocutory orders of the High Court of Kalutara that allowed PW-01 to be questioned and to give evidence by reference to her prior police statement, including through leading questions and after threats of prosecution for alleged false testimony. The Court of Appeal held that sections 159 and 160 of the Evidence Ordinance do not authorise a lay witness in a criminal trial to refresh memory by reading a police statement recorded under section 110 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, which may only be used to contradict or explain testimony and is not substantive evidence. Relying on constitutional fair trial guarantees and comparative case law, the Court found the procedure adopted by the prosecuting State Counsel and sanctioned by the High Court to be illegal, unconstitutional, and fundamentally unfair to the accused, rendering PW-01's evidence devoid of legal value. It accordingly set aside the impugned orders, ordered PW-01's evidence to be expunged, and directed the High Court to recommence the trial afresh following correct legal principles.
defence_counsel: Navodya Ganegoda
hc_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal observed that the High Court Judge misapplied the law on the use of police statements by treating section 159 of the Evidence Ordinance as permitting PW-01 to refresh her memory from her police statement and by relying on section 110(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure to justify broader use of such statements. It held that this interpretation ignored the limited, non-substantive role of police statements and that by endorsing leading questions and allowing the witness to read and base her testimony on the police statement, the High Court had disregarded the rules of evidence and contributed to an unfair trial. The Court therefore set aside the orders P-02, P-03 and P-04 and declared PW-01's evidence given on 05-10-2021 and 13-01-2022 to be of no legal value.
precedents_cited_list: Simon v. State of Kerala – 1996 (1) KLT 406; 1996 (1) KLJ 348 | Chinnammal v. State of Tamil Nadu and Others – 1997 (1) SCC 145 | Varkey Joseph v. State of Kerala – 1993 AIR 1892; 1993 SCR (3) 390
standard_of_review_applied: Misdirection on law and improper application of the Evidence Ordinance and Code of Criminal Procedure leading to an illegal, unfair trial procedure that shocked the conscience of the Court.
final_charge_after_appeal: Murder under section 296 read with section 32 of the Penal Code

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Sections 54(A)(b) and 54(A)(d) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance as amended by Act No. 13 of 1984
brief_facts_summary: The appellant, the mother-in-law of a woman named Nilanthi, was alleged to have been trafficking heroin based on information received by IP Chandana of the Colombo Crime Division. A police party went to Stacepura, where a female constable searched the appellant and recovered a parcel of brown powder from the pocket of her frock, which tested positive for heroin, was weighed at 25.110 grams at a jewellery shop, and later sent to the Government Analyst who found 24.74 grams containing 5.58 grams of heroin. At trial the prosecution led eight witnesses, including the detecting officers, while the appellant gave only a dock statement admitting the arrest but denying possession of drugs and claiming she was arrested at her residence.
evidence_type_primary: Police eyewitness testimony and physical drug production
evidence_type_secondary: Government Analyst report and documentary chain of custody evidence
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 54(A)(d) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court of Colombo convicted the appellant on the second count of possession of heroin under Section 54(A)(d) while acquitting her on the trafficking count. Relying on the evidence of the detecting officers and the Government Analyst report, the court found the prosecution case proved and sentenced the appellant to life imprisonment on 2019-03-01, without addressing the discrepancy in the weight of the production or the implications of her dock statement.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: On appeal, the appellant contended that the prosecution had failed to prove the charges beyond reasonable doubt and that the raid was not a genuine one. She argued that the significant variation between the weight of the heroin at detection and at analysis showed that the chain of custody was not proved and that the productions could have been tampered with. She further complained that the High Court failed to consider her dock statement in the light of applicable case law, thereby denying her a fair trial.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Prosecution failed to prove the charge beyond reasonable doubt and the raid was alleged to be not genuine. | Variation in the quantity of the drug production between detection and analysis showed that the chain of custody was not proved beyond reasonable doubt. | The High Court failed to properly consider the appellant's dock statement in accordance with decided cases, resulting in an unfair trial.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal scrutinized the evidence of the detecting officer, noting that he went to Stacepura to arrest the appellant without knowing her residence or whereabouts and only knowing the address of Nilanthi, which cast doubt on the genuineness of the raid. The court also emphasized the unexplained discrepancy between the weight of the heroin at the time of detection (25.110 grams) and at analysis (24.74 grams), finding that the prosecution had failed to prove an unbroken chain of custody. In contrast, the appellant's dock statement that she was arrested at her residence and that no drugs were recovered from her was found to create a serious doubt when viewed in the totality of the evidence.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal held that the unexplained weight discrepancy and doubts about the manner of the raid, together with the appellant's dock statement, created a reasonable doubt in the prosecution case and entitled the appellant to the benefit of that doubt.
defence_version_summary: The appellant made an unsworn dock statement in which she admitted being arrested on the date mentioned in the indictment but denied that any illegal substance was recovered from her possession and stated that she was arrested at her residence, not on the road. No defence witnesses were called. The Court of Appeal, applying authority on the evidential value of dock statements, held that her version, when considered alongside weaknesses in the prosecution case, created reasonable doubt and had to be given due weight.
legal_errors_description: The Court of Appeal found that the High Court failed to address the significant discrepancy in the weight of the production between detection and analysis and failed to consider the implications for the chain of custody. It also held that the High Court did not properly evaluate the appellant's dock statement in light of established case law, resulting in the appellant not being afforded a fair trial.
procedural_defects_description: Procedural defects included the omission by the High Court to comment on or resolve the discrepancy in the weights of the heroin production and the failure to consider the appellant's dock statement in the totality of the evidence. These omissions undermined the fairness of the trial and the reliability of the conviction.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analysed the prosecution evidence on the raid and seizure, noting that the detecting officer went to Stacepura without knowing the appellant's residence and that the evidence did not satisfactorily explain how she was located, which cast doubt on the genuineness of the detection. The court placed particular emphasis on the difference between the weight of the production at the time of detection and at the Government Analyst, holding that this unexplained discrepancy meant the prosecution had failed to establish an unbroken chain of custody and the integrity of the production. Applying principles from several precedents and treating the appellant's dock statement as evidence to be weighed with the rest, the court concluded that the prosecution had not proved the case beyond reasonable doubt, and therefore the conviction and sentence could not stand.
coa_sentence_type: No sentence (acquitted)
brief_judgment_file_summary: This appeal from the High Court of Colombo concerned a conviction for possession of heroin under Section 54(A)(d) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance, where the appellant had been sentenced to life imprisonment after a police raid in Stacepura allegedly yielded 5.58 grams of heroin. The Court of Appeal identified serious doubts about the genuineness of the raid, noting that the detecting officer set out without knowing the appellant's residence and that the prosecution did not clearly establish how she was located at Stacepura Road. The court further held that the substantial and unexplained discrepancy between the weight of the production at detection (25.110 grams) and at the Government Analyst (24.74 grams, containing 5.58 grams of heroin) meant that the chain of custody was not proved beyond reasonable doubt. Giving due consideration to the appellant's dock statement that she was arrested at home and that no drugs were found on her, and applying established authorities on chain of custody and dock statements, the Court of Appeal set aside the conviction and sentence and acquitted her of the possession charge, thereby allowing the appeal.
defence_counsel: Rushdie Habeeb with Waseemul Akram and A. Perera
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court accepted the evidence of the detecting officers and the Government Analyst report and convicted the appellant on the possession charge, sentencing her to life imprisonment while acquitting her of trafficking, but did not discuss the discrepancy in the weight of the production or the defence version. The Court of Appeal criticized this approach, pointing out that the failure to address the weight discrepancy and to evaluate the dock statement deprived the appellant of a fair assessment of the evidence. It held that, in drug cases, careful proof of the inward journey of productions and proper consideration of the defence are essential, and that the High Court's omissions amounted to errors warranting interference.
precedents_cited_list: Mohamed Nimnaz v. Attorney General – CA/95/94 | Perera v. Attorney General – [1998] 1 Sri L.R. 378 | Witharana Doli Nona v. The Republic of Sri Lanka – CA/19/99 | Don Samantha Jude Anthony Jayamaha v. The Attorney General – CA/303/2006 (11/07/2012) | Kathubdeen v. Republic of Sri Lanka – [1998] 3 SLR 107
standard_of_review_applied: Failure to establish an unbroken chain of custody and to preserve the integrity of productions, coupled with failure to properly evaluate the defence evidence and resulting reasonable doubt in the conviction.
final_charge_after_appeal: None (acquitted of all charges)

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | Amal Ranaraja, J.
offence_sections: Section 140 of the Penal Code; Section 296 read with Section 146 of the Penal Code; Section 300 read with Section 146 of the Penal Code; Section 296 read with Section 32 of the Penal Code; Section 300 read with Section 32 of the Penal Code
offence_category: Murder, attempted murder and unlawful assembly
location_of_offence: Alubomulla village on Gramodya Mawatha, within the jurisdiction of the High Court of Panadura
brief_facts_summary: The appellants and several others, residents of Alubomulla, allegedly formed an unlawful assembly on 14.04.2003 on Gramodya Mawatha and attacked PW-03 Lakshman Thomas and his brother, the deceased Galahitiyawage Ranjith Thomas, using a steel pole, a sword and a dagger. According to PW-01 and PW-03, the 2nd appellant first struck the deceased with a steel pole causing him to fall, the 1st appellant then cut PW-03 with a sword, and the 3rd appellant finally stabbed the deceased twice in the chest with a dagger, leading to his death. There had been a prior incident on 22.03.2003 where the 1st to 3rd appellants and others assaulted PW-03 over an allegation that he had tipped off law enforcement, giving rise to animosity and a suggested motive for the later attack.
evidence_type_secondary: Prior police statements and omissions used to impeach the eyewitnesses
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Count 1 – Section 140 of the Penal Code; Count 2 – Section 296 read with Section 146 of the Penal Code; Count 3 – Section 300 read with Section 146 of the Penal Code
hc_sentence_type: Death sentence for murder on Count 2, together with terms of imprisonment and fines imposed on Counts 1 and 3
hc_judgment_summary: At the conclusion of the second trial, the High Court of Panadura accepted the eyewitness accounts of PW-01 and PW-03, found the 1st to 3rd accused guilty on Counts 1, 2 and 3, and acquitted the 4th and 5th accused of all charges. The 1st to 3rd accused were sentenced to death on the murder count and to imprisonment and fines on the unlawful assembly and attempted murder counts.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellants contended that they had been denied a fair trial when, after the prosecution case was heard by one High Court Judge who reserved an order under section 200(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, a successor Judge took over without obtaining that order and refused to recall key prosecution witnesses. They argued that the trial judge failed to evaluate numerous contradictions and omissions in the testimony of PW-01 and PW-03, particularly regarding the presence and complicity of the 4th and 5th accused and the formation of an unlawful assembly of five persons. Further grounds alleged misdirection on the law relating to corroboration, common object, burden of proof, the application of the Ellenborough dictum to an eyewitness case, and unfair treatment of the 2nd appellant's dock statement and defence evidence.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Alleged denial of a fair trial due to the successor Judge proceeding without obtaining the predecessor Judge's reserved order under section 200(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure. | Complaint that the successor Judge refused to recall prosecution witnesses heard by the predecessor Judge, despite recorded notes on demeanor and deportment. | Challenge to the sufficiency and evaluation of evidence, highlighting multiple contradictions and omissions in PW-01 and PW-03's testimony, especially about the presence and role of the 4th and 5th accused. | Argument that failure to prove an unlawful assembly of five members rendered Count 1 unproved and thereby undermined convictions on Counts 2 and 3 based on common object. | Alleged failure of the trial judge to properly evaluate probability and credibility of prosecution witnesses and to consider defence evidence in its correct perspective. | Grounds that the trial judge misdirected himself on corroboration, burden of proof, and misapplied the Ellenborough principle to what was essentially an eyewitness case. | Complaint that the trial judge treated the 2nd appellant's dock statement with contempt, drew adverse inferences from the failure to call defence witnesses, and thus unfairly shifted the burden of proof.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal observed that the prosecution case rested primarily on the eyewitness accounts of PW-01 Indrani and PW-03 Lakshman, whose credibility had been heavily challenged through cross-examination. It noted that around thirty omissions were highlighted between their testimony and initial police statements, including discrepancies about the number of persons present at the scene, casting doubt on aspects of their evidence. The Court further held that, given these weaknesses and the long lapse of time since the incident, the likelihood of reliable testimony and a safe conviction at any retrial was significantly reduced.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal considered that the credibility of the key eyewitnesses had already been seriously undermined by numerous omissions and that, after more than twenty years since the offence, the chances of safely relying on their testimony at a fresh trial were remote, justifying an acquittal rather than a retrial.
defence_version_summary: The appellants pleaded not guilty and sought to undermine the prosecution case mainly by cross-examining PW-01 and PW-03 on contradictions and omissions between their testimony and police statements, arguing that the presence of five participants and an unlawful assembly had not been proved and that their own implication was doubtful. The 2nd appellant delivered a dock statement, and it was contended on appeal that the trial judge treated that statement with undue contempt and drew adverse inferences from the absence of defence witnesses, thereby placing an improper burden on the appellants. The defence maintained that, properly evaluated, the probability and credibility of the prosecution evidence did not justify convictions for unlawful assembly, murder or attempted murder.
legal_errors_description: The Court of Appeal held that the successor High Court Judge erred in proceeding without obtaining the predecessor Judge's reserved order under section 200(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure despite the latter remaining in office, and in refusing the defence request to recall key prosecution witnesses whose demeanor and deportment had been recorded by the predecessor Judge. These misdirections and omissions were found to have denied the appellants a fair trial.
procedural_defects_description: Procedurally, the second trial was conducted before two different High Court Judges, with the prosecution case concluded before the first and the defence case before the second, yet the successor Judge declined to obtain the predecessor's pending section 200(1) order or to recall crucial prosecution witnesses for re-examination. The Court considered that, given the recorded observations on demeanor and the availability of the predecessor Judge, the successor Judge's refusal to take such steps constituted a serious procedural irregularity affecting the fairness of the trial.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal first addressed the complaint that the second trial had been conducted unfairly, noting that the predecessor High Court Judge who heard the entire prosecution case had reserved an order under section 200(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure and recorded the demeanor of key witnesses, yet the successor Judge neither sought that order nor recalled those witnesses despite requests by the defence. It held that, since the predecessor Judge remained in office and could have been nominated to deliver the order, the successor Judge's refusal amounted to a misdirection that denied the appellants a fair trial, a position conceded by the Additional Solicitor General. In considering whether to order a retrial, the Court examined the prosecution case, which depended almost entirely on the eyewitness testimony of PW-01 and PW-03, and observed that cross-examination had exposed about thirty omissions between their trial testimony and police statements, including significant discrepancies over how many assailants were present. Emphasizing that more than twenty years had passed since the offence and that credibility problems with the eyewitnesses would only worsen with time, the Court, guided by authorities such as King v. H. R. S. Fernando, Peter Singho v. Werapitiya, The Queen v. G. K. Jayasinghe and Hon. Attorney General v. Bimbirigodage Sujith Lal, concluded that the chances of a safe conviction at a fresh trial were remote. It therefore set aside the convictions and sentences and directed that the appellants be acquitted without ordering a third trial.
coa_sentence_type: Acquitted – no sentence imposed
brief_judgment_file_summary: Three appellants convicted by the High Court of Panadura on charges of unlawful assembly, murder and attempted murder arising from a 2003 village assault appealed against a second-trial judgment of 19.12.2019 that imposed the death penalty and other sentences. The Court of Appeal found that the second trial had been conducted before two different High Court Judges, with the predecessor Judge having heard all prosecution evidence and reserved an order under section 200(1) while noting the demeanor of key eyewitnesses, but the successor Judge refused to obtain that order or recall those witnesses despite defence requests. Accepting the Additional Solicitor General's concession that this deprived the appellants of a fair trial, the Court nevertheless considered whether a retrial was appropriate and analyzed the strength of the prosecution case, which was based almost entirely on PW-01 and PW-03 whose statements were shown to contain about thirty omissions on material matters, including the number of assailants. Relying on precedent, and stressing that over twenty years had elapsed since the offence and that the appellants had already faced two long trials, the Court held that ordering a third trial after such a long delay would be unjust and that the prospects of a safe conviction were remote. Accordingly, it set aside the High Court convictions and sentencing order and acquitted the appellants of all charges, allowing the appeal in full.
prosecution_counsel: Dilan Ratnayake, P.C., Additional Solicitor General, for the State
defence_counsel: Darshana Kuruppu with Dineru Bandara, Tharushi Gamage, Buddhika Thilakarathna, Sudarsha P. de Silva and Sahan Weerasinghe for the 1st Accused-Appellant; Indica Mallawarachchi for the 2nd Accused-Appellant; Nihara Randeniya for the 3rd Accused-Appellant
weapon_type: Steel pole, sword, dagger and a knife alleged to have been used in the assault
cause_of_death_exact_text: The deceased died after being first struck with a steel pole and then stabbed twice in the chest with a dagger during the assault.
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court in the second trial, sitting without a jury, accepted the evidence of PW-01 and PW-03, convicted the 1st to 3rd accused on the first three counts and sentenced them to death on the murder count while acquitting the 4th and 5th accused. The Court of Appeal criticized the manner in which the second trial was conducted, holding that the successor Judge's failure to obtain the predecessor Judge's reserved section 200(1) order and to recall key witnesses, despite recorded observations on their demeanor and the predecessor Judge remaining in office, amounted to serious error. Because these procedural defects rendered the trial unfair, the Court did not carry out a detailed reassessment of the High Court's factual reasoning but instead focused on whether a further retrial would be just.

judges: P. Kumararatnam J. | Sampath B. Abayakoon J.
offence_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code
location_of_offence: Silusavi tile factory housing scheme at Punchi Lida Road, Haldanduwana and an adjacent plantation plot
brief_facts_summary: The 1st Appellant, the mother of the infant Iswaralage Kaushalya, and the 2nd Appellant, who was legally married to PW1 but also living with the 1st Appellant, resided with PW1 in a line room at the Silusavi tile factory housing scheme in Haldanduwana. On a morning when PW1 had gone to work and returned for breakfast, she heard the infant crying and saw the 2nd Appellant strangling the child while the 1st Appellant was present but did nothing to intervene. Later that day the child was missing, and after PW1 complained to the Koswatte Police, the infant’s body was found dumped in a nearby plantation and a postmortem revealed death due to pressure on the neck and mouth. The Appellants were later apprehended while hiding under a bridge, denied the charge in dock statements at trial, but were convicted of murder by the High Court.
evidence_type_primary: Eyewitness testimony of PW1 and circumstantial evidence
evidence_type_secondary: Medical expert evidence from the JMO and evidence of the Appellants' suspicious conduct before and after the incident
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court of Chilaw conducted a non-jury trial after the Appellants initially pleaded guilty but the judge ordered the trial to proceed as if they had not pleaded guilty. Relying on PW1's evidence that she saw the 2nd Appellant strangling the infant, together with corroborating surrounding circumstances and the JMO's opinion that the child died from pressure applied to the neck and mouth, the court found both Appellants guilty of murder under Section 296 of the Penal Code. On 2017-05-31 the High Court sentenced each Appellant to death.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The Appellants argued that the circumstantial evidence led at trial was insufficient to establish beyond reasonable doubt that they alone committed the murder. They contended that the prosecution failed to prove the date of the offence beyond reasonable doubt and that the learned High Court Judge did not properly consider alleged contradictions and inconsistencies in the prosecution witnesses' testimony. In addition, counsel complained that the High Court judgment was devoid of proper judicial analysis and evaluation of the evidence and showed a total disregard of Section 283 of the Code of Criminal Procedure.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Alleged insufficiency of circumstantial evidence to establish that the Appellants committed the murder | Alleged failure of the prosecution to prove the date of the offence beyond reasonable doubt | Alleged failure of the High Court Judge to consider contradictory and inconsistent versions of prosecution witnesses | Allegation that the High Court judgment lacked proper judicial analysis and evaluation of evidence and disregarded Section 283 of the Code of Criminal Procedure
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal considered PW1, the legally wedded wife of the 2nd Appellant, to be a competent witness for the prosecution in terms of Section 81 of the Children and Young Persons Ordinance and accepted her testimony that she saw the 2nd Appellant strangling the infant while the 1st Appellant did nothing to stop it. It relied on the JMO's medical evidence confirming that death resulted from pressure applied to the neck and mouth and regarded the Appellants' subsequent conduct, including their failure to explain the child's disappearance and their attempt to hide, as strongly incriminating circumstantial evidence. The Court treated the alleged discrepancies in PW1's evidence as minor, attributable to the lapse of about seven years between the incident and her testimony, and noted that no material contradictions or omissions had been properly marked to undermine the prosecution case.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal held that the proved circumstances, including PW1's observations, the medical findings, and the Appellants' conduct, formed a complete chain that was consistent only with their guilt and totally inconsistent with any reasonable hypothesis of innocence, so that no reasonable doubt or benefit of doubt arose in their favour.
defence_version_summary: After the close of the prosecution case, each Appellant made a brief dock statement in which they simply denied the charge and did not call any defence witnesses or advance an alibi or alternative version of events. The Court of Appeal regarded these bare denials as insufficient to cast doubt on the strong prosecution evidence, especially in light of PW1's eyewitness account and the corroborating medical and circumstantial evidence. It therefore found the defence version lacking in credibility.
legal_errors_description: The Court observed that the High Court Judge had not expressly resolved the legal issue arising from Section 120(2) of the Evidence Ordinance regarding the competency of PW1 as the spouse of the 2nd Appellant, but held that Section 81 of the Children and Young Persons Ordinance clearly made her a competent prosecution witness in an offence against a child. It also addressed counsel's complaint that the judgment lacked proper analysis by referring to Section 436 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and Article 138 of the Constitution and concluded that any such errors or omissions in the judgment did not prejudice the substantial rights of the parties or occasion a failure of justice.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal reaffirmed the principles governing circumstantial evidence and held that PW1's evidence of seeing the 2nd Appellant strangling the infant, combined with the JMO's findings on cause and timing of death and the Appellants' suspicious conduct in not explaining the child's disappearance and subsequently hiding, formed an unbroken chain pointing only to their guilt. It rejected the complaint about the date of the offence, noting that the date specified in the indictment, PW1's testimony, and the medical opinion that death occurred four to five days before the postmortem were consistent and that the Appellants had been given sufficient notice under Section 165 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The Court also found that no material contradictions or omissions in the prosecution evidence had been established and that the High Court had correctly applied the law on circumstantial evidence. Applying Section 436 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and Article 138 of the Constitution, it held that no error or irregularity had caused a failure of justice and accordingly affirmed both the conviction for murder and the sentence of death.
coa_sentence_type: Death
brief_judgment_file_summary: This appeal arose from the conviction and death sentence imposed on the 1st and 2nd Appellants by the High Court of Chilaw for the murder of a three-month-old infant, Iswaralage Kaushalya, under Section 296 of the Penal Code. The prosecution case was based on PW1's evidence that she saw the 2nd Appellant strangling the child in the shared line room at the Silusavi tile factory housing scheme, the child's subsequent disappearance and the discovery of her body in a nearby plantation, and the JMO's opinion that death resulted from pressure on the neck and mouth consistent with homicidal strangulation. On appeal, the Appellants challenged the sufficiency of circumstantial evidence, the proof of the date of the offence, and the treatment of alleged contradictions, and further complained that the High Court judgment lacked proper analysis and ignored Section 283 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The Court of Appeal held that PW1 was a competent witness in an offence against a child, that the circumstantial evidence formed a complete and compelling chain pointing only to the Appellants' guilt, that the date of the offence was adequately proved and notified, and that no material contradictions or procedural irregularities had been shown to cause a failure of justice. Accordingly, it affirmed the conviction for murder and the sentence of death and dismissed the appeal.
defence_counsel: Tenny Fernando for the 1st Appellant; K.A. Upul Anuradha Wickramaratne for the 2nd Appellant
cause_of_death_exact_text: Difficulty of breathing caused by pressure applied on the neck and mouth of the infant child.
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court treated the matter as a serious case of homicide of a very young child and convicted both Appellants of murder based on PW1's testimony, the medical evidence, and supporting circumstantial evidence, including their conduct after the incident. The Court of Appeal noted that while the High Court had not explicitly discussed certain legal questions, such as the competency of PW1 as the spouse of the 2nd Appellant and the detailed evaluative requirements under Section 283 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, its factual conclusions and application of the law on circumstantial evidence were correct. The appellate court therefore held that any shortcomings in the reasoning did not prejudice the Appellants' substantial rights or cause a failure of justice and upheld the High Court's conviction and sentence.
precedents_cited_list: C. Chenga Reddy and others v. State of A.P. – (1996) 10 SCC 193 | McGreevy v. Director of Public Prosecution – [1973] 1 WLR 276 | Attorney General v. Potta Naufer and others – [2007] 2 SLR 144 | Kusumadasa v. State – [2011] 1 SLR 240 | Premawansha v. Attorney General – [2009] 2 SLR 205 | Bhoginbhai Hirjibhai v. State of Gujarat – citation not specified | R. v. Dossai – 13 Cr. App. R. 158 | The Attorney General v. Sandanam Pitchi Mary Theresa – (2011) 2 Sri L.R. 292
standard_of_review_applied: Review of the sufficiency of circumstantial evidence, evaluation of alleged contradictions and proof of the date of the offence, coupled with the failure of justice standard under Section 436 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and Article 138 of the Constitution.
final_charge_after_appeal: Murder under Section 296 of the Penal Code

judges: P. Kumararatnam, J. | K. M. G. H. Kulatunga, J.
offence_sections: Sections 54A(b) and 54A(d) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance as amended by Act No. 13 of 1984
brief_facts_summary: On 26 April 2013 a team from the Crime Prevention Unit of Borella Police Station, led by IP Priyadharshana, was on routine crime prevention duty when they allegedly received information about a drug courier. They set up an ambush on Baseline Road and apprehended the Appellant, recovering a pink cellophane bag with a brown substance from the pocket of his shorts. The substance reacted positively for heroin and was weighed first at the police station and then again at a pawn shop, with the indictment alleging trafficking and possession of 2.6 grams of heroin. The Appellant denied ever possessing heroin and claimed he was falsely implicated after being arrested elsewhere.
evidence_type_primary: Police eyewitness testimony and physical recovery of heroin
evidence_type_secondary: Forensic analysis by the Government Analyst and related documentary police records
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Sections 54A(b) and 54A(d) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance as amended by Act No. 13 of 1984
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court of Colombo convicted the Appellant on both counts under sections 54A(b) and 54A(d) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance, accepting the police evidence regarding the raid and recovery of heroin. The court rejected the dock statement of the Appellant and defence version and on 28 June 2023 imposed life imprisonment on the Appellant for each count.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: On appeal the Appellant challenged the trial judge's failure to properly evaluate the credibility of PW1 and the material contradictions and omissions in the prosecution evidence. It was further contended that the judge misdirected himself in law in treating PW2 as corroborative and material evidence and in rejecting the defence case. The Appellant also complained that the benefit of reasonable doubt and of section 114(f) of the Evidence Ordinance was not afforded and that the conviction and sentence were bad in law.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Trial judge failed to consider the credibility of PW1 in the prosecution case. | Trial judge failed to consider material contradictions and omissions in the evidence. | Trial judge misdirected himself on the law in accepting PW2 as corroborative and material evidence. | Trial judge failed to extend the advantage of reasonable doubt to the defence. | Trial judge failed to give the Appellant the benefit of section 114(f) of the Evidence Ordinance. | Conviction and sentence were alleged to be bad in law.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal noted that the raid was conducted by a small group of police officers who left the station without prior specific information and received the tip off while on routine duty, and that only police officers supported the recovery. It highlighted the unexplained double weighing of the heroin parcel, the use of a personal weighing machine at a pawn shop, and the failure to search the Appellant's house or investigate any alleged supplier, finding that these factors weakened the prosecution version. The court considered the defence suggestions in cross examination and the dock statement that the arrest occurred elsewhere and the case was an introduction and found that this account created serious doubt about the prosecution case.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal explicitly applied a principle of probability, holding that the unexplained double weighing, lack of follow up investigation into the Appellant's residence or alleged supplier, and the manner of the raid made the prosecution narrative improbable and thus insufficient to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt.
defence_version_summary: The Appellant did not call witnesses but made a dock statement asserting that he was not arrested on Baseline Road as claimed, that he was arrested at Modera, and that he never possessed heroin and had been introduced into the case. Defence counsel had put this version to the prosecution witnesses in cross examination, contrary to the High Court's finding that no such case was suggested. The Court of Appeal held that the dock statement was wrongly rejected, that it had to be treated as evidence subject to its infirmities, and that together with the cross examination it created serious doubt about the prosecution case.
legal_errors_description: The Court of Appeal found that the High Court judge completely misdirected himself regarding the legal status and proper treatment of a dock statement, wrongly rejecting the Appellant's unsworn statement instead of evaluating it as evidence capable of creating reasonable doubt. It also held that the judge erred in concluding that the defence case had not been put to prosecution witnesses and in relying on that mistaken premise to reject the defence version, which resulted in denial of a fair trial.
procedural_defects_description: The misdirection on the admission and assessment of the dock statement and the erroneous finding that the defence version was not suggested in cross examination amounted to procedural unfairness, depriving the Appellant of a fair trial as guaranteed by Article 13(3) of the Constitution and recognised in authorities such as Attorney General v Segulebbe Latheef.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal carefully reviewed the police evidence, emphasising the importance of probability in assessing criminal proof and finding the unexplained double weighing of the heroin, the use of a personal weighing machine at a pawn shop, and the absence of basic follow up inquiries to be significant weaknesses. It held that the High Court had misdirected itself in law by rejecting the dock statement, mischaracterising the defence cross examination, and thereby denying the Appellant a fair trial. Giving due weight to the defence version and the deficiencies in the prosecution case, the court concluded that the prosecution had not proved trafficking and possession beyond reasonable doubt and therefore set aside the conviction and sentence and acquitted the Appellant.
coa_sentence_type: None (Appellant acquitted and sentence set aside)
brief_judgment_file_summary: This judgment of the Court of Appeal concerns an appeal from a conviction in the High Court of Colombo for trafficking in and possession of heroin under sections 54A(b) and 54A(d) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance. The prosecution relied mainly on the testimony of police officers who claimed to have apprehended the Appellant on Baseline Road with a parcel of heroin, supported by a Government Analyst report, while the defence maintained through a dock statement that he was arrested elsewhere and falsely implicated. The Court of Appeal scrutinised the circumstances of the raid, the unexplained double weighing of the drugs, the failure to conduct basic investigative steps, and the High Court's treatment of the dock statement and defence case. It held that the trial judge had misdirected himself in law, denied the Appellant a fair trial, and that the prosecution had failed to prove the charges beyond reasonable doubt, resulting in the conviction and sentence being set aside and the Appellant being acquitted.
prosecution_counsel: Anoopa De Silva, DSG with Jehan Gunasekera, SC for the Respondent
defence_counsel: Radha M. Kuruwitabandara for the Appellant
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court accepted the prosecution version of a routine crime prevention raid leading to the Appellant's arrest on Baseline Road with heroin and rejected the dock statement as having no evidential value, concluding that the defence had not put its stance to the prosecution witnesses. The Court of Appeal criticised this reasoning as a complete misdirection on the law relating to dock statements and as factually incorrect in light of the cross examination and held that these errors caused serious prejudice to the Appellant. It found that a proper evaluation of the evidence, including the defence version and the deficiencies in the police investigation, should have led the High Court to entertain reasonable doubt and acquit.
precedents_cited_list: Queen v Buddharakkitha Thero 63 NLR 433 | King v Vellayan 1918 20 NLR 251 at 266 | Queen v Kularatne 71 NLR 529 | The Attorney General v Segulebbe Latheef and Another 2008 1 SLR 225 | R v Hepworth 1928 AD 265 at 277
standard_of_review_applied: The Court of Appeal reviewed the case for misdirection on the law regarding dock statements, failure to properly evaluate defence evidence and cross examination, and for unreasonable or perverse findings on probability and proof beyond reasonable doubt.
final_charge_after_appeal: Sections 54A(b) and 54A(d) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance (trafficking and possession of heroin), with the Appellant acquitted of these charges.

judges: B. Sasi Mahendran, J. | Amal Ranaraja, J.
offence_sections: Section 364(1) of the Penal Code as amended by Act No. 22 of 1995
