brief_facts_summary: The accused, a 42-year-old neighbour, was indicted in the High Court of Puttalam for raping 72-year-old Asurana Pathiranage Sumanawathi, an elderly woman who lived alone. The prosecution led evidence through six witnesses and marked documents P1 to P7, after which the High Court found him guilty under section 364(1) of the Penal Code. The present appeal to the Court of Appeal concerns only the severity of the sentence imposed by the High Court.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 364(1) of the Penal Code as amended by Act No. 22 of 1995
hc_judgment_summary: By judgment dated 30.04.2024, the High Court of Puttalam convicted the accused of rape under section 364(1) of the Penal Code. The court sentenced him to 18 years' rigorous imprisonment, imposed a fine of 15000, and ordered 200000 as compensation to the victim in default of further imprisonment.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The accused lodged an appeal challenging the conviction, the sentence of fine, and the compensation. At the hearing, however, his counsel withdrew the appeal against conviction and confined the challenge to the sentence, contending that the High Court failed to properly consider mitigating factors and that the 18-year term was excessive within the statutory range.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Appeal initially filed against conviction, fine, and compensation. | At the hearing, appeal against conviction was withdrawn and only the sentence was canvassed. | It was argued that the High Court Judge failed to adequately consider mitigating factors when imposing sentence. | It was contended that the sentence of 18 years' rigorous imprisonment was excessive within the 7–20 year statutory range under section 364(1).
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The prosecution called six witnesses and produced seven documents in the High Court, while the accused gave a dock statement and called one defence witness. In this judgment the Court of Appeal does not re-evaluate that evidence because the appeal against conviction was withdrawn. The analysis is confined to sentencing, with no detailed discussion of witness credibility or evidentiary contradictions.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal did not revisit the issue of guilt after the appellant withdrew the challenge to conviction and focused solely on whether the sentence properly reflected the aggravating and mitigating circumstances.
defence_version_summary: At trial the accused gave a dock statement and called one defence witness, but the judgment does not set out the substance of that evidence. On appeal he abandoned any challenge to the conviction and sought only a reduction of sentence, effectively accepting the High Court's findings on guilt. The Court of Appeal therefore did not assess the defence version or credibility in detail and confined itself to sentencing considerations.
legal_errors_description: The Court of Appeal found that the trial judge had failed to indicate the reasons and aggravating factors justifying the imposition of an 18-year term of rigorous imprisonment, so that the sentencing discretion was exercised without adequate reasoning and on an improper basis.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court examined the statutory range for rape under section 364(1), noting that the starting point for sentencing is seven years' rigorous imprisonment and that this should be adjusted for aggravating and mitigating factors. It observed that the High Court had considered certain aggravating factors, including the victim's advanced age and the neighbour relationship, as well as mitigating factors such as the accused's lack of previous convictions and family responsibilities, but had not explained why these warranted a sentence of 18 years close to the 20-year maximum. Referring to both local and foreign authorities on sentencing discretion and appellate intervention, the Court held that the absence of adequate reasons and the weight of mitigating factors justified interference with the quantum of sentence. It accordingly reduced the custodial term while affirming the financial penalties.
coa_sentence_type: Rigorous Imprisonment 10 years
brief_judgment_file_summary: This Court of Appeal judgment arises from an appeal by Kurugamage Lalith Priyadarshana alias Chaminda against the sentence imposed by the High Court of Puttalam on a conviction for rape under section 364(1) of the Penal Code. The appellant ultimately abandoned his challenge to the conviction and argued only that the sentence of 18 years' rigorous imprisonment was excessive and that the trial judge had insufficiently considered mitigating factors such as his lack of prior convictions and family responsibilities. The Court reviewed the statutory sentencing range, the concept of a seven-year starting point, the role of aggravating and mitigating factors, and several authorities on when an appellate court may interfere with sentencing discretion. Concluding that the High Court had not given adequate reasons for imposing a term close to the maximum and that the mitigating factors justified a lower penalty, the Court of Appeal varied the custodial sentence to 10 years' rigorous imprisonment while affirming the fine and compensation orders.
defence_counsel: Amila Palliyage with Sandeepani Wijesooriya, Savani Udugampola, Lakitha Wakishta and Subaj de Silva.
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court of Puttalam convicted the accused of rape and, after hearing submissions on aggravating factors such as the victim's advanced age, her status as a neighbour, and the fact that she lived alone, as well as mitigating factors including the accused's clean record and family responsibilities, imposed 18 years of rigorous imprisonment together with a fine and compensation. The Court of Appeal noted that although some factors were mentioned, the trial judge did not articulate why a sentence close to the 20-year maximum was appropriate or clearly demonstrate the balancing of aggravating and mitigating considerations. On that basis, the appellate court concluded that the sentencing discretion had not been properly exercised and that interference with the length of the custodial term was warranted.
precedents_cited_list: Archbold: Sentencing Guidelines (2019) | Attorney General v. Ranasinghe and Others – (1993) 2 SLR 81 | Kieth Billiam – (1986) 82 Criminal Appeal Reports 347 | King v. Rankira – 42 NLR 145 | The Attorney General v. Mendis – 1995 1 SLR 138 | Illakotulena Gamaralalage Thilakerathna v. Officer in Charge, Motor Traffic Division and The Attorney General – SC Appeal No. 173/2017, decided 22/10/2024 | Bed Raj v. State of Uttar Pradesh
standard_of_review_applied: Failure to properly exercise sentencing discretion and to give adequate reasons for the chosen term, thereby permitting appellate interference with sentence.
sentencing_principles_applied: The Court applied a starting-point and range approach for sexual offences, considered the interplay of aggravating and mitigating factors, and followed authorities stressing that appellate courts interfere with sentence only where the trial judge acts on a wrong principle or omits adequate reasons for departing from an appropriate starting point.
final_charge_after_appeal: Rape under Section 364(1) of the Penal Code as amended

judges: B. Sasi Mahendran, J. | Amal Ranaraja, J.
offence_sections: Section 365B(2)(b) of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The accused, an uncle of the victim, was indicted in the High Court of Kegalle on three counts of grave sexual abuse of a 14 year old girl under Section 365B(2)(b) of the Penal Code. He tendered an unqualified plea of guilty to all three counts. The abuse occurred on several occasions at the victim's residence and was not the result of an intimate relationship between the parties, with a considerable age disparity between the accused and the victim. The case remained pending for over a decade, and at the time of sentencing the accused relied on his age, ill health, lack of previous convictions and responsibility for elderly parents as mitigating factors.
evidence_type_secondary: Sentencing submissions by prosecution and victim's counsel
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 365B(2)(b) of the Penal Code
hc_sentence_type: Rigorous imprisonment of 7 years on each of 3 counts (to run concurrently) plus a fine on each count
hc_judgment_summary: Upon the accused tendering an unqualified plea of guilty to all three counts of grave sexual abuse, the High Court of Kegalle convicted him and imposed the statutory minimum of 7 years rigorous imprisonment on each count with a fine of 2000 per count, ordering the custodial terms to run concurrently. The court did not order compensation as the victim indicated she did not seek compensation. In its sentencing order, the High Court distinguished other authorities cited to support suspension of sentence, having regard to the age gap, the uncle guardian relationship and repeated abuse of the child.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The accused appealed only against the sentence, contending that the High Court should have suspended the custodial term despite the statutory minimum. He argued that the High Court failed to follow a prior Court of Appeal decision in CA Appeal 120/2001 and the principle in Queen v. Kularatne allowing suspension when there is a long lapse of time and potential hardship to the accused's family. He further submitted that the court failed to consider Supreme Court authority (SC Appeal 89A/2009) asserting a discretion to suspend sentence even where a minimum mandatory sentence is prescribed. The appeal therefore focused on alleged misapplication of sentencing principles and failure to give due weight to delay and family circumstances.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Complaint that the High Court failed to suspend the sentence in line with the Court of Appeal decision in CA Appeal 120/2001. | Reliance on Queen v. Kularatne 71 NLR 529 to argue that, given more than 10 years had elapsed since the offence, the court should consider disturbance to the accused's family and the grave repercussions and could have suspended the sentence. | Allegation that the High Court failed to apply the principle in SC Appeal 89A/2009 that a court may suspend a sentence notwithstanding a statutory minimum mandatory term. | Reliance on delay (over a decade) and the accused being the breadwinner caring for elderly parents as grounds for mitigation and suspension of the custodial sentence.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: Because the accused tendered an unqualified plea of guilty, there was no contested trial and no detailed analysis of oral or forensic evidence in the judgment. The sentencing and appellate analysis turned instead on admitted facts such as the victim's age, the familial relationship, repeated acts of abuse and the circumstances advanced in mitigation. The Court of Appeal focused on these aggravating and mitigating factors rather than on the credibility of witnesses or evidentiary conflicts.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal did not engage in a probability based assessment of competing versions of events, as the conviction rested on the accused's guilty plea. Instead, it weighed the aggravating features of repeated grave sexual abuse of a minor niece against the mitigation advanced and concluded that public interest and the seriousness of the offence justified the custodial sentence imposed.
defence_version_summary: The defence did not contest the facts of the charges and the accused entered an unqualified plea of guilty to all three counts. In mitigation, counsel emphasized that the plea was tendered at the outset, that the accused had no previous convictions, suffered from a nerve ailment, was responsible for looking after his elderly parents, and that the incident had occurred about 13 years earlier and the case had been pending for around 14 years. On appeal, it was further argued that in light of these circumstances and relevant precedents, the High Court should have exercised discretion to suspend the sentence. The Court of Appeal found that no sufficient mitigating facts had been pleaded to displace the need for an immediate custodial sentence.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal examined the statutory framework, noting that Section 365B(2)(b) prescribes a minimum sentence of 7 years rigorous imprisonment, a fine and compensation for grave sexual abuse of a person under 18 years. It referred to leading authorities on sentencing, including Attorney General v. H.N. De Silva, Attorney General v. Mendis and Attorney General v. Ranasinghe, as well as English guidance in Roberts and the principle in King v. Rankira that appellate intervention in sentencing is warranted only where discretion is exercised on a wrong principle. The court emphasized public interest, deterrence and the aggravating factors present: the victim's young age, repeated acts of abuse, the uncle guardian relationship, the age disparity and the mental impact on the victim. It held that the High Court appropriately considered these factors, correctly distinguished authorities where suspension was granted in very different factual contexts, and had not erred in declining to suspend the sentence, so there was no basis to interfere with the sentence imposed.
coa_sentence_type: Rigorous imprisonment of 7 years on each of 3 counts (to run concurrently) with a fine of 2000 on each count, sentence affirmed
brief_judgment_file_summary: This Court of Appeal judgment concerns an appeal against sentence by an accused who pleaded guilty in the High Court of Kegalle to three counts of grave sexual abuse of his 14 year old niece under Section 365B(2)(b) of the Penal Code. The High Court convicted him on his plea and imposed 7 years rigorous imprisonment on each count, to run concurrently, together with fines, declining to suspend the custodial term in light of the seriousness and aggravating circumstances of the offences. On appeal, the accused relied on delay, his personal and family circumstances and several precedents to argue that the High Court should have suspended the sentence despite the statutory minimum. The Court of Appeal, after reviewing the statutory scheme and key sentencing authorities on sexual offences, held that the High Court had properly exercised its sentencing discretion, that public interest and deterrence required an immediate custodial sentence and that no wrong principle had been applied, and accordingly dismissed the application without costs.
prosecution_counsel: Malik Azeez, Senior State Counsel for the State
defence_counsel: Dr. Sunil Abeyratne with H. Gunathilake for the Accused-Appellant
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court of Kegalle convicted the accused on his own plea of guilty and applied the minimum mandatory sentence under Section 365B(2)(b), imposing 7 years rigorous imprisonment on each of three counts and fines, to run concurrently. In its sentencing order, it distinguished Supreme Court authority (SC Appeal 03/08) on the basis that that case involved a love affair whereas here the victim was a minor niece, there was a substantial age gap, and the accused occupied a guardian like position, having repeatedly abused the child when her parents were absent. The Court of Appeal endorsed this reasoning and found that, in light of the aggravating factors and the nature of the offence, the High Court was justified in declining to suspend the sentence.
precedents_cited_list: CA Appeal 120/2001 – Court of Appeal decision dated 20.05.2004 (Nanayakkara J and Abeyratne J) | Queen v. Kularatne – 71 NLR 529 | SC Appeal 89A/2009 – Supreme Court of Sri Lanka | SC Appeal 03/08 – Supreme Court of Sri Lanka | The Attorney General v. H.N. De Silva – 57 NLR 121 | The Attorney General v. Mendis – 1995 1 SLR 138 | The Attorney General v. Ranasinghe and Others – 1992 2 SLR 81 | Rex v. Boyd – (1908) 1 Cr. App. Rep. 64 | Roberts – Court of Appeal of England rape sentencing case (referred to at page 244) | King v. Rankira – 42 NLR 145
standard_of_review_applied: The Court of Appeal reiterated that it will not interfere with a sentencing judge's discretion unless that discretion has been exercised on a wrong principle, relying in particular on King v. Rankira and related sentencing authority, and found no such misdirection or wrongful principle in this case.
sentencing_principles_applied: The court applied principles that sentencing must reflect the gravity of the offence, statutory ranges, deterrence, public disapproval, protection of vulnerable victims and public interest, and that reformation of the offender, while relevant, is subordinate where serious sexual offences against minors with aggravating factors are concerned. It also endorsed the view that sentence bargaining should not be encouraged and that for rape and grave sexual abuse an immediate custodial sentence is ordinarily required except in wholly exceptional circumstances.
final_charge_after_appeal: Grave sexual abuse under Section 365B(2)(b) of the Penal Code on three counts

judges: Menaka Wijesundera J | Wickum A. Kaluarachchi J
offence_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: PW-1, an 11-year-old boy living in Enderamulla with his parents and two younger siblings, was sexually abused by the accused-appellant, a 25-year-old neighbour. The accused wanted PW-1 to live with him and repeatedly suggested killing PW-1's family by setting fire to their house. On the day before the incident he obtained sleeping tablets and petrol, had sleeping pills mixed into the family's dinner, and in the early hours of 01.02.2002 he removed PW-1 from the house and set it on fire. PW-1's parents and two younger siblings, who were sleeping inside, died in the blaze.
evidence_type_primary: Eyewitness testimony of child victim PW-1
evidence_type_secondary: Medical evidence and other corroborative witness testimony
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code (four counts)
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court of Gampaha tried the appellant in absentia under section 241 of the Code of Criminal Procedure while he was absconding but represented by counsel. Relying principally on PW-1's testimony, supported by medical and other evidence, the judge held that PW-1 was not an accomplice, that his evidence was credible, and that the prosecution had proved the four counts of murder beyond reasonable doubt. The court convicted the appellant on all four counts under section 296 and imposed the death sentence.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: On appeal, counsel argued that the High Court judge erred in law by applying section 76 of the Penal Code to PW-1 and by holding that PW-1 was not an accomplice whose evidence required corroboration. They claimed PW-1's evidence was unreliable because of contradictions and because no conditional pardon was tendered to him under section 256 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. They further submitted that the police investigations lacked integrity, citing alleged fabrication surrounding the recovery of a flambeau at the scene. The appeal thus challenged both the legal characterization of PW-1 and the evaluation of the prosecution evidence.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Alleged misapplication of section 76 of the Penal Code to PW-1 when assessing his culpability. | Challenge to the finding that PW-1 was not an accomplice and that his evidence could be acted upon without corroboration. | Allegation that PW-1's testimony was not credible due to contradictions and inconsistencies. | Complaint that no conditional pardon was granted to PW-1 under section 256 of the Code of Criminal Procedure despite treating him as effectively involved. | Allegation that the integrity and credibility of the police investigation were compromised, including issues relating to the recovery of a flambeau.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal examined PW-1's evidence in detail, noting his account of the sexual abuse, the preparatory acts involving sleeping tablets and petrol, and the events around 3.00 a.m. when the accused took him out of the house and the fire started. It held that although some minor contradictions and omissions were marked, the core narrative about the crime was not effectively challenged in cross-examination. Medical and other witness evidence were seen as corroborating PW-1 on material aspects, and the court concluded that he was a credible witness whose testimony could be safely relied upon without corroboration.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal found the prosecution version, particularly PW-1's account supported by medical and other evidence, to be consistent and compelling, while the defence offered no alternative explanation and merely attacked credibility and investigation. It held that alleged investigative defects and minor contradictions did not create a reasonable doubt and therefore declined to extend the benefit of the doubt to the appellant.
defence_version_summary: The appellant did not call any defence witnesses after the close of the prosecution case, and there is no record of a positive defence version beyond suggestions put in cross-examination challenging PW-1's credibility and the integrity of the investigation. Counsel argued that PW-1 was an accomplice whose uncorroborated evidence could not sustain a conviction and that investigative bias undermined the case. Both the High Court and the Court of Appeal rejected these contentions, finding no credible alternative account of events and treating the appellant's challenges as insufficient to displace the prosecution case.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal first addressed the complaint about investigative integrity, concluding that even if there were irregularities concerning the flambeau, they did not affect the trial judge's reasoning because he had not relied on any connection between that item and the appellant, and no miscarriage of justice was shown. It then considered the main grounds regarding PW-1's status, holding that as an 11-year-old child who lacked sufficient maturity and who acted under fear and domination by the appellant, he fell within section 76 of the Penal Code and could not be treated as an accomplice, so no pardon or corroboration was legally required. The court emphasized that PW-1 was a victim and witness, not a guilty associate, and that his testimony was consistent on the central events, with minor contradictions and omissions properly evaluated by the High Court. Applying authorities on defective investigations and accomplice evidence, the Court of Appeal upheld the trial judge's assessment of credibility, found the prosecution case proved beyond reasonable doubt, and affirmed both conviction and sentence.
coa_sentence_type: Death
brief_judgment_file_summary: The Court of Appeal heard an appeal by the accused-appellant, who had been tried in absentia and sentenced to death by the High Court of Gampaha on four counts of murder for setting fire to the home of an 11-year-old boy, killing the boy's parents and two siblings. After reviewing the facts, it rejected defence arguments that the main witness PW-1 was an accomplice requiring a pardon and corroboration, holding that as an 11-year-old victim of continuing sexual abuse who acted out of fear and without criminal intent, he fell within section 76 of the Penal Code and could not be treated as an accomplice. The court held that minor contradictions and alleged investigative defects, including issues over the recovery of a flambeau, did not undermine the credibility of PW-1 or cause any miscarriage of justice, especially as the trial judge had not relied on the impugned item. Endorsing the High Court's careful evaluation of evidence and legal reasoning, the Court of Appeal affirmed the convictions and death sentences and dismissed the appeal.
prosecution_counsel: Disna Warnakula, Deputy Solicitor General, for the State
defence_counsel: Amila Palliyage with Sandeepani Wijesooriya, Savani Udugampola, Lakitha Wakishta Arachchi and Subaj De Silva for the Accused-Appellant
weapon_type: Flambeau (torch) and petrol used to set fire to the house
cause_of_death_exact_text: Death of the four victims caused by the house being set on fire while they were sleeping inside.
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court judge analyzed PW-1's age, vulnerability and relationship with the appellant, concluded that he lacked the maturity and intent necessary to be an accomplice within section 76, and treated him as an ordinary witness whose credible testimony did not require corroboration. The judge considered contradictions and alleged investigative shortcomings but found that they did not affect the core prosecution narrative or the proof of the four murders beyond reasonable doubt. The Court of Appeal reviewed this reasoning and held that the trial judge had correctly applied the law and properly evaluated the evidence, finding no error warranting appellate intervention.
precedents_cited_list: Dissanayake Mudiyanselage Jayasiri v. The Hon. Attorney General – S.C. Appeal 73/2015 (18.09.2018) | Panangalage Don Nilanka and another v. The Hon. Attorney General – S.C. Appeal 139/2014 (21.11.2018) | Ajith Fernando alias Konda Ajith and others v. The Attorney General – (2004) 1 Sri L.R. 288 | Union of India v. Prakash P. Hinduja – AIR 2003 SC 2612 | H.N. Rishbud v. The State of Delhi – 1955 SCR 1150 | Amar Singh v. Balwinder Singh – AIR 2003 SC 1164 | King v. Pieris Appuhamy – 43 NLR 412 | Rekumal v. Emperor – 1934 AIR 183 | Peiris v. Dole – 49 NLR 142 | Emperor v. Burn – 11 Bombay Law Reports | Galagamage Indrawansa Kumarasiri and three others v. W.M.M. Kumarihamy and Hon. Attorney General – S.C. TAB Appeal 02/2012 (02.04.2014)
standard_of_review_applied: The Court of Appeal examined whether there was any misdirection on the law regarding section 76 and accomplice status, whether investigative defects or contradictions caused a miscarriage of justice, and whether the High Court's evaluation of credibility and evidence was perverse or unreasonable.
final_charge_after_appeal: Murder of four persons under Section 296 of the Penal Code (four counts).

judges: P. Kumararatnam J | K.M.G.H. Kulatunga J
brief_facts_summary: The petitioner and another accused were tried in the Magistrate’s Court of Colombo on charges of cheating and misappropriation of 800000, and the petitioner, who had absconded, was tried in absentia under Section 192(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, convicted and sentenced on 2010-08-27 while an open warrant was issued against him. Nearly six years later he filed an appeal to the Provincial High Court of the Western Province relying on the ICCPR Act to challenge the Magistrate’s judgment, but the High Court dismissed the appeal as being out of time and pointed to the specific procedure under Section 192(2) to vacate an in absentia determination. In 2024 the petitioner invoked the Court of Appeal’s revisionary jurisdiction seeking to set aside the High Court’s 2017 judgment and to obtain the same lenient treatment and suspended sentence that had been afforded to the first accused. The State opposed the application on grounds of extreme delay, continued absconding and lack of clean hands.
hc_judgment_summary: The Provincial High Court of the Western Province, sitting at Colombo, held that the appeal filed by the petitioner against the Magistrate’s conviction and sentence was governed by the time limits in the Code of Criminal Procedure. It found that the appeal, lodged about six years after the Magistrate’s judgment, was hopelessly out of time and that Section 192(2) of the Code provided the proper procedure to vacate an in absentia conviction. On that basis the High Court rejected the appeal for want of jurisdiction.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: Before the Court of Appeal, the petitioner contended that the Provincial High Court should not have dismissed his appeal because it had been filed under Section 4(2) of the ICCPR Act, which he claimed conferred a right of appeal without a prescribed time limit. He argued that the High Court erred in applying the Code of Criminal Procedure time limits and in refusing to entertain his appeal on that basis. In addition, he sought to obtain the same concession as the first accused, namely the opportunity to repay half of the allegedly misappropriated sum with a suspended sentence. The State countered that the petitioner was guilty of extreme laches, had absconded for years, and had not approached the court with clean hands.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Alleged that an appeal brought under Section 4(2) of the ICCPR Act is not subject to the usual time limits in the Code of Criminal Procedure and therefore the Provincial High Court erred in rejecting the appeal as out of time. | Contended that the Provincial High Court misapplied the law on appeals and failed to recognise the broader right of appeal guaranteed by the ICCPR Act. | Requested that the petitioner be afforded the same concession given to the first accused, namely the opportunity to pay half of the misappropriated sum to the virtual complainant and receive a suspended sentence. | Implicitly challenged the procedural route adopted by the High Court, arguing that it should have entertained the appeal rather than directing the petitioner to the mechanism under Section 192(2) for in absentia convictions.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal order does not re-evaluate the trial evidence or discuss individual witnesses, focusing instead on the long procedural history, delay and jurisdictional questions. There is no analysis of credibility, contradictions or reliability of any prosecution or defence witnesses. The merits of the original conviction are left untouched as the Court confines itself to whether the appeal and revision applications are maintainable.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal treats the extreme delay and lack of jurisdiction as dispositive and therefore does not engage in weighing probabilities or considering the benefit of the doubt on the underlying charges. It emphasises that without a valid, timely appeal or demonstrated exceptional circumstances in revision, the conviction and sentence must stand without re-examination of the evidence.
defence_version_summary: At trial the petitioner had absconded and was tried in absentia, so no detailed defence version or alibi is recorded in this judgment. In the later proceedings he claimed that he had pursued the wrong remedy and relied on the ICCPR Act to justify a late appeal, while also asking to receive the same suspended sentence and restitution arrangement that had been granted to the first accused. The Court of Appeal regarded his conduct as demonstrating laches and a lack of clean hands rather than a credible substantive defence and refused to interfere.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal stresses that revisionary jurisdiction is discretionary and can only be invoked upon proof of exceptional circumstances such as a miscarriage of justice or patent illegality; mere dissatisfaction with a time-bar ruling does not suffice. It endorses the Provincial High Court’s view that appeals from Magistrates’ Courts are subject to the time limits in the Code of Criminal Procedure and that appeals filed years out of time leave the appellate court without jurisdiction. The Court rejects the argument that Section 4(2) of the ICCPR Act creates a freestanding, timeless right of appeal, holding instead that the general procedural framework and time limits continue to apply. It also finds that the petitioner’s long delay, continued absconding and failure to seek appropriate remedies earlier preclude any exercise of revisionary powers or grant of sentencing concessions.
coa_sentence_type: Not applicable
brief_judgment_file_summary: This Court of Appeal order concerns a revision application by a convicted accused who had been tried in absentia for cheating and misappropriation and who, after many years of absconding, sought to challenge an adverse Provincial High Court decision and obtain lenient sentencing similar to his co-accused. The Court traces the procedural history, noting that the Magistrate’s conviction and sentence were delivered in 2010, that an appeal to the Provincial High Court was lodged about six years late, and that the High Court rejected that appeal as time-barred and directed attention to the specific procedure for vacating in absentia convictions. Analysing principles of revisionary jurisdiction, exceptional circumstances and statutory time limits for appeals, the Court of Appeal concludes that Section 4(2) of the ICCPR Act does not displace the general appeal time limits or confer jurisdiction to entertain an appeal filed after such a long delay. Finding no exceptional circumstances, no legal error in the High Court’s reasoning and significant laches by the petitioner, the Court refuses to issue notice and dismisses the revision application in limine.
defence_counsel: Tenny Fernando
hc_analysis_summary: The Provincial High Court treated the petitioner’s appeal from the Magistrate’s conviction as an ordinary criminal appeal governed by the Code of Criminal Procedure and found that, having been filed roughly six years after the Magistrate’s judgment, it was hopelessly out of time. It also observed that where a conviction is entered in absentia under Section 192(1), the proper course is to invoke Section 192(2) to seek to vacate that determination, rather than to file a late appeal. The Court of Appeal expressly endorses this analysis, holding that the High Court correctly declined jurisdiction over the out-of-time appeal and committed no reviewable error.
precedents_cited_list: Dharmaratne and Another v Palm Paradise Cabanas Ltd. and Others – (2003) 3 SLR 24 | Wijesinghe v Tharmaratnam – Sri Skantha’s Law Reports Vol. IV 47 | Attorney General v Podisingho – 51 NLR 385 | Tirimanne v Commissioner of Income Tax – 59 NLR 304 | Ekanayake Mudiyanselage Upali Herath v Aluthge Wijedasa – CA (PHC) 163/2002
standard_of_review_applied: Revisionary jurisdiction based on exceptional circumstances, laches and absence of jurisdiction where an appeal is filed out of time
final_charge_after_appeal: Cheating and misappropriation

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 3 of the Animals Act
offence_category: Offence under the Animals Act (illegal transportation of cattle)
brief_facts_summary: The registered owner of vehicle SP-LE-5212 had the vehicle released on a bail bond of Rs. 1,000,000 after it was seized for transporting cattle without a permit. The registered owner initially denied receiving the vehicle but later admitted it was released to him and that he had sold it, and failed to produce it for a court inquiry. The Magistrate ordered the registered owner to deposit the bond value and the High Court dismissed the revision application; the Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal and upheld the Magistrate's order.
evidence_type_primary: Admission by the registered owner and court record of the Registrar's inquiry
evidence_type_secondary: Registrar's report and documentary bail bond record
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 3 of the Animals Act
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court considered the facts and circumstances and found no reason to interfere with the Magistrate's order requiring the registered owner to deposit the bond value, therefore dismissing the revision application.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant challenged the Magistrate's order to deposit Rs. 1,000,000 on the basis that he was not the person to whom the vehicle was released and disputed the factual basis for ordering deposit, initially denying release and later offering an alternative account involving a finance company.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Appellant initially denied that the vehicle was released to him | Appellant alleged the finance company had released the vehicle | Appellant contested the Magistrate's order to deposit the bond value after failing to produce the vehicle | Appellant sought revision of the Magistrate's order in the High Court
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Registrar's inquiry established that the vehicle was released to the appellant and the appellant gave inconsistent statements, initially denying and later admitting he had sold the vehicle. The court found the appellant attempted to mislead the court and relied on documentary and procedural records rather than viva voce eyewitness testimony.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court evaluated documentary and admission evidence and found the appellant's admissions and the Registrar's report sufficiently probable to uphold the Magistrate's factual finding; no benefit of doubt was extended to the appellant.
defence_version_summary: The appellant initially denied receiving the vehicle and later claimed the finance company had released it; he then admitted selling the vehicle. There was no alibi and no defence witnesses were called. The court found the appellant's statements not credible and viewed them as attempts to mislead the court.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found that the Magistrate followed correct procedure in ordering the appellant to deposit the bond value because the appellant had signed the bail bond and taken charge of the vehicle. The Court accepted the Registrar's inquiry and the appellant's inconsistent statements, rejected the appellant's alternative explanation involving the finance company, and upheld the High Court's refusal to interfere with the Magistrate's order. The Court noted the vehicle had been used previously in similar offences which supported the Magistrate's view and considered the appellant's conduct as necessitating enforcement of the bond.
coa_sentence_type: Order to deposit bond value (Rs. 1,000,000)
brief_judgment_file_summary: Appeal against the Provincial High Court judgment dismissing a revision application concerning a Magistrate's order that the registered owner of vehicle SP-LE-5212 deposit Rs. 1,000,000 because he failed to produce the vehicle for an inquiry into confiscation under the Animals Act. The appellant initially denied receiving the vehicle, later admitted it was released to him and sold, and failed to produce it. The Magistrate ordered deposit of the bond value and the High Court dismissed the revision. The Court of Appeal found no merit in the appeal and dismissed it, directing communication of the judgment to the High Court and Magistrate's Court for implementation.
defence_counsel: Migara Kodithuwakku instructed by Manjula Kalupahana
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court reviewed the facts and circumstances and found no reason to interfere with the Magistrate's order to require the registered owner to deposit the bond value, thereby dismissing the revision application; the Court of Appeal agreed with that assessment.
standard_of_review_applied: Review of correctness of the Magistrate's procedure and factual findings, and whether there was reason for the High Court to interfere with the Magistrate's order
final_charge_after_appeal: Offence under the Animals Act (Section 3)

judges: Menaka Wijesundera | Wickum A. Kaluarachchi
offence_sections: Section 386
brief_facts_summary: The complainant entered into a tenancy in 1999 and later an agreement to purchase the property for Rs.2,700,000, paying amounts which he alleges total Rs.2,200,000 or Rs.22,00,000. The High Court convicted the accused-appellant for dishonest misappropriation under Section 386 and imposed sentence by judgment dated 2016-08-30. On appeal the Court of Appeal found that the prosecution did not prove dishonest intention beyond reasonable doubt and allowed the appeal, setting aside the conviction and sentence.
evidence_type_primary: Eyewitness testimony (complainant) and documentary evidence (agreement, cheques)
evidence_type_secondary: Documentary evidence (cheques, district court settlement, agreement to sell)
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 386
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court accepted the complainant's evidence that large sums were paid and concluded the accused dishonestly misappropriated the money by executing an unregistered agreement and attributing knowledge and culpability to the accused (and his wife as a lawyer). The High Court convicted under Section 386 and imposed sentence on 2016-08-30.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant submitted that the trial judge failed to consider uncontroverted evidence negating dishonest intention and erred in law and fact in concluding that the appellant dishonestly misappropriated funds. The appellant also contended the transaction was essentially civil and the High Court misapplied legal principles regarding unenforceable agreements and the Prevention of Frauds Ordinance.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Failure to attach significance to uncontroverted evidence negating dishonest intention | Error in fact and law in concluding dishonest misappropriation | Transaction is civil in nature and not criminal | High Court accepted unproven cash payments contrary to District Court findings | Misapplication of Prevention of Frauds Ordinance and inference of fraud from non-registration
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The complainant (PW-1) testified to multiple payments and produced three cheques for portions of the sum while also claiming cash payments which lacked receipts and precise dates. The appellant gave a dock statement and called three witnesses and offered to return the money; the Court of Appeal found the evidence did not establish dishonest misappropriation beyond reasonable doubt and noted inconsistencies between District Court findings and the High Court acceptance of unproven cash payments.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal assessed probabilities against the prosecution where key cash payments were unproven and held that the prosecution failed to exclude reasonable doubt; the High Court's acceptance of the complainant's fuller payment claim was considered unsafe and not supported by evidence.
defence_version_summary: The defence denied dishonest misappropriation, gave a dock statement and proposed to repay the amounts, and called three witnesses; no alibi was advanced. The Court of Appeal found the defence evidence and the lack of clear proof by the prosecution sufficient to create reasonable doubt about dishonest intention.
legal_errors_description: The Court of Appeal found the High Court erred by treating an unregistered agreement entered into by mutual consent as proof of fraudulent intent, by attributing non-registration to the accused alone despite mutual agreement, and by accepting unproven cash payments contrary to District Court findings, thereby misdirecting itself on the law and facts.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed whether dishonest intention was proved and concluded it was not. Key reasons included that the agreement was unregistered by mutual consent, non-registration alone did not establish fraud, the High Court wrongly attributed knowledge and culpability to the accused and his wife as a lawyer, and the prosecution failed to prove cash payments conclusively. The COA found the High Court's inference of dishonest misappropriation perverse, weighed prosecution credibility unfavorably on contested items, and considered the defence offer to repay and defence witnesses sufficient to raise reasonable doubt.
brief_judgment_file_summary: Appeal against conviction under Section 386 for alleged misappropriation of funds paid under an agreement to sell. High Court convicted on 2016-08-30 accepting complainant's broader payment claims and inferring dishonest intent from lack of notarial registration. Court of Appeal held prosecution failed to prove dishonest misappropriation beyond reasonable doubt, found legal and factual errors in the High Court's reasoning regarding non-registration and attribution of intent, set aside the conviction and sentence and allowed the appeal on 2024-02-28.
defence_counsel: Dr. Ranjith Fernando with Champika Monarawila and Michelle Fernando
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court accepted the complainant's testimony that substantial payments were made and concluded the accused dishonestly misappropriated the funds by executing an unregistered agreement and relying on the accused's wife as a lawyer to have known registration was required. The Court of Appeal found these conclusions erroneous because the agreement was unregistered by mutual consent and non-registration did not itself establish dishonest intent.
standard_of_review_applied: Court reviewed for misdirection on law and perverse findings in evaluation of evidence
final_charge_after_appeal: Misappropriation under Section 386 (same) but acquitted

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Forest Ordinance (proviso to section 40(1)); Mines and Minerals Act (section not specified)
offence_category: Illegal transport of timber and sand (breach of Forest Ordinance and Mines & Minerals Act)
brief_facts_summary: The registered owner of a tipper vehicle sought to prevent confiscation after the vehicle was used to transport timber and sand without permits. The driver/accused pleaded guilty and was sentenced by the Magistrate; the Magistrate ordered confiscation of the vehicle under section 40(1) of the Forest Ordinance. The owner filed revision proceedings in the High Court which were dismissed, and the Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal.
evidence_type_primary: Oral testimony of the vehicle owner (appellant)
evidence_type_secondary: Court record including accused's guilty plea and police detention records
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Forest Ordinance and Mines and Minerals Act (sections not explicitly stated in judgment)
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court dismissed the appellant's revision application, agreeing with the Magistrate that the appellant failed to prove on the balance of probability that he had taken all precautions to prevent use of his vehicle for the offence. The High Court found no merit in the appellant's contentions and upheld the confiscation order.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant argued the Magistrate applied an unduly high burden of proof beyond the balance of probabilities and rejected his evidence without sufficient basis. He also contended the accused was convicted on a defective charge and that this defect was relevant to the inquiry into confiscation.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Claim that Magistrate imposed an excessively high burden of proof on the appellant | Submission that accused was convicted on a defective charge impacting the inquiry | Claim that evidence of the appellant was wrongly discredited
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: Only the appellant (vehicle owner) gave evidence at the inquiry; his testimony contained multiple inconsistencies and improbabilities which undermined its reliability. The court found the evidence to be essentially hearsay without corroboration and noted the appellant's failure to call the friend alleged to have custody of the vehicle.
probability_assessment_by_court: The court applied the balance of probabilities standard and found the appellant failed to prove he had taken all reasonable precautions; inconsistencies and lack of corroborating witnesses led the court to reject the appellant's version.
defence_version_summary: The appellant claimed he had handed the vehicle to a friend (named inconsistently as Duminda/Mahinda), instructed it not be used illegally, collected monthly payments, and was unaware the vehicle transported timber and sand. There was no alibi; only the appellant testified and the court found his credibility weak due to material inconsistencies and failure to call the friend to corroborate.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal upheld the Magistrate and High Court findings, emphasizing that the owner had to prove on the balance of probability that he took all reasonable precautions to prevent misuse of the vehicle. The COA highlighted inconsistencies in the appellant's evidence (wrong registration number, inconsistent dates and friend names), the absence of corroborative witnesses, and that any defects in the charge did not prejudice the accused. The court found no misdirection in law and no reason to interfere with confiscation.
coa_sentence_type: Unchanged (sentence as imposed by Magistrate; details not specified)
brief_judgment_file_summary: Appeal by the registered owner of a tipper vehicle against confiscation under section 40(1) of the Forest Ordinance after the vehicle was used to transport timber and sand without permits. The Magistrate ordered confiscation after the accused pleaded guilty; the High Court dismissed the owner's revision application. The Court of Appeal found the owner's testimony inconsistent and uncorroborated, applied the balance of probabilities standard, and dismissed the appeal.
defence_counsel: Jagath Abeynayake with Aranya Dewanarayana and Ishani Gunathilaka
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court dismissed the appellant's revision application after considering the Magistrate's order and the evidence, finding the appellant failed to prove he had taken all precautions required by the proviso to section 40(1) of the Forest Ordinance. The COA agreed that the High Court properly considered the law and facts.
precedents_cited_list: The Finance Company PLC Vs. Priyantha Chandra and Five Others (2010) 2 SLR 220
standard_of_review_applied: Balance of probabilities for the proviso to section 40(1); review for misdirection or perversity in Magistrate's factual findings
final_charge_after_appeal: Original charges upheld

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Penal Code Sections 386, 389, 392, 400, 402, 454; Offences Against Public Property Act Section 5
brief_facts_summary: The Petitioner, a Court Clerk in charge of the production room, was arrested regarding the loss of 308.14 grams of gold jewels. It is alleged that an individual impersonating a police constable surreptitiously took the jewels. The Petitioner was charged under the Public Property Act.
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court Judge refused the revision application to grant bail to the Petitioner by order dated 24.05.2023.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The Petitioner argued that he is the sole breadwinner for his family, including three children and sick parents. He contended that he has been in remand for over 9 months and that the items in question might not legally constitute 'Public Property'.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Long period of remand (over 9 months). | Humanitarian grounds (sole breadwinner, sick parents). | Legal argument that court productions claimed by third parties may not be 'Public Property'. | Presumption of innocence.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court did not analyze witness evidence in depth as this was a bail application. It considered the B reports and the lack of incriminating evidence presented so far.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court noted that any benefit of doubt regarding the strength of the case must accrue to the suspect at the bail stage.
defence_version_summary: The Petitioner denies the charges, attributing the theft to an impersonator. He emphasizes his clean record, family responsibilities, and the potential legal argument regarding the definition of public property.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court allowed the bail application based on exceptional circumstances, citing the long remand period, the presumption of innocence, and the lack of strong prima facie evidence. The Court emphasized that remand should not be used as punishment before conviction.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The Court of Appeal granted bail to a suspect charged under the Public Property Act for missing court productions. The Court found exceptional circumstances in the 9-month remand period and the absence of strong incriminating evidence.
defence_counsel: Rushdie Habeeb with Rizwan Uwaiz and Supun Dissanayake
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court had refused bail, impliedly finding that no exceptional circumstances existed to overcome the statutory bar in the Public Property Act.
precedents_cited_list: Ramu Thamodarampillai v. The Attorney General [2004] 3 SLR 180 | CA(PHC)APN 107/2018
standard_of_review_applied: Evaluation of exceptional circumstances for bail

judges: Menaka Wijesundera, J | Wickum A. Kaluarachchi, J
offence_sections: Section 365 B(2)(b) of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The accused-appellant, a three-wheeler driver transporting school children, was charged with sexually abusing an eight-year-old girl. The victim testified that after dropping off other children, the accused took her to a forest area and forced her to perform oral sex. The abuse occurred on multiple occasions during the first half of 2014.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 365 B(2)(b) of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court acquitted the accused on counts two and three due to lack of specific proof regarding the dates but convicted him on the first count. He was sentenced to eight years rigorous imprisonment, fined, and ordered to pay compensation.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant argued that the prosecution failed to prove the offence occurred within the stipulated time and that the charges were vague regarding the specific place and incident. He also contended that the acquittal on two counts should have precluded conviction on the first and that the trial judge failed to properly evaluate evidence and probabilities.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Failure to prove commission of offence within the time period stipulated in charges | Insufficient notice of place and incident (Section 165(1) CPC) | Inconsistency: Conviction on count 1 despite acquittal on counts 2 and 3 | Failure to apply the test of probability | Improper evaluation of evidence and failure to consider contradictions
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The court accepted the child victim's testimony, noting that delay in reporting and minor inconsistencies are natural for a child of that age (8 years old) and do not undermine credibility. The court cited guidelines on child witnesses and accepted the mother's explanation for the delay in making a police complaint.
probability_assessment_by_court: The court rejected the defense argument that the presence of other children made the abuse improbable, accepting that the accused could have chosen a day when the victim was alone.
defence_version_summary: The accused made a dock statement denying the allegations, claiming they were fabricated due to a financial dispute over 'seettu salli'. The court and the victim's mother rejected this motive as implausible for fabricating such a serious charge.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal affirmed the conviction, ruling that the indictment properly specified a time period under Section 174(1) and that exact dates are not essential unless material. The court upheld the trial judge's evaluation of the child witness, finding the delay in reporting understandable due to fear. The dock statement was found insufficient to cast reasonable doubt.
coa_sentence_type: Rigorous Imprisonment 8 years
brief_judgment_file_summary: The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal of an accused convicted of sexually abusing an 8-year-old girl in a three-wheeler. The court upheld the High Court's findings, rejecting arguments regarding vague charges and the probability of the incident, and affirmed the 8-year rigorous imprisonment sentence.
defence_counsel: Harshana Matara Arachchi
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court correctly convicted on the first count while acquitting on the others due to technical proof of dates, which did not contradict the finding of guilt. The trial judge's assessment of the child witness's credibility and the rejection of the defense's fabrication theory were deemed correct.
precedents_cited_list: Thimbirigolle Sirirathana Thero v. OIC Police Station Rasnayakepura - CA No.194/2015 | A.K.K.Rasika Amarasinghe v. O.I.C. Special Investigating Unit - SC Appeal No.140/2010 | King v. Kitchilan - 45 NLR 82 | R. v. Dossi - 13 Cr. App.R. 158 | Bharwada Bhoginbhai Hirjibhai v. State of Gujarat - 1983 AIR 753 | Daradadagamage Chandraratne Jayawardane alias Shantha v. The Attorney General - CA/85/2013
standard_of_review_applied: Evaluation of evidence credibility (child witness) and procedural validity of charges.
sentencing_principles_applied: The sentence was deemed reasonable and lawful.

judges: M. T. Mohammed Laffar, J. | S. U. B. Karalliyadde, J.
offence_sections: Police Disciplinary Code Section 1, Section 5(B), Section 16
offence_category: Disciplinary Offences (Aiding cattle theft, False statement)
brief_facts_summary: The Petitioner, a Police Inspector, was charge-sheeted for aiding and abetting the theft of 5 heads of cattle and making false statements. Following a formal disciplinary inquiry, he was found guilty and demoted to Sub-Inspector. He appealed to the National Police Commission and the Administrative Appeal Tribunal (AAT), both of which upheld the decision, leading him to file this Writ Application.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The Petitioner argued that the AAT decision contained an error of law on the face of the record because the evidence of key witnesses was not corroborated and they harbored animosity towards him. He claimed the prosecution failed to prove charges on the balance of probability.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Error of law on the face of the record | Evidence of PW1 and PW2 not corroborated | Lack of direct or circumstantial evidence | Witness animosity/hatred | Prosecution failed to prove charges on balance of probability
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court observed that the AAT had properly considered whether the Inquiring Officer evaluated the evidence correctly. The Petitioner's claim that witnesses PW1 and PW2 testified due to hatred was noted, but the tribunal's reliance on the evidence was deemed reasonable.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court noted that the charges were proved on the balance of probability at the Formal Disciplinary Inquiry.
defence_version_summary: The Petitioner pleaded not guilty and alleged that witnesses Jayasiri (PW1) and his wife (PW2) implicated him falsely due to hatred because the Petitioner had previously arrested the brother of Jayasiri's wife for possession of a hand grenade.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court held that the AAT's reasons were consistent, intelligible, and not bad in law. It found that the tribunal had not acted with manifest unreasonableness in evaluating the evidence. Additionally, the Court noted that quashing the AAT decision would be futile as the Petitioner had not challenged the underlying decisions of the National Police Commission and the Inquiring Officer.
coa_sentence_type: Demotion from Inspector to Sub-Inspector
brief_judgment_file_summary: The Petitioner sought a Writ of Certiorari to quash the Administrative Appeal Tribunal's decision upholding his demotion for disciplinary offences involving cattle theft. The Court of Appeal dismissed the application, finding no error of law on the face of the record and noting that the relief sought would be futile as the original disciplinary decisions were not challenged.
defence_counsel: P. K. Perera
hc_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal reviewed the AAT's decision and found it had properly considered the Inquiring Officer's evaluation of the evidence. The Court found no error of law or erroneous legal approach in the tribunal's findings.
precedents_cited_list: Gunasekera Vs. De Mel, Commissioner of Labour - 79 (2) NLR 409 | Chas Hayley and Co. Ltd., Vs. Commercial and Industrial Workers - [1995] 2 Sri LR 42 | Samastha Lanka Nidahas Grama Niladhari Sangamaya Vs Dissanayake - [2013] BLR 68 | Siddeek Vs Jacolyn Seneviratne - [1984] 1 Sri LR 83 | Ratnasiri and others Vs Ellawala and others - (2004) SLR 180
standard_of_review_applied: Error of law on the face of the record; manifest unreasonableness.

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 364(1) of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The victim, a married woman, was walking through a rubber plantation when the appellant dragged her into a ditch and raped her. She identified him at an identification parade. The appellant denied involvement, claiming he was 16 at the time and at home.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 364(1) of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the accused based on the victim's testimony and positive identification at the parade. He was sentenced to 10 years rigorous imprisonment, a fine of Rs. 10,000, and compensation of Rs. 100,000.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant argued that the prosecution's evidence was unfairly based on leading questions. He further contended that the identification was unsatisfactory, citing Turnbull guidelines, lack of prior acquaintance, and discrepancies in the description given to the police versus the accused's appearance.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Evidence elicited through leading questions denied fair trial | Unsatisfactory identification (Turnbull guidelines) | Contradictions regarding description (age, squint eye, skin color) | Failure to consider dock statement properly
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The court found the victim's evidence credible, viewing leading questions as necessary clarifications for an uneducated witness. Medical evidence of nail marks supported her account of a struggle. The identification was deemed reliable as the victim had ample time to view the assailant in daylight.
probability_assessment_by_court: The court assessed the identification as reliable, noting the incident occurred in daylight with close contact, rejecting the view that it was a fleeting glance requiring strict Turnbull warnings.
defence_version_summary: The accused made a dock statement denying the offence, claiming he was 16 years old at the time and sleeping at home. He also alleged police assault and being forced to sign a statement.
procedural_defects_description: The court found that leading questions were clarification attempts and did not prejudice the appellant.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court dismissed the appeal, holding that the 'leading questions' were acceptable clarifications for an uneducated witness. It ruled that the identification was reliable given the daylight conditions and struggle, distinguishing it from fleeting glance cases requiring strict Turnbull warnings. Contradictions in description were deemed minor and not properly challenged by the defence.
coa_sentence_type: Rigorous Imprisonment 10 years
brief_judgment_file_summary: The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal of Thanthrige Don Shantha Alwis against his conviction for rape by the High Court of Gampaha. The Court upheld the conviction based on the victim's testimony and identification parade evidence, rejecting arguments about leading questions and unsatisfactory identification. The sentence of 10 years rigorous imprisonment was affirmed.
defence_counsel: Suhada Gamlath, P.C. with Sumudu Hewage
hc_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found that the High Court Judge correctly evaluated the evidence and identification. Any potential infirmities were deemed not to have occasioned a failure of justice.
precedents_cited_list: State of Punjab Vs. Gurmeet Singh and others (1996) 2 SCC 384 | Regina Vs. Turnbull (1977) Q.B. 224 | Sigera Vs. The Attorney General (2011) 1 SLR 201 | The Attorney General Vs. Sanadnam Pitchi Theresa (2011) 2 SLR 292 | Bogm Bhai Hirji Bhai Vs. State of Gujarat, AIR (1983) SC 753 | Stirland Vs. D. P. P.- (1944) А.С. 315
standard_of_review_applied: Substantial miscarriage of justice test (Article 138 proviso / Section 436)

judges: Menaka Wijesundera J. | Wickum A. Kaluarachchi J.
offence_sections: Section 296, Section 380
brief_facts_summary: The deceased was found dead in his home with injuries from a blunt weapon. The prosecution alleged that the two appellants and an absconding accused committed the murder and robbed the deceased's vehicle, basing the case on circumstantial evidence including the recovery of a pestle and the 1st appellant's arrest with the deceased's motorcycle. The accused admitted presence but claimed a fight occurred between the deceased and the absconding accused.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 296, Section 380
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the 1st and 3rd appellants along with the absconding 2nd accused for murder and robbery based on circumstantial evidence. The trial judge utilized the evidence given by the defence to fill gaps in the prosecution's case to establish guilt.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The 1st appellant argued that the trial judge evaluated the evidence erroneously and failed to properly consider Section 32 of the Evidence Ordinance. The 3rd appellant argued that the case was based on circumstantial evidence which was not proved beyond a reasonable doubt.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Erroneous evaluation of prosecution and defence evidence. | Improper consideration of Section 32 of the Evidence Ordinance. | Circumstantial evidence insufficient to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt. | Trial judge erred by using defence evidence to fill gaps in the prosecution case.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The prosecution presented family members (mother, brother, brother-in-law) and official witnesses (army, police, doctor). The defence presented the evidence of the appellants on oath, which remained uncontradicted. The court found the prosecution witnesses established presence but not the murderous intention or participation of the appellants.
probability_assessment_by_court: The court found the prosecution failed to prove the case beyond reasonable doubt and that the defence version was plausible and uncontradicted.
defence_version_summary: The appellants testified they visited the deceased for a vehicle transaction. They claimed the deceased, who was drunk, attacked the absconding 2nd accused with a pestle. The 2nd accused retaliated in self-defence. The appellants claimed to be bystanders who fled the scene.
legal_errors_description: The trial judge erred by using the evidence of the defence to fill in the gaps of the prosecution and reversed the presumption of innocence.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal held that the circumstantial evidence did not lead to an irresistible inference of guilt and that common intention was not proved. The Court criticized the trial judge for using defence testimony to bolster the prosecution's case, which violates the presumption of innocence. The uncontradicted evidence of the appellants suggested they were mere bystanders.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The Court of Appeal overturned the High Court's conviction of two appellants for murder and robbery. The case relied on circumstantial evidence, which the appellate court found insufficient to establish common intention. The court emphasized that defence evidence cannot be used to fill gaps in the prosecution's case and acquitted both appellants.
defence_counsel: Nalin Ladduwahetty, P.C. with Kavithri Ubeysekara; Neranjan Jayasinghe
cause_of_death_exact_text: shock and hemorrhage due to injuries caused from a blunt weapon
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court had concluded the appellants shared a common murderous intention based on inadequate circumstances. The Court of Appeal stated the trial judge erred by examining the truthfulness of the defence evidence in light of the prosecution's evidence rather than considering the totality properly.
precedents_cited_list: Mapalagama Acharige Ariyaratne vs The Attorney General SC 31-1992 | James Silva vs The Republic of Sri Lanka (1980) 2SLR 167 | Jayasena vs The Queen 72 NLR 313
standard_of_review_applied: Review of evidence evaluation and burden of proof application

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 296
brief_facts_summary: The appellant assaulted his 80-year-old father following a verbal altercation over a land deed after both had consumed alcohol. Eyewitnesses saw the appellant beating the deceased with his hands, feet, and a wooden plank. The deceased sustained 13 injuries, including fractured ribs, and succumbed to them.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 296
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court Judge found the appellant guilty of murder, accepting the eyewitness and medical evidence. The Judge rejected the appellant's defence of lack of intention and provocation, partly relying on contradictions in the appellant's police statement.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant argued that the trial judge failed to consider the aspect of provocation or cumulative provocation and did not properly evaluate the defence version. It was also submitted that the judge relied on inadmissible evidence regarding intention and failed to recognize the appellant's lack of intention to kill.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Failure to consider provocation or cumulative provocation | Failure to consider the defence version of events in correct perspective | Consideration of inadmissible evidence in the judgment | Failure to consider that the appellant had no intention
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court found the evidence of eyewitnesses (PW-01, PW-04, PW-06) to be cogent and trustworthy, establishing that quarrels were common between the father and son. The medical evidence (JMO) confirmed the severity of the beating with 13 contusions and fractured ribs.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court assessed the probability of a sudden fight based on the established history of alcohol-fueled quarrels and the specific dispute over the deed on the day of the incident.
defence_version_summary: The appellant testified that he cared for his father, but they frequently quarreled when drunk. He claimed his father scolded him over a refusal to hand over a land deed, leading to a sudden loss of temper and the assault, without any intention to kill.
legal_errors_description: The High Court Judge erroneously relied on inadmissible confessionary statements (marked X-1, X-2, X-3) to reject the appellant's credibility. The Judge also failed to consider the exception of sudden fight and provocation which arose from the prosecution's own evidence.
procedural_defects_description: Consideration of inadmissible confessionary statements from the police investigation during the trial findings.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal held that the trial judge erred by relying on inadmissible portions of the appellant's police statement. The Court found that the evidence, including prosecution witnesses, supported a finding of a sudden fight and cumulative provocation. Consequently, the conviction for murder was set aside and replaced with culpable homicide not amounting to murder.
coa_sentence_type: Rigorous Imprisonment 12 years
brief_judgment_file_summary: The appellant appealed a death sentence for murdering his father. The Court of Appeal found that the High Court improperly considered inadmissible confessionary evidence and failed to address the defense of sudden fight and provocation. The conviction was modified to culpable homicide not amounting to murder under Section 297, and the sentence was reduced to 12 years rigorous imprisonment.
defence_counsel: Ershan Ariaratnam
cause_of_death_exact_text: death had been due to the injuries sustained by the deceased
hc_analysis_summary: The COA criticized the High Court for failing to consider the exception under Section 294 regarding sudden fights, despite evidence supporting it. The HC was also found to have misdirected itself by using inadmissible confessionary statements to discredit the accused's testimony.
precedents_cited_list: Rathnayake Mudiyanselage Karunarathne Vs. The Attorney General C.A. 181/2009 | Gamini vs. The Attorney General (2011) 1 SLR 236
standard_of_review_applied: Misdirection on law regarding admissibility of evidence and failure to consider statutory exceptions supported by evidence.
sentencing_principles_applied: Sentencing under Section 297 considering the nature of injuries and the time already served.
final_charge_after_appeal: Culpable homicide not amounting to murder (Section 297)

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 9A (1) read with Section 10(d) of the Fauna and Flora Protection Ordinance as amended by Act No.22 of 2009
brief_facts_summary: The Petitioner, owner of a backhoe, sought the release of his machine which was confiscated after its operator pleaded guilty to excavating gravel in Wilpattu National Park without authority. The Petitioner claimed he was unaware of the offence and had taken necessary precautions. The Magistrate confiscated the machine, and the High Court refused to issue notice on the Petitioner's revision application.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 9A (1) read with Section 10(d) of the Fauna and Flora Protection Ordinance as amended by Act No.22 of 2009
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court Judge refused to issue notice to the Respondents, effectively dismissing the revision application. The Judge held that the Petitioner had failed to submit plausible reasons to revise the Learned Magistrate's order confiscating the vehicle.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The Petitioner argues that the High Court erred in refusing notice despite a prima facie case and exceptional circumstances. He contends that he proved ownership and lack of knowledge of the offence on a balance of probabilities and took all precautions. He further argues his right to a fair hearing was violated.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Failed to consider that on the date of supporting, the Petitioner had only to put forward a prima facie case | Failed to appreciate that there were exceptional circumstances warranting the exercise of revisionary jurisdiction | Misdirected themselves with regard to the rights of the absolute owner to be heard | Failed to consider that the Petitioner has proved ownership on a balance of probability | Failed to consider that the Petitioner has proved that the Petitioner had no knowledge of the commission of the offence | Failed to consider that the Petitioner had taken all precautions to prevent the use of the vehicle for the commission of the offence | Misdirected themselves by imposing a higher burden of proof on the Petitioner in a vehicle confiscation inquiry | Failed to consider and properly apply the accepted legal principles and judicial precedents
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal accepted the evidence of the Petitioner and the operator, noting it was consistent and showed the operator acted on his own without the owner's knowledge. The Court criticized the Magistrate for ignoring this evidence and demanding an impossible standard of precaution.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court reaffirmed that the standard of proof for a claimant in a confiscation inquiry is the balance of probabilities.
defence_version_summary: The Petitioner maintained he hired the operator for legitimate work with instructions against illegal activities. The operator admitted to excavating gravel at the request of villagers without the Petitioner's knowledge or permission.
legal_errors_description: The High Court erred in refusing notice when a prima facie case was shown. The Magistrate erred by imposing an excessively high burden of proof on the owner regarding precautions and misdirected on the number of witnesses required.
procedural_defects_description: High Court refused notice summarily, denying a fair hearing.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal held that an innocent owner who proves on a balance of probabilities that they were unaware of the offence and took precautions is entitled to the release of the vehicle. The Court found the Petitioner had satisfied this burden through his testimony and the operator's evidence. The Court emphasized that precautions should be assessed subjectively and not artificially, and that the High Court erred in not exercising its revisionary jurisdiction to correct the Magistrate's erroneous order.
coa_sentence_type: Confiscation order set aside; Vehicle released to Petitioner
brief_judgment_file_summary: The Petitioner appealed against the refusal of the High Court to issue notice on a revision application regarding the confiscation of his backhoe. The backhoe had been used by an employee to commit an environmental offence without the Petitioner's knowledge. The Court of Appeal set aside both the High Court's refusal and the Magistrate's confiscation order, ruling that the Petitioner had established his bona fides and lack of complicity on a balance of probabilities. The vehicle was ordered to be released.
defence_counsel: Asanka Dissanayake with Ershan Ariaratnam
hc_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the High Court failed to appreciate the exceptional circumstances and the prima facie case presented by the Petitioner, wrongfully refusing to issue notice.
precedents_cited_list: Commissioner of Police v. Tanes (1957-58) 68 CLR 383 | The Orient Financial Services Corporation Ltd v. The Range Forest Officer, Ampara and Hon. Attorney General [2013] 1 SLR 208 | Mudankotuwa v Attorney General [1996] 2 SLR 77 | CA/PHC/203/17 | Mallawa Arachchige Supun Malhara v The Attorney General CA(PHC) 09/2015 | Ceylinco Leasing Corporation v M.H. Harrison and others SC Appeal 43/2012 | Vadivelu Thevar Vs. State of Madras SIR S C 614
standard_of_review_applied: Revisionary Jurisdiction
sentencing_principles_applied: Confiscation of a vehicle should not occur if the owner is innocent and took reasonable precautions.

judges: M. T. Mohammed Laffar, J. | K. K. A. V. Swarnadhipathi, J.
brief_facts_summary: The Petitioner was ordered to pay maintenance to his wife and child by the Magistrate's Court of Colombo. Upon his failure to do so, the Magistrate imposed a jail term on 11-10-2017. The Petitioner unsuccessfully sought revision in the High Court before applying to the Court of Appeal.
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court affirmed the order of the Magistrate regarding the jail term imposed for failure to pay maintenance and dismissed the Petitioner's revision application.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The Petitioner sought to revise the lower court orders but the case turned on preliminary objections raised by the State. The State argued the Petitioner failed to establish exceptional circumstances, failed to exercise the statutory right of appeal, and was guilty of laches.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Petitioner claimed inability to appeal due to mental stress | Petitioner claimed lack of awareness of the right to appeal | Petitioner cited financial difficulties preventing family assistance
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The judgment does not analyze witness evidence as it was decided on preliminary objections regarding the maintainability of the revision application.
probability_assessment_by_court: The court did not assess factual probabilities but focused on the legal threshold for revision.
defence_version_summary: The Petitioner admitted to not filing an appeal in time but offered excuses including mental stress, ignorance of the law, and financial difficulties.
