procedural_defects_description: The Petitioner failed to explain the 9-month delay in filing the revision application and failed to exercise the statutory right to appeal without valid reason.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court upheld the State's preliminary objections, emphasizing that revision is an extraordinary remedy available only in exceptional circumstances, which the Petitioner failed to establish. The Court noted the Petitioner had a right of appeal which was not exercised, and the reasons provided (stress, ignorance) were insufficient. Additionally, the unexplained delay of 9 months was deemed unreasonable.
coa_sentence_type: Jail term
brief_judgment_file_summary: The Petitioner filed a Revision Application against the High Court's affirmation of a Magistrate's order imposing a jail term for non-payment of maintenance. The State raised preliminary objections regarding the lack of exceptional circumstances, failure to exercise the right of appeal, and unexplained delay. The Court of Appeal upheld these objections, citing settled law that revision is discretionary and requires prompt action and exceptional grounds. The application was dismissed with costs.
defence_counsel: Rushdie Habeeb with Rizwan Uwais
hc_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal did not review the High Court's factual findings but implicitly supported its decision by refusing to grant revisionary relief.
precedents_cited_list: Thilagaratnam Vs. E.A.P. Edirisingha [1982] 1 SLR 56 | Cadaman Pulle Vs. Ceylon Paper Sacks Ltd. [2001] 3 SLR 112 | Dharmaratne Vs. Palmparadise cabanas Ltd. [2003] 3 SLR 24 | Rasheed Ali Vs. Mohamed Ali [1981] 1 SLR 262 | AG. Vs. Najimudeen (SC. Appeal No. 62/2016) | Geethani Nilushika Vs. Waruni Harshika (SC Appeal No. 93/2017) | Seylan bank Vs. Thangaveil [2004] 2 SLR 101 | Rajapakse Vs. The State [2001] 2 SLR 161
standard_of_review_applied: Revisionary jurisdiction (Exceptional Circumstances)

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 364(2) read with section 364(2)(g) of the Penal Code as amended
brief_facts_summary: The victim, a 52-year-old woman, was dragged to a shrub area by the 1st and 2nd Respondents while returning from work. The 1st Respondent raped her while the 2nd Respondent stood by, threatening to kill her. Witnesses arrived upon hearing her wails, interrupting the accused who then claimed the act was consensual for money.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 364(2) read with section 364(2)(g) of the Penal Code
hc_sentence_type: Rigorous Imprisonment 10 years suspended for 15 years, Fine, Compensation
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the 1st Respondent of Gang Rape but acquitted the 2nd Respondent. The judge imposed a 10-year rigorous imprisonment term but suspended it for 15 years, alongside a fine and compensation, contrary to the mandatory minimum sentencing laws.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The Attorney General challenged the legality of the suspended sentence, arguing that Gang Rape carries a mandatory minimum term of 10 years which cannot be suspended. The default sentence for compensation was also challenged as exceeding the legal limit.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Sentence illegal as Gang Rape carries a minimum mandatory punishment of 10 years | Section 303(2)(a) of CPC prohibits suspending sentences where a mandatory minimum is prescribed | Section 303(2)(d) of CPC prohibits suspending sentences where the term exceeds two years | Default sentence for compensation illegal under Section 291(d) of CPC
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The court accepted the victim's testimony which was corroborated by witnesses PW2 and PW3 who arrived at the scene and observed her distressed state and torn clothes. The defence version of consent was rejected.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal focused on the legality of the sentence rather than factual probability, implicitly accepting the High Court's factual findings that established guilt.
defence_version_summary: The accused claimed they were drunk and the victim consented to sexual intercourse for money, but they were interrupted by witnesses before any sexual act occurred.
legal_errors_description: The High Court illegally suspended a mandatory minimum sentence of 10 years contrary to Section 303(2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure Act. The default sentence for compensation also exceeded the statutory limit.
procedural_defects_description: Sentencing procedure violated mandatory statutory provisions prohibiting suspension of sentences for Gang Rape.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal held that the High Court Judge acted illegally by suspending the sentence for Gang Rape, which carries a mandatory minimum of 10 years. Citing the Code of Criminal Procedure Act, the Court ruled that sentences cannot be suspended when a mandatory minimum exists or when the term exceeds two years. The Court emphasized the legislative intent to punish heinous crimes against women severely and corrected the sentence to 10 years rigorous imprisonment.
coa_sentence_type: 10 years Rigorous Imprisonment, Fine Rs. 30,000 (default 6 months RI), Compensation Rs. 100,000 (default 2 years RI)
brief_judgment_file_summary: The Attorney General filed a revision application challenging the suspended sentence imposed on the 1st Respondent for Gang Rape. The High Court had convicted the accused but suspended the 10-year term, which the AG argued was illegal due to the mandatory minimum sentencing laws. The Court of Appeal agreed, citing clear statutory prohibitions against suspending such sentences. The Court modified the sentence to 10 years rigorous imprisonment and reduced the default sentence for compensation.
hc_analysis_summary: The COA criticized the HC Judge for misdirecting himself on the law and failing to impose the mandatory punishment prescribed by the legislature. The COA noted the HC Judge's sentence was illegal and allowed a perpetrator of a heinous crime to avoid proper punishment.
precedents_cited_list: Attorney General and Others v. Sumathipala [2006] 2 SLR 126 | R.S.Nayak v.A.R.Antulay, AIR 1984 SC 684 | Tennakoon v. Dissanakayake 50 NLR 403 | Nandasena v Senanayake and Others [1981] 1 SLR 238 | Dhananjay Chatterjee alias Dhana v State of West Bengal [1194] 2 SCC 220
standard_of_review_applied: Legality of sentence
sentencing_principles_applied: Deterrence, Legislative Intent, Protection of Women

judges: Menaka Wijesundera J. | Wickum A. Kaluarachchi J.
offence_sections: Grave sexual abuse under the provisions of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The accused-appellant, the paternal grandfather of the victim, was indicted for grave sexual abuse of his 5-year-old granddaughter. The prosecution alleged the victim ran into the appellant's house while playing hide and seek, where the appellant allegedly held her and rubbed her genitals against his penis. The defense argued the case was fabricated due to a land dispute between the appellant and the victim's father.
evidence_type_secondary: Medical evidence (JMO), testimony of the victim's brother and father
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Grave sexual abuse under the provisions of the Penal Code (Count 1)
hc_sentence_type: Unknown (Sentence details not provided in text)
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court Judge convicted the appellant on the first count and acquitted him on the second count. The trial judge concluded the prosecution proved its case beyond reasonable doubt before analyzing the defense evidence, which the Court of Appeal found to be a grave error.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant argued that the prosecution failed to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt and that the trial judge failed to consider material contradictions and omissions. Additionally, it was argued that the trial judge erred by concluding the prosecution's case was proved before evaluating the defense evidence, violating the presumption of innocence.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The prosecution had not proved its case beyond a reasonable doubt | The learned trial judge had not considered the omissions and the contradictions in the story of the prosecution satisfactorily | The story of the prosecution being highly improbable | Trial judge erred by examining defense evidence only after concluding prosecution proved its case | Trial judge failed to appreciate the demeanor and deportment of witnesses correctly
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court found significant contradictions between the victim's testimony and that of her brother and the JMO. The victim claimed she stood while the act occurred, but her brother claimed she was seated on the appellant's lap. The JMO stated the victim only reported touching the penis (Count 2, acquitted), not the act in Count 1.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court held that the contradictions created a reasonable doubt, especially given the unchallenged defense evidence regarding a land dispute.
defence_version_summary: The appellant testified on oath, denying the allegations and attributing them to a land dispute with the victim's father regarding the distribution of paddy lands. This version was corroborated by his wife and remained unchallenged during cross-examination.
legal_errors_description: The trial judge violated the presumption of innocence by concluding the prosecution proved its case beyond reasonable doubt before considering the defense evidence. The judge also failed to properly evaluate contradictions between the victim's evidence and corroborating witnesses.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal held that the trial judge fundamentally erred by deciding the prosecution had proved its case prior to analyzing the defense evidence. The Court noted vital contradictions between the victim (PW-1), her brother (PW-3), and the JMO (PW-9) regarding the nature of the act and the victim's position. The defense evidence regarding a land dispute was consistent and unchallenged, casting reasonable doubt on the prosecution's case. Consequently, the conviction on Count 1 was unsafe.
coa_sentence_type: Acquitted
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused-appellant appealed a conviction for grave sexual abuse of his granddaughter. The High Court had convicted him on one count despite contradictions in the prosecution evidence and a consistent defense regarding a land dispute. The Court of Appeal set aside the conviction, ruling that the trial judge erred by deciding guilt before evaluating the defense evidence and by failing to address material contradictions between the victim and other prosecution witnesses. The appellant was acquitted.
defence_counsel: U.R. de Silva, PC with Hiruni Rubereu and M. Hannadige
hc_analysis_summary: The COA criticized the HC for reversing the burden of proof by evaluating defense evidence only after finding the prosecution case proved. The COA also found the HC failed to appreciate the demeanor of witnesses and ignored vital contradictions.
precedents_cited_list: Wickremasinghe vs Dedolina and others 1996 (2) SLR | The Republic of Sri Lanka vs. Thimbirigolle Sirirathana Thero CA 194-2015 | James Silva vs The Republic of Sri Lanka 1980 (2) SLR page 167 | Anthony Michael Morril V. Attorney General Court of Appeal Case No. CA 26/06
standard_of_review_applied: Review of evidence evaluation and application of burden of proof principles.

judges: Menaka Wijesundera J. | Wickum A. Kaluarachchi J.
offence_sections: Sections 140, 146-296, 146-410 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The accused-appellant, along with others, formed an unlawful assembly armed with katties and attacked the deceased at the house of Farook around 10:30 PM. They also damaged a vehicle and property at the scene. The incident was witnessed by three eyewitnesses, and the motive was linked to a previous murder case involving the witnesses.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Sections 140, 146-296, 146-410 of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The trial judge convicted the appellant along with the 1st and 2nd accused for charges of unlawful assembly and murder. The judge accepted the prosecution evidence and rejected the defence.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant argued that the trial judge failed to properly consider Section 48 of the Judicature Act No. 2 of 1978 before adopting evidence recorded by a predecessor. Additionally, the appellant contended that the identification of the accused was unsatisfactory and unreliable.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The trial judge had not considered section 48 of the Judicature act no 2 of 1978 before adopting the evidence led before his predecessor | Lack of identification of the appellant
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The court relied on the testimony of three eyewitnesses, including two brothers of the deceased, who identified the appellant with the aid of light from the house and torches. The court found the identification reliable despite the incident occurring at night.
probability_assessment_by_court: The court held that the identification of the appellant was established by the prosecution beyond a reasonable doubt.
defence_version_summary: The appellant gave evidence on oath denying the entire incident.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found that the trial judge had correctly exercised discretion under Section 48 of the Judicature Act to adopt evidence recorded by a predecessor, noting that a retrial would cause injustice given the 1986 offence date. The Court also affirmed the identification evidence, citing the presence of artificial light and multiple witnesses. The Court concluded the prosecution proved the case beyond reasonable doubt.
coa_sentence_type: Original sentence affirmed
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused-appellant appealed a High Court conviction for murder and unlawful assembly related to an incident in 1986. The appeal challenged the identification evidence and the trial procedure where the judge adopted evidence recorded by a predecessor under Section 48 of the Judicature Act. The Court of Appeal upheld the conviction, ruling that the judge properly exercised discretion to avoid delay and that the eyewitness identification was reliable. The appeal was dismissed.
defence_counsel: K. Kugaraja
hc_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the High Court's reasoning sound, particularly regarding the acceptance of eyewitness testimony and the procedural decision to continue the trial on adopted evidence.
precedents_cited_list: SC appeal SC-CHC-37-2013 | Bandaranaike vs Jagathesan and others 1984 2 SRI L. R 397
standard_of_review_applied: Beyond reasonable doubt

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: section 365B(2)(b) of the Penal Code as amended by the Penal Code (Amendment) Act No. 22 of 1995, 29 of 1998 and 16 of 2006
brief_facts_summary: The appellant was indicted for committing grave sexual abuse on a male minor (12 years old) between February and March 2012 at a rubber estate. The victim, who had low IQ, identified the appellant as 'Beeri Kalu Ayya' but could not recall the specific date. The incident came to light after the victim was abused by another person and examined by a JMO.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: section 365B(2)(b) of the Penal Code as amended by the Penal Code (Amendment) Act No. 22 of 1995, 29 of 1998 and 16 of 2006
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court Judge found the appellant guilty based on the reliable evidence of the victim child, despite the child's inability to specify the date. The Judge considered the child's limitations and found the evidence truthful.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant argued that the prosecution failed to prove the specific date and place of the offence. Additionally, it was argued that there was no evidence establishing the accused's presence at the alleged place on the alleged date.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The date of the offence and the place of offence has not been proved by the prosecution. | The prosecution has failed to adduce any evidence to establish that the accused was present on the alleged date and place of the offence.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court found the victim's evidence highly reliable and cogent despite his low IQ and inability to recall the date. The medical evidence supported the history given by the child. Minor discrepancies were deemed immaterial.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court held that the prosecution proved the case beyond reasonable doubt, as the date is not material without prejudice to the accused.
defence_version_summary: The accused made a dock statement merely denying the allegations and asking to be discharged. He did not dispute his identity or residence in the same area as the victim.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal affirmed the conviction, ruling that the date of the offence is not a material particular unless it prejudices the accused's defence (citing Rex v Dossi). Since the accused's defence was a mere denial and he lived in the same village, the lack of a specific date did not cause prejudice. The Court upheld the trial judge's assessment of the victim's credibility.
coa_sentence_type: Rigorous Imprisonment 12 years (deemed to commence from 30-07-2021)
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused appealed a conviction for grave sexual abuse of a minor, arguing the date and place were not proved. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal, holding that under Section 165 of the Criminal Procedure Code and case law like Rex v Dossi, a specific date is not essential unless prejudice is shown. The conviction and sentence of 12 years rigorous imprisonment were affirmed.
defence_counsel: Yuwin Matugama
hc_analysis_summary: The COA found the High Court Judge correctly evaluated the evidence, including the victim's testimony and the dock statement. The Judge's findings on facts and credibility were deemed sound.
precedents_cited_list: Rex Vs. Dossi 13 Cr. App. R. 158 | D. R. M. Pandithakoralage (Excise Inspector) Vs. V. Κ. Selvanayagam 56 NLR 143 | Mahathun and Others Vs. Attorney General (2015) 1 SLR 74 | Alwis Vs. Piyasena Fernando (1993) 1 SLR 119
standard_of_review_applied: Appellate courts will not lightly disturb findings of primary fact by a trial judge unless manifestly wrong.

judges: D.N. Samarakoon, J. | K. K. A. V. Swarnadhipathy, J.
offence_sections: Inland Revenue Act No. 10 of 2006; Tax Appeals Commission Act No. 23 of 2011; Value Added Tax Act No. 14 of 2002
brief_facts_summary: The Appellant, Reckitt Benckiser (Lanka) Limited, appealed against a determination regarding Value Added Tax (VAT) and penalties confirmed by the Tax Appeals Commission. The core dispute was whether the Appellant constituted a 'manufacturer' under the VAT Act when utilizing third-party contract manufacturers (MOS Lanka and Lalan) for products like 'Mortein' and 'Harpic'. Procedural issues were raised concerning whether the determinations by the Tax Appeals Commission and the Commissioner General of Inland Revenue were time-barred under the relevant statutes.
hc_judgment_summary: The Tax Appeals Commission (the tribunal below) determined that the Appellant was a manufacturer and confirmed the VAT and penalty payable. It rejected the argument that the determinations were time-barred.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The Appellant argued that the Tax Appeals Commission's determination was time-barred as it was made 526 days after the hearing commenced, exceeding the 270-day limit. They also argued the Commissioner General's determination was time-barred due to invalid acknowledgment of the appeal. Substantively, they contended they were not the 'manufacturer' but merely the brand owner purchasing from contract manufacturers.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Is the determination of the Tax Appeals Commission time barred? | Is the determination made by the Commissioner General of Inland Revenue time barred? | Did the Tax Appeals Commission err in law in concluding the appellant was a manufacturer within the contemplation of the Value Added Tax Act? | Is the determination of the Tax Appeals Commission against the weight of evidence? | Is the amount of Value Added Tax and penalty payable excessive, arbitrary and unreasonable?
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court analyzed the statutory interpretation of 'manufacturer' and the procedural timelines rather than witness credibility in a criminal sense. The Court accepted the Appellant's position that they purchased goods from contract manufacturers (MOS Lanka and Lalan) who physically manufactured the products.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court applied statutory interpretation principles, holding that tax statutes must be strictly construed and benefits of doubt given to the taxpayer.
defence_version_summary: The Appellant maintained they were not the manufacturer but the purchaser of goods from contract manufacturers. They argued the statutory time limits for the Tax Appeals Commission and Commissioner General were mandatory and had been violated, rendering the determinations void.
legal_errors_description: The Court found the Tax Appeals Commission erred in interpreting the 270-day time limit as directory rather than mandatory. The Court also found legal error in classifying the Appellant as a 'manufacturer' when they were outsourcing production.
procedural_defects_description: The Tax Appeals Commission failed to make its determination within the mandatory 270-day period. The Commissioner General of Inland Revenue failed to properly acknowledge the appeal or determine it within the statutory time limit.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal held that the time limit of 270 days in Section 10 of the Tax Appeals Commission Act is mandatory, and failure to comply renders the determination void. It distinguished tax statutes from fundamental rights cases, emphasizing strict construction in favor of the taxpayer. The Court also held that the Commissioner General's determination was time-barred because the acknowledgment of the appeal by an Assessor was invalid without specific delegation. On the substantive issue, the Court ruled that the Appellant was not a 'manufacturer' under the VAT Act, as the physical manufacturing was done by third-party contract manufacturers (MOS Lanka and Lalan), and ownership/branding did not equate to manufacturing under the statutory definition.
coa_sentence_type: Tax liability and penalties vacated
brief_judgment_file_summary: This is a tax appeal case where Reckitt Benckiser (Lanka) Ltd challenged VAT and penalties imposed by the Commissioner General of Inland Revenue and confirmed by the Tax Appeals Commission. The Court of Appeal allowed the appeal on both procedural and substantive grounds. Procedurally, the Court held that the statutory time limits for the Tax Appeals Commission to make a determination are mandatory, and the Commission's decision made after 526 days was time-barred and void. Substantively, the Court ruled that the Appellant, who outsourced production to contract manufacturers, did not fit the statutory definition of a 'manufacturer' under the VAT Act and was therefore not liable for the tax.
defence_counsel: Dr. Shivaji Felix P.C. with Mr. Shanaka Amarasinghe and Mr. Nivantha Satharasinghe
hc_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found that the Tax Appeals Commission (acting as the lower tribunal) erred in law by treating mandatory time limits as directory and by misinterpreting the definition of 'manufacturer' to include a brand owner using contract manufacturers.

Tax 04/2013 | Unilever Sri Lanka Limited vs. Commissioner General of Inland Revenue C. A. Tax 23/2029
standard_of_review_applied: Question of Law

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 22(3) read with section 22(1) of Act No-37 of 1916 as amended by Amendment Act No- 22 of 1996 and Section 27 read with section 9 of the Explosives Act No- 21 of 1956
brief_facts_summary: On May 22, 2005, acting on a tip-off, PW-01 and a police team raided a house in Peliyagoda where they found the appellant in a room on the upper floor. A T-56 gun and 29 live ammunitions were discovered under the mattress of the bed used by the appellant. The appellant was arrested and subsequently indicted for illegal possession of the firearm and ammunition.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 22(3) read with section 22(1) of Act No-37 of 1916 as amended by Amendment Act No- 22 of 1996 and Section 27 read with section 9 of the Explosives Act No- 21 of 1956
hc_sentence_type: Life imprisonment and six months imprisonment
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court found the appellant guilty on both counts. He was sentenced to life imprisonment for the possession of the T-56 gun and six months imprisonment for the possession of ammunition.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appeal argued that the prosecution failed to prove the case beyond reasonable doubt and that the trial judge failed to properly evaluate the evidence or appreciate witness credibility. A key ground was that the judgment violated Section 283 of the Code of Criminal Procedure by not providing proper reasons and by analyzing the defence before the prosecution case. It was also argued that the burden of proof was misapplied.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The case has not been proved beyond reasonable doubt. | The conviction cannot be supported having regard to the evidence led at the trial. | There is no evaluation of the prosecution evidence. | The learned High Court Judge has failed to appreciate the credibility of PW-01 and PW-09 especially in the context that the raid was a planned detection. | The learned High Court Judge misdirected himself of the burden of the prosecution and that of the defence, and the Ellenborough dictum was applied erroneously. | There was no proper analysis of the dock statement. | The judgment was totally contrary to section 283 of the Code of Criminal Procedure Act. | The absence of notes by the police officers in the context of fact that this was a planned detection has not been considered. | Whether it is safe to convict the accused under the circumstances.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal did not deeply analyze the specific testimonies of PW-01 and PW-09 but focused on the High Court Judge's failure to evaluate them. The COA noted that the trial judge did not scrutinize the prosecution evidence to establish a prima facie case before considering the defence.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court found the High Court failed to properly assess probability or reasonable doubt, instead relying on the weakness of the defence to convict.
defence_version_summary: The accused made a dock statement. The specific content is not detailed, but the judgment notes the trial judge rejected the defence as untenable and false in light of prosecution evidence without proper independent evaluation.
legal_errors_description: Violation of Section 283 of the Code of Criminal Procedure by failing to provide reasons and points for determination. Misdirection on burden of proof by examining the defence evidence in light of prosecution witnesses rather than evaluating prosecution evidence independently.
procedural_defects_description: The judgment did not follow the mandatory legal requirements for a judgment, failing to analyze evidence or give reasons for the decision.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal held that the High Court Judge committed a fatal irregularity by determining the case based on the weakness of the defence rather than the strength of the prosecution. The judgment was found to be in violation of Section 283 of the Code of Criminal Procedure as it lacked proper evaluation of evidence and reasons for the decision. The Court cited established case law emphasizing that the prosecution must stand on its own legs. Due to the reversal of the presumption of innocence and the defective judgment structure, the conviction was set aside. A retrial was deemed inappropriate given the 18-year lapse since the incident and the accused's long incarceration.
coa_sentence_type: Acquitted
brief_judgment_file_summary: The appellant appealed against a conviction for illegal possession of a T-56 gun and ammunition, for which he received a life sentence. The Court of Appeal found that the High Court Judge failed to write a proper judgment in accordance with Section 283 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, specifically by analyzing the defence's weakness to support the conviction rather than establishing the prosecution's case independently. This approach reversed the burden of proof and presumption of innocence. Consequently, the conviction was set aside, and no retrial was ordered due to the significant delay of over 18 years since the incident.
defence_counsel: Kalinga Indatissa P.C. with Ms. Rashmini Indatissa, Ms. Razana Salih
hc_analysis_summary: The COA criticized the HC for not following the conventional or legal approach to judgment writing. The HC judge was faulted for compartmentalizing the evidence and deciding the case based on the untenability of the defence.
precedents_cited_list: Chandrasena and Others Vs. Munaweera (1998) 3 SLR 94 | Ibrahim Vs. Inspector of Police 59 NLR 235 | Thusaiya Vs. Pathihamy 15 CLW 119 | Narender Kumar Vs. The Queen 72 NLR 313 | State of Uttar Pradesh Vs. Anthony (1984) SCJ 236 | Nandasena Vs. Attorney General (2008) 1 SLR 51 | L.C. Fernando Vs. The Republic of Sri Lanka 79-II NLR 313
standard_of_review_applied: Review of compliance with mandatory statutory provisions (Section 283) and fundamental principles of burden of proof.
sentencing_principles_applied: Considered principles for ordering retrial: time duration, period of incarceration, trauma to accused, and interests of justice.

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 296 read with Section 32 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: On June 8, 2001, the deceased was traveling in a three-wheeler when the Appellant and another accused forcibly entered the vehicle and stabbed him to death. The incident was witnessed by the three-wheeler driver (PW2), who identified the Appellant as a neighbor. The Appellant was indicted for murder and robbery but convicted only of murder.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 296 read with Section 32 of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court accepted the evidence of the sole eyewitness (PW2) as convincing and credible, finding no reason to disbelieve him. The Appellant was convicted of murder and sentenced to death, while being acquitted of the robbery charge.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The Appellant contended that the evidence of the sole eyewitness (PW2) failed the test of credibility and probability. The defence argued that the witness's testimony did not inspire the confidence of the Court.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Evidence of sole eyewitness PW2 fails the test of credibility, probability and does not inspire the confidence of the Court
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the sole eyewitness (PW2) reliable as he knew the Appellant well and had no motive to falsely implicate him. The Court noted that alleged contradictions regarding the witness's statement to the police were not properly marked at the trial.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court found the prosecution version probable and the eyewitness account convincing beyond reasonable doubt.
defence_version_summary: The Appellant and the 4th accused remained silent and did not offer any defence evidence. The defence counsel argued that the eyewitness was unreliable due to alleged inconsistencies with his police statement.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal affirmed the High Court's findings, emphasizing that the credibility of the sole eyewitness was not impeached. The Court noted that the Appellant was well-known to the witness and there was no motive for false implication. The Court also held that contradictions must be properly marked at trial to be considered, citing relevant legal precedents.
coa_sentence_type: Death
brief_judgment_file_summary: The Appellant appealed against his conviction for murder and death sentence, arguing that the sole eyewitness lacked credibility. The High Court had convicted him based on the testimony of a three-wheeler driver who witnessed the stabbing. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal, upholding the eyewitness's reliability and the conviction. The death sentence was affirmed.
defence_counsel: Kasun Chamara Munasinghe
cause_of_death_exact_text: haemorrhage and shock following multiple stab injuries on the chest and abdomen penetrating lungs, liver and severing the inferno vane Cora
hc_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found that the High Court Judge correctly analyzed the evidence and rightly convicted the Appellant based on convincing eyewitness testimony.
precedents_cited_list: The Queen v. K.A. Santin Singho 65 NLR 447 | State Rep. by Inspector of Police v. Saravanan AIR 2009 SC 152 | Acharaparambath Pradeepan & Anr. v. State of Kerala 2006 13 SCC 643 | Kehar Singh & Ors v. State (Delhi Admn.) [3] AIR 1988 SC 1883
standard_of_review_applied: The Court reviewed whether the evidence of the sole eyewitness inspired confidence and whether the trial judge properly evaluated credibility.

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 19(b) and 19(c) of the Bribery Act
brief_facts_summary: The accused was indicted for accepting a gratification of Rs. 12,500/- for performing an official act. The trial had proceeded to the conclusion of evidence and was fixed for final submissions when the High Court Judge raised a jurisdictional issue regarding the sanction of the Commissioners. The Judge subsequently dismissed the action and discharged the accused based on this issue.
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court Judge dismissed the case and discharged the accused, ruling that the failure to obtain the sanction of all three Commissioners created a patent lack of jurisdiction, rendering the proceedings void ab initio. Ten days later, the Judge issued an 'edited' order to correct the initial order.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The petitioner argued that the High Court Judge misdirected himself by treating the lack of sanction as a patent lack of jurisdiction rather than a procedural (latent) defect. Furthermore, the petitioner contended that the Judge acted illegally and without jurisdiction (functus officio) by altering the signed judgment ten days after its pronouncement.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: High Court Judge misdirected as to the question of jurisdiction and law regarding patent vs latent lack of jurisdiction. | High Court Judge violated section 283(4) of the Code of Criminal Procedure Act by altering a signed judgment.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal did not analyze the witness evidence as the appeal focused solely on the legal validity of the dismissal order. The trial evidence had been concluded in the High Court before the dismissal.
probability_assessment_by_court: The assessment was purely legal regarding the distinction between patent and latent jurisdiction and the powers of a judge to review their own order.
defence_version_summary: The accused pleaded not guilty. The defence counsel had informed the High Court that they objected to any withdrawal of the case and were agreeable to the continuation of the trial.
legal_errors_description: The High Court Judge erred in classifying the lack of three Commissioners' sanction as a patent lack of jurisdiction (void ab initio) instead of a latent procedural defect. The Judge also erred by altering the signed judgment 10 days later, violating section 283(4) of the Code of Criminal Procedure.
procedural_defects_description: The High Court Judge purported to issue an 'edited' order after the original order was signed and delivered, despite being functus officio.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal held that the failure to get the sanction of all three Commissioners is a procedural defect (latent lack of jurisdiction), not a patent one, and does not render the action void ab initio. The Court cited 'P. Beatrice Perera' to distinguish between patent and latent jurisdiction. The Court also ruled that the High Court Judge became functus officio after signing the judgment and had no power to issue a second 'edited' order, citing section 283(4) of the Code of Criminal Procedure and 'Hari Singh Mann Vs. Harbhajan Singh Bajwa'. The dismissal was termed a positive miscarriage of justice.
coa_sentence_type: Directed the High Court to proceed with the action commencing from where it stood before the order was pronounced.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The Director General of CIABOC filed a revision application against the High Court's order dismissing a bribery case and discharging the accused due to an alleged patent lack of jurisdiction regarding commissioner sanctions. The Court of Appeal set aside the High Court's order, ruling that the defect was latent rather than patent and that the Judge acted illegally by altering the signed judgment. The case was remanded to the High Court to continue the trial from the final submissions stage.
defence_counsel: Asanka Mendis with Sandeepani Wijesooriya
hc_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found that the High Court Judge misdirected himself by raising a jurisdictional objection suo moto on a wrong premise of law. The Judge also erred procedurally by attempting to review and alter his own signed judgment.
precedents_cited_list: Anoma S. Polwatte Vs. The Commission to Investigate Allegations of Bribery and Corruption SC/Writ Application No 01/2011 | P. Beatrice Perera Vs. The Commissioner of National Housing 77 NLR 361 | Hari Singh Mann Vs. Harbhajan Singh Bajwa AIR 2001 SC 43 | Indiketiya Hewage Kusumadasa Mahanama Vs. The Commission to Investigate allegations of Bribery or Corruption, SC TAB- 1A and 1B/2020 | Hotel Galaxy (Pvt) Ltd. Vs. Mercantile Hotels Management Ltd (1987) 1 SLR 5 | Wijesinghe Vs. Thamararatnam (Sriskantha Law Report Vol. IV page 47) | Vanik Incorporation Ltd. Vs. Jayasekare (1997) 2 SLR 365
standard_of_review_applied: Revisionary powers exercised due to exceptional circumstances and a positive miscarriage of justice.

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 365(B) 2 (b) of the Penal Code as amended by Acts No.29 of 1998 and No. 16 of 2016
location_of_offence: A nearby house near the mosque
brief_facts_summary: The accused took the 5-year-old victim to a nearby house under the pretext of giving biscuits and committed grave sexual abuse (anal intercourse). The victim later revealed the incident to his mother, and medical examination confirmed injuries consistent with anal abuse. The victim testified at age 17 regarding the incident which occurred around 2009.
evidence_type_secondary: Medical evidence (JMO Report), Testimony of the victim's mother
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 365(B) 2 (b) of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the accused based on the victim's credible testimony and corroborative medical evidence, rejecting the defence. The court imposed 9 years rigorous imprisonment, taking into account the tender age of the victim and the gravity of the offence.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant argued that the prosecution failed to prove the date and place of the offence beyond reasonable doubt and that there were contradictions in the witness testimonies. The appellant further contended that the prosecution's version was improbable and the sentence imposed was excessive.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Whether the Learned High Court Judge has correctly assessed that the prosecution has proved the offence... beyond reasonable doubt. | Has the Learned High Court Judge misdirected himself in evaluating evidence... by failing to identify the clear-cut contradictions... | Has the Learned Hogh Court Judge failed to consider the improbabilities of the version of the prosecution. | Did the Learned High Court Judge err in sentencing the Appellant for an unreasonable and excessive term...
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The court accepted the victim's evidence as credible, noting that his inability to recall the exact date was natural given his young age (5 years) at the time of the offence. The medical evidence (PW6) showing three anal injuries and evidence of intercourse strongly corroborated the victim's account. Contradictions were deemed immaterial to the core facts.
probability_assessment_by_court: The court held that precise dates are not essential if the accused is given reasonable notice, especially with child witnesses testifying years later. The prosecution's case was found to be proved beyond reasonable doubt.
defence_version_summary: The accused pleaded not guilty and made a dock statement denying the incident. During the incident time, he had allegedly told the grandmother the victim was injured climbing an iron post, but in court, he simply denied the charge.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal affirmed the High Court's findings, agreeing that the discrepancy regarding the date was not fatal given the victim's age and the specific date provided by the mother (PW2). The court found the sentence of 9 years reasonable within the statutory range of 7-20 years, considering the aggravating factor of the victim's age. The contradictions raised were considered minor and not affecting the substance of the case.
coa_sentence_type: Rigorous Imprisonment 09 years, Fine Rs. 15,000/-, Compensation Rs. 200,000/-
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused appealed a conviction for grave sexual abuse of a 5-year-old boy, challenging the proof of date/place and the severity of the sentence. The Court of Appeal upheld the conviction, ruling that the victim's uncertainty about the date was understandable and cured by other evidence. The 9-year sentence was affirmed as appropriate given the victim's tender age.
defence_counsel: Ruwan S.Jayawardena
hc_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal concluded that the High Court Judge correctly evaluated the evidence, properly addressing the delay and the child witness's memory limitations. The trial judge's sentencing was also found to be fair and proportionate.
precedents_cited_list: Bhoginbhai Hirjibhai v. State of Gujarat | R. v. Dossai 13 Cr.App.R. 158 | Ranjeet Kumar Ram v. State of Bihar [2015] SCC Online SC 500 | The Attorney General v. Sandanam Pitchai Mary Theresa [2011] 2 SLR 292
standard_of_review_applied: Review of evidence credibility and sentencing discretion
sentencing_principles_applied: Proportionality, protection of minors, statutory ranges

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 357 of the Penal Code and Section 365B (2) (b) of the Penal Code as amended Act No.22 of 0995
brief_facts_summary: The Appellant was indicted for kidnapping and sexually abusing an under-aged girl who attended the school where his daughters studied. The prosecution relied principally on a video-recorded statement of the victim given to the Child Protection Authority, in which she implicated the Appellant. However, during the trial, the victim recanted her statement, testifying that the Appellant did not commit the acts and that she had been coerced by her school principal to implicate him, while the true perpetrator was her boyfriend.
evidence_type_primary: Video recorded statement of the child victim
evidence_type_secondary: Testimony of the School Principal and Probation Officer
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 357 of the Penal Code and Section 365B (2) (b) of the Penal Code as amended Act No.22 of 0995
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the Appellant on both counts, sentencing him to 07 and 12 years rigorous imprisonment respectively. The trial judge relied on the victim's video-recorded statement, concluding it was corroborated by the evidence of the school principal and a probation officer, despite the victim's retraction in court.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The Appellant argued that the trial judge erred in law by accepting the video recording without the independent corroboration required by Section 163A(5) of the Evidence (Special Provisions) Act, given that the witness contradicted the recording. The Appellant also contended that the evidence of the principal and probation officer established only consistency, not corroboration, and that the victim's evidence was inconsistent.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Prosecution failed to prove the ingredients of the charges beyond reasonable doubt | Victim's evidence was inconsistent and contradictory | Video recording of the victim was not corroborated in material particulars by evidence from an independent source as required by Section 163A (5) of the Evidence (Special Provisions) Act No. 32 of 1999 | Learned Trial Judge erred in law by concluding upon considering the evidence-in-chief of the victim that it is proved beyond reasonable doubt | Learned High Court Judge erred in law by concluding that the evidence given by the victim at the video conference proved that the Accused committed a sexual act | Learned High Court Judge erred by concluding that the evidence of the probation officer had corroborated the evidence of the victim
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The prosecution called 31 witnesses, but the case hinged on the victim's video evidence. The victim expressly contradicted this video evidence in court, stating the Appellant was innocent and she was coerced by the principal. The Court of Appeal found that the witnesses used by the trial judge for corroboration (Principal and Probation Officer) could only prove the consistency of the victim's earlier story, not independent corroboration of the accused's involvement.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court concluded the prosecution failed to prove the case beyond reasonable doubt because the statutory requirement for independent corroboration of a retracted video statement was not met.
defence_version_summary: The Appellant pleaded not guilty and made a dock statement. The defence maintained that the Appellant was innocent and had been falsely implicated due to the instigation of the school principal (PW3), a version supported by the victim's own testimony at trial where she named her boyfriend as the perpetrator.
legal_errors_description: The High Court Judge misdirected himself by treating evidence of consistency (testimony of PW3 and PW5 regarding what the victim told them) as independent corroboration required under Section 163A(5) of the Evidence (Special Provisions) Act. The Judge also erroneously classified the offence under Section 365(2)(b) as falling under Section 363(A)(5) of the Penal Code.
procedural_defects_description: Admission of hearsay evidence regarding influence on the victim's mother without calling the relevant witnesses, affecting the right to a fair trial.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal emphasized that under Section 163A(5) of the Evidence (Special Provisions) Act, if a child witness contradicts their video-recorded statement, the court can only act on the recording if it is corroborated by independent evidence in material particulars. The Court held that the High Court erred in considering the evidence of the Principal (PW3) and Probation Officer (PW5) as corroboration; their testimony merely established that the victim had made the statement (consistency), but did not independently connect the Appellant to the crime as required by law. Citing authorities like 'Sana v. Republic', the Court ruled that a complaint cannot corroborate the witness herself. Consequently, the conviction could not stand.
brief_judgment_file_summary: Harold Rex Jansen appealed his conviction for kidnapping and grave sexual abuse of a minor. The prosecution's case relied on a video-recorded interview of the victim, which she later retracted in court, claiming the Appellant was innocent and she was coerced by her principal. The High Court convicted the Appellant, finding corroboration in the testimony of the principal and a probation officer. The Court of Appeal set aside the conviction and acquitted the Appellant, ruling that the supporting witnesses only showed consistency, not the independent corroboration required by Section 163A(5) of the Evidence (Special Provisions) Act for a retracted video statement.
defence_counsel: Shanaka Ranasinghe, PC with Niroshana Mihindukulasuriya
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court Judge correctly noted the victim contradicted her video evidence but incorrectly applied the law on corroboration. The Judge mistook evidence of the victim's prior consistency (statements to PW3 and PW5) for independent corroborative evidence required by statute.
precedents_cited_list: Director of Public Prosecutions v. Hester [1972] 3 A.E.R 1056 | Fernando v. The Republic [1978] 79 (II) NLR 313 | Ariyadasa v. Queen 70 NLR 3 | Sana v. Republic of Sri Lanka [2009] 1 SLR 48 | King v. Atukorale 50 N.L.R. 256 | S. Rajaratnam v. The Republic of Sri Lanka 79(1) N.L.R. 73 | R v. Hepworth 1928 (AD) 265
standard_of_review_applied: Review of legal misdirection regarding corroboration and analysis of evidence sufficiency.

high_court_case_no: HC of Colombo Case No: B 1964/2013
judges: Menaka Wijesundera, J. | B. Sasi Mahendran, J.
offence_sections: Section 19 (b) and Section 19 (c) of the Bribery Act
brief_facts_summary: The accused, a Superintendent of Works at Kalutara Urban Council, was charged with soliciting and accepting a gratification of Rs. 15,000 from an insurance agent. The prosecution alleged this sum was 5% of insurance premiums demanded as an inducement to allocate council insurance work to the agent. The accused was arrested during a sting operation while accepting the money but claimed it was a loan repayment.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 19 (b) and Section 19 (c) of the Bribery Act
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the accused on all four counts, imposing fines and simple imprisonment. The Judge accepted the prosecution witnesses' evidence as corroborative and rejected the defense's explanation, finding the charges proved beyond reasonable doubt.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The Appellant argued that the main prosecution witness provided contradictory evidence regarding the calculation of the bribe (commission vs. premium), which the trial judge failed to address. They also contended that the prosecution failed to prove the specific demand for Rs. 15,000 and the element of inducement. Furthermore, the defense argued the trial judge erred by not properly evaluating the defense's loan repayment version.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Contradictory evidence by PW1 regarding the nature of the bribe | Failure to prove solicitation of the specific sum of Rs. 15,000 | Failure to prove the element of inducement | Failure to evaluate the defense version of a loan repayment | Reversal of the presumption of innocence
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the complainant's (PW1) evidence unreliable due to inconsistent statements about whether the bribe was 5% of the commission or the premium. The Court noted that the trial judge failed to subject this credibility issue to judicial evaluation. The evidence was deemed insufficient to prove the specific demand for Rs. 15,000.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court held the prosecution failed to prove the case beyond reasonable doubt, noting that the trial judge's selective consideration of evidence and failure to analyze contradictions compromised the verdict.
defence_version_summary: The accused denied soliciting a bribe, stating the Rs. 15,000 received was the repayment of a loan he had previously given to the complainant. He also alleged the case was fabricated due to political animosity from a local UNP MP.
legal_errors_description: The trial judge erred by failing to evaluate material contradictions in prosecution testimony and by examining the defense evidence only in light of the prosecution's case, thereby reversing the presumption of innocence.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal determined that the High Court Judge failed to evaluate the totality of the evidence, specifically overlooking material contradictions in PW1's testimony regarding the bribe's calculation. The Court found no evidence of a specific demand for Rs. 15,000 or the alleged inducement act. Citing established case law, the Court held that the trial judge improperly shifted the burden of proof by testing the defense version against the prosecution's case rather than independently.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused appealed a High Court conviction for bribery involving the alleged solicitation of Rs. 15,000. The Court of Appeal set aside the conviction, citing the trial judge's failure to address significant contradictions in the complainant's testimony regarding the bribe amount. The Court also ruled that the trial judge erred in law by not properly evaluating the defense's claim of loan repayment and by shifting the burden of proof onto the accused. The accused was acquitted of all charges.
defence_counsel: Nalin Ladduwahetty, PC with Kavithri Ubeysekara, Yasas Hewapathirana and Menuka Premashantha
hc_analysis_summary: The COA found the HC judgment invalid due to the judge's failure to discuss contradictory versions of the witness's testimony and provide reasoning. The HC was criticized for mechanically accepting prosecution evidence without evaluating the defense's loan explanation.
precedents_cited_list: Padmatilake (Sgt) V. Director General, Commission to Investigate Allegations of Bribery/Corruption 2009 2 SLR Page 151 | James Silva V The Republic of Sri Lanka (1980) 2SLR Page 167 | Jayasena V the Queen 72 NLR Page 313
standard_of_review_applied: Evaluation of evidence in totality; Presumption of innocence.

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 296 read with Section 32 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The deceased was allegedly attacked by the Appellants and others while walking with his father (PW1) on a forested route at night. PW1 claimed the accused emerged from the forest and attacked the deceased with weapons, causing him to fall. PW1 fled the scene and later claimed to have fainted, while the defence challenged his identification and version of events.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 296 read with Section 32 of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the 1st, 2nd, and 3rd Appellants on the 3rd count of murder based on common intention and sentenced them to death. The judge relied on the sole eyewitness testimony of the deceased's father (PW1), finding it convincing under Section 134 of the Evidence Ordinance despite excluding the dying declaration.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The Appellants argued that the sole eyewitness's testimony failed the test of credibility due to inherent probabilities and contradictions. They also raised issues regarding the misapplication of common murderous intention principles, burden of proof, and procedural errors in evaluating evidence.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The evidence of sole eye witness fails the test of credibility and probability. | The principle governing on common murderous intention is not properly applied by the Learned High Court Judge. | The Learned High Court Judge has failed to consider the 2nd limb of Section 293 of the Penal Code. | The Dock statement of the 2nd Appellant has been rejected on unreasonable grounds. | Evidence of sole eye witness does not inspire the confidence of the Court. | The Learned High Court Judge flawed in the evaluation of the evidence by firstly evaluating the defence and rejecting same and thereafter proceeding to evaluate the prosecution evidence. | The Learned High Court Judge flawed relating to the principles of burden of proof. | Contradictory evidence between police evidence and PW1 creates a serious doubt with regard to the veracity of the prosecution version as narrated by PW1.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court found the sole eyewitness (PW1) unreliable due to significant contradictions and omissions between his testimony, police statement, and the evidence of other witnesses. Specifically, inconsistencies regarding who attacked, who shouted, and the transport of the deceased created serious doubts about the prosecution's version.
probability_assessment_by_court: The court concluded that the contradictions were material and affected the root of the case, making it unsafe to convict based on the sole witness.
defence_version_summary: The accused pleaded not guilty, opted for a non-jury trial, and made dock statements. They relied on proving contradictions and omissions in the prosecution witnesses' testimony to challenge their credibility.
legal_errors_description: The High Court Judge erred in assessing the evidence by failing to properly consider material contradictions and omissions, and by incorrectly concluding that guilt could be inferred despite these flaws.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed the testimony of the sole eyewitness, PW1, and found it lacked credibility due to numerous contradictions and omissions compared to his police statement and other evidence (PW2, PW3). The Court emphasized that while minor discrepancies are acceptable, the contradictions here went to the root of the case. Citing relevant case law, the Court held that the prosecution failed to prove the case beyond reasonable doubt.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The 2nd and 3rd Appellants appealed against their conviction for murder and death sentence imposed by the High Court of Panadura (the 1st Appellant died pending appeal). The conviction relied on the sole eyewitness testimony of the deceased's father. The Court of Appeal allowed the appeal and acquitted the Appellants, finding the eyewitness testimony unreliable due to material contradictions and omissions that the trial judge failed to properly evaluate.
defence_counsel: Neranjan Jayasinghe with Harshana Ananda, Indica Mallawarachchi
hc_analysis_summary: The COA found the HC Judge erred in evaluating the evidence by dismissing significant contradictions and omissions. The HC Judge incorrectly held that despite these flaws, the guilt of the accused could still be inferred.
precedents_cited_list: The Queen v. K.A. Santin Singho 65 NLR 447 | State Rep. by Inspector of Police v. Saravanan AIR 2009 SC 152 | Acharaparambath Pradeepan & Anr. v. State of Kerala 2006 13 SCC 643 | Kehar Singh & Ors v. State (Delhi Admn.) [3] AIR 1988 SC 1883
standard_of_review_applied: Review of evidence credibility and burden of proof satisfaction

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The appellant and the deceased were relatives and fishmongers who had a dispute over a selling spot. On the day of the incident, the appellant chased the deceased and attacked him with a manna knife, causing eight cut injuries, including a fatal one to the head. The appellant admitted to the act in a dock statement but claimed it was a result of a sudden fight and private defence.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court Judge found the appellant guilty of murder after a trial without a jury. The Judge accepted the prosecution evidence, including the deposition of the deceased eyewitness, and rejected the appellant's claim of private defence and provocation raised in the dock statement.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The counsel for the appellant initially formulated a ground questioning whether the prosecution proved the case beyond reasonable doubt. However, the counsel subsequently conceded that there was no basis to challenge the judgment as it was well-considered.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Whether the prosecution has proved the case against the appellant beyond reasonable doubt.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The prosecution relied on the deposition of the sole eyewitness (PW-01), who was deceased at the time of trial, admitted under Section 33 of the Evidence Ordinance. The court noted that PW-01 had been cross-examined during non-summary proceedings. The medical evidence confirmed fatal injuries consistent with the weapon recovered.
probability_assessment_by_court: The court found the prosecution proved the case beyond reasonable doubt, relying on the consistency of the eyewitness account and physical evidence against the appellant's unsubstantiated dock statement.
defence_version_summary: The appellant made a dock statement admitting to causing injuries but claimed he acted in private defence during a sudden fight initiated by the deceased. He asserted the deceased attacked him first with the knife.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal accepted the counsel's concession that the appeal lacked merit. The Court reviewed the evidence, noting that the trial judge correctly evaluated the eyewitness deposition which showed the appellant chasing the pleading victim, negating the defence of sudden fight or private defence. The Court affirmed that the trial judge, having observed the witnesses, made correct findings of fact.
coa_sentence_type: Death
brief_judgment_file_summary: The appellant appealed against a death sentence for murder committed in 1993. The prosecution case rested on the deposition of a deceased eyewitness and medical evidence. The appellant's counsel conceded the appeal at the hearing. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal, affirming the High Court's findings that the appellant's claim of private defence was unfounded.
defence_counsel: I. B. S. Harshana
hc_analysis_summary: The COA found the High Court Judge correctly analyzed the evidence and law, particularly regarding the rejection of the private defence plea and the evaluation of the Section 33 deposition.
precedents_cited_list: Alwis Vs. Piyasena Fernando (1993) 1 SLR 119
standard_of_review_applied: Appellate court will not disturb findings of primary facts by a trial judge unless manifestly wrong.

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 113A of the Penal Code, Section 25(3) and 19C of the Bribery Act
brief_facts_summary: The Director General for the Prevention of Bribery and Corruption indicted four accused on 14 counts including conspiracy, solicitation, and acceptance of a gratification of Rs. 125 Million. During the trial, the prosecution sought to introduce audio/video recordings (marked P-25 and P-27) of conversations between the key witness (PW-01) and the 1st and 4th accused. The High Court rejected this evidence because the original mobile phone was not produced and there was no scientific voice analysis. The Petitioner filed a revision application against this refusal.
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court Judge refused to allow the production of digital recordings (P-25 and P-27) as evidence. The Judge reasoned that the original recording device (mobile phone) was not listed as a production or in working condition, and there was no scientific analysis to identify the voices, relying on the best evidence rule.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The Petitioner argued that the High Court erred in applying the strict English 'best evidence rule' to digital recordings, which has been whittled down in modern law. They contended that under the Evidence (Special Provisions) Act No. 14 of 1995, contemporaneous recordings or copies are admissible, and issues regarding the original device or voice identification go to weight rather than admissibility.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The High Court erred in refusing to admit P-25 and P-27 based on the best evidence rule | The High Court failed to consider section 4 of the Evidence (Special Provisions) Act No. 14 of 1995 regarding contemporaneous recordings | The High Court incorrectly determined that scientific evidence is required for admissibility of voice recordings
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed the admissibility of the digital recordings P-25 and P-27. It determined that under the Evidence (Special Provisions) Act, the non-production of the original device or lack of scientific voice analysis does not preclude admissibility but affects the weight of the evidence.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court assessed that the Evidence (Special Provisions) Act allows for copies of recordings to be admitted, and the authenticity is a matter of weight.
defence_version_summary: The accused-respondents objected to the Revision application on preliminary technical grounds (defective affidavit, notice issues). At trial, they objected to the digital evidence because the original phone was not a production, was broken, and voices were not scientifically verified.
legal_errors_description: The High Court incorrectly applied the 'best evidence rule' to exclude digital recordings, failing to recognize that under the Evidence (Special Provisions) Act, copies are admissible and lack of original/expert analysis goes to weight.
procedural_defects_description: Preliminary objections regarding the date of the affidavit and notice were raised but overruled by the Court of Appeal as technicalities not prejudicing substantial rights.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal held that the 'best evidence rule' is no longer strictly applicable to exclude relevant evidence, especially digital recordings. Citing the Evidence (Special Provisions) Act No. 14 of 1995, the Court ruled that contemporaneous recordings and their copies are admissible. The Court emphasized that objections regarding the unavailability of the original device or lack of voice identification should address the weight of the evidence, not its admissibility. The High Court's order was set aside.
coa_sentence_type: None (Interlocutory Revision)
brief_judgment_file_summary: The Director General of the Bribery Commission filed a revision application challenging a High Court order that refused to admit digital recordings (P-25 and P-27) in a bribery trial. The High Court had rejected the evidence based on the absence of the original recording device and scientific voice analysis. The Court of Appeal set aside the High Court's order, ruling that under the Evidence (Special Provisions) Act, such recordings are admissible and the objections raised pertain to weight, not admissibility. The High Court was directed to allow the evidence.
prosecution_counsel: Janaka Bandara, D.S.G. with Udara Karunathilake, S.S.C., Ms. Bandara, A.D.G. and Anusha Sammandapperuma, A.D.L.
defence_counsel: Ashan Nanayakkara, Chamara Wannisekara with D. Kaushalya, Dumesh Kariyawasam, Maithri Gunaratne P.C. with Chan Godakumbura
hc_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found that the High Court Judge incorrectly relied on the 'best evidence rule' to reject digital evidence. The COA clarified that statutory provisions allow for such evidence and that the trial judge should have admitted it and considered its weight later.
precedents_cited_list: Kiriwanthe and Another Vs. Navaratne and Another (1990) 2 SLR 393 | Roylin Fernando Vs. Christian Gamini Fernando And Others SC/Appeal No. 18A-09 | Distilleries Company Ltd. Vs. Kariyawasam And Others (2001) 3 SLR 119 | Indiketiya Hewage Kusumadasa Mahanama and another Vs. Attorney General and another | King Vs. Peter Nonis (1947) 49 NLR 16 | Vanderbona Vs. Perera (1985) 2 SLR 62 | Kajala Vs. Noble (1982) 75 Cr.A.R. 149
standard_of_review_applied: Revisionary Jurisdiction (Article 138) - Failure of Justice / Prejudice to Substantial Rights

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 354 of the Penal Code and Section 365B(2)(b) of the Penal Code as amended by Amendment Act No. 22 of 1995, 29 of 1998 and 16 of 2006
brief_facts_summary: The accused kidnapped a 9-year-old girl from her home garden and took her to a nearby cinnamon cultivation. He forced her to lie down and sexually abused her by placing his penis on her vagina, but fled when her mother arrived and called out. The victim and her mother gave consistent evidence regarding the identity of the accused, who was a relative and neighbor living nearby.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 354 of the Penal Code and Section 365B(2)(b) of the Penal Code as amended by Amendment Act No. 22 of 1995, 29 of 1998 and 16 of 2006
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court Judge convicted the appellant on both counts, finding the victim's and mother's evidence credible despite the delay in testimony and lack of physical injuries. The Judge rejected the defence's argument that the charges were fabricated due to a land dispute and sentenced the accused to concurrent terms of imprisonment.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant argued that the High Court failed to consider the probability factor that favors the appellant, specifically the lack of injuries given the rough terrain. They also contended that the judge erred in finding corroboration in the medical evidence and relied on surmises and conjectures not supported by evidence.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The learned High Court Judge has erred in law by failing to consider the probability factor that favors the appellant. | The findings of the learned High Court Judge on material points favorable to the appellant have been based on mere surmises and conjectures not supported by evidence. | The learned High Court Judge has come to a wrong finding that the medical evidence corroborates the version of the prosecution.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court accepted the evidence of the victim (PW-01) and her mother (PW-02) as consistent and credible, noting that the lack of physical injuries did not disprove the act given the presence of leaves on the ground. The timeline discrepancies were considered minor and not affecting the core case, and the child's delayed testimony was handled with appropriate caution.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court found the defence's probability argument (lack of injuries on rough terrain) unconvincing because the ground had fallen leaves and the incident was brief.
defence_version_summary: The accused denied the incident completely, claiming he was arrested and assaulted by police. He alleged false implication due to a land dispute with the victim's family and provided a contradictory statement regarding his whereabouts.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal affirmed the High Court's findings, agreeing that the lack of injuries was explained by the presence of leaves and the brevity of the assault. The Court cited case law regarding memory recall of witnesses, dismissing minor discrepancies in the timeline. The defence of false implication due to a land dispute was rejected as it was deemed unlikely a mother would use a child to concoct such a serious allegation.
coa_sentence_type: Conviction and sentence affirmed; sentence deemed to commence from 18-01-2021 (2 years RI on Count 1, 10 years RI on Count 2 to run concurrently).
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused appealed against his conviction for kidnapping and grave sexual abuse of a 9-year-old girl. The prosecution relied on the testimony of the victim and her mother, who caught the accused fleeing the scene. The defence argued that the lack of physical injuries on the rocky terrain made the story improbable and alleged false implication due to a land dispute. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal, holding that the medical evidence did not contradict the victim's account and that the minor discrepancies in testimony were natural. The conviction and sentence were affirmed.
defence_counsel: Amila Palliyage with Buddhika Serasinghe, Sandeepani Wijesooriya, S. Udugampola, and J. de Silva
hc_analysis_summary: The COA found the HC Judge's analysis of the evidence to be sound, particularly the rejection of the defence's probability arguments. The HC Judge correctly evaluated the credibility of the child witness and her mother despite minor discrepancies.
precedents_cited_list: Bhoginbhai Hirjibhai Vs State of Gujarat (AIR 1983-SC 753) | D. Tikiri Banda Vs. The Attorney General Bar Association Law Report 2010 (BLR 92)
standard_of_review_applied: Appellate review of factual findings and evidence appreciation.
sentencing_principles_applied: Consideration of mitigatory circumstances and lack of previous convictions led to concurrent sentences.

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Poisons Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance as amended by Amendment Act No. 13 of 1984
brief_facts_summary: The 1st accused-appellant was arrested following a police raid on a boat at Thoduwawa Beach. Police observed a sack being transferred from a larger boat to a smaller boat, which then came ashore. The police recovered 5 parcels containing 1110 grams of heroin from the boat; the appellant was apprehended while two others escaped.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Poisons Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance as amended by Amendment Act No. 13 of 1984
hc_sentence_type: Sentence affirmed (Details not specified in judgment)
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court found the 1st accused guilty of trafficking and possession of heroin. The 4th to 7th accused were acquitted due to lack of proof beyond reasonable doubt against them. The conviction was based on the testimony of the raiding officer and the recovery of drugs.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant argued that the prosecution failed to prove the charges based on true facts and that the identification was doubtful since co-accused were acquitted despite being identified by the same witness. They also challenged the credibility of the main witness (PW-03).
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The learned High Court Judge was misdirected by failing to consider that the prosecution did not prove the ingredients of the charges against the appellant based on true facts. | Without prejudice to the above, learned High Court Judge misdirected that the 1st accused-appellant along with the 5th and the 7th accused had been identified at the time of the detection, yet the 5th and the 7th accused were acquitted which creates a doubt as to the credibility of the evidence. | The learned High Court Judge was misdirected by failing to scrutinize the credibility of PW-03 based on principles and established law of the country.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The main raiding officer (OIC) was deceased, so another officer (PW-03) testified. The court accepted PW-03's testimony regarding the observation of the boat under moonlight (Poya day). A weight discrepancy between the field test and lab analysis was explained by the Government Analyst and accepted by the court.
probability_assessment_by_court: The court found the prosecution proved the case beyond reasonable doubt, accepting the visual observation under moonlight and the recovery of drugs from the boat occupied by the appellant.
defence_version_summary: The appellant made a dock statement claiming he was sleeping, heard a noise, went to inquire, and was then apprehended, denying knowledge of the offence. He claimed to be an innocent person arrested without basis.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal affirmed the conviction, finding PW-03's evidence reliable despite being the sole testifying officer from the raid. The court accepted that visibility was possible due to the full moon and that the discrepancy in drug weight was scientifically explained. The court held that the acquittal of co-accused did not undermine the identification of the appellant, who was caught at the scene.
coa_sentence_type: Conviction and sentence affirmed (Details not specified)
brief_judgment_file_summary: The 1st Accused-Appellant appealed against his conviction for trafficking and possessing 1110g of Heroin. He was arrested on a boat during a raid, while two others escaped. The Court of Appeal upheld the conviction, rejecting arguments about identification and witness credibility, noting the arrest occurred at the scene and evidence was corroborated by the Government Analyst.
defence_counsel: Tenny Fernando with Asiri Weerakkodi and Thanya Perera
hc_analysis_summary: The COA found the HC Judge correctly evaluated the evidence and the appellant's dock statement. The HC's reasoning for acquitting others while convicting the appellant was deemed logical as the others were not apprehended at the scene.
standard_of_review_applied: Review of evidence credibility and reasonable doubt

judges: M. Sampath K. B. Wijeratne J. | M. Ahsan. R. Marikar J.
offence_sections: Section 296 read with Section 32 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The deceased was shot and killed while seated on a motorcycle in front of his home after returning with his family around 8:30 p.m. The prosecution alleged that three individuals arrived on a motorcycle, and the third person (identified as the 1st Accused) fired the shots. The deceased had a prior land dispute with the 1st Accused earlier that day. The prosecution relied on the eyewitness testimony of the deceased's step-daughter and wife.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 296 read with Section 32 of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court Judge convicted the 1st Accused of murder and sentenced him to death. The Judge rejected the alibi defense, holding that no evidence was presented to support who was with the accused, and accepted the identification evidence despite the lack of an identification parade.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant argued that the High Court Judge misdirected himself on the burden of proof regarding the alibi and failed to apply the Turnbull principle regarding identification. It was also argued that there were serious contradictions between the ocular evidence and medical evidence regarding the number of shots fired and the trajectory of the bullets.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The learned High Court Judge failed to give due credit to the alibi of the Appellant and totally rejected the evidence of the 1st Accused - Appellant. | The learned High Court Judge misdirected himself as to the burden of proof. | The learned High Court Judge failed to direct himself according to the turnbull principle. | The learned High Court Judge failed to consider the presumption of innocence.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the identification evidence unsatisfactory as the witness did not know the accused prior to the incident and observed the gunman briefly under poor lighting conditions without a subsequent identification parade. The medical evidence (multiple entry wounds, upward trajectory) significantly contradicted the eyewitness accounts of a single shot fired while seated. These inconsistencies cast substantial doubt on the prosecution's version.
probability_assessment_by_court: The contradictions regarding the number of shots (witnesses heard one, medical evidence showed multiple wounds/cartridges) and the lack of reliable identification created reasonable doubt.
defence_version_summary: The 1st Accused-Appellant pleaded not guilty and raised a defense of alibi, giving evidence on his own behalf. He denied involvement in the crime.
