The Court of Appeal found no errors in the High Court's consideration of evidence relating to the Appellant's conduct, the recovery of bodies under Section 27 of the Evidence Ordinance, and the overall assessment that the circumstances pointed only to the Appellant's guilt.

Attorney General (2010) 2 Sri L.R. 113 at 115 | Zahira Habibullah Sheikh and Others v. State of Gujarat [Appeal (crl.) 446-449 of 2004]
standard_of_review_applied: The Court reviewed whether the circumstantial evidence was consistent with the guilt of the accused and inconsistent with any reasonable hypothesis of innocence, applying the cumulative effect test for circumstantial evidence.

judges: Menaka Wijesundera J. | B. Sasi Mahendran J.
offence_sections: Rape under the provisions of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The victim, a married woman living separately from her husband, collected her sick child from the husband at night. The appellant gave the victim and child a lift on his motorbike, dropped the child at the victim's parents' place, then allegedly took the victim to the jungle and raped her twice without consent. The victim's father assaulted the appellant with a club upon their return, and the victim complained to police at 2:30 am the same night.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Rape under the provisions of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the appellant of rape. The trial judge analyzed the prosecution evidence and concluded that although the victim's evidence had contradictions and omissions, these did not go to the root of the case. The judge believed the victim's testimony and convicted the appellant.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The main ground of appeal was that there was no rape but sexual intercourse with consent. The appellant argued that he had an intimate relationship with the victim and that the sexual intercourse on the day of the incident was consensual. The defense contended that the victim's evidence was uncorroborated and contained contradictions and omissions.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: There was no rape but sexual intercourse with consent | The victim's evidence was uncorroborated | The victim's evidence contained contradictions and omissions | The appellant stood the test of cross-examination without contradictions or omissions
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The victim was the sole witness to the incident. The Court of Appeal noted that the victim's evidence contained contradictions and omissions and was uncorroborated. In contrast, the appellant's evidence was uncontradicted and he stood the test of cross-examination well. The trial judge failed to consider improbabilities in the prosecution case.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal found that the evidence of the appellant created a serious doubt in the case for the prosecution regarding the issue of consent, which is the core element that must be proven beyond reasonable doubt in a rape charge.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty and testified that he had a very intimate relationship with the victim. He claimed that on the day of the incident, the victim refused to get down from the bicycle and suggested they go somewhere, after which they selected a lonely plot of jungle and had consensual sexual intercourse. He stated the victim wanted to leave quickly and upon their return, the victim's father assaulted him with a club. The appellant stood the test of cross-examination very well without any contradictions or omissions. The Court of Appeal found his testimony credible.
legal_errors_description: The trial judge failed to consider the improbabilities in the case for the prosecution and wholeheartedly and blindly believed the evidence of the victim, which denied a fair trial to the appellant. The judge also failed to observe that the appellant stood the test of cross-examination without any contradiction or omission.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found that the trial judge failed to properly evaluate the evidence. The victim was the sole witness to the incident and her evidence was uncorroborated and contained contradictions and omissions. In contrast, the appellant's evidence was uncontradicted and he performed well under cross-examination. The COA noted that the victim's father acted in a very violent manner soon after the incident, raising questions about whether this sparked the complaint. The trial judge failed to consider improbabilities in the prosecution case and blindly believed the victim's testimony, denying the appellant a fair trial. The COA applied precedents requiring corroboration in rape cases and found that the appellant's evidence of consent created serious doubt about whether the prosecution proved lack of consent beyond reasonable doubt. The core issue was consent, and the prosecution failed to prove its absence beyond reasonable doubt.
coa_sentence_type: Conviction and sentence set aside
brief_judgment_file_summary: The appellant Imbulpitiya Gamage Anura was convicted by the High Court of Hambantota of rape. He appealed claiming the sexual intercourse was consensual. The victim testified she was taken to the jungle and raped twice without consent, while the appellant testified they had an intimate relationship and consensual intercourse. The Court of Appeal found the trial judge failed to properly evaluate the evidence, noting the victim was the sole witness with uncorroborated testimony containing contradictions, while the appellant's evidence was uncontradicted and he performed well under cross-examination. The COA held that the appellant's evidence created serious doubt about consent, which the prosecution must prove beyond reasonable doubt. The appeal was allowed and the conviction and sentence were set aside.
prosecution_counsel: Chethiya Gunasekara, ASG with Jayalakshi De Silva, SC
defence_counsel: Gamini Perera with Manjula Nimesh, Kumara De Silva and Aruni De Silva Instructed by Vijitha Salpitikorala
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court analyzed the prosecution evidence and concluded that although the victim's evidence had contradictions and omissions, these did not go to the root of the case. However, the Court of Appeal found that the trial judge failed to consider improbabilities in the prosecution case, failed to observe that the appellant stood the test of cross-examination without contradictions, and wholeheartedly and blindly believed the victim's evidence, thereby denying the appellant a fair trial.
precedents_cited_list: Gurcharan Singh vs State of Haryana AIR 1972 SC 2661 | Premasiri vs The Queen 77NLR 86
standard_of_review_applied: The Court of Appeal reviewed the evidence and applied the standard that in rape cases, courts should look for corroboration of the victim's testimony and should only convict on uncorroborated evidence when it is sufficient to convince that the victim is speaking the truth. The prosecution must prove lack of consent beyond reasonable doubt.

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The Appellant was married to the 1st deceased Pushpa Priyadharshani and they had a daughter, the 2nd deceased Thihari Udayangani. On 24 April 2011, the Appellant went to PW1's house alone, claiming his wife went to buy medicine, but was wearing a T-shirt with blood marks, mud patches and grass particles, and behaving suspiciously. Police investigation led to recovery of the bodies of both deceased buried near the Appellant's house based on his statement under Section 27 of the Evidence Ordinance.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court Judge convicted the Appellant under Section 296 of the Penal Code for committing double murder and sentenced him to death on 01 June 2020. The conviction was based on strong circumstantial evidence including the last seen doctrine, suspicious conduct, and recovery of bodies pursuant to the Appellant's statement.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The Appellant argued that the prosecution failed to prove that the only inference is that he committed the offence. He contended his right to fair trial was infringed by biased investigations. He also argued the High Court Judge erred by holding that rules relating to Section 27 inquiry under the Evidence Ordinance were duly complied with.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The prosecution has failed to prove that the only inference is that the Appellant committed the offence | The Appellant's right to a fair trial has been infringed by biased investigations | The Learned High Court Judge has erred in law by holding that rules relating to Section 27 inquiry under the Evidence Ordnance has been duly complied
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The prosecution called PW1, PW2, PW3, PW4, PW5, PW6, and PW8. The evidence established the last seen doctrine, suspicious conduct of the Appellant, recovery of bodies based on his statement, and medical evidence of violent deaths. The Court found the circumstantial evidence formed a strong chain consistent only with guilt.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court held the circumstances were consistent only with the Appellant's guilt and totally inconsistent with his innocence, applying the reasonable hypothesis of innocence test.
defence_version_summary: The Appellant made a dock statement only and did not call any witnesses. He denied the allegation and claimed unknown persons entered his house and assaulted him and his wife, and he ran away and hid in the thicket. However, he failed to put this position to prosecution witnesses during cross-examination. The Court found his explanation false and contradictory to his earlier statement.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed the circumstantial evidence applying established principles from Rex v Exall, King v Abeywickrama, and Tamil Nadu v Rajendran. The Court found the last seen doctrine was proved, shifting burden to the Appellant to explain what happened. The Appellant gave contradictory explanations - first telling PW1 his wife went to buy medicine, then in dock statement claiming unknown persons attacked them. His suspicious behavior with blood-stained clothing and the recovery of bodies based on his Section 27 statement formed strong links. The Court held the evidence under Section 27 was properly admitted per Somaratne Rajapakse principles. The Court rejected claims of biased investigation, finding police followed correct procedures. The Court emphasized the Appellant failed to cross-examine prosecution witnesses on his defence version, strengthening the prosecution case.
coa_sentence_type: Death
brief_judgment_file_summary: Ekanayaka Mudiyanselage Gamini Bandara was convicted by the High Court of Kalutara for double murder under Section 296 of the Penal Code and sentenced to death for killing his wife Pushpa Priyadharshani and daughter Thihari Udayangani on 24 April 2011. The conviction was based on strong circumstantial evidence including last seen doctrine, suspicious conduct with blood-stained clothing, contradictory explanations, and recovery of bodies based on his statement under Section 27 of the Evidence Ordinance. The Appellant appealed arguing insufficient circumstantial evidence, biased investigation, and errors in Section 27 application. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal on 10 January 2024, holding the circumstances were consistent only with guilt and inconsistent with innocence, and that all legal procedures were properly followed.
defence_counsel: Naveen Maha Arachchige
cause_of_death_exact_text: 1st deceased: hemorrhage and shock following injury to the abdomen; 2nd deceased: asphyxia
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court Judge correctly considered the evidence pertaining to the conduct of the Appellant and properly evaluated the circumstantial evidence. The COA affirmed the HC's findings that the evidence was consistent only with guilt and inconsistent with innocence.

Abeywickrama Et Al 44 NLR 254 | Tamil Nadu v Rajendran Appeal (1996) 917(Cr.L) | Basanti v State of UP, AIR 1987 SC 1572 | Somaratne Rajapakse Others v. Hon. Attorney General (2010) 2 Sri L.R. 113 | Zahira Habibullah Sheikh and Others v. State of Gujarat [Appeal (crl.) 446-449 of 2004]
standard_of_review_applied: The Court reviewed whether the High Court properly evaluated circumstantial evidence and whether the circumstances were consistent only with guilt and inconsistent with any reasonable hypothesis of innocence.

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Poisons Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance as amended by Amendment Act No. 13 of 1984
brief_facts_summary: On 23-08-2000, police officers from the Vice Prevention Unit of Elpitiya were searching a thicket near Ahungalle railway station for illicit liquor. They observed a female walking suspiciously and apprehended her. She was holding a camera reel container in her right-hand palm containing a brown powder identified as Heroin. The substance was weighed at 8.404 grams gross weight and later analyzed to contain 3.21 grams of pure Heroin. The appellant was arrested at the scene.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Poisons Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance as amended by Amendment Act No. 13 of 1984
hc_judgment_summary: After trial, the High Court of Balapitiya found the appellant guilty on both counts of possession and trafficking of 3.21 grams of Heroin. The court sentenced her to life imprisonment on both counts on 13-01-2021.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant argued that there were inter se contradictions between prosecution witnesses PW-02 and PW-04 which the High Court failed to consider. She contended that WPC2686 Sandya, a member of the police party, was not called as a witness creating doubt. The appellant challenged the probability of the incident as narrated by witnesses and alleged the High Court Judge was misdirected as to the place of arrest. She also claimed denial of fair trial due to being remanded during trial.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Inter se contradictions between PW-02 and PW-04 evidence not considered as relevant | WPC2686 Sandya not called as witness creating doubt | Probability of alleged incident as narrated questionable | High Court Judge misdirected as to alleged place of arrest | Denial of fair trial due to remand during trial
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The prosecution relied on PW-02 and PW-04, both police officers who participated in the detection. Their evidence was consistent regarding the arrest and recovery of Heroin from the appellant's palm. The Court of Appeal found their testimony cogent, probable and trustworthy, rejecting claims of contradictions.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal found the prosecution version highly probable. The court found it improbable that police would falsely implicate the appellant or that a drug trafficker would hide drugs in a thicket in a small container. The defence version was deemed improbable.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty. She took the position in her dock statement that police found drugs in a thicket and came to her mother's house where they falsely arrested her. She denied having anything in her possession. The court found her defence not credible and rejected it as improbable.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal examined all grounds of appeal and found them without merit. The court held that the appellant's remand during trial did not deny her a fair trial as no evidence was led during that period. The court found no material contradictions between PW-02 and PW-04 regarding where the appellant lived. The failure to call WPC2686 Sandya was not a missing link as her role was minimal and two officers already testified. The court assessed the probability of events and found the prosecution version credible while rejecting the appellant's version as improbable. The court applied the principle from Jayasena v. Queen that evidence must be considered in totality, and cited Devundarage Nihal v. AG and other precedents on the number of witnesses required. Finding the prosecution evidence cogent and trustworthy, the Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal and affirmed the conviction and sentence.
coa_sentence_type: Life imprisonment on both counts affirmed
brief_judgment_file_summary: The appellant Induwadura Anusha de Silva was convicted by the High Court of Balapitiya for possession and trafficking of 3.21 grams of Heroin on 23-08-2000 at Ahungalle and sentenced to life imprisonment on both counts. She appealed challenging contradictions in witness evidence, failure to call WPC2686 Sandya, improbability of the prosecution case, misdirection on place of arrest, and denial of fair trial due to remand during trial. The Court of Appeal comprehensively examined each ground, found the prosecution evidence of two police officers cogent and probable, held that not calling WPC Sandya did not create a missing link, rejected claims of contradictions, and found no denial of fair trial. The appeal was dismissed and the conviction and sentence were affirmed.
defence_counsel: Harshana Mataraarachchi
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court evaluated the prosecution evidence after the defence closed and found the appellant guilty on both counts. The Court of Appeal noted that the High Court properly considered the evidence and reached a correct conclusion on guilt and sentence.
precedents_cited_list: Jayasena Vs. Queen 72 NLR 313 | Devundarage Nihal Vs. A.G., S.C. Appeal 154/2010 | Vadivelu Thewar Vs. State of Madras SIR SC 614 | King Vs Chalo Singho 42 NLR 269 | Walimunige John Vs. The State 76 NLR 488
standard_of_review_applied: The Court of Appeal considered whether the evidence as a whole, viewed in totality rather than isolation, supported the conviction. The court applied the principle from Jayasena v. Queen that a prudent man must consider all matters in totality to determine guilt.

judges: B. Sasi Mahendran, J. | Amal Ranaraja, J.
offence_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The accused, son-in-law of the deceased Wijesundara Mudiyanselage Punchi Appuhamy, visited the deceased's residence on 14.09.2012 seeking his wife. After conversing with the deceased for half an hour, the accused called the deceased closer claiming to share a secret and then launched a sudden attack on his neck with a cleaver, inflicting multiple injuries. The deceased's wife PW01 witnessed the attack and fled to seek help. The JMO found 13 incised injuries concentrated on the head, neck, and chest consistent with a curved instrument.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court Judge convicted the accused of murder and imposed the death sentence. The Judge excluded the evidence of PW10 regarding the recovery of the weapon but found PW01's narrative of the stabbing incident to be consistent and credible, deeming it sufficient to support the conviction.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The accused appealed challenging whether the High Court Judge failed to give the benefit of arising doubts to the accused. The appeal also raised issues regarding the previous and post behavior of the accused. During oral submissions, the defence counsel argued that the accused should have been convicted of culpable homicide not amounting to murder based on grave and sudden provocation.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Whether the Learned High Court Judge of Kegalla has failed to give the benefit of the arising doubts to the benefit of the Accused-Appellant? | The previous and the post behaviour of the Accused
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The prosecution called 12 witnesses and marked productions P1 to P7. PW01, the sole eyewitness and wife of the deceased, consistently maintained her testimony that she witnessed the accused stab the deceased. The Court found her evidence credible and trustworthy despite defence suggestions that she had not observed the incident. PW11, the JMO, provided expert medical evidence corroborating PW01's account.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court found no reasonable doubt about the accused's guilt based on the consistent and credible eyewitness testimony of PW01 corroborated by the medical evidence showing 13 incised injuries consistent with the attack described.
defence_version_summary: The accused made only a dock statement and did not call any witnesses. The defence argued during oral submissions that the accused should be convicted of culpable homicide based on grave and sudden provocation. However, there was no evidence of provocation from the deceased or PW01, and the Court found the accused brought the weapon to the scene, negating any claim of loss of self-control.
procedural_defects_description: The High Court Judge excluded PW10's evidence regarding the recovery of the weapon due to contradictions with PW01's testimony about how the cleaver was found.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal carefully examined whether the defence of grave and sudden provocation under Exception 1 to Section 294 of the Penal Code could apply. The Court applied the test from K.D.J. Perera v. The King requiring the accused to establish provocation was given, was sudden and grave, resulted in loss of self-control, and the act was committed while deprived of self-control. The Court found no evidence of any provocative behavior by the deceased or PW01 at the time of the incident. The postmortem revealed 13 severe injuries to the head and neck consistent with use of a weapon. Significantly, the accused brought the weapon with him to the scene rather than picking it up in the heat of the moment. The Court evaluated PW01's testimony and found she remained consistent throughout cross-examination, making her evidence credible and trustworthy. The Court concluded there was no basis to reduce the conviction from murder to culpable homicide and affirmed both the conviction and death sentence.
coa_sentence_type: Death sentence
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused Pathirannahalage Nimal Weerasinghe was convicted by the High Court of Kegalle for murdering his father-in-law Wijesundara Mudiyanselage Punchi Appuhamy on 14.09.2012 under Section 296 of the Penal Code and sentenced to death. The prosecution presented 12 witnesses including PW01 who witnessed the attack and the JMO who found 13 incised injuries on the deceased. The accused appealed challenging the conviction and argued for a reduced charge of culpable homicide based on grave and sudden provocation. The Court of Appeal held that there was no evidence of provocation and the accused brought the weapon to the scene, negating any claim of loss of self-control. Finding PW01's testimony credible and consistent, the Court dismissed the appeal and affirmed both the conviction and death sentence.
defence_counsel: Jagath Nanayakkawa
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court Judge excluded PW10's evidence regarding weapon recovery due to contradictions but found PW01's narrative of the stabbing to be consistent and credible. The Court found her testimony sufficient to support the conviction and imposed the death sentence for murder.
precedents_cited_list: K.D.J. Perera v. The King, 53 NLR 193
standard_of_review_applied: The Court of Appeal reviewed whether there was any basis to interfere with the High Court's decision by examining whether the defence of grave and sudden provocation could apply and whether the conviction and sentence were supported by the evidence and legal principles.
sentencing_principles_applied: The Court applied the principles for grave and sudden provocation under Exception 1 to Section 294 of the Penal Code, requiring the accused to establish on a balance of probabilities that provocation occurred, was grave and sudden, deprived the accused of self-control, and the death was caused while in that state.

judges: B. Sasi Mahendran, J. | Amal Ranaraja, J.
offence_sections: Section 5(2) of the Offences Against Public Property Act No.12 of 1982
brief_facts_summary: The appellant deceived Ratnadeshapriya Samaraweera, manager of People's Bank Ginthupitiya branch, between May 1, 2000 and June 30, 2000. The appellant dishonestly induced the manager to hand over bills of lading and invoices related to a consignment imported by Durga Agencies by falsely asserting that payment of Rs.850,000 would be made to the International Division of People's Bank. The documents were released based on the appellant's assurance to ensure payment before the goods were cleared, but the consignment was cleared and additional payment documents were later discovered to be forged.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 5(2) of the Offences Against Public Property Act No.12 of 1982
hc_sentence_type: 26 months simple imprisonment and fine of Rs. 2,550,000 with 3 years simple imprisonment in default
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the appellant of the first charge of cheating and sentenced him to 26 months simple imprisonment and imposed a fine of Rs. 2,550,000 with 3 years simple imprisonment in default. The second accused was acquitted of the second charge. The fine imposed was three times the amount related to the offence committed in accordance with section 5(2) of the Offences Against Public Property Act.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant challenged the conviction on multiple grounds including that the indictment was defective as necessary ingredients of cheating were not contained in the charges, prosecution failed to prove damage or loss to government, the High Court Judge failed to consider PW01 as not credible, and failed to properly evaluate defence evidence. The appellant also argued the Judge misdirected himself by coming to erroneous conclusions making the judgment bad in law, and that the sentence was excessive.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Whether the indictment is defective as the necessary ingredients of the offence of cheating are not contained in the charges of the indictment | Whether the prosecution has failed to prove the ingredient of damage or loss caused to the government in the offence of cheating | Whether the Learned High Court Judge has failed to consider PW01 is not a credible witness and his evidence should not be relied upon | Whether the Learned High Court Judge has failed to properly consider and evaluate the evidence of the defence | Whether the Learned High Court Judge has misdirected himself by coming to erroneous or irrelevant conclusions/findings in the judgment and therefore whether the judgment is bad in law | Whether the sentence imposed on the appellant is excessive considering the circumstances of the appellant
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court found that the defence failed to demonstrate any animosity between PW01 and the appellant, and the appellant failed to identify material contradictions in PW01's testimony or provide reasons to challenge PW01's credibility. The Court concluded that the argument asserting PW01 is an unreliable witness lacked merit.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court found that the appellant induced belief in PW01 that a commitment was made which was subsequently breached, and engaged in deceptive practices causing wrongful gain to the business entity involved in importing the consignment
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty and maintained his innocence throughout proceedings. He asserted that he was manipulated by the second accused into participating in transactions that appeared innocuous on the surface. The appellant's defence was that he was misled and coerced into dealings which he believed to be legitimate exchanges with PW01. The Court found the High Court Judge properly evaluated the appellant's evidence and other defence witnesses holistically and provided clear reasons for not relying on specific evidence.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed the offence under section 398 of the Penal Code and determined that the appellant's conduct fell under the second limb of cheating, which does not require establishing actual damage or harm. The Court noted that the appellant had established trust with the bank through regular visits representing other customers, which contributed to PW01's decision to release the documents. The Court found that by undertaking to make payments to the international branch, the appellant induced belief in PW01 that a commitment was made which was subsequently breached. The Court rejected arguments that PW01 was not credible, finding no animosity demonstrated and no material contradictions identified by the defence. The Court upheld the High Court's holistic evaluation of evidence and found the sentence was in line with statutory provisions. The appeal was dismissed with no order as to costs.
coa_sentence_type: 26 months simple imprisonment and fine of Rs. 2,550,000 with 3 years simple imprisonment in default
brief_judgment_file_summary: Gnanaiyah Jeyagaran was convicted by the High Court of Colombo for cheating under section 5(2) of the Offences Against Public Property Act No.12 of 1982, for deceiving a bank manager to obtain bills of lading and invoices by falsely promising payment of Rs.850,000 between May and June 2000. He was sentenced to 26 months simple imprisonment and fined Rs. 2,550,000 with 3 years imprisonment in default. The appellant challenged the conviction on grounds including defective indictment, failure to prove loss to government, credibility of prosecution witness, improper evaluation of defence evidence, misdirection of law, and excessive sentence. The Court of Appeal found the offence fell under the second limb of cheating which does not require proof of damage, upheld the credibility of the bank manager witness, found the High Court properly evaluated all evidence holistically, and determined the sentence was in line with statutory provisions being three times the amount involved. The appeal was dismissed.
defence_counsel: Kaneel Maddumage with Praveen Premathilaka
hc_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found that the Learned High Court Judge meticulously evaluated the evidence presented by the appellant and other defence witnesses holistically rather than in piecemeal fashion. The High Court Judge provided clear and cogent reasons for conclusions drawn and for not relying on specific evidence, demonstrating commitment to transparency and fairness. The Court of Appeal found no basis to interfere with the High Court's findings.
precedents_cited_list: AG vs. Wijerama [1937] 17 CLR 160 | Smith and Hogan - Criminal Law 10th edition (2003) at pages 568 to 569
standard_of_review_applied: Appellate review of conviction and sentence with assessment of whether High Court properly evaluated evidence and applied law correctly
sentencing_principles_applied: The sentence was in line with section 5(2) of the Offences Against Public Property Act No.12 of 1982, with the fine being three times the amount related to the offence committed

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 141 of the Penal Code read together with Section 32 of the Penal Code, Section 146 read together with Section 383 of the Penal Code, Section 32 read together with Section 383 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The 3rd Accused-Petitioner along with three other accused were indicted for being members of an unlawful assembly armed with deadly weapons and committing multiple robberies on 12th October 2001 at Mauara. The robberies involved theft of money, gold rings, gold chains, and wrist watches from multiple victims. The Petitioner absconded after service of the indictment and the trial proceeded in absentia, resulting in conviction on five counts.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 141 of the Penal Code read together with Section 32 of the Penal Code, Section 146 read together with Section 383 of the Penal Code
hc_sentence_type: 15 years rigorous imprisonment on each count, to run concurrently
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court tried the Petitioner in absentia after he absconded. The High Court found the Petitioner guilty on counts 1st, 3rd, 6th, 8th, and 9th, and acquitted him on counts 2nd, 5th, and 7th. The Court imposed a sentence of 15 years rigorous imprisonment on each count, with sentences to run concurrently.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The Petitioner submitted exceptional circumstances for revision: (a) The High Court judgment dated 13.03.2021 is contrary to law; (b) The High Court failed to consider the severity of death threats and that the Petitioner ran for his life; (c) The High Court failed to consider the notable disparity in punishment between the 2nd and 4th Accused who received 5 years versus the Petitioner who received 15 years.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The judgment of the Learned High Court Judge dated 13.03.2021 is contrary to law | The Learned High Court Judge failed to consider the severity of the death threats and neglected to consider that the Petitioner had run for his life due to death threats | The Learned High Court Judge had failed to consider the notable disparity in the punishment given to 2nd and 4th Accused as oppose to the punishment of the Petitioner
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The judgment does not provide detailed analysis of witness evidence. The Court focused primarily on the procedural issue of the Petitioner's absconding and the Section 241(3) CPC inquiry rather than evaluating the substantive evidence that led to the original conviction.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court focused on the mala fide nature of the Petitioner's absence and found his explanation regarding death threats to be insufficient, noting he returned to Sri Lanka twice without checking his case status
defence_version_summary: The Petitioner did not plead guilty and absconded after service of the indictment. His defence at the revision stage was that he absconded due to death threats from an underworld figure. The Court rejected this explanation as mala fide, noting he returned to Sri Lanka in 2015 and 2018 without checking his case status.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal examined whether exceptional circumstances existed to warrant exercise of its revisionary jurisdiction under Article 138 of the Constitution. The Court found that the High Court correctly conducted the Section 241(3) CPC inquiry and properly concluded the Petitioner's absence was mala fide. The Court addressed the sentencing disparity argument by explaining that the 2nd and 4th Accused received reduced sentences because they pleaded guilty on 14.11.2011, which saves court time and protects victims from secondary victimization. In contrast, the Petitioner absconded and was arrested seven years after the warrant was issued. The Court applied precedents establishing that revision is discretionary and requires exceptional circumstances, which were not present here. The Court concluded the Petitioner failed to demonstrate sufficient exceptional grounds warranting intervention.
coa_sentence_type: 15 years rigorous imprisonment on each count (counts 1st, 3rd, 6th, 8th, and 9th), to run concurrently
brief_judgment_file_summary: The 3rd Accused-Petitioner was convicted in absentia by the High Court of Embilipitiya on five counts of robbery as member of an unlawful assembly armed with deadly weapons and sentenced to 15 years rigorous imprisonment on each count to run concurrently. The Petitioner absconded after service of indictment and was arrested seven years later. He filed a revision application arguing the judgment was contrary to law, the High Court ignored death threats that caused him to flee, and there was disparity compared to co-accused who received 5 years. The Court of Appeal dismissed the revision application, holding no exceptional circumstances existed to warrant intervention. The Court found the High Court correctly determined the Petitioner's absence was mala fide and properly explained that co-accused received reduced sentences for pleading guilty early.
prosecution_counsel: Sudharshana De Silva, SDSG with I.M.M.Fahim, SC
defence_counsel: K.A.D.K. Jayalath
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court conducted a Section 241(3) CPC inquiry after the Petitioner was arrested on an open warrant. The High Court correctly considered that the Petitioner had absconded in 2008, returned to Sri Lanka twice in 2015 and 2018 without checking his case, and claimed death threats from a deceased underworld figure. The Court of Appeal affirmed the High Court's finding that the Petitioner's absence was mala fide.
precedents_cited_list: Ramu Thamodarampillai v. The Attorney General [2004] 3 SLR 180 | Marian Beebee v. Seyed Mohamed 69 CLW 34 | Rasheed Ali v. Mohammed Ali and Others [1981] 1 SLR 262 | Commissioner of Police v. Tanes (1957-58) 68 CLR 383
standard_of_review_applied: Revisionary jurisdiction under Article 138 of the Constitution requiring demonstration of exceptional circumstances
sentencing_principles_applied: The Court applied the principle that accused who plead guilty receive reduced sentences because it encourages early guilty pleas, saves court time and money, and protects witnesses and victims from secondary victimization. Sentencing is the prerogative of the court.

judges: P. Kumararatnam, J. | R. P. Hettiarachchi, J.
offence_sections: Sections 54(A)(b) and 54(A)(d) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance as amended by Act No.13 of 1984
brief_facts_summary: On 16th August 2013, IP/Antony (PW1) arrested the Appellant at Thoppuwa Junction, Kochchikade, based on information from an informant. PW2 Kekulandara checked the Appellant and uncovered a cellophane bag with 09 packets containing a substance suspected to be Heroin from his trouser pocket. The Appellant was brought to the Police Narcotics Bureau where the substance was weighed at 48 grams gross, properly sealed with fingerprints, entered in the Production Register, and handed to the reserve police officer.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Sections 54(A)(b) and 54(A)(d) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance as amended by Act No.13 of 1984
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court of Chilaw found the Appellant guilty on both counts of trafficking and being in possession of 16.52 grams of Heroin on 16th August 2013. The learned High Court Judge imposed life imprisonment on the Appellant for both counts on 13th September 2023.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The Appellant raised two main grounds. First, the prosecution failed to prove the chain of inward journey beyond reasonable doubt due to a discrepancy in the total weight of the powder weighed by PW1 and the weight indicated by the Government Analyst's Department. Second, the learned High Court Judge failed to consider material inter se contradictions of the main prosecution witnesses who conducted the inquiry.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The prosecution has failed to prove the chain of inward journey beyond reasonable doubt, as there is a discrepancy in the total weight of the powder contained in the production sent by the Police Narcotics Bureau which was weighed by PW1 and the weight indicated by the Government Analyst's Department. | The learned High Court Judge has failed to consider the material inter se contradictions of the main prosecution witnesses who had conducted the inquiry.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The prosecution called PW1 IP/Antony who arrested the Appellant and PW2 SI/Kekulandara to corroborate PW1's evidence. The Court found significant discrepancies in the weight of the substance between what was recorded by police (16.100 grams gross aggregate) and the Government Analyst Report (8.64 grams), creating serious doubt about the chain of custody and integrity of the evidence.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court found that the evidence presented by the prosecution regarding the inward journey of the productions creates a serious doubt on the conviction. The weight discrepancy of 8.46 grams between police records and Government Analyst Report, coupled with the absence of the Appellant's signature on the sealed envelope, undermined the prosecution's case beyond reasonable doubt.
defence_version_summary: The Appellant pleaded not guilty. In his dock statement, the Appellant denied being in possession of any dangerous drugs as claimed by the prosecution. The Appellant gave only a dock statement and did not call witnesses. The Court found that the evidence supported the Appellant's defence stance due to serious doubts in the prosecution case.
legal_errors_description: The learned High Court Judge failed to analyse the weight discrepancy of the substance (8.46 grams difference between police weighing and Government Analyst Report), which disturbs the production chain. The HC Judge also concluded that production was properly sealed despite one of the Appellant's signatures being absent on the sealed envelope. These misdirections deprived the Appellant of a fair trial.
procedural_defects_description: One of the Appellant's signatures was absent on the sealed envelope, despite PW1 and PW2 stating that fingerprints were taken to seal the production after weighing. The learned High Court Judge nevertheless concluded that production had been properly sealed in the presence of the Appellant.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal applied the principle from Woolmington v. DPP that prosecution must prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt. The Court emphasized that in drug cases, the inward journey of productions must be established with cogent evidence, citing Mohamed Nimnaz V. Attorney General CA/95/94 and Perera V. Attorney General [1998] 1 Sri.L.R. The COA found that the prosecution failed to establish the chain of custody due to a significant weight discrepancy of 8.46 grams (16.100 grams recorded by police versus 8.64 grams in Government Analyst Report). The Deputy Solicitor General admitted the discrepancy and could not explain it. The Court found that the High Court Judge made no comment about this weight discrepancy in his judgment, causing great prejudice to the Appellant and refusing him a fair trial. Additionally, the absence of one signature on the sealed envelope, despite the HC Judge's finding that production was properly sealed, constituted a clear misdirection. The COA concluded that these contradictions and improbabilities in prosecution evidence created serious doubt about the conviction and supported the Appellant's defence stance, affecting the root of the case.
coa_sentence_type: Acquittal from all charges
brief_judgment_file_summary: Mapatunage Dhammika was charged in the High Court of Chilaw under Sections 54(A)(b) and 54(A)(d) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance for trafficking and possession of 16.52 grams of Heroin on 16th August 2013. The High Court found him guilty and imposed life imprisonment on both counts on 13th September 2023. On appeal, the Appellant challenged the chain of custody and contradictions in prosecution evidence. The Court of Appeal found a significant unexplained weight discrepancy of 8.46 grams between police records (16.100 grams) and the Government Analyst Report (8.64 grams), which the Deputy Solicitor General admitted but could not explain. The COA also found that the High Court Judge misdirected himself by failing to analyse this discrepancy and by concluding the production was properly sealed despite a missing signature. The Court of Appeal set aside the conviction and sentence, acquitted the Appellant from all charges, and allowed the appeal on 31st July 2025.
defence_counsel: Isuru Somadasa
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court Judge convicted the Appellant and imposed life imprisonment on both counts without addressing the weight discrepancy between police records and the Government Analyst Report. The COA found that the HC Judge misdirected himself by failing to analyse this significant discrepancy and by concluding that production was properly sealed despite the absence of one of the Appellant's signatures on the sealed envelope, causing great prejudice and denying a fair trial.
precedents_cited_list: Woolmington v. DPP [1935] A.C.462 | Mohamed Nimnaz V. Attorney General CA/95/94 | Perera V. Attorney General [1998] 1 Sri.L.R | Koushappis v. The State of WA [2007] WASCA 26; (2007) 168 A Crim R 51
standard_of_review_applied: The Court applied the standard that prosecution must prove the case beyond reasonable doubt and establish the chain of custody with cogent evidence, ensuring the inward journey of productions has not been disturbed at all material points.

judges: Menaka Wijesundera J. | Wickum A. Kaluarachchi J.
brief_facts_summary: The appellant was indicted along with the deceased Somapala (husband of the deceased victim) for the murder of the appellant's sister. On 03-06-2006, the deceased-accused Somapala entered the house with a sword and cut the deceased victim while the appellant walked in with a knife hidden in his shirt, told everyone not to move, and gave chase to witness Nilmini with the knife. The appellant and Somapala arrived together and left the scene together. The police recovered a knife subsequent to the appellant's statement.
hc_judgment_summary: Upon conclusion of trial, the learned trial judge convicted the appellant for murder and sentenced accordingly. The trial judge found that the appellant shared a common murderous intention with the deceased-accused Somapala based on evidence that the appellant arrived with a knife hidden in his shirt, brandished it telling everyone not to move, gave chase to a witness, and left the scene with Somapala.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant raised three grounds: (1) the trial judge usurped the role of the prosecutor by allowing defence witness examination in chief to proceed in the absence of state counsel, (2) the appellant did not share a common murderous intention with the deceased-accused Somapala at the time of the incident, and (3) the trial judge failed to consider contradictions and omissions in the prosecution evidence.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The trial judge has usurped the role of the prosecutor | The appellant has not shared a common murderous intention with the dead-accused, Somapala, at the time of the incident | The trial judge has failed to consider the contradictions and omissions
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found that PW-01 (Nilmini) stood the test of cross examination satisfactorily and was corroborated by PW-02 and PW-04. The lay witnesses and investigative officers observed sufficient illumination at the scene. The appellant's dock statement was rejected because the line of defence was not taken up during cross examination of witnesses, and the defence witness spoke in line with prosecution witnesses.
probability_assessment_by_court: The court found sufficient direct and circumstantial evidence to establish common intention between the appellant and deceased-accused, including the appellant arriving with a hidden knife, brandishing it, giving chase to witness, and leaving the scene together with Somapala.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty, made a dock statement, and called one defence witness. In his dock statement, the appellant admitted going to the scene and giving chase to PW-01 but denied sharing a common murderous intention with Somapala, claiming the cutting of the deceased took place while he was giving chase to witness No. 02. The trial judge rejected this dock statement because the line of defence was not taken up during cross examination of witnesses. The defence witness corroborated the prosecution's story.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal thoroughly examined all three grounds of appeal. On the first ground regarding the trial judge usurping the role of prosecutor, the COA found no prejudice was caused when the defence witness examination in chief proceeded without state counsel present, as only examination in chief occurred, cross examination was postponed for two months giving the Attorney General ample time to prepare, and the trial judge asked no questions. On the second ground regarding common intention, the COA found overwhelming evidence that the appellant shared a common murderous intention with Somapala: the appellant walked in with a knife hidden in his shirt, brandished it telling everyone not to move, gave chase to witnesses, left the scene with Somapala, and had a bad relationship with witness Nilmini. The COA applied precedents from The King v Asappu (1948) 50 NLR 324 and The Queen v J Mahatun (1959) 61 NLR 540 establishing that common intention need not be pre-arranged but can arise at the spur of the moment. The COA rejected the appellant's dock statement because this defence line was not put to prosecution witnesses during cross examination. On the third ground regarding contradictions, the COA found the trial judge considered contradictions v1-v4 lucidly and clearly. The COA dismissed the appeal finding no merit in any ground.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The appellant Yaapa Mudiyanselage Nihal alias Edmond Nihal was convicted by the High Court of Kuliyapitiya for the murder of his sister committed on 03-06-2006 along with co-accused Somapala (the victim's husband). The appellant appealed raising three grounds: procedural impropriety in allowing defence witness examination without state counsel, lack of common murderous intention with Somapala, and failure to consider contradictions. The Court of Appeal dismissed all grounds finding: no prejudice occurred from the procedural matter, overwhelming evidence established common intention (appellant arrived with hidden knife, brandished it, gave chase, and left with Somapala), and the trial judge properly considered contradictions. The COA affirmed the conviction applying precedents on common intention and finding the appellant's dock statement inconsistent with his cross examination strategy.
defence_counsel: Tenny Fernando
hc_analysis_summary: The trial judge thoroughly considered all items of evidence against the appellant including that he walked into the scene with a knife hidden in his shirt, Somapala followed soon after, the appellant brandished his knife telling everyone to stay in place, he left the scene with Somapala, and he had a bad relationship with witness Nilmini. The trial judge rejected the appellant's dock statement because the line of defence was not taken up during cross examination of witnesses. The COA found the trial judge considered contradictions v1-v4 lucidly and clearly.
precedents_cited_list: The King v Asappu et al (1948) 50 NLR 324 | The Queen v J Mahatun (1959) 61 NLR 540
standard_of_review_applied: Appellate review of trial court's factual findings and legal conclusions on conviction and common intention

judges: Menaka Wijesundera J. | B. Sasi Mahendran J.
brief_facts_summary: The appellant and his mother (1st accused) were indicted for the murder of the appellant's wife, who was 19 years old at the time. On 30 December 2007, the appellant made a threatening phone call to the victim's father. The victim suffered 65% burn injuries after the 1st accused poured kerosene on her and set her on fire following an argument, while the appellant slapped her, banged her head on the wall, and refused to help extinguish the flames. The victim was admitted to hospital on 30 December 2007 and died on 3 January 2008 from burn injuries.
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted both accused of murder after finding that three dying declarations and medical evidence clearly demonstrated they acted in furtherance of a common murderous intention. The trial judge found the type of injuries inflicted and the appellant's threatening phone call to the victim's father prior to the incident demonstrated murderous intentions.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The main ground of appeal was that the trial judge had not considered the dying declaration properly and the case for the prosecution had not been proved beyond a reasonable doubt. The appellant argued that the dying declarations were deficient and contradicted each other, the police statement was questionable because proper permission from medical authorities was not obtained, and the statement to the relative was coached as it was made after the victim's death.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The trial judge had not considered the dying declaration properly | The case for the prosecution had not been proved beyond a reasonable doubt | The dying declarations of the deceased are deficient and contradict each other | The dying declaration made to the police is questionable because he had not obtained permission from the medical authorities | The relative to whom the deceased had made a dying declaration had not made a statement until the victim had died and therefore it is coached
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the dying declarations to be very consistent, clearly demonstrating the cause of death and how the two accused acted to commit the act. The police had obtained permission from the nurse in charge before recording the statement from the victim. The witnesses who quoted the dying declaration stood the test of cross-examination satisfactorily.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal found the prosecution proved beyond a reasonable doubt that the appellant acted with a common murderous intention with the first accused and committed the murder.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty and gave evidence on oath. He claimed the deceased was of quarrelsome nature and on the day of the incident she fought with him for not having ginger at home to serve ginger tea when her parents came. He admitted hitting her, then went to the toilet, and when he returned she had set fire to herself. The court rejected this version and found the prosecution case proved.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal thoroughly reviewed the evidence and found no merit in the appellant's submissions. The court held that the three dying declarations were very consistent and clearly demonstrated the cause of death and how the accused acted. The deceased was in a position to speak according to the doctor who conducted the post-mortem and she identified the assailants. The police had properly obtained permission from the nurse in charge before recording the statement. The witnesses who quoted the dying declarations stood the test of cross-examination satisfactorily. The court applied established precedents on dying declarations including the requirement that the deceased was able to speak, could identify the assailant, and the statement was true and could be accepted beyond reasonable doubt. The medical evidence confirmed 65% burn injuries which was undoubtedly fatal. The court emphasized that a criminal trial serves justice to the accused, victim and society, ensuring both that no innocent person is punished and that a guilty person does not escape.
brief_judgment_file_summary: Mohammed Hussain Mohamed Firnas and his mother Abdul Kareem Kurrathul Ain were convicted by the High Court of Colombo for the murder of the appellant's 19-year-old wife who died from 65% burn injuries on 3 January 2008. The prosecution case was based on three dying declarations made by the victim to her father, a relative, and police, stating that after an argument the 1st accused poured kerosene on her and set her on fire while the appellant assaulted her and refused to help. The appellant appealed arguing the dying declarations were not properly considered, contradicted each other, and the case was not proved beyond reasonable doubt. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal on 25 July 2024, finding the dying declarations were consistent and reliable, the victim was able to speak and identify her assailants, the witnesses stood the test of cross-examination, and the prosecution proved the case beyond reasonable doubt. The conviction and sentence were affirmed.
defence_counsel: N. M Shaheid with Zaid Ali and Wazeem Amhar
cause_of_death_exact_text: the deceased had died of burn injuries and the totality of the burn injuries had been 65%
hc_analysis_summary: The trial judge referred to the evidence of both sides and found that three dying declarations and medical evidence clearly demonstrated that the appellant and 1st accused acted in furtherance of a common murderous intention. The type of injuries inflicted demonstrated murderous intentions. The Court of Appeal agreed with this analysis and found no errors in the High Court's reasoning.
precedents_cited_list: CA-41-2009 | Gamini Attanayake vs the Attorney General CA-3-2011 | Somasundera vs The Queen 76 NLR 10 | Perera vs Jayasinghe 48 NLR 17 | Sigera v Attorney General (2011) 1 Sri.L.R. 201 | Ambika Prasad vs State of New Delhi 2000 SCC Crl 522
standard_of_review_applied: The Court of Appeal reviewed whether the prosecution proved beyond a reasonable doubt that the appellant acted with common murderous intention and committed murder, applying established guidelines for evaluating dying declarations.

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code (Murder) and Section 382 of the Penal Code (Robbery)
brief_facts_summary: The appellant came to the victim's building site on 22-05-2002 inquiring about satalin planks advertised for sale. He went upstairs with the deceased son (aged 19) to view additional planks. The appellant stabbed the deceased with a knife, came down with a blood-soaked knife, threatened the mother (PW-01) at knife point, and robbed her gold chain before fleeing. The deceased died from his injuries hours later. The appellant was arrested on 28-05-2002, and a gold chain was recovered from a jewellery shop in Sea Street based on his statement under section 27 of the Evidence Ordinance.
evidence_type_secondary: Recovery of gold chain and knife under section 27, Medical evidence, Identification parade
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code (Murder) and Section 382 of the Penal Code (Robbery)
hc_sentence_type: Death sentence for Count 1 (Murder) and 12 years rigorous imprisonment for Count 2 (Robbery), with fine and compensation
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court of Colombo found the appellant guilty on both counts after trial without a jury. The HC sentenced him to death for murder and 12 years rigorous imprisonment for robbery, with a fine of Rs. 50,000 (default 2 years RI) and compensation of Rs. 25,000 (default 1 year RI). The HC accepted the eyewitness testimony of the victim's mother and the evidence of identification parade, recovery of the gold chain from the jewellery shop, and the recovery of the knife.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant challenged his conviction and sentence arguing that the learned High Court Judge erred in law by failing to consider contradictions and omissions in the prosecution case in favour of the defence, erred in evaluating evidence relating to identification of the appellant, failed to consider discrepancies in the evidence of PW-01 in favour of the appellant, and disregarded the dock statement made by the appellant.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Did the learned High Court Judge err in law by failing to consider contradictions and omissions in the prosecution case in favour of the defence | Did the learned High Court Judge err in evaluating the evidence in relation to the identification of the appellant | Did the learned High Court Judge err in failing to consider the discrepancies in the evidence of PW-01 in favour of the appellant | Did the learned High Court Judge err in disregarding the dock statement of the appellant
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal held that PW-01 (mother and eyewitness) had sufficient time to observe the appellant as he conversed with her and her son for 5-10 minutes before going upstairs, and she witnessed him coming down with a blood-soaked knife and robbing her chain. The identification parade was properly conducted and admitted under section 420. The jewellery shop owner (PW-05) positively identified the appellant as the person who sold him the chain. The COA found the contradictions and omissions to be trivial and not material to the core of the case.
probability_assessment_by_court: The COA held that the prosecution established its case beyond reasonable doubt. The eyewitness testimony was credible, the identification was proper, and the recovery of the gold chain and knife corroborated the prosecution case. The dock statement failed to create any reasonable doubt.
defence_version_summary: The appellant made a dock statement claiming he was arrested on 23-05-2002 when police visited his house. He claimed he was tortured and forced to show police to a jewellery shop and say he sold the chain there. He alleged police forced the shop owner to hand over a gold chain. He claimed he was shown to two females at the police station before the identification parade. The court rejected this defence as the appellant failed to put these allegations to the relevant witnesses during cross-examination, and he did not inform the Magistrate during the identification parade that he had been previously shown to the witness.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal thoroughly examined each ground of appeal and found no merit in any of them. The COA held that the alleged contradictions and omissions were trivial and did not touch the core of the case, citing State of Uttar Pradesh Vs. Anthony and State of U.P. Vs. M.K. Anthony. The COA applied the Turnbull Guidelines from Regina Vs. Turnbull (1977) QB 224 to assess the identification evidence and found that PW-01 had adequate opportunity to observe the appellant for 5-10 minutes in daylight. The COA emphasized that the appellant failed to cross-examine PW-05 (jewellery shop owner) on his defence that he never sold the chain, citing Sarwan Singh Vs. State of Punjab and Pilippu Mandige Nalaka Krishantha Kumara Thisera Vs A.G. The COA held that the HC Judge correctly evaluated the dock statement in accordance with Queen Vs. Kularathne (1968) 71 NLR 529, noting its infirmity as unsworn and not subject to cross-examination. The COA found that the HC Judge properly established that the prosecution proved a strong prima facie case before considering whether the defence created reasonable doubt, which it did not.
coa_sentence_type: Death sentence for Count 1 (Murder) and 12 years rigorous imprisonment for Count 2 (Robbery), with fine of Rs. 50,000 (default 2 years RI) and compensation of Rs. 25,000 (default 1 year RI)
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused-appellant Sandun Dinusha Wanigasuriya was convicted by the High Court of Colombo for the murder of 19-year-old Harshika Damith Fonseka and robbery of a gold chain from the victim's mother Lalani Fonseka on 22-05-2002 at Kaldamulla. The HC sentenced him to death for murder and 12 years RI for robbery, plus Rs. 50,000 fine and Rs. 25,000 compensation. The appellant appealed on grounds of contradictions in prosecution evidence, improper identification evaluation, and failure to consider his dock statement. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal on 25-07-2024, holding that the contradictions were trivial, the identification was proper under Turnbull Guidelines, the recovery of the gold chain and knife corroborated the prosecution case, and the dock statement failed to create reasonable doubt. The COA affirmed the conviction and sentence.
defence_counsel: Nipun Samaratunga
cause_of_death_exact_text: The deceased has received a deep stab wound just below his right side armpit, which has penetrated the heart cavity and the lungs. The cause of death had been due to the injuries suffered by the deceased as a result of the stabbing.
hc_analysis_summary: The COA found that the HC Judge properly considered the prosecution evidence to establish a strong prima facie case before evaluating whether the defence created reasonable doubt. The HC Judge correctly considered the alleged contradictions and omissions and determined they did not create reasonable doubt. The HC Judge properly evaluated the identification evidence and the dock statement in accordance with established legal principles.
precedents_cited_list: State of Uttar Pradesh Vs. Anthony 1985 AIR SC 48 | State of U.P. Vs. M. K. Anthony, AIR 1985 SC 48 | Regina Vs. Turnbull (1977) QB 224 | Sarwan Singh Vs. State of Punjab 2002 AIR Supreme Court iii 3652 | Boby Mathew Vs. State of Karnataka 2004 3 Cri. L. J.3003 | Pilippu Mandige Nalaka Krishantha Kumara Thisera Vs A.G CA 87/2005 | King Vs. Vellayan Sittambaram (1918) 20 NLR 257 | Queen Vs. Buddharakkita Thero (1962) 63 NLR 433 | Queen Vs. Kularathne (1968) 71 NLR 529
standard_of_review_applied: The Court of Appeal reviewed whether the High Court Judge properly evaluated the evidence, whether contradictions and omissions were material, whether identification evidence was properly assessed, and whether the dock statement was given appropriate weight considering its infirmity as unsworn and not subject to cross-examination.

judges: Menaka Wijesundera, J | Wickum A. Kaluarachchi, J
offence_sections: Section 355 of the Penal Code read with Section 32
brief_facts_summary: On 07 July 1989 around 11:00 p.m., a group of persons including officers in police uniform came to the house of 16-year-old Rathnachandra Liyanage at Delgoda and took him away stating they needed to record a statement. They then went to his brother PW-3's residence 2.5 miles away, got Rathnachandra to call his brother, and took both into custody. Both were put in a van and taken to Batalanda where PW-3 was tortured and heard his brother's voice. The next morning, the 1st accused informed the father that Rathnachandra had escaped, but Rathnachandra was never seen again and remains missing.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 355 of the Penal Code read with Section 32
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted all five accused on the 5th count of the indictment for abducting Rathnachandra Liyanage in order to murder him, acting in furtherance of common intention under Section 355 read with Section 32 of the Penal Code. Each accused was sentenced to five years of rigorous imprisonment. The court found that the prosecution proved the abduction and the intention to murder through circumstantial evidence.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellants challenged the conviction on multiple grounds including: failure to comply with Section 196 of the Criminal Procedure Code by not reading the indictment; wrongful evaluation of evidence; delay of six years and four months in making a complaint to police causing prejudice; improper identification of accused; failure to properly consider and evaluate common intention as required by law; and that the prosecution failed to prove the 5th charge beyond reasonable doubt.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The learned High Court Judge wrongfully evaluated the evidence at trial | The learned High Court Judge erred in not complying with Section 196 of the Code of Criminal Procedure | The learned High Court Judge failed to consider belatedness of complaint and its impact | The accused-appellants were not properly identified | The learned High Court Judge failed to consider or evaluate common intention as required by law | The prosecution did not prove charge No.5 beyond reasonable doubt | The learned High Court Judge's findings are not maintainable in law | The case against the 1st accused and other four accused are fundamentally different | The evidence given by accused from witness box was not properly considered and evaluated | The learned Trial Judge failed to properly analyze the evidence of prosecution witnesses | The learned Trial Judge failed to give benefit of doubt to accused when such doubt was created
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The prosecution case relied primarily on four main witnesses: PW-1 and PW-2 (father and mother, whose depositions from non-summary inquiry were admitted under Section 33), PW-3 (brother who witnessed the abduction and was also taken into custody and tortured), and PW-7 (cousin). The Court found their evidence credible and consistent. PW-3's voice identification of his brother at Batalanda was accepted as reliable given their close familial relationship.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court held that the circumstantial evidence was consistent only with the guilt of the 1st to 4th accused and not with any reasonable hypothesis of innocence. The victim was taken into custody, brought to Batalanda with his brother, heard shouting, and then disappeared never to be seen again. The false statement by the 1st accused that the victim escaped demonstrated guilt.
defence_version_summary: All accused pleaded not guilty. The 1st accused did not give evidence or make a dock statement but called one witness who did not state anything material. The 2nd, 3rd, 4th, and 5th accused gave evidence on oath. The 5th accused claimed he was merely the driver who did not know where they were going until instructed. The other accused spoke only about arresting PW-3 and never mentioned taking Rathnachandra into custody. The Court found their evidence did not cast reasonable doubt on the prosecution case.
procedural_defects_description: The indictment was not read to the accused before commencement of trial as required by Section 196 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. However, the Court held this did not vitiate the trial as the indictment was served to all accused, they were represented by counsel throughout, and no substantial prejudice was caused to their rights.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal extensively analyzed each ground of appeal. On the Section 196 non-compliance, following the Supreme Court decision in Hiniduma Dahanayakege Siripala case, the Court held no substantial prejudice occurred as accused were represented and could have pleaded guilty during trial. On the delay issue, the Court found the explanation acceptable given the political situation during 1989-1991 insurgency period, the father's immediate attempts to complain being refused by police, and his filing of Habeas Corpus application in 1991 when conditions improved. On identification, the Court found the 1st accused was properly identified by PW-1 and PW-2 when introduced by OIC Mahanama, and by his own admission that the victim escaped. The 2nd to 4th accused were identified by multiple witnesses at the abduction scenes and at Batalanda where PW-3 was tortured. The Court analyzed voice identification principles and accepted PW-3's identification of his brother's voice at Batalanda as reliable. On common intention, the Court found clear evidence of pre-arrangement and coordinated action by the 1st to 4th accused in taking the victim, transporting him with his brother to Batalanda, and the false statement about escape. The circumstantial evidence pointed only to guilt. However, the Court found insufficient evidence that the 5th accused shared the common intention, as he was merely the driver and not present during the torture, and therefore acquitted him. The convictions and sentences of the 1st to 4th accused were affirmed.
coa_sentence_type: The 1st, 2nd, 3rd, and 4th accused-appellants' convictions and sentences of five years rigorous imprisonment were affirmed. The 5th accused-appellant was acquitted.
brief_judgment_file_summary: Five accused were charged with abducting 16-year-old Rathnachandra Liyanage on 07 July 1989 in order to murder him. The High Court convicted all five accused under Section 355 read with Section 32 of the Penal Code and sentenced each to five years rigorous imprisonment. On appeal, the accused challenged the conviction on grounds including non-compliance with Section 196 CPC, delay in complaint, improper identification, and failure to prove common intention. The Court of Appeal held that the procedural defect did not cause substantial prejudice, the delay was adequately explained by the 1989-1991 insurgency situation and the father's Habeas Corpus application, and identification was properly established. The Court found clear circumstantial evidence and common intention among the 1st to 4th accused in abducting the victim who was never seen again. However, the 5th accused who was merely the driver was acquitted. The appeals of the 1st to 4th accused were dismissed while the 5th accused's appeal was allowed.
defence_counsel: Nalin Ladduwahetty, PC with Kavithri Hirusha Ubeysekera for 1st Accused; Ranjan Mendis with Kavinda Priyankarage for 2nd, 3rd and 5th Accused; Darshana Kuruppu with Tharushi Gamage for 4th Accused
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court analyzed the delay in making complaint and found it was during the insurgency period and the father's attempts to complain were futile. The High Court considered the defence evidence from pages 15 to 20 of the judgment. The Court found the identification was proper and that common intention was established. The Court of Appeal affirmed most of the High Court's findings but differed on the 5th accused, finding insufficient evidence of his participation in the common intention.
