standard_of_review_applied: Review of delay in filing appeal and exercise of discretionary revisionary powers under section 364 of the CCPA considering the contumacious conduct of the appellant

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Sections 54(A)(b) and 54(A)(d) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance as amended by Act No. 13 of 1984
location_of_offence: Pepiliyana Sunethradevi Raja Viharaya area, Badowita
brief_facts_summary: On 13th March 2011, PW1 IP/Epalakotuwa conducted a raid with 6 police officers from Boralesgamuwa Police Station based on information about two individuals on motorcycles distributing heroin. At about 1:00 pm, the Appellant was apprehended on motorcycle bearing No. WP UI 9114 near Pepiliyana Raja Maha Viharaya. Police recovered 25 grocery bags from his jacket pocket, containing 1000 small packets, along with Rs.50,000/- cash and two mobile phones. The substances were initially weighed at Ameesha Jewellery (158.50 grams with packaging), then the next day at Dilani Jewellery (25 grams). Government Analyst Report indicated 25.06 grams of brown powder containing 5.75 grams of pure Heroin (Diacetylmorphine).
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Sections 54(A)(b) and 54(A)(d) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance as amended by Act No. 13 of 1984
hc_judgment_summary: After trial, the High Court of Colombo found the Appellant guilty on both counts of Trafficking and Possession of 5.75 grams of Heroin (diacetylmorphine). The Learned High Court Judge imposed death sentence on 21/11/2018.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The Appellant raised four grounds of appeal: (1) that the Learned Trial Judge erred in concluding that the prosecution proved chain of custody beyond reasonable grounds; (2) that the Trial Judge violated Section 159 of the Evidence Ordinance when PW2 referred to a document not made by him; (3) that the prosecution version did not pass the test of probability given contradictions and discrepancies in police evidence; and (4) that the Trial Judge did not evaluate the defence evidence from the correct perspective and rejected it on the wrong premise.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: That the Learned Trial Judge erred in law when concluding that the prosecution proved the chain of custody beyond reasonable grounds. | That the Learned Trial Judge violated the provisions of the Section 159 of the Evidence Ordinance. | That the Learned Trial Judge failed to consider that the prosecution version did not pass the test of probability. | That the Learned Trial Judge did not evaluate the defence evidence from the correct perspective and the rejected same in the wrong premise.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The prosecution called PW1, PW2, PW4, PW7, PW8, PW10, PW12, PW13 and PW14 Government Analyst. PW2 corroborated PW1's evidence, and other police witnesses established the movement of production to the Government Analyst Department. The Court found serious issues with PW2 referring to a document not made by him (violating Section 159 of Evidence Ordinance), contradictions between PW1 and PW2's testimonies, altered police notes, weight discrepancies, and failure to obtain receipt from Dilani Jewellery Shop.
probability_assessment_by_court: Court found prosecution version did not pass the test of probability due to contradictions in police evidence, altered notes, weight discrepancies, lack of receipt from second weighing, and contradictory testimonies between PW1 and PW2
defence_version_summary: The Appellant made a dock statement (not guilty). He claimed he was falsely arrested by PW2 when making a call to purchase a three-wheeler with Rs.110,000/- in his possession. He stated that at Anderson Road near a cemetery, a motor bike collided with a three-wheeler carrying police officers. Police first checked the rider Dhammika Perera, recovered 300 grams of Heroin from him, then divided it into two parcels introducing 158 grams each to the Appellant and the other person. Police also took Rs.10,000/- for three-wheeler repair and divided the remaining Rs.100,000/- into Rs.50,000/- each for both accused. The Court found the Trial Judge failed to properly consider this dock statement and rejected it without proper analysis.
legal_errors_description: Trial Judge violated Section 159 of Evidence Ordinance by allowing PW2 to refer to a document not made by him; failed to properly evaluate chain of custody evidence despite weight discrepancy (25 grams vs 25.06 grams); failed to consider the prosecution version in light of probability test; failed to properly evaluate and analyze defence evidence before rejection
procedural_defects_description: PW2 referred to a separate paper not made by himself during evidence (Section 159 violation); no receipt obtained from Dilani Jewellery Shop for second weighing; PW1 altered departure notes (12 hours written over to 11 hours); PW1 prepared detailed notes 10 days after the raid
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal comprehensively analyzed three key issues: chain of custody, procedural violations, and probability. On chain of custody, the Court found a critical weight discrepancy - the substances weighed 25 grams at Dilani Jewellery (including cellophane bag) but the Government Analyst Report showed 25.06 grams of brown powder alone (excluding the bag), which the prosecution failed to explain. The Court cited Perera v. Attorney General holding that the inward journey to the analyst is most important, and emphasized that chain of custody must be proved by clear and specific evidence. On procedural violations, the Court found PW2 violated Section 159 of Evidence Ordinance by referring to a document not made by him, raising serious doubt about the raid conduct. The Court noted PW1 altered official notes (11 hours written over 12 hours) and prepared detailed notes 10 days after the raid. On probability, the Court found numerous contradictions: PW2 stated the Appellant was identified through identity card and handcuffed, which PW1 failed to corroborate; PW2 said police carried scales and sealing equipment to the raid, contradicted by PW1; no receipt obtained from Dilani Jewellery despite Appellant's denial of being taken there. The Court found the Trial Judge failed to evaluate defence evidence on equal footing with prosecution evidence, improperly rejecting the dock statement without proper analysis. Citing R v. Hepworth, the Court emphasized that a judge must be an administrator of justice, not merely an umpire. The Court concluded that the prosecution failed to prove the case beyond reasonable doubt.
coa_sentence_type: Acquittal - conviction and sentence set aside
brief_judgment_file_summary: Kekulandara Mudiyanselage Don Anura Weerasinghe was convicted by the High Court of Colombo on 21/11/2018 for trafficking and possession of 5.75 grams of Heroin under Sections 54(A)(b) and 54(A)(d) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance and sentenced to death. The offence occurred on 13th March 2011 when he was arrested with 1000 small packets of heroin near Pepiliyana Raja Maha Viharaya. On appeal, the Court of Appeal found multiple critical defects: a weight discrepancy in the seized substances (25 grams vs 25.06 grams) unexplained by prosecution, violation of Section 159 of Evidence Ordinance when PW2 referred to a document not made by him, altered police notes, contradictions between prosecution witnesses, lack of receipt from second weighing location, and failure to properly evaluate defence evidence. The Court held that the prosecution failed to prove chain of custody and the case beyond reasonable doubt. The appeal was allowed, and the Appellant was acquitted by judgment dated 05/07/2024.
defence_counsel: Nihara Randeniya
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court found the Appellant guilty on both counts and imposed death sentence. The Court of Appeal found that the Trial Judge erred by: concluding prosecution proved chain of custody despite weight discrepancy; allowing violation of Section 159 of Evidence Ordinance; failing to apply the probability test to prosecution evidence given the contradictions, altered notes, and lack of corroboration; and failing to properly evaluate and analyze the defence dock statement before rejecting it, instead rejecting it without proper consideration on equal footing with prosecution evidence.
precedents_cited_list: Woolmington v DPP (1935) | Mohamed Nimnaz V. Attorney General CA/95/94 | Attorney-General v. Rawther 25 NLR 385 | Miller v. Minister of Pensions (1947) 2 All E.R. 372 | Perera V. Attorney General [1998] 1 Sri.L.R 378 | Koushappis v. The State of WA [2007] WASCA 26; (2007) 168 A Crim R 51 | R v. Hepworth 1928 (AD) 265
standard_of_review_applied: Beyond reasonable doubt standard; appellate review of whether prosecution proved case beyond reasonable doubt; evaluation of chain of custody evidence; assessment of probability of prosecution version; review of proper evaluation of defence evidence

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Sections 54(A)(d) and 54(A)(b) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance as amended by Act No. 13 of 1984
brief_facts_summary: On 18/02/2018, police officers from Colombo Crime Division conducted a raid on an apartment complex at Keselwatte based on information about a person named Robinson possessing a firearm. Upon searching the Appellant's fifth-floor apartment, officers found a locked almirah which the Appellant opened with his keys. Inside were two parcels containing 62.736 grams of pure Heroin and 12.170 grams of Cannabis, along with weighing machines, a spoon with heroin traces, and small bags. The Appellant was arrested and the drugs were sent to the Government Analyst for confirmation.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Sections 54(A)(d) and 54(A)(b) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance as amended by Act No. 13 of 1984
hc_sentence_type: Death on 1st and 2nd Counts and 01-year rigorous imprisonment each on Counts 3rd and 4th
hc_judgment_summary: After considering evidence from the prosecution and defence, the Learned Trial Judge found the Appellant guilty on all counts. The High Court sentenced him to death on the 1st and 2nd counts (trafficking charges) and imposed 01-year rigorous imprisonment each on the 3rd and 4th counts (possession charges) on 13/12/2019.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The Appellant challenged the conviction on three main grounds. First, he contended that the Learned Trial Judge failed to consider the doubtfulness in relation to the raid conducted by prosecution witnesses. Second, he argued that the Trial Judge had not properly considered the evidence for the defence. Third, he claimed that the Learned High Court Judge had performed the role of the prosecutor under Section 165 of the Evidence Ordinance by asking inappropriate questions.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: That the Learned Trial Judge failed to consider the doubtfulness in relation to the raid conducted by the prosecution witnesses | That the Learned Trial Judge had not properly considered the evidence for the defence | The Learned High Court Judge had performed the role of the prosecutor under Section 165 of the Evidence Ordinance
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found that PW1 and PW2 provided clear, cogent, and unambiguous evidence that passed the probability test. The prosecution called 04 witnesses and marked productions P1-37. The Court noted that the evidence regarding the presence or non-presence of the Appellant's wife did not create doubt about the prosecution's version, and the defence could not create any plausible doubt over the evidence of PW1 and PW2.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal held that the prosecution version passed the test of probability and proved the case beyond reasonable doubt. The Learned High Court Judge accurately discussed and analysed the evidence pertaining to time consumption for the entire raid and accepted the prosecution's position.
defence_version_summary: The Appellant pleaded not guilty. In his dock statement, he claimed that PW1 intentionally implicated him in the case. He admitted the arrest but disputed that he possessed narcotics as alleged by the prosecution. The Appellant called 04 witnesses and marked documents V1 and V2. The Court noted inconsistencies between the Appellant's dock statement and his wife's evidence regarding who opened the door when police arrived. The Court rejected the defence evidence, finding it unable to create any doubt against the overwhelming evidence of the prosecution.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal thoroughly examined all three grounds of appeal and rejected them. Regarding the first two grounds about the doubtfulness of the raid and consideration of defence evidence, the Court found that PW1 and PW2 gave consistent evidence about the raid, and the defence failed to create any plausible doubt. The Court noted that inconsistencies about the Appellant's wife's presence did not affect the prosecution case, as the Appellant had exclusive possession of the locked almirah containing the narcotics. The Court held that the Learned High Court Judge correctly evaluated the defence evidence in light of the totality of evidence and properly rejected it with adequate reasons. On the third ground regarding judicial questioning under Section 165 of the Evidence Ordinance, the Court found that the Trial Judge's questions were not detrimental to the defence's rights and the findings were not based solely on those questions. The Court of Appeal affirmed that the prosecution proved the case beyond reasonable doubt, with evidence from PW1 and PW2 being clear, cogent, unambiguous and passing the probability test.
coa_sentence_type: Death on 1st and 2nd Counts and 01-year rigorous imprisonment each on Counts 3rd and 4th
brief_judgment_file_summary: Simiyon Robinson was indicted in the High Court of Colombo for possession and trafficking of 62.736 grams of Heroin and 12.170 grams of Cannabis under Sections 54(A)(d) and 54(A)(b) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance. The drugs were discovered during a police raid on 18/02/2018 at his apartment in Keselwatte. The High Court convicted him on all counts and sentenced him to death on trafficking counts and one year rigorous imprisonment on possession counts on 13/12/2019. The Appellant appealed on grounds that the Trial Judge failed to consider doubtfulness about the raid, improperly evaluated defence evidence, and performed the role of prosecutor by questioning witnesses. The Court of Appeal found that prosecution witnesses PW1 and PW2 gave clear and consistent evidence that passed the probability test, the defence evidence failed to create reasonable doubt, and the Trial Judge's questioning was within permissible limits under Section 165 of the Evidence Ordinance. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal and affirmed both the conviction and sentence on 03/07/2024.
defence_counsel: I.B.S Harshana
hc_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found that the Learned High Court Judge correctly and extensively discussed and analysed the dock statement of the Appellant and the evidence given by defence witnesses. The Trial Judge properly concluded that the defence evidence was unable to create any doubt against the overwhelming evidence of the prosecution and gave correct reasons for rejecting the defence evidence. The High Court Judge also accurately discussed and analysed the evidence pertaining to time consumption for the entire raid and accepted the prosecution's position.
precedents_cited_list: Mohamed Nimnaz v. Attorney General CA/95/94 | Attorney-General v. Rawther 25 NLR 385 | Don Samantha Jude Anthony Jayamaha v. The Attorney General CA/303/2006 | Kathubdeen v. Republic of Sri Lanka [1998] 3 SLR 107 | People v Arnold 98 N.Y.2d 63 (2002) | Senanayake v De Silva 75 NLR 409
standard_of_review_applied: The Court of Appeal reviewed whether the prosecution proved the case beyond reasonable doubt and whether the Learned Trial Judge properly evaluated all evidence in its correct perspective

judges: Menaka Wijesundera J. | Wickum A. Kaluarachchi J.
offence_sections: Section 140, 146/296, 146/315 of the Penal Code and in the alternative on the basis of Common Intention
brief_facts_summary: On 4th February 1998 around 8.45 PM, four persons including the appellant entered the deceased's house compound. The first accused Neil and appellant Titus were carrying knives. They assaulted the deceased with knives, with the appellant continuing the assault after the deceased fell down. The appellant was arrested on 29.04.2001, nearly three years after absconding.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Fourth charge in the Indictment under Section 140, 146/296, 146/315 of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the appellant on the fourth charge in the indictment after he pleaded not guilty. The trial judge found the prosecution witnesses trustworthy despite minor contradictions. The court accepted the identification parade evidence and rejected the appellant's dock statement.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The main ground of appeal raised was the identification of the appellant at the scene of crime. Defence counsel argued that the trial judge misdirected himself by not giving adequate weight to contradictions in PW1's evidence. It was contended that although the witness identified the appellant at the identification parade, she failed to mention his name in the police statement made soon after the incident.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Identification of the appellant at the scene of crime | Trial judge misdirected himself by not giving adequate weight to contradictions in PW1's evidence | Witness failed to mention appellant's name in police statement despite identifying him at identification parade | Appellant was shown to witnesses before the identification parade
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: PW1, the deceased's daughter (17 years old), was the main eyewitness who identified the appellant and witnessed the assault. PW2, the deceased's sister, also witnessed the incident and identified the first accused and appellant. The Court found both witnesses trustworthy despite minor contradictions, noting the traumatic circumstances affected their ability to recall exact details immediately after the incident.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court held that the prosecution proved their case beyond reasonable doubt. The witnesses stood the test of probability, spontaneity and trustworthiness beyond a reasonable doubt despite contradictions and omissions.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty and made a statement from the dock. He claimed he was shown to witnesses by police before the identification parade but did not provide specific details about which witnesses. The trial judge did not accept the dock statement. No defence witnesses were called.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal held that the trial judge did not misdirect himself regarding contradictions in PW1's evidence, noting that a witness cannot be expected to give an uncontradicted narration of events, especially considering the traumatic experience of a 17-year-old witnessing her father's murder. The Court cited AG v Potta Naufer and Oliver Dayananda Kalanasooriya v Republic cases establishing that criminal cases cannot be proved with mathematical accuracy and contradictions not going to the root of the case should be disregarded. Regarding the identification parade held nearly three years after the incident, the Court found it admissible because the appellant had been absconding and the parade was held at the first opportunity after his arrest on 29.04.2001. The Court rejected the appellant's claim of being shown to witnesses before the parade as becoming 'very common' and lacking specificity. The Court found the prosecution proved its case beyond reasonable doubt, with witnesses standing the test of probability, spontaneity and trustworthiness. Based on the appellant's conduct, the nature of injuries (14 injuries including one necessarily fatal), and the weapons used, the Court concluded the appellant acted with intention to cause death and shared common murderous intention with the first accused.
coa_sentence_type: Death sentence for murder affirmed
brief_judgment_file_summary: Waliweriya Wardhanage Titus was convicted by the High Court of Galle for murder under Sections 140, 146/296, 146/315 of the Penal Code committed on 4th February 1998. He appealed challenging identification at the crime scene and contradictions in witness testimony. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal on 3rd July 2024, holding that the trial judge correctly assessed witness credibility despite minor contradictions due to trauma, the identification parade held three years later was admissible as the appellant had been absconding, and the prosecution proved the case beyond reasonable doubt showing the appellant shared common murderous intention with co-accused.
defence_counsel: Anil Silva, PC with Isuru Jayawardane and Sarith Wadugedhara
cause_of_death_exact_text: Injury number 2 had been identified to be necessarily fatal
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted the appellant on the fourth charge after trial. The trial judge found PW1 to be a trustworthy witness and accepted the identification parade evidence. The Court of Appeal found the trial judge correctly assessed the evidence and did not misdirect himself on contradictions or the admissibility of the identification parade.
precedents_cited_list: AG v Potta Naufer and others (2007) 2 Sri.L.R 186 to 187 | Oliver Dayananda Kalanasooriya alias Raju v Republic of Sri Lanka, CA 28/2009 | Ranmuka Arachchilage Chaminda Roshan v The Republic of Sri Lanka, CA No. 120/2004 | Keerthi Bandara v Attorney General (2002) 3 SLR 245
standard_of_review_applied: Whether the prosecution proved the case beyond reasonable doubt and whether the trial judge misdirected himself in assessing witness credibility and admitting identification parade evidence

judges: Amal Ranaraja, J. | B. Sasi Mahendran, J.
offence_sections: Section 383 of the Penal Code read with section 32
brief_facts_summary: On March 23, 2004, two armed intruders entered PW01's residence at approximately 8:15pm. The intruders exposed their faces, gathered household members, and demanded valuables. They robbed cash amounting to Rs. 44,000.00 and various pieces of jewellery including gold-chain and gold-ring from PW01, with total value of items stolen being Rs. 137,750.00.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 383 of the Penal Code read with section 32
hc_sentence_type: Five years rigorous imprisonment with fine and compensation
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court Judge convicted the appellant of robbery with attempt to cause death or grievous hurt under section 383 read with section 32 of the Penal Code. The appellant was sentenced to five years rigorous imprisonment, a fine of Rs. 5,000.00 with six months rigorous imprisonment in default, and ordered to pay Rs. 137,750.00 as compensation with one year rigorous imprisonment in default.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant challenged the conviction arguing that the identification was not properly established, citing an 8-year delay between the incident and identification parade. The defence contended that the High Court Judge made erroneous findings and failed to properly consider the appellant's dock statement. The main argument was that the prosecution failed to prove the charge beyond reasonable doubt due to significant inconsistencies in witness testimony regarding physical features and prior encounters.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The Learned High Court Judge has failed to consider that the identification of the appellant has not been established | The erroneous findings of the Learned High Court Judge have adversely affected the appellant | The Learned High Court Judge has arrived at his judgment without properly considering the dock statement of the appellant | The prosecution has failed to prove the charge beyond a reasonable doubt
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found significant inconsistencies in the testimony of PW01 and PW03 regarding the appellant's physical features and prior encounters. Both witnesses contradicted their earlier statements to investigating officers. The identification parade was held 8 years after the incident, and both witnesses mentioned having seen the appellant on two prior occasions at the business premises, which was not included in their initial statements.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal held that the burden of proof lies squarely with the prosecution to establish the case beyond reasonable doubt, and the prosecution failed to meet this standard due to unreliable identification evidence.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty and asserted that he was falsely implicated in the charge. He made a dock statement which the High Court allegedly failed to properly consider. The Court of Appeal found that the High Court improperly relied on weaknesses in the appellant's case rather than requiring the prosecution to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt.
legal_errors_description: The High Court Judge relied on perceived weaknesses in the appellant's case to strengthen the prosecution's position, which is a misapplication of legal principles. The focus should have been on whether the prosecution met the requisite standard for conviction beyond reasonable doubt, not on inconsistencies in the defence case.
procedural_defects_description: The identification parade was held 8 years after the occurrence, which raised serious questions about its reliability and integrity, especially given the contradictions in witness testimony.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal conducted a thorough analysis of the identification evidence and found critical flaws in both the process and the witness testimony. The Court noted that PW01 and PW03 both provided contradictory descriptions of the appellant's physical features compared to their earlier statements. Both witnesses also disclosed prior encounters with the appellant at his business premises, information not included in their initial statements, raising questions about whether their identification was influenced by these encounters rather than the parade itself. The Court applied principles from Queen vs V.P.Julis regarding identification parades not being substantive evidence and Rex vs Turnball regarding the handling of disputed identification evidence. The Court emphasized that dock identification is undesirable and unsafe, citing Munirathne and Others vs. The State. The Court found that the High Court Judge improperly relied on weaknesses in the appellant's case rather than requiring the prosecution to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt. Given the 8-year delay, inconsistencies in witness testimony, absence of corroborating testimony from PW01's deceased wife, and the fundamental misapplication of legal principles regarding burden of proof, the Court of Appeal determined that the conviction was unsafe.
coa_sentence_type: Acquittal - conviction and sentence set aside
brief_judgment_file_summary: The appellant Nakulugamuwa Yapage Suraj Priyantha was convicted by the High Court of Hambantota for robbery with attempt to cause death or grievous hurt under section 383 read with section 32 of the Penal Code, arising from an incident on March 23, 2004 where two armed intruders robbed cash and jewellery valued at Rs. 137,750.00. He was sentenced to five years rigorous imprisonment with a fine of Rs. 5,000.00 and ordered to pay compensation of Rs. 137,750.00. On appeal, the Court of Appeal found serious flaws in the identification evidence, noting that the identification parade was held 8 years after the incident, witnesses PW01 and PW03 provided contradictory descriptions of the appellant's physical features, and both disclosed prior encounters with the appellant not mentioned in their initial statements. The Court held that the High Court Judge improperly relied on weaknesses in the appellant's case rather than requiring the prosecution to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt. The Court of Appeal set aside the conviction and sentence and acquitted the appellant.
defence_counsel: Asthika Devendra with Aruna Madushanka
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court Judge relied on perceived weaknesses in the appellant's case to strengthen the prosecution's position. The Court of Appeal found this approach to be a misapplication of legal principles, as the burden of proof lies with the prosecution to establish the case beyond reasonable doubt, irrespective of any shortcomings in the appellant's case.
precedents_cited_list: Queen vs V.P.Julis [1953] 65 NLR 505 at 510-511 | Rex vs Turnball [1997] QB 224 | Munirathne and Others vs. The State [2001] 2 SLR 382
standard_of_review_applied: Appellate review of conviction and sentence examining whether the prosecution proved the case beyond reasonable doubt and whether the trial judge properly applied legal principles regarding burden of proof and identification evidence

judges: B. Sasi Mahendran, J. | Amal Ranaraja, J.
offence_sections: Sections 54A(b) and 54A(d) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance, as amended by Act No. 13 of 1984
brief_facts_summary: On 12th May 2017, police received intelligence that the accused was transporting heroin by motorcycle from Ragama and Delgoda to Sedawatta. Officers conducted surveillance and intercepted the accused at approximately 14:00 hours on motorcycle BDQ-0800 on Thudugala Road. During a body search, PW1 recovered 25.77 grams of heroin from the right pocket of the accused's trousers. The accused was arrested and the substance was sent to the Government Analyst for examination.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Sections 54A(b) and 54A(d) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance, as amended by Act No. 13 of 1984
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court of Colombo found the accused guilty on both counts of possession and trafficking of 25.77 grams of Diacetylmorphine (heroin) on 10th December 2019. The prosecution led evidence from nine witnesses and produced exhibits P1 through P11. The accused made only a dock statement in his defence, and the High Court Judge sentenced him to life imprisonment on both counts.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant challenged the conviction on the basis that the version of the prosecution was highly improbable and that the learned High Court Judge had failed to apply the test of probability and improbability in evaluating the evidence. The main contention was that the manner in which PW1 claimed to have conducted the search while the accused remained seated on the motorcycle was improbable and lacked credibility.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The version of the prosecution is highly improbable | The learned High Court Judge failed to apply the test of probability and improbability in evaluating the evidence | The manner of searching the accused while he remained seated on the motorcycle is improbable and questionable
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The prosecution led evidence from nine witnesses and produced exhibits marked P1 through P11. PW1 was the key witness who testified about the intelligence received, surveillance operation, interception, and recovery of heroin from the accused's pocket. The Court of Appeal found considerable doubt regarding the plausibility of PW1's testimony about searching while the accused remained seated on the motorcycle.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal applied the test of probability and improbability and found PW1's testimony highly improbable. The court held that it was improbable that a search conducted while the accused remained seated on the motorcycle could have resulted in the recovery of the substance from the accused's pocket, and concluded that the prosecution's narrative lacked credibility.
defence_version_summary: The accused pleaded not guilty and made only a dock statement in his defence. He did not call any witnesses. The court did not provide specific details about the content of his dock statement or his credibility assessment in the judgment.
legal_errors_description: The Court of Appeal found that the learned High Court Judge did not adequately apply the test of probability to the prosecution's case. The COA held that the testimony of PW1 was improbable and the manner of search as described lacked credibility.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal conducted a careful analysis of PW1's testimony and applied the test of probability and improbability. The court found considerable doubt regarding the plausibility of searching while the accused remained seated on the motorcycle, concluding such a method appeared unnecessary and cast significant doubt on PW1's account. The COA cited Section 11(b) of the Evidence Ordinance and referenced legal authorities including Murray's English Dictionary on probability, Sarkar on Evidence, Coomaraswamy on the Law of Evidence, Wickremasuriya v Dedoleena, and Selvanayagam Carmel Jenova v Attorney General. The court held that applying the test of probability and improbability, the prosecution's narrative lacked credibility. The COA concluded that the prosecution failed to prove its case beyond a reasonable doubt and set aside both the conviction and sentence, acquitting the accused-appellant.
coa_sentence_type: Acquittal - conviction and sentence set aside
brief_judgment_file_summary: Herath Mudiyanselage Thushara was convicted by the High Court of Colombo on 10th December 2019 for possession and trafficking of 25.77 grams of heroin under Sections 54A(b) and 54A(d) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance and sentenced to life imprisonment. The appellant challenged the conviction arguing that the prosecution's version was highly improbable and the High Court Judge failed to apply the test of probability. The Court of Appeal carefully reviewed the testimony of PW1 and found it highly improbable that a search conducted while the accused remained seated on a motorcycle could have resulted in the recovery of heroin from his pocket. Applying the test of probability and improbability and citing relevant legal authorities, the COA held that the prosecution failed to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt. The appeal was allowed, and the accused-appellant was acquitted with both conviction and sentence set aside.
defence_counsel: Kalinga Indatissa, PC with Rashmini Indatissa and Razan Salih
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court Judge found the accused guilty on both counts based on the prosecution evidence from nine witnesses and sentenced him to life imprisonment. However, the Court of Appeal held that the High Court Judge did not adequately apply the test of probability to the prosecution's case and failed to identify the improbability in PW1's testimony regarding the manner of the search.
precedents_cited_list: Wickremasuriya v Dedoleena and Others [1996] 2 S.L.R. 95 | Selvanayagam Carmel Jenova Vs. The Attorney General, CA Case No. 107/2011
standard_of_review_applied: The Court of Appeal applied the test of probability and improbability to evaluate whether the prosecution proved its case beyond reasonable doubt, examining whether the prosecution's narrative was credible based on the laws of nature, human conduct patterns, and conformity to knowledge, observation, and experience.

judges: B. Sasi Mahendran, J. | Amal Ranaraja, J.
offence_sections: Section 365B(2)(b) of the Penal Code (as amended by Act No.22 of 1995 and Act No. 29 of 1998 and Act No.16 of 2006)
brief_facts_summary: On May 8, 2009, the appellant invited 12-year-old PW01 to his house under the pretext of feeling uncomfortable spending the night alone. Once inside, the appellant undressed PW01 and himself, then committed grave sexual abuse by placing his penis between her thighs. PW03, the victim's sibling, witnessed the act through a wooden window and informed the parents, who then witnessed the abuse and took PW01 to the police station immediately.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 365B(2)(b) of the Penal Code (as amended by Act No.22 of 1995 and Act No. 29 of 1998 and Act No.16 of 2006)
hc_sentence_type: 8 years rigorous imprisonment, fine of Rs. 5,000 with 4 months imprisonment in default, and Rs. 100,000 compensation with 1 year imprisonment in default
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court found the appellant guilty of grave sexual abuse under section 365B(2)(b) of the Penal Code. The court convicted and sentenced him to 8 years rigorous imprisonment with a fine of Rs. 5,000 and compensation of Rs. 100,000 to the victim. The conviction was based on the testimony of the victim, eyewitness accounts from her sibling and parents, and medical evidence.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant challenged whether the main ingredient of the charge was proven beyond reasonable doubt, contending that the victim testified to penetration rather than intercrural sex. The defence argued the High Court Judge erred by not allowing a vital contradiction to be marked during cross-examination of PW01. Additional grounds included alleged failures to properly evaluate the evidence of PW12 (medical officer), PW02, PW03, and PW08 (investigating officer).
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Has the Learned High Court Judge failed to consider that the main ingredient of the charge has not been proven beyond a reasonable doubt by the prosecution? | Has the Learned High Court Judge erred in law by not allowing to mark a vital contradiction during the cross examination of PW01? | Has the Learned High Court Judge failed to evaluate the evidence of PW12 accurately? | Has the Learned High Court Judge failed to evaluate the evidence of PW02, PW03, and PW08 accurately?
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the victim's testimony credible despite her being a reluctant witness due to the traumatic nature of the incident. The Court accepted that PW01, who was 12 at the time of the offence and from a rural village background, would naturally prefer not to discuss the harrowing experience. The eyewitness testimony of PW03 who saw the act through the window, along with the parents who also witnessed the abuse, corroborated PW01's account.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court found the evidence proved the charge beyond reasonable doubt despite minor contradictions, noting that the victim's reluctance and trauma were natural responses that did not undermine her credibility.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty to the charge. The defence challenged the proof of the main ingredient of the offence, arguing inconsistencies between the charge of intercrural sex and testimony suggesting penetration. The defence attempted to mark contradictions in the victim's testimony but was prevented by the trial judge. The Court of Appeal found the defence's credibility challenges lacked merit.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal thoroughly analyzed the grounds of appeal and found them without merit. The Court emphasized that PW01 was a reluctant witness due to the traumatic nature of the incident and her rural upbringing, requiring coaxing to extract evidence. The Court rejected the contention that intercrural sex was not proven, finding the victim's testimony consistent with the charge. Regarding the contradiction marking issue, the Court held the trial judge correctly disallowed it as the defence failed to follow mandatory procedures under Section 145 of the Evidence Ordinance. The Court found no material error in allowing PW12 to testify on the medical report prepared by another doctor, as proper admissions were recorded and the appellant had cross-examined PW12. The Court noted the appellant's actions showed preplanning and manipulation, justifying the sentence. The appeal was dismissed without interfering with the conviction or sentence.
coa_sentence_type: 8 years rigorous imprisonment, fine of Rs. 5,000 with 4 months imprisonment in default, and Rs. 100,000 compensation with 1 year imprisonment in default
brief_judgment_file_summary: Jayasinghe Arachchige Karunarathna was convicted by the High Court of Rathnapura for grave sexual abuse of a 12-year-old female child under section 365B(2)(b) of the Penal Code, committed on May 8, 2009. He was sentenced to 8 years rigorous imprisonment with a fine of Rs. 5,000 and Rs. 100,000 compensation. The appellant challenged the conviction on grounds that the charge was not proven, procedural errors in cross-examination, and improper evaluation of medical and witness evidence. The Court of Appeal found all grounds lacked merit, noting the victim was a credible reluctant witness and the defence failed to properly challenge contradictions. The Court emphasized the appellant's preplanning and manipulation as aggravating factors. The appeal was dismissed and the High Court judgment upheld.
defence_counsel: Kasun Sarathchandra
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted the appellant based on the testimony of the victim, eyewitness accounts from PW03 and the parents, and medical evidence. The Court of Appeal found the High Court's analysis sound and upheld the conviction, noting the trial judge properly managed the cross-examination and correctly evaluated all evidence.
precedents_cited_list: D. Tikiribanda vs. Attorney General, CA 64/2003 decided on 06.10.2009 | Agampodi Wijepala de Soyza vs. Officer-in-Charge and Another, SC Appeal 159/2018, S.C. minute dated 07.07.2021
standard_of_review_applied: The Court of Appeal reviewed whether the High Court properly evaluated evidence and applied correct legal procedures, examining credibility assessments and procedural compliance with the Evidence Ordinance.
sentencing_principles_applied: The Court considered aggravating circumstances including the appellant's preplanning and manipulation in luring the child victim to his house under false pretenses, justifying the sentence imposed by the High Court.

judges: B. Sasi Mahendran, J. | Amal Ranaraja, J.
offence_sections: Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance No. 13 of 1984, as amended
brief_facts_summary: The Accused, Shivanandam Muralidaran, was indicted before the High Court of Colombo for the possession and trafficking of 24.816 kilograms of Cannabis Sativa, allegedly committed on or around 2nd May 2020. On 7th February 2023, the Accused pleaded guilty, following which the Learned High Court Judge convicted and sentenced him. Subsequently, notice was issued to the Petitioner (the registered owner of the vehicle used in the offence), as she had signed a bond in connection with the vehicle inquiry.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance No. 13 of 1984, as amended
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted and sentenced the Accused after he pleaded guilty to possession and trafficking of 24.816 kilograms of Cannabis Sativa. A vehicle inquiry was held on 16th June 2023, and the registered owner (Petitioner) agreed to pay four million rupees from a bond valued at five million, as she was unable to produce the vehicle.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The Petitioner filed an application for revision seeking to set aside the order of the High Court of Colombo dated 16.06.2023. The Petitioner contested the High Court order that was based on her own agreement to pay four million rupees from the bond, as she was unable to produce the vehicle.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Seeking to set aside the order of the High Court of Colombo dated 16.06.2023 regarding the bond payment
defence_version_summary: The petitioner stated that she had previously sold the vehicle to her late brother, who had subsequently leased it to a third party prior to the incident. The vehicle had been released to her by the court under a bond valued at five million. As she was unable to produce the vehicle before the court, she agreed to pay four million in partial fulfilment of the bond obligation.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal held that the remedy of revision is discretionary and will not be exercised unless the application reveals circumstances amounting to a miscarriage of justice. The Court noted that the petitioner had entered into an agreement before the Court, undertaking to pay a sum of four million rupees. However, she was now contesting the order issued by the learned High Court Judge, which was based on the assurance she herself provided. The Court viewed this as a withdrawal from the undertaking given to the Court and a breach of contract. The Court emphasized that the conduct of the Petitioner is a pertinent factor in the determination of this application, citing Peera v. The People's Bank. The Court held that the conduct of the defendant disentitles relief by way of revision in the facts and circumstances of this case.
brief_judgment_file_summary: This is a revision application filed by Mohamed Hussaindeen Neeza, the registered owner of a vehicle used in a drug trafficking case. The Accused, Shivanandam Muralidaran, was indicted for possession and trafficking of 24.816 kilograms of Cannabis Sativa and pleaded guilty before the High Court of Colombo on 7th February 2023. The Petitioner had signed a bond valued at five million rupees for the vehicle and agreed to pay four million rupees when she could not produce the vehicle. The Court of Appeal dismissed the revision application, holding that the Petitioner was contesting an order based on her own undertaking, which amounted to a breach of contract. The Court emphasized that the conduct of the Petitioner disentitled her to relief by way of revision. The application was dismissed with state costs of Rs. 50,000.
defence_counsel: Tenny Fernando
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court held a vehicle inquiry and observed that the petitioner agreed to pay four million rupees from the bond, as she was unable to produce the vehicle. The Court of Appeal noted that the High Court's order was based on the assurance provided by the Petitioner herself.
precedents_cited_list: Peera v. The People's Bank, 1995 (2) SLR 84 at page 87
standard_of_review_applied: Discretionary remedy of revision that will not be exercised unless the application reveals circumstances amounting to a miscarriage of justice
