judges: B. Sasi Mahendran, J. | Amal Ranaraja, J.
offence_sections: Section 54A(d) and Section 54A(b) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance (as amended by Act No.13 of 1984)
brief_facts_summary: On or about June 22, 2017, the appellant was charged with possession and trafficking of 01.56 grams of heroin. The appellant was indicted in the High Court of Colombo and convicted of both charges after trial. The appellant is a sixty-five-year-old male and the sole breadwinner for his family with two children.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 54A(d) and Section 54A(b) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance (as amended by Act No.13 of 1984)
hc_sentence_type: 7 years rigorous imprisonment and fine of Rs.100,000.00 with one year simple imprisonment in default for each charge
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court Judge convicted the appellant of both charges of possession and trafficking of 01.56 grams of heroin. For each charge, the court sentenced the appellant to 7 years rigorous imprisonment and imposed a fine of Rs.100,000.00 with one year simple imprisonment in default. The court considered the legal framework and facts presented in mitigation including the appellant's age and family circumstances.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant did not wish to contest the conviction but only the sentencing order. The sole ground of appeal urged by the learned counsel was whether the sentences imposed on the appellant were disproportionate. The appellant had requested a non-custodial sentence in the High Court but did not sufficiently elaborate on the reasons or circumstances in support of such plea.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Are the sentences imposed on the appellant disproportionate?
defence_version_summary: The appellant did not contest the conviction and only appealed against the sentencing order. The appellant requested a non-custodial sentence in the High Court but did not sufficiently elaborate on the reasons or circumstances in support of such plea.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal examined whether the sentences imposed were disproportionate. The COA noted that the law at the time mandated a fine not less than one hundred thousand rupees and not exceeding five hundred thousand rupees and imprisonment of either description for a period not less than seven years and not exceeding twenty years. The High Court Judge thoroughly considered this legal framework along with pertinent facts presented in mitigation, including the appellant's age (sixty-five years old) and his role as the sole breadwinner for his family with two children. The Court of Appeal remained mindful of the legal obligations imposed by mandatory sentencing laws while weighing the personal circumstances of the appellant. Finding that the disputed sentencing order was made after comprehensive review of all relevant facts, the COA was not inclined to interfere with the sentencing order and dismissed the appeal.
coa_sentence_type: 7 years rigorous imprisonment and fine of Rs.100,000.00 with one year simple imprisonment in default for each charge, sentences to run concurrently from September 06, 2023
brief_judgment_file_summary: The appellant, Kasthuri Arrachchige Tiyulin Wickremarathna, was convicted by the High Court of Colombo for possession and trafficking of 01.56 grams of heroin on June 22, 2017, under Section 54A(d) and 54A(b) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance. The High Court sentenced him to 7 years rigorous imprisonment and a fine of Rs.100,000.00 for each charge. The appellant appealed only the sentencing order on the ground that the sentences were disproportionate. The Court of Appeal considered the mandatory sentencing laws and the appellant's personal circumstances including his age of sixty-five years and role as sole breadwinner for his family with two children. The COA found that the High Court Judge had thoroughly considered the legal framework and mitigation factors and was not inclined to interfere with the sentencing order, dismissing the appeal but ordering that the sentences run concurrently from the date of conviction.
defence_counsel: Ershan Ariaratnam
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court Judge thoroughly considered the legal framework mandating specific penalties for drug offences and the pertinent facts presented in mitigation. The HC took into account significant factors including the appellant's age of sixty-five years and his role as the sole breadwinner for his family with two children. The COA found that the sentencing order was made after comprehensive review of all relevant facts.
standard_of_review_applied: The Court of Appeal reviewed whether it should interfere with the sentencing order considering mandatory sentencing laws and the personal circumstances of the appellant
sentencing_principles_applied: The Court applied mandatory sentencing laws under the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance while balancing the personal circumstances of the appellant including age and family responsibilities. The Court considered that the law mandated a fine not less than one hundred thousand rupees and not exceeding five hundred thousand rupees and imprisonment of either description for a period not less than seven years and not exceeding twenty years.

judges: B. Sasi Mahendran, J. | Amal Ranaraja, J.
offence_sections: Section 54(a) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance, as amended by Act No. 13 of 1984
brief_facts_summary: On 11th December 2008, police received intelligence about an individual obtaining heroin. A raid team arrested the accused at Thorana Junction, Peliyagoda around 13:55 hours. Officers searched him and recovered a grocery bag containing a light brown powdery substance suspected to be heroin from his right trouser pocket, along with a Nokia mobile phone and identity card from his left pocket. The substance was weighed at Peliyagoda Police Station at 31g 400mg including wrapping, later analyzed as 4.69 grams of heroin.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 54(a) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance, as amended by Act No. 13 of 1984
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court of Colombo found the accused guilty of possession of 4.69 grams of heroin in violation of Section 54(a) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance. After hearing three prosecution witnesses and considering the accused's dock statement, the Learned Trial Judge imposed a sentence of life imprisonment.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant challenged the High Court judgment on three main grounds. First, the Trial Judge failed to appreciate discrepancies regarding the production registry. Second, the Judge failed to consider the appellant's version. Third, the Judge failed to appreciate that the prosecution's version fails the test of probability.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The learned Trial Judge failed to appreciate that there is a discrepancy about the production registry belonging to the productions of this case. | The learned Trial Judge failed to consider the version of the appellant. | The learned Trial Judge failed to appreciate that the version of the prosecution fails the test of probability.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the testimonies of PW1 and PW6 to be credible, trustworthy, and corroborative without material contradictions. The appellate court upheld that the Trial Judge, having observed witnesses firsthand, was well placed to assess credibility. The prosecution successfully established the sequence of events from intelligence receipt to arrest, recovery, and proper sealing of evidence.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court found the prosecution version passed the test of probability, with consistent timing evidence from out-entries and production registers supporting the police witnesses' account over the accused's dock statement claiming earlier arrest time.
defence_version_summary: The accused pleaded not guilty and made a dock statement claiming he was arrested at around 10:30 hours while en route to visit his grandmother on a motorbike. Defence counsel suggested another individual named Jayathissa was actually arrested and challenged the location and timing of arrest. The court found the dock statement did not raise reasonable doubt and rejected the defence version as inconsistent with documentary evidence showing officers received information around 12:30 hours and left the station after 13:00 hours.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal applied the established principle that Trial Judges who observe witnesses are best positioned to assess credibility. The appellate court conducted intrinsic and extrinsic examination of evidence as required, analyzing testimonies of PW1 and PW6 for consistency and reliability. The COA found no material contradictions between the two key prosecution witnesses and noted that defence counsel failed to establish any significant inconsistencies. The Court examined the chain of custody from arrest to sealing and found it properly maintained. Regarding the production registry discrepancy raised by the appellant, the COA noted that the Trial Judge accepted the witness's explanation. The Court rejected the appellant's dock statement version regarding arrest timing, finding it contradicted by out-entry records and production register timing. Applying precedent from King v. Gunaratne, the COA concluded the verdict was not unreasonable, no misdirection occurred, and no wrong inferences were drawn from the evidence.
coa_sentence_type: Life Imprisonment
brief_judgment_file_summary: Hewadevage Sujith Nishantha was convicted by the High Court of Colombo for possession of 4.69 grams of heroin under Section 54(a) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance and sentenced to life imprisonment. The accused appealed on grounds that the Trial Judge failed to appreciate production registry discrepancies, failed to consider his version, and that the prosecution case failed probability test. The Court of Appeal, comprising B. Sasi Mahendran, J. and Amal Ranaraja, J., found the testimonies of the two key police witnesses credible and consistent, with proper chain of custody maintained. The COA rejected the accused's dock statement as inconsistent with documentary evidence and found no legal errors or misdirection by the Trial Judge. The appeal was dismissed and conviction and sentence affirmed on 04.07.2025.
defence_counsel: Hafeel Farisz with Sanjeewa Kodithuwakku
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court Judge found the prosecution witnesses credible after observing their demeanor during examination and cross-examination. The Trial Judge accepted the explanation regarding production registry discrepancies and found the prosecution version coherent regarding timing and chain of custody. The Court of Appeal affirmed that the Trial Judge correctly evaluated evidence and reached justifiable conclusions about witness truthfulness.
precedents_cited_list: King v. Gunaratne and Another, CLR V.14 page 144
standard_of_review_applied: The Court of Appeal applied the three-part test: whether the verdict was unreasonable against the weight of evidence, whether there was misdirection on law or evidence, and whether wrong inferences were drawn from documents and evidence. The appellate court also applied the principle that findings on questions of fact are entitled to great weight, but must test evidence intrinsically and extrinsically.

judges: P. Kumararatnam, J. | R. P. Hettiarachchi, J.
offence_sections: Section 54(A)(d) and 54(A)(b) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance as amended by Act No. 13 of 1984
brief_facts_summary: On 13th March 2018, police conducted a raid at Samagama based on information about drug trafficking by the Appellant. The Appellant was stopped while walking, behaved suspiciously and tried to flee. Upon search, a small parcel containing heroin was found in his right trouser pocket and six currency notes of Rs.5000 each were found in his left pocket. The parcel was weighed at a jewellery shop showing 8.400 grams and the Appellant was arrested for possession and trafficking of heroin.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 54(A)(d) and 54(A)(b) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance as amended by Act No. 13 of 1984
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court of Kegalle found the Appellant guilty of both counts of possession and trafficking of 6.143 grams of heroin. The Appellant was sentenced to death on both counts on 06th April 2023.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The Appellant raised four grounds of appeal. First, the High Court Judge failed to consider the variation in quantity of the production which affects the root of the prosecution case. Second, the version of the prosecution is improbable. Third, the High Court Judge erred by compelling the Appellant to adduce more evidence. Fourth, the High Court Judge erred by rejecting the defence evidence on wrong premises.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The Learned High Court Judge erred in law by failing to consider the variation in quantity of the production which affects the root of the prosecution case | The version of the prosecution is improbable | The Learned High Court Judge erred in law by compelling the Appellant to adduce more evidence | The Learned High Court Judge erred in law by rejecting the defence evidence on wrong premises
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The prosecution led 5 witnesses excluding the Government Analyst. PW1 SI Gamini was the Chief Investigation Officer who conducted the raid and search. The Government Analyst Report was admitted under Section 420 of the Code of Criminal Procedure Act. The Court of Appeal noted that the prosecution failed to address the critical weight discrepancy between the initial weighing (8.400 grams) and the Government Analyst report (6.956 grams), which was a difference of 1.494 grams.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal found that the weight discrepancy of 1.494 grams created a serious doubt in the prosecution case and the prosecution failed to prove beyond reasonable doubt that the same production recovered at the time of detection reached the Government Analyst. The Court held that in the absence of any explanation for this substantial weight difference, the Appellant had not been afforded a fair trial.
defence_version_summary: The Appellant pleaded not guilty and made a dock statement denying possession of any dangerous drugs. He claimed his father was arrested first and when he visited the police station, his father was released and he was taken into custody. He contended that the drugs were introduced to him by the 1st and 2nd witnesses (police officers). His father gave evidence in support of his defence.
legal_errors_description: The Learned High Court Judge failed to make any comments about the discrepancy in weight of the substance recovered, which was a substantial fact. The Court of Appeal held that in the absence of any comment regarding this particular point, the Appellant had not been afforded a fair trial and this caused great prejudice to him. The prosecution failed to address this critical issue during trial by not putting relevant questions to PW1 or calling the Government Analyst to explain the difference.
procedural_defects_description: The prosecution failed to clarify the weight discrepancy highlighted by the Government Analyst during the trial. The prosecution did not put relevant questions to PW1 regarding the discrepancy and did not call the Government Analyst to explain the reason for the difference. This failure to address a substantial fact affecting the inward journey of the production was a significant procedural defect.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found that the weight discrepancy between the initial weighing (8.400 grams at the jewellery shop) and the Government Analyst Report (6.956 grams) was a critical issue. The difference of 1.494 grams was substantial and created serious doubt in the prosecution case. The Court emphasized that in drug-related cases, the prosecution must prove the chain relating to the inward journey and establish that productions have not been tampered with. The Court noted that the Government Analyst had made a note of the weight difference in the report, but the prosecution took no steps to explain it during trial. The Court held that considering the pure heroin detected in this case, the weight discrepancy was crucial and would certainly have an impact on the outcome. The Learned High Court Judge had not made any comments about this discrepancy in her judgment, which meant the Appellant was not afforded a fair trial and suffered great prejudice. The Court applied principles from Woolmington v. DPP, Karunadasa v. OIC Nittambuwa, Witharana Doli Nona v. Republic of Sri Lanka, Mahasarukkalige Chandani v. Attorney General, and Mohamed Nimnaz v. Attorney General regarding burden of proof and chain of custody requirements in drug cases.
coa_sentence_type: Acquittal from both charges
brief_judgment_file_summary: Hewage Rajith Kumara Sunil Jayaratne was convicted by the High Court of Kegalle for possession and trafficking of 6.143 grams of heroin under Sections 54(A)(d) and 54(A)(b) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance and sentenced to death on both counts on 06/04/2023. The Appellant appealed challenging the weight discrepancy in the production, the improbability of the prosecution version, and alleged errors by the trial judge. The Court of Appeal found that there was a critical unexplained weight discrepancy of 1.494 grams between the initial weighing (8.400 grams) and the Government Analyst Report (6.956 grams), which the prosecution failed to address during trial. The Court held that this substantial discrepancy created serious doubt about whether the same production reached the Government Analyst, and that the High Court Judge's failure to address this issue denied the Appellant a fair trial. The Court of Appeal set aside the conviction and sentence and acquitted the Appellant from both charges, allowing the appeal.
defence_counsel: Amila Palliyage with Sandeepani Wijesooriya, Savani Udugampola, Lakitha Wakishta Arachchi and Subaj De Silva
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted the Appellant and sentenced him to death on both counts. However, the Court of Appeal found that the Learned High Court Judge had not made any comments about the substantial weight discrepancy in the production, which was a critical issue. The Court of Appeal held that the failure to address this discrepancy meant the Appellant was not afforded a fair trial and suffered great prejudice.
precedents_cited_list: Woolmington v. DPP [1935] A.C.462 | Karunadasa Vs. Officer-in-Charge, Motor Traffic Division, Police Station Nittambuwa (1987) 1 SLR 155 | Witharana Doli Nona v. The Republic of Sri Lanka CA/19/99 | Mahasarukkalige Chandani v. Attorney General CA/213/2009 | Mohamed Nimnaz V. Attorney General CA/95/94
standard_of_review_applied: The Court of Appeal reviewed whether the prosecution proved the case beyond reasonable doubt and whether the inward journey of the production was established with reliable evidence, particularly focusing on whether the production recovered from the accused was the same production examined by the Government Analyst.

judges: P. Kumararatnam, J. | R. P. Hettiarachchi, J.
offence_sections: Section 140 of the Penal Code, Section 296 read with Section 146 of the Penal Code, Section 300 read with Section 146 of the Penal Code, Section 296 read with Section 32 of the Penal Code, Section 300 read with Section 32 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: On 29.01.1998 at Kahaduwa, the appellant along with others forcibly broke into a house where the family was sleeping after a function. The deceased accused Priyashantha stabbed the inmates while the appellant armed with a pole and the 2nd accused prevented the family members from escaping. Six family members were killed and one survivor PW2 aged 14 sustained serious abdominal injuries. The house was burnt and bodies were piled and burnt inside. Four suspects died in a police shootout and this was the third house attacked that night.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 140 of the Penal Code, Section 296 read with Section 146 of the Penal Code, Section 300 read with Section 146 of the Penal Code
hc_sentence_type: Death sentence for counts 2-7, 6 months rigorous imprisonment for count 1, 15 years rigorous imprisonment with fine and default sentence for count 8
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the appellant and 2nd accused for counts 1-8 after trial. The prosecution presented 8 witnesses including eyewitness PW2 who identified the accused. The court found the appellant actively participated in the unlawful assembly that caused death of six victims and attempted murder of one survivor by preventing victims from escaping the attack.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant challenged whether the prosecution proved their case beyond reasonable doubt and whether the prosecution proved the appellant's involvement beyond reasonable doubt. The defence argued that eyewitness PW2's evidence was unreliable due to omissions and contradictions, that she was an interested witness, and that her evidence was not corroborated by other witnesses.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Has the prosecution proved their case beyond a reasonable doubt? | Has the prosecution proved the involvement of the Appellant beyond a reasonable doubt?
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found eyewitness PW2's evidence convincing despite her young age of 14 at the time. The court held that minor omissions and contradictions regarding whether appellant carried a club or knife did not affect the core of the prosecution case. The court applied the principle that evidence must be weighed not counted and that a single credible witness can support conviction.
probability_assessment_by_court: The court found PW2's evidence cogent and without ambiguity on material points. The court held that discrepancies not relating to the core of the prosecution case should be disregarded when probability factors favor the witness version. The prosecution proved the case beyond reasonable doubt.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty and made a dock statement denying the charges. He called one defence witness. The court found the defence evidence failed to create a doubt over the prosecution case and rejected the defence version.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal conducted comprehensive analysis of the eyewitness testimony of PW2 who was 14 years old at the time of incident. The court acknowledged cognitive and psychological factors affecting eyewitness testimony but found PW2's evidence truthful and impressive. The court distinguished between material contradictions affecting the core case versus minor discrepancies about peripheral details like whether appellant carried a club or knife. The court applied Section 134 of Evidence Ordinance holding no particular number of witnesses is required and cited precedents that single credible witness can support conviction. The court found the High Court Judge properly analyzed the evidence of unlawful assembly and correctly convicted the appellant. The court emphasized that appellant actively prevented victims from escaping the attack which constituted active participation in the unlawful assembly. The identification was reliable through oil lamp light and investigating officer verified lighting conditions. The court held all probability factors favored the prosecution version and the defence failed to create reasonable doubt.
coa_sentence_type: Death sentence for counts 2-7, 6 months rigorous imprisonment for count 1, 15 years rigorous imprisonment with Rs.20,000 fine with default sentence of 1 year simple imprisonment for count 8
brief_judgment_file_summary: The appellant Puwakwaththa Gamage Ranjith alias Patty was convicted by the High Court of Balapitiya for being part of an unlawful assembly that murdered six family members and attempted to murder one survivor on 29.01.1998 at Kahaduwa. The High Court imposed death sentences for six murder counts, 6 months rigorous imprisonment for unlawful assembly, 15 years rigorous imprisonment with Rs.20,000 fine for attempted murder, and ordered Rs.500,000 compensation. The appellant appealed challenging the prosecution case and reliability of the 14-year-old eyewitness PW2. The Court of Appeal on 04.07.2025 dismissed the appeal holding that PW2's evidence was credible despite minor contradictions, that a single credible witness can support conviction, and that the High Court properly analyzed the evidence and correctly convicted the appellant who actively prevented victims from escaping the attack.
prosecution_counsel: Sanjeewa Dissanayake, D. S. G. with Jehan Gunasekara, SC
defence_counsel: Anil Silva, P. C. with Isuru Jayawardena, Sarith Wadugedera and Arinda Silva
cause_of_death_exact_text: Gunshot wounds and multiple cut injuries
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court Judge clearly analyzed the evidence from both parties and properly considered the legal principles of unlawful assembly. The High Court accurately considered the omission and contradiction highlighted by defence and correctly held they were insufficient to disturb the core of the case. The Court of Appeal found the High Court judgment properly analyzed evidence and gave plausible reasons for believing PW2's evidence.
precedents_cited_list: Sumanasena v. The Attorney General [1999] 3 Sri.L.R 137 | Madduma Siripala and another v. The Attorney General CA/125-126/10 decided on 27/10/2017 | Chacko Alias Aniyan Kunju & others v. State of Kerala [2004] INSC 87 | Bandara v. The State [2001] 1 SLR 63
standard_of_review_applied: Appellate review of factual findings and legal conclusions of trial court with deference to trial judge's assessment of witness credibility

judges: P. Kumararatnam, J. | Pradeep Hettiarachchi, J.
offence_sections: Section 296 read with section 32 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The accused-appellant Jagath Kumar De Silva and a second accused were charged with the murder of Bodhandi Anil De Silva on 23-01-2004. The deceased was shot near the Rajjawatte culvert at around 10:10 am while seated in a van with his wife, daughter, and one Podi Sudda. According to the prosecution, the appellant and the second accused arrived from the seaside and shot the deceased from both sides of the van using firearms. The deceased died from multiple gunshot wounds. Two eyewitnesses, the wife (PW1) and daughter (PW2) of the deceased, testified at trial.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 296 read with section 32 of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court of Balapitiya convicted the appellant of murder on 19-01-2023 after a trial without jury. The court accepted the evidence of the wife and daughter of the deceased who testified that the appellant shot the deceased. The appellant was sentenced to death.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant challenged the High Court's failure to properly evaluate prosecution witnesses using tests of consistency, probability and spontaneity. He argued there were serious inter se contradictions between PW1 and PW2's evidence. The appellant also contended that the court failed to draw an adverse inference under section 114(f) of the Evidence Ordinance for the prosecution's failure to call PW3, a crucial eyewitness. Additionally, the appellant argued that the trial judge improperly rejected the defence witness DW1's evidence based solely on her relationship to the appellant.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Failure to evaluate credibility of prosecution witnesses using accepted tests of consistency, probability and spontaneity | Failure to draw adverse inference against prosecution for not calling eyewitness PW3 | Failure to identify that a fair investigation had not been conducted | Failure to analyze the defense case properly and reject defense witness evidence lawfully | Erroneous finding that case proved beyond reasonable doubt
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found serious inter se contradictions between PW1 and PW2 regarding whether van shutters were open or closed and the sequence of shooting. PW2's statement was recorded two weeks after the incident, raising concerns about possible coaching. The court found these contradictions material and going to the root of the case, casting serious doubts on witness credibility.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal found it highly improbable that PW3 remained calm and seated while two gunmen fired simultaneously from both sides, and that he was not hit by any bullets. The court also found it improbable that PW2's belated statement was not the result of coaching by PW1.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty and made a dock statement denying involvement in the crime. He called one defence witness, Dehinga Amitha Mendis (DW1), who testified that she heard shots from her house next to the crime scene and saw PW1 approaching the scene 10-15 minutes after hearing the shots. The Court of Appeal found DW1's evidence credible, spontaneous, and consistent, noting her statement was recorded promptly and no contradictions were elicited by the prosecution.
legal_errors_description: The High Court failed to properly evaluate witness credibility using accepted tests, glossed over material contradictions as minor, failed to inquire into the delay in recording PW2's statement, improperly relied on State Counsel's speculations about PW3's evidence at non-summary inquiry, and discriminatingly rejected DW1's evidence based solely on her distant relationship to the appellant while accepting biased testimony from the wife and daughter of the deceased.
procedural_defects_description: The learned trial judge deviated from standard procedure by taking into consideration PW3's evidence at the non-summary inquiry which was not led at trial, and based his decision on State Counsel's speculations, thereby depriving the accused of the opportunity to be heard.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found that material contradictions existed between the two key prosecution witnesses (wife and daughter of deceased) regarding whether van shutters were open or closed and the sequence of shooting events. The court held these contradictions went to the root of the case and cast serious doubts on witness credibility. The daughter's statement was recorded two weeks after the incident without proper explanation, raising concerns about possible coaching. The court found it highly improbable that eyewitness PW3 remained seated calmly during simultaneous shooting from both sides and was not hit. The prosecution's failure to call PW3, who was listed as a witness and seated closest to the deceased, constituted a vital missing link warranting an adverse inference under section 114(f) of the Evidence Ordinance. The High Court improperly rejected the defence witness's evidence based solely on her distant relationship to the appellant while accepting evidence from the wife and daughter who were closely related to the deceased. The court concluded that the prosecution failed to prove the case beyond reasonable doubt.
coa_sentence_type: Acquittal - conviction and sentence quashed
brief_judgment_file_summary: The appellant Jagath Kumar De Silva was convicted of murder and sentenced to death by the High Court of Balapitiya for the shooting death of Bodhandi Anil De Silva on 23-01-2004. On appeal, the Court of Appeal found material contradictions between the two key prosecution witnesses (the deceased's wife and daughter) regarding the manner of shooting. The daughter's statement was recorded two weeks after the incident without proper explanation, raising concerns about coaching. The prosecution failed to call PW3, a crucial eyewitness seated closest to the deceased, warranting an adverse inference. The High Court improperly rejected defence witness evidence based on her distant relationship to the appellant while accepting biased testimony from the deceased's wife and daughter. The Court of Appeal allowed the appeal, quashed the conviction and sentence, and acquitted the appellant, finding the prosecution failed to prove the case beyond reasonable doubt.
prosecution_counsel: Anoopa De Silva for the Respondent
defence_counsel: Sarath Jayamanne PC with Asith Siriwardene, Vineshka Mendis, Prashan Wickremaratne, Sanjeewa Meegahawaththa and M.A. Noorie
cause_of_death_exact_text: Three categories of wounds: 1st category - burn marks from right to left behind the head from gun sparks with 3 gun shots but no skull penetration; 2nd category - bullet penetrated chest from top left to bottom from left side 3-4 feet away (would immediately result in death); 3rd category - bullet penetrated left side of abdomen from left side. The deceased was shot from opposite directions simultaneously.
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court acknowledged contradictions between PW1 and PW2 but proceeded on the basis that they did not go to the root of the case. The court made excuses for PW2's contradictions due to her age (8 years old) and traumatic experience. The court concluded PW3 was an unfavorable witness based on State Counsel's speculations about his evidence at non-summary inquiry. The court rejected DW1's evidence solely because she attempted to conceal her relationship with the appellant. The Court of Appeal found these approaches fundamentally flawed.
precedents_cited_list: Bandaranayake vs. Jagathsena [1984] 2 SLR 397 | Boghi Bhai Hirji Bhai vs. State of Gujarat AIR 1983 SC 753 | Veerasamy Sivathasan vs. AG SC Appeal 208/2012 (15 December 2021) | State of Uttar Pradesh vs. M. K. Anthony | State of Rajasthan v. Smt. Kalki and Another (1981) 2 SCC 752 | Haramanis v Somalatha [1983] 3 Sri.LR 365 | Mohamed Rasik Mohamad Minaur Alias Seenu v The Attorney General CA HCC/0185/2017 (CA Minutes of 03-03-2022) | Panchi and Others v State of Uttar Pradesh (1998) 7 SCC 177 | Sumanasena v Attorney-General [1999] 3 Sri.LR 137 | Ajith Samarakoon v The Republic [2004] 2 Sri.LR 209 | Kahandagamage Dharmasiri v AG SC Appeal 4 of 2009, SC/SPL/LA 165 of 2008 | Sinnathamby Ganeshan and Another v The Republic of Sri Lanka C.A. Appeal No. 57-58/2003 | Walimunige John & Another v The State 76 NLR 488 | Kumara de Silva v Attorney General [2010] 2 Sri.LR 169 | Ajith Fernando alias Konda Ajith and Others v Attorney General [2004] 1 Sri LR 288
standard_of_review_applied: The Court of Appeal reviewed whether the High Court properly evaluated witness credibility using accepted tests of consistency, probability and spontaneity, whether material contradictions went to the root of the case, whether proper inquiry was made into delayed statements, and whether adverse inferences should have been drawn for non-production of crucial witnesses.

judges: B. Sasi Mahendran, J. | Amal Ranaraja, J.
offence_sections: Section 354 of the Penal Code (Charge 01 - acquitted); Section 365 B (2)(b) of the Penal Code as amended by Act No.22 of 1995 and Act No.29 of 1988 and Act No.16 of 2006 (Charges 02, 03, 04)
brief_facts_summary: The appellant was an immediate neighbour of the victim (PW01). On September 27, 2016, the appellant got PW01 to accompany him under the pretence of assisting in removing a blockage from a water pipeline. At the location, the appellant armed with a knife forcibly dragged PW01 further away and subjected him to sexual abuse by placing his genitals inside the victim's mouth and placing his mouth on the victim's genitals.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 365 B (2)(b) of the Penal Code as amended by Act No.22 of 1995 and Act No.29 of 1988 and Act No.16 of 2006
hc_sentence_type: Rigorous Imprisonment 10 years per charge, Fine, Compensation
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the appellant on charges 02 and 03 for grave sexual abuse under section 365 B (2)(b) of the Penal Code and acquitted him on charges 01 and 04. The High Court sentenced the appellant to 10 years rigorous imprisonment for each charge with fines of Rs.25,000 per charge and compensation totaling Rs.300,000.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant argued that the prosecution failed to satisfy the test of consistency, spontaneity and probability in evidence. The appellant contended that the High Court Judge did not properly consider the delay in complaint, considered material not in evidence, and that contradictions were not proved. The appellant also argued that the prosecution failed to call a material witness, failed to prove the ingredients of the offence, and that the burden of proof was shifted to the accused.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Prosecution failed to satisfy the Court as to the test of consistency, spontaneity, probability, inter se and per se contradictions in evidence of prosecution witnesses | Learned High Court Judge did not consider the delay in making the complaint from the correct perspective | Learned High Court Judge considered in his judgment material which had not been elicited in the evidence | Contradictions and omissions marked by the prosecution when the accused was giving evidence had not been proved | Prosecution failed to call a material witness | Prosecution failed to prove the ingredients of the offence | Learned High Court Judge shifted the burden of proving his innocence to the accused
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found that minor inconsistencies regarding the duration of acquaintance and manner of dragging did not undermine the credibility of PW01's testimony. The Court acknowledged that the victim may have been overwhelmed during cross-examination and that psychological trauma could affect recall of certain details. The Court assessed PW01's mother's testimony noting she became emotional and may have forgotten aspects.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal assessed probability arguments regarding whether the victim would have continued attending school after the incident and whether the appellant would have visited the victim's house. The Court found these arguments did not undermine the prosecution case considering the psychological impact on a 15-year-old victim and the power imbalance.
defence_version_summary: The appellant admitted that he and PW01 went to the location where the pipe was fixed to the stream but denied committing sexual abuse against PW01. He maintained there was animosity among households regarding water usage and believed he was falsely implicated. The Court of Appeal found the appellant's account improbable when evaluated against the surrounding evidence.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal conducted a comprehensive review of all grounds of appeal. The Court found that minor inconsistencies in testimony regarding duration of acquaintance and manner of dragging were not material discrepancies. The Court acknowledged psychological factors affecting a 15-year-old victim's ability to recall details during cross-examination and the trauma's impact on disclosure. The Court rejected probability arguments about the victim continuing school or the appellant visiting the victim's house, noting the power imbalance and the appellant's possession of a knife. The Court found the delay in complaint was reasonably explained by the victim's age and fear. Regarding burden of proof, the Court found the High Court Judge meticulously assessed both parties' narratives and applied required legal principles without shifting burden to the accused. The Court concluded the High Court judgment was sustainable and dismissed the appeal.
coa_sentence_type: Rigorous Imprisonment 10 years per charge (Charges 02 and 03), Fine Rs.25,000 per charge with one year imprisonment in default, Compensation Rs.300,000 total (Rs.150,000 per charge) with six months imprisonment per charge in default
brief_judgment_file_summary: The appellant Jayalathge Vijitha was convicted by the High Court of Matara on two counts of grave sexual abuse under section 365 B (2)(b) of the Penal Code for sexually abusing a minor neighbour on September 27, 2016. The High Court sentenced him to 10 years rigorous imprisonment per charge, fines totaling Rs.50,000 and compensation of Rs.300,000. The appellant appealed arguing inconsistencies in prosecution evidence, improper consideration of delay in complaint, and shifting of burden of proof. The Court of Appeal found minor inconsistencies were not material, psychological factors explained the delay and recall issues, and the High Court properly evaluated evidence without shifting burden. The appeal was dismissed.
defence_counsel: Asanka Mendis with Sandeepani Wijesooriya
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court Judge carefully considered the appellant's narrative in conjunction with the totality of evidence presented at trial and concluded the appellant's account was improbable. The Court of Appeal found the High Court Judge meticulously assessed narratives from both parties and applied required legal principles concerning evaluation of evidence in a careful and thorough way, decisively choosing to act upon the respondent's evidence while giving less weight to the appellant's.
standard_of_review_applied: The Court of Appeal reviewed whether the High Court properly assessed credibility of witnesses, whether inconsistencies were material, whether burden of proof was properly applied, and whether the conviction was sustainable based on the totality of evidence

judges: B. Sasi Mahendran, J. | Amal Ranaraja, J.
offence_sections: Section 365B(2) of the Penal Code, as amended by Act No. 22 of 1995
brief_facts_summary: The 14-year-old victim visited Kalawana Hospital on 4th August 2005 and noticed two individuals following her. She sought refuge in a gold jewellery shop owned by the Accused, who escorted her to an inner room where he allegedly pushed her against the wall, unzipped his trousers, and subjected her to inappropriate physical contact for approximately 30 minutes. She reported the incident to her sister-in-law two days later, and a complaint was lodged at Kalawana Police Station on 7th August 2005.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 365B(2) of the Penal Code, as amended by Act No. 22 of 1995
hc_sentence_type: Twelve years rigorous imprisonment with fine and compensation
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court of Ratnapura found the Accused guilty of grave sexual abuse and imposed a sentence of twelve years rigorous imprisonment along with a fine of Rs. 20,000 and compensation of Rs. 200,000 to the victim. The co-accused Farhan was acquitted after evaluation of prosecution evidence.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The Accused-Appellant challenged the credibility of the victim's testimony, raised discrepancies regarding the location of the incident, argued the incident could not have occurred inside the gold shop, raised delay in complaint, contended no force or threat was used, claimed no evidence of gross indecency, and argued the dock statement was not properly considered. Additionally, undue delay in filing the indictment was raised as a sentencing factor.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Credibility of the witness Kaniamma (PW01) | Gross discrepancy as to where the incident took place | The purported incident could not have taken place inside the Gold shop | Delay in making the Complaint | No force, threat or intimidation or fear of death or hurt was used and she was not in lawful detention | No evidence whatsoever to suggest PW01 was subject to the said purported gross indecency | Dock statement of the Accused-Appellant was not considered in light of the attended circumstances | Undue delay in filing the indictment not considered in sentencing
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The prosecution presented six witnesses and two documents. The victim's testimony remained consistent throughout and withstood cross-examination. Minor discrepancies regarding the exact location within the premises did not go to the root of the case. The victim provided a reasonable explanation for the delay in lodging the complaint.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court held that contradictions did not give rise to reasonable doubt and that the prosecution proved the case beyond reasonable doubt
defence_version_summary: The Accused pleaded not guilty and made a dock statement only without calling witnesses. He stated that the prosecution witness had been inside an adjoining shop and he emerged with her before entering the jewellery shop. The Court rejected the dock statement as lacking sufficient evidential weight to raise reasonable doubt.
procedural_defects_description: Thirteen year delay in filing indictment from date of offence
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal affirmed the conviction, finding that the victim's testimony was credible and consistent despite minor discrepancies about the exact location within the premises. The Court held that both the jewellery shop and adjoining shop were located next to each other, and the adjoining shop contained a room. The discrepancy did not strike at the root of the prosecution case. The Court applied the principle that truthful witnesses may differ in minor details due to varying powers of observation and passage of time. The victim's evidence withstood cross-examination and she provided reasonable explanation for delay in complaint. The Court applied judicial precedents on child witnesses and corroboration. However, regarding sentencing, the Court found the thirteen-year delay in filing indictment and overall delay in concluding the case to be significant mitigating factors. Applying K.R. Karunaratne v. The State and Section 333 of the Code of Criminal Procedure Act, the Court reduced the sentence from twelve years to two years rigorous imprisonment suspended for ten years, while affirming the fine and compensation.
coa_sentence_type: Two years rigorous imprisonment suspended for ten years from the date of High Court judgment with fine and compensation affirmed
brief_judgment_file_summary: Perumal Kamaraj was convicted by the High Court of Ratnapura for grave sexual abuse of a 14-year-old girl under Section 365B(2) of the Penal Code and sentenced to twelve years rigorous imprisonment with Rs. 20,000 fine and Rs. 200,000 compensation. The incident occurred on 4th August 2005 at a jewellery shop in Kalawana. The Accused-Appellant challenged the conviction on grounds of witness credibility, location discrepancies, delay in complaint, and inadequacy of evidence, and challenged the sentence based on prosecutorial delay. The Court of Appeal affirmed the conviction, finding the victim's testimony credible despite minor discrepancies about the exact location. However, the Court reduced the sentence to two years rigorous imprisonment suspended for ten years due to the thirteen-year delay in filing the indictment and overall delay in concluding the case, while affirming the fine and compensation.
defence_counsel: Faisz Musthapha, PC with Keerthi Tillekeratne and Bishran Zibul
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court Judge properly evaluated the evidence and rejected the dock statement as lacking sufficient weight to raise reasonable doubt. The High Court correctly found the Accused guilty based on the victim's credible testimony. However, the High Court failed to consider the thirteen-year delay in filing the indictment as a mitigating factor in sentencing.

The Republic of Sri Lanka, CA No. 147/2005 | Bhoginbhai Hirjibhai Vs. Attorney General, 2007 (1) SLR 224 | K.R. Karunaratne v. The State, 78 NLR 413
standard_of_review_applied: Appellate review of evidence and conviction; consideration of delay as mitigating factor in sentencing under Section 333 of Code of Criminal Procedure Act No. 25 of 2024
sentencing_principles_applied: The Court applied the principle that undue delay in prosecution may be a mitigating factor in sentencing, citing K.R. Karunaratne v. The State. The Court also applied Section 333 of the Code of Criminal Procedure Act No. 25 of 2024 regarding consideration of time spent in custody. The thirteen-year delay in filing indictment and four years already served were considered in suspending the sentence.

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 365B(b)2(b) and Section 345 of the Penal Code as amended by Act No. 22 of 1995
brief_facts_summary: The Appellant was indicted for two counts of Grave Sexual Abuse under Section 365B(b)2(b) and one count of Sexual Harassment under Section 345 of the Penal Code committed against his 4-year-old son Kevin Heman Brito between 01/11/2012 and 30/11/2012. The Child Protection Authority video recorded the victim's statement under Section 163(c) of the Evidence Ordinance. The prosecution called 6 witnesses and marked productions P1-P5. The Appellant gave evidence and called two defense witnesses.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 365B(b)2(b) and Section 345 of the Penal Code as amended by Act No. 22 of 1995
hc_sentence_type: Count 1: 7 years rigorous imprisonment with compensation Rs. 500,000 (default 6 months simple imprisonment); Count 2: 7 years rigorous imprisonment with compensation Rs. 500,000 (default 6 months simple imprisonment); Count 3: 2 years rigorous imprisonment with compensation Rs. 200,000 (default 3 months simple imprisonment), all sentences to run consecutively
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the Appellant on all three counts after trial. The prosecution relied heavily on the video recorded testimony of the 4-year-old victim under Section 163A of the Evidence Ordinance. The High Court sentenced the Appellant to consecutive terms of imprisonment totaling 16 years rigorous imprisonment with total compensation of Rs. 1,200,000.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The Appellant challenged the conviction on multiple grounds including that the child victim was tutored by his mother (PW1) during video recording, incorrect transcript was presented, the judge improperly used the Police Information Book not in evidence, burden of proof was shifted to the Appellant, failure to produce CDs seized by authorities, PW1 had motive to implicate the Appellant, and PW1 was not a competent witness being the wife of the Appellant.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The Learned Trial Judge failed to consider that the child victim was tutored by PW1, the mother of the child during the video recording | The Appellant was denied a fair trial by presenting incorrect transcript of the interview conducted by the Child Protection Authority | The Appellant was denied a fair trial by convicting him using the Police Information Book which had not been produced as evidence | The Appellant was denied a fair trial by shifting the burden on the Appellant to rebut the evidence of the prosecution | The Learned High Court Judge failed to consider that the failure to produce the CDs taken into custody by the National Child Protection Authority warrants application of Section 114(f) of the Evidence Ordinance | The trial Judge did not consider that PW1 had strong motive to implicate the Appellant through the child who was 4 years of age | The Learned High Court Judge failed to consider that PW1, who was the wife of the Appellant, is not a competent witness to give evidence as far as the charges are concerned
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The prosecution called 6 witnesses with the primary evidence being the video recorded statement of the 4-year-old victim. The Court of Appeal found serious flaws including that the mother (PW1) prompted and tutored the child during video recording, and the transcript presented differed materially from the actual video recording. The Court found that PW1 had a motive to fabricate evidence due to domestic violence complaints and restraining orders.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal found that the prosecution failed to prove the case beyond reasonable doubt due to tutoring of the child witness, incorrect transcript, improper use of Police Information Book, shifting burden of proof, non-production of CDs, and use of incompetent witness testimony
defence_version_summary: The Appellant pleaded not guilty, gave evidence from the witness box and called two defense witnesses. The defense highlighted that the matrimonial relationship between the Appellant and PW1 was strained, and argued that PW1 had a strong motive to implicate the Appellant through the child. The Court of Appeal found merit in the defense's contentions regarding tutoring, evidentiary flaws, and procedural errors.
legal_errors_description: Multiple legal errors identified: (1) accepting video evidence where child was tutored by mother; (2) relying on incorrect transcript that differed from actual video recording; (3) improperly using and perusing Police Information Book not admitted in evidence; (4) shifting burden of proof to the Appellant; (5) failure to apply Section 114(f) for non-production of CDs; (6) accepting testimony of wife as competent witness when Sections 365B(b)2(b) and 345 not included in First Schedule of Children and Young Persons Ordinance
procedural_defects_description: The High Court Judge improperly perused the Police Information Book which was not admitted as evidence in the trial. The CDs seized by police were not produced at trial. The wife of the Appellant was allowed to testify as a competent witness despite legal prohibition.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal conducted detailed analysis and found multiple fatal flaws in the High Court proceedings. The COA examined the video recording and found that the transcript marked as P1 was materially different from the actual recording, with numerous instances where PW1 prompted and tutored the 4-year-old victim to say things against the Appellant. The Court cited American Professional Society guidelines and precedents including Panchhi v State of Uttar Pradesh and Liyana Arachchige Lesli Wijesekera v AG, emphasizing that caregivers should not influence child witnesses. The COA found that the strained matrimonial relationship and restraining orders indicated PW1 had motive to fabricate. The Court held that the High Court Judge erred in using the Police Information Book not in evidence, citing Punchimahattaya v The State and Priyal Indrajith v AG. The COA found the burden of proof was improperly shifted to the Appellant, violating the 'Golden Thread' principle from Woolmington v DPP. The Court noted that while Section 81 of Children and Young Persons Ordinance makes spouses competent witnesses, this applies only to offences in the First Schedule, which had not been amended to include Sections 365B(b)2(b) and 345 introduced by the 1995 amendment. The COA concluded these cumulative errors denied the Appellant a fair trial and the prosecution failed to prove the case beyond reasonable doubt.
coa_sentence_type: Acquitted - conviction set aside
brief_judgment_file_summary: Kalutara Koralage Hemantha Brito was convicted by the High Court of Colombo for two counts of Grave Sexual Abuse and one count of Sexual Harassment against his 4-year-old son between 01/11/2012 and 30/11/2012, and sentenced to consecutive imprisonment totaling 16 years with Rs. 1,200,000 compensation. The Court of Appeal allowed the appeal on multiple grounds, finding that the child victim was tutored by his mother during video recording, the transcript presented materially differed from the actual video, the High Court Judge improperly used Police Information Book not in evidence, the burden of proof was shifted to the Appellant, CDs seized were not produced, and the wife was allowed to testify despite not being a competent witness as the relevant sections were not included in the First Schedule of the Children and Young Persons Ordinance. The COA held that these cumulative errors denied a fair trial and the prosecution failed to prove the case beyond reasonable doubt, and accordingly acquitted the Appellant.
defence_counsel: Darshana Kuruppu with Sahan Weerasinghe and Dineru Dundara
hc_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal extensively criticized the High Court's judgment, finding that the HC Judge misdirected herself in law on multiple counts. The HC failed to properly scrutinize the video evidence and transcript for accuracy and authenticity, improperly used Police Information Book not in evidence, shifted the burden of proof to the Appellant by requiring him to rebut prosecution evidence, failed to apply adverse inference for non-production of CDs, and erroneously allowed the wife to testify as a competent witness when the law did not permit this for the charged offences.
precedents_cited_list: Panchhi and Others v State of Uttar Pradesh (1998) 7 SCC 177 | Liyana Arachchige Lesli Wijesekera v The Attorney General CA/HCC/0046/22 decided on 13.09.2023 | Punchimahattaya v The State 76 NLR 564 | Priyal Indrajith and two others v The Attorney General CA/HCC/300-302/2018 decided on 16.01.2023 | Woolmington v DPP [1935] A.C.462 | Hattuwan Pedige Sugath Karunaratne v The Attorney General SC Appeal 32 of 2020
standard_of_review_applied: Appellate review of conviction and sentence under Section 331(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure Act No.15 of 1979 read with Article 138 of the Constitution

judges: B. Sasi Mahendran, J. | Amal Ranaraja, J.
offence_sections: Section 54(a)(b) and 54A(d) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance, as amended by Act No. 13 of 1984
brief_facts_summary: PW5, officer in charge of Kitchen Department at Welikada Prison, received information on March 2, 2012 that a prisoner from Aluthkade Prison possessed heroin. On March 3, 2012 at 6:30 AM, PW5 and PW6 searched the accused-appellant in P2 ward and found a blue grocery bag containing brown powder concealed in his underwear. Government analyst confirmed the substance was 3.44 grams of pure heroin (21.94 grams total weight). The accused-appellant was a prisoner who had been transferred from Aluthkade Prison.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 54(a)(b) and 54A(d) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance, as amended by Act No. 13 of 1984
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court of Colombo found the accused guilty on both counts of possession and trafficking of heroin after trial. The prosecution led evidence from six witnesses and marked productions P1 to P11. The accused made a statement from the dock. The High Court Judge imposed the death sentence.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The defence argued that the trial judge failed to consider the improbability and suspiciousness of the prosecution's version. They challenged the credibility of PW5's evidence and highlighted contradictory positions between PW5 and PW6 regarding the alleged incident. The defence also contended that the trial judge erred in convicting the accused for trafficking heroin in the absence of contributory activity proving commercial distribution intent.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The Learned Trial Judge had failed to consider the improbability and suspiciousness of the version of the prosecution pertaining to the alleged incident | The Learned Trial Judge had not properly considered the issues relating to the credibility of the evidence by PW5 | The Learned Trial Judge had failed to consider the contradictory positions relating to this alleged incident between PW5 and PW6 | The learned Trial Judge had erred in law by convicting the Accused Appellant for the 1 count namely the trafficking of heroin count in the absence of contributory activity to by the Accused appellant to the same effect
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found PW5 and PW6 credible and consistent in their testimonies regarding the arrest and recovery of heroin. The trial judge had the benefit of observing witness demeanour and found no contradictions or significant omissions in PW5's testimony. PW6 corroborated PW5's account of the search and recovery, and both witnesses were found trustworthy.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court found no reasonable doubt regarding the prosecution's case, noting that the witnesses remained consistent and credible despite cross-examination challenges
defence_version_summary: The accused pleaded not guilty and made a statement from the dock. He claimed that the contested production was introduced when he requested to move to another room. The defence suggested PW5 had been implicated in a prior heroin possession case but presented no evidence of prior animosity between the parties. The accused did not call any witnesses.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal carefully examined the evidence and found that the trial judge properly assessed witness credibility. The appellate court noted that trial judges have the advantage of observing witness demeanour and deportment, placing them in a better position to assess credibility. The COA found PW5 and PW6's testimonies consistent and reliable, with PW6 corroborating PW5's account of the recovery. The Court addressed the defence argument about lack of evidence of trafficking intent by noting that the quantity of 3.44 grams of pure heroin recovered within prison confines indicated it was intended for distribution among inmates. Citing Mohamed Iqbal Mohamed Sadath v. Attorney General, the Court held that drug quantity is a good indicator of whether possession is for personal use or commercial purposes. The Court was satisfied that the prosecution proved the drugs were meant for distribution and trafficking.
coa_sentence_type: Death
brief_judgment_file_summary: Rathnayaka Mudiyanselage Niranjaya Kumara was convicted by the High Court of Colombo for possession and trafficking of 3.44 grams of heroin found concealed in his underwear at Welikada Prison on March 3, 2012, and sentenced to death. He appealed challenging witness credibility, alleged contradictions between prosecution witnesses, and arguing insufficient evidence of trafficking intent. The Court of Appeal found the trial judge properly assessed witness credibility, noting PW5 and PW6 provided consistent and corroborative testimony. The COA held that the quantity of heroin recovered within prison indicated intent to distribute among inmates, satisfying the trafficking element. The appeal was dismissed and the conviction with death sentence was upheld.
defence_counsel: I.B.S. Harshana
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court Judge thoroughly analysed the testimonies of PW5 and PW6 and found no material discrepancies that would undermine their credibility. The trial judge found both witnesses credible and trustworthy, and properly evaluated their evidence. The Court of Appeal found no justifiable reason to disturb the trial judge's credibility findings.
precedents_cited_list: Mohamed Iqbal Mohamed Sadath v. Attorney General, SC Appeal 110/15 (SC Minutes, 14.12.2020)
standard_of_review_applied: The Court of Appeal applied the principle that appellate courts do not have the benefit of observing witnesses who give evidence at trial, while trial courts have the benefit of observing witness demeanour and deportment, placing them in a better position to assess credibility

judges: Menaka Wijesundera, J. | Wickum A. Kaluarachchi, J.
offence_sections: Section 364(3) of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The accused-appellant was charged with raping his daughter on two occasions during 2012 when she was 13 years old and in Grade 9. The first incident occurred in February 2012 when they returned home alone from a pirith ceremony. The second incident occurred about three months later when the victim was changing clothes after returning from school. The victim did not disclose the incidents until 2015 when she sent an SMS to her boyfriend mentioning her father's harassment, which her mother discovered, leading to a complaint after the father beat the mother with an iron rod.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 364(3) of the Penal Code
hc_sentence_type: 17 years of rigorous imprisonment on each count, running concurrently
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the accused-appellant on both counts of rape under Section 364(3) of the Penal Code. The court imposed 17 years rigorous imprisonment on each count to run concurrently, with fines of Rs. 25,000 per count and compensation of Rs. 200,000 per count, with default imprisonment terms.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant challenged the conviction on grounds that the prosecutrix's testimony was inconsistent, unreliable, and contained vital omissions and contradictions. The defence argued that the 3.5 year delay in reporting was unjustified, the reasons for delay were false, and the victim's subsequent conduct was suspicious. Additional grounds included claims that the trial judge incorrectly rejected the dock statement by shifting the burden of proof, and that Section 114(f) of the Evidence Ordinance should operate against the prosecution for failing to call Saman Kumara as a witness.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Inconsistent and erratic versions in the testimony of the prosecutrix renders her evidence unworthy of credence | Testimony of the prosecutrix is peppered with vital omissions and material contradictions which consequently taints her credibility and testimonial trustworthiness | 3.5 year undue belatedness of the police complaint renders the conviction wholly unsafe | Reasons adduced by the prosecutrix to justify the said belatedness are wholly unjustifiable and/or appear to be palpably false in view of the vital omissions coupled with her subsequent conduct following the alleged 1st incident | Learned Trial Judge's conclusive finding that the evidence of the prosecutrix is wholly consistent with the history recorded by the 2 medical officers is factually and legally flawed | Evidence of the prosecutrix does not favour the test of probability in view of the suspicious subsequent conduct of the prosecutrix following the alleged 1st incident of rape | Rejection of the dock statement is legally flawed as the LTJ has shifted the burden of proof to the accused-appellant thereby reversing the presumption of innocence and occasioning in a deprivation of a fair trial | Section 114(f) of the Evidence Ordinance operates against the prosecution for its failure to list and lead the evidence of Saman Kumara who was a vital witness to the prosecution and who would have provided the missing link in the prosecution case | Judgment of the Trial Court is legally and factually flawed thereby rendering the Judgment factually and legally untenable
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found that the prosecutrix (PW-1) was a reliable witness despite some inconsistencies and omissions in her testimony. The court considered her age at the time of the incident (13 years) and the eight-year gap before giving evidence. The medical evidence from the Judicial Medical Officer showing an old tear of hymen consistent with penetration and psychiatric evidence of adjustment disorder corroborated her testimony.
probability_assessment_by_court: The court found the victim's testimony credible when analyzed with her mental condition as a daughter raped by her father. The court noted that no daughter would falsely accuse her father of rape regardless of family disputes. The court applied the reasonable doubt standard and found the defence dock statement improbable and unbelievable, raising no reasonable doubt.
defence_version_summary: The accused pleaded not guilty and made a dock statement. The trial judge extensively analyzed the dock statement from pages 80-83 of the judgment and found it improbable and unbelievable. The defence suggested through cross-examination that the victim may have had sexual intercourse with her boyfriend Saman Kumara and falsely implicated her father, but the court rejected this theory. The court found the dock statement did not raise any reasonable doubt on the prosecution case.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal comprehensively addressed all grounds of appeal. On the issue of delayed complaint, the court accepted that a 13-year-old child victim of incestuous rape by her father who threatened to kill her and her mother had justifiable reasons for the 3.5 year delay, citing international authorities on child victim behavior. Regarding the prosecutrix's credibility, the court found minor inconsistencies explained by her age and the eight-year gap before testimony, noting human tendency to forget painful memories. The court held that while corroboration in rape cases is prudent, it is not legally essential when the victim's testimony is convincing, and here medical and psychiatric evidence corroborated her account. The court rejected claims that the trial judge improperly shifted the burden of proof, finding the dock statement was properly analyzed and rejected as improbable. On the failure to call Saman Kumara, the court held his evidence was unnecessary as the facts surrounding the SMS disclosure were undisputed. The court noted significantly that the victim informing Saman Kumara of her father's harassment negated the defence theory that she had sex with Saman Kumara and falsely implicated her father. Finding no legal or factual errors in the High Court judgment, the Court of Appeal affirmed the convictions and sentences.
coa_sentence_type: 17 years of rigorous imprisonment on each count, running concurrently, with fine of Rs. 25,000 per count and compensation of Rs. 200,000 per count with default imprisonment
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused-appellant Sarath Menikpura was convicted by the High Court of Ratnapura on two counts of raping his 13-year-old daughter during 2012, punishable under Section 364(3) of the Penal Code. He was sentenced to 17 years rigorous imprisonment on each count to run concurrently, with fines totaling Rs. 50,000 and compensation totaling Rs. 400,000. The appellant challenged the conviction arguing the victim's testimony was unreliable with inconsistencies, the 3.5 year delay in reporting was unjustified, the trial judge improperly rejected the dock statement, and the prosecution failed to call a material witness. The Court of Appeal dismissed all grounds, holding that the delay was justified given the child victim's fear of her father who threatened to kill her and her mother, that minor inconsistencies were explained by her age and trauma, that corroboration while prudent was not essential and was present through medical and psychiatric evidence, and that the trial judge properly evaluated and rejected the improbable dock statement. The Court of Appeal affirmed the High Court's judgment, convictions and sentences on June 27, 2024.
defence_counsel: Indica Mallawaratchy
hc_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found that the High Court Judge correctly analyzed the evidence and reached a proper conclusion. The trial judge properly considered all inconsistencies and omissions in the victim's testimony and correctly concluded they did not affect her credibility. The trial judge appropriately evaluated the dock statement extensively and found it improbable and unbelievable. The Court of Appeal held that the High Court judgment was both factually and legally correct.
precedents_cited_list: Sumanasena v. Attorney General (1999) 3 Sri L.R. 137 | Daradagamage Chandraratne Jayawardane alias Shantha v. The Attorney General Court of Appeal case No. CA/85/2013 decided on 25.05.2018 | Gurcharan Singh v. State of Haryane AIR (1972) SC 2661 | Sunil and Another v. The Attorney General (1986) 1 Sri L.R 230 | The King v. Themis Singho 45 N.L.R 378 | Premasiri and Another v. The Queen 77 NLR 85 | Regina v. W.D Dharmasena 58 N.L.R 15 | Bhoginbhai Hirjibhai v. state of Gujarat (1983) AIR S.C 753
standard_of_review_applied: The Court of Appeal reviewed whether the trial judge properly evaluated the evidence, whether legal and factual errors were made in the judgment, and whether the convictions and sentences were justified based on the evidence. The court applied the reasonable doubt standard in assessing whether the prosecution proved its case beyond reasonable doubt.

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 296 read with section 32 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The two accused-appellants were indicted for causing the death of Mohomad Anzarge Rumesh Imran on 17-04-2007. The deceased's mother testified that four persons including the appellants came to their house searching for her husband who had failed to provide overseas jobs despite taking money. When the husband was not found, an altercation ensued resulting in the 2nd appellant stabbing the deceased in the abdominal area. The deceased later succumbed to his injuries at the hospital.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 296 read with section 32 of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: After a trial without a jury, the learned High Court Judge of Kuliyapitiya found the appellants guilty as charged for the offence of murder by judgment dated 04-09-2020. Both appellants were sentenced to death.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The 1st appellant contended that the prosecution did not prove common intention, the High Court Judge did not evaluate his dock statement, and there was evidence for culpable homicide not amounting to murder which was not considered. The 2nd appellant raised grounds including premature judgment before analyzing defence evidence, wrongly casting burden on accused, failure to correctly evaluate eyewitness evidence, errors in evaluating common intention, and failure to consider culpable homicide not amounting to murder.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The prosecution has not proven the common intention of the 1st accused-appellant | The learned High Court Judge has not evaluated the dock statement of the 1st accused-appellant | There was evidence relating to culpable homicide not amounting to murder, and the learned High Court Judge has failed to evaluate evidence in that regard | Did the learned High Court Judge err in prematurely judging the case before the analysis of the defence evidence | Did the learned High Court Judge err in wrongly casting a burden on the accused to rebut the evidence against them | Has the learned High Court Judge erred in failing to correctly to evaluate the evidence of PW-02 | Has the learned High Court Judge erred in accepting the evidence of PW-02 with regard to the omissions and other infirmities | Has the learned High Court Judge erred in wrongfully evaluating common intention or non-evaluation of common intention | Has the learned High Court Judge erred in not considering the law in relation to culpable homicide not amounting to murder | Do the failure to adopt previous proceedings fatal to sustain a conviction
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The mother of the deceased (PW-02) was the sole eyewitness to the incident. Her evidence was admitted to have omissions and infirmities, including suggestions that she failed to mention in her police statement that the 2nd appellant assaulted her son. Defence suggested she came with a knife which caused the injuries, which she denied.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court considered whether evidence showed intentional murder or culpable homicide arising from sudden fight and grave provocation
defence_version_summary: The 1st appellant made a dock statement claiming the deceased's father had cheated them of money promised for overseas employment, they came to demand return of money, and a brawl occurred which the mother started with a knife resulting in an unfortunate occurrence. The 2nd appellant remained silent and provided no statement.
legal_errors_description: The learned High Court Judge failed to consider whether the actions of the appellants would fall under exception 1 of section 294 of the Penal Code as culpable homicide not amounting to murder, despite evidence showing the incident arose from sudden fight due to grave provocation
procedural_defects_description: The trial Judge failed to consider the alternative of culpable homicide not amounting to murder when there was a basis for such finding in the evidence, which is a duty even when such defence was not raised by the accused
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found that the learned High Court Judge considered relevant factors but failed to apply section 294 exception 1 of the Penal Code. The evidence clearly established that the appellants had no intention of harming the deceased when they came to the house, and the fatal injury sparked off as a sudden fight due to grave provocation arising from cumulative frustration over the father's actions. The fact that only one stab wound was inflicted despite claims of repeated stabbing showed it was a sudden fight not an intentional attack. The Court held it was the duty of the trial Judge to consider culpable homicide even when not raised by defence. The 1st appellant's common intention was established as he was part of the group that assaulted the deceased. The death was an unfortunate incident where the deceased paid for his father's sins.
coa_sentence_type: 10 years each rigorous imprisonment and fine of Rs. 25,000 each with 1 year simple imprisonment in default
brief_judgment_file_summary: Two accused-appellants were convicted by the High Court of Kuliyapitiya for murdering Mohomad Anzarge Rumesh Imran on 17-04-2007 and sentenced to death. The incident arose when they came searching for the deceased's father who had cheated them of money for overseas employment. An altercation resulted in the 2nd appellant stabbing the deceased who died from the injury. On appeal, the Court of Appeal found the High Court Judge erred in not considering whether the evidence supported culpable homicide not amounting to murder under exception 1 of section 294 (grave and sudden provocation). The conviction was modified to culpable homicide not amounting to murder under section 297, and both appellants were sentenced to 10 years rigorous imprisonment, fines of Rs. 25,000 each, and compensation of Rs. 500,000 each to the deceased's mother.
defence_counsel: Chathura Amarathunga for the 1st Accused-Appellant; Nalin Ladduwahetty, P.C. with Kavithri Ubeysekera for the 2nd Accused-Appellant
cause_of_death_exact_text: one stab wound to his abdominal area which has resulted in loss of blood, which has contributed towards his death
hc_analysis_summary: The learned High Court Judge considered the factors including the background of the incident and provocation in the judgment but failed to draw attention to whether the actions of the appellants would fall under general exceptions stated in section 294 of the Penal Code. The trial Judge did not consider the alternative of culpable homicide not amounting to murder despite having a basis for such finding in the evidence.
precedents_cited_list: King Vs. Bellana Withanage Eddin 41 NLR 345 | Gamini vs. The Attorney General (2011) 1 SLR 236
standard_of_review_applied: Appellate review of conviction and sentence with consideration of whether trial Judge properly evaluated evidence and applied correct legal principles
sentencing_principles_applied: The Court considered the facts and circumstances in determining punishment under the 2nd limb of section 297 of the Penal Code for culpable homicide not amounting to murder. Compensation was ordered as appropriate given the mother's loss, with sentence deemed to commence from date of original conviction.
