final_charge_after_appeal: Culpable homicide not amounting to murder under exception 1 of section 294 of the Penal Code, punishable under section 297

judges: Menaka Wijesundera J. | B. Sasi Mahendran J.
brief_facts_summary: The appellant was indicted for murdering his wife along with his mother (1st accused). On 30.12.2007, the deceased, a 19-year-old woman married to the appellant and living with him and his mother, was burned with kerosene oil. The father received a threatening phone call from the appellant before the incident. The victim suffered 65% burn injuries and died on 03.01.2008, after making three dying declarations stating that the appellant and 1st accused acted together - the appellant slapped her, banged her head on the wall, and the 1st accused poured kerosene and set her on fire while the appellant refused to help.
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted both accused for murder. The trial judge found that three dying declarations and medical evidence clearly demonstrated that the appellant and 1st accused acted in furtherance of a common murderous intention. The type of injuries inflicted and the appellant's threatening phone call to the father prior to the incident demonstrated murderous intentions.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The main ground of appeal was that the trial judge had not considered the dying declaration properly and the case for the prosecution had not been proved beyond a reasonable doubt. The defence argued that the dying declarations were deficient and contradicted each other, that the police recorded the statement without proper permission from medical authorities, and that the relative's statement was coached as it was made only after the victim's death.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The trial judge had not considered the dying declaration properly | The case for the prosecution had not been proved beyond a reasonable doubt | The dying declarations of the deceased are deficient and contradict each other | The dying declaration made to the police is questionable because permission from medical authorities was not obtained | The relative's dying declaration statement was coached as it was made only after the victim died
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court found the three dying declarations to be very consistent, clearly demonstrating the cause of death and the actions of the two accused. The father's emotional testimony and the relative's statement were accepted as truthful. The doctor who conducted the post-mortem confirmed the deceased was conscious and able to speak, and ruled out accident or suicide.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court found that prosecution proved beyond a reasonable doubt that the appellant acted with common murderous intention with the first accused and committed the murder
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty and gave evidence on oath. He claimed the deceased was of quarrelsome nature and on the day of the incident fought with him for not having ginger at home to serve ginger tea when her parents came. He said he hit her and went to the toilet, and when he came back she had set fire to herself. The court rejected this version.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal thoroughly examined the validity of the dying declarations and found them consistent and reliable. The Court applied the guidelines from Gamini Attanayake vs Attorney General and other precedents, verifying that the deceased's statements were true and accurate, could be accepted beyond reasonable doubt, the witnesses quoting the declarations were truthful, the deceased was able to speak at the time, and she could identify the assailants. The Court rejected the defence's arguments about contradictions and procedural defects, finding that the police properly obtained permission from the nurse in charge before recording the statement and that the relative's delayed statement was understandable given lack of familiarity with the criminal justice system. The Court emphasized the principle from Ambika Prasad that a judge must ensure guilty persons do not escape. The medical evidence confirming 65% fatal burn injuries and the doctor's testimony that the deceased was conscious and could speak, combined with the three consistent dying declarations, proved the case beyond reasonable doubt.
coa_sentence_type: Murder conviction affirmed
brief_judgment_file_summary: Mohammed Hussain Mohamed Firnas and Abdul Kareem Kurrathul Ain were convicted by the High Court of Colombo for the murder of the appellant's wife on 30.12.2007. The victim suffered 65% burn injuries after the 1st accused poured kerosene and set her on fire while the appellant refused to help, and she died on 03.01.2008 after making three dying declarations to her father, a relative, and police. The appellant appealed arguing the dying declarations were improperly considered and contradictory. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal on 25.07.2024, finding the dying declarations were consistent and reliable, the deceased was able to speak and identify her assailants, the witnesses were truthful, and the prosecution proved the case beyond reasonable doubt. The conviction and sentence were affirmed.
defence_counsel: N. M Shaheid with Zaid Ali and Wazeem Amhar
cause_of_death_exact_text: burn injuries
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court properly evaluated the three dying declarations and medical evidence, finding they clearly demonstrated that the appellant and 1st accused acted in furtherance of a common murderous intention. The Court of Appeal found no errors in the High Court's analysis and affirmed the conviction.
precedents_cited_list: CA-41-2009 | Gamini Attanayake vs the Attorney General CA-3-2011 | Somasundera vs The Queen 76 NLR 10 | Perera vs Jayasinghe 48 NLR 17 | Sigera v Attorney General (2011) 1 Sri.L.R. 201 | Ambika Prasad vs State of New Delhi 2000 SCC Crl 522
standard_of_review_applied: The Court applied the standard of whether the prosecution proved the case beyond a reasonable doubt, examining the validity and reliability of dying declarations according to established legal principles

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code (Count 1 - Murder) and Section 382 of the Penal Code (Count 2 - Robbery)
brief_facts_summary: On 22-05-2002, the appellant came to a building site at Kaldamulla inquiring about satalin planks advertised for sale. He went upstairs with the deceased son of PW-01 Lalani Fonseka, stabbed him to death with a knife, then came down with a blood-soaked knife, robbed PW-01's gold chain at knifepoint and fled. The deceased died from stab wounds hours later. The appellant was arrested on 28-05-2002, and a gold chain was recovered from a jewellery shop in Sea Street where he allegedly sold it, and a knife was recovered from behind his house.
evidence_type_secondary: Physical evidence, Medical evidence, Recovery of stolen property
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code (Count 1 - Murder) and Section 382 of the Penal Code (Count 2 - Robbery)
hc_sentence_type: Death sentence for Count 1 (Murder) and 12 years rigorous imprisonment for Count 2 (Robbery), with fine and compensation
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court of Colombo found the appellant guilty as charged on both counts after a trial without a jury. The court accepted the prosecution's evidence including the eyewitness testimony of PW-01, the identification parade, the recovery of the gold chain and knife, and medical evidence. The appellant was sentenced to death for murder and 12 years rigorous imprisonment for robbery, with a fine of Rs. 50,000 (2 years default) and compensation of Rs. 25,000 (1 year default).
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant challenged his conviction and sentence on four main grounds: that the High Court Judge failed to consider contradictions and omissions in the prosecution case; that the Judge erred in evaluating evidence relating to the identification of the appellant; that the Judge failed to consider discrepancies in PW-01's evidence in favour of the appellant; and that the Judge erred in disregarding the appellant's dock statement.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Did the learned High Court Judge err in law by failing to consider contradictions and omissions in the prosecution case in favour of the defence | Did the learned High Court Judge err in evaluating the evidence in relation to the identification of the appellant | Did the learned High Court Judge err in failing to consider the discrepancies in the evidence of PW-01 in favour of the appellant | Did the learned High Court Judge err in disregarding the dock statement of the appellant
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found that PW-01 Lalani Fonseka was a credible eyewitness who had sufficient time to observe the appellant before and during the crime. The Court held that minor contradictions regarding whether the appellant and her son went upstairs together or separately were not material and did not shake the core of her testimony. The Court emphasized that the witness made her statement while emotionally distressed after her son was stabbed, and that the totality of her evidence had a ring of truth.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal found that the prosecution established its case beyond reasonable doubt. The Court assessed whether the alleged contradictions and omissions created reasonable doubt as to the totality of the evidence and concluded they did not. The Court found the eyewitness identification reliable, the recovery of stolen property properly established, and the defence dock statement insufficient to create reasonable doubt.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty and gave a dock statement (unsworn). He claimed he was arrested on 23-05-2002, shown to two females at the police station on the 25th, tortured by police, and forced to show a jewellery shop and say he sold a chain there. He claimed the police forced the shop owner to hand over a gold chain. He alleged one of the females identified him at the identification parade. The Court found his dock statement not credible, noting he failed to challenge prosecution witnesses on these allegations during cross-examination and failed to inform the Magistrate at the identification parade that he had been previously shown to the witness.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal conducted a comprehensive review and found no merit in any ground of appeal. The Court applied the principle from State of U.P. v. M.K. Anthony that evidence should be read as a whole to determine if it has a ring of truth, and minor discrepancies on trivial matters not touching the core of the case should not permit rejection of evidence. The Court applied the Turnbull Guidelines on identification evidence and found that PW-01 had sufficient time to observe the appellant during their conversation about the satalin planks and during the attack. The Court noted the appellant failed to properly challenge witnesses through cross-examination on his defence allegations, citing Sarwan Singh v. State of Punjab that when a party fails to put their case in cross-examination, the opponent's evidence should be accepted. Regarding the dock statement, the Court referred to Queen v. Kularathne and held that while a dock statement has evidential value, it suffers from the infirmity that it is not given under oath or subject to cross-examination. The Court found the High Court Judge correctly considered all evidence and properly applied legal principles regarding burden of proof and reasonable doubt.
coa_sentence_type: Death sentence for Count 1 (Murder) and 12 years rigorous imprisonment for Count 2 (Robbery), with fine of Rs. 50,000 (default 2 years rigorous imprisonment) and compensation of Rs. 25,000 (default 1 year rigorous imprisonment)
brief_judgment_file_summary: The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal of Sandun Dinusha Wanigasuriya against his conviction and sentence for the murder of Harshika Damith Fonseka and robbery of Lalani Fonseka at Kaldamulla on 22-05-2002. The High Court of Colombo had sentenced him to death for murder and 12 years rigorous imprisonment for robbery, plus fines and compensation. The appellant challenged his conviction on grounds of contradictions in prosecution evidence, improper evaluation of identification evidence, and failure to consider his dock statement. The Court of Appeal found that the eyewitness PW-01 had sufficient opportunity to observe the appellant, that minor contradictions did not undermine the core evidence, that the identification parade was properly conducted, and that the appellant failed to properly challenge prosecution witnesses through cross-examination. The Court affirmed the conviction and sentence, finding the High Court Judge correctly applied legal principles and properly evaluated all evidence.
defence_counsel: Nipun Samaratunga
cause_of_death_exact_text: The deceased has received a deep stab wound just below his right side armpit, which has penetrated the heart cavity and the lungs. The cause of death had been due to the injuries suffered by the deceased as a result of the stabbing.
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court Judge properly established that the prosecution proved a strong prima facie case before considering whether the defence created reasonable doubt. The Judge considered the evidence of prosecution witnesses separately and evaluated whether their evidence was cogent and believable. The Judge properly considered alleged contradictions, omissions and discrepancies to determine if they created reasonable doubt in the prosecution case. The Court of Appeal found the High Court Judge clearly understood and correctly applied legal provisions for considering evidence in criminal cases and properly evaluated the dock statement in its correct perspective.
precedents_cited_list: State of Uttar Pradesh v. Anthony 1985 AIR SC 48 | State of U.P. v. M.K. Anthony AIR 1985 SC 48 | Regina v. Turnbull (1977) QB 224 | Sarwan Singh v. State of Punjab 2002 AIR Supreme Court iii 3652 | Boby Mathew v. State of Karnataka 2004 3 Cri. L.J. 3003 | Pilippu Mandige Nalaka Krishantha Kumara Thisera v. A.G CA 87/2005 | King v. Vellayan Sittambaram (1918) 20 NLR 257 | Queen v. Buddharakkita Thero (1962) 63 NLR 433 | Queen v. Kularathne (1968) 71 NLR 529
standard_of_review_applied: The Court of Appeal reviewed whether the trial judge properly evaluated evidence, correctly applied legal principles regarding identification evidence, contradictions and omissions, and dock statements. The Court examined whether the High Court's findings were reasonable based on the evidence and whether proper directions on burden of proof and reasonable doubt were given.

judges: Menaka Wijesundera, J | Wickum A. Kaluarachchi, J
offence_sections: Section 54A (b) and 54A (d) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance (as amended)
brief_facts_summary: An informant provided information to PW-1 at Colombo Crimes Division about a woman carrying heroin in the Grandpass area. A raid team of nine police officers was organized and proceeded to Stacepura. The informant gave a second information describing the woman's clothing (black trouser and purple blouse). Police officers found the accused-appellant near a playground and PW-7 (Woman Police Constable 'Deepika') searched her, recovering a parcel of heroin (3.62 grams) from her right trouser pocket. They searched her house finding nothing, then went to Dedigama Pawning Centre to weigh and seal the heroin.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 54A (b) and 54A (d) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance (as amended)
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court Judge convicted the accused-appellant on both charges of trafficking and possession of 3.62 grams of heroin on 28.04.2023. The Judge sentenced the appellant to life imprisonment for both charges.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant challenged the conviction on multiple grounds including that the information which formed the source of the raid had inherent discrepancies and infirmities, the prosecution case was improbable, there was reasonable doubt whether a Woman Police Constable accompanied the raid team, there was insufficient evidence to prove trafficking and possession beyond reasonable doubt, and the High Court Judge misdirected himself on facts.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The learned High Court Judge failed to notice, consider, and evaluate that the 'information' which is the 'source' of present matter has inherent discrepancies/infirmities | The learned High Court Judge failed to take cognizance of the improbability of the prosecution case | The learned High Court Judge failed to consider and evaluate that there is a reasonable doubt whether a Woman Police Constable accompanied the raid team | The prosecution had failed to act under Rule 52 of the Supreme Court Rules (Conduct and Etiquette for Attorneys-at-Law) Rules 1988 | The learned High Court Judge failed to consider that there is no sufficient evidence to prove beyond a reasonable doubt, the charge of trafficking | The learned High Court Judge failed to consider whether the prosecution has proved the possession of heroin beyond a reasonable doubt | The learned High Court Judge misdirected himself on the facts and convicted the appellant | The conviction and the sentence are bad in law
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found vital discrepancies between PW-1 and PW-7's testimonies regarding the raid, including contradictions about whether the appellant kept silent or denied possessing illegal substances when questioned, the duration of the house search (40 minutes vs 10 minutes), and the distance walked. The court also found the information received by PW-1 contained infirmities - the informant allegedly did not provide identity or location details, yet PW-1 recorded these specifics in the information book.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal found the prosecution story totally improbable, particularly the timeline and logistics of the raid. The court noted that if police walked 500 meters to 1 kilometer after receiving information that the woman was leaving her house, it was impossible they could apprehend her within 50 meters of her house as claimed.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty. In her dock statement, she claimed she was arrested at her home, contradicting the prosecution's version that she was arrested near a playground. The defence suggested in cross-examination that police came to arrest the appellant's husband. The High Court wrongly stated this suggestion was not made, but it appeared at page 98 of the appeal brief.
legal_errors_description: The learned High Court Judge failed to properly analyze the evidence and identify vital discrepancies in the information received and the raid narrative. The Judge also wrongly stated that the defence did not suggest police came to arrest the appellant's husband, when this suggestion was actually made in cross-examination at page 98 of the appeal brief.
procedural_defects_description: PW-1 did not make notes in compliance with Section 1(V) of Police Departmental Order No. A16 regarding the search of the appellant's house. PW-8 (S.I. Jayathilake) also failed to make any entries despite his involvement in searching the house, claiming he did not take part in any act relating to the raid, which contradicted PW-1's evidence.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal focused primarily on the improbability of the prosecution case. The court identified a vital infirmity in the information received - PW-1's oral testimony indicated the informant did not provide identity or location details, yet the information book entry included that 'Niroshan's wife' residing in 'Stacepura' was carrying heroin. The court found the timeline improbable: if the woman was leaving her house when police received the second information, and police then walked 500 meters to 1 kilometer, it was impossible to apprehend her within 50 meters of her house. The court also found vital contradictions between PW-1 and PW-7 regarding whether the appellant spoke when questioned, the duration of the house search, and other details. These contradictions raised reasonable doubt about whether the raid occurred as described or whether the appellant was arrested at home as she claimed. The court held that the prosecution failed to prove beyond reasonable doubt that a raid was carried out in the manner described by prosecution witnesses.
coa_sentence_type: Acquitted of both charges, convictions and sentences set aside
brief_judgment_file_summary: Anthony Theresa was convicted by the High Court of Colombo on 28.04.2023 for trafficking and possession of 3.62 grams of heroin under Section 54A(b) and 54A(d) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance and sentenced to life imprisonment on both charges. She appealed arguing the information forming the basis of the raid contained discrepancies, the prosecution case was improbable, and there were contradictions in witness testimony. The Court of Appeal found vital infirmities in the information received by police, noting that PW-1's oral evidence contradicted what was recorded in the information book. The court held the raid timeline was improbable and identified multiple contradictions between PW-1 and PW-7's testimony. The Court of Appeal concluded the prosecution failed to prove beyond reasonable doubt that the raid occurred as described, set aside the conviction and sentences, and acquitted the appellant of both charges on 26.06.2024.
defence_counsel: Kavithri Hirusha Ubeysekera, Assigned Counsel
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court Judge convicted the appellant without properly analyzing the vital discrepancies and infirmities in the prosecution evidence. The Judge failed to consider contradictions between PW-1 and PW-7's testimony and did not evaluate the improbability of the prosecution's timeline for the raid. The Court of Appeal noted the High Court Judge also wrongly stated that the defence did not cross-examine PW-1 about police coming to arrest the appellant's husband, when this suggestion was actually made.
standard_of_review_applied: Review of whether prosecution proved the case beyond reasonable doubt; evaluation of whether the learned High Court Judge properly analyzed evidence and identified discrepancies

judges: Menaka Wijesundera J. | Wickum A. Kaluarachchi J.
offence_sections: Section 297 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The appellant and three others were indicted for murder under the Penal Code. The incident occurred at a funeral house late at night where mourners were playing cards. A person named Bache shuffled the cards and the appellant objected, leading to a tussle. When the deceased intervened, the appellant assaulted and held the deceased while the 1st accused stabbed him, resulting in a fatal stab injury along with four other non-grievous injuries.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 297 of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the appellant and the 1st accused for culpable homicide not amounting to murder on the basis of a sudden fight. The trial judge rejected the evidence of PW3 as unreliable but accepted the testimony of PW16. The judge considered the nature of the circumstances at the time of the incident and found the appellant guilty under section 297 of the Penal Code.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The main ground of appeal was that the trial judge had misconstrued in applying section 32 of the Penal Code. The appellant argued that he did not share a common intention with the other accused at the time of the offence and that there was no prearranged plan among the accused.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The trial judge misconstrued in applying section 32 of the Penal Code | The appellant did not share a common intention with the other accused | There was no prearranged plan among the accused and the appellant
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The prosecution relied on two eye-witnesses, PW16 and PW3. The trial judge rejected PW3's evidence as unreliable but accepted PW16's testimony. Both witnesses testified that Bache started the fight and that the appellant challenged Bache, then assaulted and held the deceased while the 1st accused stabbed him.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court found that the evidence clearly showed the appellant participated in assaulting the deceased and shared common intention with the 1st accused at the time of the incident despite no prearranged plan.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty. The appellant gave a statement from the dock which was rejected by the trial judge on the basis that it had not been put to the prosecution witnesses. The Court found no credibility in the defence version.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal held that the trial judge correctly applied section 32 of the Penal Code regarding common intention. The Court noted that liability under section 32 can take place instantaneously without premeditation, and that common intention can be formed on the spur of the moment. The Court found that although the appellant and 1st accused had no prearranged plan, the evidence clearly showed they shared common intention at the time of the offence when the appellant assaulted and held the deceased while the 1st accused stabbed him. The Court cited The Queen vs Mahathun and another at 61 NLR 540 on the principle of common intention. The Court also applied the principle from Sunil Jayaratne vs Attorney General 2011 2 Sri L.R 92 that appellate courts should not interfere with trial judge's credibility assessments unless there is grave miscarriage of justice. The Court found no merit in the appellant's submissions and dismissed the appeal.
coa_sentence_type: Conviction and sentence imposed by High Court affirmed for culpable homicide not amounting to murder under section 297 of the Penal Code
brief_judgment_file_summary: Korku Hannadige Lahiru Dilshan, the 4th accused-appellant, was indicted with three others for murder. The High Court of Homagama convicted the appellant and 1st accused for culpable homicide not amounting to murder under section 297 of the Penal Code on the basis of a sudden fight at a funeral house. The appellant appealed arguing the trial judge misconstrued the application of section 32 of the Penal Code on common intention. The Court of Appeal held that common intention can be formed instantaneously without premeditation, and the evidence showed the appellant shared common intention with the 1st accused when he assaulted and held the deceased while the 1st accused stabbed him. The appeal was dismissed.
defence_counsel: Aruna Pathirana Arachchi
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted the appellant and 1st accused for culpable homicide not amounting to murder based on a sudden fight. The trial judge accepted PW16's evidence but rejected PW3 as unreliable. The Court of Appeal found the trial judge's analysis and application of section 32 on common intention to be correct and upheld the conviction.
precedents_cited_list: The Queen vs Mahathun and another at 61 NLR 540 | Sunil Jayaratne vs Attorney General 2011 2 Sri L.R 92
standard_of_review_applied: Appellate courts should not interfere with trial judge's credibility assessments and findings unless there is grave miscarriage of justice, as the trial judge has the priceless opportunity of watching the demeanor and deportment of witnesses

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 16(b) and Section 19(c) of the Bribery Act
brief_facts_summary: The accused-appellant, an Inspector of Police and OIC of Mawanalla traffic police, stopped PW-01, a hiring van driver, for crossing the center white line on 06-09-2008. On 10-09-2008, when PW-01 came to the police station to retrieve his license, the appellant allegedly demanded Rs. 2500/- or else he would have to go to Court and pay Rs. 5000/-. On 11-09-2008, PW-01 returned with Bribery Commission officials in a raid where he handed Rs. 2500/- to the appellant who placed it in his trouser pocket. The appellant resisted arrest violently and the money was recovered on the floor near his table.
evidence_type_secondary: Decoy witness testimony and documentary evidence
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 16(b) and Section 19(c) of the Bribery Act
hc_sentence_type: 5 years rigorous imprisonment for each of four counts to run concurrently, totaling 5 years rigorous imprisonment, with fines
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court found the appellant guilty on all four counts after trial. The learned High Court Judge considered both mitigatory and aggravating circumstances and imposed 5 years rigorous imprisonment for each count to run concurrently. In addition, fines of Rs. 5000/- each were imposed on all four counts with default imprisonment of one year each.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant raised two main grounds: first, that no fair trial was afforded to him at the High Court hearing, specifically arguing that the learned Judge improperly relied on documents marked P-08(1) to P-08(6) without giving him opportunity to explain, and wrongly considered evidence of PW-05 who was treated as a hostile witness. Second, that the evidence led at trial creates reasonable doubt as to the charges and he should have been acquitted, pointing to alleged contradictions in prosecution evidence and arguing he was falsely targeted for doing his duty correctly.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: No fair trial was afforded to the appellant at the hearing of this matter before the High Court | The evidence led at the trial creates a reasonable doubt as to the charges against the appellant and therefore, he should have been acquitted of the charges
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court found no material contradictions or omissions in the prosecution evidence. The testimony of PW-01, the decoy PW-02, and raid leader PW-03 was consistent on material matters. Minor discrepancies such as who first mentioned bringing the money were found to be trivial and not affecting the core of the prosecution case.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court found the prosecution evidence cogent and truthful enough to be acted upon beyond reasonable doubt. The defence version was found to be an attempt to create a false narrative.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty. He testified under oath that he refused PW-01's requests for spot fines as the offence did not qualify for one, and instructed him to come to Court on 17-09-2008. He claimed he never accepted any bribe and resisted arrest because he was innocent. He called WPC Prabha who supported his version that she was present and heard no money transaction. However, the prosecution in rebuttal proved that the appellant and his witness had communicated via mobile phone during the trial period, undermining their credibility.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found no merit in the appeal. On the fair trial ground, the COA held that the appellant failed to cross-examine witnesses on documentary evidence marked P-08(1) to P-08(6) and could not later claim he had no opportunity. Regarding PW-05 being treated as hostile, the COA found no prejudice as the witness gave nothing detrimental in chief and what he said under cross-examination was hearsay with no evidential value. The COA emphasized that official documents produced by PW-05 were undisputed. On the evidence ground, the COA held that alleged contradictions were trivial and did not go to the core of the case, citing precedents that minor discrepancies should not discredit otherwise reliable testimony. The COA found the prosecution evidence consistent and cogent on material matters. The defence version was found to be a false narrative, especially after rebuttal evidence showed the appellant and his witness had communicated during trial despite denying contact. The COA affirmed the conviction and sentence, finding the High Court Judge had cautiously and correctly evaluated all evidence.
coa_sentence_type: 5 years rigorous imprisonment (concurrent) affirmed with fines of Rs. 5000/- on each of four counts
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused-appellant, an Inspector of Police at Mawanalla traffic police, was indicted on four counts under sections 16(b) and 19(c) of the Bribery Act for soliciting and accepting a gratification of Rs. 2500/- from a van driver in September 2008. The High Court of Colombo convicted him on all counts on 16-11-2018 and sentenced him to 5 years rigorous imprisonment (concurrent) plus fines totaling Rs. 20,000/-. On appeal, he argued he was denied a fair trial and that contradictions created reasonable doubt. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal on 24-06-2024, holding that no fair trial denial occurred as the appellant failed to cross-examine on documentary evidence and the treatment of a hostile witness caused no prejudice. The COA found alleged contradictions trivial and that the prosecution evidence was consistent and cogent while the defence narrative was false, particularly after rebuttal evidence showed improper contact between the appellant and his witness during trial.
defence_counsel: Prasantha Lal De Alwis, P.C. with Chamara Wannisekara
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court Judge carefully considered whether the appellant's position that he could not issue a spot fine for crossing the center white line was correct. While finding this legally correct, the HC examined documents P-08(1) to P-08(6) and found that in practice spot fines were issued for such offences, even by the appellant on the same day for another motorist. The HC found no material contradictions in prosecution evidence and determined the defence version was a false narrative.
precedents_cited_list: The Queen Vs. R. R. Abilinu Fernando (1967) 70 NLR 73 | Galaboda Payagalage Sanath Wimalasiri Vs. Officer-in-Charge, Police Station, Maradana and Hon. Attorney General, SC Appeal No. 32/11 | E.R.S.R.Coomaraswamy, The Law of Evidence Vol II Book 2, 818 | The King Vs. N. A. Fernando (1945) 46 NLR 254 | Profulla Kumar Saker Vs. King Emperor A.I.R. 1931 Calcutta 491 | Mahathun and Others Vs. The Attorney General (2015) 1 SLR 74 | State of Uttar Pradesh Vs. Anthony 1985 AIR SC 48 | Bhoginbhai Hirjibhai V. State of Gujarat AIR 1983 SC 753
standard_of_review_applied: The Court of Appeal will not lightly disturb findings of a trial judge regarding acceptance or rejection of testimony unless manifestly wrong. Minor discrepancies should not be given excessive weight when evidence is generally reliable.
sentencing_principles_applied: The High Court considered both mitigatory and aggravating circumstances. The sentences were ordered to run concurrently showing consideration of mitigatory factors.

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 365 B (2) (b) of the Penal Code as amended by Act No. 22 of 1995
brief_facts_summary: The victim, a 7-year-old girl, was lured by the Appellant who showed her a child's picture on his mobile and took her to a nearby abandoned house. He removed her undergarment, positioned his genitalia between her legs near her vagina, and committed grave sexual abuse while covering her mouth to prevent her from crying. She immediately informed her mother, who notified her father working in Colombo, and a complaint was lodged the next day on 04.03.2009 after her father assaulted the Appellant.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 365 B (2) (b) of the Penal Code as amended by Act No. 22 of 1995
hc_sentence_type: 14 years rigorous imprisonment with fine of Rs.25,000 subject to 06 months simple imprisonment in default, and compensation of Rs.200,000 with 01-year rigorous imprisonment in default
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court Judge, after considering evidence from both parties, convicted the Appellant as charged for grave sexual abuse. The conviction was based on the credible testimony of the child victim (PW1) who was 7 years old at the time of the incident and gave evidence 10 years later, corroborated by her parents (PW2 and PW3). The medical evidence did not exclude sexual abuse, and the court found the victim's evidence convincing and cogent.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The Appellant challenged the conviction on four main grounds: (1) creditworthiness and trustworthiness of prosecution witnesses are questionable, (2) the victim's evidence was not corroborated with other evidence, (3) contradictions, omissions, and inconsistencies in the medical officer's evidence were not considered by the High Court Judge, and (4) the prosecution failed to prove the case beyond reasonable doubt.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Creditworthiness and trustworthiness of the prosecution witnesses are questionable | The evidence of the victim has not been corroborated with other evidence | Contradictions, omissions, and inconsistencies on the evidence of medical officer is not considered by the Learned High Court Judge | The prosecution has failed to prove the case beyond reasonable doubts
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The victim (PW1) testified 10 years after the incident when she was 16 years old. Her evidence was found credible and consistent despite minor omissions attributed to her age and passage of time. Her parents PW2 and PW3 corroborated material aspects of her testimony, including immediate complaint and police report filed the next day.
probability_assessment_by_court: The court assessed the testimonial trustworthiness and credibility of the child witness with utmost care, finding no ambiguity or infirmity affecting the root of the case. The evidence was deemed convincing and cogent, sufficient on its own to prove the case beyond reasonable doubt.
defence_version_summary: The Appellant pleaded not guilty. He gave a statement from the dock and called his brother as a defence witness. The defence attempted to challenge the victim's credibility by suggesting she was coached by parents and highlighting minor omissions and contradictions. The court found the defence version unconvincing compared to the prosecution's case.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal conducted a comprehensive analysis of child witness credibility, citing multiple international precedents emphasizing that children should not be held to the same exacting standards as adults but must still be assessed carefully. The court found that the High Court Judge properly assessed the child victim's evidence with caution and care, correctly concluding it was convincing and cogent. The Court of Appeal held that the defence failed to mark any contradictions and that three minor omissions highlighted were not forceful enough to shake the credibility of the victim or the core issues. The medical evidence, while showing certain practical errors, was consistent with the victim's testimony and did not exclude sexual abuse. The court emphasized that corroboration is not a sine qua non in sexual offence cases, though the victim's evidence was well corroborated by her parents on material points. The Court of Appeal concluded the prosecution proved the case beyond reasonable doubt and that no basis existed to interfere with the High Court's judgment.
coa_sentence_type: 14 years rigorous imprisonment with fine of Rs.25,000 subject to 06 months simple imprisonment in default, and compensation of Rs.200,000 with 01-year rigorous imprisonment in default, effective from the date of High Court judgment on 22/05/2020
brief_judgment_file_summary: This is an appeal against conviction for grave sexual abuse under Section 365 B (2) (b) of the Penal Code. The Appellant sexually abused a 7-year-old girl in an abandoned house on 03/03/2009. The High Court convicted him and sentenced him to 14 years rigorous imprisonment, a fine of Rs.25,000, and compensation of Rs.200,000. The Appellant challenged the conviction on grounds of witness credibility, lack of corroboration, medical inconsistencies, and failure to prove beyond reasonable doubt. The Court of Appeal extensively analyzed child witness credibility standards and found the High Court Judge properly assessed the victim's evidence as convincing and cogent, corroborated by her parents, with medical evidence consistent with her testimony. The appeal was dismissed and the sentence was ordered effective from the date of the High Court judgment.
defence_counsel: Sanjaya Senevirathne
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court Judge carefully assessed the evidence of the child victim with appropriate caution, finding her testimony credible and consistent. The court properly disregarded minor omissions considering the victim's age at the time of incident and the 10-year delay before testimony. The court correctly applied the principle that corroboration is not required in sexual offence cases and found the victim's evidence convincing on its own, though it was further supported by parental testimony.
precedents_cited_list: R v. Brasier 168 Eng. Rep.202 [1779] | Ratansinh Dalsukhbhai Nayak v. State of Gujarat [2004] 1 SCC 64 | Ranjeet Kumar Ram v. State of Bihar [2015] SCC Online SC 500 | R v. Baker EWCA Crim 4 [2010] | R v. B. (G), 1990 CanLII 7308 (SCC); [1990] 2 S.C.R. 30 | Rameshwar v. The State of Rajasthan, [1952] S.C.R. 377 @ 386 | Gamini Dolawatte V. Attorney General [1988] 1 Sri. L. R 221 | Bhargavan v.State of Kerala AIR 2004 SC 1058
standard_of_review_applied: The Court of Appeal reviewed whether the High Court Judge properly assessed the credibility and competence of the child witness, whether findings were supported by evidence, and whether the conviction was safe based on the evidence presented
sentencing_principles_applied: The Court of Appeal ordered the sentence to be effective from the date of the High Court judgment (22/05/2020) considering all circumstances of the case

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 345 as amended by the Amendment Act No. 22 of 1995 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The accused was the Human Resource Manager of Prima Ceylon Limited and the victim (PW-01) was a clerk working under him. On three separate occasions (15-01-2011, 16-01-2011, and 30-01-2011), the accused summoned PW-01 to work alone during holidays and committed acts of sexual harassment including embracing, touching her face, stroking her head, kissing her cheek and lips, and showing pornographic material. After the third incident, she complained to company management and subsequently to police on 07-02-2011.
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court Judge acquitted the accused on 16-09-2015, giving him the benefit of doubt. The HC Judge erroneously focused on the requirement to prove sexual gratification (which is not required for section 345 offences) and found there was unexplained delay in making the police complaint, creating doubt about the genuineness of the complaint.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The aggrieved party (PW-01) appealed the acquittal after the Attorney General declined to appeal. The main grounds were that the HC judgment was a complete misdirection on law and facts, that the HC wrongly required proof of sexual gratification for sexual harassment charges, and that the HC incorrectly found there was unexplained delay in making the complaint.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The judgment was pronounced by being completely misdirected as to the relevant law and facts | The judgment cannot be termed as a proper judgment in terms of section 283 of the Code of Criminal Procedure Act | The HC wrongly considered proof of sexual gratification as a necessary ingredient whereas section 345 does not require proving sexual gratification | The HC incorrectly held there was delay by the aggrieved party to lodge a complaint when the delay was well explained
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found PW-01's evidence credible and trustworthy with no significant contradictions. Her husband PW-10's testimony corroborated her distressed state and the complaint process. Security officers confirmed her attendance on the relevant dates. The COA held that in sexual harassment cases, eyewitness corroboration of the actual incident cannot be expected as perpetrators ensure no witnesses.
probability_assessment_by_court: The COA held that the prosecution proved the case beyond reasonable doubt. The victim's evidence had the ring of truth and her behavior was consistent with someone subjected to workplace sexual harassment by a superior. The defence claim of conspiracy by the company was rejected as there was no evidence the company initiated the complaint.
defence_version_summary: The accused pleaded not guilty. He admitted calling PW-01 to work on two occasions but claimed she came on her own on the third occasion. He denied all allegations of sexual harassment and claimed there was a conspiracy by Prima Ceylon Limited management to get rid of him because he exposed corrupt practices. The COA found this defence created no reasonable doubt and rejected the conspiracy theory.
legal_errors_description: The HC Judge was totally misdirected on the ingredients of section 345 offences by requiring proof of sexual gratification (which is only required for section 365B grave sexual abuse). The HC failed to properly analyze evidence, incorrectly found unexplained delay, and bizarrely cited facts from an unrelated murder case involving one Aranolis which had nothing to do with this case.
procedural_defects_description: The HC judgment did not comply with section 283 of the Code of Criminal Procedure Act as it failed to properly consider and analyze evidence from both prosecution and defence, and failed to provide proper reasoning for the decision.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal set aside the HC judgment as it could not be allowed to stand due to complete misdirection on law and facts. The COA conducted a fresh evaluation of evidence and found PW-01's testimony credible and truthful. The COA analyzed the workplace dynamics noting PW-01 was a vulnerable young employee whose livelihood depended on her job, explaining why she continued to respond to the accused's summons despite earlier harassment. The COA held that showing pornography, unwelcome physical contact by a superior in the workplace constituted sexual harassment under section 345. The COA rejected the accused's conspiracy defence and held the prosecution proved all three counts beyond reasonable doubt. The COA emphasized that sexual harassment cases require sensitive handling and courts should not be swayed by minor contradictions but examine broader probabilities and whether the victim's evidence inspires confidence.
coa_sentence_type: 7 years rigorous imprisonment total (2 years on count 1, 2 years on count 2, 3 years on count 3, to run consecutively), fines totaling Rs. 75,000 (Rs. 25,000 per count) with 6 months simple imprisonment in default on each count, and compensation of Rs. 750,000 to the victim with 1 year simple imprisonment in default
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused, a Human Resource Manager at Prima Ceylon Limited in Trincomalee, was indicted for three counts of sexual harassment under section 345 of the Penal Code against his subordinate employee PW-01 on 15-01-2011, 16-01-2011, and 30-01-2011. The High Court acquitted him on 16-09-2015 based on wrongly requiring proof of sexual gratification and finding unexplained delay. The victim appealed after the Attorney General declined to appeal. The Court of Appeal set aside the HC judgment as fundamentally flawed due to misdirection on law and failure to properly analyze evidence. After fresh evaluation, the COA found the prosecution proved all charges beyond reasonable doubt and convicted the accused, sentencing him to 7 years rigorous imprisonment, fines totaling Rs. 75,000, and compensation of Rs. 750,000 to the victim.
defence_counsel: Anuja Premaratna, P.C. with Nayana Dissanayake, Aviska Jayawardana, Natasha de Alwis, Bandula Dissanayake, Ishan Gampolage and Ramith Dunusinghe
hc_analysis_summary: The HC failed to consider or analyze evidence from either party in proper perspective. The HC wrongly required proof of sexual gratification for section 345 offences and erroneously found unexplained delay when the victim and her husband had clearly explained the complaint timeline. The HC bizarrely referenced an unrelated murder case involving one Aranolis and cited page 304 of the brief relating to that other case.
precedents_cited_list: Muthaiyah Yogarajah alias Yoga v Attorney General CA Appeal 55/06 decided on 24-02-2009 | CA 118/2002 decided on 26-03-2008 | State of Uttar Pradesh v M.K Anthoney (1984) S.C.J 236-1985 Cri. L.J. 493 at 498 | Vishaka And Others v State Of Rajasthan And Others decided on 13-08-1997 | Mahathun and Others v The Attorney General (2015) 1 SLR 74 | Apparel Export Promotion Council v A.K. Chopra 1999 1 SCC 259 decided on 20-01-1999 | Dharmasiri v Republic of Sri Lanka (2010) 2 SLR 241 | Kumara de Silva and two others v Attorney General (2010) 2 SLR 169 | Fradd v Brown and Co. Limited 20 NLR 282 | Boginbhai Hirjibhai v State of Gujarat (1983) AIR S.C. 753
standard_of_review_applied: The Court of Appeal exercised its power under section 337 of the Code of Criminal Procedure Act to reverse the acquittal and considering the age of the case (14 years since incident), decided not to order a retrial but instead to consider the evidence itself to determine whether prosecution proved the case beyond reasonable doubt
sentencing_principles_applied: The COA considered both mitigating factors (no previous convictions, age of 59 years, loss of employment) and aggravating factors (abuse of position of authority, workplace sexual harassment of vulnerable subordinate employee, multiple incidents). The Court imposed consecutive sentences for the three separate offences and ordered substantial compensation to the victim for psychological trauma under section 345 of the Penal Code.

judges: Menaka Wijesundera, J. | Wickum A. Kaluarachchi, J.
offence_sections: Section 300 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The accused-appellant was convicted of attempting to murder Senadheera Pathiranage Samarathunga. The appellant inflicted two stab injuries and eight cut injuries on the victim, with one injury being sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death. The appellant continued stabbing even after the victim fell to the ground and threatened bystanders with a knife not to help the victim.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 300 of the Penal Code
hc_sentence_type: Rigorous Imprisonment 20 years, Fine Rs. 25,000/- with default term 3 months, Compensation Rs. 1,000,000/- with default term 2 years RI, Rs. 50,000/- deposit under Assistance to and Protection of Victims of Crime and Witnesses Act with default term 6 months
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the appellant for attempted murder under Section 300 of the Penal Code and sentenced him to twenty years rigorous imprisonment. The trial judge considered the gravity and seriousness of the offence, pre-arrangement for the commission of the offence, the impact on the victim, the several injuries caused, and the unremorseful conduct of the accused. The trial judge also considered some mitigating factors including that the accused was a woman, pregnant, and a breast-feeding mother of an infant.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant admitted that the learned Trial Judge had rightly convicted the appellant for attempted murder charge and canvassed only the sentence. The appellant contended that it is not reasonable to impose the maximum punishment of twenty years and one million compensation is also excessive. The appellant argued that the learned Trial Judge considered only limited mitigatory factors and did not consider other factors that could have reduced the punishment.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Maximum punishment of twenty years rigorous imprisonment is excessive | Compensation of one million rupees is excessive | Trial Judge failed to consider all relevant mitigating factors in sentencing
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal reviewed the evidence showing the appellant inflicted two stab injuries and eight cut injuries on PW-1. Injury No. 2 in the Medico-Legal Report marked P-1 was an injury sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death. PW-1's evidence demonstrated the appellant's fierce nature in committing the crime, including continuing to stab after the victim fell and threatening bystanders.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court found the conviction proper based on eyewitness testimony and medical evidence showing intent to murder and serious injuries inflicted.
defence_version_summary: The appellant admitted the conviction was correct and did not challenge guilt. The defence focused solely on arguing the sentence was excessive and that additional mitigating factors should have been considered.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal agreed the conviction was proper but found the sentencing required reconsideration. While acknowledging aggravating factors including the number and severity of injuries, the appellant's unremorseful conduct, and threatening bystanders, the Court found the trial judge failed to adequately consider important mitigating factors. These included the 18-year delay between the offence (2004) and conviction (2022), the appellant's age (44 at offence, 62 at conviction, would be 82 at release), and having only one previous conviction from 1994 with a suspended sentence that had ended five years before this offence. The Court cited Priyanka Perera v. Attorney General regarding the impact of delays on sentencing. Balancing these factors, the Court reduced the imprisonment from 20 to 14 years and compensation from Rs. 1,000,000 to Rs. 500,000 while maintaining other penalties.
coa_sentence_type: Rigorous Imprisonment 14 years from date of conviction (22 June 2022), Fine Rs. 25,000/- with default term 3 months, Compensation Rs. 500,000/- (reduced from Rs. 1,000,000/-), Rs. 50,000/- deposit under Assistance to and Protection of Victims of Crime and Witnesses Act with default term 6 months
brief_judgment_file_summary: Tennekoon Mudiyanselage Karunarathne was convicted by the High Court of Kandy for attempted murder under Section 300 of the Penal Code for stabbing Senadheera Pathiranage Samarathunga, causing two stab wounds and eight cut injuries. The High Court sentenced him to 20 years rigorous imprisonment, Rs. 25,000 fine, and Rs. 1,000,000 compensation. The appellant challenged only the sentence as excessive, admitting the conviction was correct. The Court of Appeal found the trial judge failed to adequately consider mitigating factors including the 18-year delay from offence to conviction and the appellant's age. The Court reduced the sentence to 14 years rigorous imprisonment and compensation to Rs. 500,000, while maintaining other penalties.
defence_counsel: Indica Mallawaratchy
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court Judge considered aggravating factors including gravity of the offence, pre-arrangement, impact on victim, multiple injuries, and unremorseful conduct. However, the Court of Appeal found the trial judge failed to adequately consider important mitigating factors such as the period the accused faced trial, the time gap between offence and conviction, and the age of the accused.
precedents_cited_list: Priyanka Perera v. Attorney General S.C. Appeal 99/2006
standard_of_review_applied: Appeal of sentence - Court of Appeal reviewed whether the trial judge properly considered both aggravating and mitigating factors in imposing sentence
sentencing_principles_applied: The Court applied the principle that when sentencing an accused, both mitigating and aggravating factors must be considered. Mitigating factors include the period facing trial, time gap between offence and conviction, age of the accused, and previous convictions. Aggravating factors include number of injuries inflicted, impact on victim including physical and psychological trauma, and lack of remorse. The Court cited Priyanka Perera v. Attorney General regarding consideration of undue delay in sentencing.

judges: B. Sasi Mahendran, J. | Amal Ranaraja, J.
offence_sections: Section 54A(b) and Section 54A(d) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance as amended by Act No. 13 of 1984
brief_facts_summary: On November 02, 2013, Inspector Chandana (PW01) and his team from Colombo Crimes Division conducted surveillance in Nawagampura to apprehend drug traffickers. They spotted the appellant in suspicious behavior near Nawagampura ground, pursued and apprehended him. During the search, officers discovered a pink cellophane bag containing 3.19 grams of heroin from the appellant's possession.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 54A(b) and Section 54A(d) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance as amended by Act No. 13 of 1984
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the appellant on both charges of trafficking and possession of 3.19 grams of heroin. The court sentenced the appellant to life imprisonment on each charge.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant challenged the conviction arguing that the High Court Judge erred by convicting for trafficking without having additional evidence beyond possession. The appellant also contended that the Judge failed to consider the improbability of the prosecution's case, particularly regarding the circumstances of apprehension and the appellant's behavior upon spotting the officers.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Did the Learned High Court Judge err in law by convicting the appellant for trafficking without having additional evidence? | Did the Learned High Court Judge err in law by failing to consider the improbability of the prosecution's case?
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal accepted the evidence of PW01 Inspector Chandana regarding the surveillance operation, pursuit and arrest of the appellant. The Government Analyst report confirmed the substance was heroin weighing 3.19 grams (gross weight 19.69 grams). The Court rejected the appellant's claim of false implication.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court determined the large quantity of heroin (19.69 grams gross) was significantly more than for personal consumption, establishing beyond reasonable doubt that the appellant possessed it for trafficking purposes rather than personal use
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty and asserted that officers questioned him about one Nona Amma's residence, searched the premises, recovered items, and when he could not provide information about her whereabouts, officers falsely implicated him with a recovered item. The Court did not find the defence version credible.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal comprehensively analyzed the trafficking charge, citing Mohamed Iqbal Mohamed Sadat vs. The Attorney General to explain that trafficking requires additional evidence beyond mere possession. The Court found that the quantity of heroin (19.69 grams gross weight) was significantly larger than what an addict would possess for personal consumption, particularly given the high cost of narcotics. This substantial quantity provided reasonable inference that the appellant possessed the substance for distribution rather than personal use. The Court rejected the defence argument about the appellant's behavioral response to seeing officers, noting that human behavior is complex and varies between individuals based on unique circumstances and psychological state. The Court found the evidence overwhelming and the prosecution case proved beyond reasonable doubt.
coa_sentence_type: Life imprisonment on both charges, commencing from the date of conviction
brief_judgment_file_summary: Rajendra Dhanendran was convicted by the High Court of Colombo for trafficking and possession of 3.19 grams of heroin on November 02, 2013, and sentenced to life imprisonment on both charges. He appealed arguing insufficient evidence to prove trafficking and improbability of the prosecution case. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal, holding that the large quantity of heroin (19.69 grams gross) was evidence of trafficking rather than personal use, and that behavioral arguments about how the appellant should have reacted to seeing officers were flawed as human behavior varies based on individual circumstances.
defence_counsel: Amila Palliyage with Sandeepani Wijesooriya, Savani Udugampola, Lakitha Wakista Arachchi and Subaj De Silva
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted the appellant on both charges based on the evidence of police surveillance, recovery of heroin from the appellant's possession, and the Government Analyst report. The Court of Appeal found no error in the High Court's reasoning and upheld the conviction and sentence.
precedents_cited_list: Mohamed Iqbal Mohamed Sadat vs. The Attorney General, SC/SPL/LA/58/15, SC Appeal 110/15 decided on December 14, 2020
standard_of_review_applied: The Court of Appeal reviewed whether the High Court erred in law in convicting for trafficking without additional evidence and whether it failed to consider improbability of the prosecution case

judges: B. Sasi Mahendran, J. | Amal Ranaraja, J.
offence_sections: Section 365B (2)(b) of the Penal Code, as amended by Acts Nos. 22 of 1995, 28 of 1998, and 16 of 2006
brief_facts_summary: The accused was charged with two counts of grave sexual abuse against a nine-year-old victim, Balapuwaduge Aruna Lakshan Mendis, who was living with the accused and his mother. In December 2015, after dropping the victim at school, the accused told him to return early to receive a bicycle, then showed him a pornographic video and committed sexual acts including anal penetration. The victim initially told his mother who took no action, then later informed his brother who contacted the father, leading to a police complaint and medical examination in March 2016.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 365B (2)(b) of the Penal Code, as amended by Acts Nos. 22 of 1995, 28 of 1998, and 16 of 2006
hc_sentence_type: 14 years of rigorous imprisonment and fined Rs. 20,000 with a default penalty of three months, and ordered to pay Rs. 200,000 as compensation to the victim with a default sentence of six months
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court found the accused guilty of the first charge of grave sexual abuse under Section 365B (2)(b) of the Penal Code after trial. The prosecution presented evidence from eight witnesses and three productions, while the accused provided only a dock statement. The accused was sentenced to 14 years rigorous imprisonment with fines and compensation, but was acquitted of the second charge.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant challenged the conviction on three main grounds. First, he argued that PW1's evidence failed to satisfy tests of spontaneity, probability, and belatedness, and was not credible. Second, he contended that the trial judge did not give reasons for convicting on one count while acquitting on the other. Third, he claimed the trial judge failed to properly analyse the accused's dock statement.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The evidence of PW1 has failed to satisfy the test of spontaneity, probability, and belatedness, hence, PW1's evidence was not credible and the learned High Court would not have acted upon such evidence to convict the accused | That the learned trial judge has not given reasons to convict the Accused for one count and acquit from the other count | That the learned trial Judge has not analysed the dock statement of the accused in the correct perspective
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the victim PW1's testimony largely consistent despite a minor contradiction about whether he attended school on the day of the incident. The court held that this discrepancy was not substantial enough to create reasonable doubt, noting that the victim testified nine years after the incident and could not be expected to recall every minor detail. The victim's medical examination findings aligned with his account, showing three healed tears in the anal area.
probability_assessment_by_court: The court found no reasonable doubt about the victim's testimony, holding that the contradiction about school attendance was not substantial. The court noted that victims of sexual abuse often choose not to discuss their experiences and that minor inconsistencies after nine years are natural and do not affect credibility.
defence_version_summary: The accused pleaded not guilty and provided only a dock statement in his defence, claiming that the victim's father brought the allegation due to personal animosity. The accused did not call any defence witnesses. The court rejected this defence, noting that the victim explicitly stated he personally informed his father about the incident and had no animosity toward the accused.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal comprehensively reviewed the evidence and found that the victim's testimony was largely consistent and credible despite a minor contradiction about school attendance. The court applied the principle that witnesses cannot be expected to possess photographic memory, especially when testifying nine years after the incident. The medical evidence corroborated the victim's account with findings of three healed tears in the anal area. The court justified the delay in reporting, noting that the nine-year-old victim initially told his mother who took no action, and it was only later that he informed his father through his brother. The court rejected the defence claim of personal animosity, finding that the victim explicitly stated he personally informed his father. The court held that none of the grounds of appeal warranted interference with the High Court's findings, as the victim's testimony remained intact despite cross-examination and the contradiction pertained only to a minor detail that did not affect the core incident.
coa_sentence_type: 14 years of rigorous imprisonment and fined Rs. 20,000 with a default penalty of three months, and ordered to pay Rs. 200,000 as compensation to the victim with a default sentence of six months
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused-appellant Naththandige Densyl Nilantha was convicted by the High Court of Puttalam on one count of grave sexual abuse against a nine-year-old victim under Section 365B (2)(b) of the Penal Code and sentenced to 14 years rigorous imprisonment with fines and compensation, but acquitted on the second count. The accused appealed challenging the credibility of the victim's evidence, the lack of reasons for the different verdicts on the two counts, and the analysis of his dock statement. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal, holding that the victim's testimony was credible and consistent despite a minor contradiction about school attendance, that the delay in reporting was justified given the victim's age and circumstances, and that the defence claim of personal animosity was properly rejected. The conviction and sentence were upheld.
defence_counsel: Asankada D. Mendis
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted the accused on the first count of grave sexual abuse based on the prosecution evidence from eight witnesses and three productions, while acquitting him on the second count. The Court of Appeal found that the High Court properly evaluated the evidence and reached a justified conclusion, noting that the trial judge rightly dismissed the defence allegation of personal animosity.
precedents_cited_list: Bhoginbhai Hirjibhai v. State of Gujarat, AIR 1983 SC 753 | Don Kuruppu Arachchige Indika Gayan v The Republic of Sri Lanka, CA 205/2007 | Dhannasiri vs. The Republic of Sri Lanka 2012 (1) SLR 268 | Dhannasiri 2010 (2) SLR 241 | Udagama vs. AG 2000 (2) SLR 103
standard_of_review_applied: Appellate review of factual findings and credibility assessments made by the trial court, with deference to the trial judge's advantage of observing witnesses

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 364(2)(e) of the Penal Code punishable in terms of section 364(2) as amended by the Penal Code Amendment Act No. 22 of 1995
brief_facts_summary: The victim, a 12-year-old girl born on 13-02-1996, went to the appellant's house in October 2008 to make a telephone call to her elder sister. The appellant, who was her neighbor, allowed her to make the call. After the call, the appellant showed her a CD on TV, removed her clothes, and forcibly raped her on a sofa. The victim informed her elder sister 2-3 days later, and subsequently revealed the incident when hospitalized for abuse by her mother's paramour.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 364(2)(e) of the Penal Code punishable in terms of section 364(2) as amended by the Penal Code Amendment Act No. 22 of 1995
hc_sentence_type: 15 years rigorous imprisonment, fine of Rs. 25,000 with 12 months rigorous imprisonment in default, and compensation of Rs. 250,000 to be recovered as a fine
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court of Chilaw found the appellant guilty of raping a minor between 07-10-2007 and 06-10-2008 in violation of section 364(2)(e) of the Penal Code. After considering mitigatory and aggravating circumstances, the court sentenced him to 15 years rigorous imprisonment with a fine of Rs. 25,000 and compensation of Rs. 250,000, though the court failed to specify the recipient of compensation and default sentence for non-payment.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant argued that the High Court Judge erred in not considering infirmities in the prosecution evidence, failed to consider section 114 of the Evidence Ordinance when the prosecution did not call the victim's sister as a witness, claimed the indefinite date of offence in the indictment impaired his right to a fair trial, contended the Judge wrongly rejected the defence evidence, and alleged procedural failures caused disadvantage to the accused.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Did the learned High Court Judge err in not considering the infirmities in the prosecution evidence | Did the learned High Court Judge fail to consider the importance of section 114 of the Evidence Ordinance as relevant when the prosecution failed to call the evidence of the sister of the victim as a witness for the prosecution | Was the accused's entitlement for a fair trial impaired by the indefinite date of offence stated in the indictment | Did the learned High Court Judge err by wrongly rejecting the defence evidence | Did the learned High Court Judge's failure to act according to the required procedural steps cause a disadvantage to the accused
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The victim child (PW-02) testified consistently that the appellant raped her when she went to his house to make a telephone call. Medical evidence from the JMO confirmed repeated sexual intercourse. The mother (PW-03) testified that the victim revealed the appellant's rape while hospitalized. The appellant and his wife denied the incident, claiming the victim only made a call in the wife's presence outside the house.
probability_assessment_by_court: The court found the victim's evidence cogent and trustworthy despite initial delay in reporting the appellant's involvement, which was explained by the child's age, dependence on her mother, and the traumatic circumstances of ongoing abuse by another person. The court rejected the defence version as it was not properly put to prosecution witnesses during cross-examination.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty. He admitted the victim child came to his house to make a telephone call but claimed his wife was present at the time. He testified that the child spoke to his wife, who asked him to give his mobile phone to the child. He stated the phone was given outside the house and the child left after making the call. The court rejected this defence as not credible, finding it was not properly put to prosecution witnesses during cross-examination.
procedural_defects_description: The High Court Judge read over the indictment to the appellant before it was served on him, contrary to sections 195 and 196 of the Code of Criminal Procedure Act. However, the Court of Appeal found this did not cause material prejudice or failure of justice as the appellant was represented by counsel and the trial commenced nearly a year later, providing adequate time to prepare.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal comprehensively analyzed all grounds of appeal and found no merit. Regarding section 114 of the Evidence Ordinance, the COA held that since the victim's sister was called as a defence witness, her evidence was before the court and no prejudice occurred. On the indefinite date issue, the court noted the appellant admitted the victim came to his house, showing no alibi was prevented and citing precedent that date specificity is not material unless it prejudices the accused. The procedural irregularity of reading the indictment before service was found not to have caused material prejudice given the appellant had counsel and adequate preparation time. The court found the victim's evidence credible despite delay in reporting, which was explained by her age, dependence, and traumatic circumstances. The COA held the High Court Judge properly evaluated evidence and correctly rejected the defence version, which was not properly put to prosecution witnesses in cross-examination, citing precedents on the importance of confronting witnesses with the defence case.
coa_sentence_type: 15 years rigorous imprisonment, fine of Rs. 25,000 with 12 months rigorous imprisonment in default, and compensation of Rs. 250,000 to PW-02 with 18 months simple imprisonment in default. Sentence deemed to have commenced from 26-06-2019.
brief_judgment_file_summary: Randeni Aarachchige Dona Indunil Samantha was convicted by the High Court of Chilaw for raping a minor in October 2008 at Marawila, sentenced to 15 years rigorous imprisonment, fined Rs. 25,000, and ordered to pay Rs. 250,000 compensation. The appellant challenged the conviction on grounds of evidentiary infirmities, procedural irregularities, and wrongful rejection of defence evidence. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal, finding the victim's testimony credible and consistent, the procedural defects not prejudicial, and the defence case improperly presented as it was not put to prosecution witnesses during cross-examination. The COA varied the sentence only to specify that compensation should be paid to the victim (PW-02) with an 18-month simple imprisonment default term, and that the sentence commenced from the date of HC judgment (26-06-2019).
defence_counsel: Nalin Ladduwahetty, P.C. with Kavithri Ubeysekera
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court Judge considered whether the delay in the victim coming forward with the allegation against the appellant created doubt but found it did not. The judge examined the defence case and found the appellant failed to properly challenge prosecution evidence through cross-examination. The Court of Appeal found the HC Judge correctly evaluated the evidence and properly applied the burden of proof, though noted the judge's statements about failure to challenge evidence should be understood in the context that the defence version was not properly put to witnesses.
precedents_cited_list: James Silva Vs. The Republic of Sri Lanka (1980) 2 SLR 167 | Rex Vs. Dossi 13 Cr. App. R. 158 | D.R.M Pandithakoralage (Excise Inspector) Vs. V.K Selvanayagam 56 NLR 143 | D. Tikiribanda Vs. Attorney General, CA 64/2003 decided on 6-10-2009 reported in Bar Association Law Journal (2010) (B.L.R.) 92 | Mahathun and Others Vs. Attorney General (2015) 1 SLR 74 | Gamage Prabath Janaka Nayana Priyantha Perera Vs. Attorney General CA 107/2012 decided on 27-05-2016 | Sarwan Singh Vs. State of Punjab (2002) AIR S.C. iii 3652 | Pilippu Mandige Nalaka Krishantha Kumara Thisera Vs. AG, CA 87/2005 decided on 17-05-2007
standard_of_review_applied: The Court of Appeal applied the constitutional and statutory standards under Article 138 of the Constitution and section 436 of the Code of Criminal Procedure Act, examining whether errors, defects, or irregularities prejudiced substantial rights or occasioned a failure of justice. The court also applied the principle that it will not lightly disturb a trial judge's findings regarding acceptance or rejection of witnesses unless manifestly wrong.
sentencing_principles_applied: The High Court considered mitigatory and aggravating circumstances in sentencing. The Court of Appeal modified the sentence to specify the compensation recipient (the victim PW-02) and impose an 18-month simple imprisonment default term for non-payment of compensation. The sentence was deemed to have commenced from the date of conviction (26-06-2019) considering the appellant had been in incarceration since that date.

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Sections 54(A)(d) and 54(A)(b) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance as amended by Act No. 13 of 1984
brief_facts_summary: On 11th January 2017, IP/Danapala and his team from the Crime Prevention Unit of Wellawatta Police Station conducted a raid at Pasalwatte, Madampitiya based on informant information. The Appellant was arrested at 5.00pm after police found a pink cellophane bag containing 132 small packets of brown substance (10610 milligrams total) in his right shorts pocket. The substance tested positive for Heroin (Diacetylmorphine). The Appellant was taken to Letchumi Jewellers to weigh the substance and then handed over to Grandpass Police Station at 8.00pm under PR No.160/2017.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 54(A)(d) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance as amended by Act No. 13 of 1984
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court of Colombo found the Appellant guilty only for the first count (possession) and acquitted him on the trafficking count. The Learned High Court Judge imposed life imprisonment on the Appellant on 21st January 2020.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The Appellant challenged the conviction on four main grounds: (1) the raid was false, (2) there was no fair investigation, (3) contradictions inter se and per se were not considered by the trial court, and (4) the manifest false narrative of the raid was not properly evaluated.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The raid is false | No fair investigation | The contradictions inter se and per se not considered | That the manifest false narrative of the raid was not considered
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The prosecution called PW1, PW2, PW5, PW6 and PW8, while the Government Analyst report was admitted under Section 420. The Court found serious contradictions in PW1's evidence regarding the Criminal Note Pad and weighing equipment. The Court noted that PW1 denied arresting another person named Dhamma on the same day, but Magistrate Court records showed a suspect was arrested on 11.01.2017 for Cannabis possession and entered under PR No.161/17, the number immediately following this case's production number.
