probability_assessment_by_court: The Court found that the prosecution failed the probability test on multiple grounds: taking two and half hours to weigh 10610 milligrams was highly improbable, PW1's claim of not having a note pad contradicted his evidence of taking one, using a jewellery shop instead of the weighing kit already available was unexplained, and the failure to investigate the source of the drugs or search the Appellant's house raised serious doubts.
defence_version_summary: The Appellant pleaded not guilty and made a statement from the Dock, claiming this was an introduction and that he never possessed the drugs. The defence suggested that a person called Dhamma was arrested first and Heroin was recovered from a toilet ceiling of an old house near Dhamma's house, not from the Appellant. The Appellant did not call any witnesses. The Court of Appeal found the defence version raised very serious doubt in the prosecution case, especially given the evidence of another arrest on the same day that PW1 denied.
legal_errors_description: The Court of Appeal found that the Learned Trial Judge failed to look into the evidence in its correct perspective and should have accepted the evidence adduced by the Appellant. The prosecution failed to prove the case beyond reasonable doubt.
procedural_defects_description: PW1 did not record the information in the Criminal Note Pad as required. The raiding officers concealed the arrest of another person for a narcotic offence on the same day in the same police area, which raised very serious doubt. PW1 failed to take meaningful action to search the Appellant's house or investigate the source of the alleged drugs.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal conducted a thorough analysis of the evidence and found multiple serious flaws in the prosecution case. The Court emphasized that the burden of proof lies with the prosecution to establish guilt beyond reasonable doubt, citing Mohamed Nimnaz v. Attorney General, Attorney-General v. Rawther, and Miller v. Minister of Pensions. The Court applied the probability test and found the prosecution case failed on several grounds: (1) taking two and half hours to weigh a small quantity was highly improbable, (2) PW1's contradictory evidence about the Criminal Note Pad, (3) unexplained decision to use a jewellery shop instead of available weighing equipment, (4) lethargic investigation with no house search or source investigation, and (5) most critically, PW1's denial of arresting another person on the same day was contradicted by Magistrate Court records showing PR No.161/17 for Cannabis possession on 11.01.2017. The Court emphasized that a trial judge must consider evidence from both sides with an open mind and act as an administrator of justice, not merely as an umpire. The Court concluded that the defence case raised very serious doubt and the prosecution failed to prove the case beyond reasonable doubt.
coa_sentence_type: Acquittal - conviction and sentence set aside
brief_judgment_file_summary: Rupasinghe Arachchilage Chaturanga Priyadharshana was indicted for possession and trafficking of 3.78 grams of Heroin on 11th January 2017. The High Court of Colombo convicted him only on the possession count and imposed life imprisonment on 21/01/2020. On appeal, the Appellant challenged the raid as false, claimed unfair investigation, and argued that contradictions were not properly considered. The Court of Appeal found multiple serious flaws: PW1's contradictory evidence about note pads and weighing equipment, the improbable two and half hour weighing time, failure to investigate or search the house, and critically, PW1's denial of arresting another person on the same day was contradicted by Magistrate Court records. The Court held the prosecution failed to prove the case beyond reasonable doubt, set aside the conviction and sentence, and acquitted the Appellant.
defence_counsel: Hafeel Farisz with Sanjeewa Kodithuwakku
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted the Appellant only on the possession count and acquitted him on trafficking, imposing life imprisonment. The Court of Appeal found that the Learned Trial Judge failed to look into the evidence in its correct perspective and should have accepted the evidence adduced by the Appellant, as the prosecution had failed to prove the case beyond reasonable doubt.
precedents_cited_list: Mohamed Nimnaz v. Attorney General CA/95/94 | Attorney-General v. Rawther 25 NLR 385 [1987] 1 SLR 155 | Miller v. Minister of Pensions (1947) 2 All E.R. 372 | R v. Hepworth 1928 (AD) 265
standard_of_review_applied: The Court of Appeal reviewed whether the prosecution proved the case beyond reasonable doubt, applying the probability test to assess the credibility and reliability of the prosecution evidence against the defence case.

judges: Menaka Wijesundera, J | Wickum A. Kaluarachchi, J
offence_sections: Section 434 of the Penal Code read with Section 32, Section 300 of the Penal Code read with Section 32, Section 317 of the Penal Code read with Section 32
offence_category: House Trespass, Attempted Murder, Grievous Hurt
brief_facts_summary: On 06 October 2005 at about 2:00 am, two accused broke into the house of PW-2 Dayarathna and his wife PW-3 in Agulugalle. The 1st accused-appellant was armed with a sword and the 2nd accused carried a gun. The 2nd accused shot and injured PW-3, while the 1st accused assaulted PW-2 with the sword causing injuries to his mouth. Both victims identified the accused as persons known to them from childhood from the same village.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 434 of the Penal Code read with Section 32, Section 300 of the Penal Code read with Section 32, Section 317 of the Penal Code read with Section 32
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court Judge convicted both accused on all three counts after trial. The 2nd accused absconded and was tried in absentia. The learned High Court Judge correctly and carefully analyzed the prosecution evidence and found the case proved beyond reasonable doubt.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant challenged the conviction on three main grounds: first, that identification of the 1st accused-appellant had not been established; second, that the prosecution has not proved the case beyond reasonable doubt; and third, that the common intention doctrine cannot be applied in this case.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The identification of the 1st accused-appellant had not been established | The prosecution has not proved the case beyond a reasonable doubt | Common intention doctrine cannot be applied in this case
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: PW-3 provided cogent evidence identifying both accused after switching on emergency light, having known them from childhood in the same village. Although PW-2's identification evidence was weaker as the accused had covered faces, PW-3's clear identification was sufficient. PW-1 corroborated that PW-3 immediately named the accused after the incident.
probability_assessment_by_court: Court found that PW-3's identification evidence was cogent and could be accepted without any doubt, establishing identity beyond reasonable doubt even without considering PW-2's weaker identification evidence.
defence_version_summary: Both accused pleaded not guilty. The appellant neither gave evidence nor made a statement from the dock. The only defence witness, a Senior Superintendent of Police, stated he could not find the file he was asked to produce. Therefore, there was no substantive evidence from the defence.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal carefully analyzed the identification issue and found PW-3's evidence cogent and reliable as she identified both accused after switching on emergency light, having known them from childhood in the same village. The Court noted that even the appellant realized he was identified when he threatened the victims not to divulge their names. Regarding common intention under Section 32, the COA held this was one of the best cases illustrating the doctrine, as both accused came armed with different weapons (gun and sword), committed different criminal acts in furtherance of their common intention, and left together threatening the victims. The Court applied the principles from Queen V. Mahatun (61 NLR 540) that common intention can be formed on the spur of the moment and must be evidenced by criminal acts. The COA found no merit in any grounds of appeal and affirmed the High Court's conviction and sentence.
coa_sentence_type: Conviction and sentence imposed by High Court affirmed
brief_judgment_file_summary: The 1st accused-appellant was indicted with another in the High Court of Balapitiya for house trespass, attempted murder, and grievous hurt arising from an incident on 06 October 2005 where two armed men broke into a house and attacked the occupants. The High Court convicted both accused on all three counts. The appellant appealed challenging identification, sufficiency of evidence, and application of common intention doctrine. The Court of Appeal dismissed all grounds, finding PW-3's identification evidence cogent as she knew both accused from childhood and identified them with emergency light, and that the case perfectly illustrated common intention as both accused came armed, committed different criminal acts in furtherance of common intention, and left together. The appeal was dismissed and conviction and sentence affirmed.
defence_counsel: Epa Aruna Shantha with Dammika Perera and Navindu Kalansooriya
hc_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found that the prosecution evidence had been correctly and carefully analyzed by the learned High Court Judge. The COA saw no reason to interfere with the High Court judgment and held that the learned High Court Judge came to a correct conclusion.
precedents_cited_list: Queen V. Mahatun - 61 NLR 540 | Queen V. Vincent Fernando and two others - 65 NLR 265
standard_of_review_applied: Whether the High Court Judge correctly analyzed the evidence and whether the conviction was established beyond reasonable doubt

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | R. Gurusinghe, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 25(2) read with sections 40(1) and 40(a) of the Forest Ordinance
offence_category: Forest Offence - Illegal Transport of Timber
brief_facts_summary: Two accused persons were charged before the Magistrate's Court of Badulla for transporting timber valued at Rs. 381,401.07 during night using lorry No. 42-5722 without a valid permit. Both accused pleaded guilty and were sentenced. The timber was confiscated and the Magistrate ordered an inquiry under section 40(1) of the Forest Ordinance to determine whether the lorry should be confiscated. The registered owner Samsudeen Nissardeen claimed the vehicle was leased and used only for transporting fruits for his business.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 25(2) read with sections 40(1) and 40(a) of the Forest Ordinance
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court dismissed the revision application filed by the registered owner challenging the Magistrate's confiscation order dated 31-10-2017. The High Court determined that the learned Magistrate made the confiscation order in accordance with the law and found no exceptional circumstances warranting revision.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The petitioner argued that the Magistrate erred in interpreting the proviso of section 40(1) of the Forest Ordinance as amended. He contended the Magistrate failed to consider the proper burden of proof and that the High Court Judge erred in determining no exceptional circumstances existed. The petitioner submitted that evidence led at the inquiry was unchallenged and should have been accepted on the balance of probability in his favour.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The learned Magistrate erred in law when interpreting the requirements of the proviso of section 40(1) of the Forest Ordinance as amended by Forest (Amendment) Act No.65 of 2009 | The learned Magistrate failed to consider the required burden of proof in an inquiry of this nature | The learned High Court Judge erred when determining that no exceptional circumstances exist for the Court to invoke revisionary jurisdiction | None of the evidence led at the inquiry had been challenged by the prosecution at any material points | The mode of proof being balance of probability, the evidence of the registered owner should have been considered in favour of the petitioner | One cannot expect a registered owner to take all possible precautions in a given scenario | The evidence has to be considered in a fact sensitive manner
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The registered owner gave evidence that he purchased the lorry to transport fruits for his business, instructed the driver not to use it for other purposes, and had no knowledge of the illegal timber transport. A finance company representative confirmed the vehicle was under lease with regular payments. The prosecution did not materially challenge this evidence but only suggested the owner used the vehicle illegally to pay rentals, which the petitioner denied.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal held that the mode of proof in such inquiries is on the balance of probability. The satisfaction of the Court as mentioned in the proviso should be assessed on the balance of probability and evidence should be considered in a fact sensitive manner.
defence_version_summary: The registered owner claimed he ran the largest fruit stall in Badulla for over 25 years and purchased the lorry only to transport fruits. He stated the driver was a trusted employee of 5 years whom he instructed not to use the vehicle for hiring or illegal purposes. He allowed the driver to take the vehicle home when returning late or leaving early. The owner maintained he had no knowledge of the timber transport and this was the first offence involving his vehicle. The Court of Appeal found his evidence credible and uncontradicted.
legal_errors_description: The Magistrate erred by giving a strict interpretation to 'had taken all precautions to prevent the use' in the proviso of section 40(1) instead of considering evidence in a fact sensitive manner. The Magistrate incorrectly determined that verbal instructions were insufficient without considering the unique circumstances and that the evidence was unchallenged. The High Court Judge erred in upholding this narrow interpretation.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal held that the revisionary jurisdiction is a discretionary remedy exercisable upon exceptional circumstances requiring intervention to remedy a miscarriage of justice. The Court found the Magistrate failed to consider evidence in proper perspective by strictly interpreting 'all precautions' instead of adopting a pragmatic, fact-sensitive approach. The Court noted the evidence was uncontradicted that the vehicle was used only for transporting fruits, the driver was trusted for 5 years, oral instructions were given not to misuse the vehicle, and there were no prior offences. The Court held that expecting an owner to take all possible precautions is unreasonable and that the standard should be whether the owner took precautions expected under the given circumstances. The Court found a miscarriage of justice occurred and exceptional circumstances existed warranting exercise of revisionary powers. The Court cited recent precedents preferring liberal interpretation over strict interpretation in such inquiries.
coa_sentence_type: Confiscation order set aside and vehicle ordered to be released to petitioner
brief_judgment_file_summary: This is a revision application by registered owner Samsudeen Nissardeen challenging the confiscation of his lorry used by his driver to illegally transport timber. The Magistrate's Court confiscated the vehicle after finding the owner failed to prove he took all precautions to prevent the offence. The High Court dismissed the revision finding no exceptional circumstances. The Court of Appeal allowed the revision, holding that the lower courts erred by strictly interpreting 'all precautions' instead of considering the uncontradicted evidence in a fact-sensitive manner. The Court found exceptional circumstances existed as the owner gave instructions, the driver was trusted for 5 years, the vehicle was used only for fruits business, and there were no prior offences. The Court set aside both the Magistrate's and High Court's orders and ordered release of the vehicle.
prosecution_counsel: Maheshika Silva, D.S.G. with Jayalakshi De Silva, S.S.C.
defence_counsel: Amila Palliyage with Sandeepani Wijesooriya, Savani Udugampola, Tharinda Ratwatte, Lakitha Wakishta Arachchi and Subaj De Silva
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court upheld the Magistrate's confiscation order finding it was made in accordance with law and no exceptional circumstances existed to warrant revision. The Court of Appeal found this judgment could not be justified as the High Court reached its decision by justifying the narrow path taken by the Magistrate without properly considering the unique circumstances and uncontradicted evidence.
precedents_cited_list: SC Appeal No-111/2015, 113/2015 and 114/2015 decided on 27-05-2020 | Caderamanpulle Vs. Ceylon Paper Sacks Ltd (2001) 3 SLR 112 | Hotel Galaxy (Pvt) Ltd. Vs. Mercantile Hotels Management Ltd (1987) 1 SLR 5 | Wijesinghe Vs. Thamararatnam (Sriskantha Law Report Vol. IV page 47) | Vanik Incorporation Ltd. Vs. Jayasekare (1997) 2 SLR 365 | Mary Matilda Silva Vs. Inspector of Police Habarana CA (PHC) 86/97 decided on 08-07-2010 | The Finance Company PLC Vs. Priyantha Chandra and Five Others (2010) 2 SLR 220 | Orient Financial Services Corporation Limited Vs. Attorney General (2013) 1 SLR 208 | The Range Forest Officer, Ampara Vs. The Attorney General, CA (PHC) 37/2007 | CA-PHC-108-2010 decided on 26-08-2014 | Sadi Banda Vs. Officer in Charge of the Norton Bridge Police Station (2014) 1 SLR 33
standard_of_review_applied: Discretionary revisionary jurisdiction under Article 138 of the Constitution requiring existence of exceptional circumstances and miscarriage of justice
sentencing_principles_applied: When considering confiscation under the proviso of section 40(1) of the Forest Ordinance, the mode of proof is balance of probability and evidence must be considered in a pragmatic, fact-sensitive manner rather than expecting all possible precautions. The Court must consider whether the owner took precautions reasonably expected under the given circumstances and assess unique factors of each case.

judges: Menaka Wijesundera J. | Wickum A. Kaluarachchi J.
offence_sections: Rape of a girl less than sixteen years of age
brief_facts_summary: The victim and her younger sister were at home when the appellant, called Nimal bappa, came to the house and sent the sister to the boutique. The victim claims she lost consciousness and when she regained consciousness she had no clothes on. She says the appellant raped her but did not tell anyone because he threatened to kill her. Six months later, when taken to a doctor for stomach ache, it was discovered she was six months pregnant, and only then did she implicate the appellant.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Rape of a girl less than sixteen years of age
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court of Anuradhapura convicted the appellant on 27.08.2020 for the offence of rape of a girl less than sixteen years of age and imposed a sentence. The specific details of the High Court's reasoning and sentence are not explicitly stated in the Court of Appeal judgment.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant challenged the conviction on four main grounds: the trial judge failed to consider the improbability in the story of the victim (PW1); the trial judge failed to consider the belatedness of the first complaint by the victim which occurred six months after the incident; the prosecution failed to prove a specific date of the offence; and the trial judge had not considered the defense adequately.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The trial judge had failed to consider the improbability in the story of PW1 | The trial judge had failed to consider the belatedness of the 1st complaint by the victim | The prosecution had failed to prove a specific date of offence | The trial judge had not considered the defense adequately
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the victim's evidence to be inconsistent and improbable, with significant contradictions. The victim's sister, who was at the scene and supposedly told the victim what happened, did not corroborate the victim's testimony. The victim's claim of unconsciousness conflicted with her subsequent detailed description of events, and the six-month delay in reporting raised serious doubts about the truthfulness of her version.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court found multiple doubts haunting the prosecution case, including inconsistencies in the victim's evidence, lack of corroboration from the sister, improbability of the mother not noticing the pregnancy, and the six-month delay in reporting. The Court held that these created reasonable doubt and the prosecution failed to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt.
defence_version_summary: The appellant gave evidence on oath and denied the entire incident. The trial judge failed to consider the defense version in the proper perspective. The Court of Appeal found that the trial judge did not adequately consider the defense.
legal_errors_description: The trial judge failed to consider the improbabilities in the prosecution story and failed to properly evaluate the credibility of the victim's testimony in totality. The trial judge also failed to consider the defense adequately and did not properly apply the standard of proof beyond reasonable doubt.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found merit in all grounds of appeal raised by the appellant. The Court held that the victim's evidence was highly improbable and inconsistent, with the sister failing to corroborate the victim's version despite being present at the scene. The victim's claim of unconsciousness contradicted her subsequent detailed description of events. The six-month delay in reporting, with the complaint only made after a doctor discovered the pregnancy, raised serious doubts about the truthfulness of the allegation. The investigating officer noted the victim was obviously pregnant when the statement was recorded, making it improbable that the mother had not noticed earlier. The Court cited precedents on witness credibility and timely complaints, holding that inconsistent testimony is unreliable and undue delay creates doubt. The trial judge failed to properly evaluate these improbabilities and did not adequately consider the defense version. The Court found the prosecution failed to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt, and the conviction and sentence were erroneous and bad in law.
coa_sentence_type: Acquittal - conviction and sentence set aside
brief_judgment_file_summary: The appellant, Anthonilage Nimal Ranasinghe, was convicted by the High Court of Anuradhapura on 27.08.2020 for rape of a girl less than sixteen years of age. He appealed on grounds that the trial judge failed to consider improbabilities in the victim's story, the six-month delay in reporting, the failure to prove a specific date of offence, and inadequate consideration of the defense. The Court of Appeal found the victim's evidence inconsistent and improbable, with no corroboration from her sister who was present at the scene, and the significant delay in reporting created reasonable doubt. The Court held that the trial judge failed to properly evaluate witness credibility and adequately consider the defense. Finding merit in the grounds of appeal, the Court of Appeal allowed the appeal, set aside the conviction and sentence, and acquitted the appellant.
defence_counsel: Darshana Kuruppu with Sahan Weerasinghe
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted the appellant based on the victim's testimony. However, the Court of Appeal found that the trial judge failed to properly consider the improbabilities and inconsistencies in the victim's evidence, did not adequately evaluate the lack of corroboration from the sister, failed to consider the significance of the six-month delay in reporting, and did not give proper consideration to the defense version.
precedents_cited_list: Padmathilake vs Director General Commission to Investigate Bribery and Corruption 2009 2SLR | Haramanis vs Somalatha 3 Sri L.R. 365
standard_of_review_applied: The Court of Appeal applied the standard that the prosecution must prove its case beyond reasonable doubt, and that witness credibility should be subject to judicial evaluation in totality. The Court also applied the test for timely complaint that it should be made as early as could reasonably be expected in the circumstances.

judges: Menaka Wijesundera, J. | Wickum A. Kaluarachchi, J.
offence_sections: Section 54A(b) and 54A(d) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance as amended by Act No.13 of 1984
location_of_offence: Near mosque close to playground called 'Somaliyawa', Henamulla camp area
brief_facts_summary: On 24.07.2014 at approximately 15:15, IP Mahinda Wanasinghe received information from an informant about a bearded man named Kasun bringing heroin to a location near a mosque. A police team of twelve officers conducted a raid and arrested the accused-appellant after he allegedly turned back upon seeing police in uniform. Upon search, police found a light pink cellophane bag containing 2.64 grams of heroin in his right trouser pocket. The heroin was weighed and sealed at Dedigama Pawning Centre on Baseline Road.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 54A(b) and 54A(d) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance as amended by Act No.13 of 1984
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court Judge convicted the accused-appellant on both counts of trafficking and possessing 2.64 grams of heroin on 15.05.2019 and imposed life imprisonment for both counts. The Judge concluded that there were no discrepancies in prosecution evidence and that the charges were proved beyond reasonable doubt. The Judge convicted the appellant for trafficking stating that 2.64 grams of heroin was not for personal consumption and thus must have been kept with intention of trafficking.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The defence contended that the prosecution story was improbable due to contradictory timing evidence where PW-1 stated the van reached Colombo Municipal Council at 3:15 p.m. but also stated the arrest occurred at 3:15 p.m. Defence argued that despite information that the accused was bringing heroin from home, no search was conducted at his residence. Defence highlighted contradictions between PW-1 and PW-2 regarding whether detection occurred on a by-road or main road, whether handcuffs were taken during the raid, and unusual note-making procedures by PW-2.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Timing contradiction: PW-1 stated van reached location at 3:15 p.m. but also stated arrest occurred at 3:15 p.m., making prosecution story improbable | No search conducted at accused's home despite information he was bringing heroin from his residence | Contradiction between PW-1 and PW-2 regarding location of detection (by-road vs main road) | Contradiction regarding whether handcuffs were taken during raid (PW-1 said yes, PW-2 said no) | Unusual note-making procedure: PW-2 made notes on crime pad at police station instead of information book, and notes were pasted three days later | Main investigating officer PW-1 was in uniform during raid, which is unusual for such operations | High Court Judge failed to analyze prosecution evidence and did not consider contradictions | High Court Judge wrongly rejected dock statement for improper reasons | Charges not proved beyond reasonable doubt
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found that the High Court Judge failed to analyze prosecution evidence and merely narrated evidence without considering contradictions. Multiple discrepancies existed between PW-1 and PW-2 testimony regarding timing, location of detection, and whether handcuffs were taken. The Judge concluded charges were proved beyond reasonable doubt without addressing these contradictions or analyzing the evidence.
probability_assessment_by_court: Court of Appeal found that High Court failed to properly assess reasonable doubt and did not analyze contradictions and improbabilities in prosecution case
defence_version_summary: Accused-appellant made a dock statement claiming he was arrested without any reason. He did not call witnesses and did not give sworn evidence. High Court rejected the dock statement solely on the ground that the accused had not complained to a higher police officer about being illegally arrested. Court of Appeal found this reason for rejection to be improper and not a valid basis to disregard the dock statement.
legal_errors_description: High Court Judge wrongly convicted accused for trafficking on the basis that 2.64 grams of heroin was excess for personal consumption, which is not the correct legal test. Under Section 54A, trafficking requires proof of selling, giving, procuring, storing, administering, transporting, sending, delivering or distributing, not merely quantity assessment. High Court Judge also improperly rejected dock statement for irrelevant reason that accused had not complained to higher police officer.
procedural_defects_description: Judgment did not comply with Section 283(1) of Code of Criminal Procedure Act which requires judgment to contain points for determination, decision thereon, and reasons for decision. The High Court judgment contained only narration of evidence up to page 15 of 17 pages, then concluded charges proved without analysis or stating reasons.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found fundamental flaws in the High Court judgment. The judgment failed to analyze prosecution evidence and merely narrated evidence without addressing contradictions pointed out by defence counsel regarding timing, location of detection, handcuffs, and note-making procedures. The High Court Judge improperly rejected the dock statement solely because the accused had not complained to a higher police officer, which the Court of Appeal found to be no valid reason. The Court emphasized that under the presumption of innocence, every accused is free to state innocence via dock statement and the Trial Judge must consider it before rejecting with proper reasons. Additionally, the High Court wrongly convicted for trafficking based on quantity rather than proof of acts defined under Section 54A. The judgment violated Section 283(1) of CCPA by not containing points for determination and reasons for decision. Given ten years elapsed since the offence, five years of incarceration, and no fault of the accused, the Court of Appeal applied the principle 'Actus Curiae Neminem Gravabit' and refused to order retrial, citing precedents that refuse retrials where substantial time has elapsed.
coa_sentence_type: Convictions and sentences set aside; accused-appellant acquitted of both counts
brief_judgment_file_summary: Kottabadhuge Kasun Madhushanka was convicted by the High Court of Colombo for trafficking and possessing 2.64 grams of heroin on 24.07.2014 under Section 54A(b) and 54A(d) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance and sentenced to life imprisonment on both counts on 15.05.2019. The accused appealed against convictions and sentences. Defence counsel highlighted multiple contradictions in prosecution evidence regarding timing, location, and procedures, and argued the High Court failed to analyze evidence. The Court of Appeal found the High Court judgment fundamentally flawed as it failed to analyze prosecution evidence, improperly rejected the dock statement, wrongly applied the law on trafficking by relying on quantity rather than statutory definition, and violated Section 283(1) of CCPA by not containing points for determination and reasons. Given ten years elapsed since the offence and five years of incarceration with no fault of the accused, the Court of Appeal allowed the appeal, set aside the convictions and sentences, and acquitted the accused-appellant of both counts without ordering retrial.
defence_counsel: R. Arsecularatne, PC with Ms. Chamindri Arsecularatne, U. Muhandiramge, Tharindu Punchihewa, Pasindu Gamage, Punsi Gamage and Eranga Yakandawala
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court Judge's judgment was found to be fundamentally defective. Up to page 15 of the 17-page judgment, there was only narration of prosecution and defence evidence without any analysis. The Judge concluded charges were proved beyond reasonable doubt without considering contradictions pointed out by defence. The Court of Appeal found the High Court failed to analyze prosecution evidence, improperly rejected dock statement, and wrongly applied the law on trafficking conviction based on quantity rather than statutory requirements.
precedents_cited_list: Nandana V. Attorney General - (2008) 1 Sri L.R. 51 | Peter Singho V. Werapotiya - 55 NLR 157 | Queen V. Jayasinghe - 69 NLR 413 | L.C. Fernando V. Republic of Sri Lanka - 79 (2) NLR 313
standard_of_review_applied: Court of Appeal reviewed whether High Court properly analyzed prosecution evidence, considered defence submissions, applied correct legal principles, and complied with procedural requirements under Section 283(1) of Code of Criminal Procedure Act
sentencing_principles_applied: Court applied principle that discretion to order retrial should be exercised judicially considering nature of evidence, time elapsed since offence, period of incarceration suffered, and trauma of second trial. Applied maxim 'Actus Curiae Neminem Gravabit' (act of Court shall prejudice no man). Followed precedents refusing retrial where substantial time (over 3-4 years) has elapsed, particularly where ten years passed since offence and accused incarcerated for five years with no fault on his part.

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 365B(2)(b) of the Penal Code as amended by Penal Code Amendment Act No. 22 of 1995, 29 of 1998 and 16 of 2006
brief_facts_summary: The appellant was accused of committing grave sexual abuse on a 12-year-old minor girl by having intercrural sex with her on or about 18-05-2007 at Hanepola. The police commenced investigations after receiving a 119-call about a child being repeatedly raped. The victim stated the appellant, who was a frequent visitor to her home, took her to a room when she was alone and had intercrural sex with her after removing her clothes. Medical examination revealed a fimbriated hymen with no injuries, but the doctor opined intercrural sex and even penile penetration could occur without leaving marks.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 365B(2)(b) of the Penal Code as amended by Penal Code Amendment Act No. 22 of 1995, 29 of 1998 and 16 of 2006
hc_sentence_type: 14 years rigorous imprisonment, fine of Rs. 10,000 with 8 months simple imprisonment in default, and Rs. 200,000 compensation with 2 years rigorous imprisonment in default
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court of Gampaha found the appellant guilty as charged of grave sexual abuse on a minor under section 365B(2)(b) of the Penal Code. He was sentenced to 14 years rigorous imprisonment, a fine of Rs. 10,000 with default imprisonment of 8 months, and ordered to pay Rs. 200,000 as compensation to the victim with 2 years rigorous imprisonment in default. The default sentences were to be served consecutively.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant challenged both conviction and sentence on two main grounds. First, he argued the High Court Judge failed to properly evaluate the evidence of the victim and failed to give him the benefit of doubt. Second, he contended the prosecution failed to prove the date of offence and led conflicting evidence regarding the date. The defence argued the victim's evidence was inconsistent regarding whether intercrural sex or penile penetration occurred, and she was uncertain about the time of day the incident occurred.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The learned High Court Judge has failed to evaluate the evidence of PW-01 properly, and thereby had failed to give the benefit of the doubt to the accused appellant | The prosecution has failed to prove the date of offence and had led conflicting evidence with regard to the date of offence
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal held that the victim's evidence should be read as a whole to assess if it had a ring of truth. The Court noted the victim was 12 years old at the time of the incident and gave evidence 9 years later, and that she could not read or write despite attending school up to grade 9. The Court found discrepancies in her evidence regarding whether intercrural sex or penile penetration occurred, and omissions regarding blood and duration were not material discrepancies that created reasonable doubt about her credibility.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court assessed that minor discrepancies and omissions in the victim's evidence did not create reasonable doubt. The Court emphasized that the evidence must be considered in totality and that the victim's social background, age, and the passage of time should be factored into evaluating her testimony. The Court found the prosecution proved the case beyond reasonable doubt.
defence_version_summary: The accused pleaded not guilty. Making a dock statement only without calling witnesses, he claimed he was working in the brick kiln industry and was arrested at 10 p.m. after assaulting someone named Wasantha Rohana with a club around 5 p.m. when he saw Rohana scolding his mother. He stated he was initially told he was wanted as a suspect in a quarrel and only learned later it was a rape case. The Court found his defence did not create any doubt as to the victim's evidence and assessed it as not credible.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal comprehensively analyzed both grounds of appeal and found no merit in them. Regarding the date of offence, the Court held that any error in stating the date is not material unless it is the essence of the offence or the accused is prejudiced, which was not the case here. The Court emphasized that the victim was 12 years old when the incident occurred and gave evidence 9 years later, and her inability to remember exact dates did not create reasonable doubt. Regarding the evaluation of evidence, the Court found the High Court Judge correctly considered the evidence in totality and properly assessed the victim's credibility. The Court applied the principle that evidence should be read as a whole to determine if it has a ring of truth, and minor discrepancies on trivial matters not touching the core of the case should not lead to rejection of evidence. The Court held the victim's inconsistencies regarding whether intercrural sex or penile penetration occurred, and omissions about blood and duration, were not material discrepancies that undermined her credibility. The Court cited several precedents on accepting child victim testimony and the natural human tendency to forget painful details. The Court affirmed the conviction and sentence, finding the prosecution proved the case beyond reasonable doubt.
coa_sentence_type: 14 years rigorous imprisonment, fine of Rs. 10,000 with 8 months simple imprisonment in default, and Rs. 200,000 compensation with 2 years rigorous imprisonment in default, with default sentences to be served consecutively. Sentence deemed to commence from date of conviction 24-01-2020.
brief_judgment_file_summary: Maarukku Kankanamalage Anura Kumarasiri was convicted by the High Court of Gampaha for grave sexual abuse of a 12-year-old minor under section 365B(2)(b) of the Penal Code and sentenced to 14 years rigorous imprisonment, a fine of Rs. 10,000, and Rs. 200,000 compensation. He appealed on grounds that the High Court failed to properly evaluate the victim's evidence and the prosecution failed to prove the date of offence. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal, holding that any error in the date was not material as the accused was not misled or prejudiced, and that the victim's evidence when read in totality had a ring of truth despite minor discrepancies. The Court emphasized the victim's age, social circumstances, and the passage of time in evaluating her testimony. The conviction and sentence were affirmed with the sentence deemed to commence from the date of conviction.
defence_counsel: Kamal Perera with A. Fernando
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court Judge considered the evidence in its totality and assessed all relevant factors to determine the victim's evidence was cogent and truthful. The High Court properly considered all discrepancies alleged in relation to the evidence and came to determinations with sound reasoning. The Court of Appeal found no reason to disagree with the High Court's evaluation and found the High Court Judge correctly analyzed the evidence.
precedents_cited_list: R. Vs. Dossi 12 Cr. App. R., 158 | D.R.M Pandithacoralage Vs. V.K Selvenayagam 56 NLR 143 | D. Tikiri Banda Vs. The Attorney General, Bar Association Law Reports 2010 (B.L.R. 92) | Attorney General Vs. Dardadagamage Chandraratna Jayawardene alias Shantha, CA 85/2013 decided on 25-05-2018 | State of Uttar Pradesh Vs. M.K Anthoney (1984) S.C.J 236-1985 Cri. L.J. 493 at 498
standard_of_review_applied: The Court of Appeal reviewed whether the High Court properly evaluated the evidence and whether the prosecution proved the case beyond reasonable doubt. The Court applied the principle that the appellate court should attach due weight to the trial court's appreciation of evidence and should not reject evidence based on minor variations or infirmities unless there are weighty and formidable reasons.

judges: Menaka Wijesundera J. | Wickum A. Kaluarachchi J.
brief_facts_summary: The accused appellant was indicted for two charges of abduction and three charges of grave sexual abuse against a child victim. The offences occurred between 1.1.2002 to 5.12.2002 when the victim was in year three. The appellant, who was related to the victim, took her to the jungle on three occasions and sexually abused her by removing her undergarment and keeping his genitals between her legs. Medical examination revealed redness in the vaginal area indicative of frequent fondling.
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the appellant for all five charges after trial. The trial judge evaluated the evidence including the victim's testimony given 18 years after the incident, the mother's testimony, and medical evidence showing physical signs of abuse. The appellant had pleaded not guilty and made a dock statement denying the incident entirely, which the trial judge rejected with reasons.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant raised three main grounds of appeal. First, that the trial judge failed to evaluate the prosecution evidence in the correct perspective. Second, that the dock statement had been wrongly considered. Third, that the prosecution failed to prove its case beyond a reasonable doubt.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The trial judge had failed to evaluate the evidence of the prosecution in the correct perspective | The dock statement had been wrongly considered | The prosecution had failed to prove its case beyond a reasonable doubt
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The victim gave evidence after 18 years and was very reluctant, having to be prompted numerous times. She testified that the appellant, who was related to her, sexually abused her three times when she was in year three. The mother corroborated that the victim complained of stomach ache and disclosed the abuse. The doctor's evidence and case history corroborated the victim's testimony, with medical findings of redness in the vaginal area indicative of frequent fondling.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal found that despite the victim's reluctance and time lapse of 18 years, the prosecution proved the case beyond reasonable doubt based on the victim's core testimony corroborated by medical evidence and the mother's testimony.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty and made a dock statement from the witness box denying the incident entirely. No defence witnesses were called. The trial judge analyzed the dock statement adequately and rejected it with reasons. The Court of Appeal found no merit in the defence version.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found that the trial judge properly evaluated the evidence being mindful of the 18-year time lapse and the victim's reluctance to testify. The Court noted that the victim, who had married and had children by the time of trial, naturally did not want old wounds to surface. Despite her reluctance, she testified to the core facts which were corroborated by medical evidence. The Court emphasized the trial judge's priceless advantage of watching the demeanor and deportment of witnesses. The Court rejected the ground that the dock statement was wrongly considered, finding the trial judge adequately analyzed and rejected it with reasons. Citing Oliver Dayananda alias Raja vs Republic of Sri Lanka, the Court noted criminal cases cannot be proved with mathematical accuracy. While affirming the conviction, the Court varied the sentences considering the time elapsed since 2002, reducing imprisonment terms but maintaining fines.
coa_sentence_type: 1st charge: 1 year imprisonment and fine; 2nd charge: 7 years RI and fine; 3rd charge: 1 year imprisonment and fine; 4th charge: 7 years RI and fine; 5th charge: 7 years RI and fine. All terms to run concurrently from 1st April 2021.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused-appellant was convicted by the High Court of Ratnapura for two charges of abduction and three charges of grave sexual abuse committed between January and December 2002 against a child victim who was in year three. The victim testified 18 years later in 2020, reluctantly stating the appellant took her to the jungle three times and sexually abused her, corroborated by her mother and medical evidence showing vaginal redness from frequent fondling. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal on conviction, finding the trial judge properly evaluated the reluctant testimony and corroborating evidence. However, considering the time lapse since 2002, the Court varied the sentences, reducing imprisonment terms from 3 to 1 year for charges 1 and 3, and from 8 to 7 years for charges 2, 4, and 5, with all terms running concurrently from the conviction date.
defence_counsel: Ashanthi De Almeida
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court trial judge meticulously analyzed the prosecution evidence and had the advantage of watching the demeanor and deportment of the victim. The trial judge was patient and mindful of the 18-year time lapse causing lapses in the victim's evidence, properly evaluated the evidence in the correct perspective, and rejected the dock statement with reasons. The Court of Appeal found no errors in the High Court's analysis.
precedents_cited_list: Oliver Dayananda alias Raja vs Republic of Sri Lanka CA 28-2009 decided on 13.02.2013
standard_of_review_applied: The Court of Appeal reviewed whether the trial judge properly evaluated the evidence and considered the priceless advantage the trial judge had in watching the demeanor and deportment of witnesses.
sentencing_principles_applied: The Court of Appeal considered the passage of time since the offence in 2002 and the changes that may have taken place in the lives of both the victim and appellant as a basis for varying the sentences while affirming the conviction.

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 403 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The accused, a Bank Manager, deceived the victim Grace Nirmala Balachandran into giving him Rs. 1,439,773.78 with the promise of providing her the ground floor of a twin house he was building. The victim contributed money from time to time for construction believing she would receive title to the ground floor. After the house was built and she occupied the ground floor, the accused failed to transfer title and eventually evicted her following a dispute over utility bills.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 403 of the Penal Code
hc_sentence_type: 2 years rigorous imprisonment suspended for 10 years, Fine of Rs. 10,000 with default sentence of 6 months simple imprisonment, Compensation of Rs. 4,000,000
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court found the appellant guilty of cheating under section 403 of the Penal Code. Considering the time period it took for the case to conclude and the age of the appellant, the court imposed a suspended sentence of 2 years rigorous imprisonment for 10 years, a fine of Rs. 10,000, and compensation of Rs. 4,000,000 to the victim.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant argued that the High Court Judge did not consider matters favorable to the accused and failed to consider inter se and per se contradictions of main witnesses. The appellant contended the prosecution did not prove the case beyond reasonable doubt. The appellant also challenged the compensation order as being contrary to law.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The learned High Court Judge has not considered the matters favourable to the accused in his judgment | The learned High Court Judge has not considered the inter se and per se contradictions of main witnesses | The prosecution has not proved the case beyond reasonable doubt | Without prejudice to the above grounds of appeal, the compensation ordered by the learned High Court Judge was contrary to law
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found that PW-01, PW-02, and PW-03 corroborated each other's evidence regarding the agreement between the appellant and victim, and the use of victim's money for house construction. The Court held that the appellant failed to challenge material points in cross-examination, and there was no reason to doubt the credibility of witnesses who had no motive to give false evidence.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court found that the prosecution established beyond reasonable doubt that the appellant deceived the victim with false promises to obtain money, and failed to fulfill the agreement to transfer title to the ground floor.
defence_version_summary: The accused pleaded not guilty initially and gave evidence under oath. He admitted receiving Rs. 729,773 and Rs. 100,000 from PW-01 but claimed Rs. 500,000 was returned and the balance Rs. 229,773 was advance rent payment. He denied having an agreement to provide part of the house to PW-01 and claimed she was merely a tenant. The court rejected this version as incredible given the corroborating evidence of PW-02 and PW-03.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal comprehensively analyzed the essential ingredients of cheating under section 403 read with section 398 of the Penal Code. The court found that the prosecution proved beyond reasonable doubt that the appellant deceived PW-01 with false promises to obtain money for house construction. The court emphasized that PW-02 and PW-03, being close friends with no reason to lie, corroborated PW-01's evidence about the agreement and money transfers. The court held that minor discrepancies in PW-01's evidence were understandable given the 10-year gap between events and testimony, and considering the war situation that existed in 2002 which affected travel and communication. The court applied the principle that failure to challenge material evidence in cross-examination means such evidence is accepted. Regarding sentencing, the court held that section 17(4) of the Code of Criminal Procedure Act imposes no limitation on compensation amounts ordered by the High Court, distinguishing it from the Assistance to and Protection of Crimes and Witnesses Act. The court found the compensation of Rs. 4,000,000 fair and reasonable considering the circumstances.
coa_sentence_type: 2 years rigorous imprisonment suspended for 10 years, Fine of Rs. 10,000 with default sentence of 6 months simple imprisonment, Compensation of Rs. 4,000,000 with default sentence of 2 years rigorous imprisonment
brief_judgment_file_summary: Ratnam Nadarajah, a Bank Manager, was convicted by the High Court of Colombo for cheating Grace Nirmala Balachandran under section 403 of the Penal Code by deceiving her with false promises of providing the ground floor of a house and obtaining Rs. 1,439,773.78. The High Court sentenced him to 2 years rigorous imprisonment suspended for 10 years, a fine of Rs. 10,000, and compensation of Rs. 4,000,000. On appeal, the accused challenged the conviction arguing contradictions in evidence, insufficient proof, and that compensation was contrary to law. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal, finding that the prosecution proved beyond reasonable doubt that the appellant deceived the victim with false promises, supported by corroborating evidence from two independent witnesses. The court held that the compensation amount under section 17(4) of the Code of Criminal Procedure Act was lawful and appropriate given the circumstances.
defence_counsel: Anil Silva, P.C. with Amaan Bandara instructed by M/S Tharmarajah Tharmaja
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court properly analyzed the evidence and found the appellant guilty of cheating. The court considered aggravating and mitigating circumstances including the time taken for case conclusion and the appellant's age before sentencing. The Court of Appeal held that the High Court correctly applied the legal principles and made findings supported by evidence.
precedents_cited_list: Carey Vs. de Silva (1887) 1 C.L.Rep. 49 | Silva (1933) II Times of Cey. 57 | Clucas (1949) 2 K.B. 266 | Zahir Vs. Cooray (1941) 42 NLR 263 | Sarwan Singh Vs. State of Punjab 2002 AIR Supreme Court iii 3652 | Boby Mathew Vs. State of Karnataka 2004 3 Cri. L. J. 3003 | Pilippu Mandige Nalaka Krishantha Kumara Thisera Vs. A.G CA 87/2005
standard_of_review_applied: The Court of Appeal reviewed whether the High Court properly evaluated the evidence and correctly applied legal principles regarding the offence of cheating under section 403 of the Penal Code
sentencing_principles_applied: The court considered the time period taken for case conclusion, the age of the appellant, the circumstances of the victim who lost her hard-earned money, and the appropriateness of compensation under section 17(4) of the Code of Criminal Procedure Act

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 54(A)(b) and 54(A)(d) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance as amended by Act No. 13 of 1984
brief_facts_summary: On 04/11/2015, police officers from Grandpass Police Station conducted a routine mobile patrol. PW1 IP/Chammika spotted the Appellant standing near a Buddha statue on Stacepura Road, and upon seeing police officers, she began walking towards her house. The Appellant was stopped and searched, and PW1 observed a pink cellophane bag in her hand containing brown substance. The substance was taken to Letchumi Jewellers for weighing (10 grams gross weight) and later tested positive for heroin (3.85 grams net).
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 54(A)(d) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance as amended by Act No. 13 of 1984
hc_judgment_summary: The Learned High Court Judge of Colombo found the Appellant guilty only on the second count of Possession of 3.85 grams of Heroin and acquitted her on the first count of Trafficking. Life imprisonment was imposed on 14/09/2018. The High Court Judge rejected the Dock Statement on the ground that it was not given under oath and was not subjected to cross-examination.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The Appellant challenged the conviction on two main grounds. First, the prosecution case does not satisfy the test of probability. Second, the defence evidence was rejected on a wrong premise, particularly the Dock Statement which was dismissed merely because it was not under oath.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The case for the prosecution does not satisfy the test of probability. | The rejection of the defence evidence on wrong premise.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The prosecution called five witnesses (PW1, PW2, PW5, PW7, PW9) and admitted the Government Analyst Report under Section 420. The Court of Appeal found the prosecution version improbable, noting that the police officers took over an hour to weigh a small amount of substance, and that PW1 admitted knowing the Appellant previously as 'Batti', which contradicted the prosecution narrative.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal found the prosecution case failed the test of probability. Key improbabilities included: officers taking over an hour to weigh 10 grams; the Appellant becoming nervous upon seeing plain-clothed officers; PW1 knowing the Appellant previously which contradicted the prosecution narrative that this was a random encounter; and the implausibility of the Appellant holding heroin while walking towards her house after seeing strangers.
defence_version_summary: The Appellant pleaded not guilty. She made a statement from the Dock (not under oath) claiming she was arrested at her house, not near a Buddha statue. She called her husband as a defence witness. The Court of Appeal noted the High Court Judge improperly rejected the Dock Statement merely because it was not under oath and not subjected to cross-examination, causing great prejudice to the Appellant.
legal_errors_description: The High Court Judge failed to properly evaluate the probability factors in conjunction with the defence evidence. He rejected the Dock Statement merely because it was not given under oath and was not subjected to cross examination, which caused great prejudice to the Appellant. The Judge failed to consider the evidence on equal footing and did not analyze the defence evidence properly.
procedural_defects_description: The High Court Judge failed to consider the Dock Statement in its correct perspective and rejected it on improper grounds. The Judge did not properly evaluate why the police took over an hour to weigh 10 grams of substance, and failed to analyze the significance of PW1 knowing the Appellant previously.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found multiple serious deficiencies in the prosecution case that failed to meet the probability test. The COA emphasized that probability plays a crucial role in criminal investigations and noted several improbable aspects: the police taking over an hour to weigh a small 10-gram substance; the Appellant becoming nervous upon seeing two plain-clothed men and walking towards her house while allegedly holding heroin; and critically, PW1 admitting he knew the Appellant previously as 'Batti' which contradicted the prosecution's narrative of a random encounter. The COA held that the High Court Judge improperly rejected the Dock Statement merely because it was not under oath, causing great prejudice. The Judge failed to consider evidence on equal footing and did not properly analyze the defence version. The COA applied the principle from R v. Hepworth that a Judge must be an administrator of justice, not merely a figure-head, and must see that justice is done. Finding that the prosecution failed to prove the case beyond reasonable doubt, the COA set aside the conviction and acquitted the Appellant.
coa_sentence_type: Acquitted - conviction and sentence set aside
brief_judgment_file_summary: George Gnanapragasam Irangani alias Batti was indicted for trafficking and possession of 3.85 grams of heroin on 04/11/2015. The High Court of Colombo found her guilty only on the possession count and imposed life imprisonment on 14/09/2018. On appeal, the Appellant challenged the conviction on grounds that the prosecution case did not satisfy the test of probability and that the defence evidence was rejected on wrong premise. The Court of Appeal found the prosecution case improbable, noting police took over an hour to weigh 10 grams of substance, PW1 knew the Appellant previously contradicting the prosecution narrative, and the High Court Judge improperly rejected the Dock Statement merely because it was not under oath. Finding the prosecution failed to prove the case beyond reasonable doubt, the COA set aside the conviction and sentence, acquitting the Appellant on 07/06/2024.
defence_counsel: Amila Palliyage with Sandeepani Wijesooriya, Sawani Udugampola, Lakitha Wakishta Arachchi and Subaj De Silva
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court Judge rejected the Dock Statement merely because it was not given under oath and was not subjected to cross-examination. The Judge failed to consider the probability factors in conjunction with the defence evidence and did not properly analyze the defence version. The rejection of defence evidence without proper analysis caused great prejudice to the Appellant.
precedents_cited_list: Mohamed Nimnaz v. Attorney General CA/95/94 | Attorney-General v. Rawther 25 NLR 385 [1987] 1 SLR 155 | Miller v. Minister of Pensions (1947) 2 All E.R. 372 | R v. Hepworth 1928 (AD) 265
standard_of_review_applied: The Court of Appeal reviewed whether the prosecution proved the case beyond reasonable doubt and whether the High Court Judge properly evaluated the probability test and considered the defence evidence on equal footing with prosecution evidence.
final_charge_after_appeal: Acquitted - no conviction stands

judges: Menaka Wijesundera J. | Wickum A. Kaluarachchi J.
offence_sections: Section 354 and 365(B) of the Penal Code
location_of_offence: Near railway line running from Nugegoda to down south
brief_facts_summary: An eight-year-old victim went to buy toffees in the evening at about 6pm when a three-wheeler stopped and the person inside boarded her and took her to his house where she was sexually abused. The victim went missing and was later found hiding inside a cupboard outside. The appellant was arrested on 21st May 2005 after the victim and mother made a complaint to Mirihana police regarding the sexual abuse.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 354 and 365(B) of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the appellant based on the victim's evidence and medical evidence. The trial judge concluded that the appellant was a well-known person to the victim based on the manner in which the child got into the three-wheeler. The High Court dismissed concerns about dock identification and contradictions in the prosecution evidence.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant challenged the High Court conviction on two main grounds. First, the trial judge failed to consider that the identification was merely a dock identification by the victim. Second, the trial judge did not consider the evidence of the prosecution in its proper perspective, particularly the contradictions and omissions in the evidence of the victim and her mother.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The trial judge had failed to consider the dock identification of the appellant | The trial judge has not considered the evidence of the prosecution in its proper perspective
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found that the evidence of the victim sounded very artificial and false, appearing to be coached. The victim and her mother's evidence revealed they were trying to concoct a story which had taken place differently. The trial judge merely glossed over the contradictions and omissions marked in the prosecution evidence.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal found the probability factor of the evidence to be doubtful and it created a reasonable doubt in the prosecution story. The evidence of the prosecution witnesses lacked clarity and truthfulness.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty and made a dock statement in which he said he knew the victim's mother and they had a relationship. He claimed that because of this relationship, the story was concocted by the victim's mother. The Court found the defence version raised reasonable doubt about the prosecution's case.
legal_errors_description: The trial judge's reasoning upon which he based his conclusion was very superficial and void of any analysis of the legal principles of deciding a criminal case of this nature. The trial judge made an unsupported assumption that the appellant was a well-known person to the victim which was not substantiated by evidence in Court.
procedural_defects_description: The identification of the appellant was merely a dock identification which was not properly addressed by the trial judge. The victim never mentioned the appellant by name nor said she had seen or known him before.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found that the victim's identification of the appellant was merely a dock identification as she never mentioned him by name nor said she had seen or known him before. The victim's evidence appeared coached and artificial. The contradictions marked during cross-examination indicated the victim's mother may have had an affair with the appellant and concocted the story. The trial judge's assumption that the appellant was well-known to the victim was not substantiated by evidence in Court. The Court found the evidence of the victim and her mother lacked clarity and truthfulness, and the probability factor of the prosecution story was doubtful, creating reasonable doubt. The trial judge merely glossed over contradictions and omissions and failed to apply proper legal principles. The Court concluded the reasoning of the trial judge was superficial and void of proper analysis.
coa_sentence_type: Acquittal
brief_judgment_file_summary: Merinchchage Janaka Perera was convicted by the High Court of Colombo under sections 354 and 365(B) of the Penal Code for sexually abusing an eight-year-old child in May 2005. The appellant appealed on grounds that the trial judge failed to consider the dock identification issue and did not properly evaluate the prosecution evidence. The Court of Appeal found the victim's identification was merely dock identification, the victim's evidence appeared coached and artificial, and contradictions suggested the victim's mother may have concocted the story due to a prior relationship with the appellant. The Court found reasonable doubt in the prosecution case and held that the trial judge's reasoning was superficial and void of proper legal analysis. The appeal was allowed and the appellant was acquitted.
defence_counsel: Shanaka Ranasinghe P.C. with Mihindukulasooriya and Sandamali Peiris
hc_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found that the High Court's reasoning was very superficial and void of any analysis of the legal principles of deciding a criminal case of this nature. The trial judge merely glossed over the contradictions and omissions marked in the evidence of the prosecution. The trial judge's affirmations on the probability factor of the prosecution story did not appear to be with merit and reason acceptable to the Court of Appeal.
standard_of_review_applied: The Court of Appeal reviewed the trial judge's evaluation of evidence and application of legal principles, finding the reasoning superficial and lacking proper analysis of legal principles for deciding criminal cases of this nature.

judges: Menaka Wijesundera, J | Wickum A. Kaluarachchi, J
offence_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: On 24.03.1996, the 2nd accused-appellant along with two other accused assaulted the deceased Perimasamy Sadasivam Subramanium with clubs at or near the 2nd accused's house. PW-1 and PW-2 witnessed the assault and took the deceased to Chilaw hospital. The deceased died on 31.03.1996 after seven days from injuries sustained. A dying declaration was recorded by police while the deceased was undergoing treatment.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court of Chilaw convicted the 1st and 2nd accused for murder after trial. The HC Judge relied upon the dying declaration admitted under Section 32 of the Evidence Ordinance and the evidence of eyewitnesses PW-1 and PW-2. Death sentence was imposed on both convicted accused on 15.06.2015.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant argued that the learned High Court Judge misdirected himself on facts and law in reaching his conclusion. The main contentions were that the Trial Judge wrongly relied upon the dying declaration, and that even if the prosecution story were true, the appellant could only be convicted of culpable homicide not amounting to murder, not murder.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The learned High Court Judge misdirected himself on facts and law | The learned Trial Judge wrongly relied upon the dying declaration | Even if prosecution story is believed, accused could only be convicted for culpable homicide not amounting to murder
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The prosecution led six witnesses including two eyewitnesses PW-1 and PW-2. The Court of Appeal found vital contradictions between the dying declaration and eyewitness evidence regarding the place of assault. Medical evidence contradicted the dying declaration as no head injury was found despite the deceased claiming he was struck on the head.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal found that vital contradictions between the dying declaration and eyewitness evidence regarding place of assault cast reasonable doubt on the prosecution case. Medical evidence contradicted the dying declaration rendering it unreliable.
defence_version_summary: The 2nd accused-appellant gave evidence on oath. His defence was that the deceased was assaulted only by the 1st accused when the deceased was at the 2nd accused-appellant's house. His mother was called as a defence witness to corroborate his evidence. The Court of Appeal found that the defence evidence was rejected by the HC Judge on a completely wrong and illegal basis.
legal_errors_description: The HC Judge made incorrect legal observations regarding admissibility of hearsay evidence. He used a confessionary statement from police records (marked X-1) that was inadmissible under Section 25(1) of the Evidence Ordinance to reject defence evidence. He failed to analyze defence evidence properly.
procedural_defects_description: The HC Judge used evidence (portion of police statement) that was not actually led during trial. He rejected defence evidence using a confessionary statement which is inadmissible under Section 25(1) of Evidence Ordinance. The judgment was entered without properly considering the defence case.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found multiple fatal errors in the High Court judgment. First, there was a vital contradiction between the dying declaration (stating assault commenced at deceased's home) and eyewitness evidence (stating assault occurred at 2nd accused's house verandah) that goes to the root of the case. Second, medical evidence contradicted the dying declaration as no head injury was found despite the deceased claiming he was struck on the head with a club. Third, the HC Judge erroneously rejected defence evidence by relying on a portion of the appellant's police statement (X-1) that was not led as evidence and constituted an inadmissible confessionary statement under Section 25(1) of the Evidence Ordinance. The COA held that the judgment was entered without properly considering the defence evidence and that the prosecution failed to prove the charge beyond reasonable doubt due to contradictory evidence and infirmities in the prosecution case.
coa_sentence_type: Acquittal - conviction and death sentence set aside
brief_judgment_file_summary: The 2nd accused-appellant was convicted of murder under Section 296 of the Penal Code by the High Court of Chilaw and sentenced to death for the murder of Perimasamy Sadasivam Subramanium on 24.03.1996. The prosecution case relied on eyewitness testimony of PW-1 and PW-2 and a dying declaration. The Court of Appeal allowed the appeal finding vital contradictions between the dying declaration and eyewitness evidence regarding the place of assault, medical evidence contradicting the dying declaration, and serious errors by the HC Judge in using an inadmissible confessionary statement to reject defence evidence. The COA held the HC Judge misdirected himself on law and facts, set aside the conviction and death sentence, and acquitted the 2nd accused-appellant of the charge of murder.
defence_counsel: Anil Silva, PC
hc_analysis_summary: The HC Judge accepted both the dying declaration and the eyewitness evidence of PW-1 and PW-2 despite vital contradictions between them. He made incorrect legal observations regarding hearsay evidence admissibility. He erroneously rejected defence evidence by relying on an inadmissible confessionary statement from police records that was not even led as evidence during trial, violating Section 25(1) of the Evidence Ordinance.
