judges: Menaka Wijesundera J. | Wickum A. Kaluarachchi J.
offence_sections: Poisons Opium and Dangerous drugs Ordinance
brief_facts_summary: Police Narcotics Bureau officers led by PW1 received a tip off regarding the appellant and went to St Johns Market in Colombo around 1pm. They waited until the appellant arrived around 6pm or 7pm, searched him, and found 15.68 grammes of heroin. The appellant was taken into custody and officers searched three houses habituated by him, recovering jewelry and money from his Wattala house which was later handed over to his sister on his instructions.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Poisons Opium and Dangerous drugs Ordinance
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court of Colombo convicted the accused appellant for possession and trafficking of 15.68 grammes of heroin under the Poisons Opium and Dangerous drugs Ordinance. The appellant had pleaded not guilty and stood trial, but was convicted and sentenced accordingly after the trial concluded.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant raised three main grounds: first, that the trial judge failed to consider the improbability of the prosecution story regarding officers waiting for hours and the handing over of money to the appellant's sister; second, that the trial judge followed wrong procedure to cover gaps in the prosecution by allowing the Government Analyst Report to be marked after the defense had closed; third, that the trial judge commented on the demeanor of PW1 who had not been led before him, thereby denying a fair trial.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The learned trial judge had failed to consider the improbability of the prosecution story | The trial judge had followed wrong procedure to cover the gaps of the prosecution | The trial judge had commented on the demeanor of witnesses who had not been led before him and thereby denying a fair trial to the appellant
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: PW1 was corroborated by PW3 who assisted him and all witnesses of the raid were very lengthily cross-examined but stood the test of cross examination well. The Court of Appeal found the prosecution witnesses credible but held that procedural irregularities vitiated the trial.
probability_assessment_by_court: Court of Appeal found nothing unusual in the prosecution story and no improbability, but held procedural errors vitiated the conviction
defence_version_summary: The accused appellant pleaded not guilty to the indictment and stood trial. He made a dock statement on 31st October 2017. The defense objected to the improbability of the prosecution story, particularly regarding officers waiting for hours and the handling of recovered money. Whether the defense objected to marking the Government Analyst Report after closure was questionable due to an undated alteration in the proceedings.
legal_errors_description: The trial judge allowed the Government Analyst Report to be marked in evidence after both prosecution and defense had closed their cases, which violated proper procedure. The trial judge also commented on the demeanor of PW1 who had not been led before him. These procedural irregularities were found to be erroneous and illegal.
procedural_defects_description: The Government Analyst Report was admitted by both parties on 30th August 2017 but was not marked in evidence until after the defense had closed on 31st October 2017. The trial judge allowed it to be marked on 13th March 2018 when the matter was due for submissions. There was also an undated alteration in the proceedings from 'does not object' to 'objects' which was not reflected in the journal entry.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal examined all three grounds of appeal raised by the appellant. On the first ground regarding improbability, the Court found nothing unusual in the prosecution story, noting that handing over money to the appellant's sister on his request was not improbable, and that officers waiting for several hours to avoid missing the appellant was reasonable. The Court noted that prosecution witnesses were well corroborated and stood cross-examination well. However, on the second ground, the Court found serious procedural errors. The Government Analyst Report, though admitted by both parties during trial, was not marked in evidence until after the defense had closed, which violated established legal principles. The Court cited precedents including Ponnaiya vs Abdul Cader 38 NLR 281 and The King vs Ariyadasa 43 NLR 289 which held that calling evidence after closure to fill gaps in prosecution is irregular and can vitiate a trial. The Court noted that the GAR was the most vital piece of evidence and allowing it to be marked after the defense closed denied the appellant the opportunity to present his defense with all facts. The Court also agreed with the third ground that the trial judge inappropriately commented on the demeanor of PW1 who had not been led before him. While the learned DSG argued that no injustice was caused since the report was admitted during trial, the Court rejected this, holding that the findings of the trial judge were erroneous and illegal, sufficient to vitiate the conviction and sentence.
coa_sentence_type: Acquittal
brief_judgment_file_summary: Thangaiah Paul Owen Kanagaraj Kadosha was convicted by the High Court of Colombo for possession and trafficking of 15.68 grammes of heroin under the Poisons Opium and Dangerous drugs Ordinance. He appealed to the Court of Appeal on three main grounds: improbability of the prosecution story, procedural irregularities in marking the Government Analyst Report, and improper judicial comments. The Court of Appeal found the prosecution story credible but held that the trial judge committed serious procedural errors by allowing the vital Government Analyst Report to be marked in evidence after the defense had closed, violating established legal principles that prohibit filling gaps in prosecution after closure. The Court also found that the trial judge inappropriately commented on a witness's demeanor without having seen the witness. These procedural irregularities were held to be erroneous and illegal, vitiating the conviction and sentence. The appeal was allowed and the accused was acquitted of all charges.
defence_counsel: Rienzie Arsecularatne, P.C. with Chamindrie Arsecularatne, Thiliina Punchihewa, Punsisi Gamage and Eranga Kahandawala
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted the appellant after finding the prosecution case proven beyond reasonable doubt. However, the Court of Appeal found that the High Court committed serious procedural errors by allowing the Government Analyst Report to be marked after the defense closed and by commenting on the demeanor of a witness who had not appeared before the trial judge. The Court of Appeal held these findings were erroneous and illegal, vitiating the conviction.
precedents_cited_list: Ponnaiya vs Abdul Cader 38 NLR 281 | The King vs Ariyadasa 43 NLR 289
standard_of_review_applied: The Court of Appeal reviewed whether procedural irregularities and legal errors by the trial judge vitiated the conviction and sentence

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code and Section 4(2) of the Offensive Weapon Act No.18 of 1996
brief_facts_summary: On August 4, 2001, following two earlier confrontations, a mob of 12-15 persons including PW1 went to 'Bosevena Watta' in search of the Appellant. According to PW1, the Appellant hurled a bomb at the mob which exploded, causing the death of Vidana Silvisthirige Dhammika Fonseka and injuring several persons. The Appellant was arrested and tried for murder and using an offensive weapon.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code and Section 4(2) of the Offensive Weapon Act No.18 of 1996
hc_sentence_type: Death Sentence for Count 1; 10 years Rigorous Imprisonment and fine for Counts 5, 6, and 7 running concurrent
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court Judge convicted the Appellant on Counts 1, 5, 6, and 7 after finding that the prosecution evidence warranted a case to answer. The Judge relied on the evidence of PW1 as a solitary eyewitness under Section 134 of the Evidence Ordinance, finding it convincing and proving the charge beyond reasonable doubt. The Appellant was sentenced to death for the murder charge and concurrent sentences of 10 years rigorous imprisonment with fines for the offensive weapon charges.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The Appellant challenged the conviction primarily on the basis that the High Court Judge erred in convicting him on the uncorroborated evidence of PW1. Additional grounds included failure to prove the identity of the dead body, failure to consider conviction for a lesser offence under exceptions to Section 294 of the Penal Code, and improper evaluation and rejection of the dock statement.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The Learned High Court Judge erred in law by convicting the Appellant on the uncorroborated evidence of PW1 | The Learned High Court Judge had failed to take into consideration that the prosecution had failed to prove the identity of the dead body | The Learned High Court Judge had failed to take into consideration whether the Appellant could be convicted for a lesser offence under one of the special exceptions to Section 294 of the Penal Code | The Learned High Court Judge had failed to evaluate the dock statement according to the law and had failed to give proper reasons in rejecting the dock statement
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The prosecution led 11 witnesses. PW1 testified to directly seeing the Appellant throw the bomb. However, PW2 stated he saw a person resembling the Appellant throw the bomb. PW4 saw the bomb thrown from the direction where the Appellant was but did not identify who threw it. PW16 also did not see who threw the bomb. The Court of Appeal found material contradictions between PW1 and other prosecution witnesses.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal found that the prosecution failed to prove the case beyond reasonable doubt due to contradictions in eyewitness testimony and lack of corroboration
defence_version_summary: The Appellant pleaded not guilty and made a dock statement. He did not call any witnesses. The Court of Appeal noted that the High Court Judge failed to properly evaluate the dock statement and give proper reasons for rejecting it, though this ground was not specifically analyzed as the first ground was dispositive.
legal_errors_description: The High Court Judge failed to properly scrutinize the testimony of the sole eyewitness and assess credibility and reliability. The Judge incorrectly found PW1's evidence was corroborated by PW2 when in fact PW2's testimony contradicted PW1. The Judge failed to consider material contradictions affecting the root of the case.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal focused on evaluating the credibility and reliability of the eyewitness testimony, particularly PW1. The Court noted that while a conviction can be based on the evidence of a single witness if cogent and impressive, in this case PW1's evidence was contradicted by other prosecution witnesses on material points. PW2 only saw someone resembling the Appellant, PW4 saw the bomb thrown from the Appellant's direction but did not identify the thrower, and PW16 did not see who threw the bomb. The Court found these contradictions affected the root of the case and concluded that PW1's evidence should have been corroborated given that a group went to attack the Appellant. The Court held that the prosecution failed to establish who threw the bomb and that PW1's evidence was not cogent and impressive enough to act upon alone. The Court cited precedents on eyewitness testimony evaluation, burden of proof, and single witness evidence.
coa_sentence_type: Acquitted of all charges; conviction and sentence quashed
brief_judgment_file_summary: Mahamaddumage Don Eranda Suresh Kumara was convicted by the High Court of Colombo for murder under Section 296 of the Penal Code and three counts of using an offensive weapon under Section 4(2) of the Offensive Weapon Act for a bomb attack on August 4, 2001 at Borella that killed one person and injured several others. He was sentenced to death for murder and concurrent 10-year rigorous imprisonment terms with fines totaling Rs.30,000 for the weapon charges. On appeal, the Appellant challenged the conviction primarily on the ground that it was based on uncorroborated evidence of a single eyewitness (PW1). The Court of Appeal found that PW1's testimony was contradicted by other prosecution witnesses on material points regarding who threw the bomb, and that the High Court Judge erred in finding the evidence cogent enough to convict without corroboration. The Court of Appeal allowed the appeal, quashed the conviction and sentence, and acquitted the Appellant of all charges on the basis that the prosecution failed to prove the case beyond reasonable doubt.
defence_counsel: Neranjan Jayasinghe
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court Judge considered the judicial principles relating to acting upon the evidence of a solitary witness and concluded that PW1's evidence was convincing under Section 134 of the Evidence Ordinance. The Court of Appeal found this to be erroneous as the Judge failed to properly scrutinize the testimony, assess credibility and reliability, and consider material contradictions with other prosecution witnesses that affected the root of the case.
precedents_cited_list: The Queen v. K.A. Santin Singho 65 NLR 447 | Sumansena V Attorney General [1999] 3 Sri L.R. at 137
standard_of_review_applied: The Court reviewed whether the High Court Judge properly evaluated eyewitness testimony credibility and reliability, and whether the prosecution proved the case beyond reasonable doubt

judges: B. Sasi Mahendran, J. | Amal Ranaraja, J.
offence_sections: Section 296 read together with Section 32 of the Penal Code as amended
brief_facts_summary: Four accused were charged with murdering Hettige Premajiwa alias Ranji on 23.06.2007. The deceased had prior complaints against the accused for cutting his bike tire and death threats. On the day of the incident, the deceased was attacked and found bleeding on an estate road. He made three separate dying declarations to his wife (PW1), brother-in-law (PW3), and a friend (PW4), naming all four accused as his assailants. The deceased suffered nine external injuries including skull fractures and brain bleeding, and died the same day.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 296 read together with Section 32 of the Penal Code as amended
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court of Kalutara found all four accused guilty of murder based on three consistent dying declarations made by the deceased and medical evidence. The court accepted the dying declarations as credible evidence and imposed the death sentence on 07.09.2020.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The accused argued that the High Court failed to consider contradictions in the prosecution case and did not properly evaluate the defence case. They contended that the judge did not adequately assess weaknesses and credibility issues with prosecution witnesses. The defence also claimed the order contradicted the evidence and that the dying declarations required corroboration.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The High Court has not considered the contradictions in the prosecution case | The Court did not properly consider the defence case | The Learned High Court Judge has not properly considered the weaknesses and the non-credibility of the Prosecution witnesses | The order was given in contradiction to the evidence placed before the Court
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The prosecution presented eleven witnesses and relied primarily on three dying declarations made by the deceased to PW1 (wife), PW3 (brother-in-law), and PW4 (friend). All three witnesses consistently testified that the deceased named all four accused as his attackers. The Court found these dying declarations credible, noting they were consistent across all three witnesses and the deceased was able to speak and identify his assailants.
probability_assessment_by_court: Court applied established legal principles for dying declarations and found them to be true, voluntary, and not the result of tutoring or prompting. The consistency across three separate declarations and medical evidence supporting the deceased's ability to speak satisfied the court beyond reasonable doubt.
defence_version_summary: The accused pleaded not guilty. They gave evidence from the dock and called one defence witness. The defence primarily challenged the prosecution case by arguing lack of corroboration for dying declarations and suggesting the injuries resulted from a fall from a moving vehicle rather than an assault. The Court found the defence version not credible.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal extensively analyzed the law on dying declarations, citing Queen vs. Anthonypillai, Gamini Mahaarachchi vs. The Attorney General, Sigera vs. Attorney General, and Indian precedents. The COA held that dying declarations do not require corroboration as a matter of law if they are found to be true, voluntary, and reliable. The court noted the defence did not dispute that the deceased made the declarations or that witnesses were truthful, but only challenged the lack of corroboration. The COA found all three dying declarations were consistent in naming the four accused, the deceased was able to speak and identify assailants, and the declarations were true and accurate. Medical evidence supported the deceased's ability to speak and showed defence injuries including a stab wound, contradicting the fall theory. The COA affirmed the High Court's decision.
coa_sentence_type: Death
brief_judgment_file_summary: Four accused were convicted of murdering Hettige Premajiwa alias Ranji on 23.06.2007 by the High Court of Kalutara and sentenced to death. The prosecution case relied on three consistent dying declarations made by the deceased to his wife, brother-in-law, and a friend, all naming the four accused as attackers. The accused appealed arguing contradictions in prosecution evidence, lack of corroboration for dying declarations, and improper consideration of the defence case. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal, holding that dying declarations do not require corroboration if found to be true, voluntary, and reliable, and affirmed the conviction and death sentence.
defence_counsel: Charith Calhena
cause_of_death_exact_text: The injuries done to the head and the effect those had on the brain were the cause of death
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court accepted the three dying declarations as credible and consistent evidence. The HC found the deceased was able to speak and identify his assailants, and the declarations were true and accurate. The Court of Appeal found no error in the High Court's analysis and reasoning.

judges: B. Sasi Mahendran, J. | Amal Ranaraja, J.
offence_sections: Section 54(a)(b) and Section 54 A(d) of the Poisons, Opium, and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance as amended by Act No.13 of 1984
brief_facts_summary: On 13.08.2011, police officers from Kotahena Police Station were conducting routine surveillance at Maha Vidyala Mawatha when they encountered the appellant coming from a shanty town called 146waththa. Upon search, PW1 recovered a pink plastic bag containing 2.59 grams of heroin mixed powder from the appellant's possession, along with Rs. 63,000 in cash. The substance was weighed, sealed, and sent to the Government Analyst for testing.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 54(a)(b) and Section 54 A(d) of the Poisons, Opium, and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance as amended by Act No.13 of 1984
hc_sentence_type: Life imprisonment in respect of each charge
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court Judge found the appellant guilty on both charges of trafficking and possessing 2.59 grams of heroin without authorization. The appellant was convicted and sentenced to life imprisonment in respect of each charge after pleading not guilty at trial.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant contended that the chain of custody was not proved due to the unexplained loss of the Police property receipt no. 91/2011 and suspect property receipt no. 15/2011. The defence also argued that the notes on the raid were vague, making the prosecution version improbable.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The chain of custody has not been proved by the respondent due to the unexplained loss of the production and property receipts | The notes on the raid are vague, therefore, the prosecution version is improbable
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The prosecution case relied on two police witnesses (PW1 and PW2) who testified about the arrest and recovery of heroin. The Court of Appeal found that the prosecution failed to establish the chain of custody through compelling evidence, particularly due to the missing Police property receipt and suspect property receipt.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal held that the prosecution failed to prove beyond reasonable doubt the inward journey of the production due to missing property receipts and lack of compelling evidence that they were misplaced.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty and maintained that he was taken into custody at 146waththa when he went there to perform manual labour. He claimed he was arrested, taken to Kotahena Police Station, detained overnight, and only realized he was falsely implicated when an officer obtained his fingerprints the following day. The court does not provide a credibility assessment of the defence version in the judgment.
legal_errors_description: The Learned High Court Judge misdirected himself when he concluded that the prosecution had proved beyond reasonable doubt the inward journey of the production, despite the absence of the Police property receipt and suspect property receipt and failure to establish through compelling evidence that they were misplaced.
procedural_defects_description: The prosecution failed to produce the Sri Lanka Police property receipt no. 91/2011 and suspect property receipt no. 15/2011 in Court, despite them being listed as evidence in the indictment. The prosecution attempted to add PW10 to explain the missing receipts but that witness never testified, and no formal application was made to produce copies of the receipts.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal carefully examined the chain of custody issue raised by the appellant. The court noted that while the Police property receipt and suspect property receipt were listed as evidence in the indictment, the prosecution failed to produce them at trial and merely stated they had been misplaced without providing compelling evidence of this claim. The prosecution's attempt to call PW10 to explain the situation was unsuccessful as the witness never testified. The Court held that these receipts are important documents to manifest the inward journey of the production and custody of suspect property, and that it was dangerous to rely solely on oral testimony of reserve officers without documentary evidence. The court found the High Court Judge misdirected himself in concluding the prosecution proved the chain of custody beyond reasonable doubt. Additionally, the Court noted that 14 years had lapsed since the alleged offence in 2011, making it unjust to call upon the appellant to defend himself again. Citing The Queen vs. G.K. Jayasinghe, the Court declined to order a retrial due to the time lapse and the unreliable nature of the prosecution case.
coa_sentence_type: Acquittal - conviction and sentence set aside
brief_judgment_file_summary: Abdul Hameed Mohammed Niyaz was convicted by the High Court of Colombo for trafficking and possessing 2.59 grams of heroin on 13.08.2011 and sentenced to life imprisonment on each charge. He appealed to the Court of Appeal challenging the conviction on grounds that the chain of custody was not proved due to missing Police property receipts. The Court of Appeal found that the prosecution failed to produce the Police property receipt and suspect property receipt at trial and did not establish through compelling evidence that they were misplaced, making it dangerous to rely solely on oral testimony regarding chain of custody. The Court held the High Court Judge misdirected himself in finding the prosecution proved its case beyond reasonable doubt. Noting that 14 years had passed since the alleged offence, the Court of Appeal set aside the conviction and sentence and acquitted the appellant.
defence_counsel: Nayantha Wijesundara
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court found the appellant guilty and convicted him on both charges after trial, sentencing him to life imprisonment on each count. The Court of Appeal held that the High Court Judge misdirected himself by concluding the prosecution proved beyond reasonable doubt the inward journey of the production despite the missing property receipts and lack of compelling evidence explaining their absence.
precedents_cited_list: The Queen vs. G.K. Jayasinghe 69 NLR 314
standard_of_review_applied: The Court of Appeal reviewed whether the prosecution proved its case beyond reasonable doubt, particularly examining the chain of custody of evidence and procedural compliance.

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 54(A)(d) and Section 54(A)(b) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance as amended by Act No. 13 of 1984
brief_facts_summary: On 15.05.2010, police received information about heroin trafficking in Thalahena area. At around 8.15 am, police stopped a scooter with the 2nd Appellant as rider and 1st Appellant as pillion rider. Upon search by woman police officer, a parcel wrapped in blue cellophane containing suspected heroin weighing 154 grams was found concealed in the right side pocket of the 1st Appellant's frock. Both appellants were arrested and Rs.250,000 cash was found at their house and handed to the 1st Appellant's mother.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 54(A)(d) and Section 54(A)(b) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance as amended by Act No. 13 of 1984
hc_sentence_type: Death sentence on all three counts
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court of Colombo found both appellants guilty on all three counts after trial. The 1st Appellant was convicted for possession of 22.91 grams of heroin, the 2nd Appellant for aiding and abetting, and both for trafficking 22.91 grams of heroin. Death sentence was imposed on all three counts on 29.09.2015.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The 1st Appellant challenged the lawfulness of amending the date of offence in the indictment, insertion of Sinhala text after both parties closed their cases, and allowing the prosecution to call a retired Government Analyst under Section 439 after defence closed. A key ground was the unexplained weight discrepancy where heroin with covers weighed 154 grams but without covers weighed 156.5 grams at Government Analyst Department. The 2nd Appellant argued that the trial judge failed to consider the likelihood of false implication due to enmity between him and PW1.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Whether it was lawful for the Learned High Court Judge to amend the date of offence in Count number one in the indictment to read as 15.10.2010 instead of 15.10.2011 by placing his signature dated 07.03.2013 | Whether it was lawful for the Learned High Court Judge to insert the words 'ixfYdaê; fpdaokdj lshjd myod foñ'' under his signature dated 04.09.2014 after the prosecution closed its case on 15.05.2013 and after the defence closed its case on 07.08.2013 | Whether it was lawful for the Learned High Court Judge to rely on Section 439 of the Code of Criminal Procedure Act No.15 of 1979 to allow the prosecution to call witness Nihal Mapitigama Liyanarachchi (retired Government Analyst) after both parties closed their cases | The prosecution failed to explain how the weight of Heroin along with the covers which weighed 154 grams purportedly weighed without covers 156.5 grams when the Government Analyst weighed on 06.01.2011 | The Learned High Court Judge has failed to take into consideration that there is a strong likelihood for the prosecution witnesses specially PW1 Rangajeewa to falsely implicate the 2nd Appellant due to the enmity prevailed between him and PW1
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The prosecution called 5 witnesses including the Government Analyst. The Court of Appeal found serious issues with the evidence including unexplained weight discrepancy in the heroin and improper handling of the chain of custody. The Court noted that the prosecution failed to establish the inward journey of the production beyond reasonable doubt, particularly regarding the weight difference between initial seizure (154 grams with cover) and Government Analyst's measurement (156.5 grams without cover).
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal found that the weight discrepancy created reasonable doubt over the prosecution case. The Court held that the prosecution failed to prove beyond reasonable doubt that what was analyzed was exactly the same substance detected at the time of arrest, as the inward journey of the production was not established as safe.
defence_version_summary: Both appellants opted to give evidence from the witness box and pleaded not guilty. The 2nd Appellant claimed there was enmity between him (an ex-police officer) and PW1 Rangajeewa which led to false implication. The Court of Appeal found merit in the defence arguments particularly regarding the unexplained weight discrepancy and procedural violations.
legal_errors_description: The High Court Judge committed clear violations of Section 167 of the Code of Criminal Procedure Act by failing to read and explain the amended charge to the appellants. The Judge also misdirected himself by invoking Section 439 of the CPC to allow the prosecution to call PW5 (Government Analyst) nearly 2 years after defence closed their case, which improperly filled gaps in the prosecution case and put the accused at unfair disadvantage.
procedural_defects_description: The indictment was amended on 07.03.2013 but was never read over and explained to the appellants as required by Section 167 of the CPC. The Sinhala text was inserted on 04.09.2014 claiming the amendment was read and explained, but this was not reflected in proceedings or journal entries. Additionally, the prosecution was improperly allowed to call a fresh witness under Section 439 after both parties had closed their cases.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found multiple serious legal and procedural errors in the High Court proceedings. The COA emphasized that the prosecution must prove beyond reasonable doubt that the substance analyzed was exactly what was seized, and the inward journey of production plays a dominant role. The Court found the weight discrepancy of 2.5 grams (154 grams with cover versus 156.5 grams without cover) to be a substantial and unexplained fact that created reasonable doubt. The COA held that this discrepancy was very significant considering the pure heroin detected, and the prosecution failed to question either PW1 or the Government Analyst to explain this anomaly. The Court also found clear violations of Section 167 regarding amendment procedures and misdirection in invoking Section 439 to call evidence after defence closed. Citing precedents including Mohamed Nimnaz v Attorney General and Faiza Hanoon Yoosuf v Attorney General, the COA held that prosecutors should not be given a second chance to fill gaps of badly handled prosecutions. The Court concluded that since the inward journey of production was not established as safe, it was unnecessary to consider other appeal grounds. The conviction and sentence were set aside and both appellants were acquitted.
coa_sentence_type: Acquittal - conviction and sentence set aside
brief_judgment_file_summary: The 1st and 2nd Appellants were convicted by the High Court of Colombo for possession and trafficking of 22.91 grams of heroin and sentenced to death on all three counts on 29.09.2015. On appeal, the appellants challenged procedural violations including improper amendment of the indictment, calling of prosecution witness after defence closed, and unexplained weight discrepancy in the heroin evidence. The Court of Appeal found serious legal errors including violation of Section 167 of the CPC for failing to read amended charges to appellants, and misdirection in invoking Section 439 to allow prosecution to fill gaps after defence closed. Most significantly, the COA found that the prosecution failed to explain how heroin initially weighed at 154 grams with cover subsequently weighed 156.5 grams without cover at the Government Analyst Department, creating reasonable doubt about the chain of custody. The Court held that the prosecution failed to establish the inward journey of production as safe and beyond reasonable doubt. The appeal was allowed, conviction and sentence set aside, and both appellants were acquitted.
defence_counsel: Rienzie Arsekularatne, PC with Chamindri Arsekularatne, Udara Muhandiramge, Thilina Punchihewa, Punsisi Gamage, C. Fernando and Himasha Silva for the 1st Appellant; Neranjan Jayasinghe with Harshana Ananda for the 2nd Appellant
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted both appellants on all three counts and imposed death sentences. However, the Court of Appeal found that the High Court Judge committed clear violations of Section 167 by failing to properly read and explain amended charges to the appellants, misdirected himself on law by invoking Section 439 to allow prosecution to call witness after defence closed, and failed to properly analyze the substantial weight discrepancy in the heroin evidence which created reasonable doubt about the chain of custody and identity of the production.
precedents_cited_list: Woolmington v DPP (1935) | M.K. Francis Alwis v The Queen 70 NLR 558 | David v Idroos 45 NLR 300 | Vendendriesen v Houwa Umma 39 NLR 65 | Mohamed Nimnaz v Attorney General CA/95/94 | Faiza Hanoon Yoosuf v Attorney General CA/121/2002 | Mahasarukkalige Chandani v Attorney General CA/213/2009
standard_of_review_applied: Beyond reasonable doubt standard for criminal prosecutions; appellate review of legal errors and misdirection on law by trial judge; assessment of whether prosecution established chain of custody and inward journey of production as safe

judges: B. Sasi Mahendran, J. | Amal Ranaraja, J.
offence_sections: Section 365 B (2)(b) of the Penal Code as amended by Act No. 22 of 1995 and Act No. 29 of 1998
brief_facts_summary: The victim PW 01 was 14 years old and in grade 8 when the appellant, her father, committed grave sexual abuse against her. The first incident occurred when the appellant took her to a jungle to pick cashews and had intercrural sex with her. Three days later, at around midnight at home, the appellant again had intercrural sex with PW 01 while she was sleeping. The victim disclosed the abuse to PW 02, who informed PW 03 (the mother), who then complained to police.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 365 B (2)(b) of the Penal Code as amended by Act No. 22 of 1995 and Act No. 29 of 1998
hc_sentence_type: 15 years rigorous imprisonment on each of two charges with fines and default imprisonment
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court Judge convicted the appellant on the first and second charges of grave sexual abuse and acquitted him of the third charge. The Judge carefully evaluated all evidence including witness testimonies and expert reports, considering the age and background of witnesses, and concluded the prosecution established a strong case with compelling evidence creating a coherent narrative supporting the allegations.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant challenged both the conviction and sentencing order. The appellant argued that the prosecution evidence revealed a strong motive for false implication, claiming PW 01 and PW 03 brought his alleged bad character into evidence while PW 02 displayed bias. The appellant maintained his position that his wife was having an extramarital affair and planned the case to mislead police and imprison him.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Prosecution evidence reveals strong motive for false implication | PW 01 and PW 03 brought appellant's bad character into the case | PW 02 displayed bias | Case was fabricated due to wife's illicit affair
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found that the High Court Judge thoroughly evaluated evidence taking into account the age and background of witnesses. The Court acknowledged discrepancies in victim's testimony due to passage of 12 years and psychological factors, but deemed contradictions immaterial as they did not fundamentally undermine credibility. The combined testimony of PW 01, PW 02, and PW 03 showed clear consensus challenging the appellant's assertions.
probability_assessment_by_court: Court found prosecution succeeded in creating coherent narrative with compelling evidence establishing case beyond reasonable doubt, while appellant's dock statement failed to create reasonable doubt
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty and gave a dock statement maintaining he was not mentally retarded to have sex with his daughter. He claimed his wife was having an extramarital affair and planned the false allegations to mislead police and imprison him. The Court found the dock statement failed to create reasonable doubt and noted the appellant failed to suggest his position to PW 02 while PW 01 and PW 03 categorically rejected his stance.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal extensively discussed the complexities of child testimony and memory over time, noting PW 01 was examined in court 12 years after the incidents. The Court found discrepancies understandable given the victim's age, psychological development, trauma, and passage of time. The Court cited Section 166 of the Code of Criminal Procedure Act and precedent D.R.M.Pandithakoralege vs. V.K.Selvanayagam 56 NLR 143 to establish that the lack of exact dates did not mislead the appellant and was not material. The Court evaluated the dock statement principles and found the High Court Judge properly assessed why it failed to create reasonable doubt. The Court noted the appellant failed to suggest his position regarding fabrication to PW 02, and that PW 01, PW 02, and PW 03's combined testimony showed clear consensus rejecting the appellant's assertions. The Court concluded the High Court Judge thoroughly evaluated all evidence considering witness age and background, ensured no undue burden on appellant, and properly found prosecution established a strong case. Finding no basis to interfere, the Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal.
coa_sentence_type: 15 years rigorous imprisonment on each of two charges with fines of Rs.10,000 per charge and six months simple imprisonment in default of payment
brief_judgment_file_summary: Mapa Hamilage Sunil Premasiri Mapa was convicted by the High Court of Kurunegala of two counts of grave sexual abuse under Section 365 B (2)(b) of the Penal Code against his 14-year-old daughter, and sentenced to 15 years rigorous imprisonment and Rs.10,000 fine per count. The appellant challenged the conviction and sentence arguing false implication motivated by his wife's extramarital affair. The Court of Appeal extensively analyzed issues of child testimony reliability over time, finding discrepancies understandable given 12 years passed between incidents and court testimony. The Court held the lack of exact dates was not material under Section 166 and cited precedent that mistaken dates do not require amendment unless the accused is prejudiced. Finding the High Court Judge properly evaluated all evidence and the appellant's dock statement failed to create reasonable doubt, the Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal.
defence_counsel: Dineru Bandana
hc_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal affirmed the High Court Judge's thorough evaluation of evidence, noting the Judge properly considered the age and background of witnesses, carefully evaluated background facts, and ensured no undue burden was placed on the appellant. The High Court Judge correctly assessed why the appellant's dock statement failed to create reasonable doubt in the prosecution's case.
precedents_cited_list: D.R.M.Pandithakoralege (Excise Inspector) vs. V.K.Selvanayagam 56 NLR 143 | William Edward James | Dossi
standard_of_review_applied: Appellate review of conviction and sentence with consideration of whether High Court properly evaluated evidence and whether appellant was misled by any procedural defects

judges: B. Sasi Mahendran, J. | Amal Ranaraja, J.
offence_sections: Section 54 A (b) and Section 54 A (d) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance as amended by Act No.13 of 1984
brief_facts_summary: On 04.04.2014, police officers from the narcotics bureau received a tip about drug transportation in Wellampitiya. At about 22.50 hrs, an informant pointed out a three-wheel scooter driven by the appellant. Officers stopped the appellant in Seeyawatha, Maligawaththa and discovered a black plastic bag containing four silver foiled bags with brown powder identified as heroin (693.9 grams). The appellant was arrested and a weighing scale was recovered from his house.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 54 A (b) and Section 54 A (d) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance as amended by Act No.13 of 1984
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court Judge convicted the appellant on both charges of trafficking and possessing 693.9 grams of heroin and sentenced him to death. The HC gave credence to prosecution witnesses' testimony over the appellant's dock statement and rejected the defence version.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant challenged whether the prosecution version was inherently impossible and whether the HC Judge erred in using different yardsticks to analyze prosecution versus defence cases. The appellant argued the HC Judge wrongly concluded the prosecution version was more probable than the defence version and improperly rejected the dock statement without proper reasons. The appellant also raised whether he received a fair trial.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Is the prosecution version inherently impossible? | Did the Learned High Court Judge err in using a different yardstick in analysing the prosecution's case as against the defendant's case? | Did the Learned High Court Judge err in coming to the conclusion that the prosecution version is more probable than the defence version? | Did the Learned High Court Judge err in rejecting the dock statement without proper reasons? | In those circumstances, did the appellant receive a fair trial in the High Court.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The COA found the testimony of PW1 and PW5 strange, peculiar, odd and unusual. The Court noted the informant's ability to identify the three-wheel scooter at night for four hours without knowing registration details was implausible. The officers' conduct in exposing the informant and not stopping the vehicle at the earliest opportunity did not harmonize with expected police procedure.
probability_assessment_by_court: The COA found the prosecution narrative implausible and not convincing. The Court applied the principle from Alim vs. Wijesinghe that where facts are capable of inference in favour of the accused and against him, the inference consistent with innocence should be preferred.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty and gave a dock statement claiming he travelled to Avisawella High Court to stand surety for someone named Lalitha. After returning to Colombo, he was stopped near Samantha Cinema Hall in Dematagoda, blindfolded, taken to an isolated area, assaulted and questioned about drugs. He was then taken to two houses in Wanniwatha, Wellampitiya where drugs were purportedly found and he was falsely implicated. The COA found the HC Judge improperly rejected this dock statement without proper reasons.
legal_errors_description: The COA held the Learned High Court Judge misdirected himself when he concluded prosecution witnesses were creditworthy and it was safe to act on their testimony. The HC Judge erred in using a different yardstick to analyze prosecution versus defence cases and wrongly rejected the dock statement without proper reasons.
procedural_defects_description: Law enforcement officers failed to protect the informant's identity by having the informant present at the roadside when the appellant passed by, which is unusual and not normal police procedure. Officers also failed to explain precautions taken to avoid detection during the extended pursuit.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the prosecution witnesses' narratives implausible, strange, and unusual. The COA noted it was uncertain how the informant could identify the appellant in a three-wheel scooter at night without knowing the registration number and for an extended surveillance period of over four hours. The officers' failure to protect the informant's identity and their decision not to stop the vehicle at the earliest opportunity were inconsistent with normal police conduct. The HC Judge improperly gave credence to prosecution testimony when facts were capable of inference favoring the appellant's innocence, in violation of the principle in Alim vs. Wijesinghe. Given nine years had lapsed since the offence and the unreliable nature of the evidence, the COA found it unjust to order a retrial, citing The Queen vs. G.K.Jayasinghe as precedent.
coa_sentence_type: Acquittal - conviction and sentence set aside
brief_judgment_file_summary: The appellant Seyed Ibrahim Mohomed Uvais was convicted by the High Court of Colombo for trafficking and possessing 693.9 grams of heroin on 04.04.2014 at Maligawaththa and sentenced to death. He appealed arguing the prosecution version was implausible and he did not receive a fair trial. The Court of Appeal found the testimony of police witnesses strange and implausible, noting the informant's unlikely ability to identify the vehicle at night and the officers' improper exposure of the informant. The COA held the HC Judge misdirected himself in favoring prosecution testimony when facts supported the defence version. Given nine years had lapsed since the offence and the unreliable evidence, the COA set aside the conviction and sentence and acquitted the appellant.
defence_counsel: Shavindra Fernand, P.C. with Thivanka Attygalle, Mirthula Skandarajah and Rishnie Fernandopulle
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court Judge gave credence to prosecution witnesses' testimony and rejected the appellant's dock statement. However, the COA found the HC Judge misdirected himself by not applying the principle that where facts are capable of inference favoring the accused, that inference should be preferred. The HC used different yardsticks for analyzing prosecution versus defence cases.
precedents_cited_list: Alim vs. Wijesinghe (S.I.Police, Batticaloa) 38 CLW 95 | The Queen vs. G.K.Jayasinghe 69 NLR 314
standard_of_review_applied: The Court of Appeal applied appellate review standards examining whether the HC Judge properly assessed credibility and applied correct legal principles, particularly the principle that facts capable of dual inference should favor the accused's innocence.

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code read with Section 32 of the Penal Code
location_of_offence: Near the deceased's house in a paddy field, Kadawata area
brief_facts_summary: On 11-07-2000, two men were attacked with a sharp cutting instrument near a paddy field. The deceased Nimal Indrasiri Rohana Mayadunna was found with fatal cut injuries after going out to buy cigarettes. Before death, he identified three attackers including the appellant. His wife saw three persons running away and the brother also heard the dying declaration naming the same three persons.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code read with Section 32 of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court found the appellant guilty on the first count for causing the death of Nimal Indrasiri Rohana Mayadunna based on dying declarations and eyewitness testimony. The appellant was acquitted on the second count due to lack of evidence. The court sentenced him to death for murder.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant argued that the High Court Judge convicted him on insufficient and doubtful evidence. He challenged the reliability of the dying declarations claiming they were different from each other. He also contested the eyewitness identification stating there was insufficient light for positive identification and the defence evidence was rejected on unreasonable grounds.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The learned High Court Judge has convicted the accused-appellant on insufficient and doubtful evidence of the prosecution | Defence evidence has been rejected on unreasonable grounds
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court analyzed dying declarations made to two witnesses and evaluated their consistency. The JMO confirmed the deceased could speak for 30 minutes to one hour after injuries. Minor contradictions about timing and seeing the second deceased were attributed to 19-year delay in testimony and did not affect credibility.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court assessed the dying declarations were consistent and corroborated. The identification was reliable given bright moonlight conditions and familiarity with accused persons. The JMO evidence supported that deceased could speak after injuries.
defence_version_summary: Plea: Not guilty. Alibi: Yes - claimed he was drinking liquor at Sisira's shop until 11 p.m. Defence called one witness (Sisira) to support alibi. Made dock statement only, did not give sworn evidence. Court rejected alibi as it did not create impossibility of presence at crime scene since shop was in same village.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed whether dying declarations were admissible and reliable under Section 32(1) of the Evidence Ordinance. It found the two declarations consistent with each other, not contradictory. The COA affirmed the JMO evidence that deceased could speak for 30 minutes to one hour given his age and physical strength. The Court accepted the identification was positive given bright moonlight five days before full moon and familiarity with accused. Minor contradictions were explained by 19-year delay. The alibi was properly rejected as it did not establish impossibility of presence at crime scene. The Court found no legal or factual errors in the High Court judgment.
coa_sentence_type: Death
brief_judgment_file_summary: The appellant was the 3rd accused charged with murder of Nimal Indrasiri Rohana Mayadunna on 11-07-2000 along with two co-accused. The High Court convicted him to death based on dying declarations and eyewitness testimony. On appeal, he challenged the reliability of dying declarations and identification evidence. The Court of Appeal held the dying declarations were consistent and admissible, medical evidence supported the deceased's ability to speak after injuries, and identification was reliable given moonlight and familiarity. The alibi defence was properly rejected. The appeal was dismissed and conviction affirmed.
defence_counsel: Niranjan Jayasinghe
cause_of_death_exact_text: 15 inches long cut injury caused to the heart cavity and the lung cavity on the right side of the heart, and the stomach, which has caused cut injuries to the liver, several ribs, and other internal organs - described as necessarily fatal injury
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court properly evaluated the dying declarations under Section 32(1) of the Evidence Ordinance and found them reliable. It correctly assessed the identification evidence and medical evidence supporting the deceased's ability to speak. The HC properly rejected the alibi as it did not create reasonable doubt about the prosecution case.
precedents_cited_list: Ranasinghe Vs. The Attorney General (2007) 1 SLR 218 | Gunapala and Others Vs. The Republic of Sri Lanka (1994) 3 SLR 180 | Martin Singho Vs. Queen 69 CLW 21 | The King Vs. Marshall (1948) 51 NLR 157 | Rex vs. Chandrasekera (1942) 44 NLR 126 | Rex vs. Fernando (1947) 48 NLR 251 | E.R.S.R Coomaraswamy, The Law of Evidence Volume 1 at page 466
standard_of_review_applied: The Court of Appeal reviewed whether the High Court convicted on insufficient and doubtful evidence, whether dying declarations were properly admitted and evaluated, whether identification evidence was reliable, and whether the alibi was properly considered. The standard applied was whether the prosecution proved the case beyond reasonable doubt.

judges: Menaka Wijesundera, J. | Wickum A. Kaluarachchi, J.
offence_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: On 13th October 2008 around 7 a.m., the accused-appellant and another person entered the victims' house and shot Chandralatha (mother) and Dinesh Prasanna (son), resulting in both deaths. PW-4, the daughter and sister of the deceased, witnessed the accused-appellant leaving the scene after hearing gunshots. Dinesh Prasanna died at hospital admission, while Chandralatha died nearly a month later from septicemia caused by firearm injuries. One day after the incident, Chandralatha made a dying declaration to Police Constable Saman Kumara identifying 'Sampath' from Bandaranayakepura as the shooter.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court of Colombo convicted the accused-appellant on two counts of murder for killing Chandralatha and Dinesh Prasanna and imposed the death sentence. The conviction was based on eyewitness testimony of PW-4 and the dying declaration of Chandralatha, both identifying the accused-appellant as the shooter.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant challenged the conviction arguing that the Trial Judge failed to adequately consider facts in his favor and infirmities in the prosecution case. He contended the dying declaration was not evaluated using proper legal tests and his alibi defense was not adequately considered. The defense also argued that chain of causation regarding Chandralatha's death was not properly examined and the accused was denied a fair trial.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The learned Trial Judge has failed to adequately consider the facts in favour of the accused-appellant as required by law | The obvious infirmities in the case for the prosecution have not been considered adequately and reasons for acting upon the evidence notwithstanding such infirmities have not been given | The dying deposition of the deceased has not been considered utilizing the tests laid down by our courts | The defence of alibi taken up by the accused throughout the trial has not been adequately considered | There has not been adequate consideration of the defence case as required by law | The accused has been denied a fair trial, which is a constitutionally guaranteed fundamental right
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court found PW-4 credible, noting she made a prompt statement to police on 14.10.2008 and saw the appellant at close proximity (six feet) in good morning lighting. The dying declaration of Chandralatha was deemed true and reliable as she explicitly identified 'Sampath' as the shooter, with no reason for false implication. Both pieces of evidence corroborated each other regarding the identity of the accused-appellant.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court found the prosecution proved the two charges beyond reasonable doubt based on corroborated eyewitness and dying declaration evidence. The alibi was rejected as it failed to cover the time of the offence and the dock statement was unbelievable.
defence_version_summary: The accused pleaded not guilty and raised an alibi defense claiming he was on official duty at Kotte Municipal Council at the time of the incident. He made a dock statement claiming his brother 'Upul' came to the incident location and PW-4 misidentified him due to their similar appearance. He also claimed he was arrested the day after the incident by a police officer named 'Saman'. The Court rejected the dock statement as unbelievable because it failed to specify the time he was at work, provided no documentary evidence, and contradicted unchallenged prosecution evidence that he was arrested on 25.10.2008 after absconding.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal thoroughly examined whether the dying declaration met legal standards from Ranasinghe v. Attorney General. While noting the Trial Judge did not explicitly enumerate all tests, the Court found the Judge properly considered key matters including that Chandralatha had no opportunity for tutoring before making the declaration. The Court emphasized Chandralatha saw the shooter in very close proximity, knew the appellant well, and explicitly identified 'Sampath' in her signed statement. Regarding the alibi, the Court found it failed because it did not cover the specific time of the offence (around 7:10-7:15 a.m.), lacked documentary support, and the dock statement contradicted unchallenged evidence about the arrest date and the appellant absconding. The Court held the dying declaration and PW-4's testimony corroborated each other, establishing guilt beyond reasonable doubt. The Court rejected the chain of causation argument because the defense admitted the cause of death.
coa_sentence_type: Death sentence
brief_judgment_file_summary: Mahawanni Arachchige Sampath Chaminda was convicted by the High Court of Colombo for murdering Chandralatha and her son Dinesh Prasanna on 13th October 2008 and sentenced to death. He appealed arguing the Trial Judge failed to properly evaluate the dying declaration, inadequately considered his alibi defense, and denied him a fair trial. The Court of Appeal affirmed the conviction on 26th March 2024, finding that the dying declaration was reliable and corroborated by eyewitness PW-4, while the alibi failed to cover the time of the offence and the dock statement was unbelievable. The appeal was dismissed and the death sentence was upheld.
defence_counsel: Palitha Fernando, P.C.
cause_of_death_exact_text: Death of Chandralatha was due to Septicemia occurred as a result of firearm injuries. Death of Dinesh Prasanna was due to cranio-cerebral injuries following discharge from a firearm or firearms.
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court accepted the dying declaration as independently made without tutoring and relied on PW-4's eyewitness testimony to convict the appellant. The Court noted the appellant was a well-known person to the victims and PW-4 identified him fleeing the scene. The High Court also considered and rejected the alibi defense, finding the dock statement unconvincing.

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code for double murder and Section 380 of the Penal Code for robbery
brief_facts_summary: The Appellant was engaged in tile work at the victims' house on the day of the incident. The victims, Wimal Malaviarachchi and Nanda Srimathi, were found murdered in their home by their son and relatives when they failed to pick up the children from tuition class. A DVD player, gold jewelry belonging to the deceased mother, and a phone belonging to the deceased father were missing. The Appellant was arrested after investigation revealed that the deceased's mobile phone was recovered from him, and stolen jewelry was recovered from a pawn shop under a receipt in the Appellant's name.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code for double murder and Section 380 of the Penal Code for robbery
hc_sentence_type: Death on counts 1 and 2, 10 years rigorous imprisonment and fine of Rs.2500 with default sentence of 3 months simple imprisonment on count 3
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court Judge convicted the Appellant of double murder under Section 296 of the Penal Code and robbery under Section 380 of the Penal Code. The Appellant was sentenced to death on the first and second counts for the murders of Wimal Malaviarachchi and Nanda Srimathi. On the third count of robbery, the Appellant was sentenced to 10 years rigorous imprisonment and a fine of Rs.2500 with a default sentence of 3 months simple imprisonment.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The Appellant challenged the conviction on four grounds: insufficient circumstantial evidence to convict beyond reasonable doubt, failure by the High Court Judge to explain and record the Appellant's rights under Section 200(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure Act, improper admission of PW3's evidence in absence of a police statement and inquest evidence, and failure to properly consider the Appellant's dock statement.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The Learned High Court Judge has failed to consider the items of circumstantial evidence beyond reasonable doubt as the circumstantial evidence led in the trial is insufficient to convict the Appellant | The Learned High Court Judge has failed to explain and record the rights of the Appellant as per section 200(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure Act No. 15 of 1979 | The Learned High Court Judge erred in law by allowing the prosecution to lead the evidence of PW3 in absence of statement given to police and in absence of his evidence in the NS proceedings | The Learned High Court Judge has not considered the dock statement of the Appellant in its correct perspective
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The prosecution called 12 witnesses including lay witnesses, official witnesses, and medical witnesses. PW3, the 12-year-old son of the deceased, identified the Appellant as the person doing tile work at the house and identified stolen items. PW1 and PW2 corroborated the discovery of the bodies. The Court of Appeal found the circumstantial evidence strong and incriminating, noting that the failure to cross-examine PW22 on the phone recovery indicated acceptance of that testimony.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal held that the items of circumstantial evidence led in the trial were sufficient to reach the conclusion that the Appellant only committed the murder of the deceased persons and robbed the items recovered from him, and that the evidence adduced by the prosecution was potent and conclusive
defence_version_summary: The Appellant pleaded not guilty and made only a dock statement to end the defence case without calling any witnesses. The Court of Appeal held that the Learned High Court Judge had considered the dock statement extensively and given reasons why she disbelieved it, finding that the evidence adduced by the Appellant could not create any doubt over the prosecution case.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal comprehensively analyzed all four grounds of appeal and dismissed each. On the procedural ground regarding Section 200(1), the Court found that despite the proceeding not indicating compliance, the journal entry and judgment confirmed the Appellant's rights were explained. On the circumstantial evidence ground, the Court applied established principles from multiple precedents and found the evidence sufficient, noting the recovered mobile phone, jewelry pawned under the Appellant's name, and DVD player all linked the Appellant to the crime. The Court emphasized that PW22's evidence on phone recovery was not cross-examined, which constituted acceptance. On the identification ground, the Court found PW3's identification reliable as he had clearly seen the Appellant when delivering lunch and later identified him at an identification parade admitted under Section 420. On the ground regarding PW3's evidence, the Court held that inquest evidence could be used as previous statements and the prosecution had the right to call PW3. On the dock statement ground, the Court found the High Court Judge had properly considered and rejected it with reasons. The Court affirmed the conviction, finding the circumstantial evidence strong, incriminating, and sufficient to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt.
coa_sentence_type: Death on counts 1 and 2, 10 years rigorous imprisonment and fine of Rs.2500 with default sentence of 3 months simple imprisonment on count 3
brief_judgment_file_summary: The Appellant, Kurudupatabedilage Sudharshana Jayasekera, was convicted by the High Court of Panadura for the double murder of Wimal Malaviarachchi and Nanda Srimathi under Section 296 of the Penal Code and robbery under Section 380 of the Penal Code, committed on or about 23 November 2008 while he was engaged in tile work at the victims' house. He was sentenced to death on the murder counts and 10 years rigorous imprisonment with a fine of Rs.2500 on the robbery count. The Appellant appealed on four grounds: insufficient circumstantial evidence, procedural violations regarding Section 200(1), improper admission of PW3's evidence, and improper consideration of his dock statement. The Court of Appeal, comprising Sampath B. Abayakoon J. and P. Kumararatnam J., thoroughly examined each ground and dismissed the appeal on 26 March 2024. The Court found the circumstantial evidence including the recovery of the victim's mobile phone from the Appellant, jewelry pawned under his name, and the DVD player to be strong and incriminating, sufficient to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt, and affirmed both the conviction and sentence.
defence_counsel: Dharshana Kuruppu with Sahan Weerasinghe
cause_of_death_exact_text: Cranio cerebral injuries following impact to the head
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court Judge adequately dealt with and applied the principles governing the evaluation of circumstantial evidence, considered all the circumstances to reach her conclusion, correctly narrated all witnesses who gave evidence, considered the dock statement of the Appellant extensively and gave reasons why she disbelieved it. The Court of Appeal found the High Court Judge had very correctly analyzed all the evidence presented by both parties and properly concluded that the Appellant was guilty of the charges levelled against him.

judges: N. Bandula Karunarathna J. P/CA | D. N. Samarakoon, J. | M. T. Mohammed Laffar, J
brief_facts_summary: This is not a criminal case but a writ application seeking certiorari and prohibition against findings of a Presidential Commission of Inquiry into political victimization. Petitioner Anura Kumara Dissanayake challenged findings made against him by the Commission chaired by Hon. Upali Abeyrathne regarding alleged political victimization complaints.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: Petitioner challenged the Commission's jurisdiction to inquire into complaints from private individuals not falling within the mandate. Argued Commission acted ultra vires its powers, violated natural justice rules, failed to disclose evidence against him, and made unreasonable findings without evidentiary basis.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Commission lacked jurisdiction to hear complaints from private individuals | Complainants were not public officers/state corporation employees/armed forces/police as required by mandate | Petitioner does not fall within categories (a) to (d) of the mandate | Breach of natural justice - no proper disclosure of case against Petitioner | Findings ultra vires and beyond Commission's mandate | Findings unreasonable in Wednesbury sense | Violation of undertaking given to Court of Appeal | Matter sub judice - interference with ongoing judicial proceedings
defence_version_summary: Petitioner appeared before Commission and gave evidence but objected to jurisdiction. Contended he did not interfere with investigations or judicial proceedings. No evidence showed he participated in decision-making of Anti-Corruption Committee or manipulated any proceedings. Commission violated undertaking given to Court not to summon him.
legal_errors_description: Commission acted without jurisdiction by accepting complaints from persons not within its mandate, exceeded its powers by inquiring into matters outside paragraphs (a) to (d) of the Gazette, violated rules of natural justice, acted contrary to undertaking given to Court, interfered with sub judice matters, made findings without evidentiary basis
procedural_defects_description: Failed to disclose complaint and evidence to Petitioner, failed to provide fair hearing, violated undertaking to Court, did not permit Attorney General's counsel to make submissions on behalf of Petitioner, threatened counsel with contempt proceedings
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: Court held Commission lacked jurisdiction as most complainants were not public officers/state employees/armed forces/police as required by mandate. Petitioner did not fall within categories (a) to (d) of the Gazette. Commission breached natural justice by not disclosing case against Petitioner and threatening counsel. Commission violated undertaking given to Court not to summon Petitioner. Recommendations not legally binding but should be quashed to protect Petitioner's reputation. Findings unreasonable, arbitrary, mala fide, ultra vires, and without evidentiary basis. Special Presidential Commission appointed to review findings came to premature end without recommendations, showing original findings lacked merit. Cabinet decided not to implement recommendations.
brief_judgment_file_summary: Petitioner Anura Kumara Dissanayake, Leader of JVP and Member of Parliament, challenged findings of Presidential Commission of Inquiry into Political Victimization chaired by Hon. Upali Abeyrathne. Commission made findings against Petitioner in 16 complaints and recommended action under Bribery Act and other laws. Court of Appeal held Commission lacked jurisdiction as complainants were private individuals not within mandate, Petitioner did not fall within categories Commission could inquire into, Commission violated natural justice and undertaking to Court. Court quashed all findings and recommendations against Petitioner and issued prohibition preventing further action. No order for costs.

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 354 of the Penal Code (Count 1) and Section 365B(2)(b) of the Penal Code as amended by Penal Code (Amendment) Act No. 22 of 1995, 29 of 1998 and 16 of 2006 (Count 2)
brief_facts_summary: The appellant abducted a 9-year-old girl child on or about 01-01-2013 at Pesalai during a wedding at his house. He took her between two parked vans in the dark, lifted her dress, touched her thighs and genitals. The child reported it to her grandmother immediately, but the grandmother told her not to tell anyone. The incident came to light in 2014 after a child protection awareness program at school.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 354 of the Penal Code (Count 1) and Section 365B(2)(b) of the Penal Code as amended by Penal Code (Amendment) Act No. 22 of 1995, 29 of 1998 and 16 of 2006 (Count 2)
hc_sentence_type: Count 1: 2 years rigorous imprisonment and Rs.10,000 fine (in default 6 months simple imprisonment). Count 2: 7 years rigorous imprisonment and Rs.10,000 fine (in default 6 months simple imprisonment). Sentences to run concurrently. Rs.100,000 compensation to victim (in default 6 months simple imprisonment)
hc_judgment_summary: The learned High Court Judge of Mannar found the appellant guilty as charged on both counts after trial on 29-06-2022. After considering mitigatory and aggravating circumstances, the judge sentenced him to concurrent imprisonment terms on both counts along with fines and ordered compensation to the victim child.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant challenged the conviction arguing belatedness of the complaint and discrepancies in PW-01's evidence with other witnesses. He contended that the prosecution failed to prove the specific act of inserting a finger into the vagina as charged. He argued that the offence of kidnapping cannot be sustained. He further submitted that the learned High Court Judge failed to adequately consider the defence evidence, especially the appellant's testimony.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Belatedness of the complaint and discrepancies of the evidence of PW-01 taken with other witnesses renders conviction unsustainable | In light of the specific act mentioned in the indictment, the prosecution has failed to prove the charge of grave sexual abuse | The offence of kidnapping cannot be sustained in the light of the evidence | The learned High Court Judge has failed to adequately consider the defence, especially the evidence of the appellant
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court analyzed the victim child's evidence given 7 years after the incident when she was a grade 11 student. The grandmother confirmed the child reported the incident immediately but was told not to tell anyone. The Child Rights Welfare Officer confirmed disclosure after awareness program. The evidence was found cogent and trustworthy when considered in totality.
probability_assessment_by_court: Court found that the prosecution proved the case beyond reasonable doubt when considering the evidence as a whole, despite the child being unable to specify exact manner of touching. The defence of false complaint due to jealousy was found unsupported.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty and gave evidence under oath. He took the position that a false complaint was made against him due to jealousy because his family and children are well educated and the villagers are jealous. He also claimed villagers were angry because he supported a candidate opposed by them in an election. He called several defence witnesses including the grandmother, Child Rights Welfare Officer, JMO, and friend of victim. The Court found the defence positions were not put to prosecution witnesses in cross-examination and that the prosecution proved the case beyond reasonable doubt.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal comprehensively analyzed the totality of evidence from both prosecution and defence. The COA found the belatedness of complaint was explainable and justified given the child's age, the grandmother telling her not to tell anyone, and disclosure occurring after an awareness program. Minor discrepancies were not material to shake the core of the case. The COA held that although the child could not specify the exact manner of touching, her evidence established the appellant touched her vagina which satisfied the elements of grave sexual abuse. The offence of kidnapping was established as the child was taken between vans without consent of lawful guardian. The defence positions of jealousy and political enmity were not put to prosecution witnesses in cross-examination, which was held against the appellant. The COA applied precedents regarding belated complaints, photographic memory expectations, and significance of contradictions, concluding the prosecution proved its case beyond reasonable doubt.
coa_sentence_type: Count 1: 2 years rigorous imprisonment and Rs.10,000 fine (in default 6 months simple imprisonment). Count 2: 7 years rigorous imprisonment and Rs.10,000 fine (in default 6 months simple imprisonment). Sentences to run concurrently. Rs.100,000 compensation to victim (in default 6 months simple imprisonment). Conviction and sentence affirmed.
brief_judgment_file_summary: Pathinathan Consal Dias was convicted by the High Court of Mannar for abducting and committing grave sexual abuse on a 9-year-old girl child on 01-01-2013 at Pesalai. He was sentenced to concurrent imprisonment terms totaling 7 years with fines of Rs.20,000 and compensation of Rs.100,000. The appellant challenged the conviction on grounds of belatedness, discrepancies, failure to prove specific act, and inadequate consideration of defence. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal, finding the belatedness was explainable, discrepancies were not material, the elements of both offences were proved beyond reasonable doubt, and the defence positions were not properly put to prosecution witnesses in cross-examination.
defence_counsel: Saliya Pieris, P.C. with K. Kugaraja
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court Judge found the appellant guilty as charged after trial and sentenced him to concurrent imprisonment terms with fines and compensation. The COA found no errors in the High Court's analysis and affirmed that the High Court properly evaluated the evidence and correctly concluded the prosecution proved its case beyond reasonable doubt.

standard_of_review_applied: The Court of Appeal reviewed whether the conviction and sentence were manifestly wrong and whether the prosecution proved its case beyond reasonable doubt. The COA considered the totality of evidence without compartmentalizing and evaluated whether material contradictions existed that would shake the core of the case.

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 19(b) and 19(c) of the Bribery Act No. 11 of 1954 as amended
brief_facts_summary: Information was received on 03.04.2018 prompting CIABOC to authorize an investigation against the Respondent. The Investigation Officer conducted a raid on 05.04.2018 and arrested the Respondent while he was accepting Rs. 5,000 from the complainant Nagalingam Thangamma. The Respondent was charged with solicitation and acceptance of money as gratification on various occasions to perform his duty. The indictment contained 12 charges.
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court upheld a preliminary objection raised by the defence that all Commissioners of CIABOC had not given directive to the Director General to proceed with the criminal investigation. The High Court dismissed the indictment and discharged the Respondent on 21.10.2022.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The Petitioner argued that the High Court order was contrary to law and infested with illegality. The main ground was that Section 2(8) of CIABOC Act allows Commission members to exercise powers separately, and their acts are deemed acts of the Commission. The Petitioner contended that the HC erroneously applied the Anoma Polwatte case and failed to consider that no provision requires all three commissioners to sign directives.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The order dated 21.10.2022 is contrary to law | The order is infested with illegality since learned High Court Judge has entailed sanctioning of criminal investigation by all three commissioners as a prerequisite which is not known to law | The learned Trial Judge erred in law by failing to consider Section 2(8) of CIABOC Act that members may exercise powers separately | The learned Trial Judge erred in law by failing to consider that Anoma Polwatte case was regarding Section 78(1) of Bribery Act and Respondent should have used remedy under Section 24(1) of CIABOC Act | The learned Trial Judge erred in law by failing to consider that investigation and institution of proceedings constitute a Power under Section 16(3) of CIABOC Act | The learned Trial Judge misconceived in law in holding that directive is required under Sec. 3 of CIABOC Act for both investigation and institution of proceedings | The learned trial Judge misdirected himself in
