considering ratio decidendi in Anoma Polwatta case applicable to institution of proceeding and investigation | The learned trial judge misconceived in law in holding that section 78(1) of Bribery Act is applicable to institution of proceedings before High Court | The learned Trial Judge erred by failing to consider CA/PHC/APN/2/2021 which recognized distinction between criminal proceedings under CIABOC Act and Bribery Act | The Learned Trial judge erroneously determined that Supreme Court Judgement should be considered over Court of Appeal judgement | The learned trial judge erroneously determined that the criminal investigation was contrary to law | The learned Trial judge misconceived in law regarding Anoma Polwatte case and Section 78 of Bribery Act | The Court of Appeal erred in failing to consider applicability of section 114(D) of Evidence Ordinance | The Learned Trial Judge errored in law in failing to give valid reasons for the order | The order is contrary to legal maxim Ut res magis valeat quam pereat
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The case did not proceed to trial as it was dismissed at the preliminary objection stage. No witness evidence was analyzed by either the High Court or Court of Appeal. The case centered on procedural and jurisdictional issues regarding the validity of the indictment.
defence_version_summary: The defence raised a preliminary objection that the indictment was void ab initio because all Commissioners of CIABOC had not given directive to proceed with criminal investigation. The defence relied on Anoma Polwatta v CIABOC SC/Writ Application No. 01/2011 and urged the trial judge to dismiss the indictment. The High Court accepted the defence preliminary objection.
legal_errors_description: The Court of Appeal found that the High Court erred in law by requiring all three CIABOC Commissioners to sign the directive, which is not required under Section 2(8) of CIABOC Act. The HC also erred by misapplying the Anoma Polwatte case which dealt with Section 78(1) of Bribery Act regarding Magistrates Court proceedings, not High Court proceedings under CIABOC Act Sections 11 and 12. The HC failed to consider that only compliance with Sections 12(1) and (2) is required when Director General files indictment.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal conducted a comprehensive analysis of the procedural requirements for filing indictments under the CIABOC Act. The COA relied heavily on the Supreme Court decision in Indikatiya Hewage Kusumadasa Mahanama case decided on 11.01.2023, which clarified that no additional requirement of written directive from all commissioners is needed beyond compliance with Sections 12(1) and (2) of CIABOC Act. The COA found that Section 2(8) of CIABOC Act explicitly allows Commission members to exercise powers separately, and such acts are deemed acts of the Commission. The COA distinguished between proceedings under Section 78(1) of Bribery Act in Magistrates Court and proceedings under Sections 11 and 12 of CIABOC Act in High Court. The COA held that the High Court has no power to question validity of indictment beyond checking compliance with Sections 12(1) and (2), and any such challenge should be before Supreme Court under Section 24. The COA concluded that requiring written sanction from all commissioners is an unnecessary additional requirement that would obstruct the smooth functioning of the Bribery Act.
coa_sentence_type: Case remanded back to High Court for trial
brief_judgment_file_summary: This is a revision application by the Director General of CIABOC challenging the High Court of Colombo's order dismissing an indictment against Sivapadham Sadhananthan charged under Section 19(b) and 19(c) of the Bribery Act. The accused was arrested on 05.04.2018 while accepting Rs. 5,000 as gratification. The High Court upheld a preliminary objection that all three CIABOC Commissioners had not signed the directive for investigation. The Court of Appeal allowed the revision, holding that Section 2(8) of CIABOC Act permits commissioners to act separately and their individual acts are deemed Commission acts. The COA relied on Supreme Court precedent clarifying that only compliance with Sections 12(1) and (2) is required when filing indictments, and set aside the HC order directing the case back to trial.
prosecution_counsel: Anusha Sammandapperuma, Assistant Director Legal for the Petitioner
defence_counsel: Saliya Pieris, PC for the Respondent
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court upheld the defence preliminary objection based on the premise that all CIABOC Commissioners must give directive for criminal investigation. The HC dismissed the indictment discharging the Respondent. The COA found this reasoning erroneous as it imposed an additional requirement not found in law and misapplied the Anoma Polwatte precedent which dealt with different statutory provisions.
precedents_cited_list: Anoma Polwatta v The Commission to Investigate Allegation of Bribery and Corruption SC/Writ Application No. 01/2011 | CA/PHC/APN/2/2021 decided on 01/11/2021 | Indikatiya Hewage Kusumadasa Mahanama and Another v. The Commission to Investigate Allegations of Bribery or Corruption and Another SC TAB 1A and 1B/2000, decided on 11.01.2023
standard_of_review_applied: Revision jurisdiction under Article 138 of the Constitution read with Sections 364 and 365 of the Code of Criminal Procedure Act No. 15 of 1979

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 403 of the Penal Code (cheating); Section 13 of the Sri Lanka Bureau of Foreign Employment Act; Section 389 of the Penal Code (criminal breach of trust); Section 386 of the Penal Code (criminal misappropriation)
brief_facts_summary: The petitioner was charged in the Magistrate's Court of Chilaw with four offences relating to a foreign job transaction. The charges were for cheating under the Penal Code, cheating under the Sri Lanka Bureau of Foreign Employment Act, criminal breach of trust, and criminal misappropriation. The Magistrate convicted her on counts 1, 3, and 4, and acquitted her on count 2. The High Court, on appeal, acquitted her on counts 1 and 3 but upheld the conviction for criminal misappropriation (count 4) and enhanced the sentence.
evidence_type_primary: Evidence related to a foreign job transaction and the payment of Rs. 200,000.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 386 of the Penal Code (criminal misappropriation)
hc_sentence_type: On count 4: 6 months rigorous imprisonment with a fine of Rs. 1500 (default: 1 month imprisonment). Also ordered to pay Rs. 200,000 as compensation (default: 3 months simple imprisonment).
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court partly allowed the appeal, acquitting the petitioner on counts 1 and 3 but affirming the conviction on count 4 (criminal misappropriation). The High Court Judge then varied and enhanced the sentence for count 4, imposing 6 months rigorous imprisonment and a fine.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The primary submission was that the High Court Judge misdirected himself by enhancing the sentence without following due procedure, specifically by not giving the petitioner an opportunity to show cause against the enhancement. This procedural defect was argued to be illegal and a miscarriage of justice.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The High Court Judge erred in enhancing the sentence without giving the petitioner an opportunity to show cause as to why the sentence should not be enhanced.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The judgment focuses on procedural aspects of sentencing rather than detailed analysis of witness evidence. The key evidence appears to be related to the transaction and payment of Rs. 200,000.
defence_version_summary: The petitioner pleaded not guilty in the Magistrate's Court. The appeal to the High Court challenged the conviction and sentence. In the revision application, the defence argued procedural error in the enhancement of sentence.
legal_errors_description: The High Court failed to follow the mandatory procedure of giving the accused an opportunity to show cause before enhancing a sentence.
procedural_defects_description: Failure to afford the petitioner an opportunity to be heard prior to enhancement of the sentence, violating the principle of natural justice (audi alteram partem).
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found that the High Court Judge enhanced the sentence on count 4 without giving the petitioner an opportunity to show cause, which is a procedural irregularity and a miscarriage of justice. The COA held this constituted exceptional circumstances warranting revisionary intervention. Citing precedents (Bandara Vs. Republic of Sri Lanka, SC/SPL/LA No. 201/2006), the court emphasized the cardinal principle that an accused must be heard before sentence enhancement. The COA set aside the enhanced sentence and reinstated the original Magistrate's sentence for count 4.
coa_sentence_type: On count 4: Fine of Rs. 1500 (default: 1 month simple imprisonment). The order to pay Rs. 200,000 compensation (default: 3 months simple imprisonment) remains.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The petitioner was convicted in the Magistrate's Court for fraud-related offences. The High Court acquitted her on some counts but enhanced the sentence for criminal misappropriation. The Court of Appeal, on revision, found the High Court procedurally erred by enhancing the sentence without giving the petitioner a chance to show cause. The COA partly allowed the revision, setting aside the enhanced sentence and restoring the original Magistrate's sentence for the remaining count.
defence_counsel: Anil Silva, P.C. with A. Bandara
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court correctly affirmed the conviction on count 4 but erred in procedure by enhancing the sentence without giving the accused an opportunity to be heard on enhancement. The COA viewed this as a fundamental procedural defect.
precedents_cited_list: Buwaneka Aluvihare, J. in SC Appeal No. 111-2015 with SC Appeal No. 113-15 and SC Appeal No. 114-15 | Hotel Galaxy (Pvt) Ltd. Vs. Mercantile Hotels Management Ltd (1987) 1 SLR 5 | Wijesinghe Vs. Thamararatnam (Sriskantha Law Report Vol. IV page 47) | Vanik Incorporation Ltd. Vs. Jayasekare (1997) 2 SLR 365 | Bandara Vs. Republic of Sri Lanka (2002) 2 SLR 277 | SC Appeal No. 115-2019 (Shiran Gooneratne, J.) | SC/SPL/LA No. 201/2006 | Pharmadasa Vs. Piyadasa (2008) BLR 208
standard_of_review_applied: Revisionary jurisdiction under Article 138 of the Constitution, exercised only in exceptional circumstances where there is a miscarriage of justice due to a fundamental procedural violation.
sentencing_principles_applied: The principle that before enhancing a sentence, the appellate court must give the accused an opportunity to show cause against enhancement, as per natural justice (audi alteram partem).

judges: Menaka Wijesundera, J | Wickum A. Kaluarachchi, J
offence_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The accused-appellant was indicted for the murder of Maduppuli Hewage Susantha by fatal firearm injuries to the chest. The prosecution relied on eyewitnesses PW-1 (the deceased's wife) and PW-2 (the deceased's sister-in-law), who claimed to have seen the accused running from the scene. The defence challenged the identification evidence and the credibility of the witnesses.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court Judge convicted the accused-appellant of murder and sentenced him to death. The judge concluded that strong circumstantial evidence proved beyond reasonable doubt that the accused shot the deceased.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant argued that the High Court Judge misdirected himself by failing to properly evaluate the first information (119 call), failed to consider lighting conditions for identification, erred in evaluating circumstantial evidence, and failed to apply the presumption of innocence correctly. The primary issues were identification and the judge's observations on evidence evaluation.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The learned High Court Judge gravely misdirected himself as he failed to consider/evaluate the first information which is the 119-emergency call. | The identity of the appellant has not been proved beyond a reasonable doubt. | The learned High Court Judge had failed to consider/evaluate that the prosecution has not established the lighting condition at the time of the incident to prove a positive identification. | The learned High Court Judge had erred in law in failing to evaluate the evidence under the legal principles governing circumstantial evidence and had rather acted on suspicious circumstances. | The learned High Court Judge failed to provide the benefit of Section 114(f) of the Evidence Ordinance for the appellant. | The learned High Court Judge had been influenced by facts and circumstances not elicited during the trial. | The learned High Court Judge has misdirected himself on the infirmities in prosecution evidence. | The conviction and sentence are bad in law.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found PW-1's testimony not credible due to contradiction with her first information. PW-2's identification was deemed unreliable as she only saw the back of the fleeing person. The prosecution did not establish sufficient lighting conditions for positive identification.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal held that the identification evidence was insufficient to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt, creating a reasonable doubt regarding whether PW-2 actually identified the appellant.
defence_version_summary: The accused-appellant pleaded not guilty. He made a statement from the dock, which the High Court Judge rejected. No defence witnesses were mentioned. The Court of Appeal did not assess the credibility of the defence version, focusing instead on flaws in prosecution evidence.
legal_errors_description: The High Court Judge held a wrong view that the presumption of innocence is operative only until the prosecution builds a strong case. The judge also misdirected himself regarding the first information and failed to properly evaluate identification evidence.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the High Court Judge erred in law regarding the presumption of innocence, misdirected himself on the first information, and failed to properly evaluate identification evidence. PW-1's credibility was undermined by her first information stating 'unidentified persons'. PW-2's identification was unreliable as she only saw the back of the fleeing person. The prosecution failed to establish sufficient lighting conditions. The court held the identification was not proved beyond reasonable doubt, and the conviction based on circumstantial evidence was unsafe.
coa_sentence_type: Acquitted of murder charge; conviction and sentence set aside.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused-appellant was convicted of murder by the High Court of Matara and sentenced to death. He appealed on grounds including misdirection on the first information, faulty identification, and errors in evaluating circumstantial evidence. The Court of Appeal found the High Court Judge erred on the presumption of innocence and identification. PW-1's testimony was contradicted by her first information. PW-2 only saw the back of the fleeing person. The court held identification was not proved beyond reasonable doubt. The appeal was allowed, the conviction and death sentence were set aside, and the accused was acquitted.
defence_counsel: Kavithri Ubeysekara
cause_of_death_exact_text: fatal firearm injuries on the chest
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court concluded strong circumstantial evidence proved the accused shot the deceased beyond reasonable doubt. The Court of Appeal found this analysis flawed, citing errors in handling the first information, presumption of innocence, and identification evidence.
precedents_cited_list: Anthony Michael Morril V. Attorney General – Court of Appeal Case No. CA 26/06, decided on 25.05.2010
standard_of_review_applied: Evaluation of whether the High Court's conviction was based on evidence proving guilt beyond reasonable doubt.

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Poisons Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance as amended by Amendment Act No. 13 of 1984
brief_facts_summary: The accused-appellant was arrested on 27-01-2001 by Police Narcotic Bureau (PNB) officers based on an informant's tip that a female named Mary would be bringing drugs to Stace Road, Colombo 14. Officers observed and followed a female, later identified as the appellant. Upon searching a purse she was carrying, they found a cellophane bag containing a brown powder suspected to be heroin. A field test was positive. The substance was later analyzed and found to contain 11.8 grams of heroin. The appellant claimed she was arrested inside her home while caring for her sick daughter and that the drugs were planted.
evidence_type_secondary: Government Analyst Report, Eyewitness testimony (police officers)
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Poisons Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance as amended by Amendment Act No. 13 of 1984
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court Judge found the appellant guilty as charged, holding that the prosecution proved its case beyond reasonable doubt. After considering the previous conviction record and other relevant factors, the judge sentenced the appellant to life imprisonment.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant appealed on grounds that the prosecution witnesses' evidence lacked credibility and probability, the chain of custody of the drug productions was not proven, and the High Court Judge rejected the appellant's defence on unreasonable grounds.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The evidence of the prosecution witnesses fails the test of credibility and the probability. | The prosecution has failed to prove the chain of custody of productions. | The evidence given by the accused-appellant has been rejected on unreasonable grounds.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed the prosecution witnesses' evidence as a whole, finding minor discrepancies not material to the core of the case. It found their evidence credible and consistent on material points.
probability_assessment_by_court: The court assessed the probability of the prosecution version against the defence, found the prosecution version more probable, and held no reasonable doubt was created by minor contradictions or the defence.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty. She gave a sworn dock statement claiming she was arrested inside her home while with her sick daughter, that the police found nothing, and that the drugs were planted from a previous raid. The High Court and Court of Appeal found her defence inconsistent and not credible, failing to create reasonable doubt.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed the grounds systematically. It found the prosecution witnesses credible despite minor discrepancies in timing and descriptions, which were not material. It held the chain of custody was proven, with productions continuously in PW-01's custody until handover. It found the defence version inconsistent and improbable, especially the claim about planted drugs, which lacked basis. The court applied principles that minor contradictions do not undermine credible evidence and that the prosecution's case must be considered as a whole. It affirmed the High Court's finding that the prosecution proved guilt beyond reasonable doubt and the sentence was appropriate.
coa_sentence_type: Life Imprisonment
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused-appellant was convicted by the High Court of Colombo for possessing 11.8 grams of heroin and sentenced to life imprisonment. She appealed, challenging witness credibility, chain of custody, and rejection of her defence. The Court of Appeal thoroughly analyzed the evidence, finding the prosecution witnesses credible on material points and the chain of custody intact. It found the defence version inconsistent and failed to create reasonable doubt. The appeal was dismissed, affirming the conviction and sentence.
defence_counsel: Niranjan Jayasinghe with Harshana Ananda
hc_analysis_summary: The COA found the High Court Judge correctly considered the totality of evidence, assessed witness credibility, and properly applied the burden of proof. No errors in the HC's reasoning or conclusions were identified.
precedents_cited_list: Don Samantha Jude Anthony Jayamaha Vs. The Attorney General, C.A. 303/2006 | Jayasena Vs. Queen 72 NLR 313 | The Attorney General Vs. Potta Naufar and Others (Ambeptitya Murder Case) (2007) 2 SLR 144 | Mahathun and Others Vs. The Attorney General (2015) 1 SLR 74 | State of U.P. Vs. M. K. Anthony, AIR 1985 SC 48 | SC Appeal No. 99/2007 decided on 30.07.2009 | Narender Kumar Vs. State (NCT of Delhi), AIR 2012 SC 2281
standard_of_review_applied: The court will not lightly disturb findings of a trial judge regarding acceptance or rejection of witness testimony unless manifestly wrong. Evidence must be considered as a whole.
sentencing_principles_applied: Life imprisonment imposed based on the offence and consideration of previous conviction record and other relevant factors. No specific sentencing principles discussed in detail.

judges: Menaka Wijesundera, J. | Wickum A. Kaluarachchi, J.
offence_sections: Poisons Opium and Dangerous drugs Ordinance
brief_facts_summary: On 21 December 2003, police received a tip-off and conducted a raid at Maradana. The accused-appellant was arrested on Siemen’s Road. A body search found a substance suspected to be heroin in his right trouser pocket. The substance weighed around 3 grammes and was sealed. The appellant was indicted for possession and trafficking of 2.40 grammes of heroin.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Poisons Opium and Dangerous drugs Ordinance
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court found the appellant guilty of possession and trafficking of heroin and sentenced him to rigorous imprisonment. The trial judge was satisfied with the prosecution evidence and found it proved beyond reasonable doubt.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The main grounds were that the trial judge did not consider prosecution evidence in correct perspective, did not look for corroboration, and did not consider the defense case at all. Specific challenges were raised regarding the weight discrepancy of the heroin, custody of productions at the Government Analyst, and procedural irregularities.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Trial judge had not considered the prosecution evidence in the correct perspective. | Trial judge had not looked for corroboration. | The defense case not being considered at all. | The deference in the weight of the heroin had not been explained by the prosecution. | Where were the productions kept in the Government Analyst department. | Why the preparation of the report was delayed. | Adoption of evidence had been done after the trial judge who delivered the judgment started hearing PW1.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed the evidence of PW1, the main investigative officer, and found him trustworthy and reliable. The failure to call PW2 did not undermine the prosecution as per Section 134 of the Evidence Ordinance. The Government Analyst's evidence was accepted regarding custody and weight discrepancy.
probability_assessment_by_court: Court found the evidence of PW1 credible and sufficient to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty. He made a statement from the dock claiming the narcotics were introduced to him and that he was arrested while having lunch with his father. The father testified to corroborate the appellant but also stated the appellant was arrested for not knowing a person called 'Lala'. The Court of Appeal found the trial judge had considered the defense evidence at length.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found no merit in the appeal grounds. It held that the evidence of PW1, a police officer, was credible and did not require corroboration under Section 134 of the Evidence Ordinance. The Government Analyst adequately explained the weight discrepancy and custody. The adoption of evidence, though documented out of order, did not cause a miscarriage of justice. The trial judge had properly considered the defense. The conviction and sentence were affirmed as reasonable and within the law.
coa_sentence_type: Rigorous Imprisonment (affirmed)
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused appealed his High Court conviction for possession and trafficking of 2.40 grammes of heroin. The High Court found him guilty and sentenced him to rigorous imprisonment. Grounds of appeal included lack of corroboration, chain of custody issues, and procedural errors. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal, finding the police evidence credible and corroboration not required. The Government Analyst's evidence was accepted. The conviction and sentence were affirmed.
defence_counsel: Rienzie Arsecularatne, P.C. with Chamindri Arsecularatne and Himasha Silva
hc_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the High Court judgment reasonable. The trial judge properly analyzed the evidence, was mindful of the accused's rights and the prosecution's burden of proof. No errors were identified.
precedents_cited_list: SC Appeal 154-2010 (Aluvihare J interpreting Section 134 of the Evidence Ordinance)
standard_of_review_applied: Review of evidence and trial judge's findings for reasonableness and legality.

judges: Menaka Wijesundera J. | Wickum A. Kaluarachchi J.
offence_sections: sections 140, 104435, 146-296, 146-382 of three charges, 146-383 and in the alternative on the basis of common intention the same charges of murder, 382 and 383 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: On 12.2.2000, a group of about five persons armed with a pistol and knives looted a jewelry shop in Nuwara-Eliya, injuring people inside. While fleeing, the 3rd appellant dropped stolen items. The deceased tried to assault him, and the 3rd appellant stabbed the deceased. The appellants fled in a vehicle which later toppled near Gregory Lake. Police arrested the 3rd, 4th, and 5th accused from the vehicle and recovered jewelry. The 1st appellant was later arrested at Borella based on information received, and a pawning receipt and jewelry were recovered from his custody and his wife's house.
evidence_type_primary: Eyewitness testimony, Physical evidence (recovered jewelry), Dock identification
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: sections 140, 104435, 146-296, 146-382 of three charges, 146-383 and in the alternative on the basis of common intention the same charges of murder, 382 and 383 of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court found the 1st to 5th accused guilty on all charges based on common object. The 2nd and 5th accused were tried in absentia as they were absconding. The trial judge convicted them accordingly.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellants challenged the reliability of identification parade evidence and the trial judge's evaluation of evidence and common object. The 1st appellant argued the parade procedures were improper and evidence was not adequately considered. The 3rd appellant argued his identification was unreliable. The 4th appellant argued non-evaluation of his identification and the common object.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The evidence of the identification parades held not being adequately considered | The evidence in entirety not being properly considered (1st appellant) | Identification of the 3rd appellant not being reliable (3rd appellant) | Non evaluation of the identification of the 4th appellant | Non evaluation of the common object (4th appellant)
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: Witnesses inside the shop identified the appellants in broad daylight with shop illumination. They gave evidence 14 years after the incident but stood cross-examination well. The Court found dock identification reliable due to ample opportunity to observe the appellants during the 10-minute incident.
probability_assessment_by_court: Court concluded witnesses had sufficient opportunity to identify appellants in good lighting, making dock identification reliable.
defence_version_summary: The appellants pleaded ignorance of the incident. The 3rd appellant admitted in his dock statement he was in the vehicle but denied the rest. They did not call defence witnesses. The Court held they could not be exonerated as their ignorance was not put to witnesses in cross-examination.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found identification parade evidence had infirmities but not grave enough to reject. It emphasized dock identification was substantive. The incident lasted about 10 minutes in broad daylight with additional shop lighting, providing ample opportunity for identification. The stabbing occurred while appellants fled together after robbery, indicating it was in furtherance of common object. The recovery of jewelry from appellants and their immediate arrest supported guilt. The Court applied precedents on identification parades and unlawful assembly liability.
coa_sentence_type: Sentence and conviction entered by trial judge affirmed
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused-appellants (1st, 3rd, 4th) appealed their High Court conviction for robbery and murder based on common object. The High Court found them guilty after a trial where two accused were tried in absentia. Grounds of appeal focused on unreliable identification parade evidence and inadequate evaluation of evidence. The Court of Appeal upheld the conviction, finding dock identification reliable due to witnesses' ample opportunity to observe during the 10-minute daylight robbery. It ruled the stabbing during escape was in furtherance of common object. The appeal was dismissed, affirming the trial judge's sentence and conviction.
defence_counsel: U. R. De Silva P.C. with Savithri Fernando and Pradeepa Kaluarachchi for the 1st Accused-Appellant, Chathura Amarathunga for the 3rd Accused-Appellant, Anuja Premaratne, P.C. with Nayana Dissanayake and Natasha De Alwis for the 4th Accused-Appellant
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted the accused based on common object. The COA found no error in this conclusion, agreeing the evidence established common object and that the stabbing occurred during the unlawful assembly's progression.
precedents_cited_list: CA-120-2004 Rannnuka Arachchige Chaminda Roshan vs The Attorney General | Tanayake Mudiyanselage Sunil Ratnayake vs Attorney General SC TAB 1-2006 | SC Special Appeal 7-2018 | Muniratne & Others v State, [2001] 2 SLR 382 | K.M. Premachandra & Others v Attorney General, C.A. 39-41/97 | Roshan v Attorney General, [2011] 1 SLR 364
standard_of_review_applied: Evaluation of evidence and identification reliability

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 3(1) of the Prevention of Money Laundering Act No. 5 of 2006 as amended by Amendment Act No. 40 of 2011
brief_facts_summary: The accused-petitioner was indicted before the High Court of Colombo for knowingly engaging in money laundering through the use of her bank account for a sum of Rs. 20,700,200/- between 18-03-2010 and 24-11-2010. The charge was based on an amendment to the Prevention of Money Laundering Act. The accused-petitioner raised a preliminary objection, arguing the amendment had no retrospective effect and thus the charge relating to a period before the amendment came into effect could not be maintained.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 3(1) of the Prevention of Money Laundering Act No. 5 of 2006 as amended by Amendment Act No. 40 of 2011
hc_judgment_summary: The learned High Court Judge overruled the preliminary objection raised by the petitioner, holding that the amendment was applicable. The matter was fixed for pre-trial conference.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The petitioner sought revision against the High Court order overruling the preliminary objection. The primary ground was that the amendment to the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, under which the charge was formulated, had no retrospective effect. The petitioner argued that since the alleged offence occurred before the amendment came into effect, the indictment was invalid.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The amendment under which the charge was preferred had no retrospective effect. | The petitioner was charged for an offence that was not in existence at the time of the alleged acts. | The learned High Court Judge failed to appreciate the relevant legal provisions correctly.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: This case did not proceed to trial as it was disposed of on a preliminary legal objection regarding the retrospective application of a statute. No witness evidence or physical evidence was analyzed.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal applied rules of statutory interpretation to determine that the amendment had no retrospective effect, creating reasonable doubt about the validity of the charge.
defence_version_summary: The petitioner pleaded not guilty by raising a preliminary objection against the maintainability of the indictment. The defence argued the law under which she was charged was not in force at the time of the alleged acts. The court agreed with the petitioner's legal argument.
legal_errors_description: The High Court Judge erred in law by holding that the amendment to the substantive law (Prevention of Money Laundering Act) had retrospective effect without any express or implied provision to that effect in the amending Act.
procedural_defects_description: The High Court Judge proceeded with the indictment based on an incorrect interpretation of the law, thereby initiating proceedings that were not maintainable in law.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal conducted a detailed analysis of the rules of statutory interpretation regarding retrospectivity. It referred to authoritative texts and Indian Supreme Court judgments, establishing the presumption against retrospectivity for substantive laws. The court found no basis, express or implied, for the amendment to have retrospective effect. It concluded the High Court Judge was completely misdirected in law by applying the amendment retrospectively, which shocked the conscience of the court and occasioned a miscarriage of justice. The amendment was held to be a change to substantive law, affecting vested rights, and thus purely prospective.
coa_sentence_type: Case dismissed, accused discharged from proceedings
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused-petitioner was charged in the High Court of Colombo with money laundering under an amended law for acts occurring before the amendment. The High Court overruled her preliminary objection on retrospectivity. On revision, the Court of Appeal held that the amendment to the substantive law had no retrospective effect. It found the High Court order legally erroneous, occasioning a miscarriage of justice. The Court of Appeal allowed the revision, set aside the High Court order, upheld the preliminary objection, dismissed the action, and discharged the accused.
prosecution_counsel: Sudharshana De Silva, S.D.S.G for the Respondent (Attorney General)
defence_counsel: Sandeepani Wijesooriya with Randeepa Wijesooriya for the Petitioner
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court Judge overruled the preliminary objection, finding the amendment applicable. The Court of Appeal found this analysis flawed, as the judge incorrectly applied the law on retrospectivity, misconstrued cited judgments, and reached a finding without a legally tenable basis.
precedents_cited_list: Hotel Galaxy (Pvt) Ltd Vs. Mercantile Hotels managements Limited (1987) 1 SLR 5 | Mariam BeeBee Vs. Seyed Mohamed 68 NLR 36 | Bank of Ceylon Vs. Kaleel, and others (2004) 1 SLR 284 | Sarath Wimalaweera Vs. The Attorney General (2015) 1 SLR 379 | Mrs. Dorothy Silva Vs. Inspector Of Police, City Vise Squad Pettah 78 NLR 553 | Maharaja Organization Limited Vs. Viacom International Inc. and Another SC Appeal No: SC/CHC/Appeal/4/2002 decided on 20-06-2021 | Leechman and Company Ltd Vs. Rangalla Consolidated Limited (1981) 2 SLR 373 | Punjab Tin Supply Co. Vs. Central Government AIR 1984 SC 87 | Hitendra Vishnu Thakur Vs. State of Maharashtra 1994 AIR 2623
standard_of_review_applied: Revisionary jurisdiction under Article 138 of the Constitution, requiring exceptional circumstances such as a miscarriage of justice, a manifestly erroneous order, or an order that shocks the conscience of the court.

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 140, Section 296 read with section 146, Section 314 read with section 146, Section 296 read with section 32, Section 314 read with section 32 of the Penal Code
location_of_offence: Near a well near the deceased's house
brief_facts_summary: On 14 August 1996, a group of 20-30 people, including the accused, came in an agitated state towards the deceased Padmasiri and his friends while they were bathing. The deceased was assaulted by the group, leading to his death. Another person, Chaminda Nalin Kumara, was also injured in the incident. The incident was witnessed by PW-03 Priyantha Senadeera from hiding.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 140, Section 296 read with section 146 of the Penal Code
hc_sentence_type: 6 months rigorous imprisonment on count 1 and death sentence on count 2
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court found the accused guilty on counts 1 and 2 (unlawful assembly and murder as a member of unlawful assembly). They were acquitted on count 3. Counts 4 and 5 were considered alternate counts, so no order was pronounced. The accused were sentenced to 6 months rigorous imprisonment on count 1 and death on count 2.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: Appellants challenged the conviction based on contradictions and unreliability of eyewitness testimonies (PW-03 and PW-04). They argued the trial Judge failed to properly evaluate evidence, including dock statements, and failed to assess witness credibility. A key ground was that the judgment did not comply with Section 283 of the Criminal Procedure Act, lacking proper analysis and reasoning.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Serious doubt as to participation of 1st accused due to contradictions | Reasonable doubt as to existence of an unlawful assembly with five or more people and common object | Dock statement not evaluated separately and rejected based on prosecution evidence strength | Evidence of PW-03 wholly contradictory, unsafe, unreliable | Evidence of PW-04 erratic, no reliance could be placed | Trial Judge failed to assess credibility and testimonial trustworthiness of witnesses | Conflict of evidence between PW-03 and PW-04 creates serious doubt | Judgment violates Section 283 of Criminal Procedure Act due to failures to assess eyewitness trustworthiness, reason out reliance on eyewitness, apply relevant law on unlawful assembly, and address conflicts/infirmities in testimony
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: COA found the trial Judge's analysis inadequate. Key eyewitnesses (PW-03, PW-04) gave evidence long after the event, leading to contradictions and omissions. The trial Judge failed to properly analyze whether the evidence established an unlawful assembly and the accused's membership.
probability_assessment_by_court: COA found the trial Judge failed to properly analyze evidence to establish guilt beyond reasonable doubt, particularly regarding unlawful assembly.
defence_version_summary: All accused pleaded not guilty. They made dock statements denying involvement and claimed they were falsely implicated due to political rivalry. The trial Judge rejected this defence, stating it was not credible in light of prosecution evidence.
legal_errors_description: The High Court judgment was found not to be a proper judgment in terms of Section 283 of the Criminal Procedure Act. It failed to contain proper points for determination, decision, and reasons for the decision. It also misdirected itself by examining the defence evidence in the light of prosecution evidence, reversing the presumption of innocence.
procedural_defects_description: Failure to comply with mandatory requirements of Section 283 of the Criminal Procedure Act regarding judgment writing.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: COA held the High Court judgment deficient under Section 283 of the Criminal Procedure Act. It lacked proper analysis of evidence, especially regarding the establishment of an unlawful assembly and the specific participation of each accused. The trial Judge failed to evaluate contradictions, assess dock statements properly, and provide reasoned findings. COA cited precedents on proper judgment writing and evidence evaluation. Considering the 28-year delay since the offence, witnesses' faded memories, and the appellants' incarceration since 2017, COA found no purpose in a retrial and acquitted the appellants.
coa_sentence_type: Acquitted and set aside conviction and sentence
brief_judgment_file_summary: Seven accused were indicted for unlawful assembly, murder, and causing injuries relating to an incident on 14 August 1996. The High Court of Kuliyapitiya convicted the available accused on counts of unlawful assembly and murder as a member of unlawful assembly, sentencing them to imprisonment and death. The accused appealed, arguing witness unreliability, contradictions, and that the judgment failed to meet legal standards under Section 283 of the Criminal Procedure Act. The Court of Appeal found the High Court judgment legally deficient, lacking proper evidence analysis and reasoning. Due to the 28-year delay, faded witness memory, and time served, the COA set aside the conviction and sentence and acquitted the appellants, declining to order a retrial.
defence_counsel: Neranjan Jayasinghe with Harshana Ananda (1st Accused), Indica Mallawaratchy (2nd Accused), Jagath Abeynayake (5th and 6th Accused)
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court Judge summarized evidence and dock statements but failed to provide proper analysis and reasoning as required by law. He concluded the prosecution proved its case beyond doubt but did not adequately address contradictions or analyze whether the evidence established an unlawful assembly with the accused as members. COA found this approach legally flawed.
precedents_cited_list: Ibrahim Vs. Inspector of Police 59 NLR 235 | Thusaiya Vs. Pathihamy 15 CLW 119 | C.A. Appeal No. 62-65/2005 decided on 07-06-2011 | Fraad Vs. Brown and Company 20 NLR 282 | Piyasena Vs. Alwis (1993) 1 SLR 119 | Wikramasooriya Vs. Dedolina (1996) 2 NLR 95 | James Silva Vs. The Republic of Sri Lanka (1980) 2 SLR 167 | Jayasena Vs. The Queen 72 NLR 313 | State of Uttar Pradesh Vs. Anthony (1984) SCJ 236/(1985) CRI L.J. 493 | L.C. Fernando Vs. The Republic of Sri Lanka 79-II NLR 313 | Nandasena Vs. Attorney General (2008) 1 SLR 51 | Chandrasena and Others Vs. Munaweera (1998) 3 SLR 94
standard_of_review_applied: COA reviewed whether the High Court judgment complied with Section 283 of the Criminal Procedure Act and whether the conviction was based on proper analysis of evidence. It applied principles from precedents on proper judgment writing and evidence evaluation.

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: On 07 June 2003 at Dehiwala, the Accused-Appellant allegedly stabbed the deceased, Muththirigala Kankanamlage Seeman Singho, resulting in his death. The prosecution's case relied primarily on the eyewitness testimony of PW1, who saw the Appellant stabbing the deceased and trying to remove the knife. The deceased later told PW1 he was stabbed after refusing to give money. The Appellant surrendered the next day, and a knife and T-shirt with human blood were recovered. The post-mortem confirmed fatal stab injuries.
evidence_type_secondary: Medical evidence, Government Analyst Report, Physical evidence recovery
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court Judge found the evidence of the sole eyewitness PW1 convincing and corroborated by medical and forensic evidence. The Judge was satisfied the prosecution proved the case beyond reasonable doubt and convicted the Appellant as charged, sentencing him to death.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The Appellant argued the High Court Judge failed to properly scrutinize the sole eyewitness's testimony and assess her credibility. He also contended the Judge misdirected himself by anticipating defence evidence and shifting the burden of proof, and failed to properly evaluate discrepancies and contradictions in the evidence.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The Learned High Court Judge failed to scrutinize testimony of sole eye witness according to principles established in law and failed to evaluate the creditworthiness of the said witness. | The Learned High Court Judge has anticipated certain evidence be led on behalf of the defence and thereby shifted the burden on certain material issue. | The Learned High Court Judge misdirected himself by failing to properly evaluate the discrepancies, inter se contradictions on material points.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the eyewitness PW1's testimony clear, cogent, and corroborated by the JMO's evidence of defence injuries and the recovery of a blood-stained knife and T-shirt. The court considered minor omissions in her statement immaterial and found her credible.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal held the prosecution proved its case beyond reasonable doubt, based on the convincing eyewitness testimony, corroborating medical and forensic evidence, and the Appellant's conduct.
defence_version_summary: The Appellant opted for a non-jury trial, made dock statements, and closed his case without calling witnesses. He pleaded not guilty. The court found the prosecution evidence credible and the defence arguments lacking merit.
legal_errors_description: The Court of Appeal noted the High Court Judge made a misdirection by commenting that the defence failed to call the Appellant's mother to prove the knife was handed over by her, but held this did not affect the root of the case.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal thoroughly analysed the evidence, affirming the High Court's reliance on the sole eyewitness under Section 134 of the Evidence Ordinance. It found her testimony credible, corroborated by medical evidence (defence injuries) and forensic evidence (blood on knife and T-shirt). The court considered the Appellant's conduct (preventing help, absconding) incriminating. It dismissed the grounds of appeal, finding the minor omissions immaterial, the misdirection on burden of proof harmless, and the evidence proving guilt beyond reasonable doubt.
coa_sentence_type: Death
brief_judgment_file_summary: The Accused-Appellant was convicted of murder under Section 296 of the Penal Code by the High Court of Colombo and sentenced to death. He appealed, arguing the High Court Judge failed to properly assess the sole eyewitness's credibility, misdirected on the burden of proof, and ignored contradictions. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal, finding the eyewitness testimony credible and corroborated by medical and forensic evidence, the Appellant's conduct incriminating, and any errors by the High Court not prejudicial. The conviction and death sentence were affirmed.
defence_counsel: Teny Fernando
cause_of_death_exact_text: three stab injuries to abdominal cavity and resulting haemorrhage and blood loss
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court Judge relied on the convincing eyewitness testimony of PW1, corroborated by medical and forensic evidence, to convict. The Court of Appeal found the analysis adequate, though it noted a minor misdirection regarding the burden of proof, which it deemed not prejudicial.
precedents_cited_list: The Queen v. K.A. Santin Singho 65 NLR 447 | Basanti v State of UP, AIR 1987 SC 1572 | Sumanseña v Attorney General [1999] 3 Sri L.R. 137 | The Attorney General v. Sandanam Pitchai Mary Theresa [2011] 2 SLR 292
standard_of_review_applied: The court reviewed whether the High Court properly evaluated the evidence, particularly the sole eyewitness testimony, and whether the conviction was supported by evidence proving guilt beyond reasonable doubt.

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 63(1)(a) of the Mines and Minerals Act No.33 of 1992 as amended by Act No.66 of 2009
brief_facts_summary: The accused was charged for mining sand without a valid license using an excavator machine. He pleaded guilty and was convicted and fined by the Magistrate's Court. The Magistrate also ordered an inquiry to decide whether to confiscate the excavator. The registered owner (the Petitioner) appeared at the inquiry and gave evidence. The Magistrate decided to confiscate the machine. The Petitioner, aggrieved by the confiscation order, filed a revision in the High Court, which was dismissed. The Petitioner then appealed to the Court of Appeal.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 63(1)(a) of the Mines and Minerals Act No.33 of 1992 as amended by Act No.66 of 2009
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court dismissed the Petitioner's revision application to set aside the Magistrate's confiscation order. The High Court held that the Petitioner failed to prove he had no knowledge of the offence and failed to take necessary precautions to prevent misuse of the excavator. It also applied reasoning from a case under the Excise Ordinance.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The Petitioner argued the High Court order was void, bad in law, and illegal. He contended the High Court erroneously concluded he failed to take precautions and wrongly applied a test from an Excise Ordinance case. He argued the High Court failed to consider the difference in wording between the Excise Ordinance and the Mines and Minerals Act regarding confiscation, and incorrectly assigned the burden of proof to him.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The High Court order is void, bad in law and illegal as it did not give due courtesy to Section 63(b)(1) of the Mine and Minerals Act. | The High Court erroneously inferred the Petitioner could not take any precaution to prevent the offence. | The High Court erroneously applied the test from Aruna Pradeep Prasanna vs Attorney General (Excise Ordinance case). | The High Court erroneously concluded the burden of proof under the Excise Ordinance is the same as under the Mines and Minerals Act. | The High Court failed to consider the different wording ('shall be liable' vs 'may make order to be confiscated') between the two Acts. | The High Court erroneously assigned the burden of proof to the applicant, which was not intended by Parliament. | The High Court erroneously used the Excise Ordinance judgment without considering the relevant facts of this case. | The High Court concluded the Petitioner's evidence was contrary to law.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The primary evidence was the accused's guilty plea. At the confiscation inquiry, only the Petitioner (owner) gave evidence, stating he rented the machine to a license holder, gave instructions against illegal use, and was unaware of the offence. The Court of Appeal found this credible.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal assessed that the Petitioner, lacking knowledge or benefit from the crime, could not be deemed behind the illegal operation.
defence_version_summary: The accused pleaded guilty. The Petitioner (owner) claimed a not guilty stance regarding the confiscation, providing an alibi of ignorance. He testified he rented the machine to a license holder, gave specific instructions against illegal use, and trusted the accused. The Court found his version credible and that he took necessary precautions.
legal_errors_description: The High Court erred in law by incorrectly applying the burden of proof and legal tests from the Excise Ordinance to the Mines and Minerals Act, and by failing to properly consider the Petitioner's evidence and the discretionary nature of confiscation under the Act.
procedural_defects_description: The High Court failed to give due consideration to the specific wording and intent of Section 63(b)(1) of the Mines and Minerals Act and incorrectly applied precedent from a different statute.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal held that the High Court and Magistrate erred. It distinguished the Mines and Minerals Act from the Excise Ordinance, noting the former uses 'may' for confiscation, indicating discretion. It cited Manawadu V. The Attorney General, emphasizing that forfeiture is not automatic and an owner must be heard. It found the Petitioner's evidence credible: he rented the machine to a purported license holder, gave instructions against illegal use, and had no knowledge of the offence. The Court concluded the Petitioner took necessary precautions and, lacking knowledge or benefit, should not be penalized. The confiscation orders were set aside.
coa_sentence_type: The accused's conviction and fine stand. The confiscation order against the Petitioner's excavator is set aside.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The registered owner (Petitioner) appealed to the Court of Appeal against the High Court's dismissal of his revision, which upheld the Magistrate's order confiscating his excavator used by the accused for illegal sand mining. The High Court found the Petitioner failed to prove lack of knowledge or take necessary precautions. The Court of Appeal allowed the appeal, finding legal errors. It held the High Court wrongly applied Excise Ordinance precedent and burden of proof to the Mines and Minerals Act. Citing Manawadu, it emphasized confiscation is discretionary and an innocent owner must be heard. Accepting the Petitioner's evidence of renting to a license holder and giving proper instructions, the Court set aside the confiscation orders and directed the excavator's release.
defence_counsel: Sandamal Rajapaksha
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court dismissed the revision, finding the Petitioner failed to prove lack of knowledge or take precautions, and applied a test from an Excise Ordinance case. The COA found this analysis erroneous, as it misapplied the law and burden of proof specific to the Mines and Minerals Act.
precedents_cited_list: Marian Beebee v. Seyed Mohamed 69 CLW 34 | Rasheed Ali v.Mohammed Ali and Others [1981] 1 SLR 262 | Commissioner of Police v. Tanes (1957-58) 68 CLR 383 | Aruna Pradeep Prasanna vs Attorney General CA (PHC) No 61/2012 | Manawadu V. The Attorney General (1987) 2 SLR 30
standard_of_review_applied: Revisionary jurisdiction invoked due to exceptional circumstances and errors of law leading to a miscarriage of justice.
sentencing_principles_applied: Principles regarding discretionary confiscation of property, burden of proof on the owner to show lack of knowledge/non-participation, and the requirement to hear the owner (audi alteram partem) before forfeiture.

judges: Menaka Wijesundera, J. | Wickum A. Kaluarachchi, J.
offence_sections: Poisons Opium and Dangerous drugs Ordinance
brief_facts_summary: On 13.9.2003, police officers received a tipoff and went to the Peliyagoda area. The appellant arrived carrying a shoulder bag which was searched, and a pink grocery bag containing a substance suspected to be heroin was found. The appellant was taken into custody. Officers then went to the appellant's mother-in-law's house and the house of the person alleged to have supplied the heroin but found no suspicious items at either location, though the alleged supplier was arrested.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Poisons Opium and Dangerous drugs Ordinance
hc_sentence_type: Conviction entered but specific sentence type not detailed in judgment extract
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the appellant on both charges of possession and trafficking of 196.1 grammes of heroin. The trial judge relied on the evidence of the prosecution's single witness (PW2).
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant challenged the conviction on several grounds: the prosecution relied on a single witness's evidence; PW2 improperly refreshed memory using PW1's notes; the trial judge failed to look for corroboration; the defense case was not analyzed; and the chain of productions was not established.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The prosecution has relied on a single witness's evidence | PW2 had relied on the notes made by PW1 which is a violation of section 159 of the Evidence Ordinance | The trial judge had not looked for corroboration | Defense case not being analyzed | Chain of productions not being established
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The prosecution's case relied heavily on the testimony of PW2, who was present during the raid. The COA found PW2's use of PW1's notes to refresh memory was permissible under Section 159 of the Evidence Ordinance. The defense called the appellant's wife and daughter, whose consistent and uncontradicted evidence supported the appellant's alibi.
probability_assessment_by_court: The COA found improbabilities in the prosecution's story, such as the failure to properly search relevant houses, and noted the trial judge was too eager to accept the prosecution's version without adequately considering the defense evidence, creating reasonable doubt.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty and made a statement from the dock denying the entire incident, claiming he was arrested at home. This alibi was corroborated by the sworn testimony of his wife and daughter, who withstood cross-examination with no contradictions. The court assessed their evidence as consistent and uncontradicted.
legal_errors_description: The COA found the trial judge erred by failing to properly analyze the defense case and its corroborating witnesses, and by not duly considering improbabilities in the prosecution's narrative.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found no violation of Section 159 of the Evidence Ordinance by PW2 refreshing memory from another's notes, citing precedent (King vs Navasivayam). It held that a conviction can be based on a single credible witness and corroboration is not mandatory. However, the COA identified critical flaws: the trial judge failed to analyze the consistent, corroborated defense alibi and did not consider the improbability of the police officers' actions (failing to search relevant houses). The COA concluded the trial judge was too eager to believe the prosecution, disregarded the defense, and thereby denied the appellant a fair trial, causing a miscarriage of justice.
coa_sentence_type: Conviction and sentence set aside
brief_judgment_file_summary: The appellant was convicted in the High Court of Colombo for possession and trafficking of 196.1g of heroin. He appealed on grounds including reliance on a single witness, improper memory refreshing, lack of corroboration, and failure to analyze the defense. The Court of Appeal found PW2's use of notes was legal and a single witness can suffice. However, it found the trial judge failed to consider the improbabilities in the police story and the consistent, corroborated defense alibi, denying a fair trial. The appeal was allowed, the conviction and sentence were set aside, and the appellant was acquitted.
defence_counsel: Rienzie Arseculeratne, PC with Chamindri Arseculeratne, Thilina Punchihewa, Punsisi Gamage, Eranga Yakandawala, Himasha Silva, Erandi Pathiranage
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted the appellant based on the prosecution's single witness. The COA found the trial judge erred by not analyzing the defense case and its corroborating witnesses, and by not considering the improbability of the police officers' failure to search relevant houses, instead being too eager to agree with the prosecution.
precedents_cited_list: The King vs Navasivayam 49 NLR 294 | Rajapaksha Pathirage Justin Rajapaksha VS Prasanna Rathnayake & Others SC/FR 689/2012 | SC-SPL-LAN0100-2010
standard_of_review_applied: The COA reviewed the trial judge's findings on evidence and procedure, assessing the correctness of the conviction and whether a fair trial was denied.

judges: WICKUM A. KALUARACHCHI, J | MENAKA WIJESUNDERA, J
offence_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The 2nd accused-appellant was indicted for the murder of Arumugam Chandrasekeran on or about 7th February 2014. The prosecution case was that the day before the murder, the appellant threw stones at the deceased's house and threatened him. On the morning of the murder, while the deceased and others were about to get into a three-wheeler to go to the police, the appellant and the 1st accused arrived. The appellant stabbed the deceased in the chest, while the 1st accused allegedly held the deceased's hands behind his back. The appellant denied the charge, claiming he was asleep at home and that a relative, 'Raja' (PW-11), confessed to the stabbing.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court Judge acquitted the 1st accused and convicted the 2nd accused-appellant of murder. The judge found the evidence that the 1st accused held the deceased's hands unbelievable, but accepted the evidence that the 2nd accused-appellant stabbed the deceased. The 2nd accused-appellant was sentenced to death.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant's counsel argued that contradictions and omissions in the prosecution evidence were not properly considered by the High Court Judge. Specifically, he pointed to a contradiction marked as V-1 in the evidence of PW-7 and two omissions in the evidence of PW-1.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Contradictions and omissions were not properly considered by the learned High Court Judge.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed the credibility of prosecution witnesses. It found PW-1 and PW-7 unreliable due to omissions and a contradiction. PW-3's testimony was found to be inextricably linked to a false part about the 1st accused holding the deceased, making her entire account unreliable. PW-11 contradicted a key part of PW-3's evidence regarding the knife. The defence evidence, including the appellant's alibi and claim that PW-11 was the real perpetrator, was considered.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court found that the prosecution's failure to provide credible, consistent evidence created a reasonable doubt as to the appellant's guilt.
defence_version_summary: The 2nd accused-appellant pleaded not guilty. He gave evidence on oath denying the charge, claiming an alibi that he was sleeping at home at the time. His defence was that 'Raja' (PW-11) committed the murder and confessed to him. Two other defence witnesses also testified. The High Court Judge rejected the defence evidence, but the Court of Appeal found the Judge's analysis of it was erroneous and it raised a reasonable doubt.
legal_errors_description: The Court found the High Court Judge erred in applying the concept of 'divisibility of credibility' to the evidence of PW-3 and in rejecting the defence evidence based on incorrect findings.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal conducted a thorough re-evaluation of the evidence. It agreed with the High Court that PW-1 and PW-7 were not credible. It then focused on PW-3, the only other witness to describe the murder. The Court found PW-3's evidence about the appellant stabbing the deceased was indivisible from her false testimony about the 1st accused holding the deceased, making her entire account unreliable. PW-11's testimony contradicted PW-3's account of the knife handover. The Court found the High Court Judge erred in rejecting the defence evidence and in concluding PW-11 could not have been the perpetrator. The prosecution case, resting on unreliable witnesses, failed to prove guilt beyond a reasonable doubt.
coa_sentence_type: Acquitted, no sentence imposed.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The 2nd accused-appellant, Wellupilain Thyagaraja alias Shivaraja, was convicted of murder by the High Court of Kegalle and sentenced to death. He appealed to the Court of Appeal. The prosecution case relied on eyewitnesses, including PW-3, who claimed she saw the appellant stab the deceased while the 1st accused held him. The High Court acquitted the 1st accused, finding that part of the evidence false. The Court of Appeal found the evidence of the key eyewitness, PW-3, was indivisible and unreliable because it contained a proven falsehood. Other prosecution witnesses were also found unreliable or contradictory. The Court held the prosecution failed to prove the appellant's guilt beyond a reasonable doubt. The appeal was allowed, the conviction and death sentence were set aside, and the appellant was acquitted.
defence_counsel: Thushara Dissanayake
cause_of_death_exact_text: hemo-pneumothorax due to a stab injury to the chest
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court Judge accepted part of PW-3's evidence (against the appellant) while rejecting another part (against the 1st accused) and dismissed the defence version. The Court of Appeal found this analysis was erroneous because the two parts of PW-3's testimony were indivisible for the single event of the stabbing, and the Judge failed to properly consider the defence evidence and contradictions.
precedents_cited_list: Samaraweera V. Attorney General – (1990) 1 Sri L.R. 256 | Siriuvardena and another V. The Attorney General, (1998) 2 Sri L.R. 222 | Baksh V. The Queen (1958) AC 167 (P.C.) | Dudh Nath Pandey V. The State of U.P, 1981 AIR 911, 1981 SCR (2) 771
standard_of_review_applied: The Court of Appeal examined whether the Trial Judge correctly evaluated the evidence and came to a correct conclusion, re-assessing the credibility and reliability of witnesses.

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 300 read with section 32 of the Penal Code
location_of_offence: Katkovalam, within the jurisdiction of the High Court of Jaffna
brief_facts_summary: The appellants, along with the 1st accused, attacked the victim (Rasathurai Arulprasath) with a knife, a club, and a hand clip, causing grievous injuries on 7th November 2015. The victim was called out of his house by the appellants and then assaulted. The incident resulted in life-threatening injuries and fractures to the victim's skull, requiring hospitalization. The appellants and the victim were known to each other from a young age.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 300 read with section 32 of the Penal Code
hc_sentence_type: 8 years rigorous imprisonment each, plus a fine and compensation
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the appellants for attempted murder. It found that the appellants, acting with common intention, attacked the victim causing grievous injuries. The court imposed 8 years rigorous imprisonment, a fine of Rs. 5000 each, and compensation of Rs. 200,000 each to the victim.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellants argued that the conviction was against the weight of evidence, contradictions between the injured person's evidence and the medical evidence were not considered, and the sentences imposed were excessive. They contended that the medical evidence (MLR) only showed two cut injuries, which could be attributed solely to the 1st accused who pleaded guilty, and that the evidence did not warrant conviction against them.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The conviction is against the weight of evidence led at the trial. | Doubts in the prosecution case was not considered by the learned High Court Judge. | The evidence of the injured was not properly evaluated by the learned High Court Judge. | The medical evidence, if properly analyzed by the learned High Court Judge could have resulted in the acquittal of both accused-appellants. | The contradiction between the medical evidence given by the doctor and the evidence of the injured was not taken into account by the learned High Court Judge. | The sentence imposed on both appellants are excessive and unreasonable, when the evidence led against both appellants does not warrant the sentences imposed by court.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the evidence of the injured victim (PW-01) credible, consistent, and uncontradicted on material points. The medical evidence (JMO PW-04 and MLR P-02) corroborated the victim's account of the attack and the seriousness of the injuries, including life-threatening cut injuries and skull fractures.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal found the prosecution evidence established the appellants' guilt beyond reasonable doubt. It held that minor discrepancies in testimony do not shake the core of the case and that the evidence, viewed in its totality, was trustworthy and cogent.
defence_version_summary: The appellants pleaded not guilty. The 1st appellant made a dock statement claiming the 1st accused (who pleaded guilty) alone attacked the victim. The 2nd appellant made a dock statement claiming he was not present at the scene. The Court found these defences did not create reasonable doubt or provide a reasonable explanation in their favor.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal thoroughly evaluated the evidence, applying established legal principles on evaluating witness contradictions from Mahathun and Others Vs. The Attorney General and State of U. P. Vs. M. K. Anthony. It found the victim's evidence credible and consistent with the medical report. The Court held that the appellants acted with common intention, referencing precedents on common intention (Rishideo Vs. State of U.P., Mahabub Shah Vs. Emperor, The Queen Vs. J. Mahatun and Another). It rejected the argument that the medical evidence contradicted the victim's account, noting the JMO's findings were consistent with the described assault. The Court found the sentences imposed by the High Court were reasonable considering the severity of the injuries.
coa_sentence_type: 8 years rigorous imprisonment each, fine of Rs. 5000 each, compensation of Rs. 200,000 each to the victim (PW-01). Default sentences: 3 months simple imprisonment for fine default, 12 months simple imprisonment for compensation default.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The 2nd and 3rd accused (appellants) were convicted by the Jaffna High Court for the attempted murder of Rasathurai Arulprasath, sentenced to 8 years rigorous imprisonment, a fine, and compensation. They appealed, challenging the conviction based on alleged contradictions between the victim's testimony and medical evidence, and the sentence as excessive. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal, upholding the High Court's judgment. It found the victim's evidence credible and consistent with the medical evidence, established common intention among the assailants, and deemed the sentence appropriate given the grievous, life-threatening injuries inflicted.
defence_counsel: G. Jeyakumar with Rudani
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court considered the evidence and found the appellants guilty of attempted murder, acting with common intention. It imposed a sentence reflecting the severity of the injuries. The Court of Appeal found no error in the High Court's analysis, reasoning, or sentencing, and affirmed its judgment in full.
precedents_cited_list: Mahathun and Others Vs. The Attorney General (2015) 1 SLR 74 | State of U. P. Vs. M. K. Anthony, AIR 1985 SC 48 | E.R.S.R. Coomaraswamy, The Law of Evidence Volume I at page 224 (citing Emperor Vs. Bataram Das 49 Cal. 358) | Rishideo Vs. State of U.P. (1955) AIR 331 | Mahabub Shah Vs. Emperor A.I.R. (1945) Privy Council 118 | The Queen Vs. J. Mahatun and Another 61 NLR 540
standard_of_review_applied: The Court of Appeal will not lightly disturb the trial judge's findings on witness credibility unless manifestly wrong. Evidence must be considered in its totality, and minor discrepancies not touching the core of the case are not fatal.
sentencing_principles_applied: The sentence for attempted murder can extend to 10 years imprisonment, and up to 20 years if hurt is caused. The Court considered the severity of the life-threatening injuries sustained by the victim in upholding the sentence.

judges: Menaka Wijesundera, J | Wickum A. Kaluarachchi, J
offence_sections: Section 296, 300, 317, and 314 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: On 23.06.2006, the appellant and his twin brother (1st accused, deceased before trial) went to the deceased's house. Both were armed, one with an iron bar and the other with a dagger. They assaulted the deceased. The fatal head injury was caused by the iron bar. After the deceased fell, they continued beating him. Police arrived, saw two people beating the deceased, who then fled. The 1st accused died before trial; the 3rd accused was acquitted.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the 2nd accused-appellant for murder under Section 296 of the Penal Code. The Judge acted on the evidence of PW-1 and PW-4, finding them reliable despite minor discrepancies after 12 years. The Judge found the appellant acted with common intention with the 1st accused.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant challenged the identification evidence, argued the Judge failed to evaluate evidence regarding his injuries, expected proof of the defence case, and failed to properly consider the dock statement. The main contention was that it was not established whether the appellant or the 1st accused caused the fatal injury, and that common intention was not proven.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The learned High Court Judge failed to evaluate the evidence regarding the identification of the 2nd accused-appellant. | The learned High Court Judge failed to evaluate the evidence regarding the injuries sustained by the 2nd accused-appellant. | The learned High Court Judge expected proof of the defence case. | The learned High Court Judge failed to consider the dock statement properly.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The COA found PW-1 and PW-4 reliable. Minor discrepancies were expected after 12 years. PW-3's evidence was not considered due to unsigned inquest record. PW-12 (police officer) corroborated the attack. Evidence established the appellant's presence was participatory, not mere.
probability_assessment_by_court: The COA found the prosecution proved its case beyond reasonable doubt. The appellant's participatory presence and common intention with the 1st accused were established.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty. He gave a dock statement claiming he went to settle a dispute between the deceased and his brother and was himself attacked. The court found this an unacceptable afterthought as it was not suggested to prosecution witnesses.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The COA analyzed the doctrine of common intention under Section 32 of the Penal Code. It found the appellant's presence was participatory: he and his brother came armed looking for the deceased, jointly assaulted him, continued beating after he fell, and fled together. The COA held that even if the fatal blow was by the 1st accused, the appellant was liable under common intention. Minor witness discrepancies were natural after 12 years. The dock statement was an afterthought. The prosecution case was unchallenged on key points. The appeal grounds lacked merit.
coa_sentence_type: Conviction and sentence affirmed
brief_judgment_file_summary: The 2nd accused-appellant was convicted of murder by the High Court for the 2006 killing of Wasantha Ranjith Abeysinghe. He appealed on grounds including misidentification and lack of common intention. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal, finding he acted with common intention with his twin brother (1st accused). The COA held his presence was participatory, making him liable under Section 32 of the Penal Code regardless of who inflicted the fatal blow. The conviction and sentence were affirmed.
defence_counsel: Sumith Senanayake, PC with Nisali Balachandra
hc_analysis_summary: The COA found the High Court Judge correctly acted on the evidence of PW-1 and PW-4, treating minor discrepancies as natural after 12 years. The Judge correctly applied the law on common intention. No errors were identified.
precedents_cited_list: Queen V. Vincent Fernando and two others – 65 NLR 265 | Richard V. State – 76 NLR 534 | Sarath Kumara V. Attorney General – C.A. No. 207/2008 | Queen V. Mahathun - 61 NLR 540 | Bhoginbhai Hirjibhai V. State of Gujarat - AIR 1983 SC 753 | Himachal Pradesh V. Thakur Dass (1983) 2 Cri. L.J. 1694 | Motilal V. State of Madhya Pradesh (1990) Criminal Law Journal NOC 125 MP | Sarvan Singh V. State of Punjab (2002 AIR SC (iii) 3652) | Ratnayake Mudiyanselage Premachandra V. The Hon. Attorney General C.A. Case No. 79/2011
standard_of_review_applied: Evaluation of evidence and application of legal principles (common intention)

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 296 of Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The accused-appellant, a workmate of the deceased who paid salaries to workers he employed, visited the deceased's house. The deceased's 9-year-old son (PW1) witnessed the appellant strike the deceased, pour kerosene oil on her, and set her on fire. The deceased suffered 95% burns and died in hospital. The appellant gave a dock statement claiming he was unaware how the deceased got burnt.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 296 of Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The Learned High Court Judge convicted the appellant of murder after a non-jury trial and sentenced him to death. The judge extensively analyzed the evidence of the child eyewitness (PW1) and the appellant's dock statement, finding the eyewitness credible and rejecting the appellant's version.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant argued the trial judge failed to properly evaluate the evidence, failed to consider whether non-compliance with Section 109 of the Criminal Procedure Act resulted in an unfair trial, and failed to appreciate the prosecution's failure to call fingerprint evidence from the kerosene bottle.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Did the Learned trial Judge fail to properly evaluate the evidence of the prosecution and the defence? | Did the Learned Trial Judge fail in considering whether complying with Section 109 (1) (2) and (3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure Act No.15 of 1979 by the prosecution amounts to an unfair trial for the accused? | Did the Learned Trial Judge failed to appreciate and give the benefit of the prosecution’s failure not calling the fingerprint on the Kerosene oil bottle marked P2 as stated by PW7, as it creates a reasonable doubt of prosecution’s case as to whether the deceased herself set fire on her?
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed the child eyewitness testimony, considering the witness's age, the circumstances of the incident, and the lack of material contradictions. The court upheld the trial judge's finding that the evidence was clear, believable, and unambiguous.
