probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal found the prosecution's case established beyond reasonable doubt based on the eyewitness testimony and medical evidence, finding no merit in the grounds of appeal challenging the evidence.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty and made a dock statement claiming he was unaware how the deceased got burnt. He offered an alibi that he was leaving the house when he saw the deceased engulfed in flames and later surrendered to police. The court found his version not credible.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal comprehensively reviewed the grounds of appeal. It found the trial judge properly evaluated the evidence, particularly that of the child eyewitness (PW1), applying the correct legal principles for child witnesses. It found no procedural unfairness regarding the recording of statements under Section 109, as a translator was used and provided at trial. The failure to take fingerprints from the kerosene bottle was deemed irrelevant as the eyewitness account was clear and believable. The court concluded the prosecution established a strong prima facie case based on direct eyewitness testimony and medical evidence, finding no reason to interfere with the High Court's findings.
coa_sentence_type: Death
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused-appellant appealed his High Court conviction for murder and death sentence for killing his workmate by setting her on fire. The High Court relied heavily on the eyewitness account of the deceased's 9-year-old son. The appellant argued grounds including improper evidence evaluation, procedural unfairness in recording statements, and failure to call fingerprint evidence. The Court of Appeal analyzed each ground, upheld the trial judge's credibility assessments and procedural compliance, and found the prosecution's case based on eyewitness testimony and medical evidence was strong. The appeal was dismissed, confirming the conviction and death sentence.
defence_counsel: Harishka Samaranayake
cause_of_death_exact_text: 95% burn injuries on her body surface area caused by short lasted intense flame burn due to oxidative and ignition of clothing of victim
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court judge extensively analyzed the eyewitness evidence and the appellant's dock statement, found the child witness reliable, and rejected the appellant's version. The Court of Appeal found no errors in this analysis.
precedents_cited_list: Ranjeet Kumar Ram v. State of Bihar [2015] SCC Online SC 500 | The Queen v. K.A. Santin Singho 65 NLR 447
standard_of_review_applied: Review of the trial judge's evaluation of evidence and application of law, assessing whether findings were reasonable and based on credible evidence.

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 3A of the Animals Act as amended by Amendment Act No. 20 of 1968
brief_facts_summary: The appellant's vehicle (No. 250-1359) was used by his father, Mohammed Yoosuf Mohammed Iqbal, to transport a cow without a valid permit on 03-08-2015. The father pleaded guilty before the Magistrate's Court of Mt. Lavinia, was convicted, and the cow was confiscated. Subsequently, the Magistrate held an inquiry to determine whether the vehicle should also be confiscated from its registered owner (the appellant). The appellant gave evidence claiming he had no knowledge of the offence and that his father took the vehicle without permission on the day, while it was parked at his aunt's house.
evidence_type_primary: Physical evidence (vehicle, cow) and admission of guilt by driver
evidence_type_secondary: Owner's testimony regarding his knowledge and precautions
hc_judgment_summary: The Provincial High Court dismissed the appellant's revision application without issuing notice to the respondents. The High Court found the appellant failed to explain a two-month delay in filing the revision application. It overruled the appellant's objection that the charge against his father was defective and that therefore the vehicle inquiry was invalid.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant appealed the High Court's dismissal of his revision application without issuing notice. He argued the High Court should have considered the merits of his application (focusing on whether he knew of the offence or took precautions) rather than relying on a technical objection regarding the charge. He contended the Magistrate's confiscation order should be vacated as he established he had no knowledge of the offence.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: High Court erred in dismissing revision application without issuing notice. | Magistrate's confiscation order was made in error as appellant established he had no knowledge of the offence. | The charge against the driver in the Magistrate's Court was defective, making the subsequent vehicle inquiry invalid.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The primary evidence was the appellant's own testimony at the inquiry before the Magistrate. He stated he had no knowledge his father would use the vehicle for the offence and that the vehicle was taken without his permission. The Court of Appeal found his evidence on lack of knowledge was not materially challenged and that the Magistrate's conclusions were based on surmises rather than evidence.
probability_assessment_by_court: Court of Appeal applied balance of probability standard as required by proviso to section 3A of Animals Act, finding appellant had sufficiently established he had no knowledge of the offence.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not liable for confiscation. He gave evidence, called no other witnesses. He claimed he had no knowledge of the offence being committed by his father, who took the vehicle without permission. He also stated he did not engage in illegal activities and used the vehicle for legitimate hiring work. The Court of Appeal found his testimony credible on the lack of knowledge.
legal_errors_description: Magistrate failed to properly apply the legal test under section 3A proviso of Animals Act, which requires owner to prove EITHER lack of knowledge OR taking all precautions. Magistrate incorrectly required both. High Court erred in dismissing revision application without considering merits.
procedural_defects_description: High Court dismissed revision application without issuing notice to respondents, based on delay and a technical objection, without considering merits of the application regarding knowledge/precautions.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed the requirements under section 3A proviso of the Animals Act, distinguishing it from the Forest Ordinance. It held the owner need only prove either lack of knowledge OR taking all precautions on a balance of probability. It found the appellant's evidence that he had no knowledge of the offence was credible and not materially challenged. The Court concluded the Magistrate's order was based on surmises and failed to properly consider the 'lack of knowledge' limb. The High Court also erred procedurally by not issuing notice and considering merits. Precedents Faris v The Officer in Charge and Nizar v Inspector of Police were applied.
coa_sentence_type: Order for confiscation of vehicle set aside. Vehicle to be released to appellant.
brief_judgment_file_summary: This is an appeal against the confiscation of a vehicle used to transport a cow without a permit. The driver (appellant's father) pleaded guilty. The Magistrate ordered vehicle confiscation after an inquiry, finding the owner (appellant) failed to prove he had no knowledge or took precautions. The High Court dismissed his revision application without notice. The Court of Appeal allowed the appeal, finding the Magistrate misapplied the law by not properly considering the appellant's evidence of lack of knowledge, which only required proof of one factor. The High Court also erred procedurally. Both lower court orders were set aside and the vehicle was ordered released.
defence_counsel: Ruwantha Cooray instructed by Ramzi Bacha
hc_analysis_summary: High Court dismissed revision application without issuing notice, focusing on appellant's delay and a technical objection about the charge against the driver. The COA found the High Court failed to consider whether the Magistrate had correctly applied the legal principles regarding confiscation under the Animals Act.
precedents_cited_list: Faris Vs. The Officer in Charge, Police Station Galenbindunuwewa and Another (1992) 1 SLR 160 | Nizar vs. Inspector of Police Waththegama (1978-79) 2 SLR 204
standard_of_review_applied: Review of correctness of legal interpretation and application by lower courts, and evaluation of evidence on a balance of probability.
sentencing_principles_applied: Principles governing confiscation of vehicles under section 3A proviso of Animals Act, specifically that confiscation cannot be made if owner proves either lack of knowledge OR taking all precautions on a balance of probability.

judges: B. Sasi Mahendran, J. | Amal Ranaraja, J.
offence_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The deceased, a three-wheeler driver, was found dead near Marakarampalai School. His wife received a call about an accident around 2 AM on 29.01.2013. Two accused, also three-wheeler drivers, were arrested. Blood stains matching the deceased's DNA were found on the first accused's three-wheeler. The prosecution case was based on circumstantial evidence. The High Court convicted the 1st accused of murder and sentenced him to death, acquitting the 2nd accused. The 1st accused appealed.
evidence_type_secondary: Medical evidence; Witness testimony (PW12 SOCO officer)
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the 1st accused of murder based on DNA evidence linking blood in his three-wheeler to the deceased, and sentenced him to death.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant argued that the conviction was unsafe due to uncertainty regarding the blood sample origin; weakness of prosecution case; misdirection on burden of proof; failure to eliminate accident as cause of death; unreliability of PW03; insufficiency and improper evaluation of circumstantial evidence.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Uncertainty/ambiguity regarding origin of blood sample allegedly from deceased. | Failure to consider inherent weakness of prosecution case. | Misdirection in law by examining defence evidence in light of prosecution evidence, shifting burden of proof. | Failure to eliminate possibility of accident as cause of death. | PW03 is not a credible witness. | Circumstantial evidence items inadequate to support conviction. | Failure to apply proper principles for evaluating circumstantial evidence.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: Prosecution led 14 witnesses. Key issues: PW12 (SOCO) clarified blood samples were taken from the scene ground, not from the deceased's body, creating doubt about sample exclusivity. Medical evidence suggested injuries could have resulted from an accident (blunt force/heavy fall). No direct eyewitness to murder.
probability_assessment_by_court: Yes - Court applied principle that circumstantial evidence must be incompatible with innocence and must only be consistent with guilt.
defence_version_summary: Accused made dock statements. Defence challenged prosecution evidence, particularly origin of blood sample and cause of death, suggesting accident as possible cause.
legal_errors_description: High Court Judge misdirected himself regarding origin of blood sample (thinking it was from body, but it was from scene ground). Potential error in evaluating circumstantial evidence and burden of proof.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: Court of Appeal analyzed principles for circumstantial evidence cases, citing several precedents. Held that evidence must be reliable and form a chain leading only to guilt, excluding reasonable hypotheses of innocence. Found serious doubt about exclusivity of blood sample (not from body, but scene). Medical evidence did not establish murder as only cause. Prosecution failed to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The Court of Appeal allowed the appeal, acquitting the accused. It found the prosecution failed to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt. Key reasons: doubt over origin/exclusivity of blood sample used for DNA match; medical evidence did not rule out accident; circumstantial evidence did not form an inescapable chain pointing only to guilt.
defence_counsel: K. Kugaraja
cause_of_death_exact_text: "When the deceased person had been subjected to a very strong attack and or that deceased person, if he had fallen down and when a force becomes heavy through that fall, such a death could take place."
hc_analysis_summary: High Court convicted based on DNA match of blood in accused's vehicle to deceased. However, COA found error in assuming blood sample was from deceased's body; it was from the scene ground. Also, medical evidence was not conclusive of murder.
precedents_cited_list: E.R.S.R. Coomaraswamy, The Law of Evidence | B.R.R.A. Jagath Pramawansha v. The Attorney General, CA Appeal No. 173/2005 | King v. Abeywicrama 44 NLR 254 | King v. Appuhamy 46 NLR 128 | Podisingho v. King 53 NLR 49 | Junaideen Mohamed Haaris v. Attorney General, SC Appeal 118/17 | R vs. Blom 1939 A.D. 188 | Miller vs. Minister of Pensions, 1947 All England Law Reports
standard_of_review_applied: Appellate review of conviction based on circumstantial evidence; whether verdict is unsafe.
sentencing_principles_applied: Not applicable (appeal allowed on conviction)
final_charge_after_appeal: Acquitted

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 300 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The 1st accused-appellant was charged with attempted murder for shooting the injured party (PW-01) in the head and chest using a gun. The appellant pleaded guilty. The injured party sustained serious, life-threatening injuries and had lasting physical impairments. The appellant had a previous conviction for culpable homicide not amounting to murder.
evidence_type_secondary: Government Analyst Report, Medico Legal Report, Observation of injured party's condition
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 300 of the Penal Code
hc_sentence_type: Fifteen years rigorous imprisonment, Fine, Compensation
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the appellant after he pleaded guilty. The judge considered the serious gunshot injuries to the head, the lasting medical condition of the injured, the appellant's previous conviction record, and the appellant's offer to pay compensation. The judge imposed 15 years RI, a fine, and compensation.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant's counsel argued the sentence was excessive because the appellant pleaded guilty without wasting court time and offered to pay compensation. He contended the High Court Judge did not consider mitigatory factors correctly and made inappropriate comments against the appellant in the sentencing order.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The learned High Court Judge has not considered the mitigatory factors in the correct perspective when imposing the sentence on the appellant.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal noted the injured party (PW-01) was shot at close range with a firearm, causing injuries sufficient to cause death. The Government Analyst Report confirmed a gun was used. The court observed PW-01's lasting impairments and considered the appellant's previous conviction as an aggravating factor.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal found the appellant had clear intention to kill based on the nature of the attack and injuries caused.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded guilty to the charge. He offered to pay compensation and claimed he and the injured were now friends. No alibi or defence witnesses were mentioned.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal held that while a guilty plea can be a mitigatory factor, it is not the sole criterion for a lenient sentence. The court agreed the High Court Judge correctly balanced aggravating factors (seriousness of injuries, lasting impact on victim, use of a firearm, previous conviction) against mitigatory factors (guilty plea, compensation offer). The COA found the sentence was within legal limits, reduced from the maximum, and was fair. The judge's comments on the proper charge were seen as administrative observations, not influencing the sentence. The appeal was dismissed.
coa_sentence_type: Fifteen years rigorous imprisonment, Fine of Rs. 25,000, Compensation of Rs. 1,000,000 (with default simple imprisonment of 2 years if compensation not paid). Sentence deemed commenced from 06-04-2023.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The 1st accused-appellant appealed against his High Court sentence for attempted murder. He had pleaded guilty to shooting the victim, causing severe injuries. The High Court imposed 15 years RI, a fine, and compensation. On appeal, he argued the sentence was excessive given his guilty plea and compensation offer. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal, finding the sentence fair and reasonable after considering the serious aggravating factors, including the victim's lasting condition and the appellant's previous conviction.
defence_counsel: Neranjan Jayasinghe with Randunu Heellage, Lahiru Vidushanke and Imangsi Senarath
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court considered the mitigatory and aggravating circumstances. The COA found the HC Judge correctly assessed the facts, including the victim's injuries and the appellant's record, and reduced the sentence from the maximum allowable. The COA saw no error in the HC's reasoning.
precedents_cited_list: Attorney General Vs. H.N.De Silva 57 NLR 121 | Sevaka Perumal et al. Vs. State of Tamil Nadu AIR 1991 SC 1463 | Attorney General Vs. Ranasinghe and others (1993) 2 SLR 81
standard_of_review_applied: Review of sentence for excessiveness within legal parameters.
sentencing_principles_applied: Balancing aggravating and mitigatory factors, deterrence, protection of society, consideration of gravity of offence, effect on victim, and offender's previous record.

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: section 296 of the Penal Code
location_of_offence: Kamburugoda within the jurisdiction of the High Court of Kalutara
brief_facts_summary: The appellant (elder brother) was indicted for the murder of his brother on 5th January 2010. The deceased's wife (PW-01) heard screams, saw the appellant leaving their house with a mamoty, and found the deceased with serious head injuries. The appellant prevented them from taking the injured to the hospital and later consumed poison. Police found a blood-stained mamoty (P-01) and admitted both men to the hospital where the deceased died.
evidence_type_secondary: Medical evidence (JMO postmortem), Physical evidence (mamoty P-01)
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: section 296 of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court Judge, after a trial without a jury, found the appellant guilty of murder under section 296 of the Penal Code. The judge sentenced him to death based on the prosecution's evidence, including circumstantial evidence and witness testimonies.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant's counsel argued the High Court Judge misdirected himself on the burden of proof and that the prosecution failed to prove the case beyond reasonable doubt. He contended the circumstantial evidence was insufficient, there were discrepancies about the location where the deceased fell, and the weapon was not properly identified.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The learned High Court Judge has misdirected himself as to the burden of proof and thereby erred in delivering the impugned judgment. | The prosecution has failed to prove the case beyond reasonable doubt against the appellant and the learned High Court Judge has failed to analyze the evidence in the correct perspective.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The prosecution relied on witnesses PW-01 (wife), PW-02 (sister-in-law), PW-03 (relative), and a police officer. Their evidence established the appellant's presence, possession of the mamoty, prevention of medical help, and subsequent poisoning. The JMO's evidence linked the mamoty to the fatal injuries. The appellant did not challenge key evidence during cross-examination.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal applied principles of circumstantial evidence, holding that the totality of evidence irresistibly pointed to the appellant's guilt and was inconsistent with any reasonable hypothesis of innocence. The appellant's explanation was found improbable and he failed to explain incriminating circumstances.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty and gave evidence under oath. He denied causing his brother's death, claimed the deceased had a mental ailment, and said he only hit him once in 2008. He alleged witnesses were lying. He claimed he found his brother already injured, became stunned, and accidentally drank insecticide. He did not cross-examine material prosecution evidence.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The COA examined the grounds together. It confirmed the correct legal principles for circumstantial evidence were applied. It found a strong prima facie case: the appellant was seen leaving the scene with a mamoty, prevented help, and the weapon was found nearby. The appellant's failure to challenge key evidence and his improbable defence story were noted. The COA held the evidence, taken cumulatively, proved guilt beyond reasonable doubt, was consistent only with guilt, and met the standard set out in precedents. The HC Judge was not misdirected on the burden of proof.
coa_sentence_type: Death
brief_judgment_file_summary: The appellant was convicted of murder by the High Court of Kalutara and sentenced to death for killing his brother in 2010. He appealed, arguing misdirection on the burden of proof and insufficient evidence. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal, finding the High Court correctly analyzed the circumstantial evidence, which included eyewitness accounts of the appellant fleeing with the weapon and preventing medical aid, recovery of the blood-stained mamoty, and medical evidence linking it to the fatal injury. The COA held the evidence proved guilt beyond reasonable doubt and affirmed the conviction and sentence.
defence_counsel: Rajinda Kandegedara
cause_of_death_exact_text: injury number one had been a deep cut injury, which has resulted in the death of the deceased
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court considered the totality of evidence and found the prosecution proved the case beyond reasonable doubt. The COA found no misdirection or error in the HC's analysis, agreeing it was correctly conducted.
precedents_cited_list: The King Vs. Abeywickrama 44 NLR 254 | Don Sunny Vs. The Attorney General (1998) 2 SLR 01 | The King Vs. Gunaratne 47 NLR 145 | Regina Vs. Exall (176 English Reports, Nisi Prius at page 853) | Sumanasena Vs. The Attorney General (1999) 3 SLR 137 | Rex Vs. Lord Cochrane and others (1814) Gurneys Reports 479 | Rex Vs. Burdett (1820) B & Ald 161 | Sarawan Singh Vs. State of Punjab AIR 2002 SC III 3655 | Pilippu Mandige Nalaka Krishantha Thisera Vs. The Attorney General, CA 87/2005 | Motilal Vs. State of Madya Pradesh (1990) (CLJ NOC 125 MP) | Ramakant Rai Vs. Madan Rai AIR 2004 SC at 84
standard_of_review_applied: Review based on whether the High Court properly applied the law on burden of proof and circumstantial evidence, and whether the conviction was supported by evidence proving guilt beyond reasonable doubt.

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 19(b) and section 19(c) of the Bribery Act
brief_facts_summary: The complainant (PW-01), a funeral undertaking businessman, won a tender to remove body parts from Mahamodara hospital laboratory. When he went to remove the samples, the two appellants, laborers at the laboratory, demanded Rs.10,000 as a bribe to release the samples without delay. The complainant lodged a complaint with the Bribery Commission, leading to a raid on 18-05-2009 where marked money was given to the 1st appellant and later allegedly to the 2nd appellant. Both were arrested by Bribery Commission officials.
evidence_type_primary: Eyewitness testimony (complainant PW-01 and decoy PW-02)
evidence_type_secondary: Official evidence regarding tender, claim voucher, and employment status of appellants
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 19(b) and section 19(c) of the Bribery Act
hc_sentence_type: 4 years simple imprisonment per count (8 counts total; grouped to total 8 years per appellant), fines, and additional payment under section 26 of Bribery Act
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court found the appellants guilty on all counts. The 1st appellant was convicted on counts 1-4 (soliciting and accepting a bribe). The 2nd appellant was convicted on counts 5-8 (aiding and abetting). Sentences were structured to result in a total of 8 years simple imprisonment for each appellant, plus fines and an order to pay Rs.10,000 each under section 26 of the Bribery Act.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The 1st appellant argued the trial judge predetermined guilt, failed to properly evaluate evidence, and failed to analyze the complainant's credibility. The 2nd appellant argued the prosecution failed to prove the charges beyond reasonable doubt, the judge failed to consider contradictions in prosecution evidence, failed to apply section 114(f) of the Evidence Ordinance for missing phone details, and sought corroboration after doubting the complainant's credibility.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The learned High Court Judge predetermined the charges were proved beyond reasonable doubt before considering defence evidence. | The learned High Court Judge failed to properly evaluate the evidence of the whole case. | The credibility of the complainant was not properly analyzed. | The prosecution failed to establish ingredients of charges against 2nd appellant beyond reasonable doubt. | The learned High Court Judge failed to consider inter se and per se contradictions of prosecution witnesses. | Failure to call phone details warrants application of section 114(f) of Evidence Ordinance. | The learned High Court Judge misdirected himself by seeking corroboration after finding the complainant not credible.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found minor discrepancies in PW-01's evidence (e.g., initially saying money was given to both appellants, then correcting to only the 1st appellant) were not material and did not affect the core of the prosecution case. The Court accepted the evidence of PW-01 and PW-02 as credible and corroborated, establishing the incident and acceptance of money beyond reasonable doubt.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court held minor discrepancies did not create reasonable doubt. The evidence as a whole had the 'ring of truth'. Reasonable doubt was defined as not being imaginary, trivial, or based on abstract speculation.
defence_version_summary: Both appellants pleaded not guilty and made statements from the dock, denying any wrongdoing. The 1st appellant claimed PW-01 framed him because he prevented PW-01's fraudulent claim. The 2nd appellant also denied accepting any bribe. The Court rejected these defences, finding no basis for the claim of being framed.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed the grounds together. It found the trial judge did not misdirect himself by using the phrase 'beyond reasonable doubt' during evidence analysis, as the judgment read as a whole showed proper consideration of defence. Minor contradictions in PW-01's evidence were found not material. The claim that appellants blocked PW-01's payment was disproven, as payment was made months after their arrest. The Court held the non-production of phone details did not attract section 114(f) of the Evidence Ordinance. The trial judge's search for corroboration was proper, not a misdirection. The Court of Appeal dismissed the conviction appeal for want of merit. However, it varied the sentence, ordering all sentences for each appellant to run concurrently, reducing total imprisonment from 8 to 4 years per appellant.
coa_sentence_type: 4 years rigorous imprisonment (concurrent on all counts) per appellant, plus fines and additional payment under section 26 of Bribery Act with default sentences.
brief_judgment_file_summary: Two appellants, hospital laborers, were convicted by the High Court of Colombo for soliciting, accepting, and aiding/abetting a Rs.10,000 bribe from a funeral undertaker. They were sentenced to a total of 8 years imprisonment each, fines, and an additional payment. They appealed on grounds including misdirection, evidence contradictions, and excessive sentence. The Court of Appeal dismissed the conviction appeal, finding the prosecution proved its case beyond reasonable doubt and minor discrepancies were not material. However, it allowed the sentence appeal in part, varying the sentences to run concurrently, reducing the total imprisonment to 4 years each, while upholding the fines and additional payment.
defence_counsel: U.R. de Silva, P.C. with Pradeepa Kaluarachchi for 1st Accused-Appellant, Darshana Kuruppu with Tharushi Gamage for 2nd Accused-Appellant
hc_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found no prejudice to the appellants' substantial rights or failure of justice due to any alleged defects in the High Court judgment. It affirmed the High Court's reasoning on credibility and evidence, though it corrected the sentencing structure.
precedents_cited_list: State of U.P. Vs. M. K. Anthony, AIR 1985 SC 48 | Jayasena Vs. Queen 72 NLR 313 | State of Punjab Vs. Karnail Singh (2003) 11 SCC 271 | Stirland Vs. Director of Public Prosecution (1944 AC(PC) 315) | State of U.P. Vs. Anil Singh (AIR 1988 SC 1998)
standard_of_review_applied: Appellate jurisdiction under Article 138 of the Constitution; judgment not to be reversed for error, defect or irregularity unless it prejudices substantial rights or occasions a failure of justice.
sentencing_principles_applied: Consideration of facts and circumstances of the case; proportionality of sentence; concurrent vs. consecutive sentencing.

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 354 of the Penal Code; Section 365B(2)(b) of the Penal Code as amended by Penal Code (Amendment) Act No. 22 of 1995, 29 of 1998 and 16 of 2006
location_of_offence: Pesalai within the jurisdiction of the High Court of Mannar
brief_facts_summary: The accused-appellant was charged with abducting a minor girl on or about 01-01-2013 and committing grave sexual abuse by inserting his finger into her vagina. The victim (PW-01), aged around 9 at the time, reported the incident to her grandmother soon after but was told not to tell anyone. The matter came to light over a year later after a school awareness program, prompting police investigation and charges. The victim testified that the appellant took her between parked vans, lifted her dress, and touched her genitals.
evidence_type_secondary: Medical evidence (Medico-Legal Report), Testimony of grandmother, Child Welfare Officer
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 354 of the Penal Code; Section 365B(2)(b) of the Penal Code as amended by Penal Code (Amendment) Act No. 22 of 1995, 29 of 1998 and 16 of 2006
hc_sentence_type: Count 01: 2 years rigorous imprisonment and fine; Count 02: 7 years rigorous imprisonment and fine; sentences concurrent; compensation ordered
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court found the appellant guilty on both counts. The judge considered mitigating and aggravating circumstances, sentencing him to imprisonment and fines, ordering the sentences to run concurrently, and ordering compensation to the victim.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant argued the conviction was unsafe due to the belated complaint and discrepancies in evidence. He contended the prosecution failed to prove the specific act of grave sexual abuse (finger insertion), that the kidnapping charge was unsupported by evidence, and that the High Court judge failed to adequately consider the defence case.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: In view of the belatedness of the complaint and the discrepancies of the evidence of PW-01 taken with other witnesses, whether the conviction could be sustained. | In the light of the specific act mentioned in the indictment, whether the prosecution has failed to prove the charge of grave sexual abuse. | The offence of kidnapping cannot be sustained in the light of the evidence. | Whether the learned High Court Judge has failed to adequately consider the defence, especially the evidence of the appellant.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court considered the totality of evidence, including testimony from the victim, her mother, grandmother, the Child Rights Welfare Officer, and the JMO. Minor discrepancies were deemed immaterial, and the victim's testimony was found credible despite the delayed complaint and her reluctance.
probability_assessment_by_court: Court found prosecution proved case beyond reasonable doubt; no reasonable doubt created by defence; delay in complaint was justified and explained.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty, gave evidence under oath, and called witnesses. He alleged the complaint was false due to jealousy (envy of his educated family, rejection of a marriage proposal, political enmity). The court found his defence not credible and noted failure to put specific allegations to prosecution witnesses in cross-examination.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal reviewed the evidence as a whole, applying the principle that prosecution must prove its case beyond reasonable doubt. It found the victim's testimony credible and trustworthy, despite minor discrepancies and delayed complaint, which was satisfactorily explained by her age, trauma, and grandmother's instruction. The court held the essential ingredients of both abduction and grave sexual abuse were met, as the act of touching the genitals fell within the definition of grave sexual abuse, even without specific proof of finger insertion. The defence allegations of false complaint due to jealousy were not put to relevant witnesses and were unsupported. The High Court's conviction and sentence were upheld as based on cogent evidence and proper legal principles.
coa_sentence_type: Conviction and sentence affirmed; sentences to run concurrently: Count 01: 2 years rigorous imprisonment and Rs.10,000 fine (default 6 months simple imprisonment); Count 02: 7 years rigorous imprisonment and Rs.10,000 fine (default 6 months simple imprisonment); compensation of Rs.100,000 to victim (default 6 months simple imprisonment).
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused-appellant was convicted by the High Court of Mannar for abducting and committing grave sexual abuse on a minor girl. He appealed, challenging the conviction based on belated complaint, discrepancies, insufficient proof of specific act, and inadequate consideration of defence. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal, finding the victim's testimony credible and the prosecution's case proved beyond reasonable doubt. The High Court's conviction and sentence were affirmed.
defence_counsel: Saliya Pieris, P.C. with K. Kugaraja
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court found the appellant guilty based on the victim's testimony and other evidence, sentencing him to imprisonment, fines, and compensation. The COA found no error in the HC's analysis, concluding it properly considered the evidence and defence.
precedents_cited_list: Pantis Vs. The Attorney General (1998) 2 SLR 148 | Narender Kumar Vs. State (NCT of Delhi), AIR 2012 SC 2281 | James Silva Vs. The Republic of Sri Lanka (1980) 2 SLR 167 | D. Tikiribanda Vs. Attorney-General CA 64/2003 decided 06-10-2009 reported in the Bar Association Law Journal (2010) (B.L.R.) 92 | Gamage Prabhath Janaka Nayana Priyantha Perera Vs. Attorney General [CA/107/2012] decided on 27.05.2016 | Bhoginbhai Hirjibhai Vs State of Gujarat (AIR 1983-SC 753 at pp 756-758) | Mahathun and Others Vs. The Attorney General (2015) 1 SLR 74 | Sarwan Singh Vs State of Punjab 2002 AIR Supreme Court iii 3652 at 36755,3656 | Boby Mathew Vs State of Karnataka 2004 3 Cri. L. J.3003 | Pilippu Mandige Nalaka Krishantha Kumara Thisera Vs A.G CA 87/2005 decided on 17-05-2007
standard_of_review_applied: Review of evidence as a whole to determine if prosecution proved case beyond reasonable doubt; will not lightly disturb trial judge's findings unless manifestly wrong.
sentencing_principles_applied: Consideration of mitigatory and aggravating circumstances; sentences ordered to run concurrently; compensation to victim.

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 364(2) of the Penal Code as amended
brief_facts_summary: The victim, a 12-year-old girl living with her father and brother, was raped multiple times by the Appellant in 2009. The Appellant was married to the victim's sister and used the opportunity while his wife was hospitalized to commit the offences, threatening the victim to keep silent. The victim became pregnant and later gave birth to a child, whose paternity was confirmed by a DNA report as belonging to the Appellant.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 364(2) of the Penal Code as amended
hc_sentence_type: Rigorous imprisonment for 13 years on each of 3 counts (total 39 years)
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the Appellant after he pleaded guilty based on the DNA report. The court sentenced him to 13 years rigorous imprisonment for each count of statutory rape, to run consecutively, resulting in 39 years total. The court also imposed a fine of Rs. 10,000 per count and compensation of Rs. 250,000.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appeal contested only the sentence, specifically the order for the sentences to run consecutively. The Appellant argued that the sentence was excessive, especially given his guilty plea which saved court time, and his personal circumstances as a married person with children.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Sentence is excessive | Sentences should run concurrently rather than consecutively
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The victim gave clear evidence in chief regarding the incidents. Her testimony, combined with the DNA report confirming the Appellant's paternity of the child born from the rape, formed the core of the prosecution case. The court noted the trauma suffered by the victim as a child and the delay in testifying.
probability_assessment_by_court: The DNA report provided conclusive proof of paternity, confirming the victim's account and leaving no reasonable doubt.
defence_version_summary: The Appellant pleaded guilty to all charges unconditionally upon presentation of the DNA report. He did not contest conviction, only the sentence. No alibi or other witnesses were called by the defence.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal noted that sentencing is a court prerogative and must balance the seriousness of the offence with the offender's circumstances. While the maximum sentence for statutory rape is 20 years, the Court held that imposing 13 years per count and ordering them to run consecutively (totalling 39 years) was inappropriate. It considered the Appellant's guilty plea (saving court time) and his family circumstances as mitigating factors. The Court found the High Court judge did not properly exercise sentencing discretion regarding concurrency and thus varied the sentence.
coa_sentence_type: Rigorous imprisonment for 13 years on each count, to run concurrently. Fines and default sentences remain. Compensation enhanced to Rs. 500,000 with default sentence of 2 years. Sentence operative from 18.01.2023.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The Appellant was convicted in the High Court of Hambantota on three counts of statutory rape of a 12-year-old girl and sentenced to 39 years rigorous imprisonment (13 years per count, consecutive). He appealed only the sentence, arguing it was excessive. The Court of Appeal found the total effective sentence of 39 years was disproportionate. Considering his guilty plea and personal circumstances, it ordered the sentences to run concurrently, resulting in a 13-year term. The conviction was affirmed, compensation was increased, and the appeal was partly allowed.
defence_counsel: Neranjan Jayasinghe with Randunu Heellage and Imangsi Senarath
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court imposed consecutive sentences of 13 years per count. The COA found the judge erred in not properly considering the total period (39 years) and mitigating factors, thereby failing to exercise sentencing discretion appropriately.
standard_of_review_applied: Court's discretion in sentencing, principle of proportionality and fairness
sentencing_principles_applied: Proportionality to the seriousness of the crime, consideration of offender's circumstances (guilty plea, family status), and fairness in sentencing.

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: section 296 read with section 32 of the Penal Code
location_of_offence: Iddamalgama within the Jurisdiction of the High Court of Chilaw
brief_facts_summary: The two accused-appellants were charged with the murder of Herath Jayasinghe Mudalige Anuruddika Jayasinghe alias Bandara on 23-03-2022 at Iddamalgama. The prosecution relied on eyewitness testimony from PW-02 and PW-16, who witnessed the stabbing attack. The appellants pleaded not guilty, gave evidence under oath, and claimed innocence. The High Court found them guilty and sentenced them to death.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: section 296 read with section 32 of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: After a judge-alone trial, the High Court Judge found both appellants guilty of murder as charged. The court relied on the eyewitness testimony of PW-02 and PW-16. Both appellants were sentenced to death.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellants argued that the evidence of the two eyewitnesses was contradictory, internally inconsistent, and incompatible with the medical evidence. They also challenged the High Court Judge's failure to consider the possibility of a sudden fight, properly evaluate contradictions, analyze improbabilities, and consider omissions and the evidence of a defence witness. They argued the judge erred in accepting the reasons for the delayed statements and not considering an uninvestigated alternative attack.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Evidence of the two eyewitnesses is contradictory to each other. | Contradiction in relation to other witnesses, especially the medical evidence, not considered. | Failure to consider the possibility of a sudden fight. | Failure to evaluate correctly inter se contradictions between PW-02 and PW-16. | Error in accepting testimonies of PW-02 and PW-16 as both are incompatible with medical evidence. | Failure to consider that PW-02 admitted in a statement he did not observe the accused at the scene. | Failure to properly analyze the improbabilities of PW-02's evidence. | Failure to consider omissions from PW-02's testimony. | Failure to consider per se contraindications of PW-02. | Failure to consider the evidence of defence witness Dhadallage Janaka Sujeewa. | Failure to analyze contradictions from the testimony of PW-16. | Failure to identify a different type of attack gone uninvestigated. | Error in accepting reasons for delay in making statements in light of improbabilities. | Failure to properly analyze improbabilities of PW-16's evidence. | Failure to recognize the non-calling of Asoka creates a doubt. | Consideration of inferences in favour of the defence.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed the credibility of eyewitnesses PW-02 and PW-16, finding their delayed statements were sufficiently explained by fear. The court found no material contradictions affecting the core of the case and held that minor discrepancies in witnesses' recollections are normal. The medical evidence was found to be consistent with the eyewitness accounts of a stabbing to the chest area.
probability_assessment_by_court: Court found the prosecution proved its case beyond reasonable doubt and the appellants failed to create a reasonable doubt.
defence_version_summary: Both appellants pleaded not guilty and gave evidence under oath. The 1st appellant claimed he attended a party, returned home, slept, and later fled out of fear after being accused. He claimed someone set him up. The 2nd appellant claimed he attended the fair, returned home, and was later assaulted and handed over to police, denying involvement. The court found their defences not credible.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal conducted a detailed review of the evidence. It found the eyewitnesses credible despite their initial delay in coming forward, attributing it to fear in a village setting. The court applied the principle that minor discrepancies do not undermine credibility if the witness is truthful on material matters. It rejected arguments about contradictions with medical evidence, noting the JMO's findings of stab wounds to the chest were consistent with witness accounts. It also held there was no evidentiary basis to consider the possibility of a sudden fight reducing the charge. The COA concluded the High Court Judge correctly analyzed the evidence and reached a sound verdict.
coa_sentence_type: Death sentence affirmed
brief_judgment_file_summary: The two accused-appellants were convicted of murder by the High Court of Chilaw and sentenced to death. They appealed to the Court of Appeal on multiple grounds, including contradictions in eyewitness testimony, inconsistency with medical evidence, and failure to consider a possible sudden fight. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal, finding the eyewitnesses credible despite initial delays, no material contradictions, and no basis to alter the charge. The conviction and death sentence were affirmed.
defence_counsel: Champika Monarawila with Michelle Fernando (for 1st Accused-Appellant), Punraji D. Karunasekara (for 2nd Accused-Appellant)
cause_of_death_exact_text: The 1st stab injury which has damaged the heart of the deceased has caused this death.
hc_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the High Court Judge correctly evaluated the evidence, accepted the credible eyewitness testimony, and properly considered whether there was material to support a finding of culpable homicide not amounting to murder. The COA agreed with the HC's determination.
precedents_cited_list: Attorney General Vs Potta Naufar and Others (Ambeptitya Murder Case) (2007) 2 SLR 144 | Mahathun and Others Vs. The Attorney General (2015) 1 SLR 74 | The Attorney General Vs. Sanadnam Pitchi Theresa (2011) 2 SLR 292 | Bharwada Bhoginbhai Hirjibhai Vs. State of Gujarat, AIR (1983) SC 753 | State of Uttar Pradesh Vs. Anthony 1985 AIR SC 48 | State of U.P. Vs. M. K. Anthony, AIR 1985 SC 48 | Bhoginbhai Hirjibhai Vs. Statee of Gujarat AIR 1983 753
standard_of_review_applied: The Court of Appeal will not lightly disturb the findings of a trial judge with regard to the acceptance or rejection of testimony of a witness unless it is manifestly wrong. Evidence must be viewed in its totality.

judges: Menaka Wijesundera, J | Wickum A. Kaluarachchi, J
offence_sections: Section 54A (b) and Section 54A (d) of the Poisons, Opium, and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance as amended by Act No. 13 of 1984
location_of_offence: Grandpass area, near Mahawatta rail gate, Colombo
brief_facts_summary: On 13 September 2012, army surveillance officers (PW-1 and others) received information from an informant that a young man was carrying heroin near the Mahawatta rail gate in Grandpass. They proceeded to the location, where the informant pointed out the accused-appellant. The appellant was searched and a parcel containing a brown substance (later confirmed as heroin) was found in his right trouser pocket. The appellant was handed over to the Police Narcotics Bureau.
evidence_type_secondary: Government Analyst Report, Eyewitness testimony of army officers
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 54A (d) of the Poisons, Opium, and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court acquitted the appellant on the trafficking count (Count 1) but convicted him on the possession count (Count 2) for possessing 27.02 grams of heroin. The appellant was sentenced to life imprisonment.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant appealed against conviction and sentence on three main grounds: (1) The Trial Judge failed to consider inconsistencies in the prosecution case. (2) The prosecution failed to establish the last link of the inward journey of the production beyond reasonable doubt. (3) The Trial Judge rejected the dock statement on a wrong premise.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The learned Trial Judge failed to consider the inconsistencies in the prosecution case. | Prosecution has failed to establish the last link of the inward journey of the production beyond a reasonable doubt. | The learned Trial Judge has rejected the dock statement on a wrong premise.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the evidence of the prosecution witnesses, particularly PW-1 and PW-2, to be credible and probable. Minor inconsistencies were held not to be material. The chain of custody was sufficiently established through PW-8. The dock statement was found to be improbable.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court held the prosecution proved its case beyond reasonable doubt. The minor inconsistencies did not create reasonable doubt, and the accused's dock statement was improbable.
defence_version_summary: Accused pleaded not guilty. He made an unsworn statement from the dock alleging he was apprehended by a group of people, taken to the Narcotics Bureau, a heroin parcel was introduced, and his fingerprint was forcibly taken. He called one defence witness. The court found his statement wholly improbable and not raised in cross-examination of prosecution witnesses.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal methodically addressed each ground of appeal. It found no material inconsistencies between PW-1 and PW-2 regarding the informant. It held the chain of custody was proven beyond reasonable doubt as PW-8 testified the seals were intact when she received the production. The court rejected the dock statement as improbable and noted it was not put to prosecution witnesses in cross-examination, citing the rule in Sarvan Singh v. State of Punjab. Applying precedents on reasonable doubt (Veerasamy Sivathasan, Shivaji Bobade, Dharm Das Wadhwani, Wijesekera v. Arnolis), it found the prosecution proved its case beyond reasonable doubt and affirmed the High Court judgment.
coa_sentence_type: Life Imprisonment
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused-appellant, Selvaraj Ranjith Kumara, was indicted in the High Court of Colombo for trafficking and possessing 27.02 grams of heroin. He was acquitted of trafficking but convicted of possession and sentenced to life imprisonment. He appealed on grounds of inconsistencies in prosecution evidence, failure to prove chain of custody, and wrongful rejection of his dock statement. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal, finding the prosecution evidence credible, the chain of custody established, and the dock statement improbable and not properly put to witnesses. The conviction and life sentence were affirmed.
prosecution_counsel: Azard Navavi, S.D.S.G. for the Respondent
defence_counsel: Amila Palliyage with Sandeepani Wijesooriya, Savani Udugampola, Lakitha Wakishta Arachchi and Subaj De Silva for Accused-Appellant
hc_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found no material error in the High Court's reasoning. The High Court had correctly evaluated the evidence, acquitted on the trafficking count, and convicted on possession based on credible evidence. The COA agreed with the HC's assessment of the dock statement, despite noting a minor incorrect observation in the HC judgment.
precedents_cited_list: Sarvan Singh V. State of Punjab (2002 AIR SC (iii) 3652) | Ratnayake Mudiyanselage Premachandra V. The Hon. Attorney General C.A. Case No. 79/2011 | Veerasamy Sivathasan V. Hon. Attorney General - SC Appeal 208/2012 | Shivaji Sahebrao Bobade & Arr. V. State of Maharashtra – equivalent citations: 1973 AIR 2622, 1974 SCR (1) 489 | Dharm Das Wadhwani V. The State of Uttar Pradesh, 1974 Cri. LJ (SC) 1249 | Wijesekera (Excise Inspector) V. Arnolis, (1940) (17 CLW 138)
standard_of_review_applied: Appeal against conviction and sentence; review of evidence for material inconsistencies, chain of custody, and correctness of findings.

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 296 read with Sections 113B and 102 of the Penal Code; Section 296 read with Section 32 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The deceased Raja Ananda Edirisinghe was murdered in his Rajagiriya residence on 17 November 2008. The 2nd Appellant, a long-time employee, lived in the upper floor. The 1st Appellant was seen departing the scene. The killing involved ligature strangulation, blunt head trauma, and a stab wound. Evidence included witness testimonies placing the Appellants at the scene, financial transactions between them, a prior hand grenade attack, and a confession by the 3rd Appellant (not party to this appeal).
evidence_type_secondary: Confession (by 3rd Appellant), Witness testimony, Identification parade notes, Medical evidence, Physical evidence from crime scene, Fingerprint report, Financial records
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 296 read with Sections 113B and 102 of the Penal Code; Section 296 read with Section 32 of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court Judge found the case rested entirely on circumstantial evidence. After considering prosecution and defence evidence, the Judge convicted the Appellants as charged and sentenced them to death on 17 October 2018. The 2nd Accused was acquitted due to lack of evidence.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: Appellants contended the High Court Judge erred in law by failing to correctly apply principles for cases based solely on circumstantial evidence, convicted them based on suspicious circumstances, took an erroneous approach to interpreting conspiracy and common intention, and failed to evaluate defence evidence from the correct perspective. The 1st Appellant also separately contended his identity was not established beyond reasonable doubt.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Failure to follow settled law and principles relating to a case entirely based on circumstantial evidence. | Conviction based only on suspicious circumstances. | Erroneous approach in interpreting conspiracy and common intention. | Failure to evaluate defence evidence from the correct perspective and rejected it on wrong premise. | (1st Appellant separately) Identity was not established beyond reasonable doubt.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed the evidence, finding the prosecution led 20 witnesses and the circumstantial evidence formed a complete chain pointing to guilt. The High Court Judge correctly evaluated all evidence, including the Appellants' dock statements.
probability_assessment_by_court: Court found the only reasonable inference from the established circumstances implicated the guilt of the Appellants, excluding every reasonable hypothesis of innocence.
defence_version_summary: The Appellants pleaded not guilty and made dock statements denying the charges. The 1st Appellant claimed he had visited the deceased's house before and that a cheque was for a lease. The 2nd Appellant did not deny presence at the scene. The High Court Judge evaluated and rejected their statements as lacking credibility and failing to challenge prosecution evidence on material points.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal comprehensively reviewed the High Court judgment and evidence. It held the High Court Judge correctly identified the case as entirely circumstantial and meticulously applied the required legal tests. The COA analyzed the principles from King v Abeywickrama, Gunawardena v the Republic, and Hanumant v State of M.P., finding the High Court had properly required the proven facts to be consistent only with guilt and to exclude every other possibility. The COA found the combined circumstantial evidence – including presence at scene, suspicious conduct, financial links, prior attack, and identification – formed a complete rope of evidence establishing guilt beyond reasonable doubt. The separate identity challenge by the 1st Appellant was rejected as witnesses had ample opportunity for identification. All appeal grounds were found meritless.
coa_sentence_type: Death sentence upheld
brief_judgment_file_summary: The Attorney General indicted the Accused-Appellants for the murder of Raja Ananda Edirisinghe in Rajagiriya on 17 November 2008. The High Court of Colombo, after a non-jury trial, convicted the Appellants based on circumstantial evidence and sentenced them to death. They appealed on grounds including misapplication of circumstantial evidence principles, conviction on suspicion, errors in interpreting conspiracy, and faulty evaluation of defence evidence. The Court of Appeal meticulously reviewed the evidence and legal principles, concluding the High Court Judge correctly applied the law and the circumstantial evidence formed a complete chain proving guilt beyond reasonable doubt. The appeal was dismissed and the death sentence upheld.
defence_counsel: Nihara Randeniya for the 1st Appellant. Sahan Kulatunga with Thilini Samarasekara for the 2nd Appellant.
cause_of_death_exact_text: ligature strangulation, blunt weapon trauma to the head and stab injury to the abdomen
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court Judge correctly held the case rested on circumstantial evidence, meticulously considered all evidence, applied the correct legal tests, and found the only reasonable inference was guilt. The Court of Appeal found no error in this analysis.
precedents_cited_list: King v Abeywickrama [1943] 44 NLR 254 | Gunawardena v the Republic [1981] 2 SLR 315 | Hanumant v State of M.P [1952] AIR SC 343; 1953 Cri LJ 129
standard_of_review_applied: Review of whether the trial judge correctly applied legal principles to the evidence, particularly regarding circumstantial evidence.

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 40(1) of the Forest Ordinance as amended by Forest (Amendment) Act No.65 of 2009
brief_facts_summary: The case concerns vehicles (tractor NP RG-1489 and trailer 46-8609) used in the illegal collection and transport of sand from a reserve forest area. The accused (petitioner's son) pleaded guilty and was sentenced. The Magistrate Court initiated proceedings for the forfeiture of the vehicles to the state under Section 40(1) of the Forest Ordinance, requiring the registered owner (the petitioner) to show cause. Despite multiple opportunities, the petitioner repeatedly failed to appear in court or substantiate his claim that he took all precautions to prevent the offence, leading to the Magistrate ordering confiscation.
hc_sentence_type: Order refusing to issue notice on revision application
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court Judge refused to issue notice on the petitioner's revision application. The judge found the petitioner failed to show due diligence in the Magistrate Court proceedings and failed to establish exceptional circumstances warranting the Court's intervention. The refusal was based on the petitioner's repeated failure to appear and substantiate his claim, even after considering a medical certificate for absence.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The petitioner argued the High Court order was contrary to law and evidence. He claimed the judge erred in refusing to issue notices, in finding no exceptional circumstances, and in failing to properly consider documents explaining his absence. He also argued the Magistrate's confiscation order was illegal and caused irreparable loss and a miscarriage of justice.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: High Court order contrary to law and evidence. | High Court judge erred in law in refusing to issue notices. | Finding of no exceptional circumstances was erroneous. | Failed to consider documents M-03 and M-04 showing reason for absence on 03-08-2023. | Erred in stating petitioner could have informed court if ill. | Failed to consider illegality of Magistrate's order and irreparable loss as exceptional grounds.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The primary evidence was the son's guilty plea to the forest offence. The Court of Appeal's analysis focused on the petitioner's conduct, not witness testimony. The court found the petitioner failed to diligently pursue his claim or establish the statutory defence under Section 40(1).
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal assessed that the petitioner, by his own inaction and laches, had disentitled himself to the discretionary relief of revision.
defence_version_summary: The petitioner (registered owner) did not plead guilty to any offence; his son (the accused) pleaded guilty. The petitioner's defence before the Magistrate was a claim for release of vehicles under the proviso to Section 40(1), requiring proof he took all precautions to prevent the offence. He failed to substantiate this claim due to repeated non-appearance and lack of diligence. The court assessed his conduct as showing scant disregard for the process.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal held that revision is a discretionary remedy requiring exceptional circumstances or a miscarriage of justice. It found no such circumstances. The court analyzed the petitioner's repeated failure to appear before the Magistrate to establish his statutory defence under Section 40(1), despite multiple opportunities and indulgences granted. It applied the principle that one who sleeps over his rights and is guilty of laches cannot use revision to overcome his own actions. The court agreed with the High Court's finding that the petitioner showed no due diligence and that the Magistrate had no option but to confiscate the vehicles once the petitioner failed to prove his claim.
coa_sentence_type: The Court of Appeal affirmed the High Court order (refusing notice) and the Magistrate Court order (confiscating the vehicles). No new sentence imposed.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The case involves a revision application regarding the confiscation of vehicles used in a forest offence. The petitioner's son pleaded guilty. The Magistrate, after the petitioner repeatedly failed to appear and show cause, ordered confiscation under the Forest Ordinance. The High Court refused to intervene in revision. The Court of Appeal dismissed the petitioner's further revision application, finding no exceptional circumstances and that the petitioner, through his own laches and lack of diligence, had disentitled himself to discretionary relief. The confiscation order was upheld.
prosecution_counsel: Jayalakshi de Silva, S.S.C., with I.M.M. Fahim
defence_counsel: Sriranganathan Ragul
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court analyzed the petitioner's conduct and found a lack of due diligence and failure to establish exceptional circumstances for revision. The Court of Appeal agreed with this analysis, finding the High Court judge correctly understood the law and the petitioner's failure to diligently pursue his claim.
precedents_cited_list: Caderamanpulle Vs. Ceylon Paper Sacks Ltd (2001) 3 SLR 112 | Hotel Galaxy (Pvt) Ltd. Vs. Mercantile Hotels Management Ltd (1987) 1 SLR 5 | Wijesinghe Vs. Thamarartnam (Sriskantha Law Report Vol. IV page 47) | Vanik Incorporation Ltd. Vs. Jayasekare (1997) 2 SLR 365 | Biso Manike Vs. C.R. de Alwis (1982) 1 SLR 368 | Perera Vs. People’s Bank (1995) 2 SLR 84 | Siripala Vs. Lanerolle and another (2012) 1 SLR 105 | Liyanage and another Vs. Rathnasiri – Divisional Secretariat, Gampaha and others (2013) 1 SLR 6
standard_of_review_applied: Revisionary jurisdiction is a discretionary remedy exercised only upon exceptional circumstances requiring intervention to remedy a miscarriage of justice.

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: 1. Section 296 read with Section 32 of the Penal Code. 2. Section 380 read with 32 of the Penal Code. 3. Section 394 read with Section 32 of the Penal Code.
brief_facts_summary: The deceased, a businesswoman, was found dead in her home on 07.06.2009. The 1st Appellant worked as her laborer/gardener and the 2nd Appellant worked in her kitchen. On the day of the incident, the deceased was alone with the Appellants. The deceased was found with cut injuries on her neck, and cash and jewelry were missing. The Appellants were arrested days later in Ja-ela, with stolen property recovered. Evidence included footprints matching the Appellants found at the scene and a confession from the 2nd Appellant.
evidence_type_primary: Circumstantial evidence, Confession (2nd Appellant), Physical evidence (footprints, recovered stolen property)
evidence_type_secondary: Medical evidence (post-mortem), Fingerprint analysis report, Photographic evidence
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: 1. Section 296 read with Section 32 of the Penal Code. 2. Section 380 read with 32 of the Penal Code.
hc_sentence_type: Death (Count 1), 10 years rigorous imprisonment with a fine of Rs.10,000/- each (Count 2), 06 months simple imprisonment in default of fine
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court Judge convicted the Appellants on counts 1 (murder) and 2 (robbery) after a non-jury trial. The judge found the prosecution's circumstantial evidence, including matching footprints and recovered stolen property, sufficient to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt. The judge sentenced them to death for murder and 10 years rigorous imprisonment with a fine for robbery.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The Appellants argued the conviction was based on insufficient and suspicious circumstantial evidence, failure to exclude third-party involvement, and failure to consider contradictions and omissions in prosecution evidence. The 2nd Appellant also challenged the admission of her confession, claimed the indictment was not read to her, and argued the judge failed to analyze common intention and the second charge properly.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: That the Learned High Court Judge failed to consider the well-settled principles of law relating to a case entirely based on circumstantial evidence. | That the Learned High Court Judge convicted the 1st Appellant based only on suspicious circumstances and speculations. | That the Learned High Court Judge failed to exclude the involvement of a third party. | That the Learned High Court Judge failed to analyse credibility of the prosecution witnesses and the entirety of the prosecution case. | That the Learned High Court Judge failed to consider the important contradictions and omissions of the prosecution witnesses. | That the Learned High Court Judge failed to analyse the defence evidence in the correct perspective and rejected the same on wrong premise. | The indictment was not read over to the 2nd Appellant. | The dock statement made by 2nd Appellant was not considered and analysed in the judgment. | The Learned High Court Judge erred in law by failing to consider the statement under Section 127 of the CPC which is an exculpatory statement and not a confession. | The Learned High Court Judge erred in law by failing to consider the items of circumstantial evidence led against the 2nd Appellant is not sufficient to draw an irresistible and inescapable inference the 2nd Appellant entertain common murderous intention with the 1st Appellant. | That the Learned High Court Judge failed to consider that the suspicious circumstances do not establish the guilt of 2nd Appellant. | That the Learned High Court Judge has not analysed the 2nd charge in the judgment and not given reasons for the conviction against the 2nd Appellant as per Section 283 of the CPC.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the High Court Judge correctly analyzed the evidence, including the credibility of witnesses and the circumstantial evidence chain. The judge had the advantage of observing witness demeanor. Minor contradictions were found not to affect the prosecution case.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal held the circumstantial evidence was consistent only with the guilt of the Appellants and inconsistent with any reasonable hypothesis of innocence, following established precedents.
defence_version_summary: Both Appellants pleaded not guilty and made dock statements denying the charges, blaming the police for fabrication. They did not call witnesses. The High Court Judge disbelieved their defence and accepted the prosecution version.
procedural_defects_description: Ground raised that indictment was not read to the 2nd Appellant, but COA considered it an oversight not prejudicing substantial rights.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal thoroughly reviewed the High Court judgment and evidence. It found the High Court Judge correctly applied the law on circumstantial evidence, properly analyzed witness credibility, and itemized 21 points of circumstantial evidence leading to the only reasonable conclusion of guilt. The COA held the confession of the 2nd Appellant was properly admitted after a voir dire inquiry and was voluntary. It found no failure of justice regarding the procedural oversight of reading the indictment. The collective weight of circumstantial evidence, including matching footprints, recovery of stolen property, and the confession, firmly established common intention to commit murder and robbery. The appeal was dismissed.
coa_sentence_type: Death sentence for murder (Count 1) and 10 years rigorous imprisonment with a fine of Rs.10,000/- each for robbery (Count 2) affirmed.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The Attorney General indicted two Appellants for murder and robbery of a businesswoman in Kurunegala. The High Court convicted them on both counts after a non-jury trial and sentenced them to death and imprisonment with fines. The Appellants appealed, challenging the sufficiency of circumstantial evidence, procedural errors, and the admission of a confession. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal, finding the High Court Judge correctly analyzed the evidence, the circumstantial evidence conclusively pointed to guilt, and any procedural oversight did not cause a failure of justice. The convictions and sentences were affirmed.
defence_counsel: Nihara Randeniya for the 1st Appellant. Sandeepani Wijesooriya for the 2nd Appellant.
cause_of_death_exact_text: Death was caused due to ligature strangulation and a cut of the throat.
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court Judge analyzed the circumstantial evidence, listed 21 points supporting guilt, and found it consistent only with the Appellants' guilt. The Court of Appeal agreed with this analysis, finding no error in the High Court's reasoning or conclusions.
precedents_cited_list: King v Abeywickrama 44 NLR 254 | Podisingho v King 53 NLR 49 | Attorney General v Sandanam Pitchi Mary Theresa SC Appeal S.C. Appeal No. 79/2008 | Nuwan de Silva v The Attorney General [2005] 1 SLR 2004
standard_of_review_applied: Appellate court reviewed for errors in fact or law, considering the trial judge's unique advantage in observing witness demeanor, and applied the proviso that errors not prejudicing substantial rights or causing a failure of justice do not warrant reversal.

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 433 of the Penal Code; Section 364(1) of the Penal Code as amended by Amendment Act No.22 of 1995
brief_facts_summary: The prosecutrix (PW-01) was alone in her house at night when the accused-appellant, a person known to her, came to her door, identified himself, and threatened to smash the house if she did not open. When she refused, he forced open the back door, entered, held her by the neck, forced her onto a bed, and had forcible sexual intercourse with her. After the incident, she went to a neighbor's house out of fear. Her son returned home later, was informed, and took her to the police and hospital. The accused claimed the sexual intercourse was consensual and part of a long-standing affair, which was instigated as a false complaint by the prosecutrix's son.
evidence_type_secondary: Medical evidence (Judicial Medical Officer), Testimony of neighbor and son (PW-03), Police investigation evidence
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 433 of the Penal Code; Section 364(1) of the Penal Code as amended by Amendment Act No.22 of 1995
hc_sentence_type: Count 01: 3 months simple imprisonment; Count 02: 15 years rigorous imprisonment
hc_judgment_summary: After a trial without a jury, the High Court Judge found the appellant guilty on both counts. The judge considered mitigatory and aggravating circumstances, imposing sentences of imprisonment and fines for both counts, and ordered compensation to the victim. The judge also ordered police supervision for 4 years post-release.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant's counsel argued that the prosecution had not proved the case beyond reasonable doubt. It was contended that favorable matters pertaining to the defence were not considered and that the High Court Judge did not properly evaluate the appellant's dock statement, particularly regarding consent and the duration of the incident.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The prosecution had not proved the case beyond reasonable doubt. | Matters favorable to the accused pertaining to his defence have not been taken into consideration by the learned High Court Judge. | The dock statement of the accused has not been properly evaluated by the learned High Court Judge.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed the evidence of the prosecutrix, her neighbor, her son, and the JMO. It found minor discrepancies (e.g., where the prosecutrix was when her son returned) were not material and did not create reasonable doubt. The court held the prosecution's version was credible and corroborated.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court assessed that minor discrepancies were expected and did not create reasonable doubt. The totality of evidence supported the prosecution's case beyond reasonable doubt.
defence_version_summary: The accused pleaded not guilty. He made a statement from the dock, claiming a long-standing consensual affair with the prosecutrix, and that the rape complaint was fabricated by her son after he discovered the affair. The court found this defence inconsistent, not put to key witnesses in cross-examination, and lacking evidentiary support.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal dismissed all grounds of appeal. It found the High Court Judge correctly considered the totality of evidence. The COA held that the prosecutrix's estimate of the incident's duration (1.5 hours) was a subjective perception under traumatic circumstances, not proof of consent. The appellant's dock statement was an inadequate defence as it did not admit to the act on the specific night and key allegations were not put to relevant witnesses in cross-examination. Minor contradictions in witness statements were not material. The prosecution proved its case beyond reasonable doubt.
coa_sentence_type: Appeal dismissed. Sentence to be deemed commenced from 31-10-2019. High Court sentences stand: Count 01 - 3 months simple imprisonment and fine of Rs.100 with default sentence; Count 02 - 15 years rigorous imprisonment and fine of Rs.25,000 with default sentence; Compensation of Rs.250,000 to victim with default sentence; 4 years police supervision post-release.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused-appellant was convicted by the High Court of Kuliyapitiya for house trespass by night and rape, and sentenced to imprisonment, fines, and compensation. He appealed, arguing the prosecution failed to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt, his defence was not considered, and his dock statement was not properly evaluated. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal, finding the High Court correctly assessed the evidence. Minor discrepancies did not create doubt, the appellant's defence was inconsistent and not properly put to witnesses, and the prosecution's case was proven. The sentence was upheld but deemed to run from the date of conviction.
defence_counsel: Anil Silva, P.C. with Amaan Bandara
hc_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the High Court Judge diligently considered the defence and the prosecution evidence. The HC arrived at its findings after considering the totality of evidence correctly, and no errors were identified warranting interference.
precedents_cited_list: Mahathun and Others Vs. The Attorney General (2015) 1 SLR 74 | State of U.P. Vs. M. K. Anthony, AIR 1985 SC 48 | Sarwan Singh Vs State of Punjab 2002 AIR Supreme Court iii 3652 | Boby Mathew Vs State of Karnataka 2004 3 Cri. L. J.3003 | Pilippu Mandige Nalaka Krishantha Kumara Thisera Vs A.G CA 87/2005 decided on 17-05-2007 | Jayasena Vs. Queen 72 NLR 313 (PC)
standard_of_review_applied: The Court of Appeal will not lightly disturb the findings of a trial judge regarding witness credibility unless manifestly wrong. The case was reviewed by considering all evidence in its totality.
sentencing_principles_applied: The High Court considered mitigatory and aggravating circumstances. The Court of Appeal upheld the sentence, ordering it to run from the date of conviction.

judges: Menaka Wijesundera J. | Wickum A. Kaluarachchi J.
offence_sections: provisions of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The victim, an 11-year-old girl, was alone at home around 5:30 pm when the appellant, a neighbor, entered her house and committed the act of grave sexual abuse. After the incident, she ran to her friend's house and narrated the story. The friend, father, doctor, and police gave evidence. The appellant denied the allegations from the dock.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: provisions of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The trial judge found the appellant guilty of grave sexual abuse. The judge considered the victim's evidence to be without contradiction or omission, and the corroborative evidence of her friend and father as satisfactory.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant's counsel argued that the trial judge failed to adequately consider the victim's evidence, the dock statement, and the defense case.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The evidence of the victim not being considered adequately. | The dock statement not being adequately considered. | The case for the defense not being considered by the trial judge adequately.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The victim's evidence was explicit and consistent. She was cross-examined lengthily but stood the test well. Her friend and father corroborated her story without creating doubt.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court found the prosecution's case proved beyond reasonable doubt. The victim's evidence was credible and corroborated.
