brief_facts_summary: The accused was charged for possessing 11,250 milliliters of illicit liquor. He pleaded not guilty. During the trial, the prosecution's evidence included a police raid (PW-01) and the accused's previous conviction record was improperly submitted to the court before conviction. The Magistrate found the accused guilty and fined him Rs. 25,000. The High Court dismissed his appeal. The accused then sought revision from the Court of Appeal.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: section 47(1) of the Excise Ordinance
hc_judgment_summary: The Provincial High Court of Kurunegala dismissed the appeal, finding no reason to interfere with the conviction and sentence imposed by the Magistrate. The High Court justified the Magistrate's handling of the evidence and the dock statement.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The petitioner argued that the police improperly submitted his previous conviction record, prejudicing the Magistrate. He also challenged the admission of bad character evidence by PW-01 and the Magistrate's incorrect assessment of his dock statement. He claimed these actions denied him a fair trial.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Improper submission of previous conviction record causing prejudice. | Admission of irrelevant bad character evidence by PW-01. | Misdirection in considering the accused's dock statement.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The primary evidence was from PW-01, the police officer who conducted the raid. The Court found the admission of the accused's previous conviction record and bad character evidence was improper and prejudicial. The Magistrate's handling of the accused's dock statement was also found to be erroneous.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court found a miscarriage of justice due to procedural errors and prejudice, leading to acquittal.
defence_version_summary: The accused pleaded not guilty. He made a statement from the dock but did not call witnesses. The Court found the Magistrate misdirected herself in assessing the evidential value of his dock statement.
legal_errors_description: The Magistrate erred in allowing bad character evidence and considering the accused's previous conviction record. She also misdirected herself on the legal value of an accused's dock statement.
procedural_defects_description: Improper submission of the accused's previous conviction record to the court before conviction. Admission of irrelevant bad character evidence during trial.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found exceptional circumstances warranting revision. It held that the submission of the accused's previous conviction record and the admission of bad character evidence (contrary to Section 54 of the Evidence Ordinance) violated fair trial principles and prejudiced the accused. The Magistrate also erred in her assessment of the accused's dock statement, failing to accord it proper evidential value. The High Court failed to correct these errors. Given the nature of the procedural violations and the risk of further unfairness in a retrial with police witnesses, the Court acquitted the accused.
coa_sentence_type: Acquittal
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused was convicted by the Magistrate's Court for possessing illicit liquor and fined. His appeal to the Provincial High Court was dismissed. He sought revision from the Court of Appeal, arguing denial of a fair trial due to improper admission of previous conviction record and bad character evidence, and misdirection regarding his dock statement. The Court of Appeal found these were exceptional circumstances violating fair trial principles. It set aside the lower courts' judgments and acquitted the accused, declining to order a retrial due to the risk of further prejudice.
defence_counsel: Isuru Jayawardana
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court dismissed the appeal, justifying the Magistrate's actions. The COA found the High Court erred in failing to recognize the procedural violations (improper character evidence and record submission) and the misdirection on the dock statement, which amounted to a denial of a fair trial.
precedents_cited_list: Thilagaratnam Vs. Edirisinghe (1982) 1 SLR 56 | Jonita Vs. Abeysekara (Sriskantha Law Report Vol IV Page 22) | Hotel Galaxy (Pvt) Ltd Vs. Mercantile Hotels Management Ltd (1987) 1 SLR 5 | Wijesinghe Vs. Thamararatnam (Sriskantha Law Report Volume IV page 47) | Vanik Incorporation Ltd Vs. Jayasekare (1997) 2 SLR 365 | Sadi Banda Vs. Officer In Charge of Norton Bridge Police Station | Queen Vs. Kularathne (1968) 71 NLR 529 | King Vs. Vellayan Sittambaram (1918) 20 NLR 257 | Queen Vs. Buddharakkita Thero (1962) 63 NLR 433
standard_of_review_applied: Revisionary jurisdiction exercised due to exceptional circumstances warranting intervention, specifically procedural errors causing a miscarriage of justice.

judges: Menaka Wijesundera J. | K.M.G.H Kulatunga J.
offence_sections: sections 354 and 364(2) of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The accused-appellant was indicted for kidnapping from lawful guardianship and statutory rape of a victim who was between 15-16 years old at the time. The prosecution alleged a love affair and three instances of sexual intercourse in 2005/2006, resulting in pregnancy and an abortion. The victim complained to police in July 2007. The appellant denied the allegations, claiming he was at work during key dates and that the victim was in a relationship with another person.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: sections 354 and 364(2) of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court of Trincomalee convicted the appellant on both counts in the indictment after trial. The appellant pleaded not guilty. The trial judge accepted the prosecution evidence and rejected the defence position, sentencing the appellant accordingly.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant's counsel argued the charge was defective for not specifying a specific date but only a time period, violating Section 165(1) of the Criminal Procedure Code. The second ground was that the prosecution failed to prove its case beyond a reasonable doubt, particularly regarding the date of the offence and the overall unreliability of the victim's evidence.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The charge being defective. | The prosecution has not proved their case beyond a reasonable doubt.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The victim's evidence was inconsistent regarding the year of the offence (2005 vs 2006). The Court found her evidence on the time period doubtful. The appellant gave evidence denying the acts and presented an alibi for specific dates. The trial judge rejected the appellant's position primarily because prosecution witnesses were not cross-examined on those points.
probability_assessment_by_court: Court found a reasonable doubt existed regarding the date of the offence, as the prosecution failed to prove it beyond reasonable doubt. The victim's inconsistent timeline and the medical history created doubt.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty. He denied any sexual acts with the victim. He gave evidence and called witnesses. He presented an alibi, stating he was at work on specific dates alleged by the victim. The court noted his evidence created a reasonable doubt which the trial judge failed to properly analyze.
legal_errors_description: The trial judge misdirected himself on the law regarding the admissibility of evidence of multiple acts of rape under Section 54 of the Evidence Ordinance. He also failed to properly consider the reasonable doubt created by inconsistencies in the prosecution's case regarding the date of the offence.
procedural_defects_description: The indictment specified a time period (between 1st January 2005 and 31st December 2005) instead of a specific date. The Court of Appeal judges differed on whether this constituted a fatal defect, but agreed the prosecution failed to prove the offence occurred within that period.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: Justice Wijesundera found the prosecution failed to prove the date of the offence beyond reasonable doubt due to inconsistencies in the victim's evidence and medical history. She also held the trial judge misdirected himself on the law by admitting evidence of three acts of rape without proper consideration of the Evidence Ordinance. Justice Kulatunga agreed the appeal should be allowed due to the prosecution's failure to prove the offence within the charged period and the unreliability of the victim's evidence, but disagreed that a charge must always specify a specific date, arguing that stating a time period can be valid under Section 165(1). Both judges concluded the trial judge seriously misdirected himself on law and fact.
coa_sentence_type: Conviction and sentence set aside.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused-appellant appealed his High Court conviction for kidnapping and statutory rape. The Court of Appeal allowed the appeal. Justice Wijesundera found the prosecution failed to prove the date of the offence beyond reasonable doubt and that the trial judge misdirected himself on the law regarding evidence of similar acts. Justice Kulatunga concurred in the result but provided a detailed dissenting rationale on the validity of a charge specifying a time period versus a specific date. The conviction and sentence were set aside.
defence_counsel: Senarath Jayasundara and Rehani Chandrasiri
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted the appellant based on the prosecution evidence, rejecting the defence. The Court of Appeal found the trial judge failed to properly analyze the reasonable doubt created by the defence evidence and inconsistencies in the prosecution case, particularly regarding the date, and misdirected himself on the law of evidence.
precedents_cited_list: Baiya Dewayalage Sugathapala alias Sugathe Seeya v. Attorney General [CA/HCC/0007/2024] | Kumburawela Kankanamge Dayarathne v. Attorney General, CA/188/2015 | R. H. M. S. Prematunga alias Ananda v. AttorneyGeneral,CA 01/2013 | A.N. Mukergi v. State [A.I.R 1969 All 489] | Ram Asrey v. Stateof U.P. [1982 A.L.J. 1138] | Sukhdev v. State M.P. [1995(2) Crimes 336] | Attorney General v. Viraj Aponso and Others, SC 24/2008 | Madawala Gedara Premadasa v. AttorneyGeneral, CA/261/2009 | Madduma Ralalage Gunasena v. Attorney General, CA/HCC/0082/2020 | Keerawella Palliyaguruge Dinesh Indika v. Attorney General, CA/88/2013 | Jayawardana v. Attorney General, CA/HCC/0431/2019 | Siripala v. Attorney General, CA/HCC/0156/18 | R v. Douglas [1991 CanLII 81 (SCC)]
standard_of_review_applied: Appeal against conviction and sentence, reviewing errors of law and fact.

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 296 read with Section 32 of the Penal Code (for murder); Section 300 read with Section 32 of the Penal Code (for attempted murder)
location_of_offence: Near deceased's restaurant in Egaluoya/Galhena Junction/playground area
brief_facts_summary: On 15.04.2007, the Appellants were alleged to have attacked the deceased Loku Gamage Jayantha Victor and attempted to murder Don Rohitha (PW2). According to the prosecution, the incident occurred after the deceased had attended a New Year festival. The main prosecution eyewitness (PW1, nephew of the deceased) stated that the 3rd Appellant stopped the motorbike, assaulted the deceased from behind, and the 1st Appellant attacked the deceased on the head with a sword. The 2nd Appellant allegedly threatened with a sword. PW2, who was with the deceased, was assaulted by the 3rd Appellant but did not witness the murder. The Appellants were convicted and sentenced by the High Court, and they appealed.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 296 read with Section 32 of the Penal Code (for murder); Section 300 read with Section 32 of the Penal Code (for attempted murder)
hc_sentence_type: Death sentence on 1st count (murder); 05-years rigorous imprisonment and fine of Rs.25,000/- with default sentence of 01-year simple imprisonment on 2nd count (attempted murder). Additionally, compensation of Rs.100,000/- to PW2 with default sentence of 01-year simple imprisonment.
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court Judge convicted the Appellants as charged after a non-jury trial. The Judge found the evidence of the prosecution witnesses (especially PW1) convincing and proved the charges beyond reasonable doubt. The Appellants were sentenced to death for murder and rigorous imprisonment with a fine for attempted murder, and ordered to pay compensation.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The Appellants argued that the evidence of the sole eyewitness (PW1) was not credible, consistent, or probable. They highlighted contradictions and omissions in PW1's testimony and the failure of PW2 to corroborate the murder. They also argued that the High Court Judge wrongly assessed the evidence, incorrectly applied the law on common intention, relied on demeanour of a witness who did not testify before him, and denied a fair trial. They claimed the Judge imposed liability without proper analysis of infirmities in the prosecution case.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The evidence of PW1 and PW2 fails the test of credibility, probability and consistency. | The learned High Court Judge rejected the defence on unreasonable grounds. | There has been totally inadequate analysis of the case for the prosecution in the light of the many infirmities. | The learned Trial Judge has laid much emphasis on the fact that the accused had absconded after the incident in concluding on their culpability without considering the circumstances under which they had to surrender to Court. | The learned Trial Judge has relied upon the demeanour of the first witness for the prosecution when in fact he did not testify before the learned Judge. | The learned Trial Judge has imposed liability on the basis of common intention without considering the law pertaining to common intention as laid down in decided cases. | There has been total inadequacy in the case for the defence, thereby causing much prejudice to the Accused Appellant. | Due to one or more of the reasons, the Accused Appellants had been denied a fair trial, a Fundamental Right Constitutionally guaranteed.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed the credibility of the sole eyewitness (PW1). It found numerous contradictions and omissions between PW1's court testimony and his previous statements to police, in the inquest, and non-summary inquiry. PW2, who was present, did not witness the murder and could not properly identify the 3rd Appellant. The COA held the prosecution evidence contained serious doubt and ambiguity.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal found that the evidence of PW1 and PW2 was not convincing, reliable, or strong enough to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt. The contradictions and omissions created serious doubt.
defence_version_summary: The Appellants pleaded not guilty. The 1st Appellant gave evidence from the witness box and called two witnesses. The 2nd and 3rd Appellants made dock statements. The High Court Judge wrongly recorded that the 3rd Appellant gave evidence from the witness box. The Court of Appeal found the defence arguments on contradictions and omissions valid.
legal_errors_description: The High Court Judge misapplied the law on common intention without proper consideration of the facts and judicial pronouncements. The Judge also relied on the demeanour of a witness who did not testify before him.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal conducted a thorough analysis of the eyewitness testimony. It found that PW1's evidence was riddled with contradictions and omissions (e.g., who blocked the road, details of the attack) when compared to his previous statements. PW2 did not witness the murder and failed to properly identify the 3rd Appellant. The COA emphasized the burden of proof remains on the prosecution and that the High Court Judge failed to adequately consider these infirmities. The Judge also erred in imposing common intention without sufficient evidence of a common murderous intention. Citing principles from cases like The Queen v. K. A. Santin Singho, the COA held the prosecution failed to prove the case beyond reasonable doubt due to the unreliable evidence.
coa_sentence_type: Acquitted. All convictions and sentences set aside.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The 1st, 2nd, and 3rd Accused-Appellants were convicted by the High Court of Kalutara for murder and attempted murder and sentenced to death and imprisonment. They appealed, challenging the credibility of the sole eyewitness (PW1) and the application of the law on common intention. The Court of Appeal found serious contradictions and omissions in PW1's testimony, and that PW2 did not witness the murder. The COA held the prosecution failed to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt, set aside the High Court conviction and sentence, and acquitted all Appellants.
defence_counsel: Neranjan Jayasinghe with Randunu Heelllage and Imangsi Senerath (for 1st and 2nd Appellants); Palitha Fernando, PC with Harshana Ananda (for 3rd Appellant)
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court Judge concluded the prosecution evidence (especially PW1) was convincing and proved the charges beyond reasonable doubt. However, the COA found the HC Judge failed to properly consider the contradictions and omissions in PW1's evidence and wrongly applied the law on common intention. The HC Judge also made a factual error regarding which accused gave evidence.
precedents_cited_list: The Queen v. K. A. Santin Singho 65 NLR 447 | State Rep. by Inspector of Police v. Saravanan AIR 2009 SC 152 | Acharaparambath Pradeepan & Anr. v. State of Kerala 2006 13 SCC 643 | Kehar Singh & Ors v. State (Delhi Adam.) [3] AIR 1988 SC 1883
standard_of_review_applied: Review of evidence to determine if prosecution proved guilt beyond reasonable doubt; assessment of witness credibility, contradictions, and omissions.

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 365B (2) (b) of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The Appellant was a class teacher at B/Arawa Maha Vidyalaya. He was accused of committing grave sexual abuse on a 10-year-old female student (PW1) during afternoon Mathematics classes between 01.12.2013 and 03.02.2014. The acts involved squeezing her breasts and digital penetration of her vagina. The victim disclosed the incidents to her mother on 04.02.2014, and a complaint was lodged at Mahiyangana Police Station on 05.02.2014.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 365B (2) (b) of the Penal Code
hc_sentence_type: 10 years rigorous imprisonment, fine of Rs.10,000 with default 6 months simple imprisonment, compensation of Rs.100,000 with default 12 months rigorous imprisonment
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the Appellant only on the 3rd count of grave sexual abuse. He was acquitted on the 1st and 2nd counts. The Judge considered the evidence presented and found the victim's testimony convincing and cogent.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The Appellant challenged the conviction on grounds of inconsistencies in the victim's evidence, improper evaluation of prosecution evidence, consideration of unmarked defence statements, and reversal of the burden of proof.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Did the learned High Court Judge fail to consider the inconsistencies and contradictions between PW1's evidence and the short history given to the Medical Officer. | Did the learned High Court Judge fail to properly evaluate the prosecution evidence particularly on the consideration of improbability. | Has the learned High Court Judge erred in law by considering the portion of the statement made by the Appellant which were not marked during the defence. | The learned Trial Judge erred in law by placing the burden on the Appellant to prove his innocence.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal carefully assessed the victim's testimony and found it creditworthy and consistent with medical evidence. Minor contradictions (e.g., how the mother learned of the incident) were not considered to affect the core of the case. The JMO's finding of a superficial hymenal tear was consistent with the allegation of digital penetration.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court assessed the probability of events as recounted by the child victim and found her evidence convincing and sufficient to prove the case beyond reasonable doubt.
defence_version_summary: The Appellant pleaded not guilty, gave evidence from the witness box denying the charges, and closed his case. The court found his defence not credible and accepted the prosecution evidence.
legal_errors_description: The COA noted a potential misdirection regarding consideration of an unmarked portion of the Appellant's statement, but found it did not prejudice the Appellant's substantial rights.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal dismissed all grounds of appeal. It held that the victim's testimony was credible, consistent with medical evidence, and sufficient to prove the charge. Minor inconsistencies did not affect the core of the case. The alleged misdirection regarding an unmarked statement did not prejudice the Appellant. The Court found no error in the High Court's application of the burden of proof. Guided by precedents on medical evidence admissibility and the constitutional provision on non-prejudicial errors, the COA concluded the HC judgment was sound.
coa_sentence_type: 10 years rigorous imprisonment, fine of Rs.10,000 with default 6 months simple imprisonment, compensation of Rs.100,000 with default 12 months rigorous imprisonment (sentence operative from 02.12.2022)
brief_judgment_file_summary: The Appellant, a teacher, was convicted by the Badulla High Court on one count of grave sexual abuse against a 10-year-old student and sentenced to 10 years RI, a fine, and compensation. He appealed on grounds of evidential inconsistencies, misdirection, and burden of proof. The Court of Appeal, after analyzing the victim's testimony, medical evidence, and legal arguments, found the conviction sound, the victim credible, and no prejudicial error. The appeal was dismissed, and the High Court sentence upheld.
defence_counsel: Shanaka Ranasinghe,PC with Niroshan Mihidukulasuriya and V. Abeysooriya
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court carefully considered the evidence, found the victim's testimony convincing and cogent, and convicted on one count. The COA agreed with this analysis, finding the HC had properly evaluated the evidence and applied the correct legal standards, with any minor error being non-prejudicial.
precedents_cited_list: Gamini Dolawatte V. Attorney General [1988] 1 Sri. L. R 221 | Bhargavan v. State of Kerala AIR 2004 SC 1058 (Supreme Court of India)
standard_of_review_applied: Appellate jurisdiction for correction of errors in fact or in law, considering whether errors prejudiced substantial rights or occasioned a failure of justice under Article 138 of the Constitution.

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Sections 54(A)(b) and 54(A)(d) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance as amended by Act No.13 of 1984
brief_facts_summary: The appellant, a Jail Guard, was arrested on 25 May 2013 at Bogambara Prison after a jailor suspected him and found a cellophane bag with packets believed to be heroin in his possession. The police were informed, and PW1 took custody of the appellant and the alleged drugs. The recovered substances were initially weighed as 11 grams. The appellant was later tried and convicted in the High Court of Kandy for trafficking and possession of heroin.
evidence_type_secondary: Police testimony, Government Analyst Report, Prison official testimony
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Sections 54(A)(b) and 54(A)(d) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance as amended by Act No.13 of 1984
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court Judge found the appellant guilty on both counts of trafficking and possession of 2.80 grams of heroin and imposed a sentence of life imprisonment on each count. The judgment was delivered on 07 June 2023.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant argued that the High Court Judge failed to consider inconsistencies in prosecution evidence and a vital discrepancy regarding the quantity of heroin recovered. The judgment was also challenged as lacking proper reasoning and basic legal principles.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The learned High Court Judge erred in law by failing to consider the inconsistencies of evidence presented by the prosecution. | The learned High Court Judge erred in law by failing to consider the vital discrepancy with regard to the quantity of Heroin recovered from the Appellant. | The judgment of the learned High Court Judge is void of any reasoning and lack basic principle of law.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal identified serious contradictions between prosecution witnesses, particularly regarding where and when the alleged drugs were weighed, and regarding the custody of the appellant after arrest. These contradictions, along with a significant weight discrepancy, cast doubt on the integrity of the prosecution's evidence chain.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court found serious contradictions and a broken chain of custody created reasonable doubt, meaning the prosecution failed to prove the case beyond reasonable doubt.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty. He gave a dock statement denying possession of any drugs and claimed he was never shown any parcel allegedly recovered from him, nor was anything sealed or weighed in his presence. The court found his version was supported by the identified contradictions in the prosecution case.
legal_errors_description: The High Court Judge erred by failing to consider material inconsistencies in prosecution evidence and a vital discrepancy in the quantity of drugs, and by delivering a judgment lacking proper reasoning.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed serious contradictions in prosecution evidence: PW1 testified the drugs were weighed at the prison, but his B Report said they were weighed at a welfare shop, and PW10 confirmed they were not weighed in prison. There was also a contradiction between PW1 and PW2 regarding the appellant's movements after arrest. A significant weight discrepancy existed (11 grams initially vs. 12.84 grams in the Analyst Report), which the prosecution could not explain. The chain of custody was compromised as PW1 stored the drugs in his personal locker. Citing Woolmington v. DPP and Mohamed Nimnaz, the Court held the prosecution failed to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt due to these flaws, which undermined the evidence's reliability.
coa_sentence_type: Acquitted; conviction and sentence set aside
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused-appellant, a jail guard, was convicted by the High Court of Kandy for trafficking and possession of 2.80 grams of heroin and sentenced to life imprisonment. He appealed, arguing inconsistencies in prosecution evidence and a discrepancy in the weight of the recovered drugs. The Court of Appeal found serious contradictions among prosecution witnesses regarding the weighing and custody of the drugs, and a broken chain of custody. The prosecution could not explain a significant weight difference. The Court held the prosecution failed to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt, set aside the conviction and sentence, and acquitted the appellant.
defence_counsel: Amila Palliyage with Sandeepani Wijesooriya, Savani Udugampola, Lakitha Wakishta Arachchi and Subaj De Silva
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court Judge convicted the appellant based on the prosecution evidence. The Court of Appeal found the HC judgment failed to properly analyze or even acknowledge the material contradictions in the prosecution evidence and the chain of custody issues, which rendered the conviction unsafe.
precedents_cited_list: Woolmington v. DPP [1935] A.C.462 | Mohamed Nimnaz V. Attorney General CA/95/94 | Perera V. Attorney General [1998] 1 Sri.L.R | Koushappis v. The State of WA [2007] WASCA 26; (2007) 168 A Crim R 51
standard_of_review_applied: Appeal based on errors of law and fact, reviewing whether the prosecution proved its case beyond reasonable doubt.

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: section 34(1)(a) and/or section 34(1)(b) of the National Authority on Tobacco and Alcohol Act No. 27 of 2006 as amended by the Amendment Act No. 3 of 2015
brief_facts_summary: The petitioner (2nd accused-petitioner-petitioner, D.S. Gunasekara (Pvt) Ltd) was charged along with Ceylon Tobacco Company PLC before the Magistrate's Court for failing to display required pictorial warnings on large cardboard boxes used to transport cigarette packets, as per the NATA Act. The prosecution was initiated by an Authorized Officer/Public Health Inspector. The accused argued the Act did not require warnings on such boxes, leading to a prior writ application to the Court of Appeal, which clarified the requirement. After the Court of Appeal judgment, the accused complied by adding the warnings.
evidence_type_primary: Physical evidence (cardboard boxes without pictorial warnings)
evidence_type_secondary: Testimony of Authorized Officer/Public Health Inspector
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court Judge dismissed the revision application, holding the Magistrate was correct in refusing to allow withdrawal of charges under Section 189 of the Code of Criminal Procedure Act. The Court found the accused failed to establish sufficient exceptional circumstances for judicial intervention.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The petitioner argued the Magistrate failed to appreciate the special circumstances: the offence arose from a genuine ambiguity in interpreting the NATA Act (difference between official Sinhala text and English translation), and the accused took immediate corrective steps after the Court of Appeal clarified the law. They also contended the Attorney General properly exercised prosecutorial discretion to withdraw charges.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Magistrate failed to appreciate special circumstances and ambiguity in the Act | High Court Judge should have intervened to set aside Magistrate's order refusing withdrawal | Attorney General correctly exercised prosecutorial discretion to withdraw charges
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The primary evidence was the testimony of the Public Health Inspector (PW-01) who conducted the raid and seized the boxes. He admitted the accused's initial legal interpretation and confirmed corrective action after the Court of Appeal judgment. The Court accepted the offence stemmed from a legal misinterpretation, not intentional violation.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court found the accused acted under a genuine misapprehension of law due to ambiguity between Sinhala and English texts of the Act, not with criminal intent.
defence_version_summary: The accused pleaded not guilty, arguing no legal requirement for pictorial warnings on large transport boxes. They filed a writ application challenging the charges. After the Court of Appeal clarified the law, they immediately complied. The Court accepted their actions were based on a legal misinterpretation.
legal_errors_description: The Magistrate erred in refusing to allow withdrawal of charges under Section 189 CrPC by not properly considering the Attorney General's prosecutorial discretion, the technical/ambiguous nature of the offence, and the accused's post-judgment compliance.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal held the revisionary jurisdiction should be exercised due to exceptional circumstances. It found the offence was highly technical, arising from ambiguity in the Act's translation. The Attorney General properly exercised discretion to withdraw charges after the accused complied post-interpretation. The Magistrate and High Court failed to consider these special circumstances rationally. The Court set aside the lower courts' orders, allowed withdrawal of charges, and acquitted the accused.
coa_sentence_type: Acquittal, charges withdrawn
brief_judgment_file_summary: D.S. Gunasekara (Pvt) Ltd (petitioner) and Ceylon Tobacco Company PLC were charged for not displaying pictorial warnings on cigarette transport boxes under the NATA Act. The Magistrate and High Court refused the prosecution's application to withdraw charges. The Court of Appeal, in revision, found exceptional circumstances: the offence stemmed from legal ambiguity, the accused complied after a clarifying judgment, and the Attorney General properly exercised prosecutorial discretion. The Court allowed the revision, set aside the lower courts' orders, permitted withdrawal of charges, and acquitted the accused.
prosecution_counsel: Maheshika Silva, D.S.G. for the 2nd Respondent; Hon. Attorney General represented
defence_counsel: Saliya Pieris, P.C. with Manoj Bandara, Hasitha Gamage and Chinthaka Kulathunga for the Petitioner
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court dismissed the revision application, agreeing with the Magistrate that no exceptional circumstances warranted intervention under Section 189 CrPC. The COA found this was an error, as the High Court should have considered the legal ambiguity, post-compliance, and prosecutorial discretion as sufficient grounds for withdrawal.
precedents_cited_list: Hotel Galaxy (Pvt) Ltd Vs. Mercantile Hotels Management Ltd (1987) 1 SLR 5 | Wijesinghe Vs. Thamararatnam (Sriskantha Law Report Volume IV page 47) | Vanik Incorporation Ltd Vs. Jayasekare (1997) 2 SLR 365 | Sadi Banda Vs. Officer In Charge of Norton Bridge Police Station (supra)
standard_of_review_applied: Revisionary jurisdiction exercised only in exceptional circumstances where a miscarriage of justice occurs or where circumstances 'shock the conscience of the Court'

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 34(1)(a) and/or section 34(1)(b) of the National Authority on Tobacco and Alcohol Act No. 27 of 2006 as amended by the Amendment Act No. 3 of 2015
offence_category: Violation of Tobacco and Alcohol Act
brief_facts_summary: The petitioners (Ceylon Tobacco Company PLC and D.S. Gunasekara (Pvt) Ltd) were charged for failing to display required pictorial warnings on large cardboard boxes used to transport cigarette packets, as required by the NATA Act. They initially argued that the Act did not require warnings on such boxes, relying on the English translation. The Court of Appeal, after examining the official Sinhala version, clarified that warnings were required. After that judgment, the petitioners complied by adding the warnings.
evidence_type_primary: Physical evidence (large cardboard boxes without pictorial warnings)
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 34(1)(a) and/or section 34(1)(b) of the National Authority on Tobacco and Alcohol Act No. 27 of 2006 as amended by the Amendment Act No. 3 of 2015
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court dismissed the revision application, agreeing with the Magistrate that the prosecution's application to withdraw charges under section 189 of the Criminal Procedure Code should not be allowed. The High Court held that the Magistrate was correct and that no sufficient exceptional circumstances existed for intervention.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The petitioners argued the Magistrate failed to appreciate the special circumstances: the ambiguity in the NATA Act's language (Sinhala vs. English) that led to the violation, their immediate compliance after the Court of Appeal's clarification, and the Attorney General's proper use of prosecutorial discretion to withdraw charges. They claimed both the Magistrate and High Court Judge erred in not allowing the withdrawal.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Magistrate failed to appreciate special circumstances and ambiguity in law | High Court Judge should have intervened to set aside Magistrate's order refusing withdrawal | Attorney General properly exercised prosecutorial discretion to withdraw charges | Sufficient exceptional circumstances exist for revisionary jurisdiction
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The complainant (Authorized Officer and Public Health Inspector) testified about the raid and seizure of cardboard boxes without pictorial warnings. He admitted the petitioners' initial contention was based on a misinterpretation of the Act. After the Court of Appeal judgment, the petitioners complied.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court found the petitioners acted due to a misinterpretation of law, not intentional violation, and immediately corrected the error after legal clarity.
defence_version_summary: Petitioners pleaded not guilty. Their defence was that the NATA Act, based on its English translation, did not require pictorial warnings on large cardboard boxes. They argued the violation was unintentional and based on legal ambiguity, not criminal intent.
legal_errors_description: The Magistrate and High Court failed to properly consider the Attorney General's prosecutorial discretion and the exceptional circumstances (legal ambiguity, immediate compliance) when refusing the withdrawal of charges under section 189 CrPC.
procedural_defects_description: Magistrate's refusal to allow withdrawal of charges despite the Attorney General's request and the existence of sufficient grounds under section 189 CrPC.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal held that the petitioners established sufficient exceptional circumstances for revisionary intervention. It found the Magistrate should have permitted the withdrawal under section 189 CrPC, given the legal ambiguity in the NATA Act (Sinhala vs. English texts), the petitioners' immediate compliance after the Court of Appeal's clarification, and the Attorney General's proper exercise of prosecutorial discretion. The Court emphasized revision is discretionary and granted only in exceptional circumstances, which were present here due to the technical nature of the offence and lack of criminal intent.
coa_sentence_type: Acquittal and withdrawal of charges allowed
brief_judgment_file_summary: The petitioners were charged for not displaying pictorial warnings on cigarette transport boxes under the NATA Act. They argued the requirement was ambiguous due to differences between the Sinhala and English texts. After the Court of Appeal clarified the law, they complied. The Attorney General sought to withdraw charges under section 189 CrPC, but the Magistrate and High Court refused. The Court of Appeal allowed the revision, finding exceptional circumstances existed: legal ambiguity, immediate compliance, and proper prosecutorial discretion. It set aside the lower court orders, allowed withdrawal of charges, and acquitted the petitioners.
defence_counsel: Saliya Pieris, P.C. with Manoj Bandara, Hasitha Gamage and Chinthaka Kulathunga
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court dismissed the revision, agreeing with the Magistrate that no sufficient exceptional circumstances existed to allow withdrawal. The COA found the High Court erred in not recognizing the legal ambiguity, the petitioners' compliance, and the Attorney General's proper discretion as exceptional circumstances warranting intervention.
precedents_cited_list: Hotel Galaxy (Pvt) Ltd Vs. Mercantile Hotels Management Ltd (1987) 1 SLR 5 | Wijesinghe Vs. Thamararatnam (Sriskantha Law Report Volume IV page 47) | Vanik Incorporation Ltd Vs. Jayasekare (1997) 2 SLR 365 | Sadi Banda Vs. Officer In Charge of Norton Bridge Police Station (supra)

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 140, Section 296 read with Section 146, Section 316 read with Section 146, Section 410 read with Section 146 of the Penal Code; Section 296 read with Section 32, Section 316 read with Section 32, Section 410 read with Section 32 of the Penal Code
offence_category: Murder, Unlawful Assembly, Grievous Hurt, Mischief
brief_facts_summary: On 15-06-2012 around 7:00 p.m., a JVP political meeting in Katuwana was attacked by a group arriving on motorbikes. A tall person armed with a T-56 weapon fired indiscriminately, resulting in two deaths and one grievous injury. The appellant was identified by eyewitnesses at the scene and at an identification parade. The appellant later surrendered to court. Evidence linked him to a mobile phone lost by the chief guest and a T-56 weapon hidden at a relative's house, which was recovered by police and matched to spent cartridges from the scene.
evidence_type_primary: Eyewitness testimony, Physical evidence (weapon, mobile phone)
evidence_type_secondary: Government Analyst Report (ballistics), Identification parade evidence
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 140, Section 296 read with Section 146, Section 316 read with Section 146, Section 410 read with Section 146 of the Penal Code; Section 296 read with Section 32, Section 316 read with Section 32, Section 410 read with Section 32 of the Penal Code
hc_sentence_type: Death (counts 2, 3, 6, 7); Rigorous Imprisonment 6 months (count 1), 7 years (count 4), 2 years (count 5), 7 years (count 8), 2 years (count 9); Fines with default sentences; Compensation ordered
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court found the appellant guilty on all nine counts after trial without a jury. The judge sentenced him to death on four murder counts, imposed various terms of rigorous imprisonment, fines, and compensation. The court accepted the eyewitness identifications and circumstantial evidence linking the appellant to the weapon and stolen mobile phone.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant challenged his conviction primarily on two grounds: (1) The High Court Judge failed to properly evaluate the identification of the accused, criticizing the conduct of the identification parade and the reliability of witness identification. (2) The High Court Judge rejected defence evidence without proper evaluation, including the appellant's alibi and witness testimony.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The learned High Court Judge has failed to properly evaluate the identity of the accused-appellant. | The learned High Court Judge has rejected the defence evidence without a proper evaluation.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the eyewitness identification credible. Witnesses observed the appellant in good light, he made no attempt to conceal his identity, and he remained at the scene for about 30 minutes. The identification parade was properly conducted. Circumstantial evidence, including recovery of the murder weapon and the victim's mobile phone from the appellant's relative, strongly corroborated the eyewitness accounts.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal held the prosecution proved its case beyond reasonable doubt. The combination of positive eyewitness identification, recovery of the weapon and stolen phone, and the appellant's failure to provide a credible explanation for the incriminating circumstantial evidence left no reasonable doubt.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty and gave sworn evidence. His defence was an alibi: he claimed he was at another location (Middeniya and Thanamalwila) at the time of the incident. He called two defence witnesses, including Ramani Ishwarage. The High Court and Court of Appeal rejected the defence as not creating a reasonable doubt or offering a credible explanation for the strong prosecution evidence.
legal_errors_description: The Court of Appeal found a sentencing error. The High Court sentenced the appellant separately on counts 1-5 (based on common object/unlawful assembly) and counts 6-9 (based on common intention under Section 32). The COA held counts 6-9 should have been treated as alternative counts to 1-5. Sentencing on both sets for the same acts amounted to sentencing the appellant twice for the same offence.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal against conviction. It thoroughly analyzed the identification evidence, finding the parade was properly conducted and witness identification was reliable given good lighting, prolonged observation, and the appellant's lack of disguise. It affirmed the High Court's evaluation of evidence, including the compelling circumstantial evidence of the recovered T-56 weapon (matched to the crime) and mobile phone (stolen from the victim). The court referenced the Turnbull guidelines and Sigera v AG but found they were not applicable as identification conditions were favorable. It held the prosecution proved its case beyond reasonable doubt. On sentencing, the COA found a misdirection: sentencing on both sets of counts (1-5 and 6-9) for the same transaction was improper. It set aside the sentences on counts 6-9 but affirmed the sentences on counts 1-5, including the death sentences on counts 2 and 3.
coa_sentence_type: Death (counts 2, 3); Rigorous Imprisonment 6 months (count 1), 7 years (count 4), 2 years (count 5); Fines with default sentences; Compensation ordered. Sentences on counts 6, 7, 8, 9 set aside.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused-appellant was convicted by the Tangalle High Court for murder, unlawful assembly, grievous hurt, and mischief arising from an armed attack on a political meeting in 2012, resulting in two deaths. He was sentenced to death on four counts and imprisonment on others. He appealed to the Court of Appeal, challenging his identification and the rejection of his defence evidence. The COA dismissed the appeal against conviction, upholding the reliability of eyewitness and circumstantial evidence. However, it partly allowed the appeal against sentence, finding that the High Court erred by sentencing him separately on two sets of charges for the same transaction. The COA set aside the sentences on four counts but affirmed the remaining sentences, including the death penalty.
defence_counsel: U.R. de Silva, P.C. with Savithri Fernando
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted the appellant based on eyewitness identification and circumstantial evidence. The Court of Appeal agreed with the HC's analysis of the evidence and its conclusion of guilt. However, the COA identified a legal error in the HC's sentencing approach, specifically the failure to treat certain counts as alternatives, leading to double punishment for the same acts.
precedents_cited_list: Regina Vs. Turnbull and Another (1977) QB 224 | Sigera Vs. The Attorney General (2011) 1 SLR 201 | SC Appeal No. 99/2007 decided on 30.07.2009 | Sumanasena Vs. The Attorney General (1999) 3 SLR 137 | Rex Vs. Lord Cochrane and others (1814) Gurneys Reports 479 | Rex Vs. Burdett (1820) B & Ald 161
standard_of_review_applied: The Court of Appeal reviewed whether the High Court properly evaluated the evidence, applied correct legal principles, and reached a verdict sustainable on the evidence. It examined identification evidence with reference to Turnbull guidelines and assessed if guilt was proved beyond reasonable doubt.
sentencing_principles_applied: The Court discussed the principle against double punishment for the same offence. It held that when charges are based on the same transaction but formulated under different legal provisions (common object vs. common intention), sentences should be imposed on alternative counts, not cumulatively.

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 364(2)(g) of the Penal Code as amended by the Penal Code (Amendment) Act No-22 of 1995, 29 of 1998 and 16 of 2006
brief_facts_summary: The prosecutrix, an 18-year-old female, was allegedly forced into a three-wheeler by two men (the appellant and another) while walking home from church on 29-05-2011. She claims they covered her face, she lost consciousness, and awoke in a jungle where she was raped by both men. The accused were arrested soon after near the scene in a matching three-wheeler. The appellant's defence was that he knew the prosecutrix from school, she and the 2nd accused had an affair, and they all went together voluntarily; he claimed the rape allegation arose from a dispute over a stolen chain.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 364(2)(g) of the Penal Code as amended by the Penal Code (Amendment) Act No-22 of 1995, 29 of 1998 and 16 of 2006
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the appellant of gang rape (Count 1) and sentenced him to 10 years rigorous imprisonment, a Rs. 5000 fine, and compensation of Rs. 500,000 to the prosecutrix. The conviction was based on the evidence of the prosecutrix and medical corroboration.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant's counsel argued that no identification parade was held causing prejudice, the High Court wrongly rejected the defence version, and the prosecutrix's version was improbable. The focus was on lack of corroboration, inconsistencies in the evidence, and procedural fairness.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: No identification parade was held, which caused prejudice towards the appellant. | The learned High Court Judge has rejected the defence version of events on a wrong premise. | The version of the prosecutrix does not favour the test of probability.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found inconsistencies between the prosecutrix's court testimony and her initial history to the JMO, and noted a lack of sufficient corroboration from other prosecution witnesses regarding how the incident was reported. The defence evidence, while not contradicted, was not given equal weight by the High Court.
probability_assessment_by_court: The COA found the prosecutrix's version improbable given inconsistencies, lack of corroboration, and the unusual behavior of the accused traveling back with her. It concluded the prosecution failed to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty, gave sworn evidence, and called no other witnesses. He claimed the prosecutrix was known to him, they met voluntarily, and the rape allegation was false, arising from a dispute over a stolen chain. The COA noted the High Court did not give equal weight to his evidence.
legal_errors_description: The High Court failed to properly assess the need for corroboration of the prosecutrix's testimony given inconsistencies and improbabilities, and relied on weaknesses of the defence rather than establishing the prosecution case beyond reasonable doubt.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed the evidence holistically, noting significant inconsistencies in the prosecutrix's account (e.g., church vs. work, one vs. two rapists), the improbability of the accused returning her in the same vehicle, and lack of corroborative witness alignment. It cited precedents on the need for careful scrutiny of uncorroborated sexual assault testimony and the principle that a conviction cannot be based on defence weaknesses. The COA found the prosecution evidence not cogent or probable enough to establish guilt beyond reasonable doubt.
coa_sentence_type: Acquitted, conviction and sentence set aside
brief_judgment_file_summary: The 1st accused-appellant appealed his High Court conviction and sentence for gang rape. The High Court of Vavuniya had sentenced him to 10 years RI, a Rs. 5000 fine, and Rs. 500,000 compensation. Appeal grounds included lack of identification parade, wrongful rejection of defence, and improbability of the prosecutrix's version. The Court of Appeal found material inconsistencies in the prosecutrix's evidence, insufficient corroboration, and that the High Court erred by not requiring stronger proof. It allowed the appeal, set aside the conviction and sentence, and acquitted the appellant.
defence_counsel: K. Kugaraja
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted based on the prosecutrix's testimony and medical evidence. The COA found the HC failed to properly weigh inconsistencies, require corroboration where needed, and erroneously bolstered a weak prosecution case by referencing defence weaknesses.
precedents_cited_list: Wanasingle Vs. The Attorney General and Another (2011) 1 SLR 01 | James Silva Vs. The Republic of Sri Lanka (1980) 2 SLR 167 | Jayasena Vs. The Queen 72 NLR 313 (PC) | Kamal Addararachchi Vs. The State (2000) 3 SLR 393 | Narender Kumar Vs. State of Delhi (NCT of Delhi), AIR 2012 SC 2281
standard_of_review_applied: Holistic assessment of all evidence to determine if prosecution proved guilt beyond reasonable doubt, with particular scrutiny for uncorroborated sexual assault testimony.

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 365B 2 (b) of the Penal Code amended by Act No. 22 of 1995 and Act No 29 of 1998 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The victim was a 13-year-old male child who had entered into priesthood and was attached to the Sri Subhodarama Privena in Mahawanawella under the care of the accused, the Chief Priest. The indictment alleged three counts of Grave Sexual Abuse, committed by inserting the accused's penis into the victim's mouth within a specified period. The victim was diagnosed as depressed due to continuous sexual abuse. A preliminary objection regarding the time frame in the indictment was raised at the Pre-Trial Conference.
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court Judge discharged the accused from the 2nd and 3rd charges in the indictment at the Pre-Trial stage. The Judge also directed the prosecution to amend the 1st charge by including a specific date of offence, upholding the defence's preliminary objection that the lack of specific dates affected the accused's ability to raise an alibi defence.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The petitioner (Attorney General) argued the High Court Judge erred in law by failing to consider that specifying a period in the indictment is legally permissible under the Code of Criminal Procedure and relevant case law. The judge misdirected himself by discharging counts at the pre-trial stage, depriving the victim of a fair trial, and by wrongly interpreting the concept of fair trial and the purpose of a Pre-Trial Conference.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The Learned High Court Judge has erred in law by failing to consider that the period specified in the indictment is in compliance with sections 165, 166 and 174 of the Code of Criminal Procedure Act No 15 of 1979 as amended and with the decided case law of the appellate courts of Sri Lanka. | The Learned High Court Judge has misdirected himself in law by discharging the Accused-Respondent from counts 2 and 3 at the pre-trial stage depriving the victim of a fair trial. | The Learned High Court Judge erred in law by entertaining an erroneous interpretation of the concept of fair trial by arriving at the conclusion that unless an exact date is specified in a case of child abuse, a child victim is not even entitled to have the case taken up for trial. | The Learned High Court Judge erred in law by failing to consider that his decision to discharge the Accused Respondent at a Pre Trial Conference deprived the opportunity for the prosecution to act in terms of section 167 of the Code of Criminal Procedure Act No. 15 of 1979 based on the evidence of Prosecution witnesses. | The decision of the Learned Trial Judge to discharge the Accused Respondent from counts 2 and 3 of the indictment prior to consideration of any evidence of the Prosecution was, premature, unlawful, arbitrary, unreasonable, and capricious. | The Learned High Court Judge misdirected himself on the purpose of a Pre- Trial conference as well as on the nature & extent of powers conferred on the High Court Judge at a Pre-Trial conference by directing the Prosecution to amend the 1st charge by inserting a specific date of offence.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal did not evaluate the evidence on its merits, as the appeal was on a revision application concerning a pre-trial order. The analysis focused on the legality of the High Court's procedural decision.
probability_assessment_by_court: No assessment of reasonable doubt was made at this procedural stage.
defence_version_summary: The accused pleaded not guilty. The defence raised a preliminary objection regarding the time frame in the indictment at the Pre-Trial Conference, arguing it prejudiced the accused's ability to raise an alibi. The accused had not raised an alibi defence during the investigation stage.
legal_errors_description: The High Court Judge erred in law by holding that an exact date must be specified in the indictment, failing to consider that specifying a period is legally sufficient under Sections 165 and 166 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The Judge also erred by entertaining an alibi defence as a preliminary objection at the pre-trial stage, contrary to Section 126A which governs when such a defence can be raised.
procedural_defects_description: The High Court Judge exceeded the powers conferred at a Pre-Trial Conference by directing the prosecution to amend the indictment and by discharging the accused from counts 2 and 3 prior to any evidence being led. This was a premature intervention into prosecutorial discretion.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal held that the High Court Judge misdirected himself on the law. Citing Sections 165 and 166 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and relevant precedents, the COA found that specifying a period, not an exact date, in a charge is legally permissible if it gives the accused reasonable notice. The Judge also erred in considering an alibi defence at the pre-trial stage, as Section 126A provides a specific procedure for raising it, which can only be invoked during the trial proper. The COA concluded the Judge's orders were a clear misdirection, exceeding his powers at the Pre-Trial Conference and improperly curtailing the prosecution's case.
coa_sentence_type: Order of High Court set aside. Case remitted to High Court to proceed with trial on original indictment.
brief_judgment_file_summary: This was a revision application by the Attorney General challenging a High Court of Ampara order. The High Court Judge had discharged the accused (a Buddhist monk) from two counts of Grave Sexual Abuse against a child and directed amendment of the remaining charge to specify a date. The Court of Appeal allowed the revision, finding the High Court Judge erred in law by holding an exact date was required in the indictment and by prematurely considering an alibi defence at the pre-trial stage. The COA set aside the High Court order and directed the trial to proceed on the original three-count indictment.
defence_counsel: Nalin Laduwahetty, PC with Ranjith Samarasekera
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court Judge upheld the defence's preliminary objection that the lack of specific dates in the charges prejudiced the accused's right to a fair trial, particularly the ability to raise an alibi. The COA found this reasoning erroneous, as the law does not mandate exact dates and alibi defences have a specific procedural framework not applicable at the pre-trial stage.
precedents_cited_list: Director General of Commission to Investigate Allegation of Bribery or Corruption v. Punchi Banda and another CA (PHC) APN No. 142/2014 decided on 12.09.2017 | M.G.Premadasa v. The Attorney General CA 261/2009 decided on 26.05.2014 | R v Dossi 13 Cr.App.R.158
standard_of_review_applied: Revision under Article 138 of the Constitution, reviewing the legality and correctness of the High Court's pre-trial order.

judges: Sampath B. Abeykoon, J. | Amal Ranaraja, J.
offence_sections: Section 354 of the Penal Code (Kidnapping); Section 365(B)(2)(b) of the Penal Code as Amended by Act No. 22 of 1995 and Act No. 29 of 1998 and Act No. 16 of 2006 (Grave Sexual Abuse)
brief_facts_summary: The accused-appellant was a frequent visitor to the victim's (PW1) home. He would take PW1's toys and hide them in a wooded area, then take PW1 there on the pretext of searching for them. In the wooded area, the appellant undressed himself and PW1, laid PW1 on the ground, and placed his penis between PW1's thighs, committing sexual acts on multiple occasions when PW1 was less than 16 years old. The victim could not recall the exact dates.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 354 of the Penal Code; Section 365(B)(2)(b) of the Penal Code
hc_sentence_type: 1 year rigorous imprisonment for Count 1; 7 years rigorous imprisonment for Count 2; Fines imposed with default simple imprisonment terms
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the accused-appellant upon his guilty plea to both charges of kidnapping and grave sexual abuse. He was sentenced to one year's rigorous imprisonment for kidnapping and the minimum mandatory sentence of seven years' rigorous imprisonment for grave sexual abuse. Fines and default prison terms were also imposed.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant appealed only against the sentence. Counsel argued the High Court Judge had discretion to impose a non-custodial sentence under Section 306 of the Code of Criminal Procedure Act. Counsel also argued the Judge should have considered the appellant's age, educational background, and other extenuating circumstances, and the long delay in concluding the case as mitigating factors.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: High Court Judge had discretion to impose a non-custodial sentence under Section 306 of the Criminal Procedure Code. | Judge failed to consider appellant's age, educational background, and other extenuating circumstances as grounds for a non-custodial sentence. | Delay in concluding the case kept the appellant in suspense and should be a mitigating factor.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The prosecution case relied primarily on the victim's (PW1) testimony regarding the sexual abuse and kidnapping. The Court of Appeal noted the appellant's actions involved pre-planning and manipulation.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded guilty to both charges in the High Court. The appeal was based solely on the sentence, not the conviction.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal rejected the argument that Section 306 of the Criminal Procedure Code (discharge with a warning) applied, citing precedent that it is only for Magistrate's Courts. The Court found significant aggravating circumstances: the appellant was a repeat offender for similar crimes, the offence involved pre-planning and manipulation of a 9-year-old child, and the second charge carried a mandatory minimum sentence. The delay in the case was not considered a sufficient mitigating factor to reduce the lawful sentence imposed by the High Court.
coa_sentence_type: 1 year rigorous imprisonment for Count 1; 7 years rigorous imprisonment for Count 2; Fines of Rs.1500 and Rs.5000 with default simple imprisonment terms of 3 months and 6 months respectively. Sentences to run concurrently with existing sentence from case no. 107/2017.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused-appellant pleaded guilty in the Badulla High Court to kidnapping and grave sexual abuse of a minor under 16 years. He was sentenced to 1 and 7 years rigorous imprisonment plus fines. He appealed only against the sentence, arguing for a non-custodial sentence based on discretion, personal circumstances, and trial delay. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal, finding Section 306 inapplicable to High Court cases, noting aggravating factors including prior similar convictions, pre-planning, and the mandatory minimum sentence for grave sexual abuse. The High Court's sentence was upheld.
defence_counsel: Ariyapala T. Hewage
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted based on a guilty plea and imposed the statutory minimum sentence for grave sexual abuse. The Court of Appeal found no error in the High Court's sentencing decision, agreeing that the serious nature of the offence and the presence of aggravating factors warranted the custodial sentence.
precedents_cited_list: Attorney General vs. Ranasinghe and Others [1993] 2 SLR 81 | Attorney General vs. Mendis [1995] 1 SLR 138
standard_of_review_applied: Appellate review of sentencing discretion and applicability of legal provisions.
sentencing_principles_applied: Consideration of aggravating and mitigating circumstances, mandatory minimum sentences, public interest vs. offender reformation, and precedent on sentencing for serious planned crimes.

judges: Menaka Wijesundera J. | K.M.G.H Kulatunga J.
brief_facts_summary: The accused-appellant was charged with the rape of a girl under 16 years. The prosecution case was that the victim, then 14, was alone at home when the appellant, a neighbor she called 'kiri atta,' called her to his house, showed her a knife, and raped her. The victim's testimony contained significant contradictions regarding the number of times the incident occurred and her enjoyment of a subsequent act. The incident was allegedly witnessed by two boys, whose accounts also differed. The prosecution also presented evidence from the victim's sister and a Judicial Medical Officer.
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court judge found the appellant guilty of rape. The judge reproduced the relevant penal section and analyzed how a criminal case should be proved. The judge acknowledged contradictions and omissions in the victim's evidence but concluded they did not go to the root of the prosecution case. Notably, the judge delivering the judgment had not heard any of the witnesses at trial.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant's counsel argued that the High Court judge failed to properly consider the evidence of the victim (PW-01), which was inconsistent and vacillating. The second ground was that the judge placed an undue burden on the defence by requiring the appellant to prove his defence of being falsely implicated due to a monetary transaction.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: PW-01’s evidence has not been considered properly. | Defence has been given an undue responsibility.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the victim's (PW-01) evidence to be inconsistent, vacillating, and contradictory. She changed her account of how many times she was raped and admitted to lying in court. Other prosecution witnesses (a neighbor and the victim's sister) also gave contradictory evidence. The prosecution evidence was described as 'a ball of confusion.' The defence evidence, where the appellant claimed false implication over a monetary transaction, was not contradicted.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal held that the inconsistencies and contradictions in the prosecution evidence created a reasonable doubt regarding the credibility of the witness and the prosecution's story.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty. He testified that he was falsely implicated because of a monetary transaction with the victim's father. He was cross-examined but did not contradict his police statement. The court found he stood the test of cross-examination.
legal_errors_description: The High Court judge misdirected on the burden of proof by requiring the appellant to prove his defence (false implication due to monetary transaction), thereby shifting the burden from the prosecution and violating the presumption of innocence.
procedural_defects_description: The High Court judge who delivered the judgment had not heard any of the witnesses, which deprived the court of the advantage of observing witness demeanor, a critical factor given the inconsistencies in the evidence.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the prosecution evidence, particularly from the victim (PW-01), to be inconsistent, contradictory, and lacking credibility. It highlighted the procedural defect that the trial judge who wrote the judgment did not hear the witnesses, a critical shortcoming given the credibility issues. The COA also found a fundamental legal error where the High Court judge improperly placed the burden of proof on the appellant to prove his defence, violating the presumption of innocence. Citing precedents on the burden of proof and the importance of the trial judge observing witnesses, the COA held the appeal had merit.
coa_sentence_type: Conviction and sentence set aside.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused-appellant was convicted by the Matable High Court for the rape of a girl under 16. He appealed on grounds that the victim's evidence was not properly considered and an undue burden was placed on the defence. The Court of Appeal found the victim's testimony was inconsistent, contradictory, and she admitted to lying. The High Court judge who delivered the verdict had not heard the witnesses, a critical flaw. The COA also ruled the High Court erred by shifting the burden of proof to the appellant. The appeal was allowed, and the conviction and sentence were set aside, resulting in an acquittal.
defence_counsel: Ershan Ariaratnam
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court judge found the appellant guilty, acknowledging contradictions in the victim's evidence but concluding they were not fatal. The COA criticized this analysis, finding the inconsistencies went to the root of the case. The COA also criticized the judge for not hearing the witnesses and for misdirecting on the burden of proof.

standard_of_review_applied: The court reviewed the High Court's factual findings, emphasizing the disadvantage of an appellate court when the trial judge did not observe witness demeanor, and reviewed for errors of law, particularly regarding the burden of proof.

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 20(b)iv of the Bribery Act
brief_facts_summary: PW1 (Punchi Nona), a villager, requested the Appellant, a local politician and attorney, to secure a government job for her son-in-law (PW2). The Appellant solicited Rs. 50,000/- for the job. PW1 mortgaged her land to obtain the money and gave it to the Appellant on 26.12.2007. When the job was not secured, PW1 requested the money back. The Appellant issued a cheque which bounced. After partial repayment and a complaint to the Bribery Commission, the Appellant sent the remaining amount. The Appellant claimed the money was a donation for his political party office construction.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 20(b)iv of the Bribery Act
hc_sentence_type: For Count 1: 04 years rigorous imprisonment with a fine of Rs.5,000/- and default sentence of 01-month simple imprisonment. For Count 2: 04 years rigorous imprisonment with a fine of Rs.5,000/- and default sentence of 01-month simple imprisonment. Sentences to run concurrently.
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court Judge found the Appellant guilty on both counts of soliciting and accepting gratification. The prosecution proved the case beyond reasonable doubt. The sentences were imposed to run concurrently.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The Appellant argued the prosecution failed to prove the case beyond reasonable doubt, the evidence was insufficient, his evidence was not considered, the trial judge failed to evaluate evidence considering infirmities and contradictions, the failure to consider the date of offence reflected bias, and the judge who wrote the judgment failed to observe the demeanour of witnesses.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The prosecution has failed to prove the case beyond reasonable doubt. | The evidence led at the trial is insufficient to make an order of conviction. | The evidence of the Appellant had not been given any consideration. | The trial judge failed to evaluate the evidence taking into consideration the obvious infirmities and contradictions. | The failure to consider the date of commission of the offence reflects partial bias. | The judge who wrote the judgment failed to observe the demeanour and deportment of the witnesses.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal held the trial judge meticulously evaluated evidence and found prosecution witnesses consistent and probable. The credibility of witnesses was accepted.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court assessed the totality of evidence and found prosecution proved the case beyond reasonable doubt, with no reasonable doubt created.
defence_version_summary: The Appellant pleaded not guilty. He gave evidence, called five witnesses, and marked productions. His defence was that the money received was a donation for party office construction, not gratification. The court rejected this as implausible given PW1's financial circumstances and the purpose of the loan.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal reviewed the evidence and found the High Court Judge correctly applied the law. The prosecution proved solicitation and acceptance of gratification beyond reasonable doubt. The trial judge properly considered the evidence, including contradictions, and found prosecution witnesses credible. The defence argument regarding the date of offence was addressed under CPC Section 165. The change of judges did not prejudice the trial as Section 48 of the Judicature Act was complied with. The appeal grounds lacked merit.
coa_sentence_type: Conviction and sentence affirmed. For Count 1: 04 years rigorous imprisonment with a fine of Rs.5,000/- and default sentence of 01-month simple imprisonment. For Count 2: 04 years rigorous imprisonment with a fine of Rs.5,000/- and default sentence of 01-month simple imprisonment. Sentences to run concurrently.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The Accused-Appellant was convicted in the High Court of Colombo for soliciting and accepting a bribe of Rs. 50,000/- from PW1 to secure a government job for her son-in-law. He was sentenced to concurrent terms of rigorous imprisonment and fines. He appealed on grounds including insufficient evidence, procedural errors, and bias. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal, upholding the conviction and sentence, finding the prosecution proved the case beyond reasonable doubt and the trial was fair.
defence_counsel: Kalinga Indatissa, P.C., with A. Wasantha Akram, Ravindu Jayakody and Rashmini Indatissa
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court Judge considered evidence from both sides, found prosecution witnesses credible and consistent, and convicted the Appellant. The Court of Appeal found no error in this analysis.

Republic of Sri Lanka CA/307/2006 decided on 17/07/2013 | Case No.CA/HCC/0168/2015 decided on 24/02/2022
