judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 113B, 102 and 380 of the Penal Code read with section 44(a) of the Firearms Ordinance as amended by Firearms (Amendment) Act No. 22 of 1966. (Count 2: section 380 read with section 44(a))
location_of_offence: Narangoda, Bogala Pathala, within the jurisdiction of the High Court of Kegalle
brief_facts_summary: The office premises of Bogala Graphite Limited were robbed in the early hours of 24-03-2000. A group of robbers tied up security officers, removed an iron safe containing Rs. 1,900,000/- intended for worker salaries, and loaded it into the factory's jeep (31⏱-1183), which they also took, firing shots in the process. Investigations led police to a hotel (Madilanda Walawwa) where the iron safe (now empty) was recovered from a toilet pit, and a T-56 type firearm, hand grenade, and other weapons/ammunition were found. Money totaling Rs. 633,240/- was recovered from various accused. The appellant was the lessee and manager of the hotel.
evidence_type_secondary: Physical evidence (firearm, safe, jeep, money), Government Analyst Report, Fingerprint evidence
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 113B, 102 and 380 of the Penal Code read with section 44(a) of the Firearms Ordinance as amended by Firearms (Amendment) Act No. 22 of 1966. (Count 2: section 380 read with section 44(a))
hc_sentence_type: Life Imprisonment (on both Counts 1 and 2). Fine of Rs. 5000 on each count.
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the appellant (9th accused) based on his possession and control of the hotel where the weapons and looted safe were found, and the unchallenged evidence of PW-25 placing him at the hotel on the day of the incident, leaving at night and returning. The 1st to 8th accused were acquitted due to insufficient evidence.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant argued the High Court Judge wrongly rejected his alibi defence that he was in Anuradhapura on the day of the incident. He also argued the judge misdirected himself on circumstantial evidence by holding the productions were in the appellant's exclusive possession when evidence showed others were present at the hotel.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The learned High Court Judge has wrongly rejected the alibi taken up by the appellant. | The learned High Court Judge has misdirected himself on the circumstantial evidence in holding that the productions were in exclusive possession of the appellant since there was evidence that several other persons were also present in the premises.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The case relied heavily on the unchallenged evidence of PW-25, a painter at the hotel, who placed the appellant and others at the scene, described their movements on the night of the robbery, and detailed sounds heard upon their return. No eyewitnesses to the robbery could identify the perpetrators. Fingerprint evidence linked the 2nd accused to the stolen jeep. The Government Analyst linked spent cartridges from the crime scene to a weapon found at the hotel.
probability_assessment_by_court: Court analyzed if circumstantial evidence was consistent only with guilt and inconsistent with innocence, citing precedents like The King Vs. Abeywickrama, Don Sunny Vs. The Attorney General, and Karunaratne Vs. Attorney-General.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty and made a dock statement. He claimed he was in Anuradhapura fulfilling a vow on the day of the incident, not at the hotel. He stated he leased the hotel from a friend and visited only 2-3 days a week. The Court found the alibi defence failed as he did not comply with section 126A notice requirements and his mere statement did not exclude the possibility of participation.
legal_errors_description: The High Court Judge may have been misdirected in convicting the appellant solely on the basis of possession and control of the hotel. Also, the Judge misdirected by imposing separate life sentences for two counts arising from the same incident.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the prosecution proved the case against the appellant beyond reasonable doubt based on circumstantial evidence. It upheld the conviction, agreeing with the High Court that the appellant's alibi failed due to non-compliance with section 126A of the Code of Criminal Procedure and his failure to challenge PW-25's evidence. The Court held the circumstantial evidence, particularly PW-25's testimony and the recovery of weapons and the safe from the hotel under the appellant's control, pointed irresistibly to his guilt. However, the COA noted the HC Judge was misdirected in acquitting the other accused and in sentencing the appellant on both counts for the same incident. Applying the proviso to Article 138 of the Constitution and section 436 of the CCP, the COA found no substantial miscarriage of justice occurred in convicting the appellant.
coa_sentence_type: Life Imprisonment on Count 1 and a fine of Rs. 5000 (with 3 months simple imprisonment in default). The life imprisonment sentence on Count 2 is set aside.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The 9th accused-appellant was convicted by the Kegalle High Court for conspiring and committing an armed robbery at Bogala Graphite Limited, based on circumstantial evidence linking him to a hotel where stolen items and weapons were found, and the testimony of PW-25. He was sentenced to life imprisonment on two counts and fined. The 1st to 8th accused were acquitted. On appeal, the Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal against conviction, finding the circumstantial evidence overwhelming and the alibi defence invalid. However, the appeal against sentence was partly allowed, setting aside the life sentence on Count 2 as it was an alternative count for the same incident.
defence_counsel: Saliya Pieris, P.C. with Pasindu Thilakarathna and Nisal Hennadige
weapon_type: Firearm resembling a T-56 weapon, hand grenade
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted the appellant based on his control of the hotel and PW-25's evidence, but acquitted other accused due to insufficient evidence. The COA found the HC Judge misdirected in acquitting the others and in imposing separate sentences for two counts from the same transaction.
precedents_cited_list: The King Vs. Abeywickrama 44 NLR 254 | Don Sunny Vs. The Attorney General (1998) 2 SLR 01 | King Vs. Gunaratne 47 NLR 145 | Regina Vs. Exall (176 English Reports, Nisi Prius at page 853) | Karunaratne Vs. Attorney-General (2005) 2 SLR 233 | Krishantha de Silva Vs. The Attorney General (2003) 1 SLR 162 | Banda and Others Vs. The Attorney General (1999) 3 SLR 168 | Stirland Vs. D. P. P.- (1944) A.C. 315 | Lafeer Vs. Queen 74 NLR 246 | Rex Vs. Muller (1864) 60 C.C.C. Sess. Pap. 461 | Punchi Banda Vs. The State (1973) 76 NLR 293
standard_of_review_applied: Examined whether errors/irregularities occasioned a failure of justice or prejudiced substantial rights, applying the proviso to Article 138 of the Constitution and section 436 of the Code of Criminal Procedure Act.
sentencing_principles_applied: Principle that separate sentences should not be imposed for alternative counts arising from the same incident.

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 16(b) and Section 19(c) of the Bribery Act
brief_facts_summary: The Accused-Appellant, an Excise Guard, solicited and accepted bribes from PW-01 Premawathi (a boutique owner selling unlicensed White Beedi) to avoid prosecution for her illegal trade. He demanded Rs. 5,000 upfront and Rs. 1,000 monthly. A trap was set by the Bribery Commission (CIABOC) leading to his arrest while accepting the Rs. 5,000. The appellant also separately solicited bribes from PW-05 Lionel, a supplier of White Beedi, not to prosecute him for illegal manufacture.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 16(b) and Section 19(c) of the Bribery Act
hc_sentence_type: Rigorous Imprisonment 2 years each for 8 counts (served concurrently resulting in total 8 years), Fine of Rs. 3,000 for each of the 8 counts, and an additional fine of Rs. 5,000 under section 26 of the Bribery Act
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court found the appellant guilty on counts 1 to 7 and 9, and acquitted him on counts 8, 10, 11, and 12. He was sentenced to rigorous imprisonment and fines. The sentences for related counts were ordered to run concurrently, resulting in a total of 8 years rigorous imprisonment.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: Appellant challenged conviction on grounds of misjoinder of charges (counts 7-12 being a separate transaction), contradictions and falsehood in prosecution witness testimony, failure to correctly evaluate witness credibility, discrepancies in trap evidence, and failure to consider the defence case.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The indictment is contrary to law as the joinder of charges is contrary to section 174 and 175 of the Code of Criminal Procedure Act No. 15 of 1979. | It has been proven that Piyadasa (PW-02) and Lionel (PW-05) have deliberately uttered falsehood before the Court, therefore, their evidence cannot be relied upon. | The evidence of PW-01 Premawathi cannot be relied upon. | The evidence of PW-02 cannot be relied upon. | The learned High Court Judge has failed to correctly and independently evaluate the credibility of the evidence of PW-05 Lionel. | The evidence of PW-01 concerning the trap is contrary to the evidence of PW-03. | The learned High Court Judge while accepting that there is a discrepancy regarding the location where the trap took place, has failed to give the benefit of the doubt to the appellant. | The learned High Court Judge has failed to consider the defence case.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: Court of Appeal found prosecution witnesses (PW-01, PW-02, PW-05, decoy) credible. Minor discrepancies in their testimonies regarding location and sequence were deemed natural and not material. Their evidence was consistent on the core demand and acceptance of bribes.
probability_assessment_by_court: Court held that minor discrepancies in witness testimony did not create reasonable doubt. Evidence of demand and acceptance of bribe was clear and consistent on material points.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty. He made a lengthy dock statement denying all charges, claiming false implication due to his detection of illegal drugs on the complainants. He claimed the money was forcibly attempted to be put into his pocket during the raid. The defence called one witness (a Development Officer) regarding the location of a wine store. The court found the defence version unconvincing and lacking credibility.
legal_errors_description: Misjoinder of charges relating to counts 7-12, which pertained to a separate transaction involving PW-05 Lionel.
procedural_defects_description: Misjoinder of charges under the Code of Criminal Procedure Act.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The COA first addressed the legal issue of misjoinder. Relying on Lionel Vs. Officer-In-Charge, Meetiyagoda Police Station and section 436 of the CCP, it held the misjoinder of counts 7-12 was an irregularity curable as it caused no prejudice to the appellant regarding counts 1-6. The COA then comprehensively analyzed witness credibility, applying principles from Indian and Sri Lankan precedents (Bhoginbhai Hirjibhai Vs State of Gujarat, Attorney General Vs. Potta Naufar, Mahathun and Others Vs. The Attorney General, State of U.P. Vs. M. K. Anthony). It found the prosecution witnesses credible on material points, minor discrepancies were natural and did not create reasonable doubt. The COA affirmed the HC's rejection of the defence version and its evaluation of evidence. It found the conviction on counts 1-6 safe but set aside convictions on counts 7 and 9 due to misjoinder.
coa_sentence_type: Rigorous Imprisonment 2 years each for counts 1 to 6 (sentences for counts 1 & 3, 2 & 4, 5 & 6 to run concurrently), Fine of Rs. 3,000 for each of the 6 counts, and an additional fine of Rs. 5,000 under section 26 of the Bribery Act. Sentences to commence from date of pronouncement of COA judgment.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The Accused-Appellant, an Excise Guard, was convicted by the High Court of Colombo on multiple counts of soliciting and accepting bribes under the Bribery Act. He was sentenced to 8 years rigorous imprisonment and fines. He appealed, challenging the conviction on grounds including misjoinder of charges and witness credibility. The Court of Appeal found a misjoinder regarding counts 7-12 but held it was a curable irregularity that caused no prejudice to counts 1-6. After a thorough analysis of witness evidence and applying relevant precedents, the COA dismissed the appeal regarding counts 1-6, affirming the conviction and sentence. However, it allowed the appeal regarding counts 7 and 9, setting aside the conviction and sentence on those counts due to the misjoinder.
prosecution_counsel: Ruvini Wickramasinghe, Deputy Director General of CIABOC for the Respondent
defence_counsel: Kapila Waidyaratne, P.C. with Akkila Jayasundara and Akhila Mathishi for the Accused-Appellant
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court found the appellant guilty on counts 1-7 and 9 after evaluating witness credibility and rejecting the defence. The COA found the HC's analysis of evidence for counts 1-6 to be correct. However, the COA identified an error in the HC's joinder of charges for counts 7-12, which involved a separate transaction.
precedents_cited_list: Lionel Vs. Officer-In-Charge, Meetiyagoda Police Station (1987) 1 SLR 210 | Bhoginbhai Hirjibhai Vs State of Gujarat (AIR 1983-SC 753) | The Attorney General Vs. Potta Naufar and Others (Ambeptitya Murder Case) (2007) 2 SLR 144 | Mahathun and Others Vs. The Attorney General (2015) 1 SLR 74 | State of U.P. Vs. M. K. Anthony, AIR 1985 SC 48
standard_of_review_applied: The COA applied a standard of review that examines whether the trial judge's findings on witness credibility and facts are manifestly wrong, and whether any procedural errors occasioned a failure of justice.
sentencing_principles_applied: The COA did not alter the sentence for the affirmed counts, implicitly accepting the HC's sentencing approach. It applied section 436 of the CCP regarding curable irregularities.

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Sections 54(A)(d) and 54(A)(b) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance as amended by Act No. 13 of 1984
location_of_offence: Campbell Car Park at Borella, near the main gate of the Oval Play Ground
brief_facts_summary: On 08/01/2012, based on information, police officers including PW1 went to Campbell Car Park, Borella. They spotted a person matching the description given by the informant. Upon inquiry and body check, a parcel containing a brown substance was recovered from his right-side trouser pocket. The substance reacted positively for heroin, leading to his arrest. The gross weight was 24 grams, later sealed and handed over. The High Court convicted him for possession and trafficking.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Sections 54(A)(d) and 54(A)(b) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance as amended by Act No. 13 of 1984
hc_judgment_summary: The Learned Trial Judge found the Appellant guilty on the 1st count (Possession and Trafficking of 3.42 grams of Heroin) and sentenced him to life imprisonment on 07/11/2018. The Appellant was acquitted from the 2nd count. The Judge accepted the prosecution evidence, finding it credible and sufficient.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The Appellant argued that the trial judge failed to analyse improbabilities in the prosecution version and contradictions between prosecution witnesses, making the conviction unsafe. He also contended that the judge misdirected himself by not correctly analysing his dock statement in line with his defence.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: That the Learned Trial Judge failed to analyse the improbabilities of the prosecution version and thereby the conviction is unsafe. | That the Learned Trial Judge failed to analyse inter se and per se contradictions of the prosecution witnesses which creates a reasonable doubt on the prosecution case. | That the Learned Trial Judge misdirected himself by failing to correctly analyse the dock statement in line with the defence eversion.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the evidence of PW1 and PW2, the key witnesses, to be clear, cogent, and unambiguous. It concluded that their evidence passed the probability test and that no material contradictions undermined the prosecution case. The chain of custody and handling of evidence were properly explained and accepted.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal analyzed the time factor and circumstances of the raid, concluding the prosecution case passed the probability test without material contradictions. It affirmed the High Court's finding that the case was proven beyond reasonable doubt.
defence_version_summary: The Appellant pleaded not guilty. He made a dock statement claiming he was wrongly implicated. He alleged he was arrested while talking to a person named Chamara Srimal, and that the heroin recovered was from Srimal, not him. The court found his dock statement did not create any reasonable doubt against the overwhelming prosecution evidence.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal thoroughly examined the grounds of appeal. It found no merit in the claims of improbability or contradictions in the prosecution evidence, noting PW1 and PW2's evidence was clear and corroborated. It analyzed the time factor of the raid and the method of arrest, finding them credible and explained. It evaluated the Appellant's dock statement in light of the totality of evidence and concluded it created no reasonable doubt. The court affirmed the High Court's correct application of the burden of proof beyond reasonable doubt and its analysis of the evidence. The appeal was dismissed.
coa_sentence_type: Life Imprisonment
brief_judgment_file_summary: The Appellant was convicted in the High Court of Colombo for Possession and Trafficking of heroin and sentenced to life imprisonment. He appealed, challenging the conviction on grounds of improbabilities, witness contradictions, and misdirection regarding his dock statement. The Court of Appeal found the evidence of the key prosecution witnesses clear and credible, the prosecution case proven beyond reasonable doubt, and the Appellant's defence version insufficient to create a doubt. The appeal was dismissed, and the conviction and sentence were affirmed.
defence_counsel: Tenny Fernando with H. Silva
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court Judge analyzed the evidence, found the prosecution witnesses credible, and concluded the case was proven beyond reasonable doubt. The Court of Appeal reviewed this analysis and found no errors, agreeing with the High Court's reasoning and conclusions.
precedents_cited_list: Mohamed Nimnaz V. Attorney General CA/95/94 | Attorney-General v. Rawther 25 NLR 385 | Stirland v. Director of Public Prosecution [1944] AC (PC) 315 | Don Samantha Jude Anthony Jayamaha v. The Attorney General CA/303/2006 | Kathubdeen v. Republic of Sri Lanka [1998] 3 SLR 107
standard_of_review_applied: The court applied the standard of reviewing whether the High Court's verdict was reasonable based on the evidence and whether any legal misdirection occurred.
sentencing_principles_applied: The judgment does not discuss specific sentencing principles in detail beyond affirming the life sentence imposed by the High Court for the drug trafficking conviction.

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance as amended by Amendment Act No. 13 of 2004
brief_facts_summary: The accused-appellant was arrested on 01-02-2014 when a police vice-prevention team, while on patrol in Colombo, observed her behaving suspiciously on Locket Lane. Upon searching her, police recovered a pink cellophane bag containing a powder from the right pocket of her dress, which was later confirmed to be 4.73 grams of pure heroin. The police team subsequently searched her house, weighed the substance at a pawning center, and followed procedural steps to seal and submit the evidence.
evidence_type_secondary: Eyewitness testimony (police officers), Government Analyst Report
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance as amended by Amendment Act No. 13 of 2004
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court acquitted the appellant of trafficking (1st count) but found her guilty of possession of heroin (2nd count). After considering aggravating and mitigatory circumstances, the judge sentenced her to life imprisonment.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant's counsel argued that the High Court Judge failed to consider improbabilities in the prosecution evidence and failed to properly consider the appellant's dock statement in line with her defence version. The defence claimed the police were looking for another person (Lena Paba) and falsely implicated the appellant.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The learned High Court Judge failed to consider the improbabilities in the evidence adduced by the prosecution. | The learned High Court Judge failed to consider the dock statement of the appellant in line with the defence version of events.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the evidence of the police witnesses (PW-01 and PW-09) credible and consistent regarding the recovery of heroin from the appellant. Minor discrepancies in the evidence, such as the exact weight recorded and the routes taken, were deemed not material. The chain of custody was admitted by the defence.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court applied the standard of proof beyond reasonable doubt, distinguishing it from fanciful doubt, and found the prosecution evidence met that standard.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty. Her defence was that the police came looking for a drug dealer named Lena Paba and, failing to find her, falsely arrested the appellant and planted heroin. She gave a dock statement but called no defence witnesses. The court found her defence version did not create reasonable doubt.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal thoroughly reviewed the evidence and the High Court's reasoning. It found no merit in the appeal grounds. It held that minor inconsistencies in the prosecution evidence were not material and did not create reasonable doubt. The court affirmed that the prosecution proved its case beyond reasonable doubt, referencing precedents on the standard of proof. The High Court Judge was found to have correctly considered the evidence and the defence. The appeal was dismissed.
coa_sentence_type: Life Imprisonment
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused-appellant was convicted in the High Court of Colombo for possession of 4.73 grams of heroin and sentenced to life imprisonment. She appealed, arguing the High Court Judge failed to consider improbabilities in the prosecution evidence and her dock statement. The Court of Appeal found the police evidence credible and the minor discrepancies immaterial. It affirmed the conviction and sentence, dismissing the appeal.
defence_counsel: Tenny Fernando with Terin Marasinghe
hc_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the High Court Judge correctly analyzed the evidence, applied the burden of proof properly, and considered the defence version. No errors in the HC's reasoning were identified.
precedents_cited_list: State of Punjab Vs. Karnail Singh (2003) 11 SCC 271 | Ramakant Rai Vs. Madan Rai AIR 2004 SC at 84 | Stirland Vs. Director of Public Prosecution (1944 AC(PC) 315) | State of U.P. Vs. Anil Singh (AIR 1988 SC 1998)
standard_of_review_applied: Review of whether the High Court's verdict was reasonable and based on evidence proving guilt beyond reasonable doubt.
sentencing_principles_applied: Consideration of aggravating and mitigatory circumstances before imposing life imprisonment.

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 54(A)(b) and Section 54(A)(d) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance as amended by Act No. 13 of 1984
brief_facts_summary: The accused-appellant was arrested on 26th July 2012 while driving a red three-wheeler at Kimbula Ela Junction. Police recovered a parcel containing substances which reacted for heroin from his trouser pocket. The 2nd accused was also arrested as he tried to flee. The substance was weighed at 20 grams at the Bureau, sealed, and handed over. The investigation also involved a search for a person named Ubayatulla in the Wanawasala area, but he was not found.
evidence_type_primary: Physical evidence (recovery of parcel with heroin)
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 54(A)(b) and Section 54(A)(d) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance as amended by Act No. 13 of 1984
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court Judge found the appellant guilty on counts 1 and 2 for trafficking 5.39 grams of heroin and sentenced him to life imprisonment on both counts on 21 March 2018. The 2nd accused was acquitted for want of evidence.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant contended that the evidence of the prosecution witnesses (PW1 and PW2) was contradictory and failed the test of credibility and probability. He also argued that an unexplained amendment was made to the Government Analyst Report. The appeal was based on the prosecution's failure to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Evidence given by PW1 and PW2 is contradictory and thereby failed the test of credibility. | Amendment made to the Government Analyst Report was not explained by the prosecution.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The court found the prosecution evidence, particularly from PW1 and PW2, lacked credibility and consistency. The sequence of events supported the appellant's dock statement. The unexplained amendment to the crucial Government Analyst Report and the failure to produce supporting documentary evidence created reasonable doubt.
probability_assessment_by_court: Court found defence evidence sufficient to create reasonable doubt in the prosecution case, particularly regarding contradictions in evidence and unexplained amendment to the Government Analyst Report.
defence_version_summary: The appellant made a dock statement claiming he was arrested at his residence around 9.30 pm, questioned about Ubayatulla, taken to Ubayatulla's house, and then to the Police Narcotics Bureau where he was falsely charged. His three-wheeler was stationed near his house at arrest. He pleaded not guilty.
legal_errors_description: The High Court Judge erred in rejecting the defence evidence which was sufficient to create a reasonable doubt in the prosecution case.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the prosecution evidence contradictory and unreliable. The first information about a red three-wheeler was doubtful, and no documentary proof was produced. The second information led to arrest, but police failed to search the appellant's house. The sequence of events matched the appellant's dock statement. An unexplained amendment to the crucial Government Analyst Report further weakened the prosecution case. Considering the grounds of appeal and the burden of proof, the defence evidence created reasonable doubt. Citing precedents on credibility assessment and appellate review, the COA held the prosecution failed to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt and acquitted the appellant.
coa_sentence_type: Acquitted, sentence set aside
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused-appellant was convicted by the High Court of Colombo for trafficking 5.39 grams of heroin and sentenced to life imprisonment. He appealed, arguing contradictions in police evidence and an unexplained amendment to the Government Analyst Report. The Court of Appeal found the prosecution evidence unreliable and inconsistent, noting failures in police procedure and documentation. The defence version created reasonable doubt. The COA allowed the appeal, set aside the conviction and sentence, and acquitted the appellant from both charges.
defence_counsel: Faisz Musthapha, PC with K.Thilakaratne
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted the appellant based on the prosecution evidence. The COA viewed this as an error, finding the HC should not have rejected the defence evidence which created reasonable doubt regarding the credibility of prosecution witnesses and the unexplained amendment to the Government Analyst Report.
precedents_cited_list: Mohamed Nimnaz v. Attorney General CA/95/94 | Girija Prasad (dead) by LRs. v. State of M.P., AIR [2007] SCW 5589 (2007) 7 SCC 625 | Vadivelu Thevar v. State of Madras AIR 1957 SC 614 | Kumara De Silva and two others v The Attorney General [2010] 2 SLR 169 | Lal Mandi v. State of West Bengal (1995) 3 SCC 603
standard_of_review_applied: Appellate Court's duty to appreciate evidence on record and give benefit of reasonable doubt if two views are possible.

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: section 296 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The accused-appellant was convicted for the murder of his wife (Phimbiyage Sachethana Sandamali) and two young children on 16-12-2012 at their house in Ratmalana. The prosecution case relied on circumstantial evidence and a confessional statement made to a Magistrate. Initially thought to be deaths by accidental fire, postmortems revealed the mother and elder child died by manual strangulation, and the younger child by burn injuries. The appellant had commenced a romantic relationship with another woman (PW-10) shortly before the incident.
evidence_type_secondary: Postmortem reports, Government Analyst Report, Police investigation, Phone records and SMS details
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: section 296 of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: After a trial without a jury, the High Court Judge found the appellant guilty of three counts of murder. The judge relied on the circumstantial evidence and the confessional statement made to the Magistrate. The appellant was sentenced to death on all three counts.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant's counsel argued the prosecution failed to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt. Grounds included failure to consider plausible alternative inferences from circumstantial evidence, improper analysis of witness evidence, judicial prejudice, defects in investigation, and failure to properly consider the defence. The core argument was that a fair trial was denied, leading to a miscarriage of justice.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The learned trial Judge failed to apply his judicial mind to arrive at a finding whether the prosecution proved its case beyond reasonable doubt. | The learned High Court Judge drew incorrect inferences and failed to consider plausible alternative inferences from circumstantial evidence. | The learned High Court Judge failed to properly analyze and consider doubtful, false, and inconclusive evidence of prosecution witnesses, failing to recognize reasonable doubt. | The learned High Court Judge was prejudiced from commencement, failing to evaluate circumstantial evidence fairly, denying a fair trial. | The learned High Court Judge failed to consider defects and improbabilities in the investigation, causing doubt and amounting to a miscarriage of justice. | The learned High Court Judge failed to properly analyze the defence narration and improperly rejected it.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed the evidence of key witnesses, including the brother of the deceased (PW-01), the appellant's mother (PW-02), the domestic servant, and PW-10 (the appellant's romantic interest). The court also evaluated the expert evidence of the JMO (PW-34), the Government Analyst (PW-35), and the Magistrate (PW-36) who recorded the confession. The COA found the trial judge correctly assessed witness credibility and the chain of circumstantial evidence.
probability_assessment_by_court: The COA applied the principle that circumstantial evidence must be inconsistent with any reasonable hypothesis of innocence. The court found the cumulative circumstantial evidence, including the appellant's conduct and confession, pointed irresistibly to guilt.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty. He made a lengthy dock statement denying the charges, claiming the confessional statement was made under duress after police assault. He admitted a connection with PW-10 but claimed it was not a motive for murder. He called no defence witnesses. The court found his defence lacked credibility and was an afterthought.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The COA conducted a thorough review. It first upheld the trial judge's voir dire ruling, finding the confessional statement (P-12) was voluntary, noting the Magistrate followed proper procedure and the appellant had opportunities to report any duress. The COA then analyzed the circumstantial evidence, applying precedents like The King Vs. Abeywickrama and Don Sunny Vs. The Attorney General. It found the evidence—including the appellant's suspicious conduct (giving money to PW-06, statements to PW-01 about fingerprints), his relationship with PW-10 and attempts to distance himself, the lack of forced entry, the JMO's findings, and the SOCO's observations—formed a cohesive rope of guilt, excluding any reasonable hypothesis of innocence. The COA rejected arguments about investigation flaws (DNA tests, statements of other boarders) as without merit. It affirmed the trial judge's advantage in observing witnesses and found no basis to disturb the findings.
coa_sentence_type: Death sentence on all three counts affirmed
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused-appellant appealed against his High Court conviction and death sentence for murdering his wife and two children. The prosecution case was based on circumstantial evidence and a confessional statement. The appellant challenged the voluntariness of his confession, sufficiency of circumstantial evidence, fairness of trial, and investigation defects. The Court of Appeal, after detailed analysis, held the confession was voluntary and the circumstantial evidence, viewed cumulatively, proved guilt beyond reasonable doubt. The appeal was dismissed, and the High Court judgment and death sentence were affirmed.
prosecution_counsel: Ayesha Jinasena, P.C., Solicitor General, with Malik Azeez, S.C.
defence_counsel: Kapila Waidyaratne, P.C. with Akkila Jayasundara and Akhila Mathishi
cause_of_death_exact_text: Sandamali: 'died due to application of pressure on her neck'; Kushan (3-year-old): 'died due to manual strangulation of the neck'; Ishan (younger child): 'died due to complications of burn injuries'.
hc_analysis_summary: The COA found the High Court Judge correctly conducted the trial, held a proper voir dire on the confession, and analyzed the evidence meticulously. The COA agreed with the HC's reasoning that the circumstantial evidence led to the only inference of the appellant's guilt and saw no error in the HC's approach or findings.
precedents_cited_list: SC/TAB/1A and 1B/2020 | Mahadevan Yogakanthan Vs. Republic of Sri Lanka, C.A. Appeal 41/2010 | S. Vivekanadan and Another Vs. S. Selvaratnam 79 (1) NLR 337 | The King Vs. Abeywickrama 44 NLR 254 | Don Sunny Vs. The Attorney General (1998) 2 SLR 01 | The King Vs. Guaratne 47 NLR 145 | Regina Vs. Exall (176 English Reports, Nisi Prius at page 853) | Mahathun and Others Vs. The Attorney General (2015) 1 SLR 74 | State of U.P. Vs. M. K. Anthony, AIR 1985 SC 48 | Ramakant Rai Vs. Madan Rai AIR 2004 SC at 84 | Bhoginbhai Hirjibhai Vs. State of Gujarat (AIR 1983 SC 753) | Chaminda Vs. The Republic (2009) 1 SLR 144
standard_of_review_applied: The appellate court will not lightly disturb findings of fact by a trial judge who observed witness demeanor and deportment, unless the determination is manifestly wrong and occasions a failure of justice.

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 364(2) of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The accused-appellant was convicted of raping the victim (PW-01), who was his wife's niece, on 15 December 2002 when she was 15 years old. The victim had been living with the appellant's family since childhood. She testified that the appellant, who was drunk, raped her while his wife was overseas. She reported the incident to a neighbor (PW-03) and the grama niladhari (PW-04) the next day and later to the police. The Judicial Medical Officer found old tears and contusions consistent with sexual intercourse.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 364(2) of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court Judge found the appellant guilty of rape under section 364(2) of the Penal Code. The judge sentenced him to 15 years rigorous imprisonment, a fine of Rs. 25,000, and ordered compensation of Rs. 250,000 to the victim. Default imprisonment terms were also imposed.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant argued the High Court Judge failed to properly evaluate vital omissions and contradictions in the prosecution evidence (marked V-01, V-02, V-03). It was submitted the evidence lacked consistency, probability, and spontaneity, and that taken as a whole, it created reasonable doubt. The judge was also faulted for not properly considering the appellant's dock statement and defence evidence.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The learned High Court Judge has failed to evaluate the vital omissions and the relevant contradictions marked V-01, 02 and 03. | Totality of the evidence has not been taken into account and as a result, the learned High Court Judge has failed to evaluate the evidence on the basis of lack of consistency, probability and spontaneity.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the High Court Judge correctly considered the evidence in its totality. Minor contradictions and omissions (V-01 to V-03) were not material. The victim's evidence was considered cogent and truthful, supported by the JMO and other witnesses.
probability_assessment_by_court: The COA applied the standard of proof beyond reasonable doubt, finding no actual or substantial doubts arose from the evidence. Doubts must be reasonable, not vague apprehensions.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty and made a statement from the dock, denying the offence. He claimed the victim made false allegations because he opposed her love affair with a neighbor. His wife testified in his defence, denying the rape and suggesting the victim had a mental disorder.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the High Court Judge correctly evaluated the evidence, including contradictions and omissions. The COA cited precedents on witness reliability and the standard of proof beyond reasonable doubt. It held the victim's evidence was credible, consistent, and supported by the JMO and other witnesses. The appellant's defence was unpersuasive and did not create reasonable doubt. The COA found no legal or procedural errors in the HC judgment.
coa_sentence_type: 15 years rigorous imprisonment (deemed commenced from 16-01-2023), fine of Rs. 25,000, compensation of Rs. 250,000 to victim with default imprisonment terms affirmed.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused-appellant appealed his conviction and sentence for raping a 15-year-old minor (his niece) in 2002. The High Court of Matara sentenced him to 15 years rigorous imprisonment, a fine, and compensation. On appeal, he argued the HC failed to properly evaluate contradictions and the totality of evidence. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal, finding the HC correctly assessed the evidence, the victim was credible, and the defence did not create reasonable doubt. The conviction and sentence were affirmed.
defence_counsel: Razik Zarook, P.C. with Rohana Deshapriya and Chanakya Liyanage
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court Judge methodically considered the evidence, including contradictions and omissions, and found the prosecution proved its case beyond reasonable doubt. The COA agreed with this analysis and found no error in the HC's reasoning or approach.
precedents_cited_list: D. Tikiribanda Vs. The Attorney General (B.L.R. 2010 92) | Bhoginbhai Hirjibhai Vs. State of Gujarat (AIR 1983 SC 753) | Ramakant Rai Vs. Madan Rai (AIR 2004 SC 84)
standard_of_review_applied: Review of evidence evaluation and application of legal principles, focusing on whether the High Court Judge correctly applied the standard of proof beyond reasonable doubt and considered the totality of evidence.
sentencing_principles_applied: The COA affirmed the sentence but ordered it be deemed to have commenced from the date of the HC sentence (16-01-2023), considering the appellant had been incarcerated since conviction.

judges: Menaka Wijesundera, J | K.M.G.H. Kulatunga, J
offence_sections: 1. Section 54A(b) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Act for trafficking of 634kg of Cannabis Sativa L. 2. Section 54A(b) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Act for possessing the said 634kg of Cannabis Sativa L. 3. Section 22(3) read with Section 22(1) of the Firearms Ordinance No. 33 of 1916 for being in possession of a locally made firearm. 4. Section 27 read with Section 09(2) of the Explosives Act No. 21 of 1956 for being in possession of a live cartridge.
offence_category: Drug Trafficking, Firearms and Explosives Offences
brief_facts_summary: On 06.09.2004, a police team observed a suspicious vehicle and gave chase. The vehicle stopped and the 2nd accused-appellant, a Reserve Police Constable in uniform, fled the scene. The 1st accused was arrested in the vehicle. Searches recovered 30 bags of Cannabis (634kg total), a locally made firearm, and a live cartridge. The Appellant absconded for over a month before being apprehended in a hospital.
evidence_type_primary: Physical evidence and Eyewitness testimony (police officers)
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Same as field 9.
hc_sentence_type: Rigorous Imprisonment 2 years each for counts 1 and 2 (consecutively). Rigorous Imprisonment 1 year with fine of Rs.10,000 for count 3. Rigorous Imprisonment 1 year with fine of Rs.25,000 for count 4 (with default imprisonment). Sentences for counts 3 and 4 concurrent with each other and with sentences for counts 1 and 2.
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court found the 2nd accused guilty on all four counts after trial. He was sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for counts 1 and 2 (2 years each, consecutive) and for counts 3 and 4 (1 year each with fines, concurrent with other sentences), resulting in an aggregate sentence of 4 years RI.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appeal was limited to the sentence. The appellant sought a reduction of sentence based on his current medical condition and the disparity in sentence between him and the 1st accused (co-accused). The Respondent argued the sentence should not be reduced and could be enhanced due to the seriousness of the offence, the appellant being a serving police officer in uniform, his absconding, and the large quantity of drugs.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The current medical condition of the Appellant. | The disparity in the sentence between the 1st accused and the appellant.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: Prosecution evidence was from police officers who observed the vehicle, gave chase, saw the appellant flee, and recovered the drugs, firearm, and cartridge. The appellant was identified as a fellow Reserve Police Constable. The court obtained a Medico Legal Report to assess the appellant's health for serving the sentence.
probability_assessment_by_court: No analysis of reasonable doubt as the appeal was limited to sentence.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty and proceeded to trial. The co-accused (1st accused) pleaded guilty. The appellant did not present a specific defence version; his appeal contested only the sentence. The court did not assess the credibility of a defence story.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The COA examined the medical report which indicated the appellant had a surgical history and some limb weakness but was capable of serving his sentence. It addressed the sentence disparity, noting the 1st accused received a concurrent one-year aggregate sentence after an early guilty plea, a factor recognized by law. The appellant, a police officer, had his role considered an aggravating factor. The court upheld the minimum mandatory two-year sentences for the drug counts but considered the totality of circumstances, including the 18-year delay and the co-accused's concurrent sentences. It ordered all sentences for the appellant to run concurrently.
coa_sentence_type: Rigorous imprisonment for two years (aggregate). Sentences for counts 1 to 4 ordered to run concurrently.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The appellant, a Reserve Police Constable, was convicted of trafficking 634kg of cannabis, possession of the same, and possession of a firearm and live cartridge. The High Court sentenced him to an aggregate of 4 years RI. He appealed only against the sentence, citing medical grounds and sentence disparity with the co-accused who pleaded guilty. The Court of Appeal upheld the convictions and the individual sentences but ordered all sentences to run concurrently, reducing the aggregate term to 2 years RI, partially allowing the appeal.
defence_counsel: J.P. Gamage with Theekshana Ranawecra
hc_analysis_summary: The HC convicted the appellant after trial, considering his role as a police officer an aggravating factor and imposing the statutory minimum sentences for the drug offences. The COA found the differentiation in sentences between the appellant and the co-accused was justified based on their different culpability and circumstances (guilty plea vs. trial, aggravating role).
precedents_cited_list: SC No. 03/2008 | A.G. Vs. Rohana | Hirimuthugoda
standard_of_review_applied: Review of sentence discretion, consideration of statutory minimum mandatory sentences and relevant circumstances.
sentencing_principles_applied: Consideration of minimum mandatory sentences, early guilty plea as a mitigating factor (Section 197(2) CPC), abuse of office as an aggravating factor, totality principle, and disparity in sentences among co-accused.

judges: Menaka Wijesundera, J | Wickum A. Kaluarachchi, J
offence_sections: Section 5(1) of the Offences against Public Property Act No. 12 of 1982 as amended by Act No.76 of 1988
brief_facts_summary: The accused-appellant was the Officer in Charge of the Pawning Division at People's Bank, Kalpitiya Branch. He was charged with criminally misappropriating Rs. 2,685,550 by repeatedly pawning the same fake jewelry items through intermediaries and obtaining money. The prosecution alleged he pawned the items 55 times through various individuals.
evidence_type_secondary: Physical evidence (fake jewelry items), Circumstantial evidence
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 5(1) of the Offences against Public Property Act No. 12 of 1982 as amended by Act No.76 of 1988
hc_sentence_type: 10 years simple imprisonment and a fine
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the accused-appellant on the first count of criminal misappropriation and sentenced him to 10 years simple imprisonment and a fine of Rs. 8,056,650 with a default sentence of 10 years. The court found he misappropriated the entire amount of Rs. 2,685,550.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant argued the High Court judgment was not in terms of Section 283 of the Criminal Procedure Act, that the judge misapplied principles of circumstantial evidence, and improperly rejected the defence case. Specifically, counsel argued the appellant had no access to the safe keys and thus no opportunity to retrieve and re-pawn the jewelry.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The Judgement of the learned High Court Judge is not a Judgment in terms of Section 283 of the Code of Criminal Procedure Act. | The learned High Court Judge has misconceived in law and facts as he has failed to appreciate the evidence in the light of the principles applicable for evaluation of circumstantial evidence. | The learned Trial Judge has improperly rejected the defence case.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed testimony from prosecution witnesses (PW-3, PW-16, PW-17, PW-20) who stated the appellant gave them the same jewelry to pawn repeatedly, they obtained money from the bank, and handed it to him. The court found no link between the appellant and the fake jewelry or 38 receipts produced through a retired Credit Officer.
probability_assessment_by_court: The court found the circumstantial evidence irresistibly pointed to the appellant's guilt regarding Rs. 843,000, leaving no room for reasonable doubt about his involvement.
defence_version_summary: The accused-appellant pleaded not guilty, gave evidence denying any involvement, but called no witnesses. The court found his denial created no reasonable doubt given the prosecution evidence.
legal_errors_description: The High Court incorrectly concluded the appellant misappropriated the entire Rs. 2,685,550. The prosecution only proved misappropriation of Rs. 843,000 related to 18 receipts.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the High Court erred in finding misappropriation of the full charged amount. It upheld the conviction based on proved misappropriation of Rs. 843,000 from 18 receipts, applying precedents that a conviction can stand for a lesser proved amount. It rejected the argument on circumstantial evidence, finding the evidence irresistibly pointed to the appellant taking back and re-pawning jewelry. It affirmed the imprisonment sentence but reduced the fine to three times the proved amount as required by law.
coa_sentence_type: 10 years simple imprisonment affirmed. Fine reduced to Rs. 2,529,000 with a default sentence of 6 years simple imprisonment.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused-appellant, a bank officer, was convicted by the High Court of Puttalam for criminally misappropriating Rs. 2,685,550 from the bank's pawning division and sentenced to 10 years imprisonment and a heavy fine. On appeal, the Court of Appeal found the prosecution only proved misappropriation of Rs. 843,000 related to 18 pawn receipts. It upheld the conviction for that lesser amount and affirmed the 10-year imprisonment. However, it reduced the fine to Rs. 2,529,000 (three times the proved amount) with a 6-year default sentence. The appeal was partly allowed regarding the fine.
defence_counsel: U.R. De Silva, PC with Savithri Fernando, Thilini Athapaththu
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court found the appellant guilty of misappropriating the entire Rs. 2,685,550. The COA found this conclusion incorrect as the prosecution only proved misappropriation of Rs. 843,000, but held the error did not vitiate the conviction for the proved amount.
precedents_cited_list: M. E. A. Cooray v. The King-53 N.L.R. 73 | Regina v. Thomas Wright 1 [169 E. R. 1070] | Emperor v Byramji Jamsetji Chevalla 3 [A.I.R. 1928 Bom. 148]
standard_of_review_applied: The court reviewed whether the conviction was sustainable based on the evidence, applying principles for circumstantial evidence and precedents on conviction for a lesser proved amount.
sentencing_principles_applied: The fine was calculated as three times the value of the misappropriated property as mandated by Section 5(1) of the Offences Against Public Property Act.

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Sections 54(A)(b) and 54(A)(d) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance as amended by Act No. 13 of 1984
location_of_offence: Cardernanawatta, Borella Police area, Serpentine Road, Borella
brief_facts_summary: On 18/04/2013, police officers from the Police Narcotics Bureau conducted a raid based on information from an informant that the Appellant was selling heroin. The Appellant was arrested near his house. A cellophane bag containing a substance that tested positive for heroin (11.54 grams) was recovered from his right-side trouser pocket. Police also recovered Rs. 317,000 from his left-side trouser pocket and later, from his wife's almirah, Rs. 297,000 and some jewelry. His wife was also arrested but later released with the cash and jewelry returned.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Sections 54(A)(b) and 54(A)(d) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance as amended by Act No. 13 of 1984
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court found the Appellant guilty on both counts of trafficking and possession of 11.54 grams of heroin. The learned High Court Judge imposed the death sentence for both counts.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The Appellant argued the High Court judge failed to consider material contradictions in prosecution evidence, failed to assess that the prosecution version failed the probability test, wrongly concluded the prosecution proved the chain of custody, and erroneously rejected the dock statement while shifting the burden of proof onto the Appellant.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The learned High Court Judge had failed to take into consideration material contradictions in the evidence of the prosecution witnesses. | The learned High Court Judge had failed to take into consideration that the version of the prosecution fails the test of probability. | The learned High Court Judge had arrived at the wrong conclusion that the prosecution had proved the chain of productions. | The learned High Court Judge had erroneously rejected the dock statement and the learned High Court Judge had expected the Appellant to prove his case by calling witnesses and thereby shifted the burden on the Appellant to prove his innocence.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found serious contradictions and improbabilities in the prosecution evidence, including discrepancies in where the informant met police and where the arrest occurred, and the lack of notes regarding the informant's identity. The chain of custody evidence was deemed insufficient.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal found the prosecution version, including the informant's actions and the recovery of cash, failed the test of probability, creating reasonable doubt.
defence_version_summary: The Appellant pleaded not guilty. He made a dock statement but absconded afterwards. He did not call any witnesses. His explanation was that the large sum of cash found was from selling a vehicle to repair his house. The COA found the prosecution failed to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt.
legal_errors_description: The High Court judge failed to properly assess contradictions and probability in prosecution evidence, erred on chain of custody proof, and improperly shifted the burden of proof to the accused.
procedural_defects_description: The Appellant was not present for the closing stages of the trial after absconding, but was represented. The COA also found he was not afforded a fair trial as guaranteed by the Constitution.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed contradictions between PW1 and PW7 regarding the arrest location and the informant's role, finding the prosecution story improbable. It highlighted the lack of proper notes on the informant and inconsistencies in the recovery of cash. The court emphasized the prosecution's burden to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt never shifts and found the High Court had erred by expecting the Appellant to prove his innocence. Citing precedents on fair trial and burden of proof, the COA concluded the prosecution failed to meet its standard, the chain of custody was not proven, and the Appellant did not receive a fair trial.
coa_sentence_type: Acquitted, conviction and sentence set aside
brief_judgment_file_summary: The Accused-Appellant was convicted in the High Court of Colombo for trafficking and possessing 11.54g of heroin and sentenced to death. He appealed, arguing material contradictions, failure of probability test, unproven chain of custody, and shifting of burden of proof. The Court of Appeal found serious discrepancies in police testimony regarding the informant and arrest location, and that the prosecution failed to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt. The court also found the Appellant was denied a fair trial. The conviction and death sentence were set aside, and the Appellant was acquitted.
defence_counsel: Neranjan Jayasinghe with Randunu Heellage and Imansi Senarath
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court accepted the prosecution evidence and convicted the Appellant. The COA found the HC failed to properly evaluate contradictions and improbabilities in the evidence, and erred in its application of the burden of proof.
precedents_cited_list: Mohamed Nimnaz V. Attorney General CA/95/94 | Attorney-General v. Rawther 25 NLR 385 | Miller v. Minister of Pensions (1947) 2 All E.R. 372 | R v. Hepworth 1928 (AD) 265
standard_of_review_applied: Review of whether prosecution proved its case beyond reasonable doubt, focusing on factual contradictions, probability, chain of custody, and fair trial principles.

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 140, Section 296 read with Section 146, Section 296 read with Section 32 of the Penal Code (Original charges). Convicted under Section 297 of the Penal Code.
offence_category: Culpable Homicide not amounting to Murder
location_of_offence: Buwaliara, within the jurisdiction of the High Court of Tangalle
brief_facts_summary: On or about 28-08-1996, the accused-appellants, along with two others, were indicted for being members of an unlawful assembly with intent to cause injuries to Jasin Arachchige Karunasena and for causing his death. After a lengthy trial, the High Court acquitted the appellants of the unlawful assembly and murder charges but convicted them of culpable homicide not amounting to murder under section 297 of the Penal Code. The incident arose from a sudden quarrel and fight, during which the appellants attacked the deceased with a knife he was carrying. The deceased died from his injuries, which were exacerbated by a lack of timely medical treatment.
evidence_type_secondary: Medical evidence (Judicial Medical Officer's post-mortem report)
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 297 of the Penal Code (Culpable homicide not amounting to murder)
hc_sentence_type: Rigorous Imprisonment 15 years each plus Fine
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court Judge convicted the appellants for culpable homicide not amounting to murder under section 297 of the Penal Code, sentencing each to 15 years rigorous imprisonment and a fine of Rs. 100,000/- with a 6-month default sentence. The judge acquitted them of the unlawful assembly and murder charges and also acquitted the 4th and 5th accused for lack of evidence. The conviction was based on an assessment of the act causing death but falling short of murder.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellants challenged only the sentence, not the conviction. Their counsel argued that the sentence should have been imposed under the 2nd limb of section 297 of the Penal Code, as the act was done with knowledge it was likely to cause death, but without the intention to cause death, and the incident occurred in a sudden fight without undue advantage or cruelty.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Sentence should have been under the 2nd limb of section 297 of the Penal Code (act done with knowledge likely to cause death but without intention). | Incident occurred as a result of a sudden fight without the offender having taken undue advantage or acted in a cruel or unusual manner. | Appellants were young at the time of the incident. | Medical evidence indicated injuries were not fatal in the ordinary course of nature; death resulted from delay in medical treatment.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The primary evidence included eyewitness testimony (PW-03 and PW-04). The medical evidence from the Judicial Medical Officer indicated the injuries were not fatal in the ordinary course of nature; death occurred due to delay in medical treatment. The Court of Appeal found the evidence established knowledge that the act was likely to cause death but no intention to cause death.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal found that the evidence established the appellants had knowledge their actions were likely to cause death but did not establish an intention to cause death. The benefit of the doubt was given regarding intention.
defence_version_summary: The appellants pleaded not guilty. The defence did not call witnesses but challenged the sentence on appeal. The Court of Appeal accepted the defence argument that the incident occurred in a sudden fight without premeditation or cruelty, and that the sentence should reflect the absence of murderous intent.
legal_errors_description: The High Court Judge failed to specify under which exception of section 294 of the Penal Code the offence was determined to be culpable homicide not amounting to murder, and failed to properly reason out the determination.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed the evidence and found the High Court Judge correctly convicted under section 297 but erred in sentencing under the 1st limb. The COA held the act was done with knowledge it was likely to cause death but without intention, falling under Explanation 4 to section 294 (sudden fight). Citing Indian and Sri Lankan precedents, the COA distinguished between 'knowledge' and 'intention'. The JMO's opinion that injuries were not ordinarily fatal and death resulted from lack of medical attention supported the absence of murderous intent. Therefore, the sentence should be under the 2nd limb of section 297.
coa_sentence_type: Rigorous Imprisonment 10 years each under the 2nd limb of section 297 of the Penal Code, plus fine of Rs. 100,000/- each with default sentence of 6 months simple imprisonment.
brief_judgment_file_summary: Three accused-appellants were convicted by the Tangalle High Court of culpable homicide not amounting to murder under section 297 of the Penal Code for the 1996 death of Karunasena, and sentenced to 15 years rigorous imprisonment each plus a fine. They appealed only against the sentence, arguing it should be under the 2nd limb of section 297. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal against conviction but partly allowed the sentencing appeal. The COA found the High Court Judge failed to specify the legal exception applied but held the offence fell under Exception 4 (sudden fight). The COA reduced the imprisonment to 10 years each under the 2nd limb, maintaining the fines.
defence_counsel: Anuja Premaratna, P.C. with Imasha Senadeera
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court Judge convicted under section 297 but did not specify under which exception of section 294 the offence fell, and sentenced under the 1st limb. The COA found this reasoning deficient and re-evaluated the evidence to conclude the appropriate exception was Exception 4 (sudden fight) and the sentencing limb should be the 2nd.
precedents_cited_list: Jai Prakash Vs. State (Delhi Administration) 1991 SCR (1) 202 | The King Vs. Aldon (1943) 44 NLR 575
standard_of_review_applied: Review of sentencing determination based on evidence and application of legal principles.
sentencing_principles_applied: Consideration of aggravating and mitigatory circumstances; distinction between knowledge and intention in culpable homicide; application of exceptions under section 294; benefit of doubt regarding intention.
final_charge_after_appeal: Culpable Homicide not amounting to Murder under Section 297 of the Penal Code

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code
location_of_offence: Randiya Uyana Housing Scheme (Elakanda area implied)
brief_facts_summary: The appellant's wife eloped with the deceased and lived with him for three months. On the day of the incident, the appellant brought his wife back. In the evening, she attempted to elope again with the deceased in a three-wheeler. The appellant intercepted them, a fight ensued between him and the deceased, resulting in the deceased sustaining 16 stab wounds and dying. The appellant was arrested, and a blood-stained shirt was recovered.
evidence_type_primary: Eyewitness testimony (PW1, PW5), Physical evidence (blood-stained shirt)
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court concluded the prosecution proved the murder charge beyond reasonable doubt. The appellant was convicted under Section 296 of the Penal Code and sentenced to death on 07.02.2023.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant argued the High Court erred in convicting for murder and failing to consider culpable homicide not amounting to murder based on a sudden fight. He also claimed his dock statement was wrongly disbelieved and he was denied a fair trial.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The Learned High Court Judge has erred in law by deciding that the prosecution has proved the case beyond reasonable doubt. | The Learned High Court Judge erred in law by disbelieving the dock statement of the Appellant in toto. | The Appellant was not afforded a fair trial. | Has the Learned High Court Judge erred in law by deciding that the alleged act committed by the Appellant falls under murder when there is evidence suggesting that the act committed falls under culpable homicide not amounting to murder.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the High Court judge acknowledged a sudden fight occurred but failed to apply Exception 4 to Section 294 of the Penal Code, which was a misdirection. The prosecution relied on eyewitnesses and medical evidence.
probability_assessment_by_court: Court of Appeal found the High Court's failure to consider Exception 4 for sudden fight caused prejudice, leading to a conviction for murder instead of culpable homicide.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty. He made a dock statement claiming he stopped the three-wheeler, pleaded with his wife, and the deceased started a fight. He stated he pulled the deceased's hand and ran away after being assaulted. The High Court disbelieved his dock statement in toto.
legal_errors_description: High Court judge failed to consider the alternative verdict of culpable homicide not amounting to murder under Exception 4 to Section 294 of the Penal Code, despite evidence of a sudden fight.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal held that the High Court judge misdirected himself in law by not considering the defence of sudden fight under Exception 4 to Section 294, even though the judge acknowledged a fight occurred. Citing precedent (The King v Bellana Vitanage Eddin, Luvis v. The Queen), the COA emphasized it is the judge's duty to consider alternative verdicts based on evidence, even if not raised by the defence. The COA concluded the act fell under culpable homicide not amounting to murder, set aside the death sentence, and imposed a term of imprisonment.
coa_sentence_type: 10 years rigorous imprisonment, Fine of Rs.5000/- with 06 months default sentence
brief_judgment_file_summary: The appellant was convicted of murder and sentenced to death by the High Court for stabbing the deceased, who had eloped with his wife. He appealed, arguing the High Court erred by not considering culpable homicide not amounting to murder based on a sudden fight. The Court of Appeal found the High Court judge failed to apply Exception 4 to Section 294 despite evidence of a sudden quarrel, constituting a misdirection. The appeal was partly allowed: the conviction was modified to culpable homicide not amounting to murder, the death sentence was set aside, and a sentence of 10 years rigorous imprisonment with a fine was imposed.
defence_counsel: Rahul Jayathilaka
cause_of_death_exact_text: death had occurred due to two stab injuries to heart and lungs due to multiple stab injuries to the chest
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court concluded the prosecution proved murder beyond reasonable doubt and sentenced the appellant to death. The Court of Appeal found the High Court erred by not considering the alternative of culpable homicide not amounting to murder under Exception 4 for sudden fight, despite acknowledging a fight occurred.
precedents_cited_list: The King v Bellana Vitanage Eddin 41 NLR 345 | Luvis v. The Queen 56 NLR 442
standard_of_review_applied: Review of legal misdirection by trial judge regarding application of Exception 4 to Section 294 of the Penal Code.
sentencing_principles_applied: Consideration of diminished responsibility due to sudden fight under Exception 4 to Section 294, substituting a lesser sentence for the death penalty.
final_charge_after_appeal: Modified from Murder to Culpable Homicide not amounting to murder

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 296 read with Section 32 of the Penal Code (murder); Section 300 read with Section 32 of the Penal Code (attempted murder); Section 315 read with Section 32 of the Penal Code (grievous hurt)
location_of_offence: Near the house of DW3 Palika, daughter of the 1st Appellant
brief_facts_summary: A long-standing family dispute culminated in an incident on 23 May 2005, resulting in the death of Dilshan Pushpakumara and injuries to several others. The prosecution alleged that the appellants attacked the deceased with a sword and knife. The defence claimed the deceased's party initiated the attack at the 1st Appellant's daughter's house, leading to a sudden fight where the appellants acted in self-defence but exceeded its limits.
evidence_type_secondary: Medical evidence (Medico Legal Reports), B/Report of police investigation
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 296 read with Section 32 of the Penal Code (murder); Section 300 read with Section 32 of the Penal Code (attempted murder); Section 315 read with Section 32 of the Penal Code (grievous hurt)
hc_sentence_type: Death sentence (for 1st Appellant on count 1; for 2nd Appellant on count 1); Rigorous imprisonment (varying terms for other counts); Fines; Compensation; Suspended imprisonment (for 1st Accused)
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court acquitted the 4th Accused. It convicted the 1st Accused on counts 3 and 4, the 1st Appellant (2nd Accused) on counts 1 and 2, and the 2nd Appellant (3rd Accused) on counts 1, 3, and 4. It imposed death sentences on both appellants for murder, along with prison terms, fines, and compensation for other counts.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: Appellants argued the trial judge failed to adequately consider the facts, did not consider common intention, and failed to consider evidence of provocation and sudden fight, thereby depriving them of a fair trial. Counsel argued the case should have been considered under Section 297 of the Penal Code (culpable homicide not amounting to murder) based on provocation and sudden fight.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: 1. There is no adequate consideration of the facts of the case. | 2. The Common Intention was not considered in the judgment of the learned trial judge. | 3. According to the facts of the case, evidence transpired of provocation but no consideration given in the judgment. Thereby the Appellants were deprived of a fair trial.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found omissions and contradictions in prosecution witness testimony (PW1, PW3, PW4). It noted the prosecution failed to explain the injuries on the 1st Appellant and defence witness DW3, and failed to explain why the deceased's party went 1.5 km to the incident location. Defence evidence, including from DW3 and a visiting lawyer/Acting Magistrate, supported the claim of an initial attack and struggle inside DW3's house.
probability_assessment_by_court: The COA found the prosecution version doubtful due to unexplained injuries on the accused, contradictions, and the failure to explain the genesis of the incident, creating reasonable doubt.
defence_version_summary: Not guilty plea. The 1st and 3rd Accused made statements from the dock, the 2nd Accused (1st Appellant) gave evidence from the witness box, and the 4th Accused remained silent. The defence called four witnesses. They claimed the deceased's party initiated the attack at the daughter's house, they acted in self-defence to save their lives, but exceeded the right of private defence. The court found the defence version probable in light of the prosecution's failure to explain injuries on the accused.
legal_errors_description: High Court judge failed to consider the legal exception of sudden fight and provocation under Section 294 Exception 4 of the Penal Code, and failed to properly apply Section 297 (culpable homicide not amounting to murder) instead of Section 296 (murder).
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The COA focused primarily on the third ground of appeal (provocation/sudden fight). It found ample evidence of a sudden fight and provocation, which the HC judge failed to consider. Applying Exception 4 to Section 294 and Section 105 of the Evidence Ordinance, the COA held the appellants, while provoked and acting in private defence, exceeded its limits. Therefore, the offence should be culpable homicide not amounting to murder under Section 297, not murder under Section 296. The COA cited Lakshmi Singh v State of Bihar regarding the importance of the prosecution explaining injuries on the accused. It found the prosecution case doubtful due to contradictions, omissions, and failure to explain injuries and the reason for the deceased's party being at the scene.
coa_sentence_type: For the 1st Appellant (2nd Accused): 12 years rigorous imprisonment on count 1 (modified from death); 1-year rigorous imprisonment with fine and compensation on count 2 (unchanged). Sentences on counts 1 and 2 to run concurrent. For the 2nd Appellant (3rd Accused): 12 years rigorous imprisonment on count 1 (modified from death); sentences on counts 1, 3, and 4 (1-year and 2-year rigorous imprisonment with fines/compensation) to run concurrent. Sentences operative from 29/09/2020.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The appellants, convicted of murder and other charges by the Balapitiya High Court and sentenced to death, appealed. They argued the trial judge failed to consider provocation, sudden fight, and self-defence. The Court of Appeal found the High Court erred by not considering evidence of a sudden fight and the appellants exceeding the right of private defence. Applying legal principles on provocation and citing precedent on unexplained accused injuries, the COA modified the conviction from murder to culpable homicide not amounting to murder under Section 297 of the Penal Code. It set aside the death sentences, imposing 12 years rigorous imprisonment for murder, while upholding other convictions and sentences. The appeal was partly allowed.
defence_counsel: Neranjan Jayasinghe with Harshana Ananda, Imansi Senaratne and Randunu Heellage for the 1st Appellant. Palitha Fernando, PC with Harshana Ananda for the 2nd Appellant.
weapon_type: Sword, knife, pole, mamoty, katty, axe
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court accepted the prosecution version, convicting the appellants of murder. The COA found the HC judge failed to consider crucial evidence supporting a sudden fight and provocation, failed to explain injuries on the appellants, and erroneously relied on the investigating officer's opinion about the incident location, leading to a wrong legal classification of the offence.
precedents_cited_list: Lakshmi Singh And Other v State of Bihar 1976 AIR SC 2263
standard_of_review_applied: Review of factual findings and legal classification of the offence, focusing on errors in considering evidence of provocation, sudden fight, and right of private defence.
sentencing_principles_applied: Principles regarding modification of offence from murder to culpable homicide not amounting to murder under Section 297 based on sudden fight and exceeding private defence.
final_charge_after_appeal: Murder under Section 296 modified to Culpable Homicide not amounting to Murder under Section 297 of the Penal Code for count 1.

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 54(A) (d) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance as amended by Act No. 13 of 1984
brief_facts_summary: Based on information received, police from the Narcotics Bureau raided a location near Thotalanga on 04.07.2000. The Appellant was identified and arrested. A search allegedly revealed a cellophane bag containing 2.67 grams of Heroin in his trouser pocket. The Appellant's defense was that he was arrested at his residence while having lunch, and no illegal substances were found on him.
evidence_type_secondary: Eyewitness testimony (Police officers), Government Analyst Report
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 54(A) (d) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance as amended by Act No. 13 of 1984
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court found the Appellant guilty of possessing 2.67 grams of Heroin. The Appellant was sentenced to life imprisonment. The conviction was based on the evidence of police witnesses and the Government Analyst report.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The Appellant argued that the High Court Judge erred in law by refusing his application to be represented by counsel in absentia, failed to fairly evaluate defence evidence, and that key prosecution witnesses (PW1 and PW4) were not credible. It was also contended that the refusal of counsel deprived the Appellant of the benefit of a previous revision order rectifying an erroneous alibi ruling.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Whether the learned High Court Judge erred in law in refusing the application made under Section 241(2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure Act No. 15 of 1979. | Whether the learned High Court Judge fairly and squarely evaluated the evidence of the defence. | Whether PW1 and PW4 are credible witnesses. | Whether the learned High Court Judge by disallowing the Appellant to be represented and defended by counsel deprived the Appellant of the benefit of the outcome in CA (PHC) APN 116/2010 and thus permitted the previous erroneous order pertaining to alibi to remain.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found infirmities in the evidence of PW1 and PW4, including discrepancies about the arrest location, weight of the substance, and procedural entries. The defence evidence, including testimony about a prior arrest and beating, was deemed sufficient to create reasonable doubt.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court found the defence evidence created a reasonable doubt over the prosecution case, leading to acquittal.
defence_version_summary: The Appellant pleaded not guilty. He testified he was arrested at his residence while having lunch, wearing a sarong, and that nothing illegal was found. Defence called witnesses and challenged prosecution witness credibility. The Court found the defence version created reasonable doubt.
legal_errors_description: The High Court Judge erred in law by refusing the Appellant's application under Section 241(2) to be defended by counsel in absentia, violating his fundamental right to a fair trial.
