procedural_defects_description: Refusal to allow counsel to represent the Appellant in his absence; previous erroneous order concerning alibi evidence that was later rectified but the benefit was allegedly lost due to lack of representation.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The COA held that refusing the Appellant's statutory right to be defended by counsel in absentia under Section 241(2) was a serious legal error causing prejudice. It found the High Court Judge did not fairly evaluate defence evidence and that infirmities in the testimony of PW1 and PW4 created reasonable doubt. Considering the 24-year delay since the offence and that evidence had been led twice, a re-trial was not appropriate. The defence evidence was sufficient to acquit.
coa_sentence_type: Acquitted, no sentence imposed.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The Accused-Appellant was convicted by the Colombo High Court for possession of 2.67g of Heroin and sentenced to life imprisonment. On appeal, he argued procedural errors, unfair evaluation of defence evidence, and witness credibility issues. The Court of Appeal found the High Court erred in law by refusing his right to counsel in absentia, creating a serious procedural defect. It also found the defence evidence created reasonable doubt and, given the 24-year delay, a re-trial was not warranted. The conviction and sentence were set aside, and the Appellant was acquitted.
defence_counsel: Saliya Peiris, PC, with Pasindu Thilakaratne and Mark Fernando
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted based on prosecution evidence from police and the Analyst. The COA found the HC Judge erred in refusing counsel in absentia, failed to properly evaluate defence evidence, and that credibility issues with prosecution witnesses undermined the case.
precedents_cited_list: Mohamed Ninmaz V. Attorney General CA/95/94 | Attorney-General v. Rawther 25 NLR 385 | Miller v. Minister of Pensions (1947) 2 All E.R. 372 | Mohamed Buhary Mohamed Asmin v Attorney General CA/240/2010 | Thilakaratne v Attorney General [1989] 2 SLR 191 | Martin v Queen 69 CLW 21 | Kumara De Silva v The Attorney General [2010] 2 SRI LR. 169
standard_of_review_applied: Review for legal error, procedural fairness, and evaluation of evidence to determine if prosecution proved its case beyond reasonable doubt.

judges: B. Sasi Mahendran, J. | Amal Ranaraja, J
offence_sections: Section 138 of the Penal Code (Unlawful Assembly) read with Section 26(1) (b) and 26(1) (c) of the Emergency (Miscellaneous Provisions and Powers) Regulation No. 4 of 1994 published in Gazette Extraordinary No. 843/12 of 04.11.1994
brief_facts_summary: On or around 01 February 1998, a group of masked individuals abducted several civilians during a reported terrorist attack near the Bharatipuram police checkpoint. The bodies of the abducted civilians were later found deceased near the checkpoint. The accused, police officers and others, were indicted for being members of an unlawful assembly with the common object of committing murder.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 138 of the Penal Code (Unlawful Assembly) read with Section 26(1) (b) and 26(1) (c) of the Emergency (Miscellaneous Provisions and Powers) Regulation No. 4 of 1994
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court Judge convicted the 1st, 2nd, 4th, 5th, and 8th Accused on the first count (unlawful assembly with common object of murder) and sentenced them to life imprisonment. They were acquitted of all other charges (murder, abduction). The 3rd and 6th Accused were acquitted of all charges. The Judge concluded the accused were members of an unlawful assembly.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellants argued the conviction was against the weight of evidence and contrary to law. They primarily contended the prosecution failed to establish the existence of an unlawful assembly with a shared common object to commit murder, as there was no evidence all accused were present together at the time of the shootings or shared the unlawful object.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Judgment is against the weight of evidence and is contrary to the law | The High Court Judge erred in law by receiving evidence on a faulty indictment, on two separate unlawful assemblies contrary to the rules of joinder of charges | The High Court Judge erred in law by convicting the appellant when there was no evidence in relation to the constitution of an unlawful assembly | The High Court Judge misdirected himself and erred in law by his failure to apply the legal principles in relation to elements of unlawful assembly | The High Court Judge failed to consider and erred in law, as the prosecution had failed to lead evidence of unlawful assembly | The High Court Judge erred in law by his failure to consider that the appellant had a reason to be present at the scene. | The High Court Judge misdirected himself and erred in law on the object of unlawful assembly when the appellant had not subscribed to any unlawful object | The High Court Judge had misdirected himself on the burden of proof | The High Court Judge had failed to evaluate and adduce proper reasons for rejecting the dock statements.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed the testimony of key prosecution witnesses (PW37, PW38). It found their evidence did not establish the accused acted in concert as an unlawful assembly. Witnesses could not identify all accused together at the scene of the killings, and there was no evidence of a shared common object.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal found the prosecution failed to prove beyond reasonable doubt that the appellants were members of an unlawful assembly with a common object of murder. Evidence showed discrete, uncoordinated actions by individuals, not collective intent.
defence_version_summary: The accused pleaded not guilty and made dock statements. They called two witnesses in support of their defence. They denied being part of an unlawful assembly and argued their presence was for a lawful purpose (responding to a terrorist attack). The Court of Appeal found the High Court failed to properly evaluate and give reasons for rejecting the dock statements.
legal_errors_description: The High Court Judge misdirected himself on the legal principles governing unlawful assembly, particularly regarding the requirement for a shared common object and the simultaneous presence of members. He failed to properly apply the burden of proof and evaluate the evidence in light of these principles.
procedural_defects_description: The indictment was faulty for potentially alleging two separate unlawful assemblies contrary to joinder rules. The charge sheet made no reference to an 'unknown person' whose presence was noted in evidence, creating a discrepancy.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal held the High Court Judge misappreciated the factual matrix and misapplied the law on unlawful assembly. It examined precedents and scholarly commentary, emphasizing that mere presence does not make one a member of an unlawful assembly; the prosecution must prove intentional joining with a common object. The evidence from PW37 and PW38 failed to establish the appellants acted in concert with a shared unlawful object. The actions described were discrete and uncoordinated. The initial gathering was for a lawful purpose (responding to attack). The prosecution did not lead cogent evidence that all appellants were present together at the time of the killings or shared the specific common object of murder.
coa_sentence_type: Conviction and sentence set aside
brief_judgment_file_summary: Thirteen individuals were indicted in the High Court of Anuradhapura on various charges including murder and unlawful assembly. The High Court convicted the 1st, 2nd, 4th, 5th, and 8th Accused of unlawful assembly with the common object of murder and sentenced them to life imprisonment, acquitting them of murder and other charges. The accused appealed. The Court of Appeal found the prosecution evidence, primarily from police eyewitnesses, failed to prove the existence of an unlawful assembly with a shared common object to commit murder. It held the High Court Judge misdirected himself on the law of unlawful assembly and misappreciated the facts. The Court of Appeal allowed the appeal, set aside the convictions and sentences, and acquitted the appellants.
defence_counsel: Neranjan Jayasinghe with Randunu Heellage and Imangsi Senarath (for 2nd & 8th), Shavindra Fernando, PC with Thivanka Attygalle, Nipun Samaratunga and Natasha Wijayasekara (for 4th), Priyantha Nawana, PC with Ravihansa Wijesinghe (for 5th)
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court Judge concluded the accused were members of an unlawful assembly with murder as its common object. However, he acquitted them of the actual murder charges. The COA found the HC Judge's reasoning legally unsustainable as it was based on a misapplication of the law regarding the essential elements of an unlawful assembly, particularly the need for a proven common object and the simultaneous presence of members at the material time.
precedents_cited_list: Samy and Others v. Attorney General, 2007 (2) SLR 216 | Rex v. Dias, Ceylon Law Record Volume 17, page 16 | Police Sergeant Kulatunga v. Mudalihamy, 42 NLR 33 | Andrayas v. The Queen, 67 NLR, 425
standard_of_review_applied: Review of the High Court's application of legal principles and assessment of evidence regarding the offence of unlawful assembly.

judges: B. Sasi Mahendran, J. | Amal Ranaraja, J
offence_sections: Section 138 of the Penal Code (Unlawful Assembly) read with Section 26(1) (b) and 26(1) (c) of the Emergency (Miscellaneous Provisions and Powers) Regulation No. 4 of 1994 published in Gazette Extraordinary No. 843/12 of 04.11.1994
brief_facts_summary: On or around 01 February 1998, a group of masked individuals abducted several civilians during a reported terrorist attack near the Bharatipuram police checkpoint. The bodies of the abducted civilians were later found deceased near the checkpoint. The accused, police officers and others, were indicted for being members of an unlawful assembly with the common object of committing murder.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 138 of the Penal Code (Unlawful Assembly) read with Section 26(1) (b) and 26(1) (c) of the Emergency (Miscellaneous Provisions and Powers) Regulation No. 4 of 1994
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court Judge convicted the 1st, 2nd, 4th, 5th, and 8th Accused on the first count (unlawful assembly with common object of murder) and sentenced them to life imprisonment. They were acquitted of all other charges (murder, abduction). The 3rd and 6th Accused were acquitted of all charges. The Judge concluded the accused were members of an unlawful assembly.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellants argued the conviction was against the weight of evidence and contrary to law. They primarily contended the prosecution failed to establish the existence of an unlawful assembly with a shared common object to commit murder, as there was no evidence all accused were present together at the time of the shootings or shared the unlawful object.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Judgment is against the weight of evidence and is contrary to the law | The High Court Judge erred in law by receiving evidence on a faulty indictment, on two separate unlawful assemblies contrary to the rules of joinder of charges | The High Court Judge erred in law by convicting the appellant when there was no evidence in relation to the constitution of an unlawful assembly | The High Court Judge misdirected himself and erred in law by his failure to apply the legal principles in relation to elements of unlawful assembly | The High Court Judge failed to consider and erred in law, as the prosecution had failed to lead evidence of unlawful assembly | The High Court Judge erred in law by his failure to consider that the appellant had a reason to be present at the scene. | The High Court Judge misdirected himself and erred in law on the object of unlawful assembly when the appellant had not subscribed to any unlawful object | The High Court Judge had misdirected himself on the burden of proof | The High Court Judge had failed to evaluate and adduce proper reasons for rejecting the dock statements.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed the testimony of key prosecution witnesses (PW37, PW38). It found their evidence did not establish the accused acted in concert as an unlawful assembly. Witnesses could not identify all accused together at the scene of the killings, and there was no evidence of a shared common object.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal found the prosecution failed to prove beyond reasonable doubt that the appellants were members of an unlawful assembly with a common object of murder. Evidence showed discrete, uncoordinated actions by individuals, not collective intent.
defence_version_summary: The accused pleaded not guilty and made dock statements. They called two witnesses in support of their defence. They denied being part of an unlawful assembly and argued their presence was for a lawful purpose (responding to a terrorist attack). The Court of Appeal found the High Court failed to properly evaluate and give reasons for rejecting the dock statements.
legal_errors_description: The High Court Judge misdirected himself on the legal principles governing unlawful assembly, particularly regarding the requirement for a shared common object and the simultaneous presence of members. He failed to properly apply the burden of proof and evaluate the evidence in light of these principles.
procedural_defects_description: The indictment was faulty for potentially alleging two separate unlawful assemblies contrary to joinder rules. The charge sheet made no reference to an 'unknown person' whose presence was noted in evidence, creating a discrepancy.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal held the High Court Judge misappreciated the factual matrix and misapplied the law on unlawful assembly. It examined precedents and scholarly commentary, emphasizing that mere presence does not make one a member of an unlawful assembly; the prosecution must prove intentional joining with a common object. The evidence from PW37 and PW38 failed to establish the appellants acted in concert with a shared unlawful object. The actions described were discrete and uncoordinated. The initial gathering was for a lawful purpose (responding to attack). The prosecution did not lead cogent evidence that all appellants were present together at the time of the killings or shared the specific common object of murder.
coa_sentence_type: Conviction and sentence set aside
brief_judgment_file_summary: Thirteen individuals were indicted in the High Court of Anuradhapura on various charges including murder and unlawful assembly. The High Court convicted the 1st, 2nd, 4th, 5th, and 8th Accused of unlawful assembly with the common object of murder and sentenced them to life imprisonment, acquitting them of murder and other charges. The accused appealed. The Court of Appeal found the prosecution evidence, primarily from police eyewitnesses, failed to prove the existence of an unlawful assembly with a shared common object to commit murder. It held the High Court Judge misdirected himself on the law of unlawful assembly and misappreciated the facts. The Court of Appeal allowed the appeal, set aside the convictions and sentences, and acquitted the appellants.
defence_counsel: Neranjan Jayasinghe with Randunu Heellage and Imangsi Senarath (for 2nd & 8th), Shavindra Fernando, PC with Thivanka Attygalle, Nipun Samaratunga and Natasha Wijayasekara (for 4th), Priyantha Nawana, PC with Ravihansa Wijesinghe (for 5th)
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court Judge concluded the accused were members of an unlawful assembly with murder as its common object. However, he acquitted them of the actual murder charges. The COA found the HC Judge's reasoning legally unsustainable as it was based on a misapplication of the law regarding the essential elements of an unlawful assembly, particularly the need for a proven common object and the simultaneous presence of members at the material time.
precedents_cited_list: Samy and Others v. Attorney General, 2007 (2) SLR 216 | Rex v. Dias, Ceylon Law Record Volume 17, page 16 | Police Sergeant Kulatunga v. Mudalihamy, 42 NLR 33 | Andrayas v. The Queen, 67 NLR, 425
standard_of_review_applied: Review of the High Court's application of legal principles and assessment of evidence regarding the offence of unlawful assembly.

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR) Act No-56 of 2007 and sections 120, 291(a), 291(b) of the Penal Code and section 6 of the Computer Crimes Act No. 24 of 2007
brief_facts_summary: The first and second suspects were arrested and produced before the Magistrate's Court of Colombo Fort on 28-05-2023 based on a B-report alleging they made defamatory and hateful statements to disturb religious harmony. They were later released on bail on 06-07-2023. An Attorney-at-Law, representing an organization called Sinhala Rawaya, subsequently informed the Court on 07-06-2023 that a person named Widarshana Kannangara and others, including the petitioner, had conducted a press briefing criticizing the suspects' remand, which amounted to contempt of Court. The Magistrate then ordered an investigation into the alleged contempt.
evidence_type_primary: Video recording and photographs of alleged press conference
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court Judge refused to issue notice on the petitioner's revision application, finding that the petitioner failed to establish any matter that shocks the conscience of the Court or amounts to a positive miscarriage of justice.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The petitioner challenged the High Court's refusal to issue notice on his revision application and the Magistrate's orders. Key arguments were that the Magistrate lacked jurisdiction to order an investigation into contempt allegedly occurring outside his court, that the correct forum for such contempt was the Court of Appeal, that the press conference occurred in the jurisdiction of a different Magistrate's Court, and that the Magistrate acted without a proper complaint.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The learned Magistrate had no jurisdiction under section 55(1) of the Judicature Act to take cognizance of alleged contempt of Court occurring outside his jurisdiction. | For alleged contempt of this nature, only the Court of Appeal has jurisdiction under Article 105(3) of the Constitution. | The alleged press conference was held in the Maradana police area, within the jurisdiction of the Maligakanda Magistrate's Court. | Without a proper complaint under section 136(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure Act, the Magistrate had no jurisdiction to act on a statement made by an Attorney-at-Law. | The High Court Judge erred in law by analyzing section 9(b)(i) to justify the Magistrate's actions and by failing to consider the lack of exceptional circumstances was not required as there is no right to appeal.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed the basis of the Magistrate's orders, finding they were based on a statement by an Attorney-at-Law and a video/photographs of a concluded press conference. The Court found there was nothing to investigate further, only a matter for contempt proceedings in the correct forum.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal found the Magistrate acted without jurisdiction as the alleged contempt did not occur in his presence or in the course of proceedings in his court.
defence_version_summary: The petitioner pleaded not guilty by way of a revision application, arguing the Magistrate's orders were made without jurisdiction. The Court found the petitioner's arguments had merit.
legal_errors_description: The High Court Judge erred in law by applying section 9(b)(i) of the Code of Criminal Procedure Act and failing to consider the specific contempt jurisdiction under section 55(1) of the Judicature Act. The Magistrate lacked jurisdiction to order an investigation into contempt allegedly committed outside his court.
procedural_defects_description: The Magistrate ordered an investigation based on a mere statement by an Attorney-at-Law without a proper complaint under section 136(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure Act and for an alleged offence occurring in the jurisdiction of another Magistrate's Court.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal held that the Magistrate's Court's jurisdiction over contempt is strictly limited by section 55(1) of the Judicature Act to contempt committed in the presence of the court or in the course of its proceedings. The alleged press conference occurred outside the Magistrate's presence and jurisdiction (Maradana area under Maligakanda Magistrate's Court). For contempt ex facie curiae, the proper forum is the Court of Appeal under Article 105(3) of the Constitution. The Magistrate therefore acted without jurisdiction in ordering the CID and Computer Crimes Investigation Division to investigate. The High Court Judge erred by not recognizing this jurisdictional flaw and by misapplying other procedural provisions. The petitioner established exceptional circumstances warranting revisionary intervention.
brief_judgment_file_summary: This is a revision application to the Court of Appeal challenging the High Court's refusal to issue notice on a revision against Magistrate's Court orders. The Magistrate had ordered an investigation into alleged contempt of court based on a press conference criticizing the remand of two suspects. The Court of Appeal held the Magistrate lacked jurisdiction as the alleged contempt occurred outside his court's presence and territorial jurisdiction, and such contempt falls under the Court of Appeal's purview. The High Court erred in law in its analysis. The Court of Appeal allowed the revision, setting aside the High Court order and the relevant parts of the Magistrate's orders.
prosecution_counsel: Jehan Gunasekara, S.C. for the Attorney General
defence_counsel: Saliya Pieris, P.C. with Jhanuka Nandasiri and Manujaya De Silva for the Petitioner
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court Judge refused notice, finding no exceptional circumstances or miscarriage of justice. The COA found the High Court Judge erred by misapplying section 9(b)(i) of the Code of Criminal Procedure Act and failing to properly consider the jurisdictional limits of the Magistrate under section 55(1) of the Judicature Act regarding contempt.
precedents_cited_list: Sadi Banda Vs. Officer In Charge of Norton Bridge Police Station (supra) | Hotel Galaxy (Pvt) Ltd Vs. Mercantile Hotels Management Ltd (1987) 1 SLR 5 | Wijesinghe Vs. Thamararatnam (Sriskantha Law Report Volume IV page 47) | Vanik Incorporation Ltd Vs. Jayasekare (1997) 2 SLR 365 | Regent International Hotels Ltd Vs. Siril Gardiner and Others (1978-79-80) 1 SLR 278
standard_of_review_applied: Revisionary jurisdiction under Article 138 of the Constitution, requiring exceptional circumstances or a miscarriage of justice.

judges: S.U.B. Karallyadde, J | Mayadunne Corea, J
offence_sections: violation of the Parliamentary Elections Act, No. 1 of 1980
brief_facts_summary: The Petitioner, a politician and former Chairman of the Central Provincial Council, was convicted in the High Court of Kandy for election-related violence under the Penal Code and Parliamentary Elections Act, No. 1 of 1980. He was sentenced to two years and six months imprisonment. On appeal, the Court of Appeal affirmed the conviction but reduced the sentence to two years and suspended it for five years, effective from December 2, 2021. Following the initial conviction, the Petitioner was removed from office in March 2015 and claims deprivation of salary from that date. He filed a writ application seeking a mandamus to compel payment of salary arrears from March 2015 to October 2018 and reinstatement as Chairman.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: violation of the Parliamentary Elections Act, No. 1 of 1980 and Penal Code
hc_sentence_type: Rigorous Imprisonment for two years and six months
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the Petitioner for election-related offences and sentenced him to two years and six months imprisonment. This conviction led to his disqualification and removal from the office of Chairman of the Central Provincial Council in March 2015.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The Petitioner sought a writ of mandamus for two main reliefs: 1) payment of compensation for unpaid salary from the date of his removal from office, and 2) reinstatement as Chairman of the Central Provincial Council. His arguments centered on the suspension of his sentence by the Court of Appeal, which he claimed restored his entitlement to salary and office.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Delay in filing the application | The Appellate Court affirmed the conviction and only varied the sentence on sympathetic grounds | No grounds urged and the Application is misconceived | Petitioner's Application cannot be maintained in view of Articles 89 and 91 of the Constitution
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: This is a writ application, not a criminal trial appeal. No witness testimony or physical evidence from the original criminal trial was analyzed in this judgment. The Court focused on procedural and legal issues surrounding the mandamus application.
defence_version_summary: The Petitioner pleaded not guilty in the original High Court trial. In the writ application, his defence was that the suspension of his sentence restored his rights to salary and office. The Court found he failed to prove his case, suppressed material facts, and lacked clean hands.
procedural_defects_description: The Court found the Petitioner failed to name necessary parties (the newly elected Chairman), failed to first demand the relief from the relevant authority, and was guilty of undue delay in filing the application.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed the writ application on multiple grounds. It found the Petitioner guilty of undue delay, as he filed the application 1.5 years after the Court of Appeal's judgment. The Court held that the conviction was affirmed, not set aside, and the suspended sentence only applied from December 2021, not retrospectively to 2015. It found the Petitioner suppressed material facts by not disclosing that a new Chairman had been elected. The Court held that a salary is for work performed; since the Petitioner did not work after 2015, he had no legal entitlement. It further found the Petitioner disqualified under Article 91 of the Constitution and Section 3 of the Provincial Councils Act due to his conviction. The application was also premature as the suspended sentence operational period was still running. The Court concluded the Petitioner failed to establish a prima facie case for mandamus, which requires a pre-existing right and a prior demand and refusal, neither of which were proven.
coa_sentence_type: Sentence of two years imprisonment suspended for five years, effective from December 2, 2021 (as per earlier Court of Appeal judgment P1). The writ application was dismissed.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The Petitioner, a former Chairman of the Central Provincial Council convicted for election offences, sought a writ of mandamus from the Court of Appeal for payment of unpaid salary from 2015-2018 and reinstatement. The High Court had convicted and sentenced him to imprisonment. The Court of Appeal affirmed the conviction but suspended the sentence. In the writ application, the Court of Appeal dismissed the petition on multiple grounds: undue delay, suppression of material facts (non-disclosure of a newly elected Chairman), failure to name necessary parties, failure to first demand the relief from authorities, lack of legal entitlement to salary for work not performed, and disqualification under the Constitution due to the conviction. The Court held the Petitioner failed to establish a prima facie case for mandamus.
prosecution_counsel: Dilan Ratnayake, A.S.G., PC, for the 5th Respondent
defence_counsel: Lakshan Dias with Imasha Fernando instructed by Dayani Panditharathne for the Petitioner
hc_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal did not analyze or criticize the High Court's criminal trial judgment in this proceeding. The writ application was based on the consequences of the conviction, not the trial's merits.
precedents_cited_list: Dissanayake v. Fernando (1986) 71 NLR 356 | Gunasekera v. Weerakoon 73 NLR 262 | Abdul Rahuman v. Mayor of Colombo 69 NLR 453 | Wijegoonawardena v. Kularatne 51 NLR 453 | W. S. Alphonso Appuhamy v. Hettiarachchi (1973) 22 NLR 77 | Nanunukula Plantations Limited Vs Minister of Lands and others (2012) 1 SLR 376 | Rawaya Publishers v. Wijedasa Rajapakse and others (2003) 3 SLR 213 | Ukwatte v DFCC (2004) 1 SLR 164 | S.I. Syndicate v. Union of India AIR 1975 Sc 460 | Rasammah & another v. A.P.B.Maumperi 65 NLR 77 | Saranguhewage Garvin De Silva v. Lankapura Pradeshiya Sabha and others SC Appeal 10/2009 | Perera v. National Housing Development Authority (2001) 3 SLR 50 | A.M.Podihamine Vs T.P.A.Hemakumara and others CA (Writ) Application No 69/2013
standard_of_review_applied: The Court applied the standard for granting a writ of mandamus, requiring the applicant to prove the existence of a legal right, a corresponding public duty, a prior demand and refusal, and to come with clean hands without suppressing material facts.

judges: M. Ahsan R. Marikar, J. (CA) | M Sampath K. B Wijeratne, J.(CA)
offence_sections: Forest Ordinance (Reserve forest entry, felling teak trees, transporting illegal timber)
location_of_offence: Reserve forest under Galgamuwa Range Forest Officer jurisdiction
brief_facts_summary: The 3rd and 4th Respondents were charged in Mahawa Magistrate's Court for entering a reserve forest, felling six teak trees, and transporting the timber in vehicle MWPA-2814. They initially pleaded not guilty but later changed their plea to guilty. The Magistrate held an inquiry on confiscation of the vehicle and ordered its confiscation. The Appellant, who claimed ownership of the vehicle via a sale dated after the offence, challenged this through revision to the High Court and then appeal to the Court of Appeal, arguing the offence was committed without his knowledge.
evidence_type_primary: Confession (Guilty plea of accused), Documentary evidence (B report, charge sheet, vehicle registration forms)
evidence_type_secondary: Testimony of Motor Traffic officials, Inquiry record
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Forest Ordinance (Reserve forest entry, felling teak trees, transporting illegal timber)
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court dismissed the Appellant's revision application. The Judge held that ownership of the vehicle had not been legally transferred at the time of the offence and the Appellant failed to prove the accused acted without his knowledge. The Judge found no exceptional circumstances to invoke revisionary jurisdiction.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The Appellant argued that the offence was committed by the 3rd and 4th Respondents without his knowledge as the registered owner of the vehicle. He contended this fact was not duly considered by the Magistrate or the High Court Judge.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The 3rd and 4th Respondents committed the offence without the knowledge of the Appellant, the registered owner. | The said facts had not been duly considered by the Learned Magistrate and or the High Court Judge.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court found the Magistrate and High Court had properly considered evidence, including the guilty plea, documents (MT6, MT8 forms), and Motor Traffic official testimony. The Court concluded the Appellant and 2nd Respondent colluded to mislead on ownership transfer timing.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court found the Appellant failed to prove he was the registered owner at the time of the offence or that he took all precautions to prevent the vehicle's misuse.
defence_version_summary: The 3rd and 4th Respondents initially pleaded not guilty but later pleaded guilty. The Appellant, in the confiscation inquiry, claimed he purchased the vehicle before the offence but registered it after, and that the offence was committed without his knowledge. The Court rejected this as collusive and an attempt to mislead.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed the disputed facts and found the Magistrate and High Court had properly conducted inquiries and considered evidence. It cited precedent that revisionary jurisdiction requires exceptional circumstances, which were absent. The Court agreed with the High Court that the Appellant failed to prove he was the registered owner at the time of offence or that he took all precautions, as required by the Forest Ordinance proviso. The Court found evidence of collusion between the Appellant and accused to mislead on ownership transfer timing.
coa_sentence_type: Fine against accused (confirmed), Confiscation of vehicle MWPA-2814 (confirmed)
brief_judgment_file_summary: The Appellant, claiming ownership of vehicle MWPA-2814, appealed against the High Court's dismissal of his revision application challenging the Magistrate's order confiscating the vehicle used to transport illegally felled teak. The 3rd and 4th Respondents had pleaded guilty to the forest offence. The Court of Appeal held that the Magistrate and High Court properly considered evidence, including registration documents showing transfer after the offence, and found no exceptional circumstances to exercise revisionary jurisdiction. The appeal was dismissed with costs.
defence_counsel: Dimuthu Bandara with Kaheliya Alahakoon and Buddhika Thilakarathna
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court Judge considered the Magistrate's order and found no exceptional circumstances to invoke revisionary jurisdiction, noting the Appellant failed to prove ownership at the time of offence or lack of knowledge. The COA concurred with this analysis.
precedents_cited_list: Hotel Galaxy Ltd v Mercantile Hotel Management Ltd (1987) 1 SLR 5 | Cademmanpulle v Ceylon Paper Sacks Ltd (2001) 3 SLR 112 | W.M Piyal Senadheera v AG Appeal No. 249/2017
standard_of_review_applied: Revisionary jurisdiction requiring exceptional circumstances for intervention
sentencing_principles_applied: Confiscation under Forest Ordinance: proviso allows owner to avoid confiscation if they prove taking all precautions or vehicle used without knowledge.

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: section 296 of the Penal Code
location_of_offence: Gonaganaara within the jurisdiction of the High Court of Monaragala
brief_facts_summary: The deceased was found dead with cut injuries near the appellant's house. The prosecution's case relied on circumstantial evidence, including the deceased's last movements toward the appellant's residence, the recovery of a knife and a bloodstained sarong from the appellant's house based on his statement, and DNA matching the deceased's blood on the sarong. The appellant was a Civil Defence Force member familiar with police work.
evidence_type_secondary: Circumstantial evidence, Government Analyst Report, Medical evidence (JMO)
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: section 296 of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court Judge found the appellant guilty of murder based on circumstantial evidence. The judge was satisfied the evidence pointed irresistibly to the appellant's guilt and sentenced him to death.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant challenged the credibility of the main investigator (PW-09) and a witness (PW-03), claimed the prosecution failed to prove the chain of custody of productions, and argued the circumstantial evidence was insufficient to conclude only he could have committed the crime. He also alleged he was illegally arrested and tortured.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The learned High Court Judge failed to consider the credibility of the main investigator, namely PW-09. | Did the learned High Court Judge fail to consider that the prosecution has failed to prove the inward journey of productions beyond reasonable doubt? | Did the learned High Court Judge fail to consider the credibility of PW-03? | Did the learned High Court Judge misdirected herself in considering the fact that it was the accused and no one else who had the opportunity to commit the crime?
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The COA found the evidence of PW-09 (investigating officer) and PW-03 (boutique owner) credible. It held that minor omissions did not undermine their truthfulness. The chain of custody of the blood sample was found secure despite minor recording lapses.
probability_assessment_by_court: The COA applied the principle that circumstantial evidence must be consistent only with guilt and inconsistent with any reasonable hypothesis of innocence. It found the totality of evidence met this standard beyond reasonable doubt.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty and made a statement from the dock. He denied the charge, claimed illegal arrest and torture by police, alleged evidence was planted (blood applied to sarong), and stated the recovered knife and clothes were taken from open areas of his house. The court found his allegations unsupported and an afterthought.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The COA meticulously analyzed each ground of appeal. It found the High Court Judge correctly applied the law on circumstantial evidence, assessing the totality like strands of a rope. The COA upheld the credibility of the investigator and key witness, finding no material contradictions. It confirmed the chain of custody of the blood sample was not compromised. The DNA match on the appellant's sarong was found compelling with no possibility of tampering. The court noted a motive (suspicion of an illicit relationship) existed, though not required. The COA concluded the prosecution proved its case beyond reasonable doubt.
coa_sentence_type: Death sentence affirmed
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused-appellant was convicted of murder by the High Court of Monaragala and sentenced to death. He appealed challenging witness credibility, chain of custody, and sufficiency of circumstantial evidence. The Court of Appeal thoroughly examined the grounds, finding the High Court correctly evaluated the circumstantial evidence, which included the deceased's last movements, recovery of the murder weapon and a bloodstained sarong from the appellant's house, and a DNA match. The appeal was dismissed, and the conviction and death sentence were affirmed.
defence_counsel: Niroshan Mihindukulasuriya
cause_of_death_exact_text: The first injury has been to the neck, which has caused serious injuries to the deceased and had been the injury that has caused his death.
hc_analysis_summary: The COA found the High Court Judge was well conversant with the legal requirements for proving a case based on circumstantial evidence. The HC correctly identified and assessed the circumstantial evidence strands and came to a proper conclusion. The COA only differed slightly on labeling one piece of evidence a 'dying declaration' but agreed on its probative value.
precedents_cited_list: The King Vs. Abeywickrama 44 NLR 254 | Don Sunny Vs. The Attorney General (1998) 2 SLR 01 | King Vs. Gunaratne 47 NLR 145 | Regina Vs. Exall (176 English Reports, Nisi Prius at page 853) | Karunaratne Vs. Attorney-General (2005) 2 SLR 233 | Sarwan Singh Vs State of Punjab 2002 AIR Supreme Court iii 3652 | Boby Mathew Vs State of Karnataka 2004 3 Cri. L. J.3003
standard_of_review_applied: The COA reviewed whether the High Court's conclusions were reasonable based on the evidence, applying principles for circumstantial evidence cases.

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code
location_of_offence: At PW2's new house under construction
brief_facts_summary: The Appellant assaulted the deceased with a pole on the head while the deceased was seated on a veranda, causing him to fall. The Appellant then dragged the deceased to adjacent land where a large rock was later found placed on his head. The police recovered an iron rod based on the Appellant's statement. The deceased had a history as an Island Reconvicted Criminal but was not involved in any brawl at the time.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court Judge found the Appellant guilty of murder after a non-jury trial. The Judge considered the evidence presented and the defence taken, and sentenced the Appellant to death.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The sole ground of appeal was the failure of the Trial Judge to properly evaluate the defence evidence regarding the plea of Cumulative Provocation. The Appellant argued that the case should be considered under Section 297 (culpable homicide not amounting to murder) due to cumulative provocation.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Failure to properly evaluate defence evidence with regard to the plea of Cumulative Provocation
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The prosecution called witnesses including eyewitnesses to the assault and dragging of the deceased, and the JMO. The defence called the Appellant and five witnesses to support the claim of cumulative provocation, but no evidence of a sudden fight or complaints against the deceased was presented.
probability_assessment_by_court: The court assessed that the Appellant failed to prove the existence of a special exception (cumulative provocation) on a balance of probabilities.
defence_version_summary: The Appellant pleaded not guilty. He gave evidence and called five witnesses. The defence claimed the incident resulted from cumulative provocation by the deceased, citing past harassment and killing a rooster. However, no complaints were made to police. The court found the defence version unsubstantiated.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed the plea of cumulative provocation under Exception-1 to Section 294 of the Penal Code. It reviewed the development of law on cumulative provocation in Sri Lankan and Indian jurisprudence. The court found no evidence that the deceased provoked the Appellant at the time of the assault. The Appellant's claim of sustained mental stress from past events was not supported by evidence of complaints or that the final incident was triggered by provocation. The COA agreed with the High Court Judge's refusal to grant the mitigatory plea.
coa_sentence_type: Death
brief_judgment_file_summary: The Appellant was convicted of murder by the High Court of Kalutara and sentenced to death. He appealed solely on the ground that the Trial Judge failed to properly evaluate the defence evidence on cumulative provocation, which should have reduced the charge to culpable homicide. The Court of Appeal examined the legal development of cumulative provocation but found no evidence of provocation at the time of the incident or that past events led to a loss of self-control. The court affirmed the conviction and sentence, dismissing the appeal.
defence_counsel: Kasun Liyanage with Thilakkana Indunil
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court Judge considered the evidence and defence, and correctly refused to award the benefit of the mitigatory plea of cumulative provocation. The COA found no error in the High Court's analysis.
precedents_cited_list: The King v Bellana Withanage Eddin 41 NLR 345 | Premalal v Attorney General [2000] 2 SLR 403 | W. A. Gamini v Attorney General CA/142/2009 | R. W. Nandana Senarathbandara v Attorney General SC/Appeal/32/2015 | Poovammal v State 2012 (2) MLJ (Crt.) 482 | Suyambukkani Vs State of Tamil Nadu [1989 LW (Crt.) 86] | K. M. Nanavathi Vs State of Maharastra [A.I.R.] 1962 S.C. 605
standard_of_review_applied: Evaluation of whether the Trial Judge properly considered the defence evidence on cumulative provocation, and whether the plea should succeed on a balance of probabilities.

judges: P. Kumararatnam, J. | R. P. Hettiarachchi, J.
offence_sections: Section 4(2) of the Offensive Weapon Act read together with Section 32 of the Penal Code; Section 300 read together with Section 32 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: PW1, a security officer at Galle Municipal Council, was ambushed on his way home on 02.09.1999. He was attacked with a hand grenade and shot at, sustaining injuries that required hospitalization. PW1 went missing before concluding his evidence, and his non-summary deposition was later marked. The Judicial Medical Officer (PW4) stated the injuries were non-grievous and insufficient to cause death.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 4(2) of the Offensive Weapon Act read together with Section 32 of the Penal Code; Section 300 read together with Section 32 of the Penal Code
hc_sentence_type: Count 1: 12 years rigorous imprisonment. Count 2: 2 years rigorous imprisonment. Sentences to run concurrently.
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the Appellant on both counts of attempted murder and sentenced him to rigorous imprisonment, fines, and compensation. The 2nd Accused was acquitted.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The Appellant argued the trial judge failed to apply her judicial mind properly, misdirected herself in evaluating contradictions and omissions, wrongly considered the incomplete testimony of PW1, and thereby deprived him of a fair trial, resulting in an erroneous conviction.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The learned Trial Judge had failed to apply her judicial mind in arriving at a finding whether the prosecution has proved its case beyond a reasonable doubt. | The learned Trial Judge had misdirected herself by failing to judicially evaluate the inter se and per se contradictions and omissions which casts a reasonable doubt on the prosecution’s case with regard to the credibility of the witnesses and thereby the conviction is bad in law. | The learned Trial Judge had failed legally to consider and evaluate the evidence of PW1 elicited at the non-summary trial adopted in terms of Section 33 of the Evidence Ordinance. Further, the learned Trial Judge had also failed to legally consider and evaluate the incomplete testimony of PW1 placed on record and had thereby erred in fact and in law. | The conviction is contrary to law and against the weight of the evidence thereby the learned Trial Judge had erroneously determined the culpability of each accused. | The learned Trial Judge had failed to properly and legally consider the totality of evidence and thereby deprived a fair trial to the Appellant.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The prosecution called 6 witnesses. The key witness PW1 gave incomplete testimony and his non-summary deposition was improperly relied upon. The medical evidence indicated non-grievous injuries.
probability_assessment_by_court: Court found the prosecution failed to prove the case beyond reasonable doubt, noting PW1's incomplete testimony and failure to name assailants to the doctor.
defence_version_summary: The Appellant pleaded not guilty, gave evidence under oath, and closed his case. The court found the prosecution evidence insufficient to sustain conviction.
legal_errors_description: The trial judge wrongfully adopted the incomplete evidence of PW1 from the non-summary inquiry under Section 33 of the Evidence Ordinance and acted on it to convict.
procedural_defects_description: Proceeding with the case and convicting based on the incomplete deposition of PW1, who went missing, constituted a serious procedural error causing prejudice.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found a serious misdirection by the High Court Judge. The judge wrongly admitted and relied on the incomplete non-summary deposition of PW1, who had gone missing, to convict the Appellant. This procedural irregularity caused great prejudice. The ASG conceded this error. The COA held the prosecution's evidence, including the incomplete testimony and medical evidence indicating non-grievous injuries where the victim did not name the assailants, failed to establish the charges beyond reasonable doubt.
coa_sentence_type: Conviction and sentence set aside. Appellant acquitted.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The Appellant was convicted by the High Court of Balapitiya on two counts of attempted murder for an attack on PW1 in 1999 and sentenced to imprisonment, fines, and compensation. He appealed, arguing the trial judge erred in law and fact by relying on the incomplete deposition of PW1, who went missing, and failing to properly evaluate evidence. The Court of Appeal agreed, finding a serious procedural misdirection prejudiced the Appellant. The prosecution evidence, including the incomplete testimony and medical evidence of non-grievous injuries, failed to prove the case beyond reasonable doubt. The appeal was allowed, the conviction and sentence were set aside, and the Appellant was acquitted.
defence_counsel: Akkila Jayasundara with Akhila Mathishi
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted based on the incomplete evidence of PW1. The COA found this was a wrongful adoption of evidence under Section 33 of the Evidence Ordinance and a failure to ensure a fair trial.
standard_of_review_applied: Review of whether the prosecution proved its case beyond reasonable doubt and whether procedural errors prejudiced the trial.

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 364(3) of the Penal Code as amended by Penal Code Amendment Act No. 22 of 1995 (incest under Section 364A)
brief_facts_summary: The appellant was convicted for raping his 8-year-old daughter multiple times between January and May 2014 while her mother was overseas. The incidents occurred in their family home. The victim disclosed the abuse to a neighbor, Priyanthi (PW-02), who lodged a police complaint. Medical evidence showed signs of penile penetration.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 364(3) of the Penal Code as amended by Penal Code Amendment Act No. 22 of 1995
hc_sentence_type: 19 years rigorous imprisonment, fine Rs. 25,000 with default sentence of one year simple imprisonment
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court found the appellant guilty of raping his daughter, considering the victim's testimony and medical evidence. The judge imposed a 19-year rigorous imprisonment term and a fine, noting aggravating and mitigating circumstances.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant challenged his conviction and sentence on multiple grounds, including failure to prove the place of incident, consideration of bad character evidence, procedural defects regarding Attorney General's sanction, inconsistency between conviction and sentencing sections, defective charge, contradictions in prosecution evidence, and improper consideration of defence evidence.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The prosecution has failed to prove the place of the incident. | The learned High Court Judge has considered bad character evidence of the accused. | Failure to annex the written sanction of the Attorney General as required in a case of incest in terms of section 364A vitiates the conviction. | The learned High Court Judge has considered the ingredients of section 364A(3) of the Penal Code when convicting the accused, but when sentencing the learned High Court Judge has considered section 364(3) of the Penal Code. | Prosecution has been conducted on a defective charge. | The prosecution has failed to satisfy Court that the evidence of prosecution witnesses passed the tests of consistency, probability, and the inter se and per se contradictions. | The learned High Court Judge has not considered the defence evidence in its correct perspective.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court found the victim's testimony credible despite omissions and contradictions, considering her young age and trauma. The JMO's medical evidence corroborated penile penetration. Defence witnesses, including the appellant's other children, were found to be favoring the appellant and lacked credibility.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court found the victim's testimony credible and consistent with medical evidence, rejecting the defence's suggestion of false implication.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty and made a dock statement denying the allegations. He claimed the neighbor Priyanthi's husband committed the abuse and that Priyanthi instigated a false complaint to keep the children and their mother's money. Defence witnesses (his other children and a neighbor) testified in his favor but were discredited by the court.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal systematically rejected all grounds of appeal. It held the minor discrepancy in the place of incident was not material, the Attorney General's filing of the indictment implied sanction, no separate sanction was needed, and sentencing under section 364(3) was correct. The Court found no improper bad character evidence and held the victim's testimony, despite minor omissions, was credible and consistent with medical evidence. It cited precedents on child witness reliability and trauma. The sentence was deemed fair considering aggravating and mitigating circumstances.
coa_sentence_type: 19 years rigorous imprisonment affirmed, fine of Rs. 25,000 with default sentence of one year simple imprisonment affirmed. Sentence deemed commenced from 18-10-2023.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused-appellant appealed his conviction and 19-year sentence for raping his 8-year-old daughter. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal, rejecting grounds concerning place of incident, Attorney General's sanction, charge defect, evidence contradictions, and consideration of defence evidence. The Court found the victim's testimony credible and corroborated by medical evidence. The sentence was upheld as fair.
defence_counsel: Asanka Mendis with Shehan Rajapakse
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court correctly considered the evidence, found the victim credible, and imposed a sentence after weighing aggravating and mitigating factors. The COA found no error in the HC's reasoning or analysis.
precedents_cited_list: King vs. Marshall Appuhamy (1949) 51 N.L.R. page 140, 45 C.L.W. pages 49 | D. Tikiribanda Vs. The Attorney General (2009) Bar Association Law Reports 2010 (B.L.R.) 92 | Bhoginbhai Hirjibhai Vs. State of Gujarat (AIR 1983-SC 753)
standard_of_review_applied: Appellate review of conviction and sentence, assessing errors of law and fact
sentencing_principles_applied: Consideration of aggravating and mitigating circumstances, mandatory minimum sentence, and maximum sentence under relevant section

judges: P. Kumararatnam, J. | R. P. Hettiarachchi, J.
offence_sections: Section 296 read with Section 32 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The incident started at the house of PW4, who sold liquor. On the day, the three appellants and the deceased consumed liquor. The 1st Appellant attempted to take something from the deceased's bag, hitting the deceased when resisted. The deceased later left but was not seen alive again. PW7 later saw all appellants coming from the deceased's house. The 1st and 2nd Appellants later threatened witnesses. A cotton tree club used in the crime was recovered and matched by the Government Analyst.
evidence_type_secondary: Dying declaration, Eyewitness testimony, Physical evidence (clubs), Medical evidence
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 296 read with Section 32 of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court Judge convicted all three appellants of murder based on the evidence and sentenced them to death on 05.04.2019.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellants challenged the conviction on multiple grounds, including the sufficiency of evidence, the reliability of prosecution witnesses, the admissibility and reliance on a dying declaration, and material contradictions and omissions in the prosecution case. They also argued the case was based entirely on circumstantial evidence.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Whether the prosecution has failed to establish the ingredients of the charge of murder beyond reasonable doubt. | Whether the High Court Judge erred in concluding that the prosecution witnesses are trustworthy. | Whether the High Court Judge erred in concluding that the deceased made a dying declaration under Section 32 of the Evidence Ordinance and basing the judgment on it. | Whether the High Court Judge failed to consider some material contradictions in the evidence of the prosecution witnesses. | That the High Court Judge failed to consider the principles of law relating to a case entirely based on circumstantial evidence. | That the High Court Judge failed to appreciate the probability factors of the prosecution witnesses. | That the High Court Judge failed to consider that the prosecution witnesses contradict each other.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The court found strong incriminating circumstantial evidence against the 1st and 2nd Appellants, including their movements, threats to witnesses, and recovery of weapons. The evidence against the 3rd Appellant was weak, relying on an omission by PW7 regarding his presence.
probability_assessment_by_court: The court assessed the cumulative weight of the circumstantial evidence and found it eliminated the hypothesis of innocence for the 1st and 2nd Appellants beyond reasonable doubt, but created a reasonable doubt for the 3rd Appellant.
defence_version_summary: The appellants opted for a non-jury trial, made dock statements, and closed their case. They pleaded not guilty. The defence did not call witnesses.
legal_errors_description: The High Court Judge failed to properly consider the omission by PW7 regarding the presence of the 3rd Appellant, which went to the root of the prosecution's case against him.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed the case as entirely based on circumstantial evidence. It affirmed the admission of the dying declaration under Section 32(1) of the Evidence Ordinance as the statement was authentic and pertained to the cause of death. The court found the cumulative circumstantial evidence strong and incriminating against the 1st and 2nd Appellants, confirming the High Court's analysis. However, it found a material omission in PW7's evidence regarding the 3rd Appellant's presence, which created reasonable doubt. Citing precedents, the court held that not every inconsistency undermines a witness's credibility, but this particular omission was material and should have been considered in favour of the 3rd Appellant.
coa_sentence_type: Death sentence affirmed for the 1st and 2nd Appellants; 3rd Appellant acquitted.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The three Accused-Appellants were convicted of murder by the High Court of Chilaw and sentenced to death. They appealed to the Court of Appeal, challenging the sufficiency of evidence, witness reliability, and the dying declaration. The Court of Appeal found the cumulative circumstantial evidence strong against the 1st and 2nd Appellants and upheld their conviction and death sentence. However, due to a material omission in a witness statement regarding the 3rd Appellant's presence, the court found reasonable doubt and acquitted him.
defence_counsel: Jagath Nanayakkara for the 1st Appellant, Nihara Randeniya for the 2nd Appellant, K.A. Upul Anuradha Wickramaratne for the 3rd Appellant
cause_of_death_exact_text: death of the deceased had resulted from a hard blow to the right side of the head which had caused severe brain damage
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court Judge convicted all three appellants based on the evidence, including the dying declaration. The COA found the High Court correctly analyzed evidence against the 1st and 2nd Appellants but erred by not considering a material omission in PW7's evidence that undermined the case against the 3rd Appellant.
precedents_cited_list: R v Waters [2023] QCA 243 | Shepherd v The Queen (1990) 170 CLR 573 | Dharmawansa Silva and Another v. The Republic of Sri Lanka [1981] 2 Sri.L.R.439 | The Attorney General v. Sandanam Pitchi Mary Theresa (2011) 2 Sri L.R. 292
standard_of_review_applied: The court assessed whether the High Court's conviction was supported by evidence and whether any legal errors were made, particularly regarding the evaluation of circumstantial evidence and witness credibility.

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 56(1) of the Finance Business Act No. 42 of 2011 read with Section 113(a)(1) of the Penal Code; Section 56(1) read with Sections 2(4), 53(1) and 2(4) of the Finance Business Act No. 42 of 2011
offence_category: Financial Crime (Operating Finance Business Without License)
brief_facts_summary: The 5th Respondent (Swarnamahal Jewellers (Pvt) Ltd) was incorporated primarily for jewellery business but engaged in finance business without registration or license. It failed to repay deposits. Following a Presidential Commission of Inquiry, the CID investigated and the Attorney General filed an indictment against the accused (the company and its directors) in the High Court of Colombo. The High Court Judge discharged the accused after upholding preliminary objections.
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court Judge upheld the 3rd preliminary objection that the Finance Business Act No. 42 of 2011 cannot be applied retrospectively to offences committed under the repealed Finance Companies Act No. 78 of 1988. The Judge held proceeding under a defective indictment was pointless and discharged the accused, but noted this was no bar to a fresh indictment.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The Petitioner (Attorney General) appealed the High Court order discharging the accused. The core ground was the High Court Judge's failure to consider Section 71(2) of the Finance Business Act No. 42 of 2011, which preserves requirements from the repealed Act and links the two laws, thereby allowing retrospective application. The Petitioner argued the offences under both Acts are identical and the new Act should not allow offenders to escape prosecution.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Failure to consider Section 71(2) of the Finance Business Act No. 42 of 2011, which links the repealed and new Acts. | Erroneous conclusion that the Finance Business Act No. 42 of 2011 cannot apply retrospectively.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The judgment is focused on a legal revision application concerning preliminary objections. No analysis of witness evidence is provided.
probability_assessment_by_court: No assessment of reasonable doubt made; the appeal was decided on a pure legal point.
defence_version_summary: The Accused-Respondents pleaded not guilty. Their defence was raised via preliminary objections challenging the legality of the indictment, including the retrospective application of law and the principle of alter ego.
legal_errors_description: The High Court Judge failed to consider Section 71(2) of the Finance Business Act No. 42 of 2011, which links the repealed Finance Companies Act with the new Act, thereby making the requirements of the repealed Act continue under the new Act where not inconsistent. This failure led to the erroneous conclusion that the new Act could not apply retrospectively to the alleged offences.
procedural_defects_description: The High Court discharged the accused based on preliminary objections before trial, which the Court of Appeal found was done without proper consideration of a relevant legal provision (Section 71(2)).
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal focused on the legal interpretation of Section 71(2) of the Finance Business Act No. 42 of 2011. It held that this provision explicitly links the repealed Finance Companies Act (No. 78 of 1988) with the new Act, preserving its requirements where not inconsistent. Therefore, the requirement to register and obtain a license for finance business continued under the new Act. The COA found the High Court Judge's failure to consider this provision was an error in law. It set aside the discharge order and remitted the case for the High Court to consider the remaining preliminary objections.
coa_sentence_type: Order of discharge set aside; case remanded to High Court to consider remaining preliminary objections.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The Attorney General filed a revision application challenging the Colombo High Court's order discharging the accused (directors and their company) from charges of operating a finance business without a license. The High Court had upheld a preliminary objection that the Finance Business Act 2011 could not apply retrospectively. The Court of Appeal allowed the appeal, finding the High Court erred by not considering Section 71(2) of the 2011 Act, which links it to the repealed 1988 Act. The COA set aside the discharge order and directed the High Court to consider the other preliminary objections before proceeding to trial.
defence_counsel: Shavindra Fernando, PC with Anil Silva, PC, Anuja Premaratne, PC, Amman Bandara and Natasha De Alwis
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court analyzed the retrospective application of the Finance Business Act 2011 and concluded it did not specifically provide for retrospective effect for offences under Section 56. The COA found this analysis erroneous because it failed to consider Section 71(2), which provides a bridge between the old and new Acts.
standard_of_review_applied: Revision under Article 138 of the Constitution; review of legal error in High Court order.

judges: Menaka Wijesundera J. | Wickum A. Kaluarachchi J.
brief_facts_summary: The case concerns a land sale where the real owners (PW-01 and PW-02), orphaned siblings, entrusted their documents to the 1st accused, their brother-in-law, to sell their land. The 1st accused, with a land broker (PW-06), engaged a notary (PW-03). A forged sales agreement was later discovered, executed by impersonators posing as the owners, with PW-03's wife (PW-04) as the beneficiary. The real owners discovered the fraud when development began on the land. The accused appellants were charged with aiding and abetting forgery.
evidence_type_secondary: Documentary evidence (forged agreement), Expert evidence (handwriting analysis)
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the accused-appellants on charges of aiding and abetting forgery and sentenced them accordingly. The trial judge relied on the evidence, particularly that of PW-06, to find guilt.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellants argued that the trial judge erred by not considering the failure of attesting witnesses to verify identities, inadequacies in the evidence of PW-06, failing to properly consider the defense case, and that the charges were defective.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The trial judge had not been mindful of the fact that the two witnesses who attested the alleged document had failed to discharge their duty of ascertaining the identity of the attesting vendor. | The trial judge had failed to consider the inadequacies in the evidence of PW-06. | The trial judge has failed to consider the defense case in its proper perspective. | Charges being defective.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the key prosecution witness (PW-06) unreliable due to vital omissions and contradictions, particularly his failure to tell the CID about the 2nd accused's involvement. The notary (PW-03) was found to have shirked his duties. The real owners (PW-01, PW-02) did not allege the 1st accused's involvement in forgery.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court found the prosecution failed to prove charges beyond reasonable doubt, highlighting unreliable witness testimony and lack of direct evidence linking the 1st accused to the impersonation act.
defence_version_summary: The 1st accused pleaded not guilty, testified on oath that he acted honestly to help the owners sell the land, and denied the charges. He stated he gave documents to a broker (Sooriyaarachchi) who then engaged the notary. He called a witness (Mahendra Wellkala) in support. The 2nd accused made a statement from the dock. The Court found the 1st accused's evidence withstood cross-examination.
legal_errors_description: The trial judge failed to properly assess the reliability of PW-06's evidence, which contained vital omissions and contradictions, and failed to appreciate the failure of duty by the attesting witness and notary.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed the evidence and found the prosecution's case rested heavily on the unreliable testimony of PW-06, who had serious omissions (not informing CID about the 2nd accused's role). The Court noted the 1st accused was not present at the key attestation where impersonation occurred, and the real owners did not accuse him of forgery. The notary (PW-03) failed his duty. The trial judge erred by relying on PW-06's infirm evidence and not properly considering the defense case and the reasonable doubt created. The prosecution did not prove the charges beyond reasonable doubt.
coa_sentence_type: Acquitted. No sentence imposed.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The 1st and 2nd accused were convicted by the High Court of Colombo for aiding and abetting forgery concerning a land sale using impersonators. They appealed. The Court of Appeal found the key prosecution witness (PW-06) unreliable due to omissions, and the notary (PW-03) negligent. The real owners did not blame the 1st accused. The Court held the prosecution failed to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt, allowed the appeal, and acquitted both appellants.
defence_counsel: Sarath Jaymanne P.C with Ms. Vineshka Mendis, Prashan Wickramaratne, Sujeewa Meegahawatte, Dakshin Abeykoon and D. Ratnayake
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court heavily relied on the evidence of PW-06 to convict. The Court of Appeal found this was an error, as PW-06's evidence was unreliable and contained vital omissions which the trial judge failed to properly consider, leading to a miscarriage of justice.
standard_of_review_applied: Assessment of whether the prosecution proved its case beyond reasonable doubt based on the evidence on record.

judges: Sobhitha Rajakaruna J. | Menaka Wijesundera J. | Mayadunne Corea J.
offence_sections: Article 105 (3) of the Constitution and the law of contempt of court as defined in case law
brief_facts_summary: Proceedings were initiated against the Respondent (Adambarage Desmond Chathuranga De Alwis) based on a web article he uploaded on lankanewsweb.org on 30.04.2020, containing purported accusations of bribery and corruption against judges of the Court of Appeal. The article was widely circulated on social media. The CID investigated and confirmed the Respondent uploaded the article. The Respondent absconded, having left the country while related magistrate's court proceedings were pending, leading the Court to proceed with the inquiry in his absence.
evidence_type_secondary: CID investigation reports, Digital Forensic Laboratory reports, Immigration records
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The judgment does not detail specific grounds of appeal raised by the Respondent, as the proceedings were initiated by the Court under Article 105(3) for contempt. The Respondent was absent and did not present a defence. The Court's analysis focused on whether the published article constituted contempt.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court examined several prosecution witnesses from the CID and Immigration Department. Their evidence established that the Respondent uploaded the article, acted as the website administrator, and was absconding. Digital forensic evidence linked the article to him. The Court found the evidence satisfactory and uncontroverted.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court found the charges proved beyond reasonable doubt based on direct evidence linking the Respondent to the publication and his absence indicating awareness of proceedings.
defence_version_summary: The accused did not appear and offered no defence. He did not plead guilty, present witnesses, or give a dock statement. The Court found he was evading proceedings and was aware of the charges.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed the evidence proving the Respondent authored and published the defamatory article targeting specific Appeal Court judges. It found the statements were false, malicious, and intended to insult the court and lower its authority. The Court referenced contempt precedents defining the offence as acts calculated to bring the court into disrepute or obstruct justice. It confirmed the burden of proof beyond reasonable doubt was met, noted the Respondent's absence did not hinder the inquiry due to the Court's inherent powers, and concluded the article seriously violated the duty to protect judicial integrity.
coa_sentence_type: Guilty of contempt of court; punishment to be determined (the judgment states 'the said Accused should be punished for such contempt' but does not specify the sentence)
brief_judgment_file_summary: The Court of Appeal convicted Adambarage Desmond Chathuranga De Alwis for contempt of court under Article 105(3) of the Constitution. He had published a web article falsely accusing Court of Appeal judges of bribery, which was widely circulated. The CID investigation proved his authorship and role as website administrator. The Respondent absconded, so the Court proceeded in absentia. Based on witness and digital forensic evidence, the Court found the charges proved beyond reasonable doubt, holding the publication was malicious and intended to scandalize the court. The appeal was dismissed, and he was found guilty, with punishment to follow.
prosecution_counsel: Dilan Ratnayake PC, ASG with Chaya Sri Nammuni DSG for the Attorney General
precedents_cited_list: Vijitha Herath v. Secretary to the Treasury SC Contempt 2 -2023 dated 14.11.2023 | Madiyanselage Vijit Reginald Perera v. The King 52 NLR 293 | Reg v. Gray 1900 2 Q.B. 36 | Cross and Another vs Dabrera (1999) 1 SLR 205 | Regina vs Kopito
standard_of_review_applied: Proof beyond reasonable doubt as for a criminal charge
sentencing_principles_applied: The judgment notes contempt bears a criminal character and must be satisfactorily proved. It references the need to maintain respect for the court and public faith in administration of justice.

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 296 of Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: On 22/08/2008 around 9:30am, PW1 and PW2 heard shouts and found the deceased Padmawathi fallen with the Appellant standing nearby holding a crowbar. Padmawathi uttered 'Aru Jagath, Jagath' before PW1 went to the police. The Appellant was charged with murdering two persons, his wife and another. He made a dock statement denying the charges, claiming he found the deceased upon returning home and raised cries. PW2, though named as a prosecution witness, was called as a defence witness.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 296 of Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: Following a jury trial, the High Court convicted the Appellant on both counts of murder and sentenced him to death on 12/08/2016. The jury found the Appellant guilty based on the evidence presented, including the dying declaration and recovery of the weapon.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The Appellant argued he was denied a fair trial due to procedural errors in announcing the verdict and refusal to call the Magistrate. He also claimed misdirections on the standard of proof, evidential value of his dock statement, dying declaration, Section 27 recovery, culpable homicide, and that the verdict was against the evidence.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Denial of fair trial under Article 13(3): Registrar announced verdict before Foreman; refusal to call Magistrate who conducted inquest. | Misdirection on standard of proof. | Misdirection on evidential value of dock statement. | Misdirection that weakness of defence establishes prosecution case. | Misdirection about dying declaration. | Misdirection about Section 27(1) recovery of Evidence Ordinance. | Misdirection regarding culpable homicide not amounting to murder. | Verdict is against the evidence.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal reviewed the evidence, including the dying declaration to PW1, recovery of the crowbar under Section 27, and medical evidence from JMOs (PW5, PW6). It found the High Court Judge properly directed the jury on all matters, and the evidence sufficiently established guilt beyond reasonable doubt.
probability_assessment_by_court: Court concluded prosecution proved case beyond reasonable doubt; no other reasonable verdict possible.
defence_version_summary: The Appellant pleaded not guilty. He made a dock statement denying charges, claiming he found the deceased and raised cries. He called PW2 as a defence witness. The court found his defence did not raise reasonable doubt.
procedural_defects_description: Appellant claimed Registrar announced verdict before Foreman and refusal to call Magistrate was unreasonable. Court found no prejudice or failure of justice; errors were cured by immediate correction and proper procedure.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal meticulously analyzed each ground. It found the procedural error in verdict announcement was immediately corrected without prejudice. The refusal to call the Magistrate was proper as the application was premature and sought irregular procedure. The Court held the High Court Judge correctly directed the jury on standard of proof, dock statement, dying declaration, Section 27 recovery, and culpable homicide. The evidence, including the dying declaration and recovery of the crowbar, was highly incriminating and established guilt beyond reasonable doubt. No misdirection was found. The jury's verdict was supported by the evidence.
coa_sentence_type: Death sentence upheld
brief_judgment_file_summary: The Accused-Appellant was convicted of two counts of murder under Section 296 of the Penal Code by the High Court of Embilipitiya and sentenced to death. He appealed on grounds including denial of fair trial, misdirections on law and evidence, and excessive sentence. The Court of Appeal, after analyzing the record, found no merit in the appeal grounds. It held the trial was fair, the jury was properly directed, and the evidence conclusively proved guilt. The appeal was dismissed and the death sentence confirmed.
defence_counsel: Darshana Kuruppu with Sahan Weerasinghe
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court conducted a jury trial, gave proper directions on law and evidence, and accepted the jury's guilty verdict. The COA found no errors in the HC's reasoning or conduct of the trial.
precedents_cited_list: Woolmington v. DPP [1935] A.C.462 | Hakkini Asela De Silva and two others v The Attorney General SC Appeal No. 14/2011 | King v Martin 31 NLR 124 | Queen v. Buddharakkitha Thero 63 NLR 433 | Queen v. Kularatne 71 NLR 529 | Kalinga Padmatilake alias Sergent Elpitiya v The Director General, Commission to Investigate Allegations SC Appeal No. 99/2007 | Dharmawansa Silva and Another v. The Republic of Sri Lanka [1981] 2 Sri.L.R.439 | Sigera v Attorney General [2011] 1 Sri.L.R. 201 | Somaratne Rajapakse Others v. Hon. Attorney General (2010) 2 Sri L.R. 113
