standard_of_review_applied: Appellate review for errors in fact or law, considering whether any error occasioned a failure of justice or prejudiced substantial rights.

judges: Menaka Wijesundera, J | Wickum A. Kaluarachchi, J
offence_sections: Section 365B(2)(b) of the Penal Code
location_of_offence: Ragama, near the well adjacent to the victim's house
brief_facts_summary: The victim, a seven-year-old girl at the time, alleged that on a Sunday around 11:30 a.m., the accused-appellant who lived in the adjacent land came to the well near her house. The victim had just come out of the toilet and was not wearing clothes on her lower body. The accused kissed her genital area using his mouth. The victim was fourteen when she gave evidence at the trial.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 365B(2)(b) of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the accused of grave sexual abuse. The Judge found the victim's testimony credible and convicted the accused. He was sentenced to 10 years rigorous imprisonment, fined Rs. 25,000/- with a default sentence, and ordered to pay Rs. 100,000/- compensation with a default sentence.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant raised a primary legal issue that the judge who wrote the judgment never heard the evidence, violating Section 283(1) of the CCPA. Other grounds included failure to evaluate evidence properly, findings contrary to PW-1's evidence, and failure to evaluate legal elements of the offence.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The learned Trial Judge had failed to evaluate the evidence properly and failed to apply the legal principles. | The findings of the learned High Court Judge are not supported and contrary to the evidence of PW-1. | Hon. High Court Judge had failed to evaluate the required legal elements of the offence of grave sexual abuse and convicted the appellant for the said offence.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed the victim's testimony (PW-1) and found the discrepancy between her court evidence (kissing) and the charge (inserting tongue) was a minor omission after seven years. The court held the act of kissing the genitalia with the mouth satisfied the legal elements of grave sexual abuse.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal found no reasonable doubt and held the victim's testimony credible. The minor omission after seven years did not create doubt.
defence_version_summary: The accused-appellant pleaded not guilty. He made a statement from the dock. The defence counsel requested to adopt evidence from the previous judge and proceed. The court considered his dock statement.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal addressed the main legal issue: whether a judge who did not hear evidence can write a judgment. It held that under settled law, a succeeding judge can act on evidence recorded by a predecessor after notifying parties, which was complied with here. The court analyzed the victim's testimony, finding the discrepancy between 'kissed' and 'inserted tongue' was a minor omission after seven years and did not mislead the accused. It found the act of kissing the genitalia with the mouth constituted grave sexual abuse under Section 365B. The court upheld the High Court's credibility findings and saw no reason to interfere with the conviction or sentence.
coa_sentence_type: 10 years rigorous imprisonment, fine of Rs. 25,000/- with default sentence of 6 months simple imprisonment, and compensation of Rs. 100,000/- with default sentence of 1 year simple imprisonment
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused-appellant was convicted by the High Court of Gampaha for grave sexual abuse of a seven-year-old girl and sentenced to 10 years rigorous imprisonment, a fine, and compensation. He appealed, raising grounds including that the judge who wrote the judgment never heard the evidence. The Court of Appeal held that a succeeding judge can lawfully write a judgment based on evidence recorded by a predecessor after notifying parties, which was done here. It found the victim's testimony credible and that the act of kissing the genitalia with the mouth constituted the offence despite a minor discrepancy in description. The appeal was dismissed, affirming the conviction and sentence.
defence_counsel: Senarath Jayasundera with Chathurangi Wedage and Rehani Chandrasiri
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court Judge correctly analyzed the evidence, found the victim credible, and concluded the offence was proved. The Court of Appeal agreed with this analysis and found no errors in the High Court's reasoning.
precedents_cited_list: Nimal Pinsiri Godakandeniyage alias Nimal pinsiri V. Hon. Attorney General – Court of Appeal No. CA 77/2014 | Somapala V. The Commissioner to Investigate Bribery and Corruption- (CA (PHC) APN 37/2009, CA Minutes of 03.02.2010) | The Hon. Attorney General V. Chandana Sri Lal Gurusinghe (SC/APPEAL/139/2019) | Hettiarachchilage Wasantha Rathna V. OIC Yakkala Police Station and The Hon. Attorney General (SC/APPEAL/2/2022) | Rajapakse Gedara Nandasena alias kirikolla V. The Hon. Attorney General (SC SPL LA No: SC/SPL/LA/267/2018) | Central Finance Company PLC V. Chandrasekera – (2020) 1 Sri L.R. 161
standard_of_review_applied: The court reviewed whether the High Court judgment complied with procedural law (Section 283(1) CCPA) and whether the evidence supported the conviction.
sentencing_principles_applied: The court did not modify the sentence. The appellant's counsel did not challenge the sentence specifically. The court found no reason to interfere with the sentence imposed by the High Court.

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 317 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The appellants were tenants in a house owned by PW1's husband. A dispute arose over their suspected sale of cannabis and illicit liquor from the rental premises, leading to PW1 and her husband complaining to police and requesting they vacate. On the day of the incident, the appellants ambushed PW1 near her toilet and threw acid on her, causing severe injuries including complete blindness. PW1 identified both appellants at the scene.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 317 of the Penal Code
hc_sentence_type: 7 1/2 years rigorous imprisonment and a fine
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the appellants based on the evidence, including PW1's identification and the medical evidence. The judge found the prosecution had proved its case beyond reasonable doubt and sentenced each appellant to 7 1/2 years rigorous imprisonment, a fine, and compensation.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellants argued the High Court judge erred in law by failing to consider material discrepancies regarding visual identification, rejecting the defence on a wrong premise, and considering the unreliable evidence of the victim to convict.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The learned High Court Judge erred in law by failing to consider the material discrepancy with regard to the visual identification of the Appellants beyond reasonable doubt. | The learned High Court Judge erred in law by rejecting the defence on wrong premise. | The learned High Court Judge erred in law by considering the unreliable evidence of the victim to convict the Appellants.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The prosecution case rested primarily on PW1's eyewitness testimony. The Court of Appeal found the identification reliable despite PW1's blindness at trial, as she knew the appellants well. The medical evidence corroborated her injuries.
probability_assessment_by_court: Court found identification reliable beyond reasonable doubt, considering PW1 knew appellants well, and common intention established.
defence_version_summary: The appellants pleaded not guilty and made dock statements denying the charges. They called one defence witness. The court found their defence lacked merit, noting the 2nd appellant's confession to PW1 and the 1st appellant's failure to answer a key question.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The COA affirmed the High Court's decision. It held the identification was reliable as PW1 knew the appellants well as tenants. It applied Turnbull guidelines on identification, noting the judge was cautious. It found evidence of common intention based on planning and the 2nd appellant's confession. The COA concluded the High Court correctly analyzed evidence and proved the case beyond reasonable doubt.
coa_sentence_type: 7 1/2 years rigorous imprisonment and a fine of Rs.1500 with a default sentence of 03 months rigorous imprisonment. Compensation of Rs.150,000 each to PW1 with a default sentence of 01 year simple imprisonment. Sentence to commence from the day judgment is pronounced upon the appellants by the High Court Judge.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The appellants were convicted by the Balapitiya High Court for committing grievous hurt by throwing acid on PW1 under Section 317 of the Penal Code and sentenced to imprisonment, a fine, and compensation. They appealed on grounds of erroneous identification, unreliable evidence, and wrong premise for rejecting defence. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal, affirming the conviction and sentence. The COA found the identification reliable, common intention established, and the High Court's analysis of evidence correct.
defence_counsel: Amila Palliyage with Sandeepani Wijesooriya, S. Udugampola, Lakitha Wakishta Arachchi and Subaj De Silva
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court extensively discussed the identification by PW1, considered the defence evidence, and found the prosecution proved its case beyond reasonable doubt. The COA found the High Court's analysis accurate and without error.
precedents_cited_list: R v. Turnbull [1977] QB 224 | King v. Ranasinghe et al 47 NLR 373
standard_of_review_applied: Review of evidence and identification based on Turnbull guidelines and common intention principles.
sentencing_principles_applied: The judgment mentions the common intention principle under Section 32 of the Penal Code and joint liability.

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance as amended by the Amendment Act No. 13 of 1984
brief_facts_summary: The accused was arrested after a police raid on Dam Street on 11-08-2013 based on information that he would be handing over a heroin parcel. A parcel concealed in his undergarment was recovered and confirmed to be heroin (4.03 grams). He was indicted for trafficking and possession.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance as amended by the Amendment Act No. 13 of 1984
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court found the appellant guilty on both counts (trafficking and possession) after analyzing the evidence. The judge rejected the defence version as having no merit and improbable, concluding the prosecution proved its case beyond reasonable doubt.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant argued the trial judge denied him a fair trial by excessively questioning defence witnesses and encroaching into the prosecutor's role. The defence was not given a fair opportunity, and the judge failed to properly consider the defence version and the dock statement.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: That the learned High Court Judge has acted contrary to the provisions of section 165 of the Evidence Ordinance as he has encroached into the role of the prosecutor and thereby denied a fair trial to the appellant. | That the learned High Court Judge has not given a fair opportunity to the appellant to present the defence case. | That the learned High Court Judge has failed to consider whether the defence version passes the test of probability rather than that of the prosecution, and the dock statement of the appellant has not been considered properly.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The prosecution relied on the evidence of police officers (PW-01 and PW-02) regarding the raid, recovery, and arrest. The defence called the appellant's sister and his young daughter, whose evidence was heavily questioned by the trial judge. The COA found the judge's excessive questioning of the child witness (then 11) deprived the appellant of a fair trial.
probability_assessment_by_court: The HC judge found the defence version improbable and without merit. The COA focused on the fairness of the trial procedure rather than reassessing the probability of the defence.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty. He claimed he was walking to hand over shop collection money to his employer when arrested, assaulted, and falsely implicated. The heroin was introduced by the police. He made a dock statement and called his sister and daughter as witnesses. The HC judge rejected this defence as a built-up story.
legal_errors_description: The Court of Appeal found the trial judge acted contrary to section 165 of the Evidence Ordinance by excessively questioning defence witnesses, encroaching on the prosecutor's role, and creating an appearance of bias, thereby denying a fair trial.
procedural_defects_description: The trial judge's excessive and aggressive questioning of the defence witnesses, particularly the child witness, during her examination-in-chief and cross-examination, violating the spirit of section 165 and principles of fair trial.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The COA analyzed whether the trial judge's questioning of defence witnesses, especially the appellant's young daughter, caused prejudice and denied a fair trial under Article 13(3) of the Constitution. Citing Sri Lankan and Commonwealth precedents (State of Rajasthan v Ani, Ram Chander v State of Haryana, Sisilinona v Balasuriya, The Queen v V.P. David Perera, Jones v National Coal Board, SC (SPL) LA 184/2017, The King v Namasiwayam), the court held that while a judge has wide powers under section 165 of the Evidence Ordinance to ascertain truth, this must not be exercised to the point of appearing biased or taking over the prosecutor's role. The COA found the trial judge's intrusive questioning of the child witness—implying she was tutored and questioning her based on evidence from another witness—deprived the appellant of a manifestly fair trial, vitiating the judgment.
coa_sentence_type: Acquitted, no sentence imposed
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused was convicted by the High Court of Colombo for trafficking and possessing 4.03 grams of heroin and sentenced to life imprisonment. He appealed, arguing the trial judge denied him a fair trial by excessively questioning defence witnesses, especially his 11-year-old daughter. The Court of Appeal found the judge's questioning crossed the line under section 165 of the Evidence Ordinance, creating an appearance of bias and vitiating the trial. The conviction and sentence were set aside. Considering the incident occurred in 2013 and the appellant had been incarcerated for over 5 years, the COA declined to order a retrial and acquitted the appellant.
defence_counsel: Neranjan Jayasinghe with Randunu Heellage
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court analyzed the evidence, found the prosecution case proved beyond reasonable doubt, and rejected the defence as improbable and without merit. The COA criticized the HC judge's method, finding that his excessive and prejudicial questioning of defence witnesses, particularly a child witness, undermined the fairness of the trial and the resulting judgment.
precedents_cited_list: State of Rajasthan Vs. Ani, AIR 1997 SC 1023, 1025: 1197 CrILJ 1529 | Ram Chander Vs. The State of Haryana (AIR 1981 SC 1036) | Sisilinona Vs. Balasuriya (2002) 1 SLR 404 | The Queen Vs. V.P. David Perera 66 NLR 553 | Yuill Vs. Yuill (1945) 1 All E.R. 183 | Jones Vs. National Coal Board (1957) 2 WLR 760 | SC (SPL) LA 184/2017 – decided on 26.06.2020 | The King V. Namasiwayam Et Al. Appeals Nos. 21-24 of 1948 49 NLR 289
standard_of_review_applied: Whether the trial judge's conduct denied the appellant a fair trial guaranteed under the Constitution, examining the application of section 165 of the Evidence Ordinance and principles of judicial impartiality.

judges: Menaka Wijesundera J. | Wickum A. Kaluarachchi J.
brief_facts_summary: The accused-appellant was charged with two counts of grave sexual abuse alleged to have occurred between 01/04/2014 and 16/10/2014. The prosecution case relied mainly on the victim's evidence, stating the accused, a known elderly person, sexually abused her after she asked him for money to buy a phone card to communicate with her boyfriend. The victim reported the incident to her grandmother about three weeks after it occurred, leading to a police complaint on 17/10/2014. The accused denied the allegations, claiming false implication due to a land dispute with the victim's family.
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the accused-appellant on the first charge and acquitted him on the second charge. The conviction and sentence led to the instant appeal.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The main grounds of appeal were that the prosecution failed to prove a specific date of offence, placing an undue burden on the appellant to prove his innocence, the trial judge failed to consider contradictions in evidence, and the judgement was contrary to Section 283 of the Code of Criminal Procedure Act.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: A specific date of offence had not been proved by the prosecution. | The accused-appellant had been given an undue burden to prove his innocence. | Contradictions has not been considered by the trial judge. | The judgement is contrary to Section 283 of Code of Criminal Procedure Act.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The prosecution evidence relied on the victim, her family members, a doctor, and the police. The victim's evidence contained a vital contradiction regarding the time of the offence (telling the doctor it happened before the August vacation, but in court suggesting after). The Court of Appeal found this seriously affected her credibility.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal found the prosecution failed to establish beyond reasonable doubt that the offence was committed during the lengthy period specified in the charge, especially given the victim's contradictory statements on timing.
defence_version_summary: The accused pleaded not guilty. He made a statement from the dock denying the entire incident and claiming false implication due to a land dispute. His wife gave evidence corroborating his dock statement. The defence did not raise an alibi specifically due to the lack of a specific date.
legal_errors_description: The High Court failed to ensure the charge specified a precise date as required by Section 165(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure Act for a fair trial, and proceeded on a charge framed on vague and contradictory evidence.
procedural_defects_description: The indictment specified a period (01/04/2014 to 16/10/2014) without a specific date, violating Section 165(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure Act and denying the appellant a fair chance to formulate his defence.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed the requirement under Section 165(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure Act for charges to specify time and place to ensure a fair trial. It found the prosecution failed to prove a specific date, relying on a vague period derived from contradictory victim statements. Citing precedents like Kamburawela Kankanamalage Dayarathne v The Attorney General and Indian cases, the Court held that framing a charge on such vague evidence denied the appellant a fair trial. The vital contradiction in the victim's evidence regarding the timing further undermined the prosecution case. The Court concluded no fair trial was awarded and the appellant had no proper charge to answer.
coa_sentence_type: Acquitted of the charge in the indictment.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused-appellant was convicted by the Kurunegala High Court on one count of grave sexual abuse alleged to have occurred between 01/04/2014 and 16/10/2014. He appealed on grounds including failure to prove a specific date, contradictions in evidence, and procedural errors. The Court of Appeal, analyzing Section 165 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and relevant precedents, found the charge was framed on a vague period and contradictory evidence, denying the appellant a fair trial. The Court allowed the appeal and acquitted the appellant.
defence_counsel: Dharshana Kuruppu with Tharushi Gamage and Sahan Weerasinghe
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted the appellant based on the prosecution evidence. The Court of Appeal found the High Court failed to observe that the charge lacked a specific date as required by law and was based on vague and contradictory evidence, thereby denying a fair trial.
precedents_cited_list: Kamburawela Kankanamalage Dayarathne alias 'Chuti mama' v The Attorney General, CA 188/2015 | Attorney General v Viraj Aponso and Others S.C 24/2008 | R.H.M.S Premathunga alias Ananda v Attorney General CA 01/2013 | A.N Mukergi v State A.I.R 1969 All 489 | Ram Asrey v State of U.P 1982 A.L.J 1138 | Sukhdev v State of M.P 1995(2) Crimes 336
standard_of_review_applied: Review of legal requirements for framing charges under Section 165 of the Code of Criminal Procedure Act and assessment of evidence for fair trial violations.

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code
location_of_offence: Pallekada (Ayagama) within the jurisdiction of the High Court of Ratnapura
brief_facts_summary: A dispute arose when the deceased and his son were collecting compost fertilizer near a common boundary. The appellant's mother and sister protested, leading to a verbal altercation and physical brawl. The appellant arrived, cut filled fertilizer bags with a kathy knife, and ultimately attacked the deceased with the knife, causing a fatal head injury. The appellant claimed he acted in private defence to save his sister from being attacked by the deceased.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 294 exception 4 and section 297 of the Penal Code
hc_sentence_type: 12 years rigorous imprisonment, fine of Rs. 15,000/-, compensation of Rs. 300,000/-
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court Judge found the appellant guilty of culpable homicide not amounting to murder under section 294 exception 4, convicting him under section 297. The Judge rejected the defence of private defence, finding the appellant had exceeded his right. Considering mitigating and aggravating circumstances, the Judge imposed a sentence of 12 years rigorous imprisonment.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant argued the High Court Judge failed to give due consideration to his right of private defence exercised to save his sister from attack by the deceased. The judgment was also claimed to be contrary and in excess of the law.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The learned High Court Judge has caused grave miscarriage of justice to the accused-appellant by failing to give due consideration and importance to the right of private defence exercised by the accused-appellant. | The judgment of the learned High Court Judge is contrary and in excess to law.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The prosecution presented eyewitnesses including the deceased's wife and son. The appellant gave a dock statement and called his injured sister and a JMO as defence witnesses. The Court analyzed the conflicting accounts regarding who had the weapon and who initiated the attack.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court found no reasonable doubt regarding the appellant's role in causing death, rejecting the private defence claim and finding the act fell under sudden fight provisions.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty. He gave a dock statement claiming he acted in private defence to rescue his sister from an attack by the deceased. He called his sister and a JMO as defence witnesses. The High Court did not find his version credible, finding he had exceeded his right of private defence.
legal_errors_description: The Court of Appeal found a sentencing error: the High Court applied the first limb of section 297 (up to 20 years) when the facts warranted application of the second limb (up to 10 years).
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The COA reviewed the High Court's findings on private defence under sections 89, 90, and 92 of the Penal Code and burden of proof under section 105 of the Evidence Ordinance. It agreed with the HC that the appellant failed to establish private defence and had exceeded his right. The COA affirmed the conviction for culpable homicide not amounting to murder under exception 4 of section 294, as it was a sudden fight without premeditation. However, it found a sentencing error, holding the second limb of section 297 (up to 10 years) applied, not the first (up to 20 years). The COA cited precedents on appellate deference to trial judges' witness credibility assessments (De Silva and Others Vs. The Attorney General, Chaminda Vs. The Republic).
coa_sentence_type: 9 years rigorous imprisonment, fine of Rs. 15,000/- (default 6 months simple imprisonment), compensation of Rs. 300,000/- to PW-01 (default 1-year simple imprisonment)
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused-appellant was convicted by the High Court of Ratnapura for culpable homicide not amounting to murder, receiving 12 years rigorous imprisonment. He appealed, arguing the High Court failed to consider his right of private defence. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal against conviction, agreeing the appellant exceeded his right of private defence and the killing occurred during a sudden fight. However, it partially allowed the appeal against sentence, reducing the imprisonment to 9 years as it fell under the second limb of section 297 of the Penal Code.
defence_counsel: Hafeel Farisz with Sanjeewa Kodithuwakku, Shannon Thilakaratne and Shermina Bangsjayah
cause_of_death_exact_text: one serious cut injury to his head, which has resulted in his death
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court correctly rejected the private defence claim and convicted under section 297 for culpable homicide not amounting to murder, finding the act was committed in a sudden fight without premeditation. However, the COA found the High Court erred in applying the first limb of section 297 for sentencing instead of the second limb.
precedents_cited_list: De Silva and Others Vs. The Attorney General (2010) 2 SLR 169 | Chaminda Vs. The Republic (2009) 1 SLR 144
standard_of_review_applied: Appellate Courts are hesitant to interfere with trial judge's findings on witness credibility and fact unless determinations are contrary to evidence and law.
sentencing_principles_applied: Consideration of mitigatory and aggravating circumstances; correct application of statutory sentencing limbs under section 297 of the Penal Code.
final_charge_after_appeal: Culpable homicide not amounting to murder

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: section 364(1) of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The prosecutrix, a 53-year-old married woman, was forcibly raped by an unknown person on July 10, 2012, after returning from bathing in a canal. She noted the motorcycle number and, with help, apprehended the suspect, who was later identified as the accused. The victim was medically examined two days after the incident. The accused claimed consent as his defence.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: section 364(1) of the Penal Code
hc_sentence_type: 10 years rigorous imprisonment and a fine of Rs. 10000 with a default sentence of 1 year rigorous imprisonment
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the accused for rape under section 364(1) of the Penal Code after a non-jury trial. The judge relied on the victim's evidence, held that medical evidence cannot override ocular testimony, and disregarded minor contradictions.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant argued the victim's story was contradicted by medical evidence and that she was not a credible witness due to numerous contradictions. The defence also argued the judge failed to consider the lack of credibility and the need for corroborating evidence.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The learned trial Judge has failed to consider that the story of the prosecutrix has been contradicted by medical evidence. | The learned Trial Judge has failed to take into consideration that the prosecutrix is not a credible witness and it is unsafe to act upon the evidence owing to numerous inter se and per se contradictions that go to the very root of the prosecution case.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court found the victim's testimony consistent and credible despite some contradictions regarding injuries. The medical evidence was considered but not allowed to override her direct testimony. The court held the contradictions were minor and did not go to the root of the case.
probability_assessment_by_court: The court assessed that minor contradictions did not create reasonable doubt, and the victim's testimony was consistent and credible.
defence_version_summary: The accused pleaded not guilty and gave evidence from the witness box, taking up the defence of consent. The High Court judge rejected the defence evidence after considering it.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal upheld the High Court decision, finding no merit in the appeal grounds. The COA agreed the trial judge correctly considered the medical evidence and found it does not override the victim's ocular testimony. The contradictions in the victim's evidence were minor, did not go to the root of the case, and were properly addressed. The COA found the victim's testimony credible and consistent, and there was no reason for her to falsely implicate the appellant. The conviction and sentence were affirmed.
coa_sentence_type: 10 years rigorous imprisonment and a fine of Rs. 10000 with a default sentence of 1 year rigorous imprisonment, operative from 02.12.2022
brief_judgment_file_summary: The appellant was convicted by the High Court of Hambantota for rape under section 364(1) of the Penal Code and sentenced to 10 years rigorous imprisonment and a fine. He appealed on grounds of contradictions in the victim's story with medical evidence and lack of credibility. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal, holding the trial judge correctly evaluated the evidence, the contradictions were minor, and the victim's testimony was credible. The conviction and sentence were affirmed and ordered to run from the date of the High Court sentence.
defence_counsel: Darshana Kuruppu with Buddhika Thilakarathna
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court judge extensively considered medical evidence and contradictions, concluding medical evidence cannot override ocular testimony and that minor contradictions did not affect the case's root. The COA found this analysis correct.
precedents_cited_list: Mazur Ivegen & Iana Bereznah vs AG SC/TAB/1/2015 | The Attorney General v. Sandanam Pitchi Mary Theresa [2011] SLR Vol. 2 pg. 292 | Sunil and others v. Attorney General [1986] 1 Sri.L. R 230 | Bhoginbhai Hirjibhai v. State of Gujarat [1983] AIR 753 | State of Karnataka v S.Raju (2007) 11 SCC 490 | State of MP v Dayal Sahu (2005) 8 SCC 122
standard_of_review_applied: Appellate court review of trial judge's findings on evidence and credibility
sentencing_principles_applied: The sentence was affirmed with consideration of the time spent in remand, ordering it to run from the date of the High Court sentence.

judges: Menaka Wijesundera J. | Wickum A. Kaluarachchi J.
brief_facts_summary: The appellant was indicted for possession and trafficking of 3.43 grammes of heroin. Police received a tip-off, followed an informant, and observed the appellant receive a parcel from a three-wheeler driver. The appellant was arrested, and a parcel (N1) was found clutched in her hand. A second parcel (N2) was found in a bottle in her kitchen. Both parcels were sealed separately and sent for analysis; heroin was detected only in N1.
evidence_type_primary: Physical evidence (recovery of parcel with heroin)
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court acquitted the co-accused but convicted the appellant on charges of possession and trafficking of heroin. The trial judge found the prosecution had proved its case beyond reasonable doubt and sentenced the appellant to life imprisonment.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant argued the prosecution failed to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt due to improper analysis of evidence, contradictions and omissions in the prosecution's case, and wrongful rejection of the dock statement.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The prosecution has not proved its case beyond a reasonable doubt and the trial judge has failed to properly analyse the evidence | The trial judge has failed to consider the contradictions and omissions in the prosecution’s case | The trial judge has wrongly rejected the dock statement.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The prosecution evidence primarily consisted of testimony from the raiding officers (PW-01, PW-02) and the Government Analyst. The Court of Appeal found contradictions between PW-01 and PW-02 were not material to the root of the case.
probability_assessment_by_court: The court referenced Shivaji Sahebrao Bobade and held the standard of proof beyond reasonable doubt should not be stretched morbidly to embrace every degree of doubt.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty and made a statement from the dock denying the whole incident. The trial judge rejected the dock statement as untruthful.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found no merit in the grounds of appeal. It held that the separate sealing and handling of parcels N1 and N2 did not create reasonable doubt. Contradictions between PW-01 and PW-02 were minor and did not go to the root of the case. The trial judge properly exercised discretion in rejecting the untruthful dock statement. The court cited precedents on dock statements and appellate non-interference where the trial judge applied correct principles.
coa_sentence_type: Life Imprisonment (affirmed)
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused-appellant appealed against a High Court conviction and life sentence for possession and trafficking of 3.43g of heroin. She argued the prosecution failed to prove its case, the trial judge ignored contradictions, and her dock statement was wrongly rejected. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal, finding the separate handling of drug parcels did not create doubt, contradictions were immaterial, and the trial judge properly assessed the dock statement. The conviction and life sentence were affirmed.
defence_counsel: Neranajan Jayasinghe with Harshana Ananda, Randula Heelage and Imanzi Senarath
hc_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the trial judge meticulously considered the evidence and contradictions, and correctly applied the law. No errors were identified in the High Court's analysis.
precedents_cited_list: Shivaji Sahebrao Bobade and Anr. V State of Maharashtra 1973 AIR 2622, 1974 SCR(1) 489 | Devundarage Nihal v Attorney General CA 125/2008 | Senaka Priyantha v Attorney General, CA 91/2008 | Mataralage Nishantha Sampath v Hon Attorney General, CA Appeal No. 82/2011 | Kularatne v Queen 71 NLR 529 | Fattal v Wallbrooke Trustee (Jersey) Ltd, CA (2008) EWCA Civ 427 | Kahandagamage Dharmasiri v The Republic of Sri Lanka, SC Appeal 4/2009 | Ambikar Prasad and another v State of New Delhi 2000 SCCCrl.522
standard_of_review_applied: Appellate court should not interfere with case management decisions where the trial judge applied correct principles and considered relevant matters.
sentencing_principles_applied: Reference to principle that a criminal trial aims to do justice for accused, victim, and society, ensuring the guilty do not escape punishment.

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: section 296 of the Penal Code
location_of_offence: Rathmalakandiya within the jurisdiction of the High Court of Ampara
brief_facts_summary: The accused-appellant was charged with murdering Samantha Jagath Kumara on or about 01-12-2012. The deceased's wife (PW-01) and daughter (PW-04) witnessed a tall, dark-clothed intruder attack the deceased in their home. The appellant, who was known to the witnesses as a former neighbor, was arrested after police investigations. A knife (P-08) recovered based on his statement was found to have blood matching the deceased's DNA. The deceased allegedly had an affair with the appellant's wife, providing a motive. The appellant raised an alibi defence, which was challenged by phone records.
evidence_type_secondary: Eyewitness testimony, DNA evidence, Medical evidence, Phone records, Physical evidence (knife, clothing)
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: section 296 of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court Judge found the appellant guilty based on the eyewitness accounts of PW-01 and PW-04, who identified the appellant as the attacker, and on the circumstantial evidence. The Judge determined the prosecution proved its case beyond reasonable doubt and sentenced the appellant to death.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant challenged the conviction on two main grounds: (1) that the High Court Judge failed to properly evaluate the improbabilities and infirmities regarding the identification of the appellant by the eyewitnesses, and (2) that the Judge failed to properly evaluate the defence evidence, particularly the defence of alibi.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Has the learned High Court Judge failed to evaluate the improbabilities and infirmities regarding the identity of the appellant. | Has the learned High Court Judge failed to properly evaluate the defence evidence, especially the defence of alibi taken by the appellant.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the High Court Judge misdirected himself on the eyewitness identification, as the witnesses were well-acquainted with the appellant, undermining the need for an identification parade and the reliability of their identification. However, the COA found the circumstantial evidence, taken cumulatively, was strong enough to sustain the conviction.
probability_assessment_by_court: The COA held that the totality of the circumstantial evidence, when taken together, irresistibly pointed to the appellant's guilt and was inconsistent with any reasonable hypothesis of innocence, establishing the case beyond reasonable doubt.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty, gave notice of alibi, and made a statement from the dock. He called his wife as a defence witness. The defence claimed he was elsewhere at the time of the crime, having worked until 10 PM on 1st December and traveling home, arriving around 6:30 AM on 2nd December. He alleged police assault leading to a false admission. The COA found his alibi not credible and contradicted by phone records.
legal_errors_description: The COA found the High Court Judge misdirected himself on the issue of eyewitness identification, incorrectly relying on their positive identification at the crime scene despite evidence they knew the appellant well and initially failed to identify him.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The COA agreed the High Court Judge erred regarding eyewitness identification. However, it conducted an independent assessment of the circumstantial evidence. This included: the DNA match on the knife (P-08) recovered based on the appellant's statement; clothing matching the eyewitness description; mobile phone records placing the appellant near the crime scene around the relevant time; a clear motive arising from the deceased's affair with the appellant's wife; and the JMO's evidence linking the knife to the fatal injuries. Applying principles from cases like The King Vs. Abeywickrama and Don Sunny Vs. The Attorney General, the COA concluded the cumulative circumstantial evidence was consistent only with the appellant's guilt and inconsistent with innocence, proving the case beyond reasonable doubt. The error on identification was found not to prejudice substantial rights or cause a failure of justice under Article 138 of the Constitution.
coa_sentence_type: Death (sentence of the High Court upheld)
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused-appellant was convicted of murder by the High Court of Ampara and sentenced to death. He appealed, arguing the High Court Judge erred in evaluating eyewitness identification and his alibi defence. The Court of Appeal found the Judge misdirected himself on the identification issue, as the witnesses knew the appellant. However, the COA independently evaluated the circumstantial evidence, including DNA-matched murder weapon recovery, phone records contradicting the alibi, matching clothing, and a clear motive. Applying established principles on circumstantial evidence, the COA held the evidence cumulatively proved guilt beyond reasonable doubt. The appeal was dismissed, and the conviction and death sentence were upheld, as the identification error did not prejudice substantial rights.
defence_counsel: Mirthula Skandarajah (Assigned Counsel)
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court Judge convicted based on positive eyewitness identification and circumstantial evidence. The COA found the Judge erred in his analysis of the eyewitness identification evidence but agreed with the ultimate conclusion of guilt based on a correct, independent assessment of the strong circumstantial evidence.
precedents_cited_list: Martin Singho Vs. Queen 69 CLW 21 | The King Vs. Marshall (1948) 51 NLR 157 | Rex vs. Chandrasekera (1942) 44 NLR 126 | Rex vs. Fernando (1947) 48 NLR 251 | The King Vs. Abeywickrama 44 NLR 254 | Don Sunny Vs. The Attorney General (1998) 2 SLR 01 | King Vs. Gunaratne 47 NLR 145 | Regina Vs. Exall (176 English Reports, Nisi Prius at page 853) | Karunaratne Vs. Attorney-General (2005) 2 SLR 233
standard_of_review_applied: The COA conducted an independent assessment of the evidence, particularly the circumstantial evidence, to determine if the only reasonable inference was guilt, applying the principles for convictions based on circumstantial evidence.

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: section 296 of the Penal Code
location_of_offence: near Weddagala Temple, in the village (Poththekanda/Weddawala area)
brief_facts_summary: The accused-appellant was charged with murdering Dangampola Mudiyanselage Gunapala Munasinghe on 3 June 2001. The deceased was stabbed and later died in hospital. Key evidence included the deceased's dying declarations to his wife (PW-01) and other villagers that 'Korala' (the appellant) stabbed him, and the appellant's admission to a relative (PW-03) soon after the incident. The appellant absconded during trial, was convicted in absentia in 2012, and was sentenced to death upon arrest in 2021.
evidence_type_secondary: Medical evidence (JMO report), Circumstantial evidence (appellant's admission to relative)
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: section 296 of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court found the appellant guilty of murder based on the evidence, particularly the dying declaration. Since the appellant had absconded, the trial proceeded under section 241 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. Upon his later arrest and production, the court imposed the mandatory death sentence.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant argued he was denied a fair trial because an alleged first statement by the deceased's wife was not provided. He also challenged the proof of his identity as the perpetrator and the validity of the dying declaration, claiming the prosecution failed to prove the charge beyond reasonable doubt.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The appellant was denied a fair trial. | The prosecution has failed to prove the identity of the appellant. | The prosecution failed to prove the dying declaration of the deceased. | The charge was not proved beyond reasonable doubt against the appellant.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court found the dying declaration credible and consistent. Multiple witnesses (PW-01, PW-04, PW-07, PW-08, PW-09) corroborated that the deceased identified 'Korala' (the appellant) as his assailant. PW-03, a relative of the appellant, saw him with a knife and heard his admission soon after the incident. The JMO evidence supported the deceased's ability to speak post-incident.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court found the dying declaration consistent and corroborated by other evidence, leaving no reasonable doubt. The appellant's identity was never in serious question during trial.
defence_version_summary: The appellant did not plead guilty and did not call a defence as he absconded before the defence stage. At appeal, his counsel argued procedural unfairness (missing statement) and challenged evidence sufficiency. The court found his defence arguments lacked merit.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal rejected all grounds of appeal. It found no denial of fair trial, as PW-01's alleged first 'statement' was merely an oral report not formally recorded, so no statement was withheld. The appellant's identity was proven through the deceased's consistent dying declarations to multiple witnesses and the appellant's own admission to PW-03. The dying declaration was admissible under Section 32(1) of the Evidence Ordinance and was reliable. The prosecution proved the charge beyond reasonable doubt based on this declaration and corroborative evidence. The appeal was devoid of merit.
coa_sentence_type: Death sentence affirmed
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused-appellant was convicted of murder by the High Court of Kegalle and sentenced to death. He appealed, arguing denial of fair trial, failure to prove identity and dying declaration, and insufficient proof. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal. It held the dying declaration was reliable and admissible, the appellant's identity was clear, and there was no procedural unfairness. The conviction and death sentence were affirmed.
defence_counsel: Nalaka Samarakoon with Rajinda Kandegedara
cause_of_death_exact_text: injury number 01, which has been to the right side of the chest as the fatal stab injury
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted based on the dying declaration and corroborative evidence. The Court of Appeal found no error in the HC's analysis, agreeing that the evidence proved guilt beyond reasonable doubt.
precedents_cited_list: The King Vs. Asirvadan Nadar, 51 NLR 322
standard_of_review_applied: Review of conviction and sentence based on evidence adduced and legal grounds raised.
sentencing_principles_applied: Mandatory death sentence for murder under section 296 of the Penal Code.

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 63 (1) of the Mines and Minerals Act No. 33 of 1992 as amended by the Amendment Act No. 66 of 2009
brief_facts_summary: On 25 August 2017, the first accused used a loader (EP ZA-5559) to dig soil without a permit. The second accused transported the dug soil using a lorry without a permit. Both accused pleaded guilty in the Magistrate's Court. The magistrate confiscated the loader but released the lorry, prompting an appeal by the loader's owner.
hc_judgment_summary: The appellant challenged the Magistrate's confiscation order via a revision application to the High Court of Ampara. The High Court Judge, after considering legal principles, legislative intent, and case law, dismissed the revision application, affirming the confiscation order.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant argued that the loader, being registered as a vehicle under the Motor Traffic Act, does not fall within the category of items (machinery, equipment) that can be confiscated under the Mines and Minerals Act. He contended that the High Court Judge incorrectly interpreted the law by classifying the loader as machinery used in the offence.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Whether the confiscated item comes within a meaning of a vehicle or not. | Was the interpretation given by the learned High Court Judge in that regard correct.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The appellant (owner) gave evidence and called witnesses before the Magistrate to support his claim against confiscation. The court found he failed to show sufficient cause. The facts of the offence were not contested.
probability_assessment_by_court: Court found appellant failed to show cause against confiscation; loader's use as digging machinery was clear from the charge to which the accused pleaded guilty.
defence_version_summary: The accused pleaded guilty to the charges. The appellant (owner) pleaded not guilty to the confiscation, claiming the loader is a vehicle not liable to forfeiture. He gave evidence and called witnesses but the court found his cause insufficient.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal held that the loader, though registered as a vehicle, was used as machinery/equipment to dig soil in commission of the offence under the Mines and Minerals Act. It distinguished prior cases involving vehicles used solely for transport. The Court found the Magistrate and High Court correctly interpreted section 63B(1), which allows forfeiture of 'machinery, equipment or material' used in the offence, and that the legislative omission of 'vehicle' did not preclude confiscation of a vehicle used as machinery. The appeal was devoid of merit.
coa_sentence_type: Confiscation of loader (vehicle EP ZA-5559) affirmed.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The appellant, owner of a loader, appealed against the High Court's dismissal of his revision application challenging the Magistrate's order confiscating the loader used in illegal soil digging. The Court of Appeal examined whether the loader, registered as a vehicle, could be confiscated as 'machinery or equipment' under the Mines and Minerals Act. It held that the loader was used as digging machinery, not merely for transport, and thus fell within the confiscation provision. The appeal was dismissed, affirming the lower courts' orders.
defence_counsel: Chathura Galhena with Dharani Weerasinghe and Deymini Bulegoda
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court Judge considered legal principles, legislative intent, and case law, and agreed with the Magistrate's order. The COA found the HC judgment well-considered and saw no reason to disagree.
precedents_cited_list: Nishantha and Three Others Vs. The State (2014) 1 SLR 2005 | Punchirala Danapala Vs. OIC Police Station Horowpathana and two Others CA (PHC) APN 106/15 decided on 19-02-2016
standard_of_review_applied: Review of legal interpretation (whether loader qualifies as confiscable machinery/equipment under the Act).
sentencing_principles_applied: Forfeiture principles under section 63B(1) of Mines and Minerals Act.

judges: Menaka Wijesundera J | Neil Iddawala J
offence_sections: Section 298 of the Penal Code and offences under the Motor Traffic Act
brief_facts_summary: On 20/09/2010, the petitioner was driving car WP KD-9026 when an accident took place, killing one passenger. The evidence indicates the road was wet, the driver saw something like a stone ahead, and when trying to avoid it, the vehicle slipped, knocked, and toppled. The petitioner was convicted of negligently causing a deadly road accident.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 298 of the Penal Code and offences under the Motor Traffic Act
hc_sentence_type: 1-year rigorous imprisonment suspended for 5 years and fines
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court affirmed the Magistrate's order convicting the petitioner for negligently causing a deadly road accident under Section 298 of the Penal Code and for two offences under the Motor Traffic Act. The sentence included a suspended imprisonment and fines, and compensation was ordered.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The petitioner argued the Magistrate erred in finding the accident was due to negligent driving at high speed. The petitioner claimed the road was wet, and the accident occurred when trying to avoid an object like a stone.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Error in finding that fatal accident took place due to accused negligently driving in high speed
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court considered evidence from witnesses including the accused and a passenger. Both stated the road was wet, and an object like a stone was ahead. The Court found that if the accused was driving at a controllable speed, he could have avoided the stone and the accident.
probability_assessment_by_court: Court found no reasonable doubt; the evidence supported the conclusion of negligent driving.
defence_version_summary: The petitioner pleaded not guilty. The defence claimed the road was wet, and the accident happened when trying to avoid a stone-like object. The Court found the defence not credible as the accident could have been avoided with proper speed control.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal applied revisionary jurisdiction to assess irregularities, illegalities, or improprieties. It found no exceptional circumstances warranting revision. The Court agreed with the lower courts that the petitioner was driving negligently. The evidence indicated that with proper speed control, the accident could have been avoided. The compensation was considered nominal and not excessive. No errors were found in the Magistrate's or High Court's orders.
coa_sentence_type: 1-year rigorous imprisonment suspended for 5 years, fines of Rs. 5000, and compensation of Rs. 100000
brief_judgment_file_summary: The petitioner was convicted for negligently causing a deadly road accident under Section 298 of the Penal Code and for two offences under the Motor Traffic Act. The Magistrate sentenced him to suspended imprisonment, fines, and compensation. The High Court affirmed this. The petitioner filed a revision application arguing the accident was not due to high-speed negligent driving. The Court of Appeal found no exceptional circumstances or errors in the lower courts' orders and dismissed the application.
defence_counsel: Dishan Dharmasena
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court affirmed the Magistrate's conviction and sentence. The Court of Appeal found no errors in the High Court's analysis and agreed with its reasoning.
precedents_cited_list: Kulatilake v Attorney General (2010) 1 SLR 212 p. 215 | Attorney General vs. Ranasinghe and others (1993) 2 SLR p.81 | Abdul Hassan Mohamed Kaleel v Mohamed Kaleel Mohamed Imithiyas CA/PHC/APN/141/16 CA Minute dated 25.01.2017
standard_of_review_applied: Revisionary jurisdiction to assess irregularities, illegalities, or improprieties, exercised only in exceptional circumstances.

judges: Prasantha De Silva, J. | K.K.A.V. Swarnadhipathi, J.
offence_sections: Sections 454, 457 and 462
brief_facts_summary: The Appellant was charged in the Magistrate's Court of Wariyapola under Sections 454, 457 and 462. The original plaint was amended, naming the Appellant as the sole accused and the other two accused as prosecution witnesses. The Appellant agreed to transfer a deed to witness number one (his brother) as part of a proposed settlement. The case proceeded, and the Appellant was found guilty on one count. He received a suspended sentence.
hc_judgment_summary: The Magistrate's Court found the Appellant guilty on the 1st count and acquitted him on the 2nd count, imposing a suspended sentence. The Appellant appealed to the Kurunegala High Court (HCA/76/2010), which dismissed the appeal on 31 May 2013. The High Court later refused permission to proceed with a revision application on 29 January 2018.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The Appellant argued that he was deprived of a fair trial because the prosecution witnesses were examined before one Magistrate but the judgment was written by another, leading to an unfair evaluation of evidence. He also argued that the plaint was improperly amended in a criminal case and that the handwriting evidence against him was not proved by an expert, raising doubt about the case being proved beyond reasonable doubt.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Witnesses examined before one Magistrate, judgment delivered by another, leading to unfair evaluation. | No provision to amend the plaint in criminal cases after filing; charges can be amended, not the plaint. | Handwriting of Appellant not proved by expert evidence, creating reasonable doubt.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The judgment notes that the evaluation of witness evidence was potentially unfair because different magistrates handled the examination and the judgment. The lack of expert proof for handwriting evidence was also raised as an issue creating doubt.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal did not assess the probability of guilt, as the appeal was dismissed on procedural grounds of functus officio.
defence_version_summary: The Appellant pleaded not guilty. The defence argued procedural errors and unfair trial. No alibi or defence witnesses are mentioned in the provided text.
procedural_defects_description: Appellant argued improper amendment of plaint and unfair evaluation due to different magistrates handling witness examination and judgment.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found that the Appellant had exhausted his right of appeal when the High Court dismissed his earlier appeal. The principle of functus officio applies: once a judicial order is final, the same court cannot re-activate or reconsider it. The Court cited precedents establishing finality in litigation. The Appellant's delay of nearly three years in seeking a revision, after being dismissed from service, was not considered an exceptional ground. Therefore, the High Court Judge was correct in refusing to entertain the revision application.
coa_sentence_type: Suspended sentence (as per original Magistrate Court sentence)
brief_judgment_file_summary: The Appellant, a police officer, was convicted in the Magistrate's Court of Wariyapola on one count and given a suspended sentence. His appeal to the Kurunegala High Court was dismissed. Years later, after being dismissed from service, he sought revision in the High Court, which was refused. He appealed that refusal to the Court of Appeal. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal, holding that the High Court Judge was functus officio after dismissing the first appeal and could not entertain a revision. The Appellant's procedural and fairness arguments were not examined on merits due to this procedural bar.
defence_counsel: Anil Silva (P.C) with S. Neranga
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court dismissed the Appellant's initial appeal. Later, it correctly refused to entertain a revision application on the grounds that it was functus officio after the dismissal. The Court of Appeal agreed with this analysis.
precedents_cited_list: Finnegan Vs. Galladari Hotels (Lanka) Ltd., (1989) 2 SLR 272-281 | Sinnatangum Vs. Sinnen, (1985) 1 NLR 220-221 | Hettiarachchi Vs. Senevirathna (N02), (1994) SLR 293-297 | Jeyaraj Fernandopulle Vs. Premachandra De Silva, (1996) 1 SLR 70-88
standard_of_review_applied: Application of the legal principle of functus officio and finality of litigation to determine if a revision application was permissible.

judges: Menaka Wijesundera, J. | B. Sasi Mahendran, J.
offence_sections: offences punishable under the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance as amended by Act No. 13 of 1984
brief_facts_summary: Accused was indicted for possession and trafficking of 2.11 grams of Heroin on 7th May 2013. Police received information from Army intelligence, raided the location, searched the Accused, and allegedly found a parcel of heroin in his trouser pocket. The Accused, in his dock statement, claimed he was arrested by army officers while washing his vehicle and later handed over to police, with the heroin being retrieved from a goat shed near the house.
evidence_type_secondary: Eyewitness testimony of police and army officers
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: offences punishable under the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance as amended by Act No. 13 of 1984
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court Judge found the Accused guilty on both counts of possession and trafficking of heroin, convicted him, and sentenced him to life imprisonment.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: Appellant argued the trial Judge failed to consider vital contradictions among prosecution witnesses and wrongly rejected the dock statement and defence witness evidence. The third ground alleging judicial bias was withdrawn at the hearing.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The learned trial Judge had failed to consider the vital contradictions of the Prosecution witnesses. | The learned trial judge had wrongly rejected the dock statement and the evidence of Defence witness. | The learned trial judge has been biased towards the Prosecution and has abused Defence witnesses. (Withdrawn)
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found material contradictions in prosecution evidence regarding the time and place of receiving information, time of arrival at the police station, and distance to the jeweler. It considered the improbability of the prosecution story and found the evidence lacked cogency.
probability_assessment_by_court: Court found prosecution version improbable in light of contradictions and defence version, creating reasonable doubt.
defence_version_summary: Accused pleaded not guilty. He made a dock statement claiming he was arrested by army officers, not at his house, and the heroin was retrieved from a goat shed. He called one defence witness (Weerasingha Arachchilage Gnanasiri) who corroborated his version. The Court of Appeal found the defence version created reasonable doubt.
legal_errors_description: Trial Judge failed to properly consider vital contradictions in prosecution evidence and wrongly dismissed defence evidence, effectively reversing the presumption of innocence.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: COA found material contradictions in prosecution evidence (timing, locations, conduct) that went to the root of the case. It assessed credibility per Onassis v Vergottis principles and Wickremasuriya v Dedoleena, concluding contradictions were not trivial. It found prosecution version improbable, noting failure to search others at scene and illogical actions of army officers. Citing James Silva v Republic of Sri Lanka, it held that evaluating defence evidence in light of prosecution evidence reversed the presumption of innocence. The evidence did not meet the beyond reasonable doubt threshold.
coa_sentence_type: Conviction and sentence set aside
brief_judgment_file_summary: The Accused-Appellant was convicted by the High Court of Colombo for possession and trafficking of 2.11g of heroin and sentenced to life imprisonment. He appealed, arguing the trial Judge failed to consider contradictions in prosecution evidence and wrongly rejected his defence. The Court of Appeal found material contradictions regarding the raid timing, police station arrival, and distance to the jeweler, and deemed the prosecution story improbable. It held the evidence did not prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt, set aside the High Court judgment, and acquitted the Accused.
prosecution_counsel: Azard Navavi, DSG for the State
defence_counsel: Neranjan Jayasinghe with Harshana Ananda for the Accused Appellant
hc_analysis_summary: High Court Judge found the prosecution evidence credible and convicted the Accused. COA found the HC failed to properly evaluate contradictions and improbabilities in prosecution evidence and wrongly dismissed the defence version, leading to a miscarriage of justice.
precedents_cited_list: Onassis and Calogeropoulos v. Vergottis [1968] 2 Lloyd's Rep. 403 | Wickremasuriya v. Dedoleena and Others 1996 [2] SLR 95 | James Silva v. The Republic of Sri Lanka [1980] 2 SLR 167 | Barwada Boginbhai Hirjibhai v. the State of Gujarat | Munasighe Arachchilage Samanalee Perera v. The Republic of Sri Lanka CA 270/2006
standard_of_review_applied: Evaluation of whether prosecution proved its case beyond reasonable doubt, assessing credibility, contradictions, and probabilities.

judges: P. Kumararatnam, J. | Sampath B. Abayakoon, J.
offence_sections: Sections 54A (d) and 54A (b) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance as amended by Act No.13 of 1984
location_of_offence: Samagipura housing scheme at Kosgashandiya in Grandpass
brief_facts_summary: Police received information about heroin trafficking and went to Samagipura. The informant pointed out the accused. Two parcels wrapped in cellophane were recovered from the accused's underwear. The parcels were weighed and sent for analysis, which confirmed 51.9 grams of heroin. The accused was later arrested at his house. Another person, Jamaldeen Roomy, was also arrested with a separate packet of heroin. The accused absconded during trial, which proceeded in his absence.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Sections 54A (d) and 54A (b) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance as amended by Act No.13 of 1984
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court found the accused guilty on both counts of possession and trafficking of 51.9 grams of heroin. The judge imposed the death penalty on each count. The trial was conducted in absentia after the accused absconded.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appeal was argued on two main grounds: denial of a fair trial and failure to prove the chain of custody of the productions. Specific complaints included the admission of prejudicial bad character evidence, unequal treatment of the defence, failure to properly evaluate defence evidence, and contradictions in prosecution evidence regarding the raid, recovery, and handling of the heroin.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The version of the defence was rejected contrary to law and the principles of evaluating the defence. | The Learned High Court Judge has failed to judicially scrutinize the version of the defence. | The Learned High Court Judge permitted illegal and inadmissible evidence including evidence of bad character of the accused causing grave miscarriage of justice. | The presumption of innocence was reversed by the Learned Trial Judge denying the right to a fair trial. | The prosecution and the defence were not treated with equality of arms. | The Learned High Court Judge has failed to apply the long held dictas and principles in evaluating the evidence of trained police officers and disregarded the contradictions inter se and per se causing grave miscarriage of justice. | The Learned High Court Judge has failed to appreciate the discrepancies of the productions itself as described by the prosecution. | The production chain has not been proved. | The judgment is contrary to law and against the weight of the evidence adduced in the case.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: COA found serious contradictions in prosecution evidence (PW1 & PW3) regarding timing of raid, number of parcels recovered from second person, and time of handing over productions. Defence evidence from accused's wife and co-arrested person was improperly rejected. The judge was influenced by inadmissible bad character evidence.
probability_assessment_by_court: COA found prosecution version improbable due to highlighted contradictions and discrepancies, creating reasonable doubt.
defence_version_summary: The accused pleaded not guilty. The defence called two witnesses: his wife and the co-arrested person. The wife testified the accused was arrested at home, beaten, and police took underwear; no heroin was recovered from him. The co-arrested person testified police brought parcels from an abandoned house. The High Court judge rejected the defence evidence partly because the accused did not testify personally, which the COA found a misdirection.
legal_errors_description: Admission of bad character evidence contrary to Section 54 of Evidence Ordinance; failure to properly evaluate defence evidence; misdirection on accused's right to silence; unequal treatment of parties.
procedural_defects_description: Trial continued in absentia after accused absconded; prosecution led inadmissible prejudicial evidence; lack of equality of arms between prosecution and defence.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: COA held the accused was denied a fair trial due to admission of bad character evidence, failure to properly consider defence evidence, and prosecution's failure to prove chain of custody. The judge erred by rejecting defence evidence because accused did not testify, ignoring his right to silence. Serious contradictions in prosecution evidence (timings, number of parcels, handling of productions) created reasonable doubt and broke the chain of custody. Relying on precedents about fair trial and equality of arms, the COA found the conviction unsustainable.
coa_sentence_type: Acquitted, sentence set aside.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused was convicted in the High Court of Colombo for possession and trafficking of 51.9g heroin and sentenced to death on each count. He appealed, arguing denial of fair trial and failure to prove chain of custody. The Court of Appeal found the trial judge admitted prejudicial bad character evidence, failed to properly evaluate defence testimony, and there were serious contradictions in prosecution evidence regarding the raid and handling of the drugs. The COA held the chain of custody was broken and the accused was denied a fair trial. The conviction and sentence were set aside, and the accused was acquitted on both charges.
defence_counsel: Hafeel Fariz with Sanjeewa Kodithuwakku
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court accepted prosecution evidence from PW1 and PW3 as true before considering other evidence. It rejected defence evidence partly because accused did not testify. COA found this approach was a misdirection, showed influence of inadmissible evidence, and violated fair trial principles.
precedents_cited_list: Devage Thusitha Chamara alias Thilan v. The Attorney General CA/HCC/0050/2020 decided on 01/11/2022 | R.G.Moses v. The Queen 75 NLR 121 | Kithsiri v. Attorney General [2014] 1 SLR 38 | Shiv Kumar v. Hukam Chand and Anr [1999] 7 SCC 104 | C.A.Sisira alias Mahatun CA/122/2006 decided on 09/10/2014
standard_of_review_applied: Evaluation of whether fair trial was denied and whether chain of custody was proven based on evidence and legal principles.

judges: Prasantha De Silva, J. | K.K.A.V. Swarnadhipathi, J.
offence_sections: Section 66 of the Primary Court Procedure Act No 44 of 1979
offence_category: Dispute affecting land / Threat to peace
brief_facts_summary: The Officer-in-charge of Kaluthara Police filed information in the Magistrate's Court under Section 66 of the Primary Court Procedure Act concerning a dispute over premises at No. 138, Palathota Road, Kaluthara South. The 1st Party Respondent (sister) had leased the premises, which she claimed to own via a 1999 deed of gift from her father. The 2nd Party Respondent (brother) claimed ownership via a last will and probate. The lessee voluntarily vacated and handed keys to the 2nd Party Respondent at the police station. The police filed information due to a threatened breach of peace.
evidence_type_primary: Documentary evidence (deed of gift, lease agreement, probate, affidavits)
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 68(3) of the Primary Court Procedure Act No 44 of 1979
hc_sentence_type: Restoration of possession to 1st Party Respondent
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court Judge, exercising revisionary jurisdiction, dismissed the 2nd Party Respondent-Petitioner's application. The Judge upheld the Magistrate's order that the 1st Party Respondent was entitled to possession of the disputed premises under Section 68(3) of the Primary Court Procedure Act, finding no merit in the revision application.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The Appellant (2nd Party Respondent) argued that there was no threatened breach of peace to invoke jurisdiction under Section 66, and that there was no forcible dispossession as required by Section 68(b) because the lessee voluntarily handed over possession. He also contended that physical possession was with the lessee, not the 1st Party Respondent, at the time.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: No breach of the peace threatened or likely to justify jurisdiction under Section 66. | No forcible dispossession as required by Section 68(b) because lessee handed over possession voluntarily. | Physical possession was with the lessee, not the 1st Party Respondent, at the time of alleged dispossession.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court analyzed documentary evidence including the deed of gift, lease agreement, probate, and affidavits. It emphasized the legal concepts of actual vs. constructive possession, finding the 1st Party Respondent retained constructive possession and control through the valid lease.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court found the 1st Party Respondent was forcibly dispossessed as the dispossession occurred against her will and without her knowledge, while she retained constructive possession via the lease.
defence_version_summary: The 2nd Party Respondent (Appellant) pleaded not liable, claiming lawful ownership via probate and that the lessee voluntarily handed over possession, so no forcible dispossession occurred. He did not call witnesses but relied on documentary evidence (probate, will). The court found his legal interpretation unsustainable.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal. It held that under Section 66(1)(a), the police's opinion on a threatened breach of peace is sufficient for jurisdiction; the Magistrate need not inquire. Relying on Iqbal vs Majedudeen, it distinguished between actual and constructive possession, finding the 1st Party Respondent had constructive possession via the lease. The dispossession was 'forcible' as defined in Section 68(3) because it was against the will of the person entitled to possess (the 1st Party Respondent) and without legal authority, even though the lessee acted voluntarily. The probate did not prove the Appellant's possession relevant to the dispute. The Court saw no reason to interfere with the lower courts' orders.
coa_sentence_type: Restoration of possession to 1st Party Respondent; costs awarded against Appellant.
brief_judgment_file_summary: This appeal concerned a land dispute between siblings over premises at Kaluthara South. The High Court and Magistrate Court had ordered possession restored to the 1st Party Respondent (sister/lessor) under the Primary Court Procedure Act. The 2nd Party Respondent (brother/Appellant) appealed, arguing no threatened breach of peace and no forcible dispossession as the lessee voluntarily handed over keys. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal, upholding that police jurisdiction under Section 66 was properly invoked and that the sister was forcibly dispossessed in law as the dispossession was against her will while she retained constructive possession via the lease.
defence_counsel: K. Herath A.A.L with V. Gunasekara A.A.L for the 2nd Party Respondent-Petitioner-Petitioner (Appellant); Nalin Laduwahetti P.C with K.Ubeysekara A.A.L for the 1st Party Respondent-Respondent-Respondent
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court Judge upheld the Magistrate's finding that the 1st Party Respondent was entitled to possession under Section 68(3) and that the Appellant had no right to possess the premises. The COA agreed with this analysis and found no error.
precedents_cited_list: Velupillai and Others Vs. Sivanathan [1993(1) S.L.R 123] | Iqbal vs Majedudeen and other [1999 (3) S.L.R 213]
standard_of_review_applied: Revisionary jurisdiction / appellate review of lower court orders.
sentencing_principles_applied: Principles under Section 68(3) of the Primary Courts Procedure Act regarding restoration of possession after forcible dispossession.

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Sections 54A(d) and (b) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance as amended by the Act No.13 of 1984
brief_facts_summary: The accused was arrested by Police Narcotics Bureau officers on 25.02.2020 based on information from the 1st suspect. He was found in possession of 1.10 kilograms of a substance believed to be heroin. The Government Analyst report confirmed 225.1 grams of pure heroin (Diacetylmorphine) from the substance recovered from the accused. Other suspects were also arrested and later some were discharged or granted bail.
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court refused bail to the accused on 28.07.2022, citing the lack of exceptional circumstances as required under the relevant law for drug offences involving a pure quantity of 10 grams or more of heroin.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The petitioner filed a revision application seeking bail for her husband, the accused. She argued exceptional circumstances existed, including: delay in trial (over 3 years remand), bail granted to co-suspects with larger quantities of drugs, the accused being the sole breadwinner with a special needs child, the accused suffering from ailments, and the 1st suspect's statement under section 127 of the CPC describing the arrest manner.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Delay in trial (over 30 months remand) as exceptional circumstance | Bail granted to principal suspect (1st suspect with 600g pure heroin) | Prosecution version not credible / accused falsely implicated | 3rd and 4th suspects discharged by Attorney General | 1st suspect's statement under section 127 of CPC describing arrest | Accused is sole breadwinner; child has special needs | Accused suffers from ailments
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The primary evidence is the physical recovery of drugs and the Government Analyst report confirming 225.1 grams of pure heroin. The court considered the delay in trial and the bail granted to other suspects as factors in the revision application.
probability_assessment_by_court: The court assessed the delay of over three years in remand as excessive and oppressive, constituting an exceptional circumstance for granting bail, considering the presumption of innocence.
defence_version_summary: The accused pleaded not guilty. The defence argued false implication and highlighted exceptional circumstances for bail: delay, bail to co-accused, family hardship, and health issues. No alibi or defence witnesses are detailed in the bail revision judgment.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed the bail revision application under Section 83 of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Act (amended). It found the delay of over three years without trial commencement to be excessive and oppressive, constituting an exceptional circumstance. It noted the High Court failed to consider this delay while granting bail to the principal suspect. Citing precedents on delay and the right to trial without undue delay, and balancing the seriousness of the offence with the presumption of innocence, the COA decided to grant bail with strict conditions.
coa_sentence_type: Bail granted with strict conditions
brief_judgment_file_summary: The petitioner sought revision of the High Court's bail refusal order for her husband, accused under the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance for possessing 225.1g pure heroin. The High Court refused bail, citing lack of exceptional circumstances.
