The Court of Appeal allowed the revision, finding the over three-year remand delay without trial commencement to be an exceptional circumstance, especially since the principal suspect with more drugs was granted bail. The COA granted bail with conditions including Rs. 100,000 cash bail, two sureties, travel ban, and reporting to police.
defence_counsel: Tenny Fernando
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court refused bail, finding no exceptional circumstances. The COA found the HC erred by not considering the prolonged remand delay as an exceptional circumstance, especially when it had considered similar delay for the principal suspect's bail.
precedents_cited_list: Ramu Thamodarampillai v. The Attorney General [2004] 3 SLR 180 | CA(PHC)APN 107/2018 decided on 19.03.2019 | Nasher v. Director of Public Prosecution [2020] VSCA 144
standard_of_review_applied: Revisionary jurisdiction under Article 138 of the Constitution read with Section 404 of the Code of Criminal Procedure Act No.15 of 1979, considering whether exceptional circumstances exist for bail under the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Act.
sentencing_principles_applied: Bail principles: presumption of innocence, bail not to be withheld as punishment, discretion exercised with care considering facts, delay as a factor constituting exceptional circumstances.

judges: Menaka Wijesundera, J. | B. Sasi Mahendran, J.
offence_sections: Section 294(3) of the Penal Code (murder), Section 32 and Section 140 (unlawful assembly, common intention)
location_of_offence: At or near the house of the deceased (Mathalge Weerasinghe), likely in the Panadura area
brief_facts_summary: On 30 October 2001, a group including the accused approached the house of the deceased Mathalge Weerasinghe. Eyewitnesses (the deceased's parents) stated the accused were armed and entered the house. The deceased was brought out and attacked; his shoulder was severed. The deceased died from multiple injuries inflicted by sharp-edged weapons. The accused were arrested, and weapons (swords and a manna) were recovered from a cesspit. The High Court convicted the 1st, 2nd, and 3rd accused of murder and imposed the death sentence.
evidence_type_secondary: Medical evidence, Recovery of weapons (physical evidence)
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 294(3) of the Penal Code (murder)
hc_judgment_summary: The Learned High Court Judge convicted the 1st, 2nd, and 3rd Accused of murder and imposed the death sentence. The judge accepted the eyewitness evidence, finding the accused were part of an unlawful assembly with a common intention to commit murder. The 4th and 5th accused were acquitted.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellants challenged the conviction on multiple grounds, including that the prosecution failed to establish their specific acts as members of an unlawful assembly, that the trial judge relied on uncorroborated and inconsistent evidence, that the charge of unlawful assembly was untenable, and that the judge failed to consider provocation and the influence of liquor. They also argued the judge neglected witness demeanor and incorrectly applied legal principles to the dock statement.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The Prosecution failed to establish the specific act or omission by the Appellant that would categorize him as a member of an unlawful assembly. | The Learned Trial Judge relied on uncorroborated and inconsistent evidence to convict the Appellant. | The charge of unlawful assembly is untenable, as only three accused were charged. | The Learned Trial Judge failed to consider the Appellants acted under grave and sudden provocation while under the influence of liquor. | The Learned Trial Judge neglected to consider the demeanor and deportment of prosecution witnesses. | The Learned Trial Judge incorrectly applied legal principles related to the dock statement and did not give it due consideration.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found significant inconsistencies and contradictions in the eyewitness testimonies (PW1 and PW2), particularly regarding identification, presence at the scene, and details of the attack. PW1 was deemed inconsistent and unreliable. The court also noted the lack of clear evidence linking the 2nd and 3rd accused to any overt criminal act.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court applied the standard of proof beyond a reasonable doubt. It found the prosecution failed to prove the common object of an unlawful assembly or that the injuries inflicted by the 1st accused alone caused death, creating reasonable doubt.
defence_version_summary: The 1st Accused pleaded not guilty, gave evidence from the witness box, denying the allegation and claiming an argument with the deceased ended amicably. The 2nd, 3rd, 4th, and 5th Accused made dock statements. The court found the prosecution failed to prove the case against the 2nd and 3rd accused beyond reasonable doubt.
legal_errors_description: The High Court judge erred in law by inadequately analyzing evidence, applying the theory of photographic memory to excuse witness inconsistencies, misapplying legal principles on unlawful assembly and common intention, and failing to properly consider the dock statement.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal meticulously analyzed the evidence. It found the eyewitness testimonies (PW1 and PW2) inconsistent and unreliable on key details. Applying precedents (Kumara de Silva, Jagathsena, Queen v. Vincent Fernando), the court held the prosecution failed to prove the existence of an unlawful assembly with a common object, as mere presence was insufficient. Regarding the 1st accused, medical evidence indicated multiple weapons caused the fatal injuries; it could not be conclusively proven his single act caused death. Therefore, murder was not established, but his culpability for causing grievous hurt was proven. The appeal of the 2nd and 3rd accused was allowed (acquittal). The 1st accused's conviction was modified from murder to voluntarily causing grievous hurt.
coa_sentence_type: 7 years of rigorous imprisonment (for the 1st Accused under section 317 of the Penal Code). The 2nd and 3rd Accused are acquitted.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The 1st, 2nd, and 3rd Accused were convicted of murder by the High Court of Panadura and sentenced to death. They appealed. The Court of Appeal found the prosecution evidence, particularly eyewitness testimony, inconsistent and unreliable. It ruled the prosecution failed to prove the accused formed an unlawful assembly with a common intention to murder. Applying relevant precedents, the court acquitted the 2nd and 3rd accused. For the 1st accused, it found the medical evidence did not conclusively prove his act alone caused death, reducing the conviction to voluntarily causing grievous hurt with a dangerous weapon and imposing 7 years rigorous imprisonment. The death sentence was set aside.
defence_counsel: Kolitha Dharmawardana with Chamindi Diloka Mannakkara for the 1st Accused-Appellant; Neranjan Jayasinghe with D.D.K.Katugampola for the 2nd Accused-Appellant; Saliya Pieris, PC with Yohan Pieris and Farhad Jiffry for the 3rd Accused-Appellant
cause_of_death_exact_text: loss of heart rate and lung function due to bleeding and trauma inflicted by cuts to the head and neck from a sharp-edged weapon... the possibility of death was mainly due to the 5th injury recorded, which could result in instant death.
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court accepted the eyewitness evidence and found the accused guilty of murder as part of an unlawful assembly. The Court of Appeal criticized this, finding the High Court judge erred by not properly analyzing witness inconsistencies and by misapplying legal principles on unlawful assembly and common intention.
precedents_cited_list: Kumara de Silva and 2 others vs. Attorney General [2010] 2 S.L.R. 169 | Attorney General vs. Somadasa | Jagathsena and others v G.D.P Perera and others [1992], 1 S.L.R 375 | Queen v. Vincent Fernando 65 NLR 265 | Piyathilaka and 2 Others v. Republic of Sri Lanka [1996] 2 S.L.R
standard_of_review_applied: Review of evidence and legal principles applied by the trial court, assessing whether conviction was safe and based on evidence proving guilt beyond reasonable doubt.
sentencing_principles_applied: Consideration of the appropriate offence based on proven acts and intention. For the 1st accused, sentencing under section 317 of the Penal Code for voluntarily causing grievous hurt with a dangerous weapon.
final_charge_after_appeal: For 1st Accused: Modified from Murder to Voluntarily causing grievous hurt by dangerous weapons under section 317 of the Penal Code.

judges: Menaka Wijesundera, J. | B. Sasi Mahendran, J.
offence_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code
location_of_offence: At or near the deceased's residence, Tissamaharama area
brief_facts_summary: The deceased was shot at his home on 7 April 2005 while preparing to depart for Colombo. His wife (PW2) testified she heard a gunshot, saw her husband rush back into the house stating 'Ajith shot him', and then saw the accused Ajith Priyantha Weerathunga fleeing from near the toilet holding an object like a gun. A prior unresolved dispute existed between the accused and deceased, and the deceased had reportedly been threatened by the accused. The accused was convicted of murder and sentenced to death by the High Court.
evidence_type_secondary: Medical evidence, Police evidence, Dying declaration
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court found the accused guilty of murder based on the evidence, including the eyewitness identification by the deceased's wife (PW2) and the dying declaration. The court rejected the accused's alibi defense and convicted him, imposing the death sentence.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant argued that his identification was not established beyond reasonable doubt, the trial judge failed to properly consider evidence and relied on defense submissions, erred in law by rejecting the alibi defense and shifting the burden of proof, and failed to consider inherent weaknesses in the prosecution case.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The learned High Court Judge has failed to consider that the identification of the Accused-Appellant has not been established beyond reasonable doubt. | The learned High Court Judge has not properly considered the evidence led at the trial but has written the judgment based on the written submissions filed by the defence. | The learned High Court Judge has erred in law by rejecting the defence of Alibi and by shifting the burden to the defence to prove the defence of Alibi. | The learned High Court Judge has failed to consider the inherent weaknesses of the prosecution case.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the testimony of PW2 (the wife) to be credible, consistent, and sufficient to establish the accused's identity beyond reasonable doubt. Her account was corroborated by the dying declaration, the medical evidence (PW6), and police observations (PW8) regarding adequate lighting at the scene.
probability_assessment_by_court: The court held that the prosecution evidence, particularly the consistent and unchallenged eyewitness identification and dying declaration, proved guilt beyond reasonable doubt.
defence_version_summary: The accused pleaded not guilty. He gave evidence under oath and called one defence witness (DW1) to support an alibi defense, claiming he was at a party at Chinthaka's house at the time of the incident. The court found the alibi to be an afterthought and rejected it, noting the accused failed to suggest this alibi to prosecution witnesses during cross-examination.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal conducted a thorough analysis of the evidence. It found the High Court judge correctly evaluated the evidence, particularly the credible and consistent testimony of PW2 who identified the accused fleeing the scene. The court noted the area was well-lit, PW2 knew the accused as a neighbour, and her evidence was corroborated by the deceased's dying declaration and medical evidence. The court rejected the alibi defense, citing the accused's failure to suggest it to prosecution witnesses and referenced the precedent Sarwan Singh vs. State of Punjab regarding the effect of such silence. No infirmities were found in the prosecution case or the High Court's reasoning.
coa_sentence_type: Death sentence upheld
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused-appellant, Ajith Priyantha Weerathunga, was convicted of murder under Section 296 of the Penal Code by the High Court of Hambantota and sentenced to death for shooting the deceased on 7 April 2005. The prosecution's case relied heavily on the eyewitness testimony of the deceased's wife (PW2), who identified the accused fleeing the scene, and the deceased's dying declaration. The accused appealed on grounds including faulty identification and erroneous rejection of his alibi defense. The Court of Appeal found the identification was established beyond reasonable doubt, the alibi was rightly rejected, and the High Court judgment was sound. The appeal was dismissed, and the conviction and death sentence were upheld.
defence_counsel: Darshana Kuruppu with Buddhika Thilakaratne and Sahan Sanketha Weerasinghe
cause_of_death_exact_text: excessive loss of blood and hemorrhagic shock
hc_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the High Court judge correctly analysed and evaluated the evidence, arriving at the conclusion that the accused committed the offence. The High Court had rightly rejected the accused's evidence and alibi defense.
precedents_cited_list: Gunasiri, Jayarathna Silva, Gnanasiri v. Republic of Sri Lanka 2009 (1) SLR 39 | Sarwan Singh vs. State of Punjab | Bobby Mathew vs. State of Karnataka
standard_of_review_applied: Review of evidence and legal conclusions of the High Court

judges: Sasi Mahendran, J. | Menaka Wijesundera, J.
offence_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code
location_of_offence: At or near the deceased's residence
brief_facts_summary: The accused was indicted for the murder of Katapodi Kankanamge Bandula Senarathna on 7 April 2005. The deceased was shot at his home and later died in hospital. The deceased's wife (PW2) testified she heard a gunshot, saw the accused fleeing, and the deceased stated 'Ajith shot him' before collapsing. There was a prior unresolved dispute between the accused and the deceased.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The Learned High Court Judge found the accused guilty of murder based on the evidence, including the dying declaration and eyewitness identification. The judge convicted the accused and imposed the death sentence.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The accused appealed on grounds including failure to establish identification beyond reasonable doubt, improper consideration of evidence, error in rejecting the defence of alibi and shifting the burden of proof, and failure to consider inherent weaknesses of the prosecution case.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The learned High Court Judge has failed to consider that the identification of the Accused-Appellant has not been established beyond reasonable doubt. | The learned High Court Judge has not properly considered the evidence led at the trial but has written the judgment based on the written submissions filed by the defence. | The learned High Court Judge has erred in law by rejecting the defence of Alibi and by shifting the burden to the defence to prove the defence of Alibi. | The learned High Court Judge has failed to consider the inherent weaknesses of the prosecution case.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the prosecution witnesses credible and their evidence trustworthy. The testimony of PW2 (eyewitness) was consistent and corroborated by the dying declaration. The alibi defence was rejected as an afterthought.
probability_assessment_by_court: The court held the evidence established the accused's identity beyond reasonable doubt and found no infirmities in the prosecution case.
defence_version_summary: The accused pleaded not guilty, gave evidence under oath, and raised an alibi defence, claiming he was at Chinthaka's party. The court rejected this defence as a mere afterthought, noting he failed to suggest it to prosecution witnesses.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal thoroughly analyzed the evidence, finding the eyewitness (PW2) credible and her identification reliable due to adequate lighting and prior familiarity with the accused. The dying declaration was corroborated. The alibi defence was rejected based on the failure to suggest it to prosecution witnesses, citing precedent (Gunasiri, Jayarathna Silva, Gnanasiri v. Republic of Sri Lanka). The COA found the High Court correctly evaluated the evidence and saw no merit in the appeal.
coa_sentence_type: Death sentence upheld
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused appealed his High Court conviction for murder and death sentence. Grounds included identification issues and erroneous rejection of alibi. The Court of Appeal found the eyewitness testimony and dying declaration reliable, the identification was established beyond reasonable doubt, and the alibi defence was properly rejected. The appeal was dismissed, upholding the conviction and death sentence.
defence_counsel: Darshana Kuruppu with Buddhika Thilakaratne and Sahan Sanketha Weerasinghe
cause_of_death_exact_text: excessive loss of blood and hemorrhagic shock
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court correctly analyzed and evaluated the evidence, finding the accused guilty of murder. The COA agreed with the HC's reasoning and found no errors in its judgment.
precedents_cited_list: Gunasiri, Jayarathna Silva, Gnanasiri v. Republic of Sri Lanka 2009 (1) SLR 39 | Sarwan Singh vs. State of Punjab | Bobby Mathew vs. State of Kamataka
standard_of_review_applied: Review of evidence and legal correctness of High Court judgment

judges: N. Bandula Karunarathna, J. (P/CA) | M.A.R. Marikar, J.
brief_facts_summary: The Accused-Petitioner sought to transfer Case No. HCV/2923/2019 from the Vavuniya High Court, alleging bias and lack of impartiality by the specially appointed High Court Judge M.M.M. Mihal. The application was based on claims that the judge allowed ex parte communication with a witness, ordered investigations under the Witness Protection Act, cancelled the petitioner's bail without considering health, and refused requested trial dates. The case, originating from an incident in 2011, commenced hearings in November 2022.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The Accused-Petitioner argued that the High Court Judge was biased and not impartial, citing specific instances of alleged unfair conduct including ex parte meetings with witnesses, ordering investigations under the Witness Protection Act, cancelling bail without considering health, refusing requested trial dates, and making controversial comments.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: High Court Judge allowed State Counsel to bring Prosecution Witness No.3 to chambers without representation of Accused-Petitioner. | Judge directed SSP to investigate matters under Witness Protection Act without proper hearing. | Judge cancelled bail of Accused-Petitioner under Witness Protection Act and failed to consider health condition. | Judge refused to grant trial dates requested by Accused-Petitioner's Counsel and made controversial comments.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court reviewed proceedings and found the High Court Judge acted to expedite the case and address witness interference concerns. Witness testimony indicated threats and potential tampering, leading to judicial orders for investigation. The Court found no evidence of bias in the judge's actions.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court found no reasonable suspicion or real likelihood of bias, and the petitioner failed to adduce sufficient grounds for transfer.
defence_version_summary: The Accused-Petitioner pleaded not guilty and alleged judicial bias. No alibi or defence witnesses are mentioned in the transfer application. The court assessed the credibility of the bias claims and found them insufficient.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed the petition and proceedings, finding that the High Court Judge was specially appointed by the Chief Justice to expedite the case. The court reviewed the alleged instances of bias and concluded they were part of normal judicial management, including addressing witness threats and ensuring timely trial progress. The court applied tests for disqualifying bias (real likelihood and reasonable suspicion) and found no evidence to support the claims. Precedents on transfer applications were cited, emphasizing that transfer requires sufficient grounds and is not granted lightly.
coa_sentence_type: Petition dismissed with costs
brief_judgment_file_summary: The Accused-Petitioner, Jeyaratnam Sri Ranga, sought to transfer Case No. HCV/2923/2019 from Vavuniya High Court, alleging bias by Judge M.M.M. Mihal. The Court of Appeal examined the grounds, including ex parte witness interactions, bail cancellation, and trial date refusals. It found the judge was properly appointed to expedite the long-pending case and acted appropriately on witness interference concerns. Citing precedents, the court held the petitioner failed to prove bias or provide sufficient grounds for transfer. The petition was dismissed subject to payment of costs.
defence_counsel: Thishya Weragoda with Sanjaya Marambe and P.H. Weilkumbura instructed by Niluka Dissanayake
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court was managing a long-delayed case, taking steps to expedite proceedings and address witness protection issues. The Court of Appeal found no errors in the High Court's conduct and viewed its actions as appropriate judicial case management.
precedents_cited_list: Abdul Hasheeb V Mendis Perera and Others [1991] 1 SLR 243 | Sivasubramaniam V Sivasubramaniam [1980] 2 SLR 58
standard_of_review_applied: Tests for disqualifying bias: (i) real likelihood of bias and (ii) reasonable suspicion of bias; sufficient grounds required for transfer, not granted lightly.

judges: Menaka Wijesundera, J. | B. Sasi Mahendran, J.
offence_sections: Count 1: Section 364(2) of the Penal Code as amended by Act No. 22 of 1995. Count 2: Section 296 of the Penal Code. Count 3: Section 380 of the Penal Code.
location_of_offence: House in front of the Mavadivedum Army camp
brief_facts_summary: The accused was indicted for raping a minor girl, murdering her, and robbing money and jewellery from the house. An eyewitness (PW1) saw the accused follow the victim into her house, cut her neck, and rape her. The victim's grandmother (PW3) found the body and reported missing items. PW2, a pastor, was alerted at the scene and called the police. The Judicial Medical Officer (PW7) confirmed death by neck wound and evidence of rape.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Count 1: Section 364(2) of the Penal Code as amended by Act No. 22 of 1995. Count 2: Section 296 of the Penal Code. Count 3: Section 380 of the Penal Code.
hc_sentence_type: Count 1: 10 years rigorous imprisonment and fine. Count 2: Death Sentence. Count 3: 10 years rigorous imprisonment and fine.
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court Judge found the accused guilty on all three counts after trial. The judge accepted the eyewitness and medical evidence, convicting the accused of rape, murder, and robbery. Sentences were imposed accordingly.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant argued that the English translation brief did not show compliance with the 'Jury Option' procedure under Section 195(e) of the Criminal Procedure Code, which would vitiate the High Court proceedings. He also contended that the trial judge erred in admitting the deposition evidence of PW1 under Section 33 of the Evidence Ordinance, as the legal criteria were not satisfied.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The approved/accepted English translation brief does not appear to indicate due compliance of Section 195(e) of the Criminal Procedure Code relating to 'Jury Option' which would vitiate the entire preceding before the High Court. | The learned Trial Judge erred in fact and law by permitting the admission of the Deposition Evidence of Krishnapulle as it did not satisfy the laid down legal criteria under Section 33 of the Evidence Ordinance.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court found the eyewitness (PW1) credible and his evidence consistent with the medical findings. The prosecution led evidence of eight witnesses. The defense did not cross-examine PW1 on key points like the rape, and the accused's dock statement was rejected.
probability_assessment_by_court: Court held prosecution proved guilt beyond reasonable doubt for murder and rape, but not for robbery.
defence_version_summary: The accused pleaded not guilty and gave a dock statement claiming he only arrived at the crime scene to see what was happening. The court rejected this as inconsistent with prosecution evidence and noted the defense failed to cross-examine on material points like the rape.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal examined the grounds of appeal and found no merit. It confirmed the trial judge correctly handled the jury option issue and properly admitted PW1's deposition under Section 33 of the Evidence Ordinance after evidence showed the witness was untraceable. The COA evaluated the totality of evidence, including credible eyewitness testimony, consistent witness accounts, and strong medical evidence confirming rape and murder. It found the prosecution proved murder and rape beyond reasonable doubt but acquitted the accused on the robbery count due to insufficient evidence. The High Court's reasoning was upheld, and the appeal was dismissed for counts 1 and 2.
coa_sentence_type: Count 1: 10 years rigorous imprisonment and fine of 5000 LKR. Count 2: Death Sentence upheld. Count 3: Acquitted.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused was convicted by the High Court of Batticaloa for raping and murdering a minor girl and robbery. He was sentenced to death for murder, imprisonment for rape, and imprisonment and fines for robbery. He appealed on procedural grounds regarding jury option and admission of deposition evidence. The Court of Appeal dismissed both grounds, finding the procedures were correctly followed. The COA upheld the convictions for rape and murder, finding the evidence sufficient and credible, but acquitted the accused on the robbery charge due to insufficient evidence. The appeal was dismissed.
defence_counsel: Dr. Ranjith Fernando with Maleesha Meera
cause_of_death_exact_text: a 15-inch-long cut wound under the Deceased’s chin which slit opened her throat cutting off the blood vessels in her trachea, resulting in the complete blockage of blood circulation and breathing, categorically succumbing to instantaneous death
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted based on eyewitness and medical evidence. The COA found the HC correctly assessed evidence and applied the law, with no errors identified in its analysis or reasoning.
precedents_cited_list: Annavi Muthiriyan v Emperor 1915, 16 Cr. L.J 294
standard_of_review_applied: Review of trial court's factual and legal determinations, assessing if evidence supports conviction beyond reasonable doubt.

judges: Menaka Wijesundera, J. | B. Sasi Mahendran, J.
offence_sections: Section 54A(d) and 54A(b) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance as amended by Act No. 13 of 1984
brief_facts_summary: On 23rd December 2013, PW1 (Police Inspector Chandana Mahendra Bandara) and his team went to Orugodawatta Majeed Place. They saw a woman in a yellow floral dress who turned away suspiciously upon seeing them. She was apprehended and searched by PW10, Lady Officer Anusha, who found a light pink cellophane bag containing a brown powder in her right pocket. The powder was identified as heroin and weighed 20.340 grams. The Accused was arrested and the production was processed, eventually being sent to the Government Analyst.
evidence_type_secondary: Government Analyst Report, Police testimony regarding chain of custody
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 54A(d) and 54A(b) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance as amended by Act No. 13 of 1984
hc_judgment_summary: The Learned High Court Judge pronounced the Accused guilty on both counts of possession and trafficking of 5.77 g of Diacetylmorphine (heroin). She was sentenced to life imprisonment for each count.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The main ground of appeal was that the Learned Trial Judge failed to consider that the prosecution had not established a chain of inward journey for the drug evidence. The defence argued this created doubt about whether the production was tampered with before reaching the Government Analyst.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Failure to consider prosecution's failure to establish chain of inward journey of the production
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The prosecution led evidence from sixteen witnesses. The Court of Appeal examined the evidence concerning the chain of custody, particularly the timing of handling productions 107/13 and 108/13. It found the officers were clear about what they received, despite attempts by defence counsel to sow confusion.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court concluded the prosecution proved beyond reasonable doubt that there was no opportunity for tampering with the production until it reached the Government Analyst.
defence_version_summary: The Accused gave a dock statement. The defence challenged the chain of custody, arguing the prosecution failed to establish the inward journey of the drug evidence, creating doubt about tampering. The court found the defence evidence did not cast doubt on the prosecution's version.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed the evidence regarding the chain of custody, referencing precedents (Perera v. The Attorney General, Witharana Doli Nona v. The Republic of Sri Lanka, Mariyanayagan Norbertsingam v. Attorney General) which emphasize proving the inward journey to exclude tampering. It examined the testimony of PW1, PW11, and PW12 regarding the timing of handling productions 107/13 and 108/13, noting attempts by defence counsel to create confusion. The Court found the officers were unequivocal about what they received and that the prosecution proved beyond reasonable doubt there was no opportunity for tampering. It affirmed the High Court's analysis of the evidence and the conviction.
coa_sentence_type: Life imprisonment for each count (affirmed)
brief_judgment_file_summary: The Accused-Appellant, Mohammed Thaha Nurul Sifaya, was convicted in the High Court of Colombo for possession and trafficking of heroin and sentenced to life imprisonment on each count. She appealed, primarily arguing the prosecution failed to establish the chain of inward journey for the drug evidence. The Court of Appeal examined the testimony of police witnesses regarding the custody of the production, referencing relevant precedents on chain of custody. It found the prosecution proved beyond reasonable doubt there was no opportunity for tampering. The Court affirmed the conviction and sentence, dismissing the appeal.
defence_counsel: Amila Palliyage with Sandeepani Wijesooriya and S. Udugampola
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court Judge correctly analyzed the evidence concerning the chain of production and found the Accused guilty. The Court of Appeal agreed with this analysis and found no error.
precedents_cited_list: Perera v. The Attorney General (1998) 1 SLR 378 | Witharana Doli Nona vs. The Republic of Sri Lanka C.A. 19/99 | CA 16/2010 Mariyanayagan Norbertsingam v. Attorney General decided on 13.07.2015
standard_of_review_applied: Evaluation of evidence and application of established legal principles regarding chain of custody in drug cases.

judges: Menaka Wijesundera, J. | B. Sasi Mahendran, J.
offence_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The Accused-Appellant and the Deceased were employed at a hotel in Ottamavady and resided in a house rented by the hotel owner. The hotel owner (PW1) discovered the Deceased's body after forcing entry into the padlocked house when the Deceased did not report for work. Police investigation led to the arrest of the Accused, who was found in possession of a set of keys to the house and a mobile phone.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The Learned High Court Judge found the Accused guilty of murder, convicted him, and imposed the death sentence.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appeal was against the conviction and death sentence. The main argument centered on the insufficiency of circumstantial evidence to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The prosecution led evidence of six witnesses. The Court of Appeal found no direct evidence and the circumstantial evidence insufficient to prove guilt.
probability_assessment_by_court: Court held the prosecution failed to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt as the circumstantial evidence did not form a complete chain pointing irresistibly to guilt and left room for reasonable doubt.
defence_version_summary: The Accused made a dock statement asserting he had left the residence to stay at his cousin's house and that there was no animosity between him and the Deceased. The court found the prosecution case unproven.
legal_errors_description: The High Court erred in convicting based on insufficient circumstantial evidence that did not meet the required legal standard.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal applied established principles on circumstantial evidence, citing Hanumant Govind Nargundkar and Sudu Hakuruge Jamis. It held that the proved circumstances must be fully established, consistent only with guilt, and exclude every other hypothesis. The prosecution failed to establish that the mobile phone belonged to the Deceased or that only the Accused and Deceased had keys. No evidence excluded other persons. The chain of evidence was incomplete and left reasonable grounds consistent with innocence.
coa_sentence_type: Acquitted - conviction and sentence set aside
brief_judgment_file_summary: The Accused-Appellant was convicted of murder by the High Court of Batticaloa and sentenced to death. He appealed to the Court of Appeal. The case was based on circumstantial evidence. The Court of Appeal found the evidence insufficient, as it did not form a complete chain pointing irresistibly to guilt and left room for reasonable doubt. The appeal was allowed, the conviction and sentence were set aside, and the Accused was acquitted.
defence_counsel: Dr. Ranjith Fernando with Champika Monarawila
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted based on circumstantial evidence. The Court of Appeal found the High Court erred as the evidence was insufficient and did not meet the legal standard for circumstantial evidence convictions.
precedents_cited_list: Hanumant Govind Nargundkar and another v. State of Madhya Pradesh, AIR 1952 SC 343 | Sudu Hakuruge Jamis and 1 Other v. The Attorney General, CA 204/2010 | H.K.K.Habakkala v. Attorney General CA Appeal 107/2005 | Don Sunny v. AG 1998 2 SLR Page 1
standard_of_review_applied: Review of circumstantial evidence based on established legal principles requiring proof beyond reasonable doubt and exclusion of every hypothesis consistent with innocence.

judges: Prasantha De Silva,J. | K.K.A.V. Swarnadhipathi,J.
offence_sections: Section 13B (1) of the Industrial Disputes Act No. 43 of 1950 as amended
brief_facts_summary: The Applicant filed an application to the Labour Tribunal of Galle regarding an industrial dispute. A settlement was reached on 21.11.2014, reinstating the Applicant at Ketandala Estate from 01.12.2014 without back pay. The Respondents later alleged the Applicant failed to report for work and had suppressed material facts, including prior employment with Kelani Valley Plantation PLC. They filed a motion to set aside the settlement. The Labour Tribunal President refused this motion on 09.07.2015. The Respondents successfully revised this order in the Provincial High Court of Galle on 07.11.2017, which set aside the settlement and ordered an inquiry into the Applicant's prior employment. The Applicant appealed this order to the Court of Appeal.
evidence_type_secondary: Allegations of material fact suppression regarding prior employment
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 13B (1) of the Industrial Disputes Act No. 43 of 1950 as amended
hc_sentence_type: Order to hold an inquiry and set aside settlement
hc_judgment_summary: The Provincial High Court allowed the revision application, set aside the Labour Tribunal's settlement order dated 21.11.2014, and ordered an inquiry to ascertain if the Applicant was working at Kelani Valley Plantation PLC when he applied to the Labour Tribunal.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The Appellant appealed the Provincial High Court's order. The Respondents raised a preliminary objection challenging the Court of Appeal's jurisdiction to hear the appeal, arguing that under the Industrial Disputes Act, appeals from the Provincial High Court in labour matters lie directly to the Supreme Court.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Whether the Court of Appeal has jurisdiction to hear and determine this appeal in respect of the Industrial Dispute matters when an order was made by the Learned High Court Judge of the Provincial High Court of Galle.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The case revolves around the interpretation of jurisdictional statutes. The Court of Appeal analyzed constitutional provisions and specific laws like the Industrial Disputes Act to determine the correct appellate pathway.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court applied a literal rule of statutory interpretation to determine the legislature's intent regarding appellate jurisdiction.
defence_version_summary: The Applicant (Appellant) argued the Court of Appeal had jurisdiction under Article 154P(6) of the Constitution. The Respondents argued jurisdiction lay exclusively with the Supreme Court under the Industrial Disputes Act. The Court found the Respondents' interpretation correct.
procedural_defects_description: The appeal was filed in the wrong court; the correct appellate court for the Provincial High Court's order in a labour matter is the Supreme Court, not the Court of Appeal.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal conducted a detailed analysis of Article 154P of the Constitution, the High Court of the Provinces (Special Provisions) Act No. 19 of 1990, and the Industrial Disputes Act. It applied the literal rule of interpretation, finding the plain meaning of Section 31DD of the Industrial Disputes Act grants exclusive appellate jurisdiction to the Supreme Court for orders from the Provincial High Court in labour matters. It distinguished the precedent in Gunarathna v Thambiyagam as given per incuriam regarding the Industrial Disputes Act and followed more recent authority (Duro Pipe, Sunil Jayawardana) affirming the Supreme Court's exclusive jurisdiction. Consequently, it upheld the preliminary objection on jurisdiction.
coa_sentence_type: The appeal was dismissed for lack of jurisdiction. The order of the Provincial High Court dated 07.11.2017 remains valid, and the Labour Tribunal is ordered to conduct the inquiry as directed.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The Applicant-Appellant challenged a Provincial High Court order which set aside a Labour Tribunal settlement and ordered an inquiry. The Respondents raised a preliminary objection on the Court of Appeal's jurisdiction. The Court of Appeal analyzed constitutional and statutory provisions, particularly Section 31DD of the Industrial Disputes Act, concluding that appeals from Provincial High Court orders in labour matters lie exclusively to the Supreme Court. It upheld the objection, dismissed the appeal for lack of jurisdiction, and affirmed the High Court's order for an inquiry by the Labour Tribunal.
defence_counsel: Chamara Nanayakkarawasam AAL with Dinuka Fernando AAL, for the Applicant-Respondent-Appellant; Samantha Vitharana AAL with Hiranya Fernando AAL for the Respondent-Petitioner-Respondents
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court allowed the revision application, finding merit in the Respondents' claim that the Applicant suppressed material facts. It set aside the Labour Tribunal's settlement and ordered a factual inquiry. The Court of Appeal did not critique the High Court's substantive reasoning but focused solely on the jurisdictional issue for the appeal.
precedents_cited_list: Duport Steel v Sirs (19980) 1 WLR 142 | Balasooriya Mudiyanselage Soorathunga Balasooriya v Saman Piyasiri and Others (2012) CA (Writ) No. 342/2012 CAM 29.04.2019 | Gunarathna v Thambiyagam 1993 2 SLR 355 | Bulathsinhala Arachoñige Indrani Mallika V Bulathsinhala Arachoñige Sirivardane of Dummalasooriya, SC Appeal No 160/2016 [SC Minutes 02.12.2022] | Duro Pipe (Private) Ltd v Hetitge Pradeep Silva and 38 Others, CA PHC 91/2015 [CAM 27.02.2017] | Sunil Jayawardana vs. Puttalam Cement Company Limited CA (PHC) APN 265/2004 [CA Minutes dated 05.08.2005] | Ramanathan Chettiar v. Wickramarachchi and Others [1978-79] 2 Sri LR 395
standard_of_review_applied: Literal rule of statutory interpretation to determine jurisdictional intent.

judges: Menaka Wijesundera, J. | B. Sasi Mahendran, J.
offence_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code (Count 1); Section 317 of the Penal Code (Counts 2 & 3)
location_of_offence: At the residence of PW1 (house of PW1 Sudu Menika)
brief_facts_summary: On 20 June 1993, the Accused, a relative, proposed to PW2 (aged 15) at her home. After she rejected him, he left and returned with a large pole hidden behind his back. He struck PW2, her mother PW1, and her brother (the Deceased). The Deceased died from brain damage and skull fracture. PW1 and PW2 were hospitalized with injuries.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code (Count 1); Section 317 of the Penal Code (Counts 2 & 3)
hc_sentence_type: Death sentence (Count 1); Five years rigorous imprisonment with fine (Count 2); One year rigorous imprisonment with fine (Count 3)
hc_judgment_summary: The Accused was convicted by a unanimous jury verdict on all three counts. The High Court Judge sentenced him to death for murder, and imposed terms of rigorous imprisonment and fines for causing grievous hurt and hurt.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The Accused appealed on grounds including: the High Court Judge's failure to discharge the jury due to alleged misconduct; misdirection on the evidentiary value of prosecution witnesses (PW2, PW3, PW4); failure to direct on defence evidence; failure to appreciate contradictions; and failure to give the benefit of doubt.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Failure to discharge jury over alleged discussion between juniors and court staff. | Misdirection on evidentiary value of PW3 (Geethani Manel). | Failure to analyse and misdirection on evidence of PW2 (Ramani). | Failure to direct on importance of documents marked for defence. | Failure to appreciate contradictions and omissions and give benefit of doubt. | Failure to direct on hearsay evidence of PW4 (Wimalawathi). | Failure to direct on defence case and defence witnesses.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found that the contradictions in the testimony of lay witnesses, who gave evidence after 18 years, did not go to the root of the case. The court held the prosecution evidence was credible and established the charges.
probability_assessment_by_court: Court held Accused failed to prove insanity on balance of probability. Prosecution evidence left no reasonable doubt.
defence_version_summary: Accused pleaded not guilty and raised defence of insanity under Section 77, Penal Code. He made a dock statement and led one defence witness (Doctor). Defence argued he was of unsound mind. Court rejected this, finding he acted with rational thought and failed to prove insanity.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The COA found no misdirection or non-direction by the HC Judge causing miscarriage of justice. It held contradictions in lay witness testimony after many years were not material. The defence of insanity was correctly rejected as the doctor's evidence was from 2001 and did not address mental state in 1993. The Accused's premeditated actions showed rational thought. The conviction based on unanimous jury verdict and the sentence were affirmed.
coa_sentence_type: Death sentence affirmed (Count 1); Five years rigorous imprisonment with fine affirmed (Count 2); One year rigorous imprisonment with fine affirmed (Count 3)
brief_judgment_file_summary: The Accused was convicted of murder and assault in the High Court of Monaragala and sentenced to death and imprisonment. He appealed to the Court of Appeal on grounds including jury misconduct, misdirection on evidence, and failure to consider the defence of insanity. The COA found no legal errors or misdirection. It held the insanity defence was not proven, the eyewitness evidence was credible despite minor contradictions, and the jury's unanimous verdict was sound. The appeal was dismissed, affirming the conviction and sentence.
defence_counsel: Chathura Amarathunga
cause_of_death_exact_text: brain damage with a fractured skull following the assault to the head with a blunt weapon
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court Judge correctly directed the jury on the law and evidence, including the insignificance of contradictions and the rejection of the insanity defence. The COA found the HC analysis and directions were proper.
precedents_cited_list: Bhoginbhai Hirjibhai V. State of Gujarat AIR 1983 SC 753 | Nandaseena v Attorney General 2007, 1 S.L.R 237
standard_of_review_applied: Reviewed for misdirection or non-direction causing miscarriage of justice; examined whether verdict was unreasonable or unsupported by evidence.
sentencing_principles_applied: Imposed sentences as per Penal Code sections; affirmed the HC sentence which included death penalty and imprisonment.

judges: Menaka Wijesundera, J. | B. Sasi Mahendran, J.
offence_sections: 54A(b) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance as amended by Act No. 13 of 1984, Section 54A(d) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance as amended by Act No. 13 of 1984
location_of_offence: House at end of narrow lane adjacent to St. Anthony’s Shrine in Blumendhal
brief_facts_summary: Police received information about heroin trafficking at a house in Blumendhal. A team led by PW1 raided the location on foot and found the Accused inside. The Accused attempted to escape but was apprehended. A pink cellophane bag containing brown powder, identified as heroin, was found in his pants pocket. The Accused was arrested and the substance was sealed as evidence.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: 54A(b) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance as amended by Act No. 13 of 1984, Section 54A(d) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance as amended by Act No. 13 of 1984
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court Judge found the Accused guilty on both counts of trafficking and possession of heroin and sentenced him to life imprisonment on each count.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The Appellant argued the High Court Judge failed to consider contradictions between prosecution witnesses, did not give due regard to the dock statement, and did not account for untrustworthiness and weaknesses in the prosecution evidence. The judgment was claimed to be contrary to the evidence.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Has the learned High Court Judge not given due regard to the contradictions between the Prosecution witnesses? | Has the learned High Court Judge not given due regard to the dock statement of the Appellant? | Has the learned High Court Judge not give due regard to the untrustworthiness and weaknesses of the prosecution? | Is the Judgment contrary to the evidence?
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court found significant contradictions and implausibilities in the testimonies of PW1 and PW2, including inconsistencies in timelines, the sealing of evidence, and the identification of the substance. The Court deemed the evidence unreliable.
probability_assessment_by_court: Court found that the prosecution evidence did not establish guilt beyond reasonable doubt due to contradictions and implausibilities.
defence_version_summary: The Accused made a dock statement. He did not plead guilty. No alibi or defence witnesses were mentioned. The Court found the prosecution evidence unreliable.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal carefully examined the evidence, focusing on inconsistencies in the police testimony (PW1 and PW2) regarding timelines, the sealing of evidence, the identification process, and the route taken to the location. The Court found the prosecution evidence contradictory and implausible, and concluded that the charges were not proved beyond reasonable doubt.
coa_sentence_type: Sentence and conviction set aside
brief_judgment_file_summary: The Accused was convicted by the High Court of Colombo for trafficking and possession of heroin and sentenced to life imprisonment. He appealed, arguing contradictions in prosecution evidence and failure to consider his dock statement. The Court of Appeal found significant inconsistencies in police testimony regarding the timeline, sealing of evidence, and identification, rendering the evidence unreliable. The appeal was allowed, the conviction and sentence were set aside, and the Accused was acquitted.
defence_counsel: Vishwa De Livera Tennakoon with Lilani Ganegama
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court Judge found the Accused guilty based on prosecution evidence. The Court of Appeal found the High Court failed to address vital contradictions and implausibilities in the evidence of PW1 and PW2.
standard_of_review_applied: Review of evidence for contradictions and reliability to determine if guilt was proved beyond reasonable doubt.

judges: Sasi Mahendran, J. | Menaka Wijesundera, J.
offence_sections: Section 365 B (2) of the Penal Code as amended by Act, No. 22 of 1995, and as further amended by No. 29 of 1998 and No. 16 of 2006
brief_facts_summary: The Accused-Appellant was indicted for committing grave sexual abuse on a girl under 16 years (PW1), who lived in his house with her family. The abuse occurred multiple times at the accused's house when no one else was home. The victim reported the abuse to her English teacher, leading to police involvement and a medical examination. She was later placed in an orphanage.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 365 B (2) of the Penal Code as amended by Act, No. 22 of 1995, and as further amended by No. 29 of 1998 and No. 16 of 2006
hc_sentence_type: 12 years of rigorous imprisonment, along with a fine of Rs. 25,000/-, with a default sentence of six months of simple imprisonment
hc_judgment_summary: The Learned High Court Judge found the Accused guilty based on the prosecution evidence, particularly the consistent testimony of PW1. The Accused was convicted and sentenced to 12 years rigorous imprisonment, fined, and ordered to pay compensation.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appeal argued that the prosecution failed to prove the exact date of the offence and failed to exclude the possibility that someone else could have committed the offence. The defence contended that contradictions in the victim's evidence created reasonable doubt.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The Learned Trial Judge had failed to consider that the date of the alleged offence had not been proved by the Prosecution. | The Learned Trial Judge had failed to consider that the prosecution failed to exclude the possibility of the instant offence being committed by someone else when the evidence of the prosecution itself leads to a reasonable inference that either someone else could have done the same.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found PW1's testimony consistent and truthful, despite minor contradictions. The court noted that victims of child sexual abuse may have memory lapses and should not be expected to recall events with photographic precision.
probability_assessment_by_court: The court held the prosecution proved its case beyond reasonable doubt. Minor inconsistencies did not create doubt given the victim's age and trauma.
defence_version_summary: The Accused pleaded not guilty and made a dock statement. He claimed the victim and her family lived at his house only 10 days, that his house was too small for such acts, and that he had reported the father's abuse to a teacher. The court found his version unconvincing and not capable of raising reasonable doubt.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The COA analyzed the evidence, noting PW1 was consistent about being abused in grade six. It applied precedents stating victims cannot be expected to recall details with photographic memory and that minor contradictions are natural in child abuse cases. The COA found the High Court correctly assessed credibility and that the defence did not create reasonable doubt. The objection regarding the date was overruled as the victim was certain about her grade level at the time.
coa_sentence_type: 12 years rigorous imprisonment, fine of Rs. 25,000 with default simple imprisonment of 6 months, compensation of Rs. 100,000 with default rigorous imprisonment of 2 years
brief_judgment_file_summary: The Accused-Appellant was convicted by the High Court of Rathnapura for grave sexual abuse of a minor under Section 365B(2) of the Penal Code and sentenced to 12 years rigorous imprisonment, a fine, and compensation. He appealed on grounds that the date was not proved and that the prosecution failed to exclude others. The Court of Appeal found the victim's testimony consistent and credible, applied relevant precedents on child witness memory, and dismissed the appeal, affirming the conviction and sentence.
defence_counsel: I.B.S. Harshana
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court correctly considered PW1's evidence and found her truthful. The COA agreed with the HC's assessment and its rejection of the accused's dock statement.
precedents_cited_list: D.Tikiribanda v. Attorney General, 2010 BLR 92 | Bhoginbhai Hirjibhai V. State of Gujarat AIR 1983 SC 753 | Don Kuruppu Arachchige Indika Gayan v The Republic of Sri Lanka, CA 205/2007 | Warnakulasuriya Lakshman Thisera alias Jayakody Don Lakshman Appuhamy v. Attorney General, CA 13/2015
standard_of_review_applied: Beyond reasonable doubt standard; evaluation of witness credibility and consistency.

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 308(A)(2) of the Penal Code as amended for committing an offence of Cruelty
brief_facts_summary: The victim, a 15-year-old girl from an impoverished family, was brought by the Appellant's husband to the Appellant's house in Ranpokunugama, Nittambuwa. The Appellant subjected the victim to cruel treatment, including assault with blunt and sharp weapons, burning, and deprivation of proper care, over a period between 03.09.1999 and 25.10.1999. The victim returned home with numerous injuries, corroborated by her mother, brother, and medical evidence. The Appellant was arrested after an inquiry by IP/Rajapaksha.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 308(A)(2) of the Penal Code as amended for committing an offence of Cruelty
hc_sentence_type: Two years rigorous imprisonment and a fine of Rs.1000/-, default two weeks simple imprisonment. Compensation of Rs.50,000/- to victim, default three months simple imprisonment.
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the Appellant on the third count of cruelty and acquitted her on the second count of aiding rape. The court sentenced her to two years rigorous imprisonment with a fine and compensation to the victim, believing the evidence of the victim and the corroborating witnesses despite some contradictions.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The Appellant's counsel argued that the High Court Judge failed to properly evaluate the evidence, did not apply the maxim 'Falsus in uno, falsus in omnibus', wrongly expected proof from the defence, and failed to consider grave discrepancies in the prosecution case.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The Learned High Court Judge has not evaluated the evidence properly. | The Learned High Court Judge has failed to follow the maxim Falsus in uno, falsus in omnibus. | The Learned High Court Judge had expected some proof from the defence. | The Learned High Court Judge has failed to consider grave discrepancies of the prosecution case.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal carefully evaluated the victim's evidence, acknowledging the need for caution with a child witness. It found the High Court Judge had properly analyzed the evidence, correctly addressed contradictions, and applied the maxim 'Falsus in uno, falsus in omnibus' as per superior court guidance.
probability_assessment_by_court: The court found no reasonable doubt regarding the charge of cruelty and held the victim's evidence credible despite minor discrepancies.
defence_version_summary: The Appellant pleaded not guilty, gave evidence from the witness box, and called two witnesses on her behalf. She denied assaulting the victim, stating the victim already had injuries when she arrived. The court found the defence evidence failed to create a doubt in the prosecution case.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed the appeal grounds comprehensively. It found the High Court Judge properly evaluated the evidence, correctly applied the divisibility of witness credibility principle, and did not misapply the 'Falsus in uno' maxim. The Court found no proof was expected from the defence and the contradictions in the prosecution case were not grave. It upheld the conviction but, considering the passage of 23 years, the age of the Appellant (54), and the circumstances, decided to suspend the sentence while increasing compensation.
coa_sentence_type: Two years rigorous imprisonment suspended for 10 years. Compensation increased to Rs.500,000/- with a default sentence of two years.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The Appellant (2nd Accused) was convicted by the High Court of Gampaha for cruelty to a child (victim) under her care. She appealed on grounds of improper evidence evaluation, failure to apply a legal maxim, expecting defence proof, and ignoring prosecution discrepancies. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal, upholding the conviction. However, considering the long delay (23 years) and the Appellant's age, the Court suspended the two-year sentence for 10 years and increased the compensation to the victim from Rs.50,000 to Rs.500,000.
defence_counsel: Sumith Senanayake, P.C. with Madhushani De Soysa, Nirmani Wickramasinghe with Damitha Wickrama Arachchi
hc_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the High Court Judge correctly analyzed the evidence, considered witness credibility as divisible, and gave plausible reasons for disregarding minor contradictions. The COA found no error in the HC's approach.
precedents_cited_list: Panchhi and Others v. The State of U.P and Others [1998] 7 SCC 177 | Kumara De Silva and 2 Others v. Attorney General [2010] 2 SLR 169 | Samarawcera v Attorney General [1990] 1 SLR 256 | Viraj v The Attorney General [2010] 2 SLR 251
standard_of_review_applied: Evaluation of whether the High Court Judge properly considered evidence, applied legal principles correctly, and addressed contradictions reasonably.
sentencing_principles_applied: Consideration of delay in prosecution (23 years), age of the accused (54), circumstances of the case, and the mandatory minimum sentence under Section 308(A)(2), leading to suspension of sentence and increase in compensation.

judges: Menaka Wijesundera, J. | B. Sasi Mahendran, J.
offence_sections: Section 54A(d) and 54A(b) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance as amended by Act No. 13 of 1984
location_of_offence: Babapulla bridge at Kettarama, Kettarama Temple Rd, Malligawatta, Colombo
brief_facts_summary: The Accused-Appellant was arrested on August 22, 2016, after police received information about a man carrying heroin. He was apprehended near the Babapulla bridge, Kettarama, matching the informant's description. Police searched him and found a package containing brown powder later confirmed to be 13.23g of pure diacetylmorphine (heroin) within 45.290g of powder. He was also found with cash and gold jewelry. The prosecution presented evidence from fourteen witnesses, and the High Court convicted and sentenced him to death for possession and trafficking.
evidence_type_secondary: Eyewitness testimony of police officers, Government Analyst Report
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 54A(d) and 54A(b) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance as amended by Act No. 13 of 1984
hc_sentence_type: Death sentence for each offense (possession and trafficking)
hc_judgment_summary: The Learned High Court Judge found the Accused guilty of both charges based on prosecution evidence and sentenced him to death for each offense. The judge did not accept the defence's version of events.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant argued that the High Court judge failed to consider discrepancies in the production chain, contradictions in prosecution evidence, the probability of the prosecution case, and the consistency of the defence. The judge also erred in rejecting the defence version on a wrong basis.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The learned High Court Judge has failed to consider the discrepancies in the production chain in favour of the Accused-Appellant. | The Learned High Court Judge has failed to consider and properly evaluate vital inter partes contradictions. | The Learned High Court Judge has erred in considering the probability of the case of the Prosecution. | The Learned High Court Judge has failed to consider and grant due weightage to the consistency of the defence of the Accused. | The Learned High Court Judge has erred in refusing to Act upon the defence version and rejecting in on a wrong and erroneous basis.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The prosecution presented evidence from fourteen witnesses. The Court of Appeal found the evidence of PW1 and PW2 consistent and without marked contradictions regarding the arrest and recovery of drugs. The chain of custody evidence was also found to be reliable.
probability_assessment_by_court: The court considered the totality of evidence, including the prosecution case and the dock statement. It held that the defence evidence did not create a reasonable doubt in the prosecution's case.
defence_version_summary: The Accused pleaded not guilty. His defence was an alibi, claiming he was arrested at his wife's residence earlier in the day and assaulted. He gave a dock statement and called one defence witness (his mistress). The court found his version not credible and insufficient to create a reasonable doubt.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal thoroughly examined the evidence, including witness testimonies and the chain of custody. It found no discrepancies regarding the arrest location and that the prosecution evidence was consistent. The chain of custody, despite a minor omission in PW1's testimony, was confirmed by PW11 and the Government Analyst. The court cited precedent (Don. Shamantha Jude Anthony Jayamaha v. Attorney General) on evaluating dock statements in light of the totality of evidence. It found the trial judge had properly considered all evidence and reasons for disbelieving the defence. The defence failed to create reasonable doubt.
coa_sentence_type: Death sentence for each offense affirmed
brief_judgment_file_summary: The Accused-Appellant was convicted by the High Court of Colombo for possession and trafficking of 13.23g of heroin and sentenced to death. He appealed on grounds including discrepancies in the production chain and contradictions in evidence. The Court of Appeal reviewed the evidence, found the prosecution case strong and the chain of custody reliable, and held the defence version did not create reasonable doubt. The appeal was dismissed, and the High Court's conviction and death sentence were affirmed.
defence_counsel: Anuja Premaratna, PC with Imasha Senadeera
hc_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found that the High Court judge thoroughly considered all material evidence, scrutinized the defence evidence, and provided reasons for disbelieving the defence version. No errors were identified in the HC's analysis.
precedents_cited_list: Don. Shamantha Jude Anthony Jayamaha v. Attorney General, CA 303/2006, decided on 11.07.2012
standard_of_review_applied: The court reviewed whether the conviction could be reached based on the evidence led before the trial court, considering the totality of evidence.

judges: Menaka Wijesundera, J. | B. Sasi Mahendran, J.
offence_sections: Unlawful assembly to commit murder and hurt, and in the alternative common intention to commit murder and hurt
brief_facts_summary: The deceased and others went to inspect a three-wheeler. A group of police officers, led by the first accused appellant, arrived, assaulted them accusing them of treasure hunting, and took them to the police station. The deceased later developed breathing difficulties, was admitted to the remand hospital, and died on May 9. The prosecution alleged assault by the police, while the defense claimed they were performing a lawful duty and used force to control a group fighting among themselves in a suspicious location.
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the accused appellants based on unlawful assembly to commit murder and hurt, or alternatively common intention. The trial judge found them guilty, but specific details of the sentence are not provided in the appeal judgment.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appeals were lodged to set aside the High Court judgment. The main grounds challenge the prosecution's narrative on the time of the incident, the formation of an unlawful assembly, the reliability of the dying declaration, contradictions in witness testimony, and the lack of evidence linking the 2nd to 6th accused to the assault or a common murderous object.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Discrepancy in time of incident between prosecution and defense (6:30 p.m. vs. 8:45 p.m./9 p.m.) | Failure to prove formation of an unlawful assembly with common object | Contradictions in prosecution witness testimony (especially the brother of the deceased) | Dying declaration reliability and failure to implicate other accused | Lack of evidence against 2nd to 6th accused appellants | Defense acting in lawful duty and using necessary force
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court found serious contradictions in prosecution witness testimony, especially the brother of the deceased who initially implicated all accused but later said only the first accused assaulted them. The defense evidence, including police station notes and testimony of the OIC, challenged the prosecution's timeline. The dying declaration was considered but found insufficient to implicate all accused.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court found the prosecution's story improbable and lacking merit, with serious doubts about the time of incident and common object among accused. Prosecution failed to prove charges beyond reasonable doubt.
defence_version_summary: The accused pleaded not guilty. The first accused appellant stated he was performing a lawful duty, used slaps to control a group fighting among themselves, and bought them food. Other accused supported this version in their dock statements. The defense claimed they did not share an illegal common object.
legal_errors_description: High Court erred in finding unlawful assembly and common intention without sufficient evidence. Failed to properly assess contradictions in prosecution evidence and reliability of dying declaration.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed the time discrepancy (prosecution: 6:30 p.m., defense: 8:45 p.m./9 p.m.), finding defense evidence corroborated by police notes. It found no unlawful assembly as accused were performing a lawful duty and lacked a common illegal object. Witness contradictions and unreliable dying declaration weakened the prosecution case. For the 1st accused, the Court found no murder intent but knowledge of causing death due to his experience, convicting him of culpable homicide not amounting to murder.
coa_sentence_type: 07 years rigorous imprisonment for culpable homicide not amounting to murder (for 1st accused appellant); Acquittal for 2nd to 6th accused appellants
brief_judgment_file_summary: Six police officers were convicted by the Badulla High Court for unlawful assembly to commit murder and hurt. The Court of Appeal partly allowed the appeals. It acquitted the 2nd to 6th accused due to lack of evidence and no common unlawful object. For the 1st accused, it set aside the murder conviction but found him guilty of culpable homicide not amounting to murder, sentencing him to 7 years rigorous imprisonment. The Court highlighted contradictions in prosecution evidence, unreliable dying declaration, and the defense's lawful duty claim.
defence_counsel: Anil Silva, P.C. with Shaluka Neranga (1st accused); Neranjan Jayasinghe with D.D.K. Katugampola (2nd and 4th accused); Sallya Peiris, P.C. with Thanuka Nandasiri (3rd accused); Nalin Ladduwahetty, P.C. with Kavithri Ubeysekera, Rajitha Samarasekera and Menuka Premashantha (5th accused); Multiple counsel for 6th accused (Nandasiri Yapa, Rohitha Rajapaksha, Pradeep Fernando, Bhagya Herath)
cause_of_death_exact_text: Extensive damage to the brain caused by a fatal injury on the head
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted all accused based on unlawful assembly/common intention. The COA found the HC erred by not properly considering the time discrepancy, witness contradictions, and lack of evidence for a common unlawful object among the accused, especially the 2nd to 6th.
precedents_cited_list: Mendis vs. Paramaswami (62 NLR 302) | Jagathsena and others vs G.D.P.Perea and others ((1992) 1 Sri L.R. 375)
standard_of_review_applied: Evaluation of evidence for sufficiency and reliability, burden of proof beyond reasonable doubt
sentencing_principles_applied: Consideration of intention vs. knowledge in murder vs. culpable homicide, sentencing based on the degree of culpability and circumstances of the offence
final_charge_after_appeal: Murder modified to Culpable Homicide not amounting to murder (for 1st accused)

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 25(2) read with section 40(1) of the Forest Ordinance
brief_facts_summary: The accused was charged in the Udugama Magistrate’s Court for transporting Venivelgeta (a forest produce) without a permit in a three-wheeler owned by the petitioner. The accused pleaded guilty and was convicted. The Magistrate then initiated an inquiry regarding confiscation of the vehicle under section 40(1) of the Forest Ordinance. The vehicle owner (the petitioner) gave evidence, calling a representative from the leasing company, as the vehicle was under a lease. The Magistrate, by order dated 27-01-2022, ordered confiscation, finding the owner failed to establish he took all necessary precautions to prevent the offence.
evidence_type_primary: Owner and leasing company representative testimony
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court Judge of Galle refused the revision application on 22-02-2022 without issuing notice to the respondents, holding there were no exceptional circumstances and no miscarriage of justice to warrant interference with the Magistrate's confiscation order.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The petitioner challenged the Magistrate's confiscation order and the High Court's refusal to issue notice on the revision. Main arguments: The Magistrate erred in finding the owner failed to take all precautions, especially when evidence showed instructions were given to the driver. The High Court Judge erred in dismissing the revision without notice and a hearing, despite property rights being at stake. The prosecution failed to specify the quantity and value of the Venivelgeta, relevant to assessing gravity and exceptional circumstances.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Learned Magistrate erred in concluding owner failed to take all necessary precautions. | Learned High Court Judge erred in refusing to issue notice and grant a hearing on the revision application. | Prosecution failed to mention quantity and value of transported Venivelgeta, a relevant factor. | Confiscation order not justifiable given owner's evidence and lack of knowledge.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed the Magistrate's findings, noting the Magistrate implicitly acknowledged the owner gave instructions to the driver (his brother). The Court found the Magistrate failed to consider other relevant factors like the quantity/value of the produce and the owner's lack of prior knowledge or illegal use of the vehicle.
probability_assessment_by_court: Court applied balance of probability as the standard of proof for the confiscation inquiry, as settled by precedent.
defence_version_summary: The accused pleaded guilty to the charge. The vehicle owner (petitioner) pleaded not to confiscation, testifying he gave instructions to the driver (his brother) and had no knowledge of the offence. The Magistrate accepted the owner had no knowledge but still confiscated the vehicle for failing to prove sufficient precautions.
legal_errors_description: The Magistrate erred by not considering all relevant facts (quantity/value of produce, owner's lack of knowledge, no prior illegal use) when deciding confiscation. The High Court Judge erred in law by refusing to issue notice on the revision application without properly considering exceptional circumstances and property rights.
procedural_defects_description: High Court Judge dismissed revision application without issuing notice to respondents and without granting a hearing, despite the matter involving third-party property rights.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal held the confiscation inquiry requires proof on a balance of probability. The Magistrate's own findings implied the owner gave instructions and had no knowledge, which should have satisfied the requirement of taking precautions under section 40(1) proviso. The Magistrate failed to consider other relevant factors like the unspecified quantity/value of the produce. The High Court Judge erred procedurally by dismissing the revision without notice and a hearing. Citing precedent (Sadi Banda), the COA found exceptional circumstances existed (property rights, procedural unfairness) to invoke revisionary jurisdiction. The confiscation was not justifiable.
coa_sentence_type: Order for release of vehicle to petitioner; Magistrate's confiscation order and High Court's dismissal order set aside.
brief_judgment_file_summary: This is a revision application to the Court of Appeal by the owner of a three-wheeler confiscated after the driver (the owner's brother) was convicted for transporting Venivelgeta without a permit. The Udugama Magistrate ordered confiscation, finding the owner failed to prove he took all precautions. The Galle High Court dismissed the owner's revision without notice. The Court of Appeal allowed the appeal, holding the Magistrate erred in not considering all relevant facts and the High Court erred procedurally. The COA set aside both lower court orders and directed the Magistrate to release the vehicle to the owner.
defence_counsel: Kamal Suneth Perera
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court Judge refused the revision application without issuing notice, finding no exceptional circumstances. The COA found this was an error, as property rights were at stake and the Judge should have issued notice and granted a hearing before dismissal. The COA also noted the High Court considered irrelevant factors (like lease rental amounts and parking location) not central to the Magistrate's confiscation reasoning.
precedents_cited_list: Sadi Banda Vs. Officer-in-Charge of Norton Bridge Police Station (2014) 1 SLR 33 | The Finance Company PLC Vs. Priyantha Chandra and Five Others (2010) 2 SLR 220
standard_of_review_applied: Revisionary jurisdiction under Article 138 of the Constitution; Court examines if lower courts committed errors of law or fact warranting interference, focusing on exceptional circumstances and miscarriage of justice.

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 40 of the Forest Ordinance
brief_facts_summary: The accused was charged with transporting timber without a permit under the Forest Ordinance. He pleaded guilty and was sentenced. An inquiry was held regarding the vehicle used, a tractor and trailer. The registered owners (the Appellants) were summoned to show cause why the vehicles should not be confiscated. The Magistrate ordered confiscation, which was upheld by the High Court on revision. The owners appealed to the Court of Appeal.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 40 of the Forest Ordinance
hc_sentence_type: Confiscation of vehicle to the State
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court affirmed the Magistrate's order confiscating the tractor and trailer. The High Court dismissed the revision application on the ground that the Appellants had failed to adduce exceptional circumstances.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The Appellants contended the orders were contrary to law and against the evidence. They argued both lower courts erred in concluding they failed to establish taking precautions to prevent illegal use, and failed to properly evaluate evidence regarding lack of knowledge and lack of habitual offending.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The orders are contrary to law and against the weight of evidence. | Both courts erred in law and fact in concluding Appellants failed to establish taking precautions. | The Magistrate failed to consider evidence of the 2nd Appellant's conscious efforts. | Both courts failed to evaluate evidence regarding previous illegal activities not being recorded. | Both courts failed to evaluate evidence that Appellants/Accused are not habitual offenders. | Both courts failed to evaluate the fact Appellants had no knowledge about transporting timber without permit. | The Magistrate arrived at a conjectural view that the 2nd Appellant had knowledge of the offence.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed the evidence of the vehicle owners regarding precautions taken. It found the Magistrate failed to properly evaluate this evidence, particularly the 1st Appellant's instructions and inspections, and the 2nd Appellant's steps to prevent illegal use.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal found the lower courts failed to properly evaluate the evidence showing the owners took precautions and lacked knowledge.
defence_version_summary: The Accused pleaded guilty.
