judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: section 296 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The accused-appellant was convicted of murdering his 9-year-old nephew, Munasinghe Arachchilage Indunil Chamara, on 09-11-2001. Neighbor witnesses observed the appellant assaulting the child with bare hands and a club, dragging him and causing his head to strike a wall. The child succumbed to injuries. The Judicial Medical Officer observed 18 injuries, including a head injury deemed essentially fatal. The appellant's defense was a denial, stating he found the child unconscious and took him to the hospital.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: section 296 of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court Judge found the appellant guilty of murder under section 296 of the Penal Code. The judge determined the appellant caused injuries with the intention of causing death, falling under the 2nd limb of section 294. The judge found no basis for the appellant's defense of denial and sentenced him to death.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The sole ground of appeal argued was that the evidence warranted a conviction for culpable homicide not amounting to murder under section 297, based on the 3rd limb of section 293 (knowledge). The appellant's counsel contended the actions fell short of murder as defined in section 294. The respondent argued there was no evidence to bring the case within any exception to murder under section 294 and moved for dismissal.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The evidence led at the trial warrants the consideration of a lesser culpability on the basis of knowledge.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the eyewitness testimonies of PW-04 and PW-06 credible and supported by the police officer's observation that they could see the incident. The appellant did not effectively challenge the evidence linking him to the injuries. The JMO's evidence strongly corroborated the eyewitness accounts regarding the nature and severity of the fatal injuries.
probability_assessment_by_court: The court found the prosecution evidence established the appellant's guilt beyond reasonable doubt. The appellant failed to provide a sufficient explanation for the incriminating evidence against him.
defence_version_summary: The accused pleaded not guilty. His defense was a total denial given in a dock statement, claiming he found the child unconscious and took him to the hospital. He did not call any witnesses. The court found his defense to have no basis and not credible in light of the strong prosecution evidence.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The COA analyzed whether the High Court should have considered the lesser charge of culpable homicide not amounting to murder. It held that simply arguing the actions fall under section 293 is insufficient; the appellant must show they fall within one of the exceptions to murder in section 294. The COA reviewed the evidence, including the JMO's opinion on the fatal nature of the head injury and the number of injuries, and found no basis to conclude the case fell within any exception. It cited precedent (King Vs. Bellana Withanage Eddin, King Vs. Albert Appuhamy) on the trial judge's duty to consider lesser charges but found no evidence in the record to support such a conclusion here. The COA affirmed the High Court's analysis and finding of murder under section 294(2).
coa_sentence_type: Death
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused-appellant appealed his murder conviction and death sentence for the 2001 killing of his 9-year-old nephew. The High Court of Kurunegala convicted him based on eyewitness and medical evidence. The sole appeal ground argued for a lesser conviction of culpable homicide not amounting to murder. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal, finding no evidence to place the case within the exceptions to murder under section 294 of the Penal Code. It affirmed the High Court's judgment, conviction for murder, and death sentence.
defence_counsel: Indica Mallawaratchy
cause_of_death_exact_text: blunt trauma caused to the head
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court correctly analyzed the evidence, found the appellant caused injuries with the intention of causing death (section 294, 2nd limb), and convicted for murder. The Court of Appeal agreed with this analysis and found no error.
precedents_cited_list: King Vs. Bellana Withanage Eddin 41 NLR 345 | King Vs. Albert Appuhamy 41 NLR 505
standard_of_review_applied: Appellate review of conviction and sentence based on evidence and legal interpretation of sections 293, 294, and 297 of the Penal Code.

judges: Sampath B.Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The accused-appellant, a police officer, was on night duty searching suspicious vehicles near Karamatiara Junction. A motorbike with two riders approached and ignored orders to stop. The appellant and PW1 saw what they believed to be a gun-like object. The appellant fired shots to stop the bike, striking the deceased in the head, causing his death. The incident attracted a hostile crowd which was later controlled by police.
evidence_type_primary: Eyewitness testimony (police officer PW1 and rider PW2)
evidence_type_secondary: Medical evidence (post mortem report), Scene observation (investigating officers)
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court judge, after a non-jury trial, convicted the appellant of murder under Section 296 of the Penal Code and sentenced him to death on 20.05.2022. The judge found the prosecution evidence sufficient to establish guilt beyond reasonable doubt.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant argued that the High Court judge failed to properly evaluate the appellant's lack of intention to commit murder, his actions done in good faith while performing duties, and the credibility of prosecution witnesses. The appellant contended the evidence showed he was acting under legal duty and should be protected under Section 69 of the Penal Code.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Whether the Learned High Court Judge failed to evaluate the evidence pertaining to the intention of the Appellant. | Whether the Appellant has acted upon his powers in good faith. | Whether the evidence given by PW2 and the circumstances of the incident make PW2 a trustworthy witness. | Whether the Learned High Court judge has properly evaluated the Dock Statement of the Appellant and the evidence favorable for the Appellant.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal reevaluated the evidence, focusing on PW1 and PW2's testimonies and the scene description. The court found the appellant acted on a reasonable suspicion while on duty, seeing a gun-like object, and shot to stop the fleeing bike without intent to kill.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal assessed that the appellant lacked criminal intent and acted in good faith under a mistaken belief of legal duty, negating the probability of guilt for murder.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty. He made a dock statement explaining he fired shots to stop a suspicious motorbike while on duty, believing one rider had a gun, without intending to kill. The court found his version credible in the circumstances.
legal_errors_description: The High Court judge erred in law by not considering the applicability of Section 69 of the Penal Code (act done under legal duty or mistaken belief) to the appellant's actions as a police officer acting in good faith.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed the evidence in light of the appellant's duties under the Police Ordinance and the legal protections for public servants. It found the High Court judge failed to properly assess the absence of criminal intent and the appellant's good faith belief in performing his duty. The court cited legal authorities including Tennessee v. Garner on use of deadly force and principles from 'Criminal Law in Sri Lanka'. Considering the circumstances—the appellant's reasonable suspicion of a weapon, the fleeing bike, and the difficult terrain—the COA held the appellant was entitled to protection under Section 69 of the Penal Code and should have been acquitted.
coa_sentence_type: Acquitted; conviction and sentence set aside
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused-appellant, a police officer, was convicted of murder by the High Court of Embilipitiya and sentenced to death for shooting and killing a motorcycle rider while on night duty. He appealed, arguing he acted in good faith under his duties with no murderous intent. The Court of Appeal found the High Court judge erred by not considering Section 69 of the Penal Code, which protects acts done under a legal duty or mistaken belief in good faith. The COA held the appellant, acting on reasonable suspicion of a weapon, was discharging his duty to maintain law and order. The appeal was allowed, the conviction and death sentence were set aside, and the appellant was acquitted.
defence_counsel: Saliya Pieris, PC with Thanuka Nandasiri
cause_of_death_exact_text: gunshot entry wound in the back of the head of the deceased which had damaged the brain and caused the death
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court judge convicted the appellant of murder based on the shooting incident. The COA found the HC judge failed to properly evaluate the appellant's lack of intention, his actions in good faith as a police officer, and the applicability of statutory protections, leading to an erroneous finding of guilt.
precedents_cited_list: Tennessee v Garner, 471 U.S. 1(1985)
standard_of_review_applied: Review of evidence and legal principles to determine if High Court erred in not applying Section 69 of Penal Code and in assessing intent and good faith.

judges: Menaka Wijesundera, J. | B. Sasi Mahendran, J.
offence_sections: Section 54A (d) and Section 54A (b) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance
brief_facts_summary: The accused was arrested on 19.08.2008 at a checkpoint on the Dehiwala-Wellawatte bridge after a random search. Police officers recovered 2.60 grams of heroin (360 packets) from a green shopping bag in his pocket. The accused was taken to Wellawatte police station and the productions were handed over. The prosecution alleged possession and trafficking of heroin and morphine.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 54A (d) and Section 54A (b) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance
hc_sentence_type: Life Imprisonment for counts 1 and 2, 2 years each for counts 3 and 4 to run concurrently
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the accused on all four counts. He was sentenced to life imprisonment for possession and trafficking of heroin (counts 1 and 2) and 2 years each for possession and trafficking of morphine (counts 3 and 4) to run concurrently.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant argued the prosecution failed to prove the chain of custody of the productions beyond reasonable doubt, particularly the inward journey to the Government Analyst. He also contended the trial judge misdirected himself on the burden of proof, failed to consider contradictions in prosecution evidence, and failed to appreciate that the prosecution did not call key witnesses.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Failure to prove inward journey of productions beyond reasonable doubt | Failure to consider contradictions, omissions, and inconsistencies in prosecution evidence | Misdirection on law relating to burden of proof | Failure to appreciate evidence insufficient to rebut presumption of innocence | Failure to appreciate burden of proof is on prosecution | Imposing unnecessary burden on defence in a case of bare denial | Erred in failing to properly consider and evaluate evidence in totality | Failed to consider defence evidence | Prosecution failed to call key witnesses depriving fair trial | Failed to prove trafficking to requisite standard | Prosecution evidence contradicted itself on morphine charges | Conviction and sentence cannot be supported by evidence | Denied a fair trial
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed the evidence of prosecution witnesses regarding the handling of the productions. It found discrepancies in the testimony about who handled the productions and when, particularly the inward journey to the Government Analyst. The clerk who received the productions (Inoka) was not called as a witness, and PW11 could not identify her signature.
probability_assessment_by_court: Court found reasonable doubt due to break in chain of custody of productions to Government Analyst.
defence_version_summary: The accused made a statement from the dock and closed his case. He did not plead guilty. The defence was a bare denial, challenging the prosecution's evidence, particularly the chain of custody.
legal_errors_description: The High Court judge failed to consider that the evidence did not establish the chain of custody of the productions to the Government Analyst beyond reasonable doubt. The judge also failed to appreciate the possibility that the morphine could have reformed from heroin during the 15-month delay before analysis.
procedural_defects_description: Prosecution failed to call key witness (clerk Inoka) who received the productions, and PW11 could not identify her signature, breaking the chain of evidence.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal applied precedents establishing that in drug cases, the prosecution must prove the inward journey of the productions to the Government Analyst without break to rule out tampering. It found discrepancies in the evidence regarding who handled the productions and when, especially the handover from PW10 to PW06 and the reception by the clerk Inoka, who was not called as a witness. The court also found the conviction for morphine unsustainable as the Government Analyst evidence indicated it could have reformed from heroin during the 15-month delay. The prosecution failed to prove the chain of custody beyond reasonable doubt.
coa_sentence_type: Conviction and sentence set aside.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused was convicted in the High Court of Colombo for possession and trafficking of heroin and morphine and sentenced to life imprisonment and concurrent terms. He appealed. The Court of Appeal found the prosecution failed to prove the chain of custody of the drug productions, especially the inward journey to the Government Analyst, beyond reasonable doubt. Key handling witnesses gave conflicting evidence, and a crucial clerk was not called. The court also found the morphine conviction unsustainable due to possible chemical reformation. The appeal was allowed, and the conviction and sentence were set aside.
defence_counsel: Samantha Premachandra
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted based on the prosecution evidence. The Court of Appeal found the High Court judge failed to properly evaluate the evidence regarding the chain of custody and the possibility of chemical change in the drugs, thereby erring in law.
precedents_cited_list: Perera v Attorney General 1998 (1) SLR page 379 | CA 99-101/96 Decided on 12.11.1997 | Witharana Doli Nona v. The Republic of Sri Lanka, CA 19/99 | Faiza Hanoon Yoosuf v. Attorney General CA/121/002 decided on 22.11.2010
standard_of_review_applied: Whether prosecution proved case beyond reasonable doubt, particularly chain of custody of productions to Government Analyst.

judges: Menaka Wijesundera, J. | B. Sasi Mahendran, J.
offence_sections: Section 54A(d) and 54A(b) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance, as amended by Act No. 13 of 1984
location_of_offence: a certain place on the Chilaw-Colombo road in the Mahawewa area
brief_facts_summary: On 09.03.2006, a police team received information about a drug transfer and observed a suspicious van. Around 5:55 am, a motorcycle approached and a parcel was passed to the rear of the van. Police obstructed the van, searched it, and recovered two parcels of heroin from the two accused, who were trying to hide them. The Government Analyst confirmed the substance was 333.7g of pure heroin.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 54A(d) and 54A(b) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance, as amended by Act No. 13 of 1984
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court Judge found both accused guilty on both counts of possession and trafficking of heroin and imposed the death sentence. The conviction was based on their presence at the scene and their conduct in trying to hide the parcels during the raid.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellants challenged the conviction on several grounds, including the prosecution's failure to produce the alleged van and call its driver as a witness, failure to consider improbabilities in the prosecution version, misdirection on the law regarding drawing inferences from non-production of evidence, and that the judge erred by placing an undue burden on the accused and considering unproven facts.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The learned trial judge has failed to consider the need to adduce evidence of the Driver of the Van alleged to have been used by the accused. | The learned trial judge has failed to consider the glaring improbabilities and lapses in the prosecution version of the alleged raid which warrant calling of the said driver of the van as an independent witness. | The learned trial Judge has not considered the gravity of the failure by the prosecution to submit the vehicle alleged to have been used by the accused to be identified at the trial. | The learned trial judge has misdirected himself in law by not forming an inference under sec 114(f) of the Evidence Ordinance with regard to non-production of the van of the accused in the trial and failure to call its driver as a witness. | The learned trial judge has unduly burdened the accused by expecting them to prove certain facts, which is against establishes law. | The learned judge has erred in law, by considering against the accused, several facts which have not been proved in Court, and which also irrelevant to the matter.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The prosecution examined six witnesses. Both accused gave dock statements and called no witnesses. The Court of Appeal found the evidence, including police testimony and the Government Analyst report, was sufficient and credible. The conduct of the accused in trying to hide the parcels indicated knowledge and possession.
probability_assessment_by_court: Court held the prosecution discharged its burden and the accused failed to create a real doubt. Their conduct suggested knowledge of the parcel's contents.
defence_version_summary: Both accused pleaded not guilty and gave dock statements vehemently denying the accusations. The second accused admitted he was inside the van at the time of the raid. They called no witnesses. The court found their denial insufficient to create reasonable doubt.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal reviewed the grounds of appeal and found them without merit. It held that the prosecution had established the accused had joint possession and knowledge of the heroin, based on their presence in the van, the timing and manner of the transfer, and their attempt to hide the parcels. The failure to produce the van or call its driver was not prejudicial as the second accused admitted being in the van. The court applied legal principles on possession from cited precedents and concluded the High Court judgment was sound. No reason was found to interfere with the conviction or sentence.
coa_sentence_type: Death sentence affirmed
brief_judgment_file_summary: The two accused were convicted by the High Court of Chilaw for possession and trafficking of 333.7g of heroin and sentenced to death. They appealed, arguing the prosecution failed to produce the vehicle or call its driver, and that the judge misdirected himself. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal, finding the prosecution evidence sufficient, the accused's conduct indicative of knowledge and joint possession, and the grounds of appeal without merit. The conviction and death sentence were affirmed.
defence_counsel: Malindu Peiris with Dimuthu Bandara
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court found the accused guilty based on their presence at the scene and their attempt to hide the drug parcels. The Court of Appeal agreed with this reasoning and found no errors in the High Court's analysis or conclusions.

Attorney General, SC Appeal 110/15, (SC Minutes 14.12.2020) | James MC Namara, 1988 (87) Cr. App. R. 246 | R. v Martindale [1986] 1 W.L.R. 1042 | R. v Bland [1988] Crim. L.R. 41 | R. v McNamara (1988) 87 Cr.App.R. 246 | R. v Lewis (1988) 87 Cr.App.R. 270 | Thompson (1869) 21 L.T. 397
standard_of_review_applied: Review of evidence and legal findings of the High Court to determine if conviction was safe and sentence appropriate.
sentencing_principles_applied: Affirmed the death sentence imposed by the High Court as the conviction for drug trafficking under the relevant provisions was upheld.

judges: Menaka Wijesundera J. | B. Sasi Mahendran J.
offence_sections: grave sexual abuse under the provisions of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The victim was six years old at the time of the offense. The accused-appellant is the father of the victim. The incidents occurred in November 2008 or 2009 when the mother was in the hospital with a newborn. The victim described two incidents of sexual abuse, including genital touching and pressing. The mother later partially witnessed an act and questioned the victim and appellant. After numerous fights and failed family attempts to settle the matter, the mother reported the incident to the police on 28 March 2009.
evidence_type_secondary: Medical evidence (Judicial Medical Officer report), Mother's testimony
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: grave sexual abuse under the provisions of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court of Balapitiya found the accused-appellant guilty of grave sexual abuse. The trial judge sentenced him accordingly. The judgment was delivered on 15 February 2018.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant's counsel challenged the conviction on two main grounds: the improbability of the prosecution's story, which they argued was not properly considered by the trial judge, and the delay in lodging the first complaint with the police.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: 1) The improbability of the story for the prosecution which he alleges has not been considered by the trial judge. | 2) The delay in making the 1st complaint to police.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The victim, despite her young age, was consistent in her narration. The mother's delay in complaining was acceptably explained by the context of family disputes and attempts at settlement. The prosecution witnesses withstood lengthy cross-examination and were found credible.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court found the prosecution version proved beyond reasonable doubt. The victim's consistency, the acceptable explanation for the delay in complaint, and the medical evidence supporting the history outweighed the defense's claim of improbability.
defence_version_summary: The accused-appellant pleaded not guilty. He claimed the prosecution story was concocted. No alibi or defence witnesses are mentioned. The court found his defense and dock statement unconvincing compared to the credible and consistent prosecution evidence.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal thoroughly analyzed the grounds of appeal. It found the victim's testimony consistent and credible despite her age. The delay in complaint was acceptably explained by the rural family context and attempts at internal settlement, negating claims of tutoring. The medical evidence, while not conclusively proving penetration, supported the victim's history and could not be ruled out. The court rejected the defense's claim that the story was invented for a monetary dispute as unbelievable. Applying precedent on delayed complaints, the COA found no merit in the appeal grounds and was satisfied the prosecution proved its case beyond reasonable doubt.
coa_sentence_type: Affirmed the conviction and sentence of the High Court
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused-appellant, father of the victim, was convicted by the High Court of Balapitiya for grave sexual abuse of his six-year-old daughter. He appealed, arguing the prosecution story was improbable and the first police complaint was delayed. The Court of Appeal found the victim's testimony credible and consistent, the delay in complaint acceptably explained by family circumstances, and the medical evidence supportive. It dismissed the appeal and affirmed the High Court's conviction and sentence.
defence_counsel: Prasantha Lal De Alwis, P.C. with L.A.D. Samith Kalhara
hc_analysis_summary: The COA found no error in the High Court's judgment. It agreed with the HC's assessment of witness credibility and its conclusion that the prosecution proved the charge beyond reasonable doubt.
precedents_cited_list: Arachchige Mahinda Dharma Sri Muthuarachchi vs Attorney General CA-485-2017 | Haramanis vs Somalatha (1998) # Sri L.R. 365
standard_of_review_applied: Review of evidence and grounds of appeal as presented.

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 296 read with Section 32 of the Penal Code and Section 300 read with Section 32 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The Appellant was convicted for the attempted murder of PW1 and the murder of PW1's wife (the deceased). The incident stemmed from a long-standing land dispute. PW1 was attacked while returning home by the Appellant and unknown persons. PW2, the 15-year-old son, witnessed the Appellant assault his mother inside their house. The Appellant fled after the incident and was arrested 14 days later.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 296 read with Section 32 of the Penal Code (murder) and Section 300 read with Section 32 of the Penal Code (attempted murder)
hc_sentence_type: Death sentence for murder (Count 5) and 12 years rigorous imprisonment with fine for attempted murder (Count 4)
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court Judge acquitted the Appellant on charges related to unlawful assembly (Counts 1-3) but convicted him on charges of murder and attempted murder based on common intention (Counts 4-5). The conviction relied on eyewitness identification by PW1 and PW2, and the suspicious conduct of the Appellant after the incident.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The Appellant argued that the prosecution story was improbable and did not inspire confidence, and that the defence story was more probable. The grounds are interrelated, focusing on the tenability of the prosecution case compared to the defence.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The Learned High Court Judge has failed to consider that the story of the prosecution is improbable and does not inspire confidence. | The Learned High Court Judge has failed to consider that the story of the Appellant is more probable.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court carefully evaluated identification evidence. PW1 identified the Appellant during the attack on him using torchlight. PW2, a child witness, clearly identified the Appellant assaulting his mother inside the house by the light of oil lamps and moonlight. The Court considered the traumatic context and found their evidence credible and corroborated.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court found the prosecution evidence strong and incriminating, and the defence evidence failed to create a reasonable doubt over the prosecution case.
defence_version_summary: The Appellant pleaded not guilty. He made a dock statement and called four witnesses. Initially, he took a position of total denial. Later, he suggested PW1 started the first incident due to the land dispute. He did not suggest any third party was responsible for the death.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the High Court Judge correctly analyzed all evidence. It emphasized the importance of identification evidence, citing precedents like Turnbull, but found the identification in this case reliable as the Appellant was a known neighbor. The Court considered PW2's age and trauma but found his core account credible and corroborated. The Appellant's suspicious conduct after the incident was also relevant. The defence failed to cast doubt on the prosecution case. Therefore, the convictions were sound.
coa_sentence_type: Death sentence for murder (Count 5) and 12 years rigorous imprisonment with a fine of Rs. 5000 for attempted murder (Count 4) affirmed.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The Accused-Appellant was convicted by the High Court of Galle for the murder of Opatha Kankanamge Nandawatnie and attempted murder of Thumbagoda Ganithage Wilson, receiving death and 12-year imprisonment sentences respectively. He appealed, arguing the prosecution case was improbable. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal, upholding the High Court's analysis. It found the eyewitness identification by the victim's husband and son, who knew the Appellant as a neighbor, was reliable despite the lack of an identification parade. The Appellant's suspicious post-incident conduct and the defence's failure to create reasonable doubt further supported the conviction.
defence_counsel: Darshana Kuruppu with Rahul Jayathilaka and Sahan Weerasinghe
hc_analysis_summary: The COA found the HC Judge properly analyzed evidence from both parties. The HC correctly applied the law on common intention, acquitted on unlawful assembly charges, and convicted based on strong eyewitness evidence and the Appellant's conduct. The COA affirmed this analysis and finding of guilt.
precedents_cited_list: Karunaratne Mudiyansege Madduma Bandara v. The Attorney General CA/190-192/11 | Gorle S. Naidu v. State of A.P. [1997] Appeal (Cri) 232-234 | R v. Turnbull [1977] QB 224 | Daradala Ganage Chandralatha Jayawardena alias Shantha v AG CA 85/2013
standard_of_review_applied: The Court reviewed whether the High Court Judge properly considered and analyzed the evidence to arrive at the conviction.

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 364(1) of the Penal Code as amended by the Penal Code (Amendment) Act No. 22 of 1995
brief_facts_summary: The accused-appellant, a watcher of a coconut estate, forcibly entered the house of the prosecutrix and her husband about three weeks after they started working there. He raped the prosecutrix after her husband left for work, threatened her, and left. The prosecutrix promptly informed the estate manager and her husband, and they reported the incident to the police. The prosecution case relied primarily on the testimony of the victim, her husband, and the estate manager's deposition.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 364(1) of the Penal Code as amended by the Penal Code (Amendment) Act No. 22 of 1995
hc_sentence_type: 10 years rigorous imprisonment, Fine of Rs. 20000, Compensation order
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court Judge found the accused guilty of rape. He was convicted and sentenced to 10 years rigorous imprisonment, fined Rs. 20,000, and ordered to pay Rs. 400,000 compensation. As the offence occurred during the operative period of two prior suspended sentences, the Judge ordered the new sentence to commence after the suspended sentences were served, effectively revoking the suspension.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant's counsel argued that the prosecutrix's version was not credible or probable. The trial judge placed an unwarranted burden of proof on the appellant, unreasonably rejected the dock statement, and the judge's interventions denied the appellant a fair trial.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The learned High Court Judge has failed to consider the credibility and the probability of the prosecutrix’s version. | The learned High Court Judge has placed an unwarranted burden of proof on the appellant. | The learned High Court Judge has unreasonably rejected the dock statement without considering the fact that the dock statement creates a doubt on the prosecution case. | The learned High Court Judge’s intervention and interjections resulted in the denial of a fair trial towards the appellant.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the prosecutrix's evidence credible, noting her prompt complaint to the manager and husband. The lack of physical injuries did not undermine her testimony. The dock statement was an afterthought and did not create a reasonable doubt.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal assessed the probability and found the victim's version credible. The prompt complaint and corroborating circumstances supported her testimony. The absence of injuries was not fatal to the prosecution case.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty. His defence was one of consent. He gave a dock statement, claiming the estate manager instigated the complaint due to a prior dispute. He called no witnesses. The court found his defence to be an afterthought and lacking credibility.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal comprehensively reviewed the evidence and grounds of appeal. It found the victim's testimony credible and consistent, noting her prompt complaint to the manager and husband. The lack of physical injuries was not determinative, especially given the legal position under the amended Penal Code. The court found the defence of consent and the claim of instigation by the manager to be afterthoughts. It held that the trial judge's questions were aimed at clarification and did not cause prejudice or deny a fair trial. It affirmed the High Court's assessment of evidence and conviction.
coa_sentence_type: 10 years rigorous imprisonment affirmed, Fine of Rs. 20000 affirmed, Compensation order of Rs. 400000 affirmed. Sentence deemed effective from the date of the High Court sentence, 22-10-2021.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused-appellant was convicted by the High Court of Chilaw for the rape of a co-worker's wife in a coconut estate and sentenced to 10 years RI, a fine, and compensation. He appealed on grounds including credibility of the victim, burden of proof, rejection of his dock statement, and unfair trial due to judicial intervention. The Court of Appeal found the victim's evidence credible and corroborated by prompt complaint and circumstances. It held the lack of injuries did not negate the offence and the trial judge's interventions were for clarification. The appeal was dismissed, and the conviction and sentence were affirmed, with the sentence backdated to the original sentencing date.
defence_counsel: Ershan Ariaratnam
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court Judge found the prosecutrix's evidence credible and convicted the appellant. The COA agreed with the HC's reasoning, finding no error in its assessment of evidence, handling of the defence of consent, or its conclusions on credibility.
precedents_cited_list: Gurcharan Singh Vs. State Of Haryana AIR 1972 SC 266 L | Bhoginbhai Hirijibai Vs. State Of Gujarat (1983) AIR 753 | Sunil Vs. The Attorney General (1986) 1 SLR 230 | D. Tikiribanda Vs. The Attorney General- Bar Association Law Reports 2010 BLR 92
standard_of_review_applied: The Court of Appeal reviewed the evidence and findings of the High Court to determine if there were any errors in the assessment of credibility, probability, or procedural fairness that would warrant intervention.
sentencing_principles_applied: The Court considered the appellant's previous convictions (suspended sentences) and ordered the new sentence to be served consecutively, effectively revoking the suspension. It also backdated the sentence to the date of the High Court judgment.

judges: Sobhitha Rajakaruna J. | Dhammika Ganepola J.
offence_sections: Rule 12 of the SEC Rules published in Gazette Extraordinary No. 1215/2 on 18.12.2001. Section 147 of the Securities and Exchange Commission of Sri Lanka Act, No. 19 of 2021.
brief_facts_summary: The Securities and Exchange Commission of Sri Lanka (SEC) investigated trading activity in shares of Browns Investments PLC (BIL) between 08.12.2020 and 04.01.2021. The SEC alleged the 2nd Petitioner, through Capital Trust Group, engaged in wash trades and other activities creating a false or misleading appearance of active trading, violating SEC Rule 12. After show-cause letters, the SEC directed initiating criminal proceedings, which the Petitioners challenged via writ application.
evidence_type_primary: Documentary evidence (trading records, show cause letters, responses)
evidence_type_secondary: Surveillance reports from Colombo Stock Exchange (CSE) and SEC
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The Petitioners challenged the SEC's decisions to initiate criminal proceedings via writs of certiorari and prohibition. Primary grounds include that the SEC violated natural justice by failing to provide sufficient details of allegations in show-cause letters, that the alleged wash trades did not violate Rule 12 or cause market distortion, and that the SEC's decision was predetermined.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Violation of natural justice due to insufficient particulars in show-cause letters | Alleged wash trades did not violate Rule 12 or artificially affect share price | SEC's decision to prosecute was a predetermined fait accompli | SEC failed to prove actions were 'calculated' to create false/misleading appearance
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court analyzed documentary evidence including show-cause letters, responses, and trading data ('P21'). It found the SEC failed to provide adequate specifics, making it impossible for the Petitioner to properly respond, violating natural justice.
probability_assessment_by_court: Court found insufficient material to conclude the Petitioner's actions were 'calculated' to distort the market as required by Rule 12, and noted the SEC failed to discharge its burden in providing clear information.
defence_version_summary: The 2nd Petitioner pleaded not guilty to the allegations. He denied market manipulation, provided detailed written responses to show-cause letters, explained some trades as genuine errors (e.g., placing BUY instead of SELL), and argued wash trades were due to margin calls. The Court found his explanations plausible given the lack of specific contrary evidence from the SEC.
legal_errors_description: The SEC violated the rules of natural justice by failing to provide the accused with sufficient details of the allegations to enable a proper defense, infringing the 'right to know the opposing case'.
procedural_defects_description: Procedural defect in the investigation/prosecution process: SEC issued show-cause letters and Notices of Action without providing adequate particulars of the alleged violations, curtailing a fair hearing.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed whether the SEC's decision to prosecute violated natural justice. It found the show-cause letters ('P3', 'P8') lacked specific details (dates, times, transaction IDs) of the alleged violations, making it impossible for the Petitioner to respond effectively. The Court rejected the SEC's argument that causality between conduct and market outcome was unnecessary for a Rule 12 violation, emphasizing the need to prove actions were 'calculated' to create a false appearance. On the limited material, the Court could not find compelling evidence that the nine wash trades violated Rule 12 or were calculated to distort the market. The Court upheld the principle of 'right to know the opposing case' as fundamental to natural justice, especially in criminal proceedings. It concluded the SEC's failure to disclose full allegations rendered its decision procedurally flawed.
coa_sentence_type: No sentence imposed. Writ of Certiorari issued quashing the Notices of Action ('P10' and 'P17') and the decision to institute criminal proceedings.
brief_judgment_file_summary: Capital Trust Holdings Limited and its Chairman challenged the SEC's decision to initiate criminal proceedings for alleged market manipulation of Browns Investments PLC shares. The SEC alleged wash trades and other activities violated Rule 12. The Court of Appeal found the SEC violated natural justice by not providing sufficient details of the allegations in show-cause letters, infringing the Petitioner's right to know the case against him. The Court also found, on the limited material, no compelling evidence the trades were 'calculated' to manipulate the market. The Court allowed the appeal, quashed the SEC's decision to prosecute via a Writ of Certiorari, but clarified this does not prevent the SEC from taking future lawful action.
prosecution_counsel: Vikum de Abrew P.C. with Manohara Jayasinghe D.S.G.
defence_counsel: Sanjeewa Jayawardana P.C. with Suren Gnanaraj and Rukshan Senadecra
precedents_cited_list: Kanda v. Government of Malaya, (1962) AC 322 | Free Trade Zone and General Services Employees Union (FTZGSEU) and Others v. B.K.P. Chandrakeerthi, CA / WRIT / 303 / 2022 | Ganeshan Samson Roy v. M.M. Janaka Marasinghe and Others S.C (F/R) 405/ 2018
standard_of_review_applied: Judicial review of administrative action for violations of natural justice and procedural fairness.

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 365 B (2) (b) of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The appellant, a Buddhist priest, was convicted of committing grave sexual abuse on the male victim, PW1, who was 17 years old at the time. The victim was called to the appellant's room on the pretext of receiving bananas, where the appellant performed anal and oral intercourse on him. PW3 witnessed the incident from a higher elevation. The victim did not shout out, and his mental condition was described as substandard with low IQ. He only complained after his mother, PW2, inquired.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 365 B (2) (b) of the Penal Code
hc_sentence_type: 1st Count - 20 years rigorous imprisonment with fine. 2nd Count - 20 years rigorous imprisonment with fine. Sentences to run concurrently.
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court Judge convicted the appellant on two counts of grave sexual abuse after considering evidence from both parties. The judge found the prosecution evidence credible despite contradictions and omissions, and imposed the maximum sentence of 20 years rigorous imprisonment per count, to run concurrently, with fines and compensation.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant argued that the judge failed to consider implied consent as the victim was 17, that medical evidence suggested consent due to lack of injuries, that the Ellenborough Dictum was erroneously applied, and that the sentence was excessive.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The Learned High Court Judge has failed to consider the element of implied consent in the impugned judgment as the victim had admitted that he was 17 years of age at the time of the incident. | Even the medical evidence is suggestive of the consent of the part of the victim as there were no injuries observed by the Judicial Medical Officer suggestive of force. | The Learned High Court Judge has erroneously applied Ellenborough Dictum in the impugned judgment. | The sentence imposed by the Learned High Court Judge is excessive.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal carefully assessed the credibility of the child victim (PW1), considering his mental condition and the circumstances. It found his testimony truthful and supported by the eyewitness (PW3) and medical evidence, and held contradictions and omissions were not material.
probability_assessment_by_court: The court assessed that contradictions and omissions did not create reasonable doubt, and the victim's testimony was credible despite his mental condition.
defence_version_summary: The defence was total denial initially, but at trial the appellant advanced a defence of consent. He gave evidence under oath and called witnesses. The court found his consent defence an afterthought and not credible.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The COA reviewed the grounds of appeal comprehensively. It dismissed arguments on consent, finding the victim did not consent and was deceived, and his mental condition explained his reaction. It found no prejudice from applying the Ellenborough Dictum. It upheld the conviction on the first count (as the prosecution conceded the second count lacked evidence). On sentencing, it found the 20-year maximum excessive given the appellant's clean record, age, priesthood, and circumstances, and reduced it to 12 years rigorous imprisonment. It affirmed the fine and compensation.
coa_sentence_type: 12 years rigorous imprisonment on first count, fine of Rs.1000 and compensation of Rs.100,000 with default sentences. Second count conviction and sentence set aside.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The appellant, a Buddhist priest, was convicted by the High Court of Panadura on two counts of grave sexual abuse of a 17-year-old male with low intelligence and sentenced to 20 years rigorous imprisonment per count (concurrent), fines, and compensation. He appealed on grounds of implied consent, medical evidence, misapplication of law, and excessive sentence. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal on conviction for the first count (the prosecution conceded the second count lacked evidence). It upheld the conviction but reduced the sentence to 12 years rigorous imprisonment, maintaining the fine and compensation, finding the maximum sentence inappropriate given the appellant's circumstances.
defence_counsel: Amila Palliyage with Sandeepani Wijesooriya, S.Udugampola and Subaj De Silva
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court Judge considered all evidence, found the victim credible despite contradictions, and convicted the appellant. The COA agreed with the HC's credibility assessment and conviction reasoning, but found the HC's imposition of the maximum 20-year sentence excessive and an error in sentencing discretion.
precedents_cited_list: R v. Brasier168 Eng. Rep.202 [1779] | Ratansinh Dalsukhbhai Nayak v. State of Gujarat [2004] 1 SCC 64 | R v. Baker EWCA Crim 4 [2010] | R v. B. (G),1990 CanLII 7308 (SCC); [1990] 2 S.C.R. 30 | Bharwada Bhoginbhai Hirjibhai v State of Gujarat 1983 AIR SC 753
standard_of_review_applied: Assessment of witness credibility and sentencing discretion, considering the trial judge's findings and circumstances of the case.
sentencing_principles_applied: Consideration of mandatory minimum sentence, circumstances of the case, appellant's background (priest, clean record, age), and proportionality.

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 365(b)2(b) of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The Petitioner was convicted on two counts under Section 365(b)2(b) of the Penal Code. He was sentenced to 10 years RI and fined Rs.10,000 on each count, with a compensation order of Rs.100,000 to PW1. The Petitioner's application for bail pending appeal was refused by the High Court.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 365(b)2(b) of the Penal Code
hc_sentence_type: 10 years Rigorous Imprisonment and a fine on each count; sentences to run concurrently
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the Petitioner on both counts, sentencing him to 10 years RI and a fine on each count, with compensation to PW1. The Court later refused bail pending appeal, stating the Petitioner failed to prove exceptional circumstances.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The Petitioner challenges the High Court's refusal of bail pending appeal, arguing the order is contrary to law, the judge misdirected himself on exceptional circumstances, and the Petitioner's health condition constitutes exceptional circumstances.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The order is contrary to law. | The judge misdirected himself in holding no exceptional circumstances were averred. | The judge erred in refusing bail as continuous incarceration would endanger the Petitioner's life, constituting exceptional circumstances.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal reviewed the High Court's refusal of bail pending appeal. It noted the settled principle that bail pending appeal is granted only in exceptional circumstances. The Court considered the Petitioner's health condition (history of Myocardial Infarction) and the High Court's directions for medical care, concluding this was not an appropriate case to issue notice. It found no error in the High Court's refusal, emphasizing the seriousness of the offence and punishment.
coa_sentence_type: Bail refused; main appeal to be fixed for early hearing.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The Petitioner, convicted on two counts under Section 365(b)2(b) of the Penal Code and sentenced to imprisonment and fines, applied for bail pending appeal. The High Court refused bail, finding no exceptional circumstances. The Petitioner challenged this refusal in the Court of Appeal, citing health issues and misdirection. The Court of Appeal dismissed the application, upholding the principle that bail pending appeal requires exceptional circumstances and directing the main appeal to be fixed for early hearing.
defence_counsel: Anil Silva, PC with Amaan Bandara
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court refused bail pending appeal, finding the Petitioner failed to prove exceptional circumstances. It considered the Petitioner's health condition and directed medical care. The Court of Appeal found no error in this analysis.
precedents_cited_list: King vs. Keerala 48 N.L.R. 202 | The Queen vs. B. Rupasingha Perera 62 N.L.R.238 | The Queen vs. Koranelis Silva 74 N.L.R. 113
standard_of_review_applied: Review of High Court's bail refusal order for legal correctness and exercise of discretion.

judges: Menaka Wijesundera, J. | B. Sasi Mahendran, J.
offence_sections: Section 354 of the Penal Code, Section 364 (2) (e) of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The accused-appellant was indicted for abducting a girl under 16 years (Count 1) and raping her (Count 2) on or about 13.09.2011 in Pondukalchenai. The victim (PW01) testified she was returning from school with others when the accused approached, threatened them, and dragged her into the jungle where she lost consciousness and later alleged rape. The High Court convicted on both counts. The Court of Appeal considered the appeal based on grounds including improper leading questions, lack of credibility, and medical evidence inconsistency.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 354 of the Penal Code, Section 364 (2) (e) of the Penal Code
hc_sentence_type: Count 1: 2 years Rigorous Imprisonment suspended for 10 years. Count 2: 10 years Rigorous Imprisonment, a fine of Rs.5000, compensation of Rs.50,000.
hc_judgment_summary: The Learned High Court Judge convicted the accused on both counts of abduction and rape. The judge sentenced him to 2 years Rigorous Imprisonment suspended for 10 years on the abduction count, and 10 years Rigorous Imprisonment with a fine and compensation on the rape count.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant argued the High Court Judge erred in allowing leading questions by the prosecution, failed to consider that the prosecutrix was warned about false evidence, and failed to consider infirmities in the prosecution case as required by precedent.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The Learned High Court Judge erred in law in allowing the prosecution to ask leading questions to the detriment of the appellant contrary to the principle upheld in S.C. Appeal 118/17. | The Learned High Court Judge erred in law in failing to consider that the prosecutrix was admonished and warned by the prosecution that if false evidence is given, she will receive punishment. | That the Learned High Court Judge failed to consider the infirmities of the prosecution case as required by the judgments in the cases Wijepala v. The Attorney General.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed the prosecutrix's testimony, noting she initially could not recall events due to unconsciousness and later provided details of rape after prosecution questioning. The court found the questioning involved leading questions which diminished the probative value of her testimony. Medical evidence from Dr. Rahuman showed no injuries or bleeding in the genital area, contradicting the prosecutrix's claim of bleeding.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal held the prosecution failed to prove the rape charge beyond reasonable doubt due to leading questions undermining witness credibility and medical evidence contradicting the victim's account. The abduction charge was proven based on consistent eyewitness testimony.
defence_version_summary: The accused pleaded not guilty. The defence challenged the prosecution's evidence, particularly the credibility of the prosecutrix and the use of leading questions. No alibi or defence witnesses are mentioned. The court found the prosecutrix's evidence on rape not credible.
legal_errors_description: The High Court Judge erred in allowing leading questions by the prosecution, which prompted the witness and diminished the evidentiary value of her testimony.
procedural_defects_description: Improper questioning through leading questions allowed by the judge, and failure to properly evaluate witness credibility and infirmities in the prosecution case.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal carefully analyzed the evidence, particularly the prosecutrix's testimony and the medical evidence. It found that the prosecution used leading questions to elicit the rape allegation after the witness stated she was unconscious, which undermined her trustworthiness. Citing Junaiden Mohamed Haaris and others v. Attorney General, the court emphasized that leading questions diminish probative value. It also reviewed judicial precedents on uncorroborated evidence in rape cases, concluding that the victim's evidence was not credible enough to convict without corroboration, especially given the contradictory medical evidence showing no injuries or bleeding. For the abduction charge, the court found consistent, unchallenged testimony from the victim and other eyewitnesses (PW11, PW03) sufficient to uphold the conviction.
coa_sentence_type: Count 1 (Abduction): Conviction and sentence affirmed (2 years Rigorous Imprisonment suspended for 10 years from 07.12.2023). Count 2 (Rape): Acquitted.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused-appellant was convicted by the High Court of Batticaloa for abduction and rape of a girl under 16. He appealed on grounds including improper leading questions and medical evidence inconsistency. The Court of Appeal found the prosecution used leading questions to elicit the rape allegation, undermining the victim's credibility, and medical evidence contradicted her account. It acquitted the appellant of rape but upheld the abduction conviction based on consistent eyewitness testimony. The sentence for abduction was suspended for 10 years from the appeal judgment date.
defence_counsel: Arunandam, PC with Thambiraja Dayamduraja
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted based on the prosecutrix's testimony. The Court of Appeal found the High Court erred in allowing leading questions and failing to properly assess the credibility of the prosecutrix and the infirmities in the prosecution case, particularly the lack of medical corroboration for rape.

standard_of_review_applied: The court reviewed whether the High Court judgment was based on proper evaluation of evidence and correct application of law, particularly regarding leading questions, witness credibility, and corroboration requirements in rape cases.
sentencing_principles_applied: The court considered the suspension of sentence for the abduction conviction, maintaining the High Court's suspended sentence but re-starting the suspension period from the appeal judgment date.

judges: M. T. Mohammed Laffar, J. | S. U. B. Karalliyadde, J.
offence_sections: Navy Act, No. 33 of 1976, and Sri Lanka Navy Order 0501
offence_category: Disciplinary (Consumption of narcotic substances - cannabis, and selling foreign cigarettes)
brief_facts_summary: The Petitioner, a Leading Seaman, was arrested on 21.01.2021 after a search of the junior sailors' mess found him in possession of foreign cigarettes and two other sailors with cannabis. Urine tests from all three sailors were positive for THC. A Board of Inquiry recommended disciplinary action for consumption of cannabis and selling foreign cigarettes. A Summary Trial was held on 09.03.2021, where the Petitioner pleaded not guilty to cannabis consumption but admitted to selling cigarettes. He was convicted and sentenced to dismissal without disgrace. The Petitioner appealed to the President, who approved the sentence on 03.08.2021.
evidence_type_secondary: Medical evidence (rapid urine test report positive for THC), Board of Inquiry report
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The Petitioner challenges the Summary Trial conviction and sentence on grounds that the trial was conducted in a manner ultra vires, against principles of consistency, contrary to law and Navy Order, violating fundamental principles of law and his right to representation. He alleges he was not served a charge sheet, not given opportunity to choose a Defending Officer, and not given adequate time to prepare his defence.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Summary Trial conducted ultra vires, against principles of consistency, contrary to law and Sri Lanka Navy Order | Violation of fundamental principles of law | Violation of right of representation | Not served with a charge sheet | Not given opportunity to choose a Defending Officer or Counsel | Not given adequate time to prepare defence
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court focused on procedural defects rather than witness testimony. Evidence considered included the urine test report (P-1), Board of Inquiry report (P-2), and Summary Trial records (R-6, R-7). Ambiguity in trial records regarding charges and pleas was noted.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court found the Summary Trial proceedings violated procedural rules and natural justice, creating doubt about their legality, but did not assess probability of guilt.
defence_version_summary: Petitioner pleaded not guilty to charge of cannabis consumption but guilty to selling foreign cigarettes at Summary Trial. He did not call witnesses but submitted written submissions (P-4). He alleged procedural violations: no charge sheet, no choice of Defending Officer, inadequate time to prepare.
legal_errors_description: The Court found the Summary Trial proceedings violated the Sri Lanka Navy Order 0501 (R3) and fundamental principles of natural justice, rendering the proceedings a nullity.
procedural_defects_description: Failure to serve charge sheet, failure to provide adequate time to prepare defence, violation of Navy Order 0501 provisions regarding right to be defended by a defending officer of accused's will (subject to service exigencies), ambiguity in trial record regarding charges and plea.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed the writ jurisdiction under Article 140 of the Constitution and Section 132(1) of the Navy Act, establishing its power of judicial review over Summary Trial proceedings. It distinguished between judicial review (concerned with legality of decision-making process) and appeal (concerned with merits). The Court held that the President's immunity under Article 35 did not oust its jurisdiction as the Petitioner was challenging the Summary Trial proceedings, not the President's order. The Court found procedural errors: ambiguity in the trial record regarding charges (R-6 showed only one charge but language implied multiple), failure to serve charge sheet as required by Navy Order 0501, and failure to ensure the Petitioner's right to be defended by an officer of his choice (subject to exigencies). The Court concluded the proceedings violated the Navy Order and natural justice, rendering the conviction and sentence a nullity.
coa_sentence_type: Conviction and sentence quashed (P-7 nullified). No retrial ordered.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The Petitioner, a Leading Seaman, challenged his conviction and sentence of dismissal by a Navy Summary Trial for consumption of cannabis and selling foreign cigarettes. He alleged procedural violations including no charge sheet, no choice of Defending Officer, and inadequate time to prepare. The Court of Appeal held it had jurisdiction via writ under Article 140 and Navy Act Section 132(1). It found the Summary Trial proceedings violated Sri Lanka Navy Order 0501 and principles of natural justice due to ambiguity in charges, failure to serve charge sheet, and infringement of right to defence. The Court quashed the conviction and sentence (P-7) as a nullity. No costs were ordered.
prosecution_counsel: Ms. A. Gajadheera SC for the Respondents
defence_counsel: Shavindra Fernando, PC with Mirthula Skandaraja and Sandani Wijendra for the Petitioner
