probability_assessment_by_court: Court applied balance of probabilities standard to assess whether appellant discharged burden under Section 40. Found appellant failed to prove he took all necessary precautions.
defence_version_summary: The accused pleaded guilty. The appellant (vehicle owner) claimed not guilty of enabling the offence, stating he gave instructions to the accused not to use the vehicle beyond Moratuwa and inquired about its whereabouts. The court found his testimony uncorroborated and not credible.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed Section 40 of the Forest Ordinance, which places the burden on a third-party owner to prove to the court's satisfaction that all precautions were taken to prevent the vehicle's use in the offence. It upheld the lower courts' findings that the appellant's uncorroborated statement about giving instructions was insufficient. Citing precedent (Samarasinghege Dharmasena v W. P. Wangasinghe), it emphasized that mere instructions are inadequate; the owner must take steps to implement them. The Court also noted discrepancies in the appellant's evidence regarding his knowledge of the vehicle's whereabouts, revealing a lackadaisical attitude. It concluded the appellant failed to discharge the statutory burden.
coa_sentence_type: Confiscation of vehicle bearing registration no. 48-4853 affirmed
brief_judgment_file_summary: This appeal challenged the confiscation of a vehicle used to transport jack fruit logs without a permit, under the Forest Ordinance. The accused pleaded guilty. The vehicle owner (appellant) argued he took precautions by instructing the driver. The Magistrate and High Court ordered confiscation, finding the owner failed to prove he took all necessary precautions. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal, upholding the lower courts' orders, ruling that uncorroborated statements about instructions are insufficient to discharge the statutory burden under Section 40.
prosecution_counsel: Nishantha Nagaratnam, SC for the Hon. Attorney General
defence_counsel: Pradeep Perera with Dilmi Pieris for the Appellant. Diana Rodrigo for the Accused Respondent Respondent
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court dismissed the revision application, finding no exceptional circumstances and no illegality in the Magistrate's order. It agreed the appellant failed to show necessary precautions were taken to prevent the offence.
precedents_cited_list: Samarasinghege Dharmasena v W. P. Wangasinghe CA(PHC) 197/2013 CA Minute dated 22.01.2019 | S. D. N. Premasiri v Officer In Charge, Mawathagama C A (PHC) 46/2015 Court of Appeal Minute dated 27.11.2018
standard_of_review_applied: Revisionary jurisdiction - examining legality and correctness of lower court orders
sentencing_principles_applied: Mandatory confiscation under Section 40 of Forest Ordinance unless third-party owner proves all precautions taken

judges: D.N. Samarakoon, J. | B. Sasi Mahendran, J.
offence_sections: Section 403 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The petitioner was indicted along with his sister for cheating. He was residing in Italy on a foreign permit since 1979 and was unaware of the case. The High Court proceeded with a trial in absentia under Section 241(1)(b) of the Code of Criminal Procedure Act, finding him guilty and sentencing him. He was later arrested in Madrid in October 2022 pursuant to an international warrant. The petitioner sought to set aside the conviction and sentence and applied for a trial de novo under Section 241(3).
evidence_type_secondary: Witness testimony (brother, Grama Niladharis, CID officer)
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 403 of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court proceeded with a trial in absentia under Section 241(1)(b) of the Code of Criminal Procedure Act on the ground that the petitioner had absconded. The petitioner was found guilty and sentenced. An open warrant was issued. The High Court later refused an application under Section 241(3) to set aside the conviction and sentence, insisting on the petitioner's personal attendance.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The petitioner sought revision and/or restitution under Article 138(1) of the Constitution, arguing there was no basis to commence the trial in absentia as he was not absconding and was unaware of the case. He also challenged the High Court's refusal of his application under Section 241(3) to set aside the conviction and order a de novo trial, arguing the judge wrongly insisted on personal attendance without exercising discretion.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Trial in absentia under Section 241(1)(b) was improper as petitioner was not absconding and was unaware of the case | High Court erred in refusing application under Section 241(3) by rigidly insisting on personal attendance without exercising discretion | The initial order to try the case in absentia was a nullity, rendering all subsequent proceedings bad
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal reviewed the case record and found no concrete evidence that the petitioner was absconding. Evidence showed he had left for Italy in 1979, long before the case. The High Court judge had evidence from the petitioner's brother, Grama Niladharis, and a CID officer but erroneously concluded the petitioner had absconded.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court found no reasonable basis to infer the petitioner was absconding, as he was not notified of the case and had left the country in 1979. The circumstances did not support a finding that he avoided trial.
defence_version_summary: The petitioner pleaded not guilty (inferred from trial in absentia). He asserted he was unaware of the case, having been in Italy since 1979, and did not abscond. He sought to set aside the conviction and be tried de novo. The Court accepted his lack of awareness and bona fide absence.
legal_errors_description: The High Court erred in concluding the petitioner had absconded under Section 241(1)(b) without concrete evidence, and in refusing his Section 241(3) application by rigidly insisting on personal attendance without exercising discretion.
procedural_defects_description: The High Court proceeded with a trial in absentia based on an erroneous finding of absconding, which the Court of Appeal deemed a nullity. The High Court also failed to exercise discretion to allow the petitioner's lawyer to appear on his behalf under Section 241(3).
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal held there was no concrete and cogent evidence that the petitioner had absconded or left the island to avoid trial. He had left in 1979 and was unaware of the case. The initial order for trial in absentia was a nullity, rendering subsequent proceedings invalid. The High Court judge also erred by not exercising discretion to allow the petitioner's lawyer to appear under Section 241(3) despite the petitioner being in foreign custody. The Court cited Sudharman De Silva v. The Attorney General on the right to be heard by an attorney-at-law. The circumstances warranted revision, shocking the conscience of the court.
coa_sentence_type: Trial de novo ordered
brief_judgment_file_summary: The petitioner, accused of cheating, was tried and convicted in absentia by the High Court of Colombo. He was residing in Italy and unaware of the case. After arrest in Madrid, he sought revision. The Court of Appeal found no evidence he absconded, as he left Sri Lanka in 1979. The High Court's order for trial in absentia was a nullity, and the judge erred in refusing his application under Section 241(3). The Court set aside the conviction, sentence, and warrants, ordering a trial de novo.
defence_counsel: Asthika Devendra with Kaneel Maddumage
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court concluded the petitioner absconded and proceeded with a trial in absentia under Section 241(1)(b). It later refused his application under Section 241(3) for a de novo trial, insisting on personal attendance. The Court of Appeal found these decisions erroneous, as there was no evidence of absconding and the judge failed to exercise discretion.
precedents_cited_list: Sudharman De Silva v. The Attorney General [1986] 1 SLR 9 | Samarasekera Mudiyanselage Priyantha Peiris v. the Attorney General CA Case No. 52/2012 decided on 28.07.2015
standard_of_review_applied: Revisionary jurisdiction under Article 138(1) of the Constitution

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The deceased, Balapuwaduge Antony Mendis, was assaulted on the head with a wooden pole by the Appellant at the Indibedda Community Centre on or about 1st November 2008. The sole eyewitness, PW2, a carpenter who knew both the deceased and the Appellant, witnessed the incident under light from a street lamp. The deceased died from cranio-cerebral injuries. The Appellant was convicted and sentenced to death by the High Court of Panadura.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court Judge convicted the Appellant of murder under Section 296 of the Penal Code and sentenced him to death. The conviction was based primarily on the eyewitness testimony of PW2, corroborated by medical and police evidence.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The Appellant challenged the conviction as unsafe, arguing it was based solely on the evidence of a single eyewitness, PW2. The main contention was that the identification of the Appellant under the prevailing lighting conditions was difficult and unreliable.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The conviction arising solely on the evidence of PW2, namely Thelge Sunil Lakxman Peiris is unsafe as the purported identification of the Appellant was made under difficult external circumstances.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the sole eyewitness PW2's evidence to be cogent, trustworthy, and corroborated by medical and police evidence. His identification of the Appellant, whom he knew, was deemed reliable despite the lighting conditions.
probability_assessment_by_court: The court assessed the reliability of the sole eyewitness and found no reasonable doubt as to the Appellant's identity as the perpetrator.
defence_version_summary: The Appellant pleaded not guilty, made a dock statement denying the charge, but admitted being at the crime scene watching a group singing. He called no defence witnesses.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal carefully assessed the identification evidence of the sole eyewitness PW2, considering the lighting conditions and the witness's prior knowledge of the Appellant. It referenced legal principles on identification from Alexander v. R and the sufficiency of a single witness from Sumanasena v. The Attorney General. The court found PW2's evidence cogent, corroborated, and sufficient to establish guilt beyond reasonable doubt. It saw no reason to interfere with the trial judge's findings.
coa_sentence_type: Death
brief_judgment_file_summary: The Accused-Appellant was convicted of murder and sentenced to death by the High Court of Panadura for killing Balapuwaduge Antony Mendis with a wooden pole. He appealed, arguing the conviction based solely on a single eyewitness's identification under difficult lighting was unsafe. The Court of Appeal found the eyewitness's evidence cogent, trustworthy, and corroborated, dismissing the appeal and affirming the conviction and death sentence.
defence_counsel: K.Kugarajah
cause_of_death_exact_text: Cranio-cerebral injuries following blunt impact
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted the Appellant based on the sole eyewitness's evidence, which it found credible and corroborated. The Court of Appeal reviewed this analysis and found no error, agreeing with the trial judge's assessment.
precedents_cited_list: Alexander v. R (1981) 145 CLR 395 | Sumanasena v. The Attorney General [1999] 3 SLR 137
standard_of_review_applied: Assessment of whether the prosecution proved the Appellant's identification beyond reasonable doubt.

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 300 of Penal Code (attempted murder); Section 315 of Penal Code (voluntarily causing grievous hurt)
offence_category: Attempted Murder, Voluntarily Causing Grievous Hurt
location_of_offence: Land where the Appellants were residing
brief_facts_summary: A fight erupted between family members over land and harvesting crops. PW2 entered land claimed by the 1st Appellant to harvest bananas and coconuts. The 1st Appellant assaulted PW2. The 2nd Appellant, arriving later, assaulted PW2 and also assaulted PW1 (PW2's son) on the head, causing severe brain injury. The 3rd accused (mother/wife) was acquitted.
evidence_type_secondary: Medical evidence (PW14, JMO; PW15, doctor); Police observation (PW6)
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 300 and Section 315 of the Penal Code
hc_sentence_type: Count 1: 12 years rigorous imprisonment with fine; Count 2: 1 year rigorous imprisonment with fine; Compensation order
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted both Appellants on counts of attempted murder and causing grievous hurt, acquitting the 3rd accused. It sentenced them to imprisonment, fines, and ordered compensation. The judge attributed common intention between the 1st and 2nd Appellants.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: Appellants challenged the conviction on grounds that the prosecution failed to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt, the trial judge failed to consider lesser culpability, and improperly evaluated evidence on common intention.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Has the prosecution proved the case against the Appellants beyond reasonable doubts. | Has the learned Trial Judge failed to consider lesser culpability in this case. | Has the learned High Court Judge properly evaluated the evidence pertains to Common Intention.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The prosecution case relied heavily on PW2, the purported eyewitness. PW1 could not testify due to injury. PW17 was treated as adverse. The Court of Appeal found the High Court erred in relying solely on PW2 and in attributing common intention.
probability_assessment_by_court: Court found no common intention proven and prosecution case rested solely on PW2, whose testimony did not prove the charges beyond reasonable doubt in its entirety.
defence_version_summary: Appellants pleaded not guilty and gave evidence. They claimed PW2 and PW1 were armed, and PW1's injury was caused accidentally by a blow from PW2 during the fight. The defence argued the fight was sudden and between close relations.
legal_errors_description: Misdirection on law regarding common intention. The High Court incorrectly attributed common intention between the Appellants where evidence showed only similar intention in a sudden fight.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The COA analyzed the evidence, finding the prosecution case rested on the single eyewitness PW2. It held the High Court erred in inferring common intention, as per King v. Ranasinghe, as there was no evidence of pre-planning; the Appellants acted with similar but separate intentions in a sudden fight. Considering the familial context and nature of the fight, the COA found the 2nd Appellant's actions fell under Section 301 (attempted culpable homicide not amounting to murder) rather than Section 300 (attempted murder). It quashed the 1st Appellant's conviction on the first count and modified the 2nd Appellant's conviction.
coa_sentence_type: 1st Appellant: Acquitted on Count 1; sentence on Count 2 (1 year rigorous imprisonment + fine) remains. 2nd Appellant: Conviction on Count 1 modified to Section 301, sentenced to 7 years rigorous imprisonment with fine; sentence on Count 2 (1 year rigorous imprisonment + fine) remains. Sentences for each Appellant to run concurrently. Default sentences to run consecutively. Compensation for 2nd Appellant modified to Rs. 750,000 payable to PW2.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The Appellants, father and son, were convicted by the High Court of Gampaha for attempted murder and causing grievous hurt following a familial fight over land. They appealed, arguing the prosecution failed to prove its case, the judge erred on common intention and sentencing. The Court of Appeal partly allowed the appeal. It quashed the 1st Appellant's attempted murder conviction for lack of common intention. It modified the 2nd Appellant's conviction from attempted murder to attempted culpable homicide not amounting to murder (Section 301), reducing his sentence. The sentences for causing grievous hurt were upheld.
defence_counsel: Anil Silva, P.C. with Amaan Bandara and Shaluka Neranga
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted based on the eyewitness PW2 and attributed common intention. The COA found the HC erred in its evaluation of common intention and in relying solely on PW2 without sufficient corroboration, misdirecting itself on the law.
precedents_cited_list: King v. Ranasinghe et al 47 NLR 373 | Regina V. Periyasamy 58 NLR 433
standard_of_review_applied: Review of evidence and legal correctness of High Court judgment, including evaluation of common intention and appropriate charge.
sentencing_principles_applied: Consideration of lesser culpability under Section 301 for sudden fight among close relations, and ordering sentences to run concurrently.
final_charge_after_appeal: For 2nd Appellant: Attempted murder (Section 300) modified to attempt to commit culpable homicide not amounting to murder (Section 301).

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: section 296 read with section 32 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The appellant and another were charged with three counts of murder allegedly committed on 2nd November 2006. The prosecution case relied primarily on the evidence of a single eyewitness (PW-01), who claimed the incident resulted from gang-related violence targeting him. PW-01, who had been released from remand custody a day prior, was with the three deceased when they were fired upon. He claimed to have pretended to be dead, identified the appellant as one of the assailants, and made a statement to police three months later. The appellant denied any involvement and claimed he was unaware he was a suspect until receiving High Court summons.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: section 296 read with section 32 of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: After a trial without a jury, the High Court Judge found the appellant guilty of three counts of murder as charged in the indictment. The 2nd accused was acquitted of all charges. The conviction was based solely on the evidence of PW-01, the sole eyewitness.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appeal was based on the contention that the High Court Judge convicted the appellant without considering the reasonable doubts created about his involvement. The main argument focused on the belatedness and unreliability of the sole eyewitness's statement, and that the appellant had been denied a fair trial due to irregularities in the investigation and proceedings.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The learned High Court Judge convicted the appellant without considering the reasonable doubts that have been created as to the involvement of the appellant to the crime. | The appellant has not been afforded a fair trial in accordance with the due process of the law.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed the reliability of PW-01, the sole eyewitness. It noted the three-month delay in his police statement, contradictions between his claim of informing the OIC and the OIC's denial, and his familiarity with the legal system. The Court found his belated evidence, without corroboration, unsafe to rely upon for a conviction in a serious crime.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court held that relying on a belated statement from a single witness without sufficient corroboration was highly unsafe. It applied the principle that where facts can be interpreted for or against the accused, the inference consistent with innocence should be preferred.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty. His defence was that he was never involved in the crime, never arrested, and only learned of the charges upon receiving High Court summons. No defence witnesses are mentioned as being called. The Court accepted the appellant's position that police failed to properly investigate or arrest him.
legal_errors_description: The High Court erred in convicting the appellant based on the uncorroborated and belated evidence of a single witness, failing to consider reasonable doubt, and failing to ensure a fair trial.
procedural_defects_description: Police failed to properly investigate, inform the Magistrate of the eyewitness statement, or arrest the appellant. They misinformed the Magistrate that the appellant was evading arrest, while he was living at the address to which High Court summons were successfully served. Non-summary proceedings were commenced based on incorrect information.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the conviction unsafe. It scrutinized the reliability of the sole eyewitness (PW-01), highlighting the three-month delay in his statement, the contradiction regarding his alleged call to the OIC, and his legal awareness. The Court noted serious investigative and procedural irregularities: the appellant was never arrested or his statement recorded, police incorrectly claimed he was evading arrest, and he was denied a fair trial. Applying the principle from Alim Vs. Wijesinghe that inferences consistent with innocence should be preferred, the Court concluded the charges were not proved beyond reasonable doubt based solely on PW-01's belated testimony.
coa_sentence_type: Acquitted and set aside
brief_judgment_file_summary: The appellant was convicted by the High Court of Colombo for three counts of murder based solely on the eyewitness account of PW-01. He appealed, arguing the conviction was unsafe due to reasonable doubt and procedural irregularities denying him a fair trial. The Court of Appeal found the eyewitness's belated statement unreliable and noted serious flaws in the police investigation and court proceedings, including a false claim that the appellant was evading arrest. The appeal was allowed, the conviction and sentence were set aside, and the appellant was acquitted.
defence_counsel: Sheron Serasinghe, Assigned Counsel
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted the appellant based on the sole testimony of PW-01. The COA found this reasoning flawed, as the HC failed to adequately assess the witness's credibility, the delay in his statement, and the investigative failures that deprived the appellant of a fair trial.
precedents_cited_list: Alim Vs. Wijesinghe, S.I. Police Batticaloa, 38 CLW 95
standard_of_review_applied: Assessment of whether the conviction was safe and based on reliable evidence, considering reasonable doubt and procedural fairness.

judges: N. Bandula Karunarathna J. | R. Gurusinghe J.
offence_sections: Section 386 of the Penal Code read with section 5 (I) of the Public Property Act No. 12 of 1982; Section 196 read with section 190 of the Penal Code; Section 400 of the Penal Code read with section 5(1) of the Public Property Act No. 12 of 1982
offence_category: Fraud, False Declaration, Misappropriation of Public Funds
brief_facts_summary: The accused-appellant, a Notary Public, attested a Mortgage Bond (Deed No. 734) valued at Rs. 6,000,000 on 15.02.1991, requiring Rs. 60,000 in stamp duty. The prosecution alleged the original monthly list submitted erroneously listed the deed as a Last Will, not a Mortgage Bond, and the duplicate deed with proper stamps was submitted over a year late, causing loss of stamp duty revenue.
evidence_type_primary: Documentary evidence (Deed, Day Book, monthly lists)
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 196 read with section 190 of the Penal Code (two counts) and Section 400 of the Penal Code read with section 5(1) of the Public Property Act
hc_sentence_type: Total imprisonment of 24 months suspended for 5 years and fines on each count
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court acquitted the accused on charges under the Public Property Act but convicted her on four counts of making false declarations and misleading officials. The court imposed a total suspended sentence of 24 months and a total fine of Rs. 95,000.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant argued the prosecution failed to prove charges beyond reasonable doubt, relied on inadmissible hearsay evidence, and that convictions on certain charges were erroneous. The appellant also contended the Trial Judge failed to consider lack of dishonest intention for misappropriation and failed to properly evaluate evidence.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Prosecution failed to prove charges beyond reasonable doubt. | The only evidence against the accused-appellant is hearsay evidence which is inadmissible. | Convictions in relation to charges 1 and 4 are erroneous.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The prosecution relied on documentary evidence and testimony from Land Registry officials. The Court of Appeal found key parts of the evidence, particularly regarding the original monthly list and the entry in the Notaries Book, to be hearsay and not properly tested.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal found the prosecution evidence did not establish dishonest intention beyond reasonable doubt and that reliance on hearsay evidence created reasonable doubt.
defence_version_summary: The accused pleaded not guilty, gave evidence, and denied guilt. She claimed her deceased Law Clerk, Jayantha Pieris, handled the preparation and submission of the monthly list and deeds. She stated she was pre-occupied with her job and entrusted these matters to him.
legal_errors_description: The Court of Appeal found the Trial Judge failed to properly evaluate the evidence, misdirected himself by not considering the hearsay nature of key evidence, and failed to require the prosecution to prove dishonest intention for misappropriation beyond reasonable doubt.
procedural_defects_description: The Trial Judge rejected an application under section 200 of the Criminal Procedure Code made by the defence and called for the defence. The COA noted this affected the right to a fair trial based on presumption of innocence.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal held the prosecution failed to prove the charges beyond reasonable doubt. Key evidence regarding the original monthly list and the Notaries Book entry was hearsay, as the original list was not produced and the official who made the entry was deceased. The prosecution did not establish the requisite dishonest intention for misappropriation. The Trial Judge erred in law by not properly analyzing the evidence, relying on probabilities instead of proof beyond reasonable doubt, and failing to give reasons for rejecting the accused's explanation. The conviction was therefore unsafe.
coa_sentence_type: Acquitted and discharged from all counts. No sentence imposed.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused-appellant, a Notary Public, was convicted in the High Court for making false declarations and misleading officials regarding a Mortgage Bond and its stamp duty. She was given a suspended sentence and fined. On appeal, the Court of Appeal found the prosecution evidence was insufficient and relied on hearsay, failing to prove dishonest intent or the charges beyond reasonable doubt. The Trial Judge was found to have erred in law. The appeal was allowed, the conviction and sentence were set aside, and the accused was acquitted on all counts.
defence_counsel: Razik Zarook, PC with Rohana Deshapriya AAL and Chanakya Liyanage AAL
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted based on documentary evidence and witness testimony, acquitting on some charges. The COA found the HC judgment was unsound in law as it failed to properly evaluate the evidence, considered inadmissible hearsay, and did not require the prosecution to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt.
precedents_cited_list: Dissanayake vs. Attorney-General II Sri. L.R 150 (CA/SC/279/78-MC Kuliyapitiya/92043) | The King vs. Cassim 48 NLR 116 | Kodituwakku Chaminda Vs Republic of Sri Lanka CA /248/2004, dated 19.11.2009 | Alwis Vs Piyasena Fernando 1993 (1) SLR 119 | Wijekoon Mudiyanselage Appuhamy Vs. Republic CA 61/98 dated, 11.01.2001 | Mahinda Herath Vs AG CA 21/2001, dated 13-09-2005 | Shavul Hameed Badurdeen Vs AG CA 167/2006, dated 23.02.2010 | Dr. Karunadasa Vs Open University of Sri Lanka 2006 (3) SLR 226
standard_of_review_applied: The Court of Appeal reviewed whether the Trial Judge properly evaluated the evidence and correctly applied the burden of proof (beyond reasonable doubt). It intervened where the findings were based on hearsay or an incorrect legal standard.

judges: Menaka Wijesundera, J. | Neil Iddawala, J.
offence_sections: Section 298 of the Penal Code and Section 151 (3), Section 149 (1), Section 224, Section 131 and Section 99 of the Motor Traffic Ordinance
brief_facts_summary: The Accused-Appellant-Petitioner (Petitioner) was involved in a fatal head-on collision while driving a jeep. He attempted to overtake a vehicle and collided with a motorcyclist coming from the opposite direction. The motorcyclist was caught under the front right tire of the jeep and died as a result. The incident occurred in 2001.
evidence_type_primary: Eyewitness testimony and physical evidence of the accident scene
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 298 of the Penal Code and Section 151 (3), Section 149 (1), Section 224, Section 131 and Section 99 of the Motor Traffic Ordinance
hc_sentence_type: 01-year rigorous imprisonment for the first charge under Section 298 of the Penal Code; other sentences under Motor Traffic Ordinance unspecified
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court Judge affirmed the conviction and sentence imposed by the Magistrate. The High Court considered only the sentence, as the Petitioner had stated in the High Court that he was only challenging the sentence and not the conviction.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The Petitioner's counsel submitted that the High Court Judge did not properly consider the evidence from the Magistrate's Court. He argued the prosecution failed to prove the charge of criminal negligence under Section 298 of the Penal Code, as there was insufficient evidence to establish the Petitioner drove at a very high speed or with a high degree of negligence. The absence of brake marks on the road was also cited.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: High Court Judge did not consider evidence led at Magistrate's Court | Prosecution failed to prove high speed or high degree of negligence | No reliable evidence to establish facts for Section 298 charge | No brake marks on road or grass to support prosecution case
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Magistrate considered the evidence, noting it was a head-on collision. The Magistrate disregarded the Petitioner's evidence due to contradictions and omissions in his police statement. The Court of Appeal found no illegality or exceptional conclusion contrary to law or facts.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal found no reasonable doubt created by the defence; the prosecution's evidence was sufficient.
defence_version_summary: The Petitioner pleaded not guilty. He gave evidence but it was disregarded by the Magistrate due to contradictions and omissions in his police statement. The defence argued the prosecution failed to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt.
procedural_defects_description: The Petitioner failed to divulge all facts relating to the application, specifically not mentioning that in the High Court he only challenged the sentence and not the conviction.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal noted the Petitioner's inconsistency in submissions between the High Court and the revision application. Despite procedural shortcomings, the Court examined the case in the interest of justice. It found the Magistrate had properly considered evidence, concluding the Petitioner's jeep was mostly on the wrong side of the road, causing the fatal collision. No illegality or exceptional reason was found to reverse the lower courts' orders. Considering the 2001 incident and changes in the Petitioner's life, the Court varied the sentence.
coa_sentence_type: Suspended sentence of 01-year rigorous imprisonment for the first charge under Section 298, suspended for 10 years from the date of conviction; other sentences under Motor Traffic Ordinance remain unchanged.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The Accused-Appellant-Petitioner was convicted by the Magistrate's Court and the High Court for criminal negligence under Section 298 of the Penal Code and traffic offences, following a fatal 2001 collision. He filed a revision application challenging the conviction and sentence. The Court of Appeal found no legal error in the lower courts' decisions but noted the Petitioner failed to disclose he only challenged the sentence in the High Court. Nevertheless, considering the age of the case, the Court suspended the one-year rigorous imprisonment for 10 years, dismissing the revision application otherwise.
defence_counsel: L. Amarasinghe with N. Malkumara
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court affirmed the Magistrate's conviction. The High Court only considered the sentence, as the Petitioner had limited his challenge to the sentence at that stage. The Court of Appeal found no error in the High Court's approach.
standard_of_review_applied: Revision jurisdiction under Article 138 of the Constitution; discretionary power requiring full disclosure and clean hands.
sentencing_principles_applied: Consideration of the time elapsed since the offence (2001) and changes in the Petitioner's life, leading to suspension of sentence.

judges: Menaka Wijesundera, J. | Neil Iddawala, J.
offence_sections: Assistance to and Protection of Victims of Crime and Witnesses Act, No. 04 of 2015
brief_facts_summary: A girl named Punsika Mayaumi complained that the suspect kidnapped and sexually abused her. The suspect allegedly videotaped the sexual activities and threatened to make the footage public if she disclosed them. The magistrate directed police to investigate under the specified Act, and the suspect has been in remand since May 2022.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The suspect-petitioner pleaded for bail citing his tender age as an exceptional circumstance. The respondents vehemently objected to the bail application.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Tender age of suspect as exceptional circumstance | Consequences of youth being in remand
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The judgment focuses on the suspect's alleged conduct (videotaping and threatening) and the nature of the offence. The conclusion of investigations is not yet known.
probability_assessment_by_court: The court considered the suspect's subsequent conduct and the nature of the offence as factors against bail.
defence_version_summary: The suspect-petitioner pleaded for bail, not guilty. No alibi or defence witnesses mentioned. The court did not assess credibility of a substantive defence as it was a bail hearing.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed the bail application under the relevant Act, which permits bail only upon exceptional circumstances. It considered the petitioner's argument of tender age but found the nature of the principal offence (kidnapping and sexual abuse) and the suspect's subsequent conduct (alleged videotaping and threats) to be clear violations of the Act's objectives. Despite investigations being incomplete, the court concluded it was fair to refuse bail.
brief_judgment_file_summary: This is a bail application in the Court of Appeal by Sirimanna Arachchige Hasitha Hansaka, who is accused of kidnapping and sexually abusing a girl and allegedly videotaping the acts and threatening her. The suspect has been in remand since May 2022. He sought bail citing his tender age as an exceptional circumstance. The Court of Appeal, after considering the nature of the offence and the suspect's alleged subsequent conduct, refused the bail application.
defence_counsel: Ranil Samarasooriya with Madhava De Alwis
standard_of_review_applied: Bail application review under specific statute requiring exceptional circumstances.

judges: N. Bandula Karunarathna J. | R. Gurusinghe J.
offence_sections: sections 16(b) 19(c) of the Bribery Act
location_of_offence: Gokarella (police raid context); solicitation via telephone
brief_facts_summary: The accused, a police sergeant, solicited and accepted a bribe of Rs. 5,000 from the complainant (a businessman) to release the complainant's friend (Palitha Wijerathne) who was in custody for illegal timber cutting. The complainant informed the Bribery Commission, and a trap was set leading to the accused's arrest while accepting the money. The accused initially pleaded not guilty in the High Court.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: sections 16(b) 19(c) of the Bribery Act
hc_sentence_type: 02 years rigorous imprisonment for each of 4 charges (concurrently), Fine Rs. 3,000 per charge, Compensation Rs. 5,000 under section 26 of Bribery Act, with default simple imprisonment sentences
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the accused on all four counts of soliciting and accepting a bribe. The trial judge imposed custodial sentences, fines, and compensation. The accused appealed the sentence.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant did not challenge the conviction. The appeal focused solely on requesting a non-custodial sentence due to mitigating circumstances, specifically the need to care for his mentally retarded child.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Appeal against sentence only | Request for non-custodial sentence based on mitigating family circumstances
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The prosecution led nine witnesses, including the complainant and others involved in the trap. The Court of Appeal noted the conviction was not challenged, thus the evidence was accepted as sufficient for conviction.
probability_assessment_by_court: Conviction was not challenged; appeal focused solely on sentence.
defence_version_summary: The accused pleaded not guilty. He gave a dock statement denying the charges but admitted opposing bail for the suspects and calling the suspect's wife. The defence did not challenge the conviction on appeal.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal noted the appeal was only against sentence. It considered the mitigating circumstances: the appellant's mentally retarded child requiring special care, his repentance, and lack of previous convictions. The court exercised leniency by suspending the custodial sentence, allowing a non-custodial outcome to enable the appellant to care for his child.
coa_sentence_type: Six months rigorous imprisonment for each count (4 counts), total 2 years imprisonment suspended for 7 years. Fine of Rs. 3,000 per count (default 3 months imprisonment per count, to run concurrently). Penalty of Rs. 5,000 under section 26 of Bribery Act.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused, a police sergeant, was convicted by the High Court on four counts of soliciting and accepting a bribe. He was sentenced to imprisonment, fines, and compensation. He appealed only against the sentence. The Court of Appeal, considering his mitigating family circumstances (a mentally retarded child needing care), suspended the custodial sentence for 7 years while maintaining the fines and penalty. The appeal was dismissed but the sentence was altered to a non-custodial one.
prosecution_counsel: Gayan Madawage, AAL with Udari Kumarihamy, AAL
defence_counsel: Anil Silva, PC with Shaluka Veranga, AAL
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted based on evidence of solicitation and acceptance of bribe via a trap. The Court of Appeal did not critique the HC's reasoning on conviction, as it was not challenged.
standard_of_review_applied: Discretionary review of sentence based on mitigating circumstances.
sentencing_principles_applied: Consideration of mitigating circumstances (family situation, first offence, repentance) to impose a non-custodial suspended sentence.

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 140, Section 296 read with Section 146, and Section 296 read with Section 32 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The deceased Rajgopal Wijeratnam was brutally murdered on 14th March 2001 in broad daylight. His wife (PW-01) and daughter (PW-02) claimed to be eyewitnesses. The appellants allegedly had a grudge against the deceased for visiting a murder suspect in remand. They were seen threatening a neighbor and later attacking that neighbor's house. When the deceased approached, they chased and stabbed him. The 1st accused later admitted stabbing the deceased during a sudden fight, claiming others were not involved.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 140, Section 296 read with Section 146, and Section 296 read with Section 32 of the Penal Code
hc_sentence_type: Death sentence on count 2, 6 months rigorous imprisonment and a fine on count 1
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the appellants on charges of unlawful assembly and murder based primarily on the eyewitness testimony of the wife and daughter. They were sentenced to death for murder and received a prison term and fine for unlawful assembly.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellants argued the evidence of the eyewitnesses (PW-01 and PW-02) was unreliable due to contradictions in their statements. They also challenged the trial judge's refusal to call a crucial witness (PW-06), misdirections on the law (including on common object and alibi), and failure to ensure a fair trial.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Evidence does not support PW-02 being an eyewitness. | Weaknesses in PW-01's evidence create reasonable doubt. | Judge erred in certifying demeanor of PW-02 when not the trial judge. | Section 114(f) of Evidence Ordinance operates against prosecution for not calling PW-06. | Denial of fair trial by refusing to call PW-06 as prosecution witness. | Misdirection in concluding evidence of PW-01 and PW-02 is believable. | Judge compartmentalized evidence by accepting prosecution evidence before considering defence. | Judge misdirected by mixing up liability based on common object and vicarious liability. | Judge misdirected in law by construing evidence of 2nd and 4th appellants as an alibi. | Misdirection on proof beyond reasonable doubt. | Judge failed to call PW-06 in the interests of justice violating section 199(4) of CrPC.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the testimonies of PW-01 and PW-02 unreliable due to significant contradictions between their court evidence and prior statements. The failure to call PW-06, a key independent neighbor, further undermined the prosecution case.
probability_assessment_by_court: The COA held the prosecution failed to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt due to unreliable eyewitnesses and lack of corroboration. Reasonable doubt existed regarding the participation of all accused.
defence_version_summary: The 1st accused pleaded not guilty but admitted to stabbing the deceased, claiming it was a sudden fight and he acted alone. The 2nd accused claimed an alibi, stating he was on a hire to Wellawatte. The 3rd, 4th, and 5th accused denied involvement, with the 4th claiming he did not live in the area. The 2nd and 5th accused called defence witnesses. The COA found the 1st accused's version regarding a sudden fight credible, but disbelieved the prosecution's case against the others.
legal_errors_description: Misdirection on the law regarding alibi, misdirection on mixing up common object liability with vicarious liability, misdirection on the burden of proof, and procedural error in not calling PW-06.
procedural_defects_description: Refusal of the trial judge to call PW-06 as a prosecution witness in the interests of justice, violating the duty to assist the court in dispensing justice.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The COA analyzed the contradictions in the eyewitness testimonies (PW-01 and PW-02), finding them unreliable and insufficient for conviction. It criticized the prosecution for not calling PW-06, applying the presumption under Section 114(f) of the Evidence Ordinance. The court distinguished between an alibi and a mere denial of presence, finding the trial judge erred in law. The conviction was unsafe without independent corroboration. For the 1st accused, based on his own admission, the COA found the offense fell under culpable homicide not amounting to murder (sudden fight).
coa_sentence_type: The 2nd to 4th accused appellants are acquitted of all charges. The 1st accused appellant is acquitted of murder but convicted of culpable homicide not amounting to murder under section 297 of the Penal Code. He is sentenced to 15 years rigorous imprisonment and a fine of Rs. 50,000, with 18 months simple imprisonment in default.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The appellants were convicted by the High Court of Colombo for unlawful assembly and murder based on the eyewitness accounts of the deceased's wife and daughter. They appealed, challenging witness reliability and procedural errors. The Court of Appeal found the eyewitness evidence unreliable and contradictory, and criticized the prosecution for not calling a key neighbor witness. It acquitted the 2nd to 4th appellants. For the 1st appellant, who admitted to the stabbing but claimed a sudden fight, the COA modified the conviction from murder to culpable homicide not amounting to murder, sentencing him to 15 years imprisonment and a fine.
defence_counsel: Indica Mallawaratchi for the 1st Accused Appellant. Rienzie Arsekularatne, P.C. with N. Karunaratne, Thilina Punchihewa and P. Gamage for the 2nd to 4th Accused Appellants.
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court relied on the uncorroborated and contradictory evidence of PW-01 and PW-02 to convict the appellants. The COA found this approach erroneous, as the evidence was unreliable and the prosecution failed to call a vital independent witness, rendering the conviction unsafe.
standard_of_review_applied: The COA reviewed whether the conviction was safe based on the evidence, applying the standard of proof beyond reasonable doubt and assessing witness credibility and contradictions.
sentencing_principles_applied: For the modified conviction of culpable homicide, the COA considered the facts, circumstances, and nature of injuries (multiple stab wounds) to determine the offense fell under the second limb of section 297 (knowledge likely to cause death). It also considered the time already served.
final_charge_after_appeal: For 1st appellant: Culpable homicide not amounting to murder under section 297 of the Penal Code.

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: On 8 September 2005, the deceased and PW-01 were traveling on a motorbike to buy toddy. They saw three persons walking ahead, including the appellant. A strong torch light was directed at them, causing the rider to lose control and fall. While on the ground, PW-01 saw the appellant approach and stab the deceased once. The deceased died from a fatal chest injury. The appellant surrendered the next day and produced a pointed knife. The motive was a dispute over the murder of the appellant's brother.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the appellant of murder after a judge-alone trial and sentenced him to death. The court relied on the eyewitness testimony of PW-01, who identified the appellant as the assailant.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant challenged the conviction solely on the ground of identity. Counsel argued that PW-01 was the only eyewitness and the incident occurred at night. Relying on the investigating officer's evidence that the streetlight was not functioning and the officer not mentioning a nearby wedding function, it was contended that a serious doubt arises as to whether PW-01 clearly identified the appellant. Counsel also pointed to a discrepancy between the medical evidence of six injuries and PW-01's account of only one attack.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Whether the prosecution has proved the identity of the appellant as the person who committed the crime beyond reasonable doubt.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the sole eyewitness (PW-01) credible and reliable. The court held that the witness, being a fellow villager well-known to the appellant, could positively identify him even in the available light conditions (motorbike headlight, wedding function lights, streetlight). The discrepancy between one seen stab and six medical injuries was explained by the circumstances and nature of the injuries.
probability_assessment_by_court: Court found no reasonable doubt. It held that the positive identification by a known witness under adequate lighting was credible. The medical evidence was consistent with the eyewitness account when viewed in totality.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty. The defence at trial and on appeal primarily challenged the identification by the sole eyewitness, suggesting he was lying. The appellant did not lead evidence or call witnesses but challenged the prosecution case through cross-examination.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal thoroughly analyzed the identification issue. It found that PW-01, being well-known to the appellant, could identify him even from behind and under the prevailing light conditions (motorbike headlight, nearby wedding function lights, streetlight). The court held that the investigating officer's later observation of a non-functioning streetlight did not undermine PW-01's identification at the time of the incident. It reconciled the medical evidence (six injuries) with PW-01's account of one stab, explaining that three injuries resulted from the fall, two were defensive, and one was the fatal stab wound. The court referenced but found the Turnbull guidelines not directly applicable as this was a recognition case between known persons. It affirmed that a conviction can be based on the sole testimony of a credible witness. No legal or procedural errors were found in the High Court judgment.
coa_sentence_type: Death (affirmed)
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused-appellant was convicted of murder by the High Court of Gampaha and sentenced to death. He appealed to the Court of Appeal challenging the conviction on the sole ground of identity, arguing the sole eyewitness could not have reliably identified him at night. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal, finding the eyewitness credible as he knew the appellant well and there was sufficient light from the motorbike headlight, a nearby wedding function, and a streetlight. The medical evidence was found consistent with the eyewitness account. The conviction and death sentence were affirmed.
defence_counsel: Amila Palliyage with Nihara Randeniya and Sewani Udugampola
cause_of_death_exact_text: Injury number 6 had been to the front upper chest, which has penetrated the skin, subcutaneous tissues, zip sternum, costal ventricular wall... an essentially fatal injury, which has resulted in the death.
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted based on the sole eyewitness testimony, finding it credible. The Court of Appeal found no error in this analysis, agreeing that the witness was reliable and the identification was sound under the circumstances.
precedents_cited_list: Regina Vs. Turnbull (1977) QB 224 | Sigera Vs. The Attorney General (2011) 1 SLR 201 | Mulluwa Vs. The State of Madhya Predesh 1976 AIR 989 | Ramratan Vs. State of Rajasthan AIR (1962) S.C. 424
standard_of_review_applied: Evaluation of whether the High Court's conviction was safe, particularly regarding the reliability of eyewitness identification and the sufficiency of evidence.

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 403 of the Penal Code (in relation to the offence of cheating as described in section 398 of the Penal Code)
brief_facts_summary: The Accused-Appellant, a vehicle dealer, was indicted for cheating the complainant (PW-01) by fraudulently inducing him to deposit Rs. 25 million into two bank accounts with the promise of delivering two Toyota Prado jeeps. The money was deposited as instructed on 11 October 2007, but the vehicles were not delivered. The complainant, also a vehicle dealer, had a prior business relationship with the appellant involving over 50 vehicle transactions. After failing to obtain the vehicles or a refund, the complainant lodged a complaint with the Criminal Investigations Department.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 403 of the Penal Code (Cheating)
hc_sentence_type: Simple imprisonment for 4 years, fine of Rs. 25,000, default sentence of 5 months simple imprisonment. Compensation order of Rs. 25 million to PW-01 with a default sentence of 18 months simple imprisonment.
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court Judge found the appellant guilty of cheating. The judge accepted the prosecution's evidence that the appellant fraudulently induced PW-01 to deposit Rs. 25 million for two jeeps which were never delivered. The conviction and sentences were based on this finding.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant argued the prosecution failed to prove the case beyond reasonable doubt. He contended the transaction was of a civil nature (a business partnership/investment) and not criminal cheating. He also argued the High Court Judge failed to properly consider a contradiction in the complainant's evidence and had predetermined the matter.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: 1. The prosecution failed to prove the case beyond reasonable doubt against the appellant. | 2. The learned High Court Judge has failed to give due concession to the contradiction marked V-01. | 3. The learned High Court Judge has predetermined the matter.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed the evidence of PW-01 (complainant), PW-02, and PW-03 (account holders). The core facts—the deposit of Rs. 25 million into the accounts of PW-02 and PW-03 and its subsequent handover to the appellant—were undisputed. The Court found the appellant's defence version (that the money was for a joint investment) was not properly put to the relevant witnesses and was inconsistent with his earlier position.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court assessed that the prosecution evidence was credible and consistent. It found the contradiction (V-01) regarding whether PW-01 had 'firm orders' for the jeeps was minor and did not create reasonable doubt, especially given the admission of the receipt of the large sum. The appellant's failure to properly put his defence to witnesses weakened his version.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty. He made a statement from the dock (no defence witnesses called). His defence was that the Rs. 25 million was not for the two Prado jeeps but was an investment in a vehicle import/sale partnership with PW-01 to share profits, which failed to materialize. The Court found this version not credible and not properly put to prosecution witnesses.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal conducted a comprehensive review. It referenced the legal definition of cheating from section 398 of the Penal Code and the precedent Zahir Vs. Cooray. The Court analyzed the undisputed fact of the money transfer and the appellant's shifting defence. It found the contradiction (V-01) in PW-01's evidence was trivial and did not undermine the core prosecution case. The Court held that the High Court Judge correctly assessed the evidence, did not predetermine the matter, and properly applied the burden of proof. The appeal was dismissed as without merit.
coa_sentence_type: Conviction and sentence affirmed (4 years simple imprisonment, fine of Rs. 25,000 with 5 months default imprisonment, compensation of Rs. 25 million to PW-01 with 18 months default imprisonment).
brief_judgment_file_summary: This is an appeal by Thajudeen Mohomad Fahim against his High Court conviction and sentence for cheating PW-01 of Rs. 25 million by promising two Toyota Prado jeeps. The High Court sentenced him to 4 years imprisonment, a fine, and ordered compensation. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal, finding the prosecution proved its case beyond reasonable doubt. The Court rejected grounds alleging failure to consider a contradiction, predetermination, and insufficiency of evidence, affirming the High Court's judgment in full.
defence_counsel: Ranil Samarasooriya with Nalaka Samarakoon and Rajinda Kandegedara
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court analyzed the evidence and found the appellant guilty, accepting the complainant's version. The COA reviewed this analysis and found no error, agreeing that the High Court Judge correctly considered the evidence and the defence, applied the law properly, and did not predetermine the outcome.
precedents_cited_list: Zahir Vs. Cooray (1941) 42 NLR 263
standard_of_review_applied: Review of whether prosecution proved its case beyond reasonable doubt; evaluation of evidence and legal principles applied by the High Court.

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code
location_of_offence: At the residence of the deceased (and the Appellant)
brief_facts_summary: The Appellant was accused of murdering his wife, the deceased, on or about 09 February 2006. Witnesses testified hearing the Appellant beating the deceased at their residence on the night of the incident, with pleas from her to stop. The deceased's naked body was found wrapped in a mat inside her house the next day. The Appellant was arrested with a bag containing a blood-stained shirt and sarong, and an axe recovered near the body was identified by the deceased's mother as having been borrowed by the Appellant.
evidence_type_primary: Eyewitness testimony, Physical evidence, Circumstantial evidence
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court Judge convicted the Appellant under Section 296 of the Penal Code for murder and sentenced him to death. The conviction was based on witness testimony of the assault, recovery of the murder weapon (axe) and blood-stained clothes, and the Appellant's failure to credibly challenge the prosecution case.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The Appellant raised nine grounds, primarily contending that the High Court Judge erred in law by imposing a burden on him to prove his alibi and misdirected himself on the burden of proof. Other grounds challenged the link between the weapon and the accused, the failure to establish the time of death, erroneous application of Section 106 of the Evidence Ordinance, inadequate circumstantial evidence, failure to send items for forensic analysis, denial of fair trial, and unwarranted application of the Ellenborough principle.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The Learned High Court Judge has flawed in law by imposing a burden on the Accused-Appellant to support his plea of alibi. | The Learned High Court Judge has factually misdirected himself when evaluating the dock statement, thereby causing serious prejudice to the Accused-Appellant. | The Learned High Court Judge has misdirected himself on the burden of proof on an accused by imposing a burden on the Accused-Appellant to rebut the prosecution version. | When the prosecution has not established a link between the weapon recovered from the scene and the accused, the Learned High Court Judge has arrived at a conclusive finding that the Accused-Appellant had murdered the deceased using the said weapon. | The prosecution has totally failed to establish the time of death, which is vital in the backdrop of the defense of alibi embarked upon by the Accused-Appellant. | The Learned High Court Judge has erroneously applied Section 106 of the Evidence Ordinance. | Accused-Appellant has been denied a fair trial as the prosecution has failed to conduct the investigations with due diligence by sending the blood-stained sarong and shirt to the Government Analyst. | Items of Circumstantial evidence are wholly inadequate to support the conviction. | Application of the Ellenborough principle is wholly unwarranted.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed witness testimonies (PW1, PW3, PW4, PW7) which consistently placed the Appellant with the deceased on the night of the murder, hearing the assault. The Appellant's dock statement claiming an alibi was found to be an afterthought as he failed to cross-examine prosecution witnesses on this defense. The medical evidence (PW9) corroborated the violent cause of death.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal concluded the circumstantial evidence chain was complete, consistent only with the guilt of the Appellant and inconsistent with innocence, establishing guilt beyond reasonable doubt.
defence_version_summary: The Appellant pleaded not guilty and made a dock statement claiming an alibi, stating he had gone to work in Kokkuvil after dinner and was drinking in a bar the next morning. He called no defence witnesses. The court found his alibi was an afterthought, not put to prosecution witnesses, and contained blatant lies, rendering it not credible.
legal_errors_description: The Court of Appeal noted the High Court Judge initially erred in law by appearing to impose a burden on the Appellant to prove his alibi. However, the COA found this error did not vitiate the conviction as the evidence overwhelmingly established guilt beyond reasonable doubt.
procedural_defects_description: The prosecution failed to send the blood-stained sarong and shirt to the Government Analyst and failed to show the axe to the medical witness for opinion. The COA held these lapses did not cause prejudice or deny a fair trial given the overall strength of evidence.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal systematically dismissed all appeal grounds. It held that while the High Court Judge may have misstated the burden regarding alibi, the Appellant's failure to suggest his alibi to prosecution witnesses and the afterthought nature of the defense rendered it meritless. The circumstantial evidence—eyewitness accounts of the assault, recovery of the borrowed axe near the body, blood-stained clothes, and the Appellant's presence with the deceased—formed a complete chain pointing solely to his guilt. The COA affirmed that the prosecution proved its case beyond reasonable doubt, and the procedural lapses did not prejudice the Appellant. The conviction and death sentence were upheld.
coa_sentence_type: Death
brief_judgment_file_summary: The Accused-Appellant was convicted of murdering his wife by the High Court of Jaffna and sentenced to death. He appealed on nine grounds, including misdirection on alibi burden, insufficient circumstantial evidence, and procedural lapses. The Court of Appeal found the alibi defense was an afterthought and unsubstantiated. It held the circumstantial evidence—witness testimony, recovery of the murder weapon and blood-stained clothes, and medical evidence—formed a conclusive chain of guilt. While noting some prosecutorial lapses, the COA found no prejudice or denial of fair trial. The appeal was dismissed, affirming the conviction and death sentence.
defence_counsel: Indica Mallowaratchy
cause_of_death_exact_text: shock and hemorrhage due to Primary Brain Damage and Transaction of Spinal Cord due to multiple cut injuries
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court Judge convicted based on witness testimony, medical evidence, and recovered weapon. The COA found the HC may have erred in placing a burden on the Appellant regarding alibi but held this was not material as the evidence overwhelmingly proved guilt. The COA affirmed the HC's overall reasoning and conclusion.
precedents_cited_list: Jayatissa v. The Attorney General [2010] 1 SLR 279 | Hakkini Asela De Silva v. AG SC Appeal No.14/2011 | Gunasiri and Two Others v. Republic of Sri Lanka [2009] 1 SLR 31 | Mannar Mannan v. The Republic of Sri Lanka [1987] 2 SLR 94 | Sanitary Inspector, Mirigama v. Thangamani Nadar 55 NLR 302 | C.Chenga Reddy and others v. State of A.P.(1996) 10 SCC 193 | Attorney General v. Potta Naufer & others (2007) 2 SLR 144
standard_of_review_applied: The Court of Appeal reviewed whether the High Court judgment was correct in law and fact, assessing if the conviction was safe despite any misdirections, applying the principle that a conviction can stand if a reasonable tribunal properly directed would have reached the same conclusion on the evidence.

judges: N. Bandula Karunarathna J. | R. Gurusinghe J.
offence_sections: section 296 read with section 32 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The accused-appellant (1st accused) and another were convicted for the murder of Seiathu Ismail Razeek on or around 16.09.1985 in Akkareipattu. The prosecution case rested solely on circumstantial evidence, including that the deceased was last seen with the 2nd accused. Key evidence involved confessions made by the accused, leading to recovery of the body from water. The accused opted for a jury trial, remained silent, and were convicted and sentenced to death by the High Court.
evidence_type_secondary: Recovery of body, Post-mortem report, Police evidence
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: section 296 read with section 32 of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court, after a jury trial, convicted both accused persons for murder based on circumstantial evidence and confessions. The jury found the charges proven beyond reasonable doubt. Both accused were sentenced to death.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant argued multiple grounds including non-compliance with Criminal Procedure Code sections, misdirection on burden/standard of proof, evaluation of circumstantial evidence, common intention, admissibility of confessions under Evidence Ordinance, failure to call vital witnesses, and insufficiency of circumstantial evidence. Several grounds were later abandoned or not proceeded with at argument.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Non-compliance of section 199 (3) of the Criminal Procedure Code (later not proceeded with) | Learned Trial Judge failed to comply with section 200 of the Criminal Procedure Code (later not proceeded with) | Medical evidence was hearsay evidence | Misdirection on principles relating to overall burden of proof and the Ellenborough principle | Misdirection relating to standard of proof | Misdirection relating to the principles governing the evaluation of circumstantial evidence cases | Misdirection relating to the concept of common intention | Misdirection relating to section 24 of the evidence ordinance | Misdirection relating to section 27 recoveries | Non-direction on distinction between murder and culpable homicide not amounting to murder | Non-direction relating to the general and special exceptions | Non-direction relating to last seen theory | Confession made by the appellant is inadmissible under section 24 of the evidence ordinance | Section 114(f) of the Evidence Ordinance operates against the prosecution by failure to call vital witnesses | Prosecution failed to establish time of death | Items of circumstantial evidence are inadequate to support conviction
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The prosecution relied on circumstantial evidence and confessions. The JMO gave evidence based on a post-mortem report prepared by another doctor. The Court of Appeal found the prosecution case weak and the evidence not sufficiently proving guilt beyond reasonable doubt.
probability_assessment_by_court: Court found the circumstantial evidence inadequate and not inconsistent with innocence. The prosecution failed to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt.
defence_version_summary: The accused pleaded not guilty. They opted for a jury trial and remained silent, neither giving evidence nor making a statement from the dock. The Court of Appeal noted their silence but held it could not be used against them as the prosecution case was weak.
legal_errors_description: Misdirection on burden and standard of proof, misdirection on evaluation of circumstantial evidence, misdirection on admissibility of confessions under Evidence Ordinance sections 24 and 27, non-direction on last seen theory and distinctions between murder and culpable homicide.
procedural_defects_description: Non-compliance with Criminal Procedure Code sections (grounds later abandoned but initially raised), failure of trial judge to properly direct jury on key legal principles.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the trial judge misdirected the jury on the burden and standard of proof, improperly invoked the Ellenborough dictum without a strong prima facie case, and failed to properly direct on circumstantial evidence evaluation and confession admissibility. The prosecution case was weak, relying on insufficient circumstantial evidence. The Court held the proved facts were compatible with innocence and inconsistent with guilt. Applying precedents on circumstantial evidence, the Court concluded the prosecution failed to prove the charge beyond reasonable doubt.
coa_sentence_type: Acquitted and discharged
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused-appellant appealed against his High Court conviction and death sentence for murder. The Court of Appeal found multiple misdirections by the trial judge, including on burden of proof, standard of proof, evaluation of circumstantial evidence, and confession admissibility. The prosecution case was weak and based on insufficient circumstantial evidence. The Court allowed the appeal, set aside the conviction and sentence, and acquitted and discharged the appellant.
defence_counsel: Indica Mallawaratchy, AAL
cause_of_death_exact_text: drowning in water
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted based on jury verdict following a trial where the judge was found to have misdirected the jury on key legal principles. The Court of Appeal criticized the HC judge for misdirection on burden/standard of proof, circumstantial evidence, and confession admissibility, and for applying the Ellenborough dictum without a strong prima facie case.
precedents_cited_list: Rex vs. Cochmne and others (Ellenborough dictum) | Inspector Arendsta vs. Wilfred Pieris, 10 Ceylon Law Weekly 121 | The King vs. Seeder de Silva (1940) 41 NLR. 337 | The King vs. Wickremasinghe (1941) 42 NLR. 313 | The king vs. Peiris Appuhamy (1942) 43 NLR. 412 | Prematilleke vs. The republic of Sri Lanka (1972) 75 NLR. 506 | Illangatilleke vs. The Republic (1984) 2 SLR 38 | Mohamed Niyas Naufar vs. The Attorney General TAB-01/2006 | The King vs. Ellyatamby (1937) 39 NLR. 53 | The Queen vs. Santin Singho 65 N.L.R. 445 | The Queen vs. Sumanasena 66 NLR 350 | The Queen vs. Murugan Ramasamy 64 NLR 433 | The Queen vs. Mapitigama Buddharakkita Thera and 2 others 63 NLR 433 | Rex vs. Jinadasa 51 NLR 529 | Kusumadasa vs. State CA 72/2005 (DB) dated 28.02.2011 | King vs Abeywickrama 44 NLR 254 | King Vs Appuhamy 46 NLR 128 | Podisingho Vs King 55 NLR 49 | Emperor Vs Browning 1918 - 18 Cr LI 482
standard_of_review_applied: Review for errors of law, misdirection, and sufficiency of evidence, particularly regarding circumstantial evidence and burden of proof.

judges: N. Bandula Karunarathna, J. | R. Gurusinghe, J.
offence_sections: section 296 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The appellant was indicted with another for murdering Gannini Gunawardena on 27 February 2003. The prosecution case was that the deceased and PW1 were returning from dropping off an elderly person when the two accused were near a jak tree. The appellant shot the deceased. PW1 witnessed the incident and informed PW2 (the deceased's wife) and others. PW2 had made a police complaint two days prior that the accused had threatened to kill the deceased. The appellant was arrested the same night, and a gun was recovered from his kitchen. The Judicial Medical Officer confirmed death was due to fatal firearm injuries.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: section 296 of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the appellant as charged and sentenced him to death. The judge considered the eyewitness testimony of PW1 to be credible and consistent, and found the recovery of the gun under section 27 of the Evidence Ordinance to be lawful.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant appealed on three grounds: (1) The evidence of the sole eyewitness (PW1) is wholly unsafe to form the basis of conviction. (2) The Trial Judge failed to properly evaluate the testimonial trustworthiness of PW1. (3) The Trial Judge erred in law on the principles relating to section 27 recoveries.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The evidence of the sole eye-witness is wholly unsafe to form the basis of the conviction. | The learned Trial Judge failed to evaluate the testimonial trustworthiness of PW1 in its correct judicial perspective. | The learned Trial Judge erred in law on the principles relating to section 27 recoveries.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal upheld the High Court's evaluation of PW1's evidence, finding it consistent and credible despite one minor contradiction. The court emphasized that minor discrepancies do not render evidence unreliable.
probability_assessment_by_court: The court found no reasonable doubt created by minor contradictions in the prosecution case.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty. He made a dock statement denying the recovery of the gun. He did not call any witnesses and did not provide an explanation for how the gun came to be in his house.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal rejected all grounds of appeal. It found the eyewitness testimony of PW1 was safe, credible, and consistent across proceedings. The minor contradiction in his evidence was not material. Regarding the section 27 recovery, the court found no misdirection, citing precedent that recovery of an object based on an accused's statement is admissible even if the confession itself is not. The court affirmed that the case was not solely circumstantial and relied on acceptable eyewitness testimony.
coa_sentence_type: Death (affirmed)
brief_judgment_file_summary: The second accused-appellant was convicted of murder by the High Court of Kegalle and sentenced to death. He appealed on grounds of unsafe eyewitness evidence and error in law regarding the recovery of the murder weapon. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal, finding the eyewitness testimony credible and the recovery of the gun under section 27 lawful. The conviction and death sentence were affirmed.
defence_counsel: Indica Mallawaratchy
cause_of_death_exact_text: necessary fatal injuries caused by a firearm
hc_analysis_summary: The COA agreed with the HC's careful consideration of PW1's evidence and its handling of the minor contradiction. It also agreed with the HC's application of the law on section 27 recoveries, finding no misdirection.
precedents_cited_list: State Of U.P. vs M.K. Anthony AIR 1985 SC 48 | Oliver Dayananda Kalansuriya alias Raja vs The Democratic Socialist Republic of Sri Lanka CA 28/2009 HC Galle 2900 | King vs Pakir Thambi 32 NLR 262 | Nissanka vs The State 2001 3 SLR 78 | Chuin Pong Shiek vs The Attorney General 1999 2 Sri Lanka law report 277 | Queen vs Murugam Ramasamy 66 NLR 265 | State of Uttar Pradesh Vs MK Anthony [1984] SCJ 236
standard_of_review_applied: The appellate court attached due weight to the trial court's appreciation of evidence, requiring weighty and formidable reasons to interfere.

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: section 296 of the Penal Code
location_of_offence: Seetha Peella, within the jurisdiction of the High Court of Avissawella
brief_facts_summary: The deceased suffered over 90% burn injuries after the house he cohabited in with the accused-respondent caught fire. They had a history of quarrels, and the deceased was a habitual drinker who frequently assaulted the respondent. On the night of the incident, neighbours heard them quarreling until early morning. A fire subsequently engulfed the house, and the deceased, while escaping, made statements implicating the respondent as the one who set him on fire. The prosecution case relied heavily on several alleged dying declarations made by the deceased.
evidence_type_secondary: Post-mortem report, Eyewitness testimony, Neighbour testimony
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: section 296 of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court Judge acquitted the accused-respondent. The judge found that despite several dying declarations, the prosecution failed to prove the charge beyond reasonable doubt. The judge considered the defence version and the attendant circumstances, including the deceased's prior suicide attempt and the accused's potential loss of all her possessions in the fire.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The Attorney General filed a revision application, not a regular appeal, arguing the High Court Judge was misdirected in evaluating the evidence. The petitioner contended the judge wrongly considered the defence evidence before and to discredit the prosecution evidence, failing to properly apply the law on dying declarations. The petitioner sought a retrial.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: High Court Judge misdirected on the way evidence in a criminal trial should be considered. | Judge considered defence evidence before prosecution evidence, reversing the presumption of innocence. | Judge failed to properly consider the law applicable to dying declarations.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: Key prosecution witnesses included neighbours who testified about the quarrel and fire, and a police officer who recorded a dying declaration. The evidence of PW-05 differed, stating the accused shouted words implying the deceased's own actions. The mother of the deceased testified about a prior suicide attempt. The prosecution case rested almost entirely on dying declarations which required careful scrutiny.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal considered whether the accused would risk destroying all her possessions by setting fire to the house with the deceased inside, and whether the deceased might have set the fire himself. Where inferences could be drawn for or against the accused, the inference favouring innocence was preferred.
defence_version_summary: The accused pleaded not guilty. The defence highlighted the unreliable nature of the dying declarations and the deceased's history of violence and prior suicide attempt. The defence argued it was improbable the accused would set fire to her own house, losing all her hard-earned possessions, with the deceased inside.
legal_errors_description: The High Court Judge was misdirected in his approach to evaluating evidence by considering the defence version first and using it to discredit the prosecution evidence, thereby reversing the presumption of innocence.
procedural_defects_description: The petitioner (Attorney General) failed to follow the proper appeal procedure under Section 15 of the Judicature Act after the acquittal, instead filing a revision application.
