A 192/2017 decided on 27.02.19
standard_of_review_applied: Appellate review of evidence to determine if prosecution proved its case beyond reasonable doubt, with focus on identification reliability, circumstantial evidence principles, and proper evaluation of defence evidence.

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: in terms of the Poisons Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance
brief_facts_summary: The accused was indicted for possessing 1.08 grams of heroin. He was on bail but failed to appear before the High Court, and summons could not be served as he had left his provided address without informing the court. A warrant was issued. After an inquiry under section 241(1) where evidence indicated the accused was absconding, the trial proceeded in absentia. He was convicted and sentenced. He was later apprehended in 2022 and applied under section 241(3) to purge default, which was dismissed.
evidence_type_secondary: Police evidence regarding execution of warrant and inquiries into accused's whereabouts
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: in terms of the Poisons Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court, after being satisfied the accused was absconding under section 241(1), proceeded with the trial in his absence. Based on the evidence presented, the accused was found guilty and sentenced to 20 years rigorous imprisonment. An open warrant was issued for his arrest.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The accused-petitioner sought revision to set aside: (1) the order to continue trial in absentia under section 241(1), (2) the conviction and sentence, and (3) the order dismissing his application under section 241(3) to purge default. He contended the initial determination he was absconding was wrong and without proper basis, and that the court should not have relied on only one witness.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Set aside order dated 07-12-2012 continuing trial in absentia under section 241(1). | Set aside conviction and sentence dated 12-03-2015, seeking acquittal or retrial. | Set aside order dated 09-11-2022 refusing application under section 241(3) to purge default.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the trial judge correctly determined the accused was absconding based on the evidence of the officer executing the warrant, who detailed unsuccessful attempts to locate the accused, his sureties, and inquiries with the new house occupier and Grama Niladari. The court held the quality, not quantity, of evidence matters.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court found no reasonable doubt; the accused's conduct in leaving his address without notice established he was absconding, and his failure to explain his absence or take steps to inform the court undermined his claim of bona fide absence.
defence_version_summary: The accused did not plead at the Court of Appeal stage. His counsel argued his absence was not deliberate, as he had appeared in Magistrate's Court and was unaware of the High Court summons. He did not give evidence or call witnesses to substantiate his bona fides under section 241(3). The court found his explanation unconvincing and his conduct evasive.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal upheld the High Court's decisions under both sections 241(1) and 241(3). It found the single police witness's evidence was sufficient and of good quality to establish the accused was absconding. It emphasized the accused's duty to keep the court informed of his address and his failure to provide any credible evidence of bona fide reasons for his absence. The court agreed with the trial judge's reasoning that the accused's actions showed evasion, not innocent absence, and that his story was developed to suit the circumstances. No legal or procedural errors were found.
coa_sentence_type: 20 years rigorous imprisonment (upheld)
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused-petitioner was convicted in absentia by the Panadura High Court for heroin possession and sentenced to 20 years rigorous imprisonment. He applied for revision, challenging the in absentia trial order, the conviction/sentence, and the refusal of his application to purge default. The Court of Appeal found the trial judge correctly determined the accused was absconding based on police evidence of failed attempts to locate him. It also found the accused failed to establish his absence was bona fide under section 241(3). The appeal was dismissed, upholding the conviction and sentence.
defence_counsel: Shavindra Fernando, P.C. with S. Wijendra
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court, after an inquiry under section 241(1), was satisfied the accused was absconding and proceeded with the trial in absentia. It later dismissed his section 241(3) application, finding he failed to establish bona fide absence. The Court of Appeal found no error in the High Court's analysis and reasoning, agreeing with its conclusions on the evidence and the accused's conduct.
standard_of_review_applied: Revisionary jurisdiction under Article 138 of the Constitution and assessment of whether the High Court's determinations under sections 241(1) and 241(3) were correct based on the evidence.

judges: Menaka Wijesundera, J. | B. Sasi Mahendran, J.
offence_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The accused-appellant was charged with the murder of his daughter. The prosecution evidence indicated he came home intoxicated, quarreled, and then stabbed his sleeping daughter and another daughter (PW1) who tried to intervene. The deceased died from excessive bleeding due to abdominal stab wounds. The accused later surrendered to police and made a dock statement denying knowledge of the events.
evidence_type_secondary: Medical evidence (JMO), Physical evidence (knife), Police evidence
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the accused of murder and imposed the death sentence. The trial judge concluded the accused was under the influence of liquor and not in a state to understand his actions, and that he failed to explain his case or take up the defence of voluntary intoxication.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant argued the trial judge erred by not properly considering the plea of voluntary intoxication, as evidence showed he was drunk at the time. He contended the judge wrongly concluded he did not take this defence and was duty-bound to explain his case, and that the judge should have considered intoxication as a defence.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Evidence shows appellant was drunk at time of incident. | Trial judge concluded appellant was under influence of liquor and not in state to understand his actions. | Trial judge concluded appellant did not take defence of intoxication and was duty-bound to explain his case. | Trial judge failed to consider plea of voluntary intoxication.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found PW1's evidence consistent, with no contradictions or discrepancies, and no reason to disbelieve her or for her to falsely implicate her father. The evidence of PW4 (police) and PW8 (SOCO) corroborated regarding the knife. The JMO's evidence confirmed cause of death and weapon type.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court found no reason to doubt the prosecution evidence, which proved the case beyond reasonable doubt. The accused's dock statement did not create any doubt about the prosecution case.
defence_version_summary: The accused made a dock statement saying he did not know what happened. He did not call witnesses. The defence was a denial. The High Court rejected his evidence, finding it did not create doubt. The Court of Appeal agreed, noting he did not take up the defence of voluntary intoxication in a manner that required judicial consideration.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal carefully reviewed the evidence, particularly that of PW1, finding it consistent and credible. It noted the absence of contradictions and the corroboration from police and medical evidence. The court held the trial judge correctly evaluated the evidence and the accused's failure to substantiate any defence, including intoxication. It found no misdirection on the law regarding voluntary intoxication, as the accused did not properly raise it as a defence. The prosecution proved its case beyond reasonable doubt.
coa_sentence_type: Death sentence (upheld)
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused-appellant was convicted of murdering his daughter and sentenced to death by the Vavuniya High Court. He appealed, arguing the trial judge failed to consider voluntary intoxication as a defence. The Court of Appeal found the eyewitness testimony credible and consistent, corroborated by medical and police evidence. It upheld the conviction and death sentence, finding no error in the trial judge's analysis.
defence_counsel: K.Kugaraja
cause_of_death_exact_text: due to excessive bleeding where 2 ½ to 3 litres of blood was found in the abdominal cavity
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court considered the evidence, found the accused was intoxicated but did not properly raise intoxication as a defence, and concluded the prosecution proved the case beyond reasonable doubt. The Court of Appeal agreed with this analysis and found no error.
standard_of_review_applied: Appellate review of conviction and sentence under Article 138(1) of the Constitution and section 331(1) of the Criminal Procedure Code.

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: sections 314 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The complainant-appellant filed a private plaint alleging the accused-respondent assaulted a toddler, Sabir Mohomed Haros, by lifting him by his jaw on 17-02-2013. At trial, the appellant gave evidence but did not witness the incident. The two sisters of the alleged victim testified no such incident occurred. The Magistrate acquitted the respondent due to lack of evidence.
hc_judgment_summary: The Provincial High Court of Kalmunai dismissed the revision application, upholding the Magistrate's acquittal. It found no merit in the appeal as there was no evidence to prove the charge.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant argued the Magistrate and High Court erred by failing to consider his evidence (as PW-01) and by not applying section 114 of the Evidence Ordinance to presume certain facts from his testimony. He claimed his evidence, if properly considered, would lead to a conviction.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The learned Magistrate and the learned High Court Judge erred in law by failing to consider the evidence of the appellant recorded at the trial. | The learned Magistrate and the learned High Court Judge failed to consider the evidence as per the section 114 of the Evidence Ordinance.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court found the appellant's evidence was hearsay as he did not witness the incident. The victim's sisters testified no incident occurred. There was no direct evidence to prove the charge.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court found no evidence whatsoever to prove the charge. The appellant's evidence was hearsay and insufficient, and the witnesses called did not support the allegation.
defence_version_summary: The accused-respondent pleaded not guilty. The defence argued the appellant's evidence was hearsay and no witnesses supported the allegation. The court accepted the defence, finding no evidence to convict.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal held the appellant failed to adduce any evidence to prove the charge. The appellant's testimony was hearsay as he did not witness the incident. The victim's sisters testified no incident occurred. The Court found no misapplication of section 114 of the Evidence Ordinance, as presumptions cannot replace the lack of direct evidence. The Magistrate correctly acquitted the respondent, and the High Court correctly dismissed the revision. The appeal was deemed meritless and filed to harass the respondent.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The complainant-appellant filed a private plaint for assault on a toddler. The Magistrate acquitted the accused due to lack of evidence, as the appellant did not witness the incident and the victim's sisters denied it. The High Court upheld the acquittal. The appellant appealed, arguing his evidence was not considered and section 114 of the Evidence Ordinance should apply. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal, finding the evidence was hearsay and insufficient, and the lower courts correctly decided the case.
defence_counsel: Shihar Hassan
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court well considered the factual and legal provisions, correctly dismissing the revision application as there was no evidence to prove the charge. The Court of Appeal agreed with this analysis.
standard_of_review_applied: Appellate review of revision application under Section 331 of the Code of Criminal Procedure Act.

judges: Menaka Wijesundera, J. | B. Sasi Mahendran, J.
offence_sections: Section 54A of the Poisons, Opium, and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance (as amended by) Act No. 13 of 1984
brief_facts_summary: The accused-appellant was arrested at Katunayake Airport upon arrival from India on 28-09-2007. Police, acting on information, inspected her suitcase which had a false bottom containing a parcel of 2 kg 20g of substance, later found to contain 193.4 grams of pure heroin. She had packed the suitcase with sarees, knew the combination lock (000), and had traveled to India multiple times. She claimed she was coerced and unaware of the drugs.
evidence_type_primary: Physical evidence (drugs in suitcase), Eyewitness testimony (police officers)
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 54A of the Poisons, Opium, and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance (as amended by) Act No. 13 of 1984
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the accused on all three counts (possession, trafficking, importing) and sentenced her to life imprisonment. The judge found the prosecution evidence credible and consistent.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The accused argued the trial judge's judgment was contrary to law and legal principles, the evidence of the accused was not properly evaluated, material issues were not properly addressed, and prosecution evidence was not correctly analysed.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The Learned Trial Judge has arrived at a judgement that is contrary to law and legal principles. | The Learned Trial Judge has not properly evaluated the evidence of the Accused. | The Learned Trial Judge has not Properly addressed material issues raised. | The Learned Trial Judge has failed to correctly analyse the Prosecution evidence.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court found the evidence of PW1 and PW3 consistent and without contradictions. The accused's evidence contained inconsistencies and new versions not put to witnesses. The Court applied legal principles on possession to infer knowledge.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court applied the legal principle from Warner's case and subsequent Sri Lankan precedents to determine that the accused had the requisite knowledge (mens rea) for possession, based on her actions (packing suitcase, knowing combination, frequent travel).
defence_version_summary: The accused testified under oath that she was coerced by Nimal with indecent photos, traveled to India multiple times, packed sarees into an empty suitcase given by Upananda, and was unaware of the drugs. She claimed she asked police to break open the suitcase. The court found her evidence inconsistent and not put to witnesses, and inferred she had knowledge of the contents.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal reviewed the evidence, finding no contradictions between prosecution witnesses. It analyzed the accused's testimony, noting inconsistencies and failure to put her version to witnesses. The court applied the legal principle from Warner v. Metropolitan Police Commissioner and subsequent Sri Lankan cases (K. Sumanawathi Perera v. Attorney General, Mohamed Iqbal Mohamed Sadath v. Attorney General) regarding possession and requisite knowledge. It held that possession requires knowledge of control, not necessarily knowledge of the exact nature of the substance. Based on the accused's actions (acquiring suitcase, packing it, knowing combination, frequent travel), the court inferred she had the requisite knowledge. It found no error in the High Court's judgment and dismissed the appeal.
coa_sentence_type: Life imprisonment (affirmed)
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused-appellant was convicted and sentenced to life imprisonment for importing, trafficking, and possessing 193.4g of heroin at the airport. She appealed, arguing misdirection on law and improper evidence evaluation. The Court of Appeal found the prosecution evidence consistent and applied legal precedents on possession, concluding she had requisite knowledge based on her conduct. The appeal was dismissed, upholding the conviction and sentence.
defence_counsel: Tenny Fernando
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court evaluated the evidence, found it consistent, and convicted the accused. The Court of Appeal agreed with this analysis, finding no errors in the evaluation or application of law.
precedents_cited_list: Warners case (Warner v. Metropolitan Police Commissioner (1968) 52 Criminal Appeal Report 373) | K. Sumanawathi Perera v. Attorney General 1998 2 SLR 20 | R v Boyesen 82 AC 768 | Gareth Edmund Lewis 1988 87 Cr.App.R 270 | Mohamed Iqbal Mohamed Sadath v. Attorney General, SC Appeal 110/15, (SC Minutes 14.12.2020)
standard_of_review_applied: Appellate review under section 333(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure Act and Article 138 of the Constitution.

The High Court upheld the acquittal. The appellant appealed, arguing his evidence was not considered and section 114 of the Evidence Ordinance should apply. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal, finding the evidence was hearsay and insufficient, and the lower courts correctly decided the case.

judges: Menaka Wijesundera, J. | B. Sasi Mahendran, J.
offence_sections: Section 296 read with section 32 of the Penal Code
location_of_offence: At or near the Accused's house
brief_facts_summary: The deceased left home on 20.10.1997 saying he was going to the Accused's house with a bottle of Kassipu. He did not return. His body was later discovered in a cesspit in front of the Accused's house after the Accused, upon being summoned and interrogated by police, gave a statement leading to the discovery. The body had cut wounds and broken bones, and the cause of death was shock from bleeding to the brain from a blow to the head with a sharp weapon. The Accused was convicted of murder by the High Court and sentenced to death.
evidence_type_secondary: Medical evidence and eyewitness testimony (last seen)
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 296 read with section 32 of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court acquitted and discharged the 2nd Accused but convicted the 1st Accused-Appellant for murder and imposed the death sentence. The conviction was based on the evidence, including the recovery of the body from a pit based on the Accused's statement and other circumstantial evidence.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appeal was based on multiple grounds including errors in law regarding the admissibility of the recovery under Section 27 of the Evidence Ordinance, misapplication of legal principles (Lucas and Ellenborough), failure to establish the exact time of death or exclude third-party involvement given the circumstantial and last-seen theory case, reliance on hearsay, and that the evidence was insufficient for conviction. A specific ground regarding non-compliance with the Judicature Act was later withdrawn.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Non-compliance of section 48 of the Judicature Act relating to the adoption of proceedings. (The said ground was later withdrawn). | Learned Trial Judge has erred in law on the principles relating to Section 27 Recoveries. | Learned Trial Judge erred in law by applying the Lucas principle thereby causing serious prejudice to the Accuse-Appellant. | The Application of the Ellenborough Principle is wholly unwarranted in the instant case. | The case being projected on the last seen theory, prosecution has failed to establish the exact time of death. | The case being on circumstantial evidence, prosecution has failed to exclude the possibility of 3rd party being the perpetrator of the crime. | Learned Trial Judge has erred on a critical issue of fact causing prejudice to the Accused-Appellant. | Learned Trial Judge has erred in law by relying upon hearsay evidence thus violating the evidence ordinance. | Items of circumstantial evidence are not weighty enough to support the conviction. | Items of evidence favorable to the accused-appellant has not been considered by the learned trial Judge consequently denying him of a fair trial.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: Prosecution led evidence of eight witnesses. Key witnesses included the deceased's wife (PW1), the investigating officer (PW8), the constable who recorded the statement (PW7), and the Judicial Medical Officer (PW5). The Court of Appeal analyzed the admissibility of the Accused's statement leading to discovery under Section 27 of the Evidence Ordinance, finding it was given while he was a person accused and in police custody.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal found the prosecution had established its case beyond reasonable doubt. It held the Accused's statement leading to discovery was admissible under Section 27 and that the circumstantial evidence was sufficient.
defence_version_summary: The Accused pleaded not guilty and made a dock statement. He stated the deceased was at his place, left at 8:30 pm after drinking with others, and he did not see him again. He claimed PW1 visited later looking for her husband. He said he was summoned to the police station on 23.10.1997, beaten by police before giving his statement, had no animosity with the deceased, and was innocent. The court did not find his version credible.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal focused on the admissibility of the Accused's statement under Section 27 of the Evidence Ordinance. It analyzed precedents from India and Sri Lanka to conclude that the phrase 'a person accused of any offence' is descriptive and does not require a formal accusation at the time of the statement. It also held that 'custody' includes situations where a suspect voluntarily submits to police and is under restraint, not just formal arrest. Applying these principles, the COA found the Accused was a person accused and in police custody when he gave the information leading to the discovery of the body. It found no reason to disturb the High Court's finding that the prosecution proved its case beyond reasonable doubt.
coa_sentence_type: Death sentence upheld
brief_judgment_file_summary: The Accused-Appellant was convicted of murder by the High Court of Embilipitiya and sentenced to death. He appealed on grounds including errors in law regarding the admissibility of his statement under Section 27 of the Evidence Ordinance, insufficiency of circumstantial evidence, and unfair trial. The Court of Appeal analyzed the legal requirements for Section 27, citing several precedents, and held that the Accused was a person accused and in police custody when he gave the information leading to the discovery of the deceased's body. The COA found the High Court's conviction was sound and dismissed the appeal, upholding the death sentence.

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: section 365B (2) (b) of the Penal Code, as amended by Penal Code (Amendment) Act No. 22 of 1995 and 29 of 1998
brief_facts_summary: The accused-appellant, a neighbor known as 'uncle', was charged with three counts of grave sexual abuse against a minor girl (PW01) between 11th April and 11th June 2004. The victim, a 10-year-old at the time, lived with her father and stepmother. She testified that the appellant would send her sister away and take her to a bed, removing her clothes and engaging in intercrural sex multiple times at her house and his. She did not report initially due to threats but later told a teacher, leading to a police complaint on 11th June 2004. Medical examination found no visible signs of abuse, which the doctor explained could be due to the time elapsed. The appellant denied the charges, claiming the grandmother fabricated the story to get the children into probation care.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: section 365B (2) (b) of the Penal Code, as amended by Penal Code (Amendment) Act No. 22 of 1995 and 29 of 1998
hc_sentence_type: 12 years rigorous imprisonment for each of the three counts, to run concurrently
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court Judge found the prosecution proved its case beyond reasonable doubt. He found the victim's evidence sufficiently corroborated, rejected the defence claim of false complaint, and accepted the doctor's explanation for the lack of visible injury. The appellant was convicted on all three counts and sentenced.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant challenged his conviction on grounds including: error in law by using the negative aspect of medical evidence as corroboration; failure to specify or prove the exact dates of offence in the indictment; insufficient identification of the appellant; findings in the judgment not supported by evidence; and failure to properly consider and evaluate defence evidence.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The error in law by applying the negative aspect of medical evidence as corroborative or supportive of the prosecution evidence. | The charges in the indictment does not specify a date but states only a period, however the prosecution failed to lead evidence regarding that period either. | The identification of the appellant was not sufficient to convict him. | Some findings in the judgement does not support by evidence. | The defence evidence had not been considered and evaluated properly.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The prosecution called the victim (PW01), her grandmother (PW04), the examining doctor (PW10), and police officers (PW07, PW08). The victim's evidence was central. The doctor found no visible signs of abuse but explained this could be due to the time elapsed. The COA found the victim's evidence credible and consistent, and that minor factual misdirections by the HC Judge did not cause prejudice.
probability_assessment_by_court: The COA found the prosecution proved its case beyond reasonable doubt. The victim's evidence was credible and trustworthy, and the lack of eyewitnesses or visible medical evidence did not create reasonable doubt given the explanations provided.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty. He made a dock statement claiming the complaint was false, concocted by the grandmother to get the children into probation care. He called one witness (Hewabattage Sunil) who stated he believed the appellant was innocent but had no knowledge of the incidents. The court found the defence version not credible and rejected it.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The COA considered the grounds cumulatively. It held that the exact date of offence was not an essential element and the period was sufficiently established by the victim's evidence that it happened in 2004 after the New Year and about a month before the medical exam. The COA found the victim's identification of the appellant was sufficient despite her inability to recall his name years later. It found no error in the HC Judge's consideration of the medical evidence, which was used to assess consistency, not as strict corroboration. The COA acknowledged minor factual misdirections in the HC judgment (e.g., stating the father was dead instead of the mother) but found they did not prejudice the appellant's substantial rights or cause a failure of justice. The COA affirmed the HC's evaluation of the defence evidence as inadequate to create doubt. Applying precedents on victim credibility in sexual assault cases and the constitutional proviso (Article 138), the COA dismissed the appeal.
coa_sentence_type: 12 years rigorous imprisonment for each of three counts, to run concurrently, and compensation of Rs. 150,000 affirmed. Sentence deemed effective from 31-08-2017.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The Accused-Appellant was convicted by the High Court of Hambantota on three counts of grave sexual abuse of a minor and sentenced to 12 years RI per count (concurrent) plus compensation. He appealed on grounds including erroneous use of medical evidence, failure to prove dates, insufficient identification, unsupported findings, and improper evaluation of defence evidence. The Court of Appeal analyzed each ground, found the victim's testimony credible and sufficiently corroborated, held date was not an essential element, and concluded that minor factual misdirections in the HC judgment did not cause prejudice or a failure of justice. The appeal was dismissed, and the conviction and sentence were affirmed.
defence_counsel: Senarath Jayasundara with Chathurangi Wedage
hc_analysis_summary: The COA found the HC Judge correctly analyzed the evidence, found the victim credible, and provided sound reasoning for conviction. The COA acknowledged the HC Judge made some minor factual misdirections (e.g., confusing which parent was deceased) but concluded these did not prejudice the appellant's substantial rights or cause a failure of justice.

judges: Menaka Wijesundera, J. | B. Sasi Mahendran, J.
offence_sections: Section 459 of the Penal Code
offence_category: Using as genuine a forged document
brief_facts_summary: The accused obtained a loan from Peoples Bank, Ampara, after submitting a document (P1) which was a financial undertaking form for salary deduction. The bank manager (PW1) later discovered the monthly installments were not being sent. The accountant (PW2) from the Police Department (the relevant authority) denied signing or sealing the document, stating it was forged. The prosecution alleged the accused fraudulently used the forged document. The accused testified he submitted the form to the Chief Clerk (PW3) for processing and later received it back signed and sealed, which he then gave to the bank.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 459 of the Penal Code
hc_sentence_type: 5 years Rigorous Imprisonment and a fine
hc_judgment_summary: The learned High Court Judge convicted the accused on the charge of using a forged document as genuine under Section 459 of the Penal Code. He was sentenced to 5 years RI and a fine of Rs. 25,000.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant argued the trial judge failed to appreciate that PW3 was an instrumental witness for the defence, failed to consider the defence version, and imposed an excessive sentence.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: That the learned trial judge has failed to determine that the PW3 namely Puwapilleyi Thawamani is an instrumental witness in proving the innocence of the Appellants; | That the learned trial judge has not considered the version of the defense at all times; | In any event, the sentence imposed on the appellant is excessive.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: Prosecution called 8 witnesses (PW1, PW2, PW5, PW6, PW7, PW9, PW10, PW11). Key witnesses were the bank manager (PW1) and the accountant (PW2) who denied authorizing the document. The defence hinged on the non-calling of PW3, the Chief Clerk, who allegedly received and date-stamped the document. The COA found the prosecution failed to prove the accused's knowledge or involvement in the forgery, especially given the missing testimony of PW3 and the presence of a date stamp on the document.
probability_assessment_by_court: The COA found the prosecution failed to prove the case beyond reasonable doubt. The absence of the vital witness (PW3) and the evidence of the date stamp on the document created reasonable doubt as to whether the accused knew the document was forged.
defence_version_summary: The accused pleaded not guilty and gave evidence. He stated he submitted the form (P1) to the Chief Clerk (PW3) for processing, received it back signed and sealed after a few days, and then submitted it to the bank. He claimed he did not see who signed it. The court found his version created reasonable doubt, especially as the prosecution failed to call PW3 to contradict it.
legal_errors_description: The learned High Court judge misdirected himself by shifting the burden of proof to the accused.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The COA analyzed the elements of the offence under Section 459, citing The Queen v Kapurala. It found the prosecution failed to prove the accused knew or had reason to believe the document was forged. The COA emphasized the burden of proof remains on the prosecution, citing Pantis v. The Attorney General and Rex v. Burdett (followed in Baddewithana v. The Attorney General). It held the failure to call PW3, the Chief Clerk who allegedly received and date-stamped the document, was a critical lapse. The accused's testimony that he submitted the form to PW3 and the presence of a date stamp on P1 created reasonable doubt. The COA concluded it would be unsafe to uphold the conviction as the prosecution did not prove the accused's knowledge of the forgery.
coa_sentence_type: Conviction and sentence set aside. Accused acquitted.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The Accused-Appellant was convicted by the High Court of Ampara for using a forged document as genuine under Section 459 of the Penal Code to obtain a loan and sentenced to 5 years RI and a fine. He appealed on grounds including the trial judge's failure to consider the importance of an uncalled witness (PW3), failure to consider the defence version, and excessive sentence. The Court of Appeal found the prosecution failed to prove the accused knew the document was forged, especially given the lapse in not calling PW3 and the evidence of a date stamp on the document. The COA held the High Court misdirected itself on the burden of proof. The appeal was allowed, the conviction and sentence were set aside, and the accused was acquitted.
defence_counsel: Saliya Pieris, PC with Eshan De Zilva
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court Judge convicted the accused, finding the prosecution proved its case. The COA found the HC Judge erred by misdirecting himself on the burden of proof and by failing to adequately consider the defence evidence and the significance of the missing witness (PW3), which created reasonable doubt.
precedents_cited_list: The Queen v Kapurala 2 NLR 330 | Pantis v. The Attorney General 1998 2 SLR 148 | Rex v. Burdett 1820 4 B & Ald 95, 120 | Baddewithana v. The Attorney General 1990 1 SLR 275
standard_of_review_applied: Review for errors of law (misdirection on burden of proof) and assessment of whether the prosecution proved its case beyond reasonable doubt.

judges: Pradeep Hettiarachchi, J | P. Kumararatnam, J
offence_sections: section 54 A(b) and section 54 A(d) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance as amended by Act No 13 of 1984
brief_facts_summary: On 3rd April 2013, the Accused-Appellant was arrested at 19:45 hours at Wattala. According to PW1, the raiding party recovered 5.33g of heroin packed in a pink-colored bag from the right-side pocket of his trousers. The sealed substance was then taken to the Police Narcotics Bureau. The prosecution alleged trafficking and unauthorized possession of heroin. The defense challenged the chain of custody and credibility of prosecution witnesses.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: section 54 A(b) and section 54 A(d) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance as amended by Act No 13 of 1984
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court of Negombo convicted the Accused-Appellant on both counts of trafficking and unauthorized possession of 5.33g of heroin. The learned High Court Judge sentenced him to life imprisonment.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appeal was limited to three main grounds: the High Court Judge erred by failing to consider that the defense version was more probable; the prosecution failed to prove the chain of custody beyond reasonable doubt; and the Judge rejected defense evidence on a wrong premise, denying a fair trial.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The Learned High Court Judge erred in law by failing to consider that the defense version is more probable than the prosecution | Prosecution has failed to prove the chain of custody beyond reasonable doubt | The Learned High Court Judge rejected the defense evidence on the wrong premise and therefore denied a fair trial
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found material and vital contradictions between PW1 and PW2 regarding the number of parcels recovered and the subsequent handover of the production. These contradictions severely undermined the credibility of the prosecution's case and broke the chain of custody.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court found the prosecution failed to prove the chain of custody beyond reasonable doubt, creating reasonable doubt as to whether the substance analyzed was the same as that seized from the Appellant.
defence_version_summary: The Accused-Appellant pleaded not guilty. The defense included a dock statement by the accused and testimony from three defense witnesses. The Court of Appeal did not reach a credibility assessment of the defense evidence, as it allowed the appeal based on prosecution failures.
legal_errors_description: The High Court Judge failed to properly consider material contradictions in prosecution evidence regarding the chain of custody and the number of parcels recovered.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal focused on the prosecution's failure to prove the chain of custody beyond reasonable doubt. It highlighted glaring contradictions between PW1 and PW2: PW1 stated one pink parcel was recovered and kept in his locker for three days before handover, while PW2 stated three pink parcels were recovered and handed over immediately upon arrival at the Police Narcotics Bureau. The Government Analyst received only one parcel. These inconsistencies severed the link between the seized substance and the evidence produced in court. The Court emphasized that the prosecution must establish all links in the chain of custody from seizure to analysis to exclude tampering. Citing precedents (Witharana Doli Nona vs Republic of Sri Lanka, Perera vs Attorney General, Mahasarukkalige Chandrani vs AG, and S v Matshaba), the Court held the prosecution's case was irreparably damaged. The Deputy Solicitor General conceded the discrepancies. The Court did not examine other evidence, finding the conviction unsustainable.
coa_sentence_type: Acquitted – No sentence imposed
brief_judgment_file_summary: The Accused-Appellant, Liyanage Sachith Ruchira Sandaruwan, was convicted by the High Court of Negombo for trafficking and unauthorized possession of 5.33g of heroin and sentenced to life imprisonment. He appealed to the Court of Appeal, arguing the High Court Judge erred in assessing probabilities, the prosecution failed to prove the chain of custody, and he was denied a fair trial. The Court of Appeal found fatal contradictions between two key prosecution witnesses (PW1 and PW2) regarding the number of drug parcels recovered and the subsequent handling of the evidence, which broke the chain of custody. The Court held the prosecution failed to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt, set aside the conviction and sentence, and acquitted the Appellant.

hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted the Appellant based on the prosecution evidence. The Court of Appeal found the High Court Judge failed to adequately address material contradictions between PW1 and PW2 regarding the chain of custody, which went to the root of the prosecution's case.

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 354 of the Penal Code; Section 365B(2)(b) of the Penal Code as amended by the Penal Code (Amendment) Act No. 22 of 1995 and 29 of 1998
brief_facts_summary: The Accused-Appellant, a known 'uncle' to the 6.5-year-old victim, took her from a neighbour's house to an abandoned house on 31-07-2008 under the pretense of picking mandarins. There, he removed her clothes, spat on her vagina, and committed intercrural sex. The victim screamed but was not heard. After the act, he gave her two mandarins and sent her home. She immediately reported the incident to her father, who took her to the police and then to the hospital for examination. The child consistently identified the appellant as the perpetrator, initially referring to him as 'uncle' and later as 'Wimale Maama'. The father corroborated the report and identified the appellant as a known neighbour.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 354 of the Penal Code; Section 365B(2)(b) of the Penal Code as amended by the Penal Code (Amendment) Act No. 22 of 1995 and 29 of 1998

hc_judgment_summary: The High Court found the appellant guilty on both counts. After considering aggravating and mitigatory circumstances, the Judge sentenced him to 1 year rigorous imprisonment on count 1 and 9 years rigorous imprisonment on count 2, to run consecutively. He was also fined Rs. 2,500 and Rs. 5,000 on the respective counts, with default sentences. He was ordered to pay Rs. 250,000 as compensation to the victim.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant's counsel argued that the burden of proof was improperly shifted to the appellant by the High Court Judge. He also contended that the identification of the appellant was doubtful, that the Judge failed to consider improbabilities in the prosecution evidence, and failed to address omissions and contradictions highlighted during the trial.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The burden of proof has been shifted to the appellant by the learned High Court Judge. | Identification of the accused-appellant is doubtful. | The learned High Court Judge has failed to consider the improbabilities and impossibilities of the prosecution evidence. | The learned High Court Judge has failed to consider omissions and contradictions highlighted during the trial in his judgment.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the victim child's (PW-01) evidence cogent, trustworthy, and consistent. Her testimony was corroborated by her father (PW-02) on material points and by the consistent history given to the JMO (PW-15). The court found no material contradictions among witnesses.
probability_assessment_by_court: Court analyzed and rejected claims of improbability (e.g., no one hearing the scream was not improbable given the location and nature of the act). Found prosecution proved its case beyond reasonable doubt.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty. His defence was a dock statement only, denying the allegations and claiming he was arrested on suspicion and never took the child anywhere. The High Court and Court of Appeal found this mere denial insufficient to create a reasonable doubt in the prosecution's case.
legal_errors_description: The COA noted the HC Judge used wrong wording suggesting the appellant should have produced acceptable evidence, which could be seen as shifting the burden of proof. However, the COA found that when the judgment was read as a whole, no such burden was actually placed on the appellant.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The COA methodically addressed each ground of appeal. It held the victim's identification of the appellant as the known 'uncle' was reliable, dismissing the Turnbull guidelines as inapplicable. It found the child's evidence consistent, credible, and corroborated. It analyzed claims of improbability (e.g., no one hearing screams) and omissions (e.g., police not recording statements from friends) and found they did not create reasonable doubt. Regarding burden of proof, the COA acknowledged infelicitous wording in the HC judgment but held, reading it as a whole, the HC correctly applied the law and the appellant's substantial rights were not prejudiced. The COA applied the proviso to Article 138 of the Constitution and Section 436 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, finding no error occasioning a failure of justice.
coa_sentence_type: Rigorous Imprisonment 10 years (consecutive: 1 year on count 1, 9 years on count 2), Fine, Compensation. Sentence deemed to have commenced from 12-09-2022 (date of HC conviction).

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 454 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The accused (3rd to 7th) were charged with preparing a forged deed (Deed No. 577). The 3rd accused pleaded guilty and was sentenced. The 4th to 7th accused were discharged by the Magistrate under Section 186 of the Code of Criminal Procedure Act No.15 of 1979. The Appellant, the virtual complainant, challenged this discharge order through a revision application in the High Court, which was dismissed. The Appellant then appealed to the Court of Appeal.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 454 of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court dismissed the Appellant's revision application. The High Court held that the Appellant failed to adduce exceptional circumstances and that the Magistrate's order under Section 186 CPC was not in violation of legal provisions. The High Court also noted the Appellant did not invoke the appellate remedy under Section 318 CPC.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The Appellant argued the Magistrate failed to examine whether Deed No. 577 was forged and failed to properly evaluate investigation material and frame fresh charges. She also argued she was not afforded a full opportunity to present her case, which was an exceptional circumstance the High Court should have considered.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The Learned Magistrate has failed to examine whether Transfer Deed No. 577 is forged document. | The need for the Learned Magistrate to properly evaluate the material elicited during the criminal investigation, and frame proper fresh charges at a re-trial. | Appellant was not afforded an opportunity to present her case fully, an exceptional circumstance which should have been considered by the Learned High Court Judge.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: Evidence from the Appellant did not reveal that the 4th and 5th accused contributed to preparing the deed in furtherance of common intention. The 6th and 7th accused were mere witnesses to the deed. No evidence of conspiracy, common intention, or aiding and abetting was found against the 4th to 7th accused.
probability_assessment_by_court: Court found no evidence linking the 4th to 7th accused to the offence. The discharge order was proper.
defence_version_summary: The 3rd accused pleaded guilty. The 4th to 7th accused applied for discharge under Section 186 CPC, arguing they were merely witnesses to the deed. The Magistrate discharged them, finding no evidence of their involvement in the offence.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal affirmed the High Court's dismissal of the revision application. It held that the revision is a discretionary remedy to be invoked only in exceptional circumstances, which the Appellant failed to demonstrate. The Court analyzed the evidence and found no fault in the Magistrate's reasoning for discharging the 4th to 7th accused, as the evidence did not establish their involvement in the forgery. The Court also noted the Appellant failed to use the statutory appeal remedy under Section 318 CPC and raised new grounds not canvassed in the High Court.
coa_sentence_type: No sentence (Appeal dismissed, discharge of 4th to 7th accused affirmed)
brief_judgment_file_summary: The Appellant, Gallage Shirani Susantha De Silva, appealed against the High Court's dismissal of her revision application challenging the Magistrate's discharge of the 4th to 7th accused from forgery charges under Section 454 of the Penal Code. The High Court found no exceptional circumstances to justify revision. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal, upholding the lower courts' orders. The COA held that the Appellant failed to show exceptional circumstances for revision, the evidence did not implicate the discharged accused, and she had not availed herself of the proper appellate remedy.
prosecution_counsel: Jayaluxshi De Silva, SSC for the 1st and 2nd Respondents
defence_counsel: Asela Serasinghe for the Appellant; Asthika Devendra with Vimukthi Karunaratne for the 4th to 7th Respondents
plea_of_accused: Guilty (3rd Accused); Not Guilty/Discharged (4th to 7th Accused)
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court correctly found the Appellant failed to adduce exceptional circumstances for revision and that the Magistrate's order under Section 186 CPC was legally sound. The COA agreed with this analysis.

Seyed Mohamed 69 CLW 34 | Rasheed Ali v.Mohammed Ali and Others [1981] 1 SLR 262 | Commissioner of Police v. Tanes (1957-58) 68 CLR 383 | Colombo Apothecaries Ltd v Commissioner of Labour 1998(3) SLR 320
standard_of_review_applied: Revisionary jurisdiction, to be exercised only in exceptional circumstances to avoid miscarriage of justice.

judges: P Kumaratnam, J. | Pradeep Hettiarachchi, J.
offence_sections: grave sexual abuse (Penal Code as amended)
brief_facts_summary: The Appellant and a second accused were indicted for grave sexual abuse of Pradeep Maduranga Jayasuriya around 09-11-1998. The Appellant absconded after being granted bail in 2001. The High Court conducted an inquiry and proceeded to trial in absentia under section 241 of the CCPA. The Appellant was convicted and sentenced in 2005. He was arrested in 2022 and assigned counsel, who unsuccessfully applied for a trial de novo. The Appellant then filed this appeal, which the Court of Appeal found was filed 17 years out of time.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: grave sexual abuse (Penal Code as amended)
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court proceeded to trial in absentia after an inquiry where a police constable testified that the Appellant's whereabouts could not be found. The Appellant was convicted and sentenced to 10 years rigorous imprisonment, a fine of Rs. 5000, and a default sentence of 12 months if the fine was not paid.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The Appellant challenged the conviction and sentence through the chief jailor. The assigned counsel argued there were several grounds of defense and contradictions that could have been highlighted, and moved for a trial de novo. The Appellant's counsel also argued that if the appeal was out of time, the Court should exercise its inherent revisionary powers under section 364 of the CCPA.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Delay in filing appeal | Request for trial de novo under section 241(3)(b) of CCPA | Invocation of revisionary powers under section 364 of CCPA | Alleged lack of evidence for proceeding under section 241 of CCPA
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The judgment mentions an inquiry prior to the in absentia trial where a police constable gave evidence about unsuccessful efforts to locate the Appellant. No detailed analysis of trial evidence is provided in the Court of Appeal judgment.
defence_version_summary: The Appellant absconded and was tried in absentia. He did not plead guilty. After arrest in 2022, his assigned counsel argued there were grounds of defense and contradictions but did not adduce evidence to show his absence was bona fide. The Court found his conduct was contumacious.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the appeal was filed 17 years out of time, far beyond the 14-day limit under section 331 of the CCPA. The Court refused to exercise its revisionary powers under section 364 due to the Appellant's inordinate delay and contumacious conduct in absconding for nearly 17 years. The Court upheld the High Court's procedure for holding the trial in absentia after a proper inquiry. The Court noted the Appellant failed to adduce any evidence that his absence was bona fide, a requirement for ordering a trial de novo under section 241(3)(b). Accordingly, the Court saw no reason to interfere with the High Court judgment.
coa_sentence_type: 10-year rigorous imprisonment, fine of Rs. 5000, and default sentence of 12 months if fine not paid
brief_judgment_file_summary: The Appellant Nassar Mohammed Hussain was convicted in absentia by the Hambanthota High Court in 2005 for grave sexual abuse and sentenced to 10 years rigorous imprisonment and a fine. He absconded for nearly 17 years before being arrested in 2022. His appeal to the Court of Appeal was filed in 2022, 17 years after the judgment. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal as out of time and refused to exercise revisionary powers due to the Appellant's contumacious conduct and undue delay. The Court also found no error in the High Court's procedure for holding the trial in absentia.
defence_counsel: Ershan Ariyaratnam
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court conducted an inquiry, heard evidence from a police constable about unsuccessful efforts to locate the Appellant, and then proceeded to trial in absentia under section 241 of the CCPA. The Court of Appeal found no error in this procedure and upheld the High Court's findings.

Priyantha Jayakody v OIC, Police station, Mawarala and Another CA/PHC/119/2004 | Camillus Ignatious vs OIC, Uhana Police Station CA (Rev) 907/89 | Opatha Mudiyanselage Nimal Perera vs A.G – CA (Rev) 532/97 | Rajapakse v The State [2001] 2 Sri LR 161 | Gunasiri and Others and Albara Dura Ananda v The State [1990] 2 Sri LR 265
standard_of_review_applied: Review of timeliness under section 331 of CCPA and discretion to exercise revisionary powers under section 364 of CCPA, considering contumacious conduct and delay.

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Sections 54(A)(b) and 54(A)(d) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance as amended by Act No. 13 of 1984
location_of_offence: Badowita area, Pepiliyana-Nedimala Road in front of Pepiliyana Sunethradevi Raja Viharaya
brief_facts_summary: Acting on information, police raided the area and apprehended the Appellant riding a motorcycle. They recovered 25 grocery bags containing 1000 small packets of a substance from his jacket pocket, along with cash and mobile phones. The substances were later weighed and analyzed, revealing 5.75 grams of heroin. The prosecution's case relied on the police raid evidence and the Government Analyst report.
evidence_type_secondary: Government Analyst Report, Police witness testimony
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Sections 54(A)(b) and 54(A)(d) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance as amended by Act No. 13 of 1984
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court found the Appellant guilty on both counts of trafficking and possession of heroin. The Judge imposed the death sentence on the Appellant.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The Appellant argued the prosecution failed to prove chain of custody beyond reasonable doubt, citing a weight discrepancy. He also contended the trial judge violated evidence rules by allowing a witness to refresh memory improperly, failed to consider the improbability of the prosecution version, and wrongly rejected the defence evidence.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The Learned Trial Judge erred in law when concluding that the prosecution proved the chain of custody beyond reasonable grounds. | The Learned Trial Judge violated the provisions of the Section 159 of the Evidence Ordinance. | The Learned Trial Judge failed to consider that the prosecution version did not pass the test of probability. | The Leaned Trial Judge did not evaluate the defence evidence from the correct perspective and the rejected same in the wrong premise.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court found serious issues with prosecution evidence: weight discrepancies in recovered drugs, a police witness refreshing memory contrary to procedure, and lack of receipts from a jeweller where drugs were weighed. These undermined the chain of custody.
probability_assessment_by_court: Court held prosecution version did not pass probability test; weight discrepancy and procedural issues created reasonable doubt.
defence_version_summary: The Appellant pleaded not guilty and made a statement from the Dock. He claimed false arrest, alleging police recovered drugs from another person, divided them, and planted them on him along with cash. The High Court rejected his statement without proper analysis.
legal_errors_description: Trial judge erred in concluding chain of custody was proven; violated Section 159 of Evidence Ordinance; failed to properly evaluate defence evidence and probability.
procedural_defects_description: Witness PW2 referred to a separate paper not his notes, violating Section 159 of Evidence Ordinance; police altered timings in report.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the prosecution failed to prove the case beyond reasonable doubt. Key issues included a significant weight discrepancy in the recovered drugs (25g at jeweller vs 25.06g at analyst) unexplained by prosecution, undermining chain of custody. Procedural defects included a witness improperly refreshing memory and police altering report timings. The trial judge failed to consider the defence version and probability factors. Citing precedents on burden of proof, the COA held the prosecution's duty was not discharged, and the conviction was unsafe.
coa_sentence_type: Acquitted, sentence set aside.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The Accused-Appellant was convicted in the High Court of Colombo for trafficking and possessing 5.75g of heroin and sentenced to death. He appealed. The Court of Appeal found the prosecution failed to prove the case beyond reasonable doubt due to a critical weight discrepancy in the evidence, procedural errors including a violation of evidence rules, and the trial judge's failure to properly assess the defence case and probability. The appeal was allowed, the conviction and sentence were set aside, and the Appellant was acquitted.
defence_counsel: Nihara Randeniya
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted based on police and analyst evidence, imposing death sentence. The COA found the HC erred by accepting flawed evidence with chain of custody issues, violating evidence procedures, and failing to consider defence or probability, resulting in an unsafe conviction.
precedents_cited_list: Woolmington v DPP (1935) | Mohamed Nimnaz V. Attorney General CA/95/94 | Attorney-General v. Rawther 25 NLR 385 | Miller v. Minister of Pensions (1947) 2 All E.R. 372 | Perera V. Attorney General [1998] 1 Sri.L.R 378 | Koushappis v. The State of WA [2007] WASCA 26; (2007) 168 A Crim R 51 | R v. Hepworth 1928 (AD) 265
standard_of_review_applied: Whether prosecution proved guilt beyond reasonable doubt; evaluation of evidence and chain of custody.

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Sections 54(A)(d) and 54(A)(b) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance as amended by Act No. 13 of 1984
brief_facts_summary: Police received information that a person named Robinson possessed a firearm. A raid was conducted on 18/02/2018. The appellant was arrested outside an apartment complex after a packet of heroin was found in his trouser pocket. A search of his fifth-floor room revealed a locked almirah containing parcels of heroin and cannabis, a spoon with traces of heroin, two electric weighing machines, and 17 small bags.
evidence_type_primary: Physical evidence (drugs, weighing machines, spoon, bags), Police testimony
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Sections 54(A)(d) and 54(A)(b) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance as amended by Act No. 13 of 1984
hc_sentence_type: Death on 1st and 2nd Counts; 01-year rigorous imprisonment each on 3rd and 4th Counts
hc_judgment_summary: The Learned Trial Judge found the Appellant guilty on all counts of Possession and Trafficking of 62.736 grams of Heroin and Possession and Trafficking of 12.170 grams of Cannabis. He was sentenced to death on the first two counts and one-year rigorous imprisonment on the third and fourth counts.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The Appellant argued the trial judge failed to consider doubts about the raid, did not properly evaluate defence evidence, and acted as a prosecutor under Section 165 of the Evidence Ordinance.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: That the Learned Trial Judge failed to consider the doubtfulness in relation to the raid conducted by the prosecution witnesses. | That the Learned Trial Judge had not properly considered the evidence for the defence. | The Learned High Court Judge had performed the role of the prosecutor under Section 165 of the Evidence Ordinance.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court found the evidence of PW1 and PW2 to be clear, cogent, consistent, and passing the probability test. The defence evidence, including the dock statement and witness testimonies, was considered but found insufficient to create a doubt against the prosecution's overwhelming evidence.
probability_assessment_by_court: Court found prosecution version passed test of probability and proved the case beyond reasonable doubt. Defence evidence failed to create any plausible doubt.
defence_version_summary: The Appellant pleaded not guilty. He made a dock statement claiming he was intentionally implicated by PW1 and disputed possessing the narcotics. He called 04 defence witnesses. The court found inconsistencies in his and his wife's accounts and rejected the defence as not credible against the prosecution evidence.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The COA found no merit in the appeal grounds. It held the trial judge correctly analyzed the raid evidence, finding it consistent and probable. The defence evidence was properly considered and found wanting. The trial judge's questions under Section 165 of the Evidence Ordinance were not improper or prejudicial. The prosecution's key witnesses were credible and their evidence proved the case beyond reasonable doubt. The conviction and sentence were therefore affirmed.
coa_sentence_type: Death on Counts 1 and 2; 01-year rigorous imprisonment each on Counts 3 and 4 (affirmed)
brief_judgment_file_summary: The Accused-Appellant, Simiyon Robinson, was convicted in the High Court of Colombo for Possession and Trafficking of Heroin and Cannabis and sentenced to death on two counts and imprisonment on two others. He appealed, arguing doubts about the raid, improper evaluation of defence evidence, and judicial bias. The Court of Appeal found the prosecution evidence, including consistent police testimony and a Government Analyst report, was credible and proved guilt beyond reasonable doubt. It rejected all grounds of appeal, affirmed the High Court's conviction and sentence, and dismissed the appeal.
defence_counsel: I.B.S Harshana
hc_analysis_summary: The HC correctly discussed and analyzed the evidence, including time consumption of the raid and inconsistencies in the defence. The COA found the HC's reasoning and conclusions to be accurate and based on a proper perspective of all evidence.
precedents_cited_list: Mohamed Nimnaz V. Attorney General CA/95/94 | the Attorney-General v. Rawther 25 NLR 385 | Don Samantha Jude Anthony Jayamaha v. The Attorney General CA/303/2006 | Kathubdeen v. Republic of Sri Lanka [1998] 3 SLR 107 | People v Arnold 98 N.Y.2d 63 (2002) | Senanayake v De Silva 75 NLR 409
standard_of_review_applied: Whether prosecution proved case beyond reasonable doubt; whether trial judge properly evaluated evidence.

judges: Menaka Wijesundera J. | Wickum A. Kaluarachchi J.
offence_sections: Section 140, 146/296, 146/315 and in the alternative on the basis of Common Intention under the provisions of the Penal Code
location_of_offence: In the house of the deceased
brief_facts_summary: On the evening of February 4, 1998, four accused entered the house of the deceased. The accused-appellant, along with others, assaulted the deceased with weapons, including a kriss knife. The appellant was identified by witnesses, including the deceased's daughter. The appellant absconded for nearly three years before being arrested. The deceased suffered 14 external injuries, one of which was necessarily fatal.
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the appellant for murder. The trial judge found the identification evidence of PW1 to be trustworthy despite some contradictions. The appellant was found guilty of the charge of murder based on common intention with the first accused.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The main ground of appeal was the identification of the appellant at the scene of crime. The appellant's counsel argued that the Trial Judge misdirected himself by not giving adequate weight to contradictions in PW1's evidence. The appellant also objected that he was shown to witnesses before the identification parade.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The main ground was the identification of the appellant at the scene of crime. | The Trial Judge misdirected himself by not giving adequate weight to contradictions in PW1's evidence. | The appellant objected that he was shown to the witnesses by the police before the identification parade.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court found PW1, despite being traumatized and some contradictions, to be a trustworthy witness who identified the appellant at the parade and in court. PW2 also identified the appellant at the scene. The Court noted that contradictions are expected given the traumatic nature of the event and do not undermine the overall trustworthiness of the witnesses.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court found the prosecution proved its case beyond reasonable doubt. The witnesses' evidence, despite minor contradictions, stood the test of probability, spontaneity, and trustworthiness.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty. He made a dock statement, claiming he was shown to witnesses before the identification parade. He called no witnesses. The trial judge and Court of Appeal did not accept his dock statement.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found no misdirection by the trial judge. It accepted the identification parade evidence, noting the delay was due to the appellant absconding. The Court cited precedent that contradictions not going to the root of the case should be disregarded and that criminal cases cannot be proved with mathematical accuracy. The Court found the witnesses credible and the prosecution's case proved beyond reasonable doubt, considering the appellant's conduct, the nature of injuries and weapons, and the common murderous intention with the first accused.
coa_sentence_type: Conviction and sentence affirmed
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused-appellant, along with three others, was charged with murder based on common intention. The High Court of Galle convicted him. He appealed, challenging his identification and alleging procedural errors with the identification parade. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal, upholding the trial judge's assessment of witness credibility and finding the prosecution proved its case beyond reasonable doubt. The conviction and sentence were affirmed.
prosecution_counsel: Shanil Kularatne, SDSG for Hon. Attorney General
defence_counsel: Anil Silva, PC with Isuru Jayawardane and Sarith Wadugedhara
hc_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the trial judge correctly accepted the identification evidence, was mindful of the witness's traumatic experience, and correctly rejected the appellant's dock statement. No errors were identified in the High Court's reasoning.
precedents_cited_list: AG VS Potta Naufer and others (2007) 2 Sri.L.R 186 to 187 | Oliver Dayananda Kalanasooriya alias Raju v Republic of Sri Lanka, CA 28/2009 decided on 13/02/2013 | Rannuka Arachchilage Chaminda Roshan V The Republic of Sri Lanka, CA No. 120/2004 | Keerthi Bandara v Attorney General (2002) 3 SLR 245
standard_of_review_applied: The Court reviewed whether the trial judge misdirected himself on the evidence, particularly regarding witness credibility and identification.

judges: N. Bandula Karunarathna J. P/CA | B. Sasi Mahendran J.
brief_facts_summary: The petitioner was a senior officer in the Prisons Department. Following a deadly prison riot in 2012, he faced criminal charges for the murder of inmates but was later acquitted. He fled the country in 2018 due to serious threats to his life and liberty. He was deemed to have vacated his post, leading to his removal from service and a subsequent legal challenge.
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court acquitted the petitioner (third accused) in case HC/TAB/493/19 on 15 July 2020, as there was no evidence to proceed against him for the deaths of 8 persons during the Wellkada prison riot.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The petitioner argued the AAT erred in: 1) wrongly accepting there was a valid vacation of post when the petitioner acted under duress to save his life; 2) failing to consider whether the PSC should have exercised discretion to accept his out-of-time appeal given the extraordinary circumstances; 3) uncritically accepting the PSC's reasons without independent analysis.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: AAT erred in accepting there was a valid Vacation of Post (VOP). | AAT failed to decide if PSC's rejection for being out of time was valid and reasonable. | AAT failed to independently scrutinize PSC's reasons and surrendered its discretion to PSC.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The judgment reviews administrative decisions and evidence of threats, not criminal trial evidence. No analysis of witness testimony is present.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court found the petitioner's explanation for leaving the country reasonable and negated any intention to abandon his post.
defence_version_summary: The petitioner pleaded not guilty in the criminal case and was acquitted. He claimed he left the country under duress due to death threats and a fear of unfair arrest, not to abandon his post.
legal_errors_description: The AAT erred by failing to exercise its independent discretion, wrongly accepting the PSC's position on VOP, and failing to properly consider the extraordinary circumstances.
procedural_defects_description: The AAT failed to independently decide the case and surrendered its discretion to the PSC.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed the legal concept of 'vacation of post' (requiring both physical absence and intent to abandon) and found the petitioner acted under extreme duress to save his life, negating intent. It criticized the AAT for failing to exercise independent discretion and for unreasonably accepting the PSC's stance. The Court considered the petitioner's acquittal, departmental recommendations for reinstatement, and the extraordinary circumstances justifying his appeal despite delay.
coa_sentence_type: Reinstatement to service with all outstanding salary payments, promotions, and salary increments from 29 January 2018.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The petitioner, a senior prison officer, challenged the decision of the Administrative Appeals Tribunal (AAT) upholding his removal from service for 'vacation of post'. He argued he fled due to death threats and an unjust arrest following his work against organized crime. The High Court had acquitted him of related murder charges. The Court of Appeal found the AAT erred in law by not independently assessing his case and by wrongly accepting the vacation of post. The Court allowed the appeal, quashed the AAT's decision and the notice of vacation of post, and ordered his reinstatement with full back pay and promotions.
defence_counsel: Hijaz Hizbullah with Piyumi Senevirathne instructed by D. Kuruppuarachchi
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court acquitted the petitioner due to lack of evidence. The Court of Appeal viewed this acquittal as supporting the petitioner's claim that the case against him was a setup.
