Appeal No. 90/2009, S.C Minutes dated 1202.2016] | Nelson De Silva v State Engineering Corporation Limited [1996 2 SLR 342] | Jathika Sevaka Sangamaya v Sri Lanka Transport Board SC Appeal 133/2016 SCM July 9th 2021 | Agricultural and Agrarian Insurance Board v Ilyas SC Appeal 164/2013 SCM March 28th 2016 | Jayawardena vs. People's Bank 2002 3SLR 17 | Credit Information Bureau of Sri Lanka vs M/S Jafferjee and Jafferjee (Pvt) Limited 2005 ISLR Pg 89 | R v Home Secretary ex parte Walsh [1992] COD 240
standard_of_review_applied: Review of administrative tribunal decision for errors of law, jurisdiction, and failure to exercise discretion.

judges: B. Sasi Mahendran, J. | Amal Ranaraja, J.
offence_sections: section 383 of the Penal Code read with section 32
brief_facts_summary: On March 23, 2004, two armed intruders entered the residence of PW01 (a businessman) and robbed cash and jewellery valued at Rs. 137,750.00 using firearms. The accused-appellant was later identified as one of the perpetrators. The appellant denied the charges, claiming false implication.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: section 383 of the Penal Code read with section 32
hc_sentence_type: Rigorous Imprisonment 5 years, Fine Rs.5000.00 with default sentence of 6 months rigorous imprisonment, Compensation Rs.137,750.00 to PW01 with default sentence of 1 year rigorous imprisonment
hc_judgment_summary: The Learned High Court Judge convicted the appellant of robbery and sentenced him to 5 years rigorous imprisonment, a fine, and compensation. The default sentences were ordered to run consecutively.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant challenged the conviction on the basis of unreliable identification, erroneous findings by the High Court, failure to properly consider the dock statement, and the prosecution's failure to prove the charge beyond reasonable doubt. The appeal focused on inconsistencies in witness testimony and the integrity of the identification parade.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The Learned High Court Judge has failed to consider that the identification of the appellant has not been established. | The erroneous findings of the Learned High Court Judge have adversely affected the appellant. | The Learned High Court Judge has arrived at his judgment without properly considering the dock statement of the appellant. | The prosecution has failed to prove the charge beyond a reasonable doubt.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found significant inconsistencies in the testimonies of PW01 and PW03 regarding their identification of the appellant. The identification parade was held 8 years after the incident, and the witnesses had prior encounters with the appellant, casting doubt on the reliability of the identification.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court found the prosecution failed to prove the charge beyond reasonable doubt due to unreliable identification evidence and inconsistencies in witness testimony.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty and asserted false implication. He did not call witnesses but made a dock statement. The Court found the defence credible in highlighting the prosecution's weaknesses.
legal_errors_description: The High Court misapplied the burden of proof by relying on weaknesses in the appellant's case instead of requiring the prosecution to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt. The High Court also failed to properly assess the reliability of the identification evidence.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed the identification evidence and found it unreliable due to inconsistencies in witness testimonies, the 8-year delay in holding the identification parade, and the witnesses' prior encounters with the appellant. The Court cited Queen vs V.P.Julis and Rex vs Turnbull to emphasize that identification parade evidence is not substantive and that honest witnesses can be mistaken. The Court held that the prosecution failed to meet the burden of proof, and the High Court erred by focusing on the appellant's inconsistencies rather than the prosecution's evidence. The conviction was set aside.
coa_sentence_type: Acquitted, no sentence imposed
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused-appellant was convicted in the High Court of Hambantota for robbery and sentenced to imprisonment, a fine, and compensation. He appealed to the Court of Appeal, challenging the conviction on grounds of unreliable identification and prosecution's failure to prove the charge. The Court of Appeal found the identification evidence flawed due to inconsistencies and delay, and held that the prosecution did not prove the case beyond reasonable doubt. The appeal was allowed, the conviction set aside, and the appellant acquitted.
prosecution_counsel: Hiranjan Pieris, S.D.S.G for the State
defence_counsel: Asthika Devendra with Aruna Madushanka for the Accused-Appellant
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted the appellant based on identification evidence. The Court of Appeal found the High Court erred by relying on the weaknesses of the appellant's case and failing to properly assess the reliability of the identification evidence, which did not meet the required standard of proof.
precedents_cited_list: Queen vs V.P.Julis [1953] 65 NLR 505 | Rex vs Turnball [1997] QB 224 | Munirathne and Others vs. The State, [2001] 2 SLR 382
standard_of_review_applied: Review of evidence and legal principles regarding identification and burden of proof

judges: Menaka Wijesundera J. | K.M.G.H Kulatunga J.
offence_sections: Section 294(3) of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The accused-appellant was indicted for the murder of his stepfather on or about 11.01.2011. The main witness, PW-01 (the appellant's sister), provided circumstantial evidence. She testified that on the night of the incident, she heard the accused tapping on her door, saw him with a blood-stained knife, and he stated 'uncle problem' and that he had to go to the police station to hand over the knife. The deceased was found injured and died five days later. The accused surrendered to the police with the knife. The case was based entirely on circumstantial evidence.
evidence_type_secondary: Medical evidence, Government Analyst Report, Witness testimony (neighbour)
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 294(3) of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The learned trial judge found the appellant guilty of murder based on the evidence and sentenced him to death. The judge concluded that the circumstances pointed irresistibly to the appellant's guilt.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant's counsel argued that the trial judgment was legally and factually flawed. Specifically, the prosecution failed to prove that the injuries inflicted were sufficient to substantiate a murder conviction under Section 294(3), as the medical evidence did not establish a high probability of death, only a likelihood. The counsel also challenged the trial judge's misdirection on law regarding recoveries and the application of the Ellenborough Dictum.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The judgement of the trial judge is legally and factually flawed. | The prosecution has failed to prove that the injuries inflicted on the deceased were sufficient to substantiate the final finding of the trial judge.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The prosecution's main witness was PW-01, the appellant's sister, who provided circumstantial evidence. Her testimony was corroborated by PW-02, a neighbour. The Court of Appeal found her evidence credible and sufficient to draw an irresistible inference that the appellant caused the injuries.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal assessed that the prosecution proved beyond reasonable doubt that the appellant caused the injuries. However, it found the medical evidence insufficient to prove a 'high probability of death' required for murder under Section 294(3), reducing the conviction to culpable homicide.
defence_version_summary: The appellant remained silent and did not give evidence when the defence was called. The prosecution witnesses were cross-examined, but not as to a possible defence. The defence did not challenge the prosecution evidence on the facts, only on legal interpretation and medical evidence.
legal_errors_description: The trial judge misdirected himself by considering the Ellenborough Dictum before evaluating circumstantial evidence and by incorrectly treating clothes recovered by police as recoveries under Section 27(1) of the Evidence Ordinance.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the circumstantial evidence, particularly from PW-01, proved beyond reasonable doubt that the appellant inflicted the injuries causing death. However, it held the prosecution failed to establish through medical evidence that the injuries carried a 'high probability of death' as required under Section 294(3) for murder. Citing precedents (Chandrasena vs AG, Bandara vs AG, Farook v AG, Rajwant Single vs State of Kerala), the Court distinguished between 'high probability' and 'mere likelihood'. Due to this deficiency, the conviction was varied to culpable homicide not amounting to murder under Section 297, considering the appellant attacked a sleeping man, his post-act behavior, and the nature of the weapon and injuries.
coa_sentence_type: 8 years rigorous imprisonment
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused-appellant appealed his murder conviction and death sentence from the High Court of Trincomalee for killing his stepfather. The Court of Appeal agreed the circumstantial evidence proved he caused the fatal injuries but found the medical evidence insufficient to establish the 'high probability of death' required for murder under Section 294(3). Citing legal precedents, the Court varied the conviction to culpable homicide not amounting to murder under Section 297, set aside the death sentence, and imposed an 8-year prison term.
defence_counsel: Indika Mallawarachci
cause_of_death_exact_text: The doctor identified 5 cut injuries as the cause of death, stating they were 'sufficient to cause death in the ordinary course of nature'.
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court found the appellant guilty of murder based on circumstantial evidence and sentenced him to death. The Court of Appeal found the HC erred in its legal application regarding the standard of 'sufficiency to cause death' under Section 294(3) and in misdirecting itself on the law concerning recoveries and the Ellenborough Dictum.
precedents_cited_list: Chandrasena vs AG[2008] 2 Sri L. R. 255 at 256 | Bandara vs AG [2006] 2 Sri L. R | Farook v AG [2006] 3 Sri L. R. 174 at 181 | Rajwant Single vs State of Kerala AIR 1966
standard_of_review_applied: The court reviewed whether the prosecution proved all ingredients of the offence beyond reasonable doubt, particularly focusing on the legal standard for 'sufficiency in the ordinary course of nature to cause death' under Section 294(3).
sentencing_principles_applied: The Court considered the nature of the act (attacking a sleeping man), the appellant's post-offence conduct (surrendering with the weapon), the type of weapon used, and the nature of injuries to determine the appropriate sentence for culpable homicide.
final_charge_after_appeal: Culpable homicide not amounting to murder under Section 297 of the Penal Code

judges: B. Sasi Mahendran, J. | Amal Ranaraja, J.
offence_sections: Sections 54A(b) and 54A(d) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance, as amended by Act No. 13 of 1984
brief_facts_summary: Acting on intelligence, police officers intercepted the accused on a motorcycle. A search conducted while the accused was seated on the motorcycle allegedly led to the recovery of 25.77 grams of heroin from his trouser pocket. The accused was arrested and the substance was sent to the Government Analyst.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Sections 54A(b) and 54A(d) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance, as amended by Act No. 13 of 1984
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court found the accused guilty of possession and trafficking of 25.77 grams of heroin. He was convicted on both counts and sentenced to life imprisonment.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The main ground of appeal was that the prosecution's version of events, specifically the search leading to the recovery of heroin, was highly improbable. It was argued that the High Court Judge failed to properly apply the test of probability and improbability to the evidence.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The prosecution's version is highly improbable. | The Learned High Court Judge failed to apply the test of probability and improbability in evaluating the evidence.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal scrutinized the testimony of PW1, the lead police officer, and found his account of searching the accused while seated on the motorcycle and recovering heroin to be highly improbable, casting significant doubt on the prosecution's case.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court applied the test of probability and improbability, finding the prosecution's narrative of the search and recovery lacked credibility and was highly improbable.
defence_version_summary: The accused made a dock statement in his defence. The judgment does not detail its content. The court did not find the defence version needing assessment as the prosecution case was rejected.
legal_errors_description: The High Court Judge failed to adequately apply the test of probability and improbability to the prosecution's evidence.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal carefully analyzed PW1's testimony regarding the search. It found the described method of searching the accused while he remained seated on the motorcycle to be highly improbable and unnecessary, casting doubt on the entire recovery story. Applying legal principles on probability from precedent and academic texts, the Court concluded the prosecution failed to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt. The conviction was therefore unsafe.
coa_sentence_type: Acquitted. No sentence imposed.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused-appellant was convicted by the High Court of Colombo for possession and trafficking of 25.77 grams of heroin and sentenced to life imprisonment. On appeal, he challenged the conviction, arguing the prosecution's story was improbable. The Court of Appeal found the police testimony describing the search and recovery of drugs to be highly improbable and lacking credibility. The appeal was allowed, the conviction and sentence were set aside, and the accused was acquitted.
defence_counsel: Kalinga Indatissa, PC with Rashmini Indatissa and Razan Salih
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court accepted the prosecution evidence and convicted the accused. The Court of Appeal found the High Court Judge erred by failing to properly apply the test of probability and improbability to the evidence, leading to an unsafe conviction.
precedents_cited_list: Wickremasuriya v Dedoleena and Others [1996] 2 S.L.R. 95 | Selvanayagam Carmel Jenova Vs. The Attorney General, CA Case No. 107/2011
standard_of_review_applied: Review of evidence based on test of probability and improbability, assessing whether the High Court properly applied this test.

judges: B. Sasi Mahendran, J. | Amal Ranaraja, J.
offence_sections: Section 365B(2)(b) of the Penal Code (as amended by Act No.22 of 1995 and Act No. 29 of 1998 and Act No.16 of 2006)
brief_facts_summary: On May 8, 2009, the accused appellant took the 12-year-old female child (PW01) to his house, under the pretext of needing company. He undressed her and himself, and placed his penis between her thighs/vagina, committing grave sexual abuse. PW03 witnessed the act by peeping through a wooden window and informed his parents, who caught the appellant in the act and took PW01 to the police. PW01 was medically examined, and a medico-legal report was prepared.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 365B(2)(b) of the Penal Code (as amended by Act No.22 of 1995 and Act No. 29 of 1998 and Act No.16 of 2006)
hc_sentence_type: Rigorous Imprisonment 8 years, Fine Rs. 5000 with 4 months imprisonment in default, Compensation Rs. 100,000 with 1-year imprisonment in default
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the appellant of grave sexual abuse under section 365B(2)(b) of the Penal Code. The judge found the prosecution proved the case beyond reasonable doubt and sentenced the appellant to 8 years rigorous imprisonment, a fine, and compensation.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant argued that the main ingredient of the charge was not proven beyond reasonable doubt, as PW01's testimony varied. He also claimed the High Court Judge erred in law by not allowing marking of a vital contradiction during cross-examination of PW01, and failed to accurately evaluate the evidence of PW12, PW02, PW03, and PW08.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Has the Learned High Court Judge failed to consider that the main ingredient of the charge has not been proven beyond a reasonable doubt by the prosecution? | Has the Learned High Court Judge erred in law by not allowing to mark a vital contradiction during the cross examination of PW01? | Has the Learned High Court Judge failed to evaluate the evidence of PW12 accurately? | Has the Learned High Court Judge failed to evaluate the evidence of PW02, PW03, and PW08 accurately?
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found PW01's testimony credible despite her reluctance as a victim of child sexual abuse. PW03's eyewitness account was corroborated by his parents (PW02). The medical report was properly admitted through PW12. Minor contradictions were deemed immaterial.
probability_assessment_by_court: Court held prosecution proved case beyond reasonable doubt; minor inconsistencies do not create reasonable doubt; victim's reluctance is natural.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty. He did not lead evidence or call witnesses. The defence challenged the prosecution evidence on contradictions and proof of the specific sexual act. The court found the defence arguments lacked merit.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The COA analyzed each ground of appeal. It held that the victim's (PW01) testimony, though requiring coaxing due to trauma, was credible and proved the sexual act. It found no error in the trial judge's handling of contradictions, as defence counsel failed to properly confront PW01 with prior statements per Section 145 of the Evidence Ordinance. The medical evidence was properly admitted through PW12. Minor lapses in investigation (PW08 not testing visibility at night) and contradictions in PW03's account were immaterial. The COA noted the appellant's actions showed pre-planning. It applied the precedent D. Tikiribanda vs. Attorney General regarding victim reluctance. The COA found no reason to interfere with the HC judgment.
coa_sentence_type: Rigorous Imprisonment 8 years, Fine Rs. 5000 with 4 months imprisonment in default, Compensation Rs. 100,000 with 1-year imprisonment in default
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused-appellant was convicted by the High Court of Rathnapura for grave sexual abuse of a 12-year-old girl and sentenced to 8 years RI, a fine, and compensation. He appealed on grounds including failure to prove the charge beyond reasonable doubt, errors in handling contradictions, and inaccurate evaluation of witness evidence. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal, upholding the conviction and sentence. It found the victim's testimony credible, minor contradictions immaterial, medical evidence properly admitted, and the defence's procedural challenges unfounded.
defence_counsel: Kasun Sarathchandra
hc_analysis_summary: The COA found the High Court judge correctly evaluated the evidence, properly applied the law on proof and contradictions, and imposed an appropriate sentence. No material errors were identified in the HC's reasoning or process.
precedents_cited_list: D. Tikiribanda vs. Attorney General, CA 64/2003 decided on 06.10.2009 | Agampodi Wijepala de Soyza vs. Officer-in-Charge and Another [SC Appeal 159/2018, S.C. minute dated 07.07.2021]
standard_of_review_applied: The COA reviewed whether the HC judgment was based on evidence and correct in law, examining specific grounds raised regarding proof, contradictions, and evaluation of witness evidence.
sentencing_principles_applied: The COA noted the presence of aggravating circumstances (preplanning and manipulation) and upheld the sentence imposed by the HC.

judges: B. Sasi Mahendran, J. | Amal Ranaraja, J
offence_sections: Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance No. 13 of 1984, as amended
brief_facts_summary: Accused Shivanandam Muralidaran was indicted for possession and trafficking of 24.816 kg of Cannabis Sativa. He pleaded guilty on 7 February 2023 and was convicted and sentenced. The petitioner, registered owner of the vehicle involved, had signed a bond for the vehicle and later agreed before the High Court to pay four million rupees as she could not produce the vehicle.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance No. 13 of 1984, as amended
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the accused after a guilty plea. The petitioner (registered owner) was notified as she had signed a bond for the vehicle. She testified that she sold the vehicle to her late brother, who leased it. The court noted her agreement to pay four million rupees as she could not produce the vehicle.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The petitioner filed an application seeking to set aside the High Court order dated 16.06.2023, which ordered payment of four million rupees based on her undertaking. She is contesting the order based on her own prior assurance.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Petitioner seeks to set aside High Court order dated 16.06.2023
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: No detailed evidence analysis in the judgment. The petitioner testified before the High Court about the vehicle's history and her agreement to pay.
defence_version_summary: Accused pleaded guilty. Petitioner (registered owner) claimed she sold vehicle to late brother who leased it, and agreed to pay four million rupees as she could not produce vehicle.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal held that revision is discretionary and will not be exercised unless miscarriage of justice is shown. The petitioner had given an undertaking to the High Court to pay four million rupees and was now challenging the order based on her own assurance. The court viewed this as withdrawal from the undertaking and breach of contract. The conduct of the petitioner is relevant; citing Peera v. The People’s Bank, the court held the petitioner is not entitled to revisionary jurisdiction.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The petitioner, registered owner of a vehicle involved in a drug trafficking case, sought revision of a High Court order requiring her to pay four million rupees based on her bond undertaking. The accused had pleaded guilty. The Court of Appeal dismissed the application, holding revision is discretionary and the petitioner's conduct—withdrawing from her own court undertaking—disentitled her to relief. The court ordered state costs of Rs. 50,000.
defence_counsel: Tenny Fernando
hc_analysis_summary: High Court accepted petitioner's undertaking to pay four million rupees after she testified she could not produce the vehicle. Court of Appeal found no error; the order was based on petitioner's own assurance.
precedents_cited_list: Peera v. The People’s Bank, 1995 (2) SLR 84
standard_of_review_applied: Discretionary revision jurisdiction; will not be exercised unless miscarriage of justice shown

judges: B. Sasi Mahendran, J. | Amal Ranaraja, J.
offence_sections: section 54A(d) and 54A(b) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance (as amended by Act No.13 of 1984)
brief_facts_summary: The appellant was indicted for possessing and trafficking 1.56 grams of heroin. He was convicted and sentenced in the High Court. The appellant appealed only against the sentencing order, not the conviction. The Court of Appeal considered the mandatory sentencing framework and personal circumstances before dismissing the appeal.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: section 54A(d) and 54A(b) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance (as amended by Act No.13 of 1984)
hc_sentence_type: Charge 01: 7 years rigorous imprisonment and fine of Rs.100,000.00 with 1 year simple imprisonment in default. Charge 02: 7 years rigorous imprisonment and fine of Rs.100,000.00 with 1 year simple imprisonment in default.
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the appellant on both charges. The judge considered the mandatory penalty provisions and mitigating factors including the appellant's age (65) and his role as sole breadwinner before imposing sentence.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant appealed only against the sentencing order, contending that the sentences imposed were disproportionate. He did not contest the conviction.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Are the sentences imposed on the appellant disproportionate?
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The judgment does not detail witness evidence as the appeal was limited to sentencing.
defence_version_summary: The appellant did not contest the conviction at appeal. A request for a non-custodial sentence was made in the High Court but not sufficiently elaborated.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal acknowledged the mandatory sentencing framework requiring a fine between Rs.100,000 and Rs.500,000 and imprisonment between 7 and 20 years. It noted the High Court judge considered this framework and mitigating factors (appellant's age, family breadwinner status). The COA balanced the legal obligations with personal circumstances and found no reason to interfere with the sentencing order.
coa_sentence_type: The 7-year rigorous imprisonment sentences on each charge are to run concurrently from the date of conviction (06.09.2023). Fines and default sentences remain.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The appellant was convicted in the High Court of Colombo for possessing and trafficking 1.56 grams of heroin and sentenced to 7 years rigorous imprisonment and a fine of Rs.100,000 per charge. He appealed only against the sentence, arguing it was disproportionate. The Court of Appeal examined the mandatory sentencing law and the mitigating factors considered by the High Court. It concluded the sentence was appropriate and dismissed the appeal, ordering the prison terms to run concurrently.
defence_counsel: Ershan Ariaratnam
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court applied the mandatory sentencing provisions and considered mitigating factors. The Court of Appeal found the High Court's reasoning and sentencing order to be comprehensive and correct.
standard_of_review_applied: The COA reviewed whether the sentence was disproportionate, considering the mandatory sentencing law and the personal circumstances of the appellant.
sentencing_principles_applied: The court applied the mandatory minimum sentencing provisions under the relevant law, while also considering mitigating factors such as the appellant's age and family responsibilities.

judges: B. Sasi Mahendran, J. | Amal Ranaraja, J
offence_sections: Section 54(a) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance, as amended by Act No. 13 of 1984
brief_facts_summary: On 11 December 2008, police received intelligence about an individual obtaining heroin. A raid was conducted at Thorana Junction, Peliyagoda, where the accused was pointed out by an informant. Officers followed and arrested the accused. A search of his right trouser pocket revealed a grocery bag containing a light brown powdery substance suspected to be heroin, weighing 31g 400mg including wrapping. The accused was taken to Peliyagoda Police Station.
evidence_type_primary: Physical evidence (recovery of heroin), Police testimony
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 54(a) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance, as amended by Act No. 13 of 1984
hc_judgment_summary: The Learned High Court Judge found the accused guilty of possessing 4.69 grams of heroin based on prosecution evidence. The judge accepted the testimonies of the police witnesses regarding the raid, arrest, and recovery of the substance. The accused was sentenced to life imprisonment.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant argued the Trial Judge failed to appreciate a discrepancy in the production registry, failed to consider the appellant's version, and failed to appreciate that the prosecution's version failed the test of probability. The defense also challenged the timing and location of the arrest, and suggested a different individual was arrested.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The learned Trial Judge failed to appreciate that there is a discrepancy about the production registry belonging to the productions of this case. | The learned Trial Judge failed to consider the version of the appellant. | The learned Trial Judge failed to appreciate that the version of the prosecution fails the test of probability.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the testimonies of PW1 and PW6 to be credible, trustworthy, and consistent. Their evidence covered the receipt of information, execution of the raid, arrest, recovery, sealing, and chain of custody. No material contradictions were found between them.
probability_assessment_by_court: The COA assessed the prosecution's version as credible and probable, and found the accused's dock statement version (arrest around 10:30) to be inconsistent with the documented evidence (officers left after 13:00), thus not raising a reasonable doubt.
defence_version_summary: The accused pleaded not guilty and made a dock statement. He claimed he was arrested around 10:30 hours while on his way to visit his grandmother on a motorbike, and suggested a person named Jayathissa was actually arrested. The court found his version inconsistent with the evidence and not credible.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The COA applied the appellate standard of review from King v. Gunaratne, respecting the trial judge's advantage in seeing witnesses. It thoroughly analyzed the evidence of PW1 and PW6, finding them credible and consistent, with no material contradictions. The COA found the trial judge correctly evaluated the evidence and the chain of custody issue was explained. The accused's dock statement did not create reasonable doubt. No legal misdirection or wrong inferences were found.
coa_sentence_type: Life Imprisonment
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused-appellant was convicted by the High Court of Colombo for possessing 4.69 grams of heroin and sentenced to life imprisonment. He appealed, challenging discrepancies in the production registry, the court's consideration of his version, and the probability of the prosecution case. The Court of Appeal found the police witnesses' testimonies credible and consistent, upheld the trial judge's findings, and dismissed the appeal, affirming the conviction and sentence.
defence_counsel: Hafeel Farisz with Sanjeewa Kodithuwakku
hc_analysis_summary: The COA found no errors in the High Court's reasoning. The trial judge correctly accepted the credible prosecution evidence regarding the raid, arrest, and recovery. The COA agreed with the HC's assessment of witness reliability and the rejection of the accused's version.
precedents_cited_list: King v. Gunaratne and Another, CLR V.14 page 144
standard_of_review_applied: The three tests from King v. Gunaratne: whether verdict was unreasonable against weight of evidence, whether there was misdirection on law or evidence, and whether wrong inferences were drawn from evidence.

judges: P. Kumararatnam, J. | R. P. Hettiarachchi, J.
offence_sections: Sections 54(A)(d) and 54(A)(b) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance as amended by Act No. 13 of 1984
brief_facts_summary: On 13/03/2018, police received information about drug trafficking by the Appellant. Police conducted a raid at Samagama, saw the Appellant acting suspiciously, caught him when he tried to flee, and searched him. A small parcel was found in his right trouser pocket, and six Rs.5000 notes were found in his left pocket. The parcel was tested for heroin, and he was arrested. The substance was weighed at a jewellery shop at 8.400 grams. The parcel was registered and eventually sent to the Government Analyst. The Government Analyst Report noted the parcel weight as 6.956 grams, a discrepancy of 1.494 grams.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Sections 54(A)(d) and 54(A)(b) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance as amended by Act No. 13 of 1984
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court found the Appellant guilty of both counts of Possession and Trafficking of 6.143 grams of Heroin. The Judge sentenced the Appellant to death on both counts on 06/04/2023.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The Appellant appealed on grounds including the Learned High Court Judge failing to consider a variation in the quantity of the production which affects the prosecution case, the prosecution version being improbable, compelling the Appellant to adduce more evidence, and rejecting defence evidence on wrong premises. The core argument centered on a weight discrepancy in the heroin parcel.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The Learned High Court Judge erred in law by failing to consider the variation in quantity of the production which affects the root of the prosecution case. | The version of the prosecution is improbable. | The Learned High Court Judge erred in law by compelling the Appellant to adduce more evidence. | The Learned High Court Judge erred in law by rejecting the defence evidence on wrong premises.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The prosecution led 05 witnesses. The Government Analyst Report was admitted under Section 420 of the CPC. The defence called the Appellant's father. The Court of Appeal focused on the weight discrepancy between the initial police weighing (8.400g) and the Government Analyst's weight (6.956g), finding it crucial.
probability_assessment_by_court: Court of Appeal found the weight discrepancy created a reasonable doubt regarding the integrity of the production chain.
defence_version_summary: The Appellant pleaded not guilty and made a dock statement. He claimed he never possessed any drugs and that drugs were introduced to him by the police witnesses after he visited the station regarding his father's arrest. He called his father as a witness in support.
legal_errors_description: The High Court Judge failed to consider the crucial weight discrepancy affecting the chain of custody and inward journey of the evidence.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The COA emphasized the prosecution's duty to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt and the specific requirement in drug cases to establish the undisturbed inward journey of the production from accused to Government Analyst. It found the unexplained weight discrepancy (8.400g vs 6.956g) of the heroin parcel was a substantial fact that the prosecution failed to clarify. The failure of the High Court to address this discrepancy in its judgment denied the Appellant a fair trial. The COA set aside the conviction and acquitted the Appellant on this basis, without needing to address other appeal grounds.
coa_sentence_type: Acquitted
brief_judgment_file_summary: The Accused-Appellant was convicted by the Kegalle High Court for Possession and Trafficking of heroin and sentenced to death. He appealed. The Court of Appeal focused on a weight discrepancy in the heroin parcel between police weighing (8.400g) and the Government Analyst's report (6.956g). The COA held this discrepancy, which the prosecution failed to explain and the High Court failed to address, broke the chain of custody and created reasonable doubt. The conviction and sentence were set aside, and the Appellant was acquitted.
defence_counsel: Amila Palliyage with Sandeepani Wijesooriya, Savani Udugampola, Lakitha Wakishta Arachchi and Subaj De Silva
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted the Appellant based on the prosecution evidence, including the Government Analyst Report. The COA found the HC judgment erred by failing to analyze the significant weight discrepancy in the evidence, which affected the integrity of the production chain and prejudiced the Appellant.
precedents_cited_list: Woolmington v. DPP [1935] A.C.462 | Karunadasa Vs. Officer-in-Charge, Motor Traffic Division, Police Station Nittambuwa (1987) 1 SLR 155 | Witharana Doli Nona v. The Republic of Sri Lanka CA/19/99 | Mahasarukkalige Chandani v. Attorney General CA/213/2009 | Mohamed Nimnaz V. Attorney General CA/95/94
standard_of_review_applied: Review of legal errors and evaluation of whether prosecution proved case beyond reasonable doubt, particularly regarding chain of custody in drug cases.

judges: P. Kumararatnam, J. | R. P. Hettiarachchi, J.
offence_sections: Section 140 of the Penal Code, Section 296 read with Section 146 of the Penal Code, Section 296 read with Section 32 of the Penal Code, Section 300 read with Section 146 of the Penal Code, Section 300 read with Section 32 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: On 29.01.1998, the appellant was a member of an unlawful assembly that attacked a house in Kahaduwa. The deceased father and five siblings were killed, and another sibling (PW2) was seriously injured. The appellant allegedly prevented the inmates from escaping while other deceased accused carried out the attack. The incident was witnessed by a 14-year-old survivor (PW2) under the light of a bottle lamp. The house was subsequently set on fire.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 140 of the Penal Code, Section 296 read with Section 146 of the Penal Code, Section 300 read with Section 146 of the Penal Code
hc_sentence_type: Death sentence for counts 2-7, 6 months rigorous imprisonment for count 1, 15 years rigorous imprisonment with fine for count 8
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the appellant and the second accused (tried in absentia) on counts 1-8. The judge found the evidence of the eyewitness (PW2) credible and concluded the prosecution proved the case beyond reasonable doubt. The judge sentenced the appellant to death for the murders and imposed imprisonment and fines for other counts, as well as compensation.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant argued that the prosecution failed to prove the case beyond reasonable doubt and failed to prove his involvement beyond reasonable doubt. The defence specifically challenged the credibility of the sole eyewitness (PW2), highlighting contradictions and omissions in her evidence, and argued her evidence was uncorroborated.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Has the prosecution proved their case beyond a reasonable doubt? | Has the prosecution proved the involvement of the Appellant beyond a reasonable doubt?
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed the evidence of PW2, the 14-year-old eyewitness. It acknowledged potential inconsistencies (omission of a weapon in her police statement, contradiction between knife and club in different proceedings) but found these did not relate to the core of the prosecution case and were insufficient to discredit her evidence given the circumstances.
probability_assessment_by_court: The court assessed the reliability of the sole eyewitness (PW2). It considered her age, trauma, injuries, and the lighting conditions, concluding her evidence was cogent, impressive, and sufficient to establish guilt beyond reasonable doubt despite minor contradictions.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty. He made a dock statement denying the charges. He called one witness in his defence. The court found the defence evidence failed to create a doubt over the prosecution case.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal conducted a thorough review. It analyzed the credibility of the sole eyewitness (PW2), a 14-year-old survivor. It addressed the defence arguments regarding omissions and contradictions in her evidence, applying legal principles from Sri Lankan and Indian precedents that a conviction can be based on the testimony of a single reliable witness. The court found the contradictions were minor, did not affect the core of the prosecution case, and were understandable given PW2's age and ordeal. It upheld the High Court judge's analysis of unlawful assembly and the identification of the appellant. The COA concluded the High Court correctly analyzed the evidence and reached a sustainable finding of guilt.
coa_sentence_type: Death sentence for counts 2-7, 6 months rigorous imprisonment for count 1, 15 years rigorous imprisonment with Rs.20,000 fine (with default sentence) for count 8, and Rs.500,000 compensation affirmed.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The appellant was convicted by the Balapitiya High Court for his role as a member of an unlawful assembly that resulted in the murder of six family members and the attempted murder of another in 1998. He was sentenced to death on multiple counts, along with imprisonment and fines. He appealed, challenging the conviction primarily on the grounds that the prosecution case, which relied heavily on the testimony of a single 14-year-old eyewitness (PW2), was not proved beyond reasonable doubt. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal, finding the eyewitness testimony credible and reliable despite minor contradictions, and upheld the High Court's conviction and sentence.
prosecution_counsel: Sanjeewa Dissanayake, D. S. G. with Jehan Gunasekara, SC
defence_counsel: Anil Silva, P. C. with Isuru Jayawardena, Sarith Wadugedera and Arinda Silva
cause_of_death_exact_text: gunshot wounds and multiple cut injuries
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court judge considered the evidence of the eyewitness (PW2) and other lay witnesses. He analyzed the legal principles of unlawful assembly, found the evidence convincing, and concluded the prosecution had proved its case beyond reasonable doubt. The Court of Appeal found no error in this analysis and agreed with the High Court's findings and reasoning.
precedents_cited_list: Sumanasena v. The Attorney General [1999] 3 Sri.L.R 137 | Madduma Siripala and another v. The Attorney General CA/125-126/10 decided on 27/10/2017 | Chacko Alias Aniyan Kunju & others v. State of Kerala [2004] INSC 87 (21st January 2004) | Bandara v. The State [2001] 1 SLR 63
standard_of_review_applied: Review of the High Court's factual findings and application of law, with particular scrutiny of the eyewitness evidence and its credibility.

judges: P Kumararathnam, J. | Pradeep Hettiarachchi, J.
offence_sections: Section 296 read with section 32 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The Accused-Appellant and a 2nd Accused (deceased) were indicted for the murder of Bodhandi Anil De Silva on 23-01-2004. The shooting occurred near a culvert at around 10:10 am while the deceased was in a van with his wife (PW1) and daughter (PW2). The prosecution alleged the Appellant and 2nd Accused shot the deceased from both sides of the vehicle. The High Court convicted the Appellant of murder and sentenced him to death.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 296 read with section 32 of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court Judge found the Appellant guilty of murder after a trial without a jury. The judge concluded the prosecution had proved its case beyond reasonable doubt and sentenced the Appellant to death on 19-01-2023.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The Appellant argued the trial judge failed to properly evaluate prosecution witness credibility using tests of consistency, probability and spontaneity. He also contended the judge failed to draw an adverse inference against the prosecution for not calling eyewitness PW3, and failed to properly evaluate the defence witness evidence.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Failure to evaluate prosecution witness credibility using accepted tests of consistency, probability and spontaneity | Failure to evaluate role of eyewitness PW3 and draw adverse inference for prosecution not calling him | Failure to properly evaluate and reject evidence of defence witness DW1
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found serious contradictions between PW1 and PW2 regarding shutter positions and sequence of events. It noted PW2's statement was belated and her evidence as a child witness required greater scrutiny. The court also criticized the failure to call PW3.
probability_assessment_by_court: Court found improbabilities in prosecution version, including PW3 remaining seated during shooting and not being hit, casting reasonable doubt.
defence_version_summary: The Appellant made a dock statement denying involvement and called one defence witness (DW1). The defence argued DW1's evidence was spontaneous and credible, but the High Court discredited it based on her distant relationship to the Appellant.
legal_errors_description: Failure to properly evaluate witness credibility using tests of consistency, probability and spontaneity; failure to draw adverse inference for not calling PW3; failure to properly evaluate defence witness evidence.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal conducted a thorough analysis of witness contradictions, finding material discrepancies between PW1 and PW2 regarding shutter positions and sequence of events. It applied tests from authorities like Bandaranayake vs. Jagathsena and Panchi v State of Uttar Pradesh regarding child witness evaluation. The court found the prosecution failed to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt due to credibility issues, belated statement of PW2, and failure to call crucial witness PW3. It also found the High Court erred in discrediting DW1 based on a distant relationship.
coa_sentence_type: Acquitted - convictions and sentences quashed
brief_judgment_file_summary: The Accused-Appellant was convicted of murder by the Balapitiya High Court and sentenced to death. He appealed on grounds including improper evaluation of prosecution witness credibility, failure to draw adverse inference for not calling eyewitness PW3, and improper evaluation of defence witness evidence. The Court of Appeal found material contradictions between key prosecution witnesses, issues with a child witness's belated statement, and failure to call a crucial witness. The court allowed the appeal, quashed the conviction and sentence, and acquitted the Appellant.
prosecution_counsel: Anoopa De Silva for the Respondent
defence_counsel: Sarath Jayamanne PC with Asith Sirivardene, Vineshka Mendis, Prashan Wickremaratne, Sanjeewa Meegahawaththa and M.A. Noorie for the Accused-Appellant
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court Judge noted contradictions between PW1 and PW2 but considered them minor and not going to the root of the case. He accepted PW2's evidence despite her being a child witness and traumatic experience. The COA found this analysis erroneous as the contradictions were material and cast doubt on prosecution's version.

judges: B. Sasi Mahendran, J. | Amal Ranaraja, J.
offence_sections: Section 354 of the Penal Code; Section 365 B (2)(b) of the Penal Code (as amended by Act No.22 of 1995 and Act No.29 of 1988 and Act No.16 of 2006)
location_of_offence: Within jurisdiction of High Court of Matara (location where pipeline connected to stream)
brief_facts_summary: The appellant, a neighbour, took the 15-year-old victim (PW01) under the pretence of clearing a water pipe blockage. At the location, the appellant allegedly armed himself with a knife, dragged the victim away, and subjected him to multiple acts of grave sexual abuse. The prosecution case relied on the victim's testimony, while the appellant denied the allegations, claiming false implication due to animosity over water usage.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 365 B (2)(b) of the Penal Code (as amended by Act No.22 of 1995 and Act No.29 of 1988 and Act No.16 of 2006)
hc_sentence_type: Rigorous Imprisonment 10 years each for charges 02 and 03; Fine Rs. 25,000 each charge with default imprisonment; Compensation Rs. 150,000 each charge with default imprisonment
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the appellant on charges 02 and 03 (grave sexual abuse) and acquitted on charges 01 and 04. The judge imposed 10 years rigorous imprisonment per convicted charge, fines, and compensation to the victim.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: Appellant's counsel argued the prosecution failed to prove consistency and reliability of witness testimony, the High Court judge did not properly consider delay in complaint, considered material not in evidence, failed to prove contradictions, failed to call material witnesses, failed to prove offence ingredients, and improperly shifted the burden of proof to the accused.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The prosecution has failed to satisfy the Court as to the test of consistency, spontaneity, probability, inter se and per se contradictions in the evidence of the prosecution witnesses. | The Learned High Court Judge has not considered the delay in making the complaint from the correct perspective. | The Learned High Court Judge has considered in his judgment material which had not been elicited in the evidence. | Contradictions and omissions marked by the prosecution when the accused was giving evidence had not been proved. | The prosecution has failed to call a material witness. | The prosecution has failed to prove the ingredients of the offence | The Learned High Court Judge has shifted the burden of proving his innocence to the accused.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the victim's (PW01) testimony credible despite minor inconsistencies, attributing them to trauma, fear, and confusing cross-examination. The court accepted that the psychological impact of the assault could overshadow details like physical assault when recounting events to a doctor or mother.
probability_assessment_by_court: Court found victim's account probable, rejecting arguments that his continued schooling or appellant's later visit undermined credibility, emphasizing power imbalance, fear from weapon, and trauma responses.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty, denied all sexual abuse allegations, and claimed false implication due to animosity between households over water usage. He gave evidence from the dock, but his narrative was found improbable by the High Court and Court of Appeal against the totality of evidence.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal conducted a holistic assessment, finding no merit in the appeal grounds. It held the High Court judge properly evaluated evidence, did not shift the burden of proof, and gave sufficient reasons for convicting. The COA found minor witness inconsistencies non-material, explained the delay in complaint by the victim's age and trauma, and held the High Court's assessment of contradictions and witness credibility was sound. The appeal was dismissed.
coa_sentence_type: Rigorous Imprisonment 10 years each for charges 02 and 03; Fine Rs. 25,000 each charge with default imprisonment; Compensation Rs. 150,000 each charge with default imprisonment (Upheld High Court sentence)
brief_judgment_file_summary: The appellant was convicted in the High Court of Matara on two counts of grave sexual abuse against a minor neighbour and sentenced to 10 years rigorous imprisonment per count, fines, and compensation. He appealed on grounds including witness inconsistencies, delay in complaint, failure to prove contradictions, and improper burden of proof. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal, finding the High Court judgment thorough, the victim's testimony credible despite minor inconsistencies explained by trauma, and no legal error in the trial process. The conviction and sentence were upheld.
defence_counsel: Asanka Mendis with Sandeepani Wijesooriya
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court Judge meticulously assessed narratives, engaged with evidence, and applied legal principles carefully. The COA found the judgment comprehensive and fair, with no improper shifting of burden of proof or reliance on unproven contradictions.
standard_of_review_applied: Holistic assessment of evidence and trial judge's findings

judges: B. Sasi Mahendran, J. | Amal Ranaraja, J
offence_sections: Section 365B(2) of the Penal Code, as amended by Act No. 22 of 1995
brief_facts_summary: The victim (PW1), a 14-year-old girl, visited Kalawana Hospital on 4th August 2005. After leaving, she felt followed by two individuals and sought refuge in a gold jewellery shop owned by the accused, a friend of her brother. The accused took her to an inner room where he allegedly pushed her against a wall, unzipped his trousers, and subjected her to inappropriate physical contact for about 30 minutes. She later disclosed the incident to her sister-in-law, and a police complaint was lodged on 7th August 2005. Medical examinations followed.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 365B(2) of the Penal Code, as amended by Act No. 22 of 1995
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court found the accused guilty of grave sexual abuse based on the testimony of the victim (PW1) and other prosecution evidence. The court sentenced him to twelve years' rigorous imprisonment, a fine of Rs. 20,000, and ordered compensation of Rs. 200,000 to the victim.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant challenged the conviction on grounds including credibility of the child witness (PW1), discrepancies about the incident location, lack of evidence of force or detention, and that the incident could not have happened inside the gold shop. He also argued that his dock statement was not properly considered and that undue delay in filing the indictment was not accounted for in sentencing.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Credibility of the witness Kaniamma (PW01) | Gross discrepancy as to where the incident took place | The purported incident could not have taken place inside the Gold shop | Delay in making the Complaint. | No, force, threat or intimidation or fear of death or hurt was used and she was not in lawful detention. | No evidence whatsoever to suggest that PW01 was subject to the said purported gross indecency. | Dock statement of the Accused-Appellant was not considered in light of the attended circumstances. | Undue delay in filing the indictment not considered in sentencing.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court found the testimony of the child victim (PW1) credible and consistent. Minor discrepancies regarding the exact location (room in the jewellery shop vs. adjoining shop) were considered immaterial. The court referenced judicial principles on evaluating child witness testimony and delay in complaint.
probability_assessment_by_court: Court found PW1's evidence credible and consistent, with minor discrepancies not creating reasonable doubt. The accused's dock statement lacked evidential weight to raise a doubt.
defence_version_summary: The accused made a dock statement only (called no witnesses). The High Court and Court of Appeal rejected his statement as lacking sufficient evidential weight to raise a reasonable doubt against the incriminating evidence.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed the evidence, particularly the child victim's testimony. It acknowledged minor discrepancies in describing the location but held they did not go to the root of the case. The court affirmed the conviction, finding PW1 credible and consistent. On sentencing, it considered the inordinate delay of over 13 years in filing the indictment (for which the accused bore no responsibility) as a significant mitigating factor warranting interference with the sentence under Section 333 of the Code of Criminal Procedure Act.
coa_sentence_type: Two years’ rigorous imprisonment, suspended for ten years from 01.04.2021. Fine, compensation, and default term affirmed.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused-appellant was convicted by the High Court of Ratnapura for grave sexual abuse of a 14-year-old girl and sentenced to 12 years' rigorous imprisonment, a fine, and compensation. He appealed on grounds including witness credibility, location discrepancies, and sentencing delay. The Court of Appeal affirmed the conviction, finding the victim's testimony credible despite minor inconsistencies. However, it reduced the sentence to 2 years' rigorous imprisonment (suspended for 10 years) due to the undue delay of over 13 years in filing the indictment, which was a mitigating factor under Section 333 of the Code of Criminal Procedure Act. The fine and compensation orders were upheld.
defence_counsel: Faisz Musthapha, PC with Keerthi Tillekeratne and Bishran Zibul
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted the accused based on the victim's testimony and other evidence. The Court of Appeal found the High Court judge correctly evaluated the evidence and rejected the accused's dock statement. No material errors in the HC's reasoning were identified.
