Sita Ram, 1936 AIR, page 60 | Renuka Subasinghe v. Attorney General, 2007 (1) SLR 224 | K.R. Karunaratne, v. The State, 78 NLR 413
standard_of_review_applied: Appeal on conviction and sentence; reviewed evidence for credibility, consistency, and whether contradictions created reasonable doubt.
sentencing_principles_applied: Considered undue delay in indictment (over 13 years) as a significant mitigating factor warranting sentence reduction, referencing precedents on delay.

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 365B (b) 2 (b) of the Penal Code as amended by Act No.22 of 1995 (two counts) and Section 345 of the Penal Code as amended by Act No.22 of 1995 (one count)
offence_category: Grave Sexual Abuse and Sexual Harassment
brief_facts_summary: The Appellant was charged with committing two counts of Grave Sexual Abuse and one count of Sexual Harassment against a child (Kevin Heman Brito) between 01/11/2012 and 30/11/2012. The victim was 4 years old at the time. The prosecution's key evidence included a video-recorded preliminary interview of the child conducted by the Child Protection Authority under Section 163(c) of the Evidence Ordinance (Special Provisions) Act No. 32 of 1999, marked as P2, with a translated script marked as P1. The Appellant and the victim's mother (PW1) had a strained marital relationship, and a restraining order had been issued against the Appellant for domestic violence.
evidence_type_secondary: Witness testimony (including mother of victim, officials from Child Protection Authority), Police Information Book extracts
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 365B (b) 2 (b) of the Penal Code (two counts) and Section 345 of the Penal Code (one count) as amended
hc_sentence_type: Counts 1 and 2: 7 years rigorous imprisonment each with compensation of Rs.500,000; Count 3: 2 years rigorous imprisonment with compensation of Rs.200,000; sentences to run consecutively
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the Appellant on all three counts. The court relied heavily on the video-recorded interview of the child victim (P2) and its transcript (P1). The Learned High Court Judge also perused the Police Information Book, which was not formally produced as evidence, and appeared to shift the burden of proof onto the Appellant to rebut the prosecution's case.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The Appellant raised seven grounds of appeal, primarily focusing on procedural unfairness and evidential flaws. Key arguments included: the child victim was tutored by the mother (PW1) during the video recording; the transcript of the video interview (P1) was inaccurate and omitted parts; the High Court Judge improperly used the Police Information Book, which was not in evidence; the burden of proof was wrongly shifted onto the Appellant; and the wife (PW1) was not a competent witness under the law.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The Learned Trial Judge has failed to consider the fact that the child victim was tutored by PW1, the mother of the child during the video recording. | The Appellant was denied a fair trial by presenting incorrect transcript of the interview conducted by the Child Protection Authority. | The Appellant was denied a fair trial by convicting him by using and perusing the Police Information Book by the Learned High Court Judge, as it had not been produced as evidence in the trial. | The Appellant has been denied a fair trial by shifting the burden on the Appellant to rebut the evidence of the prosecution. | The Learned High Court Judge has failed to consider that the failure to produce the CD’s which were taken into custody by the National Child Protection Authority warrants the Application of Section 114(f) of the Evidence Ordinance. | The trial Judge has not considered that PW1 had strong motive to implicate the Appellant through the child who was 04 years of age at the time of the incident. | The Learned High Court Judge had failed to consider that PW1, who was the wife of the Appellant is not competent witness to give evidence as far as the charges are concern.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the video evidence (P2) and its transcript (P1) unreliable due to discrepancies and the presence and prompting of the child's mother (PW1) during the recording. The court also found the High Court improperly relied on the Police Information Book not in evidence and shifted the burden of proof.
probability_assessment_by_court: Court found prosecution failed to prove case beyond reasonable doubt due to unreliable video evidence, improper use of non-evidence, shifting burden of proof, and witness competency issues.
defence_version_summary: The Appellant pleaded not guilty, gave evidence from the witness box, and called two defence witnesses. The defence challenged the credibility and admissibility of the prosecution's key evidence (video interview), alleging tutoring and inaccuracies.
legal_errors_description: High Court Judge misdirected on law by: 1) allowing and relying on the video evidence despite tutoring and inaccuracies; 2) using the Police Information Book not in evidence; 3) shifting the burden of proof onto the Appellant; 4) accepting PW1 (wife) as a competent witness when she was not under the relevant law.
procedural_defects_description: Failure to ensure accurate transcript of video evidence; perusing and relying on Police Information Book not produced as evidence; failure to apply Section 114(f) of Evidence Ordinance for non-production of obscene CDs.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal conducted a thorough review, finding multiple fundamental errors. It compared the original video recording (P2) with the prosecution's transcript (P1) and found significant omissions and inaccuracies, particularly showing the mother (PW1) prompting the child. The court held the video evidence was tainted by tutoring and could not be safely accepted. It also found the High Court Judge improperly relied on the Police Information Book (not in evidence) and wrongly shifted the burden of proof. On the legal issue of witness competency, the court found PW1 (the wife) was not a competent witness against the Appellant for the charged offences under Section 120(2) of the Evidence Ordinance, as the relevant schedule of the Children and Young Persons Ordinance had not been amended to include Sections 365B(b)2(b) and 345. The prosecution failed to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt.
coa_sentence_type: Conviction set aside; Appellant acquitted
brief_judgment_file_summary: The Appellant was convicted by the High Court of Colombo on two counts of Grave Sexual Abuse and one count of Sexual Harassment against a 4-year-old child and sentenced to consecutive terms of imprisonment with compensation. He appealed on grounds including tutoring of the child witness, inaccuracies in the video transcript, improper use of the Police Information Book, shifting of the burden of proof, and the incompetency of his wife as a witness. The Court of Appeal found the video evidence unreliable due to the mother's prompting and discrepancies between the recording and transcript. It also identified serious legal errors, including misdirection on the burden of proof and witness competency. The court concluded the prosecution failed to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt, allowed the appeal, set aside the conviction, and acquitted the Appellant.
defence_counsel: Darshana Kuruppu with Sahan Weerasinghe and Dineru Dundara
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court relied heavily on the video-recorded interview of the child and its transcript, and also perused the Police Information Book. The Court of Appeal found this approach fundamentally flawed, as the video evidence was tainted, the transcript inaccurate, and the Police Information Book was not in evidence. The HC also misdirected on the burden of proof and witness competency.
precedents_cited_list: Panchhi and Others v State of Uttar Pradesh (1998) 7 SCC 177 | Liyana Arachchige Lesli Wijesekera v The Attorney General CA/HCC/0046/22 | Punchimalattaya v The State 76 NLR 564 | Priyal Indrajith and two others v The Attorney General CA/HCC/ 300-302/2018 | Woolmington v. DPP [1935] A.C.462 | Hattuwan Pedige Sugath Karunaratne v. The Attorney General SC Appeal 32 of 2020
standard_of_review_applied: Review for errors of law and fact, assessing whether prosecution proved case beyond reasonable doubt, evaluating fairness of trial procedures and admissibility of evidence.

judges: B. Sasi Mahendran, J. | Amal Ranaraja, J.
offence_sections: Section 54 (a)(b) and 54A(d) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance, as amended by Act No. 13 of 1984
brief_facts_summary: PW5, a prison officer, received information on 2 March 2012 about a prisoner possessing heroin. On 3 March, he and PW6 located the accused prisoner in a ward, searched him, and recovered a blue grocery bag containing a brown powder from inside his underwear. The substance was later confirmed to be 3.44 grams of pure heroin. The accused was taken into custody. Prosecution evidence included witness testimonies and the sealed drug parcel.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 54 (a)(b) and 54A(d) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance, as amended by Act No. 13 of 1984
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court found the accused guilty of possession and trafficking of 3.44 grams of heroin. The judge convicted the accused on both counts and imposed the death sentence.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant argued the trial judge failed to consider improbabilities and contradictions in prosecution evidence, particularly regarding PW5's credibility and inconsistencies between PW5 and PW6. A further ground was that conviction for trafficking was erroneous due to lack of direct evidence of commercial intent.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: That the Learned Trial Judge had failed to consider the improbability and suspiciousness of the version of the prosecution pertaining to the alleged incident. | That the Learned Trial Judge had not properly considered the issues relating to the credibility of the evidence by PW5. | That the Learned Trial Judge had failed to consider the contradictory positions relating to this alleged incident between PW5 and PW6 and alternatively | The learned Trial Judge had erred in law by convicting the Accused Appellant for the 1 count namely the trafficking of heroin count in the absence of contributory activity to by the Accused appellant to the same effect.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: COA found the trial judge properly assessed witness credibility, noting no material discrepancies between PW5 and PW6. The court deferred to the trial judge's advantage in observing witness demeanor. PW5's testimony remained consistent despite cross-examination. PW6 corroborated the recovery of the drugs.
probability_assessment_by_court: COA accepted prosecution version as credible and found no reasonable doubt. It considered the quantity of heroin (3.44g pure) within a prison as indicative of trafficking intent.
defence_version_summary: The accused made a statement from the dock. Defence argued the prosecution story was improbable, the search was delayed, and the drugs could have been planted when accused was moved. No prior animosity was alleged. Defence challenged witness credibility but called no witnesses.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: COA analyzed the evidence, finding no material contradictions between PW5 and PW6. It upheld the trial judge's credibility assessments, noting the advantage of observing witness demeanor. On trafficking, COA applied precedent (Mohamed Iqbal Mohamed Sadath) and held the quantity (3.44g pure heroin) recovered inside a prison was circumstantial evidence of intent to distribute, thus proving trafficking. It found no error in the High Court judgment.
coa_sentence_type: Death sentence upheld
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused was convicted by the High Court of Colombo for possession and trafficking of 3.44 grams of heroin and sentenced to death. On appeal, he challenged witness credibility, contradictions, and the trafficking conviction due to lack of direct evidence of commercial intent. The Court of Appeal found the trial judge properly assessed witness credibility and that the quantity of heroin found in prison constituted circumstantial evidence of trafficking. The appeal was dismissed, and the conviction and death sentence were upheld.
defence_counsel: I.B.S. Harshana
hc_analysis_summary: COA found the High Court judge thoroughly analyzed testimonies, identified no material discrepancies, and correctly found the witnesses credible. COA saw no reason to disturb these findings.
precedents_cited_list: Mohamed Iqbal Mohamed Sadath v. Attorney General, SC Appeal 110/15 (SC Minutes, 14.12.2020)
standard_of_review_applied: COA deferred to trial judge's assessment of witness credibility where no material errors were found. Reviewed legal issues de novo regarding trafficking intent.
sentencing_principles_applied: Consideration of quantity of drugs as indicator of trafficking intent vs. personal use, as per cited precedent.

judges: Menaka Wijesundera, J | Wickum A. Kaluarachchi, J
offence_sections: Section 364(3) of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The accused-appellant, father of the victim, was charged with raping his daughter (PW-1) on two occasions in 2012. The victim was 13 years old at the time. She first disclosed the incidents via SMS to her boyfriend, Saman Kumara, in 2015. Her mother (PW-2) saw the reply SMS, confronted the victim the next day after a quarrel, and the victim then revealed the rapes. The mother subsequently filed a police complaint.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 364(3) of the Penal Code
hc_sentence_type: Rigorous Imprisonment 17 years on each count, sentences to run concurrently. Fine of Rs. 25,000 with 6 months default simple imprisonment on each count. Compensation of Rs. 200,000 with 1 year default simple imprisonment on each count.
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the accused-appellant on both counts of rape. The judge found the victim's testimony credible and consistent with the medical evidence. Sentences were imposed for each count with fines, compensation, and default sentences, ordered to run concurrently.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: Appellant's counsel argued the victim's testimony was unreliable due to inconsistencies, omissions, and contradictions. They challenged the justification for the 3.5-year delay in complaint, claimed the dock statement was improperly rejected, and contended that failure to call witness Saman Kumara created an adverse presumption under Section 114(f) of the Evidence Ordinance.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Inconsistent and erratic versions in the testimony of the prosecutrix renders her evidence unworthy of credence. | Testimony of the prosecutrix is peppered with vital omissions and material contradictions which consequently taints her credibility and testimonial trustworthiness. | 3 1/2 year undue belatedness of the police complaint renders the conviction wholly unsafe. | Reasons adduced by the prosecutrix to justify the said belatedness are wholly unjustifiable and/or appear to be palpably false. | LTJ's conclusive finding that the evidence of the prosecutrix is wholly consistent with the history recorded by the 2 medical officers is factually and legally flawed. | Evidence of the prosecutrix does not favour the test of probability in view of suspicious subsequent conduct. | Rejection of the dock statement is legally flawed as the LTJ has shifted the burden of proof. | Sec. 114(f) of the E.O. operates against the prosecution for its failure to list and lead the evidence of Saman Kumara. | Judgment of the Trial Court is legally and factually flawed.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the victim's testimony reliable despite minor inconsistencies, considering her age, fear of the father, and the trauma. Her evidence was corroborated by medical and psychiatric evidence.
probability_assessment_by_court: Court found no reasonable doubt. The victim's reasons for delay were plausible given her age and fear. Her testimony was credible and corroborated.
defence_version_summary: Accused pleaded not guilty. The defence relied on a dock statement denying the charges, alleging false implication due to family disputes. The court found the dock statement improbable and unbelievable.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal meticulously analyzed the grounds. It found the delay in complaint justified due to the victim's young age and fear of her father, referencing legal principles on child witnesses. It held minor inconsistencies in the victim's testimony did not affect her credibility, given the circumstances and time elapsed. The court found her evidence credible and corroborated by medical and psychiatric evidence. It rejected the claim that the trial judge shifted the burden of proof via the dock statement, finding it properly rejected as improbable. It held there was no necessity to call Saman Kumara as a witness. No legal errors were found in the High Court judgment.
coa_sentence_type: Rigorous Imprisonment 17 years on each count (concurrent). Fine of Rs. 25,000 per count with 6 months default simple imprisonment. Compensation of Rs. 200,000 per count with 1 year default simple imprisonment.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused-appellant, Sarath Menikpura, was convicted by the Ratnapura High Court on two counts of raping his daughter in 2012. He appealed, challenging the victim's reliability, the delay in complaint, the rejection of his dock statement, and the failure to call a key witness. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal. It found the victim's testimony credible and consistent with medical evidence, the delay justified given her age and fear, no error in the rejection of the dock statement, and no need to call the additional witness. The High Court's convictions and sentences were affirmed.
defence_counsel: Indica Mallawaratchy
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court found the victim's testimony credible, consistent, and corroborated by medical evidence. The Court of Appeal agreed with this analysis and found no legal or factual errors in the High Court judgment.
precedents_cited_list: Sumanasena V. Attorney General – (1999) 3 Sri L.R. 137 | Daradagamage Chandraratne Jayawardane alias Shantha v. The Attorney General - Court of Appeal case No. CA/85/2013 | Gurcharan Singh v. State of Haryane - AIR (1972) SC 2661 | Sunil and Another v. The Attorney General - (1986) 1 Sri L.R 230 | The King v. Themis Singho - 45 N.L.R 378 | Premasiri and Another v. The Queen - 77 NLR 85 | Regina v. W.D Dharmasena - 58 N.L.R 15 | Bhoginbhai Hirjibhai v. state of Gujarat - (1983) AIR S.C 753
standard_of_review_applied: The court reviewed the High Court's factual findings and legal conclusions for correctness, applying principles on child witness testimony, delay in complaint, and corroboration in rape cases.
sentencing_principles_applied: The Court of Appeal affirmed the concurrent sentences imposed, finding them appropriate. It did not modify the sentence.

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: section 296 read with section 32 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The deceased's father was involved in recruiting for overseas jobs and failed to secure promised jobs after taking money from the appellants. On 17-04-2007, the appellants and two others visited the deceased's house demanding money. An altercation ensued, leading to a physical fight. The deceased was stabbed in the abdomen and later died in hospital. The mother of the deceased was the sole eyewitness.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: section 296 read with section 32 of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court Judge found both appellants guilty of murder after a trial without a jury. Both were sentenced to death.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: Appellants argued the High Court Judge failed to consider common intention, did not evaluate the dock statement, did not consider culpable homicide not amounting to murder as an alternative, prematurely judged the case, wrongly placed a burden on the accused, and mis-evaluated the eyewitness evidence.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The prosecution has not proven the common intention of the 1st accused-appellant. | The learned High Court Judge has not evaluated the dock statement of the 1st accused-appellant. | There was evidence relating to culpable homicide not amounting to murder, and the learned High Court Judge has failed to evaluate evidence in that regard. | Did the learned High Court Judge err in prematurely judging the case before the analysis of the defence evidence. | Did the learned High Court Judge err in wrongly casting a burden on the accused to rebut the evidence against them. | Has the learned High Court Judge erred in failing to correctly to evaluate the evidence of PW-02. | Has the learned High Court Judge erred in accepting the evidence of PW-02 with regard to the omissions and other infirmities. | Has the learned High Court Judge erred in wrongfully evaluating common intention or non-evaluation of common intention. | Has the learned High Court Judge erred in not considering the law in relation to culpable homicide not amounting to murder. | Do the failure to adopt previous proceedings fatal to sustain a conviction.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The prosecution relied heavily on the eyewitness account of PW-02, the mother of the deceased. The Court of Appeal found her evidence established the sequence of events but noted the incident arose from a sudden fight due to provocation.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court found the fatal injury resulted from a sudden fight sparked by grave and sudden provocation, falling under culpable homicide not amounting to murder.
defence_version_summary: The 1st appellant made a dock statement admitting they visited to demand money back, a verbal and physical altercation ensued, and PW-02 came with a knife. The 2nd appellant remained silent. They did not directly admit causing the fatal injury but admitted a brawl occurred.
legal_errors_description: High Court Judge failed to consider whether the evidence supported a conviction for culpable homicide not amounting to murder, and failed to direct attention to the relevant exception under section 294 of the Penal Code.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The COA found the High Court Judge erred by not considering the alternative of culpable homicide not amounting to murder. It analyzed the facts, finding the incident was a sudden fight resulting from grave and sudden provocation caused by the deceased's father's actions. Common intention was established. Applying Exception 1 of section 294 of the Penal Code and precedents, the COA modified the conviction from murder to culpable homicide not amounting to murder. It also addressed and confirmed the common intention of both appellants.
coa_sentence_type: 10 years rigorous imprisonment each and a fine of Rs. 25,000 each. Default of fine: 1 year simple imprisonment each. Additional compensation of Rs. 500,000 each to PW-02, default recoverable as a fine, with a further default sentence of 2 years rigorous imprisonment each.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The two appellants were convicted of murder by the High Court of Kuliyapitiya and sentenced to death for the 2007 stabbing death of the deceased. They appealed on grounds including failure to consider common intention, mis-evaluation of evidence, and not considering culpable homicide not amounting to murder. The Court of Appeal found the High Court Judge erred by not considering the alternative offence. The COA re-evaluated the evidence, concluding the fatal injury resulted from a sudden fight due to grave and sudden provocation. It set aside the murder conviction and sentence, convicting the appellants instead for culpable homicide not amounting to murder. They were sentenced to 10 years rigorous imprisonment, fines, and ordered to pay compensation.
defence_counsel: Chathura Amarathunga for the 1st Accused-Appellant; Nalin Ladduwahetty, P.C. with Kavithri Ubeysekera for the 2nd Accused-Appellant
cause_of_death_exact_text: one stab wound to his abdominal area which has resulted in loss of blood, which has contributed towards his death.
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court found the appellants guilty of murder based on eyewitness testimony. The COA criticized the HC for not considering whether the facts supported the lesser offence of culpable homicide not amounting to murder, particularly regarding the exception of grave and sudden provocation.
precedents_cited_list: King Vs. Bellana Withanage Eddin 41 NLR 345 | Gamini vs. The Attorney General (2011) 1 SLR 236
standard_of_review_applied: The COA reviewed the evidence in its totality to determine if the High Court correctly applied the law, particularly regarding the availability of the lesser offence.
sentencing_principles_applied: The COA considered the facts and circumstances, the nature of the offence (culpable homicide not amounting to murder), and the period already spent in incarceration when imposing the sentence.
final_charge_after_appeal: Modified from Murder to Culpable Homicide not amounting to murder under Exception 1 of section 294 of the Penal Code.

judges: Menaka Wijesundera, J | Wickum A. Kaluarachchi, J
offence_sections: Section 54A (b) and 54A (d) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance (as amended)
brief_facts_summary: An informant told police a woman in the Grandpass area was carrying heroin. A raid team went to Stacepura. Police saw a woman matching a description, searched her, and found a parcel of heroin in her trouser pocket. They then searched her house but found nothing. The substance was weighed and sealed at the Dedigama Pawning Centre. The accused was arrested and later convicted for trafficking and possession of 3.62 grams of heroin.
evidence_type_primary: Physical evidence (parcel of heroin recovered from accused)
evidence_type_secondary: Police testimony regarding raid and search
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 54A (b) and 54A (d) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance (as amended)
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court Judge convicted the accused-appellant on both charges of trafficking and possession of heroin and sentenced her to life imprisonment for each charge by judgment dated 28.04.2023.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant argued the source information had discrepancies, the prosecution story was improbable, and there was doubt about the presence of a Woman Police Constable. It was also argued the prosecution failed to follow a Supreme Court Rule, and there was insufficient evidence for trafficking and possession charges. The judge allegedly misdirected himself on facts.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The learned High Court Judge failed to notice, consider, and evaluate that the 'information' which is the 'source' of present matter has inherent discrepancies/infirmities. | The learned High Court Judge failed to take cognizance of the improbability of the prosecution case. | The learned High Court Judge failed to consider and evaluate that there is a reasonable doubt whether a Woman Police Constable accompanied the raid team. | The prosecution had failed to act under Rule 52 of the Supreme Court Rules (Conduct and Etiquette for Attorneys-at-Law) Rules 1988. | The learned High Court Judge failed to consider that there is no sufficient evidence to prove beyond a reasonable doubt, the charge of trafficking. | The learned High Court Judge failed to consider whether the prosecution has proved the possession of heroin beyond a reasonable doubt. | The learned High Court Judge misdirected himself on the facts and convicted the appellant. | The conviction and the sentence are bad in law.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed testimonies of PW-1 (OIC) and PW-7 (Woman Police Constable), finding material contradictions regarding what the accused said upon arrest, the duration of house search, and the distance walked. It also noted improbabilities in the raid timeline and a vital infirmity in the recorded information.
probability_assessment_by_court: Court found the prosecution case improbable and full of vital discrepancies, creating reasonable doubt. The story of arresting the accused after walking 500m-1km from her house, when she was allegedly just leaving, was deemed totally improbable.
defence_version_summary: The accused pleaded not guilty. She gave a dock statement claiming she was arrested at home. The defence suggested police came to arrest her husband. The High Court Judge rejected her dock statement partly because this suggestion was not made in cross-examination, but the COA found this observation was wrong as the suggestion had been made.
legal_errors_description: The High Court Judge failed to properly analyze evidence and consider material contradictions and improbabilities, leading to an erroneous conclusion. The judge also incorrectly stated a defence suggestion had not been made in cross-examination.
procedural_defects_description: Failure to make notebook entries regarding the house search as required by Police Departmental Order No. A.16. The prosecution also failed to adequately explain a vital infirmity in the recorded source information.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found vital infirmities and improbabilities in the prosecution case that created reasonable doubt. It noted discrepancies between PW-1 and PW-7's evidence on key events, contradictions in timelines and distances, and a failure to follow procedural rules for notebook entries. The COA held the High Court Judge erred by not properly analyzing this evidence and failing to see how the improbabilities cast doubt on whether the raid occurred as described. The prosecution failed to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt.
coa_sentence_type: Acquitted. Convictions and sentences set aside.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused-appellant, Anthony Theresa, was convicted by the High Court of Colombo for trafficking and possessing 3.62g of heroin and sentenced to life imprisonment. She appealed, arguing the prosecution case was improbable and riddled with contradictions. The Court of Appeal found material discrepancies in police testimony regarding the raid, arrest, and search, and a vital infirmity in the source information. The COA held the prosecution failed to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt, set aside the convictions and sentences, and acquitted the accused.
defence_counsel: Kavithri Hirusha Ubeysekera, Assigned Counsel
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted the accused based on the prosecution's raid story. The COA found the HC Judge failed to properly analyze the evidence, overlooked material contradictions and improbabilities, and came to an erroneous conclusion without considering reasonable doubt raised by the discrepancies.
standard_of_review_applied: Appeal on facts and law, assessing whether the prosecution proved its case beyond reasonable doubt.

judges: Menaka Wijesundera J. | Wickum A. Kaluarachchi J.
offence_sections: Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The incident occurred at a funeral house where two groups were playing cards late at night. The appellant objected when a person named Bache shuffled cards, leading to a tussle. The deceased intervened and was assaulted by the appellant and stabbed by the 1st accused. The appellant was indicted for murder with three others.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 297 of the Penal Code
hc_sentence_type: Culpable homicide not amounting to murder, sentence not specified in detail
hc_judgment_summary: The trial judge convicted the appellant and 1st accused for culpable homicide not amounting to murder based on a sudden fight. The judge sentenced the appellant accordingly, rejecting the evidence of PW3 as unreliable but accepting PW16's testimony.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The main ground was that the trial judge misconstrued and misapplied section 32 of the Penal Code regarding common intention. The appellant's counsel argued the appellant did not share a common intention with others and there was no prearranged plan.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Trial judge misconstrued in applying section 32 of the Penal Code (common intention) | Appellant did not share common intention with other accused at time of offence | No prearranged plan among accused and appellant
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The prosecution case relied on two eyewitnesses (PW16 and PW3). The trial judge rejected PW3's evidence as unreliable but accepted PW16's. The Court of Appeal deferred to the trial judge's credibility assessment of PW3 but found PW16's evidence credible and sufficient for conviction.
probability_assessment_by_court: Court found evidence of PW16 credible and established common intention beyond reasonable doubt based on eyewitness account of appellant holding deceased while 1st accused stabbed.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty. He made a dock statement, which the trial judge rejected as it was not put to prosecution witnesses. The defence argued no common intention or prearranged plan.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the trial judge correctly applied the principle of common intention under section 32 of the Penal Code, citing Queen vs Mahathun. It held common intention can be formed spontaneously. It deferred to the trial judge's assessment of witness credibility (PW3) and found no miscarriage of justice. The evidence showed appellant assaulted deceased and held him while 1st accused stabbed, establishing shared intention.
coa_sentence_type: Culpable homicide not amounting to murder, sentence upheld (details not specified)
brief_judgment_file_summary: The 4th accused-appellant appealed his High Court conviction for culpable homicide not amounting to murder. The High Court found him guilty based on eyewitness testimony of a sudden fight at a funeral house. The appellant argued the trial judge misapplied the common intention principle. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal, finding the trial judge correctly applied the law and that common intention was established from the appellant's actions during the incident.
defence_counsel: Aruna Pathirana Arachchi
hc_analysis_summary: The trial judge convicted based on eyewitness PW16, rejected PW3 as unreliable, and found culpable homicide not murder due to sudden fight. The Court of Appeal found no error in this analysis and upheld the conviction.
precedents_cited_list: The Queen vs Mahathun and another at 61 NLR 540 | Sunil Jayaratne vs Attorney General 2011 2 Sri L.R 92
standard_of_review_applied: Appellate court will not interfere with trial judge's findings on witness credibility unless grave miscarriage of justice.
final_charge_after_appeal: Culpable homicide not amounting to murder

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 16(b) and Section 19(c) of the Bribery Act
brief_facts_summary: The accused-appellant, a police inspector, solicited and accepted Rs. 2500 as a bribe from a van driver (PW-01) to avoid a traffic charge. On 10-09-2008, the appellant solicited the bribe at Mawanalla police station. On 11-09-2008, during a raid by the Bribery Commission, the appellant accepted the marked money and was arrested. The prosecution case relied on the evidence of the driver (PW-01), a decoy officer (PW-02), and the raiding team leader (PW-03).
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 16(b) and Section 19(c) of the Bribery Act
hc_sentence_type: 5 years rigorous imprisonment on each count, to run concurrently. Fine of Rs. 5000 for each count.
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court found the appellant guilty on all four counts of soliciting and accepting a bribe. The court considered mitigatory and aggravating circumstances, imposing concurrent sentences of 5 years rigorous imprisonment and fines totaling Rs. 20,000.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant argued he was denied a fair trial, specifically regarding the trial judge's reliance on certain documentary evidence and consideration of a witness treated as hostile. He also contended that evidence created reasonable doubt, pointing to alleged contradictions in prosecution evidence and lack of corroboration from the vehicle owner.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: No fair trial was afforded to the appellant at the hearing before the High Court. | The evidence led at the trial creates a reasonable doubt as to the charges against the appellant and therefore, he should have been acquitted.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the evidence of the key prosecution witnesses (PW-01, PW-02, PW-03) to be consistent, cogent, and credible despite minor discrepancies. The court also found the defence evidence, including that of the appellant and a fellow police officer, was an attempt to create a false narrative.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court found no reasonable doubt was created by the defence. The prosecution evidence was cogent and truthful, and the appellant's version was a false narrative.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty, gave evidence, and called one witness (a fellow police officer). His defence was that he never solicited or accepted a bribe; he refused the request for a spot fine, directed the complainant to court, and was falsely accused. The court found his evidence and that of his witness not credible.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The COA meticulously analyzed the evidence, finding the testimonies of PW-01, PW-02, and PW-03 consistent and credible. It held that the trial judge correctly considered evidence from a witness treated as hostile (PW-05), applying principles from cited precedents. The court found minor discrepancies were not material and did not create reasonable doubt. It also found the appellant was not denied a fair trial, as the documentary evidence in question was properly admitted and the appellant had the opportunity to cross-examine. The appeal was dismissed for lack of merit.
coa_sentence_type: Conviction and sentence dated 16-11-2018 affirmed. The sentence is 5 years rigorous imprisonment on each of four counts (to run concurrently) and a fine of Rs. 5000 for each count.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused-appellant, a police inspector, was convicted by the High Court of Colombo for soliciting and accepting a Rs. 2500 bribe from a van driver and sentenced to 5 years rigorous imprisonment and fines. He appealed on grounds of unfair trial and reasonable doubt. The Court of Appeal thoroughly examined the evidence, found the prosecution witnesses credible and the minor discrepancies immaterial. It upheld the High Court's handling of evidence and application of law, concluding the appellant received a fair trial and the conviction was sound. The appeal was dismissed.
defence_counsel: Prasantha Lal De Alwis, P.C. with Chamara Wannisekara
hc_analysis_summary: The COA found the High Court Judge correctly analyzed the evidence, properly considered the testimony of a hostile witness, and made no material errors in law or fact. The COA agreed with the HC's conclusions on witness credibility and sufficiency of evidence.
precedents_cited_list: The Queen Vs. R. R. Abilinu Fernando (1967) 70 NLR 73 | Galahoda Payagalage Sanath Wimalasiri Vs. Officer-in-Charge, Police Station, Maradana and Hon. Attorney General, SC Appeal No. 32/11 decided on 30-11-2016 | The King Vs. N. A. Fernando (1945) 46 NLR 254 at 255 | Profulla Kumar Saker Vs. King Emperor A.I.R. 1931 Calcutta 491 | Mahathun and Others Vs. The Attorney General (2015) 1 SLR 74 | State of Uttar Pradesh Vs. Anthony 1985 AIR SC 48 | Bhoginbhai Hirjibhai V. State of Gujarat AIR 1983 SC 753
standard_of_review_applied: The COA reviewed the HC judgment for legal errors and evaluated the evidence to determine if it created reasonable doubt, applying the principle that it would not lightly disturb the trial judge's findings on witness credibility.
sentencing_principles_applied: The COA implicitly affirmed the HC's consideration of mitigatory and aggravating circumstances in sentencing. It did not modify the sentence, finding no error.

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 365 B (2) (b) of the Penal Code as amended by Act No. 22 of 1995
brief_facts_summary: The victim, about 7 years old at the time, was playing when the Appellant called her, showed her a picture on his mobile phone, and took her to a nearby abandoned house. There he removed her undergarment, positioned his genitalia near her vagina, and committed severe sexual abuse, preventing her from crying for help. The victim immediately informed her mother, who told her father; the father assaulted the Appellant the next day and lodged a police complaint.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 365 B (2) (b) of the Penal Code as amended by Act No. 22 of 1995
hc_sentence_type: 14 years of rigorous imprisonment, fine, and compensation
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court Judge convicted the Appellant as charged after considering the evidence. He sentenced the Appellant to 14 years rigorous imprisonment, imposed a fine of Rs. 25,000, and ordered compensation of Rs. 200,000 with default sentences.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The Appellant challenged the credibility and trustworthiness of prosecution witnesses, argued the victim's evidence was uncorroborated, claimed contradictions in the medical evidence were not considered, and asserted the prosecution failed to prove the case beyond reasonable doubt.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Creditworthiness and trustworthiness of the prosecution witnesses are questionable | The evidence of the victim has not been corroborated with other evidence. | Contradictions, omissions, and inconsistencies on the evidence of medical officer is not considered by the Learned High Court Judge. | The prosecution has failed to prove the case beyond reasonable doubts.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court carefully assessed the child victim's credibility, noting no material contradictions in her evidence and that minor omissions were understandable given her age and the time lapse. The evidence of the victim's parents (PW2 and PW3) supported her account, particularly regarding the immediate complaint and assault on the Appellant.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court assessed the victim's testimony as convincing, cogent, and sufficient on its own, finding no reason to doubt her account. It noted that corroboration is not a sine qua non in sexual offence cases.
defence_version_summary: The Appellant pleaded not guilty, gave a statement from the dock, and called his brother as a defence witness. The Court found the defence arguments unpersuasive and the victim's evidence credible.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed the grounds cumulatively. It reviewed principles on child witness credibility from several jurisdictions, concluding the trial judge correctly assessed the victim's testimony. The Court found no material contradictions, held that minor omissions did not affect the core case, and noted the victim's evidence was supported by her parents' actions. It affirmed that corroboration is not mandatory in sexual offence cases if the victim's evidence is credible. The medical evidence, while not excluding sexual abuse, was consistent with the victim's account. The Court found the prosecution proved its case beyond reasonable doubt and saw no reason to interfere with the High Court judgment.
coa_sentence_type: 14 years rigorous imprisonment, fine of Rs. 25,000 with default sentence of 6 months simple imprisonment, compensation of Rs. 200,000 with default sentence of 1 year rigorous imprisonment. Sentence effective from 22/05/2020.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The Appellant was convicted by the High Court of Ratnapura for Grave Sexual Abuse of a 7-year-old girl and sentenced to 14 years rigorous imprisonment, a fine, and compensation. He appealed on grounds of witness credibility, lack of corroboration, medical evidence inconsistencies, and failure to prove the case beyond reasonable doubt. The Court of Appeal, after reviewing principles on child witness testimony and the evidence, found the victim's testimony credible and corroborated by her parents' actions. It held that corroboration is not essential in sexual offence cases and dismissed the appeal, affirming the conviction and sentence.
defence_counsel: Sanjaya Senevirathne
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court Judge carefully considered the evidence, found the victim's testimony credible and without exaggeration, and convicted the Appellant. The Court of Appeal found no error in this analysis and agreed with the High Court's reasoning.
precedents_cited_list: R v. Brasier168 Eng. Rep.202 [1779] | Ratansinh Dalsukhbhai Nayak v. State of Gujarat [2004] 1 SCC 64 | Ranjeet Kumar Ram v. State of Bihar [2015] SCC Online SC 500 | R v. Baker EWCA Crim 4 [2010] | R v. B. (G),1990 CanLII 7308 (SCC); [1990] 2 S.C.R. 30 | Rameshwar v. The State of Rajasthan, [1952] S.C.R. 377 | Gamini Dolawatte V. Attorney General [1988] 1 Sri. L. R 221 | Bhargavan v.State of Kerala AIR 2004 SC 1058
standard_of_review_applied: Assessment of trial judge's findings on witness credibility and evidence, guided by principles on child witness testimony.

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: section 345 as amended by the Amendment Act No. 22 of 1995 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The accused was the Human Resource Manager of Prima Ceylon Limited, Trincomalee. The prosecutrix (PW-01), a clerk under him, was allegedly subjected to three incidents of sexual harassment on separate days in January 2011 at the office. The incidents involved unwanted touching, embracing, stroking of the head, and on the third occasion, showing pornographic material and kissing. The prosecutrix reported the incidents to company management and later lodged a police complaint. The High Court acquitted the accused. The prosecutrix, as aggrieved party, appealed the acquittal.
evidence_type_primary: Eyewitness testimony (victim - PW-01), Corroborative testimony (husband - PW-10)
evidence_type_secondary: Security officer testimony, Police investigation records
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: section 345 as amended by the Amendment Act No. 22 of 1995 of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court Judge acquitted the accused, giving him the benefit of the doubt. The judgment incorrectly stated that prosecution needed to prove sexual gratification for sexual harassment under section 345 and focused on an alleged delay in complaint, finding it created reasonable doubt.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appeal was by the aggrieved party/victim (PW-01) against acquittal. Main grounds were that the High Court judgment was completely misdirected on law and facts, requiring proof of sexual gratification for sexual harassment (which is not an ingredient under section 345), and wrongly treated an alleged delay in complaint as fatal. It was argued the judgment did not properly analyze the evidence as a whole.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Misdirection on law: wrongly considered proof of sexual gratification necessary for offence under section 345 | Misdirection on facts: wrongly determined there was an unexplained delay in complaint | Failure to consider and analyze the evidence as a whole | Failure to provide a proper judgment in terms of section 283 of the Criminal Procedure Code
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the testimony of the victim (PW-01) cogent and trustworthy, corroborated by her husband (PW-10) and security officers. The defense claim of a company conspiracy was rejected. Minor contradictions were deemed not material.
probability_assessment_by_court: Court of Appeal found the victim's evidence credible and consistent, and that the defense failed to create a reasonable doubt. The prosecution proved its case beyond reasonable doubt.
defence_version_summary: Accused pleaded not guilty. He gave evidence denying all charges. Defense claimed the complaint was a fabrication by the company (Prima Ceylon Limited) to get rid of him because he exposed corrupt practices. Court found this defense version unsubstantiated and not credible.
legal_errors_description: High Court Judge misdirected himself by requiring proof of sexual gratification for sexual harassment under section 345 of the Penal Code, which is not an ingredient. He also misapplied case law related to a different offence (grave sexual abuse under section 365B).
procedural_defects_description: Judgment did not comply with section 283 of Criminal Procedure Code: failed to properly analyze evidence as a whole, considered irrelevant facts from another case (Aranolis in a murder case), and focused only on selected parts of evidence.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal conducted a de novo analysis of the evidence. It found the victim's (PW-01) testimony credible, consistent, and corroborated by her husband and security personnel. It rejected the defense of company conspiracy as baseless. It corrected the High Court's legal error regarding the need to prove sexual gratification under section 345. The Court applied principles from Indian Supreme Court cases (Vishaka, Apparel Export Promotion Council, Boginbhai Hirjibhai) regarding sexual harassment and witness credibility. It held that in sexual harassment cases, corroboration is not mandatory if the victim's evidence is cogent. It found the prosecution proved all three counts beyond reasonable doubt.
coa_sentence_type: Count 1: 2 years rigorous imprisonment + Rs. 25,000 fine. Count 2: 2 years rigorous imprisonment + Rs. 25,000 fine. Count 3: 3 years rigorous imprisonment + Rs. 25,000 fine. All imprisonment terms to run consecutively (total 7 years rigorous imprisonment). Default on fine for each count: 6 months simple imprisonment. Additional compensation of Rs. 750,000 to victim (PW-01). Default on compensation: recoverable as fine, with 1 year simple imprisonment in default.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused, Human Resource Manager of Prima Ceylon Limited, was acquitted by the Trincomalee High Court on three counts of sexually harassing a female subordinate (PW-01). The aggrieved party/victim appealed the acquittal. The Court of Appeal found the High Court judgment fatally flawed, being misdirected on law (wrongly requiring proof of sexual gratification) and facts (wrongly focusing on complaint delay). Re-analyzing the evidence, the COA found the victim's testimony credible and corroborated, and rejected the defense claim of a company conspiracy. The COA convicted the accused on all three counts and imposed a total sentence of 7 years rigorous imprisonment, fines totalling Rs. 75,000, and compensation of Rs. 750,000 to the victim.
defence_counsel: Anuja Premaratna, P.C. with Nayana Dissanayake, Aviska Jayawardana, Natasha de Alwis, Bandula Dissanayake, Ishan Gampolage and Ramith Dunusinghe
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court acquitted the accused based on two main errors: (1) wrongly requiring proof of sexual gratification for sexual harassment under section 345, and (2) finding an unexplained delay in complaint created reasonable doubt. The COA found this analysis fundamentally flawed, as the judge failed to consider evidence as a whole and applied law from a different offence.
precedents_cited_list: Muthaiyah Yogarajah alias Yoga Accused-Appellant, Hon Attorney General Respondent, CA. Appeal 55/06 decided on 24-02-2009 | CA 118/2002 decided on 26-03-2008 | State of Uttar Pradesh Vs. M.K Anthoney (1984) S.C.J 236-1985 Cri. L.J. 493 | Vishaka And Others Vs.
