Republic of Sri Lanka (2010) 2 SLR 241 | Kumara de Silva and two others Vs. Attorney General (2010) 2 SLR 169 | Fradd Vs. Brown and Co. Limited 20 NLR 282
standard_of_review_applied: De novo consideration of evidence and law, as the High Court judgment was found fundamentally flawed and not in accordance with law.
sentencing_principles_applied: Considered aggravating factors (seriousness of offences, abuse of authority), mitigating factors (no previous convictions, age 59), and need for compensation to victim. Applied principle of consecutive sentences for separate offences.

judges: Menaka Wijesundera, J | Wickum A. Kaluarachchi, J
offence_sections: Section 300 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The accused-appellant was convicted of attempting to commit the murder of Senadheera Pathiranage Samarathunga. The appellant inflicted multiple injuries on the victim, including two stab injuries and eight cut injuries, one of which was sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death. The appellant demonstrated a fierce nature, continuing to stab the victim after he fell and threatening bystanders with a knife. The offence was committed in 2004, and the appellant was convicted in 2022 after facing trial and continuously appearing in court from 2008 to 2022.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 300 of the Penal Code
hc_sentence_type: Twenty years Rigorous Imprisonment, Fine of Rs. 25,000, Compensation of Rs. 1,000,000, and an order to deposit Rs. 50,000 under the Assistance to and Protection of Victims of Crime and Witnesses Act
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court Judge convicted the appellant for attempted murder under Section 300 of the Penal Code. The Judge considered the gravity and seriousness of the offence, pre-arrangement, impact on the victim, multiple injuries, and the appellant's unremorseful conduct. The maximum punishment of 20 years rigorous imprisonment and substantial compensation was imposed.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant's counsel admitted the conviction was correct but contested the sentence as excessive. She argued the High Court Judge imposed the maximum punishment of 20 years without considering all relevant mitigating factors, such as the appellant's age, the lengthy trial period, and the time gap between the offence and conviction. The imposition of one million rupees compensation was also contended as excessive.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Sentence excessive - maximum punishment of 20 years RI imposed unreasonably | Compensation of Rs. 1,000,000 excessive | Mitigating factors (age, trial delay, single old conviction) not adequately considered by the trial judge
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The court relied on the evidence of the victim (PW-1) and the medical report (P-1). The medical report detailed the injuries, with one injury being sufficient to cause death. The appellant's conduct during and after the attack demonstrated his fierce nature and lack of remorse.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal found the conviction for attempted murder was correctly based on the evidence and was not challenged by the appellant.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty. He was convicted by the High Court. The appeal focused only on sentence. No alibi or new defence version was presented in the appeal.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal agreed the conviction was proper. On sentencing, it found the High Court Judge did not adequately consider mitigating factors like the appellant's age (62 at conviction, 44 at offence), the 18-year delay between offence and conviction, the lengthy trial period (2008-2022), and that he had only one old previous conviction. The court noted the aggravating factors (serious injuries, fierce nature, lack of remorse) but held imposing the maximum 20-year sentence was unjustifiable. It reduced the sentence based on a balancing of these factors.
coa_sentence_type: Fourteen years Rigorous Imprisonment operative from 22nd June 2022, Fine of Rs. 25,000, Compensation of Rs. 500,000, and an order to deposit Rs. 50,000 under the Assistance to and Protection of Victims of Crime and Witnesses Act (default terms unchanged)
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused-appellant was convicted by the High Court of Kandy for attempted murder under Section 300 of the Penal Code and sentenced to 20 years RI, a fine, and substantial compensation. He appealed only against the sentence, arguing it was excessive and mitigating factors were not considered. The Court of Appeal upheld the conviction but found the maximum sentence unjustifiable. Considering the appellant's age, trial delay, and limited criminal record, it reduced the imprisonment to 14 years RI and halved the compensation. The appeal was partly allowed.
defence_counsel: Indica Mallawaratchy
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court Judge considered the gravity of the offence, pre-arrangement, impact on victim, injuries, and lack of remorse as aggravating factors. The Court of Appeal held that while these were valid considerations, the Judge failed to adequately weigh mitigating factors like the appellant's age and the lengthy trial delay, making the maximum sentence unreasonable.
precedents_cited_list: Priyanka Perera V. Attorney General – S.C. Appeal 99/2006
standard_of_review_applied: Review of sentencing discretion, considering aggravating and mitigating factors
sentencing_principles_applied: Consideration of aggravating factors (nature of injuries, impact on victim, lack of remorse) and mitigating factors (age of accused, trial delay, time between offence and conviction, previous convictions) to arrive at a just and proportionate sentence.

judges: B. Sasi Mahendran, J. | Amal Ranaraja, J.
offence_sections: section 54A(b) and 54A(d) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance as amended by Act No.13 of 1984
brief_facts_summary: On November 2, 2013, police officers on surveillance in Nawagampura spotted the appellant behaving suspiciously near a locked gate. Upon apprehension, a search revealed a pink cellophane bag containing a powdered substance. The substance was seized, weighed, sealed, and sent for analysis. The Government Analyst report confirmed it contained 3.19 grams of heroin.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: section 54A(b) and 54A(d) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance as amended by Act No.13 of 1984
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the appellant on both charges of trafficking and possessing 3.19 grams of heroin. The judge sentenced the appellant to life imprisonment on each count.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant's counsel argued that the High Court judge erred by convicting for trafficking without sufficient additional evidence beyond possession. Counsel also contended the judge failed to consider the improbability of the prosecution's case, specifically questioning the appellant's behavior upon seeing the police.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Did the Learned High Court Judge err in law by convicting the appellant for trafficking without having additional evidence? | Did the Learned High Court Judge err in law by failing to consider the improbability of the prosecution's case?
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court relied on the testimony of police officers (PW01) regarding the arrest and seizure. The key evidence was the physical recovery of drugs and the Government Analyst report confirming heroin.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal found the quantity of drugs (19.69 grams of powdered substance containing 3.19g heroin) was too large for personal use, supporting an inference of trafficking. It rejected arguments about the appellant's behavior as unconvincing generalisations.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty. His defence was that police questioned him about another person's house, searched it, found items, and then falsely implicated him with a recovered item. He did not call witnesses. The court rejected his version as lacking merit.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed the definition of 'traffic' under section 54A and cited precedent (Mohamed Iqbal Mohamed Sadat). It held that the large quantity of drugs (19.69g total mixture) was circumstantial evidence indicating possession for commercial purposes, not personal use, thus satisfying the additional act requirement for trafficking. It rejected the defence argument about the appellant's reaction to police as an unreliable generalization of human behavior. The COA found no error in the HC judgment.
coa_sentence_type: Life imprisonment on both counts, to run from date of conviction.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The appellant was convicted by the Colombo High Court for trafficking and possessing 3.19g of heroin and sentenced to life imprisonment on both counts. He appealed, arguing insufficient evidence for trafficking and improbability of the prosecution case. The Court of Appeal, citing precedent, held the large quantity of drug mixture (19.69g) was circumstantial evidence of commercial intent, transforming possession to trafficking. It dismissed the appeal, upholding the conviction and sentence.
defence_counsel: Amila Palliyage with Sandeepani Wijesooriya, Savani Udugampola, Lakitha Wakista Arachchi and Subaj De Silva
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted based on police testimony, recovery of drugs, and analyst report. The Court of Appeal found no error in this analysis, agreeing that the quantity supported a trafficking inference.
precedents_cited_list: Mohamed Iqbal Mohamed Sadat vs. The Attorney General, SC/SPL/ LA/ 58/ 15, SC Appeal 110/ 15 decided on December 14, 2020
standard_of_review_applied: Review of legal sufficiency of evidence for trafficking charge.
sentencing_principles_applied: Life imprisonment deemed appropriate for drug trafficking offences.

judges: B. Sasi Mahendran, J. | Amal Ranaraja, J
offence_sections: Section 365B (2)(b) of the Penal Code, as amended by Acts Nos. 22 of 1995, 28 of 1998, and 16 of 2006
brief_facts_summary: The accused was convicted on one count of grave sexual abuse against a minor, Balapuwaduge Aruna Lakshan Mendis, who was nine years old at the time of the incident in December 2015. The prosecution's case was that the accused showed the victim a pornography video, then removed his clothes and placed his male organ to the victim's anus when no one else was at home. The victim initially informed his mother but later reported to his brother and father, leading to a police complaint and medical examination.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 365B (2)(b) of the Penal Code, as amended by Acts Nos. 22 of 1995, 28 of 1998, and 16 of 2006
hc_sentence_type: Rigorous Imprisonment 14 years and Fine Rs. 20,000 with default penalty of 3 months
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court found the Accused guilty of the first charge of grave sexual abuse and sentenced him to 14 years rigorous imprisonment, a fine, and compensation. The Accused was acquitted on the second charge.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appeal was based on the credibility of the victim's testimony, alleged lack of reasons for convicting on one count and acquitting on another, and improper analysis of the accused's dock statement. The defence also argued delay in complaint and that the complaint was motivated by personal animosity.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The evidence of PW1 has failed to satisfy the test of spontaneity, probability, and belatedness, hence, PW1's evidence was not credible. | That the learned trial judge has not given reasons to convict the Accused for one count and acquit from the other count. | That the learned trial Judge has not analysed the dock statement of the accused in the correct perspective.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court found the victim's (PW1) testimony consistent and credible despite minor contradictions regarding school attendance. The medical evidence from the JMO corroborated the victim's account with findings of healed tears. The defence claim of personal animosity was rejected.
probability_assessment_by_court: Court found no reasonable doubt created by minor contradictions in victim's evidence, considering the time lapse and nature of the offense.
defence_version_summary: Accused pleaded not guilty. Defence was based on a dock statement. Defence claimed victim's evidence was not credible, the complaint was delayed and motivated by personal animosity from the victim's father (PW2). Court rejected these claims.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal dismissed all grounds of appeal. It found the victim's testimony credible and consistent, noting minor contradictions (e.g., school attendance) were not material to the core incident and were understandable given the 9-year lapse. The delay in complaint was justified due to the victim's age and inaction by his mother. The defence claim of personal animosity was rejected as the victim explicitly stated he informed his father himself. The medical evidence (healed anal tears) supported the victim's account. The Court upheld the High Court's conviction and sentence.
coa_sentence_type: Rigorous Imprisonment 14 years, Fine Rs. 20,000 with default penalty of 3 months, Compensation Rs. 200,000 to victim with default sentence of 6 months
brief_judgment_file_summary: The Accused-Appellant appealed his High Court conviction on one count of grave sexual abuse of a minor, for which he was sentenced to 14 years rigorous imprisonment, a fine, and compensation. The appeal grounds challenged the credibility of the child victim's evidence, the judge's reasoning, and alleged delay and improper motive for the complaint. The Court of Appeal found the victim's testimony credible and consistent, supported by medical evidence, and justified the delay. It dismissed the appeal, upholding the High Court's judgment.
defence_counsel: Asankada D. Mendis
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted on one count and acquitted on another. The Court of Appeal found no error in the High Court's reasoning, assessment of evidence, or dismissal of the defence's animosity claim.
precedents_cited_list: Bhoginbhai Hirjibhai V. State of Gujarat, AIR 1983 SC 753 | Don Kuruppu Arachchige Indika Gayan v The Republic of Sri Lanka, CA 205/2007 | Dhamasiri vs. The Republic of Sri Lanka 2012 (1) SLR 268 | Udagama Vs. AG 2000 (2) SLR 103
standard_of_review_applied: The Court reviewed the evidence and applied principles regarding witness credibility, delay in complaint, and belated evidence, as established in cited precedents.

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 364(2)(e) of the Penal Code punishable in terms of section 364(2) as amended by the Penal Code Amendment Act No. 22 of 1995
brief_facts_summary: The accused-appellant was convicted for raping a minor child in October 2008 at Marawila. The victim (PW-02), a 12-year-old at the time, went to the appellant's house to make a phone call. When alone, the appellant showed her a CD, removed her clothes, and forcibly raped her on a sofa. The victim initially did not report the incident but informed her sister 2-3 days later about being raped by her mother's paramour and subsequently, at the hospital, revealed the rape by the appellant. Medical evidence confirmed repeated sexual intercourse.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 364(2)(e) of the Penal Code punishable in terms of section 364(2) as amended by the Penal Code Amendment Act No. 22 of 1995
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court found the appellant guilty of raping a minor. After considering mitigatory and aggravating circumstances, the judge sentenced him to 15 years rigorous imprisonment, a fine of Rs. 25,000, and compensation of Rs. 250,000. The judgment noted procedural omissions regarding the compensation order.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant challenged the conviction and sentence on several grounds. Key arguments included infirmities in prosecution evidence, the prosecution's failure to call the victim's sister as a witness, impairment of fair trial due to an indefinite offence date in the indictment, wrongful rejection of defence evidence, and procedural errors by the High Court Judge in reading the indictment before serving it.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Did the learned High Court Judge err in not considering the infirmities in the prosecution evidence. | Did the learned High Court Judge fail to consider the importance of section 114 of the Evidence Ordinance as relevant when the prosecution failed to call the evidence of the sister of the victim as a witness for the prosecution. | Was the accused's entitlement for a fair trial impaired by the indefinite date of offence stated in the indictment. | Did the learned High Court Judge err by wrongly rejecting the defence evidence. | Did the learned High Court Judge's failure to act according to the required procedural steps cause a disadvantage to the accused.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal considered the totality of evidence, including the victim's testimony, JMO report, police statements, and defence witnesses. It found the victim's evidence cogent and trustworthy despite initial delay in reporting. The court noted the defence failed to properly challenge key prosecution witnesses on material points.
probability_assessment_by_court: Court assessed that prosecution proved case beyond reasonable doubt, found victim's evidence credible despite minor discrepancies, and held defence failed to create reasonable doubt.
defence_version_summary: Plea: Not guilty. The appellant denied the rape. He admitted the victim came to his house to make a call but claimed his wife was present, he gave his mobile phone outside the house, and nothing else happened. He called his wife and the victim's sister as defence witnesses. The court found the defence version not credible and noted failure to confront prosecution witnesses with his story.
legal_errors_description: The High Court Judge failed to specify to whom compensation should be paid and failed to impose a default sentence for non-payment of compensation.
procedural_defects_description: The indictment was read over to the appellant before it was served on him, contrary to sections 195 and 196 of the Code of Criminal Procedure Act. However, the COA found no prejudice or failure of justice resulted.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal conducted a comprehensive review. It first addressed grounds 2, 3, and 5, finding no merit: the prosecution's failure to call the victim's sister caused no prejudice as she testified for the defence; the indefinite offence date in the indictment did not mislead the appellant or cause prejudice; and the procedural error in reading the indictment early caused no material prejudice. On grounds 1 and 4, the COA upheld the HC's acceptance of the victim's evidence as credible and cogent, explaining the delay in reporting the appellant's involvement due to her traumatic circumstances. It noted the defence failed to cross-examine prosecution witnesses on key allegations (e.g., instigation by the mother). The COA applied precedents on delayed reporting and unconfronted evidence. It found no error in the HC's assessment of evidence or burden of proof. The appeal was dismissed, but the sentencing order was varied to clarify compensation payment to the victim and add a default sentence.
coa_sentence_type: 15 years rigorous imprisonment (deemed commenced from 26-06-2019), fine of Rs. 25,000, compensation of Rs. 250,000 payable to PW-02 (victim), with default sentence of 18 months simple imprisonment for non-payment of compensation.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused-appellant was convicted by the High Court of Chilaw for raping a minor in 2008 and sentenced to 15 years rigorous imprisonment, a fine, and compensation. He appealed on grounds including infirmities in prosecution evidence, procedural errors, and unfair trial due to an indefinite offence date. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal, finding the victim's evidence credible, no prejudice from procedural irregularities, and the defence case weak due to failure to cross-examine on material points. The COA varied the sentencing order to specify compensation payment to the victim and added a default sentence.
defence_counsel: Nalin Ladduwahetty, P.C. with Kavithri Ubeysekera
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court found the appellant guilty based on the victim's testimony and medical evidence, accepting her explanation for delayed reporting. The COA agreed with the HC's reasoning and credibility findings but identified and corrected omissions in the sentencing order regarding compensation details.
precedents_cited_list: James Silva Vs. The Republic of Sri Lanka (1980) 2 SLR 167 | Rex Vs. Dossi 13 Cr. App. R. 158 | D.R.M Pandithakoralage (Excise Inspector) Vs. V.K Selvanayagam 56 NLR 143 | D. Tikiribanda Vs. Attorney General, CA 64/2003 decided on 6-10-2009 reported in Bar Association Law Journal (2010) (B.L.R.) 92 | Mahathun and Others Vs. Attorney General (2015) 1 SLR 74 | Gamage Prabath Janaka Nayana Priyantha Perera Vs. Attorney General CA 107/2012 decided on 27-05-2016 | Sarwan Singh Vs. State of Punjab (2002) AIR S.C. iii 3652 | Pilippu Mandige Nalaka Krishantha Kumara Thisera Vs. AG, CA 87/2005 decided on 17-05-2007
standard_of_review_applied: The COA reviewed whether errors or irregularities occasioned a failure of justice or prejudiced substantial rights, as per Article 138 of the Constitution and section 436 of the Code of Criminal Procedure Act.
sentencing_principles_applied: The COA considered the High Court's assessment of mitigatory and aggravating circumstances and varied the order to clarify compensation payment and add a default sentence, ensuring justice.

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Sections 54(A)(d) and 54(A)(b) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance as amended by Act No. 13 of 1984
brief_facts_summary: On 11 January 2017, a police team from the Crime Prevention Unit of Wellawatta Police Station, while on routine duty, received information that a person named Chaturanga was selling heroin at Pasalwatte, Madampitiya. The team proceeded to the location, arrested the Appellant, and recovered 132 small packets of a brown substance from his shorts pocket. The substance, weighing 10.61 grams, tested positive for heroin. The Appellant was taken to Letchumi Jewellers to be weighed, then handed over to Grandpass Police Station.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 54(A)(d) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance as amended by Act No. 13 of 1984
hc_judgment_summary: After trial, the High Court convicted the Appellant only on the first count of possession of 3.78 grams of heroin and acquitted him on the trafficking count. The Learned High Court Judge imposed a sentence of life imprisonment on 21 January 2020.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The Appellant challenged the conviction, arguing the raid was false, the investigation was not fair, the trial judge failed to consider contradictions in the prosecution evidence, and the manifest false narrative of the raid was not considered.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The raid is false. | No fair investigation. | The contradictions inter se and per se not considered. | That the manifest false narrative of the raid was not considered.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The prosecution relied on police officers from the raiding team (PW1, PW2, PW5, PW6, PW8) and the Government Analyst report. The Court of Appeal found serious issues with the credibility of the raid and the evidence, including contradictions in PW1's testimony regarding recording information and weighing the drugs, and the failure to investigate leads or search the Appellant's house.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court found the timeline of weighing the drugs (taking 2.5 hours for a small amount) highly improbable. It also noted the failure to record the informant's tip and the contradictory reason for using a jeweller's shop instead of the police kit raised serious doubts, failing the 'probability test'.
defence_version_summary: The Appellant pleaded not guilty. The defence was a dock statement only. He claimed he did not possess the drugs and suggested the police had first arrested a person named 'Dhamma' and recovered drugs from a toilet ceiling near Dhamma's house, not from him.
legal_errors_description: The High Court failed to properly consider contradictions in prosecution evidence, the improbability of the raid narrative, and the burden of proof. It did not adequately assess the impact of the defence's claim regarding another arrest on the same day.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the prosecution failed to prove the case beyond reasonable doubt. It highlighted multiple issues: the raid began without specific information; the informant's tip was not recorded; taking 2.5 hours to weigh 10.61 grams of substance at a jeweller's shop was improbable; PW1 gave contradictory reasons for not using the police weighing kit; and the police failed to investigate the Appellant's house or his source. Crucially, the defence's submission of a Magistrate's Court record showing PW1 arrested another suspect for drugs in the same area on the same day created serious doubt, which PW1 had denied. The Court held the trial judge did not properly evaluate these doubts and probabilities.
coa_sentence_type: Acquitted. Conviction and sentence set aside.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The Accused-Appellant was convicted in the High Court of Colombo for possession of 3.78g of heroin and sentenced to life imprisonment. He appealed to the Court of Appeal. The COA found the prosecution failed to prove the case beyond reasonable doubt, citing serious improbabilities in the raid narrative, contradictions in police testimony, and the emergence of evidence suggesting another arrest for drugs was made by the same officer on the same day. The Court allowed the appeal, set aside the conviction and sentence, and acquitted the Appellant.
defence_counsel: Hafeel Farisz with Sanjeewa Kodithuwakku
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted the Appellant for possession based on the prosecution evidence. The COA found the HC erred by not properly scrutinizing the contradictions and improbabilities in the prosecution's case, and by failing to consider the reasonable doubt raised by the defence regarding another arrest on the same day.
precedents_cited_list: Mohamed Ninmaz V. Attorney General CA/95/94 | Attorney-General v. Rawther 25 NLR 385 [1987] 1 SLR 155 | Miller v. Minister of Pensions (1947) 2 All E.R. 372 | R v. Hepworth 1928 (AD) 265
standard_of_review_applied: The Court reviewed whether the prosecution proved its case beyond reasonable doubt, applying the principle that the burden never shifts from the prosecution and that the evidence must establish guilt to a high degree of probability.

judges: Menaka Wijesundera, J | Wickum A. Kaluarachchi, J
offence_sections: 1. House trespass under Section 434 of the Penal Code read with Section 32. 2. Attempted murder under Section 300 of the Penal Code read with Section 32. 3. Grievous hurt under Section 317 of the Penal Code read with section 32.
offence_category: House Trespass, Attempted Murder, Grievous Hurt
brief_facts_summary: On 6th October 2005 around 2:00 am, two accused broke into the house of PW-2 and PW-3. The 1st accused-appellant assaulted PW-2 with a cutting weapon (sword) causing injuries to his mouth. The 2nd accused shot PW-3 causing gunshot injuries. Both accused then fled, threatening the victims not to disclose their names. The accused were known to the victims from the same village since childhood.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: 1. House trespass under Section 434 of the Penal Code read with Section 32. 2. Attempted murder under Section 300 of the Penal Code read with Section 32. 3. Grievous hurt under Section 317 of the Penal Code read with section 32.
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court Judge convicted both accused on all three charges after trial. The 2nd accused absconded, and the trial proceeded in his absence. The Judge sentenced both accused.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant argued that his identification was not established, the prosecution failed to prove the case beyond reasonable doubt, and the doctrine of common intention could not be applied.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The identification of the 1st accused-appellant had not been established. | The prosecution has not proved the case beyond a reasonable doubt. | Common intention doctrine cannot be applied in this case.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found PW-3's identification evidence cogent and reliable. She knew both accused from childhood, switched on a light, and identified them despite their faces being covered. Her evidence was corroborated by her immediate statement to PW-1 and the history given to the doctor.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal held that PW-3's evidence established the appellant's identity beyond reasonable doubt. No other evidence was needed.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty. He neither gave evidence nor made a statement from the dock. The only defence witness, a Senior Superintendent of Police, could not produce the file he was asked for. There was no substantive defence evidence.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal rejected all grounds of appeal. It found PW-3's identification of the appellant was clear and reliable, as she knew him from childhood and identified him with the aid of light. The prosecution case was proved beyond reasonable doubt. The doctrine of common intention applied as both accused arrived together armed, committed different criminal acts (shooting and cutting) in furtherance of their common intention to attack the victims, and left together after threatening them. The High Court Judge's analysis was correct.
coa_sentence_type: Affirmed the conviction and sentence imposed by the High Court.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The 1st accused-appellant appealed his High Court conviction and sentence for house trespass, attempted murder, and grievous hurt. The High Court had convicted him and an absconding co-accused after trial. The appellant challenged identification, proof beyond reasonable doubt, and application of common intention. The Court of Appeal found PW-3's identification evidence cogent and reliable, upheld the prosecution case, and affirmed that common intention was established from the accused's joint armed entry and attack. The appeal was dismissed, and the High Court's judgment was affirmed.
defence_counsel: Epa Aruna Shantha with Dammika Perera and Navindu Kalansooriya
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court Judge correctly analyzed the prosecution evidence, convicted both accused on all charges, and sentenced them. The Court of Appeal found no reason to interfere with this judgment.
precedents_cited_list: Queen V. Mahatun – 61 NLR 540 | Queen V. Vincent Fernando and two others - 65 NLR 265
standard_of_review_applied: The Court assessed whether the High Court judgment was correct based on the evidence and application of law.

judges: Menaka Wijesundera J. | Wickum A. Kaluarachchi J.
brief_facts_summary: The appellant was indicted for raping a girl less than sixteen years of age. The victim's version was that the appellant came to her house, sent her younger sister away, and she lost consciousness. She later found herself unclothed. She did not tell anyone for months due to threats. Her pregnancy was discovered six months later during a doctor's visit, after which a complaint was lodged. The victim's sister did not corroborate the victim's story, and the victim's account contained inconsistencies.
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court of Anuradhapura convicted the appellant for the offence of rape of a girl less than sixteen years of age on 27.08.2020. The specific sentence and fine details are not mentioned in the provided judgment text.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant's counsel raised four main grounds: the trial judge failed to consider the improbability of the victim's story, failed to consider the belatedness of the first complaint, the prosecution failed to prove a specific date of offence, and the trial judge did not consider the defence adequately. The appeal argued the prosecution failed to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The trial judge had failed to consider the improbability in the story of PW1 | The trial judge had failed to consider the belatedness of the 1st complaint by the victim | The prosecution had failed to prove a specific date of offence | The trial judge had not considered the defense adequately.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court found the victim's evidence inconsistent and improbable. The sister, who was allegedly present, did not corroborate the victim. There was a six-month delay in lodging the complaint, and the victim's account of being unconscious yet later describing events created doubt. The investigative officer noted the victim was visibly pregnant when her statement was recorded.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court found the victim's version created a reasonable doubt due to inconsistencies, lack of corroboration from the sister, and the six-month delay in complaint. The prosecution failed to prove its case beyond a reasonable doubt.
defence_version_summary: The appellant gave evidence on oath and denied the entire incident. The defence was that the victim's story was improbable and inconsistent. The trial judge failed to adequately consider the defence case.
legal_errors_description: The Court found the conviction was erroneous and bad in law because the trial judge failed to consider the improbabilities in the prosecution story and the defence case, thereby violating the cardinal rule that prosecution must prove its case beyond reasonable doubt.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the victim's evidence inconsistent and improbable, lacking corroboration. The six-month delay in lodging the first complaint, without satisfactory explanation, created serious doubt. Relying on precedents (Padmathilake and Haramanis), the Court held that a conviction based on such unreliable evidence was dangerous and unfair. The trial judge erred by not properly evaluating the evidence's credibility and the defence's case, failing to ensure the prosecution proved its case beyond reasonable doubt.
coa_sentence_type: Sentence and conviction set aside
brief_judgment_file_summary: The appellant was convicted by the High Court of Anuradhapura for raping a girl under sixteen. He appealed on grounds including improbability of the victim's story, belated complaint, lack of specific offence date, and inadequate consideration of defence. The Court of Appeal found the victim's evidence inconsistent and uncorroborated, with an unexplained six-month delay in complaint. Citing precedents on witness reliability and timely complaints, the Court held the prosecution failed to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt. The appeal was allowed, the conviction and sentence were set aside, and the appellant was acquitted.
defence_counsel: Darshana Kuruppu with Sahan Weerasinghe
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted the appellant based on the victim's testimony. The Court of Appeal found the High Court judge failed to consider the improbabilities in the prosecution story, the belated complaint, and the defence case adequately, leading to an erroneous conviction.
precedents_cited_list: Padmathilake vs Director General Commission to Investigate Bribery and Corruption 2009 2SLR | Haramanis vs Somalatha 3 Sri L.R. 365
standard_of_review_applied: Evaluation of whether the prosecution proved its case beyond reasonable doubt, assessing witness credibility and consistency.

judges: Menaka Wijesundera, J | Wickum A. Kaluarachchchi, J
offence_sections: Section 54A(b) and 54A(d) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance as amended by Act No.13 of 1984
location_of_offence: near the mosque situated close to the playground called 'Somaliyawa', Heinamulla camp area
brief_facts_summary: On 24.07.2014, IP Mahinda Wanasinghe (PW-1) received information that a bearded man named Kasun would bring heroin near a mosque. A police team of twelve officers, including PW-1 in uniform, went to the location. They observed a person matching the description who turned back upon seeing them. The team chased and caught him. A search of his trouser pocket revealed a light pink cellophane bag containing a light brown powder, later identified as heroin weighing 2.64 grams. He was arrested at 15:15 p.m. The heroin was sealed, weighed at the Dedigama Pawning Centre, and taken to the Colombo Crimes Division.
evidence_type_primary: Physical evidence (heroin recovered from accused's pocket)
evidence_type_secondary: Police testimony regarding the raid, arrest, and recovery
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 54A(b) and 54A(d) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance as amended by Act No.13 of 1984
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court Judge convicted the accused-appellant on both counts of trafficking and possessing 2.64 grams of heroin. The Judge stated the prosecution proved the charges beyond a reasonable doubt, found no discrepancies in prosecution evidence, and rejected the accused's dock statement. The accused was sentenced to life imprisonment for both counts.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant's counsel challenged the convictions on multiple grounds, including improbabilities and contradictions in the prosecution story, discrepancies in witness testimonies (e.g., timing of events, whether handcuffs were taken, location of detection), unusual note-making by PW-2, failure to search the accused's house, and the Trial Judge's failure to analyze evidence and provide reasons for the decision. It was also argued the conviction for trafficking was based on an erroneous legal basis (quantity implying intent).
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Timing discrepancies make prosecution story improbable | Failure to search accused's house after arrest makes story improbable | Contradiction between PW-1 and PW-2 on whether handcuffs were taken for the raid | Contradiction between PW-1 and PW-2 on location of detection (by road vs. main road) | Unusual method of note-making by PW-2 (on crime pad, pasted three days later) | Main investigating officer (PW-1) being in uniform during raid argued as unusual | High Court Judge failed to analyze prosecution evidence and consider contradictions | High Court Judge rejected dock statement for an invalid reason (not complaining to higher officer) | Conviction for trafficking based on wrong legal premise (quantity implying intent, not proving an act of trafficking) | Judgment not compliant with Section 283(1) of CCPA (lacks points for determination and reasons)
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found significant contradictions in prosecution witness testimonies (PW-1 and PW-2) regarding key details like timing, location of arrest, and whether handcuffs were taken. The High Court Judge failed to analyze these discrepancies or give reasons for rejecting them. The chain of custody for the heroin was not a major point of challenge in the appeal arguments.
probability_assessment_by_court: Court of Appeal found the prosecution story improbable due to timing discrepancies and other contradictions, creating reasonable doubt.
defence_version_summary: The accused-appellant pleaded not guilty. He made a dock statement claiming he was arrested without any reason. He did not call any defence witnesses. The High Court Judge rejected his dock statement for the invalid reason that he did not complain to a higher police officer. The Court of Appeal found the Trial Judge failed to properly consider this statement.
legal_errors_description: The High Court Judge erred in law by convicting for trafficking based on the quantity of heroin (implying intent for trafficking) rather than proving an act specified in the definition of 'traffick'. The Judge also erred in rejecting the dock statement for an invalid reason (failure to complain to a higher officer).
procedural_defects_description: The High Court Judgment did not comply with Section 283(1) of the CCPA as it lacked the points for determination and the reasons for the decision. It was written without analyzing the prosecution evidence.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal held the High Court Judge failed to analyze the prosecution evidence, disregarded material contradictions between PW-1 and PW-2 (timing, handcuffs, location), and gave no reasons for finding no discrepancies. The Judge wrongly rejected the dock statement based on the accused's failure to complain to a higher officer—a flawed reasoning given the suspect's remand status. The conviction for trafficking was based on an erroneous legal foundation (quantity implying intent). The Judgment did not meet the requirements of Section 283(1) CCPA. Considering the ten-year lapse since the offence, the appellant's five-year incarceration, and the principle that an act of the court shall prejudice no man (Actus Curiae Neminem Gravabit), the COA refused a retrial, allowed the appeal, and acquitted the appellant.
coa_sentence_type: Acquitted. No sentence imposed.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused-appellant was convicted by the Colombo High Court for trafficking and possessing 2.64 grams of heroin and sentenced to life imprisonment. He appealed. The Court of Appeal identified serious flaws: the High Court Judge failed to analyze evidence, disregarded witness contradictions, rejected the dock statement for an invalid reason, based the trafficking conviction on an erroneous legal premise, and delivered a judgment non-compliant with procedural law. The COA found the prosecution story improbable due to discrepancies. Applying precedents on retrials and considering the ten-year delay, the COA allowed the appeal, set aside the convictions and sentences, and acquitted the appellant, refusing a retrial.
defence_counsel: R. Arsecularatne, PC with Ms. Chamindri Arsecularatne, U. Muhandiramge, Tharindu Punchihewa, Pasindu Gamage, Punsi Gamage and Eranga Yakandawala
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court Judge concluded the prosecution proved its case beyond reasonable doubt without analyzing the evidence or addressing contradictions pointed out by the defence. The Judge rejected the dock statement for the invalid reason that the accused did not complain to a higher police officer. The COA found this reasoning flawed and the overall judgment lacking in legal analysis.
precedents_cited_list: Nandana V. Attorney General – (2008) 1 Sri L.R. 51 | Peter Singho V. Werapottya – 55 NLR 157 | Queen V. Jayasinghe - 69 NLR 413 | L.C. Fernando V. Republic of Sri Lanka – 79 (2) NLR 313 at 374
standard_of_review_applied: Review of whether the High Court judgment was in accordance with law and whether the prosecution proved its case beyond reasonable doubt, considering evidence and procedural compliance.
sentencing_principles_applied: Principles regarding ordering a retrial: considering the nature of evidence, time elapsed since offence, period of incarceration already suffered, and trauma of a second trial (citing Nandana V. Attorney General).

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 365B(2)(b) of the Penal Code as amended by Penal Code Amendment Act No. 22 of 1995, 29 of 1998 and 16 of 2006
offence_category: Sexual abuse of a minor (grave sexual abuse)
brief_facts_summary: The accused-appellant was charged with grave sexual abuse of a 12-year-old minor girl by having intercrural sex with her for sexual gratification. The incident occurred at the victim's home when she was alone. The appellant was a frequent visitor known to the victim and her family. The victim later reported the incident to her grandmother and a police complaint was initiated after a 119-call. The accused denied the allegations, claiming he was arrested for a different quarrel.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 365B(2)(b) of the Penal Code as amended by Penal Code Amendment Act No. 22 of 1995, 29 of 1998 and 16 of 2006
hc_sentence_type: 14 years rigorous imprisonment, fine, and compensation
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court found the appellant guilty of the offence and sentenced him to 14 years rigorous imprisonment, a fine of Rs.10,000, and compensation of Rs.200,000 to the victim. The court found the victim's evidence credible despite some inconsistencies.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant argued that the High Court failed to properly evaluate the evidence of the victim, particularly regarding inconsistencies between her statements. It was also contended that the prosecution failed to prove the exact date of the offence beyond a reasonable doubt.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The learned High Court Judge has failed to evaluate the evidence of PW-01 properly, and thereby had failed to give the benefit of the doubt to the accused appellant. | The prosecution has failed to prove the date of offence and had led conflicting evidence with regard to the date of offence.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court evaluated the victim's evidence as credible, considering her age, social background, and time lapse. Discrepancies regarding details of the act and date were deemed minor and not material to the core case.
probability_assessment_by_court: Court held the victim's evidence was trustworthy, inconsistencies were minor and did not create reasonable doubt.
defence_version_summary: The accused pleaded not guilty, made a statement from the dock denying any knowledge of the incident, claiming he was arrested for a different quarrel involving assault. The defence did not call witnesses. The court found his defence created no doubt in the prosecution case.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal held that the date mentioned in the indictment is not material unless it is of the essence or the accused is misled. The inability of a child victim to recall the exact date does not create reasonable doubt. The court considered the victim's evidence as a whole and found it credible, consistent, and sufficient for conviction despite minor discrepancies. The trial judge's evaluation of evidence was correct, and the conviction and sentence were justified.
coa_sentence_type: 14 years rigorous imprisonment, fine of Rs.10,000, compensation of Rs.200,000 affirmed. Sentence deemed to commence from conviction date (24-01-2020).
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused was convicted of grave sexual abuse of a minor under section 365B(2)(b) and sentenced to 14 years rigorous imprisonment, a fine, and compensation by the High Court. He appealed on grounds of improper evidence evaluation and failure to prove the exact offence date. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal, upholding the conviction and sentence, finding the victim's evidence credible and minor discrepancies immaterial.
defence_counsel: Kamal Perera with A. Fernando
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court considered the victim's evidence credible despite inconsistencies and found the prosecution proved its case beyond reasonable doubt. The COA agreed with the HC's reasoning and evaluation.
precedents_cited_list: R. Vs. Dossi 12 Cr. App. R., 158 | D.R.M Pandithacoralage Vs. V.K Selvenayagam 56 NLR 143 | D. Tikiri Banda Vs. The Attorney General, Bar Association Law Reports 2010 (B.L.R. 92) | Attorney General Vs. Dardadagamage Chandraratna Jayawardene alias Shantha, CA 85/2013 decided on 25-05-2018 | State of Uttar Pradesh Vs. M.K Anthoney (1984) S.C.J 236-1985 Cri. L.J. 493 at 498
standard_of_review_applied: Appellate court must give due weight to trial court's evidence appreciation unless there are weighty reasons to reject it.

judges: Menaka Wijesundera, J. | Wickum A. Kaluarachchi, J.
brief_facts_summary: The accused was indicted for two charges of abduction and three charges of grave sexual abuse against a child victim. The incidents occurred when the victim was in year three, between 1.1.2002 and 5.12.2002. The victim gave evidence reluctantly after 18 years, stating the appellant had taken her to the jungle and sexually abused her. Medical evidence corroborated her account, showing redness in the vaginal area indicative of intervention.
hc_judgment_summary: The trial judge convicted the appellant on all charges after evaluating the evidence, including the victim's reluctant testimony and medical corroboration. The judge was mindful of the 18-year delay and the victim's reluctance, but found the evidence sufficient for conviction.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant's counsel argued that the trial judge failed to evaluate prosecution evidence correctly, wrongly considered the dock statement, and that the prosecution failed to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The trial judge had failed to evaluate the evidence of the prosecution in the correct perspective. | The dock statement had been wrongly considered. | The prosecution had failed to prove its case beyond a reasonable doubt.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the trial judge had properly analyzed the victim's evidence, considering the 18-year delay and her reluctance. The judge had the advantage of observing her demeanor. Medical evidence corroborated the victim's account.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court held that a criminal case cannot be proved with mathematical accuracy by human witnesses, and considered the time lapse and victim's reluctance in its assessment.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty, made a statement from the dock denying the incident entirely, and called no witnesses. The trial judge analyzed and rejected the dock statement with reasons.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the trial judge had correctly evaluated the evidence, considering the victim's reluctance due to the 18-year delay and her changed circumstances. The judge had the advantage of observing witness demeanor. The COA cited Oliver Dayananda alias Raja vs Republic of Sri Lanka, noting criminal cases cannot be proved with mathematical accuracy. The dock statement was adequately considered and rejected. The appeal was dismissed, but sentences were reduced considering the passage of time.
coa_sentence_type: Concurrent imprisonment terms: 1st charge - 1 year RI, 2nd charge - 7 years RI, 3rd charge - 1 year RI, 4th charge - 7 years RI, 5th charge - same as above. All terms to run concurrently from 1st April 2021. Fines remain as imposed by HC.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused-appellant appealed against his conviction by the High Court of Ratnapura for two charges of abduction and three of grave sexual abuse against a child victim. The High Court convicted him based on the victim's reluctant testimony after 18 years and medical corroboration. The appellant argued the trial judge failed to evaluate evidence correctly, wrongly considered his dock statement, and that the prosecution failed to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt. The Court of Appeal found the trial judge properly evaluated the evidence, considering the delay and victim's demeanor, and dismissed the appeal on conviction grounds. However, it reduced the imprisonment sentences considering the time elapsed since the 2002 incident.
defence_counsel: Ashanthi De Almeida
hc_analysis_summary: The COA found the trial judge had properly analyzed the evidence, was mindful of the legal principles and the victim's reluctance due to the long delay, and had the advantage of observing witness demeanor. No errors were identified in the HC's reasoning.
precedents_cited_list: Oliver Dayananda alias Raja vs Republic of Sri Lanka CA 28-2009 decided on 13.02.2013 by Justice Sisira De Abrew
standard_of_review_applied: The Court considered whether the trial judge evaluated the evidence correctly and was mindful of the trial judge's advantage in observing witness demeanor.
sentencing_principles_applied: The Court considered the passage of time since the 2002 incident and its impact on the lives of both victim and appellant in reducing the sentences.

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: section 403 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The accused-appellant, a retired bank manager, was indicted for cheating Grace Nirmala Balachandran (PW-01) by promising to provide her a house in a twin house construction project on land purchased jointly with PW-02. PW-01, a secretary at the University of Jaffna nearing retirement, gave the appellant money from 2002 onwards for the construction. After the ground floor was completed, she occupied it. However, the appellant failed to transfer the title as agreed. A dispute over utility bills led to her eviction, and she complained to the police. The prosecution case included witness testimonies and bank records of money transfers.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: section 403 of the Penal Code
hc_sentence_type: 2 years rigorous imprisonment suspended for 10 years, and a fine of Rs. 10,000/- with a default sentence of 6 months simple imprisonment
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court found the appellant guilty of cheating PW-01. Considering aggravating/mitigating circumstances, the lengthy duration of the case, and the appellant's age, the judge imposed a suspended sentence instead of incarceration. The court also ordered compensation of Rs. 4,000,000/- for PW-01, to be recovered as a fine if unpaid, with a default sentence of 2 years rigorous imprisonment.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appeal argued the High Court judge failed to consider matters favourable to the accused and contradictions in the main witnesses' evidence. It contended the prosecution did not prove the case beyond reasonable doubt, especially regarding the amounts allegedly cheated. A separate ground challenged the compensation order as contrary to law.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The learned High Court Judge has not considered the matters favourable to the accused in his judgment. | The learned High Court Judge has not considered the inter se and per se contradictions of main witnesses. | The prosecution has not proved the case beyond reasonable doubt. | Without prejudice to the above grounds of appeal, the compensation ordered by the learned High Court Judge was contrary to law.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the testimonies of PW-01, PW-02, and PW-03 were credible and corroborated the core allegation: PW-01 gave money to the appellant expecting title to part of the house. The appellant did not materially challenge this version. Minor discrepancies in PW-01's evidence were considered understandable given the time lapse and her circumstances.
probability_assessment_by_court: The court assessed that the prosecution proved its case beyond reasonable doubt, establishing a causal nexus between the appellant's deception and PW-01 parting with her money.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty. He gave evidence under oath, admitting receipt of some money (Rs. 729,773/- and Rs.100,000/-) but claimed part was an advance rent payment and denied any agreement to transfer title. The court found his version not credible and noted his failure to challenge material points of prosecution witnesses in cross-examination.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal conducted a thorough analysis of the evidence and legal requirements for cheating under section 403 of the Penal Code. It found the prosecution proved the essential ingredients: the appellant deceived PW-01 with a promise to provide a house, dishonestly induced her to deliver money, and caused her loss. The testimonies of PW-01, PW-02, and PW-03 were consistent on the core agreement and money flow. The court rejected arguments about witness contradictions and credibility, attributing minor discrepancies to the passage of time and PW-01's understandable reluctance. It affirmed the High Court's factual findings and legal application. On compensation, it held the High Court had power under section 17(4) of the Code of Criminal Procedure Act and the amount was fair. The appeal was dismissed.
coa_sentence_type: The appeal was dismissed. The suspended sentence imposed by the High Court (2 years rigorous imprisonment suspended for 10 years, fine of Rs.10,000/- with default sentence of 6 months simple imprisonment) was upheld. The suspended sentence was directed to commence from the date the appeal judgment is pronounced to the appellant.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused-appellant, a retired bank manager, was convicted in the High Court of Colombo for cheating Grace Nirmala Balachandran (PW-01) under section 403 of the Penal Code by promising her a house in exchange for money. The High Court imposed a suspended sentence and ordered substantial compensation. The appellant appealed, challenging the conviction, witness credibility, and the compensation order. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal, finding the prosecution proved the case beyond reasonable doubt, the witnesses were credible, and the compensation was lawfully ordered and reasonable. The High Court's judgment and sentence were upheld.
defence_counsel: Anil Silva, P.C. with Amaan Bandara instructed by M/S Tharmarajah Tharmaja
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court correctly analyzed the evidence, found the appellant guilty of cheating, and considered relevant factors for sentencing and compensation. The Court of Appeal found no error in the High Court's reasoning or application of law.
precedents_cited_list: Carey Vs. de Silva (1887) 1 C.L.Rep. 49 | Silva (1933) II Times of Cey. 57 | Clucas (1949) 2 K.B. 266 (cited in G.L. Peiris) | Zahir Vs. Cooray (1941) 42 NLR 263 | Sarwan Singh Vs. State of Punjab 2002 AIR Supreme Court iii 3652 at 36755,3656 | Boby Mathew Vs. State of Karnataka 2004 3 Cri. L. J. 3003 | Pilippu Mandige Nalaka Krishantha Kumara Thisera Vs. A.G CA 87/2005 decided on 17-05-2007
standard_of_review_applied: The Court reviewed whether the prosecution proved the charge beyond reasonable doubt, whether the High Court considered evidence properly, and whether the sentence/compensation was lawful and reasonable.
sentencing_principles_applied: The Court considered the need for just compensation to the victim, the nature of the deceit, the loss suffered, the time taken for the case, and the appellant's age. The power to award compensation under section 17(4) of the Code of Criminal Procedure Act was affirmed.

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Sections 54(A)(b) and 54(A)(d) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance as amended by Act No. 13 of 1984
location_of_offence: Stacepura Road near a Buddha statue
brief_facts_summary: On 04/11/2015, police officers on routine mobile patrol saw the Appellant standing near a Buddha statue on Stacepura Road. Upon seeing them, she began walking towards her house, arousing suspicion. She was stopped and searched, and a pink cellophane bag containing a brown substance was found in her hand. The substance tested positive for heroin, and she was arrested. The gross quantity recovered was 10 grams, later analyzed as 3.85 grams of heroin.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Sections 54(A)(b) and 54(A)(d) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance as amended by Act No. 13 of 1984
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court found the Appellant guilty only on the second count (Possession) and imposed a sentence of life imprisonment on 14/09/2018. The conviction was based on the evidence of the police raid and the recovery of heroin from the Appellant.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appeal was based on two main grounds: (1) the prosecution case does not satisfy the test of probability, and (2) the rejection of the defence evidence on a wrong premise. Specific arguments included the improbability of the police timeline, the Appellant's nervousness upon seeing plainclothes officers, and the trial judge's failure to properly consider the Appellant's dock statement and the fact that the arresting officer knew her previously.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The case for the prosecution does not satisfy the test of probability. | The rejection of the defence evidence on wrong premise.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The prosecution called PW1, PW2, PW5, PW7, and PW9. The defence called the Appellant's husband. The Court of Appeal found the prosecution's timeline improbable and raised doubts about the police's actions and their prior knowledge of the Appellant.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal found the prosecution's story improbable, specifically the over one-hour delay to weigh a small amount of substance and the Appellant's alleged nervousness upon seeing plainclothes officers she did not know were police.
defence_version_summary: The Appellant pleaded not guilty. She made a statement from the dock and called one defence witness (her husband). The Court of Appeal found the trial judge improperly rejected her dock statement merely because it was unsworn and not cross-examined, and failed to consider the defence evidence on equal footing.
legal_errors_description: The High Court Judge failed to consider the defence evidence properly, rejected the dock statement on the wrong premise (that it was unsworn and not cross-examined), and did not evaluate the probability factors of the prosecution case.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed the probability of the prosecution's case, finding the timeline of events (over an hour to weigh 10 grams) highly improbable. It criticized the High Court Judge for not considering the defence evidence equally, especially the dock statement and the fact that PW1 knew the Appellant previously. The COA held that the prosecution failed to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt, as the burden never shifts from the prosecution. The conviction was therefore unsafe.
coa_sentence_type: Acquitted, no sentence imposed.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The Accused-Appellant was convicted in the High Court of Colombo for possession of 3.85 grams of heroin and sentenced to life imprisonment. She appealed on grounds including the improbability of the prosecution case and wrongful rejection of defence evidence. The Court of Appeal found the prosecution's narrative improbable, noted the trial judge's failure to properly assess the defence case and dock statement, and held the prosecution failed to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt. The appeal was allowed, the conviction and sentence were set aside, and the Appellant was acquitted.
defence_counsel: Amila Palliyage with Sandeepani Wijesooriya, Sawani Udugampola, Lakitha Wakishta Arachchi and Subaj De Silva
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted based on police evidence. The Court of Appeal found the HC judgment flawed for not considering the improbability of the prosecution case, not properly evaluating the defence evidence and dock statement, and for causing prejudice to the Appellant by rejecting her statement on technical grounds.
precedents_cited_list: Mohamed Ninnaz V. Attorney General CA/95/94 | Attorney-General v. Rawther 25 NLR 385 | Miller v. Minister of Pensions (1947) 2 All E.R. 372 | R v. Hepworth 1928 (AD) 265
standard_of_review_applied: Whether the prosecution proved its case beyond reasonable doubt; evaluation of evidence and probability.

judges: Menaka Wijesundera J. | Wickum A. Kaluarachchi J.
offence_sections: section 354 and 365 (B ) of the Penal Code
location_of_offence: Near railway line from Nugegoda to down south and at the appellant's house
brief_facts_summary: The victim, aged eight at the time of the offence, stated she was taken by an uncle in a three-wheeler, driven to his house, and sexually abused. The appellant was arrested after the victim and her mother identified him. The prosecution's case relied heavily on the victim's dock identification and the mother's evidence.
evidence_type_secondary: Mother's testimony, medical evidence (via doctor reading another doctor's notes)
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: section 354 and 365 (B ) of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the appellant based on the victim's evidence, which the trial judge interpreted as showing the appellant was well-known to her. The trial judge concluded the appellant committed the offences.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant argued the trial judge failed to properly consider the dock identification and failed to assess the prosecution evidence in its proper perspective, leading to an unsafe conviction.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The trial judge had failed to consider the dock identification of the appellant. | The trial judge has not considered the evidence of the prosecution in its proper perspective.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the victim's evidence sounded artificial and false, and the mother's evidence contained contradictions. The prosecution's story created reasonable doubt.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court found the probability factor of the prosecution story doubtful, creating reasonable doubt. The victim's evidence was deemed artificial.
defence_version_summary: The appellant made a dock statement claiming he knew the victim's mother, had a relationship with her, and the story was concocted by her. The appellant pleaded not guilty. The court found his version created doubt alongside the prosecution's unreliable evidence.
legal_errors_description: The trial judge failed to properly analyze the dock identification, glossed over contradictions and omissions, and based the conclusion on superficial reasoning without proper legal analysis.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the trial judge's reasoning superficial and lacking proper legal analysis. The victim's evidence was deemed artificial and possibly coached, and contradictions in the mother's evidence were not properly considered. The prosecution's story created reasonable doubt. The evidence did not substantiate the trial judge's assumption that the victim knew the appellant. Therefore, the conviction was unsafe.
coa_sentence_type: Acquitted, no sentence imposed.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused-appellant was convicted in the High Court of Colombo under sections 354 and 365(B) of the Penal Code for sexually abusing a child. He appealed on grounds including failure to properly consider dock identification. The Court of Appeal found the victim's evidence artificial and contradictory, the mother's evidence dubious, and the trial judge's reasoning flawed. The prosecution's case created reasonable doubt. The appeal was allowed, and the appellant was acquitted.
defence_counsel: Shanaka Ranasinghe P.C. with Mihindukulasooriya and Sandamali Peiris
hc_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the High Court judge's affirmations on the probability of the prosecution story lacked merit. The judge glossed over contradictions and omissions, and the reasoning was superficial, void of proper legal analysis.
standard_of_review_applied: Review of evidence and reasoning of the trial judge for errors and sufficiency.

judges: Menaka Wijesundera, J | Wickum A. Kaluarachchi, J
offence_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The 2nd accused-appellant was indicted for murder along with two others for assaulting the deceased with clubs on 24.03.1996. Eyewitnesses PW-1 and PW-2 saw the assault and took the deceased to hospital where he died seven days later. The prosecution relied on a dying declaration recorded by police and eyewitness testimony. The defence challenged the evidence and presented an alternative version of events.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the 1st and 2nd accused of murder and imposed the death sentence. The Judge relied on the dying declaration and eyewitness evidence to conclude the charge was proved beyond reasonable doubt.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant argued the Trial Judge misdirected himself on facts and law, wrongly relied on the dying declaration, and that even if the prosecution story was true, the conviction should only be for culpable homicide not murder. The defence also challenged the use of a confessionary statement and contradictions in evidence.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Misdirection on facts and law | Wrong reliance on dying declaration | Charge should be culpable homicide not murder | Use of inadmissible confessionary statement | Contradictions between dying declaration and eyewitness evidence | Failure to consider defence evidence
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found vital contradictions between the dying declaration and eyewitness evidence regarding the place of assault. The dying declaration was inconsistent with medical evidence showing no head injury. Defence evidence was rejected by the High Court on an erroneous basis.
probability_assessment_by_court: Court found reasonable doubt due to contradictions between dying declaration, eyewitness evidence, and medical evidence.
defence_version_summary: The 2nd accused-appellant gave evidence on oath denying the murder charge. He presented a defence witness (his mother). The defence argued the deceased was assaulted only by the 1st accused. The High Court rejected the defence evidence erroneously.
legal_errors_description: The High Court Judge misdirected himself on the admissibility of hearsay evidence, used an inadmissible confessionary statement to reject defence evidence, and failed to properly analyze contradictions in prosecution evidence.
procedural_defects_description: The Trial Judge used a portion of a police statement not led in evidence and a confessionary statement inadmissible under Section 25(1) of the Evidence Ordinance to reject defence evidence.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the prosecution case had vital infirmities. There were contradictions between the dying declaration and eyewitness evidence on the place of assault. The dying declaration was improbable given medical evidence of no head injury. The High Court Judge erred in law regarding hearsay evidence admissibility and procedurally by using an inadmissible confessionary statement to reject defence evidence. The defence evidence was not properly considered, and reasonable doubt existed. The conviction was therefore unsafe.
coa_sentence_type: Acquitted of murder charge
brief_judgment_file_summary: The 2nd accused-appellant appealed his murder conviction and death sentence imposed by the Chilaw High Court. The Court of Appeal found the prosecution case flawed with contradictions between the dying declaration and eyewitness accounts, and the dying declaration inconsistent with medical evidence. The High Court made legal errors in admitting hearsay and using an inadmissible confessionary statement to reject defence evidence. The Court of Appeal allowed the appeal, set aside the conviction and death sentence, and acquitted the appellant.
defence_counsel: Anil Silva, PC
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court relied on the dying declaration and eyewitness evidence to convict. The COA found the HC failed to consider vital contradictions in evidence, misapplied the law on hearsay and dying declarations, and erroneously rejected defence evidence using an inadmissible statement.
