Emanis - 42 NLR 166 | Dudh Nath pandey V. The State of U.P., 1981 AIR 911, 1981 SCR (2) 771 | Anthony Michael Morril V. Attorney General – Court of Appeal Case No. CA 26/06, decided on 25.05.2010
standard_of_review_applied: Review of errors of law and fact, assessment of whether prosecution proved case beyond reasonable doubt.

judges: Menaka Wijesundera J. | Wickum A. Kaluarachchi J.
offence_sections: provisions of the Poisons Opium and Dangerous drugs Ordinance
brief_facts_summary: Police Narcotics Bureau officers received a tip-off about the appellant and waited for him at St Johns Market in Colombo. Upon his arrival around 6-7pm, he was searched and 15.68 grammes of heroin were allegedly found. The appellant was arrested, and a subsequent search of his houses resulted in the recovery of jewelry and money, which were later handed over to his sister.
evidence_type_secondary: Government Analyst Report, Eyewitness testimony (PNB officers)
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: provisions of the Poisons Opium and Dangerous drugs Ordinance
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the appellant for possession and trafficking of 15.68 grammes of heroin and sentenced him accordingly. The trial judge found the prosecution evidence credible.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant argued that the trial judge failed to consider the improbability of the prosecution story, followed wrong procedure to cover prosecution gaps, and commented on the demeanor of a witness not led before him, thereby denying a fair trial.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The learned trial judge had failed to consider the improbability of the prosecution story. | The trial judge had followed wrong procedure to cover the gaps of the prosecution. | The trial judge had commented on the demeanor of witnesses who had not been led before him and thereby denying a fair trial to the appellant.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the prosecution witnesses, particularly PW1 and PW3, were corroborated and withstood lengthy cross-examination. The court saw no improbability in the prosecution story regarding the wait at the market or the handing over of money.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court found no improbability in the prosecution story concerning the wait and the handing over of recovered money.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty, made a dock statement, and did not call witnesses. The defence challenged the prosecution's story as improbable and the procedure followed.
legal_errors_description: The trial judge followed a procedure not laid down in law to allow the marking of the Government Analyst Report after the defence case was closed, in order to fill gaps in the prosecution case.
procedural_defects_description: The trial judge allowed the prosecution to mark the Government Analyst Report as evidence after both prosecution and defence cases were closed. There was also an undated handwritten alteration in the proceedings regarding whether the defence objected.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the trial judge's procedure irregular for allowing the Government Analyst Report to be marked after the defence case closed, as this is not permitted to fill prosecution gaps. It also noted an unfair comment on a witness's demeanor. While the prosecution evidence itself was not improbable, the procedural errors and unfair comment vitiated the trial, leading to the acquittal.
coa_sentence_type: Acquitted, no sentence imposed.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused was convicted by the High Court for possession and trafficking of 15.68g of heroin. On appeal, grounds included improbability of the prosecution story, procedural error in marking the Government Analyst Report post-closure, and an unfair comment on a witness. The Court of Appeal found the procedural error (marking vital evidence after defence closed) and the unfair comment rendered the trial unfair, despite finding the core prosecution story credible. The appeal was allowed and the appellant acquitted.
defence_counsel: Rienzie Arsecularatne, P.C. with Chamindrie Arsecularatne, Thiliina Punchihewa, Punsisi Gamage and Eranga Kahandawala
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted based on prosecution evidence. The Court of Appeal found the High Court judge committed procedural errors by allowing the marking of the Government Analyst Report after the defence closed and making an unfair comment, which vitiated the trial.
precedents_cited_list: Ponnaiya vs Abdul Cader, 38 NLR 281 | The King vs Ariyadasa 43 NLR 289
standard_of_review_applied: Review of trial judge's findings and procedure for legal errors and fairness.

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code; Section 4(2) of the Offensive Weapon Act No.18 of 1996
offence_category: Murder; Causing hurt with offensive weapon
brief_facts_summary: On August 4, 2001, at Borella, the Appellant was accused of throwing a bomb at a mob, resulting in the death of Vidana Silvisthirige Dhammika Fonseka and injury to several persons. The incident occurred after a series of altercations involving PW1, the Appellant, and others. A group including PW1 went to 'Bosevena Watta' where the Appellant resided in search of him, and during the confrontation, a bomb was thrown.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code; Section 4(2) of the Offensive Weapon Act No.18 of 1996
hc_sentence_type: Death Sentence for Count 01; 10 years Rigorous Imprisonment and fine for Counts 05, 06, and 07 (sentences to run concurrent)
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court Judge convicted the Appellant on Counts 01, 05, 06, and 07. The judge found the evidence of PW1, the sole eyewitness, convincing and acted upon it under Section 134 of the Evidence Ordinance, concluding the charges were proved beyond reasonable doubt.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The Appellant argued the High Court Judge erred in convicting based on uncorroborated evidence of a solitary witness (PW1). Other grounds included failure to prove identity of the dead body, failure to consider conviction for a lesser offence, and failure to properly evaluate and give reasons for rejecting the dock statement.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The Learned High Court Judge erred in law by convicting the Appellant on the uncorroborated evidence of PW1. | The Learned High Court Judge had failed to take into consideration that the prosecution had failed to prove the identity of the dead body. | The Learned High Court Judge had failed to take into consideration whether the Appellant could be convicted for a lesser offence under one of the special exceptions to Section 294 of the Penal Code. | The Learned High Court Judge had failed to evaluate the dock statement according to the law and had failed to give proper reasons in rejecting the dock statement.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed the testimony of PW1, the sole eyewitness, and found contradictions with other prosecution witnesses (PW2, PW4, PW16). The COA concluded PW1's evidence was not cogent and impressive enough to act upon without corroboration, especially given the group attack context.
probability_assessment_by_court: The COA found the prosecution failed to prove beyond reasonable doubt who threw the bomb, as the sole eyewitness account was contradicted by other witnesses.
defence_version_summary: The Appellant made a dock statement and closed his case. He did not call witnesses. The High Court Judge evaluated and rejected the dock statement. The COA did not find the defence version specifically discussed in its reasoning.
legal_errors_description: The High Court Judge erred in convicting based on uncorroborated evidence of a solitary witness whose testimony was contradicted by other prosecution witnesses on material points.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal scrutinized the evidence of PW1, the sole eyewitness, and found his testimony contradicted by other prosecution witnesses (PW2, PW4, PW16) regarding the identity of the bomb thrower and the presence of groups. The COA applied the principle from Sumansena v Attorney General that a single witness's evidence must be cogent and impressive to act upon, but found PW1's evidence lacked these qualities and required corroboration in the context of a group attack. The COA concluded the prosecution failed to prove the case beyond reasonable doubt, as the identity of the assailant was not established.
coa_sentence_type: Conviction and sentence quashed. Acquitted of all charges.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The Accused-Appellant was convicted by the High Court of Colombo for murder (Section 296 Penal Code) and causing hurt with an offensive weapon (Section 4(2) Offensive Weapon Act) and sentenced to death and imprisonment. He appealed, arguing conviction was based on uncorroborated evidence of a sole eyewitness. The Court of Appeal found the eyewitness testimony of PW1 was contradicted by other prosecution witnesses and was not cogent enough to sustain conviction without corroboration. The COA held the prosecution failed to prove the case beyond reasonable doubt, allowed the appeal, quashed the conviction and sentence, and acquitted the Appellant.
defence_counsel: Neranjan Jayasinghe
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court Judge relied on the evidence of PW1 as a solitary witness under Section 134 of the Evidence Ordinance, finding it convincing and sufficient for conviction beyond reasonable doubt. The COA criticized this, finding the HC failed to properly scrutinize PW1's evidence, which was contradicted by other prosecution witnesses on material points.
precedents_cited_list: The Queen v. K.A. Santin Singho 65 NLR 447 | Sumansena V Attorney General [1999] 3 Sri L.R. at 137
standard_of_review_applied: Evaluation of eyewitness testimony reliability, considering factors like consistency, corroboration, and contradictions.

judges: B. Sasi Mahendran, J. | Amal Ranaraja, J.
offence_sections: Section 296 read together with Section 32 of the Penal Code as amended
brief_facts_summary: The four Accused-Appellants were indicted for the murder of Hettige Premajiwa alias Ranji on 23.06.2007. The prosecution case relied primarily on three dying declarations made by the deceased to his wife (PW1), his brother-in-law (PW3), and another witness (PW4), consistently naming the four accused. The deceased suffered head injuries, including skull fractures and internal brain bleeding, which were the cause of death. The defence argued the injuries resulted from a fall from a moving vehicle.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 296 read together with Section 32 of the Penal Code as amended
hc_judgment_summary: The Learned High Court Judge found the Accused guilty of murder based on the dying declarations and medical evidence. The court imposed the death sentence.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellants argued the High Court failed to consider contradictions in the prosecution case, did not properly consider the defence case, and did not adequately assess the weaknesses and non-credibility of prosecution witnesses. They also contended the order was contrary to the evidence, specifically challenging the dying declarations for lack of corroboration and suggesting the injuries resulted from a fall.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The High Court has not considered the contradictions in the prosecution case | The Court did not properly consider the defence case. | The Learned High Court Judge has not properly considered the weaknesses and the non-credibility of the Prosecution witnesses. | The order was given in contradiction to the evidence placed before the Court.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal carefully evaluated the three dying declarations, noting the deceased consistently identified all four accused to three different witnesses. The court found the deceased was able to speak and identify his assailants. Medical evidence confirmed injuries consistent with an assault, not merely a fall. The defence did not challenge the fact the declarations were made.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal was satisfied beyond reasonable doubt that the dying declarations were true and accurate, and that the deceased was capable of speaking and identifying his assailants.
defence_version_summary: The Accused gave evidence from the dock and called one defence witness. They pleaded not guilty. Their defence included that the injuries resulted from a fall from a moving vehicle. The court did not find the defence version credible in light of the medical evidence and consistent dying declarations.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal applied settled legal principles on dying declarations, referencing Sri Lankan and Indian precedents. It held that corroboration is not a strict requirement; a dying declaration can be the sole basis for conviction if found to be true, voluntary, and made by a person capable of identifying the assailant. The court analyzed whether the deceased made the statements, was able to speak and identify, and whether the statements were true and accurate. It found the three declarations consistent and reliable. It also rejected the defence's 'fall' theory based on medical evidence showing defensive injuries. The COA found no reason to overturn the HC judgment.
coa_sentence_type: Death sentence affirmed
brief_judgment_file_summary: Four accused were convicted of murder by the High Court of Kalutara and sentenced to death. Their appeal to the Court of Appeal challenged the conviction primarily on the grounds that the dying declarations were uncorroborated and that injuries could have been from a fall. The Court of Appeal, after analyzing legal principles on dying declarations and reviewing the evidence, found the declarations reliable and consistent, and the medical evidence conclusive of assault. The appeal was dismissed, and the High Court's judgment and death sentence were affirmed.
defence_counsel: Charith Calhena for the 1st-4th Accused-Appellants
cause_of_death_exact_text: The injuries done to the head and the effect those had on the brain were the cause of death.
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court accepted the dying declarations as substantive evidence and found the accused guilty of murder. The Court of Appeal found the High Court's reasoning and conclusions to be correct based on the evidence presented.

judges: B. Sasi Mahendran, J. | Amal Ranaraja, J.
offence_sections: Section 54(a)(b) of the Poisons, Opium, and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance as amended by Act No.13 of 1984, Section 54 A(d) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance as amended by Act No.13 of 1984
location_of_offence: Maha Vidyala Mawatha, Colombo, near 146waththa shanty town
brief_facts_summary: On 13.08.2011, police officers from Kotahena Police Station on surveillance saw the appellant coming from a shanty town and searched him. They recovered a pink plastic bag containing 2.59 grams of a brown powdered substance suspected to be heroin, and Rs. 63,000 in cash. The appellant was arrested. The substance was weighed, sealed, and sent for analysis, which confirmed it was heroin. The appellant claimed he was falsely implicated when arrested while performing manual labour.
evidence_type_primary: Physical evidence (recovery of suspected heroin and cash)
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 54(a)(b) and Section 54 A(d) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance as amended by Act No.13 of 1984
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court found the appellant guilty on both charges of trafficking and possessing heroin. The judge convicted him and sentenced him to life imprisonment for each charge.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant argued the prosecution failed to prove the chain of custody due to the unexplained loss of the police property receipt and suspect property receipt. He also contended the raid notes were vague, making the prosecution version improbable.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The chain of custody has not been proved by the respondent due to the unexplained loss of the production and property receipts. | The notes on the raid are vague, therefore, the prosecution version is improbable.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The prosecution relied on testimony from police officers (PW1, PW2) regarding the arrest and recovery. The Court of Appeal found the chain of custody evidence weak due to missing property receipts and lack of cogent explanation for their absence.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal found reasonable doubt due to failure to establish chain of custody and the unexplained lapse of time.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty. He claimed he was taken into custody while performing manual labour and was falsely implicated. He did not call witnesses but made a dock statement.
legal_errors_description: The High Court judge misdirected himself by concluding the prosecution proved the inward journey of the production beyond reasonable doubt despite the missing property receipts and weak chain of custody evidence.
procedural_defects_description: Failure by prosecution to produce key documents (Police property receipt and suspect property receipt) to establish chain of custody, and failure to provide a cogent explanation for their absence.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the prosecution failed to prove the chain of custody of the seized heroin due to the unexplained loss of the police property receipt and suspect property receipt. The prosecution's attempt to explain the loss through a proposed witness (PW10) who never testified was inadequate. The court held it was dangerous to rely solely on oral testimony without the receipts. Considering the 14-year lapse since the offence and the unreliable evidence on chain of custody, the court declined to order a retrial, citing prejudice from delay.
coa_sentence_type: Acquitted, no sentence imposed.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The appellant was convicted in the High Court of Colombo for trafficking and possessing 2.59 grams of heroin and sentenced to life imprisonment on each charge. He appealed, arguing the chain of custody was not proven due to missing property receipts and that the raid notes were vague. The Court of Appeal found the prosecution failed to establish a proper chain of custody and that the High Court misdirected itself. Considering the 14-year delay and weak evidence, the appeal was allowed, the conviction and sentence were set aside, and the appellant was acquitted.
defence_counsel: Nayantha Wijesundara
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court concluded the prosecution proved the charges beyond reasonable doubt. The Court of Appeal found this conclusion was a misdirection due to the prosecution's failure to prove the chain of custody of the production.
precedents_cited_list: The Queen vs. G.K.Jayasinghe 69 NLR 314
standard_of_review_applied: Review of conviction and sentence based on grounds of appeal, including evaluation of evidence and legal misdirection.

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 54(A)(b) and 54(A)(d) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance as amended by Act No. 13 of 1984
brief_facts_summary: On 15.05.2010, police received information about heroin trafficking in Thalahena. Police stopped a scooter where the 2nd Appellant was the rider and the 1st Appellant was the pillion rider. A parcel containing suspected heroin, weighing about 154 grams, was found concealed in the 1st Appellant's dress. Both were arrested and the suspected heroin was sent for analysis. The 1st Appellant was indicted for possession, the 2nd for aiding and abetting, and both for trafficking 22.91 grams of heroin.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 54(A)(b) and 54(A)(d) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance as amended by Act No. 13 of 1984
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court found the Appellants guilty on all counts and imposed the death sentence on 29.09.2015.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: Grounds included: unlawful amendment of the indictment date without reading it to the Appellants; unlawful reliance on Section 439 to call a witness after both sides closed their cases; prosecution's failure to explain a discrepancy in the weight of the heroin; and failure to consider the likelihood of false implication of the 2nd Appellant due to enmity with a prosecution witness.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Whether it was lawful for the Learned High Court Judge to amend the date of offence in Count number one in the indictment to read as 15.10.2010 instead of 15.10.2011 by placing his signature dated 07.03.2013. | Whether it was lawful for the Learned High Court Judge to insert words 'coeofo eofeo o coe ceo.' under his signature dated 04.09.2014 after the prosecution and defence had closed their cases. | Whether it was lawful for the Learned High Court Judge to rely on Section 439 of the Code of Criminal Procedure Act No.15 of 1979 to allow the prosecution to call witness Nihal Mapitigama Liyanarachchi. | The prosecution failed to explain as to how the weight of Heroin along with the covers which weighed 154 grams and purportedly the same weighed without covers 156.5 grams when the Government Analyst weighed on 06.01.2011. | The Learned High Court Judge has failed to take into consideration that there is a strong likelihood for the prosecution witnesses specially PW1 Rangajeewa to falsely implicate the 2nd Appellant due to the enmity prevailed between him and PW1.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The prosecution led 5 witnesses, including the Government Analyst. The Court of Appeal found significant issues with the evidence handling, including a weight discrepancy in the heroin and procedural errors in amending the indictment and recalling a witness.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal found reasonable doubt due to procedural errors and unexplained weight discrepancy, which impacted the prosecution's ability to prove the case beyond reasonable doubt.
defence_version_summary: The Appellants opted to give evidence from the witness box. Their defence was not detailed in the COA judgment extract, but the appeal challenged the conviction on procedural and evidence grounds.
legal_errors_description: The High Court Judge misdirected himself by invoking Section 439 CPC to fill gaps in the prosecution case after both sides had closed, and failed to ensure the amended indictment was read and explained to the Appellants.
procedural_defects_description: Amendment to the indictment date was not read or explained to the Appellants as required by Section 167 CPC; witness recalled under Section 439 after defence case closed, putting accused at unfair disadvantage.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the High Court committed serious procedural errors: amending the indictment without complying with Section 167 CPC, and improperly allowing the prosecution to call a witness under Section 439 after the defence closed its case, which is not permissible to fill prosecution gaps. The Court also found the prosecution failed to explain a significant weight discrepancy in the heroin (154g vs 156.5g), creating reasonable doubt about the chain of custody and integrity of the evidence. Citing precedents on chain of custody and the inward journey of productions, the COA held the prosecution did not prove its case beyond reasonable doubt. Due to these errors and evidentiary weaknesses, the conviction was unsafe.
coa_sentence_type: Acquitted and set aside the death sentence
brief_judgment_file_summary: The 1st and 2nd Accused-Appellants were convicted by the High Court of Colombo for possession, aiding and abetting, and trafficking 22.91g of heroin and sentenced to death. They appealed. The Court of Appeal allowed the appeal, finding procedural errors in amending the indictment and recalling a witness, and a failure by the prosecution to explain a weight discrepancy in the heroin, which raised reasonable doubt. The convictions and sentences were set aside and the Appellants were acquitted.
defence_counsel: Rienzie Arsekularatne, PC with Chamindri Arsekularatne, Udara Muhandiramge, Thilina Punchihewa, Punsisi Gamage, C. Fernando and Himasha Silva for the 1st Appellant. Neranjan Jayasinghe with Harshana Ananda for the 2nd Appellant.
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted the Appellants based on the prosecution evidence. The COA found the HC erred in law by misapplying procedural provisions and failing to address critical evidentiary weaknesses, particularly the unexplained weight discrepancy, which undermined the prosecution's case.
precedents_cited_list: Woolmington v DPP (1935) | M.K.Francis Alwis v The Queen 70 NLR 558 | David v Idroos 45 NLR 300 | Vendendriesen v Houwa Umma 39 NLR 65 | Mohamed Nimnaz V. Attorney General CA/95/94 | Faiza Hanoon Yoosuf v. Attorney General CA/121/2002 | Mahasarukkalige Chandani V. Attorney General CA/213/2009
standard_of_review_applied: The Court of Appeal reviewed for errors of law and procedure, and whether the prosecution proved its case beyond reasonable doubt.

judges: B. Sasi Mahendran, J. | Amal Ranaraja, J.
offence_sections: section 365 B (2)(b) of the Penal Code as amended by Act No. 22 of 1995 and Act No. 29 of 1998
brief_facts_summary: The accused-appellant, father of the victim (PW 01), was charged with grave sexual abuse of his daughter when she was 14 years old. The first incident occurred on or about 01.06.2008 in a jungle where he took her to pick cashews and had intercrural sex with her. A second incident occurred three days later at home around midnight while she slept. The victim disclosed the abuse to a friend (PW 02) after some delay, and eventually the mother (PW 03) made a complaint to the police.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: section 365 B (2)(b) of the Penal Code as amended by Act No. 22 of 1995 and Act No. 29 of 1998
hc_sentence_type: Rigorous imprisonment 15 years and fine per count
hc_judgment_summary: The Learned High Court Judge convicted the appellant on the first and second charges and acquitted him on the third. He imposed 15 years rigorous imprisonment and a fine of Rs.10,000 on each of the two counts, with a default term of six months simple imprisonment for non-payment.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant appealed against conviction and sentence. The appeal implied challenges to the credibility of the victim's testimony due to delays and inconsistencies, and argued a motive for false implication based on the mother's alleged extra-marital affair.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Appellant was not mentally retarded to commit such acts | Case was fabricated by wife (PW 03) due to her extra-marital affair to mislead police and imprison appellant
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal carefully evaluated the victim's testimony, acknowledging inconsistencies and memory issues due to trauma and the 12-year delay, but found them immaterial and not undermining the prosecution's case. The testimonies of PW 01, PW 02, and PW 03 were found credible and consistent in core allegations.
probability_assessment_by_court: The court held that discrepancies in victim's testimony due to trauma and delay did not create reasonable doubt, and the prosecution's narrative was coherent and compelling.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty. He made a dock statement claiming the case was fabricated by his wife (PW 03) due to her extra-marital affair. He did not call witnesses. The court found his defence not credible and rejected it.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed the victim's testimony, acknowledging memory issues and trauma-related inconsistencies but deemed them immaterial. It applied Section 166 of the Criminal Procedure Act, noting the accused was not misled by lack of exact dates. It evaluated the dock statement per established guidelines and found it failed to create reasonable doubt. The court upheld the High Court's thorough evaluation of witness credibility and evidence, finding no grounds to interfere.
coa_sentence_type: Rigorous imprisonment 15 years and fine of Rs.10,000 on each of two counts, with default simple imprisonment of six months per count for non-payment
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused-appellant, father of the victim, was convicted by the High Court of Kurunegala on two counts of grave sexual abuse of his 14-year-old daughter and sentenced to 15 years rigorous imprisonment and a fine per count. He appealed, challenging credibility due to delays and inconsistencies, and alleging fabrication by his wife. The Court of Appeal analyzed the evidence, acknowledged memory and trauma issues but found them immaterial, applied legal provisions on date discrepancies, evaluated the dock statement, and found no reasonable doubt created. The appeal was dismissed, upholding the High Court's conviction and sentence.
defence_counsel: Dineru Bandana
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court Judge thoroughly evaluated evidence, witness age and background, and found the prosecution presented compelling evidence through witness testimonies and expert reports, creating a coherent narrative. The Court of Appeal agreed with this analysis and found no error.
precedents_cited_list: D.R.M.Pandithakoralege (Excise Inspector) vs. V.K.Selvanayagam 56 NLR 143
standard_of_review_applied: Evaluation of evidence credibility, application of Section 166 CrPC on immaterial errors, and dock statement guidelines

judges: B. Sasi Mahendran, J. | Amal Ranaraja, J.
offence_sections: Section 54 A (b) and Section 54 A (d) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance as amended by Act No.13 of 1984
brief_facts_summary: The accused-appellant was arrested on 04.04.2014 after police, acting on informant tips, followed and intercepted his three-wheel scooter in Seeyawatha, Maligawaththa. Police found 693.9 grams of heroin in a black plastic bag. The accused claimed he was abducted, blindfolded, assaulted, and falsely implicated after attending court in Avisawella. The High Court convicted and sentenced him to death.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 54 A (b) and Section 54 A (d) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance as amended by Act No.13 of 1984
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the appellant of trafficking and possessing 693.9 grams of heroin. The judge accepted the prosecution witnesses as credible and sentenced the appellant to death.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant argued the prosecution version was inherently impossible, the High Court judge used a different yardstick for analyzing prosecution vs. defence evidence, wrongly concluded the prosecution version was more probable, wrongly rejected the dock statement, and questioned whether the appellant received a fair trial.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Is the prosecution version inherently impossible? | Did the Learned High Court Judge err in using a different yardstick in analysing the prosecution’s case as against the defendant’s case? | Did the Learned High Court Judge err in coming to the conclusion that the prosecution version is more probable than the defence version? | Did the Learned High Court Judge err in rejecting the dock statement without proper reasons? | In those circumstances, did the appellant receive a fair trial in the High Court.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the prosecution witnesses' narratives strange, peculiar, odd, and unusual. Their conduct did not harmonize with expected police behavior, and their testimony regarding the informant's identification and the prolonged chase was implausible. The court held the evidence should not be acted upon.
probability_assessment_by_court: The COA held that where facts are capable of an inference in favour of the accused and against him, the inference consistent with innocence should be preferred (applied Alim vs. Wijesinghe).
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty and gave a dock statement claiming he was abducted, blindfolded, assaulted, and falsely implicated. He claimed no narcotics were found on him. The High Court judge rejected his version, but the COA found his version plausible and the prosecution version improbable.
legal_errors_description: The High Court judge erred by not preferring the inference consistent with the accused's innocence when facts were capable of both inferences, and by misdirecting himself on the credibility of prosecution witnesses.
procedural_defects_description: Unusual conduct of police in not protecting informant's identity, failure to explain precautions during surveillance and chase, and delay in arresting the appellant.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed the improbability of the prosecution version, noting the informant's identification of the appellant at night under poor lighting conditions was questionable, the prolonged chase without immediate arrest was unusual, and the police's failure to protect the informant's identity was not normal. The court applied the principle from Alim vs. Wijesinghe that an inference consistent with innocence should be preferred. It also noted the nine-year delay since the offence and, citing The Queen vs. G.K. Jayasinghe, declined to order a retrial. The COA found the prosecution evidence unreliable and the conviction unsafe.
coa_sentence_type: Acquitted, sentence set aside.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused-appellant was convicted by the High Court of Colombo for trafficking and possessing 693.9 grams of heroin and sentenced to death. On appeal, he challenged the prosecution version as improbable, alleged unfair trial, and raised issues regarding informant identification and police conduct. The Court of Appeal found the prosecution witnesses' testimony implausible and the police actions unusual. Applying legal principles favouring the accused where inferences are ambiguous, and considering the nine-year delay, the COA set aside the conviction and sentence, acquitted the appellant, and declined a retrial.
defence_counsel: Shavindra Fernand, P.C. with Thivanka Attygalle, Mirthula Skandarajah and Rishnie Fernandopulle
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court accepted the prosecution witnesses as creditworthy and found the prosecution version more probable. The COA criticized this, finding the HC judge erred in his credibility assessment and failed to apply the correct legal principle regarding inferences consistent with innocence.
precedents_cited_list: Alim vs. Wijesinghe (S.I.Police, Battlealoa) 38 CLW 95 | The Queen vs. G.K.Jayasinghe 69 NLR 314
standard_of_review_applied: Review of factual findings and legal errors, assessing probability and credibility of evidence.

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 296 read with Section 32 of the Penal Code
location_of_offence: Paddy field adjoining the deceased's house
brief_facts_summary: On 11-07-2000, the deceased Nimal Indrasiri Rohana Mayadunna was attacked and suffered fatal cut injuries near a paddy field adjacent to his house. He made dying declarations to his wife (PW-01) and elder brother (PW-02), naming the 1st accused (Hernan/Heman), the 2nd accused (Raja), and the appellant (Nalin) as his assailants. The appellant was convicted of murder and sentenced to death by the High Court.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 296 read with Section 32 of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court Judge found the appellant guilty on the 1st count (murder of Nimal Indrasiri Rohana Mayadunna) based on the dying declarations and evidence of PW-01 and PW-02. The appellant was acquitted on the 2nd count (murder of Shelton) due to lack of evidence. He was sentenced to death.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant's counsel argued that the conviction was based on insufficient and doubtful prosecution evidence, specifically challenging the reliability of the dying declarations and the identification evidence. It was also contended that the defence evidence (alibi) was rejected on unreasonable grounds.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The learned High Court Judge has convicted the accused-appellant on insufficient and doubtful evidence of the prosecution. | Defence evidence has been rejected on unreasonable grounds.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the dying declarations made to PW-01 and PW-02 to be consistent and reliable. The JMO's evidence confirmed the deceased could have spoken for 30-60 minutes after the injuries. The alibi defence was considered but found insufficient to create reasonable doubt.
probability_assessment_by_court: Court found no reasonable doubt created by the defence. Prosecution evidence, especially the dying declarations and JMO's testimony, proved guilt beyond reasonable doubt.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty. He made a dock statement claiming an alibi, stating he was consuming liquor at a shop in the village at the time of the incident. He called one witness (Sisira) to support his alibi. The court found the alibi defence not credible and insufficient to create doubt.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal thoroughly analyzed the dying declarations, finding them consistent and corroborated by the JMO's evidence on the deceased's ability to speak. It evaluated the identification evidence under moonlight conditions and found it credible. The alibi defence was assessed as a question of fact but found not to create reasonable doubt. The court affirmed the High Court's careful evaluation of evidence and application of legal principles, including those regarding dock statements and common intention under Section 32 of the Penal Code.
coa_sentence_type: Death (Affirmed)
brief_judgment_file_summary: The 3rd accused-appellant was convicted by the High Court of Gampaha for the murder of Nimal Indrasiri Rohana Mayadunna and sentenced to death. He appealed, arguing insufficient evidence and unreasonable rejection of his alibi defence. The Court of Appeal found the dying declarations reliable, the identification credible, and the alibi insufficient to create doubt. The appeal was dismissed, and the conviction and death sentence were affirmed.
defence_counsel: Niranjan Jayasinghe
cause_of_death_exact_text: Cut injuries including a 15-inch long injury to the heart cavity, lung cavity, and stomach, causing injuries to liver, ribs, and other internal organs. Described as necessarily fatal injuries.
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court Judge carefully evaluated the dying declarations, witness credibility, and medical evidence. He considered the alibi defence and applied correct legal principles regarding dock statements and common intention. The COA found no errors in the HC's analysis or reasoning.
precedents_cited_list: Ranasinghe Vs. The Attorney General (2007) 1 SLR 218 | Gunapala and Others Vs. The Republic of Sri Lanka (1994) 3 SLR 180 | Martin Singho Vs. Queen 69 CLW 21 | The King Vs. Marshall (1948) 51 NLR 157 | Rex vs. Chandrasekera (1942) 44 NLR 126 | Rex vs. Fernando (1947) 48 NLR 251
standard_of_review_applied: The court reviewed whether the High Judge considered insufficient and doubtful evidence, and whether defence evidence was rejected on unreasonable grounds. It assessed the evidence as a whole and the application of legal principles.

judges: Menaka Wijesundera, J | Wickum A. Kaluarachchi, J
offence_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: On 13 October 2008, Chandralatha and her son Dinesh Prasanna were shot dead in their home. The prosecution case relied on the dying declaration of Chandralatha, who identified the accused-appellant as the shooter, and the eyewitness testimony of PW-4 (her daughter), who saw two persons fleeing, one of whom she identified as the appellant. The accused-appellant was convicted in the High Court on two counts of murder and sentenced to death.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the accused-appellant on two counts of murder based on the dying declaration and eyewitness testimony. The court imposed the death sentence.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant argued the Trial Judge failed to adequately consider facts favourable to the accused, failed to apply proper tests to the dying declaration, failed to properly consider the alibi defence, and that the conviction was based on unreliable eyewitness identification. It was also contended the chain of causation for one death was not considered and that the accused was denied a fair trial.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The learned Trial Judge has failed to adequately consider the facts in favour of the accused-appellant as required by law. | The obvious infirmities in the case for the prosecution have not been considered adequately and reasons for acting upon the evidence notwithstanding such infirmities have not been given. | The dying deposition of the deceased has not been considered utilizing the tests laid down by our courts. | The defence of alibi taken up by the accused throughout the trial has not been adequately considered. | In view of the above circumstances, there has not been adequate consideration of the defence case as required by law. | Due to one or more of the above reasons, the accused has been denied a fair trial, which is a constitutionally guaranteed fundamental right of a person accused of an offence.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found PW-4 credible, and her evidence was corroborated by the dying declaration. The dying declaration was found to be reliable and made independently. The defence of alibi was weak and unsupported.
probability_assessment_by_court: Court found prosecution proved guilt beyond reasonable doubt; no reasonable doubt created by alibi defence.
defence_version_summary: Accused pleaded not guilty. Defence was alibi (claimed to be on duty at Kotte Municipal Council at time of incident) via dock statement only. Defence also suggested eyewitness misidentified appellant for his brother. Court found alibi not credible and unsupported by evidence.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal upheld the High Court judgment. It found the dying declaration of Chandralatha reliable and properly admitted, meeting the tests from Ranasinghe v. Attorney General. It found PW-4 credible and her identification corroborated by the dying declaration. The alibi defence was weak, did not cover the precise time of the offence, and was contradicted by unchallenged prosecution evidence about the accused absconding. Citing Sigera v. Attorney General and other authorities, the court held a conviction can be based solely on a reliable dying declaration. No reasonable doubt arose from the defence. The appeal was dismissed.
coa_sentence_type: Death sentence affirmed
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused-appellant was convicted in the High Court of Colombo for the murder of Chandralatha and Dinesh Prasanna and sentenced to death. He appealed on grounds including improper consideration of the dying declaration, unreliable eyewitness identification, inadequate consideration of alibi defence, and denial of fair trial. The Court of Appeal found the dying declaration reliable and corroborated by eyewitness PW-4. It rejected the alibi defence as unsupported and found no error in the High Court's judgment. The appeal was dismissed and the convictions and death sentence affirmed.
defence_counsel: Palitha Fernando, P.C.
cause_of_death_exact_text: Septicemia occurred as a result of firearm injuries (Chandralatha); cranio-cerebral injuries following discharge from a firearm or firearms (Dinesh Prasanna).
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted based on the dying declaration and eyewitness evidence. The Court of Appeal found the High Court correctly accepted the dying declaration and eyewitness testimony, and adequately considered and rejected the alibi defence.
precedents_cited_list: Ranasinghe V. Attorney General – (2007) 1 Sri L.R. 218 | Sigera V. Attorney General – (2011) 1 Sri L.R. 201 | Kumarasinghe Hettiarachchilage Gamini Sarath V. The Hon. Attorney General – C.A. Case No. 24/2015, decided on 22.03.2019 | Jayatissa v. Hon. Attorney General - (2010)1 Sri LR 279 | Sarvan Singh V. State of Punjab (2002 AIR SC (iii) 3652) cited in Ratnayake Mudiyanselage Premachandra V. The Hon. Attorney General C.A. Case No. 79/2011, decided on 04.04.2017 | Himachal Pradesh V. Thakur Dass (1983) 2 Cri. L.J. 1694 at 1701 | Motilal V. State of Madhya Pradesh (1990) Criminal Law Journal NOC 125 MP
standard_of_review_applied: Court reviewed whether High Court properly applied legal tests for dying declaration, adequately considered evidence and defence, and whether conviction was safe beyond reasonable doubt.

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code for murder and Section 380 of the Penal Code for robbery
brief_facts_summary: The Appellant was convicted for the double murder of Wimal Malaviarachchi and Nanda Srimathi and robbery of items from their house on or about 23.11.2008. The victims' son (PW3) last saw the Appellant, who was doing tile work in the house, when he delivered lunch to him. Upon returning home, the son and others found the parents dead and items missing. Police investigation led to the arrest of the Appellant and recovery of stolen items, including a mobile phone and jewelry, based on his statement.
evidence_type_secondary: Physical evidence (recovered stolen items), Medical evidence (post-mortem)
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code for murder and Section 380 of the Penal Code for robbery
hc_sentence_type: Death on counts 1 and 2, 10 years rigorous imprisonment and fine on count 3
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court Judge, after a non-jury trial and considering prosecution evidence from 12 witnesses, convicted the Appellant. He was sentenced to death for the two murders and to 10 years rigorous imprisonment with a fine for robbery.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The Appellant argued that the circumstantial evidence was insufficient to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt. He also claimed procedural errors, including failure to explain his rights under CPC Section 200(1), improper admission of PW3's evidence, and failure to properly consider his dock statement.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The Learned High Court Judge has failed to consider the items of circumstantial evidence beyond reasonable doubt as the circumstantial evidence led in the trial is insufficient to convict the Appellant. | The Learned High Court Judge has failed to explain and record the rights of the Appellant as per section 200(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure Act No. 15 of 1979. | The Learned High Court Judge erred in law by allowing the prosecution to lead the evidence of PW3 in absence of statement given to police and in absence of his evidence in the NS proceedings. | The Learned High Court Judge has not considered the dock statement of the Appellant in its correct perspective.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the High Court Judge correctly evaluated the circumstantial evidence. It held that the recovered stolen items, especially the mobile phone linked to the deceased and jewelry identified by family members, formed a strong chain of evidence pointing conclusively to the Appellant.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court held the chain of circumstantial evidence was complete, conclusive, and pointed irresistibly to the guilt of the Appellant, leaving no room for reasonable doubt or any other inference.
defence_version_summary: The Appellant pleaded not guilty and opted for a non-jury trial. The defence case was closed after the Appellant made a dock statement. The High Court Judge considered but disbelieved the dock statement.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal systematically rejected all grounds of appeal. It found the High Court Judge had complied with Section 200(1) CPC by explaining the Appellant's rights. The circumstantial evidence, including recovery of the deceased's mobile phone and jewelry from the Appellant based on his statement under Section 27(1) Evidence Ordinance, and identification by PW3, was found to be strong, consistent, and conclusive of guilt. The Court noted the defence's failure to cross-examine PW22 on the mobile phone link amounted to acceptance of that evidence. It applied precedents on circumstantial evidence and held the proved circumstances were consistent only with guilt and inconsistent with innocence. The dock statement was properly considered but rightly disbelieved.
coa_sentence_type: Death sentence on counts 1 and 2 (murder) affirmed. 10 years rigorous imprisonment and fine of Rs.2500/- with default sentence of 03 months simple imprisonment on count 3 (robbery) affirmed.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The Appellant was convicted by the Panadura High Court for the 2008 double murder and robbery of a couple, and sentenced to death and imprisonment. He appealed, challenging the sufficiency of circumstantial evidence, procedural errors, and the treatment of his dock statement. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal, finding the chain of circumstantial evidence – including recovery of the deceased's mobile phone and jewelry from the Appellant – was strong, conclusive, and pointed irresistibly to his guilt. All procedural steps were deemed proper, and the convictions and sentences were affirmed.
defence_counsel: Dharshana Kuruppu with Sahan Weerasinghe
cause_of_death_exact_text: Cranio cerebral injuries following impact to the head for both deceased.
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court Judge analyzed the circumstantial evidence, found it sufficient and conclusive, and convicted the Appellant. The Court of Appeal agreed with this analysis, finding no error in the High Court's reasoning or evaluation of evidence.
precedents_cited_list: C.Chenga Reddy and others v. State of A.P.(1996) 10 SCC 193 | McGreevy v. Director of Public Prosecution [1973] 1 W.L.R.276 | Attorney General v. Attorney General (2010) 2 Sri L.R. 113 | Alexander v. R (1981) 145 CLR 395
standard_of_review_applied: The Court assessed whether the High Court correctly applied the law on circumstantial evidence and procedure, and whether the evidence was sufficient to sustain the conviction beyond reasonable doubt.

judges: N. Bandula Karunarathna J. | D. N. Samarakoon, J. | M. T. Mohammed Laffar, J
brief_facts_summary: The Petitioner, a retired Senior Superintendent of Police and former Director of CID, challenged a report by a Presidential Commission of Inquiry (the 1st to 3rd Respondents) which made adverse findings and recommendations against him. The Commission investigated alleged political victimization of public officers between 2015 and 2019, based on a complaint by the 7th Respondent. The Petitioner was named as a Respondent in the inquiry, and the Commission's report recommended his prosecution for offenses including fabrication of false evidence and corruption.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The Petitioner argued the Commission violated natural justice by not informing him of charges, not giving him a hearing, and acting against an undertaking given to the Court. He also contended the Commission acted ultra vires, exceeded its mandate, usurped the powers of the Attorney General and judiciary, and its findings were unreasonable and tainted by bias.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Violation of undertaking given to Court on 27.07.2020 | Violation of principles of Natural Justice and audi alteram partem rule | Commission acted ultra vires and exceeded its jurisdiction | Commission usurped powers of the Attorney General and the judiciary | Findings and recommendations are unreasonable in the Wednesbury sense | Commission showed hostility and bias | Inquiry into complaint was sub judice
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court found the Commission violated natural justice by not informing the Petitioner of charges or giving him a hearing. It held the Commission acted ultra vires, lacked impartiality, and its findings were unreasonable and without legal basis.
probability_assessment_by_court: Court found the Commission's actions violated natural justice and were ultra vires, rendering its report a nullity.
defence_version_summary: The Petitioner pleaded not guilty to the allegations before the Commission. He argued he was not served with proper charges or complaints, was not given a hearing, and the Commission acted in violation of an undertaking to the Court and principles of natural justice.
legal_errors_description: Commission acted ultra vires, violated natural justice (audi alteram partem), exceeded its mandate, usurped powers of Attorney General and judiciary.
procedural_defects_description: Failure to serve summons/notice, failure to inform of charges, failure to give a hearing, violation of undertaking to Court.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal held the Commission violated natural justice by not giving the Petitioner notice of charges or an opportunity to be heard, breaching the audi alteram partem rule. It found the Commission acted ultra vires, exceeded its mandate, and displayed bias. The Court noted the Commission's recommendations were not legally binding and that the appointing authority (President/Cabinet) had decided not to act on them, rendering the matter futile. However, given the serious impact on the Petitioner's reputation and the legal violations, the Court exercised its discretion to quash the report.
coa_sentence_type: Writ of Certiorari issued quashing the findings, decisions, material and recommendations against the Petitioner.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The Petitioner, a former police official, challenged a Presidential Commission report making adverse findings against him. The Court of Appeal found the Commission violated natural justice by not informing him of charges or giving a hearing, acted ultra vires, and exceeded its mandate. Despite arguments that the matter was futile as the recommendations were not acted upon, the Court allowed the appeal and issued a Writ of Certiorari quashing the report's findings against the Petitioner.

judges: N. Bandula Karunarathna J. P/CA | D. N. Samarakoon, J. | M. T. Mohammed Laffar, J
offence_sections: Section 70 of the Bribery Act; Sections 189, 191 and 100 of the Penal Code
offence_category: Corruption, Fabricating False Evidence, Giving False Evidence, Offences against Public Property
brief_facts_summary: The Petitioner, a politician and leader of the JVP, was subjected to an inquiry by a Presidential Commission of Inquiry (PCIPV) appointed to investigate alleged political victimization of public officers, employees of state corporations, and members of the armed forces/police between 08 January 2015 and 16 November 2019. The Commission made findings and recommendations against the Petitioner, including recommending action under the Bribery Act and consideration for civic disability. The Petitioner challenged the Commission's jurisdiction, alleging it acted ultra vires and in violation of natural justice.
evidence_type_secondary: Witness testimony before Commission, Gazette notifications, Cabinet Decision
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The Petitioner challenged the findings and recommendations of the Presidential Commission of Inquiry on multiple grounds: that the Commission lacked jurisdiction as most complainants were not public officers; that the Commission's mandate did not cover the Petitioner; that the Commission violated rules of natural justice by not providing details of complaints or a fair hearing; that the findings were unreasonable, arbitrary, and ultra vires; and that the recommendations were not legally binding.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Commission lacked jurisdiction as complainants were not public officers/employees of public corporations | Commission acted ultra vires its mandate as per Gazette notifications | Violation of rules of natural justice - no charges explained, no disclosure of complaints | Findings are unreasonable, arbitrary, capricious, and mala fide | Recommendations are not legally binding and have not been acted upon | Commission breached undertaking given to Court of Appeal | Findings based on membership in committees without evidence of wrongdoing | No evidence to support recommendations of corruption or fabricating false evidence
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court analyzed the Commission's proceedings and found the Petitioner was not informed of the complaints against him, was not given a fair opportunity to respond, and that the findings were based on insubstantial or irrelevant evidence. The Commission violated its own undertaking to the Court of Appeal by summoning the Petitioner.
probability_assessment_by_court: Court found no sufficient evidence to support the Commission's findings and recommendations against the Petitioner.
defence_version_summary: The Petitioner pleaded not guilty to the allegations before the Commission. He objected to jurisdiction, denied being a member of the Anti-Corruption Unit, and stated he never interfered with investigations or prosecutions. He argued the findings were baseless and violated natural justice.
legal_errors_description: The Commission acted without jurisdiction (ultra vires) by inquiring into complaints from individuals not falling within its mandate (private individuals, not public officers). It violated rules of natural justice by not disclosing complaints or providing a fair hearing.
procedural_defects_description: Commission failed to follow natural justice: did not inform Petitioner of complaints, did not allow fair opportunity to respond, breached undertaking given to Court of Appeal.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal held that the Commission lacked jurisdiction as most complainants (like Nissanka Senadhipathi) were not public officers/employees of public corporations as required by its mandate. The Commission acted ultra vires. It violated natural justice by not providing the Petitioner with details of complaints or a fair hearing. The findings were unreasonable, arbitrary, and without evidentiary basis. The recommendations were not legally binding and had not been acted upon by the President or Cabinet, who had instead appointed a Special Presidential Commission to review them. The Court found the Commission's conduct appalling and in violation of its undertaking to the Court.
coa_sentence_type: Writs of Certiorari and Prohibition granted; findings and recommendations quashed
brief_judgment_file_summary: The Petitioner, a politician, challenged the findings and recommendations of a Presidential Commission of Inquiry (PCIPV) which had recommended action against him for alleged involvement in political victimization. The Court of Appeal held the Commission lacked jurisdiction as its mandate was limited to complaints from public officers, etc., but it inquired into complaints from private individuals. The Commission violated natural justice by not informing the Petitioner of the complaints or giving him a fair hearing. Its findings were unreasonable and ultra vires. The Court issued Writs of Certiorari quashing the findings, recommendations, and the related Cabinet Decision, and a Writ of Prohibition restraining any steps based on them. No order for costs was made.

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 354 of the Penal Code; Section 365B(2)(b) of the Penal Code as amended by Penal Code (Amendment) Act No. 22 of 1995, 29 of 1998 and 16 of 2006
location_of_offence: Pesalai within the jurisdiction of the High Court of Mannar
brief_facts_summary: The accused-appellant was convicted of abducting a minor girl and committing grave sexual abuse by inserting a finger into her vagina on or about 01-01-2013. The victim, a child under 16, reported the incident to her grandmother soon after, but was told not to tell anyone. She disclosed the incident to a Child Rights Welfare Officer during a school awareness program about 1.5 years later. The prosecution case relied on the victim's testimony, her mother's evidence, and police investigation. The defence alleged a false complaint due to jealousy and political enmity.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 354 of the Penal Code; Section 365B(2)(b) of the Penal Code as amended by Penal Code (Amendment) Act No. 22 of 1995, 29 of 1998 and 16 of 2006
hc_sentence_type: Count 1: 2 years rigorous imprisonment + fine; Count 2: 7 years rigorous imprisonment + fine; Sentences to run concurrently
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court found the appellant guilty on both counts after trial. The Judge considered mitigatory and aggravating circumstances and imposed rigorous imprisonment, fines, and compensation to the victim. The sentences were ordered to run concurrently.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant challenged the conviction based on belated complaint and discrepancies in evidence. He argued the prosecution failed to prove the specific act of grave sexual abuse (insertion of finger) and that the kidnapping charge was not sustainable. He also claimed the High Court Judge failed to adequately consider the defence evidence.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: In view of the belatedness of the complaint and the discrepancies of the evidence of PW-01 taken with other witnesses, whether the conviction could be sustained. | In the light of the specific act mentioned in the indictment, whether the prosecution has failed to prove the charge of grave sexual abuse. | The offence of kidnapping cannot be sustained in the light of the evidence. | Whether the learned High Court Judge has failed to adequately consider the defence, especially the evidence of the appellant.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The prosecution called the victim child (PW-01), her mother (PW-02), and police investigators. The defence called several witnesses including the victim's grandmother, the Child Rights Welfare Officer, the JMO, and a friend of the victim. The Court of Appeal found the evidence taken as a whole was cogent and trustworthy, with no material discrepancies, and accepted the victim's testimony despite her initial reluctance and delayed disclosure.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court assessed that the prosecution proved its case beyond reasonable doubt. The delay in complaint was explainable and did not indicate falsity. The victim's reluctance was due to trauma, not fabrication. The totality of evidence was credible and supported the conviction.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty. He gave evidence under oath and called witnesses. His defence was that the complaint was false due to jealousy (his family being educated), refusal of a marriage proposal, and political enmity (supporting an unpopular election candidate). He did not specifically address the allegations in his evidence. The court found his defence vague and unsupported, and key suggestions were not put to prosecution witnesses.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal considered the totality of evidence, including defence witnesses who filled missing links. It held the delay in complaint was justified due to the victim's age, fear, and grandmother's instruction. Minor discrepancies were not material. The victim's testimony, though reluctant, was credible and corroborated by her grandmother. The act of touching the vagina satisfied the definition of grave sexual abuse. Kidnapping was established as the minor was taken without guardian's consent. The defence allegations of false complaint were vague and not put to witnesses, weakening their case. The prosecution proved its case beyond reasonable doubt.
coa_sentence_type: Conviction and sentence affirmed. Sentences to run concurrently: Count 1: 2 years rigorous imprisonment + Rs.10,000 fine; Count 2: 7 years rigorous imprisonment + Rs.10,000 fine; Compensation of Rs.100,000 to victim. Default sentences for non-payment of fine/compensation apply.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused-appellant was convicted by the High Court of Mannar for abducting a minor girl and committing grave sexual abuse. He was sentenced to rigorous imprisonment, fines, and compensation. He appealed on grounds of belated complaint, discrepancies in evidence, failure to prove specific act, unsustainable kidnapping charge, and inadequate consideration of defence. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal, holding the prosecution proved its case beyond reasonable doubt. The victim's testimony was credible, delay was explainable, and the defence was weak. The conviction and sentence were affirmed.
defence_counsel: Saliya Pieris, P.C. with K. Kugaraja
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court accepted the victim's testimony as credible, found the prosecution proved its case beyond reasonable doubt, and imposed sentence considering aggravating and mitigatory circumstances. The Court of Appeal found no error in the High Court's analysis and affirmed its judgment.
precedents_cited_list: Pantis Vs. The Attorney General (1998) 2 SLR 148 | Narender Kumar Vs. State (NCT of Delhi), AIR 2012 SC 2281 | James Silva Vs. The Republic of Sri Lanka (1980) 2 SLR 167 | D. Tikiribanda Vs. Attorney-General CA 64/2003 decided 06-10-2009 reported in the Bar Association Law Journal (2010) (B.L.R.) 92 | Gamage Prabhath Janaka Nayana Priyantha Perera Vs. Attorney General [CA/107/2012] decided on 27.05.2016 | Bhoginbhai Hirjibhai Vs State of Gujarat (AIR 1983-SC 753 at pp 756-758) | Mahathun and Others Vs. The Attorney General (2015) 1 SLR 74 | Sarwan Singh Vs State of Punjab 2002 AIR Supreme Court iii 3652 at 36755,3656 | Boby Mathew Vs State of Karnataka 2004 3 Cri. L. J.3003 | Pilippu Mandige Nalaka Krishantha Kumara Thisera Vs A.G CA 87/2005 decided on 17-05-2007
standard_of_review_applied: The Court reviewed whether the conviction was based on evidence proving guilt beyond reasonable doubt, considering the totality of evidence and giving benefit of doubt to the accused. It assessed witness credibility, contradictions, and explanations for delay.
sentencing_principles_applied: The High Court considered mitigatory and aggravating circumstances. The Court of Appeal did not modify the sentence, affirming the High Court's discretion.

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 4 and 5 of the Prevention of Domestic Violence Act No. 34 of 2005
brief_facts_summary: The aggrieved party applied for protection orders under the Prevention of Domestic Violence Act. The learned Additional Magistrate of Negombo issued interim protection orders on 25-04-2022 and 29-04-2022 after an inter parte inquiry. The petitioner, against whom the orders were made, was present with legal representation and allowed to cross-examine witnesses. The police initiated proceedings based on the aggrieved party's need for protection, following a previous protection order that had expired.
evidence_type_primary: Witness testimony (aggrieved party and other witnesses)
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The petitioner sought revision of interim protection orders, arguing the police initiated proceedings without recording his statement and there was insufficient evidence for the orders. He invoked the revisionary jurisdiction of the Court of Appeal, citing exceptional circumstances.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Challenging interim orders dated 25-04-2022 and 29-04-2022 | Police took steps without recording petitioner's statement | No evidence before Court to issue interim protection order | Invoking revisionary jurisdiction under Article 138 of Constitution
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Magistrate considered evidence from the aggrieved party and other witnesses. The petitioner was allowed to cross-examine witnesses. The Court found the Magistrate properly considered all relevant facts and circumstances before issuing the interim orders.
probability_assessment_by_court: Court found no miscarriage of justice or violation of fundamental procedure; petitioner had opportunity to show cause.
defence_version_summary: Petitioner challenged interim orders via revision application. He argued procedural unfairness (no statement recorded) and lack of evidence. He did not show cause before the Magistrate's Court as permitted by the Act.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal held the petitioner circumvented the constitutionally guaranteed remedy under Article 154P, which grants revisionary jurisdiction to the Provincial High Court for Magistrate's Court orders. The Court found no exceptional circumstances warranting its discretionary revisionary intervention. The interim orders were made after an inter parte inquiry where the petitioner cross-examined witnesses. The Act provides a remedy to show cause before the same Court and a right of appeal against final orders to the Provincial High Court. The petitioner failed to establish circumstances that 'shock the conscience of the Court' or a 'miscarriage of justice'.
coa_sentence_type: Revision application dismissed; interim protection orders remain.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The petitioner sought revision of interim protection orders issued under the Prevention of Domestic Violence Act. The Court of Appeal found he incorrectly invoked its revisionary jurisdiction under Article 138, as the Provincial High Court has exclusive revisionary power over Magistrate's Court orders under Article 154P. The Court held no exceptional circumstances existed to justify its intervention, as the orders were made after a fair hearing and the Act provided adequate remedies. The revision application was dismissed.
prosecution_counsel: I.M.M. Fahim, S.C. for the 1st and 2nd Complainant Respondents
defence_counsel: Kamal Perera for the Petitioner
precedents_cited_list: Hotel Galaxy (Pvt) Ltd. Vs. Mercantile Hotels Management Ltd. (1987) 1 SLR 05 | Wijesinghe Vs. Thamaratnam, (Srikantha Law Reports Vol-IV page 47) | Vanik Incorporation Ltd. Vs. Jayasekare (1997) 2 SLR 365
standard_of_review_applied: Discretionary revisionary jurisdiction requiring exceptional circumstances, circumstances that shock the conscience of the Court, or miscarriage of justice due to violation of fundamental procedure.

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 19(b) and 19(c) of the Bribery Act No. 11 of 1954 as amended
brief_facts_summary: The accused-respondent was indicted for soliciting and accepting Rs. 5,000 as a gratification from the virtual complainant. An investigation was initiated after a complaint was received on 03.04.2018. A raid was conducted on 05.04.2018, and the respondent was arrested while accepting the money. The Director General of CIABOC instituted criminal proceedings in the High Court based on the investigation.
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court upheld the preliminary objection raised by the defence that all three commissioners of CIABOC had not given a directive for the criminal investigation. The High Court dismissed the indictment and discharged the respondent.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The petitioner challenged the High Court order as contrary to law, arguing the judge erroneously required a directive from all three commissioners for investigation and institution of proceedings. The petitioner contended the judge misapplied the law and the precedent of Anoma Polwatte, which dealt with a different provision.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The order dated 21.10.2022 is contrary to law. | The said order is infested with illegality since learned High Court Judge has entailed sanctioning of criminal investigation by all three commissioners on a prerequisite to the institution of Criminal proceedings in the High Court which is not known to the Law. | The learned Trial Judge erred in law by failing to consider that in terms of Section 2(8) of the CIABOC Act, members may exercise powers separately. | The learned Trial Judge erred in law in failing to consider that Anoma Polwatte case was pursuant to a writ application challenging action under Section 78(1) of the Bribery Act. | The learned Trial Judge erred in law by failing to consider that the investigation and institution of proceedings constitutes a 'Power' of the Commission under Section 16(3). | The learned Trial Judge has misconceived in law in holding that a directive of the Commission is required under Sec. 3 of CIABOC Act for investigation and institution. | The said order is clearly in error as the learned trial Judge misdirected himself in considering the ratio decidendi in Anoma Polwatte applicable to institution of proceeding and the investigation. | The learned trial judge misconceived in law in holding that section 78(1) of Bribery Act is applicable to institution of proceedings before the High Court. | The learned Trial Judge erred in law by failing to consider the judicial pronouncement of the Court of Appeal in CA/PHC/APN/2/2021 which distinguished proceedings under CIABOC Act and Bribery Act. | The Learned Trial judge has erroneously determined that the Supreme Court Judgement Anoma Polwatte should be considered and the Court of Appeal judgement disregarded. | The learned trial judge has erroneously determined that the criminal investigation conducted by the Commission in this matter is contrary to law. | The learned Trial judge has misconceived in law in holding that the Supreme Court Case Anoma Polwatte was also decided regarding Section 78(1) of Bribery Act and erred in law by failing to consider that their Lordship had not made any observation on Section 78 of the Bribery Act. | The Court of Appeal erred in Law in failing to consider and applicability of section 114(D) of the Evidence Ordinance to the instant case. | The Learned Trial Judge has errored in law in failing to give valid reasons of the order. | The said order is contrary to the legal maxim of Ut res magis valeat quam pereat.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The judgment focuses on legal procedural grounds and interpretation of the CIABOC Act. There is no detailed analysis of witness or physical evidence presented at trial.
defence_version_summary: The accused raised a preliminary objection that the indictment was void because all three CIABOC commissioners had not given a directive for the criminal investigation. The defence relied on the precedent Anoma Polwatte v The Commission to Investigate Allegation of Bribery and Corruption.
legal_errors_description: The High Court judge erred in law by requiring a directive from all three commissioners of CIABOC to commence investigation and institute proceedings, misinterpreting Section 2(8) of the CIABOC Act and misapplying the Anoma Polwatte precedent which dealt with Section 78(1) of the Bribery Act.
procedural_defects_description: The High Court dismissed the indictment based on a procedural requirement (directive from all commissioners) not mandated by law, and failed to consider that under Section 12 of the CIABOC Act, the High Court's role is limited to verifying annexures to the indictment.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed Section 2(8) of the CIABOC Act, which allows members to exercise powers separately, and Section 12, which outlines requirements for forwarding an indictment. The COA held that no written directive from all three commissioners is required by law. It referenced the Supreme Court judgment in Indikatiya Hewage Kusumadasa Mahanama, which clarified that Anoma Polwatte did not impose an additional requirement for a written directive. The COA found the High Court judge misapplied the law and precedent, erroneously dismissed the indictment, and exceeded his jurisdiction by questioning the validity of the Commission's directive.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The Director General of CIABOC appealed against the High Court order dismissing an indictment against the accused for bribery. The High Court upheld a preliminary objection that all three CIABOC commissioners had not sanctioned the investigation. The Court of Appeal allowed the revision application, finding the High Court judge erred in law by imposing an unwritten requirement and misapplying precedent. The COA set aside the High Court order and directed the trial to recommence expeditiously.
defence_counsel: Saliya Pieris, PC
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court dismissed the indictment based on the defence's preliminary objection that a directive from all three CIABOC commissioners was required. The COA found this reasoning flawed, as the law does not mandate such a requirement and the High Court overstepped by questioning the validity of the Commission's directive instead of focusing on the annexures to the indictment as per Section 12.
precedents_cited_list: Anoma Polwatta v The Commission to Investigate Allegation of Bribery and Corruption SC/Writ Application No. 01/2011 | Anoma Polwatte Vs. Jayawickrama and others SC/Writ/1/2011 | CA/PHC/APN/2/2021 decided on 01/11/2021 | Indikatiya Hewage Kusumadasa Mahanama and Another v. The Commission to Investigate Allegations of Bribery or Corruption and Another SC TAB 1A and 1B/2000, decided on 11.01.2023 | Anoma S.Poluatte v. Director General Commission to Investigate Allegation of Bribery and Corruption
standard_of_review_applied: Revision jurisdiction under Article 138 of the Constitution and Sections 364 and 365 of the Code of Criminal Procedure Act.

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 403 of the Penal Code (cheating), Section 13 of the Sri Lanka Bureau of Foreign Employment Act (cheating), Section 389 of the Penal Code (criminal breach of trust), Section 386 of the Penal Code (criminal misappropriation)
brief_facts_summary: The petitioner was charged with four offences relating to a foreign job transaction: cheating under the Penal Code and the Foreign Employment Act, criminal breach of trust, and criminal misappropriation. She was initially convicted on three counts by the Magistrate's Court, acquitted on one, and ordered to pay compensation. On appeal, the High Court acquitted her on two counts, upheld conviction on criminal misappropriation, but enhanced the sentence without giving her an opportunity to show cause.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 386 of the Penal Code (criminal misappropriation)
hc_sentence_type: 6 months rigorous imprisonment and a fine of Rs. 1500/-
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court partly allowed the appeal, acquitting the petitioner on the 1st and 3rd counts (cheating and criminal breach of trust) but affirming her conviction on the 4th count (criminal misappropriation). It then enhanced the sentence for that count from the Magistrate's original fine to 6 months rigorous imprisonment with a fine, while also upholding the compensation order.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The primary ground was that the High Court Judge enhanced the sentence on the remaining count without following due procedure, specifically without giving the petitioner an opportunity to show cause why the sentence should not be enhanced. The petitioner argued this was illegal and caused a miscarriage of justice.
