He was sentenced to 7 years RI and fines. He appealed, arguing material contradictions in prosecution evidence and insufficient proof. The Court of Appeal found the witnesses credible, minor omissions immaterial, and the evidence, including the appellant's own admissions, proving guilt beyond reasonable doubt. The appeal was dismissed, and the High Court's conviction and sentence were affirmed.
defence_counsel: Anil Silva, P.C. with Amaan Bandara
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court considered the evidence and found the appellant guilty beyond reasonable doubt. The COA found the HC Judge correctly assessed the evidence and witness credibility, and saw no misdirection or error in the conviction.
precedents_cited_list: Bhoginbhai Hitijibhai Vs. State of Gujarat (AIR 1983-SC 753 at pp 756-758) | State of U P Vs. Ashok Kumar Srivastava AIR 1992 SC 840 | Inder Singh and Anr. Vs. State (Delhi Adam.) (AIR 1978 SC 1091) | State of Uttar Pradesh Vs. Anthony 1985 AIR SC 48 | Alwis Vs. Piyasena Fernando (1993) 1 SLR 119 | De Silva and Others Vs. The Attorney General (2010) 2 SLR 169
standard_of_review_applied: The COA reiterated that it would not disturb findings of primary facts made by the trial Judge unless manifestly wrong, as the trial Judge had the advantage of observing witness demeanor.
sentencing_principles_applied: The High Court considered mitigatory and aggravating circumstances. The COA did not modify the sentence, affirming the HC's decision.

judges: R. Gurusinghe J. | M.C.B.S. Morais J.
offence_sections: Section 83 of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs (Amendment) Act No. 41 of 2022
brief_facts_summary: The suspect was arrested on 5th October 2022 by Galle Police during a raid on a house, after attempting to escape. A body search revealed possession and trafficking of 100 grams and 250 milligrams of heroin, with a pure quantity of 26.65 grams as per the Government Analyst Report. The suspect has been in remand custody since 6th October 2022.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The petitioner (suspect's mother) applied for bail under exceptional circumstances. Grounds included the suspect's 7-year-old son being in her custody, the suspect being at the location to redeem pawned items, improbability of hiding the drug quantity in undergarments, presence of the child during the incident, delay in indictment, and family dependency on the suspect.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The 7 years old son of the suspect had been in the custody and under the maintenance of the suspect. | Suspect visited Jayasiri’s home to redeem a gold chain and a phone pawned and unfortunately suspect was caught in the raid. | Prosecution version that 100g and 250 mg was hidden inside suspect’s undergarment is improbable. | The suspect visited the Jayasiri’s house with her 7 years old child after his school. Nobody would do drug business in the presence of their child. | No indictment has been filed thus far since the receipt of the Government Analyst Report. | Suspect’s extended family is depending on the suspect.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The court considered alleged improbabilities in the prosecution case as weaknesses. No specific witness analysis provided in the bail application judgment.
probability_assessment_by_court: The court found alleged weaknesses in prosecution case and procedural delay sufficient to consider bail.
defence_version_summary: The suspect pleaded not impliedly; defence claimed she was at the location to redeem pawned items, not for drug business, and highlighted improbabilities in prosecution case.
procedural_defects_description: Gross negligence in filing objections with incorrect arrest date.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal considered the petition for bail under exceptional circumstances. It noted the suspect had been in remand for over 19 months without indictment despite the Government Analyst Report being received 15 months prior. The court identified weaknesses in the prosecution case and gross negligence by the respondents in filing incorrect objections. Taking these factors together, the court deemed them sufficient to grant bail with strict conditions.
coa_sentence_type: Bail granted with conditions
brief_judgment_file_summary: The petitioner, mother of the suspect, applied for bail under exceptional circumstances for drug possession and trafficking charges. The suspect was arrested in October 2022 with 26.65 grams of pure heroin. The Court of Appeal considered the prolonged remand without indictment, alleged weaknesses in the prosecution case, and procedural negligence by the respondents as exceptional circumstances. Bail was granted with conditions including cash bail, sureties, reporting, and travel ban.
defence_counsel: Lelani Sirisena
precedents_cited_list: Ramu Thamotharampillai V. The Attorney General [2004] 3 SLR 180 | Labynidarage Nishanthi V. Attorney General CA (PHC) APN 48/2014 | Welathanthrage Amila Sampath Botheju V. Attorney General CA/BAL/0239/23
standard_of_review_applied: Exceptional circumstances determination for bail under section 83 of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs (Amendment) Act

judges: R. Gurusinghe J. | M.C.B.S. Morais J.
offence_sections: section 83 (2) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs (Amendment) Act No. 41 of 2022
brief_facts_summary: The petitioner was indicted for possessing and trafficking 5947 grams of heroin and conspiring to traffic the same between 1-7 March 2017. His bail application before the High Court was refused. He applied for bail to the Court of Appeal under Section 83(2) of the Act, which restricts bail for serious drug offences except in exceptional circumstances.
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court refused the petitioner's bail application as there was no sufficient ground. The petitioner has been in custody for over 6 years, and the case has not been taken up for trial for approximately 2 years from the date the first witness was led.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The petitioner pleaded exceptional grounds for bail, including an approximately 2-year delay in taking up the trial beyond his control, denial of the right to an expeditious trial, denial of his family's right to a reasonable life due to his prolonged custody, and the misleading nature of the police B report regarding his humble lifestyle. Additional grounds were that the case was called but not taken up for trial for reasons beyond his control, and that all other suspects except him were enlarged on bail.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: I. Case not taken up for trial for approximately 2 years from date of leading of witness number 1 for reasons beyond petitioner's control. | II. Petitioner denied right to an expeditious trial. | III. Petitioner's family members' right to a reasonable life denied by his custody over 6 years. | IV. Police B report misleading on facts, petitioner's humble lifestyle not matching that of a narcotics peddler. | V. Case called but not taken up for trial for reasons beyond petitioner's control. | VI. All other suspects except petitioner enlarged on bail, unfair petitioner alone incarcerated over 6 years.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The judgment does not analyze the evidence for the main trial but focuses on the bail application. The petitioner's character is noted as significant, and a previous conviction for possessing 65 milligrams of heroin in 2013 was confirmed from the High Court record.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal found the petitioner breached his duty of utmost good faith by not disclosing a previous conviction, making it unnecessary to consider the merits of exceptional circumstances.
defence_version_summary: The petitioner pleaded not guilty (implied from bail application context). He claimed a humble lifestyle inconsistent with drug trafficking. The court found he breached his duty of full disclosure by concealing a previous conviction for a similar offence.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal declined to consider the merits of the alleged exceptional circumstances for bail because the petitioner breached his duty of utmost good faith (uberrima fides) to the court by failing to disclose his previous conviction for possession of 65mg of heroin in 2013. The court cited precedent stating that a party who fails to disclose all material facts or attempts to pollute justice should be denied relief. As the petitioner concealed this relevant fact, the bail application was refused in limine.
coa_sentence_type: Bail application refused in limine.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The petitioner, accused of possessing and trafficking 5947 grams of heroin, applied for bail to the Court of Appeal after his High Court bail application was refused. He pleaded exceptional grounds, including trial delays and unfairness compared to co-accused. The Court of Appeal found the petitioner had a previous conviction for a similar drug offence, which he failed to disclose. Citing the duty of utmost good faith, the court refused the bail application in limine without considering the merits of the alleged exceptional circumstances.
defence_counsel: Punarji Karunasekara
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court refused bail as there was no sufficient ground. The Court of Appeal did not analyze or criticize the High Court's reasoning, as it dismissed the application based on the petitioner's non-disclosure.
precedents_cited_list: Namunukula Plantations Limited V Minister of lands and Others SC Appeal No. 46/2008
standard_of_review_applied: Application of the principle of utmost good faith (uberrima fides) in discretionary jurisdiction.

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 389 of the Penal Code and Section 403 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The Appellant, a gem dealer, obtained five gemstones worth approximately Rs. 24,85,400 from PW1 (a businessman) under an agreement (P2) to sell them and return the proceeds or the gems. The Appellant failed to do either and issued a cheque which was dishonored. PW1 lodged a police complaint after the cheque bounced. PW3, another gem merchant, bought a gem from the Appellant on 08.06.1994 for Rs.65,000 and did not see him again. The Appellant was indicted for Criminal Breach of Trust and Cheating, absconded initially, was later arrested, and tried in absentia part of the time.
evidence_type_primary: Documentary evidence (agreement P2, dishonored cheque P1), Witness testimony (PW1, PW3, PW10)
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 403 of the Penal Code
hc_sentence_type: Two years rigorous imprisonment suspended for ten years, Fine, Compensation
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court Judge found the Appellant guilty only on the second count (Section 403 of the Penal Code). The Judge sentenced him to two years rigorous imprisonment suspended for ten years, a fine of Rs. 25,000, and compensation of Rs. 1,000,000, with a default sentence of six months simple imprisonment.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The Appellant argued that the prosecution failed to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt. It was also contended that the High Court Judge failed to consider matters favorable to the Appellant.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The prosecution has not proved its case beyond reasonable doubt. | The learned High Court Judge has not taken into consideration matters favourable to the Appellant.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the High Court Judge properly analyzed all oral and documentary evidence, gave plausible reasons for accepting/rejecting evidence, and accurately considered the Appellant's conduct. No vital contradictions or omissions were marked from prosecution witnesses.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal concluded the prosecution proved the case beyond reasonable doubt, applying tests of belatedness, consistency, corroboration, and probability.
defence_version_summary: The Appellant pleaded not guilty. He made a dock statement admitting he received gems from PW1 but claimed he settled all dues by a cheque. He called no defence witnesses. The court found his version less credible given the dishonored cheque and his conduct.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal held that the High Court Judge correctly applied legal principles regarding belatedness, consistency, corroboration, and probability. The Judge's findings on witness credibility were not manifestly wrong. The Appellant's admission in his dock statement that he received gems under agreement P2 strengthened the prosecution case. The non-production of the original cheque (P1) did not prejudice the Appellant as he admitted receiving the gems. The evidence of PW3 further corroborated the prosecution case. The appeal was dismissed as the prosecution proved its case beyond reasonable doubt.
coa_sentence_type: Two years rigorous imprisonment suspended for ten years, Fine of Rs. 25,000, Compensation of Rs. 1,000,000, with default sentence of six months simple imprisonment.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The Accused-Appellant was convicted in the High Court of Colombo for Cheating (Section 403 Penal Code) concerning gemstones worth Rs. 24,85,400 obtained from a businessman (PW1). He was sentenced to suspended imprisonment, a fine, and compensation. He appealed, arguing the prosecution failed to prove its case beyond doubt and that favorable matters were not considered. The Court of Appeal, after analyzing the evidence and the High Court Judge's reasoning, found the conviction sound, the legal tests properly applied, and the prosecution's case proved beyond reasonable doubt. The appeal was dismissed, upholding the High Court's conviction and sentence.
defence_counsel: Anil Silva, PC with Isuru Jayawardena and Amaan Bandara
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court Judge accurately analyzed evidence, gave plausible reasons, and applied proper legal tests. The Court of Appeal found no error in this analysis or in the Judge's findings on credibility and evidence.
precedents_cited_list: Dharmasiri v Republic of Sri Lanka [2010] 2 SLR 241
standard_of_review_applied: Court of Appeal will not lightly disturb trial Judge's findings on witness credibility unless manifestly wrong.

judges: Menaka Wijesundera J. | K.M.G.H Kulatunga J.
offence_sections: section 383, two charges under section 296, and in the alternative section 394 of the Penal Code.
brief_facts_summary: Two deceased persons (mother and son) were found on 25th April 2001, the son dead and the mother severely injured, with certain electrical items missing from their home. On the same morning, police at a checkpoint stopped a motorcycle, the rider fled, and the abandoned motorcycle and a bag containing electrical items and a gramasevaka certificate with the appellant's name were found. The motorcycle and items were identified by PW-02 (brother/son of deceased) as belonging to the deceased. The appellant was arrested later that day. A mamoty with bloodstains was recovered based on his statement, and the Government Analyst identified it as human blood.
evidence_type_secondary: Physical evidence (recovered stolen property, mamoty with blood), Identification evidence
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court judge presumed the appellant had committed offences under charges 1, 2, 3, and 4, convicted him for charges 2, 3, and 4, and considered charges 1 and 5 as alternatives. The judge failed to state the standard of proof applied.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appeal challenged the High Court's failure to consider the improbability of the prosecution version, the section 27(1) recovery made by police, and the erroneous evaluation of circumstantial evidence.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The improbability of the prosecution version not being considered by the High Court Judge. | Challenging the section 27(1) recovery made by the police. | Evaluation of circumstantial evidence being erroneous.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The prosecution relied on circumstantial evidence, including recovery of stolen goods soon after the offence and the appellant fleeing from police. The court found this evidence serious and cogent.
probability_assessment_by_court: Court applied principle that circumstantial evidence must be incompatible with innocence and only consistent with guilt, and that proof must be beyond reasonable doubt.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty. He made a dock statement denying the entire incident. He did not call witnesses.
legal_errors_description: The trial judge erroneously presumed guilt instead of deciding based on evidence, and failed to state the standard of proof applied.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the trial judge fundamentally erred by using the term 'presume' regarding guilt after analyzing evidence, instead of applying the 'beyond reasonable doubt' standard. However, the COA found the circumstantial evidence against the appellant was serious and cogent: he was found riding the deceased's motorcycle with stolen household items soon after the murder/robbery, and fled when approached by police. The COA applied Section 114(a) of the Evidence Ordinance to draw an adverse inference from recent possession of stolen goods. Despite the legal error on burden of proof, the COA considered the evidence strong enough to warrant a retrial rather than an acquittal.
coa_sentence_type: Conviction and sentence set aside. Ordered for retrial.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused-appellant was convicted by the High Court of Chilaw on murder and related charges from a 2001 incident. He appealed on grounds including erroneous evaluation of circumstantial evidence. The Court of Appeal found the trial judge made a fundamental error by failing to apply and state the 'beyond reasonable doubt' standard, instead 'presuming' guilt. However, the COA found the circumstantial evidence (recent possession of stolen goods, fleeing) was cogent. To avoid a travesty of justice, the COA set aside the conviction and sentence but ordered a retrial to be concluded expeditiously.
defence_counsel: Tenny Fernando
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court judge presumed the appellant's guilt for certain charges after analyzing evidence, convicted on some, and treated others as alternatives. The COA found this approach erroneous and illegal as the judge failed to state and apply the correct standard of proof ('beyond reasonable doubt').
precedents_cited_list: King v Appuhamy | Karamaratne v Attorney General (2005) 1 Sri LR 233 | State of V.P. vs Dr. Ravindra Prakash Mittal (1992) 2 SCJ 549 | Podi Singho vs King 53 N.L.R 49 | King vs Appuhamy 46 N.L.R 128 | State of Tamil Nadu vs Rajendran 1999 Cri. L.J. 4552 | Anuruddha Samaranayake and Four Others vs Attorney General CA 36-40/2007 decided on 25th March 2011
standard_of_review_applied: Review based on error of law (failure to apply correct standard of proof) and evaluation of circumstantial evidence.

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | Amal Ranaraja, J.
offence_sections: section 47(1) of the Excise Ordinance
location_of_offence: Kongoda Bridge within the jurisdiction of the Magistrate’s Court of Pilassa
brief_facts_summary: The petitioner was charged for possessing 11,250 milliliters of illicit liquor at Kongoda Bridge on 02-03-2020. He was arrested and produced before the Magistrate’s Court via a B-Report which included details of 34 previous similar offences. After trial, the Magistrate found him guilty, imposed a fine, and initiated confiscation proceedings for the motorcycle used. The petitioner appealed to the High Court, which dismissed the appeal.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: section 47(1) of the Excise Ordinance
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court dismissed the appeal, finding no reason to interfere with the Magistrate's conviction and sentence. The High Court Judge held that the previous convictions mentioned in the B-Report did not influence the Magistrate's judgment and that the character evidence from the police witness was not a sufficient ground to interfere.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The petitioner argued that the police, by attaching his previous conviction record to the B-Report and plaint, prejudiced the Magistrate and denied him a fair trial. He also contended that the police witness (PW-01) gave inadmissible character evidence, violating the Evidence Ordinance. Further, he claimed the Magistrate misdirected herself in evaluating his dock statement.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Prejudice caused by police submitting previous conviction record at the outset | Admission of bad character evidence by prosecution witness (PW-01) violating Section 54 of Evidence Ordinance | Misdirection by Magistrate in evaluating the defence dock statement
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal focused on the procedural impropriety of admitting the accused's previous conviction record and bad character evidence. It found that this, combined with the Magistrate's erroneous treatment of the dock statement, created a miscarriage of justice.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court found a reasonable doubt was created due to the procedural violations prejudicing the trial, warranting acquittal.
defence_version_summary: The petitioner pleaded not guilty. He made a statement from the dock but called no witnesses. The Magistrate erroneously discounted his dock statement on the basis that it was not subject to cross-examination.
legal_errors_description: The Magistrate and High Court erred in law by allowing and not properly disregarding evidence of the accused's bad character and previous convictions, violating Section 54 of the Evidence Ordinance and fair trial principles. The Magistrate also misdirected herself on the evidential value of a dock statement.
procedural_defects_description: Police improperly attached the accused's previous conviction record to the B-Report and plaint at the commencement of the case. The trial court allowed the prosecution to lead evidence of the accused's bad character.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal held that exceptional circumstances existed warranting revisionary intervention. It found a clear violation of the fair trial principle due to the police submitting the previous conviction record and the trial court admitting bad character evidence, which prejudiced the accused. The Court also held the Magistrate misdirected herself by failing to properly evaluate the evidential value of the accused's dock statement, applying the principles from Queen v. Kularathne. Considering these cumulative errors and the nature of the witnesses (police officers who could correct shortcomings in a retrial), the Court found a retrial would not ensure a fair trial and acquitted the petitioner.
coa_sentence_type: Acquitted, no sentence imposed.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The petitioner was convicted by the Magistrate's Court of Pilassa for possessing illicit liquor and fined Rs. 25,000. The High Court of Kurunegala dismissed his appeal. The Court of Appeal, in a revision application, found exceptional circumstances. It held that the police's submission of the petitioner's previous conviction record and the admission of bad character evidence violated fair trial principles and Section 54 of the Evidence Ordinance. The Court also found the Magistrate misdirected herself on the law regarding dock statements. Consequently, the Court set aside both lower court judgments and acquitted the petitioner, declining to order a retrial due to concerns over police witnesses correcting their evidence.
prosecution_counsel: Oswold Perera, S.C. for the 2nd Respondent (Hon. Attorney General)
defence_counsel: Isuru Jayawardana for the Petitioner
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court justified the Magistrate's conviction, holding that the previous convictions did not influence the Magistrate and the character evidence was not a ground for interference. The Court of Appeal found the High Court erred by failing to recognize that these procedural violations cumulatively denied the petitioner a fair trial.
precedents_cited_list: Thilagaratnam Vs. Edirisinghe (1982) 1 SLR 56 | Jonita Vs. Abeysekara (Sriskantha Law Report Vol IV Page 22) | Hotel Galaxy (Pvt) Ltd Vs. Mercantile Hotels Management Ltd (1987) 1 SLR 5 | Wijesinghe Vs. Thamararatnam (Sriskantha Law Report Volume IV page 47) | Vanik Incorporation Ltd Vs. Jayasekare (1997) 2 SLR 365 | Sadi Banda Vs. Officer In Charge of Norton Bridge Police Station | Queen Vs. Kularathne (1968) 71 NLR 529 | King Vs. Vellayan Sittambaram (1918) 20 NLR 257 | Queen Vs. Buddharakkita Thero (1962) 63 NLR 433
standard_of_review_applied: Revisionary jurisdiction exercised due to exceptional circumstances involving a miscarriage of justice from procedural violations and legal misdirections.

judges: Menaka Wijesundera J. | K.M.G.H Kulatunga J.
offence_sections: sections 354 and 364(2) of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The appellant was convicted of kidnapping and statutory rape involving a victim who was 15-16 years old around 2005/2006. The victim alleged they had a love affair and three instances of sexual intercourse, resulting in pregnancy and an abortion facilitated by the appellant. The complaint was made in July 2007 after the victim's cousin revealed the incident to her parents. The appellant, who worked at the Trincomalee Pradeshiya Sabha, denied the allegations and claimed he was working on dates relevant to the abortion.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: sections 354 and 364(2) of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the appellant on both counts in the indictment after trial where the prosecution led evidence and the appellant also gave evidence and called witnesses. The trial judge sentenced the appellant accordingly.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appeal was based on two main grounds: 1) The charge was defective as it specified a time period rather than a specific date, violating Section 165(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure. 2) The prosecution failed to prove its case beyond a reasonable doubt, particularly regarding the date of the offence and the reliability of the victim's evidence.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The charge being defective. | The prosecution has not proved their case beyond a reasonable doubt.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court found the victim's evidence regarding the time period of the offence inconsistent and unreliable, as she gave different years (2005, 2006) during her testimony. Her history given to the doctor (abortion date 2006.06.26) further created doubt. The appellant's evidence included an alibi for specific dates.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court found reasonable doubt existed regarding the date of the offence based on inconsistencies in the victim's evidence and the medical history, which the trial judge failed to properly consider.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty. He gave evidence denying any sexual acts with the victim. He claimed he was working on specific dates (26th and 27th June 2006) relevant to the abortion allegation. He stated he initially liked a marriage proposal brought by the victim's cousin's husband in 2006 but withdrew upon learning she was in a relationship with another man.
legal_errors_description: The trial judge misdirected himself on law and fact, particularly by not adverting to the doubt created by the victim's inconsistent evidence on the date of the offence and by admitting evidence of three acts of rape without proper consideration of the principles under the Evidence Ordinance.
procedural_defects_description: The charge was framed based on a time period ('between 1st January 2005 and 31st December 2005') rather than a specific date, which was argued to violate Section 165(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the prosecution failed to prove the date of the offence beyond reasonable doubt, noting inconsistencies in the victim's testimony and the medical history. The trial judge erred by not considering this doubt and by improperly admitting evidence of multiple rape acts. Justice Wijesundera found the charge defective for not specifying a date. Justice Kulatunga disagreed on the charge defect point but agreed the prosecution failed to prove the offence occurred within the charged period and that the victim's evidence was unreliable. Both judges agreed the appeal should be allowed.
coa_sentence_type: Conviction and sentence set aside.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused-appellant was convicted by the High Court of Trincomalee for kidnapping and statutory rape. He appealed to the Court of Appeal on grounds of a defective charge and failure of the prosecution to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt. The Court of Appeal found the prosecution failed to prove the offence date, noted inconsistencies in the victim's evidence, and identified legal misdirections by the trial judge. Both judges allowed the appeal, set aside the conviction and sentence, and acquitted the appellant.
defence_counsel: Senarath Jayasundara and Rehani Chandrasiri
hc_analysis_summary: The COA found the High Court judge failed to properly consider the reasonable doubt created by inconsistencies in the victim's evidence regarding the date of the offence. He also erred in admitting evidence of three acts of rape without proper legal analysis under the Evidence Ordinance.
