judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 296 read with Section 32 of the Penal Code; Section 300 read with Section 32 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: On 15.04.2007, the accused-appellants were charged with the murder of Loku Gamage Jayantha Victor and the attempted murder of Kathriarachchilage Don Rohitha (PW2). The incident occurred near the deceased's restaurant after a New Year festival. The prosecution alleged the 3rd appellant stopped the deceased's motorbike, assaulted him, after which the 1st appellant attacked the deceased on the head with a sword, and the 2nd appellant threatened with a sword.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 296 read with Section 32 of the Penal Code; Section 300 read with Section 32 of the Penal Code
hc_sentence_type: Death on 1st count (murder); 5 years rigorous imprisonment and fine of Rs.25000 on second count (attempted murder); 1-year default simple imprisonment for fine; Compensation order with 1-year default simple imprisonment
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court Judge, after a non-jury trial, convicted all appellants on both counts. The judge found the prosecution evidence, primarily from PW1 (the sole eyewitness to the murder) and PW2, convincing and sufficient to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt. Sentences of death and imprisonment were imposed, along with fines and compensation.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: Appellants challenged the credibility, probability, and consistency of eyewitness testimony (PW1 and PW2). They argued the trial judge failed to properly analyze contradictions and omissions, wrongly assessed common intention, relied on demeanour of a witness who did not testify before him, and denied a fair trial. The 3rd appellant also argued inadequate analysis of prosecution case and prejudice from absconding inference.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The evidence of PW1 and PW2 fails the test of credibility, probability and consistency. | The learned High Court Judge rejected the defence on unreasonable grounds. | There has been totally inadequate analysis of the case for the prosecution in the light of the many infirmities. | The learned Trial Judge has laid much emphasis on the fact that the accused had absconded after the incident in concluding on their culpability without considering the circumstances under which they had to surrender to Court. | The learned Trial Judge has relied upon the demeanour of the first witness for the prosecution when in fact he did not testify before the learned Judge. | The learned Trial Judge has imposed liability on the basis of common intention without considering the law pertaining to common intention as laid down in decided cases. | There has been total inadequacy in the case for the defence, thereby causing much prejudice to the Accused Appellant. | Due to one or more of the reasons, the Accused Appellants had had been denied a fair trial, a Fundamental Right Constitutionally guaranteed.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: Court analyzed the sole eyewitness (PW1) and PW2. Found serious contradictions and omissions in PW1's testimony regarding who blocked the road and details of the attack. PW2 did not witness the murder attack and misidentified an appellant. The Court held the evidence was not convincing or reliable.
probability_assessment_by_court: Court found the prosecution failed to prove the case beyond reasonable doubt due to serious doubt and ambiguity in the eyewitness testimony, including contradictions and omissions.
defence_version_summary: The 1st appellant gave evidence from the witness box and called two witnesses. The 2nd and 3rd appellants made statements from the dock. The defence challenged the prosecution evidence. The Court of Appeal found the defence version was not properly considered by the High Court, and the prosecution evidence was unreliable.
legal_errors_description: High Court Judge imposed common intention without proper legal analysis per precedents; failed to consider contradictions and omissions in prosecution evidence; relied on demeanour of a witness who did not testify before him.
procedural_defects_description: The High Court Judge wrongly stated which appellants gave evidence from the witness box versus dock statements. Potential denial of fair trial due to inadequate analysis and reliance on flawed evidence.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal conducted a thorough review of eyewitness testimony, noting the burden of proof remains on the prosecution. It identified significant contradictions and omissions in PW1's evidence (e.g., who blocked the road, details of the attack) which were not considered by the High Court. PW2's evidence was limited and included misidentification. The Court found the High Judge erred in imposing common intention without proper legal analysis and in relying on flawed evidence. Citing precedents on evaluating witness credibility, the COA held the prosecution evidence created serious doubt and was insufficient to convict beyond reasonable doubt.
coa_sentence_type: Conviction and sentence set aside; appellants acquitted.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The Attorney General appealed against the conviction and sentence of three appellants for murder and attempted murder. The High Court of Kalutara convicted them after a non-jury trial, imposing death and imprisonment sentences. The appellants appealed, challenging the credibility and consistency of the sole eyewitness, procedural errors, and misapplication of common intention. The Court of Appeal found the prosecution evidence, primarily from PW1 and PW2, contained fatal contradictions and omissions not properly considered by the High Court. It held the prosecution failed to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt, set aside the conviction and sentence, and acquitted all appellants.
defence_counsel: Neranjan Jayasinghe with Randunu Heelllage and Imangsi Senerath for 1st and 2nd Appellants; Palitha Fernando, PC with Harshana Ananda for the 3rd Appellant
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court Judge found the prosecution evidence, particularly from PW1, convincing and sufficient for conviction beyond reasonable doubt. The COA found the HC erred by not properly analyzing contradictions and omissions in eyewitness testimony, misapplying common intention law, and making factual errors about which appellants testified.
precedents_cited_list: The Queen v. K. A. Santin Singho 65 NLR 447 | State Rep. by Inspector of Police v. Saravanan AIR 2009 SC 152 | Acharaparambath Pradeepan & Anr. v. State of Kerala 2006 13 SCC 643 | Kehar Singh & Ors v. State (Delhi Adam.) [3] AIR 1988 SC 1883
standard_of_review_applied: Evaluation of whether prosecution proved case beyond reasonable doubt; assessment of witness credibility, contradictions, omissions, and application of law (common intention).

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 365B (2) (b) of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The Appellant, a class teacher, was accused of committing three counts of grave sexual abuse on a 10-year-old female student (PW1) between December 2013 and February 2014 during afternoon mathematics classes. The alleged acts included squeezing her breasts and digital penetration of her vagina. The victim initially did not disclose the incidents due to fear and respect for the teacher but later informed her mother, leading to a police complaint on 05.02.2014. Medical examination revealed findings consistent with digital penetration.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 365B (2) (b) of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court Judge, after considering the evidence, convicted the Appellant only on the 3rd count of the indictment. The Appellant was sentenced to 10 years rigorous imprisonment, fined Rs.10,000, and ordered to pay compensation of Rs.100,000. He was acquitted on the 1st and 2nd counts.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The Appellant's counsel argued that the High Court Judge failed to consider inconsistencies in the victim's evidence and the medical history, did not properly evaluate prosecution evidence, erred in law by considering an unmarked portion of the Appellant's statement, and reversed the burden of proof by placing it on the Appellant to prove his innocence.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Did the learned High Court Judge fail to consider the inconsistencies and contradictions between PW1’s evidence and the short history given to the Medical Officer. | Did the learned High Court Judge fail to properly evaluate the prosecution evidence particularly on the consideration of improbability. | Has the learned High Court Judge erred in law by considering the portion of the statement made by the Appellant which were not marked during the defence. | The learned Trial Judge erred in law by placing the burden on the Appellant to prove his innocence.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal carefully assessed the victim's (PW1) testimony, finding her evidence credible and cogent despite minor contradictions. The medical evidence (JMO report) corroborated her testimony regarding digital penetration. The court held that the minor inconsistencies did not undermine the core of the prosecution's case.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal found the victim's testimony probable and convincing, and the medical evidence supported her account. Minor contradictions were not considered material enough to create reasonable doubt.
defence_version_summary: The Appellant pleaded not guilty, gave evidence from the witness box denying the charges, and closed his case. The court assessed his defence and found the prosecution's case, particularly the victim's credible testimony, sufficient for conviction.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed each ground of appeal. It found no merit in the claim of inconsistencies, as the medical evidence corroborated the victim's testimony. It held that minor contradictions in the evidence were not material. Regarding the consideration of an unmarked statement, the court acknowledged a misdirection but found it caused no prejudice to the Appellant. The court rejected the argument that the burden of proof was reversed, finding the High Court Judge had correctly applied the law. Guided by precedents on medical evidence admissibility and Article 138 of the Constitution, the COA concluded there was no basis to interfere with the HC judgment.
coa_sentence_type: 10 years rigorous imprisonment operative from 02.12.2022, fine of Rs.10,000, compensation of Rs.100,000
brief_judgment_file_summary: The Appellant, a teacher, was convicted by the High Court of Badulla on one count of grave sexual abuse against a 10-year-old student and sentenced to 10 years RI, a fine, and compensation. He appealed on grounds including inconsistencies in evidence, improper evaluation of evidence, legal misdirection, and reversal of the burden of proof. The Court of Appeal, after analyzing the victim's credible testimony supported by medical evidence and dismissing the appeal grounds as lacking merit, dismissed the appeal and upheld the High Court's conviction and sentence.
defence_counsel: Shanaka Ranasinghe,PC with Niroshan Mihidukulasuriya and V. Abeysooriya
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court Judge carefully considered the evidence, found the victim's testimony convincing and sufficient for conviction on one count, and imposed sentence. The Court of Appeal found no material error in the HC's analysis or reasoning that warranted interference.
precedents_cited_list: Gamini Dolawatte V. Attorney General [1988] 1 Sri. L. R 221 | Bhargavan v. State of Kerala AIR 2004 SC 1058 (Supreme Court of India)
standard_of_review_applied: Appellate jurisdiction for correction of errors in fact or law, considering whether any error prejudiced the substantial rights of the parties or occasioned a failure of justice as per Article 138 of the Constitution.

judges: Menaka Wijesundera, J. | B. Sasi Mahendran, J.
offence_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code
location_of_offence: Weerasooriya Kanda, near a shop veranda
brief_facts_summary: The Accused-Appellant was convicted for the murder of Kongasdeniyage Ajith Kumara Sampath on 27 May 2006. The deceased was a three-wheeler driver hired by PW2. While waiting for a shop to open, the accused arrived, later returned with an umbrella, charged at the deceased, and stabbed him. The deceased was taken to the hospital where he died. The accused later surrendered to police and led them to the concealed knife.
evidence_type_secondary: Medical evidence (Post mortem report, PW14), Recovery of weapon (knife)
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The Learned High Court Judge convicted the accused for murder and imposed the death sentence. The judge found the prosecution evidence credible and rejected the defence of private defence.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appeal grounds focus on contradictions in witness testimonies (PW2 and PW3), inconsistencies with medical evidence, failure to consider the possibility of a sudden fight and right of private defence, misdirection regarding the post mortem report, improper evaluation of the dock statement, and failure to consider lesser offence of culpable homicide not amounting to murder.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Has the learned Trial Judge failed to consider contradictions between PW2 and PW3? | Has the Judge not considered infirmities between PW2 and the JMO (PW14)? | Has the Judge misdirected himself regarding the post mortem report signature? | Has the Judge erred in determining there was no fight and thus no right of private defence? | Has the Judge failed to consider that PW2 and PW3 did not see the stabbing and contradictions about the fight location? | Has the Judge failed to consider the Appellant's dock statement on self-defence? | Has the Judge erred in considering the Dock Statement in isolation? | Has the Judge erroneously considered presumptions not recognized in law? | Has the Judge failed to consider that PW3 corroborates the Dock Statement? | Has the Judge failed to consider culpable homicide not amounting to murder? | Has the Judge failed to give benefit of the doubt?
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the eyewitness testimony of PW2 credible and consistent, with minor contradictions deemed trivial and not material. PW3 corroborated key aspects. The medical evidence (PW14) established the nature of injuries and murderous intention. The accused's dock statement was rejected as an afterthought.
probability_assessment_by_court: Court found prosecution proved case beyond reasonable doubt. Minor discrepancies in witness testimony did not create reasonable doubt.
defence_version_summary: The accused pleaded not guilty. He made a dock statement claiming the deceased started the fight and had a knife, and he acted in self-defence. No defence witnesses were called. The court rejected this version as an afterthought, noting it was not put to prosecution witnesses in cross-examination.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The COA analyzed witness contradictions, applying principles from Bharwada Bhoginbhai Hirjibhai vs State of Gujarat and State of Uttar Pradesh v. M.K. Anthony, holding minor discrepancies are normal. It found PW2's testimony credible and corroborated by PW3. Medical evidence established murderous intention based on injury location and force. The accused's recovery of the knife under Section 27 of the Evidence Ordinance was unchallenged and incriminating. The dock statement was an afterthought as the defence version was not put to witnesses. The HC correctly applied the law on murderous intention per Sisira De Abrew J in Thommeyahakuru Somasiri vs. Republic of Sri Lanka. No reason to interfere with HC judgment.
coa_sentence_type: Death sentence affirmed
brief_judgment_file_summary: The Accused-Appellant was convicted of murder by the High Court of Gampaha and sentenced to death. He appealed on grounds including witness contradictions, medical inconsistencies, misdirection on law, and failure to consider private defence and lesser offence. The Court of Appeal found the eyewitness testimony credible, minor contradictions trivial, and medical evidence strong. It upheld the finding of murderous intention and rejected the dock statement as an afterthought. The appeal was dismissed, affirming the conviction and death sentence.
defence_counsel: Vishwa de Livera Tennakoon
cause_of_death_exact_text: Haemorrhage and shock from injuries sustained
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court correctly evaluated the evidence, found the prosecution proved murder beyond reasonable doubt, and rejected the defence of private defence. The COA found no error in this analysis and agreed with the HC's reasoning and conclusions.
precedents_cited_list: Bharwada Bhoginbhai Hirjibhai vs State of Gujarat 1983 AIR HC 753 | State of Uttar Pradesh v. M.K. Anthony, Supreme Court Journal 1984 (2) page 498 | Oliver Dayananda Kalansuriya alias Raja Vs The Democratic Socialist Republic of Sri Lanka, CA 28/2009 | Ariyasinghe And Others V Attorney General (G. C. Wickremasinghe Abduction Case) 2004 (2) Sri L.R 357 | CA 112.2006 Thommeyahakuru Somasiri vs. Republic of Sri Lanka | CA 186/2009 Kiribandara Muhandiramlage Rohana Tissa Kumara v. AG
standard_of_review_applied: Appellate court scrutiny of evidence, giving due weight to trial court's appreciation unless reasons are weighty and formidable.
sentencing_principles_applied: Death sentence affirmed based on conviction for murder under Section 296 of the Penal Code.

judges: Menaka Wijesundera J. | B. Sasi Mahendran J.
location_of_offence: near the world market in Fort, Colombo
brief_facts_summary: On 6 February 2006, police from the Narcotics Bureau arrested the appellant near the Fort railway station. A body search revealed 5.45 grams of heroin in his trouser pocket. The prosecution alleges he was in possession, while the defense claims the drugs were planted and the appellant was assaulted to reveal the whereabouts of a person named Ravi.
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the appellant for possession of 5.45 grams of heroin. The trial judge concluded the prosecution proved its case beyond reasonable doubt.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The main contention was that the alleged drugs were introduced/planted on the appellant by the police. The defense also claimed the appellant was assaulted to divulge the whereabouts of a person named Ravi, and that the police narrative was improbable.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Drugs were introduced/planted on the appellant. | The appellant was assaulted by narcotics officers to find Ravi. | The police version of taking the appellant to his brother's house is improbable. | The alleged assault at Galle Face Green in broad daylight is improbable.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court found the police officers' testimony corroborated and no material contradictions. The defense failed to put key allegations (assault, search for Ravi before arrest) to prosecution witnesses in cross-examination, weakening their version.
probability_assessment_by_court: Court found the defense version improbable (e.g., assault in public, taking suspect to his brother's house) and did not create reasonable doubt in the prosecution case.
defence_version_summary: Not guilty plea. The appellant gave evidence from the dock stating he never possessed drugs, was assaulted by police to find Ravi, and that drugs were planted on him. His brother also testified. The court found the defense version not credible and improbable.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found no merit in the appeal. It held the defense version did not create reasonable doubt. While noting the trial judge had not properly analyzed evidence at some points, the COA agreed the prosecution proved its case beyond reasonable doubt. The defense failed to cross-examine prosecution witnesses on key allegations (assault, search for Ravi before arrest), and the court found the defense narrative improbable (e.g., police assaulting in public, taking suspect to his brother's house). The conviction was upheld.
coa_sentence_type: Conviction and sentence of the trial judge affirmed.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The appellant was convicted by the High Court for possessing 5.45 grams of heroin. He appealed, claiming the drugs were planted and he was assaulted. The Court of Appeal found the defense version improbable and noted failure to cross-examine on material points. While observing some inadequate analysis by the trial judge, the COA upheld the conviction and sentence, dismissing the appeal.
prosecution_counsel: Chethiya Gunasekara A.S.G., P.C, with Ridma Kuruwita S.C.
defence_counsel: Neranjan Jayasinghe with Harshana Ananda
hc_analysis_summary: The COA observed that the trial judge had not properly analyzed the evidence at some points. However, it ultimately agreed with the HC's conclusion that the prosecution proved its case beyond reasonable doubt.
standard_of_review_applied: Assessment of whether defense created reasonable doubt in prosecution case; evaluation of evidence credibility and probability.

judges: Menaka Wijesundera J. | B. Sasi Mahendran J.
brief_facts_summary: The accused appellant and another were indicted for murder. PW1, the sister of the deceased, testified that she heard the deceased shouting on the road that the second accused had assaulted him. She went and saw the appellant and the second accused at the scene with her brother. She tried to take her brother away, but the appellant and the second accused confronted them with iron rods and assaulted the deceased. The deceased was hospitalized for 10 days and succumbed to his injuries. An iron rod was recovered based on the appellant's statement and was identified as capable of causing the fatal injury.
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court judge found the accused appellant guilty of murder and sentenced him to death.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The main contention was that PW1, the sole witness, told an improbable story because had she participated, she would have sustained injuries given the magnitude of the incident. The defense also argued contradictions in PW1's evidence and that the appellant had given a dock statement saying he was drinking with the deceased and the other accused, and had intervened to settle a fight.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Improbability of PW1's testimony as sole eyewitness | Contradictions in PW1's evidence | Dock statement presented by appellant giving alternative version of events
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court considered PW1's evidence to be consistent and persistent despite some contradictions, which were deemed not to go to the root of the case. The quality of her evidence was found to be more important than the number of witnesses.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court found no reasonable doubt raised by the appellant's dock statement or the contradictions in PW1's evidence.
defence_version_summary: The accused pleaded not guilty and gave a dock statement. He claimed he and the deceased and the other accused had been drinking, the other two fought, and he intervened to settle the matter. The court found his defense not credible and did not raise reasonable doubt.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the appellant acted willfully and with the intention of causing death, assaulting the deceased with an iron rod with considerable force. It held that the contradictions in PW1's evidence did not go to the root of the case and did not undermine her credibility, citing Indian precedents. The Court affirmed the principle that evidence should be weighed, not counted. The dock statement did not create reasonable doubt, and the appellant's failure to deny the recovery of the iron rod from his premises was noted.
coa_sentence_type: Death
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused appellant appealed his High Court conviction for murder and death sentence. The prosecution case relied on the eyewitness testimony of PW1, the deceased's sister, and medical evidence showing fatal injuries. The appellant argued the testimony was improbable and contradictory, and presented a dock statement claiming he intervened in a fight. The Court of Appeal found PW1's evidence credible and consistent, held contradictions were not material, and affirmed that the evidence established murder. It dismissed the appeal, upholding the conviction and death sentence.
prosecution_counsel: Riyaz Baey D.S.G for the State
cause_of_death_exact_text: Injury no. 1 was identified as the fatal injury; injuries 7, 8, 9 were defensive injuries.
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court judge considered the contradictions in PW1's evidence to be without merit and found the dock statement did not raise reasonable doubt. The Court of Appeal agreed with this assessment.
precedents_cited_list: Bojinbai Hirijibai vs State of Gujarat AIR 1983 SC 753 | State of Utra Pradesh vs Anthony AIR 1985 SC 48 | King vs N.A. Fernando 46 NLR 254 | Welimunige John vs The State 76 NLR 255
standard_of_review_applied: Weighing evidence rather than counting witnesses, assessing credibility and materiality of contradictions.

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: section 365B (2) (b) of the Penal Code as amended by Penal Code Amendment Act No. 22 of 1995, 29 of 1998 and 16 of 2006
location_of_offence: Tuition class/pre-school location (Waraya, Uswewa, Tangalle vicinity)
brief_facts_summary: The accused-appellant, a pre-school and English tuition teacher, was convicted of three counts of grave sexual abuse against a minor boy who was his student. The incidents (intercrural sex, oral sex, and compelling the victim to touch the appellant's penis) occurred over about two weeks in 2010-2011 when the victim was 10 years old. The abuse came to light approximately six months later after a school awareness program prompted the victim and another child to report to teachers, leading to a police complaint. The victim (PW-01) gave evidence in 2021 as a 20-year-old.
evidence_type_secondary: Medical evidence (Judicial Medical Report), Corroborative witness testimony (School teachers, father, police)
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: section 365B (2) (b) of the Penal Code as amended by Penal Code Amendment Act No. 22 of 1995, 29 of 1998 and 16 of 2006
hc_sentence_type: Rigorous Imprisonment 12 years each count (concurrent), Fine Rs. 12000 each count, Compensation Rs. 200000
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court Judge found the accused guilty on all three counts of grave sexual abuse based on the victim's credible testimony and supporting evidence. The appellant was sentenced to 12 years rigorous imprisonment per count (to run concurrently), fined Rs. 12,000 per count, and ordered to pay Rs. 200,000 as compensation to the victim.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant argued the complaint was belated, the time of offence was uncertain, there were inconsistencies in the victim's statement, the alleged acts were improbable, and he was denied a fair trial. He also contended the trial judge erred by not requiring corroboration for the victim's evidence.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Belatedness of the complaint. | Uncertainty of the time as to the occurrence of the incident. | Uncertainties in the statement of the victim. | The improbability of the act that has been complained. | No fair trial was afforded to the appellant.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the victim's (PW-01) testimony to be clear, credible, and cogent despite the time gap and lack of exact dates. The court noted that child victims may not recall events in perfect chronological order and that the absence of immediate complaint was explained by fear and lack of awareness. Corroboration from school teachers and the father supported the victim's account.
probability_assessment_by_court: Court found the victim's account credible and consistent with the modus operandi of a sexual predator in a position of authority. No reasonable doubt was created by the minor inconsistencies or lack of specific dates.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty, gave evidence under oath, and denied all charges. He claimed the allegations were false and motivated by a prior incident where he reprimanded and searched the victim for allegedly stealing money. He claimed his police statement was not read to him and that he was not informed of charges upon arrest. The court did not find his defence credible.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal thoroughly analyzed each ground. It held the delay in complaint was justified due to the victim's age, fear, and lack of awareness until a school program. Uncertainty of dates was not prejudicial as exact dates are not material in such offences. The victim's minor inconsistencies did not undermine credibility, and the story was not improbable given the appellant's position of authority and modus operandi (using money and threats). The court affirmed that corroboration is not mandatory if the victim's testimony is credible. It found no procedural errors, unfairness, or misdirection by the trial judge, who properly evaluated all evidence. The appeal was dismissed as meritless.
coa_sentence_type: Rigorous Imprisonment 12 years each count (concurrent), Fine Rs. 12000 each count, Compensation Rs. 200000. Sentence deemed to run from 20 May 2022.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused-appellant, a tuition teacher, was convicted by the High Court of Embilipitiya on three counts of grave sexual abuse against a 10-year-old student and sentenced to concurrent 12-year prison terms, fines, and compensation. He appealed on grounds including belated complaint, uncertainty of dates, inconsistencies, improbability, and unfair trial. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal, finding the victim's testimony credible and the delay explained by fear and lack of awareness. The court upheld the conviction and sentence, ordering the sentence to run from the original sentencing date.
defence_counsel: Dephne Peiris Vissundara with Desapriya Vissundara and V. Krishnamoorthy
hc_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the High Court Judge properly considered all evidence, correctly applied the burden of proof, and reached a sound conclusion based on credible victim testimony and supporting evidence. No errors in the High Court's analysis were identified.
precedents_cited_list: R Vs. Dossi 13 Cr.App. R 158 | D. Tikiribanda Vs. The Attorney General (2009) B.L.R. 92 | Bhoginbhai Hirjibhai Vs State of Gujarat AIR 1983 SC 753
standard_of_review_applied: The Court of Appeal reviewed whether the trial judge's findings were based on evidence and correct legal principles, and whether any prejudice or unfairness occurred.
sentencing_principles_applied: The High Court was noted to have given due regard to facts, circumstances, and mitigatory factors. The COA found no reason to interfere with the sentence.

judges: Menaka Wijesundera, J. | B. Sasi Mahendran, J.
offence_sections: Sections 100 and 102 of the Penal Code (abetment by intentionally aiding)
location_of_offence: Naramala police station and nearby shops, Narammala Town
brief_facts_summary: On 21 September 2005, two police officers (the accused) visited PW1's house in his absence and discovered illicit alcohol. They demanded a bribe of LKR 30,000 or LKR 10,000 to avoid legal action. PW1 reported the matter to the Bribery Commission. On 22 September, a trap was set. PW1 and a decoy (PW8) met the accused at the police station and nearby shops. The 1st Accused, in the presence of the 2nd Accused (Appellant), solicited and later accepted LKR 5,000 from PW8 in a room behind the police station. Both accused were arrested.
evidence_type_secondary: Official evidence (PW10 confirming Appellant's absence from duty)
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Sections 100 and 102 of the Penal Code (abetment by intentionally aiding)
hc_sentence_type: Suspended sentence along with a fine
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court Judge convicted both accused on all charges. The Judge gave a suspended sentence and a fine. The 1st Accused did not appeal. The 2nd Accused (Appellant) appealed against the conviction and sentence.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The Appellant argued that as a junior/subordinate officer, his mere passive presence, without any overt act or utterance, did not constitute abetment. He also contended that the Trial Judge failed to adequately address his evidence before rejecting it.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Whether the Learned Trial Judge failed to appreciate that the appellant was the subordinate officer of the 1st Accused and was subject to follow any command of the 1st Accused. Therefore, whether the mere presence of the Appellant in such instance amount to abetment as defined in the Penal Code. | Whether the learned Trial Judge has adequately and correctly addressed the Appellant’s evidence prior to rejecting it.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the evidence of PW1 and PW8 consistent and corroborative. PW1's evidence was spontaneous and not shaken in cross-examination. The Appellant's presence and actions from the initial demand to the final acceptance of the bribe showed intentional assistance, not mere passive presence.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court assessed that the Appellant's course of conduct, from beginning to end, showed intentional aiding. His absence from duty on the day also contradicted the claim of mere following of orders.
defence_version_summary: The Appellant pleaded not guilty. The defence argued he was a junior officer merely following the 1st Accused's commands without independent intention. The court rejected this, finding his assistance was intentional and active.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed Section 100 of the Penal Code, which defines abetment. It referenced precedents (Wijeyeratne v. Menon; The King v. Kadirgaman) to distinguish mere presence from intentional aiding. The Court found the Appellant was not merely present but intentionally assisted the 1st Accused from the initial demand to the acceptance of the bribe. His absence from duty on the relevant day further undermined his defence of being a passive subordinate. The Court agreed with the Trial Judge's acceptance of the prosecution evidence and found no reason to disturb the findings.
coa_sentence_type: Suspended sentence and fine affirmed
brief_judgment_file_summary: The Accused-Appellant, a police officer, was convicted by the High Court for abetting a senior officer in soliciting and accepting a bribe. He received a suspended sentence and fine. He appealed, arguing his mere presence as a subordinate did not constitute abetment. The Court of Appeal analyzed the evidence and relevant Penal Code sections on abetment. It found the Appellant intentionally aided the 1st Accused throughout the bribery transaction, from the initial demand to the final acceptance. Citing precedents, the Court distinguished between mere presence and intentional assistance. The appeal was dismissed, and the High Court's conviction and sentence were affirmed.
defence_counsel: Dr. Ranjith Fernando with Champika Monarawila and Maleesha Meera
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court accepted the prosecution evidence and found both accused guilty of abetment. The Court of Appeal found the Trial Judge's conclusion was properly reached based on the evidence and saw no error in the High Court's reasoning.
precedents_cited_list: Wijeyeratne v. Menon 48 N.L.R. 164 | The King v. Kadirgaman 41 N.L.R 534
standard_of_review_applied: Assessment of whether the Trial Judge's findings were supported by evidence and correct in law.

judges: Menaka Wijesundera J. | B. Sasi Mahendran J.
offence_sections: section 296 and 315 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The appellant stabbed the deceased multiple times, causing fatal injuries, and also stabbed an injured person named Anuradha who tried to intervene. The police recovered a knife based on the appellant's statement. The prosecution relied on eyewitness testimony, including that of the injured Anuradha and PW1, and medical evidence linking the injuries to the recovered knife.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: section 294 (3) and section 315 of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court found the appellant guilty of murder under section 294(3) of the Penal Code and for an offence under section 315. The trial judge concluded the appellant's actions were intentional and the evidence, including eyewitness testimony and medical reports, established guilt beyond reasonable doubt.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appeal sought to set aside the High Court conviction. The appellant's counsel requested consideration of the sentence, but the state counsel objected. The main thrust appears to be challenging the conviction based on the evidence and the trial judge's assessment of the dock statement.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found clear evidence from eyewitnesses and medical reports. The trial judge had noted discrepancies in prosecution evidence but held they did not go to the root of the case. The defense's dock statement was found not to raise a reasonable doubt.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court found the prosecution evidence was clear and the defense failed to create a reasonable doubt. The dock statement did not raise sufficient doubt.
defence_version_summary: The appellant made a statement from the dock. The defense also called a witness who the trial judge disbelieved, considering her a partisan witness. The defense did not plead guilty and did not successfully create a reasonable doubt in the prosecution's case.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed the trial judge's reasoning and the evidence. It found clear evidence of the appellant stabbing the deceased and an injured person without reason, indicating intention. It upheld the trial judge's assessment that the dock statement did not create reasonable doubt and that the defense witness was not credible. The court cited precedent (Queen vs Kularatne) on considering dock statements and Sunil Jayaratne vs Attorney General on appellate interference, finding no miscarriage of justice.
coa_sentence_type: Affirmed the conviction and sentence imposed by the High Court.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused-appellant appealed against his High Court conviction for murder under sections 296 and 315 of the Penal Code. The High Court had found him guilty based on eyewitness testimony and medical evidence. The appeal challenged the conviction and sentence. The Court of Appeal upheld the trial judge's findings, concluding the evidence was clear, the defense failed to raise reasonable doubt, and there was no miscarriage of justice. The appeal was dismissed, and the High Court's conviction and sentence were affirmed.
defence_counsel: I.B.S. Harshana
cause_of_death_exact_text: one of the said stab injuries which had been near the chest had cut a main blood vessel and the same had been the cause of death
hc_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the High Court judge carefully considered the evidence, including eyewitness testimony and medical reports, and correctly concluded the prosecution proved its case beyond reasonable doubt. The COA saw no error in the HC's analysis.
precedents_cited_list: Queen vs Kularatne 71 NLR 529 | Sunil Jayaratne vs Attorney General 2011 2 Sri LR 92
standard_of_review_applied: The appellate court should not interfere with the trial judge's judgment based on first-hand evidence unless there is a grave miscarriage of justice.

judges: Menaka Wijesundera J. | B. Sasi Mahendran J.
offence_sections: Section 294 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The deceased had come to a party at PW2's house and said the appellant's son had assaulted him. PW1 and PW2 led the deceased out and tried to take him home. On the way, they saw the accused on a pushbicycle. The accused stopped, and the witnesses then heard the deceased shout that he had been stabbed and saw the accused running away with a knife. The incident occurred around 9 p.m. with light from nearby houses. The deceased died from his injuries. The prosecution led evidence from two eye witnesses, the doctor, and investigative officers.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 294 of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The trial judge found the appellant guilty of murder based on the evidence. The judge concluded that the surrounding circumstances, including the witnesses seeing the appellant run away with a knife immediately after the stabbing, the prior scuffle with the appellant's son as motive, and the recovery of a knife consistent with the injury, proved the prosecution's case beyond reasonable doubt. The dock statement of the appellant was rejected as it did not create a doubt in the prosecution case.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The main ground of appeal is that the prosecution has not proved its case beyond a reasonable doubt.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The prosecution has not proved its case beyond a reasonable doubt.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The trial judge found the evidence of the two eye witnesses credible and spontaneous, even though they did not see the actual stabbing. Their testimony, combined with the medical evidence and the recovered knife, formed a consistent chain of evidence. The Court of Appeal agreed that the evidence was reliable and sufficient.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal held that the evidence, including eyewitness accounts, motive, and medical opinion, eliminated reasonable doubt and established the appellant's guilt.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty. He made a dock statement claiming he had been assaulted by the deceased on the day of the incident and ran away due to fear for his life. The trial judge did not accept this statement as it did not create a doubt in the prosecution case. No defence witnesses were mentioned.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found no merit in the appeal. It affirmed the trial judge's findings, noting that the evidence of the two eyewitnesses, though they did not see the actual stabbing, was credible and spontaneous. The medical evidence that the injury was 100% sufficient to cause death was strong. The recovered knife was consistent with the injury. The surrounding circumstances, including the prior altercation involving the appellant's son (motive) and the appellant fleeing with a knife immediately after the shout, pointed conclusively to the appellant as the assailant. The dock statement was rightly rejected. The Court found no legal misdirection or procedural error and saw no reason to interfere with the conviction or sentence.
coa_sentence_type: Death
brief_judgment_file_summary: The appellant was convicted of murder by the High Court of Colombo and sentenced to death. He appealed, arguing the prosecution failed to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt. The Court of Appeal reviewed the evidence, including eyewitness testimony placing the appellant at the scene fleeing with a knife, medical evidence confirming a fatal injury, a recovered knife, and a motive arising from a prior scuffle. The Court found the evidence credible and sufficient, rejected the appellant's dock statement, and affirmed the High Court's judgment, dismissing the appeal.
defence_counsel: Hemanthie Kumudu Wijesooriya with Tharana Karunathilake
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court concluded the prosecution proved its case beyond reasonable doubt based on credible eyewitness accounts, medical evidence, a recovered weapon, and motive. The Court of Appeal found this analysis correct and saw no errors.
standard_of_review_applied: Review of whether prosecution proved case beyond reasonable doubt based on evidence on record.

judges: Menaka Wijesundera | B. Sasi Mahendran
brief_facts_summary: The judgment is an appeal against sentence only. The incident took place in 2013, and the trial concluded in 2018. The appellants, both first-time offenders, expressed remorse at the appeal stage.
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the accused-appellants and imposed sentences of imprisonment.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appeal contested only the sentence, not the conviction. The appellants' counsel argued that the trial judge had not fully considered his position on sentence.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Sentence not contested, only sentence appeal.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: No detailed analysis of witnesses or evidence provided in the extract.
defence_version_summary: Accused-appellants pleaded not guilty at trial. The appeal focused solely on the severity of the sentence.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal considered the appellants' remorse, the fact they were first-time offenders, and the time elapsed since the 2013 incident and the 2018 trial conclusion. The court noted that expressing remorse earlier could have avoided a lengthy trial process. Considering these factors, the court decided to review and reduce the sentences.
coa_sentence_type: For 1st Accused-Appellant: Imprisonment reduced to one year on count 1 and one year on count 2, both terms suspended for 10 years. For 2nd Accused-Appellant: Imprisonment reduced to one year on the 5th charge and one year on the 6th charge, both terms suspended for 10 years. Rest of the sentence remains the same.
brief_judgment_file_summary: Two accused-appellants appealed against their sentences for bribery or corruption offences from 2013. The High Court had convicted and sentenced them. At the Court of Appeal, they did not contest the conviction but argued the sentence was excessive. The Court considered their remorse, first-time offender status, and the 10-year lapse since the incident. It reduced their prison terms to one year on relevant counts and suspended those terms for 10 years, while dismissing the appeal subject to this variation.
prosecution_counsel: Janaka Bandara D.S.G with S.N. Sabry
defence_counsel: Anil Silva P.C with U.S. Neranga
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted and sentenced the appellants. The Court of Appeal did not identify specific errors in the High Court's reasoning but reduced the sentence based on mitigating factors.
sentencing_principles_applied: Consideration of first-time offender status, time elapsed since offence and trial, and expression of remorse.

judges: Menaka Wijesundera, J. | B. Sasi Mahendran, J.
offence_sections: Section 2 of the Convention against Torture and other Cruel, Inhuman or Degrading Treatment Act No. 22 of 1994 read with the provisions of Section 32 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The accused persons, who were police officers, were indicted for torturing Sriskandarajah Sumanan (the deceased) while he was detained in custody on suspicion of robbery between 25th and 28th November 2011. The deceased was allegedly tied to a table, assaulted with blunt weapons, and died from the injuries. His body was disposed of in the Iranaimadu tank. The prosecution's case relied on eyewitness testimony and medical evidence.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 2 of the Convention against Torture and other Cruel, Inhuman or Degrading Treatment Act No. 22 of 1994 read with the provisions of Section 32 of the Penal Code
hc_sentence_type: 10 years of imprisonment, fined, awarded compensation
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court found the 1st, 2nd, 4th, 5th, 6th, and 7th accused guilty of torture and sentenced them to 10 years imprisonment, fined them, and awarded compensation. The 3rd and 8th accused were acquitted. The court relied on the eyewitness testimony of PW1 and corroborative medical evidence from the JMO.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellants argued that the trial judge failed to consider favorable evidence, their defence, and contradictions in prosecution evidence. They also claimed the judge misdirected himself in analyzing evidence and did not properly apply the concept of proof beyond reasonable doubt.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The Learned trial Judge has not considered the favourable evidence to the Appellants. | The Learned trial Judge has not considered the defence of the Appellants. | The Learned trial Judge has also misdirected himself in analysing the evidence against the Appellants and has failed to consider the evidence adduced by the Appellants and witnesses. | The evidence led by the prosecution, if properly evaluated by court, could have led to the acquittal of the Appellants. | The Learned trial judge has not considered the contradictions of the prosecution witnesses. | The Concept of proof beyond reasonable doubt was not properly applied to the facts of the case.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the evidence of PW1 (eyewitness) to be consistent, credible, and corroborated by the medical evidence of PW26 (JMO). The court accepted PW1's reason for delayed reporting (fear) and found minor contradictions in PW3's evidence did not create reasonable doubt.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal applied the test of proof beyond reasonable doubt. It found the prosecution evidence, particularly from PW1 and the JMO, was credible and consistent, leaving no reasonable doubt about the guilt of the appellants.
defence_version_summary: All accused pleaded not guilty. They gave dock statements denying the charges. The High Court found the dock statements of the 1st and 2nd accused corroborated prosecution evidence, while those of the 4th, 5th, and 6th were unreliable and rejected. The Court of Appeal upheld this assessment.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal conducted a thorough analysis of the evidence. It found PW1's eyewitness account credible and accepted his explanation for delayed reporting. The medical evidence from the JMO (PW26) corroborated PW1's version of a blunt force assault. The court applied legal precedents on belated witness testimony and minor contradictions, finding they did not undermine the prosecution case. It reviewed the High Court's evaluation of the dock statements and found no error. Applying the standard from Kirpal Singh v The State of Uttar Pradesh, the court found no gross miscarriage of justice, illegality, or unfairness warranting interference.
coa_sentence_type: 10 years of imprisonment, fined, awarded compensation (affirmed)
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused-appellants, police officers, were convicted by the High Court of Jaffna for torturing a detainee (Sriskandarajah Sumanan) to death in November 2011. They were sentenced to 10 years imprisonment, fined, and ordered to pay compensation. They appealed on grounds including failure to consider defence evidence and contradictions. The Court of Appeal found the eyewitness (PW1) and medical evidence (PW26) credible and consistent, accepted the reason for delayed reporting, and found no legal error or miscarriage of justice. The appeal was dismissed, and the High Court's conviction and sentence were affirmed.
defence_counsel: Dushit Johnthagan with K. Raveendran and Nipuni Jav for the Accused-Appellant in HCC 142/17
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted six accused based on credible eyewitness and medical evidence, finding their dock statements unreliable or corroborative of the prosecution. The Court of Appeal agreed with this analysis and found no errors in the High Court's reasoning or evaluation of evidence.
precedents_cited_list: Dharmasiri vs. The Republic of Sri Lanka 2012 (1) SLR 268 | Dharmasiri v Republic of Sri Lanka the Court of Appeal (2010 (2) SLR 241) | Oliver Dayananda Kalansuriya alias Raja Vs The Democratic Socialist Republic of Sri Lanka, CA 28/2009 decided on 13.2.2013 | Kirpal Singh v The State of Uttar Pradesh AIR (1965) SC 712
standard_of_review_applied: The Court applied the principle from Kirpal Singh v The State of Uttar Pradesh, stating it would not review evidence unless the trial was vitiated by illegality, procedural irregularity, violation of natural justice, unfair trial, or gross miscarriage of justice.

judges: Prasantha De Silva, J. | K.K.A.V. Swarnadhipathi, J.
offence_sections: Sections 66(1)(a) and 68 of the Primary Court Procedure Act No 44 of 1979
brief_facts_summary: Police filed an information under the Primary Court Procedure Act to prevent a breach of peace concerning possession of premises No. 16, Seethawaka Road, Avissawella. The 1st Appellant claimed to have leased and run a communication shop there, while the Respondents claimed she was their employee and had been terminated. A dispute and alleged assault led to police involvement. The Magistrate initially awarded possession to the 1st Appellant, but the High Court revised this order in favor of the Respondents.
evidence_type_secondary: Lease agreement and land registry documents
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Sections 66(1)(a) and 68 of the Primary Court Procedure Act No 44 of 1979
hc_sentence_type: Order revising Magistrate's order, awarding possession to the Respondents
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court Judge revised the Magistrate's order and held that the 1st and 2nd Respondents were entitled to possession of the disputed premises on the date the information was filed. The Judge concluded the 1st Appellant operated her business at a different address and that the lease agreement with the 2nd Appellant was executed after the dispute arose.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The Appellants appealed the High Court order, arguing it erroneously reversed the Magistrate's correct finding that the 1st Appellant was in possession on the relevant date. The appeal challenged the High Court's factual conclusions and legal application regarding possession under the Primary Court Procedure Act.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: High Court erred in revising Magistrate's order on possession | High Court failed to properly consider evidence of possession and dispossession | High Court misapplied sections 68(1) and 68(3) of the Primary Court Procedure Act
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed affidavits, police complaints, statements, and a lease agreement. It found the Magistrate correctly evaluated the evidence, noting the 1st Appellant was in possession until forcibly ousted, and her possession was later restored. The High Court failed to consider this sequence.
probability_assessment_by_court: Court assessed probabilities based on documentary and affidavit evidence to determine who was in possession on the relevant dates under the Primary Court Procedure Act.
defence_version_summary: The Respondents claimed the 1st Appellant was their terminated employee and they were in possession. The 1st Appellant claimed she leased and operated the shop independently and was forcibly dispossessed. The court found the Respondents' claim of employment unsubstantiated.
legal_errors_description: High Court erred in its application of sections 68(1) and 68(3) of the Primary Court Procedure Act by failing to correctly identify who was in possession on the date of filing the information or within two months prior.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal meticulously reviewed the evidence, including police complaints dated 16.10.2015, 02.11.2015, and 17.11.2015, and the affidavit of the 1st Respondent. It found the 1st Appellant was in possession of the disputed premises until 16.10.2015, was forcibly dispossessed, and possession was restored on 19.10.2015. The High Court erred by focusing on the 1st Appellant's other business address and the post-dispute lease agreement. The COA affirmed the Magistrate's correct factual and legal analysis under section 68.
coa_sentence_type: Order of the High Court set aside; Order of the Magistrate restored, awarding possession of the disputed premises to the 1st Appellant until adjudication by a competent civil court.
brief_judgment_file_summary: This was a revision and appeal concerning a possession dispute over premises in Avissawella under the Primary Court Procedure Act. The Magistrate initially awarded possession to the 1st Appellant. The High Court revised this in favor of the Respondents. The Court of Appeal allowed the appeals, finding the High Court erred in its factual and legal analysis. It restored the Magistrate's order, holding the 1st Appellant was in possession on the relevant date and entitled to protection under the Act.
defence_counsel: Sanjeewa Dasanayake AAL with Rishi Kamoordeen AAL for the 2nd Respondent-Respondent-Appellant in CA PHC 210/2018 | Thishya Weagoda AAL with Dilan Nalaka AAL for the 1st Respondent-Respondent-Appellant in CA PHC 210A/2018 | Pradeep Perera AAL with P.D.P. Pathirage AAL for the Respondent-Petitioner-Respondents in both appeals
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court concluded the Respondents were in possession on the filing date, focusing on the 1st Appellant's other business address and the timing of the lease agreement. The COA found this analysis flawed, as it ignored evidence of the 1st Appellant's possession and subsequent dispossession and restoration prior to the filing date.
standard_of_review_applied: Revisionary jurisdiction to correct errors of law and fact

judges: Menaka Wijesundera, J. | B. Sasi Mahendran, J.
brief_facts_summary: The accused-appellant was convicted by the High Court in his absence. He later applied to set aside the conviction and sentence under Section 241(3) of the Criminal Procedure Code, claiming his absence was bona fide, which the High Court rejected. He then filed this appeal against the substantive conviction and sentence.
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the accused on counts 1 to 8 of the indictment on 15 July 2014, and on 9 August 2016 refused his application under Section 241(3) to set aside the conviction and sentence and order a de novo trial, finding his absence was not bona fide.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appeal sought to set aside the substantive conviction or impose a lenient sentence. The appellant argued for an unconditional right to appeal despite his previous absence. The state raised a preliminary objection on maintainability, arguing the appeal against the substantive conviction was out of time and the appellant had not challenged the Section 241(3) order.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Unconditional right to appeal substantive conviction. | In the alternative, prayer for lenient sentence. | No prayer to set aside the Section 241(3) order.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The judgment does not analyze specific witness or physical evidence, as it deals with a procedural appeal concerning the right to appeal after a default.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal assessed that the appellant tried to use Section 241(3) to circumvent the time limit for a regular appeal.
defence_version_summary: The appellant claimed his absence at trial was bona fide. He applied under Section 241(3) to purge his default, but the High Court did not accept his claim. He did not testify or call witnesses in this appeal stage.
procedural_defects_description: Appellant attempted to circumvent the strict time limit for filing an appeal under Section 331(1) by applying under Section 241(3) after the High Court found his absence was not bona fide.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed the nature of appellate rights, the difference between appealing a conviction and applying to reopen proceedings under Section 241(3), and the mandatory time limit for appeals. It held that an accused who opts for Section 241(3) and fails must accept the consequences; using it to circumvent the appeal time bar is not permissible. The court cited Sudharman v. Attorney General to affirm the sanctity of the right of appeal but distinguished it, noting procedural steps like time limits must be complied with. The court found no exceptional circumstances to exercise revisionary jurisdiction.
coa_sentence_type: Substantive conviction and sentence upheld.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused-appellant, convicted in absentia, applied to the High Court under Section 241(3) to set aside the conviction, claiming bona fide absence, which was rejected. He then appealed to the Court of Appeal against the substantive conviction and sentence, without challenging the Section 241(3) order. The state objected, arguing the appeal was out of time. The Court of Appeal analyzed the interplay between the right to appeal and the procedure to purge default under Section 241(3), concluding the appellant attempted to circumvent the appeal time limit. It upheld the state's preliminary objection and dismissed the appeal.
defence_counsel: Kalinga Indatissa, PC, Ashanti De Almeida and Naveen Jayamanne
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court found the appellant's absence at trial was not bona fide and refused his application under Section 241(3). The Court of Appeal did not find any error in this conclusion, noting the appellant did not challenge it.
precedents_cited_list: Sudharman v. Attorney General [1986] 1 SLR 9 | H.K. Sumanasena v. Mallawarchchige Kanishka Gunawadhana SC Appeal No. 201/2014 S.C. Minute 15.03.2018 | N. Arumugam v. T. Kumaraswamy [2000] BLR 55 | De Silva v. Edward 30 CLW 81 and 82 | Attorney General v. Letchchemi [2006] BLR 16 | Gunasekara v. Attorney General [2012] BLR 215 | Rankothpedige Harindra Prasad v. Attorney General CA PHC APN 81/2015 CA Minutes 26.01.2018
standard_of_review_applied: Analysis of appellate jurisdiction, right of appeal, and revisionary jurisdiction in light of procedural compliance and statutory time limits.
sentencing_principles_applied: The court did not review sentencing principles as the appeal was dismissed on preliminary maintainability grounds.

judges: Menaka Wijesundera, J. | B. Sasi Mahendran, J.
offence_sections: Section 2 of the Convention against Torture and other Cruel, Inhuman or Degrading Treatment Act No. 22 of 1994 read with the provisions of Section 32 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The deceased, Sriskandarajah Sunnanan, was detained on suspicion of robbery between 25th and 28th November 2011 at Chunnakam Police Station and was allegedly tortured by police officers, resulting in his death. The body was disposed of in Iranaimadu tank. Key eyewitness PW1 was also detained and claimed to have witnessed the torture, including the deceased being tied to a table, assaulted, and bleeding from his nose and mouth before his body was removed.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 2 of the Convention against Torture and other Cruel, Inhuman or Degrading Treatment Act No. 22 of 1994 read with the provisions of Section 32 of the Penal Code
hc_sentence_type: 10 years of imprisonment, fined, awarded compensation
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court found the 1st, 2nd, 4th, 5th, 6th and 7th Accused guilty of torture and imposed a sentence of 10 years imprisonment, a fine, and compensation. The 3rd and 8th Accused were acquitted. The court considered the dock statements, rejecting those of the 4th, 5th, and 6th Accused as unreliable, while finding the 1st and 2nd Accused's statements corroborated prosecution evidence.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellants argued that the trial judge failed to consider favourable evidence and their defence, misdirected himself in analyzing evidence, did not properly apply proof beyond reasonable doubt, and did not consider contradictions in prosecution witnesses. They claimed proper evaluation of evidence would have led to acquittal.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The Learned trial Judge has not considered the favourable evidence to the Appellants. | The Learned trial Judge has not considered the defence of the Appellants. | The Learned trial Judge has also misdirected himself in analysing the evidence against the Appellants and has failed to consider the evidence adduced by the Appellants and witnesses. | The evidence led by the prosecution, if properly evaluated by court, could have led to the acquittal of the Appellants. | The Learned trial judge has not considered the contradictions of the prosecution witnesses. | The Concept of proof beyond reasonable doubt was not properly applied to the facts of the case.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the eyewitness testimony of PW1 consistent and credible, with no reason to disbelieve him. The court accepted his explanation for delayed reporting due to fear. His testimony was corroborated by medical evidence from PW26, the Judicial Medical Officer, and by PW3, who saw the deceased injured.
probability_assessment_by_court: The court applied the standard of proof beyond reasonable doubt, found the prosecution evidence credible and consistent, and held that the accused failed to create any reasonable doubt in the prosecution case.
defence_version_summary: The accused pleaded not guilty. They gave dock statements denying the charges. The High Court rejected the dock statements of the 4th, 5th, and 6th accused as unreliable, while noting the 1st and 2nd accused's statements corroborated prosecution evidence. No defence witnesses were mentioned.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal thoroughly analyzed the evidence, finding PW1's eyewitness testimony credible, consistent, and corroborated by medical evidence (PW26) and another witness (PW3). The court applied precedents on belated witness testimony (Dharmasiri cases) and minor contradictions (Oliver Dayananda Kalansuriya), accepting PW1's delay due to fear. It reviewed the High Court's evaluation of dock statements and found no misdirection. The court affirmed that the prosecution proved the charge of torture beyond reasonable doubt and that no gross miscarriage of justice occurred, citing Kirpal Singh v The State of Uttar Pradesh. The appeal was dismissed.
coa_sentence_type: 10 years of imprisonment, fined, awarded compensation (affirmed)
brief_judgment_file_summary: This appeal concerns the conviction and sentence of six police officers (Accused-Appellants) for torturing Sriskandarajah Sunnanan to death while in custody at Chunnakam Police Station in November 2011. The High Court of Jaffna convicted them under the Convention against Torture Act and sentenced them to 10 years imprisonment, a fine, and compensation. The appellants appealed on grounds including failure to consider defence, misdirection on evidence, and improper application of reasonable doubt. The Court of Appeal found the eyewitness testimony (PW1) credible and corroborated by medical evidence, accepted the reason for delayed reporting, and found no legal errors or miscarriage of justice. The appeal was dismissed, and the High Court's conviction and sentence affirmed.
defence_counsel: Dushit Johnthagan with K. Raveendran and Nipuni Jav for the Accused-Appellant in HCC 142/17
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted the appellants based on credible eyewitness and medical evidence, rejecting some dock statements as unreliable. The Court of Appeal found the High Court's analysis correct, with no misdirection or failure to consider the defence, and that it properly applied the burden of proof.
precedents_cited_list: Dharmasiri vs. The Republic of Sri Lanka 2012 (1) SLR 268 | Dharmasiri v Republic of Sri Lanka the Court of Appeal (2010 (2) SLR 241) | Oliver Dayananda Kalansuriya alias Raja Vs The Democratic Socialist Republic of Sri Lanka, CA 28/2009 decided on 13.2.2013 | Kirpal Singh v The State of Uttar Pradesh AIR (1965) SC 712
standard_of_review_applied: The court reviewed whether the trial was vitiated by illegality, irregularity, violation of natural justice, unfair trial, or gross miscarriage of justice, as per Kirpal Singh. It also assessed the credibility of belated witnesses and minor contradictions.

judges: Menaka Wijesundera, J. | B. Sasi Mahendran, J.
offence_sections: Section 54 A (b), 54 A (c) and 54 A (d) respectively of the Poisons, Opium, and Dangerous Drugs (as amended by) Ordinance No. 13 of 1984
brief_facts_summary: On 8th June 2005, the accused was intercepted at Katunayake airport by police after receiving information she was there to collect mishandled baggage containing heroin in men's waist belts. She collected nine bags from the mishandled baggage office. Upon questioning, she identified a specific bag which, when searched, was found to contain 74 belts holding a brown powder. The powder was later confirmed to be 144.8 grams of heroin. The accused claimed the bag belonged to a person named Sarina.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 54 A (b), 54 A (c) and 54 A (d) respectively of the Poisons, Opium, and Dangerous Drugs (as amended by) Ordinance No. 13 of 1984
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court Judge found the accused guilty on all three counts of trafficking, importing, and possessing heroin. The judge accepted the consistent evidence of the police officers and found the accused's explanation that she was collecting another person's baggage to be improbable. The accused was convicted and sentenced to death.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appeal grounds argued that the High Court Judge misdirected himself by failing to consider improbabilities and contradictions in the police testimony, failing to properly evaluate the accused's dock statement, and failing to consider that the chief investigation officer had not entered notes on material instances during the raid. It was also argued that the prosecution failed to produce best evidence and the judge failed to make an adverse inference in favour of the accused.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Learned High Court Judge misdirected himself by not considering the improbabilities of the narration of the Police Officers which cast a reasonable doubt on the prosecution version. | Learned Trial Judge misdirected by failure to evaluate the dock statement in proper context and thereby caused a miscarriage of justice. | Learned High Court Judge misdirected himself by failure to consider that the chief investigation officer had not entered notes on very material instances in the course of the raid and that creates a reasonable doubt on the version of the prosecution case. | Learned High Court Judge misdirected himself by failure to consider that dock statement very clearly corroborates the version of the defence suggested to the prosecution witnesses and thereby cast a reasonable doubt on the prosecution version. | Learned High Court Judge misdirected himself by not considering the material inter se contradiction which casts a doubt on the prosecution version and its credibility. | Learned High Court Judge has misdirected himself by neither considering the fact that prosecution has failed to produced best evidence nor has made adverse inference under section 114 of the evidence ordinance in favour of the appellant and thereby accused a miscarriage of justice.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the evidence of the main police witnesses consistent and without material contradictions. The court focused on whether the accused had knowledge of the heroin, applying principles from precedent. The accused's actions in identifying and collecting the bags and pointing out the specific bag were deemed indicative of knowledge.
probability_assessment_by_court: The court applied the principle from Warner v. Metropolitan Police Commissioner to assess whether the accused had possession with knowledge, not mere custody. Considering her actions, the court found she failed to create a reasonable doubt regarding her knowledge of the heroin's presence.
defence_version_summary: The accused pleaded not guilty. She gave a dock statement claiming the bag containing the heroin belonged to a woman named Sarina and that she was merely collecting it. The court found this version improbable and not credible, noting she identified and collected the bags as her own and knew which bag contained the belts.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal carefully reviewed the evidence and the grounds of appeal. It found the evidence of the police officers consistent and credible. The court applied the legal test for possession and knowledge from K. Sumanawathi Perera v. Attorney General and Warner v. Metropolitan Police Commissioner. It concluded the accused's actions—coming to collect the bags, identifying them as hers, and immediately pointing out the bag with belts—demonstrated the requisite knowledge of the heroin. The court found no merit in the appeal grounds and saw no reason to interfere with the High Court's judgment.
coa_sentence_type: Death
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused-appellant, W.A.D. Chandrani, was convicted by the High Court of Negombo on three counts of trafficking, importing, and possessing 141.8 grams of heroin and sentenced to death. She appealed, arguing misdirection by the trial judge regarding improbabilities in police testimony, evaluation of her dock statement, and procedural lapses. The Court of Appeal reviewed the evidence, found the police testimony consistent and the accused's defence improbable. Applying precedent on possession and knowledge, the court dismissed the appeal, affirming the conviction and death sentence.
defence_counsel: Tenny Fernando
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court accepted the consistent evidence of the police witnesses and found the accused's story that she was collecting someone else's baggage to be improbable. The Court of Appeal agreed with this analysis and found no errors in the High Court's reasoning or conclusion.
precedents_cited_list: K. Sumanawathi Perera v. Attorney General CA Appeal,No: 152/96 | Warner v. Metropolitan Police Commissioner (1968) 52 Criminal Appeal Report 373
standard_of_review_applied: The court reviewed whether the High Court Judge misdirected himself on the evidence and the law, and whether the conviction was safe.
sentencing_principles_applied: The judgment affirms the death sentence imposed by the High Court without specific discussion of sentencing principles.

judges: D.N. Samarakoon,J. | B. Sasi Mahendran, J.
offence_sections: Article 105(3) of the Constitution of the Democratic Socialist Republic of Sri Lanka
brief_facts_summary: The Respondent had won a district court case regarding her matrimonial rights. She was granted the right to occupy part of the premises. After the judgment, she attempted to gain access to her room and take possession, which led to conflicts including allegations of harassment, breaking locks, changing locks, and threatening the Petitioner. The Petitioner filed a contempt application alleging the Respondent willfully violated the district court judgment.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The application sought punishment for contempt of court, alleging the Respondent willfully violated a specific district court judgment. The Respondent denied the charges and argued the Petitioner failed to meet the standard of proof beyond reasonable doubt. The Respondent maintained her conduct did not constitute contempt.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Failure to establish conduct constitutes contempt of court | Failure to prove beyond reasonable doubt that acts brought court authority into disrespect | Acts alleged do not meet the legal standard for contempt
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Petitioner led evidence of five witnesses, including herself. The Respondent called no witnesses and remained silent. The Court of Appeal found the evidence did not establish beyond reasonable doubt that the acts constituted contempt.
probability_assessment_by_court: Court found Petitioner failed to establish beyond reasonable doubt that acts constituted contempt. Acts of breaking locks and harassment, while reprehensible, were not calculated to bring court authority into disrepute.
defence_version_summary: The Respondent pleaded not guilty to all contempt charges. She filed a statement of objections and written submissions, refrained from calling witnesses, and remained silent. She argued the Petitioner failed to meet the standard of proof beyond reasonable doubt and her conduct did not constitute contempt.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed whether the Petitioner proved beyond reasonable doubt that the Respondent's conduct constituted contempt of court. It referenced legal definitions from precedent and Oswald's Contempt of Court. The court distinguished between acts that disregard legal procedure and acts calculated to bring court authority into disrespect. It found the Respondent's acts of breaking locks, changing locks, and harassing the Petitioner were impatient and unlawful attempts to enforce a judgment, but they did not meet the threshold for contempt. The standard of proof was not satisfied. The court noted such acts may amount to other criminal offences but are not contempt. The application was dismissed with costs.
coa_sentence_type: Application dismissed with costs.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The 1st Defendant-Petitioner filed an application under Article 105(3) of the Constitution seeking to punish the Plaintiff-Respondent for contempt of court, alleging willful violation of a district court judgment. The Respondent denied the charges. The Court of Appeal heard evidence from five prosecution witnesses; the Respondent called none. The court held that while the Respondent acted impatiently and took the law into her own hands by breaking locks and harassing the Petitioner, these acts did not constitute contempt of court as they were not calculated to bring the court's authority into disrepute. The Petitioner failed to prove the case beyond reasonable doubt. The application was dismissed with costs.
prosecution_counsel: Anuja Pramarathna, PC with Asha Rathnayake for the 1st Defendant Complainant-Petitioner
defence_counsel: Harindra Dhammage with Sudesh Madanayaka for the Plaintiff-Accused-Respondent
precedents_cited_list: Kahapola Arachchige Prabath Anurada Nilupul Fernando v. Urban Council, Kesbewa & Others CA Contempt 05/2018 decided on 08.11.2019 | Oswald’s, ‘Contempt of Court’ (3rd edition)
standard_of_review_applied: Beyond reasonable doubt

judges: Menaka Wijesundera, J. | B. Sasi Mahendran, J.
offence_sections: Section 365 B (2) of the Penal Code as amended by Act, No. 22 of 1995, and as further amended by No. 29 of 1998 and No. 16 of 2006.
brief_facts_summary: The accused was charged with Grave Sexual Abuse of a child under 16. On 17 March 2007, the victim (PW1) went to a bakery and was stopped by the accused, who dragged her to a house, forcibly removed her clothes, placed his male organ between her thighs and rubbed against her. She reported the incident to her mother four days later after experiencing a burning sensation, and a complaint was lodged. The accused was convicted by the High Court.
evidence_type_secondary: Medical evidence from the Judicial Medical Officer
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 365 B (2) of the Penal Code as amended by Act, No. 22 of 1995, and as further amended by No. 29 of 1998 and No. 16 of 2006.
hc_sentence_type: 20 years of rigorous imprisonment, fine of Rs. 50,000/- with default sentence of one-year rigorous imprisonment, compensation of Rs. 400,000/- with default sentence of two years rigorous imprisonment.
