hc_judgment_summary: After trial, the High Court convicted the accused of Grave Sexual Abuse. The judge accepted the evidence of the victim as truthful and corroborated by medical evidence, and rejected the accused's alibi defence.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The grounds argued the trial judge failed to consider infirmities in the prosecution case, conflated rape and grave sexual abuse, erred in not finding the appellant not guilty, failed to account for contradictions in medical evidence, and that the judgment was unreasonable. Also alleged failure to investigate clothing and alibi, incomplete investigations, and misdirection regarding denial of charges.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The learned trial judge of the high Court has failed to consider the intrinsic infirmities of the Prosecution Case; particularly as to the charge in the indictment and the evidence of an alleged rape. | The learned trial judge of the High court has failed to appreciate that the ingredients of the offence of rape and those of the offence of grave sexual abuse are different. | The learned judge of the High Court has erred in law in failing to conclude that the Appellant was not guilty of the offence with which latter was charged. | The learned judge of the High Court has failed to take in to account the contradictory positions of the judicial medical officer in the observations contains in ‘P1’ and the evidence given by the said witness at the trial. | The said judgment and conviction are contrary to law and the evidence adduced at the trial and hence, are completely unreasonable and unjustified. | The learned trial judge has misdirected herself by concluding that the Appellant has not denied the charged leveled against him or he has not challenged the evidence led by the prosecution. | The learned trial judge of the High Court has failed to appreciate that the investigating officers had failed to investigate in to the items of clothes alleged to have been taken in to custody as well as the alibi taken by the Appellant. | The learned trial judge has failed to appreciate that the appellant had been arraigned upon incomplete and partial investigations.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed the victim's evidence, noting her age and time lapse, found minor contradictions not material, and accepted her evidence as credible and corroborated by medical evidence.
probability_assessment_by_court: Court found no reasonable doubt created by defence and held prosecution proved its case beyond reasonable doubt.
defence_version_summary: The accused pleaded not guilty, made a dock statement and took up an alibi. The alibi was not suggested to prosecution witnesses during cross-examination. The court rejected the defence as not credible.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal held that the trial judge correctly analyzed the evidence. Minor contradictions in the victim's testimony did not go to the root of the case and were understandable given her age and the time lapse. The medical evidence corroborated her account of penile friction and rough contact. The alibi defence was correctly rejected as it was not put to prosecution witnesses. The court cited precedents on evaluating witness credibility and minor discrepancies. It found no reason to interfere with the conviction or sentence.
coa_sentence_type: 20 years rigorous imprisonment, fine of Rs. 50,000/- with default sentence of one-year rigorous imprisonment, compensation of Rs. 400,000/- with default sentence of two years rigorous imprisonment.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused was convicted by the High Court of Chilaw for Grave Sexual Abuse of a child under 16 and sentenced to 20 years rigorous imprisonment, a fine, and compensation. He appealed on grounds including failure to consider infirmities, medical contradictions, misdirection, and excessive sentence. The Court of Appeal found the victim's evidence credible and corroborated by medical evidence, minor contradictions immaterial, and the alibi defence not properly raised. The appeal was dismissed, upholding the conviction and sentence.
defence_counsel: Shyamal A. Collure with A.P. Jayaweera
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court analyzed the victim's evidence, found her truthful, and accepted medical corroboration. It rejected the accused's alibi. The COA agreed with this analysis and found no errors.
precedents_cited_list: Bhoginbhai Hirjibhai V. State of Gujarat AIR 1983 SC 753 | Simonge Ekanayake v Attorney General, CA 129/2005 | State of Uttar Pradesh v. M.K. Anthony, Supreme Court Journal 1984 (2) page 498 | Sunil and Another vs. Attorney General 1986 1 SLR 230 | Alwis v. Piyassena Fernado 1993 (i) SLR 119
standard_of_review_applied: Reluctance to interfere with trial judge's findings on primary facts and witness credibility unless perverse.
sentencing_principles_applied: The Court of Appeal noted the trial judge considered all relevant facts before pronouncing sentence and found no reason to interfere.

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 386 read with section 32 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The accused-petitioners were charged before the Magistrate of Mullaitivu for criminal misappropriation of Rs. 950,000 from the virtual complainant on the promise of sending him abroad. They were arrested, produced before the Magistrate, and a charge sheet was filed. They pleaded guilty and were sentenced to a fine of Rs. 1500 each, ordered to pay Rs. 950,000 as compensation, with a default sentence of two years rigorous imprisonment. The High Court varied the default sentence to three months. The petitioners, having paid the compensation in full, sought revision in the Court of Appeal to challenge the legality of the compensation order.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 386 read with section 32 of the Penal Code
hc_sentence_type: Fine of Rs. 1500 each, compensation of Rs. 950,000, default sentence of 3 months rigorous imprisonment
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court Judge determined the compensation amount was legal but varied the default sentence from 2 years to 3 months rigorous imprisonment to align with the law.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The petitioners challenged only the legality of the compensation amount of Rs. 950,000. They argued that a Magistrate can only order a maximum of Rs. 100,000 as compensation under Section 17 of the Code of Criminal Procedure Act, and that the order exceeded the Magistrate's powers. They also contended that the Magistrate did not follow the procedure under Section 28(2) of the Assistance to and Protection of Victims of Crime and Witnesses Act No.4 of 2015 if that Act was relied upon.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Magistrate lacks power to order compensation exceeding Rs. 100,000 under Section 17 of the Code of Criminal Procedure Act. | The Assistance to and Protection of Victims of Crime and Witnesses Act No.4 of 2015 does not apply to this type of case. | Even if the 2015 Act applied, the Magistrate failed to follow the procedure in Section 28(2) of the Act.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The case was resolved by a guilty plea and a settlement agreement between the parties. The Court of Appeal analyzed the legal authority of the Magistrate to order compensation, focusing on statutory interpretation.
defence_version_summary: The petitioners pleaded guilty unconditionally. They offered to pay the misappropriated sum of Rs. 950,000 to the complainant on an installment basis, which the complainant accepted, leading to a settlement. They were convicted based on their plea.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found that the cited precedents (Nirosh Amantha Amadoru and W.H. Thulyananda Senananda) were irrelevant as they predated the Assistance to and Protection of Victims of Crime and Witnesses Act No.4 of 2015. It held that Section 28(1) of the 2015 Act empowers a Magistrate to order compensation up to Rs. 1,000,000. The Court agreed with the High Court that Section 46 of the Act defines a victim to include one who suffers economic loss. It ruled that Section 28(2) of the Act, which prescribes a procedure for determining compensation, applies when the court acts on its own motion, not when compensation is based on a settlement offer from the accused accepted by the complainant. The Court upheld the High Court's reduction of the default sentence as correct.
coa_sentence_type: Fine of Rs. 1500 each, compensation of Rs. 950,000 (already paid), default sentence of 3 months rigorous imprisonment (as varied by High Court)
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused-petitioners were convicted of criminal misappropriation of Rs. 950,000 before the Mullaitivu Magistrate's Court after pleading guilty. They were fined and ordered to pay compensation. The High Court upheld the compensation but reduced the default sentence. The petitioners sought revision in the Court of Appeal, challenging only the legality of the compensation amount, arguing it exceeded the Magistrate's powers. The Court of Appeal dismissed the application, holding that the Magistrate had the power to order the compensation under Section 28(1) of the Assistance to and Protection of Victims of Crime and Witnesses Act No.4 of 2015, and that the procedural requirements of Section 28(2) did not apply as the order was based on a settlement.
defence_counsel: K. S. Ratnavel with Lakshan Abeywardane
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court correctly identified that the default sentence of 2 years imposed by the Magistrate was not according to law. It varied the sentence to 3 months to bring it in line with the applicable law, while upholding the compensation order as legal.
precedents_cited_list: Nirosh Amantha Amadoru Vs. Attorney General CA (PHC) APN 128/15 decided on 23-11-2016 | W. H. Thulyananda Senananda Vs. Attorney General CA (PHC) APN 28/2014 decided on 07-07-2014
standard_of_review_applied: Revisionary jurisdiction under Article 138 of the Constitution
sentencing_principles_applied: Consideration of statutory limits on compensation and default sentences under the Assistance to and Protection of Victims of Crime and Witnesses Act No.4 of 2015.

judges: Menaka Wijesundera, J | B. Sasi Mahendran, J
offence_sections: Section 140 of the Penal Code; Section 296 read with Section 146 of the Penal Code; Section 296 read with Section 32 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The case involves the fatal assault of Roshan Lasantha Gomas (alias Shan) by a group of accused persons, including neighbors. The motive stemmed from a dispute over a stolen pigeon cage and related retaliation by the deceased against drug-buying activities on his property. On the day of the incident, several accused confronted the deceased at his gate. He was later attacked with steel rods and clubs after leaving in a three-wheeler, resulting in his death. The prosecution’s case relied primarily on the eyewitness account of the deceased’s sister.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 140 of the Penal Code; Section 296 read with Section 146 of the Penal Code; Section 296 read with Section 32 of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court Judge convicted all accused on all three counts in the indictment, finding them guilty of being members of an unlawful assembly, murder in furtherance of a common object, and murder with common intention. The judge relied on the sole eyewitness testimony (PW1, the deceased's sister) and corroborating medical evidence from the Judicial Medical Officer (PW6).
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellants argued that the conviction was unsafe due to the uncorroborated and unsatisfactory nature of the sole eyewitness evidence, the trial judge’s failure in evaluating evidence, and misdirection on critical factual issues. They also contended that the prosecution failed to prove murderous intention for certain accused, unlawful assembly with a common object, and sufficient evidence for conviction under Section 32 of the Penal Code.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Conviction is wholly unsafe in view of the uncorroborated and unsatisfactory nature of the evidence of the sore eye witness. | The learned trial judge has failed to apply the principles governing the evaluation of evidence. | The learned Trial Judge when writing his judgement has seriously misdirected himself on very critical issues of the facts causing serious prejudice to the appellant. | The prosecution has not been able to prove murderous intention of the 4th, 6th Accused Appellants. | The accused persons were indicted for being members of an unlawful assembly in the prosecution of common object of which to commit murder of the deceased and thereby committing an offence under section 146 of the Penal Code, but this has not been proved by the prosecution. | The evidence available in the present case is not sufficient to convict the Accused Appellants under Section 32 of the Penal Code.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the sole eyewitness (PW1) consistent and credible despite minor contradictions, noting that such minor discrepancies are common in witness testimony. Her evidence was corroborated by the medical evidence of PW6, which confirmed the fatal head injury was caused by a heavy blunt object. The court applied established principles on sole eyewitness reliability and found her testimony trustworthy.
probability_assessment_by_court: The court assessed the evidence for common intention, finding that repeated forceful blows by multiple accused established murderous intention beyond reasonable doubt.
defence_version_summary: The accused pleaded not guilty. At trial, the 1st, 2nd, 3rd, and 6th accused made statements from the dock, while the 5th accused gave evidence from the witness box. They claimed they were falsely implicated. The High Court found the prosecution evidence credible, and the Court of Appeal agreed, rejecting the defence's arguments on unreliability.
legal_errors_description: The Court of Appeal found the High Court erred in convicting the accused for unlawful assembly (first and second counts) as the prosecution failed to establish the assembly comprised five or more persons, especially after the acquittal of the 2nd, 5th, and 6th accused, and without the indictment including the phrase 'with those unknown to the prosecution'.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal thoroughly reviewed the evidence, applying precedents on sole eyewitness reliability and common intention. It upheld the conviction for murder under Section 296 read with Section 32 (common intention) against the 1st, 3rd (deceased), and 4th accused, finding they shared a murderous common intention based on their concerted violent actions. However, it acquitted the 1st and 4th accused on the unlawful assembly counts, holding the prosecution failed to prove the assembly consisted of five or more persons. The court affirmed the High Court's reliance on the eyewitness and medical evidence, noting minor contradictions did not undermine credibility. It accepted the Senior Deputy Solicitor General's concession regarding the unlawful assembly error and acquitted the 2nd, 5th, and 6th accused on all counts.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The Court of Appeal partly allowed the appeal by six accused-appellants convicted by the High Court of Colombo for murder and unlawful assembly. The prosecution's case relied on the eyewitness account of the deceased's sister (PW1) and medical evidence. The High Court convicted all accused on all counts. On appeal, the Court of Appeal acquitted the 2nd, 5th, and 6th accused entirely. It upheld the murder conviction under Section 296 read with Section 32 (common intention) against the 1st, 3rd (deceased), and 4th accused. However, it acquitted the 1st and 4th accused on the unlawful assembly counts, finding insufficient proof of an assembly of five or more persons. The court affirmed the credibility of the sole eyewitness and the medical evidence.
defence_counsel: Rasika Samarawickrama for the 1st Accused-Appellant; Gayan Perera with Prabha Perera and P. Ekanayake for the 2nd, 4th and 6th Accused-Appellants; Dr. Ranjith Fernando with Maleesha Meera for the 05th Accused Appellant
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court Judge accepted the sole eyewitness testimony and medical evidence, concluding all accused were guilty of all charges. The Court of Appeal agreed with the conviction for murder with common intention against the 1st, 3rd, and 4th accused but found the High Court erred in convicting for unlawful assembly, as the required number of persons was not proven after acquittals.
precedents_cited_list: Bharwada Bhoginbhai Hirjibhai vs State of Gujarat 1983 AIR HC 753 | Anil Phukan v. State of Assam AIR 1993 SC II 1462 | Wjiepala v. The Attorney General, 2001 (1) SLR 45 | The Queen v. Vincent Fernando 65 NLR 265 | The King v. Assappu 50 NLR 324 | Wimalasena v. Inspector of Police, Hambanthota 74 NLR 176 | Anthony v. The Queen 55 NLR 35 | Raju and Others v. Attorney General 2003 (3) SLR 116 | Kotawila Vithanage Chandradasa and Other v. Attorney General 113-114/2016 | The Queen v. Appuhamy 62 NLR 484
standard_of_review_applied: The court reviewed whether the High Court properly evaluated evidence, applied legal principles on common intention and unlawful assembly, and assessed witness credibility, particularly regarding the sole eyewitness.
final_charge_after_appeal: Murder under Section 296 read with Section 32 of the Penal Code (for 1st, 3rd, and 4th accused). Unlawful assembly charges (first and second counts) set aside for 1st and 4th accused.

judges: Menaka Wijesundera J. | B. Sasi Mahendran J.
brief_facts_summary: The accused was indicted for three counts of murder of a mother (Chamila) and her two children in 2000. The prosecution case was based on circumstantial evidence, including an anonymous petition in 2006, statements from the deceased's mother and husband about the accused's interest in Chamila and an alleged assault, a letter purportedly from Chamila but identified as the accused's handwriting, and skeletal remains recovered near the accused's property. The Judicial Medical Officer identified the remains as from an adult and two children but could not confirm identity or gender. No DNA testing was done.
evidence_type_secondary: Medical evidence (JMO report on skeletal remains), Handwriting analysis
hc_judgment_summary: The trial judge analyzed the evidence and concluded the accused was guilty of the three murders and sentenced him to capital punishment.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The main ground was that the prosecution failed to prove the death of the three deceased persons and failed to eliminate the possibility that someone else committed the murders, a fundamental principle in circumstantial evidence cases.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The prosecution had not proved the death of the three deceased persons. | The prosecution failed to eliminate beyond reasonable doubt that another person could have committed the murders.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed circumstantial evidence, including witness statements from the deceased's mother and husband, a handwriting expert's opinion, and the JMO report. It found the evidence did not conclusively link the skeletal remains to the deceased or prove the accused's guilt beyond reasonable doubt. It also noted suspicious behavior by the deceased's husband.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court found the circumstances did not irresistibly point only to the accused's guilt and failed to exclude the possibility of another perpetrator, creating reasonable doubt.
defence_version_summary: Accused pleaded not guilty. He made a dock statement claiming he found bones on his property in 2006, reported it to police, and was falsely implicated. He suggested the deceased's husband behaved suspiciously.
legal_errors_description: The High Court erred in convicting based on circumstantial evidence that did not irresistibly point to guilt and failed to exclude other reasonable possibilities.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal applied principles from Queen vs Kularatne and Karuppaiya Servie vs The King, emphasizing that in circumstantial evidence cases, the prosecution must exclude other reasonable possibilities of guilt. It analyzed the circumstances: accused's interest in Chamila, her complaint to her husband, the letter in accused's handwriting, and recovery of skeletal bones. It found these did not prove beyond reasonable doubt that the bones were of the deceased or that the accused committed the murders. It also noted the husband's unusual behavior and the six-year investigation delay. The Court concluded the prosecution failed to eliminate the possibility another person committed the crimes.
coa_sentence_type: Conviction and sentence set aside
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused was convicted in the High Court of Gampaha for the murder of Chamila and her two children and sentenced to death. The prosecution case relied on circumstantial evidence. The Court of Appeal allowed the appeal, finding the circumstantial evidence insufficient to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt and failing to exclude the possibility of another perpetrator. The conviction and sentence were set aside.
defence_counsel: Chathura Amarathunga (Assigned Counsel)
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court concluded the circumstantial evidence pointed to the accused's guilt. The Court of Appeal found the High Court erred as the evidence did not irresistibly lead to that conclusion and failed to exclude other possibilities.
precedents_cited_list: Queen vs Kularatne 71 NLR 529 | Karuppaiya Servie vs The King 52 NLR 227
standard_of_review_applied: Assessment of whether circumstantial evidence leads irresistibly to guilt and excludes other reasonable possibilities.

judges: Menaka Wijesundera, J. | B. Sasi Mahendran, J.
brief_facts_summary: The Petitioner had been a witness in the main case and was treated adversely. The court subsequently convicted the witness and imposed a sentence.
hc_sentence_type: Rigorous imprisonment for 01 year for each count to run consecutively
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the Petitioner, who was a witness in the main case, and sentenced him to one year rigorous imprisonment for each count, to run consecutively.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: Counsel for the Petitioner urged the Court of Appeal to reconsider the sentence. The Attorney General had no objection to the reconsideration.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Request for reconsideration of sentence
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The judgment does not provide details on witness evidence analysis.
defence_version_summary: Not detailed in the judgment. The appeal was based on reconsideration of sentence.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal considered the submissions of both counsel and the Attorney General's lack of objection. It reduced the sentence on each count from one year to six months rigorous imprisonment and suspended the sentence for five years.
coa_sentence_type: 06 months rigorous imprisonment on each count, suspended for 05 years
brief_judgment_file_summary: This is an application for revision by a Petitioner who was a witness in the main case and was convicted by the High Court to one year rigorous imprisonment for each count, to run consecutively. On appeal, the Petitioner sought reconsideration of the sentence. The Attorney General had no objection. The Court of Appeal reduced the sentence to six months rigorous imprisonment on each count and suspended it for five years, while dismissing the appeal subject to this variation. The court also ordered the release of the Petitioner's passport held by the High Court registry.
prosecution_counsel: Rohantha Abeysuriya, ASG, P.C. for the State
defence_counsel: Palitha Fernando P.C. with Iranga Gunawardene for the Accused-Appellant in HCC-0357-18
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted and sentenced the Petitioner. The Court of Appeal found the sentence excessive and reduced it, suspending the sentence.

judges: Menaka Wijesundera J. | B. Sasi Mahendran J.
offence_sections: sections 140, 146/296 and in the alternative 32/296 under the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The prosecution case was that the deceased was killed at a restaurant. Witness No. 1 (PW1) was with the deceased and 1st accused at the restaurant. The 2nd accused greeted the deceased and took him into the restaurant, where the deceased locked the kitchen door. The 4th accused entered the kitchen from outside, pointed a gun at PW1, and later shot at the door, forcing it open. PW1 later found the deceased injured with firearm wounds in the restaurant verandah. The police recovered a firearm on the statement of the 4th accused and a bullet from the scene. The deceased sustained 12 injuries from firearm and contusions.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: sections 140, 146/296 under the Penal Code (Counts 1 and 2)
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the 2nd and 4th accused under counts 1 and 2 (sections 140, 146/296 of the Penal Code) and sentenced both to death. The judge acquitted all four accused on count 3 (alternative charge under section 32/296). The judge's reasoning included that the accused were part of an unlawful assembly and that the 2nd and 4th accused had actively participated in the incident.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The main ground was that with the acquittal of the 1st and 3rd accused on the charge under section 32, there was no evidence of an unlawful assembly requiring five or more persons. It was argued the prosecution failed to prove common object or common intention between the 2nd and 4th accused. Further grounds included that the trial judge started adjudication on a wrong premise, failed to properly apply principles of circumstantial evidence, erroneously considered dock statements, and drew conclusions sans evidence.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: No formation of an unlawful assembly as only three accused (including deceased) remained after acquittals, not meeting the minimum of five. | No evidence that the 2nd and 4th accused shared a common object or intention, or that they had met or communicated prior. | Trial judge failed to properly apply principles of circumstantial evidence and identify complete strands. | Trial judge incorrectly concluded the 2nd and 4th accused actively participated in the incident. | Trial judge erroneously considered the dock statements by placing an unnecessary burden on the defence to create reasonable doubt. | Trial judge made factual findings without supporting evidence (e.g., bullet from 4th accused's firearm, scuffle inside restaurant).
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the prosecution evidence insufficient to prove common object or unlawful assembly. PW1's identification evidence was tainted as the accused were shown to him before the ID parade. The medical evidence of 12 injuries was not reliably linked to the convicted accused, and the trial judge drew erroneous conclusions from it.
probability_assessment_by_court: The COA found the prosecution failed to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt. The circumstantial evidence did not form a complete chain pointing exclusively to the guilt of the appellants, and there was no evidence of common object or intention.
defence_version_summary: All accused pleaded not guilty. The 2nd and 4th accused appealed. The defence argued lack of unlawful assembly and no common object. The COA assessed the defence case and found the trial judge had cast an unnecessary burden on the defence regarding dock statements.
legal_errors_description: Misdirection on the law of unlawful assembly (requiring five members). Error in assessing dock statements (requiring them to create reasonable doubt). Failure to correctly apply principles of circumstantial evidence.
procedural_defects_description: Improper identification parade procedure where accused were shown to witness before the parade.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The COA analyzed the evidence and found the trial judge's conclusions erroneous. It held that with the acquittal of the 1st and 3rd accused, there was no unlawful assembly of five or more persons. There was no evidence the 2nd and 4th accused shared a common object or intention, or that they ever met. The trial judge incorrectly applied the law on unlawful assembly and dock statements. The medical evidence did not support a scuffle involving the appellants, and the bullet was not proven to be from the 4th accused's firearm. The identification evidence was flawed. The conviction based on unlawful assembly was unsustainable.
coa_sentence_type: Convictions and sentences set aside
brief_judgment_file_summary: The 2nd and 4th accused were convicted of murder under sections 140, 146/296 of the Penal Code by the High Court of Panadura and sentenced to death. They appealed to the Court of Appeal. The main grounds were that no unlawful assembly of five persons existed after co-accused were acquitted, and no common object between the appellants was proven. The COA found the trial judge erred in law regarding unlawful assembly, misapplied circumstantial evidence principles, and drew unsupported factual conclusions. The COA allowed the appeals, set aside the convictions and death sentences, and acquitted the appellants.
defence_counsel: Neranjan Jayasingha with Harshana Ananda for the 1st Accused-Appellant. Shavindra Fernando, PC with T. Attyagalle, Mirthula Skandaraja, N. Wijesekara for the 2nd Accused-Appellant (4th Accused in High Court).
cause_of_death_exact_text: firearm injuries
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted based on a finding of unlawful assembly and active participation. The COA found this erroneous as the numerical requirement for an unlawful assembly was not met, and there was no evidence of common object or intention linking the appellants. The HC also made unsupported findings on the medical evidence and the source of the bullet.
precedents_cited_list: B.A.Premaratne vs the Republic of Sri Lanka CA168/2009 | Jayasena & Others v. G.D.D. Perera, Inspector, Criminal Investigation Department and Mrs. Sirimavo Bandaranayake (Aggrieved Party), [1992] SRI L.R. 371. CA.
standard_of_review_applied: Review of factual findings and legal errors by the trial court.

judges: Menaka Wijesundera J. | B. Sasi Mahendran J.
brief_facts_summary: The incident took place on an estate where the deceased was known for brewing illicit liquor. The two appellants and the deceased accused were involved in a campaign on the estate to stop the brewing. On the day of the incident, around 5 pm, the deceased was cut by the deceased accused and the appellants. After causing injuries, the appellants shouted that anyone else would be cut if they came forward. Three knives were recovered by police based on statements of the appellants and the deceased accused.
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the appellants for murder and sentenced them to death. The trial judge found that the prosecution proved its case beyond reasonable doubt, considering the evidence of prosecution witnesses as cogent and acceptable, and the defense case as inconsistent and wavering.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellants argued that the trial judge failed to evaluate the defense case properly and laid an undue burden on them. They also argued that the two prosecution eyewitnesses contradicted each other and that the judge's phrasing in the judgment caused grave prejudice.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Trial judge did not evaluate the defense case in proper perspective. | Trial judge laid an undue burden on the appellants. | The two eyewitnesses of the prosecution contradicted each other. | The judge's phrasing 'prosecution had proved its case beyond a reasonable doubt' in weighing defense evidence caused grave prejudice.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The trial judge considered the evidence of prosecution witnesses as without glaring contradictions and omissions. The defense was found to be wavering and inconsistent in cross-examination and dock statements. The Court of Appeal observed that the two eyewitnesses saw the incident at different stages, which does not constitute contradiction.
probability_assessment_by_court: Court found prosecution proved its case beyond reasonable doubt and defense was inconsistent.
defence_version_summary: Appellants made dock statements. They stated the deceased was involved in brewing illicit liquor, villagers were angry with him, and they saw the deceased accused cutting the deceased. Defense witnesses called by appellants reiterated this. The court found the defense wavering and inconsistent.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found no merit in the grounds of appeal. It observed the trial judge correctly applied the burden of proof beyond reasonable doubt. It held that minor discrepancies in eyewitness accounts do not shake the basic version, citing Bhajinbai Hirijbai vs. State of Gujarat. It also stated that the judge's writing style or phrasing cannot be considered prejudicial in isolation but must be viewed in the context of the case facts. The COA affirmed the conviction and sentence.
coa_sentence_type: Death
brief_judgment_file_summary: Two appellants were convicted of murder by the High Court of Nuwara Eliya and sentenced to death. They appealed, arguing the trial judge improperly evaluated the defense, that eyewitnesses contradicted each other, and that the judgment's phrasing was prejudicial. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal, finding the trial judge correctly applied the burden of proof, that discrepancies were minor, and that the judgment's wording was not prejudicial. The conviction and death sentence were affirmed.
prosecution_counsel: H. Jayasundera, A.S.G. for the State.
defence_counsel: Amila Palliyage with S. Udugampola, Sandeepani Wijesooriya and T. Ratwatte for the 1st Accused – Appellant. U. R. de Silva with Hiru Rubera for the 2nd Accused – Appellant.
cause_of_death_exact_text: One of the cut injuries had been identified as being the cause of death.
hc_analysis_summary: The COA found the trial judge was mindful of the burden of proof beyond reasonable doubt, properly analyzed evidence, and found prosecution evidence cogent. The COA agreed with the HC's reasoning and found no errors.
precedents_cited_list: Bhajinbai Hirijbai vs. the State of Gujarat AIR 1983 SC 753 | SC\TAB\2A-D/2017
standard_of_review_applied: Appellate review of trial judge's findings of fact and law, considering whether burden of proof was properly applied and evidence evaluated.

judges: M. SAMPATH K. B. WIJERATNE, J | WICKUM A. KALUARACHCHI, J
offence_sections: Section 13 and Section 14 of Schedule 1 of Chapter XLVIII of the Establishment Code; also the offence of bringing the Public Service into disrepute
brief_facts_summary: The petitioner, an Authorized Officer at the arrival terminal of Bandaranaike International Airport, was charged with disciplinary offences related to his conduct on 24.04.2014. He stepped down from his counter without permission during a busy period to have a snack and tea, leading to a verbal altercation and indecent behavior towards a Senior Authorized Officer. A disciplinary inquiry found him guilty of three charges, resulting in a deferred salary increment and a fine (later revoked on appeal).
evidence_type_primary: Witness testimony (including Senior Authorized Officers and Assistant Controller)
evidence_type_secondary: Disciplinary inquiry evidence and petitioner's written statement
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The petitioner challenged the orders of the disciplinary authority (P-8), the Public Service Commission (P-10), and the Administrative Appeals Tribunal (P-14). The 16th respondent objected that the PSC decision cannot be reviewed by the Court of Appeal under Article 61A of the Constitution. The petitioner argued that the main relief sought was to quash the AAT order, which is reviewable.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Decision of Public Service Commission cannot be challenged under Article 61A | Petitioner seeks to quash AAT order (P-14) under Article 140 | Alleged violation of principle of uberrima fides (not substantiated)
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: Evidence from disciplinary inquiry included testimony of Senior Authorized Officers and Assistant Controller describing the petitioner's unauthorized absence, verbal altercation, and disruptive behavior in a busy airport terminal. The court found the evidence substantiated the charges.
probability_assessment_by_court: Court found evidence of guilt clear and reasonable; no reasonable doubt.
defence_version_summary: Petitioner admitted stepping down for snack/tea but claimed Senior Authorized Officer abused him first; denied being quarrelsome. He did not plead guilty to the charges but admitted some facts. Defence was not accepted by disciplinary bodies or court.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal held it cannot review the PSC decision due to Article 61A constitutional bar. It reviewed the AAT order under Article 140, finding it did not err. The court examined disciplinary inquiry evidence, found petitioner guilty of unauthorized absence and disruptive conduct, and upheld the deferred salary increment as just. The AAT's failure to give detailed reasons was not fatal as it was an appellate body reviewing sufficiency of evidence.
coa_sentence_type: Defer one salary increment that fell after 24.04.2014
brief_judgment_file_summary: Petitioner, an Authorized Officer, challenged disciplinary orders related to misconduct at Bandaranaike International Airport. The Court of Appeal dismissed the writ application, holding that the Public Service Commission decision is immune from review under Article 61A. The AAT order was upheld as lawful and reasonable based on evidence of petitioner's unauthorized absence and disruptive behavior. The disciplinary penalty of deferring one salary increment was confirmed.
prosecution_counsel: Sumathi Dharmawardena ASG, PC and Shemanthi Dunuwila SC for the 16th Respondent
defence_counsel: Bhagya Gunawardhana instructed by Senior Counsel R. Chula Bandara for the Petitioner
precedents_cited_list: Bandaranaike v. Weeraratne and Others- (1981) 1 SLR 10 at 16 | Ratnayake v. Administrative Appeals Tribunal and Others -(2013) 1 Sri. L.R 331
standard_of_review_applied: Review of AAT decision under Article 140 for jurisdictional error or illegality; PSC decision not reviewable under Article 61A.
sentencing_principles_applied: Disciplinary penalty must be just and equitable considering nature of charges; deferred increment deemed appropriate.

judges: Menaka Wijesundera, J. | B. Sasi Mahendran, J.
offence_sections: Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance No. 13 of 1984 (as amended)
brief_facts_summary: On 29th December 2013, police officers on a daily routine patrol in a drug-prone area observed the accused acting suspiciously near a house. Upon search, the police recovered an electronic scale and a pink cellophane bag containing brown powder suspected to be heroin from the accused's shirt pocket. The accused was arrested, the substance was weighed and sent to the government analyst for examination, confirming it to be 3.52 grams of heroin.
evidence_type_primary: Physical evidence and police witness testimony
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance No. 13 of 1984 (as amended)
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court found the accused guilty of possession and trafficking of 3.52 grams of heroin based on the evidence of prosecution witnesses, particularly PW1 and PW3. The court was satisfied with the consistency of their evidence and the chain of custody. The accused was convicted and sentenced to life imprisonment.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant argued that the evidence was insufficient to prove the prosecution’s case beyond reasonable doubt. He also contended that the High Court judge wrongfully rejected his dock statement and failed to correctly apply the principles governing its evaluation.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The items of evidence are not sufficient to prove the prosecution’s case against the appellant beyond reasonable doubt. | The rejection of the dock statement is wrongful and the learned judge of the high court has failed to correctly apply the principles governing the evaluation of a dock statement.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal noted the High Court judge had the opportunity to observe the demeanor of the key prosecution witnesses (PW1 and PW3) and found them consistent and credible. The chain of custody of the drug production was found to be intact with no breaks or contradictions.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal held that the prosecution evidence was consistent and credible, and that the accused's dock statement failed to create any reasonable doubt in the prosecution's case.
defence_version_summary: The accused pleaded not guilty and made a dock statement only, calling no witnesses. He claimed he was arrested at home while napping, taken to the police station, forced to sign papers, and that the prosecution story was improbable. The court found his version untrustworthy, noting failures to address key details like the recovered scale.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal reviewed the High Court judgment, giving deference to the trial judge's assessment of witness credibility. It found the prosecution witnesses consistent and the chain of custody unbroken. The court applied the principles from Queen v. Kularatne for evaluating the dock statement and found it did not raise a reasonable doubt. Citing Siddick v. The Republic of Sri Lanka, it upheld the police officer's right to search based on suspicious conduct. The appeal was dismissed as no miscarriage of justice was found.
coa_sentence_type: Life imprisonment (affirmed)
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused was convicted by the High Court of Colombo for possession and trafficking of 3.52g of heroin and sentenced to life imprisonment. He appealed, arguing insufficient evidence and wrongful rejection of his dock statement. The Court of Appeal found the prosecution evidence credible and consistent, the chain of custody intact, and the dock statement insufficient to create reasonable doubt. The appeal was dismissed, and the conviction and sentence were affirmed.
defence_counsel: Chathura Amarathunga
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court found the accused guilty based on the consistent evidence of PW1 and PW3 and the unbroken chain of custody. The Court of Appeal saw no error in this analysis, agreeing with the High Court's assessment of witness credibility and evidence.
precedents_cited_list: Queen v. Kularatne 71 NLR 529 | Siddick v. The Republic of Sri Lanka [2005] 1 SLR 383 | Kirpal Singh v The State of Uttar Pradesh AIR (1965) SC 712
standard_of_review_applied: The Court will not normally review evidence unless the trial is vitiated by illegality, procedural irregularity, violation of natural justice, unfair trial, or gross miscarriage of justice.
sentencing_principles_applied: Life imprisonment for drug trafficking under the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance.

judges: Menaka Wijesundera, J. | B. Sasi Mahendran, J.
offence_sections: Section 216(a) and Section 218 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The accused-respondents were prison guards of Negombo prison. On 23 January 1995, they were escorting a suspect named Umargool, a Pakistani national suspected of importing and possessing 12,308 grams of morphine, to the Negombo Magistrate's Court while he was in custody. Umargool escaped. The accused were indicted for intentionally aiding the escape (Section 216(a)) and negligently suffering the escape (Section 218) of a person lawfully committed to custody.
evidence_type_primary: Circumstantial evidence of escape during escort duty
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 216(a) and Section 218 of the Penal Code
hc_sentence_type: Conditional discharge under Section 306(2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure Act No. 15 of 1979 with suspended sentences for three years
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court Judge convicted both accused-respondents on 31 July 2009. On 28 August 2009, despite noting the grave nature of the offence, the judge conditionally discharged them under Section 306(2) of the Criminal Procedure Code and imposed suspended sentences for three years.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The Hon. Attorney General appealed on the basis that the sentences imposed by the High Court Judge were inadequate and inappropriate given the serious nature of the offences. The main argument was that the judge misdirected herself by invoking Section 306(2) of the Criminal Procedure Code, which is meant for trivial offences or extenuating circumstances, and failed to impose an appropriate sentence.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The sentences imposed are inadequate and inappropriate for the serious nature of the offences. | The High Court Judge misdirected herself by invoking Section 306(2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure Act. | The judge failed to impose an appropriate sentence other than the sanctions in Section 306(2), having regard to the serious nature of the offences.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The judgment does not detail the evidence presented at trial. The focus of the appeal is solely on sentencing principles and the application of Section 306(2) of the Criminal Procedure Code.
defence_version_summary: The judgment does not state the plea of the accused at the High Court trial. The appeal focuses on sentencing after conviction.
legal_errors_description: The Court of Appeal found the High Court Judge erred in law by failing to appreciate the imperative provisions governing the law of sentencing and by misapplying Section 306(2) of the Criminal Procedure Code to a serious offence.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed sentencing principles from precedents, noting that punishment must be proportionate to the gravity of the offence, serve as a deterrent, and protect public interest. It acknowledged the High Court Judge's legal error in applying Section 306(2) for a serious offence involving a public servant in a position of trust. However, considering the inordinate delay of 14 years since the erroneous suspended sentence and the fact the accused completed the sentence period without blemish, imposing a custodial sentence now would be against principles of justice and equity and the conscience of the court.
coa_sentence_type: The Court of Appeal declined to set aside the High Court's conditional discharge order. The suspended sentence imposed by the High Court stands.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The Attorney General appealed against the conditional discharge and suspended sentences given to two prison guard accused-respondents convicted for aiding/negligently allowing the escape of a suspect in a major drug case. The High Court had imposed a three-year suspended sentence under Section 306(2) of the Criminal Procedure Code. The Court of Appeal agreed the High Court Judge erred by applying this provision meant for trivial offences to a serious one. However, due to an inordinate 14-year delay in the appeal process, during which the accused completed their sentence period without issue, the Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal, holding that imposing a custodial sentence now would be unjust.
defence_counsel: Dr. Ranjith Fernando with Maleesha Meera
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court Judge convicted the accused but then conditionally discharged them under Section 306(2), considering it expedient. The COA found this was an error, as the judge failed to consider the seriousness of the offence, the position of trust held by the accused as public servants, and the need for deterrent punishment.
precedents_cited_list: Attorney General v. H.N. De Silva, 57 NLR 121 | M. Gomes v. W.V.D. Leelaratna, 66 NLR 233 | Attorney General v. Ranasinghe and Others, 1993 2 SLR 81 | Attorney General v. Jinak Sri Uluwaduge and Another, 1995 1 SLR 157 | Attorney General v. Walgma Kodithuwakkuge Ruksiri alia Sudumalli CA 306/2012 | K.R. Karunaratne vs. The State, 78 NLR 413 | Attorney-General vs. Devapriya [1990] 2 Sri L.R. 212 | Tenison Ridway Kern v. Attorney General, CA Appeal No. 222/2005
standard_of_review_applied: Review of sentencing discretion and legal error in applying Section 306(2) of the Criminal Procedure Code.
sentencing_principles_applied: Proportionality between punishment and gravity of offence, deterrence, protection of society, public interest, character/antecedents/age of offender, extenuating circumstances, and the impact of inordinate delay in justice.

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: section 380 of the Penal Code
location_of_offence: victim's shop, location in Kottawa police jurisdiction
brief_facts_summary: The accused-appellant-petitioner was charged with robbing a gold chain from a female victim in her shop on 3 March 2016. The victim (PW-01) testified that the robber entered her shop as a customer, snatched her chain, and fled; she struggled with him and saw him clearly. The gold chain was never recovered. The victim identified the petitioner at an identification parade. The investigating officer died before trial, and his notes were produced via another officer under section 32(2) of the Evidence Ordinance.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: section 380 of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court dismissed the petitioner's appeal, finding no basis to interfere with the Magistrate's conviction and sentence. The High Court Judge considered the grounds of appeal and determined that the trial court's findings were sound.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The petitioner argued the High Court Judge erred by failing to properly analyze the case circumstances, not considering the unrecovered gold chain, not proving the case beyond reasonable doubt, wrongly analyzing the arrest date, and failing to analyze identification evidence correctly. He also claimed a previous appeal was filed in the wrong court due to his attorney's default.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The learned High Court Judge has erred in law by failing to properly analyze the circumstances of the case. | The learned High Court Judge has erred in law by not considering the fact that the gold chain was not found in the possession of the appellant and no investigation had been conducted to that effect. | The has erred in failing to consider that the prosecution had not proved the case beyond reasonable doubt. | The learned High Court Judge has erred on facts by wrongly analyzing that the appellant was arrested on 07-03-2016. | The learned High Court Judge has erred in law by failing to analyze the evidence adduced by the witnesses according to what was stated in the identification parade marked X-3 and the evidence of witnesses as to the identification of the accused.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the evidence of PW-01 (victim) cogent and trustworthy. The trial court and High Court properly evaluated her testimony and the identification parade notes. The court held that a conviction can be based on the testimony of a single witness if reliable.
probability_assessment_by_court: Court found the victim's evidence credible and sufficient to establish guilt beyond reasonable doubt, rejecting claims of prior showing or photograph influence.
defence_version_summary: The petitioner pleaded not guilty. The defence challenged the identification, suggesting the victim was shown the petitioner or his photo before the parade. The trial court and High Court found these claims unsubstantiated and did not create doubt in the prosecution evidence.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal held that revision is a discretionary remedy for exceptional circumstances, which were not present. The grounds raised were factual challenges, not exceptional. The court noted the petitioner failed to appeal to the Supreme Court as required and delayed. It affirmed that a conviction can rest on a single credible witness (PW-01) under section 134 of the Evidence Ordinance. The identification parade notes were properly admitted under section 414(2) of the Criminal Procedure Code. No procedural irregularity or miscarriage of justice was found. Precedents on revisionary jurisdiction and single-witness testimony were applied.
coa_sentence_type: 1-year rigorous imprisonment and fine of Rs. 1500/= (as imposed by Magistrate and affirmed by High Court)
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused was convicted of robbery under section 380 of the Penal Code for snatching a gold chain from a shopkeeper. The Magistrate sentenced him to 1-year rigorous imprisonment and a fine. The High Court dismissed his appeal. He then sought revision in the Court of Appeal, arguing identification flaws, unrecovered chain, and procedural errors. The Court of Appeal dismissed the application, finding no exceptional circumstances for revision, affirming the reliability of the single eyewitness, and noting the proper admission of identification evidence.
defence_counsel: Sachira Andrahamnadi
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court considered the appeal grounds and found no basis to interfere with the Magistrate's conviction and sentence. The Court of Appeal agreed with this analysis, finding no error in the High Court's judgment.
precedents_cited_list: Mulluwa Vs. The State of Madhya Predesh 1976 AIR 989 | Ramratan Vs. State of Rajasthan AIR (1962) S.C. 424 | Wijesinghe Vs. Tharmaratnam (Srikantha Law Reports Vol. IV page 47) | Vanik Incorporation Ltd. Vs. Jayasekara (1997) 2 SLR 365
standard_of_review_applied: Revisionary jurisdiction under Article 138 of the Constitution, discretionary remedy for exceptional circumstances or miscarriage of justice.

judges: Menaka Wijesundera, J. | B. Sasi Mahendran, J.
brief_facts_summary: The Accused-Appellant was indicted for two charges of sexual abuse under the Penal Code. The judgment text does not provide details of the arrest, incident, or evidence. The appeal focused solely on the sentence.
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the Accused-Appellant on two charges of sexual abuse. The date of conviction was 04/08/2021. The judgment does not detail the High Court's specific sentence or reasoning.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appeal was against the sentence only. The Accused-Appellant's counsel stated he was not contesting the conviction, only the sentence. The appeal sought to set aside the High Court judgment dated 04/08/2021.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Not contesting the conviction. | Appealing only the sentence.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The judgment provides no analysis or details regarding the witnesses or evidence presented at the High Court trial.
defence_version_summary: The appeal record indicates the Accused-Appellant did not contest the conviction at the Court of Appeal stage. No details of the original plea, alibi, or defence witnesses are provided.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal considered the submissions of both parties regarding the sentence. The Court backdated the sentence to be operative from the date of the High Court conviction (04/08/2021). Subject to this variation, the appeal was dismissed.
coa_sentence_type: Sentence backdated to be operative from 04/08/2021.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The Accused-Appellant appealed against the High Court of Embilipitiya's conviction and sentence on two charges of sexual abuse. The appeal was limited to challenging the sentence, not the conviction. The Court of Appeal considered the submissions and varied the sentence to be operative from the date of the High Court conviction. Subject to this variation, the appeal was dismissed.
defence_counsel: Laknath Senevirathne
hc_analysis_summary: The judgment does not detail the High Court's reasoning. The Court of Appeal's order suggests the only issue was the operative date of the sentence, which it backdated to the conviction date.
standard_of_review_applied: The Court considered submissions on the sentence.
sentencing_principles_applied: Backdating the sentence to the date of conviction.

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 389 and 386 of the Penal Code
offence_category: Criminal Breach of Trust and Criminal Misappropriation
brief_facts_summary: The accused appellant, who operated a clearing agency called Janaranjana Enterprises, was entrusted with pay orders by Singer Sri Lanka Ltd to clear goods from Sri Lanka Customs. The appellant used the pay orders to clear goods belonging to other companies, instead of clearing the goods of Singer Sri Lanka Ltd. The company discovered the misuse when their goods were not released, and the pay orders had been used for other importers, leading to a complaint to the CID.
evidence_type_primary: Circumstantial evidence and documentary evidence (pay orders, bank records)
evidence_type_secondary: Testimony of company officials and bank officials
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 389 of the Penal Code
hc_sentence_type: 30 months rigorous imprisonment, fine, default sentence, and compensation
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court found the appellant guilty of count 1 (criminal breach of trust) for misusing a pay order for Rs. 825,094/= intended for Singer Sri Lanka Ltd to clear goods for another company. The appellant was acquitted on other counts due to insufficient evidence or alternative charging. The judge considered mitigatory circumstances in sentencing.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant argued that the High Court judge erred in applying principles of circumstantial evidence regarding entrustment, a key element of the offence. The appellant contended that the circumstantial evidence was insufficient and only created suspicion, not proof beyond reasonable doubt, and pointed to another person as potentially responsible.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The learned Trial Judge has erred in law in applying principles relevant to the circumstantial evidence with regard to the entrustment being the threshold ingredient of section 389 of the Penal Code.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The prosecution's case relied on the testimony of the Items Manager of Singer Sri Lanka Ltd (PW-01) and bank officials. The evidence established the issuance and misuse of pay orders. The appellant's defence, blaming a company clerk, was rejected as an afterthought without basis.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal found the circumstantial evidence, taken together, proved entrustment and misuse beyond reasonable doubt, rejecting the argument that it only created suspicion.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty and made a dock statement. He admitted running the clearing agency and working for Singer Sri Lanka Ltd but denied misappropriation, blaming a clerk named Kapila Yatawara. The court found his defence was an afterthought and did not create reasonable doubt.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal reviewed the High Court's analysis of circumstantial evidence regarding entrustment. It agreed that the totality of evidence—the business relationship, handling of pay orders, subsequent misuse, and evasive behavior—proved entrustment and criminal breach of trust beyond reasonable doubt. The court found no misdirection by the High Court judge, rejected the defence as baseless, and upheld the conviction and sentence as legally sound and factually justified.
coa_sentence_type: 30 months rigorous imprisonment, fine, default sentence, and compensation to Singer Sri Lanka Ltd affirmed
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused appellant, a clearing agent, was convicted by the High Court of Colombo for criminal breach of trust for misusing a pay order from Singer Sri Lanka Ltd to clear goods for another company. He was sentenced to 30 months rigorous imprisonment. On appeal, he argued the High Court erred in relying on circumstantial evidence to prove entrustment. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal, finding the circumstantial evidence was sufficient and proved guilt beyond reasonable doubt, and affirmed the conviction and sentence.
defence_counsel: Kasun Liyanage
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court correctly analyzed the circumstantial evidence to prove entrustment and criminal breach of trust. The Court of Appeal found no error in this analysis and agreed that the prosecution proved its case beyond reasonable doubt.
standard_of_review_applied: Assessment of whether circumstantial evidence was sufficient to prove entrustment and guilt beyond reasonable doubt
sentencing_principles_applied: Consideration of mitigatory circumstances and relevant facts

judges: Menaka Wijesundera J. | B. Sasi Mahendran J.
offence_sections: grave sexual abuse under the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The appellant was living with the victim's mother. On the day of the incident, the appellant brought the victim from his sister's house to his home and allegedly sexually abused her. The victim told her mother the same day, and the incident was reported to the police. The victim was examined by a doctor.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: grave sexual abuse under the Penal Code
hc_sentence_type: 12 years rigorous imprisonment with a fine and a default sentence
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court found the appellant guilty of the charge of grave sexual abuse. He was convicted and sentenced to 12 years rigorous imprisonment with a fine and a default sentence.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant's counsel argued the victim's police statement was unsigned, the time of the offence was unclear, the lay witness and police evidence were contradictory, the victim's history to the doctor contradicted the doctor's findings, and the prosecution's story was highly improbable.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The victim had not signed the statement to the police. | The time of the offence not being clearly established by the prosecution. | The evidence of the lay witnesses and the police observations being contrary to each other. | The case history given by the victim to the doctor being contrary to the observations of the doctor. | As such the story of the prosecution being highly improbable.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court found the victim's unsigned police statement weakened its value, the time of the incident was not certain, and contradictions existed between the victim's and her mother's evidence regarding where she was brought from. The medical history given by the victim was also contrary to the doctor's findings.
probability_assessment_by_court: Court found the prosecution's story highly improbable and not proven beyond reasonable doubt, due to multiple infirmities in the evidence.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty. He testified on oath, denying the charge. He stated he met the victim's mother at a bus halt, brought her and her begging children home, started a family, but there were disputes. He claimed he was later arrested after the mother went to hospital with two children.
procedural_defects_description: Failure to have the victim's police statement signed as required by Section 110(10) of the Code of Criminal Procedure Code.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found multiple infirmities in the prosecution case. The unsigned victim statement reduced its evidential value. The time of the incident was unclear. There were contradictions between the victim's and her mother's evidence regarding where the victim was brought from, which cast doubt on the opportunity to commit the offence and the credibility of the victim's account. The medical history given by the victim was contrary to the doctor's clinical findings (redness possibly due to bacterial infection). The Court held the prosecution failed to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt and the trial judge did not analyze the evidence to notice these infirmities.
coa_sentence_type: Conviction and sentence set aside
brief_judgment_file_summary: The appellant was convicted by the High Court of Matara for grave sexual abuse and sentenced to 12 years rigorous imprisonment. He appealed, challenging the conviction on grounds including an unsigned victim statement, unclear timing, contradictory witness evidence, and inconsistencies in medical evidence. The Court of Appeal found the prosecution's case highly improbable and not proven beyond reasonable doubt due to these infirmities. The appeal was allowed, the conviction and sentence were set aside, and the appellant was acquitted.
defence_counsel: Jagath Abeynayake with Sachin Jayalath and Aranga Dewanarayana
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted the appellant based on the prosecution evidence. The Court of Appeal found the trial judge narrated the evidence but failed to analyze it and notice the infirmities, such as the unsigned statement, contradictions, and medical inconsistencies.
standard_of_review_applied: Assessment of whether prosecution proved its case beyond reasonable doubt.

judges: Menaka Wijesundera J. | B. Sasi Mahendran J.
offence_sections: possession and trafficking of 3.34 grams of heroin under the provisions of the Poisons Opium and dangerous drugs act
brief_facts_summary: Police received a tip-off that a white car would transport narcotics to Galle on 7.5.2010. A police team led by witness no 1 conducted a raid on the Colombo Galle Road at Hikkaduwa around 10.30 am. The accused appellant arrived at 2.45 pm, was searched, and an alleged substance suspected to be heroin was found in his right trouser pocket. The vehicle was later searched at Dodanduwa but nothing incriminating was found.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: possession and trafficking of 3.34 grams of heroin under the provisions of the Poisons Opium and dangerous drugs act
hc_sentence_type: Conviction and sentences (specific types not detailed)
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the accused appellant on both charges of possession and trafficking of heroin. The trial judge reproduced the prosecution evidence but failed to analyze discrepancies and defense evidence.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant argued that the evidence of prosecution witnesses was contradictory and improbable, the trial judge failed to consider the defense evidence and the improbabilities in the prosecution's timeline, and that these failures denied him a fair trial.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The evidence of prosecution witnesses no 1 and 4 being contradictory and the trial judge had failed to consider the same. | The time frame led by prosecution in evidence being improbable. | The evidence of the appellant not being considered by the trial judge. | The defense witness had cut across the version of the prosecution and the trial judge had failed to analyze the same and there by the appellant had been denied a fair trial.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court found contradictions between PW1 and PW4 regarding the time of events and sequence of actions. The defense witness (jewelry shop owner) contradicted the prosecution's story about weighing the substance, casting doubt on the chain of custody.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court found the prosecution's timeline highly improbable and identified contradictions that created reasonable doubt.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty. His defense was that he was arrested at Seenigama around 4 pm without any drugs, and that the police introduced the alleged substance on the instigation of Charith Manoj. He gave evidence and called two witnesses, including the jewelry shop owner, to support his claim.
legal_errors_description: Failure to consider contradictions in prosecution evidence, failure to analyze improbabilities in the prosecution's timeline, failure to properly consider and rule on the defense evidence, resulting in a denial of fair trial.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the trial judge failed to analyze significant contradictions between prosecution witnesses (PW1 and PW4) regarding key timings and the sequence of events. The prosecution's timeline was deemed highly improbable. The trial judge also failed to properly consider the defense evidence, including the jewelry shop owner who contradicted the prosecution's story about weighing the substance, thereby casting doubt on the chain of custody. The COA applied the principle that the prosecution must prove its case beyond reasonable doubt and that police evidence should be scrutinized with caution. It found the trial judge's omissions deprived the appellant of a fair trial.
coa_sentence_type: Conviction and sentences set aside
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused appellant was convicted by the High Court of Galle for possession and trafficking of 3.34 grams of heroin. He appealed on grounds including contradictory prosecution evidence, an improbable timeline, and the trial judge's failure to consider the defense. The Court of Appeal found serious lapses in the trial judge's analysis, including failure to address contradictions between prosecution witnesses, the improbable timeline, and failure to properly evaluate defense evidence that challenged the chain of custody. The COA allowed the appeal, set aside the conviction and sentences, and acquitted the appellant.
defence_counsel: Saliya Pieris, PC with Thanuka Nandasiri
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted the appellant but merely reproduced prosecution evidence without analyzing contradictions, improbabilities, or the defense case. The COA found this was a fundamental error that denied a fair trial.
precedents_cited_list: Wickramasuriya vs Dedolina and others 1996 (2) SLR page 95 | Sinnaiya vs AG CA 128-2005 BaslCriminal Law 2010 Vol 111 page 31 | Nalleperuma Thanthirige Danuka Roshan vs AG CA 216-2015 | Karuppiah Pankhudi vs AG CA 11-2005
standard_of_review_applied: Assessment of whether the trial judge properly evaluated evidence, considered contradictions and defense, and ensured a fair trial.

judges: Menaka Wijesundera J. | B. Sasi Mahendran J.
offence_sections: section 364 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The victim was returning home from work when she was dragged into the woods and raped by the appellant. She later told her mother, who observed blood dripping from her legs. The mother stated the appellant held a knife to the victim's neck, a detail the victim did not mention. The appellant was identified by the victim as 'Isuru' after several attempts, but she gave an incorrect date.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: section 364 of the Penal Code
hc_sentence_type: 20 years rigorous imprisonment with a fine and compensation and a default sentence
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the appellant of rape under section 364 of the Penal Code after a full trial. The judge found the victim's evidence credible and sentenced the appellant to 20 years rigorous imprisonment with a fine and compensation.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant argued that the High Court judge who wrote the judgment did not observe the demeanor of the victim, did not properly analyze the evidence, and that the appellant was denied a fair trial. Specific issues included inconsistent identification, lack of illumination evidence, and coaching of the victim.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The learned High Court Judge not being able to observe the demeanor and the deportment of the victim | The learned High Court Judge had not analyzed the evidence properly | The appellant not being given a fair trial
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the victim's evidence waivered, unnatural, and that she admitted to being coached. Identification was inconsistent, and the judge who convicted did not observe the lay witnesses, affecting credibility assessment.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court found the evidence not consistent or cogent enough to establish guilt beyond reasonable doubt.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty. The defence argued the victim's evidence was coached, identification was flawed, and the trial was unfair. No alibi was explicitly mentioned; the defence focused on challenging prosecution evidence.
legal_errors_description: The High Court judge failed to properly assess identification evidence, illumination at the scene, and the victim's demeanor. The prosecution did not prove the case beyond reasonable doubt.
procedural_defects_description: The judge who wrote the judgment did not observe the victim's demeanor; a different judge heard her evidence. The victim was not administered an oath initially due to perceived mental condition.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal held that the victim's evidence was inconsistent, wavered, and appeared coached. Identification was problematic due to lack of illumination evidence and inconsistent statements. The High Court judge who convicted did not observe the lay witnesses, which was critical given the victim's mental inadequacies noted by the hearing judge. The prosecution failed to prove the case beyond reasonable doubt, making corroborative evidence inconclusive.
coa_sentence_type: Conviction and sentence set aside
brief_judgment_file_summary: The appellant was convicted of rape by the High Court of Gampaha and sentenced to 20 years rigorous imprisonment with fine and compensation. He appealed on grounds including lack of demeanor observation by the convicting judge, improper evidence analysis, and unfair trial. The Court of Appeal found the victim's evidence inconsistent and possibly coached, identification unreliable due to illumination issues, and the prosecution's case not proven beyond reasonable doubt. The appeal was allowed, and the conviction and sentence were set aside.
defence_counsel: Palitha Fernando P.C with B.C. Balasuriya
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court relied heavily on the victim's evidence, believing it despite inconsistencies. The Court of Appeal found the High Court failed to adequately address issues of identification, illumination, and the victim's demeanor, leading to an unsafe conviction.
standard_of_review_applied: Beyond reasonable doubt

judges: Menaka Wijesundera J. | B. Sasi Mahendran J.
offence_sections: Section 364(2) of the Penal Code, Section 345 of the Penal Code, Section 364(2) of the Penal Code, Section 364 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The accused appellant was indicted on four counts of rape and other related offences. He pleaded guilty. The victim was 15 years old at the time, and the appellant was 25, married, and a father. The High Court convicted and sentenced him. On appeal, the Court of Appeal found the High Court failed to allow submissions in mitigation before sentencing.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 364(2) of the Penal Code, Section 345 of the Penal Code, Section 364(2) of the Penal Code, Section 364 of the Penal Code
hc_sentence_type: Rigorous Imprisonment 27 years in totality; sentences for first and second charges consecutive, sentences for third and fourth charges concurrent but after the first two.
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the appellant on all four counts after his guilty plea and imposed a total sentence of 27 years rigorous imprisonment with an ordered sequence for serving the sentences.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant's counsel only canvassed the sentence, not the conviction, arguing that the total sentence was excessive. He also averred that the High Court failed to give both parties a chance to make submissions in mitigation before sentencing.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The sentence in totality is excessive. | The High Court Judge failed to give an opportunity for both parties to make submissions in mitigation.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The conviction was based on the appellant's guilty plea. No witness testimony or other evidence is discussed in the provided judgment text.
probability_assessment_by_court: No assessment of reasonable doubt as conviction was based on a guilty plea.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded guilty to all charges. There was no alibi or other defence raised. No witnesses were called. The court accepted the plea.
legal_errors_description: The High Court Judge failed to give both parties an opportunity to make submissions in mitigation before sentencing.
procedural_defects_description: Failure to allow submissions in mitigation prior to sentencing.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal agreed that the sentence imposed by the High Court was excessive. It found a procedural defect in the High Court's failure to allow submissions in mitigation. Considering the appellant's age (25), marital status, fatherhood, and the victim's age (15), the Court varied the sentences to run concurrently and reduced the total effective imprisonment period.
coa_sentence_type: 1) 10 years rigorous imprisonment for count 1; 2) 1 year rigorous imprisonment for count 2; 3) 10 years rigorous imprisonment for count 3; 4) 10 years rigorous imprisonment for count 4. All sentences to run concurrently, backdated to the date of conviction.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The appellant Rasakumar Thirukumar appealed against his sentence for four counts of rape and related offences. The High Court of Vavuniya had convicted him after a guilty plea and imposed a 27-year total sentence. The Court of Appeal found the High Court failed to allow submissions in mitigation, making the sentence excessive. It varied the sentences to run concurrently, resulting in a reduced effective term of 10 years rigorous imprisonment, and dismissed the appeal.
defence_counsel: Ershan Ariaratnam
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted based on a guilty plea and imposed a consecutive sentence structure totalling 27 years. The Court of Appeal found the High Court erred procedurally by not allowing mitigation submissions and that the resultant total sentence was excessive.
standard_of_review_applied: Review of sentencing procedure and appropriateness.
sentencing_principles_applied: Consideration of submissions in mitigation, age of victim and accused, personal circumstances of accused.

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Sections 54(A) (d) and 54(A) (b) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance as amended by Act No. 13 of 1984
brief_facts_summary: On 14 March 2004, based on informant information, IP Vijith Jayantha (PW1) and a police team stopped a three-wheeler and arrested the female appellant. She was taken to Ambalangoda Police Station where a body search by PW3 allegedly recovered a parcel containing 36 plastic bags with 680 packets of a substance suspected to be heroin, weighing 10.500 grams. The appellant admitted her arrest but denied possession of any illegal substance.
evidence_type_secondary: Police testimony regarding search and recovery
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Sections 54(A) (d) and 54(A) (b) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance as amended by Act No. 13 of 1984
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court found the appellant guilty on both counts of possession and trafficking of 5.3 grams of heroin. The learned High Court Judge imposed a sentence of life imprisonment on both counts on 26 February 2018.
