grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellants challenged the conviction on grounds that the identification parade evidence should not have been admitted, the trial judge erroneously sought corroboration from police statements, and the judge's conclusion was against the norms of the Evidence Ordinance.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The evidence of the identification parade should never have been placed before Court. | The trial judge erroneously seeking corroboration from the police statement. | Conclusion of the trial judge against the norms of the evidence ordinance.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the identification parade evidence unsafe due to lack of proper notes and reliance on memory after 15 years. It also questioned the reliability of the dock identification given the traumatic circumstances and brief duration of the incident.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court found the evidence of identification was unsafe and created reasonable doubt.
defence_version_summary: The appellants pleaded not guilty, made statements from the dock denying involvement and the identification at the parade. No defence witnesses were called.
legal_errors_description: The High Court judge erred by relying on identification parade evidence without proper notes, seeking corroboration from police statements, and failing to consider omissions and contradictions in prosecution evidence.
procedural_defects_description: Failure to properly consider the admissibility and reliability of identification parade evidence; failure to consider omissions and contradictions in witness evidence.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal disregarded the identification parade evidence as unsafe due to the acting magistrate's reliance on memory after 15 years and lack of parade notes. It found the dock identification unreliable given the traumatic, brief nature of the incident and the witnesses' mental state. The trial judge failed to consider these factors and improperly relied on the parade evidence. The appeal was allowed, and the conviction set aside.
coa_sentence_type: Conviction and sentence set aside
brief_judgment_file_summary: The two accused appellants were convicted of murder by the High Court of Rathnapura based on eyewitness identification. They appealed, challenging the identification parade evidence and the trial judge's evaluation. The Court of Appeal found the identification evidence unsafe due to lack of proper parade notes and unreliable dock identification given the traumatic circumstances. The appeal was allowed, the conviction and sentence were set aside, and the appellants were acquitted.
defence_counsel: Palitha Fernando, P.C. for the 1st Accused – Appellant. Neranjan Jayasinghe for the 2nd Accused – Appellant.
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court relied heavily on the identification parade evidence and dock identification, concluding the prosecution evidence was cogent. The Court of Appeal found this reasoning flawed as the judge failed to consider the unreliability of the parade evidence, omissions/contradictions in witness testimony, and the traumatic context affecting identification.
precedents_cited_list: Attorney General Vs Joseph Alloysius and other1992 2 Sril.R 264 | SC (spI)Appeal 7/2018 dated 4.10.2019
standard_of_review_applied: Review of evidence evaluation and legal errors by the trial judge.

judges: Menaka Wijesundera | B. Sasi Mahendran
offence_sections: Section 364 (1) of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The accused-appellant was indicted for an offence under Section 364(1) of the Penal Code. The High Court found him guilty and sentenced him to ten years rigorous imprisonment with a fine and compensation. The appeal was filed to set aside the High Court judgment, but the appellant contested only the sentence, not the conviction.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 364 (1) of the Penal Code
hc_sentence_type: Ten years rigorous imprisonment with a fine of Rs.10,000 (default one year rigorous imprisonment) and compensation of Rs.50,000 (default another two years imprisonment)
hc_judgment_summary: The learned High Court Judge found the accused guilty of the offence under Section 364(1) of the Penal Code after trial and sentenced him to ten years rigorous imprisonment with a fine and compensation.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The counsel for the accused-appellant stated that he was not contesting the conviction but only the sentence. The appeal sought to set aside the High Court judgment dated 23.03.2021.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Appeal against sentence only, not conviction
defence_version_summary: The accused-appellant did not contest the conviction in the appeal, focusing only on challenging the sentence.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: Upon consideration of submissions from both parties, the Court of Appeal decided to vary the sentence, reducing the ten-year rigorous imprisonment to seven years rigorous imprisonment to be operative from the original sentencing date. The rest of the sentence remained the same.
coa_sentence_type: Seven years rigorous imprisonment (operative from 23.03.2021), with fine of Rs.10,000 (default one year rigorous imprisonment), and compensation of Rs.50,000 (default another two years imprisonment)
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused-appellant appealed the High Court judgment convicting him under Section 364(1) of the Penal Code and sentencing him to ten years rigorous imprisonment with fine and compensation. In the Court of Appeal, counsel contested only the sentence, not the conviction. After hearing submissions, the Court of Appeal varied the sentence by reducing the imprisonment term from ten to seven years, effective from the original sentencing date, while keeping the fine and compensation portions unchanged. The appeal was dismissed subject to this variation.
defence_counsel: Buddhika Thilakarathna
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court found the accused guilty and imposed a sentence of ten years rigorous imprisonment with fine and compensation. The Court of Appeal did not explicitly criticize the HC's reasoning but considered the sentence excessive enough to warrant a reduction.

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The deceased was the owner of Melgahawatte Coconut Estate. On 12/07/2008, the Appellant along with two others went to the house of PW1 and PW2 (employees of the deceased) seeking to assault PW2 after an earlier altercation involving PW2's son. The Appellant carried a sword. When PW2 locked himself inside, the deceased intervened. The Appellant then dealt several blows to the deceased's head with the sword, causing fatal injuries. PW1 and PW2 witnessed the incident. The Appellant was arrested on 19.07.2008.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court Judge found the Appellant guilty of murder under Section 296 of the Penal Code and sentenced him to death on 29/02/2016. The 1st and 3rd accused were acquitted. The conviction was based on the evidence of prosecution witnesses.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The Appellant appealed on three main grounds: (1) The conviction was unsustainable due to the failure of the succeeding trial judge to formally adopt the evidence recorded by his predecessor as required by Section 48 of the Judicature Act. (2) The Appellant was denied effective assistance of counsel and thereby a fair trial, due to counsel's deficient performance and potential conflict of interest. (3) The High Court should have considered a mitigatory plea under Section 297 of the Penal Code.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: In the absence of adoption of evidence can the conviction be sustained in this case. | Has there being a denial of an effective assistance of a Counsel, and thereby denied a fair trial. | In the circumstances of this case should a mitigatory plea under Section 297 of Penal Code should have been considered.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal considered the evidence of PW1 and PW2, who both witnessed the incident. PW1 saw the Appellant strike the deceased with a sword. PW2 corroborated this, watching through a hole in the door. The medical evidence (PW4) confirmed death from deep incised wounds to the head. The COA found the evidence cogent and convincing, sufficient to sustain the conviction.
probability_assessment_by_court: The COA found the evidence of the eyewitnesses cogent and convincing, leaving no reasonable doubt about the Appellant's guilt.
defence_version_summary: The Appellant pleaded not guilty. The defence consisted of a dock statement from the Appellant. No defence witnesses were called. The court assessed the defence as lacking credibility against the strong prosecution evidence.
procedural_defects_description: Appellant claimed procedural error due to non-adoption of evidence by succeeding judge and denial of fair trial due to ineffective assistance of counsel.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal dismissed all grounds of appeal. On the first ground, it held, following precedent, that formal adoption of evidence by a succeeding judge is not a mandatory requirement. On the second ground, while noting a potential issue with counsel's performance, the COA applied the proviso to Article 138 of the Constitution, finding no prejudice to the Appellant's substantial rights or failure of justice given the overwhelming evidence of guilt. The COA also noted the High Court Judge's serious flaw in not considering PW2's evidence in the judgment, but found this did not affect the outcome. On the third ground, the COA found no mitigatory circumstances in the evidence. The COA concluded the High Court judgment was sound and required no interference.
coa_sentence_type: Death
brief_judgment_file_summary: The Appellant was convicted of murder by the High Court of Chilaw and sentenced to death. He appealed to the Court of Appeal on grounds including failure to adopt evidence, denial of fair trial due to ineffective counsel, and failure to consider mitigation. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal. It held that formal adoption of evidence was not mandatory, and that any deficiency in counsel's performance did not prejudice the Appellant's substantial rights given the strong eyewitness and medical evidence. No mitigatory circumstances were found. The death sentence was upheld.
defence_counsel: Anil Silva, PC with Aman Bandara and S.Neranga
cause_of_death_exact_text: multiple deep incised wounds involving scalp, skull bone and underlying brain substance
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court carefully considered the prosecution evidence and found the Appellant guilty of murder. However, the COA identified a serious flaw: the HC Judge failed to consider the evidence of PW2 in the judgment. Despite this, the COA found the overall conclusion was correct and caused no prejudice.
precedents_cited_list: Herath Mudiyanselage Aruyaratna v. Republic of Sri Lanka CA/307/2006 decided on 17/07/2013 | Case No.CA/HCC/0168/2015 decided on 24/02/2022
standard_of_review_applied: Appellate jurisdiction for correction of errors in fact or in law, subject to the proviso in Article 138 of the Constitution that no judgment shall be revised for an error that has not prejudiced substantial rights or occasioned a failure of justice.
sentencing_principles_applied: Consideration of mitigatory circumstances under Section 297 of the Penal Code.

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 296 and 316 of the Penal Code
location_of_offence: House at the scene of the incident (location not further specified)
brief_facts_summary: The Appellant was accused of murdering Nigamuni Lalitha Mendis and causing grievous hurt to Thommadura Nadun Buddhika Mendis on or about 29 March 2003. PW1 witnessed the Appellant coming from the deceased's room brandishing a sword after hearing her cries. He later found the deceased with bleeding injuries. PW3, the injured son of the deceased, stated the Appellant woke him up, took him near a railway track, and attacked him with a sword. The Appellant absconded and was tried in absentia.
evidence_type_secondary: Medical evidence, Identification of murder weapon
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 296 and 316 of the Penal Code
hc_sentence_type: Death for Count 1 (Murder). Rigorous imprisonment 02 years and fine for Count 2 (Grievous Hurt). Additional default and compensation sentences.
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court Judge convicted the Appellant based on the evidence of PW1 and PW3, which was found to be credible and trustworthy. The judge accepted the direct and circumstantial evidence linking the Appellant to the murder and grievous hurt. The Appellant was sentenced to death for murder and imprisonment with a fine for grievous hurt.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The Appellant's Counsel argued the conviction was contrary to the evidence, that the trial judge wrongly concluded the evidence of PW1 and PW3 was credible despite material omissions and discrepancies, and that there was insufficient direct and circumstantial evidence to link the Appellant to the murder. It was also contended the prosecution failed to establish the case beyond reasonable doubt and that corroborative evidence was lacking.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The conviction is contrary to the weight of the evidence adduced in the case. | The Learned Trial judge has reached a wrong conclusion that the evidence of PW1 is credible when there are material omissions and discrepancies quite apparent upon his evidence. | The Learned Trial Judge has reached a wrong conclusion that the evidence of PW3 is credible when there are material omissions and discrepancies quite apartment upon his evidence. | The Learned Trial Judge has failed to appreciate that there that there are no strong direct and circumstantial evidence to link the accused-appellant to the charge of murder. | The Learned Trial Judge has disregarded the absence of corroborative evidence to establish both charges. | The Learned Trial Judge has wrongly come to a finding that the prosecution has establish their case beyond reasonable doubt. | The Learned Trial Judge has failed to properly and lawfully evaluate omissions and contradictions highlighted and marked on behalf of the accused-appellant.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the trial judge correctly analyzed and accepted the evidence of PW1 and PW3 as convincing and trustworthy. The Court noted that the omissions and contradictions were not material and did not go to the root of the case, especially considering the evidence was given about 13 years after the incident. Corroborative evidence existed from PW4 and the JMOs.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court held the evidence was totally inconsistent with the innocence of the accused and consistent with his guilt, establishing the case beyond reasonable doubt.
defence_version_summary: The Appellant absconded and was tried in absentia. He was represented by counsel. The defence challenged the credibility and sufficiency of the prosecution evidence, claiming omissions, discrepancies, and lack of corroboration.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found no merit in the appeal grounds. It held the trial judge correctly analyzed the evidence, including omissions and contradictions, and properly found them not to be material. The Court cited precedents (Kumara De Silva v AG, Attorney General v Sandanam Pitchi Mary Theresa, Podisingho v The King) to support its reasoning on witness credibility, handling of contradictions, and circumstantial evidence. The COA affirmed that the prosecution led strong corroborative evidence, including eyewitness identification of the weapon and corroboration from other witnesses and medical experts. The appeal was dismissed.
coa_sentence_type: Death sentence for Count 1 (Murder) and rigorous imprisonment of 02 years with a fine of Rs. 5000 for Count 2 (Grievous Hurt) affirmed. Default sentences and compensation order of Rs. 200,000 to PW3 also affirmed.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The Accused-Appellant was convicted by the High Court of Balapitiya for murder and grievous hurt, sentenced to death and imprisonment with a fine. He appealed, challenging the credibility of eyewitnesses (PW1 and PW3), sufficiency of evidence, and lack of corroboration. The Court of Appeal found the trial judge's analysis of evidence and handling of contradictions was correct, and sufficient corroborative evidence existed. Citing relevant precedents, the COA dismissed the appeal, affirming the conviction and sentence.
defence_counsel: Nagitha Wijesekera
cause_of_death_exact_text: Severe brain damage due to homicidal cut injuries over the head.
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court Judge analyzed the evidence of PW1 and PW3, found them credible, and concluded the prosecution proved its case beyond reasonable doubt. The COA agreed with this analysis and found no errors in the HC's reasoning or evaluation of evidence.
precedents_cited_list: Kumara De Silva and 2 others v. Attorney General [2010] 2 SLR 169 | The Attorney General v. Sandanam Pitchi Mary Theresa (2011) 2 Sri L.R. 292 | Podisingho v. The King 53 NLR 49
standard_of_review_applied: The Court reviewed whether the trial judge's conclusions on witness credibility and evidence sufficiency were correct, applying principles on circumstantial evidence and handling of contradictions.

judges: Menaka Wijesundera, J. | B. Sasi Mahendran, J.
offence_sections: the Poisons, Opium, and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance No. 13 of 1984, as amended
brief_facts_summary: The accused was arrested on 10th January 2014 after STF officers, acting on information, raided an area near Siriyansiri Hotel. A search found two parcels containing 2.44 grams of heroin in his trouser pocket. The accused was arrested, and the drugs were seized, weighed, and sealed.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: the Poisons, Opium, and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance No. 13 of 1984, as amended
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court found the accused guilty on both counts of possession and trafficking of heroin. The learned High Court Judge considered the evidence of the prosecution witnesses, including the government analyst, and convicted and sentenced the accused to life imprisonment.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appeal argued that the Trial Judge incorrectly applied probability tests, failed to consider contradictions and weaknesses in the prosecution case, and wrongly rejected the defence evidence. The defence also contended the accused should benefit from reduced punishment under a subsequent amending act.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The Learned Trial Judge had not correctly applied the test of probability and improbability in order to determine the creditworthiness of the Prosecution Witnesses | The Trial Judge had failed to consider the vital contradictions of the Prosecution Witnesses | The Learned Trial Judge had failed to consider the weaknesses of the Prosecutions’ case | The Learned Trial Judge had wrongly rejected the dock statement and the evidence of the Defence witness
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The court analyzed contradictions between PW1 and PW2 regarding details of the raid and arrest. It found these were minor, not vital, and did not undermine the prosecution's core case. The government analyst's evidence was accepted despite a minor weight discrepancy.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal considered whether contradictions created reasonable doubt. It held minor discrepancies in witnesses' accounts, given the lapse of time and their roles, did not assail the prosecution's probable version.
defence_version_summary: The accused pleaded not guilty and made a dock statement. He claimed he was at the location to receive money for a friend, was forcibly taken by unknown persons, and only met PW1 at the police station. He called one defence witness (a priest) whose evidence contained a time discrepancy. The court found the defence version vague, inconsistent, and not credible.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal thoroughly analyzed the grounds of appeal. It found the contradictions between PW1 and PW2 were minor and did not go to the root of the case, citing precedents on witness memory. It upheld the Trial Judge's evaluation of the dock statement and defence evidence as not creating reasonable doubt. The court also considered the appeal for a reduced sentence under a new law but was constrained by Section 7 of the Amending Act, which explicitly prohibited its retrospective application to offences committed before its enactment. The court found no merit in the appeal grounds and saw no reason to interfere with the High Court judgment.
coa_sentence_type: Life imprisonment affirmed
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused was convicted by the High Court of Colombo for possession and trafficking of 2.44 grams of heroin and sentenced to life imprisonment. He appealed on grounds including improper assessment of prosecution evidence, contradictions, and rejection of defence evidence. The Court of Appeal analyzed the witness contradictions, found them non-vital, and upheld the High Court's credibility findings. It also declined to apply a subsequent law reducing penalties, as the amending act expressly barred retrospective application. The appeal was dismissed, and the conviction and sentence were affirmed.
defence_counsel: Neranjan Jayasinghe with Harshana Ananda and Dulshan Katugampola
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court Judge considered the evidence of the trained STF officers and the government analyst, found the prosecution version probable despite minor discrepancies, and convicted the accused. The Court of Appeal found the High Court's reasoning and evaluation of evidence to be correct.
precedents_cited_list: Bharwada Bhoginbhai Hirjibhai v. State Of Gujarat 1983 AIRHC 753 | State of Uttar Pradesh v. M. K. Anthony 1984 (2) SCJ 236 | Nanediri Devage Wilman CA 122/2005 | Queen Vs. Kularatne (1968) 71 NLR 529 | Don Samantha Jude Anthony Jayamaha Vs. The Attorney General, C.A. 303/2006 | Weddikkarage Thusharika Priyadarshani v. AG CA/HCC/0080/2020 | James Silva v. The Republic of Sr Lanka [1980] 2 SLR 167 | Walakada Gamage Priyantha v. Attorney General CA/HCC/261/2014
standard_of_review_applied: The appellate court considered whether the Trial Judge's appreciation of evidence and findings were correct, giving due weight to the trial court's assessment of witness demeanor and credibility.
sentencing_principles_applied: The court considered the principle against ex post facto laws under Article 13(6) of the Constitution and the legislative intent in the amending act regarding retrospective application of reduced penalties.

judges: Menaka Wijesundera J. | B. Sasi Mahendran J.
offence_sections: theft under the Public Property act
brief_facts_summary: The appellant, a court clerk, was indicted for theft of a case record from the Attangalla Magistrates Court. The case record was last called on 24.10.2000, an open warrant was issued, and the record subsequently went missing. The record was later found on top of a cupboard in the office. Witness evidence suggested the appellant was seen tearing a page from a delivery book related to the date the record was sent, and the appellant later admitted to this. The appellant was arrested, and the police recovered the missing case record based on his statement.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: theft under the Public Property act
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the appellant for theft of the case record. The trial judge applied the presumption under section 114 of the Evidence Ordinance alongside the section 27 recovery of the record to conclude the appellant was guilty.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant argued the trial judge failed to consider the prosecution evidence, failed to consider the appellant's dock statement, and did not give reasons for her findings.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Learned trial judge had not considered the evidence led by the prosecution. | The trial judge had failed to consider the dock statement by the appellant. | Not given reasons for her findings.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed witness testimonies, including that of the day book clerk and others, noting contradictions but ultimately finding the prosecution evidence strong. The appellant's conduct, admission of tearing the delivery book page, and knowledge of the record's location were key.
probability_assessment_by_court: Court found the prosecution evidence, including appellant's conduct and admissions, proved the charge beyond reasonable doubt.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty, made a lengthy dock statement denying involvement, but admitted to tearing and rewriting a page in the delivery book. No defence witnesses were called, and the court found his denial not credible in light of the prosecution evidence.
legal_errors_description: The Court of Appeal found the trial judge wrongly applied the presumption under section 114 of the Evidence Ordinance along with section 27 recovery to prove theft.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal held that although the trial judge erred in her legal analysis regarding the application of presumptions, the prosecution had presented ample evidence, including the appellant's knowledge of the record's location, his actions of tearing the delivery book page, and his conduct after the record went missing. This evidence, which was not reasonably contradicted, was sufficient to uphold the conviction. The appellant's dock statement did not create reasonable doubt. Therefore, despite the flawed reasoning, the conviction was correct.
coa_sentence_type: Conviction and sentence affirmed, with sentence operative from the date of conviction.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The appellant, a court clerk, appealed his High Court conviction for theft of a case record. The High Court had convicted him based on witness evidence and applying legal presumptions. On appeal, grounds included failure to consider evidence and the dock statement. The Court of Appeal found the trial judge's legal analysis flawed but upheld the conviction based on strong circumstantial evidence, including the appellant's admission to tampering with records and knowledge of the stolen item's location. The appeal was dismissed.
defence_counsel: Dr. Jayatissa de Costa, PC with Chamila Ekanayaka and D.D.P Dasanayake
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court concluded guilt by applying a presumption under the Evidence Ordinance alongside the recovery of the record. The Court of Appeal found this specific legal application was wrong but agreed the underlying evidence was sufficient for conviction.
standard_of_review_applied: Review of evidence and legal analysis

judges: Menaka Wijesundera | B. Sasi Mahendran
brief_facts_summary: The Accused-Appellant was indicted for possession and trafficking of 1.33 grams of heroin in two separate charges. He was found guilty and sentenced by the High Court of Colombo (Negombo). The appeal was against the sentence only.
hc_sentence_type: Rigorous Imprisonment 10 years and Fine for both charges, sentences to run consecutively
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court found the Accused-Appellant guilty of two charges of possession and trafficking of 1.33 grams of heroin. He was sentenced to a fine of Rs. 250,000 for each charge (default 2 years imprisonment) and 10 years rigorous imprisonment for each charge, with the sentences to run consecutively.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appeal was filed only against the sentence, not the conviction. Counsel for the Accused-Appellant argued in mitigation for a reduction of the sentence. The Respondent did not object to this application.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Not contesting conviction | Appeal against sentence only
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The judgment does not detail evidence analysis. The appeal was solely on sentencing grounds.
defence_version_summary: The appeal did not contest the conviction, indicating acceptance of guilt. No alibi or specific defence version is discussed. The hearing focused solely on sentence mitigation.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal considered the mitigation submissions regarding the sentence. It found basis to reduce the rigorous imprisonment term from ten years to seven years, ordering the sentences to run concurrently instead of consecutively. The fines and default terms remained unchanged.
coa_sentence_type: Fine of Rs. 250,000 per charge (default 2 years imprisonment), and 7 years rigorous imprisonment per charge, sentences to run concurrently from 06.08.2021.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The Accused-Appellant was convicted by the High Court of Negombo on two charges of possession and trafficking of 1.33 grams of heroin, receiving a total fine of Rs. 500,000 and consecutive 10-year rigorous imprisonment sentences. He appealed against the sentence only. The Court of Appeal reduced the rigorous imprisonment to 7 years per charge and ordered them to run concurrently, while keeping the fines intact. The appeal was otherwise dismissed.
defence_counsel: Sanjith Senanayake with Upul Dissanayake
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court imposed consecutive 10-year rigorous imprisonment sentences and fines. The Court of Appeal found the consecutive sentences excessive in the circumstances and modified them to run concurrently, reducing the imprisonment term to 7 years.
standard_of_review_applied: Sentence mitigation review
sentencing_principles_applied: Principles of proportionality and mitigation considered for drug offences.

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 365B (2)(b) of the Penal Code, as amended by Amendment Act No. 22 of 1995, 29 of 1998 and 16 of 2006.
brief_facts_summary: The accused-appellant was convicted for committing grave sexual abuse on a 9-year-old female victim by inserting his penis into her anus on or about 23-03-2017 at her home in Galenbindunuwewa. The victim was alone at home when the appellant, known to her as 'Akku mama', arrived, forced himself on her, and threatened her. The victim initially did not disclose the incident due to fear, but her strange behavior led her mother and aunt to question her, after which she revealed the abuse. Medical evidence confirmed injuries consistent with the abuse. The appellant denied being the perpetrator, claiming mistaken identity.
evidence_type_secondary: Medical evidence (Judicial Medical Officer's report and testimony)
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 365B (2)(b) of the Penal Code, as amended by Amendment Act No. 22 of 1995, 29 of 1998 and 16 of 2006.
hc_sentence_type: Rigorous Imprisonment 8 years and fine Rs. 25,000
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court Judge found the appellant guilty of grave sexual abuse based on the victim's evidence, corroborated by her mother and aunt, and supported by medical findings. The appellant was sentenced to 8 years rigorous imprisonment, a fine of Rs. 25,000, and ordered to pay Rs. 100,000 as compensation to the victim.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant challenged his conviction and sentence on five grounds: (1) wrongful admission of the Judicial Medical Officer's internal notes under section 32(2) of the Evidence Ordinance; (2) failure to evaluate discrepancies between prosecution witnesses; (3) misdirection on identification of the accused; (4) failure to consider improbabilities in evidence; (5) failure to consider admissions by the appellant in sentencing.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The learned High Court Judge has wrongly admitted internal notes made by the Judicial Medical Officer (PW-07) in terms of section 32 (2) of the Evidence Ordinance. | The learned High Court Judge has misdirected himself by failing to evaluate the clear discrepancies between the evidence of PW-01, 03, 04 and 07. | The learned High Court Judge was misdirected as to the identification of the accused. | Improbabilities of the evidence were not considered. | The learned High Court Judge has failed to consider and give due credit to the admissions by the appellant in his sentencing order.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed the evidence holistically, finding the victim's testimony credible and consistent with medical findings. Minor contradictions in witness statements were considered natural and not material. The victim's identification of the appellant as 'Akku mama' was corroborated by her mother and aunt, and her fearful reaction upon seeing the appellant further supported identification.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal assessed the totality of evidence and found no reasonable doubt about the appellant's guilt. Minor discrepancies were deemed not to affect the core credibility of the prosecution case.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty and gave evidence under oath. His defence was one of mistaken identity, claiming he was not the 'Akku' who committed the offence and that there were other persons in the village with that nickname. He also claimed the victim was unknown to him. The court found his defence unconvincing and not credible.
legal_errors_description: The Court of Appeal found a misdirection by the High Court Judge in admitting the Judicial Medical Officer's internal notes (P-02-e) under section 32(2) of the Evidence Ordinance, as the JMO himself testified in court, making such admission unnecessary. However, the COA held this error did not prejudice the appellant's substantial rights or cause a failure of justice.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal comprehensively reviewed the evidence and appeal grounds. It rejected each ground: (1) The admission of JMO notes under s.32(2) was a technical misdirection but not prejudicial; (2) Discrepancies between witnesses were minor and did not undermine the core prosecution case; (3) The victim's identification of the appellant was clear, consistent, and corroborated; (4) Time discrepancies were natural for witnesses recalling traumatic events; (5) Sentencing was lawful and considered mitigating factors. The COA emphasized evaluating evidence in totality, not in isolation, and referenced the principle from Jayasena Vs. Queen. It also cited Bhoginbhai Hitijibhai Vs State of Gujarat regarding witness memory limitations. The conviction was found safe, and the sentence, though lenient given the mandatory minimum, was upheld.
coa_sentence_type: Rigorous Imprisonment 8 years, fine of Rs. 25,000, and compensation of Rs. 100,000 to victim (upheld from High Court sentence). Sentence deemed effective from 10th December 2021.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused-appellant appealed his conviction and sentence for grave sexual abuse of a minor under section 365B(2)(b) of the Penal Code. The High Court of Anuradhapura had sentenced him to 8 years rigorous imprisonment, a fine, and compensation. The Court of Appeal, after analyzing five grounds of appeal including alleged misdirection on evidence admission, witness discrepancies, identification issues, improbabilities, and sentencing, dismissed the appeal. The COA found the victim's testimony credible and corroborated, minor contradictions immaterial, and no legal error causing prejudice. The sentence was upheld and deemed effective from the original sentencing date.
defence_counsel: Ruwan S. Jayawardena
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court Judge convicted the appellant based on the victim's credible testimony, corroborative witness evidence, and medical findings. The COA found a technical misdirection in admitting the JMO's notes under s.32(2) of the Evidence Ordinance but concluded it did not prejudice the appellant or affect the soundness of the conviction.
precedents_cited_list: Jayasena Vs. Queen 72 NLR 313 | Bhoginbhai Hitijibhai Vs State of Gujarat (AIR 1983-SC 753 at pp 756-758)
standard_of_review_applied: The Court of Appeal reviewed whether the High Court judgment was sustainable based on the evidence and whether any legal errors caused prejudice or a failure of justice, as per the proviso to Article 130 of the Constitution.
sentencing_principles_applied: The Court noted the minimum mandatory sentence for the offence was rigorous imprisonment of not less than 7 years and not exceeding 20 years, plus fine and compensation. The High Court Judge was found to have considered all mitigatory factors in imposing an 8-year sentence.

judges: Menaka Wijesundera J. | B. Sasi Mahendran J.
offence_sections: Section 363 of the Penal Code, as amended by Penal Code (Amendment) Act No.22 of 1995 (sexual intercourse with a woman under sixteen years of age is rape irrespective of the consent of the women). Also referenced Section 364 (2) (e) of the Penal Code.
brief_facts_summary: The appellant was indicted for committing rape on an underage girl. He pleaded not guilty. The trial judge convicted him on both charges. The appellant's counsel argued that the appellant had been indicted for the same offence more than once. The respondent's counsel submitted the offences occurred repetitively and noted the appellant's age was twice that of the victim, despite the appellant's claim of a love affair.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 363 of the Penal Code, as amended by Penal Code (Amendment) Act No.22 of 1995 (sexual intercourse with a woman under sixteen years of age is rape irrespective of the consent of the women). Also referenced Section 364 (2) (e) of the Penal Code.
hc_sentence_type: 10 years' rigorous imprisonment, with a fine of Rs 3000 in default 01 month simple imprisonment.
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the appellant for both charges of rape on an underage girl. The trial judge imposed a sentence of 10 years' rigorous imprisonment and a fine, which was the minimum mandatory sentence prescribed by law at the time.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appeal primarily canvassed the sentence imposed by the trial judge. The appellant's counsel submitted that the appellant had been indicted for the same offence more than once. The appellant also claimed there was a love affair between him and the victim.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Sentence imposed by the trial judge is challenged. | Appellant had been indicted for the same offence more than once. | Claim of a love affair between appellant and victim.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty. The defence claimed there was a love affair between the appellant and the victim. The court noted the appellant's age was twice that of the victim.
legal_errors_description: The High Court considered itself bound by the mandatory minimum sentence, which the Court of Appeal determined was in conflict with the Constitution and that judicial discretion in sentencing was not inhibited.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal considered the legal principle established in Maramba Liyanage Rohana alias Loku vs AG (SC Appeal No 89A-2009). It noted that the Supreme Court had determined that the minimum mandatory sentence in Section 364 (2)(e) was in conflict with Articles 4(c), 11 and 12(1) of the Constitution and that the High Court retained judicial discretion to impose an appropriate sentence. Applying this principle, the COA found the trial judge had imposed the minimum sentence without exercising full discretion. The COA varied the sentence considering the circumstances.
coa_sentence_type: 7 years Rigorous Imprisonment, with a fine of Rs 3000 in default 01 month simple imprisonment (rest of the sentence remains the same, operative from the date of conviction).
brief_judgment_file_summary: The appellant appealed his conviction and sentence for rape of an underage girl from the High Court of Vavuniya. The High Court had sentenced him to 10 years' rigorous imprisonment and a fine. The appeal primarily challenged the sentence. The Court of Appeal, citing precedent (Maramba Liyanage Rohana alias Loku vs AG), held that mandatory minimum sentences for this offence conflict with the Constitution and judges retain sentencing discretion. The COA varied the sentence to 7 years' rigorous imprisonment, upholding the fine and default sentence, and dismissed the appeal subject to this variation.
defence_counsel: Samantha Premachandra – Assigned Counsel
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court imposed the mandatory minimum sentence of 10 years' rigorous imprisonment. The Court of Appeal identified an error in the HC's approach, as it failed to exercise judicial discretion in sentencing, being under the mistaken impression it was bound by the mandatory minimum, which precedent had declared unconstitutional.
precedents_cited_list: Maramba Liyanage Rohana alias Loku vs AG SC Appeal No 89A-2009 decided on 12.5.2011 | SC Reference 3/2008, H.C. Anuradhapura Case No.333/2004, SCM 15.10.2008 | SC Appeal 890-2009 decided on 12.5.2011 | SC Appeal 17-20013 decided on 12.3.20015
standard_of_review_applied: Review of sentencing discretion and application of legal principles regarding mandatory minimum sentences.
sentencing_principles_applied: Judicial discretion in sentencing, unconstitutionality of mandatory minimum sentences that conflict with Articles 4(c), 11 and 12(1) of the Constitution.

judges: Menaka Wijesundera J. | B. Sasi Mahendran J.
offence_sections: Penal Code (Murder)
brief_facts_summary: The accused appellant was the brother of the deceased's wife. The deceased had a habit of harassing his wife when drunk. On the day of the incident, the deceased came drunk and started his usual fight with his wife. The appellant intervened, which led to an altercation and the death of the deceased.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Penal Code (Murder)
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court of Chilaw convicted the accused of murder and imposed the death sentence after a trial where the accused pleaded not guilty. The conviction and sentence were based on the evidence presented.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appeal was lodged to set aside the High Court's conviction and death sentence. At argument, both parties agreed to request the Court of Appeal to consider convicting the appellant of culpable homicide not amounting to murder based on a sudden fight, rather than murder.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court considered submissions from both parties regarding the deceased's injuries and the nature of the fatal injury. The Court noted the deceased's habitual drunken quarrels and beatings of his wife, and the appellant's intervention leading to an unexpected altercation.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court accepted the defence that the incident arose from a sudden fight during the appellant's intervention in a domestic dispute, which he did not expect.
defence_version_summary: The accused pleaded not guilty at trial. The defence argued that the appellant intervened to protect his sister from the deceased's drunken harassment, which escalated into a sudden fight. The Court accepted this version as credible for reducing the charge.
legal_errors_description: The High Court erred in convicting for murder instead of culpable homicide not amounting to murder, given the circumstances of a sudden fight arising from intervention in a domestic dispute.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal considered the agreed position of both parties to reduce the charge based on a sudden fight. It examined the facts: the deceased's habitual drunken abuse of his wife, the appellant's intervention as her brother, and the ensuing unexpected altercation. The Court found the circumstances fitted culpable homicide not amounting to murder under a sudden fight exception, rather than murder. It set aside the murder conviction and imposed a sentence of rigorous imprisonment and a fine.
coa_sentence_type: Seven years rigorous imprisonment and a fine of Rupees 25000, in default 6 months imprisonment
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused appealed his murder conviction and death sentence from the High Court of Chilaw. Both parties agreed the Court of Appeal should consider convicting for culpable homicide not amounting to murder based on a sudden fight. The Court found the deceased habitually harassed his wife when drunk, the appellant intervened as her brother, and a sudden fight ensued. The murder conviction was set aside, and the appellant was convicted of culpable homicide, sentenced to 7 years rigorous imprisonment and a fine. The appeal was otherwise dismissed.
defence_counsel: Saliya Peiris PC with Chamara Wannisekara and Savithri Fernando
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted for murder and imposed the death sentence. The Court of Appeal found the High Court erred in not considering the mitigating circumstance of a sudden fight arising from the appellant's intervention in a domestic dispute, warranting a lesser charge.
final_charge_after_appeal: Culpable homicide not amounting to murder

judges: Menaka Wijesundera, J. | B. Sasi Mahendran, J.
offence_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code read with Section 32 of the Penal Code
location_of_offence: Road near residence of the deceased in the vicinity of Kelaniya
brief_facts_summary: The Accused was at a pub/restaurant on 5th January 2013. He left agitatedly after a call. Around 7:30 pm, two persons on a motorcycle shot and killed the deceased near his residence. The Accused made confessionary statements to PW2 and PW7 afterwards. He then absconded, was assisted with foreign currency and a ticket to Singapore, and was arrested at the airport on 8th January 2013.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code read with Section 32 of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the Accused for murder under Section 296 of the Penal Code read with Section 32 and sentenced him to death. The 2nd Accused was convicted for conspiracy and sentenced to five years rigorous imprisonment and a fine.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The Accused contended the Trial Judge erred in law by failing to appreciate the facts correctly and by wrongfully relying on the uncorroborated evidence of accomplices (PW1 and PW2).
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Error in law by failing to appreciate facts correctly. | Wrongful reliance on uncorroborated evidence of accomplices (PW1 and PW2).
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed the evidence of PW1, PW2 (alleged accomplices), PW7 (independent witness), and the Judicial Medical Officer (PW22). It concluded PW1 and PW2 were not accomplices, thus no corroboration was needed. Their evidence and the confessionary statements to PW2 and PW7 were deemed credible and consistent.
probability_assessment_by_court: The court held that the confessions, subsequent conduct, and lack of explanation from the accused, when fitted together like puzzle pieces, proved the case beyond reasonable doubt.
defence_version_summary: The Accused gave a dock statement, claiming he was framed and denying personal enmity with the deceased. He did not call witnesses to directly challenge the incriminating evidence against him. The court found the defence witnesses unsuccessful in creating reasonable doubt.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal conducted a thorough analysis of the legal principles regarding accomplice evidence and confessions. It held that PW1 and PW2 were not accomplices as they only assisted after the crime, thus their evidence did not require corroboration. The confessions made to PW2 and PW7 were found to be voluntary and reliable. The Accused's subsequent conduct (absconding with intent to evade arrest) and his failure to challenge incriminating evidence in cross-examination or his dock statement further strengthened the prosecution's case. The court found no legal error in the High Court's judgment and concluded the conviction was safe.
coa_sentence_type: Death
brief_judgment_file_summary: The Accused-Appellant was convicted of murder by the High Court of Gampaha and sentenced to death. He appealed, challenging the conviction on grounds including erroneous reliance on uncorroborated accomplice evidence. The Court of Appeal analyzed the evidence, particularly regarding the status of PW1 and PW2 as accomplices and the confessionary statements. It found PW1 and PW2 were not accomplices, the confessions were valid, and the Accused's subsequent conduct and failure to challenge evidence were telling. The appeal was dismissed, and the conviction and death sentence were upheld.
defence_counsel: Shyamalie Athauda
cause_of_death_exact_text: Three wounds observed to be caused by gunshots.
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court correctly analyzed the evidence, including the confessionary statements and the subsequent conduct of the Accused. The Court of Appeal found no error in the High Court's reasoning or its conclusion that the prosecution proved its case beyond reasonable doubt.

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 354 and 365B (2) (b) (Three Counts) of the Penal Code
offence_category: Kidnapping from lawful guardianship and Grave Sexual Abuse
brief_facts_summary: The victim, a 12-year-old schoolboy, was allegedly sexually abused by the Appellant, a neighbor, in a hut on the seashore between April 2003 and February 2004. The victim's brother saw the victim leaving the hut and informed their mother, leading to a police complaint. The victim stated the abuse occurred over a longer period.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 365B (2)(b) of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the Appellant only for the 4th count under Section 365B(2)(b) (Grave Sexual Abuse). He was sentenced to 7 years rigorous imprisonment and fined Rs. 15,000 with a default sentence of 2 months simple imprisonment. No compensation was ordered.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The Appellant appealed against conviction and sentence. His counsel argued the trial judge failed to consider the probability and improbability of the victim's (PW1) testimony. A preliminary issue was raised that the Appellant was a child (under 18) at the time of the offence, and the court should consider applying principles from Supreme Court determination No. 03/2008 to reconsider the mandatory sentence.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The Learned Trial Judge has failed to consider the test of probability and improbability of the testimony of PW1 in convicting the Appellant. | The Appellant was under 18 years old at the time of committing the offence.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The prosecution led all necessary witnesses. The victim's testimony was central. Medical evidence was presented but contained an anomaly as the doctor remarked the victim's hymen was intact, though the victim is male.
probability_assessment_by_court: Court noted the Appellant's plea regarding age and uniqueness of case involving children, but did not re-evaluate probability of PW1's testimony in detail.
defence_version_summary: The Appellant pleaded not guilty. He made a dock statement when the defence was called. His counsel highlighted he was 16 years old at the time of the offence.
legal_errors_description: The Court of Appeal identified that imposing the mandatory minimum sentence without considering the Appellant's status as a child at the time of the offence was an error, referencing Supreme Court determination No. 03/2008 on judicial discretion and the best interests of the child.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal focused on the sentencing aspect. It acknowledged the seriousness of the offence but emphasized the Appellant was a child (16) at the time, and the victim was also a child. The Court invoked the principle that the court is the upper guardian of a child (CRC Article 3(1), Dharma Sri Tissa Kumara Wijenaike v. AG). It held that imposing a mandatory minimum sentence without considering the child's best interests and unique circumstances (both parties being children) was inappropriate. It relied on SC Reference No. 3/2008 which held mandatory minimum sentences can conflict with constitutional rights and judicial discretion should be exercised.
coa_sentence_type: Rigorous Imprisonment 2 years (operative from 05/04/2022) and fine of Rs. 15,000 (default sentence 2 months simple imprisonment remains).
brief_judgment_file_summary: The Appellant was convicted by the Mannar High Court for Grave Sexual Abuse under Section 365B(2)(b) and sentenced to 7 years RI and a fine. He appealed, challenging the conviction and sentence, emphasizing he was 16 at the time. The Court of Appeal partly allowed the appeal. It upheld the conviction but set aside the 7-year sentence, substituting a 2-year RI term. The Court reasoned that as both parties were children at the time, and considering the Appellant's current family circumstances and the principle of the court as the upper guardian of a child, the mandatory minimum sentence should not be applied rigidly.
defence_counsel: Ershan Ariaratnam
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted the Appellant based on the evidence and imposed the statutory mandatory minimum sentence of 7 years. The Court of Appeal found the HC erred by not exercising its judicial discretion to consider a lower sentence given the Appellant was a child offender, in light of relevant Supreme Court jurisprudence.
precedents_cited_list: Supreme Court determination No. 03 of 2008 decided on 15.08.2008 | Dharma Sri Tissa Kumara Wijenaike v. Attorney General SC Appeal 179/2012 decided on 18/11/2013 | Jusabbhai Ayubbhai v. State of Gujarat CR.MA/623/2012
standard_of_review_applied: Review of sentencing discretion and application of legal principles regarding mandatory minimum sentences and the rights of child offenders.
sentencing_principles_applied: Principles from SC Ref. No.3/2008 on judicial discretion over mandatory minimum sentences; Convention on the Rights of the Child (best interests of the child); Court as upper guardian of a child; Reformation and rehabilitation over punishment for young offenders.

judges: Menaka Wijesundera, J. | B. Sasi Mahendran, J.
offence_sections: the Poisons, Opium, and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance No. 13 of 1984, as amended
location_of_offence: Satthmma Watta, Dematagoda area, Masjeed Place
brief_facts_summary: On 15 November 2013, a police patrol from the CCD in civilian attire was conducting routine duty in Satthmma Watta, an area known for drug activity. They observed a woman (the accused) walking towards them, who then turned away upon seeing them, arousing suspicion. She was searched, and a pink cellophane bag containing a brown powder (suspected heroin) was found in her right pocket. She was arrested, and the substance was weighed at 5.80 grams, sealed, and sent for analysis.
evidence_type_primary: Physical evidence (recovery of heroin), Police testimony
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: the Poisons, Opium, and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance No. 13 of 1984, as amended
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court Judge found the accused guilty on both counts (possession and trafficking of 5.80g of heroin) and sentenced her to life imprisonment. The judge accepted the prosecution's version of events and evidence.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appeal was based on the prosecution evidence failing tests of probability and credibility, failure to prove the chain of custody of the drug production, and the dock statement being unreasonably rejected.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The evidence of the prosecution fails the test of probability. | The evidence of the prosecution fails the test of credibility. | The prosecution has failed to prove the chain of custody of production. | The dock statement of the Accused has been rejected on unreasonable grounds.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The prosecution led evidence of 6 witnesses, including the OIC (PW1), other police officers involved in the raid and search (PW2-PW7), and the reserve officer who received the production (PW8). The Court of Appeal found the testimonies credible and consistent, and minor contradictions did not go to the root of the matter.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal found the prosecution's version of the raid, the accused's suspicious conduct, and the recovery of drugs to be probable and credible, given the area's reputation and the officers' experience.
defence_version_summary: The accused pleaded not guilty and gave a dock statement. She claimed she was arrested on a different date (15 June 2013) while buying buns, not on 15 November 2013 as per the prosecution. She denied any involvement with drugs and stated she was taken with her infant child. The court found her version did not create reasonable doubt.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed each ground of appeal. It found the prosecution's narrative of a routine patrol and the accused's evasive action probable. It held that minor contradictions between PW1 and PW7 regarding the direction the accused turned were not material. The chain of custody was established through signatures of PW1 and PW8, and a discrepancy in the reserve officer's name/number did not create reasonable doubt. The accused's dock statement, which referred to the wrong date and lacked corroboration, was rightly rejected as it failed to create reasonable doubt. The court affirmed the High Court's reasoning and conviction.
coa_sentence_type: Life imprisonment (affirmed)
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused-appellant was convicted by the Colombo High Court for possession and trafficking of 5.80g of heroin and sentenced to life imprisonment. She appealed on grounds including improbability, credibility issues, chain of custody, and rejection of her dock statement. The Court of Appeal, after analyzing the evidence, found the police testimony credible, the chain of custody established, and the dock statement insufficient to create reasonable doubt. The appeal was dismissed, and the conviction and sentence were affirmed.
prosecution_counsel: Dishan Warnakula, DGS for the State
defence_counsel: Neranjan Jayasinghe with Harshana Ananda and Dulshan Katugampola
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court Judge accepted the prosecution evidence, found the accused guilty on both counts, and sentenced her to life imprisonment. The Court of Appeal found no error in the High Court's analysis or its assessment of the dock statement.
precedents_cited_list: Siddick v. The Republic of Sri Lanka [2005] 1 SLR 383 | State of Uttar Pradesh v. M. K. Anthony 1984 (2) SCJ 236 | Nanadiri Devage Wilman CA 122/2005 | Perera v. AG [1998] 1 SLR 378 | Queen Vs. Kularatne (1968) 71 NLR 529 | Don Samantha Jude Anthony Jayamaha Vs. The Attorney General, C.A. 303/2006 | Weddikkarage Thusharika Priyadarshani v. AG CA/HCC/0080/2020
standard_of_review_applied: The court assessed whether the trial judge's conclusions were reasonable and whether the evidence supported the conviction, giving due weight to the trial court's appreciation of evidence.

judges: Menaka Wijesundera J. | B. Sasi Mahendran J.
offence_sections: offence of statutory rape under the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The appellant was indicted and found guilty of statutory rape. The High Court convicted and sentenced him. The appellant appealed only against the sentence. He had already served five years of his imprisonment by the time of the appeal.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: offence of statutory rape under the Penal Code
hc_sentence_type: Rigorous Imprisonment 15 years, a fine of Rs 10000 in default 2 years rigorous imprisonment, compensation of Rs 100000 in default 3 years RI.
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court Judge found the appellant guilty of statutory rape. The appellant was sentenced to 15 years rigorous imprisonment, a fine, and compensation.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: Counsel for the appellant stated he was not contesting the conviction, but only the sentence.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Appeal against sentence only.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty at trial. He did not contest the conviction on appeal, only the sentence.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal considered the submissions and the fact that the appellant had already served 5 years of his 15-year sentence. It reduced the rigorous imprisonment term from 15 to 10 years, operative from the date of conviction. The default sentences were also reduced. The appeal was otherwise dismissed.
coa_sentence_type: Rigorous Imprisonment 10 years (from date of conviction). Fine of Rs 10000 in default 1 year rigorous imprisonment. Compensation of Rs 100000 in default 1 year rigorous imprisonment.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The appellant was convicted of statutory rape by the High Court of Kandy and sentenced to 15 years RI, a fine, and compensation. He appealed only against the sentence. The Court of Appeal reduced the main prison term to 10 years, reduced the default sentences, and ordered it be operative from the conviction date. The appeal was otherwise dismissed.
defence_counsel: Asela Seresinhe
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court found the appellant guilty and imposed the sentence. The Court of Appeal did not identify errors in the conviction but reduced the sentence based on time served.

judges: Menaka WijesunderaJ. | B. Sasi MahendranJ.
offence_sections: Section 365 and two charges of 345 of the Penal Code.
brief_facts_summary: The accused was indicted under section 365 and two charges of section 345 of the Penal Code. The trial concluded with a conviction on all three charges. The High Court sentenced the accused to terms of rigorous imprisonment with fines and default sentences. The appeal was filed challenging the sentence.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 365 and two charges of 345 of the Penal Code.
hc_sentence_type: 1) for the first charge 15 years rigorous imprisonment with a fine and default sentence, 2) for the second charge 5 years rigorous imprisonment with a fine and default sentence, 3) for the 3rd charge same as above
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the appellant on all three charges. Sentences were imposed for each charge, with the sentences for the second and third charges ordered to run concurrently.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: Counsel for the appellant indicated he was only canvassing the sentence. The appeal focused on the sentence imposed by the High Court.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Only canvassing the sentence
defence_version_summary: The appellant had pleaded not guilty.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal considered submissions from both parties regarding the sentence. It found that the sentence imposed by the trial judge should be varied by reducing the imprisonment for the first charge and ordering all sentences to run concurrently from the date of conviction.
coa_sentence_type: 1) for the first charge a rigorous imprisonment of 10 years ordered and the fine and the compensation to remain the same, the sentences with regard to the second and the third not varied but all three sentences to run concurrently and from the date of the conviction.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused appellant was convicted in the High Court of Panadura on three charges under sections 365 and 345 of the Penal Code and sentenced to rigorous imprisonment with fines. The appellant appealed only against the sentence. The Court of Appeal varied the sentence by reducing the imprisonment term for the first charge from 15 to 10 years and ordered all sentences to run concurrently from the date of conviction, while dismissing the appeal.
