judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Forest Ordinance (unspecified section)
brief_facts_summary: The driver of vehicle number 48-0440 was charged for transporting sawn timber without a valid permit in violation of the Forest Ordinance. The Magistrate convicted the driver and initiated confiscation of the vehicle. The registered owner appealed, claiming she gave the vehicle to the driver for legal purposes and was unaware of the illegal use.
evidence_type_primary: Confession (guilty plea by driver) and testimony of registered owner
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Forest Ordinance (unspecified section)
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court dismissed the revision application, agreeing with the Magistrate that the registered owner failed to prove on balance of probabilities that she took all precautions to prevent the offence.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant argued that the Magistrate and High Court erred in rejecting her evidence for not calling other witnesses and misdirected on the law regarding confiscation. She contended she proved she took precautions and was unaware of the illegal use.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The Magistrate erred in rejecting the owner's evidence for not calling other witnesses. | The High Court misdirected on the law regarding the statutory requirement for confiscation. | The owner proved on balance of probabilities that she took all precautions.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the registered owner's testimony credible and unchallenged on material points. She consistently stated she gave the vehicle for legal transport and was vigilant.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal assessed the evidence on balance of probabilities and found the owner proved she took precautions and was unaware of the offence.
defence_version_summary: The registered owner pleaded not guilty to the confiscation. She testified she gave the vehicle for legal purposes, was vigilant, and had no knowledge of the illegal use. The Court found her evidence credible.
legal_errors_description: The High Court misdirected on the law by stating the statutory requirement was to confiscate the vehicle without considering the amended provision allowing the owner to prove precautions.
procedural_defects_description: The Magistrate erred in requiring the owner to call other witnesses to substantiate her evidence, contrary to section 134 of the Evidence Ordinance.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal held the owner's evidence was credible and unchallenged. It interpreted the statutory provision pragmatically, considering the totality of circumstances. Referring to precedent, it found confiscation unjustified as the owner proved she took precautions and was unaware of the offence.
coa_sentence_type: Release of vehicle to registered owner
brief_judgment_file_summary: The registered owner appealed against the confiscation of her vehicle used by the driver to transport timber illegally. The Magistrate and High Court ordered confiscation, finding she failed to prove she took precautions. The Court of Appeal allowed the appeal, holding her evidence was credible and she proved on balance of probabilities that she took precautions and was unaware of the illegal use, setting aside the confiscation orders.
prosecution_counsel: Kanishka Rajakaruna, S.C. for the Respondent
defence_counsel: Buddhika Jayakody for the Appellant
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court dismissed the revision, agreeing with the Magistrate that the owner failed to prove precautions. The Court of Appeal found the High Court misdirected on the law and failed to properly consider the owner's credible evidence.
precedents_cited_list: Manawadu Vs. The Attorney General (1987) 2 SLR 30 | Sadi Banda Vs. Officer In Charge of Nortonbridge Police Station (2014) 1 SLR 33
standard_of_review_applied: Balance of probabilities
sentencing_principles_applied: Confiscation should not be ordered if the owner proves taking all precautions to prevent the offence.

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Sections 54(A)(b), 54(A)(d) and 54(A)(c) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance as amended by Act No. 13 of 1984
brief_facts_summary: On 29.10.2013, police at Katunayake Airport arrested the appellant based on information about drug trafficking. He excreted three wraps of suspected heroin in a toilet, weighing about 145 grams. The prosecution presented evidence including witnesses and a Government Analyst Report. The appellant denied the charges in a dock statement.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Sections 54(A)(d) and 54(A)(c) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance as amended by Act No. 13 of 1984
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court found the appellant guilty on counts of possession and importing heroin, acquitted on trafficking. He was sentenced to life imprisonment on both counts. The court relied on prosecution evidence including witnesses and the Government Analyst Report.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant argued that the trial judge failed to consider favorable facts, the last link of the inward journey was not proven, the prosecution version was not credible due to lack of JMO examination, and the investigation violated Article 11 of the Constitution.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: That the Learned Trial Judge erred in law by failing to consider the fact probably favourable to the Appellant. | Last link of the inward journey is not proven beyond reasonable ground. | The version of the prosecution is not credible as the Appellant was not produced before a JMO and also the reasons given by the prosecution is not tenable. | The way the investigation carried out by the police is in violation of Article 11 of the Constitution.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The court found the evidence of PW1 and PW4 clear, cogent, and unambiguous. The prosecution proved the case beyond reasonable doubt, and the chain of custody was adequately established.
probability_assessment_by_court: The court applied the test of probability and found the prosecution case passed it beyond reasonable doubt.
defence_version_summary: The appellant made a dock statement claiming he was falsely implicated by police. He did not call witnesses. The court found the prosecution evidence credible and rejected the defence.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed each ground of appeal. They found that the prosecution evidence, including witness testimony and chain of custody, was proven beyond reasonable doubt. The court dismissed the appeal, affirming the High Court's conviction and sentence.
coa_sentence_type: Life Imprisonment
brief_judgment_file_summary: The appellant was convicted for possession and importing heroin at Katunayake Airport and sentenced to life imprisonment. He appealed on grounds including chain of custody and procedural violations. The Court of Appeal found no merit in the appeals, upheld the conviction and sentence, and dismissed the appeal.
defence_counsel: Amila Palliyage with Sandeepani Wijesooriya
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court found the appellant guilty based on prosecution evidence. The Court of Appeal agreed with the High Court's analysis and reasoning.

standard_of_review_applied: Proof beyond reasonable doubt

judges: Menaka Wijesundera, J. | B. Sasi Mahendran, J.
brief_facts_summary: On 12th August 2009, the victim (PW1) was raped by the accused in her home. She reported the incident to her mother (PW2), and they lodged a police complaint. Key evidence includes the victim's testimony, medical evidence of injuries, and blood-stained clothes. The accused is a distant relative of the victim.
hc_sentence_type: Rigorous Imprisonment 12 years with compensation and fine
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the accused based on the victim's credible testimony and medical evidence, sentencing him to 12 years rigorous imprisonment with a fine of Rs.20,000 and compensation of Rs.250,000.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant argued that the victim's evidence was unworthy of credit, the judge failed to consider corroboration principles, the investigation was unfair, defence evidence was not properly assessed, burden of proof was misapplied, and the sentence was excessive.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The evidence of the prosecutrix is unworthy of credit | The Learned High Court Judge has failed to consider the legal principles relating to 'corroboration' as it would be relevant to allegations of 'rape' | A fair and comprehensive investigation has not been conducted by the Police, which has led to a grave prejudice being caused to the Appellant | The evidence given by the Appellant, his wife and sister have not been properly assessed and analysed by the Learned Trial Judge. | The learned Trial judge has failed to apply the proper principles relating to 'burden of proof' in convicting the Appellant. | Without prejudice to the above grounds of appeal, it is argued that the custodial sentence imposed on the Appellant is excessive and deserves to be reduced considering the facts and circumstances pertaining to this case.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the victim's testimony credible and consistent, supported by medical evidence and other witnesses, and rejected the defence arguments.
probability_assessment_by_court: Court assessed credibility and found no reasonable doubt, accepting the victim's testimony as truthful.
defence_version_summary: The accused pleaded not guilty, gave evidence, and called witnesses (wife and sister). The court found his evidence inconsistent and unreliable.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed the evidence, found the victim's testimony credible and consistent, applied precedents on corroboration in rape cases, rejected defence arguments on investigation and burden of proof, and upheld the conviction and sentence.
coa_sentence_type: 12 years rigorous imprisonment with compensation of Rs.250,000 and fine of Rs.20,000
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused was convicted of raping a distant relative and sentenced to 12 years imprisonment with fines and compensation. He appealed on grounds of evidence credibility, corroboration, investigation fairness, and excessive sentence. The Court of Appeal found the victim's testimony credible, supported by medical evidence, and dismissed the appeal, upholding the conviction and sentence.
defence_counsel: Asela Serasinhe
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court properly evaluated evidence, found the victim's testimony credible, and convicted the accused. The Court of Appeal agreed with this analysis.

standard_of_review_applied: Evidence evaluation and credibility assessment

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 296 read with section 32 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The deceased Kingsley Abegunawardena was attacked on 8th June 2007 at his home in Agalawaththa after an altercation with the 1st accused at a party. PW-01, the wife, witnessed the attack and identified the accused. The accused surrendered later, and key evidence included eyewitness testimony and medical evidence.
evidence_type_secondary: Medical evidence and Government Analyst Report
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 296 read with section 32 of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court found all three appellants guilty of murder based on eyewitness testimony and common intention, sentencing them to death. The court considered contradictions in evidence but found them not material to the root of the matter.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellants challenged conviction and sentence, arguing that PW-01 had limited time and light to observe the incident, contradictions in her evidence were not considered, and common intention was not established for the 2nd and 3rd accused.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Did the learned High Court Judge erred in not considering the limited time that PW-01 had to observe the incident. | Did the learned High Court Judge erred in not considering the light available for PW-01 to observe the incident said to have been seen by her. | Did the learned High Court Judge erred in not considering the state of mind of PW-01, especially as she states that she observed the incident upon being woken up from a deep sleep. | Did the learned High Court Judge erred in not considering in favour of the accused, the omissions and contradictions in the evidence of PW-01. | Did the learned High Court Judge erred in not considering that the evidence with regard to the 2nd and 3rd accused reveals a mere presence. | Did the learned High Court Judge err in considering the words uttered by the 2nd accused as being words indicating an animosity against the deceased.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: COA analyzed PW-01's evidence using Turnbull guidelines, found her credible for identifying the 1st accused but not for proving common intention for the 2nd and 3rd accused. Contradictions were considered minor and not material.
probability_assessment_by_court: COA assessed reasonable doubt, finding that mere presence of 2nd and 3rd accused did not prove common intention beyond reasonable doubt.
defence_version_summary: The accused pleaded not guilty, made dock statements denying involvement, called no witnesses, and offered no alibi. COA found the defence not credible for the 1st accused but raised reasonable doubt for the 2nd and 3rd accused regarding common intention.
legal_errors_description: HC misinterpreted evidence regarding common intention for the 2nd and 3rd accused and misdirected on the evidence, leading to erroneous conviction.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: COA applied Turnbull guidelines to evaluate identification evidence, found PW-01 credible for the 1st accused but not for establishing common intention for the 2nd and 3rd accused. Contradictions were minor, and common intention was not proven beyond reasonable doubt for the latter two. Precedents on common intention were considered, and appeal was partly allowed.
coa_sentence_type: Death sentence affirmed for 1st accused; 2nd and 3rd accused acquitted
brief_judgment_file_summary: Three accused appealed their conviction and death sentence for murder by the High Court of Kalutara. The High Court found them guilty based on eyewitness testimony and common intention. The Court of Appeal upheld the conviction for the 1st accused but acquitted the 2nd and 3rd accused due to insufficient evidence of common intention, partly allowing the appeal.
defence_counsel: Anuja Premaratne, P.C. with Ishan Madhawa and V. Ramayage
cause_of_death_exact_text: the injuries caused to the skull and the brain
hc_analysis_summary: HC convicted all three accused based on eyewitness testimony and found common intention. COA found that HC misdirected on evidence for the 2nd and 3rd accused, misinterpreted words uttered, and erred in concluding common intention.

standard_of_review_applied: Evaluated identification evidence using Turnbull guidelines and assessed common intention based on precedents including Mahabub Shah and The King Vs. Assappu

judges: Menaka Wijesundera, J. | B. Sasi Mahendran, J.
brief_facts_summary: The appellant was accused of conspiring with the 1st accused to kill her husband. She made a confession to the Magistrate. Circumstantial evidence included an illicit affair, unusual behavior after the incident, and medical evidence of strangulation.
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the appellant for conspiracy and aiding and abetting murder based on her confession and circumstantial evidence, and sentenced her to death.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The main ground of appeal is the involuntariness of the confession made to the Magistrate, arguing that the Magistrate was involved in investigations and the appellant was not in a proper mental state.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Involuntariness of confession due to Magistrate's involvement in investigations | Appellant not in proper frame of mind | Magistrate failed to produce appellant to psychiatrist
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed the confession recording process and found it voluntary. They also considered testimony from the appellant's children, friend, and driver, along with medical evidence, concluding that the circumstantial evidence was compelling.
probability_assessment_by_court: The court found no reasonable doubt and that the circumstantial evidence drew an irresistible inference of guilt.
defence_version_summary: The appellant made a dock statement claiming she was misled to make a confession, but called no witnesses. The court found her statement to be an afterthought and not credible.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The COA examined the voluntariness of the confession, citing precedents on confession recording. They found the Magistrate properly ensured voluntariness by explaining legal implications and giving time. The circumstantial evidence, including illicit affair, appellant's behavior, and medical evidence, was reviewed and found sufficient to establish guilt beyond reasonable doubt. The dock statement was rejected.
coa_sentence_type: Death
brief_judgment_file_summary: The appellant was convicted by the High Court for conspiracy and aiding and abetting murder and sentenced to death. She appealed, challenging the voluntariness of her confession. The Court of Appeal found the confession voluntary and the circumstantial evidence sufficient, dismissing the appeal and affirming the conviction and sentence.
defence_counsel: Palitha Fernando, P.C. with Neranjan Jayasinghe
cause_of_death_exact_text: manual strangulation by a short rope
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted based on the confession and circumstantial evidence. The Court of Appeal agreed with this analysis and found no errors in the High Court's judgment.
precedents_cited_list: Rangasamy Kanaganayagum alias Attorney General CA (PHC) APN 13/2019 decided on 16.11.2020 | The Queen vs Ghanaseeha Thero and others 73 NLR 154 | S Vivekananda and another vs S Selvaratnam 79 NLR 337
standard_of_review_applied: Review of voluntariness of confession and sufficiency of evidence

judges: Menaka Wijesundera, J | B. Sasi Mahendran, J
brief_facts_summary: The victim was at home on 26 October 2010 when the appellant entered and raped her, followed by another person. She identified the appellant who was known to her husband. The husband confronted the appellant, and a police complaint was lodged. Medical evidence showed no tell-tale marks, and the victim's testimony had omissions.
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court found the appellant guilty of gang rape based on the prosecution's evidence. No detailed reasoning is provided in the judgment text.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant appealed against conviction and sentence. The main ground is the improbability of the prosecution's story, including inconsistencies in the victim's testimony and the lack of injuries to the child. The counsel argued that the act could not have occurred as described without resistance.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Prosecution story is highly improbable | Inconsistencies in victim's testimony regarding the child | Failure to indict the second culprit creates doubt
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The victim's testimony had omissions regarding a knife threat. The husband corroborated her story, but the medical evidence showed no injuries. The court found the narration highly improbable and indicative of consent.
probability_assessment_by_court: Court found prosecution story highly improbable and granted benefit of doubt to appellant.
defence_version_summary: Appellant pleaded not guilty and made a dock statement denying the allegations. No witnesses were called for defence.
legal_errors_description: High Court convicted based on improbable evidence without considering reasonable doubt.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed the evidence and found the victim's narration highly improbable, noting inconsistencies in her testimony, the absence of injuries to the child, and the prosecution's failure to indict the second culprit. They referenced legal principles on burden of proof and reasonable doubt, concluding that the prosecution failed to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt, thus granting the benefit of doubt to the appellant.
coa_sentence_type: Conviction and sentence set aside
brief_judgment_file_summary: The appellant was convicted by the High Court of Hambantota for gang rape. He appealed on grounds of improbability of the prosecution story. The Court of Appeal found inconsistencies in the victim's testimony, lack of medical evidence, and only one accused indicted, leading to reasonable doubt. The appeal was allowed, conviction and sentence set aside, and the appellant acquitted.
defence_counsel: Neranjan Jayasinghe with Harshana Ananda and Lahiru Widushanka
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted the appellant based on the victim's testimony and corroboration. The Court of Appeal found this reasoning flawed as the evidence was highly improbable and created reasonable doubt.
precedents_cited_list: Mr. Justice Mackeena in the article 'discretion' in the Irish Jurist Vol 1X 1 at 10 | State of Utra Pradesh vs Anthony AIR 1985 SC 48 | Karunadasa vs OIC Motor Traffic Division Police Station Nittambuwa 1 SLR 155
standard_of_review_applied: Applied reasonableness and burden of proof standards, referencing precedents on improbability and doubt.

judges: Menaka Wijesundera, J. | B. Sasi Mahendran, J.
offence_sections: Under the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drug Ordinance Act No. 13 of 1984
brief_facts_summary: The Accused-Appellant was indicted for possession and trafficking of 23.96 grams of heroin. He pleaded not guilty and was convicted after trial, receiving life imprisonment. The appeal was based on the Trial Judge's failure to specify offences in the judgment as required by law.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Under the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drug Ordinance Act No. 13 of 1984
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the Appellant for possession and trafficking of heroin and sentenced him to life imprisonment. The judgment did not specify which offences he was convicted of, leading to the appeal.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appeal argued that the Trial Judge's judgment was not in accordance with Section 283(2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, as it did not specify which offences the Appellant was convicted and sentenced for. The Deputy Solicitor General conceded to this position.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Judgment not in accordance with Section 283(2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure as it does not specify which offences the Appellant was convicted and sentenced for.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The trial evidence is not detailed in the appeal judgment. The Court of Appeal did not evaluate evidence but remanded for retrial due to procedural error.
defence_version_summary: The Accused pleaded not guilty. No defence witnesses or alibi are mentioned in the appeal judgment. The court did not assess credibility due to procedural remand.
legal_errors_description: The Trial Judge failed to specify the offences in the judgment as required by Section 283(2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure.
procedural_defects_description: The judgment did not specify which offences the Appellant was convicted of, violating Section 283(2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found that the Trial Judge committed a serious misdirection by not specifying the offences in the judgment as required by law. This warranted a retrial. The Court allowed the appeal, set aside the conviction and sentence, and remanded the case to the High Court for retrial.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The Accused-Appellant was convicted by the High Court of Panadura for possession and trafficking of heroin and sentenced to life imprisonment. He appealed on the ground that the judgment did not specify the offences as required by law. The Court of Appeal found a serious misdirection, allowed the appeal, set aside the conviction and sentence, and ordered a retrial in the High Court.
defence_counsel: Neranjan Jayasinghe with Harshana Ananda
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted the Appellant without specifying the offences in the judgment. The Court of Appeal found this to be a serious misdirection warranting retrial.
standard_of_review_applied: Review of judgment for compliance with procedural law

judges: Menaka Wijesundera J. | B. Sasi Mahendran J.
offence_sections: Murder under common intention
brief_facts_summary: The deceased was last seen going to the appellant's house on April 14, 1999. His decomposed body was found in a urea bag on April 23, 1999, identified by his shirt and a distinctive toe. The appellant fled after the incident, was arrested on May 1, 1999, and based on his statement, two knives were recovered. The prosecution case relied on circumstantial evidence including a confession to relatives.
evidence_type_secondary: Medical evidence and recovery of weapons
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Murder under common intention
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court found the appellant guilty of murder based on circumstantial evidence, including that the deceased was last seen with the appellant, a confession to relatives, and recovery of weapons. The trial judge concluded that the circumstantial evidence drew an irresistible inference of guilt.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The main grounds of appeal were insufficient identification of the dead body, improper handling of an adverse witness, and failure to consider recoveries under section 27 of the Evidence Ordinance. The appellant argued that these issues undermined the conviction.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Identification of the dead body was not sufficient. | Adverse witness in the prosecution had not been properly dealt by the trial judge. | The recoveries made under section 27 of the Evidence Ordinance has not been considered by the trial judge.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found that contradictions in prosecution evidence did not go to the root of the case, identification of the body was sufficient based on shirt and toe feature, and the confession to relatives was credible. The dock statement did not create reasonable doubt.
probability_assessment_by_court: The court drew an irresistible inference from the circumstantial evidence and found that the prosecution had excluded other possibilities, establishing guilt beyond reasonable doubt.
defence_version_summary: The appellant made a dock statement denying the allegations, claiming police assault, and stating that the deceased visited him with two friends. He pleaded not guilty, called no witnesses, and the court found his statement not credible.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed the grounds of appeal, finding that the identification of the body was sufficient based on medical evidence and relative testimony, there was no proper order for an adverse witness, and recoveries under section 27 were considered. They upheld the High Court's reasoning that circumstantial evidence pointed irresistibly to the appellant, and the dock statement did not create doubt. The appeal was dismissed.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The appellant appealed against his High Court conviction for murder. The High Court found him guilty based on circumstantial evidence, including last sighting, confession, and weapon recovery. Appeal grounds challenged identification, adverse witness handling, and recoveries under section 27. The Court of Appeal found no merit in these grounds, upheld the evidence, and affirmed the conviction and sentence. The appeal was dismissed.
defence_counsel: Palitha Fernando P.C. with Sachithra Harshana
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court analyzed the circumstantial evidence and concluded that it drew an irresistible inference of the appellant's guilt. The Court of Appeal agreed with this analysis and found no errors.
precedents_cited_list: AG vs. Potta Naufer and Others (2007) 2 Sri L. R. 186 to 187 p. | Oliver Dayanand Adansonia alias Raju vs. Republic of Sri Lanka CA 28th of 2009 decided on 13.02.2013 | The King vs James Chandrasekera 44 NLR page 97 | B.A Premaratne vs The Democratic Socialist Republic of Sri Lanka court of appeal 168 of 2009 decided on 20th of February 2014 | The Queen vs Kularatne (1968) 71 NLR 529 | Kuruppaiah Serveys vs The King 1960 52 NLR 227
standard_of_review_applied: The court reviewed the evidence for sufficiency and credibility, applying principles for circumstantial evidence and burden of proof.

judges: P. Kirtisinghe J | R. Gurusinghe J
offence_sections: Section 54A and 54B of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance as amended by Act No. 41 of 2022
brief_facts_summary: The petitioner was arrested for possession of heroin found in paddy sacks at his house. The heroin originated from a gas cylinder found in the sea and passed through several suspects. The pure heroin quantity was 6.3236 kg. The petitioner claims no knowledge of the drugs.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The petitioner cited his age (67 years), health issues (cancer and Multiple Myeloma), and lack of knowledge about the heroin as exceptional circumstances for bail. The respondents objected due to the large quantity of heroin, recovery of proceeds, lack of exceptional circumstances, and risk of absconding.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Petitioner arrested since 3.11.2022 and claims no knowledge of drugs. | Petitioner is 67 years old with serious health conditions including jaw cancer and Multiple Myeloma. | Respondents object: possession of 25.9 kg heroin with pure quantity 6.3236 kg. | Recovery of Rs.6,634,000 from 11th suspect's residence. | No exceptional circumstances demonstrated. | High risk of absconding due to offence gravity.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The court considered medical reports indicating the petitioner's health conditions and police reports on the investigation. No direct witnesses to the petitioner's knowledge of the drugs were mentioned.
probability_assessment_by_court: The court found that the petitioner's age, health, and lack of evidence on knowledge constituted exceptional circumstances for bail.
defence_version_summary: The petitioner pleaded not guilty through counsel, claiming no knowledge of the heroin in the paddy sacks. He presented medical evidence of his health conditions but did not call witnesses. The court considered his clean record and health issues.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed the petitioner's circumstances, including his age (67), serious health issues (cancer and Multiple Myeloma), no previous convictions, and the ongoing investigation into his knowledge. Referring to the precedent Ramu Thamodarampillai v. The Attorney General, the court held that these factors constitute exceptional circumstances warranting bail.
coa_sentence_type: Bail granted with conditions: cash bail of Rs. 50,000, two sureties of Rs. 2,000,000 each, surrender of passport, travel ban, and monthly reporting to police.
brief_judgment_file_summary: This judgment concerns a bail application by Weerathunga Arachchige Piyasena, arrested for possession of 25.9 kg of heroin. The Court of Appeal considered his age (67), health conditions, and lack of evidence on knowledge. Citing exceptional circumstances, the court granted bail with specific conditions including cash bail and sureties.
defence_counsel: Eranga Sirisena
precedents_cited_list: Ramu Thamodarampillai v. The Attorney General [2004] 3 SLR 180
standard_of_review_applied: Exceptional circumstances standard for bail under Section 83(2) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance.

judges: P. Kirtisinghe J | R. Gurusinghe J
offence_sections: Sections 54A and 54B of the Poison, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance as amended
brief_facts_summary: The 1st suspect was arrested on 19.07.2021 while packing heroin in a house at Kotugoda, Ja-ela. She was in possession of 1.225 kilograms of heroin, and Rs. 868,900 was recovered, alleged to be proceeds. The pure quantity of heroin according to the Government Analyst is 809.6 grammes.
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court of Negombo rejected the bail application, but no detailed reasoning is provided in this judgment.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The petitioner argued exceptional circumstances including failure to mention precise arrest mode, contradictions in evidence, denial of right to expeditious trial, constitutional rights, suspect's health issues, and parents' inability to provide medicine.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The police have failed to mention the precise mode of arrest which cast a reasonable suspicion of the entire version. | The police version was contradicted by circumstantial evidence and video and audio recordings. | The suspect has been denied the right to be tried expeditiously without delay. | The provisions under the Poisons, Opium, and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance do not overthrow the provisions under the Constitution that guarantee fundamental rights and substance of fair trial. | The suspect is suffering from bone fractures due to an accident and getting sufficient treatment inside the prison is extremely difficult due to the unavailability of medicines. | The parents of the suspect are unable to provide medicine for the suspect inside the prison as they are both suffering from severe health conditions.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court considered the Government Analyst report indicating pure heroin quantity of 809.6 grammes, which is a commercial quantity, and the recovery of cash, leading to high risk of absconding.
probability_assessment_by_court: Court assessed high risk of absconding due to commercial quantity and potential death or life imprisonment sentence.
defence_version_summary: The suspect, through petitioner, argued for bail based on exceptional circumstances including health issues and procedural defects.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal held that the pure heroin quantity of 809.6 grammes is commercial, and under Section 83, bail can only be granted in exceptional circumstances. The petitioner's grounds, including health issues and delay, were not considered exceptional. Citing Ranil Charuka Kulatunga case, the Court emphasized the gravity of the offence and risk of absconding, thus refusing bail.
brief_judgment_file_summary: This is a bail application by the sister of the suspect arrested for possession of 1.225 kg of heroin. The High Court rejected bail. The petitioner appealed to the Court of Appeal citing exceptional circumstances like health issues and procedural defects. The Court of Appeal found no exceptional circumstances, emphasized the commercial quantity and risk of absconding, and refused bail.
defence_counsel: Tenny Fernando
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court rejected bail, and the Court of Appeal did not find any error in that decision, upholding it based on similar reasoning.
precedents_cited_list: Ranil Charuka Kulatunga vs. Attorney General CA(PHC) APN134/2015
standard_of_review_applied: Review of exceptional circumstances for bail under Section 83 of the Poison, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance.

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 296 of Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: On 13th April 2014 in Hallawa, the appellant stabbed the deceased in the neck with a knife. PW1, an eye witness, saw the incident. The appellant was arrested while hiding in backwoods, and the knife and blood-stained clothes were recovered from his house based on his statement. The prosecution led five witnesses, including the eye witness and a medical expert.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 296 of Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the appellant for murder under Section 296 of the Penal Code and sentenced him to death. The judge found the prosecution evidence credible and proved the case beyond reasonable doubt, rejecting the defence of sudden fight and provocation.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant challenged the credibility of the sole eye witness, claiming contradictions with medical evidence and failure to explain injuries on the accused. He also argued that the High Court judge misdirected herself on defence evidence and failed to adequately consider mitigatory pleas of sudden fight, provocation, and cumulative provocation.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The testimony of the sole eye witness fails the test of credibility on the following grounds: a) The evidence of the witness contradicts with the medical evidence. b) The witness had failed to explain the injuries on the accused. | The Learned High Court Judge had misdirected herself regarding the evidence of the defence and thereby had failed to evaluate the defence evidence properly. | The Learned High Court Judge had failed to address her mind adequately to the mitigatory pleas of sudden fight, provocation and cumulative provocation which had been taken up by the defence and which is supported by the evidence of the prosecution.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the eye witness testimony credible and consistent with medical evidence. The JMO's evidence corroborated the eye witness account. The defence evidence was properly considered but found insufficient to establish sudden fight or provocation.
probability_assessment_by_court: Court concluded that the prosecution proved guilt beyond reasonable doubt based on credible evidence.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty and claimed that he stabbed the deceased due to sudden fight and provocation. He gave evidence and called a witness, but the court found his defence not credible.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal thoroughly reviewed the evidence, including the eye witness testimony, medical evidence, and defence claims. They found no contradictions in the prosecution evidence, upheld the High Court's evaluation of defence evidence, and rejected the mitigatory pleas. The recovery of the knife under section 27(1) was deemed admissible. Consequently, the appeal was dismissed, confirming the conviction and death sentence.
coa_sentence_type: Death
brief_judgment_file_summary: The appellant was convicted for murder by the High Court of Kurunegala and sentenced to death. He appealed on grounds of witness credibility, misdirection on defence evidence, and failure to consider mitigatory pleas. The Court of Appeal found the eye witness testimony reliable, medical evidence consistent, and defence properly considered. The appeal was dismissed, upholding the conviction and death sentence.
defence_counsel: Palitha Fernando, PC
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted the appellant based on eye witness and medical evidence, finding no merit in the defence of sudden fight or provocation. The Court of Appeal agreed with this analysis and found no errors.

judges: Menaka Wijesundera, J. | B. Sasi Mahendran, J.
offence_sections: Section 54A(d) and 54A(b) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance, as amended by Act No. 13 of 1984
brief_facts_summary: On August 14, 2017, police received information about a suspicious individual near Dadigama temple. They arrested the accused and found 18 small bags of heroin in his trousers, weighing 15.97 grams. The accused denied the charges, claiming he was at the temple to see the Chief Monk.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 54A(d) and 54A(b) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance, as amended by Act No. 13 of 1984
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court found the accused guilty on both counts of possession and trafficking of heroin based on prosecution evidence including recovery of drugs and witness testimonies, and imposed the death sentence.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant argued that the High Court judge failed to consider the improbability of the prosecution case, did not properly evaluate the appellant's evidence, and placed an unwarranted burden on the defense. The appellant also contended that the judge erred in applying the test of probability.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The Learned High Court Judge has failed to consider the prosecution case is improbable. | The Learned High Court Judge has failed to consider the Appellant’s evidence. | The Learned High Court Judge has cast an unwarranted burden on the Defense case.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the prosecution witnesses PW1 and PW2 truthful and consistent, with corroborated testimonies. The accused's evidence was a flat denial and did not raise any doubt about the recovery of heroin.
probability_assessment_by_court: Court applied test of probability and found prosecution evidence probable and credible.
defence_version_summary: The accused pleaded not guilty and testified that he was at Dedigama Temple to see the Chief Monk, denying any involvement with heroin. The court found his version not credible and a flat denial.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal reviewed the evidence, finding prosecution witnesses reliable and their accounts corroborated. The accused's evidence was scrutinized and found lacking in credibility. Applying the test of probability from legal precedents, the court upheld the High Court's judgment, deeming the prosecution case probable and the conviction sound.
coa_sentence_type: Death sentence upheld
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused was convicted by the High Court of Kegalle for possession and trafficking of heroin and sentenced to death. He appealed on grounds including failure to consider improbability of prosecution case and his evidence. The Court of Appeal found the prosecution witnesses credible and the evidence solid, while the accused's denial was not convincing. Applying the test of probability, the court dismissed the appeal and upheld the conviction and death sentence.
defence_counsel: Ershan Ariaratnam
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court judge examined all material evidence, evaluated the accused's testimony, and found the prosecution case credible. The Court of Appeal concurred with this analysis and found no errors.
precedents_cited_list: Wickremasuriya v Dedoleena and Others (1996) 2 S.L.R. 95 | Chaminda Jeewan Ratnayake v. A.G, CA No. 185/2016
standard_of_review_applied: Review based on evidence evaluation and test of probability.

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Forest Ordinance as amended
brief_facts_summary: The appellant's son and two others were caught transporting 5 logs of Kumbuk timber without a permit in a vehicle owned by the appellant. The accused pleaded guilty before the Magistrate's Court. The vehicle was confiscated, and the appellant appealed, claiming he had no knowledge and had given instructions to his son not to use the vehicle illegally.
evidence_type_secondary: Testimony of owner and No prior convictions
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Forest Ordinance as amended
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court dismissed the revision application, affirming the Magistrate's order to confiscate the vehicle. It held that the appellant failed to establish exceptional circumstances and that the registered owner did not take all precautions to prevent the offence.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant contended that the Magistrate correctly found he had no knowledge but misdirected on precautions; the High Court erred in not interfering and made a mistake of facts regarding the offence.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Misdirection on law regarding precautions | Mistake of facts by High Court regarding offence as transporting sand instead of timber
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the appellant's testimony credible and unchallenged on material points. It applied balance of probability and considered the specific circumstances of the case.
probability_assessment_by_court: Court applied balance of probability and found appellant took due precautions.
defence_version_summary: Appellant pleaded not responsible for confiscation, claiming he had no knowledge of the offence, gave instructions to his son not to use vehicle illegally, and testified at inquiry. Court found his evidence credible.
legal_errors_description: Lower courts applied strict interpretation of 'all precautions' instead of considering individual facts and circumstances of the case.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed the facts, including that the appellant is a retired teacher, sickly, trusted his son, vehicle not meant for heavy timber, and he gave instructions. It cited precedents moving away from strict interpretation, held that confiscation was not justified, and allowed the appeal.
coa_sentence_type: Vehicle released to appellant
brief_judgment_file_summary: This appeal concerns confiscation of a vehicle used to transport illegal timber. The appellant, the registered owner, appealed against High Court order affirming Magistrate's confiscation. Grounds included misdirection on law and mistake of facts. Court of Appeal allowed the appeal, setting aside confiscation, finding appellant took due precautions and had no knowledge, and ordered vehicle release.
defence_counsel: Chamara Nanayakkarawasam
hc_analysis_summary: High Court affirmed Magistrate's confiscation, but Court of Appeal found High Court erred in not considering exceptional circumstances and individual facts, and made a mistake of facts regarding the offence.
precedents_cited_list: Mary Matilda Silva Vs. Inspector of Police Habarana (CA PHC 86/97 decided on 08-07-2010) | Sadi Banda Vs. Officer-in-Charge of Norten Bridge Police Station (2014) 1 SLR 33
standard_of_review_applied: Balance of probability
sentencing_principles_applied: Confiscation principles under Forest Ordinance, requiring proof of all precautions taken by owner, considering individual facts and circumstances.

judges: Menaka Wijesundera, J. | B. Sasi Mahendran, J.
brief_facts_summary: The accused was charged with two counts of grave sexual abuse against a victim who was around 10 years old at the time of the offence in January 2006. The trial concluded in 2018, resulting in conviction. The appeal is only on the sentence, with the accused repenting his actions.
hc_sentence_type: 12 years rigorous imprisonment with fine and compensation for each charge, to run concurrently
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the accused-appellant for both charges of grave sexual abuse and sentenced him to 12 years rigorous imprisonment with fine and compensation for each charge, with sentences to run concurrently.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The accused-appellant contested only the sentence, not the conviction. He argued that the incident took place 17 years ago and that he is repenting his actions. The respondent objected to varying the sentence.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Sentence excessive due to passage of time | Accused repenting his actions
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The appeal did not challenge the evidence or conviction, focusing solely on sentencing. The trial court's conviction was based on evidence presented, but details are not discussed in the appeal judgment.
defence_version_summary: The accused pleaded not guilty and was convicted after trial. During appeal, he did not contest the conviction but argued for sentence reduction due to passage of time and repentance.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal considered the passage of time since the offence in 2006 and the trial conclusion in 2018, noting that 17 years had elapsed. They referenced sentencing principles from a precedent, emphasizing the seriousness of the crime. However, considering the changes over time in the lives of the appellant and victim, they reduced the sentence from 12 to 8 years rigorous imprisonment for each charge, to run concurrently, while maintaining the fine and compensation.
coa_sentence_type: 8 years rigorous imprisonment for each charge, to run concurrently from date of conviction, with fine and compensation unchanged.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused-appellant was convicted by the High Court of Ratnapura for two charges of grave sexual abuse and sentenced to 12 years rigorous imprisonment with fine and compensation. He appealed only against the sentence, citing the 17-year delay since the offence and his repentance. The Court of Appeal reduced the sentence to 8 years rigorous imprisonment for each charge to run concurrently, while upholding the fine and compensation, and dismissed the appeal subject to this variation.
defence_counsel: Saliya Pieris, P.C with Thanuka Nandasiri
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted and sentenced the accused to 12 years rigorous imprisonment. The Court of Appeal found that considering the passage of time since the offence, the sentence should be reduced to 8 years.
precedents_cited_list: C. A. Revision No. CA[PHC]APN/141/2013 decided on 25/03/2015
standard_of_review_applied: Consideration of sentencing factors including passage of time and repentance.
sentencing_principles_applied: Seriousness of the crime and passage of time as factors in sentencing.

judges: Menaka Wijesundera, J. | B. Sasi Mahendran, J.
offence_sections: Section 296 read with Section 32 of the Penal Code.
brief_facts_summary: The accused was charged with murder of Thiyagarajah Thiripuradasan. On November 24, 2011, at about 4:30 a.m., the deceased was shot in his house. PW1 and PW2, his sister and mother, heard the shot and the deceased said 'Sasidaran shot me.' They saw the accused fleeing with others. The prosecution relied on dying declarations made to PW1, PW2, and PW5.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 296 read with Section 32 of the Penal Code.
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court acquitted the 2nd and 3rd accused but convicted the 1st accused of murder based on dying declarations and imposed the death sentence.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant challenged the conviction on grounds of dying declaration validity and identification of the deceased's body. The defense argued that the dying declaration had weaknesses and that there was no proper identification of the body.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: No proper identification of the dead body | Challenges to the reliability of the dying declaration
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal evaluated the dying declarations from PW1, PW2, and PW5, found them consistent and reliable. Medical evidence from PW4 confirmed the injuries and that the deceased was able to speak, supporting the dying declarations.
probability_assessment_by_court: The court assessed the dying declarations beyond reasonable doubt, considering consistency and corroboration.
defence_version_summary: The accused pleaded not guilty and testified from the witness box. No alibi was presented. The court found the prosecution witnesses credible and the defence version not convincing.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal thoroughly analyzed the dying declarations, applying legal precedents on admissibility and reliability. They found the declarations consistent across multiple witnesses, supported by medical evidence. The court rejected the defense objection on body identification, citing relevant case law. No material contradictions were found, and the evidence was held to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt, affirming the High Court's conviction and sentence.
coa_sentence_type: Death
brief_judgment_file_summary: This appeal concerns the murder conviction of Alagan Sasitharan. The High Court of Vavuniya convicted him based on dying declarations and imposed the death sentence. On appeal, the defense challenged the dying declaration's validity and body identification. The Court of Appeal found the dying declarations reliable and consistent, upheld the conviction, and dismissed the appeal.
defence_counsel: Dr. Ranjith Fernando
cause_of_death_exact_text: gunshot injuries on the right side of the chest causing death
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted the accused based on dying declarations and medical evidence. The Court of Appeal agreed with this reasoning and found no errors in the High Court's analysis.
precedents_cited_list: Ranasinghe v Attorney-General [2007], 1 S.L.R 218 | The King v Asirvadan Nadar [1950], 51 NLR, 322 | Justimpala v. standard_of_review_applied: Review of evidence and legal correctness on dying declaration admissibility

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Poisons, Opium And Dangerous Drugs Ordinance as amended by Amendment Act No. 13 of 1984
brief_facts_summary: Police raided the appellant's house in Stespura on April 6, 2016 based on an informant's tip. They found 2.31 grams of heroin in her dress pocket and money. The key evidence included police testimony and a Government Analyst Report confirming the heroin.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Poisons, Opium And Dangerous Drugs Ordinance as amended by Amendment Act No. 13 of 1984
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court found the appellant guilty of possession of heroin, acquitted her of trafficking, and sentenced her to life imprisonment. The court considered evidence and discrepancies but found prosecution proved possession beyond reasonable doubt.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant argued that the prosecution called a witness who never participated in the raid to corroborate evidence, and that the prosecution failed to prove the case beyond reasonable doubt.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The learned High Court Judge has failed to consider the fact that the prosecution has called a witness who never participated in the raid to corroborate the evidence of the main investigation officer. | The prosecution has failed to prove the case beyond reasonable doubt.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the evidence of prosecution witnesses consistent and credible, with minor discrepancies not material to the case.
probability_assessment_by_court: The court assessed that no reasonable doubt was created and prosecution proved the case beyond reasonable doubt.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty and made a dock statement denying possession, claiming the parcel was given by someone else. She offered varying stands during cross-examination. No defence witnesses were called, and the court found her defence not credible.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed the evidence, found minor discrepancies in witness testimony but held they were not material. They upheld the High Court's credibility assessments, applied legal principles on cross-examination and reasonable doubt, and concluded that the prosecution proved the case beyond reasonable doubt. The appeal was dismissed.
coa_sentence_type: Life Imprisonment
brief_judgment_file_summary: The appellant was convicted for possession of heroin and sentenced to life imprisonment by the High Court. She appealed on grounds of witness credibility and failure to prove beyond reasonable doubt. The Court of Appeal found no merit in the grounds, affirmed the conviction and sentence, and dismissed the appeal.
defence_counsel: Isuru Somadasa
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court considered the evidence, found prosecution proved possession beyond reasonable doubt, acquitted on trafficking, and imposed life imprisonment. The Court of Appeal found this analysis correct.
precedents_cited_list: Sarwan Singh Vs. State Of Punjab (2002) AIR S.C. 111 | Motilal Vs. State Of Madhya Pradesh (1990) CLJ, NOC 125 MP
standard_of_review_applied: The court reviewed whether the prosecution proved the case beyond reasonable doubt and assessed the credibility of witnesses.
sentencing_principles_applied: The High Court considered the two mandatory sentences (death or life imprisonment) and imposed the lesser sentence of life imprisonment.

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 54A(b) and 54A(d) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance as amended by Act No. 13 of 1984
brief_facts_summary: The appellant, a senior army officer, was arrested on a bus carrying 5.919 kg of heroin. He had obtained the drugs from a house in Talaimannar area after using army resources under false pretenses. The prosecution relied on eyewitness testimony from police and army personnel, and the heroin was confirmed by Government Analyst report.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 54A(b) and 54A(d) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance as amended by Act No. 13 of 1984
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court found the appellant guilty of possession and trafficking of heroin based on evidence from witnesses and the Government Analyst. The judge rejected the defence's version and sentenced him to life imprisonment on both counts.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant argued that he did not receive a fair trial under Article 13(3) and 13(5) of the Constitution due to procedural errors, judicial bias, and contradictions in prosecution evidence. Specific grounds included failure to read indictment properly, unfair questioning by the judge, and ignoring material contradictions.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The indictment was not read and explained to the appellant in his presence before trial commenced. | The case was transferred from one High Court to another in Colombo without giving any reason and at the request of the prosecuting State Counsel. | The learned High Court Judge failed to mention any legal principles that a trial Judge should have considered before determining that the case has been proved beyond reasonable doubt. | The learned High Court Judge has only given a narration of evidence in his judgement and has failed to analyze the evidence in its correct perspective. | The learned High Court Judge has cited judgements to cover the infirmities in the evidence of the prosecution and had failed to consider a single ground that was in favour of the appellant. | The improbability of the timings from the point of receipt of information and to the arrest of the appellant, which included PW-01 going to get his pocket notebook signed by the SSP. | The learned High Court Judge asked several questions during the appellant's evidence and the questions suggest that they were asked in favour of the prosecution and not in favour of the defence. | The prosecution's failure to call Police Sergeant Ratnayake who was attached to Murukkan police and was seated next to the appellant who should have been a vital witness for the prosecution to prove the detection. | The learned High Court Judge's failure to consider the major contradiction marked V-01 in his judgement and has brushed aside the contradictions pointed out as minor differences between the witnesses for the prosecution. | The burning of the finger of the appellant was considered quite normal by the learned High Court Judge, however, the MLEF produced by the prosecution indicates no injuries, and this should have been considered in the light of the appellant's evidence that although he was taken to a place resembling a hospital but never produced before a doctor. | Glaring contradictions with regard to the bag alleged to have been carried by the appellant having a strap was not considered by the learned High Court Judge but, had made an incorrect assumption that the PW-08 had identified the bag with a strap. | The learned High Court Judge failed to consider glaring contradictions with regard to the information received. | The learned High Court Judge failed to consider in a proper manner the evidence given by the appellant that the bag was opened using a cleaning rod in the weapon and the bag being torn. | The learned High Court Judge failed to consider that the padlock and the key were introductions made by the witnesses to implicate the appellant. | The learned High Court Judge failed to consider that the padlock and the key were not kept in proper custody and was sent to the High Court by the Registrar of the Mannar Magistrate's Court separate to the other productions. | The learned High Court Judge failed to consider the contradiction between the police witnesses and army witnesses as to whether the police knew the name of Kamal Kariyawasam who is the appellant at the time of the raid. | The learned High Court Judge failed to consider the contradiction of evidence between the driver of the bus and PW-01 with regard to both the information, and the driver being out of the bus when the police arrived. | The learned High Court Judge's comment in the judgement that the defence did not challenge the evidence of the driver of the bus is untenable, because the driver's evidence was favourable to the defence as it contradicted with PW-01. | The learned High Court Judge has made an erroneous comment in the judgement that the appellant has failed to ask any questions from PW-01 of the fact that he was outside the bus when the police arrived. | There is no proper acceptance of the prosecution evidence on the basis that the prosecution has proved the case beyond reasonable doubt, nor a rejection of the appellant's evidence with reasons. The learned High Court Judge failed to consider the intermediatory position where the appellant's evidence is neither accepted nor rejected, in which case the appellant should have been acquitted.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the prosecution witnesses credible and consistent, rejecting the appellant's evidence as unreliable. The court noted that contradictions were minor and did not affect the core of the prosecution case.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal assessed the evidence and found no reasonable doubt, concluding that the prosecution proved its case beyond reasonable doubt and the appellant's version was improbable.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty and gave evidence claiming he was in the area to meet a friend for financial help, denied possessing the heroin, and alleged police fabrication. The court found his evidence not credible and rejected it.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal considered each ground of appeal, found no merit in the arguments, and upheld the High Court's conviction and sentence. The court applied the proviso to Article 138(1) of the Constitution, stating that errors must prejudice substantial rights or occasion a failure of justice, which was not the case here. The evidence was found credible, and the appellant's defence was rejected.
coa_sentence_type: Life Imprisonment affirmed
brief_judgment_file_summary: The appellant, a senior army officer, was convicted by the High Court of Colombo for possession and trafficking of 5.919 kg of heroin and sentenced to life imprisonment. He appealed on grounds of unfair trial, procedural errors, and contradictions in evidence. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal, finding no merit in the grounds and upholding the conviction and sentence.
defence_counsel: Shavindra Fernando, P.C.
hc_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found that the High Court Judge properly evaluated the evidence despite some unconventional methods, and no errors prejudiced the substantial rights of the parties. The conviction was based on credible evidence beyond reasonable doubt.
precedents_cited_list: Bhoginbhai Hirjibhai Vs. State of Gujarat 1983 AIR 753 | Gamage Vs. Attorney General And Others (2020) 1 SLR 44 | The Attorney General Vs. Devunderage Nihal (2011) 1 SLR 409 | Galagamage Indrawansa Kumarasiri and Others Vs. The Attorney General (Angulana Murder Case) S.C. TAB Appeal No. 2/2012 | Sarwan Singh Vs. State Of Punjab (2002) AIR S.C. 111 | Hiniduma Dahanayakage Siripala Alias Kiri Mahaththaya And Others Vs. Hon. Attorney General S.C. Appeal No. 115/2014 | Sunil Jayarathna v. The Attorney General, SC 97/09 (SC Minutes of 29.07.2011)
standard_of_review_applied: The Court applied the standard from the proviso to Article 138(1) of the Constitution and section 436 of the Criminal Procedure Code, that errors must prejudice substantial rights or occasion a failure of justice to warrant reversal.

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 24(1) of the Forest Ordinance
brief_facts_summary: The accused pleaded guilty to illegally transporting timber under the Forest Ordinance. The vehicle used was subject to confiscation, and the appellant, the owner, argued she was unaware of the crime and had taken preventive measures. The Magistrate ordered confiscation, which was upheld by the High Court, but the Court of Appeal set aside the order.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 24(1) of the Forest Ordinance
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court dismissed the revision application, stating that the appellant failed to prove she took all necessary precautions to prevent the offence. The court found no exceptional circumstances to grant relief.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant argued that the confiscation order ignored her lack of knowledge of the illegal act, the High Court failed to consider precedent on the value of the item, and the confiscation was unjust and violated her human rights.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The order to confiscate the vehicle was made in disregard of the appellant's explanation that she was unaware of the illegal act. | The High Court judge failed to consider existing judicial dictum pertaining to the value of the item. | The confiscation is not in line with the human rights of the appellant and is not just and equitable.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed the appellant's testimony that she took precautions and was unaware of the illegal act, and considered the timber value and precedents on confiscation.
probability_assessment_by_court: Court applied balance of probability standard to determine if owner took precautions.
defence_version_summary: The appellant argued she was unaware of the illegal act, had taken precautions by instructing against illegal use, and trusted her brother. The court found her defence acceptable.
legal_errors_description: The Magistrate and High Court failed to consider that the appellant took precautions, the timber value, and precedents on confiscation.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: COA reviewed the evidence, cited precedents, and found that the appellant had taken precautions and was unaware of the illegal act. The court held that confiscation was not justified given the circumstances, including timber value and no prior illegal use, and set aside the lower court orders.
coa_sentence_type: Vehicle released to appellant
brief_judgment_file_summary: The appellant, owner of a vehicle used for illegal timber transport, appealed against confiscation orders. The High Court dismissed her revision, but the Court of Appeal allowed the appeal, finding she took precautions and was unaware. The court cited precedents and set aside the orders, directing release of the vehicle.
defence_counsel: Asthika Devendra with Aruna Madhushanka
hc_analysis_summary: HC dismissed the revision, finding no exceptional circumstances and that appellant failed to prove precautions. COA held that HC failed to consider appellant's precautions and vehicle's clean record.
precedents_cited_list: Ramu Thamodarampillai v. The Attorney General [2004] 3 SLR 180 | Marian Beebee v. Seyed Mohamed 69 CLW 34 | Rasheed Ali v. Mohammed Ali and Others [1981] 1 SLR 262 | Commissioner of Police v. Tanes (1957-58) 68 CLR 383 | The Orient Financial Services Corporation Ltd v The Range Forest Officer, Ampara and Hon. Attorney General [2013] 1 SLR 208 | Sadi Banda v OIC of Police Station Norton Bridge [2014] 1 SLR 33 | Mallawa Arachchige Supun Malhara v The Attorney General CA(PHC) 09/2015 dated 28.08.2020 | Ceylinco Leasing Corporation v M.H. Harrison and others SC Appeal 43/2012 dated 07.12.2017
standard_of_review_applied: Discretionary review for exceptional circumstances and legal errors
sentencing_principles_applied: Principles of confiscation under Forest Ordinance, including owner's knowledge and precautions.

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code, Section 380 of the Penal Code, Section 396 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The deceased went missing on 3 September 2005 after going to her tea plantation. Her skeletal remains were discovered a year later in a cave based on information provided by the Appellant. The Appellant had pawned the deceased's gold chain and exhibited evasive conduct towards police. The prosecution case relied on circumstantial evidence including the Appellant's conduct, recovery of the remains, and medical evidence.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code, Section 380 of the Penal Code
hc_sentence_type: Death sentence for murder, 8 years rigorous imprisonment for robbery
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the Appellant for murder and robbery based on circumstantial evidence, including the recovery of the deceased's remains and pawned gold chain. The court accepted the medical evidence and the Appellant's suspicious conduct. The Appellant was sentenced to death for murder and 8 years rigorous imprisonment with a fine for robbery.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The Appellant raised three grounds: failure to establish corpus delicti beyond reasonable doubt, error in relying on the last seen theory, and that the ingredients of the charges were not proved beyond reasonable doubt.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The prosecution has failed to establish the corpus delicti beyond reasonable doubt. | The Learned High Court Judge erred by relying upon the last seen theory. | The ingredients of the charges are not proved beyond reasonable doubt.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed the circumstantial evidence, including the Appellant's conduct, recovery of remains and pawned chain, and medical evidence, and found it sufficient to establish guilt beyond reasonable doubt.
probability_assessment_by_court: The court applied the standard for circumstantial evidence that it must be consistent with guilt and inconsistent with any reasonable hypothesis of innocence, and found the evidence met that standard.
defence_version_summary: The Appellant pleaded not guilty, made a dock statement denying the charges, and did not call any witnesses. The court found his defence not credible.
legal_errors_description: The High Court Judge erred by relying upon the last seen theory when the evidence did not support that the deceased was last seen with the Appellant.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal conducted a thorough analysis of the circumstantial evidence, including the Appellant's suspicious conduct (evading police, phone call to PW1, visit to the deceased's husband in prison), recovery of the skeletal remains and pawned gold chain based on the Appellant's statement under section 27(1) of the Evidence Ordinance, medical evidence indicating homicidal death, and identification of the deceased's belongings. The court found that the chain of circumstances was complete and pointed unerringly to the Appellant's guilt. While agreeing that the last seen theory was improperly applied, the court held that this error did not vitiate the conviction as the other evidence was overwhelming. The court affirmed the High Court's conviction and sentence.
coa_sentence_type: Death sentence for murder, 8 years rigorous imprisonment for robbery with a fine of Rs.15,000
brief_judgment_file_summary: The Accused-Appellant was convicted in the High Court of Ratnapura for murder and robbery and sentenced to death and 8 years imprisonment with a fine. He appealed on grounds including failure to establish corpus delicti, error in relying on last seen theory, and insufficient proof. The Court of Appeal found the conviction was based on strong circumstantial evidence, including the Appellant's conduct, discovery of the deceased's remains and pawned chain, and medical evidence. While noting the High Court erred in applying the last seen theory, the appellate court held the error did not affect the conviction and dismissed the appeal, affirming the conviction and sentence.
defence_counsel: Indika Mallowarachchi for the Appellant
cause_of_death_exact_text: Presence of a ligature made from a meshy gunny bag with a running knot may suggest strangulation.
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted the Appellant based on circumstantial evidence, including recovery of remains and the pawned chain, and accepted the medical evidence. The Court of Appeal found the High Court correctly evaluated the evidence except for erroneously relying on the last seen theory, but this error did not affect the overall correctness of the conviction.
precedents_cited_list: King v. Abeywickrema Et Al 44 NLR 254 | Tamil Nadu v. Rajendran Appeal (Cr.L) 917 of 1996 | RM Malkani v State of Maharashtra, AIR 1973 SC 157 | Somaratne Rajapakse Others v. Hon. Attorney General (2010) 2 Sri L.R. 113 at 115 | De Saram v The Republic of Sri Lanka [2002] 1 SLR page 288
standard_of_review_applied: The court reviewed whether the circumstantial evidence was consistent with guilt and inconsistent with any reasonable hypothesis of innocence.

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: section 365B(2)(b) of the Penal Code, as amended by Penal Code (Amendment) Act No. 22 of 1995, 29 of 1998 and 16 of 2006
brief_facts_summary: The accused-appellant was charged with touching the vaginal area of a 5-year-old girl for sexual gratification. The mother witnessed the incident upon returning home from work and assaulted the appellant. The child's video recorded interview was used as evidence. The appellant denied the charge and claimed the complaint was false due to a dispute over plucking coconuts.
evidence_type_primary: Eyewitness testimony and video recorded interview of child
evidence_type_secondary: Medical evidence (JMO report) and testimony of police and child protection officers
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: section 365B(2)(b) of the Penal Code, as amended by Penal Code (Amendment) Act No. 22 of 1995, 29 of 1998 and 16 of 2006
hc_sentence_type: 7 years rigorous imprisonment, fine of Rs. 1500, compensation of Rs. 100000 with default sentences
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court found the appellant guilty based on the video recorded evidence of the child and the mother's eyewitness testimony. The court sentenced him to 7 years rigorous imprisonment, a fine, and compensation, considering the mitigatory circumstances.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant challenged the reliability and credibility of the victim's evidence, the probability of the prosecution version, and the admissibility of the video recording. He argued contradictions between the child's and mother's evidence made the prosecution case improbable.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Reliability and the credibility of the victim’s evidence. | The probability of the prosecution version. | Admissibility of the video recording in the case.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the victim child's evidence credible and consistent, and it was corroborated by the mother's direct eyewitness account. The child's video interview was properly conducted and she was cross-examined.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal found the prosecution version probable and reliable, and that the evidence proved the case beyond reasonable doubt.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty and made a dock statement. He claimed a false complaint due to a dispute over coconut plucking. He called his daughter as a witness to support his alibi that he was at home. The court did not find the defence credible.
legal_errors_description: The High Court Judge was misdirected in stating there was no direct evidence, when in fact there was eyewitness evidence from the mother.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal thoroughly analyzed the evidence, including the video recording and the mother's testimony. They found the child's evidence credible and corroborated, addressed contradictions as not material, and found the video recording properly admitted. They affirmed the conviction and sentence, noting the misdirection by the High Court did not cause prejudice.
coa_sentence_type: 7 years rigorous imprisonment, fine of Rs. 1500, compensation of Rs. 100000 with default sentences
brief_judgment_file_summary: The appellant was convicted by the High Court of Panadura for sexual abuse of a minor and sentenced to 7 years rigorous imprisonment, a fine, and compensation. He appealed on grounds of contradictions in evidence and admissibility of video evidence. The Court of Appeal found the evidence credible and the video recording properly admitted, and dismissed the appeal.
defence_counsel: Ershan Ariaratnam
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court considered the evidence and found the prosecution proved its case. The Court of Appeal found the High Court Judge was misdirected in stating there was no direct evidence, but this did not cause prejudice.
precedents_cited_list: Bhoginbhai Hirjibhai Vs. State of Gujarat (AIR 1983-SC 753 at pp 756-758)
standard_of_review_applied: The Court of Appeal reviewed the evidence and found no reason to interfere with the conviction and sentence.
sentencing_principles_applied: The High Court considered mitigatory circumstances in sentencing, and the Court of Appeal found no reason to modify the sentence.
