judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 3D of the Animals Act No. 29 of 1958 as amended by the Animals (Amendment) Act No. 10 of 2009
brief_facts_summary: Two accused were charged with transporting 68 buffaloes at night without a permit and pleaded guilty. The petitioner claimed ownership of the animals, but the Magistrate confiscated them after an inquiry. The High Court affirmed the order, and the petitioner appealed to the Court of Appeal.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 3D of the Animals Act No. 29 of 1958 as amended by the Animals (Amendment) Act No. 10 of 2009
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court affirmed the Magistrate's order confiscating the cattle. The judge discussed the legal provisions and found that the petitioner failed to prove ownership or lack of knowledge.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The petitioner argued that herding animals by foot does not constitute transportation under the Animals Act, and that the Magistrate erred in charging the accused and ordering confiscation.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Herding of animals by foot does not constitute transportation under the Animals Act | The Magistrate misdirected as to the facts and relevant law in holding an inquiry under section 3AA(3)
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The petitioner gave evidence and called a witness to prove ownership, but the court found insufficient proof. The Court of Appeal focused on the legal interpretation of 'transport'.
probability_assessment_by_court: Court found that herding animals by foot does not meet the definition of transportation under the Animals Act.
defence_version_summary: The accused pleaded guilty to the charge. The petitioner claimed ownership of the animals and that the offence was committed without his knowledge, but failed to prove it.
legal_errors_description: The Magistrate and High Court erred in interpreting 'herding' as 'transportation' under the Animals Act, and misapplied the relevant sections.
procedural_defects_description: The Magistrate issued a directive for a veterinary report but did not ensure it was carried out before pronouncing the order.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed the meaning of 'transport' in the Animals Act, concluding that herding animals by foot does not constitute transportation as envisaged by the Act. The court found that the lower courts misdirected on the law by conflating herding with transportation. The COA set aside the orders of confiscation and directed the release of the cattle to the claimant.
coa_sentence_type: Release of confiscated animals
brief_judgment_file_summary: The petitioner appealed against the confiscation of 68 buffaloes by the Magistrate's Court, which was affirmed by the High Court. The Court of Appeal held that herding animals by foot does not constitute 'transportation' under the Animals Act, and therefore the charge was incorrect. The COA set aside the lower court orders and directed the release of the animals to the claimant.
defence_counsel: Keheliya Alahakoon
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court affirmed the Magistrate's order but used the term 'taking' instead of 'transport', which the COA found to be a misdirection. The HC also misapplied the legal provisions regarding confiscation.
standard_of_review_applied: Revisionary jurisdiction under Article 138 of the Constitution to correct errors of law

judges: Sampath B.Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Sections 54(A)(b) and 54(A)(d) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance as amended by Act No. 13 of 1984
brief_facts_summary: The Appellant was arrested on 09th July 2013 during a police raid at Mahawatta area for drug-related activities. Police recovered 25.34 grams of Heroin from him and cash Rs.214,410 hidden near his house. The prosecution relied on physical evidence and the Government Analyst Report, but the defense alleged assault and fabrication of evidence.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 54(A)(d) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance as amended by Act No. 13 of 1984
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court found the Appellant guilty of trafficking heroin and sentenced him to life imprisonment. The money recovered was ordered to be confiscated by the State.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The Appellant appealed on grounds of discrepancy in the weight of heroin recovered, failure to evaluate contradictions in prosecution evidence, and the High Court Judge casting burden of proof on the Appellant.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: That there is a discrepancy in the weight of Heroin recovered from the Appellant and the Government Analyst Report. | The Learned High Court Judge has failed to evaluate the contradictions and improbabilities of the prosecution case. | That the Learned High Court Judge has cast burden on the Appellant.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The prosecution presented 4 witnesses who testified about the arrest and recovery of drugs. However, the chain of custody was weakened by weight discrepancies and improper handling of evidence.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal found reasonable doubt due to chain of custody issues and contradictions in prosecution evidence.
defence_version_summary: The Appellant denied possession of drugs in his dock statement, claiming that the drugs were introduced by the prosecution witnesses and that he was assaulted. No alibi was presented, and the court found the defence not credible in light of the evidence issues.
legal_errors_description: The High Court Judge reversed the burden of proof onto the Appellant, failed to properly evaluate contradictions in the prosecution case, and misdirected on the chain of custody requirements.
procedural_defects_description: There were defects in the chain of custody including weight discrepancy, improper sealing and handling of evidence, and failure to call the Government Analyst to testify.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed the evidence and found serious doubt in the prosecution case due to the weight discrepancy in the heroin, which disturbed the chain of custody. They also noted contradictions in the prosecution witnesses' testimonies and that the High Court Judge had erroneously placed the burden of proof on the Appellant. Applying precedents on chain of custody and burden of proof, the COA concluded that the prosecution failed to prove the case beyond reasonable doubt, leading to acquittal.
coa_sentence_type: Acquitted, no sentence imposed
brief_judgment_file_summary: This is an appeal by Kumaravel Yoganadan against his conviction and life sentence for heroin trafficking by the High Court of Colombo. The Court of Appeal allowed the appeal on grounds of weight discrepancy in the drugs, contradictions in prosecution evidence, and improper burden of proof. The COA found the chain of custody compromised and reversed the conviction, acquitting the Appellant.
defence_counsel: Udara Zoysa
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted the Appellant based on the prosecution evidence, but the Court of Appeal found that the HC failed to address key issues like weight discrepancy and improperly placed the burden of proof on the defence.
precedents_cited_list: Mohamed Nimnaz V. Attorney General CA/95/94 | Faiza Hanoon Yoosuf v Attorney General CA/121/2002 | Perera V. Attorney General [1998] 1 Sri.L.R | Woolmington v. DPP [1935] A.C.462
standard_of_review_applied: Review for legal errors and reasonable doubt based on evidence and chain of custody principles.

judges: Menaka Wijesundera J. | B. Sasi Mahendran J.
offence_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The incident occurred in 2003 when the appellant and co-accused arrived to clear land near the deceased's home. They left knives under a chair, returned later, and during an altercation, the deceased was assaulted with manna knives, leading to his death. Key evidence includes eyewitness testimony, recovery of knives based on accused statements, and medical evidence linking injuries to the knives. The accused claimed they were nearby and heard the noise but did not cross-examine witnesses on this point.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the appellant for murder under section 296 of the Penal Code based on common intention, while acquitting the co-accused. The trial judge failed to consider the improbability of the prosecution version, the inconsistency in acquitting the co-accused, and confusion in the recovery of weapons.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant argued that the trial judge failed to consider the improbability of the prosecution version, that convicting the appellant after acquitting the co-accused was inconsistent, and that there was confusion regarding the recovery of weapons based on the accused's statements.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The trial judge failed to consider the improbability of the prosecution version | The trial judge could not have convicted the appellant after acquitting the 1st accused on the evidence placed before Court | The trial judge failed to consider the confusion with regard to the recoveries made on the statements of the accused
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: Witnesses identified the appellant using a manna knife, and the doctor confirmed injuries could have been caused by the knives. The Court of Appeal found that both accused shared common intention and the trial judge failed to properly evaluate the evidence, leading to an inconsistent verdict.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal found that the trial judge failed to consider the evidence in totality and that both accused shared common intention, leading to reasonable doubt in convicting the appellant alone.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty and made a dock statement claiming they were in a nearby house and heard the noise, but this alibi was not cross-examined with witnesses, making it a belated defense.
legal_errors_description: The trial judge failed to consider the improbability of the prosecution version, the acquittal of the co-accused, confusion in recoveries, and failed to appreciate the ingredients of common intention under section 32 of the Penal Code.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed the evidence and found that both accused came to the scene armed with knives, shared a common intention to cause hurt, and acted together. The trial judge's acquittal of the co-accused while convicting the appellant was inconsistent with the evidence of common intention. Citing precedents on common intention and the need to consider all evidence together, the COA concluded that the trial judge failed to properly assess the prosecution case. Due to these legal errors and the 20-year delay since the incident, the appeal was allowed without ordering a retrial.
brief_judgment_file_summary: This appeal concerns the conviction of the appellant for murder under section 296 of the Penal Code by the High Court of Colombo, while the co-accused was acquitted. The appellant challenged the conviction on grounds including improbability of prosecution version, inconsistency with co-accused's acquittal, and confusion in weapon recoveries. The Court of Appeal found that the trial judge failed to properly consider the evidence and appreciate common intention, leading to an unjust verdict. Consequently, the appeal was allowed, the conviction and sentence were set aside, and the appellant was acquitted without a retrial due to the long delay since the 2003 incident.
defence_counsel: Shanaka Ranasinghe P.C. with Niroshan Mihindukulasooriya
cause_of_death_exact_text: shock and hemorrhage due to cut injuries
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted the appellant based on common intention but acquitted the co-accused, failing to consider that both accused acted together with shared intention. The Court of Appeal found this analysis flawed and inconsistent with the evidence.
precedents_cited_list: The Queen vs. Vincent Fernando 65 NLR 265 | James Silva v Republic of Sri Lanka 1980 2 SLR 167 | Jayasena vs. Queen 72 NLR 313
standard_of_review_applied: Consider all evidence in totality without compartmentalizing, as per precedent.

judges: Menaka Wijesundera, J. | B. Sasi Mahendran, J.
offence_sections: Section 54A(d) and 54A(b) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance, as amended by Act No. 13 of 1984
brief_facts_summary: The accused was arrested on August 1, 2013, after police received a tip and found her with 5.77g of heroin. She was holding the drugs in her palm while carrying a handbag. The prosecution presented evidence from 17 witnesses, but there were inconsistencies in testimonies and chain of custody issues.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 54A(d) and 54A(b) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance, as amended by Act No. 13 of 1984
hc_sentence_type: Rigorous Imprisonment 8 years and fine for each count
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the accused on both counts of possession and trafficking heroin. She was sentenced to 8 years rigorous imprisonment and a fine of 250,000 LKR per count, with sentences running concurrently.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant argued that the trial judge failed to evaluate infirmities in the prosecution case, including contradictions in witness testimonies, improbability of evidence, missing production pages, and chain of custody weaknesses.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The Learned Trial Judge has failed to evaluate and take cognizance of the infirmity in the case of the Prosecution. | The Learned Trial Judge has failed to evaluate and take cognizance of the impossibility in the case for the Prosecution. | The Learned Trial Judge has failed to consider that the most important production has not been handed over to the police reserve nor produced court. | The learned Trial Judge has failed to consider the improbability of the mode of transport said to have been used in the raid. | The Learned Trial Judge has failed to evaluate and take cognizance of the infirmities of the case inwards chain of the production.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found inconsistencies in prosecution witness testimonies, such as travel time discrepancies between PW1 and PW4. The chain of custody was weak due to delayed sealing of the production and missing registry pages, casting doubt on the evidence's reliability.
probability_assessment_by_court: The court assessed the improbability of the accused holding drugs in her palm and found it unlikely, creating reasonable doubt.
defence_version_summary: The accused pleaded not guilty and made a dock statement claiming she was arrested at Mount Lavinia Police Station. The defence challenged the prosecution evidence based on contradictions and chain of custody issues.
legal_errors_description: The High Court failed to properly evaluate the evidence, including contradictions in witness testimony and chain of custody deficiencies.
procedural_defects_description: Important pages in the production registry detailing handover of production to reserve are missing.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal reviewed the evidence and found significant contradictions between prosecution witnesses, such as travel time discrepancies. They highlighted the improbability of the accused holding drugs openly in her palm. The chain of custody was deficient due to delayed sealing and missing registry pages. Citing precedent, the court emphasized the need for a proven inward journey of productions. Based on these issues, the COA concluded that the prosecution failed to prove the case beyond reasonable doubt.
coa_sentence_type: Acquitted
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused was convicted by the High Court for possessing and trafficking 5.77g of heroin. She appealed on grounds of evidence infirmities, including contradictions in witness testimonies and chain of custody issues. The Court of Appeal found reasonable doubt due to improbabilities and missing evidence, leading to the appeal being allowed, conviction set aside, and accused acquitted.
defence_counsel: Anuja Premaratne, PC with Ramith Dunusinghe, Vivindra Rathnayaka, and Bandara Dissanayaka
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted the accused based on prosecution evidence, but the Court of Appeal found that the HC failed to consider contradictions in testimonies, improbabilities, and chain of custody issues, rendering the conviction unsafe.
precedents_cited_list: Witharana Doli Nona v. The Republic of Sri Lanka, CA 19/99 | Perera v. Attorney General (1998) 1 SLR 378
standard_of_review_applied: Review of evidence for reasonable doubt and compliance with chain of custody principles

judges: Menaka Wijesundera, J. | B. Sasi Mahendran, J.
offence_sections: Section 22(3) read with Section 22(1) of the Firearms Act No.33 of 1966 as amended by Act No. 22 of 1996; and Section 9(2) read with Section 27(1)(a) of Explosives Act No. 21 of 1961 as amended by Act No. 33 of 1969.
offence_category: Illegal Possession of Firearms and Explosives
brief_facts_summary: On 14 June 2009, police searched the accused's residence based on information and recovered a T-56 gun, 29 bullets, and two magazines hidden in a rice bag under a hen cage. The accused denied the allegations. The evidence was sent to the Government Analyst, but there were discrepancies in serial numbers and chain of custody issues.
evidence_type_secondary: Government Analyst report and chain of custody records
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 22(3) read with Section 22(1) of the Firearms Act No.33 of 1966 as amended by Act No. 22 of 1996; and Section 9(2) read with Section 27(1)(a) of Explosives Act No. 21 of 1961 as amended by Act No. 33 of 1969.
hc_sentence_type: Life imprisonment for count 1; 2 years rigorous imprisonment and fine for count 2
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court found the accused guilty based on prosecution evidence and imposed life imprisonment for illegal possession of a firearm and 2 years rigorous imprisonment with a fine for possession of explosives. The judge dismissed chain of custody concerns, considering them not critical for firearms.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appeal grounds include prosecution not establishing exclusive possession, contradictory and unreliable evidence from PW10, failure to address infirmities in evidence, conflicts between witnesses, and issues with identification of the weapon.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Conviction is untenable as the prosecution has not established exclusive possession on the part of the Appellant. | Evidence of PW/10 namely Gamini Jayantha is self-contradictory, erratic, and wholly unreliable casting a serious doubt in the prosecution case. | The Learned Trial Judge had totally failed to address his judicial mind to the serious infirmities in the evidence of PW10 namely Gamini Jayantha. | Conflict of evidence between PW10 namely Gamini Jayantha and PW9 namely Chandrasegara creates a serious doubt in the prosecution case. | The Learned Trial Judge has been totally oblivious to the aforementioned contradictory evidence between PW10 and PW9. | Evidence relating to the identification of the T56 weapon is infirm and the prosecution has failed to establish its identity beyond reasonable doubt.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: COA found contradictions between PW9 and PW10 regarding the handling and serial number of the firearm, and discrepancies in chain of custody, leading to reasonable doubt.
probability_assessment_by_court: COA found reasonable doubt due to discrepancies in evidence and chain of custody.
defence_version_summary: The accused gave a dock statement denying the allegations and did not call any witnesses. The court found the prosecution evidence unreliable.
legal_errors_description: High Court judge erred in dismissing chain of custody issues and not considering discrepancies in serial numbers.
procedural_defects_description: Discrepancies in serial numbers of the firearm and failure to properly maintain chain of custody.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed the evidence and found glaring discrepancies in the testimonies of PW1, PW9, and PW10 regarding the serial number and chain of custody of the firearm. They held that the prosecution failed to prove the case beyond reasonable doubt due to these inconsistencies, and the High Court judge's dismissal of chain of custody concerns was flawed.
coa_sentence_type: Acquitted, no sentence imposed
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused was convicted by the High Court of Batticaloa for illegal possession of a firearm and explosives and sentenced to life imprisonment and a fine. On appeal, the Court of Appeal found discrepancies in the evidence, particularly in the chain of custody and serial numbers, leading to reasonable doubt. The appeal was allowed, the conviction set aside, and the accused acquitted.
prosecution_counsel: Madhawa Tennakoon, DSG with Nishantha Nagaratnam, SC
defence_counsel: Indica Mallawaratchy
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted based on prosecution evidence and dismissed chain of custody issues, but the Court of Appeal found this erroneous due to discrepancies in serial numbers and evidence handling.
standard_of_review_applied: Review for reasonable doubt based on evidence inconsistencies

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 54A(a) and 54A(d) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance as amended
brief_facts_summary: The suspect was arrested on 01-02-2022 for alleged possession and trafficking of 15.85 grams of a substance suspected to be Heroin. The Government Analyst Report identified 2.44 grams of Diacetylmorphine (Heroin). The suspect has previous convictions and pending cases.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 54A(a) and 54A(d) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance as amended
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court refused bail for the suspect on the basis that he has several pending cases and previous convictions.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The petitioner argued that under the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs (Amendment) Act No. 41 of 2022, the suspect is entitled to bail as the pure quantity of Heroin is less than 10 grams and the remand period has exceeded 12 months without extension.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The High Court misapplied the bail provisions under the amended Ordinance. | The suspect should be released on bail as per sections 84 and 85 of the amended Ordinance.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court relied on the Government Analyst Report which confirmed the presence of Heroin. No witness testimony was discussed in the bail application.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court assessed that under the amended law, the suspect is entitled to bail after 12 months in remand for quantities less than 10 grams.
defence_version_summary: The suspect applied for bail, claiming entitlement under the new Amendment Act due to the pure quantity being less than 10 grams and the remand period exceeding 12 months. No plea or alibi was discussed as it is a bail application.
legal_errors_description: The High Court Judge was misdirected as to the relevant law regarding bail provisions under the amended Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed sections 83, 84, and 85 of the amended Ordinance. It found that for pure quantities of dangerous drugs less than 10 grams, the High Court must release the suspect on bail after 12 months in remand unless the Attorney General obtains an extension under section 85. Since no extension was obtained, and the suspect had been in remand for over 12 months, he was entitled to bail.
coa_sentence_type: Released on bail with conditions: cash bail of Rs. 25000, surety bail of Rs. 250000 each with 2 sureties, travel ban, and surrender of passport.
brief_judgment_file_summary: This is a revision application to the Court of Appeal challenging the High Court's refusal of bail. The suspect was arrested for possession and trafficking of Heroin. The High Court denied bail based on previous convictions and pending cases. The Court of Appeal applied the amended Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance, found that for quantities less than 10 grams, bail must be granted after 12 months in remand. Since the suspect had been in remand for over 12 months with no extension, the COA allowed the appeal, set aside the HC order, and granted bail with conditions.
defence_counsel: Janajith De Silva with Eranga Rathnayake
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court refused bail considering the suspect's previous convictions and pending cases. However, the Court of Appeal found that under the amended law, these factors should only be considered for imposing bail conditions, not for denying bail when the legal criteria for release are met.
standard_of_review_applied: Revisionary jurisdiction under sections 364 and 365 of the Code of Criminal Procedure Act

judges: Menaka Wijesundera, J. | B. Sasi Mahendran, J.
offence_sections: Unlawful assembly to commit murder and common intention to commit murder under the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: On October 30, 2001, a group of ten men approached the deceased's house and attacked him with sharp weapons, resulting in his death. Eyewitnesses, including the deceased's mother and father, identified the accused. Weapons were later recovered from a cesspit, and the accused were arrested and charged with murder.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Murder under the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the 1st, 2nd, and 3rd accused of murder and imposed the death sentence, while acquitting the 4th and 5th accused.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellants argued that the prosecution failed to establish specific acts for unlawful assembly, that the trial judge relied on uncorroborated and inconsistent evidence, and that the charge of unlawful assembly was untenable. They also claimed provocation, failure to consider witness demeanor, and incorrect application of legal principles regarding dock statements.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The Prosecution has failed to establish the specific act or omission committed by the Appellant that would categorize him as a member of an unlawful assembly, despite claiming that witnesses saw the Appellant enter the house. | The Learned Trial Judge has relied on uncorroborated and inconsistent evidence to convict the Appellant. | The charge of unlawful assembly is untenable, as only three accused were charged with being members of an unlawful assembly. | The Learned Trial Judge failed to take into account that the Appellants acted under grave and sudden provocation while under the influence of liquor during their attack on the Deceased. | The Learned Trial Judge neglected to consider the demeanor and deportment of the prosecution witnesses when evaluating their evidence. | The Learned Trial Judge incorrectly applied the legal principles related to the dock statement and did not accord the dock statement the appropriate prominence and due consideration in line with established legal principles.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found inconsistencies in the eyewitness testimonies, particularly PW1 and PW2, and noted the prosecution failed to prove common object for unlawful assembly. The medical evidence indicated multiple injuries but did not conclusively attribute death to a single injury.
probability_assessment_by_court: The court assessed whether the injuries caused death and whether there was common object for unlawful assembly, applying principles from cited cases.
defence_version_summary: The 1st accused denied the allegation, stating he played marbles with the deceased and had an argument that ended without animosity. The 1st and 2nd accused surrendered to police. The 2nd and 3rd accused made dock statements. The court found the defence version not credible for the 1st accused, but for the 2nd and 3rd, there was no evidence of active participation.
legal_errors_description: The High Court erred in accepting inconsistent eyewitness testimony and in holding there was an unlawful assembly and common intention. Also, the High Court incorrectly applied the law on dock statements.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed the evidence and found inconsistencies in the eyewitness accounts. It held the prosecution failed to prove the common object for unlawful assembly and that the medical evidence did not establish the injury caused by the 1st accused resulted in death. Citing precedents on unlawful assembly and common intention, the COA acquitted the 2nd and 3rd accused and modified the conviction of the 1st accused to voluntarily causing grievous hurt by dangerous weapons.
coa_sentence_type: For the 1st accused: 7 years rigorous imprisonment. For the 2nd and 3rd accused: acquitted.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The three accused were convicted of murder by the High Court of Panadura and sentenced to death. They appealed on grounds including inconsistent evidence, untenable charge of unlawful assembly, and provocation. The Court of Appeal found the eyewitness testimony inconsistent and the prosecution failed to prove common object for unlawful assembly. The 2nd and 3rd accused were acquitted, while the 1st accused's conviction was modified to voluntarily causing grievous hurt and sentenced to 7 years rigorous imprisonment.
defence_counsel: Kolitha Dharmawardana with Chamindi Diloka Mannakkara for 1st accused; Neranjan Jayasinghe with D.D.K.Katugampola for 2nd accused; Saliya Pieris, PC with Yohan Pieris and Farhad Jiffry for 3rd accused
cause_of_death_exact_text: loss of heart rate and lung function due to bleeding and trauma inflicted by cuts to the head and neck from a sharp-edged weapon
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted based on eyewitness testimony which the Court of Appeal found inconsistent and unreliable. The High Court failed to properly evaluate the evidence regarding unlawful assembly and common intention.
precedents_cited_list: Kumara de Silva and 2 others vs. Attorney General [2010] 2 S.L.R. 169 | Attorney General vs. Somadasa | Jagathsena and others v G.D.P Perera and others [1992] 1 S.L.R 375 | Queen v. Vincent Fernando 65 NLR 265 | Piyathilaka and 2 Others v. Republic of Sri Lanka [1996] 2 S.L.R
standard_of_review_applied: The COA reviewed the evidence and applied the principles of reasonable doubt and the legal standards for unlawful assembly and common intention.
sentencing_principles_applied: The COA considered the nature of the offence and the evidence, and applied the principle of proportionality in modifying the sentence.
final_charge_after_appeal: For the 1st accused: Voluntarily causing grievous hurt by dangerous weapons under section 317 of the Penal Code

judges: Sampath B Abayakoon, J. | K Priyantha Fernando, J.
offence_sections: Section 54A(d) and 54A(b) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance
brief_facts_summary: Appellant was arrested on 22-05-2002 based on information about an illegal heroin transaction. Excise officers found 120 small packets of brown powder (heroin) totaling 5.6 grams in his possession. The substance was analyzed by the Government Analyst, who found 2.4 grams of pure heroin. The appellant denied possession.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 54A(d) and 54A(b) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court found the appellant guilty of possession and trafficking of heroin and sentenced him to life imprisonment on both counts.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant argued break in chain of custody of productions, discrepancy in identity of productions, dock statement rejected on unreasonable grounds, and trial judge cast unnecessary burden on the accused.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Break in the chain of productions being sent to the Government Analyst | Discrepancy in the identity of the productions | Dock statement was rejected based on unreasonable grounds | The trial Judge casted unnecessary burden on the accused
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: Court of Appeal analyzed evidence of excise officers and Government Analyst. Found chain of custody properly maintained and evidence credible. Minor weight discrepancy did not prejudice appellant.
probability_assessment_by_court: Court found no reasonable doubt created by dock statement and considered totality of evidence.
defence_version_summary: Appellant pleaded not guilty. He made a dock statement denying possession of heroin but gave no reasonable explanation. He did not call witnesses. Court found dock statement not credible.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: Court of Appeal considered each ground of appeal. Found chain of custody unbroken due to admissions and proper sealing. Weight discrepancy minor and not prejudicial. Dock statement properly evaluated in totality of evidence. No unnecessary burden cast on accused. Procedural issue with indictment reading was corrected by trial de novo. Appeal dismissed.
coa_sentence_type: Life Imprisonment affirmed
brief_judgment_file_summary: Appellant convicted by High Court of Negombo for possession and trafficking of heroin and sentenced to life imprisonment. He appealed on grounds of chain of custody, identity discrepancy, dock statement rejection, and burden on accused. Court of Appeal dismissed appeal, finding no merit in grounds and affirming conviction and sentence.
defence_counsel: Tirantha Walaliyadde, P.C. with Hirandi Cooray and Sarith Pathirana
hc_analysis_summary: High Court found appellant guilty based on evidence of excise officers and Government Analyst report. Court of Appeal agreed with High Court's reasoning and found no errors.
precedents_cited_list: Perera Vs. Attorney General (1998) 1 SLR 378 | Faiza Hanoon Yoosuf Vs. The Attorney General, CA Appeal No-121/2002, HC Negombo Case No-139/93 | Queen Vs. Kularatne (1968) 71 NLR 529 | Don Samantha Jude Anthony Jayamaha Vs. The Attorney General, C.A. 303/2006 decided on 11-07-2012
standard_of_review_applied: Review of evidence and grounds of appeal to determine if prosecution proved case beyond reasonable doubt and if trial judge made errors.

judges: K. Priyantha Fernando, J. | Sampath B. Abayakoon, J.
offence_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The appellant was convicted of murder in the High Court of Ratnapura and sentenced to death. The appeal is based on the procedural error of not offering the jury option at the commencement of the trial. No detailed facts of the crime are provided in the judgment.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the appellant of murder and sentenced him to death. The trial proceeded without a jury after the defence consented to rectify the omission of offering jury option.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant argued that the High Court Judge erred in law by failing to offer the jury option at the commencement of the trial as required by section 11 of the Judicature Act. The appellant contended that this irregularity cannot be rectified at a later stage.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Failure to follow section 11 of the Judicature Act by not offering jury option at commencement of trial.
defence_version_summary: The defence consented to proceed with trial without a jury after the omission of offering jury option was noted. The plea of the accused is not explicitly stated in the judgment.
procedural_defects_description: Failure to offer jury option at the commencement of the trial as required by section 195(ee) of the Code of Criminal Procedure Act.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed the requirement to offer jury option under section 11 of the Judicature Act and section 195(ee) of the Code of Criminal Procedure Act. Citing precedents like Attorney General v. Segulebbe Latheef and Another, Palitha v. The Attorney General, and Dharmasena v. State, the court held that failure to offer jury option is an illegality, but if the defence consents or waives the right, it does not amount to nullity. In this case, the appellant consented to proceed without jury, so he is estopped from appealing on this ground. No prejudice was caused.
coa_sentence_type: Death
brief_judgment_file_summary: The appellant was convicted of murder by the High Court of Ratnapura and sentenced to death. He appealed on the ground that the High Court failed to offer the jury option at the commencement of the trial as required by law. The Court of Appeal examined the procedural defect and found that the appellant had consented to proceed without a jury when the omission was brought to light. Citing relevant precedents, the court held that the waiver of jury option prevented the appellant from raising the issue on appeal. Therefore, the appeal was dismissed, and the conviction and sentence were upheld.
defence_counsel: Duminda De Alwis with Charuni De Alwis
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court failed to offer jury option at commencement, which is an illegality. However, the defence consented to proceed without jury, so the error was rectified with waiver.
precedents_cited_list: Attorney General v. Segulebbe Latheef and Another [2008] 1 Sri LR 225 | Palitha v. The Attorney General Bar Association Law Reports 2011 (2) B.L.R 422 | Dharmasena v. State [1994] 1 Sri LR 212
standard_of_review_applied: Review of procedural error and waiver of rights

judges: N. Bandula Karunarathna, J. | R. Gurusinghe, J.
offence_sections: Section 365 (b) (2) of the Penal Code as amended by Act No. 22 of 1995 and Act No. 29 of 1998
brief_facts_summary: The accused, a teacher, was charged with grave sexual abuse of three boys at a school in Ilanthadiya between October 1996 and October 1997. The prosecution relied on victim testimonies, but there were contradictions and no medical corroboration. The accused pleaded not guilty and provided a dock statement denying the allegations.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 365 (b) (2) of the Penal Code as amended by Act No. 22 of 1995 and Act No. 29 of 1998
hc_sentence_type: Seven years imprisonment, fine of Rs. 1000, and compensation of Rs. 50,000 each to PW1 and PW2
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the appellant on counts one and two for grave sexual abuse, acquitted on count three, and sentenced him to imprisonment, fine, and compensation based on the testimonies of PW1 and PW2.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant appealed on grounds that the prosecution failed to prove the case beyond reasonable doubt, the trial judge misdirected himself in evaluating evidence, failed to consider contradictions, and improperly considered the dock statement.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The prosecution has failed to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt. | The learned Trial Judge had failed to consider and evaluate the evidence placed before Court. | The learned Trial Judge has misdirected himself with regard to the evaluation of evidence of witnesses who testified before Court. | The learned Trial Judge has failed to consider relevant and pertinent evidence of testimony of prosecution witnesses. | The learned Trial Judge has not considered the relevant evidence. | The learned Trial Judge has misdirected himself in the application of criteria to assess the credibility of witnesses. | The learned Trial Judge has failed to consider relevant and pertinent evidence in assessing the credibility of the witnesses. | The learned Trial judge has failed to consider the inter se and per se contradictions in the evidence of the prosecution witnesses. | The learned Trial Judge has failed to consider the dock statement and misdirected himself in the consideration of the dock statement made by the appellant.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The COA found contradictions in the testimonies of PW1 and PW2, lack of corroboration from other witnesses and medical evidence, and issues with the date of offence, rendering the evidence not credible.
probability_assessment_by_court: The COA assessed that the prosecution did not prove the case beyond reasonable doubt due to contradictions and lack of credible evidence.
defence_version_summary: The accused pleaded not guilty and made a dock statement denying the charges. He claimed he never stayed at the school during weekends, which contradicted the prosecution's date. The court found his defence credible in light of the evidence failures.
legal_errors_description: The indictment included Penal Code Amendment Act No. 29 of 1998, which came into effect after the offence period, causing prejudice to the appellant.
procedural_defects_description: Incorrect reference to Act No. 29 of 1998 in the charges, which was not in force at the time of the offence.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal thoroughly analyzed the evidence and found significant contradictions in the prosecution witnesses' testimonies, lack of medical corroboration, and an incorrect date of offence. Additionally, the legal charge was flawed due to inclusion of an Act not in force. Therefore, the conviction was unsafe and set aside.
coa_sentence_type: Acquitted, no sentence imposed
brief_judgment_file_summary: The appellant was convicted by the High Court of Puttalam for grave sexual abuse and sentenced to imprisonment, fine, and compensation. He appealed to the Court of Appeal on grounds of insufficient evidence and legal errors. The Court of Appeal found contradictions in witness testimonies, lack of medical evidence, and that the charges included an Act not in force at the time, leading to the appeal being allowed and the appellant acquitted.
defence_counsel: Anura Meddegoda PC. with Nadisha Kannangara
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted the appellant based on the testimonies of PW1 and PW2, but the Court of Appeal found that the trial judge failed to consider contradictions and misdirected himself in evidence evaluation.
precedents_cited_list: Nimal Senaratna v The Democratic Socialist Republic of Sri Lanka CA 126/2001 HC Anuradhapura 17/2000 Decided on 26.08.2014
standard_of_review_applied: Proof beyond reasonable doubt and review of evidence for contradictions and credibility

judges: K Priyantha Fernando, J. | Sampath B Abayakoon, J.
offence_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The appellant was accused of murdering Palaniyandi Santhanam on September 9, 1996. Witnesses heard a cry and saw the appellant with a knife near the deceased. The High Court found the appellant guilty based on circumstantial evidence and sentenced him to death.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court found the appellant guilty of murder based on circumstantial evidence, including witness testimony, and sentenced him to death.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant argued that the High Court judge failed to evaluate evidence correctly and that the circumstantial evidence was unreliable and did not point solely to the appellant.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Failure to evaluate evidence correctly | Circumstantial evidence unreliable
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the witnesses credible despite minor contradictions, and their testimony supported the circumstantial evidence against the appellant.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court applied the principle that circumstantial evidence must point irresistibly to the guilt of the accused and be inconsistent with innocence.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty, remained silent when called for defence, and did not provide an explanation for the incriminating evidence.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal reviewed the evidence, found that the High Court correctly evaluated the circumstantial evidence, upheld the credibility of witnesses, and applied legal principles from precedents to affirm the conviction.
coa_sentence_type: Death
brief_judgment_file_summary: This is an appeal by Rajagopal Gunasekaram against his conviction for murder by the High Court of Kalutara. The High Court found him guilty based on circumstantial evidence and sentenced him to death. The appellant appealed, arguing insufficient evidence evaluation. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal, upholding the conviction and sentence.
defence_counsel: Jagath Nanayakkara
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court correctly considered circumstantial evidence and found the appellant guilty beyond reasonable doubt, which the Court of Appeal affirmed.
precedents_cited_list: The King Vs. Abeywickrama 44 NLR 254 | Don Sunny Vs. The Attorney General (1998) 2 SLR 01 | Rex Vs. Lord Cochrane and Others (1814) Gurney's Report 479 | The Attorney General Vs. Potta Naufer and Others (2007) 2 SLR 144
standard_of_review_applied: Circumstantial evidence standards requiring evidence to point irresistibly to guilt and be inconsistent with innocence.

judges: N. Bandula Karunarathna, J. | R. Gurusinghe, J.
offence_sections: Section 54(a), (d) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance as amended by Act No. 13 of 1984
brief_facts_summary: The appellant was charged with possession of 31.7 grams of heroin. After being discharged in a previous case, he was re-indicted and escaped custody. Judgments were delivered in his absence, convicting him and sentencing him to death. He was apprehended in 2016 after absconding for over 20 years.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 54(a), (d) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance as amended by Act No. 13 of 1984
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the appellant of drug possession and imposed the death sentence. The judgment was delivered in the appellant's absence after he escaped custody. The judge refused a de novo trial and ordered the sentence to be implemented.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant argued that the judgment was not in conformity with Section 283 of the Criminal Procedure Code and was a nullity. Additionally, the appeal was filed with delay, but revision grounds were raised regarding the second judgment.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Judgment not in conformity with Section 283 of the Criminal Procedure Code | Second judgment delivered without jurisdiction
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The evidence involved possession of heroin, but specific witnesses or analysis are not detailed in the COA judgment. The court focused on the legal and procedural aspects of the judgments.
defence_version_summary: The appellant did not present a defence at trial as he was absconding. After apprehension, he sought a de novo trial, but the High Court rejected his application, and the COA upheld this.
legal_errors_description: The second judgment delivered on 22nd November 1996 was made without jurisdiction and is a nullity, as per Sections 341(1) and 283(4) of the Criminal Procedure Code.
procedural_defects_description: The judgment was not in conformity with Section 283 of the Criminal Procedure Code, and a second judgment was delivered without jurisdiction.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal held that the second judgment was delivered without jurisdiction and set it aside. The first judgment remained, but the appeal was filed out of time and dismissed. The court found no exceptional grounds to act in revision for the first judgment, and upheld the High Court's order to implement the sentence.
coa_sentence_type: Death
brief_judgment_file_summary: The appellant was convicted by the High Court of Colombo for possession of heroin and sentenced to death. He appealed, arguing procedural errors in the judgment. The Court of Appeal found that a second judgment was delivered without jurisdiction and set it aside, but upheld the first judgment. However, the appeal was filed out of time and dismissed, so the conviction and death sentence were upheld.
defence_counsel: R. Arsakularathne PC with Chamindri Arsakularathne
hc_analysis_summary: The COA found that the second judgment was without jurisdiction and a nullity. For the first judgment, there were infirmities but no exceptional grounds for revision.
precedents_cited_list: Rajapaksha Vs. State [2001] (2) Sri Lanka Law Report 161
standard_of_review_applied: Revision jurisdiction

judges: K Priyantha Fernando, J. | Sampath B Abayakoon, J.
offence_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The appellant was indicted for murdering Manikkuge Gunathilaka on 13th April 2016. The deceased made a dying declaration to PW-05, a police officer, describing the attack. The appellant and deceased were known to each other because the appellant's legal wife was the paramour of the deceased.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court found the appellant guilty of murder based on the dying declaration and circumstantial evidence. The judge applied the relevant legal principles for accepting dying declarations and sentenced the appellant to death.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant appealed on the ground that the High Court judge failed to properly consider the infirmities in the dying declaration. The counsel argued that the conviction based solely on the dying declaration is bad in law due to its weaknesses.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Failure to consider the infirmities of the dying declaration in its correct perspective
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal evaluated the dying declaration recorded by PW-05 and found it reliable as the deceased was able to speak and identify the appellant. The medical evidence supported the injuries, and the circumstantial evidence corroborated the declaration.
probability_assessment_by_court: The court assessed the dying declaration and circumstantial evidence and found no reasonable doubt as to the appellant's guilt.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty and challenged the prosecution evidence, particularly the dying declaration. No alibi or defence witnesses were presented, and the court found the prosecution evidence credible.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal considered the legal principles on dying declarations from cited precedents and found that the High Court judge correctly applied them. The dying declaration was reliable as the deceased was able to speak, identified the appellant, and the statement was consistent with medical evidence. No contradictions were found to create doubt, and the appeal was dismissed.
coa_sentence_type: Death
brief_judgment_file_summary: The appellant, Rathnasekaralage Nimal Anthony, was convicted of murder by the High Court of Puttalam and sentenced to death. He appealed to the Court of Appeal, arguing that the High Court failed to properly consider the infirmities in the dying declaration. The Court of Appeal reviewed the evidence, including the dying declaration recorded by PW-05 and circumstantial evidence, and found it reliable. The appeal was dismissed, affirming the conviction and death sentence.
defence_counsel: I.B. Sachitra Harshana
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court correctly applied the legal principles regarding dying declarations and circumstantial evidence. The Court of Appeal agreed with the High Court's analysis and found no errors in its reasoning.
precedents_cited_list: Somasundaram and Others Vs. The Queen 76 NLR 10 | Queen Vs. Anthony Pillai 68 CLW 57 | Sisira de Abrew, J. held in CA-106/2002 decided on 22-08-2007 | King Vs. Asirivadan Nadar 51 NLR 322 | Justin Pala Vs. The Queen 66 NLR 409 | Fradd Vs. Brown and Co. Ltd. 20 NLR, 282
standard_of_review_applied: The appellate court would not lightly disturb the findings of fact by the trial judge, recognizing the advantage of the trial judge.

judges: Arjuna Obeyesekere, J. | Mayadunne Corea, J.
offence_sections: Article 105(3) of the Constitution of the Democratic Socialist Republic of Sri Lanka
brief_facts_summary: The petitioner, a Member of Parliament, was convicted by the Supreme Court for contempt of court for statements made in a TV interview broadcast on 21st August 2017. He was sentenced to four years rigorous imprisonment. He filed a writ application to prohibit the Secretary General from declaring his Parliamentary seat vacant.
evidence_type_primary: Recording of TV interview and Supreme Court judgment
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The petitioner argued that contempt of court is not an offence under Article 89(d) of the Constitution, and that the sentence does not meet the requirements for disqualification from Parliament.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Contempt of court is not an offence that attracts disqualification under Article 89(d) | Article 89(d) requires an offence punishable with imprisonment for a term not less than two years, which contempt does not satisfy
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court relied on the Supreme Court's judgment, legal definitions, and precedents to determine the legal issues without examining witness evidence.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court assessed the legal probability based on constitutional interpretation and precedents, finding no reasonable doubt that contempt is an offence under Article 89(d).
defence_version_summary: The petitioner pleaded not guilty to the disqualification, arguing that contempt of court is not an offence under Article 89(d) and thus he remains qualified as a Member of Parliament.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed Article 89(d) and concluded that contempt of court is an offence punishable with imprisonment, satisfying the conditions for disqualification. They rejected the petitioner's arguments based on precedents and the wording of the Constitution, and held that the Secretary General must inform the Election Commission of the vacancy.
brief_judgment_file_summary: This judgment involves a writ application by a Member of Parliament convicted of contempt of court, seeking to prohibit the Secretary General from declaring his seat vacant. The Court of Appeal held that contempt is an offence under Article 89(d) of the Constitution, triggering automatic disqualification. The Court dismissed the application, upholding that the seat is vacant and must be communicated to the Election Commission.
prosecution_counsel: Ms. Indika Demuni De Silva, P.C., Senior Additional Solicitor General with Nerin Pulle, Senior Deputy Solicitor General, Ms. Suharshi Herath, Senior State Counsel, Dr (Ms.) Avanti Perera, Senior State Counsel, Suren Gnanaraj, Senior State Counsel and Ms. Indumini Randeny, State Counsel
defence_counsel: Faisz Musthapha, P.C., with M.A. Sumanthiran, P.C., Ashan Fernando, Suren Fernando, Keerthi Tillekeratne, Ms. Khyati Wikramanayake and Sanjit Dias
precedents_cited_list: A.M.E. Fernando vs. The Attorney General | SC Rule 1/2004 | Rex v. Electricity Commissioners ex parte London Electricity Joint Committee Co | Gamini Attikorale v. Dayananda Dissanayake, Commissioner of Elections and Others | Seenithamby Palkiararajah v Dayananda Dissanayake, Commissioner of Elections and Others | In Re Bramblevale Ltd | Croos vs. Daberera | S.B. Dissanayake v. Priyani Wijesekera, Secretary General of Parliament and others | Cassel & Co. Ltd Vs. Broome and Another | SC Reference No. 03/2008
standard_of_review_applied: Review of legality under writ jurisdiction for excess of jurisdiction or illegal exercise of power

judges: Devika Abeyratne, J | P. Kumararatnam, J
offence_sections: Section 433(1) of the Penal Code read with section 32 of the Penal Code; Section 296 of the Penal Code read with section 32 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The incident began when a neighbor's dog attacked PW1, the son of the deceased. The deceased went to inquire about the incident and was assaulted by the neighbor and her son. Later that night, the two appellants, armed with a pole and a sword/knife, came to the deceased's garden, assaulted him, and prevented his family from taking him to the hospital. The deceased died from a ruptured spleen caused by blunt force trauma.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 433(1) of the Penal Code read with section 32 of the Penal Code; Section 296 of the Penal Code read with section 32 of the Penal Code
hc_sentence_type: 6 months rigorous imprisonment for count 1; Death sentence for count 2
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the 1st and 2nd accused on both counts of criminal trespass and murder, sentencing them to 6 months rigorous imprisonment for trespass and death for murder. The 3rd accused was acquitted on all counts.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellants argued that the trial judge failed to consider the distinction between Section 293(2) and Section 294(3) of the Penal Code regarding knowledge versus intention. They contended that the prosecution did not prove beyond reasonable doubt that the accused had the intention to cause injuries sufficient to cause death.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Failure to consider distinction between Section 293(2) and 294(3) of the Penal Code | Lack of proof of intention to cause injuries sufficient to cause death
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal considered the eyewitness testimonies of PW1, PW2, and PW3, and the medical evidence of PW8. The medical evidence showed death resulted from a ruptured spleen due to blunt force, with no cut injuries. The court found the eyewitness accounts credible.
probability_assessment_by_court: The court assessed that the prosecution did not prove beyond reasonable doubt the intention to cause death, and thus the offense was culpable homicide not amounting to murder.
defence_version_summary: The accused pleaded not guilty. The defence did not call witnesses. The court found the prosecution evidence credible and rejected the defence.
legal_errors_description: The trial judge failed to properly consider the distinction between knowledge and intention under sections 293(2) and 294(3) of the Penal Code, leading to an erroneous conviction for murder instead of culpable homicide.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal held that the prosecution did not prove beyond reasonable doubt that the accused had the intention to cause injuries sufficient to cause death. Referring to precedents (Ranjith Wijesiri alias Wije Vs AG and King vs Mendis), the court found the offense was culpable homicide not amounting to murder under section 297. The court considered the circumstances: no prior enmity, the trivial origin of the dispute (dog attack), two assaults on the same day, and the medical evidence of a single blunt force injury causing spleen rupture. The murder conviction and death sentence were set aside, and a conviction for culpable homicide with a 10-year rigorous imprisonment sentence was substituted.
coa_sentence_type: For count 1: 6 months rigorous imprisonment (unchanged). For count 2: 10 years rigorous imprisonment.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The appellants were convicted by the High Court of Chilaw for criminal trespass and murder, receiving 6 months rigorous imprisonment and death sentence respectively. They appealed, arguing the trial judge failed to distinguish between knowledge and intention and that intention to cause death was not proven. The Court of Appeal, after considering eyewitness and medical evidence and relevant precedents, set aside the murder conviction and found the appellants guilty of culpable homicide not amounting to murder, sentencing them to 10 years rigorous imprisonment for the homicide charge while upholding the trespass conviction and sentence.
prosecution_counsel: Shanil Kularatne DSG for the Attorney General
defence_counsel: Palitha Fernando PC for the 1st Accused-Appellant; Neranjan Jayasinghe for the 2nd Accused-Appellant
cause_of_death_exact_text: excessive bleeding due to rupture of the spleen due to assault with a blunt weapon.
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted the appellants for murder. The Court of Appeal found the High Court erred by not considering the distinction between knowledge and intention, and that the evidence did not establish intention to cause death, warranting a conviction for culpable homicide instead.
precedents_cited_list: Ranjith Wijesiri alias Wije Vs AG (CA 64/94, decided on 11.03.1999) | King vs Mendis 54 NLR page 177
standard_of_review_applied: The court reviewed whether the prosecution proved the offense beyond reasonable doubt, examining both evidence and legal conclusions.
sentencing_principles_applied: The court considered the time taken to conclude the case, time already spent awaiting appeal, absence of prior animosity, trivial origin of the dispute, the victim's age (45), the threatening behavior of the accused, and the prevention of medical treatment.
final_charge_after_appeal: For count 2, murder was modified to culpable homicide not amounting to murder under section 297 of the Penal Code.

judges: Devika Abeyratne, J. | P. Kumararatanam, J.
brief_facts_summary: On 30.05.2010, the deceased was assaulted by three people with clubs on Samagi Mawatha. He was found injured in a temple and made dying declarations identifying the assailant as Nilanthi's husband. The accused was identified by one witness at an identification parade. The accused denied involvement and surrendered to court.
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the accused for murder based on the dying declaration and identification evidence, and sentenced him to death. The trial judge accepted the dying declaration as believable and found that the prosecution established Nilanthi's husband was responsible.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant argued that the circumstantial evidence, including the dying declaration and identification, created reasonable doubt. The identification parade was doubtful, and the rejection of the dock statement was wrong in law.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The dying declaration and identification create reasonable doubt. | Identification at the parade is doubtful. | Rejection of dock statement is wrong in law.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found that the prosecution failed to establish the identity of Nilanthi as the wife of the accused. The dying declaration was not corroborated, and the identification parade was questionable due to the accused being in court before the parade.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal applied principles of circumstantial evidence and found that the prosecution did not exclude reasonable inferences of innocence.
defence_version_summary: The accused pleaded not guilty and gave a dock statement denying involvement. He stated he surrendered because his name was mentioned. No alibi was presented, and no defence witnesses were called.
legal_errors_description: The High Court erroneously inferred that Nilanthi referred to by the deceased was the wife of the accused without cogent evidence.
procedural_defects_description: The identification parade was conducted after the accused was in court cell, potentially allowing witnesses to see him.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed the circumstantial evidence and found that the prosecution failed to prove beyond reasonable doubt that the Nilanthi referred to was the wife of the accused. The dying declaration was uncorroborated, and the identification parade was compromised. Applying principles from precedents, the COA held that the evidence did not irresistibly point to guilt and allowed the appeal.
coa_sentence_type: Acquitted, no sentence imposed
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused was convicted of murder and sentenced to death by the High Court. He appealed on grounds of doubtful dying declaration and identification. The Court of Appeal found that the prosecution failed to establish the identity of Nilanthi as the accused's wife and that the circumstantial evidence was insufficient. The appeal was allowed, conviction set aside, and accused acquitted.
defence_counsel: Neranjan Jayasinghe with Isansi Danthanarayana
cause_of_death_exact_text: hemorrhage and shock due to the rupture of the spleen
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted based on the dying declaration and identification, but the Court of Appeal found that the High Court erroneously inferred that Nilanthi was the wife of the accused without sufficient evidence.
precedents_cited_list: Queen vs Sumanasena 66 NLR 351 | Iyamperumel Ashokumar Vs. The Attorney General (2010 III ACI 15) (CA 167/07) | Queen vs Kularatne 71 NLR at page 534 | Don Sonny V Attorney General (1998) 2 SLR 1 | R.M Amarasiri Vs The Republic of Sri Lanka CA Appeal 107/2005 | King Vs, Gunaratne 14 Ceylon Law Recorder 174 | Fradd Vs Brown & Company 20 NLR 282 at 283 | State of Uttar Pradesh Vs M.K. Anthony [1984] SCJ 236/[1985] CRI L.J. 493 at 498/499 | Oliver Dayananda Kalansuriya alias Raja Vs Republic of Sri Lanka CA 28/2009 (13.02.2013) | B.R.R.A. Jagath Premawansa V. Attorney General CA Appeal No. 173/2005 decided on 19.03.2009 | Sarwan Singh V. State of Punjab 2002 AIR Supreme Court(iii) 3652 at 3655 and 3656 | Bobby Mathew V, State of Karanataka (2004) 3 Cri.L.J. page 3003 | Himachal Pradesh V. Thakur Dass (1983) 2 Cri.
