standard_of_review_applied: The Court of Appeal reviewed the evidence at large, considering the trial judge's findings but interfering where inferences were erroneous.

judges: N. Bandula Karunarathna, J. | R. Gurusinghe, J.
offence_sections: Section 140 of the Penal Code; Section 296 read with Section 32 of the Penal Code; Section 355 read with Section 146 of the Penal Code; Section 296 read with Section 32 of the Penal Code; Section 296 read with Section 146 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: On 19 March 1989, a group of masked individuals abducted L.M. Andirishamy from his home at night. He was later found dead on the beach with gunshot wounds. The prosecution's case relied on the testimony of the victim's son and daughter who claimed to identify the accused by their voices, as the assailants covered their faces. The accused were from the same or adjoining village.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 140 of the Penal Code; Section 296 read with Section 32 of the Penal Code; Section 355 read with Section 146 of the Penal Code; Section 296 read with Section 32 of the Penal Code; Section 296 read with Section 146 of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the accused of all charges based on the eyewitness testimony, particularly voice identification, and imposed a sentence which was appealed.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellants argued that the identification evidence was unsafe, the complaint was delayed, and other unspecified grounds.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Identification evidence is unsafe | Belatedness of complaint
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the voice identification evidence unreliable as the witnesses could not visually identify the accused, and there was no sufficient evidence that they were intimately familiar with the accused's voices. The delay in naming the accused also cast doubt on the identification.
probability_assessment_by_court: The court found that the prosecution failed to prove the identities of the accused beyond reasonable doubt due to unreliable voice identification and lack of corroborative evidence.
defence_version_summary: The defence denied the charges and argued that the identification evidence was unsafe. No alibi or defence witnesses are mentioned in the judgment.
legal_errors_description: The High Court erred in accepting voice identification evidence without ensuring that the witnesses were intimately familiar with the accused's voices and without corroborative evidence.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal conducted a detailed analysis of the voice identification evidence, referencing legal authorities that highlight the difficulties and risks of relying on voice identification. It found that the witnesses, PW1 and PW2, did not demonstrate sufficient intimacy with the accused to reliably identify them by voice, especially since the assailants covered their faces and only a few words were spoken. The court noted the delay in naming the accused and the lack of corroborative evidence. Based on this, the COA held that the prosecution failed to prove the identities of the accused beyond reasonable doubt, making the conviction unsafe.
coa_sentence_type: Acquitted, no sentence
brief_judgment_file_summary: The case involved an appeal by several accused against their conviction by the High Court of Tangalle for abduction and murder of L.M. Andirishamy in 1989. The High Court convicted them based on voice identification by the victim's son and daughter. The appellants argued that the identification evidence was unsafe and the complaint was delayed. The Court of Appeal found the voice identification unreliable due to lack of familiarity with the accused's voices and other weaknesses, citing legal precedents. Consequently, the appeal was allowed, the conviction and sentence were set aside, and all accused were acquitted.
defence_counsel: Nayantha Wijesundara for the 2nd and 5th Accused-Appellants; Rasik Zarook PC with Rohana Deshapriya, Helani de Silva and Chanakya Liyanage for the 3rd Accused-Appellant; Anil Silva PC for the 4th and 8th Accused-Appellants; Indika Mallawarachchi for the 7th Accused-Appellant; Shanaka Ranasinghe PC with Anusika Ranasinghe and R. Fernando for the 9th Accused-Appellant
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted the accused based on voice identification by witnesses who claimed to recognize the accused from their village. The Court of Appeal found this analysis flawed because the witnesses did not have sufficient opportunity or familiarity to identify the accused by voice, and the evidence was not corroborated.
precedents_cited_list: Nilesh Dinkar Paradkar vs State of Maharashtra | Pratap Singh vs The State of M.P.
standard_of_review_applied: The court reviewed the evidence to determine if the identification was established beyond reasonable doubt and if the conviction was safe.

judges: Devika Abeyratne J | P. Kumararatnam J
offence_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The appellant was accused of murdering Warnakulasuriya Mahalekamlage Mariya Katherine on April 18, 2003. Eye witness PW08 saw the appellant attack the deceased with an axe, and PW09 heard cries and saw the appellant standing with an axe. The appellant surrendered to police and confessed to PW03, and an axe was recovered.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the appellant based on eyewitness testimony, confession, and medical evidence, finding the evidence credible and sentencing him to death.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant argued that the conviction was unsafe due to uncorroborated eyewitness evidence, medical evidence conflicted with ocular testimony, and the judgment did not accord with procedural requirements under section 283 of the Criminal Procedure Code.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The conviction is wholly unsafe in the view of the uncorroborated and unsatisfactory nature of the evidence of the sole eye witness along with the other respective witnesses, led by the prosecution. | Medical evidence conflicts with ocular testimony thereby creating a grave doubt in the prosecution version. | The judgment does not accord with the provision of section 283 of the Criminal Procedure Code Act.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The court found the eyewitness testimony credible and corroborated by other witnesses and confession. Medical evidence was consistent with the assault, and no material contradictions were found.
probability_assessment_by_court: The court assessed the evidence and found it credible beyond reasonable doubt, citing precedents that a single witness can be sufficient if reliable.
defence_version_summary: The appellant made a dock statement, which was rejected by the High Court judge. He did not call witnesses, and the court found the defence not credible.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The COA analyzed each ground: for the first ground, they cited precedents that a single witness can be sufficient if reliable, and found PW08's testimony credible and corroborated. For the second ground, they held that medical evidence does not override ocular testimony when credible, and found consistency. For the third ground, they found that the HC judge properly adopted evidence under section 283. Overall, no merits in the appeal grounds.
coa_sentence_type: Death
brief_judgment_file_summary: The appellant was convicted of murder by the High Court of Chilaw and sentenced to death. He appealed on grounds of uncorroborated evidence, medical inconsistency, and procedural error. The Court of Appeal found the eyewitness testimony credible and consistent with medical evidence, and no procedural defects, thus dismissing the appeal and affirming the conviction and sentence.
defence_counsel: Mr. Rasika Samarawickrama
cause_of_death_exact_text: Cranio-Cerebral injuries due to blunt force trauma of the head (due to blow with a blunt weapon)
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court correctly evaluated evidence, found the eyewitness credible, and convicted the appellant. The COA agreed with this analysis and found no errors.
precedents_cited_list: Sumanasena v. The Attorney General [1999] 3 Sri.L.R 137 | Madduma Siripala and another v. The Attorney General CA/125-126/10 decided on 27/10/2017 | Chacko Alias Aniyan Kunju & others v. State of Kerala [2004] INSC 87 (21st January 2004) | State of Uttar Pradesh v. M.K.Anthony A.I.R (1985) S.C 48 | Menoka Malik and others v. The State of West Bengal and others (2018) 2 SCeJ 1390
standard_of_review_applied: The COA reviewed the evidence and found no reason to interfere with the High Court judgment, citing precedents on evidence evaluation.

judges: Menaka Wijesundera J. | Neil Iddawala J.
offence_sections: Sections 54A and 54B of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance
brief_facts_summary: The suspect, Mohamed Anwar Mohamed Fawaz, was a Warf Clerk at N.M.B Clearing and forwarding Agency. He was ordered to clear a consignment of potatoes, and during inspection at Luniwila, heroin was found. He claims no knowledge and was only doing his duty. He has been in remand since March 2020.
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court denied bail without considering the exceptional circumstances of the suspect's role as a warf clerk with no knowledge of the drugs and lack of evidence.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The petitioner argues that the suspect had no knowledge of the heroin and was only carrying out his duties as a warf clerk, so his incarceration is not justified and the lack of evidence constitutes exceptional circumstances for bail.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Lack of evidence against the suspect | Suspect was only performing duties as a warf clerk with no knowledge of the heroin
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The court found that the suspect had no direct involvement in the drug importation and the prosecution lacked incriminating evidence to link him to the crime.
probability_assessment_by_court: The court assessed that it is not fair to keep the suspect in remand given his role and lack of evidence.
defence_version_summary: The defence argues that the suspect is not guilty as he was unaware of the heroin and merely performed his job responsibilities as a warf clerk following orders.
legal_errors_description: The High Court failed to consider the exceptional circumstances of the suspect's minimal role and lack of evidence when denying bail.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The COA considered the provisions of the Poisons Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance regarding bail only upon exceptional circumstances. They referenced the case Ramu Thamodarumpillai vs. Attorney General for defining exceptionality. The court found that the suspect's role as a warf clerk following orders, with no direct involvement or knowledge, and the lack of incriminating evidence constituted exceptional circumstances, warranting bail.
coa_sentence_type: Bail granted with conditions: cash bail of Rs. 500,000, two sureties of Rs. 1 million each, monthly reporting to Narcotics Bureau, and surrender of passport.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The petitioner sought revision of the High Court's bail denial order for suspect Mohamed Anwar Mohamed Fawaz, charged under sections 54A and 54B for aiding heroin import. The High Court denied bail without considering exceptional circumstances. The Court of Appeal found that the suspect's role as a warf clerk with no knowledge of the drugs and lack of evidence constituted exceptional circumstances, allowing the revision and granting bail with specified conditions.
defence_counsel: Anil Silva PC with N. Perera
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court denied bail without evaluating the suspect's minimal role as a warf clerk and the lack of incriminating evidence. The COA found this omission to be an error, as these factors constitute exceptional circumstances for bail.
precedents_cited_list: Ramu Thamodarumpillai vs. Attorney General 2004 3 SLR 180
standard_of_review_applied: Revision under Article 138 of the Constitution

judges: Menaka Wijesundera J. | Neil Iddawala J.
brief_facts_summary: The High Court convicted the 1st respondent and imposed a sentence of 8 years rigorous imprisonment and a fine. The petitioner, the wife of the convicted 1st respondent, filed a revision application to set aside the High Court judgment. The Court of Appeal did not examine the merits of the case due to procedural defects in the revision application.
hc_sentence_type: 8 years Rigorous imprisonment and a fine
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the 1st respondent and imposed a sentence of 8 years rigorous imprisonment and a fine, and ordered compensation to prosecution witnesses.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The revision application did not specify the grounds for revision. The petitioner failed to aver exceptional circumstances and there was delay and non-disclosure of material facts.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal did not analyze the evidence as the revision application was dismissed on procedural grounds.
defence_version_summary: Not mentioned in the judgment.
procedural_defects_description: The petitioner failed to aver exceptional circumstances, there was inordinate delay of 4.5 years without explanation, and non-disclosure of material fact that an appeal had been filed.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed the revision application and found that the petitioner failed to aver exceptional circumstances, there was unexplained delay of 4.5 years, and non-disclosure of material facts (filing of an appeal). Therefore, the court declined to exercise its revisionary jurisdiction and dismissed the application without going into the merits.
coa_sentence_type: 8 years Rigorous imprisonment and a fine
brief_judgment_file_summary: The petitioner, wife of the convicted 1st respondent, filed a revision application to set aside the High Court judgment convicting the 1st respondent and sentencing him to 8 years rigorous imprisonment and a fine. The Court of Appeal dismissed the application because the petitioner failed to aver exceptional circumstances, there was inordinate delay of 4.5 years without explanation, and non-disclosure of material fact that an appeal had been filed. The court did not examine the merits of the case.
defence_counsel: Shiral D. Wanniarachchi

judges: N. Bandula Karunarathna, J. | R. Gurusinghe, J.
offence_sections: Section 357 read with section 32 of the Penal Code; Section 364(g) read with Section 362(2) of the Penal Code; Section 380 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The prosecutrix and her boyfriend were accosted by the accused while in a three-wheeler. The first accused abducted and raped the prosecutrix, while others restrained the boyfriend. After taking their documents, they were released, and the complaint was made five months later when the boyfriend refused to marry her.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 357 read with section 32 of the Penal Code; Section 364(g) read with Section 362(2) of the Penal Code; Section 380 of the Penal Code
hc_sentence_type: 35 years rigorous imprisonment for first accused; 27 years rigorous imprisonment each for second, third, and fourth accused; fines imposed
hc_judgment_summary: After trial by jury, all appellants were found guilty. The first accused was sentenced to 35 years rigorous imprisonment, and the others to 27 years each, with fines.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: Appellants argued that the trial Judge misdirected the jury, the verdict was unreasonable, and inadmissible confession evidence was improperly admitted. Additionally, the delay in complaint was not properly addressed.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Trial Judge misdirected the jury | Verdict of the jury was unreasonable | Inadmissible confession evidence was improperly admitted | No direction on contradictions as substantive evidence | No direction on delay in complaint
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The COA found that confession evidence was inadmissible and improperly admitted, affecting the jury's verdict. Contradictions in statements were not adequately addressed by the trial judge.
probability_assessment_by_court: COA found defence version equally probable, leading to acquittal.
defence_version_summary: Accused pleaded not guilty. First accused testified in court, denying the charges. The defence version was found equally probable by the COA.
legal_errors_description: Improper admission of confession evidence violating Section 25 of the Evidence Ordinance, and misdirection on contradictions.
procedural_defects_description: Admission of inadmissible confession evidence and lack of proper directions to jury.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The COA held that the trial judge misdirected the jury by allowing inadmissible confession evidence and failing to direct on contradictions. The delay in complaint was not properly addressed. The Deputy Solicitor General conceded the conviction could not be supported. The COA set aside the conviction and acquitted the appellants.
coa_sentence_type: Acquitted, no sentence
brief_judgment_file_summary: Four accused were convicted in High Court for abduction, gang rape, and robbery. They appealed on grounds of misdirection and improper evidence admission. The Court of Appeal found that inadmissible confession evidence was improperly admitted and the trial judge failed to direct the jury properly. The appeal was allowed, convictions set aside, and all accused acquitted.
defence_counsel: Anil Silva, PC
hc_analysis_summary: The COA found that the HC trial judge misdirected the jury and improperly admitted evidence, leading to an unsafe conviction.
precedents_cited_list: Obiyas Appuhamy v. Queen 54 NLR 32 | Anandagoda v. Queen 64 NLR 39 | The Queen v Abadda 66 NLR 397 | Punchi Banda v The State 76 NLR 293 | Babysingho v The Queen 75 NLR 451
standard_of_review_applied: Review for legal errors and miscarriage of justice

judges: Menaka Wijesundera J. | Neil Iddawala J.
offence_sections: Sections 54A and 54B of the Poisons and Opium and Dangerous Drugs Act No. 13 of 1984
brief_facts_summary: The accused was arrested on 25.3.2016 for possession of 5kg and 240 grams of heroin gross weight. He has been in remand custody for over five years. The integrity of the arresting officers is in doubt as some are now incarcerated for similar offences.
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court order dated 10.9.2020 likely related to bail or remand, which the accused is challenging as unfair.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The accused denies the allegation and argues that remand for over five years is unfair, especially since the arresting officers are now incarcerated for similar offences, casting doubt on the investigation's integrity.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Denial of allegation | Unfair remand for over five years | Doubtful integrity of arresting officers
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal considered the credibility of the investigations due to the arresting officers' incarceration, questioning the fairness of prolonged remand.
probability_assessment_by_court: Court considered the presumption of innocence and personal liberty in pre-trial detention.
defence_version_summary: The accused pleaded not guilty and denied the allegation, with no alibi or defence witnesses mentioned.
legal_errors_description: The High Court order did not adequately consider the questionable investigations and the fairness of long remand.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The COA applied revisionary jurisdiction under Article 138 and Section 404, noting the arresting officers' incarceration raises doubts on investigation credibility. It emphasized the presumption of innocence and personal liberty, finding the HC order improper and granting bail under exceptional conditions.
coa_sentence_type: Bail granted with conditions: cash bail of Rs 2 million, two sureties of Rs 1 million each, reporting to police on Sundays, and surrender of passport.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The Court of Appeal allowed a revision application against the High Court order. The accused was arrested for heroin possession and had been in remand for over five years. The court found the investigations questionable due to arresting officers' incarceration, and granted bail with specific conditions.
defence_counsel: Tenny Fernando with Prashani Matharage
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court order did not consider the doubt on investigation credibility and the fairness of prolonged remand. COA found this improper.
precedents_cited_list: Ramu Thamodarumpillai vs. Attorney General 2004 3 SLR 180 | Attorney General vs. Ranasinghe and others 1993 (2) SLR81
standard_of_review_applied: Revision under Article 138 of the Constitution and Section 404 of the Code of Criminal Procedure Act, considering illegality, impropriety, or irregularity of the order.

judges: N. Bandula Karunarathna J. | R. Gurusinghe J.
offence_sections: Section 296 read with Section 32 of the Penal Code and Section 314 read with Section 32 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: On January 9, 2001, the deceased and PW5 were attending a funeral at Gotabaya Road when the accused-appellants arrived armed with knives and cleavers. PW5 was assaulted, and the deceased was stabbed to death while fleeing. The prosecution relied on eyewitness accounts, and the accused were convicted for murder.
evidence_type_secondary: Physical evidence (knife, vehicles) and documentary evidence
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 296 read with Section 32 of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: High Court convicted the accused-appellants for murder based on eyewitness testimony, particularly PW1, and sentenced them to death. They were acquitted on the second charge of causing hurt.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: Appellants argued that the High Court failed to consider contradictions in witness testimonies, did not properly evaluate dock statements, denied a fair trial to the third accused-appellant, and erred in law by continuing the trial after requesting a predecessor.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Failure to consider contradictory versions of evidence | Failure to consider principle of common murderous intention | Failure to evaluate dock statement | Denial of fair trial | Failure to analyse evidence | Error in law by continuing trial after requesting Chief Justice | Failure to satisfy test of credibility | Error in rejecting omissions marked by defence
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: Court of Appeal found PW1's testimony credible and consistent, corroborated by PW5 and PW6. Minor contradictions were disregarded as not affecting the core case.
probability_assessment_by_court: Court assessed witness credibility and found no reasonable doubt, disregarding minor discrepancies.
defence_version_summary: Accused pleaded not guilty, made statements from the dock denying involvement, called no defence witnesses, and the court found their statements to be blanket denials without substantive defence.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: COA thoroughly reviewed evidence, found High Court correctly evaluated witness testimonies and common intention, addressed fair trial and procedural grounds citing precedents, and concluded appeal lacked merit, dismissing it.
coa_sentence_type: Death
brief_judgment_file_summary: Accused-appellants were convicted for murder by High Court of Negombo and sentenced to death. They appealed on grounds including contradictions in witness evidence, unfair trial, and procedural errors. COA analyzed evidence, found eyewitness testimony credible, upheld common intention, and dismissed appeal affirming conviction and death sentence.
defence_counsel: Neranjan Jayasinghe with Isansi Dantanarayana for 2nd Accused-Appellant; Anil Silva PC with Thaia Rulihan for 3rd Accused-Appellant; Saliya Peiris PC with Navindi Ekanayake for 4th Accused-Appellant
hc_analysis_summary: High Court convicted based on credible eyewitness testimony, particularly PW1, and properly applied law on common intention. COA agreed with this analysis.

judges: K Priyantha Fernando, J. | Sampath B Abayakoon, J.
offence_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The deceased was in an illicit relationship with the appellant and had two children. On August 19, 2009, the appellant came home drunk, assaulted her, dragged her to their house, poured kerosene on her, and set her on fire. She died seven days later. The prosecution relied on dying declarations and circumstantial evidence.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court found the appellant guilty of murder based on circumstantial evidence and dying declarations, and sentenced him to death.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant argued that the trial judge failed to adopt evidence from predecessors as required by section 48 of the Judicature Act, and failed to consider evidence of grave and sudden provocation under section 294 Exception 1 of the Penal Code.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The learned trial judge failed to adopt the evidence led before his predecessors under section 48 of the Judicature Act. | The learned trial judge failed to consider the evidence of grave and sudden provocation.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The court analyzed the dying declarations and found them reliable. The appellant did not set up a defence and made a dock statement denying knowledge of the deceased.
probability_assessment_by_court: The court found the appellant's intention established beyond reasonable doubt based on the evidence.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty, made a dock statement denying knowing the deceased, and called witnesses including his wife and Grama Niladari. The court found his defence not credible.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The COA analyzed the procedural ground and found that the trial judge complied with section 48 of the Judicature Act as the appellant did not demand to re-summon witnesses. For the provocation ground, the COA found no evidence to support grave and sudden provocation, citing precedents on burden of proof. The COA upheld the HC conviction and sentence, dismissing the appeal.
coa_sentence_type: Death
brief_judgment_file_summary: The appellant was convicted of murder and sentenced to death by the High Court of Nuwaraeliya. He appealed on grounds of procedural error under section 48 of the Judicature Act and failure to consider grave and sudden provocation. The Court of Appeal found no merit in the grounds, upheld the conviction and sentence, and dismissed the appeal.
defence_counsel: Indika Mallawarachchi
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted the appellant based on circumstantial evidence and dying declarations. The Court of Appeal agreed with this analysis and found no errors.
precedents_cited_list: K.D.J.Perera Vs. The King (1951) 53 NLR 193 | Kulanthaivel Ramesh alias Vishvalingam Sasikumar Vs. The Attorney General, C.A.Appeal Case No-16/2013 | R.M.Karunaratne Vs. standard_of_review_applied: Review of legal and factual errors

judges: N. Bandula Karunarathna J. | R. Gurusinghe J.
offence_sections: sections 370 and 394 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: On 24 July 2004, motor spare parts were found in the locker of the 2nd respondent, an employee of Sri Lanka Transport Board. He was arrested and charged under Penal Code, but acquitted by Magistrate's Court due to insufficient evidence. A disciplinary inquiry found him guilty on some charges, leading to suspension and transfer. An arbitrator awarded him back payments, which the petitioner challenges.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: Petitioner argues that the arbitrator failed to consider reasons for delay in disciplinary inquiry due to pending criminal cases, that the award includes unreasonable payments like festival and disaster advances, and that the arbitrator acted arbitrarily.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Failure to consider delay in domestic inquiry due to pending criminal cases | Failure to consider that criminal discharges were on technical grounds | Award includes festival-advance-payments and disaster-advance-payments unreasonably | Arbitrator acted arbitrarily and not judiciously
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court found that the criminal case against the 2nd respondent lacked evidence, resulting in acquittal, and the petitioner's delay in disciplinary inquiry was not justified, making the arbitrator's award mostly valid except for advance payments.
probability_assessment_by_court: Magistrate's Court acquitted due to insufficient evidence; Court of Appeal found arbitrator's award mostly justified.
defence_version_summary: The 2nd respondent was acquitted in criminal court, found guilty in disciplinary inquiry on some charges, and the arbitrator awarded him payments, which he defends in court.
legal_errors_description: Arbitrator erred in ordering festival-advance-payments and disaster-advance-payments as they were not entitlements for past periods.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal reviewed the writ application, noting that the minister's referral to arbitration was valid. The court found that the arbitrator acted within jurisdiction except for ordering advance payments, which was unreasonable as the periods had lapsed. The court held that the petitioner delayed the disciplinary inquiry without justification, and the 2nd respondent was acquitted in criminal court due to lack of evidence. Therefore, the award was affirmed except for the advance payments.
coa_sentence_type: Payment of arrears of salaries, allowances, and annual increments for the period from 29.07.2004 to 12.05.2011, excluding festival-advance-payments and disaster-advance-payments.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The Sri Lanka Transport Board petitioned the Court of Appeal to quash an arbitration award in favor of an employee, H.A. Cyril, who was acquitted of criminal charges. The Court partly allowed the writ, quashing the part of the award for festival and disaster advance payments, but upholding the payment of arrears of salaries and allowances for the suspension period.
precedents_cited_list: Queen v. The Commissioner for Special Purposes of Income Tax (1888) 21 Q.B.D. 313 | Jayaweera v. Wijeratne (1985) 2 SLR 413
standard_of_review_applied: Review based on want or excess of jurisdiction, denial of natural justice, and error on the face of the record.

judges: Devika Abeyratne, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 140, 296, 146, 300, 32 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: On November 16, 2003, at Beruwala, the deceased Mohamad Jabeer Mohamad Rizmi was assaulted by an unlawful assembly. PW2, an eyewitness, intervened and was also injured with a knife. The accused were known to the witnesses and were armed with knives and clubs. Medical evidence confirmed injuries to PW2 and the deceased.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 140, 296, 146, 300, 32 of the Penal Code
hc_sentence_type: Death sentence for murder, 18 years rigorous imprisonment for attempted murder, 6 months rigorous imprisonment for unlawful assembly
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted all accused on all five counts, imposing death sentence for murder, 18 years rigorous imprisonment for attempted murder, and 6 months for unlawful assembly. The judge found the prosecution evidence credible and established guilt beyond reasonable doubt.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellants argued that the trial judge failed to properly assess the credibility of prosecution witnesses PW1 and PW2 due to contradictions and inconsistencies. They also challenged the dock identification as bad in law and contended that the conviction under unlawful assembly was erroneous.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Evidence of prosecution witnesses lacks credibility due to contradictions | Failure to consider contradictions in medical history | Dock identification is bad in law | Error in convicting under unlawful assembly
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found PW2's eyewitness testimony credible despite minor contradictions, upheld the trial judge's assessment, and noted that failure to cross-examine on material points led to admission of evidence.
probability_assessment_by_court: The court assessed that the prosecution proved guilt beyond reasonable doubt, considering witness credibility and medical evidence, and found no material contradictions.
defence_version_summary: The accused pleaded not guilty, raised alibi for some accused (2nd, 4th, 6th, 7th), made dock statements only, and called no defence witnesses. The court found the defence not credible and inconsistent.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal thoroughly reviewed the evidence, including witness testimony and medical reports. It found that PW2's evidence was credible and consistent, minor contradictions did not affect the root of the case, and the trial judge correctly applied the law on unlawful assembly. The COA upheld the trial judge's findings based on the advantage of observing witness demeanor and the principles from cited precedents.
coa_sentence_type: Death sentence for murder (count 2), 18 years rigorous imprisonment for attempted murder (count 3), 6 months rigorous imprisonment for unlawful assembly (count 1)
brief_judgment_file_summary: This Court of Appeal judgment involves an appeal by accused-appellants against their conviction and sentence by the High Court for murder, attempted murder, and unlawful assembly. The High Court imposed death sentence and imprisonment. The appellants challenged witness credibility, identification, and legal errors. The COA dismissed the appeal, affirming the conviction and sentence, finding no material errors in the trial judge's assessment.
defence_counsel: Shanaka Ranasinghe, PC; Nalin Ladduwahetty, PC
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted based on eyewitness and medical evidence. The COA found no errors in the HC's reasoning and upheld its decision.
precedents_cited_list: Wannaku Arachchilage Gunapala vs Attorney General 2007 SLR, Volume 1, page 273 | Sarwan Singh vs State of Punjab 220 AIC SC (111)3652 at 3655, 3656 | Pattipati Venkaiah v State of Andra Pradesh AIR 1985 SC 1715 | Bhargavan v State of Kerala AIR 2004 SC 1058 | Dolawatte vs Attorney General 1986 (1) SLR 371 | Bhoginbhai vs State of Gujarat (1983) AIR SC 753 | H.K.K. Habakkala vs Attorney General 2010 BLR at page 102 | Ajith Samarakoon s The State 2994 2 SLR page 208 at page 230 | King vs Abeywickrama 44 NLR 254 | Sigera Vs Attorney General 2011 1 SLR 201
standard_of_review_applied: The COA applied a standard of not interfering with factual findings of the trial judge who observed witness demeanor, as per Sigera case.

judges: Devika Abeyratne J | P. Kumararatnam J
offence_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: Appellants, police officers, received information about illicit timber transport and went to stop a lorry. The driver defied orders and drove towards them, prompting the 2nd Appellant to fire shots, one of which killed the deceased. Key evidence includes witness accounts, recovery of gun and timber logs, and JMO report confirming gunshot wound.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 297 of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: High Court convicted Appellants under section 297 for exceeding limits of power as police officers, leading to death. Sentenced to 30 months rigorous imprisonment and fine of Rs.10,000 each.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: Appellants contend that High Court erred in finding 2nd Appellant exceeded limits of power vested in him as a police officer. They argue that since the act was committed in the course of duty, High Court ought not to have found them guilty.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: HC erred in judgement that 2nd Appellant exceeded limits of power as police officer | HC should not have found guilt as act was committed in course of duties
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: Court of Appeal considered that witnesses did not directly see the shooting, but evidence showed Appellants acted in good faith to prevent crime. The JMO report confirmed cause of death, and there was evidence of illicit timber transport.
probability_assessment_by_court: Court found that Appellants acted in good faith under section 69, so there was reasonable doubt about guilt.
defence_version_summary: Appellants pleaded not guilty and gave evidence from witness box. They claimed they were performing their duty as police officers to stop illicit timber transport, and the shooting was necessary to stop the lorry that threatened their lives. Court found their actions were in good faith.
legal_errors_description: High Court failed to apply section 69 of Penal Code, which protects acts done in good faith under legal duty.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: Court of Appeal analyzed that Appellants, as police officers, were acting under section 56 of Police Ordinance to prevent crime. The lorry driver disobeyed orders and threatened their lives, justifying the use of force. Considering section 69 of Penal Code, the act was done in good faith under legal duty, so should not be an offence. Therefore, conviction was set aside.
coa_sentence_type: Acquitted, no sentence imposed
brief_judgment_file_summary: This appeal involves two police officers convicted for murder under section 297 by High Court of Kalutara. They appealed on grounds that they acted in course of duty and did not exceed powers. Court of Appeal found that they acted in good faith under section 69 of Penal Code to prevent crime, set aside conviction, and acquitted them.
defence_counsel: Mr. A.S.M. Perera PC with Ms. Prabothini Kumarawadu for 1st Appellant; Mr. Yalith Wijesurendra for 2nd Appellant
cause_of_death_exact_text: one gunshot entry wound in the back of the head of the deceased which had damaged the brain and caused the death
hc_analysis_summary: High Court convicted Appellants for exceeding powers as police officers. Court of Appeal viewed that High Court should have considered the defence under section 69 for acts done in good faith in course of duty.
standard_of_review_applied: Court reviewed legal errors in High Court judgment regarding application of section 69 of Penal Code.

judges: K. PRIVANTHA FERNANDO, J. (P/CA) | SAMPATH B. ABAYAKOON, J.
offence_sections: Section 296 and 316 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The appellant was accused of murdering Hetitarachchige Thilaka by hitting her on the head with a katty knife. The incident occurred at the deceased's house after she mocked the appellant. The appellant claimed he acted in self-defence after being attacked with chilli powder and a club. The prosecution relied on eyewitness testimony and medical evidence.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the appellant for murder and sentenced him to death. The judge rejected the defences of grave and sudden provocation and self-defence based on medical evidence and inconsistencies in the appellant's version.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant appealed on grounds that the trial judge failed to appreciate defence evidence, consider private defence or provocation, prove murderous intention, and address contradictions in the prosecution case.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: That the learned trial Judge failed to appreciate the defence evidence. | That the learned trial Judge failed to consider that there had been grave and sudden provocation which provoked the appellant. | That the prosecution has failed to prove the murderous intention or knowledge on the part of the appellant. | That the learned trial Judge has failed to consider the contradictions and omissions of the prosecution case.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the eyewitness testimony credible and consistent. The medical evidence contradicted the appellant's self-defence claim, and any contradictions were minor and did not affect the core of the prosecution case.
probability_assessment_by_court: The court found no reasonable doubt based on credible eyewitness and medical evidence, rejecting the appellant's defences.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty and claimed self-defence, arguing he was provoked and acted in self-defence after being attacked. The court found his version inconsistent with medical evidence and not credible.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed the grounds of appeal and found that the provocation was not sudden due to the time gap between the mocking and the assault. The High Court judge properly considered the defences and evidence, with medical evidence supporting intentional killing. Contradictions in prosecution evidence were minor and did not affect credibility. Therefore, the conviction and sentence were affirmed.
coa_sentence_type: Death
brief_judgment_file_summary: The appellant was convicted of murder by the High Court of Hambantota and sentenced to death. He appealed on grounds including failure to consider defence evidence, provocation, and contradictions. The Court of Appeal found no merit in the appeals, upholding the High Court's decision based on credible eyewitness testimony and medical evidence. The appeal was dismissed, and the conviction and sentence affirmed.
defence_counsel: Nihara Randeniya
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted the appellant based on eyewitness testimony and medical evidence, rejecting the defences of provocation and self-defence. The Court of Appeal agreed with this analysis and found no errors in the High Court's judgment.

judges: Devika Abeyratne,J | P.Kumararatnam,J
offence_sections: Section 19(b) and Section 19(C) of the Bribery Act
brief_facts_summary: The accused-appellant, a school principal, was charged with soliciting a bribe of Rs. 25000 from a parent to admit her child to Grade 6. The parent did not pay the full amount, and the child was later removed from the school. A complaint was made to the Bribery Commission, leading to the prosecution.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 19(b) and Section 19(C) of the Bribery Act
hc_sentence_type: Four years rigorous imprisonment on each count to run concurrently, and a fine of Rs 2500 on each count with default imprisonment of two years rigorous imprisonment for non-payment of fine.
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the appellant on two counts of soliciting a bribe. The court found the prosecution evidence credible and sentenced the appellant to imprisonment and fine.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant argued denial of fair trial due to material non-disclosure, insufficient evidence to prove the case beyond reasonable doubt, misdirection by the trial judge, failure of prosecution to discharge its burden, and errors in the sentencing process.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The accused appellant was denied a right to Fair Trial, inter alia by material non-disclosure. | Even the evidence given and produced (though selective) there is plenty of evidence to raise a reasonable doubt in favour of the Appellant. | The serious misdirection by the learned trial judge. | Burden of proof in criminal trials; the prosecution has not discharged its burden according to law. | No evidence of the Bribery Commission having given their mind inter alia to a direction to prosecute in this case which goes to the root of the court's jurisdiction. | The Sentencing process is wrong in law
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the evidence of the main prosecution witness (PW1) contradictory and uncorroborated. The prosecution failed to call a material witness (Hansani) who could have corroborated the solicitation claim, raising reasonable doubt.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal found that the prosecution failed to prove the case beyond reasonable doubt. The evidence was contradictory and uncorroborated, and the benefit of doubt must go to the appellant.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty and denied the allegations. She stated that the money was for the School Development Fund and that she gave the account number to the parent. She did not call witnesses but made a dock statement, asserting she never solicited money or asked the child to leave school.
legal_errors_description: The trial judge misdirected himself by failing to consider vital discrepancies in the evidence and the lack of corroboration. The prosecution failed to prove the case beyond reasonable doubt.
procedural_defects_description: The prosecution failed to call a material witness (Hansani) and there was material non-disclosure of evidence such as the initial police statement, probation report, and HRC report.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal thoroughly analyzed the evidence and found contradictions between the testimonies of PW1 and PW3. The prosecution did not call a key witness (Hansani) who was present during the alleged offer of money. Citing precedents, the Court emphasized the need for corroboration in bribery cases and held that the uncorroborated and contradictory evidence of PW1 was insufficient to prove solicitation beyond reasonable doubt. Therefore, the conviction was unsafe.
coa_sentence_type: Conviction and sentence set aside; appellant acquitted.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused-appellant, a school principal, was convicted by the High Court on two counts of soliciting a bribe and sentenced to imprisonment and fine. She appealed on grounds including denial of fair trial, insufficient evidence, and misdirection. The Court of Appeal found the evidence of the main witness contradictory and uncorroborated, and the prosecution failed to call a material witness. The Court allowed the appeal, set aside the conviction and sentence, and acquitted the appellant.
prosecution_counsel: Subashini Siriwardena with Anusha Sammandapperuma for the Complainant-Respondent
defence_counsel: Eraj De Silva with Hafeel Fariz, Janagam Sundaramoorthy and Daminda Wijesuriya for the Accused-Appellant
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted the appellant based on the evidence of PW1 and PW3. The Court of Appeal found that the trial judge failed to consider vital discrepancies in their evidence and the lack of corroboration, and misdirected himself in evaluating the evidence.

The Director General, Commission to Investigate Allegations of Bribery or Corruption, 2009 2 SLR 151 SC
standard_of_review_applied: The Court of Appeal reviewed the evidence and applied the standard of proof beyond reasonable doubt, assessing whether the prosecution proved its case.

judges: K. Priyantha Fernando, J. (P/CA) | Sampath B. Abayakoon, J.
offence_sections: Section 364(1) of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The victim, a 20-year-old woman, was allegedly raped by her step-father, the appellant, while she was unconscious at home. She delayed reporting due to threats and fear, but later made a complaint after encouragement from a social worker. Medical evidence indicated vaginal penetration, but no direct evidence of penile penetration. The appellant was a 57-year-old disabled person and sole breadwinner.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 364(1) of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the appellant of rape under Section 364(1) of the Penal Code, sentencing him to 15 years rigorous imprisonment, a fine of Rs. 20,000, and compensation of Rs. 200,000 to the victim.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant argued that the trial judge failed to consider the belated complaint, assess PW1's credibility, consider material contradictions, and that prosecution failed to prove the case beyond reasonable doubt.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The learned trial Judge had failed to consider the belatedness of PW1’s complaint to the police against the appellant. | The learned trial Judge failed to assess the credibility and trustworthiness of PW1’s evidence. | The learned trial Judge failed to consider the material contradictions in the prosecution evidence. | The prosecution failed to prove the case beyond reasonable doubt.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court found the delay in complaint justifiable due to the victim's vulnerability and threats. PW1's evidence was consistent, and medical evidence confirmed penetration, but penile penetration was not proven.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court found that prosecution failed to prove penile penetration beyond reasonable doubt, but proved penetration for Grave Sexual Abuse.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty. No defence witnesses were mentioned. The court found the prosecution evidence credible for penetration but not for penile penetration.
legal_errors_description: The High Court erred in convicting the appellant for rape when prosecution failed to prove penile penetration beyond reasonable doubt.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed the delay in complaint and found it justifiable due to the victim's vulnerability and threats. The medical evidence confirmed vaginal penetration, but no evidence of penile penetration. Applying Sections 176 and 177 of the Criminal Procedure Act, the Court held that the appellant could be convicted for the lesser offence of Grave Sexual Abuse under Section 365B, as the elements were proven beyond reasonable doubt. The Court considered mitigatory factors but imposed a sentence of 10 years rigorous imprisonment, fine, and compensation.
coa_sentence_type: Rigorous Imprisonment 10 years, Fine, Compensation
brief_judgment_file_summary: The appellant was convicted by the High Court of Chilaw for rape and sentenced to 15 years imprisonment. He appealed on grounds of belated complaint, credibility issues, contradictions, and insufficient proof. The Court of Appeal found that prosecution failed to prove penile penetration for rape but proved vaginal penetration for Grave Sexual Abuse. Applying Sections 176 and 177 of the Criminal Procedure Act, the Court convicted the appellant for Grave Sexual Abuse, sentencing him to 10 years rigorous imprisonment, a fine of Rs. 5,000, and compensation of Rs. 100,000. The appeal was allowed in part.
defence_counsel: Duminda De Alwis and Charuni De Alwis
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted the appellant for rape based on victim testimony and medical evidence. The Court of Appeal found that the High Court failed to consider the lack of proof for penile penetration, which is essential for rape.
precedents_cited_list: Sumanasena v. Attorney General [1999] 3 Sri LR 137 | Sumarakooon v. The Republic [2004] 2 Sri LR 209 | King v. Piyasena [1942] 44 NLR 58 | CA appeal no. 88/2002 | Mohamed Aboobakar Ibrahim v. Hon. Attorney General CA 191/2002
standard_of_review_applied: Review based on whether prosecution proved case beyond reasonable doubt.
sentencing_principles_applied: The Court considered mitigatory factors such as appellant's age, disability, and family status, but also the seriousness of the offence and vulnerability of the victim.
final_charge_after_appeal: Grave Sexual Abuse under Section 365B of the Penal Code

judges: N. Bandula Karunarathna J. | R. Gurusinghe J.
offence_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code read with Section 32 for murder; Section 300 of the Penal Code read with Section 32 for attempted murder; Section 44(a) of the Fire Arms Act No 33 of 1916 for use of firearm
brief_facts_summary: On 28.04.2001, six individuals were murdered and others injured in a house at Balawinna. The prosecution alleged the accused were part of an unlawful assembly armed with weapons, motivated by a dispute over sheltering the first accused's mother. Key evidence included eyewitness identifications by Dinesh Sampath and Chaminda, recovery of swords and a gun, and testimony from witnesses about the accused's movements after the incident.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 296 read with Section 32 of the Penal Code for murder; Section 300 read with Section 32 of the Penal Code for attempted murder
hc_sentence_type: Death for murder; 5 years rigorous imprisonment for attempted murder
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court acquitted the 5th and 6th accused of all charges and acquitted all accused on counts based on unlawful assembly. The 1st to 4th accused were convicted for murder under Section 296 read with Section 32 and sentenced to death, and the 1st and 4th accused were convicted for attempted murder under Section 300 read with Section 32 and sentenced to 5 years rigorous imprisonment. The conviction was based on eyewitness testimony and recovered evidence.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellants argued that the trial judge failed to properly analyze evidence, overlooked contradictions in eyewitness testimony, erred in identity identification, misapplied law regarding confession admissibility, drew adverse inference from absconding without considering innocent explanation, and improperly rejected alibi defence.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The learned trial Judge failed to analyse the evidence led by the prosecution. | The learned trial Judge failed to consider that the contradictions and omissions marked specially in the evidence of the two eyewitnesses, PW 2 and PW 3, create a reasonable doubt on the case. | The learned trial Judge erred on facts that the identity of the accused-appellants by PW 2 and PW 3. | The learned trial Judge failed to consider the fact that evidence lead on behalf of the accused-appellants also creates a reasonable doubt on the prosecution case. | The learned trial Judge applied two different criteria to evaluate the evidence against the accused-appellants. | All the accused-appellants have denied any involvement in the murder incident. Therefore, the omissions and contradictions of the prosecution witnesses have to be scrutinized very carefully rather than simply disregarding them as immaterial. The trial Judge has failed to do it. | The trial Judge has adopted 2 different inequitable bases in analysing the evidence for the prosecution witnesses and the defence witnesses. He was very lenient for the prosecution witnesses and the defence witnesses, he was very strict. | This inequitable basis has deprived a fair trial to the accused-appellants. | The trial Judge has not given valid reasons for rejecting the defence evidence. | The medical evidence revealed that the injured witness told the doctor that a gang has attacked them. But he did not disclose the names of the accused persons. The doctor has to record the names of the attackers and if unknown, then it should be recorded. The trial Judge has failed to consider that aspect.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found eyewitness testimony from Dinesh Sampath and Chaminda credible, as they identified the accused under torchlight, and their evidence was consistent with medical and physical evidence. Contradictions were deemed not material to the core case.
probability_assessment_by_court: The COA assessed that the prosecution proved its case beyond reasonable doubt, and contradictions did not create doubt.
defence_version_summary: The accused pleaded not guilty. The 2nd accused gave a dock statement claiming alibi and false implication due to prior assault. The 3rd accused testified and called defence witnesses. The court found the alibi defence not properly raised under section 126A and rejected it as an afterthought.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal thoroughly analyzed the evidence, including eyewitness identification under torchlight, addressing contradictions and omissions. It found the identification reliable and supported by medical evidence and weapon recoveries. The COA rejected arguments regarding confession admissibility under Section 30, noting no violation. It considered absconding evidence but found innocent explanations insufficient. The alibi defence was rejected due to lack of notice under section 126A. Precedents on voice identification and evidence evaluation were applied. Ultimately, the COA upheld the High Court's conviction, finding no legal errors or miscarriage of justice.
coa_sentence_type: Death sentence for murder and 5 years rigorous imprisonment for attempted murder upheld
brief_judgment_file_summary: This appeal concerns the conviction and death sentence of accused-appellants for murdering six people and attempting murder of others at Godakawela in 2001. The High Court of Embilipitiya convicted the 1st to 4th accused for murder under Section 296 read with Section 32 and sentenced them to death, and for attempted murder with imprisonment. The appellants appealed on grounds including evidence analysis, identification errors, confession admissibility, absconding inference, and alibi defence. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal, finding eyewitness testimony credible, contradictions immaterial, no legal misdirection, and alibi defence improperly raised. The conviction and sentences were affirmed.
defence_counsel: Dharmasiri Karunaratne for 1st accused-appellant (appeal dismissed), Anil Silva PC with Isuru Jayawardana AAL for 2nd accused-appellant, Nihara Randeniya AAL for 4th accused-appellant (3rd appellant)
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted based on eyewitness testimony, medical evidence, and recovered weapons. The COA found no errors in this analysis and upheld the decision.

standard_of_review_applied: The COA reviewed the evidence and findings of the High Court, finding no reason to interfere as the prosecution proved its case beyond reasonable doubt.

judges: N. Bandula Karunarathna J. | R. Gurusinghe J.
offence_sections: section 54 a (d) of the Poisons, Opium, and Dangerous Drugs (amended) Ordinance
brief_facts_summary: The appellant is the registered owner of vehicle WP KD 9832, which was taken into custody on 21.11.2012 for being used to possess and traffic cannabis by the 5th accused and others. Five accused were indicted for possession and trafficking of 4 kg and 330 g of cannabis and pleaded guilty on 27.11.2017. The High Court initially did not order confiscation of the vehicle, but after an application by the appellant, an inquiry was held and the vehicle was confiscated.
evidence_type_primary: Testimony of vehicle owner and company manager, written rental agreement
evidence_type_secondary: Police evidence of arrest and accused's statement
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: section 54 a (d) of the Poisons, Opium, and Dangerous Drugs (amended) Ordinance
hc_sentence_type: For the 5 accused: For first charge - fine of Rs. 25,000 each with 6 months simple imprisonment in default; for second charge - 2 years rigorous imprisonment suspended for 10 years each. For the vehicle: Confiscation.
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the 5 accused on their guilty pleas for possession and trafficking of cannabis. Upon the appellant's application, the court held a vehicle inquiry and ordered the confiscation of the vehicle, finding the appellant had not taken adequate precautions to prevent its illegal use.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant argued there was no evidence the vehicle was used for the offence, that he had no knowledge of the offence and had given reasonable explanations, that he took precautions to prevent illegal use, and that confiscation violated his property and human rights.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: No evidence to establish that the vehicle had been used for the commission of the offence. | Confiscating the vehicle is bad in law when the appellant has given reasonable and acceptable explanations as to that he did not have any knowledge about this culpable act. | The learned Provincial High Court Judge erred in law and fact to confiscate the vehicle when the claimant has presented acceptable evidence to prove that he has taken precautions to prevent the commission of the offence using the vehicle. | The appellant has proved that he has taken necessary precautions to prevent the use of the vehicle for a crime on a balance of probability. | Confiscating the appellant's vehicle for an offence that was done without his knowledge and participation in violation of his human rights. | The concept of a property right had been violated. | The right to equal protection, the equal benefit of the law and access to equal justice had been violated.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed the testimony of the appellant and the manager of Ashan Enterprises, finding the appellant's evidence on precautions and lack of knowledge was unchallenged and credible. The prosecution led no evidence at the vehicle inquiry.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal found the appellant had, on a balance of probability, taken precautions and had no knowledge of the offence.
defence_version_summary: The appellant (vehicle owner) pleaded not involved. He testified he rented the vehicle to Ashan Enterprises, visited the company, gave verbal instructions against illegal use, and had no knowledge of the offence. The court found his evidence credible and accepted.
legal_errors_description: The High Court judge erred in law and fact by confiscating the vehicle without considering evidence that the appellant took precautions and had no knowledge, and by misapplying the law on forfeiture under Section 79 of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal held that forfeiture under Section 79 is not automatic and the owner must be heard. It found the prosecution led no evidence the vehicle was used for the offence. The appellant's evidence of precautions (visits, verbal instructions) and lack of knowledge was unchallenged in cross-examination. The manager's testimony supported the existence of internal company agreements restricting vehicle use. Applying Manawadu vs AG, the COA found the appellant discharged his burden on a balance of probability. The High Court failed to consider this evidence and misdirected itself on the law.
coa_sentence_type: Confiscation order set aside; vehicle ordered to be released to the appellant.
brief_judgment_file_summary: This appeal concerned the confiscation of a vehicle used in a drug offence. The appellant, the registered owner, argued he had no knowledge and took precautions. The Court of Appeal found the High Court erred by not considering evidence of precautions and lack of knowledge, and by misapplying forfeiture law. The appeal was allowed, the confiscation order set aside, and the vehicle ordered released.
defence_counsel: Asthika Devendra AAL with Arupa Madushanka AAL
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court confiscated the vehicle, finding the appellant failed to prove he took precautions and had no knowledge. The COA found the HC erred by not considering the appellant's evidence and misapplying the law, as the prosecution did not prove the vehicle was used for the offence or challenge the appellant's evidence.

standard_of_review_applied: Review of evidence and law, applying balance of probability for appellant's claim and requiring prosecution to prove beyond reasonable doubt.

judges: N. Bandula Karunarathna J. | R. Gurusinghe J.
offence_sections: Section 354 of the Penal Code and Section 365b(2)b of the Penal Code as amended by Act No. 22 of 1995
brief_facts_summary: The prosecatrix left her lawful guardian to go for classes and opted to meet the accused-appellant due to a love affair. The accused was convicted for kidnapping and grave sexual abuse of the prosecatrix who was under sixteen years. The court considered circumstantial evidence and the dock statement, accepting the relationship between the parties.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 354 of the Penal Code and Section 365b(2)b of the Penal Code as amended by Act No. 22 of 1995
hc_sentence_type: 2 years rigorous imprisonment for Count 1 and 15 years rigorous imprisonment for Count 2, with fines and compensation
hc_judgment_summary: High Court found accused guilty of kidnapping and grave sexual abuse, imposed sentences of imprisonment, fines, and compensation. Sentences were to run concurrently.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: Accused-appellant challenged only the sentence, arguing for reduction based on circumstances and precedents. Counsel cited cases where sentences were reduced due to love affairs and lack of harm. Also claimed prosecatrix initiated the affair and no evidence of mental distress.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Challenging only the sentence | Request for sentence reduction based on circumstances and precedents | Prosecatrix initiated the love affair | No evidence of mental harm or distress
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: Court considered circumstantial evidence and dock statement. Prosecatrix admitted to leaving guardian and having a love affair with accused. No direct evidence of force or harm was presented.
probability_assessment_by_court: Court found guilt beyond reasonable doubt based on circumstantial evidence and circumstances of the case.
defence_version_summary: Accused pleaded not guilty, relied on dock statement, and argued for sentence reduction due to love affair with prosecatrix and lack of harm.
legal_errors_description: HC judge showed bias in evidence evaluation and imposed maximum sentence without considering mitigating circumstances.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: COA reviewed the sentence appeal, noting that accused did not challenge conviction. Considered precedents where sentences were reduced for similar offences involving love affairs. Found that HC judge exhibited bias in evaluating evidence and imposed excessive sentence. COA substituted suspended sentences based on circumstances, including lack of mental harm and prosecatrix's role in initiating the affair.
coa_sentence_type: 2 years rigorous imprisonment suspended for 10 years for both counts, with fines and compensation affirmed, sentences to run concurrently
brief_judgment_file_summary: Accused-appellant was convicted by High Court of Panadura for kidnapping and grave sexual abuse of a minor and sentenced to imprisonment. He appealed only against the sentence. Court of Appeal considered the love affair between accused and victim, cited precedents, and found bias in HC judge's evaluation. COA modified sentences to suspended imprisonment, upholding conviction but reducing custodial sentence.
defence_counsel: Wasantha Fernando AAL with Dimithri Pandiwita AAL
hc_analysis_summary: HC convicted accused and imposed maximum sentences. COA found HC judge showed bias in evidence evaluation and failed to consider mitigating circumstances such as the love affair.
precedents_cited_list: CA/HCC/03/2008 | Maramba Liyanage Rohana alias Loku vs AG, S.C Appeal No 89A/2009 | AG vs Ambagala Mudiyanselage Samantha Sampath, Supreme Court appeal number 17/2013
standard_of_review_applied: Review of sentence based on factual circumstances and judicial precedents
sentencing_principles_applied: Proportionality and consideration of mitigating circumstances

judges: N. Bandula Karunarathna J. | R. Gurusinghe J.
offence_sections: Section 54A(D) and Section 54A(B) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Act No. 13 of 1984
brief_facts_summary: The accused-appellant was convicted for possession and trafficking of 4.68g of heroin. On 07.09.2014, police officers observed the appellant driving suspiciously at high speed, hitting a parked tipper truck, and then stopping at Borella junction. The police searched him and found heroin in a polythene bag in his trouser pocket and Rs. 372,000 in a bag on the rear seat of his car.
evidence_type_primary: Physical evidence (heroin and money) and eyewitness testimony of police officers
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 54A(D) and Section 54A(B) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Act No. 13 of 1984
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court found the accused guilty of two counts of possession and trafficking of heroin and sentenced him to life imprisonment on both counts.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant appealed on grounds that the trial Judge failed to consider the improbability of the prosecution version, failed to consider vital contradictions between prosecution witnesses, and did not give due prominence to the defence evidence.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The learned trial Judge has failed to consider the improbability of the prosecution version. | The learned trial Judge has failed to consider the vital contradictions between the evidence of the prosecution witnesses. | The learned trial Judge has not given due prominence to the Defence evidence.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found serious contradictions in the prosecution evidence, particularly between PW1 and PW2 regarding the damages to the car and the discovery of the money. The trial judge failed to properly consider these contradictions and the defence version, leading to reasonable doubt.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal assessed the improbabilities in the prosecution version and found that the trial judge did not properly consider them, leading to reasonable doubt.
defence_version_summary: The accused pleaded not guilty and made a dock statement. He denied possession of heroin and claimed the accident was with the police van, not a tipper. He admitted to having money but said it was rent money from tenants. The court found his defence not credible due to contradictions.
legal_errors_description: The trial judge misdirected himself by examining the tenability and truthfulness of the accused's evidence in the light of the prosecution evidence, thereby reversing the presumption of innocence.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed the evidence and found serious contradictions between PW1 and PW2, especially regarding the damages to the car and the discovery of the money. The trial judge failed to consider these contradictions and the improbabilities in the prosecution story. The COA also found that the trial judge misdirected himself by evaluating the defence evidence in the light of the prosecution evidence, reversing the presumption of innocence. Applying principles from precedents, the COA held the verdict was unreasonably against the weight of evidence and set aside the conviction.
coa_sentence_type: Acquitted, no sentence
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused-appellant was convicted by the High Court of Colombo for possession and trafficking of 4.68g of heroin and sentenced to life imprisonment. He appealed on grounds of improbability of the prosecution version, contradictions in prosecution evidence, and failure to consider defence evidence. The Court of Appeal found serious contradictions in the prosecution evidence and misdirection by the trial judge in evaluating the defence. The appeal was allowed, the conviction and sentence set aside, and the accused was acquitted.
defence_counsel: Neranjan Jayasinghe AAL
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted the accused based on the prosecution evidence without properly considering contradictions and improbabilities. The trial judge also misdirected himself by evaluating the defence evidence in the light of the prosecution evidence.

judges: K Priyantha Fernando, J. (P. / C.A.) | Sampath B Abayakoon, J.
offence_sections: Section 140 of the Penal Code, Section 296 read with Section 146 of the Penal Code, and Section 296 read with Section 32 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The deceased Lional Fernando was chased and attacked by a crowd of 10-12 persons, including the appellants, at his residence. Key eyewitnesses included PW-03 (brother of the deceased) and depositions of PW-01 and PW-02. The appellants were convicted for being members of an unlawful assembly and causing death. The defence raised was alibi, claiming they were elsewhere during the incident.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 140 of the Penal Code, Section 296 read with Section 146 of the Penal Code, and Section 296 read with Section 32 of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted all appellants as charged and sentenced them to death. The conviction was based on eyewitness evidence and depositions, finding them guilty of being members of an unlawful assembly and causing death with common intention.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: Appellants challenged the conviction on multiple grounds including misdirection on burden of proof for alibi, improper procedure in leading evidence under section 27 of Evidence Ordinance, failure to analyze prosecution evidence, considering evidence of bad character, and failure to address infirmities in depositions.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The learned High Court judge failed to follow the essential requisites of a judgment by failing to analyze prosecution evidence correctly. | The judge misdirected on law by shifting burden of proving alibi to appellants. | Proper procedure was not followed before allowing evidence of weapon recovery under section 27 of Evidence Ordinance. | The judge failed to consider if prosecution established a prima facie strong case before considering defence evidence. | Defence evidence and dock statements were considered against each other to disbelieve appellants. | The judge decided the case on defence evidence rather than prosecution evidence, misdirecting on burden of proof. | The judge failed to analyze evidence on the offence of unlawful assembly. | Evidence of bad character was considered contrary to law. | Prosecution failed to lead relevant evidence before leading depositions under section 33 of Evidence Ordinance. | The judge failed to address inherent infirmities of depositions of PW-01 and PW-02.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the High Court judge failed to properly analyze prosecution evidence, particularly eyewitness accounts and depositions. Contradictions in witness testimonies and infirmities in depositions were not adequately considered.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal found the High Court failed to assess whether prosecution evidence established guilt beyond reasonable doubt, and improperly evaluated defence alibi evidence.
defence_version_summary: All appellants pleaded not guilty and raised defence of alibi, claiming they were not at the scene. Some made dock statements, others gave sworn evidence. The defence called two witnesses. The High Court rejected the alibi defence, but the Court of Appeal found this was done incorrectly by shifting the burden of proof.
legal_errors_description: The High Court judge misdirected on law by shifting burden of proving alibi to appellants, improperly admitted evidence under section 27 of Evidence Ordinance, and considered evidence of bad character.
procedural_defects_description: Improper procedure in leading evidence under section 27 of Evidence Ordinance regarding weapon recovery, and failure to properly admit depositions under section 33.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found multiple legal and procedural errors: the High Court judge misdirected on burden of proof for alibi, improperly admitted evidence under section 27, failed to analyze prosecution evidence properly, did not consider contradictions and infirmities in witness testimonies, and based conviction on defence evidence rather than prosecution case. The Court also noted the judge failed to provide adequate reasons in the judgment as required by section 283 of Criminal Procedure Act. These errors amounted to failure of justice and denial of fair trial.
coa_sentence_type: Conviction and sentence set aside, all appellants acquitted
brief_judgment_file_summary: The appellants were convicted by the High Court of Chilaw for murder and sentenced to death. They appealed on grounds including misdirection on burden of proof for alibi, procedural errors in evidence admission, and failure to properly analyze prosecution evidence. The Court of Appeal found multiple legal errors, including shifting burden of proof, improper admission of evidence, and failure to provide adequate reasoning. The Court held these errors denied a fair trial and set aside the conviction and sentence, acquitting all appellants without ordering a retrial due to the age of the case (2001 incident).
defence_counsel: Anil Silva, P.C. for 1st and 3rd accused appellants; Shavindra Fernando, P.C. with N. Wijesekara for 4th accused appellant; Niranjan Jayasinghe for 5th, 7th and 8th accused appellants; Palitha Fernando, P.C. for 6th accused appellant; Indika Mallawarachchi for 9th accused appellant; Shehan De Silva for 10th accused appellant
cause_of_death_exact_text: injury number 07 as an essentially fatal cut injury caused to part of the head and the neck
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted based on eyewitness evidence and depositions, but failed to properly analyze prosecution evidence, misdirected on burden of proof for alibi, and admitted evidence improperly. The Court of Appeal found the judgment lacked proper reasoning and analysis as required by law.
precedents_cited_list: Mannar Mannan Vs. The Republic of Sri Lanka (1990) 1 SLR 280 | Banda and Others Vs. The Attorney General (1999) 3 SLR 168 | Jayatissaa Vs. The Hon. Attorney General (2010) 1 SLR 279 | P.M.Peter Singho Vs. M.B.Werapitiya 55 NLR 155 | Karunadasa Vs. Officer-in-Charge, Motor Traffic Division, Police Station Nittambuwa (1887) 1 SLR 155 | Chandrasena and others V. Munaweera (1998) 3 S.L.R. 94 | M. Ibrahim Vs. Inspector of Police Ratnapura 59 NLR 235 | Nandana Vs. Attorney General (2008) 1 SLR 51
standard_of_review_applied: Review for errors of law and procedure, and whether errors prejudiced substantial rights or occasioned failure of justice

judges: N. Bandula Karunarathna, J. | R. Gurusinghe, J.
offence_sections: Section 54 A(b) and 54 A(c) of the Poison Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance as amended by Act No. 13 of 1984
brief_facts_summary: The appellant was arrested during a police raid on her house in Piliyandala for allegedly possessing and trafficking 2.4 grams of heroin. Police claimed to have found 120 packets of heroin and Rs. 6,800 on a table. The appellant denied the allegations, stating she was in bed when police entered, and the heroin belonged to her son who was an addict. She had previously worked in the Middle East and received monthly remittances from her husband.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 54 A(b) and 54 A(c) of the Poison Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance as amended by Act No. 13 of 1984
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court found the appellant guilty of drug trafficking charges and sentenced her to life imprisonment on two counts. The trial judge rejected the appellant's testimony and accepted the prosecution's evidence.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant argued that the trial judge ignored evidence creating reasonable doubt, failed to evaluate discrepancies and credibility of witnesses, misapplied the burden of proof, and used defense evidence to corroborate prosecution. The presumption of innocence was not properly considered.
