grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The Learned Trial Judge has totally ignored certain evidence which created a reasonable doubt as to the prosecution case, and the Learned Trial Judge has erred inlaw by failing to consider and evaluate those evidence which amounts to the discrepancies; | The Learned Trial Judge has totally ignored certain evidence which amounts to the credibility of the witnesses and failed to apply the test of probability and improbability; | The Learned Trial Judge has used defense evidence to corroborate the prosecution evidence; | The Learned Trial Judge has not properly evaluated the evidence of the defense; | It has to be carefully considered whether the presumption of innocence of the accused-appellant has been given its due importance by the Trial Judge.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found discrepancies in prosecution witnesses' testimonies regarding timing and weighing of heroin, and deemed the appellant's version more probable, creating reasonable doubt.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal found the appellant's evidence created reasonable doubt and was more probable than the prosecution's version.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty, gave evidence denying the charges, claimed the heroin belonged to her son who was an addict, and alleged police misconduct. The court found her evidence credible.
legal_errors_description: Misdirection on burden of proof, failure to consider presumption of innocence, and ignoring discrepancies in prosecution evidence.
procedural_defects_description: Production books destroyed by termites, lack of notes on timing, discrepancies in evidence handling and weighing.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed the evidence, found numerous discrepancies in the prosecution case such as timing contradictions, weighing issues, and chain of custody problems. They applied the burden of proof principle, concluding that the prosecution failed to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt. The appellant's version was deemed more probable, leading to acquittal.
coa_sentence_type: Acquitted
brief_judgment_file_summary: The appellant was convicted by the High Court for drug trafficking and sentenced to life imprisonment. She appealed on grounds of ignored evidence, misdirection on burden of proof, and discrepancies. The Court of Appeal found the prosecution evidence unreliable, with contradictions in timing and handling of evidence, and acquitted the appellant due to reasonable doubt.
defence_counsel: Gayan Perera with Prabha Hemanthi Perera
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted based on prosecution evidence, but the Court of Appeal found the trial judge misdirected on burden of proof, ignored discrepancies, and improperly evaluated defense evidence.
precedents_cited_list: King vs James Chandrasekera 44 NLR 97 | Woolmington vs. Director of Public Prosecutions
standard_of_review_applied: Burden of proof and reasonable doubt standard

judges: N. Bandula Karunarathna, J. | R. Gurusinghe, J.
offence_sections: Section 314 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The incident occurred on December 19, 2009, in Hakmana, where the appellant, a police officer, allegedly hit PW1 with his fist, causing three teeth to shake. The prosecution presented eyewitness testimony and medical evidence, while the appellant denied the allegations and testified on oath. The High Court convicted the appellant of simple hurt under section 314 of the Penal Code.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 314 of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court found the appellant guilty of simple hurt under section 314, imposing a fine of Rs. 1,000 with a one-month default imprisonment. The judge concluded that grievous hurt was not proven due to medical evidence indicating pre-existing gum disease, but accepted the prosecution's version of the assault.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant appealed on grounds including that the conviction is bad in law, not supported by evidence, misdirection on burden of proof, failure to analyze evidence properly, contradictions in prosecution evidence, failure to evaluate defense evidence, and misdirection on contradictions in the prosecution case.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: that the conviction is bad in law | that the order of conviction is not supported by the evidence | that the Learned High Court Judge had misdirected himself on the burden of proof on the prosecution of a criminal case | that the Learned High Court Judge has failed to analyse the evidence properly | the Learned High Court Judge has failed to consider the many discrepancies and the contradictions in the prosecution evidence | the Learned High Court Judge has failed to evaluate the defense evidence | the Learned High Court Judge has misdirected himself on the contradictions inter-se in the prosecution case
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed the evidence, noting contradictions between PW1 and PW3, and that medical evidence showed no external injuries and pre-existing gum disease. The defense evidence was uncontradicted, and the prosecution witnesses' credibility was questioned due to false statements.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal found reasonable doubt based on evidence contradictions, medical inconsistency, and uncontradicted defense evidence, leading to acquittal.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty, gave evidence on oath, and called witnesses. He denied hitting PW1, explained his police training and physique, and stated that if he had hit PW1, severe injuries would have occurred. The defense evidence was uncontradicted.
legal_errors_description: The High Court wrongly applied the principle from Francis Appuhamu vs. The Queen and failed to apply the same yardstick to defense evidence as per Karuppiah Punkady vs. The Attorney General, leading to improper evaluation of evidence.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal conducted a comprehensive analysis, finding that the High Court misdirected itself on the burden of proof and failed to properly evaluate evidence. It noted contradictions in prosecution witnesses, the unreliability of PW1 due to false statements, and the uncontradicted defense evidence. Applying precedents, the COA concluded that the evidence was insufficient to support the conviction, leading to acquittal.
coa_sentence_type: Acquitted, no sentence imposed
brief_judgment_file_summary: The appellant, a police officer, was convicted by the High Court of Matara for simple hurt under section 314 of the Penal Code and fined. He appealed on grounds including misdirection on burden of proof and evidence contradictions. The Court of Appeal found errors in the High Court's analysis, particularly in evaluating witness credibility and applying legal principles. The COA allowed the appeal, acquitted the appellant, and set aside the conviction and sentence.
defence_counsel: D.S. Hewapathirana
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted the appellant based on prosecution evidence but discounted grievous hurt due to medical evidence. The COA found that the HC failed to properly assess witness credibility, contradictions, and defense evidence, leading to legal errors.
precedents_cited_list: Francis Appuhamu vs. The Queen 68 NLR 437 | Karuppiah Punkady vs. The Attorney General CA 11/2005 HC Colombo 39/00 decided 26th of August 2014
standard_of_review_applied: Review of evidence sufficiency and legal errors in application of principles

judges: N. Bandula Karunarathna J. | R. Gurusinghe J.
offence_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The accused was indicted for the murder of Wickrama Arachchige Chandrasena on 06.10.1999. Eyewitnesses P/W 01 and P/W 02 saw the incident but died before trial, so their depositions were used under Section 33 of the Evidence Ordinance. The prosecution relied on circumstantial evidence, including medical evidence from the JMO and police investigation. The accused denied the allegations in his dock statement.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the accused based on evidence including depositions of eyewitnesses and circumstantial evidence, finding guilt proven beyond reasonable doubt. The judge imposed the death sentence on 31.05.2018.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant raised five grounds: failure to judicially evaluate circumstantial evidence, failure to consider the third person at the location, failure to consider sudden fight, not rejecting the dock statement, and not properly analyzing depositions under Section 33 of the Evidence Ordinance.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The learned Trial Judge has failed to judicially evaluate the circumstantial evidence as required by law. | The learned Trial Judge failed to consider that the prosecution failed to prove the third person who was in the location. | Failure of the learned High Court Judge to consider whether there had been a sudden fight. | The learned Trial Judge did not reject the dock statement. | The learned High Court Judge did not judicially analyse the depositions of P/W01 and 02 accepted under Section 33 of the Evidence Ordinance as required by Law.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed the depositions of P/W 01 and P/W 02 under Section 33, found them properly admitted and reliable. The court upheld the conviction based on this evidence and circumstantial evidence, concluding guilt beyond reasonable doubt.
probability_assessment_by_court: The court assessed that the evidence led to guilt beyond reasonable doubt and no other reasonable hypothesis was possible.
defence_version_summary: The accused pleaded not guilty, made a dock statement denying the allegations, and did not call any witnesses. The court found the defence not credible.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal reviewed the depositions under Section 33 of the Evidence Ordinance and found them admissible. They evaluated the circumstantial evidence per legal principles from cited precedents and concluded that the prosecution proved guilt beyond reasonable doubt. The court rejected all grounds of appeal, affirming the High Court's decision.
coa_sentence_type: Death sentence
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused was convicted of murder and sentenced to death by the High Court of Gampaha. He appealed on grounds including failure to evaluate circumstantial evidence and procedural errors. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal, upholding the conviction and sentence after analyzing the depositions under Section 33 and circumstantial evidence.
defence_counsel: Shanaka Ranasinghe PC with Niroshan Mihindukulasooriya AAL, Tharakee Manchanayaka AAL and Sandamali Peiris AAL
cause_of_death_exact_text: a shock by internal bleeding caused from an attack with a blunt tool
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted based on evidence including depositions and circumstantial evidence. The Court of Appeal found the High Court's analysis correct and upheld the decision.
precedents_cited_list: Amarasiri Vs Republic of Sri Lanka CA Appeal No. 107/2005 | Gambir Vs State of Maharashtra (AIR 1982(S.C)1157) | Queen Vs Sumanasena 66 NLR 350 | Queen Vs M.G.Karolis 69 C.L.W. 47 | Manuel Vs Emperor 36 Cr LJ (1935) 1462
standard_of_review_applied: The court reviewed the evidence and legal principles, applying standards for circumstantial evidence and admissibility under Section 33 of the Evidence Ordinance.

judges: Devika Abeyratne J | P. Kumararatnam J
offence_sections: Sections 54(A) (b) and 54(A) (d) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance as amended by Act No. 13 of 1984
brief_facts_summary: Police received information about drug trafficking by the Appellant near Maradana. During a raid, the Appellant was arrested from a three-wheeler and found with a parcel containing heroin. The heroin was confirmed by the Government Analyst. The Appellant denied the charges.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Sections 54(A) (b) and 54(A) (d) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance as amended by Act No. 13 of 1984
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court found the Appellant guilty on both counts of trafficking and possession of heroin based on prosecution evidence including police testimony and Government Analyst report, and imposed life imprisonment.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The Appellant appealed on grounds that the High Court judge failed to analyze witness consistency, did not adequately consider the probability of the raid, and incorrectly rejected the accused's version.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The Learned High Court Judge has failed to satisfy the test of credibility by analysing the consistency of the testimony of witnesses | The Learned High Court Judge had not adequately considered the probability of the raid | The trial judge has incorrectly rejected the accused’s version
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed the witness evidence, found no contradictions, and upheld the High Court's credibility assessment, citing precedents that a single witness's evidence can be sufficient.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal applied the probability test and found the prosecution's version probable, with no improbabilities in the evidence.
defence_version_summary: The Appellant pleaded not guilty and made a dock statement denying the charges. No defence witnesses were called. The court disbelieved the defence version as it was contradicted by prosecution evidence.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal reviewed the evidence, found that the High Court correctly applied the credibility and probability tests, cited legal precedents on witness testimony, and concluded that the prosecution proved its case beyond reasonable doubt, thus dismissing the appeal.
coa_sentence_type: Life Imprisonment affirmed
brief_judgment_file_summary: The Appellant was convicted for trafficking and possession of heroin and sentenced to life imprisonment by the High Court. He appealed on grounds of witness inconsistency and probability of raid. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal, upholding the conviction and sentence based on credible evidence and proper legal analysis.
defence_counsel: Mr. Chamara Wannisekara with Mr. Dineth Kaushalya and Ms. Sashika Wijeratne
hc_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found that the High Court properly considered the evidence and applied the probability test, with no errors identified in the judgment.
precedents_cited_list: The Attorney General v Devunderage Nihal S.C Appeal 154/10 dated 12/05/2011 | A.G. v Mohamed Saheeb Mohamed Ismath C.A.87/97 decided on 13.7.1999 | Muulluwa v State of Madhya Pradesh AIR 1976 S.C.198 | Wallimmige John v The State 76 NLR 488 | King v N.SA. Fernando 46 NLR 255 | Gunasekara v A.G. 79 NLR 348 | Wickremasuriya v. Dedoleena and others 1996 [2] SLR 95 | Iswari Prasad v. Mohamed Isa 1963 AIR (SC) 1728 at 1734
standard_of_review_applied: The Court of Appeal reviewed the evidence for credibility and probability, applying legal precedents on witness testimony and burden of proof.

judges: N. Bandula Karunarathna J. | R. Gurusinghe J.
offence_sections: Section 449(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure Act
brief_facts_summary: The accused in the main case was charged with soliciting and accepting a bribe of Rs. 2,500 to refrain from legal action for a traffic offence. The 2nd defence witness (appellant) gave evidence in his defense. The High Court found her testimony false and convicted her for perjury, sentencing her to 12 months rigorous imprisonment for two counts to run concurrently.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 449(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure Act
hc_sentence_type: 12 months Rigorous Imprisonment for 2 counts, to run concurrently
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court found the 2nd defence witness guilty of perjury based on two allegations: false evidence about being present at the arrest and the accused not asking for money, and false evidence about not knowing the accused's telephone number and not communicating with him. The judge concluded she gave biased evidence to save the accused and imposed 12 months rigorous imprisonment.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant argued that the finding of false evidence was against the weight of evidence, the judge erred in law by neglecting the need for a glaring case of perjury, and the punishment was excessive.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The finding of the learned trial Judge to the effect that the 2nd defence witness has deliberately given false evidence is against the weight of the evidence placed before the court. | The learned trial Judge has erred in law in neglecting the need for a glaring case of perjury to proceed under section 449(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure Act. | The punishment imposed by the learned Trial Judge on the 2nd defence witness appellant is excessive.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed the evidence and found that the witness's evidence, though disbelieved by the trial judge, did not amount to deliberate falsehood required for perjury. The telephone records did not prove the content of conversations, and the witness's explanations were plausible.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal found that the evidence did not meet the high standard required for perjury and that the trial judge's conclusion was against the weight of evidence.
defence_version_summary: The 2nd defence witness pleaded not guilty to perjury. She gave evidence in her defense and provided mitigation. The Court of Appeal found her evidence did not amount to deliberate falsehood and set aside the conviction.
legal_errors_description: The trial judge erred in law by neglecting the need for a glaring case of perjury to proceed under section 449(1). Also, the inquiry under section 449(1) was invalid because one allegation was not based on a finding in the main case.
procedural_defects_description: The 1st allegation in the perjury inquiry was not based on a determination or finding of the main case, invalidating the inquiry under section 449(1).
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal held that the trial judge erred in law by neglecting the need for a glaring case of perjury. The evidence of the witness, though disbelieved, did not meet the high standard of deliberate falsehood required for perjury. The telephone records did not prove the content of conversations, and the witness's explanations were plausible. The COA set aside the conviction and sentence.
coa_sentence_type: Conviction and sentence set aside, no sentence imposed
brief_judgment_file_summary: The 2nd defence witness was convicted of perjury by the High Court for giving false evidence in a bribery case against the accused. She appealed on grounds that the finding was against the weight of evidence, the judge erred in law by not requiring a glaring case of perjury, and the sentence was excessive. The Court of Appeal allowed the appeal, holding that the evidence did not meet the high standard for perjury and that the trial judge erred in law. The conviction and sentence were set aside, and she was acquitted.
defence_counsel: Dimuth Senarath Bandara AAL with Malindu Peiris AAL and Keheliya Alahakoon AAL
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted the witness for perjury based on two allegations. The COA found that the HC erred by not requiring a glaring case of perjury and by convicting without sufficient evidence, especially since one allegation was not based on a finding in the main case.
precedents_cited_list: AG Vs. Silvan Silva (1981) 1 SLR 364 | Sinnetamby Vs. Fernando 1913 - 1 B.N.C. 25 | Duraya vs. Tissera 1914 - 3 B.N.C. 60 | Bandara Vs. Ukkuwa 1914 - 4 B.N.C. 18 | Attorney General vs Sandanam Pitchi Mary Theresa S.C. Appeal 79/2008 decided on 06.05.2010
standard_of_review_applied: The COA applied the standard that perjury requires a glaring case and deliberate falsehood, and that appellate courts are slow to interfere with factual findings but will do so if the trial judge erred in law.

judges: K Priyantha Fernando, J. | Sampath B Abayakoon, J.
offence_sections: Section 296 read with section 113B and 102, section 296 read with section 32, and section 300 read with section 32 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: On April 11, 2005, the appellants attacked the home of the deceased, throwing stones and using weapons, resulting in the death of Nissanka Wijeweera and injuries to his father Ariyadasa. The prosecution relied on eyewitness accounts from family members and medical evidence. The appellants claimed they were provoked by stones thrown at them, but the court found evidence of intentional attack.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 296 read with section 32 and section 300 read with section 32 of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court found the appellants guilty of murder and attempted murder, acquitted them of conspiracy, and sentenced them to death and imprisonment. The judge relied on eyewitness testimony and medical evidence, rejecting the defence of provocation.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellants argued that the High Court judge failed to consider the exception of sudden fight or grave provocation, convicted them on contradictory and unreliable evidence, did not properly evaluate defence statements, and inadequately considered common intention.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The learned High Court judge had failed to take into consideration the special exception of sudden fight or grave and sudden provocation. | The learned High Court judge had convicted the appellants for the count of murder on contradictory and unreliable evidence of the sole eye witness. | The learned High Court judge convicted the appellants for the charge of attempted murder on contradictory and unreliable evidence. | The learned High Court judge failed to evaluate the evidence of the defence and failed to reason out the grounds on which she rejected the dock statements of the appellants. | The learned High Court judge failed to adequately consider whether the prosecution has proved the common intention of the appellants.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed the evidence, noting contradictions but finding them minor and not affecting the overall credibility. The eyewitness testimony was supported by medical evidence.
probability_assessment_by_court: The court found the evidence overwhelming and no reasonable doubt.
defence_version_summary: The appellants pleaded not guilty, made dock statements claiming they were drunk and provoked by stones thrown at them, and denied involvement. The court found their statements not credible compared to prosecution evidence.
legal_errors_description: The HC judge misdirected by calling PW-16 an independent witness when she was related, and failed to separately consider common intention, but no prejudice caused.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The COA reviewed the evidence, found that the HC judge properly considered common intention, that contradictions were minor, and that the appellants failed to prove exceptions. The COA applied precedents on sudden fight and provocation, and found no basis to interfere with the conviction or sentence.
coa_sentence_type: Death and 10 years rigorous imprisonment
brief_judgment_file_summary: The appellants were convicted of murder and attempted murder by the High Court and sentenced to death and imprisonment. They appealed on grounds of provocation, unreliable evidence, and common intention. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal, finding no material errors or prejudice, and affirmed the conviction and sentence.
defence_counsel: Palitha Fernando PC and Neranjan Jayasinghe
cause_of_death_exact_text: Injuries 1 and 5 are necessarily fatal injuries caused to the deceased.
hc_analysis_summary: The HC convicted based on eyewitness and medical evidence, rejecting provocation defence. COA found some errors but no prejudice.
precedents_cited_list: Piyathilaka and 2 Others Vs. Republic of Sri Lanka (1996) 2 SLR 141 | King Vs. Belana Withanage Eddin 41 NLR 345 | King Vs. Vidanalage Lanty 42 NLR 317 | King Vs. Marshal Appuhamy 51 NLR 140 | The King Vs. Assappu 50 NLR 324
standard_of_review_applied: Review for errors that prejudice substantial rights or cause failure of justice under Article 138 of the Constitution

judges: Devika Abeyratne,J | P.Kumararatanam,J
offence_sections: Section 54 A (a) and 54 A (d) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Act No 13 of 1984
brief_facts_summary: The accused was arrested on 23.3.2013 near Maharoof Water tank after police received information about drug trafficking. Heroin weighing 7.21 grams was found in the knot of his sarong. The prosecution relied on police witnesses and the Government Analyst report, while the defence alleged forcible abduction and assault.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 54 A (d) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Act No 13 of 1984
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court acquitted the accused of trafficking but convicted him for possession of heroin. The court found the prosecution witnesses credible and the evidence sufficient, rejecting the defence allegations of forcible arrest and assault.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant argued that the prosecution witnesses' evidence lacked credibility and probability, that the defence evidence was unreasonably rejected, and that the prosecution failed to prove the chain of custody of the heroin.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The evidence of the main two prosecution witnesses fails the test of credibility and probability. | Rejection of the defence evidence was done on unreasonable grounds. | Prosecution failed to prove the chain of custody of the productions.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the prosecution witnesses credible and consistent, with no material contradictions. The defence evidence was properly evaluated and did not create reasonable doubt.
probability_assessment_by_court: The court assessed the probability of prosecution evidence, such as PW1 participating in two raids, and found no improbability, upholding the trial judge's findings.
defence_version_summary: The accused pleaded not guilty and made a dock statement alleging forcible abduction and assault by police. He called three defence witnesses, but the court found their evidence did not raise reasonable doubt and was not properly put to prosecution witnesses.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal thoroughly evaluated the evidence, finding the prosecution witnesses credible and consistent with no material contradictions. The defence allegations were not put to prosecution witnesses in cross-examination, and thus could not be relied upon. The chain of custody was adequately explained, and the delay in handing over the production did not undermine the case. The COA applied precedents on witness credibility and the importance of cross-examination, concluding that the High Court judgment was sound and the appeal without merit.
coa_sentence_type: Life Imprisonment
brief_judgment_file_summary: The appellant was convicted by the High Court of Colombo for possession of 7.21 grams of heroin and sentenced to life imprisonment. He appealed on grounds of credibility of witnesses, rejection of defence evidence, and chain of custody. The Court of Appeal found the prosecution evidence credible and consistent, with no material contradictions, and that the defence failed to raise reasonable doubt. The appeal was dismissed, affirming the conviction and sentence.
defence_counsel: Neranjan Jayasinghe
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court found the prosecution witnesses credible and the defence evidence insufficient. The Court of Appeal agreed, noting that the HC properly evaluated the evidence and made no errors.
precedents_cited_list: Edrick De Silva Vs Chandradasa De Silva 70 NLR at 170 | Ukkuwa v the Attorney General [2002] 3 SLR 279 | Dharmasiri V. Republic of Sri Lanka [2010] 2 Sri L.R. 241 | Sarwan Singh vs. State of Punjab AIR 2002 SC 3652 | Bobby Mathew Vs. State of Karnataka 2004 3 Cri. L.J page 3003 | Kamrudeen v AG (SC Appeal No. 90/2013 – Decided on 25.07.2019) | Devunderage Nihal Vs Attorney General, SC/Appeal 154/2010, decided on 03.01.2019
standard_of_review_applied: The court applied the standard that credibility of witnesses is primarily for the trial judge, and appellate court will not disturb findings unless manifestly wrong.

judges: N. Bandula Karunarathna, J. | R. Gurusinghe, J.
offence_sections: Section 140 of the Penal Code; Section 66 of the Parliamentary Elections Act No. 1 of 1980 read with section 146 of the Penal Code; Section 410 read with section 146 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: On December 5, 2001, at the Galaha Estate polling station, the appellant was involved in an unlawful assembly that used criminal force against officials, inserted unauthorized ballot papers, and caused mischief. The appellant was identified by witnesses including the station polling officer. The appellant had no previous convictions and is of advanced age.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 140 of the Penal Code; Section 66 of the Parliamentary Elections Act No. 1 of 1980 read with section 146 of the Penal Code; Section 410 read with section 146 of the Penal Code
hc_sentence_type: Six months imprisonment for first charge, one year each for second and third charges, total 2.5 years imprisonment
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court acquitted all other accused due to identification doubts but convicted the appellant on three counts based on evidence including the testimony of the station polling officer. The appellant was sentenced to a total of 2.5 years imprisonment.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant argued that the conviction on count two was illegal as the charge was contrary to law, that the trial judge used evidence rejected in acquitting others, that there was inadequate analysis of evidence, that the judge failed to consider necessary ingredients for unlawful assembly, and that the judge misconceived that the appellant owed an explanation.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Conviction on count two is illegal as the charge is contrary to law. | The Learned Trial Judge made use of evidence rejected in acquitting the second to fourteenth accused to convict the first accused-appellant. | There has been no adequate analysis of the evidence of the prosecution and the infirmities. The evidence of the defense witnesses has not been considered. | The Learned Trial Judge has not considered the ingredients necessary to establish the offence of unlawful assembly. | The Learned Trial Judge proceeded in the misconception that the accused owed an explanation and that the dock statement strengthens the prosecution case.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the evidence of PW5, the station polling officer, reliable despite minor omissions. The court applied principles that witnesses should not be disbelieved for trifling discrepancies and upheld the trial judge's assessment of credibility.
probability_assessment_by_court: The court assessed that the evidence as a whole justified the conclusion, and minor discrepancies did not undermine the prosecution case.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty and made a dock statement claiming he came alone to the polling station, spoke to the officer, and left peacefully, denying any incident. He called two witnesses. The trial judge rejected the defence as mere denial.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed the legal argument regarding section 38 of the Penal Code and found that the offence under the Parliamentary Elections Act falls within its ambit. They evaluated the evidence, particularly relying on PW5's testimony, and found no improper use of evidence. The court upheld the trial judge's factual findings, citing the advantage of seeing witnesses. Considering the appellant's age, clean record, and the 20-year delay, the sentence was reduced and suspended.
coa_sentence_type: Two years imprisonment suspended for five years
brief_judgment_file_summary: The appellant was convicted by the High Court of Kandy for unlawful assembly, election offences, and mischief related to an incident at Galaha Estate polling station in 2001. He appealed on grounds including illegal charge, use of rejected evidence, and inadequate analysis. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal against conviction but reduced the 2.5-year sentence to two years suspended for five years, considering the time elapsed and his age.
defence_counsel: Palitha Fernando, PC with Kaushalya Abeyratne Dias
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted the appellant based on credible eyewitness testimony, acquitting others due to identification doubts. The Court of Appeal found no error in this reasoning and upheld the conviction.
precedents_cited_list: M/s. Hirakal Ratanlal vs. STO, AIR 1973 SC 1034 | Vuchet & Sons Ltd. v. London Society of Compositors [1913] A.C. 107 | Khan vs. Ariyadasa 65 NLR 29 | Queen vs. Wellasamy 63 NLR 265 | Wickremasuriya vs. Dedoleena and Others 1996 2 Sri LR 95 | State of Uttar Pradesh v. Anthony 1985 AIR 48 (SC) | Munasinghe vs. Vidanaqe 69 NLR 97 | Watt or Thomas v. Thomas [1947] A.C. 484 (H.L.) | Bhaqwati and Ors. vs. The State of Uttar Pradesh AIR 1976 SC 1449 | Mathai Mathews v. State of Maharashtra | Labh Singh v. State of Punjab | Attorney General vs. Sandanam Pitchai Mary Theresa, [2011] 2 Sri LR 292 | R v. Paul [1977]1 SCR 181
standard_of_review_applied: Appellate court should not disturb factual findings unless unreasonable, giving weight to trial judge's assessment of witnesses who were seen and heard.
sentencing_principles_applied: Consideration of time since offence, accused's age, and lack of previous convictions in reducing and suspending sentence.

judges: N. Bandula Karunarathna, J. | R. Gurusinghe, J.
offence_sections: Section 54 A(b) and 54 A(c) of the Poison Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance as amended by Act No. 13 of 1984
brief_facts_summary: Police raided the appellant's house in Piliyandala on December 11, 1999, based on information and found 120 packets of heroin and Rs. 6,800 on a table. The appellant was arrested and claimed she was in bed when police arrived, and no heroin was hers. Key evidence included heroin packets and police testimony, but there were discrepancies in timing, weighing procedures, and evidence handling.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 54 A(b) and 54 A(c) of the Poison Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance as amended by Act No. 13 of 1984
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court found the appellant guilty of drug possession and trafficking based on prosecution evidence and sentenced her to life imprisonment on two counts. The trial judge rejected the defense's version and relied on police testimony and physical evidence.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant argued that the trial judge ignored evidence creating reasonable doubt, failed to assess witness credibility properly, used defense evidence to corroborate prosecution, did not evaluate defense evidence adequately, and did not give due importance to the presumption of innocence.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The Learned Trial Judge has totally ignored certain evidence which created a reasonable doubt as to the prosecution case | The Learned Trial Judge has totally ignored certain evidence which amounts to the credibility of the witnesses and failed to apply the test of probability and improbability | The Learned Trial Judge has used defense evidence to corroborate the prosecution evidence | The Learned Trial Judge has not properly evaluated the evidence of the defense | It has to be carefully considered whether the presumption of innocence of the accused-appellant has been given its due importance by the Trial Judge
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found discrepancies in prosecution evidence, such as inconsistent timings and weighing procedures, which created reasonable doubt. The appellant's version was deemed more probable, and the trial judge failed to properly evaluate these issues.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal assessed that the appellant's version of events was more probable than the prosecution's and that the prosecution case had reasonable doubt due to discrepancies.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty, gave evidence from the witness stand, and claimed she was in bed when police arrived, no heroin was hers, her son was a treated addict, and documents were destroyed by the Tsunami. The court found her evidence credible and created reasonable doubt.
legal_errors_description: The trial judge misapplied the burden of proof by requiring the appellant to prove her innocence, ignored prosecution discrepancies, and failed to properly evaluate evidence.
procedural_defects_description: Discrepancies in evidence handling, including timing inconsistencies, weighing procedures, and sealing of evidence.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the prosecution evidence unreliable due to contradictions in timings, weighing procedures, and failure to explain discrepancies. The appellant's version was more probable, and the trial judge erred in burden of proof and presumption of innocence. Therefore, the conviction was not proven beyond reasonable doubt and was set aside.
coa_sentence_type: Acquitted
brief_judgment_file_summary: The appellant was convicted by the High Court for drug possession and trafficking and sentenced to life imprisonment. She appealed on grounds of evidence discrepancies, burden of proof errors, and presumption of innocence. The Court of Appeal found prosecution evidence flawed and the appellant's version more probable, leading to acquittal.
defence_counsel: Gayan Perera with Prabha Hemanthi Perera
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted based on prosecution evidence, but the Court of Appeal found that the trial judge ignored discrepancies in evidence and misapplied the burden of proof, leading to an unfair trial.
precedents_cited_list: King vs James Chandrasekera 44 NLR 97 | Woolmington vs. Director of Public Prosecutions
standard_of_review_applied: Review for errors of law and evidence evaluation, focusing on burden of proof and reasonable doubt.

court_of_appeal_case_no: Democratic Socialist Republic of Sri Lanka HCC-0028-036-2019
judges: K Priyantha Fernando, J. (P. / C.A.) | Sampath B Abayakoon, J.
offence_sections: Section 140 of the Penal Code; Section 296 read with Section 146 of the Penal Code; Section 296 read with Section 32 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The deceased was chased and attacked by a crowd of 10-12 persons at his home, suffering fatal cut injuries. The appellants were charged with being members of an unlawful assembly and causing death. Key evidence included eyewitness testimony (PW-01, PW-02, PW-03) and depositions, with the prosecution also relying on medical evidence and alleged recovery of a weapon.
evidence_type_secondary: Medical evidence and recovery of weapon
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 140 of the Penal Code; Section 296 read with Section 146 of the Penal Code; Section 296 read with Section 32 of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the appellants of being members of an unlawful assembly and causing death, sentencing them to death. The judge failed to properly analyze prosecution evidence and misdirected on the burden of proof for alibi.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: Appellants challenged conviction on grounds including misdirection on burden of proof for alibi, improper admission of evidence under section 27 of Evidence Ordinance, failure to analyze prosecution evidence, consideration of bad character evidence, and procedural errors in leading depositions under section 33.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The learned High Court judge failed to follow the essential requisites of a judgment as envisaged in section 283 of the Penal Code by failing to analyze the evidence led by the prosecution in its correct perspective. | The learned High Court judge was totally misdirected as to the relevant law when she concluded that it was the burden of the appellants who pleaded the defence of alibi to prove the same, thereby shifting the burden of proof. | The proper procedure was not followed at the trial before allowing the leading of evidence as to the alleged recovery of a weapon used in the crime under section 27 of the Evidence Ordinance. | The learned High Court judge failed to consider the prosecution evidence to decide whether it has established a prima facie strong case against the appellants before considering the evidence of the appellants led in their defence. | The evidence given by some of the appellants and the dock statements of others has been considered against each other to disbelieve the evidence of the appellants, and the witnesses testified on behalf of them. | The learned High Court judge has decided the case on the basis of the defence evidence rather than the evidence led by the prosecution to prove its case, and thereby misdirected herself as to the burden of proof in a criminal action. | The learned High Court judge has failed to consider and analyze the evidence on the offence of unlawful assembly in the judgment, although the appellants were convicted based on being members of such an assembly. | Evidence of bad character has been considered in the judgment as relevant, in contrary to the established principles of law. | The prosecution failed to lead relevant evidence to satisfy the Court that PW-01 and PW-02 were not available to give evidence in Court before leading their depositions under section 33 of the Evidence Ordinance. | The learned High Court judge has failed to address her mind to the inherent infirmities of depositions of PW-01 and PW-02 before considering them as evidence at the trial.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the High Court judge failed to properly analyze prosecution evidence, especially regarding alibi and identification. Eyewitness evidence had inconsistencies and depositions were used without proper foundation, leading to unreliable convictions.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal found the High Court judge did not properly assess the evidence and the prosecution did not prove the case beyond reasonable doubt, particularly regarding alibi and identification.
defence_version_summary: The appellants pleaded not guilty and raised alibi defences, claiming they were not at the scene. Some made dock statements, others gave evidence. The defence witnesses supported the alibi of the 1st appellant and testified about events, but the High Court judge disbelieved their evidence.
legal_errors_description: The High Court judge misdirected on the burden of proof for alibi, improperly admitted evidence under section 27 of the Evidence Ordinance, and considered bad character evidence.
procedural_defects_description: The prosecution did not follow proper procedure for leading evidence under section 27 (recovery of weapon) and for admitting depositions under section 33 of the Evidence Ordinance.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal held the High Court judge failed to properly analyze prosecution evidence and misdirected on law regarding alibi and evidence admission. Identification was problematic, and the evidence was insufficient for conviction. The court also noted the long delay (incident in 2001) and refused a retrial, finding the errors resulted in a failure of justice and denial of fair trial.
coa_sentence_type: Acquitted
brief_judgment_file_summary: The appellants were convicted by the High Court of murder as members of an unlawful assembly and sentenced to death. They appealed on multiple grounds including misdirection on burden of proof for alibi, improper evidence admission, and failure to analyze prosecution evidence. The Court of Appeal found significant legal and procedural errors, acquitted all appellants, and refused a retrial due to the long delay since the 2001 incident.
defence_counsel: Anil Silva, P.C. for the 1st and 3rd accused appellants; Shavindra Fernando, P.C. with N. Wijesekara for the 4th accused appellant; Niranjan Jayasinghe for the 5th, 7th and 8th accused appellants; Palitha Fernando, P.C. for the 6th accused appellant; Indika Mallawarachchi for the 9th accused appellant; Shehan De Silva for the 10th accused appellant
cause_of_death_exact_text: injury number 07 as an essentially fatal cut injury caused to part of the head and the neck
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court judge failed to analyze prosecution evidence properly, misdirected on burden of proof for alibi, and admitted evidence improperly. The Court of Appeal found the judgment did not comply with legal requirements and resulted in a denial of fair trial.
precedents_cited_list: Mannar Mannan Vs. The Republic of Sri Lanka (1990) 1 SLR 280 | Banda and Others Vs. The Attorney General (1999) 3 SLR 168 | Jayatissaa Vs. The Hon. Attorney General (2010) 1 SLR 279 | P.M.Peter Singho Vs. M.B.Werapitiya 55 NLR 155 | Karunadasa Vs. Officer-in-Charge, Motor Traffic Division, Police Station Nittambuwa (1887) 1 SLR 155 | Chandrasena and others V. Munaweera (1998) 3 S.L.R. 94 | M. Ibrahim Vs. Inspector of Police Ratnapura 59 NLR 235 | Nandana Vs. Attorney General (2008) 1 SLR 51
standard_of_review_applied: The Court of Appeal reviewed for errors of law and fact, and considered the proviso of Article 138 of the Constitution regarding whether errors prejudiced substantial rights or occasioned a failure of justice.

judges: K Priyantha Fernando, J. | Sampath B Abayakoon, J.
offence_sections: Section 296 read with section 32 of the Penal Code for murder, and section 300 read with section 32 of the Penal Code for attempted murder
brief_facts_summary: On April 11, 2005, the appellants attacked the house of the deceased, threw stones, and chased and killed Nissanka Wijeweera with knives and swords, and injured his father Ariyadasa. Key evidence includes eyewitness testimony from family members, medical evidence of injuries, and the appellants' dock statements. The motive was alleged to be the deceased providing information to police about illicit liquor trade.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 296 read with section 32 of the Penal Code for murder, and section 300 read with section 32 of the Penal Code for attempted murder
hc_sentence_type: Death sentence for murder, and 10 years rigorous imprisonment for attempted murder
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court found the appellants guilty of murder and attempted murder, acquitted them on conspiracy, and sentenced them to death and imprisonment. The judge relied on eyewitness testimony and medical evidence, rejecting the defence of sudden fight.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellants argued that the High Court failed to consider sudden fight or provocation, relied on contradictory eyewitness evidence, failed to evaluate defence evidence and dock statements, and failed to prove common intention.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The learned High Court judge had failed to take into consideration the special exception of sudden fight or grave and sudden provocation. | The learned High Court judge had convicted the appellants for the count of murder on contradictory and unreliable evidence of the sole eye witness. | The learned High Court judge convicted the appellants for the charge of attempted murder on contradictory and unreliable evidence. | The learned High Court judge failed to evaluate the evidence of the defence and failed to reason out the grounds on which she rejected the dock statements of the appellants. | The learned High Court judge failed to adequately consider whether the prosecution has proved the common intention of the appellants.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal evaluated the eyewitness testimony and found it credible despite minor contradictions, supported by strong medical evidence establishing fatal injuries, and rejected the defence claims of provocation.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal found no reasonable doubt based on the overwhelming evidence against the appellants.
defence_version_summary: The appellants pleaded not guilty, made dock statements claiming they were provoked by stones thrown at them, and called no witnesses. The court found their statements not credible and insufficient to counter the prosecution evidence.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal held that there was no evidence of sudden fight or provocation, the eyewitness testimony was credible, medical evidence supported the prosecution, common intention was established from the appellants' actions, and any misdirections by the High Court did not prejudice the appellants or occasion a failure of justice, thus dismissing the appeal.
coa_sentence_type: Death sentence for murder and 10 years rigorous imprisonment for attempted murder, affirmed
brief_judgment_file_summary: The appellants were convicted by the High Court of murder and attempted murder and sentenced to death and imprisonment. They appealed on grounds including sudden fight, unreliable evidence, and lack of common intention. The Court of Appeal found no merit in the appeal, upheld the conviction and sentence, and dismissed the appeal.
defence_counsel: Palitha Fernando PC and Neranjan Jayasinghe
cause_of_death_exact_text: Injury 1 and 5 are necessarily fatal injuries caused to the deceased.
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted based on eyewitness and medical evidence, finding common intention. The Court of Appeal noted some misdirections but found they did not prejudice the appellants or affect the justice of the case.
precedents_cited_list: Piyathilaka and 2 Others Vs. Republic of Sri Lanka (1996) 2 SLR 141 | King Vs. Belana Withanage Eddin 41 NLR 345 | King Vs. Vidanalage Lanty 42 NLR 317 | King Vs. Marshal Appuhamy 51 NLR 140 | The King Vs. Assappu 50 NLR 324
standard_of_review_applied: The Court applied the standard from Article 138 proviso of the Constitution, considering whether errors prejudiced substantial rights or occasioned failure of justice.

judges: N. Bandula Karunarathna J. | R. Gurusinghe J.
offence_sections: section 54 A (D) and section 54 A (B) of the Poisons Opium and Dangerous Drugs Act Number 13 of 1984
location_of_offence: within the jurisdiction of the Colombo High Court
brief_facts_summary: On 07.09.2014, police observed the appellant driving suspiciously at high speed, hitting a parked tipper truck and then stopping at Borella junction. They searched him and found 4.68g of heroin in a polythene bag in his pocket and Rs. 372,000 in the car. The appellant denied the charges, claiming the money was rent from tenants and that he fled because he had no license or insurance.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: section 54 A (D) and section 54 A (B) of the Poisons Opium and Dangerous Drugs Act Number 13 of 1984
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the accused of possession and trafficking of 4.68g of heroin and sentenced him to life imprisonment. The trial judge believed the prosecution evidence and rejected the defence version.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant argued that the trial judge failed to consider the improbability of the prosecution version, contradictions in prosecution witnesses' evidence, and did not give due prominence to defence evidence.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The learned trial Judge has failed to consider the improbability of the prosecution version. | The learned trial Judge has failed to consider the vital contradictions between the evidence of the prosecution witnesses. | The learned trial Judge has not given due prominence to the Defence evidence.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found serious contradictions in the prosecution witnesses' testimonies, particularly regarding the accident details and the discovery of money. The trial judge did not properly consider these contradictions.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal found the prosecution story improbable and that material contradictions raised reasonable doubt.
defence_version_summary: The accused pleaded not guilty and made a dock statement. He claimed he was rushing to his mother's house because his child was ill, panicked and fled as he had no license or insurance, denied possessing heroin, and stated the money found was rent from tenants.
legal_errors_description: The trial judge misdirected himself by examining the defence evidence in the light of the prosecution evidence, reversing the presumption of innocence, and by not properly considering contradictions in the prosecution evidence.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found serious contradictions in the prosecution case regarding the accident location, vehicle damages, and discovery of money. The trial judge failed to properly consider these contradictions and misdirected himself by examining the defence in light of the prosecution, reversing the presumption of innocence. Applying appellate review principles, the COA held the verdict was against the weight of evidence and manifestly wrong, leading to acquittal.
coa_sentence_type: Acquitted, no sentence imposed
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused was convicted in the High Court of Colombo for possession and trafficking of 4.68g of heroin and sentenced to life imprisonment. He appealed on grounds of improbability of prosecution version, contradictions in evidence, and failure to consider defence. The Court of Appeal found material contradictions in the prosecution evidence and that the trial judge misdirected himself by reversing the presumption of innocence. The appeal was allowed, the conviction set aside, and the appellant acquitted.
defence_counsel: Neranjan Jayasinghe AAL
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted the accused based on prosecution evidence, but the Court of Appeal found the trial judge failed to consider material contradictions and misdirected himself by examining the defence in light of the prosecution, reversing the presumption of innocence.
precedents_cited_list: Attorney General v Sandanam Pitchei Mary Theresa 2011 (2) SLR 292 | Wickramasuriya vs Dedoleena and Others 1996 (2) SLR 95 | Renuka Subasinghe vs Attorney General CA 139/2001 decided on 07.05.2007 | Yaddehige Shelton vs Attorney General C.A 105/2008 decided on 16.07.2012 | Sinnaiya Kalidasa vs. The Hon. Attorney General CA 128 / 2005 BASL Criminal Law 2010 Vol. III page 31 | James Silva Vs. Republic of Sri Lanka 1980 (2) SLR 167 | King V. Guneratne 14 Ceylon Law Recorder 174 | Martin Fernando V. Inspector of police Minuwangoda 46 N.L.R 210
standard_of_review_applied: The Court of Appeal will not disturb the findings of a trial judge unless manifestly wrong. The appellate court must test evidence extrinsically and intrinsically, and if strong doubt exists as to guilt, the accused should be given the benefit of the doubt.

judges: N. Bandula Karunarathna J. | R. Gurusinghe J.
offence_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: On 06.10.1999, the deceased was murdered at Nedungahahena Temple. The prosecution relied on depositions of two eyewitnesses who died before trial, admitted under Section 33 of the Evidence Ordinance, and other circumstantial evidence. The appellant denied the allegations.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the appellant for murder under section 296 of the Penal Code and imposed the death sentence. The judge found the depositions of P/W 01 and P/W 02 credible and the circumstantial evidence consistent with guilt.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant argued that the trial judge failed to properly evaluate circumstantial evidence, did not consider the third person at the location, failed to consider sudden fight, did not reject the dock statement, and did not judicially analyse the depositions admitted under Section 33.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The learned Trial Judge has failed to judicially evaluate the circumstantial evidence as required by law. | The learned Trial Judge failed to consider that the prosecution failed to prove the third person who was in the location. | Failure of the learned High Court Judge to consider whether there had been a sudden fight. | The learned Trial Judge did not reject the dock statement. | The learned High Court Judge did not judicially analyse the depositions of P/W01 and 02 accepted under Section 33 of the Evidence Ordinance as required by Law.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed the depositions of P/W 01 and P/W 02, finding them admissible under Section 33 of the Evidence Ordinance. The circumstantial evidence was evaluated against legal guidelines and found to be consistent with guilt.
probability_assessment_by_court: Court found no reasonable doubt based on the evidence.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty and made a dock statement denying involvement. No defence witnesses were called. The court rejected the dock statement as insufficient to counter prosecution evidence.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal thoroughly analyzed the depositions of P/W 01 and P/W 02, confirming their admissibility under Section 33 of the Evidence Ordinance as the witnesses were dead and had been cross-examined during non-summary proceedings. The court applied legal principles for circumstantial evidence from precedents like Amarasiri Vs Republic of Sri Lanka and Gambir Vs State of Maharashtra, finding that the proven facts were consistent only with guilt and incompatible with innocence. The COA rejected the appellant's grounds regarding sudden fight, third person, and dock statement, holding that the High Court had properly evaluated the evidence. Ultimately, the COA found no error in the conviction or sentence.
coa_sentence_type: Death sentence
brief_judgment_file_summary: The appellant was convicted for murder under section 296 of the Penal Code by the High Court of Gampaha and sentenced to death. He appealed on grounds including improper evaluation of circumstantial evidence, failure to consider third person and sudden fight, and handling of dock statement and depositions. The Court of Appeal examined the depositions admitted under Section 33 of the Evidence Ordinance and found them properly evaluated. Applying legal standards for circumstantial evidence, the COA upheld the High Court's decision, dismissing the appeal and affirming the conviction and death sentence.
defence_counsel: Shanaka Ranasinghe PC with Niroshan Mihindukulasooriya AAL, Tharakee Manchanayaka AAL and Sandamali Peiris AAL
cause_of_death_exact_text: a shock by internal bleeding caused from an attack with a blunt tool
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court properly evaluated the depositions and circumstantial evidence, and the Court of Appeal found no errors in its analysis or conclusion.
precedents_cited_list: Amarasiri Vs Republic of Sri Lanka CA Appeal No. 107/2005 | Gambir Vs State of Maharashtra (AIR 1982(S.C)1157) | Queen Vs Sumanasena 66 NLR 350 | Queen Vs M.G.Karolis 69 C.L.W. 47 | Manuel Vs Emperor 36 Cr LJ (1935) 1462
standard_of_review_applied: Review based on sufficiency of evidence and proper application of legal principles for circumstantial evidence and admissibility of depositions.

judges: Devika Abeyratne,J | P.Kumararatanam,J
offence_sections: Section 54 A (a) and 54 A (d) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Act No 13 of 1984
brief_facts_summary: The accused was arrested on 23.3.2013 based on police information near Maharoof Water tank. He was found in possession of 7.21 grams of heroin hidden in his sarong. The prosecution relied on police testimony and the Government Analyst report. The accused denied the charges and claimed he was forcibly taken and assaulted.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 54 A (d) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Act No 13 of 1984
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court acquitted the accused on trafficking charges but convicted him for possession of 7.2 grams of heroin. The court found the prosecution witnesses credible and the evidence sufficient. The accused was sentenced to life imprisonment.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant argued that the prosecution witnesses were not credible, the defence evidence was unreasonably rejected, and the chain of custody was not proven.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The evidence of the main two witnesses of the prosecution fails the test of credibility and probability. | Rejection of the evidence of the defence had been done on unreasonable grounds. | Prosecution had failed to prove the chain of productions.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the prosecution witnesses consistent and credible, with no material contradictions. The defence evidence was evaluated but did not raise reasonable doubt. The chain of custody was adequately explained.
probability_assessment_by_court: The court found the prosecution evidence probable and credible, and the defence did not raise reasonable doubt.
defence_version_summary: The accused pleaded not guilty and made a dock statement claiming he was forcibly taken and assaulted. He called three defence witnesses. The court found the defence version not credible and insufficient to raise reasonable doubt.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal thoroughly analyzed the grounds of appeal. It found the prosecution witnesses credible and consistent, with no material contradictions. The defence evidence was adequately evaluated by the trial judge and did not raise reasonable doubt. The chain of custody was properly maintained. Citing several precedents, the COA affirmed the trial judge's findings on credibility and evidence. The appeal was dismissed as without merit.
coa_sentence_type: Life Imprisonment
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused was charged with trafficking and possession of heroin. The High Court acquitted him of trafficking but convicted him for possession and sentenced him to life imprisonment. He appealed on grounds of credibility, rejection of defence evidence, and chain of custody. The Court of Appeal found the prosecution evidence credible, the defence properly evaluated, and the chain of custody adequate. Citing precedents, the COA dismissed the appeal and affirmed the conviction and sentence.
defence_counsel: Neranjan Jayasinghe
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court found the prosecution witnesses credible and convicted the accused for possession. The Court of Appeal agreed with this analysis and found no errors in the HC's reasoning.
precedents_cited_list: Edrick De Silva Vs Chandradasa De Silva 70 NLR at 170 | Ukkuwa v the Attorney General [2002] 3 SLR 279 | Dharmasiri V. Republic of Sri Lanka [2010] 2 Sri L.R. 241 | Sarwan Singh vs. State of Punjab AIR 2002 SC 3652 | Bobby Mathew Vs. State of Karnataka 2004 3 Cri. L.J page 3003 | Kamrudeen v AG (SC Appeal No. 90/2013 – Decided on 25.07.2019) | Devunderage Nihal Vs Attorney General, SC/Appeal 154/2010,decided on 03.01.2019
standard_of_review_applied: Deference to trial judge's findings on credibility unless manifestly wrong.

judges: Hon. Justice Menaka Wijesundera | Hon. Justice Neil Iddawala
offence_sections: Section 08 and 09 of the Assistance to and Protection of Victims of Crime and Witnesses Act, No. 04 of 2015
brief_facts_summary: The Petitioner had an intimate relationship with the victim and recorded sexual activities. After the victim married another, the Petitioner released the recordings on Facebook. The victim complained, and the Petitioner was indicted. While on bail, the Petitioner threatened the victim, leading to remand based on corroborated statements.
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court remanded the Petitioner based on threats to the victim, considering investigation reports and witness statements. Bail was refused due to the seriousness of the threats and violation of bail conditions.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The Petitioner argued that the HC Judge violated the Victims Act by remanding without a proper inquiry, that the complaint is fabricated, and that the prolonged remand without completed investigations justifies bail.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: HC Judge remanded Petitioner without inquiry violating Victims Act | Evidence against Petitioner is fabricated | Petitioner's remand period of nearly one year due to incomplete investigations | Covid-19 infection is not exceptional circumstance
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court evaluated corroborated statements from the victim and witnesses regarding threats. It found the evidence credible and sufficient to deny bail, noting the Petitioner's repeated violations.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court found no exceptional circumstances for bail based on the material and Petitioner's conduct.
defence_version_summary: The Petitioner denied the allegations, claiming the complaint is fabricated. He did not plead guilty, and the Court found his claims insufficient for bail.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed the Victims Act's objectives to protect victims' rights, noting the Petitioner's repeated violations. It defined exceptional circumstances as case-specific and found that fabrication claims, remand period, and Covid-19 do not constitute exceptional grounds. The Court upheld the HC's decision, emphasizing that the Victims Act's bail provisions prevail over the general Bail Act.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The Petitioner, accused under penal code sections 354 and 364 for recording and releasing intimate content, applied for bail after being remanded for threatening the victim. The High Court denied bail based on corroborated threats. On appeal, the Petitioner argued procedural violations and exceptional circumstances like remand period and Covid-19. The Court of Appeal found no exceptional grounds, dismissed the bail application, and upheld the remand.
defence_counsel: Wasantha Navarathna Bandara, PC with Ashan Navarathna Bandara
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court remanded the Petitioner after considering investigation reports and witness statements on threats. The Court of Appeal found that the High Court had sufficient material and did not violate procedural requirements.
standard_of_review_applied: Review for exceptional circumstances under the Victims Act

judges: K. Priyantha Fernando, J. (P/CA) | Sampath B. Abayakoon, J.
offence_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The deceased was attacked by the appellant with a knife, as witnessed by his wife (PW2). The deceased sustained multiple injuries, including a deep cut to the left elbow, and later died. The prosecution relied on the eyewitness account and medical evidence.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the appellant for murder based on the eyewitness testimony and sentenced him to death. The judge found the prosecution evidence credible.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant appealed on grounds including the credibility of the main witness (PW2) and the failure to prove murderous intention under Section 294 of the Penal Code. The Court of Appeal focused on whether the prosecution proved the elements of murder.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The evidence of the main witness of the prosecution (PW2) fails the test of credibility and the test of consistency. | The evidence of PW3 regarding the dying declaration fails the test of credibility. | The reasons given by the learned High Court Judge to reject the dock statement of the accused appellant are against the law. | The learned High Court Judge has convicted the accused appellant for murder when there is evidence to bring down the culpability of the accused appellant under one or more of the exceptions in Section 294 of the Penal Code.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found PW2's evidence consistent and credible. However, the medical evidence did not establish that the injury was sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death, which was necessary for murder under Section 294.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court assessed that the prosecution failed to prove beyond reasonable doubt that the injury was sufficient to cause death, thus making it unsafe to convict for murder.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty and made a dock statement. The defence argued that the prosecution failed to prove murder, and the Court of Appeal agreed, modifying the conviction to culpable homicide not amounting to murder.
legal_errors_description: The High Court erred in convicting for murder without requiring the prosecution to prove that the bodily injury intended was sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death, as per Section 294 of the Penal Code.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed the credibility of the eyewitness (PW2) and found her testimony reliable. However, on legal grounds, they held that the prosecution did not prove the necessary intention for murder under Section 294, citing precedents like R.G. Somapala v The Queen. The medical evidence was insufficient to establish that the injury was certain to cause death, leading to a modification of the conviction to culpable homicide not amounting to murder.
coa_sentence_type: Ten years rigorous imprisonment and fine of Rupees Ten Thousand
brief_judgment_file_summary: The appellant was convicted of murder by the High Court of Kandy and sentenced to death. He appealed on grounds including witness credibility and failure to prove murderous intention. The Court of Appeal found the eyewitness credible but held that the prosecution failed to prove the injury was sufficient to cause death, thus modifying the conviction to culpable homicide not amounting to murder and sentencing him to ten years rigorous imprisonment and a fine.
defence_counsel: Palitha Fernando, PC with Neranjan Jayasinghe
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted the appellant for murder based on eyewitness testimony. However, the Court of Appeal found that the High Court erred by not ensuring that the prosecution proved the injury was sufficient to cause death under Section 294 of the Penal Code.
precedents_cited_list: Bastian Silva v Appuhamy 4 NLR 47 | R.G. Somapala v The Queen 72 NLR 121
standard_of_review_applied: The Court reviewed whether the prosecution proved the elements of murder beyond reasonable doubt, particularly the intention under Section 294 of the Penal Code.
final_charge_after_appeal: Culpable homicide not amounting to murder

judges: Menaka Wijesundera J. | Neil Iddawala J.
offence_sections: Section 2(1)(a) and 3(b) of the Prevention of Terrorism Act
brief_facts_summary: The petitioner was indicted for aiding and abetting the murder of former army commander General Sarath Fonseka. The prosecution relied on a confession recorded over six days by an Assistant Superintendent of Police under the Prevention of Terrorism Act. The petitioner objected to the voluntariness of the confession, claiming torture and improper translation, leading to a voir dire inquiry. The High Court admitted the confession as voluntary, but the Court of Appeal reviewed and set aside that order.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 2(1)(a) and 3(b) of the Prevention of Terrorism Act
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court Judge ruled that the confession was voluntary and admissible, noting that the petitioner initialed each page and did not cross-examine the ASP on key points. The judge found no evidence of torture or undue influence.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The petitioner argued that the confession was obtained under torture and inhuman treatment, making it involuntary. He also contended that the confession was dictated by the ASP and not properly translated, raising doubts about its accuracy. The respondent argued that the ASP was fluent in Tamil and the confession was voluntary, with the length of recording favoring the petitioner.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The petitioner was tortured and inhumanly treated before obtaining the confession. | The typist recorded the confession as dictated by the ASP, not by the petitioner or translator. | The ASP translating the confession caused distress and raised doubts about voluntariness.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court analyzed the evidence of the ASP, who was uncontradicted, but found that translation issues and the duration of recording raised doubts about voluntariness. The petitioner did not cross-examine the ASP on key points, but the Court still considered fairness.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court assessed that the confession recorded over six days with the ASP translating raised reasonable doubt about voluntariness under Section 24 of the Evidence Ordinance.
defence_version_summary: The petitioner denied making the confession voluntarily, claimed torture, and stated he only made a statement to another officer named Subair. He pleaded not guilty implicitly and did not call witnesses, relying on cross-examination and procedural challenges.
legal_errors_description: The High Court erred in admitting the confession without properly considering voluntariness under Section 24 of the Evidence Ordinance, given translation issues and the prolonged recording period.
procedural_defects_description: The ASP translated the confession without a proper translator over six days, causing doubt about voluntariness and procedural fairness.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal reviewed the evidence, noting that the ASP translating the confession raised doubts about its voluntariness. They referred to precedents emphasizing fairness under Section 24 of the Evidence Ordinance. The confession recorded over six days without a translator was problematic, so they set aside the High Court order, finding the confession inadmissible.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The petitioner was accused of aiding and abetting the murder of General Sarath Fonseka. The High Court admitted a confession as voluntary. The Court of Appeal revised this decision, finding that the confession was not voluntary due to translation issues and the six-day recording period, setting aside the High Court order and ruling the confession inadmissible.
defence_counsel: K.S. Ratnavel
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court found the confession voluntary based on the petitioner initialing pages and lack of cross-examination on torture claims. The Court of Appeal disagreed, citing translation issues and prolonged recording as errors in assessing voluntariness.
precedents_cited_list: Vivekanandan vs. Selvaratuum79NLR 344 | Maridasa vs. The sate 1995 1 Sri L.R.96 | Nuwan De Siva vs. The Attorney General 2005 1 Sri L.R. at 146
standard_of_review_applied: Revision under Article 140 of the Constitution, focusing on legal errors and fairness in the voluntariness of confession.

judges: Menaka Wijesundera J. | Neil Iddawala J.
offence_sections: Section 365 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The accused was convicted under Section 365 of the Penal Code and sentenced to rigorous imprisonment. An appeal has been lodged and is pending. The bail application is based on the accused's health condition after suffering a head injury in prison.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 365 of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the accused under Section 365 and sentenced him to rigorous imprisonment. Upon appeal, the High Court rejected the bail application due to absence of exceptional circumstances.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The petitioner filed a revision application against the High Court order refusing bail pending appeal. The main ground is the petitioner's health condition, specifically a serious head injury suffered in prison, which constitutes exceptional circumstances for granting bail.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Health condition of the accused due to head injury in prison
legal_errors_description: The High Court erred in not recognizing the accused's health condition as an exceptional circumstance for granting bail pending appeal.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal reviewed the concept of exceptional circumstances for bail pending appeal, citing precedents such as Ramu Thamodarum Pillai vs. Attorney General. Based on medical reports indicating traumatic brain injury and need for constant care, the court found that incarceration would endanger the accused's life, constituting exceptional circumstances. Therefore, the revision was allowed, and bail granted.
coa_sentence_type: Bail granted pending appeal; sentence remains rigorous imprisonment of seven years with fine and compensation
brief_judgment_file_summary: Dr. Anura Liyanarachchi was convicted under Section 365 of the Penal Code and sentenced to rigorous imprisonment by the High Court of Ratnapura. His bail application pending appeal was refused by the High Court. He filed a revision application to the Court of Appeal, arguing his health condition as an exceptional circumstance. The Court of Appeal, citing precedents, found that his traumatic brain injury and need for constant care constituted exceptional circumstances, endangering his life in prison. The revision was allowed, setting aside the High Court order, and bail was granted with suitable conditions.
defence_counsel: Ronald Perera, PC with S. Anthony
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court refused bail pending appeal due to lack of exceptional circumstances. The Court of Appeal found that the High Court erred in not considering the accused's health condition as an exceptional circumstance.
precedents_cited_list: King vs. Keerala 48 NLR 202 | Q vs. Caronolis Silva 74 NLR113 | Ramu Thamodarum Pillai vs. Attorney General 2004 3 SLR 180 | Attorney General vs. Gunawardena 1996 2 SLR | Attorney General vs. Ediriveera
standard_of_review_applied: Revisionary power exercised without being trammeled by technical rules, considering interests of justice.

judges: Menaka Wijesundera J. | Neil Iddawala J.
offence_sections: Section 365 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The judgment does not detail the facts of the underlying crime. It concerns a bail application pending appeal. The petitioner was convicted of kidnapping and sentenced to 8 years rigorous imprisonment with a fine and compensation to the victim. He appealed and applied for bail pending appeal, which was refused by the High Court.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 365 of the Penal Code
hc_sentence_type: 8 years rigorous imprisonment with a fine and compensation
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the petitioner under section 365 of the Penal Code and sentenced him to 8 years rigorous imprisonment with a fine and compensation to the victim. Subsequently, the High Court refused bail pending appeal on 28th January 2020, considering the risk of absconding.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The petitioner contended that the High Court Judge considered extraneous matters (the possibility of the accused travelling abroad) and not the merits of the bail application.
