brief_judgment_file_summary: The petitioner, a former senior executive of Peoples Bank, was convicted of criminal misappropriation under the Offences against Public Property Act and sentenced to 10 years rigorous imprisonment. He appealed and sought bail pending appeal on medical grounds, but the High Court rejected his bail application. The Court of Appeal, in revision, considered his severe medical condition requiring post-operative care and found exceptional circumstances compelling bail. The COA allowed the revision, set aside the HC order, and granted bail with conditions including cash bail and sureties.
defence_counsel: Shanaka Ranasinghe, PC with N. Mihindukulasuriya and A.Ranasinghe
hc_analysis_summary: High Court rejected bail application, not considering medical condition as exceptional. COA found that HC should have considered the medical recommendation compelling bail.
standard_of_review_applied: Revision under Article 138 of the Constitution, considering whether HC misdirected on law regarding bail conditions and exceptional circumstances.

judges: Menaka Wijesundera J. | Neil Iddawala J.
offence_sections: Section 54A and 54B of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance as amended by Act No. 13 of 1984
brief_facts_summary: The suspect was arrested at his home on 07.11.2018 for alleged possession of heroin. Police reported finding 5200mg on his person and 69930mg in his almirah, with the Government Analyst Report quantifying pure heroin as 3.249g and 6.735g respectively. The suspect was remanded from 14.11.2018 and his wife, as petitioner, filed a revision application against the High Court's refusal of bail.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 54A and 54B of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance as amended by Act No. 13 of 1984
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court refused bail under Section 83(1) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance, finding no exceptional circumstances warranting release.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The petitioner sought revision to set aside the High Court's bail refusal order, arguing the order was contrary to law, there was no likelihood of near-future charges, the suspect had no previous convictions but one pending case, had been in prolonged remand since November 2018, and the COVID-19 pandemic created a risk in prison. Financial hardship on the suspect's children was also cited.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The order of the learned High Court Judge is contrary to law. | There is no likelihood of charges being framed against him in near future. | The suspect has no previous convictions but has one pending case. | The suspect has been in remand for this case from 7th November 2018. | The present situation of COVID-19 pandemic has created a risk situation for the suspect to be kept in the remand prison. | The suspect being in remand for a long period of time has made the suspect’s children helpless financially.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The evidence consists of the heroin found in the suspect's possession and the Government Analyst Report. The court focused on the delay in indictment as a key factor in its analysis.
probability_assessment_by_court: The court found the unexplained delay of over two years in serving the indictment constituted an exceptional circumstance for granting bail.
defence_version_summary: The suspect has not been tried. The bail application was based on claims of exceptional circumstances including long remand, no previous convictions, family hardship, and COVID-19 risk. No plea or trial has occurred.
legal_errors_description: The High Court failed to properly consider the inordinate and unexplained delay in indictment as an exceptional circumstance under Section 83(1) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed the concept of 'exceptional circumstances' under Section 83(1) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance. It rejected grounds like financial hardship and COVID-19 risk as common to all prisoners, but found the unexplained delay of over two years in serving the indictment, after the Government Analyst Report was issued, constituted an exceptional circumstance. The court emphasized the need to avoid unreasonable delay in serious cases and, in the interest of justice, granted bail with strict conditions.
coa_sentence_type: Bail granted with conditions: cash bail of Rs. 200,000, two sureties of Rs. 500,000 each, reporting to police station every Sunday, surrender of passport, and bail cancellation for violation.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The petitioner, wife of a suspect arrested for heroin possession, filed a revision against the High Court's bail refusal. The Court of Appeal found the suspect had been in remand for over two years without indictment and the delay was unexplained. Considering this an exceptional circumstance, the court allowed the appeal and granted bail with financial conditions and reporting requirements.
defence_counsel: L.B.G Perera
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court refused bail, finding no exceptional circumstances. The Court of Appeal held the High Court erred by not giving due weight to the inordinate and unexplained delay in indictment, which constituted an exceptional circumstance warranting bail.
precedents_cited_list: Anuruddha Ratwatte and Others vs. The Attorney General 2003 2 SLR 39 | Cader vs. Officer - In - Charge Narcotics Bureau 2006 3 SLR 74 | Attorney General vs. Ranasinghe and others 1993 2 SLR p 81 @ p 85 | Gnanapandithen V. Balanayagam (1998) 1 SLR 391 | Shiyam v Officer-in-Charge, Police Narcotics Bureau & another (2006) 2 Sri L.R. 156 | Ramu Thamodarampillai Vs. The Attorney General 2004 3 SLR 180 | C.A. (PHC) APN No 16/12- CA minutes dated 14.06. 2012 | CA Application No 44/2002 CA minutes dated 06.03.2003
standard_of_review_applied: Revisionary jurisdiction under Article 138 of the Constitution and Section 364 of the Criminal Procedure Code Act, No. 15 of 1979, to examine legality, propriety, and regularity of proceedings.
sentencing_principles_applied: Principles for granting bail in exceptional circumstances under Section 83(1) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance, considering factors like delay and justice.

judges: Devika Abeyratne J | P. Kumararatnam J
offence_sections: Section 296 of Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The Appellant was convicted of murdering his wife by setting her on fire. The case relied on the dying declaration where she accused him, witness accounts of hearing cries and transporting her to hospital, and medical evidence of burn injuries. The Appellant defended by claiming suicide.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 296 of Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the Appellant based on the dying declaration and other evidence, and sentenced him to death. The judge considered the dying declaration admissible despite objections from the defence.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The Appellant argued that the conviction was bad in law as it relied solely on the uncorroborated dying declaration of the deceased. Additionally, the prosecution failed to prove that the offence was committed by the Appellant.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The conviction is bad in law as the Learned trial Judge has solely relied on the dying declaration of the deceased which is not corroborated by any other evidence. | The Learned Trial Judge has failed to consider that the prosecution has not proved that the alleged offence was committed by the accused-Appellant.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed the dying declaration, witness testimonies, and medical evidence, concluding that the dying declaration was reliable and corroborated by other evidence. The court addressed contradictions and found no prejudice to the Appellant.
probability_assessment_by_court: The court considered the dying declaration and found no reason for the deceased to falsely implicate the Appellant, thus no reasonable doubt.
defence_version_summary: The Appellant pleaded not guilty, made a dock statement claiming the deceased committed suicide, and called a defence witness. The court found the defence version not credible.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The COA analyzed the admissibility and reliability of the dying declaration under Section 32(1) of Evidence Ordinance, cited precedents on dying declarations, addressed contradictions such as time discrepancies and recording errors, and concluded that the prosecution established a strong prima facie case. The court found no material errors and upheld the High Court judgment.
coa_sentence_type: Death
brief_judgment_file_summary: The Appellant was convicted of murdering his wife and sentenced to death by the High Court of Matara. He appealed on grounds that the conviction relied solely on an uncorroborated dying declaration and the prosecution failed to prove the offence. The Court of Appeal examined the dying declaration's admissibility, witness evidence, and medical reports, dismissing the appeal and upholding the conviction and sentence.
defence_counsel: Mr.Razik Zarook PC with Mr.Chanakya Liyanage AAL
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted the Appellant based on the dying declaration and other evidence, and the Court of Appeal found no errors in this reasoning, upholding the decision.
precedents_cited_list: Dharmawansa Silva and Another v. The Republic of Sri Lanka [1981] 2 Sri.L.R.439 | Sigera v Attorney General [2011] 1 Sri.L.R. 201 | Mendis v. Paramaswami 62 NLR 302
standard_of_review_applied: Appellate review of evidence and legal issues regarding dying declaration admissibility and reliability.

judges: Arjuna Obeyesekere, J.
offence_sections: Section 160(8)(a) of the Intellectual Property Act No. 36 of 2003
brief_facts_summary: The Petitioner, a former employee of Hayleys Aventura, was accused of disclosing confidential information to his new employer after leaving. A civil case was settled with an undertaking not to disclose, but after it expired, a criminal complaint was filed under the Intellectual Property Act. The Magistrate issued summons without properly considering the material, leading to this writ application.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The Petitioner argued that the Magistrate failed to consider the material placed before him and the ingredients of the offence before issuing summons, making the decision illegal and unreasonable.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Magistrate did not consider material placed before him | Magistrate did not consider ingredients of the offence | Charge sheet is vague and defective
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court analyzed the documentary evidence, including the affidavit of the Managing Director, and found that the Magistrate did not assess whether it supported the charge. No witnesses were examined at this stage.
probability_assessment_by_court: Court applied prima facie test to determine if sufficient grounds exist based on material before Magistrate.
defence_version_summary: Petitioner filed writ application challenging Magistrate's order, arguing procedural errors. No defence version presented in Magistrate's Court as case not yet tried.
legal_errors_description: Magistrate failed to consider material and ingredients of offence before issuing summons, thus acting outside jurisdiction and illegally.
procedural_defects_description: Magistrate did not follow procedure under Section 139 of Code of Criminal Procedure Act by not forming opinion based on sufficient grounds.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The COA referenced precedents requiring Magistrates to form an opinion on sufficient grounds before issuing summons. The Magistrate's order did not demonstrate consideration of material or offence ingredients, so it was illegal and unreasonable. The writ was allowed, quashing the order.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The Petitioner, a former employee accused of disclosing confidential information, challenged the Magistrate's order issuing summons. The Court of Appeal found that the Magistrate failed to properly consider the material and ingredients of the offence, thus acting illegally. The writ was allowed, quashing the order, but the Respondent was permitted to file a fresh application if desired.
defence_counsel: Romesh De Silva, P.C., with Shanaka Cooray
precedents_cited_list: Malinie Guneratne vs Abeysinghe and another | Sundra Rajoo Nadarajah vs Menteri Luar Negeri, Malaysia & ORS | Peter Leo Fernando vs The Attorney General and Others | Derek Kelly and another vs Yasasiri Kasthuriarachchi | Kesri v. Muhammad Baksh
standard_of_review_applied: Prima facie sufficiency of grounds test as per Malinie Guneratne vs Abeysinghe

judges: K. Priyantha Fernando, J. | Sampath B. Abayakoon, J.
offence_sections: Section 364(1) of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The appellant was accused of raping PW1 in her home while her husband was out. PW1 delayed reporting the incident due to fear. The appellant claimed the sexual intercourse was consensual, and medical evidence showed injuries compatible with both forced and consensual sex.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 364(1) of the Penal Code
hc_sentence_type: 10 years rigorous imprisonment, fine of Rs. 5000, compensation of Rs. 450,000
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the appellant of rape based on the testimony of PW1 and medical evidence, sentencing him to imprisonment and fines.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant appealed on grounds including delay in making the complaint, contradictions in the prosecutrix's testimony, failure to apply the test of probability, and misapplication of legal principles regarding dock statements.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The learned Trial Judge has failed to consider the fact that the complaint is belated. | The learned Trial Judge has failed to consider the vital contradictions in the testimony of the prosecutrix. | The learned Trial Judge has failed to apply the test of probability and improbability to the version of the prosecutrix. | The learned Trial Judge has wrongly applied the principles of law relating to dock statements and has failed to offer appropriate prominence and due consideration of the dock statement in accordance with the established legal principles.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found that the delay in complaint and contradictions in PW1's testimony affected her credibility. Medical evidence was inconclusive, and key witnesses were not called, raising reasonable doubt.
probability_assessment_by_court: The court applied the test of probability and found reasonable doubt due to delay, contradictions, and lack of corroboration.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty and claimed through his dock statement that the sexual intercourse was consensual, as he had an affair with PW1. No alibi or defence witnesses were presented.
legal_errors_description: The High Court failed to consider the delay in complaint, contradictions in testimony, failed to apply the probability test, and wrongly applied legal principles regarding dock statements.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal thoroughly examined the evidence, noting that the delay in complaint and contradictions in the prosecutrix's testimony undermined her credibility. The medical evidence was compatible with both forced and consensual sex, and key witnesses were not called. The court applied legal precedents on belated witnesses and the sufficiency of prosecutrix's testimony, concluding that the prosecution did not prove the absence of consent beyond reasonable doubt, leading to acquittal.
coa_sentence_type: Acquitted, no sentence imposed
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused-appellant was convicted by the High Court of Galle for rape under section 364(1) of the Penal Code and sentenced to imprisonment and fines. He appealed on grounds including delay in complaint and contradictions in testimony. The Court of Appeal found that the prosecution failed to prove absence of consent beyond reasonable doubt due to credibility issues and lack of corroboration, allowing the appeal and acquitting the appellant.
defence_counsel: Neranjan Jayasinghe
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted the appellant based on the testimony of PW1 and medical evidence. However, the Court of Appeal criticized the High Court for failing to consider the delay in complaint, contradictions in testimony, and for misapplying legal principles regarding dock statements.
precedents_cited_list: State of Himachal Pradesh V. Asha Ram AIR [2006] SC 381: [2006] SCC(Cri)296 | Sumanasena V. Attorney General [1999] 35ri LR
standard_of_review_applied: Review based on whether prosecution proved absence of consent beyond reasonable doubt, considering evidence and legal principles.

judges: Menaka Wijesundera J. | Neil Iddawala J.
offence_sections: Section 8 and/or Section 9 of the Assistance to and Protection of Victims of Crime and Witnesses Act No 04 of 2015
brief_facts_summary: The suspect was produced for threatening Karawilakande Karunawathi and her husband and causing hurt to force them to withdraw their daughter's complaint about sexual assault and kidnapping. The complaint was lodged on 5.12.19, but the threat occurred on 7.11.2019. The suspect has been on remand for nearly 18 months without trial progress.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The petitioner applied for bail citing belated complaint and prolonged remand without trial progress. The court considered the delay and ambiguity in finality of proceedings as grounds for bail.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Belated complaint not explained | Prolonged remand without trial progress | Undue delay in proceedings
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The court examined the prima facie material under the Act and noted the lack of progress in trial, leading to bail consideration due to procedural delay.
probability_assessment_by_court: Court considered prima facie evidence and procedural delay for bail.
defence_version_summary: Suspect applied for bail denying allegations and citing procedural delays; no guilty plea or alibi discussed.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The COA analyzed the bail application under the Act, noting that suspects can be remanded only if prima facie material exists, and trials should be day-to-day without delay. Due to ambiguity in finality and 18-month remand without indictment, bail is granted with conditions.
coa_sentence_type: Bail granted with conditions: Rs 50000 cash bail each, two sureties of Rs 100000 each, report to police station every Sunday, and not to interfere with complainants.
brief_judgment_file_summary: This is a Court of Appeal bail application under the Victims and Witnesses Act. The suspect was accused of threatening victims to withdraw a sexual assault complaint. The Court granted bail due to belated complaint and undue delay in proceedings, with conditions including cash bail and reporting.
defence_counsel: Sabdika Wellappili

judges: Menaka Wijesundera J. | Neil Iddawala J.
offence_sections: Section 8(1) of the Assistance to the Protection of Victims of Crimes and Witnesses Act No. 4 of 2015
brief_facts_summary: The petitioner was initially arrested for cannabis possession and later produced for a bank robbery. While in remand, a witness complained that the petitioner threatened him via mobile phone, providing a video. The petitioner was then produced under section 8(1) of the Protection of Victims Act and has been in remand for nearly 25 months.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The petitioner argues for bail based on exceptional circumstances, including the long period of remand (nearly 25 months) and the magistrate remanding without a proper inquiry to ascertain prima facie material.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Long period of remand (nearly 25 months) | Magistrate remanded without proper inquiry to ascertain prima facie material
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The court considered the complaint and video evidence from the witness, but no detailed evidence analysis was conducted as this is a bail application. The focus was on the remand period and procedural aspects.
probability_assessment_by_court: The court assessed that the long remand period and ambiguity in indictment constitute exceptional circumstances for bail.
defence_version_summary: The petitioner sought bail on the grounds of exceptional circumstances, including prolonged remand and lack of prima facie inquiry, without pleading guilty or not guilty to the charges.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal considered the submissions, including the long period of remand (nearly 25 months), the concession by the Attorney-General's counsel, the fact that indictment filing is not yet known, and cited precedent CA(PHC) APN 64/2009. The court found exceptional circumstances and granted bail with conditions including cash bail, sureties, and reporting requirements.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The suspect petitioner applied for bail under the Assistance to the Protection of Victims of Crimes and Witnesses Act for threatening a witness in a bank robbery case. He had been in remand for nearly 25 months. The Court of Appeal found exceptional circumstances due to the long remand period and lack of indictment, and granted bail with conditions including Rs. 1 million cash bail, two sureties, and regular reporting to the police.
prosecution_counsel: Maheshika Silva SC for the State
defence_counsel: Nalin Ladduwahetty PC with C. Athukorala and Vajira Ranasinghe for the Suspect Petitioner
precedents_cited_list: CA(PHC) APN 64/2009
standard_of_review_applied: Exceptional circumstances for bail as per section 10(1)(a) of the Act

judges: Devika Aheyratne, J. | P. Kumararatanam, J.
offence_sections: Section 294 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The accused was convicted for the murder of the deceased following a land dispute. On the day of the incident, the deceased was cutting banana trees on the disputed land when the accused arrived with weapons and assaulted him, causing fatal injuries. The key evidence is the eyewitness testimony of the deceased's young son, and medical evidence confirmed the cause of death. The accused was arrested two days after fleeing the scene.
evidence_type_secondary: Medical evidence and recovery of weapons
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 294 of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the accused of murder based on the credible eyewitness testimony of the deceased's son and medical evidence. The trial judge found the child witness consistent and intelligent, and sentenced the accused to death.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant challenged the conviction arguing that the child eyewitness was not credible and his evidence creates doubt. Additionally, it was contended that the accused acted on cumulative provocation due to the land dispute and should be guilty of culpable homicide not murder under exception 4 of section 294.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Eyewitness PW2 is not credible and was lying | Child witness evidence is unreliable due to memory issues | Accused acted on cumulative provocation and should be considered for lesser offence under exception 4 of section 294 of the Penal Code
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the eyewitness PW2's testimony to be consistent, credible, and intelligent despite being a child. Medical evidence strongly supported the prosecution case, and the defence version was not believable due to contradictions.
probability_assessment_by_court: The COA found the prosecution version more probable and the accused guilty beyond reasonable doubt for culpable homicide based on the evidence.
defence_version_summary: The accused pleaded not guilty and claimed self-defence, stating that the deceased attacked him first. He suggested that the injuries occurred from falling on wooden planks or running into a jak tree. The court found his version not credible due to contradictions and inconsistent evidence.
legal_errors_description: The trial judge failed to consider the application for lesser culpability under exception 4 of section 294 of the Penal Code based on cumulative provocation.
procedural_defects_description: The assigned counsel made an application to consider lesser offence, but the trial judge did not address it properly or consider it in the background of the evidence.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal thoroughly evaluated the evidence, affirming the credibility of the child eyewitness and the medical findings. They considered the long-standing land dispute as cumulative provocation, applying precedents on sudden fight. Consequently, they modified the conviction from murder to culpable homicide not amounting to murder under section 297, setting aside the death sentence and imposing 10 years rigorous imprisonment with a fine.
coa_sentence_type: 10 years rigorous imprisonment and a fine of Rs 5000 with default one year simple imprisonment
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused was convicted of murder and sentenced to death by the High Court. On appeal, the Court of Appeal found the child eyewitness credible but considered the land dispute as cumulative provocation, reducing the offence to culpable homicide not murder. The death sentence was set aside, and the accused was sentenced to 10 years rigorous imprisonment with a fine.
defence_counsel: Sharon Serasinghe
cause_of_death_exact_text: 12 injuries inflicted by a blunt weapon have been identified and injuries No 7 and 8 on the head of the deceased were said to be necessarily fatal.
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted the accused of murder based on credible eyewitness testimony. However, the COA found that the trial judge erred by not considering the defence of cumulative provocation and the application for lesser culpability.
precedents_cited_list: Murugesu Vs The King (1951) 52 NLR 471-472 | The King Vs Jinasekere 46 NLR 246 | King VS Bellana Vithanage Eddin 41 NLR 345 | Panchehi vs the State of U.P (1998) 7 SCC 177 | M.Ajith Kumara alias Ajith Vs. Attorney General in CA No 2018/2012
standard_of_review_applied: The COA reviewed the evidence and applied legal principles on provocation and lesser offences from precedents.
sentencing_principles_applied: The COA considered the circumstances of the case, including the provocation and the time already served, in imposing the sentence.
final_charge_after_appeal: Culpable homicide not amounting to murder under section 297 of the Penal Code

judges: N. Bandula Karunarathna J. | R. Gurusinghe J.
offence_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The Appellant, a Sub Inspector at Angana Police post, had a meal with two deceased police officers on May 19, 2002. An argument broke out over a stolen farewell gift, and the Appellant shot both deceased with a T56 gun. Key evidence includes eyewitness testimony, medical evidence, and the Appellant's confession to other officers.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the Appellant of murder based on evidence including eyewitness account, dock statement, and circumstantial evidence, and sentenced him to death.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The Appellant argued denial of fair trial as judgment was delivered immediately after oral submissions, insufficient judicial evaluation, errors in burden of proof principles, and failure to consider defences of accidental firing and grave and sudden provocation.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Appellant has been denied of a fair trial as the judgement was delivered immediately after the conclusion of the oral submissions thereby demonstrating that due judicial consideration has not been given in arriving at the final verdict. | The judgement of the Learned Trial Judge is depleted of sufficient judicial evaluation as is required in a criminal trial. | The Learned Trial Judge flawed on the principles relating to overall burden of proof. | The Learned Trial Judge flawed on the principles relating to the burden of proof in a defence of accidental firing. | The evidence led at the trial warrants the consideration of the plea of grave and sudden provocation.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed eyewitness testimony, dock statement, and circumstantial evidence, and found no material to support the defence. Medical evidence contradicted the accidental firing claim.
probability_assessment_by_court: The court found that the evidence did not create reasonable doubt and rejected the defences based on medical and circumstantial evidence.
defence_version_summary: The Appellant did not deny complicity but claimed accidental firing during a fight in his dock statement. He called no witnesses. The court found his version questionable due to medical and circumstantial evidence.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The COA examined grounds of appeal including fair trial, judicial evaluation, burden of proof, and defences. They held the trial judge properly evaluated all evidence, cited precedents on fair trial and burden of proof, and found no prejudice. Medical evidence contradicted accidental firing, and provocation plea was not established. Thus, the HC decision was affirmed.
coa_sentence_type: Death
brief_judgment_file_summary: The Appellant was convicted of murdering two police officers and sentenced to death by the High Court. He appealed on grounds of fair trial, judicial evaluation, burden of proof, and defences. The Court of Appeal analyzed the evidence, including eyewitness testimony, medical evidence, and confession, and found no merit in the appeal. The conviction and death sentence were affirmed.
defence_counsel: Indica Mallawaratchy AAL
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted based on evidence including eyewitness account, dock statement, and circumstantial evidence. The COA found no fault in this analysis and affirmed the decision.
precedents_cited_list: Zahira Habibullah Sheikh and Others V. State of Gujarat | Rajesh Gupta V The State of Bihar | R V R.E.M | R V Sheppard | Woolmington V DPP | The Queen V. Buddharakkita Thera and 2 Others | Queen V. Kularatne | Jamis V. The Queen | K. D. J Perera V. The King | Fradd V. Brown & Company.
standard_of_review_applied: The appellate court will not lightly disturb findings of fact unless manifestly wrong, as per Fradd V. Brown & Company.

judges: N. Bandula Karunarathna J. | R. Gurusinghe J.
offence_sections: Section 366 of the Penal Code punishable under section 3 of the Offences Against Public Property Act No.12 of 1982
brief_facts_summary: The appellants were accused of conspiring to rob and robbing Rs.743,000 from the State Engineering Corporation. The prosecution relied on circumstantial evidence and statements made by the appellants, which led to the recovery of some money. However, the evidence was inconsistent, and no direct eyewitnesses were presented.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 366 of the Penal Code punishable under section 3 of the Offences Against Public Property Act No.12 of 1982
hc_sentence_type: Rigorous imprisonment for 3 years and a fine of Rs.743,000 with default sentence of 3 years simple imprisonment
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court judge acquitted the appellants of the original charges of conspiracy and robbery but convicted them of the lesser offence of theft. The conviction was based on circumstantial evidence and the statements made by the appellants under section 27(1) of the Evidence Ordinance.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellants appealed on grounds including the trial judge's failure to properly evaluate evidence, inconsistencies in the investigation officer's testimony, lack of independent evidence, failure to identify the stolen property specifically, and not considering the essential elements of the offence of theft.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Failure to evaluate the evidence | Failure to consider inconsistency in investigation officer's evidence | No independent evidence against appellants | No specific or identified property to establish theft | Failure to consider main components of theft offence
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found that the prosecution's evidence was inconsistent, particularly the investigation officer's testimony on the amount of money recovered. The evidence was circumstantial and did not conclusively establish the elements of theft.
probability_assessment_by_court: The court assessed that the circumstantial evidence was not incompatible with innocence and did not exclude other reasonable hypotheses, leading to doubt.
defence_version_summary: The appellants pleaded not guilty and did not present any defence evidence. The court concluded that the prosecution failed to prove the case beyond reasonable doubt.
legal_errors_description: The High Court failed to evaluate evidence properly, consider inconsistencies in testimony, identify the stolen property, and establish all elements of the offence of theft.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed the evidence and found significant inconsistencies in the investigation officer's testimony regarding the recovered money. They also noted the failure to identify the property and establish the elements of theft. Citing precedents on circumstantial evidence and credibility, the court concluded that the prosecution did not prove the case beyond reasonable doubt, leading to the quashing of the conviction.
coa_sentence_type: Acquitted, no sentence imposed
brief_judgment_file_summary: The appellants were convicted of theft by the High Court after being acquitted of robbery charges. They appealed on grounds of evidence evaluation and legal errors. The Court of Appeal found the evidence inconsistent and insufficient to prove theft, quashed the conviction, and acquitted the appellants.
defence_counsel: J.P. Gamage AAL
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted the appellants based on circumstantial evidence and accused statements, but the Court of Appeal found that the High Court failed to properly consider evidence inconsistencies and legal elements of theft.
precedents_cited_list: Sarath Fernando V Attorney General 2014(1) SLR 16 | Bhoirai V Sita Ram: (1936) 38 BOMLR 344 | R V Morrissey: (1995), 22 O.R. (3d) 514, 80 O.A.C. 161 (Ont. C.A.) | Heen Banda V The Queen; 75 NLR 54 | Pahalli Das V The State: AIR 1952 Orissa 162 | Biswanath Satpathy v The State; AIR 1967 Ori 46 | Rev Kananke Dhammadima Thero V Attorney General; CA 310/92
standard_of_review_applied: The court applied the standard for circumstantial evidence, requiring that the evidence be incompatible with innocence and exclude other reasonable hypotheses.

judges: K Priyantha Fernando, J. | Sampath B Abayakoon, J.
offence_sections: section 22(3) read with section 22(1) of the Firearms Ordinance
brief_facts_summary: The appellant was accused of possessing an automatic T-56 firearm on or about 31 March 2012. The prosecution claimed the weapon was recovered based on a statement by the appellant. The appellant denied possession and claimed he was arrested on 30 March. He was a worker at Sri Lanka Ports Authority.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: section 22(3) read with section 22(1) of the Firearms Ordinance
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court found the appellant guilty based on the recovery of the weapon and his statement, and sentenced him to life imprisonment.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appeal contended that the evidence failed to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt, the prosecution suppressed evidence and failed to call material witnesses, and the appellant provided a reasonable explanation.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Failure to prove charge beyond reasonable doubt | Suppression of evidence by prosecution | Failure to call material witnesses | Prosecution did not divulge full facts
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The COA found prosecution witnesses not truthful about the arrest date, and the appellant's version more probable. The evidence was insufficient to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt.
probability_assessment_by_court: The COA found the appellant's version more probable and that reasonable doubt was created.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty, gave evidence and called his wife. He claimed he was arrested on 30 March and no weapon was recovered from him. The court found his version credible.
legal_errors_description: The High Court did not properly evaluate the evidence and failed to give benefit of doubt.
procedural_defects_description: Prosecution suppressed evidence and failed to divulge material facts.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The COA analyzed the evidence, found contradictions in prosecution testimony regarding the arrest date, noted the suppression of evidence, and held that the prosecution failed to prove the case beyond reasonable doubt. They applied precedents on burden of proof and found the appellant's explanation reasonable.
coa_sentence_type: Sentence set aside, appellant acquitted
brief_judgment_file_summary: The appellant was convicted by the High Court of Kegalle for illegal possession of a firearm and sentenced to life imprisonment. On appeal, the Court of Appeal found prosecution evidence unreliable due to contradictions in the arrest date and suppression of evidence. The appeal was allowed, conviction set aside, and the appellant acquitted.
defence_counsel: Kalinga Indatissa P.C. with Niranjan Inyagolla, Rashmi Indatissa and Razana Salih
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted based on prosecution evidence, but the COA found that evidence was not credible and the HC should have considered the totality of evidence and given benefit of doubt.
precedents_cited_list: Queen Vs. Sumanasena 66 NLR 350 | Pantis Vs. The Attorney General (1998) 2 SLR 148 | James Silva Vs. republic of Sri Lanka (1980) 2 SLR 167
standard_of_review_applied: Evaluation of evidence and reasonable doubt standard

judges: Devika Abeyratne, J | P. Kumararatnam, J
offence_sections: Section 357 of the Penal Code read with Section 32 of the Penal Code; Section 364(2) of the Penal Code as amended by Act No. 22 of 1995
location_of_offence: Neelabemma area and Wilpattu jungle, Anuradhapura
brief_facts_summary: The prosecutrix, a married woman, was at home when the two appellants came, asked for a coin rope, drank on her veranda and left. The 2nd appellant returned, struggled with her, and the 1st appellant kicked her. They tied her husband, dragged her to a rock in Wilpattu jungle, assaulted her with a knife and bottle, and both raped her for two hours. She escaped when they fell asleep, went to a bunt, and was taken to hospital. Key evidence included her testimony, medical evidence, and statements from her husband and son.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 357 of the Penal Code read with Section 32 of the Penal Code; Section 364(2) of the Penal Code as amended by Act No. 22 of 1995
hc_sentence_type: Rigorous Imprisonment 5 years and fine for count 1; Rigorous Imprisonment 12 years and fine for counts 2 and 3; sentences to run concurrently
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the appellants on all charges, believing the prosecutrix's testimony and finding the charges proved beyond reasonable doubt. They were sentenced as above.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellants argued the trial judge erred in convicting on uncorroborated testimony, failed to consider that the doctor's testimony contradicted the prosecutrix, and that the findings were untenable and contrary to law, and failed to consider medical evidence correctly.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The learned trial judge erred in law and facts by convicting the Appellants for charge of rape on the uncorroborated testimony. | The learned trial judge has failed to consider that the testimony of the doctor who is an independent witness contradicts the evidence of the prosecutrix. | The findings of the learned trial judge in the impugned judgment are untenable and contrary to the well settled principles of law. | The learned trial judge has failed to consider the medical evidence in the correct perspective.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the prosecutrix's testimony on rape was not corroborated, as she did not mention rape to her husband, son, or doctor initially, and medical evidence did not support sexual assault.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal found the prosecution failed to prove the rape charges beyond reasonable doubt due to lack of corroboration and contradictions.
defence_version_summary: The appellants pleaded not guilty and challenged the prosecution evidence through cross-examination. The court found the prosecution evidence insufficient for the rape charges.
legal_errors_description: The trial judge failed to consider the lack of corroboration for the rape charge and the contradictions in the prosecutrix's testimony.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed the evidence and found the prosecutrix's testimony on rape was not corroborated. She did not mention rape to her husband, son, or the doctor, and medical evidence did not support it. The court cited precedents on the need for corroboration in rape cases. It upheld the abduction conviction but set aside the rape convictions due to insufficient proof beyond reasonable doubt.
coa_sentence_type: For count 1, each appellant sentenced to 5 years Rigorous Imprisonment and a fine of Rs.5000, to run from the date of conviction (13/07/2017). Convictions and sentences for counts 2 and 3 are set aside.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The two appellants were convicted in the High Court of Anuradhapura for abduction and gang rape. They appealed on grounds of uncorroborated testimony and medical evidence contradictions. The Court of Appeal upheld the abduction conviction but acquitted them of rape due to lack of corroboration and inconsistencies. The sentences for abduction were affirmed, and the rape convictions and sentences were set aside.
defence_counsel: For 1st appellant: Mr.Amila Palliyage with Mr.Duminda Alwis and Ms.Ruwanthi Doralagoda; for 2nd appellant: Mr.Neranjan Jayasinghe with Ms.Isansi Danthanarayana
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted the appellants on all charges, believing the prosecutrix's testimony. The Court of Appeal found the High Court failed to properly evaluate the need for corroboration and the inconsistencies in the evidence regarding the rape charges.
precedents_cited_list: Sunil and others v. Attorney General [1986] 1 Sri.L. R 230 | Premasiri v. Attorney General [2006] 3 Sri.L.R
standard_of_review_applied: Review of evidence and application of law on corroboration in rape cases
final_charge_after_appeal: Abduction for illicit intercourse (Section 357 read with Section 32 of the Penal Code)

judges: N. Bandula Karunarathna, J. | R. Gurusinghe, J.
offence_sections: Section 5(2) of the Offences against Public Property Act, No. 12/1982 as amended by the Act No. 28 of 1999 read with Section 403 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The appellant pawned false bangles pretending they were gold to the People’s Bank Liberty Plaza branch on three separate dates in September 2005, obtaining sums of money. He was convicted after trial. The appellant admitted to the offences under Section 420 of the Criminal Procedure Code, and is now 57 years old with a kidney disease.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 5(2) of the Offences against Public Property Act, No. 12/1982 as amended by the Act No. 28 of 1999 read with Section 403 of the Penal Code
hc_sentence_type: Rigorous Imprisonment 10 years for each count, fines as specified
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the appellant on all charges and sentenced him to 10 years rigorous imprisonment per count with fines. The sentences were to run consecutively, resulting in 36 years imprisonment, with reasons set out by the judge.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant did not challenge the conviction but sought only a reduction of the sentence, arguing that the aggregated sentence of 36 years is excessive and not proportionate.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Sentence of 36 years imprisonment is excessive | Sentence not proportionate considering appellant's age and health
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The prosecution relied on the appellant's admission under Section 420 of the Criminal Procedure Code and evidence of pawning transactions. The Court of Appeal considered this admission and mitigating factors for sentencing.
probability_assessment_by_court: The court assessed the sentence proportionality based on mitigating factors like age, health, and admission, rather than probability of guilt.
defence_version_summary: The appellant did not contest the conviction on appeal, seeking only sentence reduction. At trial, he likely pleaded not guilty, but this is not explicitly stated.
legal_errors_description: The High Court imposed consecutive sentences totalling 36 years, which the Court of Appeal found excessive and not proportionate to the offence.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal considered sentencing guidelines from precedents, the appellant's age (57), kidney disease, admission under Section 420 CPC, and compared with similar cases. They found the aggregate sentence of 36 years disproportionate and ordered sentences to run concurrently, reducing effective imprisonment to 10 years, while upholding fines.
coa_sentence_type: Ten years rigorous imprisonment for each count to run concurrently, deemed served from 14th November 2018. Fines unchanged. Default imprisonment reduced to one year rigorous imprisonment for each fine.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The appellant was convicted in the High Court of Colombo for pawning false bangles as gold on three occasions in 2005 and sentenced to 10 years rigorous imprisonment per count consecutively. He appealed only on sentence reduction. The Court of Appeal considered sentencing guidelines, his age, health, and admission, found the aggregate sentence disproportionate, and ordered sentences to run concurrently, reducing effective imprisonment to 10 years, while upholding fines and dismissing the appeal subject to sentence changes.
defence_counsel: Neranjan Jayasinghe
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court imposed consecutive sentences totalling 36 years imprisonment. The Court of Appeal found this disproportionate considering the appellant's circumstances and the nature of the offences.
precedents_cited_list: Aswan Mohamed Riswan Vs. Attorney General C.A. Revision No. C.A. (PHC) APM 141/2013, H.C. Ratnapura H.C. No. 25/2010, Decided on 25th March 2015 | Attorney General Vs. Gunaratne and others [1995] 2 SLR 240 | Soman vs State of Kerala on 14 December, 2012 | State of Punjab v. Prem Sagar
standard_of_review_applied: Review of sentence for proportionality based on sentencing guidelines and mitigating factors.
sentencing_principles_applied: Discussion of sentencing factors from precedents, including nature of offence, offender's culpability, mental state, impact, guilty plea, remorse, restitution, previous character, proportionality, reform, consistency, aggravating and mitigating factors.

judges: Devika Abeyratne,J | P.Kumararatnam,J
offence_sections: Murder under the Penal Code and Section 317 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: On 30 July 1996, the accused-appellant allegedly stabbed PW1 and PW2 and chased the deceased, who was later found dead. The prosecution relied on eyewitness testimony and medical reports. The appellant claimed self-defense, stating he was assaulted by four individuals with clubs.
evidence_type_secondary: Medical evidence and recovery of weapon
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Murder under the Penal Code and Section 317 of the Penal Code
hc_sentence_type: Death sentence for murder; for each count of grievous hurt, one year rigorous imprisonment and fine of Rs 1000
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the appellant for murder and grievous injuries based on eyewitness testimony and medical evidence. The judge found the appellant guilty and sentenced him to death for murder and imprisonment with fines for the other counts.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant appealed the convictions and sentences, arguing that the prosecution failed to prove intent for murder, that the injuries were not grievous, and that the trial judge erred in not considering self-defense.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Doubt on seriousness of injuries | Prosecution suppressed medical report | Failure to consider self-defense | Lack of evidence for murderous intention
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found that witness testimonies were corroborative but medical evidence was weak, and the prosecution failed to prove murderous intent beyond reasonable doubt.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal assessed that there was reasonable doubt regarding the intent to cause death, leading to a modification of the conviction.
defence_version_summary: The accused pleaded not guilty and claimed self-defense. He testified that he was attacked by four people with clubs and brandished a knife in self-defense, accidentally injuring them. The court found his version plausible.
legal_errors_description: The High Court failed to consider the defense of self-defense and the possibility of a lesser offence, and misdirected on the law regarding intent.
procedural_defects_description: The prosecution suppressed the medical report of the appellant, which was a material fact.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed the evidence and found that the injuries to PW1 and PW2 were not conclusively grievous, the appellant's self-defense claim was plausible, and the prosecution did not prove murderous intent beyond reasonable doubt. Citing precedents on sudden fight and lesser offences, the court modified the conviction to culpable homicide not amounting to murder.
coa_sentence_type: Eight years rigorous imprisonment for culpable homicide, and for counts two and three, one year rigorous imprisonment each to run concurrently from 12.10.2018
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused-appellant was convicted by the High Court for murder and grievous hurt, sentenced to death and imprisonment with fines. He appealed, and the Court of Appeal partly allowed the appeal, finding that the prosecution did not prove murder intent. The conviction was modified to culpable homicide not amounting to murder, with a sentence of eight years rigorous imprisonment, while maintaining the sentences for the other counts.
defence_counsel: Neranjan Jayasinghe
cause_of_death_exact_text: shock due to bleeding from heart due to a stab injury
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted based on eyewitness testimony and medical evidence, but the Court of Appeal found that the High Court failed to consider self-defense and improperly assessed the injuries and intent.
precedents_cited_list: Lakshami Singh vs State of Bihar AIR 1976 SC 2263 | Ranjit Wijesiri alias Wije vs The Attorney General CA No 64/96 | King VS Albert Appuhamy 41 NLR page 505 | King Vs. Vidanalage Lanty 42 NLR page 317 | King Vs. Bellana Vithanage Eddin 41 NLR page 345 | King Vs. Mendis 54 NLR page 177 | In re Singaram Padayachi and others [A.I.R: 1944) Mad. 223] | Ratanlal’s Law of Crimes (16th edition), page 705
standard_of_review_applied: Review based on reasonable doubt and precedents on sudden fight and lesser offences
sentencing_principles_applied: Consideration of facts, lesser culpability, and time spent in remand
final_charge_after_appeal: Culpable homicide not amounting to murder

judges: Arjuna Obeyesekere, J.
offence_sections: Sections 12, 43, 47, 75, 129, and 163 of the Customs Ordinance, and the Excise Special Provisions Act
brief_facts_summary: The petitioners imported Beehive Brandy essence, but Customs alleged it was brandy concentrate. An investigation found misdescription and failure to store goods in bonded warehouse. Key evidence included supplier correspondence, government analyst reports confirming 40% alcohol content, and customs records.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The petitioners argued that the classification of Beehive Brandy as essence was correct, and forfeiture under Section 47 requires stealth, which was not present. For storage, they claimed goods were kept outside bond due to space constraints and with consent.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Misdescription of goods as essence rather than concentrate | Forfeiture under Section 47 not applicable without stealth | Storage outside bond was due to space constraints and with consent
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court considered evidence from the supplier, government analyst, and customs inquiry. The government analyst reports confirmed 40% alcohol content, indicating the product was a spirit, not essence.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court found the inquiry officer's decision based on available material, neither illegal nor irrational.
defence_version_summary: The petitioners pleaded not guilty to the allegations, arguing that they imported essence correctly classified, and stored goods outside bond due to lack of space, with no intention to evade duties.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The COA analyzed the HS Code classification, citing precedents, and held that forfeiture under Section 47 requires stealth, which was present based on the petitioner's knowledge and actions. For storage violations, Section 75 was contravened. The COA found the inquiry officer's decision legal and rational, dismissing the application.
coa_sentence_type: Forfeiture of goods and monetary penalties as per order 'P9'
brief_judgment_file_summary: The petitioners, Free Lanka Trading Company Limited and its employees, filed a writ of certiorari to quash a customs order imposing forfeiture for misdeclaring brandy essence and storing goods outside bonded warehouse. The Court of Appeal examined the HS Code classification and found the goods were correctly classified as spirits under Code 2208, and forfeiture was justified due to stealth. The court also upheld forfeiture for storage violations under Section 75. The application was dismissed, upholding the customs order.
prosecution_counsel: Milinda Gunatilake, Senior Deputy Solicitor General
defence_counsel: Gamini Marapana, P.C., with Navin Marapana, P.C., Uchitha Wickremasinghe and Janani Peeris
precedents_cited_list: Mark Santhakumar Sandanam vs Chulananda Perera, Director General of Customs and Others | Toyota Lanka (Pvt) Limited vs Jayatilake, Director General of Customs and Others
standard_of_review_applied: Review for legality and rationality under writ of certiorari

judges: N. Bandula Karunarathna J. | R. Gurusinghe J.
offence_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The accused-appellant was convicted for the murder of Puwa Muththuraja on 06.10.2000. The prosecution's case was that the accused, armed with a knife, threatened the deceased and later killed him. The evidence included eyewitness testimony from the deceased's wife and daughter, and the appellant confessed to the wife after the incident. The appellant and the deceased were known to quarrel after drinking.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court Judge convicted the accused-appellant of murder and imposed the death sentence. The judge analyzed the evidence and rejected the appellant's dock statement.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant's counsel argued that favorable evidence was not considered, and the difference between Section 293 and 294 of the Penal Code was not properly considered. Also, the counsel highlighted a vital omission in the witness's police statement.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The trial Judge did not consider items of evidence favorable to the appellant. | The difference between Section 293 and 294 of the Penal Code was not properly considered. | There was a vital omission in the witness's police statement (failure to mention the appellant came home with a knife).
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed the eyewitness testimony and found it credible. The circumstantial evidence, including the appellant's threats and confession, was found sufficient to establish guilt beyond reasonable doubt.
probability_assessment_by_court: The court applied the standard for circumstantial evidence, that it must be inconsistent with innocence and must exclude every reasonable inference save the one of guilt. The court found the circumstantial evidence sufficient.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty and made a dock statement denying the allegation and claiming no animosity with the deceased. The trial judge rejected the dock statement as not credible and not creating doubt in the prosecution case.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal held that the trial judge correctly analyzed the evidence. The circumstantial evidence, including the appellant's threats, confession, and the medical evidence, formed a strong chain pointing to the appellant's guilt. The court also noted that the trial judge properly rejected the appellant's dock statement. The court found no miscarriage of justice.
coa_sentence_type: Death sentence
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused-appellant was convicted of murder by the High Court of Badulla and sentenced to death. He appealed to the Court of Appeal, arguing that the trial judge failed to consider favorable evidence and misapplied the law. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal, finding that the circumstantial evidence, including eyewitness testimony and the appellant's confession, was sufficient to establish guilt beyond reasonable doubt, and the trial judge's analysis was correct.
defence_counsel: Indica Mallawaratchy
cause_of_death_exact_text: extensive bleeding due to multiple-extensive cut injuries
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court Judge meticulously analyzed the evidence and rejected the appellant's dock statement. The Court of Appeal found the High Court's analysis and conclusions correct.
precedents_cited_list: Bandara v Attorney General 2006 (2) SLR 1 | Podisinghe V. King 53 N.L.R 49 | Don Sunny V. The Attorney General 1998 (2) S.L.R 1 | The Queen V. Kularatne 71 N.L.R 534 | Regina V. Exall [1866] 4 F & F 922 | Kathubdeen V. Republic of Sri Lanka [1998] 3 Sri L.R. 107 | Fradd V. Brown & Company Ltd. 20 N.L.R, at page 282
standard_of_review_applied: The Court of Appeal will not lightly disturb the findings of fact by the trial judge unless manifestly wrong.

judges: Devika Abeyratne,J | P.Kumararatnam,J
offence_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The deceased was a watcher guarding railway sleepers at Kandapola. On September 10, 2001, he did not return home, and his body was found with injuries indicating dragging and stabbing. Key evidence included testimony from PW5 who saw the accused with stolen sleepers and a body, medical evidence, and forensic evidence from the lorry. The accused were convicted of murder.
evidence_type_secondary: Medical evidence, Government Analyst Report, Physical evidence
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted all three accused of murder under Section 296 of the Penal Code and imposed the death sentence. The judge found the prosecution evidence credible, despite some contradictions, and held that the accused acted with common intention.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellants argued that the High Court judge failed to properly evaluate the evidence, including contradictions in prosecution witnesses' testimonies, the credibility of PW5, and the sufficiency of circumstantial evidence. They also raised issues regarding the identification of the body and the analysis of dock statements.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Did the learned High Court Judge fail to consider the serious infirmities in the evidence of main witness for the prosecution, Anura Wijesooriya (PW 5)? | Did the learned High Court Judge fail to consider whether the prosecution witnesses are credible and /or consistent witnesses? | Whether the learned High Court Judge has failed to fairly and properly analyze the contradictions? | Whether the learned High Court Judge has failed to fairly evaluate the dock statements of the accused? | Whether the prosecution has failed to produce sufficient circumstantial evidence? | Whether the learned High Court Judge has failed to fairly and properly analyze the uncorroborated evidence of PW 9 regarding the identification of the body of the deceased? | Whether the learned High Court Judge has delivered the judgment without sufficiently analyzing the evidence presented in this case?
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found PW5's testimony credible and unchallenged, with medical and forensic evidence corroborating the events. Contradictions in witness statements were deemed not material to the core case.
probability_assessment_by_court: The court assessed the probability of the accused's actions and found them consistent with guilt, with no reasonable doubt raised by the evidence.
defence_version_summary: The accused pleaded not guilty and gave dock statements denying involvement, alleging police coercion. The defence suggested PW5 was the perpetrator, but the court rejected this as without basis.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal thoroughly evaluated the evidence, upholding the High Court's findings. They found PW5's testimony reliable and supported by medical and forensic evidence, with contradictions not affecting the core case. The court applied precedents on circumstantial evidence and common intention, concluding that the prosecution proved guilt beyond reasonable doubt, thus dismissing the appeal.
coa_sentence_type: Death
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused were convicted of murder under Section 296 of the Penal Code for killing a watcher at Kandapola and sentenced to death by the High Court. They appealed on grounds including contradictions in evidence and insufficient circumstantial evidence. The Court of Appeal found the prosecution evidence, particularly from PW5 and forensic reports, credible and corroborated, with no material errors. The appeal was dismissed, affirming the conviction and death sentence.
defence_counsel: Asthika Devendra with Sanjeewa Ruwanpathirana
cause_of_death_exact_text: dragged on the road by tying a wire on the right side of the leg after stabbing
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted the accused based on credible witness testimony and circumstantial evidence, dismissing contradictions as immaterial. The Court of Appeal found this analysis correct and without error.
precedents_cited_list: Queen vs Sumanasena 66 NLR 351 | CA Appeal 78-80 2001 | Attorney General V Munasinghe 70 NLR 241 | Ranji Singh V State of Bihar AIR 2001 SC 3853 | State of Uttar Pradesh Vs M.K. Anthony (184) SCJ 236/(1985) CRLL.J.493 at 498/499 | Fradd vs Brown and Company 20 NLR 282 at 283 | AG Vs. Potta Naufer and others 2007(2) SLR 144 | Kusumadasa Vs. State 2011(1) SLR 240 | Sarath Fernando Vs. Attorney General 2014 (1) SLR 16 | Premawansa V Attorney General 2009 (2) SLR 205
standard_of_review_applied: Review of evidence and application of legal standards for circumstantial evidence and witness credibility.

judges: Devika Abeyratne J | P. Kumararatnam J
offence_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code read with Section 32 of the Penal Code and Section 315 of the Penal Code read with Section 32 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: On 24th July 2011, PW1 Indika and the deceased consumed liquor and went to a hotel in Rathgama. They met the appellant, an argument erupted, and the appellant stabbed the deceased twice with a knife. The appellant was known to PW1 and claimed to be from the Navy. The trial proceeded in absentia of the appellant.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 297 of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the appellant for culpable homicide not amounting to murder based on a sudden fight, sentenced to 18 years rigorous imprisonment and a fine of Rs.5000, and acquitted on the second count of hurt.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant argued that the prosecution failed to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt, specifically on identity, and that the trial was unfair due to procedural errors including trial in absentia and excessive sentence.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Has the Learned High Court Judge misdirected himself when he failed to consider that the prosecution has failed to prove its case against the Appellant beyond reasonable doubt? | Has the Learned High Court Judge misdirected himself on the question of identity of the Appellant? | Has the Learned High Court Judge failed to consider the matters favourable to the Appellant and thereby has the Appellant deprived of a fair trial? | Has the Learned High Court Judge misdirected himself when he ordered the trial to be held in absentia against the Appellant under section 241 of the Code of Criminal Procedure Act No. 15 of 1979? | In the circumstances of the case is the sentence imposed on the Appellant excessive and /or illegal?
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The COA found omissions in PW1's identification testimony, such as not mentioning the appellant's name to police initially, and criticized the hearsay in the medico-legal report. Light conditions were also unreliable.
probability_assessment_by_court: The COA held that the prosecution failed to establish identity beyond reasonable doubt, so benefit of doubt accrued to the appellant.
defence_version_summary: The appellant was tried in absentia but represented by counsel. The defence cross-examined witnesses and highlighted omissions in prosecution evidence, particularly regarding identification.
legal_errors_description: The High Court failed to properly consider omissions in witness testimony and admitted hearsay evidence from the medico-legal report case history.
procedural_defects_description: Trial was held in absentia of the appellant under section 241 of the Criminal Procedure Code.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed the evidence, noting that PW1 failed to mention the appellant's name to police initially, and the medico-legal report contained inadmissible hearsay. The light conditions at the scene were contradictory. The prosecution did not prove identity beyond reasonable doubt, so the conviction was set aside.
coa_sentence_type: Acquitted
brief_judgment_file_summary: The appellant was convicted by the High Court of Galle for culpable homicide and sentenced to 18 years RI and a fine. On appeal, the Court of Appeal found that the prosecution failed to prove the identity of the appellant beyond reasonable doubt due to omissions in witness testimony and inadmissible hearsay evidence. The appeal was allowed, and the conviction and sentence were set aside.
defence_counsel: Mr Anil Silva PC with Asela Serasinghe
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court relied on the eyewitness testimony of PW1 and the medico-legal report, but the Court of Appeal found that the High Court did not adequately address omissions in identification and admitted hearsay evidence.
precedents_cited_list: The Attorney General v. Sandanam Pitchi Mary Theresa (2011) 2 Sri L.R. 292 | Gamini Dolawatte V. Attorney General [1988] 1 Sri.L.R 221
standard_of_review_applied: Review of evidence and legal errors

judges: N. Bandula Karunarathna, J. | R. Gurusinghe, J.
brief_facts_summary: The appellant was convicted for possession and trafficking of 132.06 grams of heroin. The prosecution version is that police received information, conducted a raid, and found heroin in a bag carried by the appellant. The defence version is that the police assaulted her and planted the heroin.
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the appellant for possession and trafficking of 132.06 grams of heroin and sentenced her to life imprisonment. The conviction was based on the prosecution evidence.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant appealed on grounds that the High Court judge failed to analyze improbabilities in the prosecution case, contradictions in evidence, and misdirected himself by expecting an exculpatory explanation from the dock statement.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The learned High Court Judge has failed to analyse the improbabilities of the prosecution version of the case and thereby the conviction is unsafe. | The learned High Court Judge has failed to analyse per se and inter se contradictions in the evidence of the prosecution, which creates a reasonable doubt and thereby the conviction is unsafe. | The Trial Judge has misdirected himself expecting an exculpatory explanation in addition to the fairly long dock statement and applying irrelevant legal principles to discredit the version of the defence and thereby the conviction is unsafe.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the evidence of prosecution witnesses unsatisfactory, with contradictions and improbabilities. The evidence of PW5 was particularly unreliable.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal assessed the improbabilities in the prosecution version and found it created reasonable doubt.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty. She gave a dock statement claiming the police assaulted her and planted the heroin. She did not call any witnesses. The court found her version credible in light of the prosecution's weaknesses.
legal_errors_description: The High Court judge failed to analyze improbabilities and contradictions, and misdirected by expecting an exculpatory explanation from the dock statement.
procedural_defects_description: The Trial Judge stopped further questioning on a point, denying the defence a fair trial.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal thoroughly analyzed the evidence, highlighting contradictions and improbabilities in the prosecution case. It found the evidence of PW5 unreliable and the conduct of the raid questionable. The court also noted the failure to seal the substance at the scene and the lack of inquiry into the source of the heroin. The court concluded that the prosecution evidence was unsatisfactory and created reasonable doubt.
coa_sentence_type: Acquitted, no sentence
brief_judgment_file_summary: The appellant was convicted by the High Court of Avissawella for possession and trafficking of 132.06 grams of heroin and sentenced to life imprisonment. On appeal, the Court of Appeal found the prosecution evidence unsatisfactory, with contradictions and improbabilities, and the High Court judge had misdirected himself. The Court of Appeal allowed the appeal, set aside the conviction, and acquitted the appellant.
prosecution_counsel: D. Warnakula SSC., for the AG
defence_counsel: Tenny Fernando for the Accused-Appellant
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted the appellant based on the prosecution evidence, but the Court of Appeal found that the High Court judge failed to properly evaluate the evidence and misdirected himself, leading to an unsafe conviction.
precedents_cited_list: Punkody vs AGCA 11/2005 | Chandima vs Attorney General CA 51/2009

judges: N. Bandula Karunarathna, J. | R. Gurusinghe, J.
offence_sections: Section 54(D) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Act
brief_facts_summary: The accused-appellant was convicted for possessing and trafficking 132.06 grams of heroin. Police raided her house based on information and found heroin in a bag she was carrying. The defence alleged that the heroin was planted at the police station and that she was assaulted during the arrest.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 54(D) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Act
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the appellant based on prosecution evidence and sentenced her to life imprisonment. The judge found the prosecution witnesses credible.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant argued that the High Court judge failed to analyse improbabilities in the prosecution version, contradictions in evidence, and misdirected himself by expecting exculpatory explanation and applying irrelevant legal principles.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The learned High Court Judge has failed to analyse the improbabilities of the prosecution version of the case and thereby the conviction is unsafe. | The learned High Court Judge has failed to analyse per se and inter se contradictions in the evidence of the prosecution, which creates a reasonable doubt and thereby the conviction is unsafe. | The Trial Judge has misdirected himself expecting an exculpatory explanation in addition to the fairly long dock statement and applying irrelevant legal principles to discredit the version of the defence and thereby the conviction is unsafe.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the evidence of prosecution witnesses unsatisfactory, with contradictions and improbabilities that created reasonable doubt.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court applied the test of probability and found the prosecution version highly improbable.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty and gave a dock statement alleging that police assaulted her, found no drugs in her house, took her to the police station where heroin was planted, and took her thumb impression. No defence witnesses were called. The Court of Appeal found her version supported by prosecution contradictions.
legal_errors_description: The High Court judge failed to analyse improbabilities and contradictions in evidence, misdirected on expecting exculpatory explanation, and disallowed relevant cross-examination.
procedural_defects_description: The trial judge disallowed defence counsel from cross-examining on important points, denying a fair trial.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal thoroughly analyzed the prosecution evidence, highlighting numerous contradictions and improbabilities, such as the long wait at the junction, evasive answers from witnesses, and unsatisfactory evidence of PW5. They referenced precedent on probability and concluded that the evidence was insufficient to sustain a conviction, creating reasonable doubt. The court also noted procedural errors in disallowing cross-examination.
coa_sentence_type: Acquitted, no sentence imposed
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused-appellant was convicted by the High Court of Avissawella for possession and trafficking of heroin and sentenced to life imprisonment. She appealed on grounds of improbabilities, contradictions, and misdirection. The Court of Appeal found the prosecution evidence unsatisfactory with significant contradictions and improbabilities, creating reasonable doubt. The court set aside the conviction and sentence, acquitting the appellant.
defence_counsel: Tenny Fernando
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted the appellant based on prosecution witness testimony, which the COA found to be unreliable due to contradictions and improbabilities. The HC failed to properly analyze the evidence and disallowed relevant cross-examination.
precedents_cited_list: Punkody vs AGCA 11/2005 | Chandima vs Attorney General CA 51/2009
standard_of_review_applied: Review for safety of conviction based on evidence assessment

judges: Devika Abeyratne,J | P. Kumararatnam,J
offence_sections: Section 19(b) and Section 19(c) of the Bribery Act as amended
brief_facts_summary: The accused, the Divisional Secretary of Thalawa, was indicted for soliciting and accepting bribes in relation to a timber permit application. The complainant alleged the accused solicited Rs. 20,000, accepted an initial Rs. 10,000, and was arrested when the balance Rs. 10,000 was given in a sting operation. The accused denied the charges, claiming they were fabricated due to him reprimanding the complainant over a complaint from an accountant about timber supply issues.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 19(b) and Section 19(c) of the Bribery Act as amended
hc_sentence_type: 3 months rigorous imprisonment per count (6 counts), suspended for 7 years, plus a fine per count
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the accused on all 6 counts of soliciting and accepting bribes. He was sentenced to 3 months rigorous imprisonment per count, suspended for 7 years, and fined Rs. 5,000 per count.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant argued the prosecution failed to prove the case beyond reasonable doubt, highlighting major contradictions in the evidence of prosecution witnesses, the improbability of the alleged solicitation date being a Sunday when the accused was on leave, and the failure of the trial judge to properly evaluate defence evidence and witness credibility.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Prosecution failed to establish case beyond reasonable doubt | Major contradictions in prosecution witness evidence | Alleged solicitation date (13th May) was a Sunday and accused was on leave | Failure of trial judge to consider defence evidence and dock statement | Failure to evaluate credibility of prosecution witnesses | Unreliability of key witness (PW1) testimony
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found significant contradictions in the evidence of PW1 (complainant) regarding who paid the money and the mode of transport to the raid. PW2 did not testify to giving any money. The evidence was inconsistent and unreliable. The trial judge failed to properly analyze the defence evidence and witness credibility.
probability_assessment_by_court: The COA found the prosecution evidence created reasonable doubt due to material contradictions and inconsistencies, making it unsafe to uphold the conviction.
defence_version_summary: The accused pleaded not guilty. He denied soliciting or accepting any gratification, claiming the charges were fabricated. The defence called two witnesses. The accused also made a dock statement. The COA found the trial judge failed to give due consideration to the defence evidence and dock statement.
legal_errors_description: Failure to properly evaluate the totality of prosecution evidence and its contradictions; failure to consider defence evidence and dock statement according to law; failure to give reasons for rejecting defence evidence.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal meticulously analyzed the evidence, highlighting major contradictions in the testimony of PW1 (the complainant) regarding who paid the bribe and details of the raid. It noted the prosecution failed to explain the discrepancy regarding the investigating officer's identity (Gunawardena vs. Abeywickrama). The COA found the trial judge failed to consider the defence evidence and dock statement, and improperly rejected defence witnesses as 'partisan' without reasons. Applying the precedent in K. Padmathilake, the COA held that the prosecution witnesses' inconsistent statements rendered their testimony unreliable. Considering the totality of evidence and reasonable doubt, the conviction was deemed unsafe.
coa_sentence_type: Conviction and sentence set aside
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused, a Divisional Secretary, was convicted by the High Court on six counts of soliciting and accepting bribes related to a timber permit and sentenced to suspended imprisonment and fines.
