judges: N. Bandula Karunarathna J. | R. Gurusinghe J.
offence_sections: section 296 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The accused-appellant was indicted for causing the death of Hewage Don Dayananda by stabbing on 28.06.2002. The deceased ran to the house of PW01 stating he was stabbed by 'Ajith'. PW01 and PW05 saw the accused coming towards the house with a knife, and he threatened them. The accused was arrested six days later. A knife was recovered based on his statement, but it was not sent for analysis. The High Court convicted the appellant and sentenced him to death.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: section 296 of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court Judge convicted the accused-appellant of murder and sentenced him to death. The conviction was based on the eyewitness testimonies of PW01 and PW05, the dying declaration, and the recovery of a knife.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant argued that the prosecution case relied on circumstantial evidence with no direct witness to the stabbing. He highlighted contradictions and discrepancies in the evidence of key prosecution witnesses (PW01 and PW05), questioned the identification of the accused as the 'Ajith' mentioned by the deceased, and argued that the animosity between the witnesses and the accused affected their credibility. He also contended the prosecution failed to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Contradictions and discrepancies in prosecution witness evidence (PW01 and PW05) | Case based on circumstantial evidence with no direct witness to the act | Failure to prove the accused was the 'Ajith' referred to by the deceased | Existence of animosity between witnesses and accused affecting credibility | Prosecution failed to discharge burden of proof beyond reasonable doubt
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed contradictions in PW01's evidence but deemed them trivial and not going to the root of the matter. It found the testimonies of PW01 and PW05 credible despite suggestions of animosity, and held they clearly indicated the accused's guilt.
probability_assessment_by_court: Court held the cumulative circumstantial evidence pointed irresistibly to the guilt of the accused and was inconsistent with innocence.
defence_version_summary: The accused pleaded not guilty. The defence suggested animosity between the accused and the witnesses' family due to the accused tipping off police about their illicit liquor business. The defence challenged witness credibility and the identification. The court did not find the defence version credible.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal applied the principles for circumstantial evidence from Nandasena v Republic of Sri Lanka, requiring evidence to be inconsistent with innocence and explicable only on guilt. It found the evidence—the dying declaration, two eyewitnesses seeing the accused with a knife and threatening them, and recovery of a knife based on the accused's statement—formed a strong chain. It held that contradictions in witness testimony were minor and did not affect core credibility. The court deferred to the trial judge's advantage in assessing witness demeanor and found no misdirection or unreasonable verdict. It affirmed the conviction and sentence.
coa_sentence_type: Death
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused-appellant was convicted of murder by the High Court of Kalutara and sentenced to death for stabbing Hewage Don Dayananda in 2002. He appealed, arguing contradictions in eyewitness evidence, insufficient circumstantial evidence, and mistaken identity. The Court of Appeal analyzed the evidence, including the dying declaration, witness testimonies, and weapon recovery. It found the evidence formed a conclusive chain pointing to guilt, dismissed minor contradictions, and affirmed the trial judge's findings. The appeal was dismissed, and the conviction and death sentence were upheld.
defence_counsel: Saliya Pieris PC with Susil Wanigapura
cause_of_death_exact_text: haemorrhagic shock following stab injury to chest
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court Judge convicted based on eyewitness testimony, dying declaration, and recovered weapon. The COA found the trial judge properly evaluated evidence, considered contradictions, and correctly applied the law on circumstantial evidence and dying declarations.
precedents_cited_list: Bharwada Boghinbhai Hirjibhai v State of Gujarat AIR (1983) SC 753 | A.G. v. Visuvalingam 47 NLR 286 | State of UP v. M.K. Anthony AIR 1985 SC 48 | Queen v. Julius 1980 (2) SLR. 1 | Nandasena Vs The Republic of Sri Lanka 1994 (3) SLR 172 | R v Exall (1866)176 ER 850 | Ranasinghe Vs Attorney General 2007 (1) SLR 218 | King Vs. Gunaratne 14 Ceylon Law Recorder 174 | Fradd Vs Brown & Company 20 NLR 282 | King v. Musthapha Lebbe 44 NLR 505
standard_of_review_applied: Court of Appeal will not interfere with verdict unless there is real doubt as to guilt or conviction is unsafe, recognizing trial judge's advantage in assessing witnesses.

judges: K. PRIYANTHA FERNANDO, J. (P/CA) | SAMPATH B. ABAYAKOON, J.
offence_sections: Section 140 of the Penal Code, Section 296 read with Section 146 of the Penal Code, and Section 296 read with Section 32 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The deceased and PW1 were in a three-wheeler when they stopped at Aluth Paalama Handiya to buy cigarettes and food. A lorry arrived with several accused who got down with knives and assaulted the deceased. PW1 witnessed the assault and ran to a nearby temple to inform the priest. The deceased succumbed to injuries in the hospital.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 140 and Section 296 read with Section 146 of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the 2nd, 6th, and 7th accused on counts of unlawful assembly and murder, relying on the eyewitness testimony of PW1. The other accused were acquitted due to doubts on identity. The court found that the accused were part of an unlawful assembly with the common object of causing hurt and death.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellants argued that the trial judge erred in relying on the sole eyewitness PW1 who was not credible. They also contended that without five persons, an unlawful assembly cannot be formed, and since other accused were acquitted, the conviction is invalid. Additionally, they claimed the judge misdirected on drawing adverse inference from dock statements.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The learned trial Judge erred in law when he convicted the 2nd, 6th and 7th appellants after acquitting the rest of the accused without having five persons to form an unlawful assembly. | The learned High Court Judge erred in convicting the accused appellants on the evidence of the sole eye witness PW1 whose evidence was unworthy of credit without any evidence to corroborate his version.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found that the sole eyewitness PW1 was not credible due to contradictions in his identification of the accused. His testimony was uncorroborated and insufficient to establish guilt beyond reasonable doubt.
probability_assessment_by_court: The court found that prosecution failed to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt due to unreliable eyewitness testimony.
defence_version_summary: The accused pleaded not guilty and made dock statements without calling witnesses. The defence challenged the credibility of PW1 and highlighted contradictions in his testimony.
legal_errors_description: The High Court erred in convicting for unlawful assembly when prosecution failed to prove there were five or more persons involved, as required by law.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal thoroughly analyzed the evidence of PW1, noting significant contradictions in his identification of the accused. They applied precedents on single witness testimony, emphasizing the need for corroboration when credibility is challenged. On unlawful assembly, they held that prosecution failed to prove five or more persons were involved, making the conviction legally unsustainable. Therefore, the appeals were allowed.
coa_sentence_type: Acquitted, no sentence
brief_judgment_file_summary: The case involved seven accused charged with unlawful assembly and murder of the deceased. The High Court convicted three accused based on sole eyewitness testimony and sentenced them to death. The appellants appealed on grounds of insufficient evidence for unlawful assembly and unreliable eyewitness. The Court of Appeal found the eyewitness not credible and prosecution failed to prove five or more persons for unlawful assembly. Therefore, the appeals were allowed, convictions set aside, and accused acquitted.
defence_counsel: Shavindra Fernando, P.C., Sasikaran Perera, Umayangi Indatissa, Dharshana Kuruppu, Sajini Elvitigala, Neranjan Jayasinghe
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court relied on the sole eyewitness PW1 to convict the accused for unlawful assembly and murder. The Court of Appeal criticized this, finding PW1 not credible and the evidence insufficient to prove unlawful assembly beyond reasonable doubt.
precedents_cited_list: The Queen v Appuhamy 68 NLR 437 | Sumanasena V. Attorney General [1999] 3 Sri LR 137 | Wjepala V. Attorney General SC Appeal 104/99, SC/Spl/LA 238/99
standard_of_review_applied: Review of evidence for credibility and legal correctness

judges: Menaka Wijesundera J. | Neil Iddawala J.
location_of_offence: High seas of Sri Lanka and Boossa, Galle
brief_facts_summary: Based on a tip-off, the Sri Lankan Navy intercepted an Iranian ship on the high seas and found substances suspected to be heroin. A boat approaching the ship was intercepted, and the owner, the petitioner, was arrested at his residence in Boossa, Galle. The petitioner was not on the boat at the time of interception.
evidence_type_primary: Physical evidence (suspected heroin) and controlled delivery operation
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court order dated 23.3.2021 remanded the petitioner, but the Court of Appeal found that the Magistrate was not furnished with sufficient material to justify remand.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The petitioner argued that the B reports filed by investigative officers did not contain a synopsis of evidence as required by law, violating section 115(1) of the CPC, and that the petitioner was not physically present inside the boat at the time of arrest.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: B reports filed by investigative officers do not carry a synopsis of evidence for the magistrate to consider, violating section 115(1) of CPC | Petitioner was not physically present inside the boat which was taken into custody
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court found that no synopsis of witness statements was provided in the B reports, and thus the Magistrate lacked sufficient evidence to remand the suspect.
probability_assessment_by_court: Court assessed that there was insufficient material for remand due to procedural violations.
defence_version_summary: Petitioner argued that he was not present on the boat and that the investigative procedures were legally flawed.
legal_errors_description: Failure to provide synopsis of evidence in B reports as per section 115(1) of CPC.
procedural_defects_description: Investigative officers did not submit synopsis of statements as required by law.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal held that the Magistrate was not furnished with sufficient material to remand the suspect, violating CPC section 115(1). The Court rejected practical difficulties as justification for ignoring legal provisions and noted that the controlled delivery method is not enacted as law. The Court exercised revisionary powers to correct the error.
coa_sentence_type: Bail with suitable conditions
brief_judgment_file_summary: The petitioner, owner of a boat involved in a drug trafficking case on the high seas, applied for revision against the High Court order remanding him. The Court of Appeal found procedural errors in the investigation, including lack of evidence synopsis in B reports. The Court allowed the revision, set aside the High Court order, and directed bail with suitable conditions.
defence_counsel: Sarath Jayamanne, PC with S. Mahawanniarachchi and Vineshka Mendis
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court order remanded the petitioner, but the Court of Appeal found that the Magistrate did not have sufficient material, and the High Court failed to correct this error.

brief_facts_summary: The accused-appellants were convicted for the murder of Kiriella Arachchilage Sirisena on 28.09.2000. The key witness, Nihal Prabath Manamperi (PW 01), an accomplice with a conditional pardon, testified that the deceased was assaulted in a van with a wheel brace and beer bottles. The body was found at a bus halt, and medical evidence confirmed fatal head injuries.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 296 read with section 32 of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the 1st and 2nd accused-appellants of murder based on the evidence of PW 01, despite contradictions and omissions, and sentenced them to death. The 3rd and 4th accused were acquitted.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellants argued that the High Court judge failed to consider safeguards for accomplice evidence, delays in complaint, contradictions in PW 01's testimony, and that the evidence was not credible. They also contended that the dock statement was not properly evaluated.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The learned High Court Judge had failed to take into account the safeguards that he should have looked for in order to rely on such evidence. | The learned High Court Judge had failed to consider the delay in making a complaint to the police by the first prosecution witness and to ascertain whether he had acted in good faith in the incident. | The learned High Court Judge had failed to consider omissions and contradictions of the first prosecution witness’s testimony and the nature of the inadequate corroborative evidence. | The learned Trial Judge had convicted the accused for murder when the evidence of the first prosecution witness was not credible.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found that the contradictions and omissions in PW 01's testimony were minor and did not go to the root of the case. The medical evidence corroborated the assault, and the accomplice evidence was deemed credible with sufficient corroboration.
probability_assessment_by_court: The court assessed the credibility of PW 01 and found the prosecution version probable, with no reasonable doubt raised by the defence.
defence_version_summary: The accused pleaded not guilty and made dock statements denying the allegations. The defence argued that PW 01's evidence was not credible due to contradictions and omissions. No alibi was presented, and the court found the dock statements to be mere denials.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal conducted a thorough analysis of the evidence, focusing on the credibility of PW 01. They considered the contradictions and omissions but found them not material, citing precedents on accomplice evidence and dock statements. The medical evidence strongly supported the prosecution case, and the court concluded that the High Court correctly convicted the appellants. The appeal was dismissed, affirming the conviction and death sentence.
coa_sentence_type: Death
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused-appellants were convicted for murder and sentenced to death by the High Court of Kegalle. They appealed on grounds including credibility of the accomplice witness, contradictions in evidence, and failure to evaluate the dock statement. The Court of Appeal examined the evidence, found the witness credible despite minor discrepancies, and upheld the conviction and sentence, dismissing the appeal.

judges: Devika Abeyratne, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: On 15th May 2006, the appellant killed the deceased by cutting her throat with a knife. Eyewitnesses, including the deceased's brothers, saw the appellant at the scene and heard the deceased name him. The appellant was identified, and a knife was recovered based on his statement.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court Judge convicted the appellant based on eyewitness testimony and medical evidence, and sentenced him to death.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant argued that the trial judge failed to assess weaknesses in lay witnesses' testimony, that the identity was not properly established, and that related witnesses were lying under oath to frame him.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Failure to properly assess weaknesses of lay witness testimony | Identity of appellant not properly established | Related witnesses lying under oath to frame appellant
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the eyewitness testimony credible and corroborated by medical evidence, with no material contradictions.
probability_assessment_by_court: The court found the evidence convincing and trustworthy, leaving no reasonable doubt.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty, gave a dock statement claiming he was at a village meeting, but witnesses saw him leave. The court found his defence not credible.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed the eyewitness testimony, medical evidence, and identity issues. They upheld the High Court's credibility assessments, cited precedents on related witnesses, and found no merit in the appeal grounds, dismissing the appeal.
coa_sentence_type: Death
brief_judgment_file_summary: The appellant was convicted of murder and sentenced to death by the High Court of Kuliyapitiya. He appealed on grounds of weak witness testimony and identity issues. The Court of Appeal found the evidence credible and corroborated, dismissed the appeal, and affirmed the conviction and sentence.
defence_counsel: Mr.Nayantha Wijesundera AAL
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court correctly analyzed the evidence, accepted witness testimony as credible, and convicted the appellant. The Court of Appeal agreed with this analysis.
precedents_cited_list: Kumara De Silva and 2 others v. Attorney General [2010] 2 SLR 169 | Waman & Others v. State of Maharashtra AIR 2011 SC 3327 | Sarwan Singh and Others v. State of Punjab (1979) 4 SCC 369 | Balraje alias Trimbak v. State of Maharashtra (2010) 6 SCC 673 | Attorney General v. Sandanam Pitchi Mary Theresa [2011] 2 SRLL. R 292 | Tudor Perera v. AG (SC 23/75 D.C. Colombo Bribery 190/B – Minutes of S.C. Dated 1/11/1975)
standard_of_review_applied: The court reviewed factual findings and credibility assessments, noting that credibility is a question of fact for the trial judge.

judges: N. Bandula Karunarathna J. | R. Gurusinghe J.
offence_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The accused-appellant was involved in a fight on 17.12.2011 where he hit the deceased with a pole, leading to death. Eyewitnesses saw the assault, and the deceased was taken to hospital. The accused claimed he acted under grave and sudden provocation after seeing his mother-figure being assaulted.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the accused of murder and imposed death sentence, rejecting the plea of grave and sudden provocation.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appeal ground is that the rejection of the plea of grave and sudden provocation is factually and legally flawed, which was the only ground of appeal.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Rejection of plea of grave and sudden provocation is factually and legally flawed
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal evaluated eyewitness testimonies and defence evidence, finding that the trial judge should have considered the provocation plea based on the circumstances of the sudden fight and lack of premeditation.
probability_assessment_by_court: The COA assessed that the provocation was grave and sudden, and the death was accidental, leading to a reduction in charge.
defence_version_summary: The accused pleaded not guilty, testified that he acted under grave and sudden provocation after seeing his mother-figure being assaulted, and claimed no intention to kill, with no alibi but calling defence witnesses.
legal_errors_description: The trial judge failed to evaluate the material in favour of the accused-appellant regarding the plea of grave and sudden provocation.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed the evidence and found that the incident occurred without premeditation, in a sudden fight upon provocation, with no cooling off period, and that the accused acted in the heat of passion, justifying the plea of grave and sudden provocation, thus reducing the offence to culpable homicide.
coa_sentence_type: Rigorous imprisonment for 8 years
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused-appellant was convicted of murder by the High Court of Vavuniya and sentenced to death. He appealed on the ground that the trial judge wrongly rejected his plea of grave and sudden provocation. The Court of Appeal allowed the appeal, finding that the provocation plea was valid, and modified the conviction to culpable homicide not amounting to murder, imposing 8 years of rigorous imprisonment.
defence_counsel: Indica Mallawaratchy AAL
cause_of_death_exact_text: the death was due to blunt force trauma to head caused by cranio-cerebral injuries inflicted by a heavy blunt weapon with unlimited striking surface.
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted for murder and rejected the provocation plea, but the Court of Appeal found this erroneous as the evidence supported grave and sudden provocation and sudden fight.
precedents_cited_list: Jayasena Vs Queen; 72 NLR 313
standard_of_review_applied: Review of evidence and legal conclusions for errors in evaluating provocation plea.
sentencing_principles_applied: Consideration of provocation and sudden fight to reduce murder to culpable homicide, imposing imprisonment based on circumstances.
final_charge_after_appeal: Culpable homicide not amounting to murder under section 297 of the Penal Code

judges: Devika Abeyratne, J. | P.Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: On 26th December 2000, the deceased and his family returned to Ragama railway station. A fight broke out between the deceased's brother and the first and second accused. The third accused (appellant) was seen walking away with his arm around the deceased's neck. The deceased was later found with a stab injury and died. The prosecution relied on circumstantial evidence and the last seen theory.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the third accused (appellant) of murder and sentenced him to death, while acquitting the first and second accused. The conviction was based on circumstantial evidence, including that the appellant was last seen with the deceased.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant argued that identification was not established beyond reasonable doubt, the trial judge failed to consider vital omissions, and failed to properly evaluate the circumstantial evidence.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Identification of the accused not established beyond reasonable doubt | Failure to consider vital omissions | Failure to evaluate circumstantial evidence - evidence does not lead to irresistible inference of guilt
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the prosecution presented strong circumstantial evidence, including the last seen theory and medical evidence. The trial judge properly evaluated the evidence and omissions.
probability_assessment_by_court: The court applied the last seen theory and found the appellant failed to explain the circumstances, leading to the only inference of guilt beyond reasonable doubt.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty and gave a dock statement admitting being at the railway station and trying to settle the fight, but denied complicity. He did not call witnesses. The court found his explanation insufficient and not credible.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed the grounds and found the trial judge correctly evaluated the evidence and omissions. The court applied the last seen theory and cited precedents, holding that the prosecution established a strong circumstantial case and the appellant's failure to explain the last seen circumstance strengthened the case. The court found no reason to disturb the High Court's findings.
coa_sentence_type: Death
brief_judgment_file_summary: The appellant was convicted of murder and sentenced to death by the High Court of Gampaha. He appealed on grounds of identification, omissions, and insufficient circumstantial evidence. The Court of Appeal upheld the conviction, applying the last seen theory and finding the circumstantial evidence strong. The appeal was dismissed.
defence_counsel: Saliya Pieris, PC with Yohan Pieris
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court analyzed the evidence and omissions, concluding the prosecution proved the case beyond reasonable doubt. The Court of Appeal found the analysis correct and agreed with the conviction.
precedents_cited_list: Punchimahaththaya Vs. The State 76 NLR page 564 | State of Tamil Nadu Vs. Rajendran (1999) Cr.L.J.4552 | Rex Vs. Burdett (1820) 4 B & Ald 161 at 162 | Rajapaksha Devage Somarathna Rajapaksha And Others Vs. Attorney General (SC Appeal) 2/2002 TAB) | Surajdeo Mahto V state of Bihar (CrA 1677 of 2011 Decided on 4th August 2021-Indian SC) (Citation: LL 2021 SC 351) Surya Kant J (with CJ N.V. Ramana, Aniruddha Bose J) | Satpal V State of Haryana (2018) 6 SCC 610 | State of Rajasthan v Kashi Ram (2006) 12 SCC 254 | Godwin Igabele v the State (Supreme Court of Nigeria) [(2006) 6 NWLR (Pt. 975) 100]
standard_of_review_applied: The court reviewed the trial judge's findings of fact and law, applying principles of circumstantial evidence and the last seen theory.

judges: K. Priyantha Fernando, J. (P/CA) | Sampath B. Abayakoon, J.
offence_sections: Section 354 of the Penal Code and Section 296 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The appellant was convicted for kidnapping and murdering a 6-year-old child. The child went missing on 04.06.2009 while the appellant was present at a gathering where alcohol was consumed. The child's body was later recovered from a pit based on information from the appellant under section 27 of the Evidence Ordinance.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 354 of the Penal Code and Section 296 of the Penal Code
hc_sentence_type: Count 1: 5 years rigorous imprisonment and fine of Rs.5000; Count 2: Death sentence
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the appellant on both counts of kidnapping and murder, accepting the circumstantial evidence and the recovery of the body under section 27 of the Evidence Ordinance.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant challenged the conviction on grounds including failure to properly consider principles of circumstantial evidence, reliance on suspicious circumstances, failure to analyze credibility of prosecution witnesses, ignoring contradictions, and failure to appreciate the defence case.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The learned High Court Judge failed to consider the well settled principles of law relating to a case entirely based on circumstantial evidence. | The learned trial Judge convicted the appellant based only on suspicious circumstances and speculations. | The learned trial Judge has failed to analyze credibility of the prosecution witnesses and the entirety of the prosecution case. | The learned trial Judge failed to consider that the evidence, important contradictions and omissions of the prosecution witnesses. | The learned High Court Judge failed to appreciate the defence case and reject the same in the wrong premise.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed the circumstantial evidence and witness testimonies, finding the proved circumstances consistent only with the guilt of the appellant and that the trial judge had properly evaluated the evidence.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court applied the principle that circumstantial evidence must be consistent only with the guilt of the accused and exclude every reasonable hypothesis of innocence.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty, testified that he was drunk and could not remember events, claimed he was arrested earlier than stated by police and assaulted, and denied showing the body to police. The court found his defence not credible.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal, holding that the recovery of the body under section 27 of the Evidence Ordinance was admissible despite issues with the arrest date, and that the circumstantial evidence was sufficient and consistent only with the guilt of the appellant. The court found no merit in the grounds of appeal and affirmed the High Court's judgment.
coa_sentence_type: Count 1: 5 years rigorous imprisonment and fine of Rs.5000; Count 2: Death sentence
brief_judgment_file_summary: The appellant was convicted by the High Court of Anuradhapura for kidnapping and murder of a child. He appealed on grounds including improper handling of circumstantial evidence and illegal detention. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal, affirming the conviction and sentences, finding the circumstantial evidence sufficient and the recovery of the body under section 27 admissible.
defence_counsel: Nihara Randeniya
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted based on circumstantial evidence and recovery under section 27. The Court of Appeal found no error in the High Court's analysis and affirmed its decision.
precedents_cited_list: Shankarlal Gyarasilal Dixit V. State of Maharashtra [1981] Cri. L.J 325 | Junaiden Mohmed Haaris V. Hon. Attorney General. SC Appeal 118/17 [09.11.2018] | Sacheverell Stanley Walton Houghton Stephen Anthony Franciscoy, Criminal Appeal Reports, Vol 68, 1979 | R. V. Leathem [1861] 8 Cox CC 498 | R. V. Sang [1980] AC 402 [1979] Crim. L.R. 655
standard_of_review_applied: Review of evidence and application of legal principles for circumstantial evidence and admissibility under section 27 of Evidence Ordinance.

judges: N. Bandula Karunarathna, J. | R. Gurusinghe, J.
offence_sections: Section 364 (2) (e) of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The appellant was charged with statutory rape of a 15-year-old girl. The incident occurred a few months before the complaint was made in August 2004. The prosecutrix became pregnant and the medical evidence showed a fetus of 25-27 weeks. The appellant was known to the prosecutrix from childhood.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 364 (2) (e) of the Penal Code
hc_sentence_type: Rigorous Imprisonment 12 years, Fine Rs.15,000, Compensation Rs.250,000
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the appellant of statutory rape, relying on the credible testimony of the prosecutrix and medical evidence of pregnancy. The court accepted the prosecutrix's explanation for the delay in complaining, noting she was threatened by the appellant. The court sentenced the appellant to 12 years rigorous imprisonment, a fine, and compensation.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant argued that the prosecution evidence was not credible, there was a delay in complaining, and that the court cannot rely on circumstantial evidence when the prosecutrix's evidence is unreliable. Additionally, the appellant contended that the medical evidence was not properly evaluated and that his evidence was wrongly rejected.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The evidence is not sufficient to prove the prosecution case. | The evidence of the appellant was wrongly rejected. | The contradictions and the omissions regarding the evidence of PW1 had not been considered. | The medical evidence had not been evaluated. | The evidence of the prosecution is not credible. | Delay in complaining. | When the evidence of the prosecutrix is not reliable, Court cannot rely on circumstantial evidence.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the prosecutrix's testimony credible and without marked contradictions. The medical evidence of pregnancy was consistent with the prosecutrix's account. The court also evaluated the appellant's evidence and found no reason to accept it over the prosecution case.
probability_assessment_by_court: The court found the prosecutrix's testimony reliable and consistent with medical evidence. The delay in complaining was explained by the appellant's threats. The court found no reason to doubt the prosecution case.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty and gave evidence. He did not call any other witnesses. The court found his evidence not credible. The appellant did not provide an alibi, and his defence was that the sexual intercourse was consensual.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal held that the High Court correctly evaluated the evidence, including the prosecutrix's credible testimony and the medical evidence. The court cited precedents (State of Panjab vs. Gurnit Singh, Premasiri vs. Attorney General) to emphasize that corroboration is not mandatory in rape cases if the victim's testimony is reliable. The court found no marked contradictions in the prosecutrix's evidence and accepted the explanation for the delay in complaining. The court also evaluated the appellant's evidence and found it lacking. However, the court reduced the sentence considering the consensual nature of the intercourse and the appellant's personal circumstances.
coa_sentence_type: Rigorous Imprisonment 5 years (deemed served from 5th April 2018), Fine Rs.15,000, Compensation Rs.250,000
brief_judgment_file_summary: The appellant was convicted by the High Court of Kandy for statutory rape of a 15-year-old girl and sentenced to 12 years rigorous imprisonment, a fine, and compensation. He appealed on grounds including insufficient evidence, delay in complaining, and unreliable testimony. The Court of Appeal affirmed the conviction, finding the prosecutrix's testimony credible and consistent with medical evidence. The court reduced the sentence to 5 years imprisonment, considering the consensual nature and the appellant's personal circumstances, while maintaining the fine and compensation orders.
defence_counsel: P. Radhakrishnan
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted the appellant based on the credible testimony of the prosecutrix and medical evidence. The High Court accepted the explanation for the delay in complaining. The Court of Appeal agreed with the High Court's analysis and found no error in the conviction.
precedents_cited_list: Punchi Mahaththaya Vs. the State 76 NLR page 564 | State of Panjab Vs. Gurnit Singh and others 1996 AIR 1393 | Inder Singh & Anr. vs. The State (Delhi Administration) (1978) 4 SCC 161 | Premasiri Vs. Attorney General [2006] 3 Sri Lanka Law Report 107 | S.C. Reference 03/2008
standard_of_review_applied: The court reviewed the evidence to determine if the conviction was safe and applied sentencing principles to determine if the sentence was excessive.
sentencing_principles_applied: The court considered the consensual nature of the intercourse, the appellant's personal circumstances (no previous convictions, family responsibilities), and the principle that consent is relevant for sentencing in statutory rape cases.

judges: Devika Abeyratne J | P. Kumararatnam J
offence_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The appellant, nephew of the deceased, killed the deceased with a club after a history of conflict. The deceased had been accused of murdering the appellant's father and was acquitted after 10 years. The two families lived opposite each other and had constant quarrels. The incident occurred after an altercation involving the deceased's brother and the appellant.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the appellant of murder and imposed the death sentence. The judge did not adequately consider the plea of cumulative provocation.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The sole ground of appeal is that the trial judge failed to adequately consider the plea of cumulative provocation, which should have reduced the offence to culpable homicide not amounting to murder.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The evidence led at the trial warrants the consideration of the plea of cumulative provocation which had not been adequately dealt by the learned High Court Judge in his judgment.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal considered eyewitness testimony (PW1 and PW2) which established a history of conflict and the immediate altercation leading to the killing, supporting the plea of cumulative provocation.
probability_assessment_by_court: The court assessed that the cumulative provocation over time, including the acquittal for the father's murder and constant quarrels, deprived the appellant of self-control, justifying a reduced charge.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty. The defence argued cumulative provocation based on the history of conflict. The appellant did not testify or call defence witnesses; the argument was based on prosecution evidence. The court accepted the plea as credible.
legal_errors_description: The High Court judge failed to adequately consider the plea of cumulative provocation and did not award the benefit of that mitigatory plea to the appellant.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal extensively analyzed the doctrine of cumulative provocation, citing multiple precedents. It found the appellant, who lost his father at age 15 and endured constant quarrels with the deceased (who was acquitted of the father's murder), acted under sustained mental stress. The court held the cumulative provocation justified reducing the offence to culpable homicide. The High Court's failure to consider this plea was an error. The death sentence was set aside and replaced with imprisonment.
coa_sentence_type: 15 years rigorous imprisonment
brief_judgment_file_summary: The appellant was convicted of murder and sentenced to death by the High Court of Kuliyapitiya. He appealed on the ground that the trial judge failed to consider cumulative provocation. The Court of Appeal analyzed the history of conflict, including the deceased's acquittal for the appellant's father's murder and ongoing quarrels. It allowed the appeal in part, modifying the conviction to culpable homicide not amounting to murder and imposing 15 years rigorous imprisonment.
defence_counsel: Ms.Indika Mallawarachchi
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted for murder without adequately considering cumulative provocation. The Court of Appeal found this was an error, as the evidence warranted a reduction to culpable homicide.
precedents_cited_list: The King v Bellana Withanage Eddin 41 NLR 345 | Premalal v Attorney General [2000] 2 SLR 403 | W.A. Gamini v Attorney General CA/142/2009 | R.W.M.Nandana Senarathbandara v Attorney General SC/Appeal/32/2015 | Poovammal v State 2012 (2) MLJ (Cri.) 482 | K.M. NANAVATHI Vs STATE OF MAHARASTRA [A.I.R.] 1962 S.C. 605 | SUYAMBUKKANI Vs STATE OF TAMIL NADU [1989 LW (Crl.) 86]
standard_of_review_applied: Review of evidence and legal principles regarding cumulative provocation under Exception-1 to Section 294 of the Penal Code.
sentencing_principles_applied: Consideration of cumulative provocation to reduce murder to culpable homicide and impose a term of imprisonment based on the circumstances.
final_charge_after_appeal: Culpable homicide not amounting to murder under Section 297 of the Penal Code

judges: K Priyantha Fernando, J. (P. /C.A.) | Sampath B Abayakoon, J.
offence_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The incident occurred on 28 May 1997 at Keselwatta. The deceased was assaulted by the appellant, a relative, at a boutique using fists, a wooden club, and a knife, resulting in fatal stab wounds to the head. The deceased died in hospital. Key evidence includes eyewitness testimony and medical evidence.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court found the appellant guilty of murder and sentenced him to death. The conviction was based on eyewitness and medical evidence. The High Court did not accept the defence version.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant appealed on three grounds: inconsistencies and infirmities in the evidence of two eye witnesses; infirmities regarding the appellant carrying a knife; and absence of motive with possibility of third party involvement. The appellant also argued that the High Court should have considered culpable homicide not amounting to murder under exception 4 of section 296.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The learned trial judge has failed to address her mind to the material inconsistencies and infirmities in the evidence adduced by the two alleged eye witnesses namely, PW-02 Kanthi Samarasekara and PW-03 Puspika Samarasekara and thereby have failed to consider that the reasonable doubt generated thereby should accrue to the advantage of the accused appellant. | The learned trial judge has failed to consider the serious infirmities in the evidence of PW-02- Kanthi Samarasekara and PW-03 Pushpika Samarasekara with regard to the accused appellant carrying a knife and thereby has failed to consider that the evidence adduced by the said witnesses are highly improbable. | The learned trial judge failed to take into consideration the absence of motive on the part the accused appellant to cause the death of the deceased and thereby has failed to consider that the circumstances of the case suggest involvement of a third party in the incident.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the inconsistencies in the eyewitness accounts trivial and not material, considering the long delay between the incident and trial. The medical evidence corroborated the eyewitness accounts. The court applied principles from Bhoginbhai Hitijibhai vs State of Gujarat regarding witness memory.
probability_assessment_by_court: The court found the eyewitness evidence credible despite minor inconsistencies and held the prosecution proved its case beyond reasonable doubt.
defence_version_summary: The appellant made a dock statement claiming he was attacked by four persons including the witnesses and ran away. He called Thilak as a witness. The court did not find the defence version credible.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal, holding that inconsistencies in eyewitness accounts were minor and did not affect credibility, especially given the long delay. The court also held that motive is not essential to prove murder and there was no evidence to support the defence of sudden fight. The conviction and sentence were affirmed.
coa_sentence_type: Death
brief_judgment_file_summary: The appellant was convicted of murder by the High Court of Tangalle and sentenced to death. He appealed on grounds of inconsistencies in eyewitness evidence, infirmities regarding the knife, and absence of motive. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal, holding the inconsistencies were minor, motive is not essential, and there was no evidence to reduce the offence to culpable homicide. The conviction and sentence were affirmed.
defence_counsel: Dharshana Kuruppu with Sajini Elvitigala
cause_of_death_exact_text: the fatal nature of the stab injury suffered by the deceased to her head which has penetrated 95 mm. deep into the head.
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted based on eyewitness and medical evidence. The COA agreed with the HC's analysis and found that the HC properly considered the evidence and the alternative verdict.
precedents_cited_list: Bhoginbhai Hitijibhai Vs State of Gujarat (AIR 1983-SC 753 at pp 756-758) | The Attorney General Vs. Potta Naufer and others (2007) 2 SLR 144 at page 184 | Gangaram Vs. Emperor 62 IC 545 | King Vs. Belana Withanage Eddin 41 NLR 345 | King Vs. Vidanalage Lanty 42 NLR 317
standard_of_review_applied: The COA reviewed the evidence and applied appellate review principles to assess whether the HC's verdict was reasonable based on the evidence.

judges: K Priyantha Fernando, J. | Sampath B Abayakoon, J.
offence_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The incident occurred on 28 May 1997 at Keselwatta. The appellant, a relative, assaulted the deceased with fists and a knife, resulting in fatal stab wounds. Eyewitnesses PW-02 and PW-03 testified, and medical evidence confirmed the injuries. The appellant was convicted of murder.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court found the appellant guilty of murder based on eyewitness testimony and medical evidence, and sentenced him to death.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant argued inconsistencies and infirmities in the evidence of eye witnesses PW-02 and PW-03, that the evidence regarding the knife was improbable, and that absence of motive suggested involvement of a third party.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The learned trial judge has failed to address her mind to the material inconsistencies and infirmities in the evidence adduced by the two alleged eye witnesses. | The learned trial judge has failed to consider the serious infirmities in the evidence with regard to the accused appellant carrying a knife. | The learned trial judge failed to take into consideration the absence of motive on the part the accused appellant to cause the death of the deceased and thereby has failed to consider that the circumstances of the case suggest involvement of a third party.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found minor inconsistencies in eyewitness testimony due to the time lapse, but deemed them trivial and upheld the credibility of the witnesses.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court applied principles from Bhoginbhai case, noting that witnesses cannot be expected to have photographic memory, and found no reasonable doubt.
defence_version_summary: The appellant made a dock statement claiming he was attacked by four persons and ran away. He called one witness, Thilak, who said both sides were quarrelling. The court found the defence not credible.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal reviewed the grounds of appeal, found inconsistencies trivial due to time lapse, cited Bhoginbhai case, held motive not essential, analyzed exception under section 296 and found no evidence for sudden fight, and affirmed the conviction and sentence.
coa_sentence_type: Death sentence affirmed
brief_judgment_file_summary: The appellant was convicted of murder by the High Court of Tangalle and sentenced to death. He appealed on grounds of inconsistencies in eyewitness evidence, improbability regarding the knife, and absence of motive. The Court of Appeal found the inconsistencies trivial, motive not essential, and no basis for lesser offence, dismissing the appeal and affirming the conviction and sentence.
defence_counsel: Dharshana Kuruppu with Sajini Elvitigala
cause_of_death_exact_text: the fatal nature of the stab injury suffered by the deceased to her head which has penetrated 95 mm. deep into the head
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted based on eyewitness and medical evidence. The Court of Appeal found that the High Court correctly analyzed the evidence and considered possible defences.
precedents_cited_list: Bhoginbhai Hitijibhai Vs State of Gujarat (AIR 1983-SC 753) | The Attorney General Vs. Potta Naufer and others (2007) 2 SLR 144 | King Vs. Belana Withanage Eddin 41 NLR 345 | King Vs. Vidanalage Lanty 42 NLR 317 | Gangaram Vs. Emperor 62 IC 545
standard_of_review_applied: The Court reviewed the evidence and legal considerations, applying principles from cited cases on witness credibility and motive.

judges: Devika Abeyratne, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
brief_facts_summary: The victim, a 67-year-old Tamil lady recovering from partial paralysis, was alone at home when the accused, known as the baas, came and raped her at knife-point. She informed her husband, who lodged a complaint with the police. Medical evidence showed spermatozoa, and the accused was known to the family.
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the accused based on the victim's credible testimony and medical evidence, rejecting the defence's arguments and sentencing him to imprisonment, fine, and compensation.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant argued that evidence was insufficient to prove the case beyond reasonable doubt, the rejection of the accused's evidence and dock statement principles was wrongful, and there were errors in considering contradictions and medical evidence.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The items of evidence are not sufficient to prove the prosecution’s case against the appellant beyond reasonable doubt. | The rejection of evidence of the accused is wrongful and the learned Judge of the High Court has failed to correctly apply the principles governing the Dock Statement. | The rejection of the contradictions and omissions regarding the evidence of PW 1 is erroneous in law. | The rejection of Medical evidence is erroneous in law.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the victim's evidence clear, cogent, and convincing, corroborated by medical evidence and husband's testimony. Contradictions were immaterial and did not affect credibility.
probability_assessment_by_court: The court assessed the probability of the dock statement and found it unlikely that a false complaint would be made given the victim's age, health, and social circumstances.
defence_version_summary: The accused made a dock statement claiming he shouted in front of the victim's house due to a dispute over employment, suggesting a false complaint was lodged. No defence witnesses were called. The court found this version improbable.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal thoroughly analyzed the evidence, upholding the High Court's findings. They found the victim's testimony credible and corroborated by medical evidence, applied precedents on single witness testimony, considered the dock statement but found it did not raise reasonable doubt, and dismissed all grounds of appeal.
coa_sentence_type: 10 years rigorous imprisonment, fine of Rs 5000 with default sentence of 6 months, compensation of Rs 50,000 with default sentence of one year rigorous imprisonment.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused was convicted of rape by the High Court of Kandy and sentenced to 10 years imprisonment, fine, and compensation. He appealed on grounds of insufficient evidence and errors in evaluating evidence. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal, upholding the conviction and sentence based on credible victim testimony, medical evidence, and proper application of legal principles.
defence_counsel: Chathu Amarathunga with Oshaka Danthanarayana
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court correctly evaluated the evidence, considered contradictions immaterial, and properly assessed the dock statement. The Court of Appeal agreed with this analysis and found no errors.
precedents_cited_list: Sunil and another vs The Attorney General 1986 (I) SLR 230 | Sumanasena vs Attorney General {1999} 3 SLR 137
standard_of_review_applied: Review of evidence and application of reasonable doubt standard

judges: N. Bandula Karunarathna, J. | R. Gurusinghe, J.
offence_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The appellant was accused of murdering two persons, husband and wife, on 3rd May 2006 due to a land dispute. Eyewitnesses PW1 and PW2, the son and daughter of the deceased, saw the appellant attack their mother. The appellant claimed alibi, stating he was at Gampola at the time.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the appellant for murder based on credible eyewitness testimony from PW1 and PW2. The trial judge found the alibi defense not believable and concluded the prosecution proved guilt beyond reasonable doubt.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant argued that the Trial Judge erred in failing to evaluate alibi defense, misdirected by assuming facts not in evidence, and failed to appreciate the degree of proof required. Additionally, counsel argued that calling fresh witnesses after defense closed was prejudicial and that insufficient light affected identification.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The learned Trial Judge erred in law by failing to evaluate the evidence of alibi as a defence for the charge of a criminal offence. | The learned Trial Judge misdirected himself by assuming facts that were not transpired as evidence at the trial. | The learned Trial Judge erred in law by failing to appreciate the degree of proof required for a conviction based on principles of the law of evidence. | The Trial Judge violated the rules governing the calling of fresh witnesses after the case for the defence had been closed, which was prejudicial to the appellant. | There was no sufficient light at the time and the place of the incident, and the evidence of PW1 and PW2 cannot be relied upon.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found PW1 and PW2 credible as eyewitnesses, with prompt statements and no serious contradictions. The alibi defense was not properly confronted with prosecution witnesses and was deemed not believable.
probability_assessment_by_court: The court assessed the credibility of eyewitnesses and found no reasonable doubt; the alibi defense did not create a reasonable doubt.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty and raised an alibi defense, claiming he was at Gampola at the time. He called witnesses to support alibi, but the court found the alibi evidence not credible and an afterthought.
legal_errors_description: The Trial Judge called PW3 in rebuttal after the defense case was closed, which was irregular under criminal procedure.
procedural_defects_description: Calling fresh evidence after defense case closed without proper determination under Section 439 of Criminal Procedure Code.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The COA analyzed the eyewitness evidence of PW1 and PW2, finding them credible and corroborated. The alibi defense was not properly put to prosecution witnesses and was not believable. The procedural irregularity in calling PW3 did not cause a miscarriage of justice as the prosecution evidence was sufficient without it. The appeal was dismissed.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The appellant was convicted of murder in the High Court based on eyewitness testimony. He appealed on grounds of alibi defense evaluation, misdirection, and procedural errors. The Court of Appeal found the eyewitnesses credible, the alibi defense weak, and that any procedural irregularity did not prejudice the appellant. The appeal was dismissed, upholding the conviction and sentence.

defence_counsel: Tenney Fernando for the Accused-Appellant
hc_analysis_summary: The HC convicted based on credible eyewitness testimony. COA found the HC's evaluation of evidence correct, but noted irregularity in calling rebuttal witness, which did not affect justice.

judges: Devika Abeyratne, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
brief_facts_summary: The victim, a 67-year-old Tamil lady recovering from partial paralysis, was alone at home when the accused, known as the baas, came and raped her at knife-point. She informed her husband, who lodged a complaint with the police. Medical evidence showed spermatozoa, and the accused was known to the family.
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the accused based on the victim's credible testimony and medical evidence, rejecting the defence's arguments and sentencing him to imprisonment, fine, and compensation.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant argued that evidence was insufficient to prove the case beyond reasonable doubt, the rejection of the accused's evidence and dock statement principles was wrongful, and there were errors in considering contradictions and medical evidence.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The items of evidence are not sufficient to prove the prosecution’s case against the appellant beyond reasonable doubt. | The rejection of evidence of the accused is wrongful and the learned Judge of the High Court has failed to correctly apply the principles governing the Dock Statement. | The rejection of the contradictions and omissions regarding the evidence of PW 1 is erroneous in law. | The rejection of Medical evidence is erroneous in law.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the victim's evidence clear, cogent, and convincing, corroborated by medical evidence and husband's testimony. Contradictions were immaterial and did not affect credibility.
probability_assessment_by_court: The court assessed the probability of the dock statement and found it unlikely that a false complaint would be made given the victim's age, health, and social circumstances.
defence_version_summary: The accused made a dock statement claiming he shouted in front of the victim's house due to a dispute over employment, suggesting a false complaint was lodged. No defence witnesses were called. The court found this version improbable.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal thoroughly analyzed the evidence, upholding the High Court's findings. They found the victim's testimony credible and corroborated by medical evidence, applied precedents on single witness testimony, considered the dock statement but found it did not raise reasonable doubt, and dismissed all grounds of appeal.
coa_sentence_type: 10 years rigorous imprisonment, fine of Rs 5000 with default sentence of 6 months, compensation of Rs 50,000 with default sentence of one year rigorous imprisonment.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused was convicted of rape by the High Court of Kandy and sentenced to 10 years imprisonment, fine, and compensation. He appealed on grounds of insufficient evidence and errors in evaluating evidence. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal, upholding the conviction and sentence based on credible victim testimony, medical evidence, and proper application of legal principles.
defence_counsel: Chathu Amarathunga with Oshaka Danthanarayana
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court correctly evaluated the evidence, considered contradictions immaterial, and properly assessed the dock statement. The Court of Appeal agreed with this analysis and found no errors.
precedents_cited_list: Sunil and another vs The Attorney General 1986 (I) SLR 230 | Sumanasena vs Attorney General {1999} 3 SLR 137
standard_of_review_applied: Review of evidence and application of reasonable doubt standard

judges: Devika Abeyratne,J | P.Kumararatnam,J
brief_facts_summary: The deceased was a watcher at a saw mill and was found dead on 12th September 2010. The accused, a machine operator living at the saw mill, was convicted based on circumstantial evidence. Key evidence included a dispute over money, recovery of a wooden piece, and the presence of another person Thushara who was not called as a witness.
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the accused of murder based on circumstantial evidence, including the last seen theory and a motive over a dispute, and sentenced him to death.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The main ground is that the circumstantial evidence does not prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt. Additionally, the prosecution failed to call a key witness Thushara, and the recovery of the weapon was not conclusively linked to the crime.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Circumstantial evidence insufficient to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt | Last seen theory flawed as time of death not established | Failure to call key witness Thushara who was present at the scene | Recovery of weapon Athakoluwa not forensicly linked to the injuries
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found that the evidence was insufficient, with key witness Thushara not called, the weapon not forensicly examined, and the time of death not precisely established, leading to reasonable doubt.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court applied principles for circumstantial evidence and found that it did not exclude every reasonable inference of innocence, thus creating reasonable doubt.
defence_version_summary: The accused pleaded not guilty and gave a dock statement denying involvement, claiming he was arrested and assaulted after being informed of the death by Thushara. No alibi was presented, and the defence relied on challenging the prosecution's evidence.
legal_errors_description: The High Court misinterpreted the evidentiary value of circumstantial evidence, incorrectly applied the last seen theory, and failed to consider the failure to call key witness Thushara.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal conducted a thorough analysis of the circumstantial evidence, noting the absence of eyewitnesses, the prosecution's failure to call Thushara, the lack of forensic linking of the recovered weapon, the unestablished time of death, and the accessibility of the crime scene to outsiders. Citing several legal precedents, the court held that the evidence did not irresistibly point to the accused's guilt and did not exclude other reasonable possibilities, leading to the conclusion that the prosecution failed to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt.
coa_sentence_type: Acquitted, no sentence imposed
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused was convicted of murder by the High Court of Colombo and sentenced to death. He appealed on grounds including insufficient circumstantial evidence. The Court of Appeal found that the prosecution failed to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt due to key witness omissions, unestablished time of death, and lack of forensic evidence, and therefore allowed the appeal and acquitted the accused.
defence_counsel: Nayantha Wijesundara
cause_of_death_exact_text: cause of death is due to complications of blunt force trauma to the head and neck.
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court relied on the last seen theory and alleged motive over a dispute to convict the accused. However, the Court of Appeal found errors in this analysis, as the time of death was not established, the witness Thushara was not considered, and the evidence did not conclusively point to the accused.
precedents_cited_list: Rex v Blom | Queen v Kularatne | Don Sunny vs Attorney General | Kusumadasa Vs. State | Sarath Fernando Vs. Attorney General | Samantha Vs. Republic of Sri Lanka | AG Vs. Potta Naufer & others | Emperor v Browning | Karunaratne V AG
standard_of_review_applied: Principles for evaluating circumstantial evidence, requiring that the evidence must irresistibly point to guilt and exclude every reasonable inference of innocence.

judges: Sobhitha Rajakaruna, J. | Dhammika Ganepola, J.
offence_sections: Sections 101, 113 A, 190 of the Penal Code and Article 111 C (2) of the Constitution of the Republic of Sri Lanka
brief_facts_summary: The Petitioner, a former Chief Magistrate, was made the 2nd suspect in a Magistrate's Court case for abetment and conspiracy under the Penal Code and Constitution. The case involved the 1st suspect interfering with judicial functions by contacting the Petitioner over the telephone about a case. The 3rd Respondent (Acting IGP) affirmed that no offence was disclosed against the Petitioner based on investigations.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: Petitioner argues that the Magistrate's order making him a suspect is ultra vires as the offence under Article 111 C (2) cannot support abetment charges against the same judge who is the victim. Additionally, based on the 3rd Respondent's affidavit, there is no evidence to proceed against the Petitioner.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Magistrate's decision is ultra vires | No evidence against Petitioner | Legal error in charging abetment for the victim of the offence
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court relied on affidavits and statements from the Respondents, particularly the 3rd Respondent's assertion that no evidence exists against the Petitioner. No witness testimony was presented.
probability_assessment_by_court: Court found that the Magistrate's order was ultra vires and that no evidence supported proceedings against the Petitioner.
defence_version_summary: Petitioner denied any offence and sought to quash the Magistrate's order based on lack of evidence and legal error through writs of certiorari and prohibition.
legal_errors_description: The Magistrate erred in making the Petitioner a suspect for abetment when the offence under Article 111 C (2) involves the Petitioner as the victim, not the abettor, which is legally untenable.
procedural_defects_description: The Magistrate exceeded jurisdiction by entertaining the case against the Petitioner without proper grounds, leading to loss of legal jurisdiction.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The COA analyzed the Magistrate's order and found it ultra vires because charging the Petitioner for abetment of an offence where he is the victim is legally incorrect. The court referred to principles of criminal liability and precedents. It considered the 3rd Respondent's affidavit stating no evidence and the lack of objection from the 2nd Respondent, determining that the Magistrate lost legal jurisdiction to try the case against the Petitioner.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The Petitioner, a former Chief Magistrate, challenged a Magistrate's Court order making him a suspect for abetment and conspiracy related to judicial interference. The Court of Appeal found the order ultra vires as the offence under Article 111 C (2) could not support abetment charges against the same judge. Based on the 3rd Respondent's affidavit stating no evidence and lack of objection from the 2nd Respondent, the COA issued writs of prohibition and certiorari, quashing the order and summons, and prohibiting further proceedings against the Petitioner.
defence_counsel: Romesh De Silva PC with Sudath Caldera and N. Ankatell
precedents_cited_list: R v. Electricity Commissioner (1924) 1 KB 171 | The Queen v. D.D. Ginigandara and another (70 NLR 192) | Queen v. D.K. Dhanapala (1964) 67 NLR 450 | Re Jones v. James (1850) | Mouffet v. Washburn (1886) | Re Knowles v. Holden (1855) | Moore v. Gamgee (1890)
standard_of_review_applied: The court applied principles for issuing writs of certiorari and prohibition, focusing on jurisdiction and legal errors.

judges: K Priyantha Fernando, J. | Sampath B Abayakoon, J.
offence_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code, Section 380 of the Penal Code, and Section 383 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: On 3 November 2002, police stopped a vehicle without a windscreen, found bloodstains, and arrested the occupants (accused). The accused led police to a tank where the body of the driver was found. The deceased driver had been hired by the accused on 2 November 2002. The accused were found in possession of the stolen vehicle and were identified by a fellow driver.
evidence_type_secondary: Medical evidence (JMO report) and discovery of body based on accused's statements
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code and Section 380 of the Penal Code
hc_sentence_type: Death for murder, 10 years rigorous imprisonment for robbery, and fines
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the 1st, 2nd, and 3rd accused of murder and robbery based on circumstantial evidence and identification. The 2nd and 3rd accused were sentenced to death for murder and 10 years rigorous imprisonment for robbery. The 1st accused absconded and an open warrant was issued.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appeal was based on the ground that the trial court failed to judicially evaluate the items of circumstantial evidence by applying the standard guidelines.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Failure to judicially evaluate circumstantial evidence by applying standard guidelines.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed the circumstantial evidence, including identification by a fellow driver, possession of the stolen vehicle, broken windscreen with bloodstains, and discovery of the body based on the accused's directions.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court applied the standard for circumstantial evidence and found the evidence consistent only with guilt and inconsistent with any reasonable hypothesis of innocence.
defence_version_summary: The 2nd and 3rd accused made dock statements denying involvement, claiming they were invited by the 1st accused and were unaware of the crime until arrested. They did not call any witnesses.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal thoroughly reviewed the circumstantial evidence, including identification by PW-07, possession of the stolen vehicle soon after the robbery, the broken windscreen with bloodstains, and the discovery of the body based on the accused's directions. The court applied the standard for circumstantial evidence and found that the evidence was consistent only with the guilt of the accused and inconsistent with any reasonable hypothesis of innocence. The court also noted the applicability of section 106 of the Evidence Ordinance and the presumption under section 114 illustration (a) regarding possession of stolen goods. The court found no merit in the appeal and affirmed the conviction and sentence.
coa_sentence_type: Death for murder and 10 years rigorous imprisonment for robbery, and fines
brief_judgment_file_summary: The four accused were charged with murder and robbery of a vehicle. The High Court convicted the 1st, 2nd, and 3rd accused (the 4th accused died) and sentenced the 2nd and 3rd accused to death for murder and 10 years rigorous imprisonment for robbery. The 2nd and 3rd accused appealed on the ground that the trial court failed to properly evaluate the circumstantial evidence. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal, holding that the circumstantial evidence was strong and pointed only to the guilt of the accused, and that the trial judge had correctly applied the law.
defence_counsel: Indika Mallawarachchi
cause_of_death_exact_text: Strangulation
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court correctly evaluated the circumstantial evidence and found the accused guilty. The Court of Appeal agreed with the High Court's reasoning and found no error.

judges: Prasantha De Silva, J. | S.U.B. Karalliyadde, J.
brief_facts_summary: The Applicant initiated proceedings in the Magistrate's Court of Navalapitiya to enforce an Arbitral Award under the Co-operative Societies Law against the 1st and 2nd Accused. The Magistrate, after allowing the accused to show cause, ordered recovery of the sum mentioned in the Certificate as a fine. The 1st Accused appealed to the High Court, which dismissed the appeal on the basis that the Co-operative Law does not provide appeal rights. The 1st Accused then appealed to the Court of Appeal.
hc_sentence_type: Fine (recovery of arbitral award as a fine)
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court dismissed the appeal, holding that the Co-operative Societies Law does not provide any right of appeal against the Magistrate's order. The High Court found no statutory basis for the appeal.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The 1st Accused-Appellant argued that he has a right of appeal against the Magistrate's Order under section 4(2) of the ICCPR Act, No. 56 of 2007, which guarantees a right to appeal a conviction and sentence. He relied on the Supreme Court decision in Mallarachchige Kanishka Gunawardhana Vs. H.K. Sumanasena and the Hon. Attorney General. The Respondent argued the Co-operative Law provides no appeal right and the cited case is irrelevant.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Right of appeal exists under section 4(2) of the ICCPR Act. | The Supreme Court precedent in Mallarachchige Kanishka Gunawardhana Vs. H.K. Sumanasena and the Hon. Attorney General supports the right of appeal.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: No witness evidence was involved. The case concerned a procedural challenge to the enforceability of an arbitral award under the Co-operative Societies Law.
defence_version_summary: The 1st Accused pleaded not liable and challenged the procedure, arguing he had a right to appeal the Magistrate's order. He did not call witnesses but relied on legal submissions based on the ICCPR Act and precedent.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed whether the ICCPR Act granted a right of appeal. It distinguished the cited Supreme Court precedent, noting that case involved a criminal conviction and sentence under the Foreign Employment Bureau Act, whereas the present matter involved an administrative recovery proceeding under the Co-operative Law where the accused were not charged, tried, convicted, or sentenced for a criminal offence. The Court held that section 4(2) of the ICCPR Act applies only to persons convicted of a criminal offence under written law. Since the Magistrate's order was an administrative act to recover a debt as a fine, not a criminal conviction, the ICCPR Act right to appeal did not apply. The Co-operative Law itself provided no appeal right, so the appeal was without basis.
coa_sentence_type: Dismissal of appeal; order of the Magistrate to recover the sum as a fine affirmed; 1st Accused ordered to pay Rs. 30,000 as costs of the appeal.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The 1st Accused-Appellant appealed against the High Court's dismissal of his appeal from a Magistrate's order enforcing an arbitral award under the Co-operative Societies Law. The Appellant argued a right of appeal under the ICCPR Act, citing a Supreme Court precedent. The Court of Appeal held the ICCPR Act applies only to criminal convictions, and since the Magistrate's proceeding was administrative recovery, not a criminal trial, no right of appeal existed. The Co-operative Law also provided no appeal right. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal and ordered the Appellant to pay costs of Rs. 30,000.
defence_counsel: Mr. R. Chula Bandara
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court dismissed the appeal on the basis that the Co-operative Societies Law does not provide any right of appeal. The Court of Appeal agreed with this analysis and found no error.
precedents_cited_list: Mallarachchige Kanishka Gunawardhana Vs. H.K. Sumanasena and the Hon. Attorney General (S.C. Appeal No. 201/2014 decided on 15.03.2018)
standard_of_review_applied: Review of legal question regarding existence of statutory right of appeal and applicability of ICCPR Act.

judges: Prasantha De Silva, J. | Khema Swarnadhipathi, J.
offence_sections: Section 59(1)(c) and Section 59(4) of the Cooperative Societies Act No. 5 of 1972
brief_facts_summary: The Rathgama Multipurpose Cooperative Society deposited money with the appellant society which failed to repay. The matter was arbitrated and an award was issued. The appellant did not appeal the award. The Deputy Commissioner of Cooperative Development filed a certificate in the Magistrate's Court to recover the amount as a fine. The Magistrate ordered recovery and imposed imprisonment in default, which was upheld by the High Court.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 59(1)(c) and Section 59(4) of the Cooperative Societies Act No. 5 of 1972
hc_sentence_type: Fine and in default 6 months rigorous imprisonment
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court dismissed the appellant's revision application without issuing notice to the plaintiff, upholding the Magistrate's order.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant argued that penal law cannot be applied to recover money, that criminal law cannot be used between cooperative societies, that the plaintiff must first take steps under Section 59(3), and that the certificate under Section 59(1)(c) cannot include interest and costs.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The provisions in Penal Law cannot be applied in recovering the alleged sum of money. | When the dispute is between two different Cooperative Societies, one cannot resort to the provisions in Criminal Law. | The Plaintiff must firstly take steps under Section 59(3) of the Cooperative Societies Act and if failing, then seek relief from the Magistrate's Court. | The certificate under Section 59(1)(c) cannot include interest and costs, only the principal amount due.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The case is based on documentary evidence including the arbitration award and the certificate. The Court of Appeal analyzed the statutory provisions and found the certificate valid.
probability_assessment_by_court: The court applied principles of statutory interpretation to determine the meaning of 'amount due'.
defence_version_summary: The appellant did not appear in the Court of Appeal but had filed written submissions. The defence was that the certificate was defective and the procedure under Section 59 was not followed, and that interest and costs could not be included.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed the wording of Section 59(1)(c) and held that 'amount due' includes principal, interest, and costs. They rejected the jurisdiction objection, noting the applicable law is the 1972 Act, and distinguished the Supreme Court case cited by the appellant. They affirmed the lower courts' orders.
coa_sentence_type: Fine of Rs.20,936,863 and in default 6 months rigorous imprisonment
brief_judgment_file_summary: The Deputy Commissioner of Cooperative Development filed a certificate in the Magistrate's Court to recover money from the appellant based on an arbitral award. The Magistrate ordered recovery as a fine with imprisonment in default. The High Court dismissed the revision. The appellant appealed, arguing the certificate was defective and interest and costs could not be included. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal, holding the certificate valid and 'amount due' includes interest and costs.
prosecution_counsel: Mr. Rajin Gooneratne S.C for the Plaintiff-Respondent-Respondent
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court dismissed the appellant's revision application without issuing notice to the plaintiff. The Court of Appeal found no error in the High Court's decision.
precedents_cited_list: K. A. Dayawathie Vs D. S. Edirisinghe and 04 others [S.C F.R No.241/08] | Ambawa Thrift Credit Co-operative Society Vs D. M. Sumana Dissanayake and Co-operative Development Commissioner [C.A (PHC) 168/2011]
standard_of_review_applied: De novo review of statutory interpretation

judges: Menaka Wijesundera J. | Neil Iddawala J.
brief_facts_summary: The petitioner threatened the victim with death in the compound of the Mathugama Magistrates Court premises. The victim lodged a complaint, and the petitioner was arrested and remanded since 2017. The bail application is based on the long remand period.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The petitioner contends that he has been in remand since 2017, which is sufficiently exceptional to enlarge him on bail.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Long remand since 2017
