grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The conviction is wholly unsafe in view of the un-corroborated and unsatisfactory nature of the evidence of the main witness PW1, led by the prosecution. | The learned Trial Judge failed to consider the rules governing the test of probability to the prosecution version. | The prosecution failed to establish the chain as to the passage of production from the police station to the government analyst. | The learned Trial Judge has considered only the prosecution evidence and failed seriously to evaluate the evidence given by the defence. | The learned Trial Judge erred in law by rejecting the dock statement made by the appellant with reversing the burden of proof. | The learned Trial Judge has misdirected himself and thereby erred in law and the facts of the case, causing grave prejudice to the appellant.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the evidence of PW1 unconvincing and uncorroborated, while the defence evidence (sister's testimony) was unchallenged and corroborated the dock statement.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal applied the test of probability and found the prosecution story doubtful, while the defence story was probable and unchallenged.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty. The defence called his sister who testified that he was a three-wheeler driver, was assaulted by police, taken to his house, and his three-wheeler was handed over to his mother. The appellant made a dock statement. The Court found the defence version credible and unchallenged.
legal_errors_description: The High Court Judge erred in law by rejecting the dock statement with reversing the burden of proof, and misdirected himself on the facts and law.
procedural_defects_description: Failure to establish chain of custody, and failure to properly evaluate the defence evidence by not considering that the defence version was put to PW1.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed the evidence and found that the prosecution case was not proved beyond reasonable doubt. The evidence of PW1 was unconvincing and uncorroborated, while the defence evidence was credible and unchallenged. The Court applied the test of probability and found the prosecution story doubtful. The High Court judge erred in rejecting the defence evidence and misdirected on the burden of proof. Therefore, the conviction was unsafe.
coa_sentence_type: Acquitted, no sentence
brief_judgment_file_summary: The appellant was convicted in the High Court of Colombo for possession and trafficking of 8.64 grams of heroin and sentenced to life imprisonment. He appealed to the Court of Appeal on grounds including unreliable prosecution evidence, chain of custody issues, and misdirection on law. The Court of Appeal found the prosecution evidence unconvincing and the defence evidence credible, and set aside the conviction, acquitting the appellant.
defence_counsel: Rasika Samarawickrama
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted the appellant based on the prosecution evidence and rejected the defence evidence, including the dock statement, on the basis that the defence version was not put to PW1. The Court of Appeal found this incorrect and held that the High Court failed to properly evaluate the defence evidence and misdirected on the burden of proof.
precedents_cited_list: Attorney General v Devinduruqe Nihal (SC Appeal 154/10, decided 03.01.2019) | Hettiarachige Amila Pathum v Attorney General (CA 204/2008, decided 27.02.2013) | Queen v Kularatne (71 NLR 529)
standard_of_review_applied: The Court of Appeal reviewed the evidence and applied the test of probability, and also considered the burden of proof and the reliability of the evidence.

judges: Menaka Wijesundera J. | Neil Iddawala J.
offence_sections: Section 364 and 365 of the Penal Code
offence_category: Crimes against persons (Kidnapping/Abduction, possibly with sexual assault given context)
brief_facts_summary: The accused pleaded guilty to charges under Sections 364 and 365 of the Penal Code. The victim was an 11-year-old child who frequented the accused's house to play with his daughter of the same age. The medico-legal report substantiated the victim's injuries. The accused was 43 years old at the time of the offence.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 364 and 365 of the Penal Code
hc_sentence_type: For first charge: Five years imprisonment and a fine. For second charge: Fifteen years imprisonment, fine and compensation. Sentences to run consecutively.
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the accused based on his guilty plea to two charges under the Penal Code. It imposed consecutive sentences totalling twenty years imprisonment, plus fines and compensation.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The substituted petitioner filed a revision application seeking to set aside the sentence, not the conviction. The petitioner did not explain undue delay, lack of locus standi, or failure to exercise the right of appeal. The petition did not plead exceptional circumstances.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Delay in filing the petition. | The substituted petitioner has no locus standi. | The accused failed to exercise his right of appeal. | No exceptional circumstances pleaded.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: Evidence was based on the accused's guilty plea and a medico-legal report. No witness analysis was undertaken in this revision application.
probability_assessment_by_court: Not applicable as conviction was based on a guilty plea.
defence_version_summary: The accused pleaded guilty to both charges in the High Court. He did not appeal. A substituted petitioner filed a revision application challenging only the sentence.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal dismissed the revision application on three preliminary objections: (1) unexplained and undue delay of over one year in filing; (2) the substituted petitioner lacked locus standi as he failed to show how he was aggrieved by the sentence; and (3) the accused failed to exercise his right of appeal. The Court held that revision is an exceptional jurisdiction requiring circumstances that 'shock the conscience' of the court, which were not averred. Even on merits, the Court found the sentence for offences against an 11-year-old child by a 43-year-old man, supported by medical evidence, was neither illegal nor shocking.
coa_sentence_type: Original High Court sentence upheld: Five years imprisonment and fine for first charge; fifteen years imprisonment, fine and compensation for second charge; sentences to run consecutively.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused was convicted in the High Court of Tangalle on guilty pleas to charges under Sections 364 and 365 of the Penal Code and sentenced to consecutive totalling twenty years imprisonment, plus fines and compensation. A substituted petitioner filed a revision application in the Court of Appeal seeking to set aside only the sentence. The Court dismissed the application, upholding preliminary objections regarding undue delay, lack of locus standi, and failure to exercise the right of appeal. The Court also found no merit, as the sentence for offences against a child was neither illegal nor shocking.
defence_counsel: Shirol D. Ialamiarachchi
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted based on a guilty plea and imposed sentence. The Court of Appeal found no error in the High Court's decision that warranted revisionary intervention.
precedents_cited_list: Ellangakoon v OIC Eppawala Police Station and another (2007) 1 SLR 398 | CA/PHC/APN/21/2021 | CA/PHC/APN/78/2021 | Somnipathy v Weerasinghe (1980) 2 SLR 121 | Sriyani Silva v Iddamalgoda, Officer in Charge, Police Station, Payagala and Others (2003) SLR 14 | Sugathapala Mendis and Others v Chandrika Kumarathunga and Others (2008)2 SLR339, 391 | Gunasekara Hamini v Don Baron D.C. Colombo, 13,125 | Sello Hamy v Rapheal 1 SCR. 73 | Helena Hamline et al v Nonahamy et al 60 DC Colombo, 33,943 | Deshpande v S (1971) 13 JILI 153 | M.C. Mehta v Union of India (AIR 1988 SC 1115) | Parmanand Katara v Union of India (AIR 1989 SC 2039) | Dattaraj Nathuji Thawarev State of Maharashtra AIR2005 SC 540 | CA (PHC) APN 144/2016 HC (Rev) 76/2016 | Sonali Fernando v AG CA (PHC) APN 144/07 | E.G. standard_of_review_applied: Revisionary jurisdiction: to ascertain if there are real legal grounds to impugn the decision, not to rehear or re-evaluate evidence. Requires the order to have occasioned a failure of justice, be manifestly erroneous, or shock the conscience of the court.
sentencing_principles_applied: The Court considered the gravity of the offence, the age difference between the accused (43) and victim (11), the breach of trust, and the medical evidence.

judges: K. PRIYANTHA FERNANDO, J. (P/CA) | WICKUM A. KALUARACHCHI, J.
offence_sections: Section 54A(d) and 54A(b) of the Poisons Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance
brief_facts_summary: Police officers on patrol stopped and searched the appellant after he tried to avoid them, finding two parcels containing 38.65 grams of heroin in his trouser pocket. The appellant claimed he was with his wife buying clothes and medicine and was falsely implicated. The High Court convicted him based on prosecution evidence.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 54A(d) and 54A(b) of the Poisons Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the appellant for possession and trafficking of heroin and sentenced him to death. The judge rejected the defence version, noting the appellant's failure to call his wife as a witness and incorrectly stating that the defence was not put to prosecution witnesses in cross-examination.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant argued that the trial judge imposed an additional burden of proof on him, denying a fair trial. He also contended that the judge erred in commenting on the failure to call his wife as a witness and in stating that the defence was not put to prosecution witnesses in cross-examination.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The learned trial Judge has erred in law by imposing additional burden of proof on the accused appellant. | The learned trial Judge erred in commenting on the failure of the appellant to call his wife as a witness. | The learned trial Judge erred in stating that the defence was not put to the prosecution witnesses in cross-examination.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The prosecution relied on police testimony and physical evidence of heroin. The Court of Appeal found that the trial judge misdirected on facts by imposing burden on the accused and incorrectly assessing cross-examination.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal found that the trial judge's error in imposing burden of proof prejudiced the appellant's rights and occasioned a failure of justice, leading to acquittal.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty and made an unsworn statement from the dock, claiming he was with his wife buying clothes and medicine and was falsely implicated. No defence witnesses were called. The High Court rejected this version, but the Court of Appeal found errors in the trial judge's handling.
legal_errors_description: The trial judge imposed an additional burden of proof on the appellant to prove his innocence, contrary to the presumption of innocence under Article 13(5) of the Constitution.
procedural_defects_description: The trial judge commented on the appellant's failure to call his wife as a witness and incorrectly stated that the defence was not put to prosecution witnesses in cross-examination, when it was.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found that the trial judge erred in law by placing an additional burden of proof on the appellant, prejudicing his substantial rights and occasioning a failure of justice. They referenced the precedent Nandana v Attorney-General. The judge also misdirected on facts by stating the defence was not put to witnesses, when cross-examination showed it was. Therefore, the conviction could not stand, and the case was not fit for retrial.
coa_sentence_type: Acquitted, no sentence
brief_judgment_file_summary: The appellant was convicted by the High Court of Colombo for possession and trafficking of heroin and sentenced to death. He appealed on grounds including that the trial judge imposed an additional burden of proof. The Court of Appeal found the judge erred in law and misdirected on facts, prejudicing the appellant's rights. The appeal was allowed, and the appellant was acquitted.
defence_counsel: K. Kugaraja
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted the appellant based on prosecution evidence and rejected the defence version due to perceived failures in calling witnesses and cross-examination. The Court of Appeal found that the High Court judge erred in imposing burden of proof and misdirected on facts.
precedents_cited_list: Nandana v Attorney-General [2008] I Sri L.R | M.A.S. de Alwist v G.P.A. de Silva
standard_of_review_applied: Review under Article 138 of the Constitution, considering whether errors prejudiced substantial rights or occasioned a failure of justice.

judges: Menaka Wijesundera J. | Neil Iddawala J.
offence_sections: Sections 354 and 365 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The accused petitioner was indicted under Sections 354 and 365 of the Penal Code for alleged sexual abuse of the victim. The victim testified that he was abused by the petitioner and informed his mother around five days later. The defense highlighted three contradictions in the prosecution evidence.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Sections 354 and 365 of the Penal Code
hc_sentence_type: For first charge: Two years imprisonment with fine and compensation. For second charge: Six months imprisonment with a fine.
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the petitioner on both charges. The judge considered the victim's evidence at length, along with contradictions and omissions, and found the victim's version consistent. The defense claim that the incident was fabricated by the victim's mother over a monetary transaction was disregarded as not credible.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The petitioner filed a revision application, not an appeal, seeking to set aside the High Court judgment. He explained the delay in filing and failure to exercise the right of appeal. Arguments focused on delay in lodging the police complaint (around seventeen days) and contradictions in prosecution evidence.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Delay in lodging complaint (around seventeen days) | Contradictions in prosecution evidence
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal observed that the victim was consistent in his narration of facts. The delay in telling his mother was attributed to immaturity. The prosecution evidence was corroborated by other witnesses.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court found the victim's version credible and the defense version (fabrication over money) hard to believe, thus no reasonable doubt arose.
defence_version_summary: The petitioner pleaded not guilty. The defense claimed the incident was fabricated by the victim's mother due to a monetary dispute involving Rs. 2000. The court found this defense not credible.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal applied the revisionary jurisdiction standard, focusing on legality and propriety, not re-evaluating evidence. It found the High Court judge correctly considered the evidence, contradictions, and omissions. The victim's consistency and corroboration by other witnesses were noted. The defense allegation of fabrication was deemed not credible. No exceptional illegalities were found in the High Court judgment.
coa_sentence_type: Conviction and sentences imposed by High Court upheld (First charge: two years imprisonment with fine and compensation; Second charge: six months imprisonment with a fine).
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused petitioner sought revision to set aside the High Court conviction for sexual abuse under Sections 354 and 365 of the Penal Code. The High Court had convicted him based on the victim's consistent testimony, despite some contradictions and a delay in complaint. The Court of Appeal, exercising revisionary jurisdiction, found no legal grounds to impugn the High Court decision, upheld the conviction and sentences, and dismissed the application.
prosecution_counsel: Priyani Abeygunawardena, SC for the State
defence_counsel: Duminda De Alwis with Lakmini Amarasinghe for the Accused – Petitioner
hc_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the High Court judge correctly evaluated the evidence, including contradictions and omissions. The judge's reasoning that a witness cannot have a photographic memory and that the victim's version was consistent was endorsed.
precedents_cited_list: CA(PHC)APN 17/2006 | Browns Engineering Private Ltd. v Commissioner of Labor and others 98 SLR vol 1 pg 88 | Nissanka v the State vol.3 page No.78 | HAM Casim v GA Batticaloa (NLR vol.69 pg 403)
standard_of_review_applied: Revisionary jurisdiction: ascertaining whether there are real legal grounds relating to revisionary powers, not re-evaluating evidence or deciding if the decision is right or wrong. Focus on legality, propriety, and regularity.

judges: N. Bandula Karunarathna, J. | R. Gurusinghe, J.
brief_facts_summary: The appellant was accused of murdering Paramullage Don Karunapala on 18th October 1997 at Neboda. There was animosity between the deceased and appellant, and on that day, a fight ensued during which the deceased sustained a fatal neck injury. Key evidence came from the deposition of an eyewitness (PW1) under Section 33 of the Evidence Ordinance, as PW1 was dead by the time of trial. The appellant was a toddy tapper and had a sharp knife.
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court found the appellant guilty of murder based on the evidence, including the deposition of PW1 under Section 33 of the Evidence Ordinance, and sentenced him to death.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant appealed on grounds including denial of fair trial due to reliance on PW1's evidence under Section 33, failure to assess the trustworthiness of that evidence, failure to consider general and special exceptions under the Penal Code, and failure to properly consider the accused's evidence.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: A fair trial has been denied to the appellant because he has been convicted for murder and sentenced to death, purely on the evidence of PW1, who is dead, which evidence has been adopted purportedly in terms of section 33 of the Evidence Ordinance. | The Learned Trial Judge has failed to assess the trustworthiness and credibility of PW1’s evidence, adopted under section 33 of the evidence ordinance. | The Learned High Court Judge has failed to consider whether any general exception contained in chapter 4 of the Penal Code applied to the facts of this case. | The Learned Trial Judge has failed to consider whether any special exception contained in section 294 of the Penal Code applied to the facts of this case. | The learned Trial Judge has failed to properly consider the evidence given by the accused.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal evaluated PW1's deposition under Section 33 as admissible and probative, noting it was given on oath and subject to cross-examination. The court also considered the appellant's evidence and found contradictions, but accepted that there was a sudden fight based on the evidence.
probability_assessment_by_court: The court found the evidence credible and applied the sudden fight exception, reducing the charge to culpable homicide not amounting to murder.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty and gave evidence, claiming he grappled with the deceased during a fight where the deceased tried to use a knife, causing injury on his palm. He stated he did not know how the deceased sustained the fatal neck injury. The court noted contradictions in his testimony.
legal_errors_description: The High Court failed to consider Exception 4 of Section 294 of the Penal Code regarding sudden fight, which should have been applied to the facts.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal held that PW1's evidence under Section 33 was admissible and relevant, rejecting grounds related to fair trial and credibility. However, the court found that the High Court erred in not applying the sudden fight exception under Section 294 of the Penal Code. Based on evidence of a sudden fight, the COA modified the conviction to culpable homicide not amounting to murder and imposed a sentence of seven years rigorous imprisonment with a fine.
coa_sentence_type: Seven years rigorous imprisonment, fine of Rs. 10,000, and in default six months simple imprisonment.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The appellant was convicted of murder and sentenced to death by the High Court of Kalutara. He appealed on grounds including denial of fair trial due to reliance on deceased eyewitness evidence under Section 33 and failure to consider Penal Code exceptions. The Court of Appeal upheld the admissibility of the eyewitness evidence but found the High Court erred in not applying the sudden fight exception, modifying the conviction to culpable homicide not amounting to murder and imposing seven years rigorous imprisonment and a fine.
defence_counsel: Asela Serasinghe
cause_of_death_exact_text: a two-inch-wide ½ inch deep 4 inches long horizontal cut in front of the neck that had gone through the trachea.
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted the appellant of murder based on PW1's deposition and other evidence without considering the sudden fight exception. The Court of Appeal found this was an error and that the exception should have been applied.
precedents_cited_list: Francis Samarauickrema vs Dona Enatto Hilda Jaugasinghe Supreme Court appeal 7/2004 | Herath v. Jabbar 41 NLR 217 | Cassim v. SuppiahPulle 41 NLR 275 | Kobbekaduwa v. Seneviratne 53 NLR 354 | Sheela Sinharage v. The Attorney-General [1985] 1 Sri LR 1
standard_of_review_applied: The court reviewed the evidence and legal errors, applying precedents on evidence admissibility and Penal Code exceptions.
sentencing_principles_applied: The court applied Exception 4 of Section 294 of the Penal Code for sudden fight as a mitigatory factor, reducing the sentence from death to imprisonment.
final_charge_after_appeal: culpable homicide not amounting to murder

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 300 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The victim and Appellant are neighbours. On the day of the incident around 5 p.m., the victim was going to the well when the Appellant intercepted him, leading to an argument and fight. The Appellant stabbed the victim with a knife, and the victim was hospitalized for 18 days with surgery. The victim provided the knife to the police as evidence.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 300 of the Penal Code
hc_sentence_type: Rigorous Imprisonment 2 years, Fine Rs.1000, Default Sentence 2 months simple imprisonment
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the Appellant for attempted murder based on the victim's testimony and the knife evidence. The Appellant was tried in absentia, and no defence evidence was adduced. The judge found the prosecution proved its case beyond reasonable doubt.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The Appellant contended that the victim's evidence was not credible due to contradictions, that the High Court judge shifted the burden of proof, and that the judge failed to evaluate the defence case which created reasonable doubt.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Evidence given by the victim PW1 is not credible as it contains many contradictions inter se and per se. | The Learned High Court Judge had shifted the burden of proof on to the Appellant. | The Learned High Court Judge had failed to evaluate the defense case which creates a reasonable doubt over the prosecution’s case.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found that the contradictions in the victim's evidence did not go to the root of the case and were not material. The High Court correctly admitted the evidence and found it credible.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal held that the prosecution proved its case beyond reasonable doubt, and no reasonable doubt was created by the defence.
defence_version_summary: The Appellant was tried in absentia and adduced no evidence. Counsel appeared on his behalf but did not present any defence evidence.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal dismissed all grounds of appeal. For the first ground, they found contradictions in victim's evidence were not material. For the second ground, they held that the High Court did not shift the burden of proof. For the third ground, they noted the Appellant failed to adduce defence evidence, and the High Court properly evaluated the prosecution case. The conviction and sentence were affirmed.
coa_sentence_type: Rigorous Imprisonment 2 years, Fine Rs.1000, Default Sentence 2 months simple imprisonment
brief_judgment_file_summary: This appeal concerned a conviction for attempted murder under Section 300 of the Penal Code. The High Court convicted the Appellant, sentencing him to imprisonment and a fine. The Appellant appealed on grounds of evidence credibility, burden of proof, and evaluation of defence. The Court of Appeal found no merit in the grounds, affirmed the conviction and sentence, and dismissed the appeal.
defence_counsel: U.R. De Silva, P.C. with Savithri Fernando
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court properly analyzed the evidence, found the victim credible, and convicted the Appellant. The Court of Appeal agreed with this analysis and found no errors.
precedents_cited_list: Thilakaratne v. Attorney General [1989] 2 SLR 191 | Attorney General v. Sandanam Pitchi Mary Theresa (2011) 2 SLR 292
standard_of_review_applied: The Court of Appeal reviewed the evidence and legal grounds based on the written submissions and found no errors in the High Court judgment.

judges: Sampath B Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 296 and Section 315 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: On 08-08-2010 after an 'elle' tournament at Morakale ground the appellant and deceased were consuming liquor. The appellant suddenly attacked the deceased with a sharp cutting instrument causing fatal injuries. The appellant admitted causing injuries but claimed it was during a sudden fight over a liquor bottle.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 296 and Section 315 of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: High Court found appellant guilty of murder and causing injury based on eyewitness testimony and medical evidence sentenced to death for murder and imprisonment for causing injury.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: Appellant argued no fair trial due to counsel withdrawal and that evidence supports culpable homicide not murder under exception 4 of Section 294.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: No fair trial afforded to the appellant | Evidence establishes basis for conviction for culpable homicide not amounting to murder under exception 4 of Section 294
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: COA analyzed eyewitness and medical evidence found that prosecution evidence showed sudden fight without premeditation supporting culpable homicide not murder.
probability_assessment_by_court: COA assessed that evidence established sudden fight without premeditation so offence is culpable homicide not murder.
defence_version_summary: Appellant pleaded not guilty gave evidence claiming sudden fight over liquor bottle but changed stands during trial. COA accepted sudden fight defence based on prosecution evidence.
legal_errors_description: High Court failed to consider evidence for culpable homicide not murder under exception 4 of Section 294 of the Penal Code.
procedural_defects_description: Counsel for appellant withdrew during trial but COA did not elaborate as second ground was meritorious.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: COA held that evidence established the incident was a sudden fight without premeditation falling under exception 4 of Section 294 so conviction should be for culpable homicide not murder. HC erred in not considering this so conviction and sentence on first count set aside and modified.
coa_sentence_type: 10 years rigorous imprisonment and fine for first count 2 years rigorous imprisonment and fine for second count
brief_judgment_file_summary: Appellant was convicted of murder and causing injury by High Court of Chilaw and sentenced to death and imprisonment. He appealed on grounds of unfair trial and wrong conviction. Court of Appeal found evidence showed sudden fight so modified conviction to culpable homicide not murder sentenced to 10 years imprisonment and fine while upholding second count sentence.
defence_counsel: Anil Silva PC with A. Bandara
hc_analysis_summary: High Court convicted based on injuries and eyewitness testimony but COA found HC should have considered culpable homicide not murder due to sudden fight evidence.
precedents_cited_list: King Vs. Belana Withanage Eddin 41 NLLR 345 | King Vs. Vidanalage Lanty 42 NLLR 317
final_charge_after_appeal: Culpable homicide not amounting to murder under exception 4 of Section 294 of the Penal Code

judges: Menaka Wijesundera J. | Neil Iddawala J.
offence_sections: Section 410 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The appellant was accused of damaging 12 roof tiles by hurling rocks at the respondent's house. The Magistrate Court acquitted the appellant and ordered the respondent to pay compensation for a frivolous complaint. The High Court ordered a retrial, which was appealed to the Court of Appeal.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 410 of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court ordered a retrial, criticizing the Magistrate for considering extraneous matters and for improper handling of the case. It also suggested disciplinary action against police officers.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant argued that the High Court ordered a retrial without setting aside the acquittal, that the revision only challenged the compensation order, and that the High Court failed to appreciate jurisdictional issues.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The petitioner in the High Court did not challenge the acquittal order dated 30.12.2014, but only the order dated 31.03.2015 regarding compensation, yet the High Court ordered a re-trial. | The learned High Court failed to appreciate that Hon. Attorney General has not filed an appeal against the acquittal in the Magistrate Court | The learned High Court Judge failed to appreciate that parties only made submissions with regard to jurisdiction, but not about merits of the revision | The learned High Court Judge failed to appreciate that the order dated 2016/11/1 should have been only on whether the petitioner has rights to file a revision or not.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Magistrate used statements from third parties not named as witnesses. The Court of Appeal found the evidence weak and chances of conviction remote due to delay.
probability_assessment_by_court: COA considered conviction unlikely due to weak evidence and long delay.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty and was acquitted by the Magistrate Court. No defence witnesses were mentioned, and the defence did not present additional evidence.
legal_errors_description: The High Court erred in ordering a retrial without setting aside the acquittal and without considering the delay and nature of the offence.
procedural_defects_description: The High Court ordered a retrial without first deciding on the maintainability of the revision application and without proper jurisdictional basis.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed that a retrial is not warranted due to the substantial delay since the offence in 2009, the remote chances of conviction, and the compoundable nature of the mischief charge. It referenced precedents that retrials are ordered only in exceptional circumstances. The COA set aside the High Court's retrial order and the Magistrate's compensation order, allowing the appeal.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The appellant was charged with mischief for damaging roof tiles. The Magistrate Court acquitted the appellant and ordered the complainant to pay compensation. The High Court ordered a retrial. On appeal, the Court of Appeal allowed the appeal, set aside the retrial order due to delay and weak evidence, and upheld the acquittal.
defence_counsel: Kamal S. Perera
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court ordered a retrial without setting aside the acquittal and criticized the Magistrate's actions. The COA found this erroneous due to procedural issues and lack of merit for retrial.
precedents_cited_list: Ramalingam v Parameswary and Others (2000) 2 SLR 33 | King v Fernando 48 NLR 249 | Queen v Jayasinghe 69 NLR 314 | E. M. Gamini Edirisuriya & Others v Attorney General C.A. 228-230/2005 | Peter Singho V. Werapitiya 55 N.L.R 157
standard_of_review_applied: The Court of Appeal exercised its appellate jurisdiction to correct errors in fact or law that prejudiced substantial rights or occasioned a failure of justice.

judges: K. Priyantha Fernando, J. (P/CA) | Wickum A. Kaluarachchi, J.
offence_sections: section 296 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The appellant was charged with murder. The main eyewitness (PW1) went with the deceased to PW3's house where the deceased consumed alcohol. The appellant arrived, an argument ensued, and the deceased left. Later, while the deceased and PW1 were on a bicycle, the appellant emerged from hiding behind a tree, attacked the deceased with a knife, cutting his neck and severing three fingers. PW1 ran back to PW3's house and reported the incident. The appellant made an unsworn statement from the dock, claiming he was a fishmonger and surrendered to police after hearing they were looking for him.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: section 296 of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court Judge found the appellant guilty of murder and sentenced him to death.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant's counsel argued material contradictions between witnesses, reliance on hearsay evidence, unreliable/inconsistent prosecution evidence, failure to consider intoxication, failure to consider the dock statement, and failure to establish mens rea.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Has the learned High Court Judge gravely erred and/or misdirected himself by failing to consider the purported material contradictions between PW1 and PW3. | Has the learned High Court Judge misdirected himself by erroneously relying and acting on hearsay evidence provided by PW3 and PW4. | Has the learned High Court Judge misdirected himself by failing to consider that the evidence of the prosecution witness is unreliable and inconsistent. | Has the learned High Court Judge misdirected himself by failing to consider and/or evaluate that there was manifest evidence of intoxication of the parties. | The learned High Court Judge failed to consider that the prosecution failed to establish the intention/mens rea of the appellant. | The learned High Court Judge failed to consider the dock statement by the appellant.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The COA found the main eyewitness (PW1) to be consistent and reliable, with his evidence corroborated by PW3 and PW4. Minor contradictions on trivial matters like timing were not deemed material. The dock statement was considered and rejected by the trial judge with sufficient reasons.
probability_assessment_by_court: Court found the eyewitness evidence credible and consistent, with corroboration. Minor discrepancies did not shake the general tenor of the evidence. No reasonable doubt was raised.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty. He made an unsworn statement from the dock, claiming he was a fishmonger and surrendered to police. He did not call any defence witnesses. The court found his dock statement lacked merit and was properly rejected by the trial judge.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal meticulously analyzed each ground. It found no material contradictions between witnesses, as minor timing discrepancies were trivial. It held the eyewitness (PW1) was reliable and consistent, his evidence corroborated. There was no evidence the appellant was intoxicated. The intention (mens rea) was inferred from the nature of the attack (cutting the neck with a heavy weapon causing instantly fatal injuries). The trial judge's consideration and rejection of the dock statement were found adequate. Relying on the precedent State of Uttar Pradesh v. M.K. Anthony regarding witness appreciation, the COA affirmed the High Court's judgment, finding no reason to interfere.
coa_sentence_type: Death
brief_judgment_file_summary: The appellant was convicted of murder by the High Court of Hambantota and sentenced to death. He appealed on grounds including material contradictions, hearsay evidence, unreliable witnesses, failure to consider intoxication and his dock statement, and lack of mens rea. The Court of Appeal found the main eyewitness credible and consistent, minor contradictions immaterial, no evidence of intoxication, and mens rea clear from the fatal injuries inflicted. It affirmed the High Court's conviction and sentence, dismissing the appeal.
defence_counsel: Delan De Silva
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court Judge relied on the eyewitness testimony and medical evidence, found the appellant guilty, and sentenced him to death. The COA found the HC Judge's reasoning and evaluation of evidence to be correct, with no errors identified.
precedents_cited_list: State of Uttar Pradesh V. M.K Anthony [1984] SCJ 236/ [1985] CRI. LJ. 493
standard_of_review_applied: The appellate court attached due weight to the trial court's appreciation of evidence, requiring weighty and formidable reasons to reject it based on minor variations.

judges: Sampath B Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 365B(2)(b) of the Penal Code as amended by Act No. 22 of 1995 and 29 of 1999
brief_facts_summary: The appellant was accused of sexually abusing a minor girl over a period of time in 2010-2011. The victim was about 11 years old and the appellant was a neighbor. The victim eventually informed her grandmother, leading to a police complaint on 02-04-2011. The appellant denied the allegations, claiming they were false due to a land dispute and a dispute between his wife and the victim's relative.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 365B(2)(b) of the Penal Code as amended by Act No. 22 of 1995 and 29 of 1999
hc_sentence_type: 12 years rigorous imprisonment on each count (concurrent) and a fine of Rs. 10,000 per count
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the appellant on the first and third counts of grave sexual abuse and sentenced him to 12 years rigorous imprisonment on each count to run concurrently and a fine of Rs. 10,000 per count. The appellant was acquitted on the second count.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant argued that the charges were wrongly joined, the date of offence was incorrectly stated (31 April), the victim's evidence was not credible and required corroboration, the victim's delay in informing parents was strange, the grandmother's evidence differed, and the police evidence was concocted. The appellant contended the case was not proved beyond reasonable doubt.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The three counts were not in the same transaction and were wrongly combined. | The date 31 April does not exist, making the charges bad in law. | The victim's evidence was not credible and the judge should have looked for corroboration. | The victim did not inform her parents despite threats. | The grandmother's evidence differed from the victim's. | It was strange for the grandmother to call the appellant's house. | The police pointed to a different place and the story was concocted. | The prosecution failed to mention a particular date, causing prejudice. | The case was not proved beyond reasonable doubt.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the victim's evidence credible and cogent, considering her age and the stigma. The court noted that the victim's evidence was consistent with the medical evidence and the testimonies of the grandmother and mother, and that no corroboration was required.
probability_assessment_by_court: The court found the victim's evidence credible and consistent, and the defence version contradictory and not creating reasonable doubt.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty and gave evidence. He claimed the allegation was false due to a land dispute and a dispute between his wife and the victim's relative. The court found his explanation contradictory and not credible.
procedural_defects_description: The indictment included a non-existent date (31 April) and the appellant argued that the charges were wrongly joined. However, the court found no prejudice.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal rejected all grounds of appeal. It held that the wrong date (31 April) did not cause prejudice to the appellant. The court found the victim's evidence credible and cogent, considering her age and the stigma, and that her failure to remember exact dates was understandable. The court referred to precedents on child witness evidence and held that the evidence of the victim was consistent with the medical evidence and the testimonies of the mother and grandmother. The court found the defence version contradictory and not creating reasonable doubt.
coa_sentence_type: 12 years rigorous imprisonment on each count (concurrent) and a fine of Rs. 10,000 per count, effective from 04-09-2020
brief_judgment_file_summary: The appellant was convicted by the High Court of Kegalle on two counts of grave sexual abuse of a minor and sentenced to 12 years rigorous imprisonment and a fine. He appealed on grounds including procedural defects and credibility of the victim. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal, holding that the procedural defects did not cause prejudice and the victim's evidence was credible and corroborated by medical evidence and other witnesses. The conviction and sentence were affirmed.
defence_counsel: R. Arseckularatne, P.C. with Chamindi Arsekularatne, Evanga Yakandavala and Thilina Punchihewa
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted the appellant on two counts and acquitted on one, after evaluating the evidence. The Court of Appeal found no error in the High Court's reasoning and affirmed the decision.
precedents_cited_list: Madawala Gedara Premadasa Vs. The Attorney General C.A.261/2009 decided on 26-05-2014 | R. Vs. Dossi 13 Cr. App. R. 158 | Wright Vs. Nicholson 54 Cr. App. R. 38 | Bhoginbhai Hitijibhai Vs. State of Gujarat AIR 1983- SC 753 | D. Tikiri Banda Vs. Attorney-General CA 64/2003 decided 06-10-2009
standard_of_review_applied: The court reviewed the evidence and the law to determine if the prosecution proved the case beyond reasonable doubt and if the High Court's decision was correct.

judges: Menaka Wijesundera J | Neil Iddawala J
brief_facts_summary: The petitioner was involved in forging the seal of the Geological Survey and Mining Bureau and using fake licenses for illegal mining, causing financial loss to the State. All accused pleaded guilty to the charges. The petitioner was a first-time offender with no previous convictions.
hc_sentence_type: Rigorous Imprisonment for 6 months on Count 01 with fine, suspended sentence of 6 months Rigorous Imprisonment for 5 years on Count 02
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court varied the Magistrate's sentence, imposing rigorous imprisonment for Count 01 and a suspended sentence for Count 02, while releasing the petitioner on Count 03 as he was not charged. The court considered the nature and gravity of the forgery offences.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The petitioner argues that the sentence imposed is excessive and seeks a suspended sentence based on Section 303 of the Criminal Procedure Code. He contends that as a first-time offender with no previous convictions, he qualifies for leniency.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Sentence is excessive | Petitioner qualifies for suspended sentence under Section 303 CPC as first-time offender
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The case relied on documentary evidence of forgery, and all accused pleaded guilty. The court evaluated the gravity of the offence based on the impact on state revenue and environment, without detailed witness analysis.
probability_assessment_by_court: The court focused on sentencing factors and gravity of offence rather than probability or reasonable doubt.
defence_version_summary: The petitioner pleaded guilty to the charges. He did not present an alibi or call witnesses, relying on his guilty plea and first-time offender status for leniency in sentencing.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal extensively analyzed the criteria under Section 303 of the Criminal Procedure Code for suspended sentences. It considered the nature and gravity of the forgery offence, the premeditation involved, the financial loss to the state, and environmental damage. Citing precedents, the court emphasized that white-collar crimes with far-reaching consequences should not lightly receive suspended sentences. The court found that the petitioner's actions vitiated the purpose of the regulatory body and that the sentencing by the High Court was proportionate.
coa_sentence_type: Rigorous Imprisonment for 6 months on Count 01 with fine of Rs. 1,500 and default sentence, and suspended sentence of 6 months Rigorous Imprisonment for 5 years on Count 02 with fine of Rs. 1,500, as affirmed from High Court
brief_judgment_file_summary: The petitioner, along with others, was convicted for forging the seal of the Geological Survey and Mining Bureau and using fake licenses, causing state loss. All pleaded guilty. The High Court imposed rigorous imprisonment and fines. The petitioner appealed, arguing for a suspended sentence as a first-time offender. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal, emphasizing the gravity of the offence and its environmental impact, and affirmed the High Court's sentence.
defence_counsel: R. Wimalarathna
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court varied the Magistrate's sentence, imposing custodial sentence for serious counts based on the gravity of the offence. The Court of Appeal agreed with this approach, noting that the High Court correctly exercised discretion under Section 303 CPC.
precedents_cited_list: Karunarathne v The State 78 NLR 413 | Attorney General v H. N. De Silva 57 NLR 121 | Attorney General v Mendis (1995) 1 SLR 138 | A.M.S. Sampath Vs AG SC Appeal 17/2013 | Maraba Liyanage Rohana Vs. AG SC Appeal 89A/2009 | SC Appeal 03/2008 | Kumara Vs AG 2003 1 SLR 139 | CA PHC-184/2013 CA Minutes 15.03.2019
standard_of_review_applied: Review of sentencing discretion under Section 303 of the Criminal Procedure Code
sentencing_principles_applied: Principles under Section 303 of the CPC including nature and gravity of offence, offender's culpability, previous character, need for deterrence and denunciation

judges: Menaka Wijesundera J | Neil Iddawala J
offence_sections: Forest Ordinance (as amended)
brief_facts_summary: On 03.01.2012, vehicle No. 68-6538 was taken into custody for transporting timber without a valid license in violation of the Forest Ordinance. The accused pleaded guilty and was fined Rs. 5,000. A vehicle inquiry was then held to determine if the vehicle should be confiscated. The appellant purchased the vehicle on 13.10.2013, after the offence was committed and while the vehicle inquiry was pending, claiming to be an innocent buyer.
evidence_type_secondary: Testimony of parties to vehicle inquiry
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Forest Ordinance (as amended)
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court affirmed the Magistrate's confiscation order and dismissed the appellant's revision application in limine. The High Court upheld the Magistrate's finding that the relevant owner for the inquiry was the owner at the time of the offence, who failed to prove taking all precautions to prevent the vehicle's illegal use.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant appeals against the High Court order dismissing her revision application without issuing notice. She claims to be an innocent buyer of the vehicle after the commission of the forest offence and during the pendency of the vehicle inquiry. The central issue is whether an owner who acquired ownership after the offence is entitled to relief under the Forest Ordinance.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Whether an owner of a vehicle who got such ownership after the commission of a forest offence is entitled to relief under the Forest Ordinance (as amended).
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: Evidence was led from three persons: the owner at the time of the offence, the person in possession at the time of the offence, and the appellant. The Magistrate assessed that the appellant, as a purchaser after the offence, fell outside the purview of Section 40 of the Forest Ordinance for claiming relief.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal found it illogical for the appellant to claim redress under the Forest Ordinance as she was not privy to the vehicle at the time of the offence and failed to exercise due diligence before purchase.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded to be an innocent buyer, having purchased the vehicle after the offence. She did not plead guilty to the offence itself. The court assessed her claim lacked credibility as she purchased the vehicle while aware of a pending case and failed to verify the transferor's right to sell.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed the law governing vehicle confiscation under the Forest Ordinance, referencing its previous decisions. It held that to claim relief under Section 40, the claimant must prove on a balance of probability that all precautionary measures were taken at the time of the offence to prevent it. The appellant, acquiring the vehicle after the offence, could not satisfy this requirement. The court applied the maxim 'caveat emptor,' noting the appellant failed to exercise due diligence by purchasing the vehicle while aware of a pending case. It found no reason to interfere with the lower court orders.
coa_sentence_type: Confiscation of vehicle (to be auctioned) affirmed; fine of Rs. 5,000 (imposed earlier) stands
brief_judgment_file_summary: The Officer-in-Charge appealed against the High Court order dismissing a revision application concerning the confiscation of vehicle No. 68-6538 used in a forest offence. The appellant, who purchased the vehicle after the offence, claimed to be an innocent buyer entitled to relief. The High Court had upheld the Magistrate's confiscation order. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal, ruling that relief under the Forest Ordinance is only available to the owner at the time of the offence, who must prove taking all precautions. The appellant, as a subsequent purchaser, failed to exercise due diligence and fell outside the Ordinance's protection.
defence_counsel: Udaya Bandara
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court affirmed the Magistrate's confiscation order, finding the relevant owner for inquiry was the owner at the time of the offence. The Court of Appeal agreed with this analysis and found no error.
precedents_cited_list: CA PHC 119/18 CA Minute 15.03.2022 | CA PHC 24/17 CA Minute 03.03.2022 | CA PHC APN 139/19 CA Minute Dated 09.11.2021 | Samarasinghe Dharmasena v W. P. Wanigasinghe and Others CA PHC 197/13 CA Minute dated 22.01.2019
standard_of_review_applied: Review of lower court orders for legal correctness and application of settled law on vehicle confiscation under Forest Ordinance.
sentencing_principles_applied: Principle that confiscation under Section 40 of Forest Ordinance requires owner at time of offence to prove taking all possible precautions on a balance of probability.

judges: Menaka Wijesundera J. | Neil Iddawala J.
brief_facts_summary: The Police Narcotics Bureau, with Navy assistance, raided a vessel based on information about narcotics from Dubai. Ten people were arrested on the vessel, and three more from Sri Lankan shores. The 31st suspect surrendered himself and was taken into custody, but the B report lacked independent incriminating evidence against him.
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court granted bail to the suspect after considering that the B report filed against him did not contain any independent incriminating evidence, relying only on his statement and the narration of the raid.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The Attorney General filed for revision, arguing that in narcotics raids, it is impractical to include all details in the B report. The Court of Appeal emphasized the legal requirements for furnishing evidence to the Magistrate under Section 115 of the Criminal Procedure Code.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Contention that it is not practical to divulge all information in a B report for raids of this nature
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court found that the B report contained only the narration of the raid by police officers and summary of suspect statements, which are inadmissible under the Evidence Ordinance, with no independent evidence against the suspect.
probability_assessment_by_court: Court assessed that there is no illegality in the High Court order as the B report lacked sufficient evidence to justify detention.
defence_version_summary: The suspect surrendered himself and was granted bail; the defence likely contested the evidence, but no specific version is detailed in this judgment.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed Section 115 of the Criminal Procedure Code, which requires that when a suspect is produced before a Magistrate, a summary of witness statements must be provided. They referred to precedents including CPA/63/21, Sumanadasa v Attorney General, and Joginder Kumar v State of U.P., emphasizing that legal procedures cannot be ignored. The Court found that the B report lacked independent evidence and only contained inadmissible material, so the High Court correctly granted bail, and the revision application was dismissed.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The Attorney General filed a revision application to set aside the High Court's bail order for the 31st suspect in a narcotics raid case. The High Court had granted bail due to lack of incriminating evidence in the B report. The Court of Appeal upheld the High Court's decision, emphasizing legal requirements for evidence submission under Section 115 of the Criminal Procedure Code and dismissing the revision.
defence_counsel: Nalin Ladduwahetty, PC with Sarath Ekanayake, Vajira Ranasinghe and Kavithri Obeysekara
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court granted bail after considering that the B report did not contain independent evidence against the suspect. The Court of Appeal found this reasoning correct and in accordance with legal provisions.
precedents_cited_list: CPA/63/21 | SC SPI 1-199-200-206, Sumanadasa and 205 others v Attorney General | Joginder Kumar v State of U.P. (1994) 4 SCC 260: 1994 SCC (Cri) 1172
standard_of_review_applied: Revision under Article 138 of the Constitution, assessing the legality and propriety of the High Court's bail order.

judges: Menaka Wijesundera J | Neil Iddawala J
offence_sections: Section 402 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The petitioner was charged with cheating by obtaining Rs 350,000 from the virtual complainant by promising to secure a teaching position. He was convicted and sentenced to two years rigorous imprisonment, a fine of Rs 1,500 and compensation of Rs 100,000. The High Court affirmed the conviction and sentence, leading to this revision application.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 402 of the Penal Code
hc_sentence_type: Two years rigorous imprisonment, fine of Rs 1,500, compensation of Rs 100,000 with default sentences
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court affirmed the conviction and sentence imposed by the Magistrate Court, finding no error in the Magistrate's decision.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The petitioner sought a reduction of sentence on the grounds that he has been in remand custody for four years and is the father of four children. The respondent objected, citing the petitioner's previous similar convictions.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Sentence excessive due to family condition and time in remand custody
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Magistrate analyzed the evidence of four prosecution witnesses and found the offence proved beyond reasonable doubt. The petitioner's evidence was considered a mere denial.
probability_assessment_by_court: The court found the evidence established the offence beyond reasonable doubt.
defence_version_summary: The petitioner pleaded not guilty and gave evidence under oath. The court found his evidence to be a mere denial and not credible.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal held that it will not interfere with the sentence unless the trial judge exercised discretion on a wrong principle. The court found the Magistrate carefully analyzed the evidence and imposed a sentence within the statutory limits (up to 7 years). The mitigating factors (family condition and time in remand) were not sufficient to warrant interference, especially given the petitioner's previous similar convictions.
coa_sentence_type: Two years rigorous imprisonment, fine of Rs 1,500, compensation of Rs 100,000 (with default sentences)
brief_judgment_file_summary: The petitioner was convicted of cheating and sentenced by the Magistrate Court. The High Court affirmed the conviction. The Court of Appeal, in a revision application, dismissed the appeal, holding that the sentence was not excessive and the trial judge properly exercised discretion, considering the statutory maximum and the petitioner's previous similar convictions.
prosecution_counsel: Chathurangi Mahawaduge SC for the respondents
defence_counsel: Aruna Pathirana Arachchi for the petitioner
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court affirmed the Magistrate's decision. The Court of Appeal found no error in the High Court's judgment and agreed with its reasoning.
precedents_cited_list: King Vs Rankira 42 NLR 145 | King Vs E. M. T. De Saram 42 NLR 528 | The Attorney General v H. N. De Silva 57 NLR 121 | Meera Saheeb Mahir v OIC, Thalangama CA(PHC)APN 64/2020
standard_of_review_applied: The Court of Appeal will not interfere with the sentence unless the trial judge exercised discretion on a wrong principle or improperly.
sentencing_principles_applied: The court considered the statutory maximum sentence of seven years and the fact that the sentence imposed was within limits. It also considered the petitioner's previous convictions and the nature of the offence.

judges: K. PRIYANTHA FERNANDO, J. (P/CA) | WICKUM A. KALUARACHCHI, J.
offence_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The incident occurred at about 7:30 to 8:00 p.m. where the appellant stabbed the first deceased and cut the second deceased with a knife. Eyewitness PW4 testified to seeing the events. The appellant was controlled by villagers and later surrendered to the police.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the appellant on two counts of murder and sentenced him to death. The judge considered the prosecution evidence and rejected the appellant's dock statement.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant argued that the evidence was insufficient to prove the case beyond reasonable doubt and that the High Court wrongly rejected his dock statement. At the hearing, counsel also submitted that the judge should have considered lesser culpability based on sudden fight.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The items of evidence are not sufficient to prove the prosecution case against the appellant beyond reasonable doubt. | The rejection of the evidence of the accused is wrongful and the learned Judge of the High Court has failed to correctly apply the principles governing the evaluation of a dock statement.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found PW4 to be an independent and consistent witness whose evidence was not challenged. The injuries on the deceased reflected murderous intention, and the dock statement was properly rejected.
probability_assessment_by_court: The court assessed the evidence and found no reasonable doubt, rejecting the appellant's dock statement as not credible.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty and made an unsworn dock statement claiming he was attacked and swerved the knife unintentionally. The court found his statement not credible and rejected it.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed the evidence, found the eyewitness testimony credible and independent, and that the High Court judge properly evaluated the dock statement. The injuries indicated murderous intent, and no basis for lesser culpability was found. Thus, the appeal was dismissed.
coa_sentence_type: Death
brief_judgment_file_summary: The appellant was convicted of two counts of murder by the High Court of Embilipitiya and sentenced to death. On appeal, he argued insufficient evidence and wrongful rejection of his dock statement, also suggesting lesser culpability. The Court of Appeal found the eyewitness testimony credible and the injuries consistent with murder, affirming the conviction and sentence.
prosecution_counsel: Sudharshana De Silva, Deputy Solicitor General
defence_counsel: Chathura Amarathunga
hc_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found that the High Court judge carefully considered the evidence and dock statement, and correctly rejected the defence. No errors were identified.
precedents_cited_list: Fradd v. Brown & CO., LTD. 20 NLR 283
standard_of_review_applied: Deference to trial judge's findings on witness veracity and factual matters.

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 16(b) and 19(c) of the Bribery Act
brief_facts_summary: The complainant, a three-wheeler driver transporting illicit liquor, was stopped by police including the appellant who demanded a bribe to avoid legal action. The complainant lodged a complaint with the Bribery Commission, leading to a raid where the appellant was arrested while accepting money. The defence claimed the case was fabricated due to personal enmity with a police officer involved in the raid.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 16(b) and 19(c) of the Bribery Act
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court found the appellant guilty on all counts for soliciting bribes and imposed a fine of Rs.5,000 per count and a total of 16 months rigorous imprisonment suspended for 7 years.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant argued that the trial judge failed to consider favorable evidence, misdirected on the law of alibi, and failed to consider that the prosecution did not prove the case beyond reasonable doubt.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The Learned Trial Judge has not taken into consideration matters favourable to the Accused-Appellant and therefore has there been a miscarriage of justice? | The Learned Trial Judge misdirected himself in applying the law relating to the defence of alibi? | Has the Learned Trial Judge misdirected himself when he failed to consider that the prosecution has failed to prove the case beyond reasonable doubt?
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal noted the prosecution failed to call material witnesses (Rasika and the other police officer) and that the complainant's testimony was uncorroborated. The police station record supported the appellant's alibi, creating reasonable doubt.
probability_assessment_by_court: The court found the prosecution failed to prove the case beyond reasonable doubt due to lack of corroboration and material witnesses, giving the benefit of doubt to the appellant.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty and raised an alibi that he was at the police station during the alleged solicitation. He claimed the case was fabricated due to personal enmity with PC Wasantha, a police officer in the raiding team. The defence relied on documentary evidence (police station record) and cross-examination of prosecution witnesses without calling defence witnesses.
legal_errors_description: The High Court judge misdirected on the law of alibi by placing the burden of proof on the appellant and speculated without evidence.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal held that the prosecution failed to prove the charges beyond reasonable doubt. The court emphasized the prosecution's failure to call material witnesses and the lack of corroboration for the complainant's testimony. It found the High Court judge misdirected on the law of alibi, incorrectly placed the burden of proof on the appellant, and failed to adequately consider the possible malice due to personal enmity. The court applied the 'golden thread' principle that the prosecution must prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt and acquitted the appellant.
coa_sentence_type: Acquitted, no sentence
brief_judgment_file_summary: The appellant, a police officer, was convicted by the High Court of Colombo for soliciting bribes under the Bribery Act and sentenced to fines and suspended imprisonment. He appealed, arguing misdirection on alibi, failure to consider favorable evidence, and insufficient proof. The Court of Appeal found the prosecution failed to prove the case beyond reasonable doubt due to lack of corroboration and material witnesses, and misdirection on the burden of proof for alibi. The appeal was allowed, and the appellant was acquitted of all charges.
prosecution_counsel: Mr. Asitha Anthony, Assistant Director General of Bribery Commission
defence_counsel: Anil Silva, P.C. with Amman Bandara
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted the appellant based on the complainant's uncorroborated testimony and misdirected on the burden of proof for alibi. The Court of Appeal found the High Court failed to consider the absence of material witnesses and the documentary evidence supporting the alibi.
precedents_cited_list: Woolmington v. DPP [1935] A.C.462 | Sunil v. AG [1999] 3 SLR 191 | Walinunige John and Another v. The State 76 NLR 488 | Beddewithana v. The Attorney General [1990] 1 SLR 275 | Banda and Others v. Attorney General [1999] 3 SLR 168 | R v. Bellis [1966] 1 All E.R. 552 | R v. Richardson and Longman [1969] 1 QB 299
standard_of_review_applied: The court reviewed whether the prosecution proved the charges beyond reasonable doubt and whether the High Court correctly applied the law and evaluated the evidence.

judges: N. Bandula Karunarathna J. | R. Gurusinghe J.
offence_sections: Section 296 of the penal code read along with section 32 of the penal code
brief_facts_summary: Markkandu Sivarasa was murdered. The prosecution case relied on circumstantial evidence. The 1st accused-appellant was allegedly a frequent visitor to the deceased's house and a quarrel erupted between him and the deceased on the day of the incident. The 2nd accused-appellant was the deceased's wife. Key evidence included alleged recovery of weapons (knife, mamoty) and a blood-stained frock based on the accused's statements.
evidence_type_secondary: Recovery of physical productions (weapons, clothing), JMO evidence
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 296 of the penal code read along with section 32 of the penal code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted both accused-appellants of murder and sentenced them to death. The case was based on circumstantial evidence, including the alleged recovery of weapons and a frock following the accused's statements, and the testimony of the deceased's daughter.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellants challenged the conviction on grounds of material contradictions in police evidence regarding the arrest and recording of statements, lack of credibility in the evidence of recovery of productions (knife, mamoty, frock), and insufficiency of evidence connecting them to the offence.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: There are very material contradictions in the evidence of Woman Police Constable Priyadarshini and Sub-Inspector Thissa Senanayake, in regard to the place from where the 1st accused-appellant was arrested and his statement was recorded. | The evidence led by the prosecution in regard to the recovery of the productions P4 (knife) P5 (mamoty) and P6 (frock) lacks credibility in view of grave contradictions between police witnesses. | The evidence regarding the recovery is self-contradictory and falls short of proof required under the evidence ordinance. | Except the unreliable evidence regarding recovery of productions, there is hardly any substantial evidence incriminating the accused-appellants.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The court found major contradictions between key police witnesses regarding the arrest location, statement recording, and recovery of productions. The testimony of the child witness (PW2) was treated as adverse and found lacking credibility. The JMO evidence indicated the recovered weapons could have caused the injuries.
probability_assessment_by_court: Court found contradictions and improbabilities created reasonable doubt, and prosecution failed to prove case beyond reasonable doubt.
defence_version_summary: Both accused-appellants pleaded not guilty and gave evidence from the witness box. The 1st accused denied any relationship with the 2nd accused and claimed he was at home. The 2nd accused gave an alibi. They claimed police statements were recorded under duress. The court found the defence raised reasonable doubt.
legal_errors_description: Misapplication of Section 27(1) of Evidence Ordinance regarding the admissibility of statements and recovery of productions; failure to properly evaluate contradictions in prosecution evidence.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found grave contradictions in the evidence of the two key police witnesses regarding the arrest, place of recording statements, and recovery of productions. The prosecution failed to properly establish the recovery of productions P4, P5, P6 in consequence of the accused's statements as required by Section 27(1). The child witness's evidence was unreliable and treated as adverse. The totality of evidence was disconnected and left many questions unanswered, failing to meet the standard of proof beyond reasonable doubt for a murder case based on circumstantial evidence. The appeal was allowed.
coa_sentence_type: Acquitted, conviction quashed
brief_judgment_file_summary: The 1st and 2nd accused-appellants were convicted of murder by the Jaffna High Court and sentenced to death. They appealed to the Court of Appeal. The prosecution case relied on circumstantial evidence, including alleged recovery of a knife, mamoty, and frock based on the accused's statements, and the testimony of the deceased's young daughter. The Court of Appeal found material contradictions in police evidence regarding arrest, statement recording, and recovery of productions, and held the prosecution failed to prove the case beyond reasonable doubt. The 2nd accused-appellant died during the appeal. The appeal was allowed, the conviction of the 1st accused-appellant was quashed, and he was acquitted.
defence_counsel: N. Sri Kantha AAL with S. Panchadsaram AAL
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted based on circumstantial evidence, including the recovery of productions and the child witness's testimony. The Court of Appeal found the HC failed to properly assess the contradictions in police evidence and the unreliability of the recovery evidence, leading to a miscarriage of justice.
precedents_cited_list: King v. Thegis N.L.R. 107 | R. v. Pitt (1983) Q.B. 25 | R v Thompson (1977) 64 Cr. App.R. 96
standard_of_review_applied: Evaluation of whether prosecution proved case beyond reasonable doubt, assessment of contradictions and credibility of evidence.

judges: N. Bandula Karunarathna J. | R. Gurusinghe J.
offence_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The deceased, a 21-year-old disabled person, was last seen on 26.06.2001 going to an almsgiving. His body with 14 stab injuries was found two days later. The prosecution case relied on an extra-judicial confession made by the accused to PW4 and circumstantial evidence, including last seen with the accused. The accused denied involvement.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the accused of murder under section 296 of the Penal Code and sentenced him to death. The conviction was based on circumstantial evidence including extra-judicial confession and the last seen theory.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appeal grounds include failure to provide reasons as per section 283 of CCP, error in admitting extra-judicial confession, insufficient appreciation of circumstantial evidence, not considering the principle that suspicious circumstances do not establish guilt, and non-compliance with section 48 of the Judicature Act.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The learned trial Judge has failed to provide reasons as per section 283 of the Code of Criminal Procedure Act. | The learned trial Judge has erred in law by admitting the extra-judicial confession made by the accused. | The learned trial Judge failed to appreciate the relevant considerations that ought to be taken into account in analysing circumstantial evidence. | The learned trial Judge failed to consider the well-established principle 'suspicious circumstances do not establish guilt'. | Non-compliance with section 48 of the Judicature Act No 02 of 1978.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found that the prosecution evidence, including the belated extra-judicial confession and circumstantial evidence, was insufficient to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt. PW4's confession was uncorroborated, and PW2's evidence had contradictions and improbabilities.
probability_assessment_by_court: The COA applied principles for circumstantial evidence and found that the evidence did not exclude every reasonable hypothesis of innocence, creating reasonable doubt.
defence_version_summary: The accused pleaded not guilty and made a statement from the dock denying involvement. The defence challenged the credibility of prosecution witnesses, but did not call any witnesses.
legal_errors_description: The High Court failed to provide reasons as per section 283, erred in admitting extra-judicial confession, failed to properly analyse circumstantial evidence, and did not consider the principle that suspicious circumstances do not establish guilt.
procedural_defects_description: Non-compliance with section 48 of the Judicature Act as the successor judge did not formally adopt proceedings, violating the accused's right to a fair trial.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed the circumstantial evidence and found it insufficient to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt. The extra-judicial confession was belated and uncorroborated, and the last seen theory was weakened by failure to fix exact time of death. COA applied legal precedents on circumstantial evidence and concluded that the prosecution did not establish a complete chain of evidence. Procedural defects in not adopting proceedings under section 48 also violated fair trial rights.
coa_sentence_type: Acquitted
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused was convicted of murder by the High Court of Gampaha and sentenced to death. He appealed on grounds including insufficient circumstantial evidence, erroneous admission of extra-judicial confession, and procedural errors. The Court of Appeal found that the prosecution failed to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt, as the evidence was belated, uncorroborated, and did not exclude other possibilities. The appeal was allowed, conviction set aside, and accused acquitted.
defence_counsel: Prasantha Lal de Alwis PC with Mohan Sellaperuma AAL
cause_of_death_exact_text: death was caused due to the injuries inflicted on the neck and chest regions and excessive loss of blood.
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted based on extra-judicial confession and circumstantial evidence, but the Court of Appeal found that HC failed to properly analyze the evidence, did not provide sufficient reasons, and made legal errors in admitting confession.

judges: N. Bandula Karunarathna J. | R. Gurusinghe J.
offence_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code (murder) and Section 297 of the Penal Code (culpable homicide not amounting to murder)
brief_facts_summary: The accused, a domestic aid, unexpectedly delivered a baby alone and abandoned it near a shrub jungle. The infant was found alive but later died from injuries and sepsis. DNA evidence confirmed the accused as the biological mother, and witnesses testified to discovering the baby.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 297 of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the accused of culpable homicide not amounting to murder after plea bargaining and sentenced her to 7 years rigorous imprisonment, considering the gravity of the offence and other factors.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant appealed on the ground that the trial judge failed to appreciate mitigatory circumstances warranting a non-custodial sentence, arguing that the sentence was excessive.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The learned Trial Judge has failed to duly appreciate the mitigatory circumstances present in the case which ought to have warranted a non-custodial sentence on the appellant
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal considered the evidence, including an affidavit revealing mitigatory circumstances, and found that the accused had no evil intention and acted out of shock and fear.
probability_assessment_by_court: The court assessed that the accused had no intention to kill and acted due to sudden circumstances, reducing culpability.
defence_version_summary: The accused pleaded guilty to culpable homicide not amounting to murder. She presented an affidavit explaining she was raped and concealed the pregnancy out of shame, with no alibi or defence witnesses called.
legal_errors_description: The High Court failed to duly appreciate the mitigatory circumstances and the affidavit evidence presented by the appellant.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal considered the mitigatory circumstances, including the affidavit revealing rape, the sudden and unassisted delivery, lack of previous convictions, and the impact on her family. They found the High Court did not adequately weigh these factors and reduced the sentence to 2 years rigorous imprisonment suspended for 10 years.
coa_sentence_type: 2 years rigorous imprisonment suspended for 10 years
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused was convicted of culpable homicide not amounting to murder for abandoning her newborn who later died. The High Court sentenced her to 7 years rigorous imprisonment. She appealed on the ground of excessive sentence, presenting mitigatory circumstances.
