The Court of Appeal allowed the appeal, reduced the sentence to 2 years rigorous imprisonment suspended for 10 years, considering her lack of previous convictions and family circumstances.
defence_counsel: Kasun Liyanage AAL
cause_of_death_exact_text: shock, haemorrhage and sepsis following extensive injuries to the right knee and face associated with an unattended delivery, exposure and lack of protection
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court based its sentence on the gravity of the offence and other factors, but the Court of Appeal found it failed to consider mitigatory circumstances adequately.
standard_of_review_applied: Power under section 336 of the Code of Criminal Procedure Act to vary sentence if a different sentence should have been passed.
sentencing_principles_applied: The court considered factors such as gravity of offence, culpability, statutory punishment, and mitigatory circumstances including lack of previous convictions and family impact.

judges: Prasantha De Silva, J. | K.K.A.V. Swarnadhipathi, J.
offence_category: Criminal breach of trust / Misappropriation (Cooperative Society)
location_of_offence: Store of Panadura Multipurpose Cooperative Society
brief_facts_summary: The Appellant was employed as a storekeeper at the Panadura Multipurpose Cooperative Society. A shortage of items was discovered in the store during his tenure. The Society referred the matter to arbitration under the Cooperative Societies Act. The Appellant disputed the shortage and did not participate in the arbitration, which proceeded ex-parte. The arbitration award was made against him, and the Commissioner sought to enforce it in the Magistrate’s Court. The Appellant later sought the Minister’s intervention, which directed a fresh inquiry, but the courts did not follow this direction.
evidence_type_secondary: Registered post notices, Certificate of enforcement
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court affirmed the Magistrate’s Order which enforced the arbitration award, requiring the Appellant to pay Rs. 1,031,298.72 to the Cooperative Society. The High Court held that the ministerial direction to withdraw the case and re-inquire was not legally tenable under the Cooperative Societies Act.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The Appellant challenged the validity of the enforcement certificate filed in the Magistrate’s Court, arguing that the 1st Respondent was not entitled to claim interest and cost under Section 59(1)(c). He also contended that the Provincial High Court failed to consider the Minister’s letter directing withdrawal of the certificate and a fresh inquiry, thereby erring in law.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Certificate filed under Section 59(1)(c) is illegal and cannot include interest and cost. | The High Court erred by not considering the Minister’s direction to withdraw the case and hold a fresh inquiry. | The High Court incorrectly decided the Minister’s directive as defective.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The case relied on documentary evidence: audit reports, arbitration award, and certificates. The Court found the Appellant negligently failed to participate in arbitration or appeal the award. The certificate’s validity was upheld under Section 59(6), limiting grounds for challenge.
probability_assessment_by_court: Court found the Appellant failed to show cause against enforcement and negligently omitted statutory appeal rights.
defence_version_summary: The Appellant pleaded not liable, disputed the shortage, and claimed the amount was paid in another matter (but not proved). He did not participate in arbitration or appeal under Section 58(3). The Court found his defence unsubstantiated.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed the Cooperative Societies Act, particularly Sections 58 and 59. It held that the arbitration award became final as the Appellant did not appeal under Section 58(3). The Court clarified that Section 59(1)(c) allows recovery of the 'amount due' as a fine, which includes cost and interest. It distinguished cited cases (Bandahamy, Mohamed Ameer, Dayawathi) as inapplicable due to specific statutory wording in the Cooperative Societies Act. The ministerial direction was held to have no legal basis for interfering with the award or enforcement. The Appellant failed to show cause under the limited grounds permitted for challenging the certificate.
coa_sentence_type: Order to pay Rs. 1,031,298.72 to the 1st Respondent Society, with costs of Rs. 50,000.
brief_judgment_file_summary: This appeal arose from an arbitration award against the Appellant, a storekeeper, for shortages in a cooperative society store. The Magistrate and High Court ordered payment of Rs. 1,031,298.72. The Appellant challenged the certificate’s validity and the non-consideration of a ministerial directive for fresh inquiry. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal, holding the award was final due to no statutory appeal, the certificate was valid under Section 59, and the Minister had no power to intervene. Costs of Rs. 50,000 were awarded.
defence_counsel: Chandrasiri Wanigapura A.A.L
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court correctly affirmed the Magistrate’s Order, finding no legal basis to invalidate the arbitration award or the enforcement certificate. It properly held that the Minister’s directive was not supported by the Cooperative Societies Act.
precedents_cited_list: Sri Lanka Consumer Corporative Society’s Federation Ltd. Vs. Deputy Commissioner of Corporative Development [Southern Province] CA (PHC) 137/2013 [CA Minutes 14.10.2021] | Ambawa Thrift Credit Co-operative Society Vs. D. M. Sumana Dissanayake and Co-operative Development Commissioner [CA (PHC) 168/2011-C.A Minutes 16.01.2015] | Bandahamy Vs. Senanayake [1960] 62 NLR 313 | Mohamed Ameer and Another Vs. Yapa, Assistant Commissioner of Labour [1998] 1 SLR 156 | K.A. Dayawathi Vs. D.S. Edirisinghe [S.C. (FR) No. 241/2008] | S.H.L. Mohideen Vs. Assistant Commissioner of Cooperative Development Kalmunai [80 NLR 206]
standard_of_review_applied: Revisionary jurisdiction examining legality and procedural correctness of lower court orders.
sentencing_principles_applied: Enforcement of statutory arbitration award as per Cooperative Societies Act, finality of award if no appeal, and limited grounds for challenging enforcement certificate.

judges: N. Bandula Karunarathna J. | R. Gurusinghe J.
offence_sections: Section 296 read with section 32 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The deceased was murdered on 14.02.1999. His wife (PW1) and PW11 heard a dying declaration implicating 'Ukku Ranjith'. The accused-appellant was arrested two months later with a knife. Medical evidence confirmed fatal injuries, and the accused denied involvement.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 296 read with section 32 of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the accused-appellant based on the dying declaration and medical evidence, sentenced him to death, and acquitted the second accused.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant challenged the credibility of the dying declaration, argued that the prosecution failed to prove identity beyond reasonable doubt, and contended that the High Court wrongly rejected the dock statement and drew an adverse inference.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Evidence of PW1 and PW11 failed the test of credibility regarding the dying declaration. | Prosecution failed to prove beyond reasonable doubt that the accused-appellant was the person who committed the murder. | The learned High Court Judge had wrongly rejected the dock statement made by the accused-appellant and had wrongly drawn an adverse inference of guilt.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the dying declaration credible, spontaneous, and consistent. Medical evidence confirmed the deceased could speak, and witnesses had no animosity.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court applied tests for dying declaration and found the prosecution proved its case beyond reasonable doubt.
defence_version_summary: The accused pleaded not guilty and made a dock statement denying involvement. No witnesses were called, and the defence did not cross-examine key medical evidence on the deceased's ability to speak.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal thoroughly evaluated the dying declaration's credibility, applying tests of spontaneity, consistency, and disinterestedness. It considered medical evidence that confirmed the deceased could speak and was conscious. The Court found no infirmities in the dying declaration and upheld the High Court's conclusion that the accused was identified as 'Ukku Ranjith'. It also addressed the dock statement, finding it a bare denial that did not raise reasonable doubt.
coa_sentence_type: Death
brief_judgment_file_summary: This appeal concerns the murder conviction of Vithanage Don Ranjith alias Ukku Ranjith. The High Court convicted him based on a dying declaration and sentenced him to death. On appeal, he challenged the dying declaration's credibility, identity proof, and handling of his dock statement. The Court of Appeal found the dying declaration reliable, upheld the conviction, and dismissed the appeal.
defence_counsel: Neranjan Jayasinghe
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court relied on the dying declaration and medical evidence to convict the accused. The Court of Appeal found this analysis correct and without error.
precedents_cited_list: Queen Vs. Mendis 54 NLR 177 | Ranasinghe Vs Attorney General 2007 (1) SLR 218 | Nissanka Vs. State 2001 (3) SLR 78
standard_of_review_applied: The Court applied a thorough review of evidence, testing the dying declaration for credibility, consistency, and spontaneity, and assessed whether the prosecution proved its case beyond reasonable doubt.

judges: K. Priyantha Fernando, J (P/CA) | Wickum A. Kaluarachchi, J
brief_facts_summary: The appellants were charged with trafficking and possessing heroin based on a police raid conducted by PW1. The defence claimed that the 2nd appellant was arrested at home, supported by her daughter's testimony. Key evidence included the testimony of PW1 and the defence witnesses.
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the appellants for drug trafficking and possession, relying on the testimony of PW1. The judge denied the defence's application to call a witness and applied Section 114(f) of the Evidence Ordinance to the defence case.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellants argued that they were denied a fair trial by not allowing a defence witness. They also challenged the credibility of PW1's evidence as contradictory and insufficient for the charges against the 2nd appellant.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Denial of fair trial by not allowing defence witness | PW1's evidence is vague and contradictory | Insufficient evidence for charges against 2nd appellant | Misdirection on law regarding Section 114(f) of Evidence Ordinance
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found that PW1's evidence was not cogent due to contradictions and that the defence evidence was not properly evaluated. The prosecution relied solely on uncorroborated testimony.
probability_assessment_by_court: The court found the prosecution story improbable and that contradictions created reasonable doubt.
defence_version_summary: The appellants pleaded not guilty. The 2nd appellant claimed she was arrested at home, providing an alibi, and her daughter corroborated this. The defence called a witness but was denied another. The court found the defence version created reasonable doubt.
legal_errors_description: The High Court Judge erred by not allowing a defence witness, pre-determining evidence, and misapplying Section 114(f) of the Evidence Ordinance to the defence case.
procedural_defects_description: The High Court refused the application to call a defence witness, denying the appellants a fair trial.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal held that the High Court denied a fair trial by refusing to allow a defence witness. It identified contradictions in PW1's testimony that affected credibility and found the prosecution story improbable. The COA emphasized that the burden of proof is on the prosecution and that the defence need only create reasonable doubt. Citing precedents, it concluded that the convictions were not proven beyond reasonable doubt.
coa_sentence_type: Acquitted, sentences set aside
brief_judgment_file_summary: The appellants were convicted by the High Court for trafficking and possessing heroin. They appealed on grounds of denial of fair trial and insufficient evidence. The Court of Appeal found that the High Court erred in not allowing a defence witness and that PW1's evidence was contradictory. It held that the prosecution failed to prove the case beyond reasonable doubt, acquitted the appellants, and set aside the convictions.
defence_counsel: Shavindra Fernando, PC with Umayangi Indatissa, Tharani Mayadunne and Anika Arawwawala for the 1st Accused-Appellant; Anuja Premaratna, PC with Tarangee Mutucumarana, Senal Matugama for the 2nd Accused-Appellant
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court relied on the testimony of PW1 to convict the appellants. The Court of Appeal found that the HC failed to consider contradictions, denied fair trial, and misapplied legal principles regarding burden of proof.
precedents_cited_list: Dudh Nath Pandey vs The State Of U.P | Attorney General V. Devunderage Nihal – S.C. Appeal: 154/10 | James Silva V. The Republic of Sri Lanka – (1980) 2 Sri L.R. 167
standard_of_review_applied: The court reviewed for legal errors and sufficiency of evidence to determine if the prosecution proved its case beyond reasonable doubt.

judges: N. Bandula Karunarathna, J. | R. Gurusinghe, J.
offence_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The accused assaulted his child by dashing him on the wall, causing fatal head injuries. The mother witnessed the incident and later revealed it to doctors after the child's condition worsened. Medical evidence confirmed craniocerebral injuries from blunt force trauma and a prior greenstick fracture. The accused claimed the child fell during a fight with a paramour.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court found the appellant guilty of murder based on the credible testimony of PW1 and corroborating medical evidence. The judge considered contradictions in PW1's evidence and found them not material. The appellant was sentenced to death.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant argued that the trial judge failed to consider contradictions and omissions in PW1's evidence, erred in law by concluding PW1 was credible, failed to consider favourable defence evidence, and erred in concluding medical evidence corroborated PW1.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The learned trial judge failed to consider the vital contradictions and omissions of PW1. | The learned trial judge erred in law when concluding that PW1 is a credible witness in light of the contradictions and omissions. | The learned trial judge failed to consider favourable evidence to the defence. | The learned trial judge erred in both facts and law by concluding that the medical evidence has been corroborated by the evidence of PW1.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal evaluated contradictions in PW1's evidence and found them not material to the case. Medical evidence from the JMO strongly corroborated PW1's testimony. The trial judge's credibility assessment was given weight and upheld.
probability_assessment_by_court: The COA found no reasonable doubt, as contradictions were not material and medical evidence corroborated the prosecution case.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty. He testified for himself and called PW6 as a defence witness. His version was that the child fell during a fight with a paramour. The court found his evidence not credible and inconsistent with medical evidence.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed the contradictions in PW1's evidence and found them not material, citing precedents on witness credibility. Medical evidence from the JMO strongly corroborated PW1's testimony and ruled out the appellant's version. The trial judge's assessment of witnesses was given due weight. No legal errors were found, and the conviction and sentence were affirmed.
coa_sentence_type: Death
brief_judgment_file_summary: The appellant was convicted of murder for assaulting his child, leading to death. The High Court sentenced him to death based on eyewitness testimony and medical evidence. On appeal, he challenged contradictions in evidence and medical corroboration. The Court of Appeal found no material contradictions and affirmed the conviction and sentence.
defence_counsel: Nihara Randeniya
cause_of_death_exact_text: craniocerebral injuries due to blunt force trauma
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted based on credible eyewitness testimony and corroborating medical evidence. The Court of Appeal reviewed and found no material errors, upholding the decision.
precedents_cited_list: Barwada Bhoqinbhai Hirjibhai V. State of Gujarat AIR 1983 SC 753 | Wickramasinghe vs Dedoleena and others 1996 2 Sri LR 95 | Attorney-General v. Visuvulingam | State of Uttar Pradesh v. Anthony | Jagathsena v. Bandaranaike | Samaraweera v. The Republic | Moonesinghe vs Vidanage 69 NLR 97 | Alwis vs Piyasena Fernando 1993 1 Sri LR119
standard_of_review_applied: Appellate court gives great weight to trial judge's credibility assessments and findings of fact.

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 296 read with Section 146 and Section 315 read with Section 146 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The appellant was part of an unlawful assembly that caused hurt to PW1 and caused the death of Karawita Mudiyanselage Priyantha Nirodha Karawita on 30 March 1995. The appellant attacked PW1 with a knife, and during a scuffle, the deceased was fatally stabbed by the appellant. The deceased made a dying declaration in the hospital implicating the appellant before succumbing to his injuries.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 296 and Section 315 of the Penal Code
hc_sentence_type: Death sentence under section 296 and 1-month rigorous imprisonment under section 315
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court Judge found the appellant guilty of murder under section 296 and causing hurt under section 315. He was sentenced to death for murder and one month rigorous imprisonment for causing hurt. The other accused were acquitted.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant's counsel challenged only the sentence, arguing that the conviction under Section 296 for murder should have been considered under Section 297 for culpable homicide not amounting to murder on the basis of a sudden fight. The counsel also submitted that the medical evidence was inconclusive and contradictory.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The case should have been considered under Section 297 (culpable homicide not amounting to murder) based on a sudden fight under Exception 4 to Section 294 of the Penal Code. | The medical evidence is inconclusive and contradictory regarding the cause of death.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The court relied on the eyewitness account of PW1 and the dying declaration of the deceased. The medical evidence from the post mortem report indicated death by toxaemia, but was considered inconclusive. The court also noted evidence of a previous incident creating enmity.
probability_assessment_by_court: The court considered the evidence of a sudden fight and the fact that the appellant sustained injuries, leading to the conclusion that the case fell under Exception 4 to Section 294 for culpable homicide not murder.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty. The defence argued for the application of Exception 4 (sudden fight) to reduce the charge from murder to culpable homicide. No defence witnesses were mentioned; the argument was made by counsel. The court accepted the defence of sudden fight.
legal_errors_description: The High Court Judge failed to consider the defence of sudden fight and the alternative of culpable homicide not amounting to murder, even though there was evidence supporting it.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found that the evidence indicated a sudden fight, and the High Court Judge should have considered the alternative of culpable homicide not amounting to murder under Exception 4 to Section 294. Citing precedents, the court held that the judge has a duty to put such an alternative to the jury even if not raised by the defence. The medical evidence was found inconclusive. The court set aside the murder conviction and death sentence, convicting the appellant of culpable homicide under Section 297 and sentencing him to 10 years rigorous imprisonment.
coa_sentence_type: 10 years rigorous imprisonment
brief_judgment_file_summary: The appellant was convicted of murder and causing hurt by the High Court and sentenced to death. He appealed, arguing the case involved a sudden fight and should be culpable homicide. The Court of Appeal agreed, finding the High Court erred in not considering the sudden fight defence. It modified the conviction to culpable homicide not amounting to murder under Section 297 and imposed a 10-year rigorous imprisonment sentence. The appeal was partly allowed.
defence_counsel: Palitha Fernando, P.C.
cause_of_death_exact_text: toxaemia
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted the appellant of murder and sentenced him to death. The Court of Appeal found the High Court Judge failed to consider the evidence of a sudden fight and the applicability of Exception 4 to Section 294, which could have reduced the charge to culpable homicide.
precedents_cited_list: Mendis v. The Queen 54 NLR 177 | The King v Bellana Vitanage Eddin 41 NLR 345 | Luvis v. The Queen 56 NLR 442
standard_of_review_applied: The court reviewed the evidence to determine if the High Court should have considered the defence of sudden fight and the alternative charge of culpable homicide.
sentencing_principles_applied: The court applied Exception 4 to Section 294 (sudden fight) to reduce the offence from murder to culpable homicide, considering the circumstances of the fight and the injuries sustained by the appellant.
final_charge_after_appeal: Culpable homicide not amounting to murder under Section 297 of the Penal Code

judges: K. Priyantha Fernando, J. (P/CA) | Wickum A. Kaluarachchi, J.
offence_sections: Section 44(a) of the Fire Arms Ordinance to be read with Section 300 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The appellant, the brother-in-law of the victim Gayani Fernando, was involved in a domestic dispute while moving household items. The appellant became angry after his wife was told to feed their crying baby first. He assaulted his wife and then threw a club which hit the victim. The victim heard the sound of a gun being cocked and fired, felt her arm turn cold and bleed, and saw the appellant holding a gun before she fell unconscious. The appellant admitted to a fight and throwing a club but denied using a gun. Medical evidence confirmed a gunshot injury.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 44(a) of the Fire Arms Ordinance to be read with Section 300 of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the appellant of attempted murder and sentenced him to life imprisonment. The trial judge accepted the prosecution's version that the victim's injury was caused by a gunshot fired by the appellant.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant challenged his conviction on two main grounds: first, the High Court Judge failed to consider contradictions in the evidence of prosecution witnesses, particularly regarding hearing the gunshot; second, the judge failed to consider the defence version that the injury could have been caused by a thrown club.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The learned High Court Judge has failed to consider the contradictions in the evidence of the prosecution witnesses. | The learned High Court Judge has failed to consider the version of the defence.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the victim's evidence to be credible and consistent. Minor contradictions, such as PW2 not hearing the gunshot, did not undermine the prosecution's core case. Medical evidence confirmed a gunshot injury.
probability_assessment_by_court: The court assessed the evidence as a whole and found no reasonable doubt. Minor discrepancies did not affect the core prosecution story.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty and gave evidence. His version was that he threw a club which hit the victim, denying the use of a gun. The court found the defence version not credible and inconsistent with the medical evidence of a gunshot wound.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal reviewed the evidence and found the trial judge's assessment of witness credibility and demeanour was correct. It applied the principle that an appellate court should not lightly overturn findings based on witness demeanour unless manifestly wrong. The medical evidence supported the gunshot injury. The defence version was rejected as inconsistent with evidence. Minor contradictions did not create reasonable doubt.
coa_sentence_type: Imprisonment for life (affirmed)
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused-appellant was convicted of attempted murder in the Kurunegala High Court and sentenced to life imprisonment. He appealed on grounds of contradictions in prosecution evidence and failure to consider the defence version. The Court of Appeal found the victim's evidence credible and supported by medical evidence of a gunshot wound. It upheld the trial judge's findings on witness credibility and dismissed the appeal, affirming the conviction and sentence.
prosecution_counsel: Anoopa de Silva, Senior State Counsel
defence_counsel: Jagath Nanayakkara
hc_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found no error in the High Court judge's reasoning. The judge had given sufficient reasons for rejecting the defence version and accepting the prosecution's case based on credible evidence.
precedents_cited_list: Montgomery & Company V. Wallace-James (1904 appeal Cases 73) | Fradd V. Brown & Company, 20 NLR 282 | State of U.P. V. M.K. Anthony [1985] CR1.L.J. 493
standard_of_review_applied: Appellate court will be slow to overrule trial judge's findings on witness demeanour and credibility unless manifestly wrong.

judges: Menaka Wijesundera J | Neil Iddawala J
offence_sections: Section 25(1)(a) of the Debt Recovery (Special Provisions) Act No.2 of 1990 (as amended) for dishonoured cheques
brief_facts_summary: The petitioner Alliance Finance Company PLC filed a private plaint in the Magistrate Court of Chilaw against the 1st respondent for dishonoured cheques. The Magistrate refused to issue summons. The petitioner filed a revision application to the High Court, which was dismissed without issuing notice. The petitioner then filed this revision application in the Court of Appeal.
evidence_type_primary: Documentary evidence (dishonoured cheques and financial agreement)
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court dismissed the revision application without issuing notice, holding that the private plaint was not properly constituted. The High Court focused on the technicalities of the plaint, such as the signature and authority of the signatory.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The petitioner argued that the private plaint satisfied the requirements of Section 136(1)(a) and Section 139 of the CPC. They contended that the Magistrate and High Court erred in law by not applying the correct legal principles from Malani Gunaratne Case and Alliance Finance PLC vs Yeshan Harendra Samarasekara.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The plaint was properly constituted and satisfied Section 136(1)(a) of the CPC. | The Magistrate should have issued summons as there was sufficient ground to proceed. | The High Court erred in dismissing the revision application without issuing notice.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed the plaint and affidavit to determine if there was sufficient ground to issue summons. They found the plaint disclosed the offence and evidence, and the lower courts erred by focusing on technicalities.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court applied the test from Malani Gunaratne to see if there was prima facie sufficient ground that the offence was committed.
defence_version_summary: The 1st respondent did not appear in the Court of Appeal and refused to accept notice. No defence version was presented as the case is at a preliminary stage.
legal_errors_description: The Magistrate and High Court erred by not applying the legal principles from Malani Gunaratne Case and Alliance Finance PLC vs Yeshan Harendra Samarasekara. They focused on technicalities of the plaint instead of the offence and its ingredients.
procedural_defects_description: The High Court dismissed the revision application without issuing notice to the respondent.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal held that the Magistrate and High Court focused on the technical composition of the plaint (signature and authority) rather than considering whether the plaint disclosed the offence and its ingredients with sufficient evidence. They applied the test from Malani Gunaratne and found the plaint did disclose the offence and evidence, and there was sufficient ground to issue summons.
brief_judgment_file_summary: This is a revision application by Alliance Finance Company PLC against the order of the High Court of Chilaw which dismissed their revision without notice. The Magistrate had refused to issue summons on a private plaint for dishonoured cheques. The Court of Appeal held that the lower courts erred by focusing on technicalities of the plaint rather than the offence and its ingredients. The Court set aside the orders and directed the Magistrate to issue summons.
prosecution_counsel: Harith Adikary with Narada Amarasinghe and Dhanushika Dissanayake instructed by Achala Wanniarachchi for the Petitioner
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court focused on the technical composition of the plaint, such as the signature and authority, and dismissed the revision without notice. The COA found that the HC failed to apply the correct legal test and should have considered the offence and its ingredients.
precedents_cited_list: Malani Gunaratne, Additional District Judge Galle Vs Abeysinghe and Another (1994) 3 SLR 196 | Alliance Finance PLC vs Yeshan Harendra Samarasekara CA/PHC/APN/67/2015
standard_of_review_applied: Revisionary jurisdiction under Article 138 of the Constitution

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 354 of the Penal Code and Section 364(2) read with Section 364(2)(e) of the Penal Code as amended by Penal Code (Amendment) Act No. 22 of 1995
brief_facts_summary: On 16 August 2004, the appellant, a neighbour, lured a 10-year-old girl to his house under the pretext of offering food, where he sexually assaulted her. The victim's mother and neighbours broke into the house, found the child in shock, and took her to the police. Key evidence includes the victim's testimony, medical evidence of genital contusions and a sexually transmitted infection, and witness accounts from the mother and a neighbour.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 354 of the Penal Code and Section 364(2) read with Section 364(2)(e) of the Penal Code as amended by Penal Code (Amendment) Act No. 22 of 1995
hc_sentence_type: Two years rigorous imprisonment for count one, ten years rigorous imprisonment for count three, fines, compensation, and payment to victim fund
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the appellant on counts of abduction and rape, finding the victim's testimony credible and supported by medical evidence. He was sentenced to rigorous imprisonment, fines, and compensation, while acquitted on the second abduction count due to the absence of the other child witness.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant argued that the prosecution did not prove the case beyond reasonable doubt, highlighting omissions in the victim's evidence that undermined her credibility. He also contended that her testimony was not credible and lacked corroboration.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Whether the prosecution has discharged its duty of proving the case beyond reasonable doubt against the appellant. | Whether the omissions in the evidence of the victim go into the root of the case and hence, whether the conviction can be sustained. | Testimonial creditworthiness of PW-03 who was the victim. | The lack of corroboration to support the version of events as narrated by the victim.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the victim's testimony credible and trustworthy, noting that omissions were trivial and expected given her age and the time elapsed. Medical evidence showing contusions and infection corroborated her account, and witness testimonies from the mother and neighbour supported the sequence of events.
probability_assessment_by_court: The court held that the victim's evidence was cogent and trustworthy, and with corroboration, there was no reasonable doubt.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty and made a dock statement denying the allegations, claiming he was framed due to a land dispute. He called no witnesses, and the court found his version unconvincing and inconsistent.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal thoroughly evaluated the evidence, concluding that the victim's testimony was credible and consistent with medical findings. They applied legal precedents regarding child witnesses and rape cases, noting that minor omissions do not undermine credibility. The court found ample corroboration from other witnesses and medical evidence, thus upholding the High Court's decision and dismissing the appeal.
coa_sentence_type: Two years rigorous imprisonment for count one and ten years rigorous imprisonment for count three, to run consecutively; fines of Rs. 5,000 and Rs. 10,000; compensation of Rs. 500,000; payment of Rs. 3,000 to victim fund; with default sentences.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The appellant was convicted by the Tangalle High Court for abducting and raping a 10-year-old girl, receiving imprisonment, fines, and compensation. He appealed, challenging the evidence credibility and lack of corroboration. The Court of Appeal found the victim's testimony credible and supported by medical and witness evidence, citing relevant precedents. The appeal was dismissed, affirming the conviction and sentence.
defence_counsel: Rushdhie Habeeb, Supun Dissanayake, Hiruni Wijesinghe and Rizwan Uwais for the Accused Appellant
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court relied on the victim's testimony and medical evidence to convict the appellant, which the Court of Appeal found to be sound and correctly applied.
precedents_cited_list: Perera Vs. The Attorney General (2012) 1 SLR 69 | Bhoginbhai Hitijibhai Vs. State of Gujarat (AIR 1983-SC 753) | D. Tikiri Banda Vs. The Attorney General Bar Association Law Reports 2010 (BLR) 92
standard_of_review_applied: The court reviewed whether the prosecution proved the case beyond reasonable doubt and whether the High Court's findings were supported by evidence.

judges: N. Bandula Karunarathna J. | R. Gurusinghe J.
offence_sections: section 296 read with section 32 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The deceased was murdered on 24.06.2006. The 1st and 2nd accused-appellants were charged. An eyewitness, the deceased's sister, saw the 1st accused beat the deceased with a crowbar while the 2nd accused stood by with a rod. The prosecution relied on this witness's deposition and the wife's evidence. The incident occurred in an area under LTTE control. The accused-appellants were convicted and sentenced to death by the High Court.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: section 296 read with section 32 of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the 1st and 2nd accused-appellants of murder and sentenced them to death, relying on the deposition of the eyewitness (PW 3) and the evidence of the deceased's wife (PW 2). The court found they acted with common intention.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellants argued procedural errors in adopting proceedings and admitting the deposition of the key eyewitness, failure to properly evaluate evidence and apply principles of common intention, and failure to narrate/evaluate the defence evidence, causing prejudice and a deprivation of a fair trial.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Non-compliance of section 48 of the Judicature Act relating to adoption of proceedings. | Deposition of PW 3 (eyewitness) had been improperly admitted. | Trial Judge flawed by relying upon the said deposition to form the basis of the conviction. | Basis of the conviction (deposition of PW 3 and evidence of PW 2) is untenable. | Trial Judge failed to compartmentalize evidence against each accused and failed to apply principles of common intention. | Failure to narrate or evaluate the evidence of the accused-appellants caused serious prejudice and deprivation of a fair trial. | Rejection of evidence of the accused-appellants is flawed.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the deposition of the key eyewitness (PW 3) was improperly admitted through hearsay evidence about her unavailability and procedural flaws in its production. Without this deposition, the remaining circumstantial evidence from PW 2 was deemed insufficient to sustain a conviction beyond reasonable doubt.
probability_assessment_by_court: Court found the prosecution failed to prove the case beyond reasonable doubt after excluding the improperly admitted deposition. The remaining circumstantial evidence was inadequate to draw the necessary inference of guilt.
defence_version_summary: The accused-appellants pleaded not guilty. They denied involvement. The 1st accused claimed he was at home and was later taken by LTTE. The 2nd accused claimed he was thrashing and returned the next day. They called one defence witness who claimed the deceased's brother gave her an axe and confessed. The court considered her evidence a fabrication to safeguard the accused.
legal_errors_description: The High Court erred in law by improperly admitting the deposition of PW 3 in violation of procedural requirements and by relying on it to convict. It also failed to properly apply legal principles regarding common intention and evaluation of evidence.
procedural_defects_description: Non-compliance with section 48 of the Judicature Act regarding adoption of proceedings. Improper admission of PW 3's deposition under section 33 of Evidence Ordinance based on hearsay evidence and without producing the certified copy as required by precedent.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the High Court judgment factually untenable and flawed. It held the deposition of the key eyewitness (PW 3) was inadmissible due to procedural violations in establishing her unavailability and producing the deposition. Without this evidence, the conviction rested solely on circumstantial evidence from PW 2, which was insufficient to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt. The Court also criticized the Trial Judge for failing to compartmentalize evidence against each accused, apply principles of common intention, and narrate/evaluate the defence evidence, causing prejudice and depriving a fair trial. Considering the 16-year lapse since the offence and over 10 years of incarceration, a retrial was not ordered in the interests of justice.
coa_sentence_type: Acquitted and discharged
brief_judgment_file_summary: The 1st and 2nd accused-appellants were convicted of murder by the High Court of Batticaloa and sentenced to death. They appealed. The Court of Appeal found the High Court judgment flawed. The key eyewitness deposition was improperly admitted. Without it, the remaining circumstantial evidence was insufficient for conviction. Procedural errors, failure to evaluate defence evidence, and the long delay prejudiced a fair trial. The appeal was allowed, the conviction and sentence were quashed, and the accused-appellants were acquitted and discharged.
defence_counsel: Indica Mallawaratchy AAL
weapon_type: Crow bar, rod, pipe, iron bar (mentioned but not explicitly recovered)
cause_of_death_exact_text: Haemorrhage in the skull caused by a blow from a blunt weapon.
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted based on the deposition of PW 3 and evidence of PW 2, finding common intention. The COA found this reasoning flawed due to the inadmissible deposition and insufficient remaining evidence.
precedents_cited_list: S. Stephen and 3 others Vs. The Queen 66 NLR 264 | The King vs, Kadiragamar 40 NLR 534 | Mazur Ivegen and another vs. AG, SC Appeal No. TAB 1/2007 | R., vs. R.E.M. (2008 SCC 51 2nd October 2008) | Peter Singho Vs. Werapitiya 55 NLR 157 | Warnagodage Nandana Ratnasuriya Vs. Attorney General C.A. Appeal 58/2005
standard_of_review_applied: Appellate review to examine legality and tenability of the trial court judgment, not to rewrite it.

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 296 read with Section 32, Section 380, Section 315 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: On 16th October 1990, the deceased was stabbed and died from multiple stab injuries. PW3 saw the Appellants standing beside the deceased, with the 2nd Appellant brandishing a knife. The Appellants were charged with murder, robbery, and causing hurt.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 296 read with Section 32, Section 380, Section 315 of the Penal Code
hc_sentence_type: Death, 10 years rigorous imprisonment, 2 years rigorous imprisonment
hc_judgment_summary: High Court convicted Appellants on counts 1, 2, and 3 based on evidence, but acquitted on count 4. The judgment relied on witness testimony, though there were contradictions and rejected evidence.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: Appellants argued that evidence was insufficient to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt, the trial judge misdirected himself by using rejected evidence, and the dock statements were not properly evaluated.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Are the available items of evidence not sufficient enough to prove the case against the Appellants beyond reasonable doubt. | Has the Learned Trial Court Judge misdirected himself and had used some portions of PW1’s evidence when writing the judgement which was adopted under Section 33 of Evidence Ordinance and later rejected by the trial judge. | Has the Learned Trial Judge evaluated the two dock statements given by the Appellants.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: Evidence from PW3 and PW2 had contradictions on material points. PW1's evidence was rejected by the trial judge. No direct eyewitness to the stabbing, and medical evidence showed fatal injuries.
probability_assessment_by_court: COA found benefit of doubt should be given due to insufficient evidence and contradictions.
defence_version_summary: Appellants pleaded not guilty, made dock statements, and closed their case without calling witnesses. The defence highlighted contradictions in prosecution evidence.
legal_errors_description: High Court judge misused rejected evidence from PW1 and improperly evaluated dock statements, prejudicing fair trial.
procedural_defects_description: Evidence adopted under Section 33 of Evidence Ordinance was not properly led and later rejected, but still used in judgment.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: COA found that prosecution evidence was insufficient and contradictory, with no direct witness to the stabbing. The High Court erred by relying on rejected evidence and not properly evaluating dock statements. Benefit of doubt was accorded to the Appellants.
coa_sentence_type: Acquitted
brief_judgment_file_summary: Appellants were convicted by High Court for murder, robbery, and causing hurt, and sentenced to death and imprisonment. They appealed on grounds of insufficient evidence, misdirection, and improper evaluation of dock statements. Court of Appeal found evidence contradictory and High Court errors, allowed the appeal, and acquitted the Appellants.
defence_counsel: Gayan Perera with Prabha Perera and Panchali Ekanayake
cause_of_death_exact_text: multiple penetrating stabbed injuries to the chest
hc_analysis_summary: High Court relied on contradictory witness evidence and used rejected evidence, which COA found prejudiced the Appellants' right to fair trial.
precedents_cited_list: Queen v. Buddharakkita Thero 63 NLR 433
standard_of_review_applied: Review of evidence sufficiency and legal errors in trial judgment

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 78(5)(a) read with Section 52(1) of the Poisons Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance as amended by Act No. 13 of 1984
brief_facts_summary: The petitioner was charged with possessing 16 grams of Cannabis and transporting it. He pleaded guilty before the Magistrate. The Magistrate held an inquiry for confiscation of the vehicle used, where the petitioner stated he did not claim the vehicle. The absolute owner claimed it, but the Magistrate confiscated it to the State.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 78(5)(a) read with Section 52(1) of the Poisons Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance as amended by Act No. 13 of 1984
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court dismissed the revision application, holding that the petitioner was not an aggrieved party since he disclaimed the vehicle, and that failure to include the absolute owner as a party was a fatal defect.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The petitioner argued that there was no provision to charge for transporting under Section 52(1), and that he was charged twice for the same offence. He contended that the confiscation of the vehicle was wrong.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: No provision to charge for transporting under Section 52(1) | Charged twice for the same offence
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: For the confiscation inquiry, evidence was given by the absolute owner and the petitioner. The Court evaluated that the petitioner had no locus standi to challenge the confiscation.
defence_version_summary: The petitioner pleaded guilty to the charges. For the confiscation inquiry, he stated he was not claiming the vehicle. The court assessed he had no locus standi.
procedural_defects_description: The petitioner failed to name the absolute owner as a necessary party in the revision application.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal held that the petitioner cannot be considered an aggrieved party as he explicitly informed the Magistrate he was not claiming the vehicle. They cited precedents that revision is a discretionary remedy and requires the applicant to be aggrieved. The COA agreed with the High Court that the petitioner had no locus standi and that the procedural defect of not including the absolute owner was fatal. Therefore, the appeal was dismissed.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The petitioner appealed against the confiscation of his vehicle used in a drug offence. He had pleaded guilty to possessing and transporting Cannabis. The High Court dismissed his revision application, and the Court of Appeal upheld this decision, ruling that he was not an aggrieved party and had no standing to challenge the confiscation.
defence_counsel: Mohan Weerakoon, P.C. with Nuwan de Alwis and Sandamali Peiris
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court correctly considered that the petitioner was not an aggrieved party and that failure to include the absolute owner was a fatal defect. The COA upheld this analysis.
precedents_cited_list: Wijesinghe vs. Tharmaratnam (Sri Kantha Law Reports) Vol IV page 47 | Nonohamy Vs. Dunuwilla (Sri Kantha Law Reports) Vol IV page 30 | Appuhamy Vs. Weerathunga 23 NLR 467 | Perera Vs. People’s Bank (Bar Journal (1995) Vol IV Part 1 Page 12) | Kesara Senanayake Vs. Attorney General (2010) 1 SLR 149 | Ibrahim Vs. Nadaraja (1991) 1 SLR 131
standard_of_review_applied: Discretionary remedy standard for revision, requiring the applicant to be an aggrieved party.

judges: C.P Kirtisinghe, J | Mayadunne Corea, J
offence_sections: Section 129(1) of the Air Force Act (conduct prejudicial to air force discipline)
brief_facts_summary: The Petitioner, a Warrant Officer, was involved in a fraudulent incident at the Weerawila Air Force Camp in 2014 involving raising false vouchers to conceal a deficit in clothing stocks. An inquiry/summary trial was conducted, and he was severely reprimanded. Subsequently, in December 2014, he was issued a letter (A8) discharging him from service on the grounds that his services were 'no longer required', citing his prior disciplinary record (unauthorized absences in 1994 and 1997) and the 2014 fraud.
evidence_type_primary: Summary trial proceedings and internal inquiry findings
evidence_type_secondary: Previous warning letters and conduct sheets
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The Petitioner argued that his discharge after being reprimanded violated the principle of double jeopardy. He also contended that as a Warrant Officer, he could not be discharged under the relevant Air Force Regulations, and that discharge under section 129(1) of the Air Force Act required a conviction by court-martial, which he did not face.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Discharge after reprimand violates principle of double jeopardy | Regulations do not permit discharge of a Warrant Officer | Discharge under section 129(1) requires a court-martial conviction
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The court considered the summary trial proceedings (R3), previous warning letters (R7, R8, R9), and the discharge letter (A8). The Petitioner did not challenge the factual findings of the inquiries or the punishments meted out.
probability_assessment_by_court: The court assessed that the cumulative effect of the Petitioner's conduct warranted the administrative discharge decision.
defence_version_summary: The Petitioner pleaded not guilty to the discharge being lawful. He argued he was punished (reprimanded) for the 2014 offence and could not be punished again via discharge for the same offence. He did not deny the underlying facts of the inquiries or his prior record.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed the Air Force Act and Regulations. It held that a Warrant Officer falls under the definition of an 'airman'. It found that summary trial under section 42, read with section 129(1), was permissible. It distinguished between punishment (reprimand) and administrative discharge under the 'services no longer required' clause, relying on precedent to hold that such discharge is not a punishment and thus does not violate double jeopardy. The court also found the Petitioner guilty of suppressing material facts (failure to disclose a prior final warning letter R9) and laches, which disentitled him to discretionary relief.
coa_sentence_type: Discharge from Sri Lanka Air Force upheld (administrative decision under 'services no longer required')
brief_judgment_file_summary: The Petitioner, a Warrant Officer, challenged his discharge from the Sri Lanka Air Force after being reprimanded for involvement in a fraud at Weerawila Camp. The Court of Appeal dismissed his writ application. It held that his discharge under the 'services no longer required' clause was a lawful administrative decision, not a punishment, and thus did not violate double jeopardy. The court also found that the summary trial procedure was correct and that the Petitioner had suppressed material facts and delayed filing, barring discretionary relief.
defence_counsel: Chathura Weththasinghe
precedents_cited_list: J. H. M. L. S. Jayaweera v Air Marshall Gagana Bulathsinhala and others (CA WRIT 88/2015) | Weerathilake v Commander Sri Lanka Air Force (CA WRIT 107/2016) | Wasantha Kumara v Commander Sri Lanka Air Force (CA WRIT 171/2015) | Air Marshal G. D. Perera v K. H. M. S. Bandara (SC Appeal 104/2008) | Dissanayake v D. C. J. Weerakoon, Air Commodore (CA Minutes of 11.09.2017) | Collettes Ltd Vs. Commissioner of Labour and others (1989) 2 SLR | Moosajees Limited v Eksath Engineeru Saha Samanya Kamkaru Samithiya 79 (1) NLR 1285 | Blanca Diamonds (Pvt) Ltd v Wilfred Van Else and others (1997) 1 SLR 360 | Alphonso Appuhamy v Hettiarachchi
standard_of_review_applied: Judicial review of administrative action for legality, unreasonableness, and procedural fairness.
sentencing_principles_applied: Principles distinguishing punishment from administrative action in military discipline contexts.

judges: N. Bandula Karunarathna, J. | R. Gurusinghe, J.
offence_sections: Section 296 read with section 32 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The deceased was murdered on June 13, 2006, when two accused persons attacked him with knives outside his house. The sole eyewitness was his daughter who identified the accused as neighbors. Medical evidence confirmed deep-cut injuries sufficient to cause death.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 296 read with section 32 of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the appellants of murder based on the credible eyewitness testimony and corroborating medical evidence. The judge found that the prosecution proved the case beyond reasonable doubt and imposed the death sentence.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellants argued that the sole eyewitness was not credible, the judge failed to properly evaluate common intention and section 27 statement, and came to a premature conclusion. They also raised the defense of sudden fight and grave provocation.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Whether the learned Trial Judge was correct in his estimation with regard to the credibility of the eyewitness. | Whether the learned High Court Judge failed to evaluate common intention principles. | Whether the learned High Court Judge has failed to consider the implication of section 27 statement in law. | The learned Trial Judge was flawed by coming to a positive and premature conclusion that the prosecution had proved the case beyond reasonable doubt prior to evaluating the defence. | The learned Trial Judge has failed to address his judicial mind with regard to the veracity of the version as deposed by the sole eyewitness. | Evidence led at the trial warrant the consideration of the exception of sudden fight and/or grave and sudden provocation.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the sole eyewitness testimony credible and trustworthy, corroborated by medical evidence and police confirmation of lighting. The witness had known the accused for years and could identify them.
probability_assessment_by_court: Court found no reasonable doubt as eyewitness testimony was credible and corroborated.
defence_version_summary: The appellants pleaded not guilty. The defense suggested sudden fight and provocation, but no evidence was adduced. The court found the defense unsupported.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal thoroughly evaluated the sole eyewitness testimony, applying legal principles from Section 134 of the Evidence Ordinance and precedents like Fradd v Brown. They found the witness credible, identification reliable due to lighting and prior acquaintance, and medical evidence consistent. The court upheld the common intention finding and dismissed the sudden fight defense due to lack of evidence.
coa_sentence_type: Death
brief_judgment_file_summary: The appellants were convicted of murder by the High Court of Kandy and sentenced to death. They appealed, challenging the credibility of the sole eyewitness, common intention evaluation, and raising sudden fight defense. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal, finding the eyewitness testimony credible and corroborated by medical evidence. The court affirmed the conviction and death sentence.
defence_counsel: Sachindra De Zoysa, AAL; Indica Mallawaratchy
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted based on credible eyewitness testimony and medical evidence. The Court of Appeal found no errors in the HC's analysis and agreed with its reasoning.
precedents_cited_list: Fradd v Brown & Company Ltd. (20 NLR Page 282)
standard_of_review_applied: Deference to trial judge's assessment of witness credibility, as per appellate standards.

judges: Menaka Wijesundera J. | Neil Iddawala J.
offence_sections: Section 40 of the Forest Ordinance No. 16 of 1907 as amended by Forest (Amendment) Act No 65 of 2009
brief_facts_summary: On 24.05.2017, a tractor and trailer were taken into custody for entering a conserved forest and removing sand in violation of the Forest Ordinance. The accused persons pleaded guilty and were fined. A vehicle inquiry was held where the appellant, the registered owner, gave evidence, and the magistrate ordered confiscation of the vehicle, which was affirmed by the High Court.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 40 of the Forest Ordinance No. 16 of 1907 as amended by Forest (Amendment) Act No 65 of 2009
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court dismissed the revision application and reaffirmed the magistrate's order confiscating the vehicle.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant appealed against the confiscation, arguing that he had taken precautions to prevent the offence and that the magistrate incorrectly evaluated the evidence regarding his failure to prove precautions.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Appellant claimed he took precautions to prevent illegal use of vehicle | Magistrate incorrectly evaluated evidence on precautions
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The court analyzed the appellant's testimony and found inconsistencies, such as not always being aware of hires and a practice of not being informed, which contributed to the failure to prove precautions.
probability_assessment_by_court: The court assessed on a balance of probability that the appellant failed to take all precautions to prevent the offence.
defence_version_summary: The appellant claimed he hired the driver, checked his license, gave instructions not to engage in illegal activities, and was not informed about all hires. The court found his testimony inconsistent and insufficient to prove he took all precautions.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found that the appellant did not take all possible precautions to prevent the forest offence. They referenced precedents establishing that mere instructions are insufficient and the owner must prove active steps. The contradiction in the appellant's statements was noted, but the lack of precautions was adequate to affirm the confiscation.
coa_sentence_type: Confiscation of tractor under Forest Ordinance
brief_judgment_file_summary: The appellant, owner of a tractor confiscated for use in a forest offence, appealed against the confiscation order. The High Court affirmed the magistrate's decision. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal, finding that the appellant failed to prove he took all precautions to prevent the offence, as required by law.
defence_counsel: Vijaya Niranjan Perera PC with Oshadee Perera
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court dismissed the revision application and reaffirmed the magistrate's confiscation order. The Court of Appeal agreed with this analysis.
precedents_cited_list: Samarasinghe Dharmasena v W. P. Wanigasinghe (CA/PHC) 197/2013 | S. D. N. Premasiri v Officer in Charge, Mawathagama (CA/PHC) 46/2015 | Dewapurage Kamal Deshapriya v Officer in Charge, Police Station of Pannala CA/PHC/139/2015
standard_of_review_applied: Balance of probability as per Section 40 of Forest Ordinance
sentencing_principles_applied: Confiscation under Forest Ordinance requires owner to prove all precautions taken to prevent offence

judges: N. Bandula Karunarathna J. | R. Gurusinghe J.
offence_sections: section 23A (1) read with section 23A (3) of the Bribery Act
brief_facts_summary: The accused-appellant, an Assistant Engineer at the Irrigation Office, Kiriala, was charged under the Bribery Act for acquiring assets disproportionate to his known sources of income during the investigation period. The prosecution alleged he built a two-storied house and purchased a van for sums that could not be accounted for by his known income. The defence contended the actual costs were lower and that the appellant had substantial additional income from a backhoe loader business. The case centered on proving the value of the van and the house, and whether income from the backhoe loader was genuine.
evidence_type_primary: Documentary evidence (Valuation reports, hire purchase agreements, affidavits)
evidence_type_secondary: Witness testimony (Investigating Officer, Provincial Valuer, Car sale manager, Defence witnesses)
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: section 23A (1) read with section 23A (3) of the Bribery Act
hc_sentence_type: 2 years Rigorous Imprisonment suspended for 10 years, Fine, Penalty under section 26 of the Bribery Act
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the accused-appellant of the charge under the Bribery Act, finding that his expenditure exceeded his known income. The Judge sentenced him to suspended imprisonment, a fine, and a substantial penalty, based on the prosecution's valuation of the assets and rejection of the defence's claims regarding additional income from a backhoe loader.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant argued the High Court Judge failed to properly evaluate evidence regarding the value of the van and the construction cost of his house, and failed to consider his claimed income from a backhoe loader. The defence contended the prosecution did not establish the alleged values beyond reasonable doubt and that the appellant proved his case on a balance of probabilities.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Learned Trial Judge has failed to consider that the prosecution failed to establish the value of the vehicle in question is Rs.765,000/= beyond reasonable doubt and the appellant proved on balance of probabilities that he paid only Rs.500,000/= | The learned High Court Judge failed to consider that the value of the house built by him properly in the light of two different estimates submitted by the prosecution and the defence. | The learned High Court Judge had failed to properly evaluate the evidence in respect of the income, the appellant received from backhoe loader.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the prosecution's key witness (PW7, the car sale manager) gave contradictory and unsupported evidence regarding the vehicle's value, and the prosecution failed to properly investigate the house valuation and backhoe loader income. Defence witnesses provided uncontested, plausible testimony supporting lower asset costs and additional income.
probability_assessment_by_court: The COA held that the accused successfully rebutted the presumption under section 23A of the Bribery Act on a balance of probabilities, showing the alleged unexplained difference between his known income and expenditure was negligible and could be accounted for by the claimed adjustments in asset value and additional income.
defence_version_summary: The accused pleaded not guilty. He gave evidence and called five defence witnesses. He argued he paid only Rs.500,000 for the van (not Rs.768,000), spent Rs.1,380,000 on his house (not Rs.2,064,000), and earned significant additional income (Rs.1,225,793) from a backhoe loader business. The COA found his explanations probable and supported by witnesses.
legal_errors_description: The High Court Judge misdirected himself by failing to properly evaluate the evidence in favour of the accused, particularly regarding the valuation of assets and the income from the backhoe loader, and failed to apply the correct standard of proof for the accused to rebut the presumption under section 23A of the Bribery Act.
procedural_defects_description: The Bribery Commission indicted the accused prematurely based on an incomplete investigation, without obtaining detailed valuation reports or giving the accused an opportunity to explain alleged contradictions regarding his backhoe loader income before indictment.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The COA extensively analyzed the evidence, finding the prosecution failed to establish the value of the van (Rs.765,000) beyond reasonable doubt due to contradictory evidence from PW7 and the existence of a credible invoice (B2) for Rs.500,000. The valuation of the house was also flawed as the Commission indicted without detailed reports or comparing defence estimates. Regarding backhoe loader income, the Commission failed to investigate despite admitting some income existed, and the defence presented uncontested witness testimony and records (V12-V21). The COA held the accused successfully rebutted the statutory presumption on a balance of probabilities, reducing the unexplained difference to a negligible Rs.55,141.18 over five years. The High Court judgment was unsound in law due to misdirection and failure to properly evaluate the evidence.
coa_sentence_type: Acquitted and discharged. The conviction and sentence are set aside.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused-appellant, an Assistant Engineer, appealed his High Court conviction under the Bribery Act for acquiring assets disproportionate to his known income. The High Court sentenced him to suspended imprisonment, a fine, and a penalty. The Court of Appeal allowed the appeal, acquitting the accused. It found the High Court misdirected itself by failing to properly evaluate evidence regarding the value of the van and house, and the income from a backhoe loader. The COA held the prosecution failed to prove the asset values beyond reasonable doubt, the investigation was incomplete and premature, and the accused successfully rebutted the presumption on a balance of probabilities, explaining the negligible difference between his income and expenditure.
defence_counsel: Saliya Pieris, PC with Geeth Karunarathne AAL
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court Judge analyzed the prosecution evidence and found the case proved beyond reasonable doubt, convicting the accused. The COA found this analysis flawed, as the HC failed to properly consider the defence's credible evidence and adjustments, and misdirected itself on the law regarding the burden of proof under section 23A of the Bribery Act.
precedents_cited_list: Wanjgasekara vs. Republic of Sri Lanka 79 (1) NLR 241 | King Vs. Gunaratne 14 Ceylon Law Recorder 174 | Onnassi vs. Vergottis ((1968)2 Lloyds' R.403) | Valarshak Seth Apcar vs. Standard Coal Company Limited AIR (1943)PC 159 | Sris Chandra Nandi vs. Rakhalananda (AIR) 1941 PC 16 | D, W. Wanigasekera vs The Republic of Sri Lanka 1979 (1) NLR 241 | Attorney General vs. R.M. Karunaratne SC 16/74 D.C. Colombo B/75-SC minutes of 17.06.1977 | L.C. Fernando vs. Republic of Sri Lanka 79 (2) NLR 313
standard_of_review_applied: The appellate court applied tests to determine if the trial judge's verdict was against the weight of evidence, if there was misdirection on law or evidence, or if the trial court drew wrong inferences from the evidence. It acknowledged the trial judge's advantage in assessing witness demeanour but held it could interfere if the judgment ought not to stand and the divergence was not due to the trial judge's advantages.

judges: N. Bandula Karunarathna, J. | R. Gurusinghe, J.
offence_sections: section 296 read with section 32 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The appellant was convicted of murdering Karunapala Perera on 5 September 2001 at Naththandiya. The deceased was assaulted with a sword and died from fatal head injuries. Key evidence included eyewitness testimony, a dying declaration to the deceased's wife, and recovery of the sword based on the appellant's information.
evidence_type_secondary: Medical evidence and Recovery of weapon
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: section 296 read with section 32 of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the first accused of murder and sentenced him to death. The second accused was dead when trial commenced, and the third accused was acquitted after trial.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: Appellant's counsel argued the High Court judge failed to consider and analyze PW3's evidence, that the dying declaration to PW4 was unreliable, and that PW4's testimony was inconsistent with her previous statements to implicate the accused.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The evidence of PW3 was not considered by the learned High Court Judge. | The learned High Court Judge has failed to analyse the evidence of PW3 in totality. | The dying declaration given to the wife of the deceased (PW4) was not reliable and should not have been acted upon it. | PW4 in her statement to the police and in non-summary deposition stated something different, but in the High Court she said something else to implicate the first and second accused.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed the evidence of PW3 (three-wheeler driver) and PW4 (wife) and found the dying declaration reliable. It noted the defence failed to cross-examine PW4 properly under Section 145 of the Evidence Ordinance. The evidence of PW3 did not support the appellant's version.
probability_assessment_by_court: Court found evidence proved charge beyond reasonable doubt.
defence_version_summary: The appellant did not plead guilty. He gave a dock statement. The court found the defence version not credible and that the appellant had the sword and caused fatal injuries.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal reviewed the evidence and found the dying declaration reliable, noting the defence did not properly challenge it under Section 145 of the Evidence Ordinance. It held that the evidence, including eyewitness testimony and medical evidence, proved the appellant's guilt beyond reasonable doubt. Any omission in the High Court judgment did not prejudice the appellant's substantial rights or cause a failure of justice.
coa_sentence_type: Death sentence upheld
brief_judgment_file_summary: The appellant was convicted of murder and sentenced to death by the High Court of Chilaw. He appealed on grounds including non-consideration of evidence, unreliable dying declaration, and inconsistencies in witness testimony. The Court of Appeal found the dying declaration reliable, the evidence sufficient, and that any shortcomings in the judgment did not prejudice the appellant. The appeal was dismissed, upholding the conviction and death sentence.
defence_counsel: Neranjan Jayasinghe with Harshana Ananda
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted based on evidence including dying declaration and eyewitness testimony. The Court of Appeal found the evidence sufficient and any omission did not prejudice the appellant or cause a failure of justice.
standard_of_review_applied: Court of Appeal reviewed for errors in fact or law that prejudiced substantial rights or occasioned failure of justice under Article 138(1) proviso of the Constitution.

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: section 365B (2) (b) of the Penal Code as amended by Penal Code (Amendment) Act No- 22 of 1995, 29 of 1998 and 16 of 2006
brief_facts_summary: The accused appellant was charged with three counts of grave sexual abuse of a minor neighbor (PW-01) between November 2013 and November 2014. The incidents allegedly occurred at the appellant's house. The abuse came to light when the victim's father noticed his trouser zip open and questioned him, leading to a complaint to police. The Judicial Medical Officer found no physical evidence but did not rule out the alleged incidents.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: section 365B (2) (b) of the Penal Code as amended by Penal Code (Amendment) Act No- 22 of 1995, 29 of 1998 and 16 of 2006
hc_sentence_type: 10 years rigorous imprisonment on each of three counts to be served consecutively, fine of Rs. 10,000 per count, compensation of Rs. 200,000 per count to victim
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court Judge found the appellant guilty on all three counts. The Judge sentenced him to 10 years rigorous imprisonment per count to be served consecutively, imposed fines, and ordered compensation to the victim. In default of payment, additional simple and rigorous imprisonment terms were imposed.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant argued the High Court Judge erred by considering evidence not part of the record, failing to evaluate vital discrepancies in the evidence for the first charge, incorrectly finding the prosecution proved its case beyond reasonable doubt, and imposing an excessive sentence given the facts and circumstances.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Whether the learned High Court Judge has made a serious error in the consideration of the evidence placed before the Court by referring to some strange evidence which was never a part of the evidence, and thereby causing a denial of fair trial for the appellant. | Whether the learned High Court Judge has failed to evaluate the vital discrepancy in the evidence as to the first charge preferred against the appellant. | Whether the learned High Court Judge was in error in his consideration of the facts and the relevant law in deciding that the prosecution has proved the case beyond reasonable doubt. | In any case, whether the sentenced imposed was excessive given the facts and the circumstances.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the victim's testimony had significant discrepancies regarding the sequence and nature of the alleged incidents compared to the indictment. The evidence was deemed not cogent enough to stand alone, and the High Court Judge failed to properly analyze the infirmities.
probability_assessment_by_court: Court found the evidence of the victim was not cogent enough to act on itself. Significant discrepancies went to the root of the prosecution case, creating reasonable doubt.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty. The judgment mentions a dock statement was made and rejected by the High Court Judge. The Court of Appeal found the High Court Judge failed to properly analyze the dock statement and defence, amounting to a denial of a fair trial.
legal_errors_description: The High Court Judge erred by referring to evidence not part of the record (non-existent eyewitness 'Benjamin'), failed to properly consider vital discrepancies in the victim's evidence, and misdirected himself on the law regarding corroboration and fair trial.
procedural_defects_description: Denial of fair trial due to failure to analyze the appellant's dock statement and defence. Considering evidence not on record.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the High Court Judge committed a serious error by referring to a non-existent eyewitness, which vitiated the conviction. The victim's testimony contained major discrepancies between the indictment and his court evidence regarding the sequence and nature of the three alleged incidents. The evidence was not cogent enough to stand uncorroborated. The Court discussed the need for corroboration when a victim's evidence is weak, citing Sunil and Another Vs. The Attorney General and Sana Vs. Republic of Sri Lanka. The High Court Judge also failed to analyze the appellant's dock statement and defence, denying a fair trial. Considering the infirmities, the trauma a re-trial would cause the now-adult victim, and the time already served by the appellant, the Court declined to order a re-trial.
coa_sentence_type: Conviction and sentence set aside, appellant acquitted.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused appellant was convicted by the High Court of Colombo on three counts of grave sexual abuse of a minor and sentenced to consecutive rigorous imprisonment terms, fines, and compensation. He appealed, arguing errors in evidence consideration, discrepancies in the victim's testimony, failure to prove the case beyond reasonable doubt, and excessive sentence. The Court of Appeal found the High Court Judge erred by referring to non-existent evidence and failing to address major inconsistencies between the indictment and the victim's testimony. The COA also found the victim's evidence lacked cogency and the defence was not properly considered. The appeal was allowed, the conviction and sentence were set aside, and the appellant was acquitted. A re-trial was deemed inappropriate.
defence_counsel: Geeth Karunarathna
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court Judge found the appellant guilty based on the victim's testimony. The COA found the HC judgment flawed for referencing non-existent evidence, failing to analyze discrepancies in the victim's story, and not properly considering the defence, leading to a denial of a fair trial.
precedents_cited_list: Sunil and Another Vs. The Attorney General (1986) 1 SLR 230 | Sana Vs. Republic of Sri Lanka (2009) 1 SLR 48
standard_of_review_applied: Review of evidence, consideration of legal errors and procedural fairness, assessment of whether conviction was safe.

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
brief_facts_summary: The accused was indicted for murder and robbery of one Thelge Sumith Peiris on 04/05/2006. The main eyewitness was an 11-year-old boy who saw the accused and another person assault and stab the deceased. The witness ran home and told his mother, who sent him away for safety, so he did not give a police statement immediately but later testified at the inquest and identified the accused.
evidence_type_secondary: Medical evidence and testimony of witness's mother
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the accused based on the evidence of the sole eyewitness and medical evidence. The judge found the evidence trustworthy and convicted the accused as charged.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant argued that the conviction was unsafe because it was based on the uncorroborated evidence of a sole child eyewitness. Other grounds included no police statement by the witness, contradictory reasons for not complaining, and the identification parade being held a month later.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Conviction is wholly based on the uncorroborated evidence of a sole child eye witness. | No police statement was given by the sole eye witness. | Contradictory reasons were adduced by the eye witness and his mother for the failure in making a police complaint. | Statement of the eye witness did not lead to the arrest of the accused. | Version of the eye witness does not favour the test of probability. | Version of the eye witness is contradicted by PW1. | Trial court failed to assess the testimonial trustworthiness of the eye witness. | Learned Judge was deprived of observing the demeanour and deportment of the sole eye witness. | Identification parade was held after nearly a month from the date of the incident. No specific feature of the accused being mentioned by the eye witness.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed the eyewitness testimony and found it credible. The witness was 11 at the time of the incident and gave evidence years later. The court noted that the evidence was consistent with medical evidence and the witness had a clear view.
