probability_assessment_by_court: The court assessed the probability and found the witness's version credible and consistent with medical evidence.
defence_version_summary: The appellant opted for a non-jury trial, made a statement from the dock denying the charge, and did not call any witnesses. The court found the prosecution evidence credible and convicted.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The COA thoroughly analyzed the grounds of appeal. They found the eyewitness testimony credible and corroborated by medical evidence. They addressed each ground: the witness's failure to give a police statement was explained by fear for safety, the identification was reliable, and the judge properly assessed the evidence. The COA concluded that the conviction was safe and dismissed the appeal.
coa_sentence_type: Death
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused was convicted of murder and robbery by the High Court of Panadura and sentenced to death. The conviction was based on the testimony of a sole child eyewitness. The accused appealed on grounds including the reliability of the child witness and procedural issues. The Court of Appeal found the witness testimony credible and corroborated by medical evidence, and dismissed the appeal, upholding the conviction and sentence.
defence_counsel: Indica Mallowaratchy
hc_analysis_summary: The HC analyzed the eyewitness testimony and found it credible and consistent with medical evidence. The COA agreed with the HC's analysis and found no reason to interfere.
precedents_cited_list: The Attorney General v. Devunderage Nihal SC/Appeal/145/2010
standard_of_review_applied: The COA reviewed the evidence and found that the HC had correctly assessed the evidence, applying the standard of whether the conviction was safe.

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 19(b) and 19(c) of the Bribery Act
brief_facts_summary: The appellant, a government watcher at the Circuit Education Office of Kegalle, demanded and accepted a bribe of Rs. 10,000 from PW-01 to admit her child to a school. PW-01 complained to the Bribery Commission, and a raid was conducted where the money was recovered from the appellant. Key evidence included testimony from PW-01 (complainant) and PW-02 (decoy), who witnessed the transaction.
evidence_type_secondary: Recovery of money and witness corroboration
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 19(b) and 19(c) of the Bribery Act
hc_sentence_type: Two years rigorous imprisonment on counts 1 and 2 to run concurrently, with fines of Rs. 3000 on each count, and additional fine of Rs. 10000 under Section 26 of the Bribery Act
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court found the appellant guilty on four counts under the Bribery Act, sentenced him to imprisonment and fines, and acquitted the second accused due to lack of evidence. The court based its decision on the prosecution evidence, finding contradictions trivial.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant argued that the High Court Judge failed to consider serious contradictions in the prosecution case, that solicitation and acceptance were not proved beyond reasonable doubt, and that inadmissible evidence was considered.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The learned High Court Judge has failed to consider the serious contradictions of the prosecution case. | The learned High Court Judge has failed to consider the solicitation and the acceptance of any gratification by the appellant was not proved beyond reasonable doubt. | The learned High Court Judge has considered inadmissible evidence led by the prosecution for the purposes of the judgement.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed witness contradictions, found them to be trivial and not material to the core case, upheld the High Court's credibility assessments, and concluded that the prosecution evidence was reliable and proved the case beyond reasonable doubt.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal assessed contradictions and found no reasonable doubt, relying on the credibility of prosecution witnesses and the appellant's defence being an afterthought.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty, gave evidence under oath, claimed that the money was forcibly put into his pocket by PW-01, and denied solicitation or acceptance. The court found his version to be an afterthought and not credible, as key points were not put to witnesses in cross-examination.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal considered the grounds of appeal, reviewed the evidence for contradictions, applied precedents on witness credibility and burden of proof, found that the prosecution proved the case beyond reasonable doubt, dismissed the appellant's defence as an afterthought, and upheld the High Court's judgment.
coa_sentence_type: Two years rigorous imprisonment on counts 1 and 2 to run concurrently, with fines of Rs. 3000 on each count, and additional fine of Rs. 10000 under Section 26 of the Bribery Act
brief_judgment_file_summary: The appellant, a government watcher, was convicted for soliciting and accepting a bribe to admit a child to school. The High Court sentenced him to imprisonment and fines. He appealed on grounds of contradictions, proof beyond reasonable doubt, and inadmissible evidence. The Court of Appeal found no merit in the appeal, dismissed it, and affirmed the conviction and sentence.
defence_counsel: Darshana Kuruppu with Sajini Elvitigala, Dineru Bandara and Buddhika Thilakarathna
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted the appellant based on prosecution evidence, found contradictions to be trivial, and sentenced accordingly. The Court of Appeal upheld this analysis, finding no errors in the High Court's reasoning.
precedents_cited_list: The Attorney General Vs Potta Naufar and Others (Ambeptitya Murder Case) (2007) 2 SLR 144 | Bandara Vs. The State (2001) 2 SLR 63 at 69 | Bharwada Bhoginbhai Hirijibhai Vs. The State of Gujarat (1983) A.I.R. S.C. 753 | The Attorney General Vs. Visuwalingam 47 NLR 289 | Sarwan Singh Vs State of Punjab 2002 AIR Supreme Court iii 3652 at 36755,3656 | Pilippu Mandige Nalaka Krishantha Kumara Thisera Vs A.G, CA 87/2005 decided on 17-05-2007
standard_of_review_applied: Review of evidence for contradictions and reasonable doubt, applying precedents on witness credibility and burden of proof

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: section 296 read with section 32 of the Penal Code (Count 1); section 315 of the Penal Code (Count 2 - against 1st accused only)
location_of_offence: Ragala area (house of second accused appellant)
brief_facts_summary: The deceased, father of the second accused appellant, came to her house suspecting an illicit relationship between the appellants. An altercation ensued, resulting in injuries to the deceased, leading to his death. The first accused appellant was an employee of the second accused appellant's security service. After the incident, the first accused was seen running away with a knife.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: section 296 read with section 32 of the Penal Code (Count 1); section 315 of the Penal Code (Count 2)
hc_sentence_type: Death (Count 1); Rigorous Imprisonment 6 months (Count 2 - 1st accused only)
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court Judge convicted both appellants of murder and sentenced them to death on count one. The first appellant was also sentenced to six months rigorous imprisonment on count two. The conviction was based primarily on the dying declaration of the deceased.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellants contended that the High Court Judge failed to properly consider evidence establishing culpable homicide not amounting to murder under section 297 of the Penal Code, based on exception 4 of section 294 (sudden fight in heat of passion).
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Failure to consider evidence of culpable homicide not amounting to murder under section 297 of the Penal Code
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: No eyewitnesses apart from PW-01 (child witness) whose evidence was disregarded as adverse. PW-02 (injured) saw first accused running with a knife. The main evidence was the dying declaration, which had inconsistencies and lacked corroboration for parts implicating the second accused.
probability_assessment_by_court: Court found the incident resulted from a sudden fight without premeditation, and the dying declaration had infirmities, creating reasonable doubt for murder charge.
defence_version_summary: Not guilty plea. Defence argued the incident was a result of a sudden fight upon a sudden quarrel, with no premeditation. No witnesses called by defence mentioned, but counsel argued on legal interpretation.
legal_errors_description: High Court Judge erred in not properly considering the applicability of exception 4 of section 294 (culpable homicide not amounting to murder due to sudden fight) despite evidence supporting it.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed the dying declaration's probative value and intrinsic infirmities, noting it was not under oath and untested by cross-examination. It considered the evidence establishing a sudden fight arising from the deceased's arrival and verbal altercation, with no premeditation. The Court found the weapon (knife) was likely available at the house, indicating no undue advantage. Applying precedents, it held the High Court should have considered culpable homicide not amounting to murder. The conviction for murder was set aside and replaced with conviction under section 297.
coa_sentence_type: 10 years rigorous imprisonment each (Count 1); Fine of Rs. 20000 each (default 6 months simple imprisonment); 1st accused's 6 months rigorous imprisonment on Count 2 remains.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The first and second accused appellants were convicted of murder by the High Court of Nuwaraeliya and sentenced to death. They appealed, arguing the High Court failed to consider evidence supporting culpable homicide not amounting to murder due to a sudden fight. The Court of Appeal agreed, finding the incident resulted from a sudden quarrel without premeditation. It set aside the murder conviction, convicted them under section 297 of the Penal Code, and sentenced each to 10 years rigorous imprisonment and a fine of Rs. 20,000.
defence_counsel: Widura Ranawaka with Menaka Warnapura for 1st Accused Appellant; Shanaka Ranasinghe, PC with Niroshan Mihindukulasooriya for 2nd Accused Appellant
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court based conviction primarily on the dying declaration. The Court of Appeal found the High Court Judge considered but incorrectly rejected the applicability of the sudden fight exception, failing to properly assess the evidence supporting culpable homicide not amounting to murder.
precedents_cited_list: The King V Asirwadan Nadar 51 NLR 322 | The King Vs. Bellana Vithanage Eddin 41 NLR 345
standard_of_review_applied: Review of legal error in not considering alternative verdict of culpable homicide not amounting to murder based on evidence on record.
sentencing_principles_applied: Consideration of facts and circumstances of the case, including sudden fight, lack of premeditation, and period of incarceration since original conviction.
final_charge_after_appeal: Murder modified to Culpable Homicide not amounting to murder under section 297 of the Penal Code

judges: K. PRIYANTHA FERNANDO, J. (P/CA) | WICKUM A. KALUARACHCHI, J.
offence_sections: Section 365B(2)(b) of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The appellant, a neighbour, sexually abused a 13-year-old boy on multiple occasions when the boy visited his house to fetch water, watch television, or borrow a bicycle. The abuse came to light after probation officers inquired and took statements. The appellant denied the allegations.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 365B(2)(b) of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the appellant on two counts of grave sexual abuse based on the victim's testimony and medical evidence, finding the prosecution proved the case beyond reasonable doubt. The judge sentenced him to 10 years imprisonment with fines and compensation.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant challenged the conviction on grounds including failure to prove offences beyond reasonable doubt, denial of fair trial due to unspecified dates, misdirection in evaluating evidence, ignoring weaknesses in prosecution case, admitting inadmissible evidence, improbabilities in prosecution version, and excessive sentence and compensation.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Whether the learned High Court Judge has correctly assessed that the prosecution has proved the offences described in the indictment against the appellant were carried out by the appellant between the time period as stated in the indictment, beyond reasonable doubt? | Has the accused appellant been denied the right to a fair trial by the learned High Court Judge as the time of offences have not been specified nor provided? | Has the learned High Court Judge misdirected herself in evaluating evidence of the prosecution by failing to evaluate the deficiencies in the evidence of PW1, PW3, PW4 and PW9 and thereby has overlooked the weakness in the prosecution case? | Has the learned High Court Judge completely ignored the salient weaknesses of the prosecution case and admitted evidence which cannot be admitted under prevailing law? | Has the learned High Court Judge failed to consider the improbabilities of the version of the prosecution? | Did the learned High Court Judge err in sentencing the accused appellant for an unreasonable and excessive term of imprisonment and granted an excessive compensation to the victim?
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the victim's testimony credible despite some deficiencies and delay in complaint, which was explained by the victim's vulnerability. The medical evidence was consistent and supported the prosecution case.
probability_assessment_by_court: The court assessed that the prosecution proved the case beyond reasonable doubt, considering the victim's consistent testimony and lack of alibi defence.
defence_version_summary: The accused pleaded not guilty and made an unsworn statement from the dock denying the allegations. He did not raise an alibi defence. The court found the defence not credible.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal dismissed all grounds of appeal. For grounds 1 and 2, they held that the prosecution proved the offences during the specified period, and the lack of specific dates did not prejudice the appellant as no alibi was raised, citing precedents. For grounds 3-5, they found the victim's testimony credible and the medical evidence reliable, with delay in complaint explained. For ground 6, they found the sentence appropriate considering mitigatory factors and the prescribed punishment range. The appeal was dismissed.
coa_sentence_type: 10 years Rigorous Imprisonment concurrent with fines of Rs. 10,000 per count and compensation of Rs. 100,000
brief_judgment_file_summary: The appellant was convicted by the High Court of Monaragala for two counts of grave sexual abuse under section 365B(2)(b) of the Penal Code and sentenced to 10 years imprisonment with fines and compensation. He appealed on grounds including failure to prove offences beyond reasonable doubt, unfair trial due to unspecified dates, misdirection in evidence evaluation, and excessive sentence. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal, finding the victim's testimony credible, the lack of specific dates not prejudicial, and the sentence appropriate. The conviction and sentence were upheld.
defence_counsel: Ruwan Jayawardena, AAL
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted the appellant based on the victim's testimony and medical evidence, finding the prosecution proved the case beyond reasonable doubt. The Court of Appeal found no errors in this reasoning and upheld the decision.
precedents_cited_list: Thimbtrigolle Strirathana Thero v. Attorney General CA/194/2015 [07/05/2019] | R. V. Dossi, 13 Cr.App.R.158 | Wright V. Nicholson 54 Cr.App.R.38 | Pandithakoralage v. Selvanayagam 56 N.L.R. 143
standard_of_review_applied: Review of whether the prosecution proved the case beyond reasonable doubt and whether the trial was fair.
sentencing_principles_applied: Considered mitigatory factors and the prescribed imprisonment range of 7-20 years.

judges: K. Priyantha Fernando, J (P/CA) | Wickum A. Kaluarachchi, J
offence_sections: Section 345 of the Penal Code
location_of_offence: Dalseo Police precinct, Daegu province, Republic of Korea
brief_facts_summary: Jeong Eun Hui, a university student, was last seen on 16 October 1998 and her body was found on 17 October 1998 on Guma Expressway, having died in a motor traffic accident. Her undergarments were found nearby with semen that DNA analysis matched to the accused-respondent. There were no eyewitnesses to the incident.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 345 of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court Judge acquitted the accused under Section 200(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure Act, finding that the prosecution failed to establish the commission of the offence as there was no evidence that the accused removed the victim's undergarments or used criminal force.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant argued that the trial judge misinterpreted Section 200(1) of the CCPA and should have called for defence because a reasonable inference could be drawn from the DNA evidence that the respondent committed sexual harassment by using criminal force.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The learned trial judge misinterpreted the scope and application of section 200(1) of the CCPA | A reasonable inference could be drawn from the proven facts that the respondent committed sexual harassment
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found that there was no evidence to connect the respondent to the incident except DNA evidence on the undergarments, but this did not establish that the respondent removed the undergarments or used criminal force.
probability_assessment_by_court: The court assessed that no reasonable inference could be drawn from the evidence that the accused committed the offence as charged.
defence_version_summary: The accused was acquitted without the defence being called, as the prosecution failed to establish a case against him.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed the evidence and held that the prosecution failed to adduce evidence on the key elements of the offence, specifically that the accused removed the victim's undergarments or used criminal force. The court cited precedents on burden of proof and reasonable inferences, concluding that the High Court Judge correctly acquitted the accused without calling for defence.
coa_sentence_type: Acquitted
brief_judgment_file_summary: The Attorney General appealed against the acquittal of the accused for sexual harassment under Section 345 of the Penal Code. The High Court had acquitted the accused due to lack of evidence. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal, agreeing that the prosecution failed to prove the essential elements of the offence, and upheld the acquittal.
prosecution_counsel: Janaka Bandara, DSG with Malik Azeez, SC and Deshan Aluwihare, SC
defence_counsel: Mohan Weerakoon, PC with Nuwan De Alwis and Sandamalee Perera
cause_of_death_exact_text: motor traffic accident that caused a rapture of the brain
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court Judge acquitted the accused based on lack of evidence, but the Court of Appeal noted that some findings went beyond required limits. However, the COA agreed with the conclusion to acquit.
precedents_cited_list: Attorney General V. Baranage – (2003) 1 Sri L.R. 340 | Sunil and Another V. The Attorney General - (1986) 1 Sri L.R. 230 | Harold Rex Jansen V. Hon. Attorney General – C.A. Application No 151/13, decided on 26.02.2014
standard_of_review_applied: The Court of Appeal reviewed whether the High Court Judge correctly applied Section 200(1) of the CCPA in deciding not to call for defence, considering reasonable inferences from proven facts.

judges: Menaka Wijesundera J. | Neil Iddawala J.
offence_sections: Section 20(k) of the Forest Conservation Ordinance No. 16 of 1907 as amended
brief_facts_summary: The vehicle was seized on 23.08.2018 for unlawful forest clearing under the Forest Conservation Ordinance. The accused drivers pleaded guilty and were fined. The appellant vehicle owner claimed he instructed his son only to clear around the second accused's house but the son cleared state forest area on the second accused's insistence.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 20(k) of the Forest Conservation Ordinance No. 16 of 1907 as amended
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court affirmed the Magistrate's order to confiscate the vehicle under the Forest Conservation Ordinance, finding that the appellant failed to prove he took all precautions to prevent the offence.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant argued that Section 20(k) is a stand-alone provision and thus confiscation under Section 40 does not apply. In the alternative, he contended that he had fulfilled the burden of proving he took all precautions to prevent the use of the vehicle for the offence.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Section 20(k) of the Forest Conservation Ordinance as amended is a stand-alone Section, hence the confiscation provisions stipulated under Section 40 does not apply to the offences under Section 20. | In any case, alternatively the appellant has dispensed his burden as necessitated under Section 40.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court evaluated the appellant's testimony that he gave instructions to his son and regularly followed up on the vehicle's use. It found that the appellant took all reasonable precautions, such as constant vigilance and inquiries, thus discharging his burden under the law.
probability_assessment_by_court: Court applied balance of probability standard for burden of proof under Section 40.
defence_version_summary: The accused drivers pleaded guilty to the offence. The appellant vehicle owner claimed he instructed his son only to clear around the house and took precautions by monitoring use, but the son acted beyond instructions on the second accused's insistence.
legal_errors_description: The High Court and Magistrate erred in finding that the appellant did not discharge his burden of proving he took all precautions under Section 40 of the Forest Conservation Ordinance.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal held that Section 40 of the Forest Conservation Ordinance applies to offences under Section 20(k). However, it found that the appellant vehicle owner had proven on a balance of probability that he took all reasonable precautions to prevent the use of the vehicle for the offence, including giving instructions, regular follow-ups, and vigilance. The Court referenced precedents stating that owners need not physically monitor the vehicle at all times. Therefore, the confiscation orders were set aside.
coa_sentence_type: Fine imposed on accused; vehicle confiscation set aside.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The Range Forest Officer seized a vehicle used for unlawful forest clearing under the Forest Conservation Ordinance. The accused drivers pleaded guilty and were fined, and the Magistrate ordered confiscation of the vehicle, affirmed by the High Court. The vehicle owner appealed, arguing that Section 20(k) is stand-alone and that he had taken all precautions. The Court of Appeal held that Section 40 applies but found the owner proved he took reasonable precautions, thus allowing the appeal and setting aside the confiscation orders.
defence_counsel: L.M.K. Arulanandam, PC with T. Sivanandaraja
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court affirmed the Magistrate's confiscation order, finding that the appellant failed to discharge his burden under Section 40. The Court of Appeal found that the High Court erred in not properly evaluating the evidence of precautions taken by the appellant.
precedents_cited_list: Dewapurage Kamal Deshapriya Vs Officer in Charge, Police Station, Pannala and Others CA, PHC/139/2015 | CA/PHC/203/17
standard_of_review_applied: Correctness standard for legal issues and balance of probability for factual findings
sentencing_principles_applied: Principles under Section 40 of Forest Conservation Ordinance regarding confiscation and owner's burden of proof.

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The appellant was accused of murdering Kudadurage Simon on 2nd November 2003 at a boutique. The only eyewitness, PW-01, testified that the appellant stabbed the deceased after a verbal altercation. The postmortem report confirmed death due to multiple injuries. The appellant claimed he was provoked and suffered from depression.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court Judge found the appellant guilty of murder under section 296 of the Penal Code. The judge considered defences of mental ailment and grave and sudden provocation but found no evidence to support them, leading to a death sentence.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant appealed on grounds that the High Court wrongly rejected the plea of grave and sudden provocation. He argued that the evidence showed provocation and no preplan, which should have reduced the charge to culpable homicide under section 297.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Rejection of the plea of grave and sudden provocation is factually untenable. | Evidence on record warrant the benefit of the grave and sudden provocation to the accused appellant.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the eyewitness testimony unchallenged and clear, showing the appellant as the aggressor. Medical evidence supported the cause of death. The defence of provocation was not supported by evidence.
probability_assessment_by_court: Court found no reasonable doubt based on eyewitness and medical evidence, and rejected defences.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty and made a dock statement claiming he was provoked by the deceased and suffered from depression. He called defence witnesses including a psychiatrist, but the court found no evidence to support his claims.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed the evidence and found that the High Court Judge properly considered the defences of mental ailment and grave and sudden provocation. Referring to precedents like The King Vs. Albert Appuhamy and Gamini Vs. Attorney General, the COA held that even if not raised, the judge must consider such defences if evidence suggests. However, in this case, the evidence did not support provocation as the appellant was the aggressor and came prepared with a knife. The COA found no reason to interfere with the HC decision.
coa_sentence_type: Death
brief_judgment_file_summary: The appellant was convicted of murder under section 296 of the Penal Code for stabbing the deceased on 2nd November 2003. The High Court sentenced him to death. He appealed on grounds of grave and sudden provocation, arguing for a reduction to culpable homicide. The Court of Appeal reviewed the evidence and found no basis for provocation, as the appellant was the aggressor. The COA dismissed the appeal, affirming the conviction and death sentence.
defence_counsel: Indica Mallawaratchy
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court Judge considered defences of mental ailment and provocation but found no evidence to support them. The COA agreed with this analysis, noting that the evidence showed the appellant was the aggressor and acted with intention.
precedents_cited_list: The King Vs. Albert Appuhamy 41 NLR 505 | Gamini Vs. Attorney General (2011) 1 SLR 236
standard_of_review_applied: Review of evidence and legal defences as per precedents.

judges: Prasantha De Silva, J. | K.K.A.V. Swarnadhipathi, J.
brief_facts_summary: The 1st Party Petitioner entered into agreements to purchase land from 25 owners and took possession. The 2nd Party Respondents forcibly entered the land and claimed possession, leading to a dispute. The Petitioner filed under Section 66 of the Primary Courts’ Procedure Act, but the Magistrate and High Court dismissed the application. The Court of Appeal reviewed the case.
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court Judge dismissed the revision application without issuing notice, holding that there was no breach of peace and that the Petitioner filed out of time.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The Petitioner appealed on grounds that the High Court order is erroneous, the Judge raised new grounds not raised by Respondents, disregarded submissions, and made derogatory remarks.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The said order is erroneous and contrary to law. | All the grounds raised by the learned High Court Judge were not raised by anyone of the Respondents in the original Court and the learned High Court Judge in exercise of revisionary jurisdiction cannot raise new grounds in the exercise of appellate jurisdiction which are all questions of law. | It is the same High Court Judge who made order on 29.01.2020 to the learned Magistrate of Kaduwela to make his order considering all the material placed before him on its merits and therefore in the exercise of appellate jurisdiction by way of revision he cannot raise preliminary objection on the information filed and affidavits, and documents submitted by the parties. | The learned High Court Judge who held there was no dispute causing breach of peace, has held that the order made by the learned Magistrate on 01.06.2020 is just and reasonable when it is settled law that the jurisdiction to the learned Primary Court Judge to hear an application made under Section 66 of the Primary Courts’ Procedure Act comes only when there is breach of peace or likelihood and therefore if there is no breach of peace there is no jurisdiction to the Learned Magistrate to entertain the said application. | The learned High Court Judge totally disregarded the submissions made by the Counsel for the 1st Party Petitioner when he supported the notice on 13.08.2020 and made derogatory remarks to the Counsel erroneously blaming that he had uttered falsehood in Courts.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court analyzed affidavits and police reports to determine that there was a breach of peace and that the Petitioner was dispossessed within two months, thus entitled to restoration of possession.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court found that there was a breach of peace and that the Petitioner filed within two months, so entitled to restoration.
defence_version_summary: The Respondents claimed possession of the land and disputed the Petitioner's claims. The Magistrate and High Court found in favor of the Respondents.
legal_errors_description: The High Court Judge erred in holding no breach of peace, which is necessary for jurisdiction under the Primary Courts’ Procedure Act.
procedural_defects_description: The High Court Judge dismissed the application without issuing notice and raised new grounds not raised by the parties.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal applied revisionary jurisdiction and found that the learned Magistrate and High Court Judge erred in law. The COA held that there was a breach of peace, giving jurisdiction, and that the Petitioner was dispossessed within two months, so entitled to restoration of possession. The COA set aside the lower court orders and directed the Magistrate to issue a writ to restore possession.
coa_sentence_type: Direction to the learned Magistrate to issue a writ to restore possession of the 1st Party Petitioner and evict the Respondents from the land.
brief_judgment_file_summary: This is a revision application by Homelands Holdings (Private) Limited against Respondents regarding a land dispute. The High Court dismissed the revision without notice. The Court of Appeal allowed the appeal, finding that there was breach of peace and that the Petitioner filed within the time limit. The COA set aside the lower court orders and directed the Magistrate to restore possession to the Petitioner.
defence_counsel: Charles De Silva with K. Seneviratne
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court Judge dismissed the revision application, holding no breach of peace and that the Petitioner filed out of time. The COA found this erroneous as there was breach of peace and the filing was within time.
standard_of_review_applied: Revisionary jurisdiction under Article 138 of the Constitution

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 384 read with Section 32 of the Penal Code; Section 2(1)(b) of the Offensive Weapons Act, No. 18 of 1996
brief_facts_summary: On January 24, 1998, a group attempted to rob Sinharaja Tea Factory. The police arrested the Appellant and others in the nearby Sinharaja Forest, recovering a hand grenade from the Appellant. Key evidence includes witness identification and a Government Analyst report confirming the grenade as an offensive weapon.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 384 read with Section 32 of the Penal Code; Section 2(1)(b) of the Offensive Weapons Act, No. 18 of 1996
hc_sentence_type: Rigorous Imprisonment 10 years for count 1 and 5 years for count 2, to run concurrently; with fines
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the Appellants on both counts based on witness identification and recovery of a hand grenade. The 2nd Appellant was sentenced to 10 years rigorous imprisonment for attempted robbery and 5 years for possession of an offensive weapon, with fines, sentences to run concurrently.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The Appellant appealed on grounds that his identity was not established beyond reasonable doubt and that the prosecution failed to prove his possession of the hand grenade.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The identity of the Appellant had not been established beyond reasonable doubt. | Possession of hand bomb by the Appellant have not been proved by the prosecution.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal assessed the identification evidence using Turnbull guidelines and found it reliable despite time lapse. The recovery of the hand grenade was corroborated by the Government Analyst report, establishing the Appellant's participation.
probability_assessment_by_court: Court applied Turnbull guidelines for identification evidence and found identity established beyond reasonable doubt.
defence_version_summary: The Appellant pleaded not guilty. He absconded during trial, so his counsel made submissions on his behalf, denying the charges and challenging the prosecution evidence. No alibi or defence witnesses were called.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed the identification evidence by applying the Turnbull guidelines, considering factors like time, distance, and light, and concluded that the Appellant's identity was established beyond reasonable doubt. The recovery of the hand grenade from the Appellant upon arrest, corroborated by the Government Analyst report, proved possession. The circumstantial evidence adequately supported the conviction, and thus the HC judgment was upheld.
coa_sentence_type: Rigorous Imprisonment 10 years for count 1 and 5 years for count 2, to run concurrently; with fines, deemed effective from date of incarceration on 10/11/2021
brief_judgment_file_summary: The 2nd Accused-Appellant was convicted by the High Court of Galle for attempted robbery and possession of an offensive weapon, receiving sentences of rigorous imprisonment and fines. He appealed on grounds of mistaken identity and lack of proof of possession. The Court of Appeal applied identification guidelines, found the evidence sufficient, and dismissed the appeal, affirming the conviction and sentence to run from the date of incarceration.
defence_counsel: U.R.D. Silva, PC with Savithri Fernando
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted the Appellant based on witness identification and recovery of a hand grenade. The Court of Appeal reviewed this and found the HC's analysis correct, with sufficient evidence to support the conviction.
precedents_cited_list: Turnbull [1977] QB 224
standard_of_review_applied: Assessment of identification evidence using Turnbull guidelines and evaluation of circumstantial evidence.

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 296 read with section 32 of the Penal Code; Section 317 read with section 32 of the Penal Code
location_of_offence: Digadara junction and the road leading to the deceased's house
brief_facts_summary: The deceased and his servant (PW-02) were walking home at night when they were attacked by two assailants. The deceased was killed and PW-02 was injured with a manna knife. The prosecution's case relied heavily on the eyewitness identification by PW-02, who claimed to have recognized the appellant and another by torchlight. The appellant maintained an alibi that he was at a wedding function.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 296 read with section 32 of the Penal Code; Section 317 read with section 32 of the Penal Code
hc_sentence_type: Death sentence on first count (murder); 10 years rigorous imprisonment on second count (grievous hurt)
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court found the appellant guilty of murder and causing grievous injuries based on the evidence of PW-02. The court sentenced the appellant to death for murder and 10 years rigorous imprisonment for the second count, along with a fine and compensation to the injured witness.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant challenged the conviction on grounds of unreliable identification evidence, contradictions in prosecution testimony, failure to consider the alibi defence, and misdirection on the burden of proof.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The learned High Court Judge failed to consider that it is highly unsafe to rely on the evidence of PW-02 Hemapala as his evidence was contradicted by PW-01 and other witnesses called on behalf of the prosecution. | The identification of the appellant has not been proved beyond reasonable doubt and the possibility of mistaken identity of the appellant has not been ruled out. | The learned High Court Judge has failed to consider that the defence of the appellant is more probable, as the appellant has taken an alibi at the time of his arrest and has maintained it right throughout, which has been corroborated by the prosecution and the defence witnesses as well. | There was several misdirection in the judgement with regard to the burden of proof in a criminal case.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the identification evidence of PW-02 unreliable due to contradictions with PW-01, failure to disclose names immediately, and lack of proper lighting. The alibi defence was considered credible and created reasonable doubt.
probability_assessment_by_court: The prosecution failed to establish identity beyond reasonable doubt; the alibi created reasonable doubt entitling the appellant to an acquittal.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty and maintained an alibi that he was at a wedding function during the incident. He gave evidence on oath and called witnesses in support. The court found the alibi defence created reasonable doubt.
legal_errors_description: The High Court Judge failed to apply the Turnbull guidelines for identification and misdirected on the burden of proof regarding alibi.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal held that the High Court failed to properly apply the Turnbull guidelines for assessing identification evidence. The court found the sole identifying witness (PW-02) unreliable due to contradictions with other prosecution witnesses (especially PW-01 regarding lighting), his failure to disclose the assailants' names immediately after the incident, and the strong alibi evidence. The prosecution failed to exclude the alibi or prove identity beyond reasonable doubt, making the conviction unsafe.
coa_sentence_type: Acquitted of all charges; no sentence imposed.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The appellant was convicted by the High Court of Kalutara for murder and causing grievous injuries and sentenced to death and 10 years imprisonment. On appeal, the Court of Appeal found the identification evidence unreliable and the alibi defence credible, creating reasonable doubt. The appeal was allowed, and the appellant was acquitted of all charges.
defence_counsel: Darshana Kuruppu with Buddhika Thilakarathne and Dineru Bandara
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted based on the identification by PW-02, brushing aside infirmities in his evidence. The Court of Appeal found the High Court failed to properly assess identification using Turnbull guidelines and misdirected on the burden of proof regarding alibi.
precedents_cited_list: Rex Vs. Turnbull (1977) QB 224 | Bharwada Bhoginbhai Hirjibhai Vs. State of Gujarat 1983 AIR 753
standard_of_review_applied: Application of Turnbull guidelines for identification evidence and assessment of whether prosecution proved case beyond reasonable doubt.

judges: Menaka Wijesundera J. | Neil Iddawal J.
offence_sections: under the provisions of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Act No 13 of 1984
brief_facts_summary: The suspect was arrested on 4.5.2018 for alleged possession of 100 grams of a substance suspected to be heroin. He has been in remand custody since arrest without the trial concluding. The Court of Appeal found the delay excessive and oppressive.
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court of Panadura denied bail to the suspect in its order dated 17.9.2021.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The main contention is that the suspect has been in remand custody since his arrest without the trial concluding, and the delay is excessive and oppressive.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Delay in concluding trial | Suspect languishing in remand custody
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court considered the delay in trial and the suspect's remand period as exceptional circumstances for bail.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court found the delay in trial excessive and oppressive, justifying bail.
defence_version_summary: The suspect sought bail due to delay in trial. No details on plea or alibi provided.
legal_errors_description: The High Court failed to consider the excessive and oppressive delay as an exceptional circumstance for bail.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal cited Attorney General Vs. Edirieera on delay, and Carder vs. O.I.C Narcotics Bureau on bail. It found the suspect's remand for nearly five years excessive and oppressive, constituting exceptional circumstances for bail under section 83 of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Act. The Court held that ends of justice will be met by granting bail.
coa_sentence_type: Bail granted with suitable conditions.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The petitioner sought revision of the High Court's bail denial order for the suspect arrested in 2018 for drug possession. The suspect had been in remand for nearly five years without trial conclusion. The Court of Appeal found the delay excessive and oppressive, citing precedents, and allowed the application, setting aside the High Court order and granting bail with suitable conditions.
defence_counsel: Palitha Fernando, PC
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court denied bail. The COA found that the HC failed to properly consider the delay as an exceptional circumstance for bail.
precedents_cited_list: Attorney General Vs. Edirieera | Carder vs. O.I.C Narcotics Bureau [2006] 3 SLR 74
standard_of_review_applied: Revisionary jurisdiction under Article 138 of the Constitution and Section 404 of the Criminal Procedure Code.

judges: Menaka Wijesundera J. | Neil Iddawala J.
offence_sections: Section 54 of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Act
brief_facts_summary: The suspect was arrested on 23.08.2020 at Katunayake Airport while planning to travel abroad. Based on his statement to police, 11 kg of a substance suspected to be heroin was recovered on 17.10.2020. He has been in remand since 2020 without trial or indictment, and the main evidence against him is a section 27 recovery under the Evidence Ordinance.
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court denied bail to the suspect. The Court of Appeal found that the delay in trial and lack of indictment warranted setting aside the High Court order.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The petitioner contended that the suspect has been in remand since 2020 without trial or indictment, violating his right to personal liberty. It was argued that the main evidence, a section 27 recovery, is insufficient to prove guilt. The state failed to indicate when or if an indictment would be filed.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Suspect in remand since 2020 without trial or indictment | Main evidence is section 27 recovery, insufficient to prove guilt | Delay in prosecution causing prejudice
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The evidence against the suspect is primarily based on his statement leading to recovery of heroin. The Court of Appeal did not examine the merits but considered the delay and lack of indictment. It referenced precedent that ends of justice require bail in such circumstances.
probability_assessment_by_court: Court applied the principle that ends of justice are met by granting bail due to delay and insufficient evidence
defence_version_summary: The defence argued for bail on grounds of delay in trial and insufficient evidence. The suspect has not been indicted, and the defence contended that his personal liberty is violated.
legal_errors_description: The High Court failed to properly consider exceptional circumstances for bail under section 83 of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Act, and the excessive delay in prosecution.
procedural_defects_description: Failure to indict the suspect in a timely manner, causing excessive remand period without trial.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal considered the submissions and noted the suspect has been in custody since 2020 for an offence under section 54 of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Act. Under section 83, bail requires exceptional circumstances, which here include the delay in trial and lack of sufficient evidence. The Court referenced precedent Carder v OIC Narcotic Bureau, concluding that ends of justice require granting bail. It set aside the High Court order and directed bail on suitable conditions.
coa_sentence_type: Bail granted on suitable conditions
brief_judgment_file_summary: The petitioner sought revision of the High Court order denying bail to the suspect, who is charged under section 54 of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Act. The High Court had denied bail, but the Court of Appeal found exceptional circumstances due to delay in trial and insufficient evidence. Grounds included violation of personal liberty and procedural delays. The Court of Appeal allowed the application, set aside the High Court order, and directed bail on suitable conditions.
defence_counsel: Palitha Fernando, PC
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court denied bail, but the Court of Appeal found that the High Court failed to account for the exceptional circumstances of delay and lack of indictment. The COA held that the ends of justice require bail in this case.
precedents_cited_list: Attorney General v Ediriveera | Carder v OIC Narcotic Bureau 2006 SLR
standard_of_review_applied: Revision under Article 138 of the Constitution read with Section 404 of the Criminal Procedure Code

judges: K. Priyantha Fernando, J. (P/CA) | Wickum A. Kaluarachchi, J.
offence_sections: Section 365B(2)(b) of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The victim was an inmate at Vajira children's home and the appellant was a teacher at the Dhamma school attached to the home. The appellant sexually abused the victim continuously from 2004 until March 2007. The abuse came to light when, on 25 March 2007, the victim was abused again and other children informed a cook, leading to an investigation by a probation officer. The victim wrote a letter about the 2007 incident and later disclosed previous abuses after medical examination.
evidence_type_primary: Victim testimony and documentary evidence (letter P-1)
evidence_type_secondary: Medical evidence (JMO report) and witness testimony
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 365B(2)(b) of the Penal Code
hc_sentence_type: 12 years rigorous imprisonment, fine, and compensation
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the accused based on the evidence of the victim and other witnesses, finding the victim credible and rejecting the defence. The court sentenced the accused to 12 years rigorous imprisonment, a fine of Rs. 10,000, and compensation of Rs. 250,000.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant argued that the conviction was contrary to law and against the weight of evidence, that the trial judge failed to apply judicial mind to proof beyond reasonable doubt, failed to properly analyse prosecution evidence, and failed to consider the defence.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The conviction is contrary to law and against the weight of the evidence. | The learned trial Judge has failed to apply his judicial mind to arrive at a finding whether the prosecution has proved its case beyond reasonable doubt. | The learned trial Judge has failed to properly analyse and legally consider the fabricated and improbable evidence of the prosecution witnesses. | The learned trial Judge has failed to consider the defence and thereby improperly rejected the same.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed the victim's testimony, considered the delay in complaint justified due to the victim's vulnerable situation, and found her credible. The court also considered the letter P-1 and medical evidence.
probability_assessment_by_court: The court assessed the credibility of the victim and found her testimony reliable despite delays and inconsistencies, and held that the prosecution proved its case beyond reasonable doubt.
defence_version_summary: The accused pleaded not guilty and gave sworn evidence denying the charge. He claimed he was following a course in 2004 and did not have access to the home. The court found his evidence inconsistent and not credible.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The COA thoroughly analyzed the grounds of appeal. It held that the delay in complaint was justified given the victim's vulnerable position as an orphan in the home. The COA found the victim's testimony credible and consistent with medical evidence. It addressed the alibi defence, finding it not properly raised and not credible. The COA cited precedents on date variance in indictments and concluded no prejudice was caused. The COA affirmed the HC's conviction and sentence.
coa_sentence_type: 12 years rigorous imprisonment, fine of Rs. 10,000, and compensation of Rs. 250,000
brief_judgment_file_summary: The appellant was convicted by the High Court of Colombo for grave sexual abuse of a child at Vajira children's home and sentenced to 12 years rigorous imprisonment, a fine, and compensation. He appealed on grounds including inconsistency of evidence, delay in complaint, and failure to consider his defence. The Court of Appeal found the victim's testimony credible and the delay justified, and dismissed the appeal, affirming the conviction and sentence.
defence_counsel: Kapila Waidyaratne, P.C. with Nipuna Jagodarachchi, AAL and Akkila Jayasundara, AAL
hc_analysis_summary: The HC found the victim credible and convicted the accused. The COA agreed with the HC's analysis and found no error.
precedents_cited_list: Thimbirigolle Sirirathana Thero v. Attorney General CA/194/2015 | R. V. Dossi, 13 Cr.App.R.158 | Wright V. Nicholson 54 Cr.App.R.38 | Pandithakoralage v. Selvanayagam 56 N.L.R. 143 | State of Uttar Pradesh v. M.K.Anthony 1985 Cri LJ 493 | Ellawala Mudiyanselage Janath v. Director General Commission to Investigate Allegations of Bribery or Corruption C/A appeal 163 of 2004 (10.09.2008) | Mannar Mannan v. the Republic of Sri Lanka 1990 2 Sri LR page 280
standard_of_review_applied: The COA reviewed whether the HC's decision was correct based on the evidence and law.

judges: Menaka Wijesundera J. | Neil Iddawala J.
offence_sections: Section 3 and 4 of the Money Laundering Act
brief_facts_summary: The accused was indicted for purchasing properties valued at Rs 325 lakhs and Rs 265 lakhs from allegedly illegal money from narcotics transactions. The prosecution alleged the money came from her husband, a reputed drug dealer, while the defense claimed lawful income from businesses. The Court of Appeal found the trial judge misapplied the law on presumptions in money laundering.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 3 and 4 of the Money Laundering Act
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court acquitted the accused, concluding that the prosecution failed to prove the money used to purchase the properties was obtained from illegal activities. The trial judge found insufficient evidence to establish the predicate offence.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant argued the trial judge failed to consider the respondent's inability to generate such large sums lawfully and misdirected himself on the law regarding money laundering presumptions. The appeal emphasized that the prosecution need not prove the predicate offence under section 3(3) of the act.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The trial judge failed to consider that the money spent on properties could not be lawful given the respondent's business | The trial judge misdirected himself in concluding the prosecution failed to prove the predicate offence | The trial judge did not properly apply the rebuttable presumption under section 4 of the act
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The prosecution led evidence from 24 witnesses and documents showing large transactions from the accused's business manager's account with vague explanations. The Court of Appeal found the presumption under section 4 applied and the accused failed to rebut it.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal assessed that the rebuttable presumption under section 4 applied, shifting the burden to the accused, who failed to provide sufficient lawful explanation for the funds.
defence_version_summary: The accused pleaded not guilty and made a dock statement, claiming the money came from lawful businesses like motor vehicle sales and money lending. The court found her explanation insufficient to rebut the presumption under the Money Laundering Act.
legal_errors_description: The trial judge misdirected himself by requiring the prosecution to prove the predicate offence and failing to properly apply the rebuttable presumption under section 4 of the Money Laundering Act.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed the money laundering law, highlighting the rebuttable presumption under section 4 and that the prosecution need not prove the predicate offence under section 3(3). They found the evidence showed large, unexplained transactions from the accused's business, and the trial judge erred in law by not shifting the burden to the accused. The acquittal was set aside for a retrial.
coa_sentence_type: Retrial ordered
brief_judgment_file_summary: The Attorney General appealed the High Court's acquittal of the accused on money laundering charges related to purchasing properties with alleged illegal funds. The High Court acquitted due to insufficient proof of illegal sources. The Court of Appeal found legal errors in not applying the rebuttable presumption and set aside the acquittal, ordering a retrial in the High Court.
defence_counsel: Anil Silva, PC with Amaan Bandara
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court acquitted the accused, concluding the prosecution failed to prove the money was from illegal activities. The Court of Appeal criticized this, stating the HC misdirected on the law by not applying the rebuttable presumption and requiring proof of the predicate offence.

judges: Menaka Wijesundera J | Neil Iddawala J
offence_sections: Section 64(1) of the Fauna and Flora Protection Ordinance, as amended
brief_facts_summary: The first accused was charged for using a vehicle to construct buildings and use roads in Bellanwila Sanctuary without permission, violating the Fauna and Flora Protection Ordinance. The accused pleaded guilty and was fined Rs. 15,000. The vehicle was confiscated as the registered owner failed to prove due diligence to prevent its use in illegal activities.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 64(1) of the Fauna and Flora Protection Ordinance, as amended
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court, in revision, affirmed the Magistrate Court's confiscation order, holding that the owner failed to prove due diligence to prevent the vehicle's use in offences.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant appealed against the confiscation order, arguing that she had exercised due diligence by instructing the accused not to use the vehicle for illegal activities and that the vehicle was her only source of income.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The appellant exercised due diligence by instructing the accused not to engage the vehicle in illegal activities. | The vehicle provides the appellant's only source of income.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court analyzed the appellant's testimony and found discrepancies, including failure to mention a prior offence involving the same vehicle. The Court held that the appellant did not exercise due diligence as required.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court assessed on a balance of probability that the appellant failed to prove due diligence.
defence_version_summary: The accused pleaded guilty to the charges. The appellant, as owner, claimed she exercised due diligence by instructing the accused not to use the vehicle illegally, but the Court found her testimony insufficient and not credible.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal upheld the lower courts' decisions, finding that the appellant did not prove due diligence on a balance of probability. The Court noted the vehicle was used in a prior offence and the appellant failed to prevent its use again. The close relationship between the appellant and the accused (husband) made it easier to exercise diligence, but mere instructions were insufficient. The Court applied the principle of natural justice and cited precedent on due diligence.
coa_sentence_type: Fine of Rs. 15,000 and confiscation of vehicle
brief_judgment_file_summary: This appeal concerns the confiscation of a vehicle used in offences under the Fauna and Flora Protection Ordinance. The accused pleaded guilty and was fined. The Magistrate Court ordered confiscation, which was affirmed by the High Court. The appellant, the vehicle owner, appealed on grounds of due diligence. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal, holding that the appellant failed to prove due diligence to prevent the vehicle's use in illegal activities, especially since it was the second offence.
defence_counsel: Sandamal Rajapaksha and Sachira Andrahennadi
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court correctly dismissed the revision application, agreeing with the Magistrate that the owner failed to prove due diligence. The Court of Appeal found no error in the High Court's analysis.
precedents_cited_list: House of Lords in re Hamilton on 1981 AC 1038
standard_of_review_applied: Balance of probability for proving due diligence
sentencing_principles_applied: Due diligence and confiscation under Section 64(1) of the Fauna and Flora Protection Ordinance

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 364(2) read with Section 364(2)(e) of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The Appellant, a class teacher, was accused of raping a 10-year-old student in the school changing room. The incident was revealed 16 months later when the victim reported another rape. Key evidence included the victim's testimony, but no medical evidence or corroboration from other students was presented.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 364(2) read with Section 364(2)(e) of the Penal Code
hc_sentence_type: 18 years rigorous imprisonment, fine of Rs.25,000, and compensation of Rs.500,000
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the Appellant of rape based on the evidence presented and sentenced him to 18 years rigorous imprisonment with a fine and compensation.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The Appellant contended that the prosecution failed to prove the case beyond reasonable doubt due to lack of corroboration, contradictions in evidence, and delay in reporting. The Medico-Legal Report was also challenged as hearsay.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Prosecution evidence not proven beyond reasonable doubt | Lack of corroboration for victim's testimony | Contradictions in victim's statements | Delay in reporting the incident | Medico-Legal Report contains inadmissible hearsay
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed the victim's testimony and found it uncorroborated, with contradictions in her statements. Medical evidence was weak, and prosecution failed to call key witnesses.
probability_assessment_by_court: Court found reasonable doubt due to lack of corroboration and contradictions in evidence.
defence_version_summary: The Appellant pleaded not guilty, denied the incident, gave evidence from the witness box, and called several witnesses. The court assessed the prosecution evidence as insufficient for conviction.
legal_errors_description: High Court erred in accepting prosecutrix's evidence without corroboration for rape charge, causing prejudice to fair trial.
procedural_defects_description: Prosecution failed to call fellow students who were present at the time of the incident, despite naming them as witnesses.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: COA reviewed the evidence, applied precedents on corroboration in sexual offence cases, and found the victim's testimony uncorroborated with weak medical evidence. Noting the delay in reporting and failure to call witnesses, COA held that rape conviction was untenable but found sufficient evidence for sexual harassment under Section 345 of the Penal Code.
coa_sentence_type: Five years rigorous imprisonment, fine of Rs.10,000, and compensation of Rs.300,000
brief_judgment_file_summary: The Appellant, a teacher, was convicted by the High Court of raping a student and sentenced to 18 years imprisonment. On appeal, the Court of Appeal found the evidence insufficient for rape but sufficient for sexual harassment, modifying the conviction to sexual harassment and reducing the sentence to 5 years imprisonment with fine and compensation.
defence_counsel: A.S.M.Perera, P.C. with Uvindu Jayasiri and Chathunika Vitharana
hc_analysis_summary: High Court convicted based on victim's testimony without corroboration. COA viewed this as an error due to lack of supporting evidence and contradictions.
precedents_cited_list: Gamini Dolawatte V. Attorney General [1988] 1 Sri. L. R 221 | Sunil and Another v. The Attorney General [1986] 1 Sri.L.R. 230 | State of Andra Pradesh v. Garigula Satya Vani Murty AIR 1997 SC 1588 | Iswari Prasad v. Mohamed Isa 1963 AIR (SC) 1728 at 1734
standard_of_review_applied: Review of evidence for reasonable doubt and corroboration principles
sentencing_principles_applied: Sentencing under Section 345 of Penal Code for sexual harassment, considering compensation for injuries
final_charge_after_appeal: Section 345 of the Penal Code (sexual harassment)

judges: K. Priyantha Fernando, J (P/CA) | Wickum A. Kaluarachchi, J
offence_sections: Section 54A(b) and 54A(d) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance
brief_facts_summary: The accused-appellant was arrested by PW-3, a police officer, while traveling on a bus for possessing and trafficking 3.98 grams of heroin. PW-3 found heroin in pink cellophane bags in a black bag held by the appellant. The appellant denied possession, claiming an unknown woman handed the bag to PW-3, who then falsely implicated him.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 54A(b) and 54A(d) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the appellant for trafficking and possessing heroin based on the evidence of PW-3. The judge found the prosecution case proved beyond reasonable doubt and rejected the defence version as improbable.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: In written submissions, two grounds were raised: failure to apply correct legal principles when rejecting defence evidence and failure to consider credibility of prosecution witnesses. At the hearing, counsel focused on whether the appellant was the correct person arrested.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: That the learned trial Judge failed in applying the correct legal principles when rejecting the defence evidence. | The Learned Trial Judge erred in law by failing to consider the credibility of the evidence of prosecution witnesses.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The court analyzed PW-3's testimony as credible and consistent, while the defence version was found highly improbable. Contradictions in prosecution evidence were deemed immaterial since the appellant admitted the heroin was found.
probability_assessment_by_court: The court found the defence version highly improbable and no reasonable doubt raised on the prosecution case.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty, gave evidence denying possession, and claimed an unknown woman handed the bag to PW-3. The court found this version improbable and did not cast reasonable doubt.
procedural_defects_description: Failure to record statement of PW-3 by the HQI, but no prejudice caused to the appellant.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The COA reviewed the evidence, found PW-3's testimony credible and the defence version improbable. Contradictions in prosecution evidence were considered immaterial as the appellant admitted the heroin was found. The COA agreed with the HC that charges were proved beyond reasonable doubt and affirmed the convictions and sentences.
coa_sentence_type: Life Imprisonment
brief_judgment_file_summary: The appellant was convicted by the High Court of Panadura for trafficking and possessing heroin and sentenced to life imprisonment. On appeal, he challenged the conviction on grounds including identification issues and procedural errors. The Court of Appeal found no merit in the appeal, upheld the convictions and sentences, and dismissed the appeal.
defence_counsel: Mohan Sellapperuma with Sandeepani Wijesooriya
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted based on credible prosecution evidence and rejected the improbable defence version. The Court of Appeal agreed with this analysis and found no errors.
standard_of_review_applied: Review of evidence and legal principles

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Sections 141, 296 read with 146, 300 read with 146, 296 read with 32, and 300 read with 32 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The deceased and PW-01 were fired upon while riding a motorbike near Sugathadasa Stadium in Colombo. PW-01 identified some assailants, but eyewitness evidence was contradictory. The prosecution alleged an unlawful assembly with common object to commit murder.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Sections 141, 296 read with 146, 300 read with 146, 296 read with 32, and 300 read with 32 of the Penal Code
hc_sentence_type: Death penalty for murder, 2 years rigorous imprisonment for unlawful assembly, 20 years rigorous imprisonment for attempted murder
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted all appellants for unlawful assembly, murder, and attempted murder, sentencing them to death and imprisonment. The judge found them guilty based on eyewitness testimony and common object.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: Appellants challenged the conviction citing contradictions between PW-01 and PW-02, unreliable identification, failure to apply Turnbull principles, and lack of evidence for unlawful assembly membership.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Evidence of PW-02 regarding identification of 1st accused appellant was self-contradictory and unreliable | Learned High Court Judge failed to address contradictions in evidence of PW-01 and PW-02 | Learned High Court Judge failed to apply Turnbull principles in relation to proof of identity | Conviction based on unlawful assembly is unsustainable on evidence | Evidence of PW-01 and 02 was contradictory and prosecution failed to properly identify 3rd accused appellant | Prosecution failed to prove case beyond reasonable doubt | Learned High Court Judge acted on insufficient evidence | Learned High Court Judge failed to analyze evidence in its totality
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the evidence of PW-01 and PW-02 contradictory on material points, making it unsafe to rely on for conviction.
probability_assessment_by_court: The court found the evidence contradictory and unsafe for conviction, leading to reasonable doubt.
defence_version_summary: The appellants pleaded not guilty and contended that prosecution failed to prove their involvement. They argued that mere presence at the scene does not constitute membership in an unlawful assembly.
legal_errors_description: The High Court Judge failed to address contradictions in witness evidence and apply Turnbull principles for identification, and incorrectly found unlawful assembly without sufficient evidence.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal thoroughly examined the evidence of PW-01 and PW-02, highlighting material contradictions regarding the identification and roles of the appellants. It applied legal principles from Kulathunga Vs. Mudalihamy and Dr. Gour's Penal Law, emphasizing that mere presence does not make one a member of an unlawful assembly. The court found that the prosecution failed to establish common object or common intention, and the evidence was unreliable. Consequently, the convictions were deemed unsafe.
coa_sentence_type: Acquitted, no sentence
brief_judgment_file_summary: Four appellants were convicted by the High Court of Colombo for unlawful assembly, murder, and attempted murder, receiving death penalty and imprisonment. They appealed on grounds of contradictory eyewitness evidence and insufficient proof of unlawful assembly. The Court of Appeal found the evidence of PW-01 and PW-02 unreliable and contradictory, failing to establish common object or common intention. Referring to legal precedents, the court allowed the appeals and acquitted all appellants.
defence_counsel: Indica Mallawaratchy; Nalin Dissanayake, P.C. with Vishwa Rajapaksha and Kelum Ubeysekara; Nagitha Wijesekara
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted based on eyewitness testimony without adequately addressing contradictions. The Court of Appeal found this approach flawed, as the evidence did not prove unlawful assembly or common intention beyond reasonable doubt.
precedents_cited_list: Kulathunga Vs. Mudalihamy 42 NLR 331 | King Vs. Asarappu 50 NLR 324 | SC Appeal 20/2003 (Bindunuwewa Massacre Case)
standard_of_review_applied: The court reviewed whether the prosecution proved the case beyond reasonable doubt, assessing witness credibility and legal principles.

judges: K. PRIYANTHA FERNANDO, J. (P/CA) | WICKUM A. KALUARACHCHI, J.
offence_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The appellant was accused of murdering his father-in-law by assaulting him with a sword at the deceased's house. Key evidence includes eyewitness testimony from the deceased's wife and a neighbor, and the appellant's dock statement claiming self-defence. The appellant had a pending divorce case with the deceased's daughter.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court found the appellant guilty of murder beyond reasonable doubt and sentenced him to death. The trial judge rejected the defence version and accepted prosecution evidence.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant appealed on grounds that evidence was insufficient to prove murder beyond reasonable doubt, and the trial judge wrongfully rejected the dock statement. The appellant contended that the offence should be reduced to culpable homicide not amounting to murder due to a sudden fight.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The items of evidence are not sufficient to prove the prosecution’s case against the appellant beyond reasonable doubt. | The rejection of evidence of the accused is wrongful, and the learned Judge of the High Court has failed to correctly apply the principles governing the evaluation of a dock statement.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the prosecution evidence sufficient and credible, while the defence version was rejected due to lack of corroborating evidence. The appellant's claim of injury was not supported by witness testimony or medical reports.
probability_assessment_by_court: The court found that the prosecution proved the case beyond reasonable doubt and that the defence version did not create reasonable doubt.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty and gave an unsworn dock statement claiming self-defence, alleging the deceased struck him first. The defence called witnesses including the appellant's mother and a driver, but their testimony was discredited by the court. The court assessed the defence as not credible due to lack of corroborating evidence.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal thoroughly reviewed the evidence and found that the prosecution had proven the charge of murder beyond reasonable doubt. They rejected the appellant's claim of a sudden fight and entitlement to exception 4 under section 294, noting the absence of evidence for the appellant's injuries and the prior threats made by the appellant. The court upheld the trial judge's evaluation of the dock statement and the reasons for rejecting the defence evidence. Precedent was cited to emphasize the duty of the judge to consider alternative charges if evidence supports it, but in this case, no such basis was found. The appeal was dismissed.
coa_sentence_type: Death
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused-appellant was convicted of murder under section 296 of the Penal Code by the High Court of Kalutara and sentenced to death. He appealed on grounds of insufficient evidence and wrongful rejection of his dock statement, arguing for culpable homicide not amounting to murder due to sudden fight. The Court of Appeal examined the evidence, found no basis for sudden fight, and upheld the High Court's decision, dismissing the appeal and affirming the conviction and death sentence.
prosecution_counsel: Sudarshana De Silva, Deputy Solicitor General
defence_counsel: Chathura Amarathunga
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court found the appellant guilty of murder based on eyewitness testimony and rejected the defence version. The Court of Appeal agreed with this analysis and found no errors in the High Court's reasoning.
precedents_cited_list: King v. Bellana Vitanage Eddin 41 NLR 345
standard_of_review_applied: Appellate review of evidence and legal principles

judges: Menaka Wijesunder J. | Neil Iddawala J.
offence_sections: Poisons Opium and Dangerous drugs Ordinance
brief_facts_summary: The accused was taken into custody on July 27, 2016 for possessing 300 grams of a substance suspected to be heroin. The Government Analyst Report confirmed 145.94 grams of heroin. The accused has been in remand since 2016, and the trial has not commenced despite indictment in 2019.
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court of Negombo refused bail on December 14, 2021, based on the high amount of heroin involved and the trial postponement attributed to the defence counsel.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The petitioner argued that the accused has been in remand for an excessively long period since 2016 without trial commencement, which constitutes exceptional circumstances for bail.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Long period of remand without trial conclusion | Excessive delay in trial proceedings
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The primary evidence is the Government Analyst Report confirming heroin possession. No witness testimony is evaluated in this bail application.
defence_version_summary: Trial not commenced; bail application argued based on excessive remand period without defence version on merits.
legal_errors_description: High Court failed to consider the long remand period as exceptional circumstances for bail.
procedural_defects_description: State Counsel objected verbally but failed to file written objections as per rule 52 of the Supreme Court rules.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found that the accused has been in remand for 7 years without trial, constituting exceptional circumstances. They cited precedent on delay and noted procedural failures by the State Counsel. Consequently, the court set aside the High Court order and directed bail with suitable conditions.
brief_judgment_file_summary: This revision application challenges the High Court's refusal to grant bail. The accused, arrested in 2016 for heroin possession, has been in remand for 7 years without trial. The Court of Appeal identified excessive delay and procedural errors, set aside the High Court order, and directed the accused's release on bail with suitable conditions.
defence_counsel: I.B.S. Harshana
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court refused bail due to the high amount of heroin and trial postponement by defence counsel. The Court of Appeal found this refusal erroneous given the exceptional circumstances of prolonged remand.
precedents_cited_list: Attorney General vs. Ediriveera (2006 1 SLR Pg 25) | Christopher v. Don Paul, [1990] 2SLR L R 54 (CA)
standard_of_review_applied: Discretionary review based on exceptional circumstances for bail under the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance.

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Sections 296, 410, 315 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: On 17-09-2004, during a Kovil festival, an altercation arose over who should carry the statue. The first appellant cut the deceased's hand with a pruning knife, and all appellants followed the deceased to his house, assaulted him, damaged property, and injured his wife and another person. The accused denied involvement in the incident.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Sections 296, 410, 315 of the Penal Code
hc_sentence_type: Death sentence on count one; rigorous imprisonment on other counts with fines and compensation
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court found all appellants guilty of murder, mischief, and causing injuries. They were sentenced to death on the murder count, and rigorous imprisonment with fines and compensation on other counts. The conviction was based on the evidence presented during the trial.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellants appealed on two grounds: that the medical evidence does not support a murder conviction as injuries were not proven sufficient to cause death, and that the evidence warrants consideration of lesser culpability.
