judges: K. Priyantha Fernando, J. (P/CA) | Wickum A. Kaluarachchi, J.
offence_sections: Section 365B(2)b of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The victim, a 10-year-old girl, was sexually abused by her uncle when she was alone at home. Her father discovered the incident and found semen on the bedsheet. The complaint was delayed by about eleven months, which the prosecution explained. The appellant alleged a false complaint due to a land dispute.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 365B(2)b of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the appellant based on the victim's credible testimony, imposing 12 years rigorous imprisonment, a fine of Rs. 25,000, and compensation of Rs. 200,000. The court accepted the prosecution's explanation for the delay in reporting.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant argued that the prosecution failed to prove the charge beyond reasonable doubt, citing the delay of eleven months in reporting and the uncorroborated testimony of the child victim. He also claimed the complaint was false due to a land dispute.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Prosecution failed to prove charge beyond reasonable doubt | Delay of eleven months affects credibility of victim's testimony | Complaint was false due to land dispute
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the victim's testimony credible and consistent, noting that delay in reporting was reasonably explained due to her age and social context. The land dispute claim was rejected as an afterthought.
probability_assessment_by_court: Court assessed victim's testimony as credible and found no reasonable doubt, considering the explained delay and consistency.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty and gave an unsworn statement from the dock alleging a false complaint due to a land dispute. He called no witnesses. The court rejected this defence as an afterthought.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed the delay in complaint, citing precedents that allow for belated statements if reasonably explained. It considered the victim's young age and village setting, finding her testimony credible and sufficient for conviction without corroboration. The land dispute claim was dismissed as unconvincing. The court affirmed the High Court's judgment, emphasizing the trial judge's opportunity to observe witness demeanor.
coa_sentence_type: 12 years rigorous imprisonment, Fine of Rs. 25,000, Compensation of Rs. 200,000
brief_judgment_file_summary: The appellant was convicted by the High Court of Ratnapura for grave sexual abuse of a 10-year-old girl under section 365B(2)b of the Penal Code and sentenced to 12 years rigorous imprisonment, a fine, and compensation. He appealed, arguing that the prosecution failed to prove the charge beyond reasonable doubt due to delay and uncorroborated testimony, and alleged a false complaint due to a land dispute. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal, finding the victim's testimony credible, the delay reasonably explained, and the land dispute claim an afterthought. The conviction and sentence were affirmed.
defence_counsel: A. S. M. Perera, P.C. with Prabodhini Kumarawadu and Uvindu Jayasiri
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court accepted the victim's evidence and the prosecution's explanation for the delay in reporting. The Court of Appeal agreed, noting the trial judge's proper assessment of witness credibility.
precedents_cited_list: Haramanis v. Somalatha [1998] 3 Sri L.R 365 | Samarakoon v. The Republic [2004] 2 Sri L.R. 20 | Kahandagamage Dharmasiri v. AG SC appeal 4 of 2009, SC/SPL/LA 165 of 2008 | Anil Phukan v. State of Assam [1993] 3SCC 282 | Wijepala v. Attorney General SC Appeal 104/99 3rd October 2000
standard_of_review_applied: The Court of Appeal reviewed the evidence for sufficiency and credibility, applying principles regarding belated statements and corroboration in sexual offence cases.

judges: K. Priyantha Fernando, J (P/CA) | Wickum A. Kaluarachchi, J
offence_sections: Section 54A(b) and 54A(d) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance as amended by Act No.13 of 1984
brief_facts_summary: On February 1, 2014, police conducted a raid on a house in Panadura based on information from an informant. They found the accused-appellant sitting on a bed packing heroin into cellophane bags. He was arrested with 5 cellophane bags containing 200 packets of heroin. The prosecution relied on police eyewitness testimony and the recovered drugs.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 54A(b) and 54A(d) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance as amended by Act No.13 of 1984
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the accused-appellant for trafficking and possession of heroin based on police testimony and recovered drugs. The judge found the prosecution case proved beyond reasonable doubt and sentenced him to life imprisonment on both counts.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant argued that the prosecution failed to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt, that there was non-identification of the raid vehicle and its driver, and that there were contradictions between prosecution witnesses' evidence.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The learned trial Judge has failed to realize that the prosecution has not proved its case beyond a reasonable doubt. | The learned trial Judge has failed to appreciate the fact that non-identification of the vehicle which was used for the raid and its driver. | The learned trial Judge erred in law by failing to consider inter se contradictions between the evidence of prosecution witnesses.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal examined the contradictions in prosecution witnesses' testimonies and found them minor and not casting reasonable doubt. The evidence of PW-1 and PW-3 was consistent on key points, and the defence failed to cross-examine on material aspects, leading to acceptance of prosecution evidence.
probability_assessment_by_court: The court found that minor contradictions and improbabilities did not raise reasonable doubt, especially since the defence failed to cross-examine on material facts.
defence_version_summary: The accused pleaded not guilty and made a brief dock statement without denying the prosecution evidence. He did not call any defence witnesses. The court found the prosecution evidence unchallenged on key elements.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal rejected the appellant's grounds, holding that the use of a private vehicle for the raid was not improbable, and any contradictions in witness testimony were not material. The court emphasized that the defence did not challenge key prosecution evidence in cross-examination, and under legal principles, unchallenged evidence must be accepted. The COA found no reasonable doubt in the prosecution case and upheld the High Court's convictions and sentences.
coa_sentence_type: Life Imprisonment
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused-appellant was charged with trafficking and possession of heroin in the High Court of Panadura and convicted to life imprisonment. He appealed on grounds including failure to prove beyond reasonable doubt, non-identification of raid vehicle, and contradictions in prosecution evidence. The Court of Appeal examined these grounds, found the contradictions minor and the raid procedures acceptable, and noted the defence's failure to cross-examine material points. Citing legal precedents on unchallenged evidence, the COA held the prosecution case was proved beyond reasonable doubt and dismissed the appeal, affirming the convictions and sentences.
defence_counsel: Mohan Sellapperuma
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted the appellant based on police testimony and recovered drugs. The Court of Appeal agreed with the High Court's finding that the prosecution proved its case beyond reasonable doubt and found no merit in the appeal grounds.
precedents_cited_list: Sarvan Singh v. State of Punjab (2002 AIR SC (iii) 3652) | Himachal Pradesh v. Thakur Dass (1983) 2 Cri. L. J. 1694 | Motilal v. State of Madhya Pradesh (1990) Criminal Law Journal NOC 125 MP | Ratnayake Mudiyanselage Premachandra v. The Hon. Attorney General - C.A Case No. 79/2011
standard_of_review_applied: Review of evidence for reasonable doubt and legal errors

judges: N. Bandula Karunarathna, J. | R. Gurusinghe, J.
offence_sections: Section 54A of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance, as amended by Act No. 13 of 1984
brief_facts_summary: The appellant was arrested for possessing and trafficking 82 grams and 43 milligrams of heroin. Police received a tip-off, conducted a raid, and arrested him at Mahawatte junction. The defence claimed he was arrested at his residence and that heroin was planted.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 54A of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance, as amended by Act No. 13 of 1984
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the appellant of possession and trafficking of heroin based on prosecution evidence and sentenced him to life imprisonment.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant challenged the conviction on grounds of credibility and probability of prosecution evidence, and failure of the High Court Judge to evaluate the defence evidence and give reasons for rejecting the dock statement.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The evidence of the prosecution witnesses failed the test of credibility and test of probability. | The learned High Court Judge has failed to evaluate the evidence given by the appellant and failed to give reasons for the rejection of the dock statement made by the appellant.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found material contradictions between the testimonies of PW1 and PW4 regarding the arrest sequence, casting doubt on the prosecution case.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court assessed the probability of the informant's detailed information and found it doubtful, contributing to reasonable doubt.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty and made a dock statement claiming he was arrested at his residence, assaulted, and heroin was planted. The defence was consistent from the Magistrate's Court proceedings.
legal_errors_description: The High Court Judge failed to evaluate the defence evidence and address contradictions in prosecution evidence.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal identified glaring contradictions between prosecution witnesses, particularly PW1 and PW4, on material points such as the arrest sequence. It found the informant's information improbably detailed and doubted its truthfulness. The High Court had not evaluated the defence evidence or given reasons for rejecting the dock statement, amounting to a denial of fair trial. These issues created reasonable doubt, leading to the acquittal.
coa_sentence_type: Acquitted, no sentence imposed
brief_judgment_file_summary: The appellant was convicted by the High Court for possession and trafficking of heroin and sentenced to life imprisonment. On appeal, the Court of Appeal found material contradictions in prosecution evidence and failure to evaluate defence evidence, creating reasonable doubt. The appeal was allowed, and the appellant was acquitted.
defence_counsel: Neranjan Jayasinghe
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court relied on prosecution evidence without adequately addressing contradictions or evaluating the defence version, which the Court of Appeal found erroneous.
standard_of_review_applied: Evaluation of evidence for credibility and reasonable doubt

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: section 300 read with section 32 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: On 12-07-2005, the complainant (PW-01) was returning home by foot bicycle after attending church. Near the appellant's house, the appellant shot at him, causing a leg injury. The appellant and complainant were known to each other and had previous enmity. The other accused (appellant's brothers) were present but not involved in the shooting.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: section 300 read with section 32 of the Penal Code
hc_sentence_type: 4 years rigorous imprisonment, fine of Rs.10,000, and compensation of Rs.50,000
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the appellant of attempted murder based on the evidence of the injured eyewitness (PW-01) and medical evidence. The other accused were acquitted due to lack of evidence.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant argued that his identity was not properly established, his defence was wrongly rejected, the prosecution failed to prove the case beyond reasonable doubt, the judge considered extraneous material, and the judgment did not comply with procedural requirements. He also contended the sentence was excessive.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The learned High Court Judge has failed to consider whether the identity of the appellant has been properly established by the prosecution. | The defence put forward by the appellant has been wrongly evaluated and rejected. | The learned High Court Judge has failed to come to a finding whether the charge has been proved beyond reasonable doubt. | The learned High Court Judge has taken into consideration extraneous and irrelevant material which was not in evidence. | The learned High Court Judge has failed to fulfill the requirements of section 283 of the Code of Criminal Procedure Act. | In any event, the sentence was excessive given the facts and the circumstances of the case.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the evidence of PW-01 cogent and trustworthy, and the medical evidence consistent with his account. The investigating officer's omission regarding street lights was not considered material.
probability_assessment_by_court: The court found the prosecution proved the case beyond reasonable doubt based on the credible eyewitness identification and consistent medical evidence.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty, made a dock statement claiming he was at home and was falsely implicated due to previous enmity. The court found his defence not credible and the prosecution case established.
legal_errors_description: The High Court Judge misdirected by considering that there were lights in nearby houses, which was not in evidence, but this error did not prejudice the appellant.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed the identification evidence, noting the witness had sufficient street light and knew the appellant. It found the medical evidence consistent and the investigating officer's omissions immaterial. The court held the misdirection on light sources did not prejudice the appellant. It affirmed the conviction and sentence, finding the sentence lenient given a firearm was used.
coa_sentence_type: 4 years rigorous imprisonment, fine of Rs.10,000, and compensation of Rs.50,000
brief_judgment_file_summary: The 1st accused-appellant was convicted of attempted murder by the High Court of Negombo and sentenced to imprisonment, a fine, and compensation. He appealed on grounds including identification, misdirection, procedural error, and excessive sentence. The Court of Appeal found the identification was reliable, any misdirection did not cause prejudice, and the sentence was not excessive. The appeal was dismissed and the conviction affirmed.
defence_counsel: Nalin Ladduwahetty, P.C. with Kavithri Ubeysekara
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted based on the eyewitness and medical evidence. The Court of Appeal found a misdirection regarding light sources but held it did not prejudice the appellant or cause a failure of justice.
precedents_cited_list: Rex Vs. Turnbull and Another (1977) QB 224 | R Vs. Wood and Brown [Ann-Reg. 1784] | E.R.S.R. Coomaraswamy 'The Law of Evidence' Volume 1
standard_of_review_applied: The court reviewed whether the conviction was safe and if any errors prejudiced the appellant's substantial rights or caused a failure of justice.
sentencing_principles_applied: The court considered the use of a firearm and found the sentence lenient.

judges: N. Bandula Karunarathna J. | R. Gurusinghe J.
offence_sections: Section 365(b)(2)(b) of the Penal Code as amended by Act No. 22 of 1995 and Act No. 29 of 1998
brief_facts_summary: The accused-appellant was convicted of committing grave sexual abuse on his daughter (the victim) over a period from 2005-2007 when she was under 16 years old. The victim reported the abuse to her mother, but a police complaint was only lodged in 2007 after the mother was assaulted by the appellant. Key evidence included the victim's testimony, medical evidence from a Judicial Medical Officer, and police observations of a peephole and adult films.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 365(b)(2)(b) of the Penal Code as amended by Act No. 22 of 1995 and Act No. 29 of 1998
hc_sentence_type: 45 years rigorous imprisonment (15 years for each of 3 counts, consecutive), fine, and compensation
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court found the appellant guilty on all three counts of grave sexual abuse. The court imposed sentences of 15 years rigorous imprisonment per count, fines, and compensation, ordering the sentences to run consecutively.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant argued the conviction was unsafe due to inordinate delay in lodging the complaint, that the prosecution version failed the test of probability, and that the trial judge's assessment of witness credibility was flawed. He also contended that the basis of conviction (corroboration by medical and police evidence) was flawed, that the trial judge misdirected himself on a critical fact when evaluating the dock statement, and that the prosecution's failure to lead evidence of a witness entitled the court to draw an adverse inference.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Conviction of the appellant is unsafe in view of the inordinate delay in lodging the first complaint. | The prosecution version woefully fails the test of probability. | The assessment of the testimonial trustworthiness of the prosecution witnesses by the learned Trial Judge is deficient and flawed. | Basis of the conviction being that the evidence of the victim is corroborated by medical evidence and police evidence is flawed. | When evaluating the dock statement, the learned Trial Judge has misdirected himself on a critical issue of fact, thereby causing serious prejudice to the appellant. | Failure on the part of the prosecution to lead the evidence of PW/4 namely Akash Collure entitles the court to draw an adverse inference against the prosecution in terms of sec. 114(f) of the evidence ordinance.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the victim's testimony credible and consistent with medical and police evidence. The mother's testimony, while delayed, was accepted given the social stigma and threats. The court held the trial judge correctly assessed the evidence.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal found the prosecution version probable, accepting explanations for delay (threats, social stigma) and noting the victim's injuries were consistent with abuse.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty, made a dock statement denying the allegations, and claimed the complaint was a false implication motivated by marital disputes and an assault complaint by his wife. He called no witnesses. The court found his defence lacked credibility and was inconsistent.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal grounds, finding the delay in complaint was explained by fear and social stigma. It held the victim's evidence was credible and corroborated by medical evidence (JMO findings of hymenal wear consistent with prolonged pressure) and police evidence (peephole, adult films). The court found no misdirection by the trial judge and noted the appellant's violent nature supported the threat explanation. It affirmed the conviction but modified the sentence to run concurrently, citing lack of previous convictions.
coa_sentence_type: 15 years rigorous imprisonment for each of 3 counts to run concurrently. Fine of Rs. 10,000 per count with default sentence of 6 months simple imprisonment per count (consecutive). Compensation of Rs. 100,000 per count with default sentence of 10 months simple imprisonment per count (consecutive).
brief_judgment_file_summary: The Court of Appeal considered an appeal against a High Court conviction for three counts of grave sexual abuse on the appellant's daughter. The High Court had imposed consecutive sentences totaling 45 years rigorous imprisonment, fines, and compensation. The appellant challenged the conviction on grounds of delay, improbability, flawed evidence assessment, and misdirection. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal, affirming the conviction but modifying the sentences to run concurrently, citing lack of previous convictions.
defence_counsel: Indica Mallawaratchy AAL with Dinaru Bandara
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court found the victim's evidence credible and corroborated by medical and police evidence. The Court of Appeal agreed with the High Court's reasoning on the conviction but found the consecutive sentencing required modification, leading to a concurrent sentence.
precedents_cited_list: Athukorale vs. The Attorney General 50 NLR 256 | Rajarathnam vs. The Republic of Sri Lanka 79 NLR 73 | The King vs. Ana Sheriff 42 NLR 169 | Jarlis vs. The King 52 NLR 457 | Bandara vs. The State 2001 (2) SLR 63 | Bharvada Bhoginibhai Hilijibhai vs. State of Gujarat 1983, AIR 753 | State of Andra Pradesh vs. Garigula Satya Vani Murthy AIR 1997 SC 1588 | Mohamed Niyas Naufer & Others V. Attorney General SC Appeal. 01/2006 decided on 08.12.2006
standard_of_review_applied: The court applied a standard of not lightly interfering with factual findings of trial judges, but noted the trial judge in this case did not have the advantage of observing witness demeanor, so the COA conducted its own analysis of the evidence.
sentencing_principles_applied: The court considered the appellant's lack of previous convictions and modified the sentences to run concurrently. It also altered the default sentences for fine and compensation.

judges: K. Priyantha Fernando, J (P/CA) | Wickum A. Kaluarachchi, J
offence_sections: Sections 16(b), 19(c), and 25(2) of the Bribery Act
brief_facts_summary: The three accused-appellants were police officers who raided an illicit liquor business operated by the complainant. They solicited bribes to refrain from charging for all seized goda barrels. The complainant reported to the Bribery Commission, leading to a sting operation where bribes were allegedly accepted. The accused denied the charges.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Sections 16(b), 19(c), and 25(2) of the Bribery Act
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court found the accused guilty of soliciting and accepting bribes, accepting the prosecution version beyond reasonable doubt.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellants argued that the High Court judge failed to correctly evaluate the improbable prosecution version and the probable defense version. They contended that the prosecution evidence was contradictory and that there was motivation to fabricate charges.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Failure to correctly evaluate improbable prosecution version and probable defense version | Contradictions in prosecution evidence regarding solicitation | Lack of evidence for acceptance of bribe | Defense version more probable than prosecution version
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found contradictions in the prosecution witness testimonies, particularly regarding the purpose of the bribe, and found the defense version more probable.
probability_assessment_by_court: The court found that the prosecution evidence was contradictory and that the defense version cast reasonable doubt, leading to acquittal.
defence_version_summary: The accused pleaded not guilty and made unsworn statements from the dock denying all charges. They alleged that the complainant fabricated the story due to motivation, and that money was forcibly offered. The court found the defense version more probable than the prosecution version.
legal_errors_description: The High Court judge failed to properly evaluate the contradictions in prosecution evidence and the probability of the defense version.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal thoroughly analyzed the prosecution evidence, highlighting contradictions in the testimony regarding the solicitation and purpose of the bribe. They found that the prosecution version was improbable given the timing and circumstances, such as the case being finalized before the bribe was offered. The defense version that the charges were fabricated was deemed more probable. The court emphasized that in criminal cases, if the defense casts reasonable doubt on the prosecution case, the accused must be acquitted.
coa_sentence_type: Acquitted, no sentence imposed
brief_judgment_file_summary: Three police officers were convicted by the High Court for soliciting and accepting bribes from an illicit liquor dealer. They appealed to the Court of Appeal, arguing that the prosecution evidence was contradictory and improbable. The Court of Appeal found significant contradictions in the witness testimonies and that the prosecution version was unlikely given the circumstances. The defense version that the charges were fabricated was considered more probable. Therefore, the appeals were allowed, the convictions set aside, and all accused acquitted.
prosecution_counsel: Sudharshana De Silva, DSG with Thanuja Bandara and Gayan Madawage for the Respondent
defence_counsel: Nalin Ladduwahetti, PC with Hafeel Farisz, Kavithri Obeysekara and Rajith Samarasekara for the 1st Accused-Appellant; Duminda De Alwis with Charuni De Alwis for the 2nd Accused-Appellant; Shantha Perera, PC with Sweeni Suraweera and Mahanama Dissanayake for the 3rd Accused-Appellant
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court accepted the prosecution evidence without adequately considering contradictions and the improbability of the story. The Court of Appeal found this evaluation flawed, leading to wrongful conviction.
standard_of_review_applied: Review of evidence for reasonable doubt and probability assessment

judges: N. Bandula Karunarathna, J. | R. Gurusinghe, J.
offence_sections: Section 296 read with section 32 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The appellant was convicted for the murder of Ramalingam Balasubramaniam during a fight. The incident involved a fight between the appellant's brother and the deceased's brother, after which the appellant hit the deceased with a cricket stump, causing one injury. The appellant was 15 years old at the time of the offence.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 296 read with section 32 of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the appellant of murder and sentenced him to death, while acquitting the 2nd and 3rd accused. The judgment was based on the evidence presented.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant argued that he was only 15 years old at the time of the offence, so the death sentence should not have been imposed under section 53 of the Penal Code. Additionally, he contended that there was a sudden fight, the deceased had only one non-fatal injury, no deadly weapon was used, and he lacked murderous intention.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Appellant was 15 years old at time of offence | Death sentence should not have been imposed per section 53 of Penal Code | Sudden fight with only one non-fatal injury | No deadly weapon used | No murderous intention
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The court evaluated evidence of the fight, noting that the appellant struck only one blow with a cricket stump, and medical evidence confirmed the injury was not necessarily fatal. Mitigating factors like the appellant's age were considered.
probability_assessment_by_court: Court assessed that as a juvenile, appellant had less culpability based on precedent.
defence_version_summary: The appellant appealed conviction, arguing not guilty due to sudden fight, single non-fatal injury, and lack of murderous intention. The court considered these factors in sentencing.
legal_errors_description: High Court imposed death sentence on a juvenile, which after amendment of section 53 of Penal Code is not permitted.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: COA considered the appellant's age at the time of offence, the amended section 53 of the Penal Code, and mitigating factors. They referenced precedent on juvenile culpability, set aside the death sentence due to legal error, and imposed rigorous imprisonment after evaluating the circumstances of the fight and injury.
coa_sentence_type: Rigorous Imprisonment 7 years
brief_judgment_file_summary: The appellant was convicted of murder by the High Court of Ratnapura and sentenced to death. He appealed, arguing his juvenile age and the circumstances of the offence. The Court of Appeal partially allowed the appeal, set aside the death sentence based on amended law prohibiting death penalty for juveniles, and imposed 7 years rigorous imprisonment, considering mitigating factors and precedent.
defence_counsel: Darshana Kuruppu with Sajini Elvitigala, Dineru Bandara, Buddhika Thilakarathna, Sudanha de Silva and Chinthaka Udadeniya
hc_analysis_summary: High Court convicted the appellant of murder and sentenced him to death based on evidence. COA found that imposing death sentence on a juvenile was an error due to amended law.
precedents_cited_list: Pannangalage Don Nilanka and another vs Hon. Attorney General SC Appeal 139 /2014 | Thompson v. Oklahoma 487 U.S. 815 (1988)
standard_of_review_applied: Review of legal error in sentencing and consideration of mitigating factors
sentencing_principles_applied: Consideration of age as mitigating factor, principles from juvenile sentencing precedents

judges: N. Bandula Karunarathna, J. | R. Gurusinghe, J.
offence_sections: Section 22 of Firearms Ordinance No. 33 of 1916 as amended by Act No 22 of 1996 and Section 27(1) of Explosives Act No 21 of 1956 as amended by Act No. 33 of 1969
brief_facts_summary: On March 13, 2002, police patrolling in Pesale arrested the appellant and another person after one of three individuals fled. The appellant was found carrying a fertilizer bag containing a T56 assault rifle and 45 live cartridges. The prosecution relied on the chain of custody, but there was a significant gap. The appellant claimed that an LTTE cadre shoved the bag at him and ran away.
evidence_type_secondary: Government Analyst Report and chain of custody testimony
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 22 of Firearms Ordinance No. 33 of 1916 as amended by Act No 22 of 1996 and Section 27(1) of Explosives Act No 21 of 1956 as amended by Act No. 33 of 1969
hc_sentence_type: Life Imprisonment and One-Year Rigorous Imprisonment
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the appellant in absentia for possession of firearms and explosives, sentencing him to life imprisonment and one-year rigorous imprisonment. The trial proceeded without the appellant, and the judgment was not vacated despite his later appearance.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appeal was filed out of time and treated as a revision application. Main arguments included the irregularity of trial in absentia and gaps in the chain of custody, creating reasonable doubt.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Trial in absentia was irregular as there was no evidence the appellant was absconding | Chain of custody of the gun and cartridges had a significant gap | Reasonable doubt exists as to who was carrying the bag
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: Prosecution witnesses included police officers who arrested the appellant and those handling the chain of custody. The COA found gaps in the chain of custody and reasonable doubt due to the circumstances.
probability_assessment_by_court: COA found reasonable doubt due to gap in chain of custody and the fact that one person ran away, creating doubt about who carried the bag.
defence_version_summary: The appellant did not testify in High Court. His defence, as per police statement, was that an LTTE cadre shoved the bag at him and fled. He was tried in absentia.
legal_errors_description: High Court proceeded with trial in absentia without evidence that the appellant was absconding, which was irregular.
procedural_defects_description: Trial conducted in absence of the appellant without proper inquiry into whether he was absconding.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The COA treated the appeal as a revision application. They found the trial in absentia irregular due to lack of evidence of absconding. They identified a significant gap in the chain of custody of the gun and cartridges, which created reasonable doubt. Considering the appellant's age and time in custody, a retrial was not expedient. Thus, the conviction and sentence were set aside, and the appellant was acquitted.
coa_sentence_type: Acquitted, no sentence imposed.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The appellant was convicted in absentia by the High Court of Colombo for possession of a T56 gun and live cartridges, sentenced to life and one-year imprisonment. He appealed out of time, and the Court of Appeal treated it as a revision. The COA found the trial in absentia irregular and gaps in the chain of custody, creating reasonable doubt. Considering the circumstances, the COA acquitted the appellant and allowed the appeal.
defence_counsel: K.S. Ratnavale, AAL, with G.C. Ranitha, AAL and Suwathikka Ravichandran
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted the appellant in absentia without evidence he was absconding and refused to vacate the judgment when he appeared. The COA found this irregular and noted the chain of custody issues.
precedents_cited_list: CA.NO.96/2013, decided on 10th July 2015
standard_of_review_applied: Revisionary jurisdiction under sections 364 and 365 of the Code of Criminal Procedure Act

judges: N. Bandula Karunarathna, J. | R. Gurusinghe, J.
offence_sections: Section 54 of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance, as amended by Act No. 13 of 1984
brief_facts_summary: The accused-appellant was arrested near Dehiwela railway station for possession of 5.4 grams of heroin. Prosecution claimed a female police officer found heroin in her brassiere, but defence denied possession and alleged no female officer was present at arrest. The accused had a loan dispute with an informant who she claimed framed her.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 54 of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance, as amended by Act No. 13 of 1984
hc_judgment_summary: High Court convicted the appellant for possession of heroin and imposed death sentence based on prosecution evidence.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant argued procedural errors in amending the indictment after witnesses testified, contradictions in prosecution witnesses' testimonies, the judge decided the case before considering defence witnesses, and the dock statement was rejected without adequate evaluation.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Indictment amended after two witnesses had completed their evidence; amendment not read out to appellant nor handed over to her; judge signed amendment which should have been done by AG's department. | Learned High Court Judge failed to take into account contradictions of testimonies of prosecution witnesses. | Learned High Court Judge decided prosecution proved its case beyond reasonable doubt before considering defence witnesses. | Dock statement of appellant rejected without adequately evaluating it.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: Court of Appeal found contradictions and infirmities in prosecution evidence, especially PW9's testimony, creating reasonable doubt. Prosecution failed to prove case beyond reasonable doubt.
probability_assessment_by_court: Court found prosecution failed to prove beyond reasonable doubt due to contradictions and infirmities in evidence.
defence_version_summary: Accused pleaded not guilty, gave dock statement denying possession, claimed no female officer was present at arrest, and alleged framing due to loan dispute. No defence witnesses called, only dock statement.
legal_errors_description: High Court failed to consider contradictions in prosecution evidence and procedural errors in amending indictment.
procedural_defects_description: Indictment amended improperly after witnesses testified, not read to accused, and judge signed amendment which should be done by AG's department.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: COA analyzed prosecution evidence, found serious doubts in PW9's testimony regarding her participation and the search, noted contradictions among witnesses, and referred to precedent Wijeratne v Republic of Sri Lanka. Concluded prosecution failed to prove case beyond reasonable doubt, leading to acquittal.
coa_sentence_type: Acquitted, no sentence imposed
brief_judgment_file_summary: The appellant was convicted by High Court for possession of heroin and sentenced to death. On appeal, COA found prosecution evidence unreliable due to contradictions, especially in PW9's testimony, and procedural errors. COA allowed appeal, set aside conviction and sentence, and acquitted appellant.
defence_counsel: Rienzie Arsecularatne PC, with Thilina Punchihewa
hc_analysis_summary: High Court convicted based on prosecution evidence, but COA found HC failed to analyze infirmities and contradictions in evidence, leading to unsafe conviction.
precedents_cited_list: Wijeratne v Republic of Sri Lanka,78 NLR 49
standard_of_review_applied: Reasonable doubt standard

judges: PRASHANTHA DE SILVA, J. | K.K.A.V. SWARNADHIPATHI, J.
offence_sections: Section 44 and Section 65 of the Foreign Employment Bureau Act No.21 of 1985 (as amended)
brief_facts_summary: The accused, a licensee of an employment company, was charged for violating the Foreign Employment Bureau Act by not paying salary to an employee sent abroad and keeping her beyond the contract period. The prosecution presented evidence including the employee's testimony. The accused argued that his goodwill and business record were not considered at trial.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 44 and Section 65 of the Foreign Employment Bureau Act No.21 of 1985 (as amended)
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court affirmed the Magistrate's conviction, reasoning that the accused's responsibility extends beyond the two-year contract period under the Act, and that the employee was not free to travel, so the accused remained liable until her return.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The petitioner argued that his longstanding business record and goodwill were not considered, that the prosecution's charge should be limited to the two-year contract period, and that the prosecution failed to call witnesses to prove documents. He also contested the evidence about the employee's actions.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Goodwill and business record not considered at trial | Prosecution charge limited to two-year contract period | Evidence regarding employee running away not proven | Prosecution failed to call witnesses to prove documents
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The court evaluated the testimony of P.W.2 (the employee) and found it reliable. Documents not properly submitted were considered hearsay, and the High Court Judge correctly assessed the evidence.
probability_assessment_by_court: Court found evidence reliable and no reasonable doubt based on testimony and documents.
defence_version_summary: Accused pleaded not guilty, called defence witnesses, argued based on business record and documents, but court found evidence hearsay and not properly submitted.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal reviewed the High Court judgment and found that the Judge correctly evaluated the evidence, including the extension of liability beyond the contract period under the Foreign Employment Bureau Act. The COA held that no new material could be considered and that the HC judgment was well-settled, thus refusing leave to appeal.
brief_judgment_file_summary: This case involves an appeal by the accused, a licensee of an employment company, against conviction for violating Sections 44 and 65 of the Foreign Employment Bureau Act. The High Court affirmed the Magistrate's conviction, holding the accused liable beyond the contract period. The Court of Appeal refused leave to appeal, upholding the High Court's reasoning and evidence evaluation.
defence_counsel: Prasana Ekanayake
hc_analysis_summary: High Court reasoned that liability extends beyond contract period under the Act and evidence was properly evaluated. COA agreed with this analysis.
standard_of_review_applied: Limited review of trial record and HC evaluation

judges: N. Bandula Karunarathna J. | R. Gurusinghe J.
offence_sections: Section 400 of the Penal Code and Section 454 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The appellant, a notary public, was accused of cheating and forgery by making the plaintiff sign blank papers which were used to execute a deed renouncing his life interest in a property. The prosecution led evidence from witnesses including the plaintiff and his sister, and presented documentary evidence of deeds. The defence claimed the appellant acted on instructions and in good faith.
evidence_type_secondary: Police evidence and Land Registry records
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 400 of the Penal Code and Section 454 of the Penal Code
hc_sentence_type: 2 years rigorous imprisonment suspended for 5 years per count, fine of Rs. 5,000 per count with 3 months simple imprisonment in default
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the appellant based on prosecution evidence, finding guilt beyond reasonable doubt for cheating and forgery. The judge imposed suspended imprisonment and fines for each count.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant argued that there was no wrongful loss or dishonest intention, raised defense of mistake of fact and good faith, highlighted delay in complaint, and claimed legal errors in conviction and excessive sentencing.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: No wrongful loss to PW1 under section 21(2) of Penal Code | No dishonest intention under section 22 of Penal Code | Mistake of fact under section 72 of Penal Code | Delay in complaint raising reasonable doubt | Legal errors in HC judgment regarding validity of life interest | Sentence excessive and contrary to law | Prosecution failed to prove mens rea | HC misdirected on law and evidence
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: COA analyzed witness testimonies, found inconsistencies and delays in complaint, and raised reasonable doubt about the prosecution case. The court noted the lack of legal validity of the life interest.
probability_assessment_by_court: COA assessed reasonable doubt based on delay in complaint, witness credibility, and legal invalidity of life interest, concluding prosecution failed to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty, gave evidence under oath, claimed he acted on instructions of the parties in good faith, and raised defense of mistake of fact. No alibi was presented, and the defence relied on his dock statement and witness testimonies.
legal_errors_description: HC erred in finding guilt without valid legal basis for life interest, misapplied penal code sections on cheating and forgery, and imposed sentence exceeding maximum under section 400.
procedural_defects_description: Delay of 2 years in filing complaint without explanation, failure to consider appellant's explanation, and procedural violations in evidence handling.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: COA thoroughly reviewed the evidence, concluding that the life interest was not legally valid, thus no wrongful loss occurred. They considered the appellant's good faith, delay in complaint, and legal precedents. The court found that the prosecution failed to prove mens rea and guilt beyond reasonable doubt, and that the HC misdirected on law and evidence.
coa_sentence_type: Acquitted, no sentence imposed
brief_judgment_file_summary: The appellant, a notary public, was convicted by the High Court of Negombo for cheating and forgery related to a property deed. He appealed, arguing no legal basis for life interest, mistake of fact, procedural errors, and excessive sentence. The Court of Appeal allowed the appeal, acquitting him due to reasonable doubt, legal errors in HC judgment, and failure of prosecution to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt.
defence_counsel: G.S. Edirisinghe AAL with Nagitha Wijesekara AAL
hc_analysis_summary: HC convicted the appellant based on prosecution evidence, but COA found errors in legal interpretation of life interest validity, burden of proof, and sentencing. COA criticized HC for not considering delay and appellant's good faith defense.
precedents_cited_list: Mohammed Vs Mohammed 30 NLR 225 | Appuhamy Vs Appuhamy (1880) 3 SCC 61 | Fernando Vs Perera (1914) 17 NLR 161 | Perera Vs Perera (1956) 57 NLR 440 | Gunasekere Vs Dias Bandaranaike 39 NLR 17 | Weerakoon Vs Ranhamy 23 NLR 33 | Perera Vs Munaweera 56 NLR 433 | Kodituwakku Chaminda Vs Republic of Sri Lanka CA /248/2004 | Alwis Vs Piyasena Fernando 1993 (1) SLR 119 | Wijekoon Mudiyanselage Apouhamy Vs Republic CA 61/98 | Kamal Addaraarachchi Vs state 2000 (3) SLLR 394 | Mahinda Herath Vs AG CA 21/2001 | Shavul Hameed Badurdeen Vs AG CA 167/2006 | Dr. Karunadasa Vs Open University of Sri Lanka 2006 (3) SLR 226 | S.T.Piyasena Vs The Director General, Bribery Commission CA31/98 | Edwards Vs Butler, 244 N.C. 205, 92 S.E.2d 922 (1956) | Rex Vs Lucas [1981 2AER 1008]
standard_of_review_applied: COA reviewed evidence and law de novo, applying standard of reasonable doubt and assessing legal errors.
sentencing_principles_applied: Discussed sentencing policy, appellant's professional status as a notary with no previous convictions, and prolonged prosecution period.

judges: K. Priyantha Fernando, J. (P/CA) | Wickum A. Kaluarachchi, J.
offence_sections: section 54A(b) of the Poisons Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance and section 54A(d) of the Poisons Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance
location_of_offence: near the bridge at Leslie Ranagala Mawatha
brief_facts_summary: Acting on information, a police raiding party arrested the accused-appellant near a bridge at Leslie Ranagala Mawatha. A search revealed 11.5 grams of heroin concealed in his underwear. The accused claimed he was assaulted after arrest, but the court found the injuries occurred later while in detention.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: section 54A(b) of the Poisons Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance and section 54A(d) of the Poisons Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the accused on both counts of trafficking and possession of heroin and sentenced him to life imprisonment on each count. The judge found the prosecution evidence credible and rejected the defence version.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant argued that the prosecution version was improbable and failed the test of probability. He contended the trial judge erred in concluding the case was proved beyond reasonable doubt and incorrectly evaluated and rejected the defence evidence.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The learned trial Judge failed to consider that the prosecution version did not pass the test of probability. | The learned trial Judge erred in both facts and law when concluding that the prosecution proved the case beyond reasonable doubt. | The learned trial Judge did not evaluate the defence evidence from the correct perspective and rejected the same in a wrong premise.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the prosecution witnesses (PW1 and PW2) consistent and credible regarding the raid and recovery of heroin. The defence evidence, including the dock statement and medical testimony about injuries, did not undermine the prosecution case as the injuries occurred post-arrest.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court assessed the prosecution evidence as credible and consistent, and found no reason to doubt the recovery of heroin. The defence version did not create reasonable doubt.
defence_version_summary: The accused pleaded not guilty. He made a dock statement denying possession of heroin and claimed he was assaulted after arrest. The defence called the Judicial Medical Officer to testify about injuries. The court found the defence version not credible, noting injuries occurred during detention and did not affect the arrest evidence.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal reviewed the evidence and found the High Court judge had correctly evaluated the prosecution and defence cases. The prosecution witnesses were consistent and credible. The appellant's arguments about improbability and lack of detail in notes were insufficient to discredit the evidence. The medical evidence of injuries post-arrest did not affect the credibility of the arrest and recovery. The appeal grounds were without merit.
coa_sentence_type: Life imprisonment on both counts (upheld)
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused-appellant was convicted in the High Court of Colombo for trafficking and possession of 11.5 grams of heroin and sentenced to life imprisonment on both counts. He appealed, challenging the probability of the prosecution case, the sufficiency of evidence, and the evaluation of defence evidence. The Court of Appeal found the prosecution witnesses credible, the recovery of heroin established, and the defence version unpersuasive. The appeal was dismissed, upholding the conviction and sentence.
defence_counsel: Nihara Randeniya
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court judge considered the defence evidence and gave reasons for rejecting it, finding the prosecution proved the case beyond reasonable doubt. The Court of Appeal agreed with this analysis and found no error.
standard_of_review_applied: The Court of Appeal reviewed the evidence and the High Court's findings to determine if the prosecution proved the case beyond reasonable doubt and if the defence was properly considered.

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 296, 315, 314 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: Incident occurred on May 6, 2001, around 6.30 p.m. in an estate. Appellant had an argument with PW2 over a loan, which turned into a fight. Deceased, Appellant's mother, intervened and was stabbed by Appellant with a knife. Eyewitnessed by PW1, PW2, and PW3. Police recovered knife based on Appellant's statement.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 296, 315, 314 of the Penal Code
hc_sentence_type: Death sentence for murder; 1-year rigorous imprisonment with fine for causing hurt by dangerous weapon; 3 months rigorous imprisonment with fine for causing hurt
hc_judgment_summary: High Court Judge convicted Appellant after considering evidence. Appellant made a dock statement. Sentence included death for murder and imprisonment with fines for other counts.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: Appellant appealed conviction and sentence. Initially, counsel raised preliminary objection that jury option was not given, but withdrew after verifying record. Counsel then conceded that prosecution evidence was clear and had no grounds to support the appeal.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: COA found prosecution evidence clear and cogent. Eyewitness testimony from PW1, PW2, and PW3, supported by medical evidence and recovery of knife, established guilt beyond reasonable doubt.
probability_assessment_by_court: COA assessed evidence and found no reasonable doubt, dismissing the appeal.
defence_version_summary: Appellant pleaded not guilty and made a dock statement only. No defence witnesses called. Court found prosecution evidence credible and convicted.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: COA reviewed the record and found that jury option was properly given. Prosecution evidence was strong, including eyewitness testimony, medical reports, and recovery of knife. HC judge correctly evaluated evidence. COA applied precedent on Section 27 of Evidence Ordinance and dismissed the appeal.
coa_sentence_type: Death sentence for murder; 1-year rigorous imprisonment with fine of Rs.5000; 3 months rigorous imprisonment with fine of Rs.1000
brief_judgment_file_summary: Appellant Sengamalai Murugiah was convicted of murder and hurt charges in High Court of Kalutara and sentenced to death and imprisonment. He appealed on procedural grounds initially, but counsel withdrew objection. COA found evidence clear and cogent, including eyewitnesses and medical evidence, and dismissed the appeal, upholding the conviction and sentence.
defence_counsel: Yalith Wijesurendra
cause_of_death_exact_text: shock following severe intra thorax haemorrhage following stab injury done by a sharp pointed weapon
hc_analysis_summary: HC correctly considered evidence and convicted Appellant. COA agreed with HC's analysis and found no errors.
precedents_cited_list: Somaratne Rajapakse Others v. Hon. Attorney General (2010) 2 Sri L.R. 113 at 115
standard_of_review_applied: COA reviewed evidence and legal points, finding no error in HC judgment.

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The deceased and his wife heard knocks on their son's boutique door and went to check multiple times. On the third time, the deceased was cut by the Appellant and died on the spot. Police recovered a pole, two torch lights, and a small knife from the scene, and the Appellant was arrested later.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court Judge convicted the Appellant as charged based on the evidence, including the dying declaration, and imposed the death sentence.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The Appellant argued that the High Court Judge failed to consider contradictions in PW1's evidence, did not consider evidence favourable to the Appellant, and rejected defence evidence without proper basis.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The High Court Judge has failed to consider the contradictions and omissions of the evidence given by PW1. | The Learned High Court Judge has not considered the evidence favourable to the Appellant in his judgment. | The Learned High Court Judge has rejected the defence evidence at the wrong premises and failed to consider the evidence of the Appellant which suffices to create a reasonable doubt on the prosecution case.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found contradictions in PW1's evidence and insufficient lighting for proper identification, casting doubt on the dying declaration and overall prosecution case.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal found that the prosecution failed to prove the case beyond reasonable doubt due to inconsistencies and lack of reliable evidence.
defence_version_summary: The Appellant pleaded not guilty, gave evidence from the witness box denying the charge, and no alibi was mentioned.
legal_errors_description: The High Court Judge failed to discuss and apply the correct legal standards for dying declarations.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed the contradictions in PW1's evidence, the poor lighting conditions affecting identification, and the failure to consider third-party involvement. They applied precedents on dying declarations and concluded that the prosecution did not establish guilt beyond reasonable doubt, leading to acquittal.
coa_sentence_type: Acquitted, no sentence imposed
brief_judgment_file_summary: The Appellant was convicted of murder by the High Court of Kurunegala and sentenced to death. He appealed on grounds of evidence contradictions and unfair trial. The Court of Appeal found that the prosecution failed to prove the case beyond reasonable doubt due to issues with the dying declaration and identification, and acquitted the Appellant.
defence_counsel: Nihara Randeniya
cause_of_death_exact_text: death was caused by stab injuries to the neck and the chest
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted based on the dying declaration without proper legal analysis and failed to consider contradictions in evidence and potential third-party involvement.
precedents_cited_list: Dharmawansa Silva and Another v. The Republic of Sri Lanka [1981] 2 Sri.L.R.439 | Sigera v Attorney General [2011] 1 Sri.L.R. 201 | Emperor v. Brown [1917] 18 Cri.L.J. 482
standard_of_review_applied: Evaluation of evidence and reasonable doubt standard

judges: N. Bandula Karunarathna J. | R. Gurusinghe J.
offence_sections: regulation 29 (4) read with 29 (1) of the Emergency Regulation as issued in the Gazette (extraordinary) No. 43/12 dated 04.11.1994
brief_facts_summary: The accused was arrested on 06.12.1997 during a police raid at Bandaranayake International Airport, Katunayake, for possessing a .38 Smith & Wesson revolver without a license. The revolver was recovered from his waist by Police Sergeant Nazeer, and the chain of custody was established through police records and a Government Analyst report. The accused, alias Captain Ranji, was part of a group suspected of intimidating people with firearms.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: regulation 29 (4) read with 29 (1) of the Emergency Regulation as issued in the Gazette (extraordinary) No. 43/12 dated 04.11.1994
hc_sentence_type: 10 years Rigorous Imprisonment, Fine of Rs. 10,000, default 3 months Simple Imprisonment
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the accused of possessing a revolver without authority and sentenced him to 10 years rigorous imprisonment and a fine. The trial was conducted in absentia as the accused absconded, and the court found the prosecution evidence credible, including the recovery of the weapon and chain of custody.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant challenged the conviction on grounds of failure to prove chain of custody and contradictory evidence on the weapon's identity. Additionally, he argued that the trial in absentia was improperly ordered.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The prosecution has failed to prove the chain of custody of production | Evidence led by the prosecution on the identity of the weapon is contradictory
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found that contradictions in serial numbers were typographical errors and that the chain of custody was intact. The eyewitness testimony and forensic evidence corroborated the recovery of the revolver from the accused.
probability_assessment_by_court: The court found no reasonable doubt as contradictions were typographical and chain of custody was proven.
defence_version_summary: The accused did not plead guilty and the trial was conducted in absentia. He attempted to be represented later, but the application was rejected. No defence witnesses were called, and the court found the prosecution evidence credible.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal thoroughly examined the chain of custody, concluding that it was properly maintained from recovery to analysis. Contradictions in serial numbers were deemed typographical errors, and the eyewitness testimony was credible. The court upheld the trial in absentia as lawful under Section 241 of the Criminal Procedure Code, finding no merit in the appeal grounds. The sentence was considered legal and justifiable within the prescribed limits.
coa_sentence_type: 10 years Rigorous Imprisonment, Fine of Rs. 10,000, default 3 months Simple Imprisonment
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused appealed his conviction and sentence for possessing a revolver without authority under emergency regulations. The High Court had sentenced him to 10 years rigorous imprisonment and a fine after a trial in absentia. On appeal, he challenged the chain of custody and contradictory evidence on the weapon's identity. The Court of Appeal found the chain intact, contradictions as typographical, and upheld the trial procedure. The appeal was dismissed, and the conviction and sentence affirmed.
defence_counsel: Jagath Abenayaka AAL
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted the accused based on evidence of weapon recovery and chain of custody. The Court of Appeal found no errors in the HC's reasoning, affirming that the evidence was sufficient and the trial in absentia was proper.
standard_of_review_applied: Review of evidence and legal procedures under criminal appeal standards
sentencing_principles_applied: Proportionality and legality within statutory limits

judges: D.N. Samarakoon, J. | Pradeep Kirtisinghe, J.
brief_facts_summary: The defendant newspaper published articles on 11.06.1992 alleging plaintiff Colonel M. Dissanayake was sacked for a Rs. 8 million racket in Army Welfare Fund. Plaintiff, who was transferred, sued for defamation. Evidence showed accounts were improperly maintained and there were investigations, but plaintiff was not dismissed.
hc_judgment_summary: District Court found defendants liable for defamation and awarded Rs. 5,000 damages to plaintiff. Defendants appealed to Court of Appeal.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: Defendant appellant argued absence of animus injuriandi, that publication was privileged, and no malice or intent to injure. Plaintiff respondent defended the District Court judgment.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Absence of animus injuriandi simpliciter as defence | Publication was on privileged occasion | No malice or intent to injure
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: Court evaluated evidence from plaintiff and witnesses including retired Major General and Chartered Accountant. Evidence showed accounts were not properly kept and there were rumors of irregularities, but no proof of animus injuriandi.
probability_assessment_by_court: Court assessed absence of animus injuriandi and found publication privileged, with no reasonable doubt of liability.
defence_version_summary: Defendant pleaded not liable, argued absence of animus injuriandi and privilege. Defence did not call witnesses, relied on documents and legal arguments.
legal_errors_description: District Court erred in finding defamation without considering absence of animus injuriandi and that publication was privileged under Roman-Dutch law.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: COA analyzed Roman-Dutch law on defamation, focusing on animus injuriandi and qualified privilege. Referenced precedents like M.G. Perera vs. A.V. Peiris and Adam vs. Ward. Found that the publication was in public interest, no animus injuriandi, and thus privileged. Allowed appeal, setting aside District Court judgment.
brief_judgment_file_summary: Defendant The Associated Newspapers of Ceylon Ltd. appealed District Court judgment awarding Rs. 5,000 damages to plaintiff Colonel M. Dissanayake for defamation. COA examined defamation law, found no animus injuriandi and that publication was privileged due to public interest. Allowed appeal, set aside District Court judgment, and dismissed plaintiff's action.
prosecution_counsel: Rohan Sahabandu P.C. with Chaturika Elwitigala
defence_counsel: Kushan De Alwis P.C. with Nivantha Thilakaratne
hc_analysis_summary: District Court found defendants liable for defamation and awarded damages. COA viewed that District Court failed to properly apply Roman-Dutch law principles on animus injuriandi and privilege.

judges: N. Bandula Karunarathna J. | R. Gurusinghe J.
offence_sections: Section 354 of the Penal Code; Section 364(2)(e) of the Penal Code as amended by Act No. 22 of 1995
brief_facts_summary: The accused-appellants kidnapped a 16-year-old girl from her lawful guardian and committed rape on her. The victim's testimony indicated the incidents occurred due to her immaturity. The appellants had no prior convictions and were adults with families.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 354 of the Penal Code; Section 364(2)(e) of the Penal Code as amended by Act No. 22 of 1995
hc_sentence_type: Rigorous imprisonment for 3 years on count 1, 15 years on count 3 for 1st accused; 3 years on count 2, 12 years each on counts 4 and 5 for 2nd accused, all to run consecutively, with fines and compensation
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the appellants on all counts of kidnapping and statutory rape. The judge imposed maximum sentences considering the gravity of the offence, age difference, repetition, and need to protect children, with sentences to run consecutively.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellants challenged only the sentence, arguing it was excessive and seeking a lesser custodial sentence based on no prior convictions, consent of victim, no violence, and family circumstances.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: No previous convictions | Accused are married with children | Consent of victim | No violence or force used | No bodily injuries on victim | Seeking lesser custodial sentence
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court evaluated the victim's testimony, noting her immaturity and that consent is irrelevant due to her age. The evidence was sufficient to establish the offences of kidnapping and statutory rape.
probability_assessment_by_court: Court held that a child under 16 cannot give consent, and intercourse per se constitutes rape, so probability of guilt was high.
defence_version_summary: The accused did not plead guilty; in appeal, defence argued consent of victim, no violence, and mitigating factors like no prior convictions and family responsibilities.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal considered the sentencing principles and precedents on mandatory sentences. While acknowledging the seriousness of the offences, the court exercised discretion due to the appellants' lack of prior convictions, family circumstances, and the victim's consent. The court reduced the sentences for statutory rape counts from 15 and 12 years to 10 years each, and ordered all sentences to run concurrently, backdated to the date of conviction.
coa_sentence_type: Rigorous imprisonment for 10 years on count 3 for 1st accused, 10 years each on counts 4 and 5 for 2nd accused, and 3 years on counts 1 and 2 for both, all to run concurrently, with fines and compensation.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The Court of Appeal heard an appeal against sentences imposed by the High Court of Kalmunai for kidnapping and statutory rape of a 16-year-old girl. The High Court had convicted the appellants and imposed maximum sentences totaling 45 years rigorous imprisonment. The appellants appealed only on sentence, arguing for reduction based on consent, no violence, and family circumstances. The Court of Appeal reduced the sentences for rape counts to 10 years each and ordered all sentences to run concurrently, while maintaining convictions.
defence_counsel: Indica Mallawaratchy AAL
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court imposed maximum sentences based on the gravity of the offence, age difference, repetition, and societal need to protect children. The Court of Appeal viewed this as legally correct but exercised discretion to reduce sentences considering mitigating factors.
precedents_cited_list: Supreme Court Reference No.03 of 2008 | Attorney General Vs. Ambagala Mudiyanselage Samantha, 17 of 2003 | Attorney General Vs Ranasinghe 1993 (2) SLR 81 | Attorney General Vs Gunasena CA 110/2021 decided on 12.02.2014 | Attorney General Vs Uluwaduge 1995 (1) SLR 157 | Rizwan Vs AG CA PHC APN 141 / 2013 decided on 25.03.2015
standard_of_review_applied: Discretionary review based on sentencing principles and precedents regarding mandatory sentences.
sentencing_principles_applied: Principles included gravity of offence, culpability, statutory punishment, difficulty in detection, societal interests, denouncement, deterrence, protection of children, and just punishment.

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 40 of the Forest Ordinance
brief_facts_summary: The vehicle was confiscated after being used for illegal transportation of teak timber without a permit. The appellant, the registered owner, appealed against the confiscation, claiming he was overseas and had taken precautions by instructing the lessee not to use the vehicle illegally. He presented evidence including an agreement and testimony from a bank agent.
evidence_type_primary: Appellant's testimony and documentary evidence (agreement X-01)
evidence_type_secondary: Witness testimony (bank agent) and prosecution allegations
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 40 of the Forest Ordinance
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court dismissed the revision application, agreeing with the Magistrate that the appellant failed to take all necessary precautions to prevent illegal use of the vehicle and that no exceptional circumstances were established to warrant revisionary intervention.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant argued that he took all possible precautions, was overseas during the offence, and was unaware of the illegal use. He contended that the Magistrate and High Court erred in confiscating the vehicle and in not exercising revisionary jurisdiction.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The Magistrate erred in finding appellant failed to take sufficient precautions under Section 40 of the Forest Ordinance | The High Court erred in not exercising revisionary jurisdiction due to lack of exceptional circumstances
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the appellant's evidence credible, noting he was overseas and had instructed the lessee against illegal use. The prosecution did not dispute key facts, and the balance of probability favored the appellant.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court applied the balance of probability standard, citing Miller Vs. Minister of Pensions, and found the appellant had taken all precautions.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty to involvement in the offence; he claimed alibi by being overseas, gave evidence and called a witness, and the court found his testimony credible.
legal_errors_description: The Magistrate and High Court erred in interpreting Section 40 of the Forest Ordinance regarding the owner's duty to take precautions, and the High Court erred in not exercising revisionary jurisdiction when exceptional circumstances existed.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed the evidence and found that the appellant had taken all possible precautions, was overseas during the offence, and the vehicle was used without his knowledge. They applied the balance of probability standard and precedents like Ceylínco Leasing Corporation Ltd., concluding that the lower courts' orders should be set aside to avoid injustice.
coa_sentence_type: Release of vehicle to registered owner
brief_judgment_file_summary: This appeal concerns the confiscation of a vehicle used for illegal timber transportation. The High Court upheld the Magistrate's confiscation order. The appellant, the registered owner, appealed on grounds of taking precautions and being unaware. The Court of Appeal allowed the appeal, finding that the appellant had taken all precautions and set aside the lower court orders, directing release of the vehicle.
defence_counsel: W. Dayarathne, P.C. with Harsha Jayamini de Silva
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court dismissed the revision application, but the Court of Appeal found errors in not recognizing exceptional circumstances and misinterpreting the law on precautions.
precedents_cited_list: CA/PHC/108/2010 dated 26-08-2014 | Miller Vs. Minister of Pensions (1947) 2 AER 372 | Ceylínco Leasing Corporation Ltd. Vs. Harison CA/PHC/APN/45/2011 | Sadi Banda Vs. Officer-in charge, Police Station, Norton Bridge (2014) 1 SLR 33
standard_of_review_applied: Balance of probability and discretionary power of revision
sentencing_principles_applied: Principles under Section 40 of Forest Ordinance regarding owner's duty to take precautions to prevent illegal use of vehicle

judges: D.N. Samarakoon, J. | B. Sasi Mahendran, J.
offence_sections: Section 66(1)(b) of the Primary Courts’ Procedure Act No. 44 of 1979
offence_category: Dispute affecting land and breach of peace
brief_facts_summary: The dispute arose from an agreement between the 2nd Petitioner (Kalutara Cooperative Distilleries Society Limited) and the 2nd Respondent (Invest Lanka Investments Co. (Private) Limited) for the management of a distillery. The Cooperative Society terminated the agreement, and the Respondents filed an information under Section 66(1)(b) of the Primary Courts’ Procedure Act alleging forcible dispossession and threat of breach of peace. The Magistrate ordered restoration of possession to the Respondents.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The Petitioners challenged the Magistrate's orders on the grounds that the Magistrate did not have jurisdiction because the dispute did not affect land, there was no breach of the peace, and the Petitioners were always in possession so there could not have been forcible dispossession.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The dispute does not affect land | There was no breach of the peace | Possession was always with the Petitioners, and there could not have been forcible dispossession
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed the affidavits and documents filed by the parties. The Magistrate based her decision on the information filed by the Respondents without conducting an initial inquiry to ascertain jurisdiction.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal assessed that the Magistrate had no jurisdiction because the dispute did not affect land and there was no breach of peace.
defence_version_summary: The Petitioners contended that the Magistrate lacked jurisdiction because the dispute did not affect land and there was no breach of peace. They also argued that they were always in possession.
legal_errors_description: The Magistrate failed to conduct an initial inquiry to ascertain whether the dispute affected land and whether a breach of the peace was threatened or likely. The Magistrate incorrectly treated the commercial agreement as a lease agreement and thus wrongly found that the dispute affected land.
procedural_defects_description: The Magistrate issued notice and interim orders without first conducting an inquiry to determine jurisdiction as required by Section 66(2) of the Primary Courts’ Procedure Act.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed the jurisdictional requirements under Section 66 of the Primary Courts’ Procedure Act. The Court held that the Magistrate must conduct an initial inquiry to ascertain whether the dispute affects land and whether a breach of the peace is threatened or likely, especially when information is filed by a private party. The Court found that the Magistrate failed to do so and incorrectly determined that the dispute affected land. The Court also found that there was no breach of the peace. Therefore, the Magistrate lacked jurisdiction and the orders were set aside.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The Petitioners, the Chairman and members of Kalutara Cooperative Distilleries Society Limited, appealed against the orders of the Kalutara Magistrate’s Court which restored possession of a distillery to the Respondents. The Court of Appeal held that the Magistrate failed to conduct an initial inquiry to ascertain jurisdiction under Section 66 of the Primary Courts’ Procedure Act. The Court found that the dispute did not affect land and there was no breach of the peace. Therefore, the Magistrate lacked jurisdiction and the impugned orders were set aside.
