judges: Menaka Wijesundera J | Neil Iddawala J
offence_sections: Sections 20(b) read with 20(a)iv and 19(c) of the Bribery Act No. 11 of 1954 as amended
brief_facts_summary: The accused-appellant, an Assistant Director of Education, solicited a bribe of 300,000 LKR from PW1 and accepted 200,000 LKR from PW1's mother to facilitate employment for PW1 at the Bank of Ceylon. The prosecution presented evidence of these transactions, leading to conviction under the Bribery Act.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Sections 20(b) read with 20(a)iv and 19(c) of the Bribery Act No. 11 of 1954 as amended
hc_sentence_type: Rigorous Imprisonment 5 years per count with a fine of 5,000 LKR per count, and a penalty of 200,000 LKR under section 26 of the Bribery Act
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the appellant on four counts of bribery. For each count, 5 years rigorous imprisonment and a fine of 5,000 LKR were imposed, with sentences for counts 1 and 2 running concurrently, and counts 3 and 4 running concurrently. Additionally, a penalty of 200,000 LKR was ordered under section 26 of the Bribery Act.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant did not challenge the conviction but appealed for a variance in the sentence. The counsel argued for concurrent running of all sentences rather than separate concurrent groups, based on the discretion of the court.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Appeal against sentence only, seeking concurrent running of all sentences due to same transaction
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The prosecution relied on witness testimony from PW1 and her mother regarding the solicitation and acceptance of bribes. The Court of Appeal did not re-evaluate the evidence as the conviction was not challenged.
probability_assessment_by_court: Not assessed as conviction was not challenged
defence_version_summary: The accused pleaded not guilty in the High Court. No details of defence witnesses or alibi are provided in the appeal judgment.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal considered the appellant's request for sentence variance. Citing section 16 of the Criminal Procedure Act, the court noted its discretion to order sentences to run concurrently. Since all four charges stemmed from the same transaction, the court decided to allow all sentences to run concurrently from the date of conviction.
coa_sentence_type: Rigorous Imprisonment 5 years per count, all sentences to run concurrently from 22.01.2020, with fines of 5,000 LKR per count and penalty of 200,000 LKR under section 26 of the Bribery Act as imposed by High Court
brief_judgment_file_summary: The accused, an Assistant Director of Education, was convicted by the High Court on four counts of bribery for soliciting and accepting bribes to secure employment. The High Court imposed 5 years rigorous imprisonment per count with fines and a penalty. The appellant appealed only on sentence, seeking concurrent running of all sentences. The Court of Appeal allowed all sentences to run concurrently from the conviction date but otherwise dismissed the appeal.
prosecution_counsel: Sudarshana de Silva Deputy Solicitor General with Priyangani Jayalath Assistant Director Bribery Commission
defence_counsel: Anil Silva P.C. with Amaan Bandara
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court properly convicted the appellant based on the evidence. The Court of Appeal found no error in the conviction but exercised discretion to modify the sentence structure for concurrent running.
standard_of_review_applied: Discretionary review of sentence under section 16 of the Code of Criminal Procedure Act
sentencing_principles_applied: Principles of concurrent sentencing for offences arising from the same transaction

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code and Section 300 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The appellant was accused of murdering his wife and attempting to murder his mother-in-law on 11th March 2007. The sole eyewitness, an 11-year-old girl, testified that she saw the appellant attack the deceased with a mamoty. The appellant claimed he was at a funeral and found the victims injured, but the High Court convicted him of murder.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 296 of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the appellant of murder based on the eyewitness testimony and medical evidence, while acquitting him of attempted murder due to the death of the injured witness and disallowance of her deposition.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant appealed on grounds that the trial court failed to consider contradictions and omissions in the sole eyewitness's evidence, that the evidence was negated by medical evidence, and that there were reasonable doubts in the prosecution case.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The Trial Court was in error when it has failed to consider the serious contradictions and omissions in the evidence of the sole eye witness Kaushalya Dissanayke and thereby has caused a miscarriage of justice to the accused appellant. | The Trial Court was in error when it has failed to consider that the evidence of the sole eye witness is negated and contradicted by medical evidence. | The Trial Court was in error when it has failed to consider the existence of many reasonable doubts in the case of the prosecution and thereby causing a miscarriage of justice towards the appellant.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the sole eyewitness credible despite minor contradictions, considering her age and the traumatic event. The medical evidence was consistent with her testimony, and the appellant's defence was not put to witnesses.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal found no reasonable doubts in the prosecution case and concluded that the evidence was cogent and truthful.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty and made a dock statement claiming he was at a funeral and found the victims injured. He called one witness but failed to put his defence to prosecution witnesses. The court found his defence an afterthought and not credible.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal thoroughly analyzed the grounds of appeal, considering the contradictions in the eyewitness evidence in light of her young age and the circumstances. They applied legal principles from cited precedents regarding witness credibility and the requirement to put defence to witnesses. The medical evidence was found consistent with the eyewitness account. The appellant's failure to cross-examine on material points and his conduct after the incident, including consuming poison, were noted. The court found no merit in the appeal and dismissed it, affirming the conviction and sentence.
coa_sentence_type: Affirmed the High Court sentence
brief_judgment_file_summary: This appeal involves the appellant convicted of murdering his wife and attempting to murder his mother-in-law. The High Court convicted him of murder based on eyewitness testimony and medical evidence. The appellant appealed on grounds of contradictions in evidence and reasonable doubts. The Court of Appeal found the eyewitness credible, medical evidence consistent, and the appellant's defence lacking. The appeal was dismissed, and conviction and sentence affirmed.
defence_counsel: Dharshana Kuruppu with Sajini Elvitigala, Dinaru Bandara, Chinthaka Udadeniya, Buddhika Thilakaratne, Thanuja Dissanayake and Sudharsha Silva
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted the appellant of murder based on the credible eyewitness testimony and consistent medical evidence, while acquitting him of attempted murder. The Court of Appeal found no errors in this analysis.

State of Madya Pradesh (1990) (CLJ NOC 125 MP) | Rex Vs. Lord Cochrane and Others (1814) Gurney’s Report 479
standard_of_review_applied: The court reviewed the evidence and grounds of appeal, applying principles of witness credibility and legal standards from cited precedents.

judges: Menaka Wijesundera J. | Neil Iddawala J.
brief_facts_summary: Two abductees went to the Kamburupitiya Police Station and did not return. Witnesses claimed to have seen them in a bus with the accused and overheard the OIC (8th respondent) order their killing. The prosecution witnesses gave statements seven years after the incident, and the High Court rejected their evidence due to belatedness and unreliable identification under poor illumination.
evidence_type_secondary: Physical evidence (skulls) and witness testimony (bus driver)
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court acquitted all accused, rejecting the prosecution evidence due to belated witness statements (made seven years after the incident) and unreliable identification because of lack of illumination. The judge found the witnesses' accounts lacked spontaneity and probability.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant challenged the acquittal on two grounds: (1) the prosecution witnesses gave statements after a lapse of seven years, and (2) the High Court judge incorrectly considered the lack of proper identification due to insufficient illumination.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The statements being made by the witnesses of the prosecution after a lapse of seven years | Lack of proper identification due to lack of illumination being incorrectly considered by the High Court Judge.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The High Court judge analyzed each prosecution witness and rejected their evidence due to belated statements and lack of spontaneity. The Court of Appeal agreed, noting the improbability of the prosecution story and unreliable identification.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal found the prosecution story lacked probability and spontaneity due to the seven-year delay and unreliable identification under poor illumination.
defence_version_summary: The defence did not present evidence but challenged the prosecution evidence as belated and improbable. The High Court accepted the defence challenges and acquitted all accused.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal, agreeing with the High Court's evaluation of evidence. They found the witnesses' statements lacked spontaneity and probability due to the seven-year delay, and the identification was unreliable due to illumination issues. They cited precedents on the heavy burden in appeals against acquittal and the importance of the trial judge's firsthand observation of witnesses, concluding no grave miscarriage of justice to justify interference.
brief_judgment_file_summary: This is an appeal by the aggrieved party (wife of an abductee) against the acquittal of eight accused for abduction. The High Court acquitted all due to belated witness statements and unreliable identification. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal, upholding the acquittal, agreeing that the prosecution evidence lacked spontaneity and probability.

defence_counsel: R. Arasekularatne, PC with Punsiri Gamage for the 2nd and Accused-Respondents; Amila Palliyage with S. Utugampola for the 5th, 6th & 7th Respondents
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court analyzed the prosecution witnesses and rejected their evidence due to belated statements and lack of proper illumination for identification. The Court of Appeal found no error in this analysis.

Brown and Co Ltd | Attorney General v. D. Senevirathne 1982 (1) SLR 302

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 364(2) read with Section 364(2)(e) of the Penal Code as amended
brief_facts_summary: The Appellant was accused of raping the prosecutrix between 23/05/2012 and 02/07/2012, taking her to a guest house on Bangama Road. The prosecution led video evidence of the prosecutrix's interview, but she later contradicted her statement in court. Key evidence included video recording and testimonies from doctors and officers, with the Appellant having helped the prosecutrix with education and sports.
evidence_type_secondary: Medical evidence, Probation and psychiatric reports
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 364(2) read with Section 364(2)(e) of the Penal Code as amended
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the Appellant based on video evidence and considered it corroborated by independent witnesses. The judge sentenced him to 15 years rigorous imprisonment with a fine and compensation.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The Appellant argued that the trial judge failed to consider lack of corroboration for the video recording, that the prosecution followed illegal procedure in leading evidence, and that the investigating officer had a motive to fabricate the case.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The Learned Trial Judge has failed to consider that the video recording of the statement of the complainant has not been corroborated in material particulars by evidence from an independent source as required by Section 163A (5) of the Evidence Ordinance. | That the prosecution had followed totally illegal procedure when the evidence of the prosecutrix was led before the court. | The Learned Trial Judge had failed to consider that the chief investigating officer had a strong motive to fabricate a case against the Appellant and therefore she was an interested witness.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found that the video evidence was not corroborated by independent sources, and the prosecutrix's testimony was inconsistent. The evidence from PW4, PW18, and PW20 only showed consistency, not independent corroboration.
probability_assessment_by_court: The COA concluded that the prosecution failed to prove the case beyond reasonable doubt due to lack of corroboration and procedural errors.
defence_version_summary: The Appellant pleaded not guilty. The defence cross-examined witnesses and argued that the evidence was not corroborated and procedural errors occurred. The court found the defence arguments valid.
legal_errors_description: The High Court incorrectly considered evidence from PW4, PW18, and PW20 as corroborative when it only showed consistency, not independent corroboration as required by law.
procedural_defects_description: State Counsel led lengthy examination-in-chief without permission, violating Section 163A(3)(b) of the Evidence (Special Provisions) Act.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The COA held that the prosecution failed to adduce corroborative evidence from an independent source as required by Section 163A(5). Procedural errors in leading evidence violated fair trial principles. The video evidence was contradicted by the prosecutrix in court, and supporting evidence only showed consistency, not independent corroboration. Thus, the case was not proven beyond reasonable doubt.
coa_sentence_type: Acquitted, no sentence
brief_judgment_file_summary: The Appellant was convicted of rape by the High Court of Colombo and sentenced to 15 years rigorous imprisonment. He appealed on grounds of lack of corroboration and procedural errors. The Court of Appeal found that the video evidence was not corroborated by independent sources and procedural irregularities occurred, leading to acquittal.
defence_counsel: Sarath Jayamanne, PC with Darshana Kuruppu, Vineshka Mendis, Prashan Wickramaratne, Sanjeewa Meegahawatta
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted based on video evidence and considered it corroborated by other witnesses. COA found this erroneous as the evidence only showed consistency, not independent corroboration.

Republic of Sri Lanka [2009] 1 SLR 48 | King v. Atukorale 50 N.L.R. 256 | S. Rajaratnam v. The Republic of Sri Lanka 79(1) N.L.R. 73 | Hattuwan Pedige Sugath Karunaratne v. The Attorney General SC Appeal 32 of 2020
standard_of_review_applied: Review for legal errors and sufficiency of evidence

judges: Menaka Wijesundera J | Neil Iddawala J
offence_sections: Section 20 (1) (d), read with Section 40 and Section 40 (1) of the Forest Ordinance as amended by laws, inter alia, Act no.65 of 2009
brief_facts_summary: The accused (son of the appellant) transported one cube of granite in a lorry without a valid license within a reserved forest. He pleaded guilty and was fined. The vehicle was confiscated. The appellant (owner) claimed she gave the vehicle to the accused for servicing and was unaware of the illegal use, but the court found she did not take sufficient precautions.
evidence_type_primary: Confession/guilty plea and evidence of transporting granite
evidence_type_secondary: Evidence of prior offence (transporting sand) and appellant's admission
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 20 (1) (d), read with Section 40 and Section 40 (1) of the Forest Ordinance as amended by laws, inter alia, Act no.65 of 2009
hc_sentence_type: Fine of Rs 20000 with default imprisonment of three months and confiscation of vehicle
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court dismissed the revision application, affirming the Magistrate's confiscation order. It found that the appellant failed to show she had taken all necessary precautions to prevent the offence.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant appealed to set aside the confiscation orders, arguing she was unaware of the diversion of the vehicle and had given instructions to the accused not to use it illegally.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The appellant was uninformed of the diversion of the vehicle | The appellant had given instructions to the accused to abstain from using the vehicle for illegal activities
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal examined the appellant's evidence and found discrepancies. The appellant admitted giving the vehicle to the accused and being unaware of the illegal use. The court noted a prior offence and found that mere instructions are insufficient to discharge the burden of proof.
probability_assessment_by_court: The court applied the balance of probabilities standard for the burden of proof under the Forest Ordinance.
defence_version_summary: The appellant (owner) claimed she gave the vehicle to her son (the accused) for servicing and was unaware of the illegal use. She said she had given instructions not to use the vehicle illegally. The court did not find her credible in taking all precautions.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed the burden of proof under Section 40 of the Forest Ordinance. It held that mere instructions to the driver are insufficient to discharge the burden. The appellant failed to prove she took all precautions, especially given the accused's prior offence. The Court affirmed the lower courts' decisions, finding no reason to interfere.
coa_sentence_type: Fine of Rs 20000 and confiscation of vehicle
brief_judgment_file_summary: The appellant, owner of a lorry, appealed against the confiscation of the vehicle used by her son to transport granite illegally in a reserved forest. The son pleaded guilty and was fined. The Magistrate and High Court ordered confiscation. The Court of Appeal held that the appellant failed to prove she took all precautions to prevent the offence, as required by the Forest Ordinance, and dismissed the appeal.
defence_counsel: Aruna Pathirana with Shermila Muthalif
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court dismissed the revision application, finding that the appellant failed to show sufficient precautions. The Court of Appeal agreed with the High Court's analysis and conclusion.
precedents_cited_list: Samarasinghege Dharmasena v W. P. Wanigasinghe CA(PHC) 197/2013 CA Minute dated 22.01.2019 | S. D. N. Premasiri v Officer In Charge, Mawathagama C A (PHC) 46/2015 Court of Appeal Minute dated 27.11.2018 | H.G.Sujith Priyantha v O.I.C.Police Station, Poodala C.A (PHC) No 157/12
standard_of_review_applied: Review of lower courts' application of law and evidence on burden of proof under Forest Ordinance
sentencing_principles_applied: Confiscation under Forest Ordinance requires the owner to prove taking all precautions to prevent the offence

judges: Menaka Wijesundera J | Neil Iddawala J
offence_sections: Section 25(2) read with Section 40 of the Forest Ordinance as amended by Amendment Act, No. 65 of 2009
brief_facts_summary: The accused was convicted for transporting timber without a permit. The magistrate fined him and ordered confiscation of the vehicle after an inquiry where the owner and a witness gave contradictory evidence. The owner failed to prove he took all precautions to prevent the offence.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 25(2) read with Section 40 of the Forest Ordinance as amended by Amendment Act, No. 65 of 2009
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court dismissed the revision application and affirmed the magistrate's confiscation order, agreeing that the owner failed to prove he took all precautions to prevent the offence.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant contended that he had taken all necessary precautions to prevent the vehicle from being used illegally, and that the lower courts erred in evaluating the evidence and applying the law on burden of proof.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The learned Magistrate incorrectly applied the legal provisions and evaluated the evidence | The appellant failed to discharge the burden of proof under Section 40 of the Forest Ordinance
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The court evaluated the testimonies of the appellant and witness, noting contradictions in their accounts of who controlled the vehicle. This led to the conclusion that the appellant failed to prove he took all precautions to prevent the offence.
probability_assessment_by_court: The court applied the balance of probability standard to assess whether the owner took all precautions.
defence_version_summary: The accused pleaded guilty to the offence. The appellant owner argued he took all necessary precautions and had no knowledge of the illegal use, but the court found discrepancies in evidence and failed to discharge the burden of proof.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed the evidence presented during the confiscation inquiry, noting contradictions between the appellant's and witness's testimonies regarding control of the vehicle. It applied the burden of proof standard from Section 40 of the Forest Ordinance, requiring the owner to prove on balance of probability that all precautions were taken. Citing precedents, the court held that mere denial of knowledge is insufficient. The COA found no error in the lower courts' decisions and dismissed the appeal.
coa_sentence_type: Confiscation of vehicle
brief_judgment_file_summary: The appellant, registered owner of vehicle SG HW-4610, appealed against the confiscation order after the accused was convicted for transporting timber without a permit. The High Court affirmed the magistrate's confiscation order. The appellant argued that he had taken all precautions to prevent illegal use, but the Court of Appeal found discrepancies in evidence and upheld the lower courts' decisions, dismissing the appeal.
defence_counsel: Sanjaya Seneviratne
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court dismissed the revision application and affirmed the magistrate's confiscation order. The COA agreed with this analysis, finding no illegality.
precedents_cited_list: S. D. N. Premasiri v Officer in Charge, Mawathagama C A (PHC) 46/2015 | Jalathge Surasena v Officer in Charge, Police Station of Hikkaduwa CA (PHC) APN 100/2014
standard_of_review_applied: The court reviewed the lower courts' orders for legal correctness and evidence evaluation.
sentencing_principles_applied: Confiscation is mandatory unless the owner proves all precautions were taken to prevent the offence under Section 40 of the Forest Ordinance.

judges: K. PRIVANTHA FERNANDO, J. (P/CA) | WICKUM A. KALUARACHCHI, J.
offence_sections: Section 366 read with section 3 of the Offences Against Public Property Act No. 12 of 1982
brief_facts_summary: The appellant, a clerk in the health department, was involved in numbering question papers for a nurse promotion exam. Before the exam, question papers were leaked, and PW19 was caught trying to sell them. The appellant confessed to leaking the papers, and his confession was the primary evidence against him.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 366 read with section 3 of the Offences Against Public Property Act No. 12 of 1982
hc_sentence_type: 5 years rigorous imprisonment, fine of Rs. 1000, and compensation of Rs. 250,000 with default imprisonments
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the appellant of theft of public property based on his confession, which was found to be voluntary. He was sentenced to imprisonment and ordered to pay a fine and compensation.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant argued that the prosecution failed to prove the case beyond reasonable doubt, identification was not established, circumstantial evidence was not properly evaluated, and the confession was obtained through threat and oppression.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The prosecution has failed to prove the case beyond reasonable doubt. | Identification of the appellant as the person who committed the offence was not established. | There was no proper evaluation of the circumstantial evidence. | The established suspicious circumstances do not establish the guilt of the accused. | The learned trial Judge has erred in accepting the confession made by the appellant marked as P-X. | The learned trial Judge rejected the defence evidence on the wrong premise.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found that the confession was voluntary and not challenged in cross-examination, making it admissible. The circumstantial evidence supported the confession, and the prosecution proved the case beyond reasonable doubt.
probability_assessment_by_court: The court found the confession voluntary and true, and the prosecution proved beyond reasonable doubt.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty and gave an unsworn statement claiming the confession was obtained through threat, promise, or oppression. The court found this to be an afterthought as it was not put to witnesses in cross-examination.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal held that the confession was made voluntarily and was not challenged in cross-examination, making it admissible under Section 24 of the Evidence Ordinance. Citing precedents like Sarwan Singh and Raja Ram, the court emphasized that an extra-judicial confession can be relied upon if voluntary and true. The circumstantial evidence, including the appellant's access to question papers, supported the confession. Therefore, the prosecution proved the case beyond reasonable doubt, and no interference with the High Court's decision was warranted.
coa_sentence_type: 5 years rigorous imprisonment, fine of Rs. 1000, and compensation of Rs. 250,000 with default imprisonments
brief_judgment_file_summary: The appellant, a clerk in the health department, was convicted of theft for leaking question papers. The High Court sentenced him to imprisonment and fines. He appealed on grounds including the admissibility of his confession. The Court of Appeal found the confession voluntary and admissible, supported by circumstantial evidence, and dismissed the appeal, upholding the conviction and sentence.
defence_counsel: Malintha Jayasinghe
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted the appellant based on the confession, finding it voluntary and reliable. The Court of Appeal agreed with this assessment and found no error in the High Court's reasoning.
precedents_cited_list: Sarwan Singh v. State of Punjab 2002 AIC SC (iii) 3652 at 3655, 3656 | Himachal Pradesh v. Thakuar Dass 1993 2 Cri 1694 | Wannaku Arachchilage Gunapala v. Attorney-General [2007] 1 Sri L.R 273 | State of Rajasthan v. Raja Ram [2003] 8 SCC 180 | State v. Manjeet Singh, Sessions Case No. : 05/14, FIR No. 416/2013, Judgment Announced on : 27-09-2014
standard_of_review_applied: The court reviewed the evidence de novo, focusing on the voluntariness of the confession and whether the prosecution proved the case beyond reasonable doubt.

judges: Menaka Wijesundera J. | Neil Iddawala J.
brief_facts_summary: Suspect Buwaneswaran Rajeevan was arrested on 18.10.2020 for alleged involvement with terrorist group 'Saava' or '007'. Police recovered a sword and hand grenade from a goat-shed behind his house and found a photo of a deceased terrorist leader on his mobile phone. He denies allegations and claims coercion. He has been detained for nearly two years without trial.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: Petitioner argues that suspect has been detained for nearly two years without trial, violating Section 15B of the PTA. Suspect denies allegations and claims coercion.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Delay in trial beyond 12 months without indictment | Suspect denies allegations and claims coercion
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: Court notes absence of investigative material other than initial arrest details. Government Analyst's report received but no indictment filed.
probability_assessment_by_court: Court found no justification for continued incarceration.
defence_version_summary: Suspect denies allegations, claims coercion, and states no weapons recovered. Plea not guilty.
procedural_defects_description: Delay in investigation and failure to file indictment within reasonable time.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: COA analyzed Section 15B of PTA, noted legislative intent to use PTA only in exceptional circumstances. Found suspect detained for nearly two years without trial, fulfilling legislative prescription for bail. Granted bail due to lack of trial commencement and absence of justification for continued incarceration.
coa_sentence_type: Bail granted with conditions
brief_judgment_file_summary: Suspect Buwaneswaran Rajeevan was arrested for alleged terrorism links and detained for two years without trial. Petitioner filed bail application under Section 15B of PTA. Court of Appeal found delay unjustified and granted bail with conditions including cash bail and sureties.
defence_counsel: N.M. Shaheid and Rushdhie Habeeb
precedents_cited_list: Sukumar Vs Officer in Charge Joseph Army Camp, Vavuniya (2003) 1 S.L.R. 399
standard_of_review_applied: Discretionary review under Section 15B of PTA

judges: Menaka Wijesundera J. | Neil Iddawala J.
offence_sections: section 10(1)(a) of the Assistance to and Protection of Victims of Crime and Witnesses Act No. 4 of 2015
brief_facts_summary: The accused was arrested on 21/12/2021 and remanded for a complaint by Ajith Prasnna Senevirathne, an eye witness in a murder case that concluded 5 years ago. The other accused in the same case had been enlarged on bail. The Court of Appeal considered the bail application under the Victims and Witnesses Act.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The petitioner applied for bail under the Victims and Witnesses Act. The respondent objected on the basis that the accused has not completed one year in remand. The court found no merit in this submission as keeping the accused in remand violates his liberty.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Bail application under section 10(1)(a) of the Victims and Witnesses Act. | Objection by state counsel based on remand time less than one year. | Court held that remand for one year when substantive matter concluded five years ago violates liberty.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The court noted that the complaint was by an eye witness, but the substantive matter concluded five years ago. No detailed evidence analysis was performed for the bail application.
probability_assessment_by_court: The court assessed that keeping the accused in remand for one year when the substantive matter concluded five years ago is a definite violation of his liberty, leading to bail being granted.
defence_version_summary: The accused sought bail under the Victims and Witnesses Act. The defence argued for liberty, and the court accepted that remand was unjustified.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed that the Victims and Witnesses Act is for safeguarding victims and witnesses, but matters under this Act should be given precedence. However, keeping the accused in prison for an exact period of one year when the substantive matter has been concluded five years ago is a definite violation of his liberty to freedom. Therefore, bail was granted.
coa_sentence_type: Bail granted with conditions: cash bail of Rs. 25,000, two sureties of Rs. 50,000 each, monthly reporting to police station, and warning not to interfere with victim or family.
brief_judgment_file_summary: This judgment concerns a bail application for Randoluge Dinoj Theshan De Silva, who was arrested and remanded for a complaint by an eye witness from a murder case five years ago. The Court of Appeal allowed the bail application, finding that keeping the accused in remand for one year violates his liberty, as the substantive matter concluded long ago. Bail was granted with conditions including cash bail and sureties.
defence_counsel: Sabdhika Wellappili and Waijanthi Nandadasa
standard_of_review_applied: Application of the Victims and Witnesses Act and consideration of liberty interests for bail.

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 296 read with Section 32 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: On April 27, 2002, the deceased was at a mosque during heavy rain when a car arrived and occupants fired shots, killing him. PW1 claimed to identify the Appellant and 2nd accused with the help of car hood light, but there were contradictions in his testimony regarding the car color and exit side. The prosecution relied solely on eyewitness identification.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 296 read with Section 32 of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the Appellant and 2nd accused based on the evidence of PW1, the sole eyewitness, and sentenced them to death. The judge accepted PW1's identification despite poor light conditions.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The Appellant argued that the trial judge erred in fact and law, the prosecution failed to establish his identity beyond reasonable doubt, there was misdirection on Section 32 of the Penal Code, and relying on PW1's evidence was unsafe due to impeached character.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The Learned Trial Judge erred on facts and law. | The prosecution had failed to establish the identity of the Appellant. | The Learned Trial Judge had misdirected himself as to the proof of ingredients of the Section 32 of the Penal Code. | Relying on the evidence of PW1, the purported eye witness, is highly unsafe given the impeached character.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed PW1's identification evidence, noting contradictions in his testimony, poor light conditions, and the sole eyewitness's reliability, leading to reasonable doubt.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court assessed the probability of mistaken identity under poor light and found prosecution failed to prove identity beyond reasonable doubt.
defence_version_summary: The Appellant pleaded not guilty, denied the charge, and presented an alibi that he was at his mother's place with his wife and children during the incident. He called two witnesses to support his defence.
legal_errors_description: The High Court failed to appreciate the weak identification evidence and contradictions in PW1's testimony, leading to a miscarriage of justice.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal focused on identification evidence, citing precedents on identification uncertainty. They noted contradictions in PW1's testimony regarding car color and exit side, poor light conditions, and the sole eyewitness's reliability. COA concluded that prosecution failed to prove identity beyond reasonable doubt, thus allowing the appeal and acquitting the Appellant.
coa_sentence_type: Acquitted, no sentence imposed
brief_judgment_file_summary: The Appellant was convicted of murder by the High Court of Puttalam and sentenced to death. He appealed on grounds including misidentification and legal errors. The Court of Appeal found the identification evidence unreliable due to contradictions and poor light conditions, acquitted him and the 2nd accused, and directed the judgment to be sent to the High Court.
defence_counsel: Harishke Samaranayake
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court relied on PW1's identification to convict, but COA found that HC did not properly assess the identification evidence under poor light conditions and failed to consider contradictions.
precedents_cited_list: Alexander v. R (1981) 145 CLR 395 | Visveswaran v. State (2003) 6 SCC 73 | Turnbull [1977] QB 224
standard_of_review_applied: Assessment of whether prosecution proved identity beyond reasonable doubt, guided by identification evidence principles.

judges: Menaka Wijesundera J. | Neil Iddawala J.
offence_sections: Section 40(1) of the Forest Ordinance, No. 16 of 1907 (as amended)
brief_facts_summary: The vehicle was seized on 20.04.2015 for transporting timber without a licence. The driver pleaded guilty and was fined. The registered owner appealed against confiscation, claiming he took precautions, but the court found his evidence insufficient due to contradictions.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 40(1) of the Forest Ordinance, No. 16 of 1907 (as amended)
hc_sentence_type: Confiscation of vehicle under Forest Ordinance
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court affirmed the Magistrate's order to confiscate the vehicle, dismissing the revision application. It found that the petitioner failed to prove he took all precautions to prevent the offence.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The petitioner appealed against the confiscation orders, arguing that he had taken all necessary precautions to prevent the use of his vehicle for the offence. He contended that the lower courts incorrectly evaluated the evidence regarding his precautions.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Failure to correctly evaluate evidence on precautions taken by owner under Section 40(1) proviso of Forest Ordinance.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed the petitioner's testimony and found contradictions between his examination-in-chief and re-examination. This raised doubts about his bona fides and led to the conclusion that he failed to satisfy the burden of proof on a balance of probability.
probability_assessment_by_court: Court applied balance of probability standard to assess if owner took all precautions to prevent the offence.
defence_version_summary: The driver pleaded guilty to the offence. The owner claimed he took precautions by instructing the usual driver, but left the vehicle with the accused without similar instructions. His testimony was contradictory, and the court found it not credible.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal examined the burden of proof under Section 40(1) of the Forest Ordinance, which requires the owner to prove he took all precautions to prevent the offence. The court found contradictions in the petitioner's evidence and concluded that he failed to establish on balance of probability that he had taken all necessary precautions. Citing precedents, the COA upheld the lower courts' decisions and dismissed the appeal.
coa_sentence_type: Confiscation of vehicle under Section 40(1) of the Forest Ordinance
brief_judgment_file_summary: The registered owner of vehicle No. 227-6258 appealed against its confiscation after it was used for illegal timber transportation. The driver pleaded guilty and was fined. The Magistrate and High Court ordered confiscation under the Forest Ordinance. The Court of Appeal found the owner's evidence contradictory and insufficient to prove he took all precautions, dismissing the appeal and upholding the confiscation.
defence_counsel: Dinesh de Silva
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court affirmed the Magistrate's confiscation order, finding the petitioner failed to prove he took all precautions. The Court of Appeal reviewed this and found no error, agreeing with the High Court's analysis.
precedents_cited_list: The Finance Company PLC v. Agampodi Mahapedige Priyantha Chandana and others (2010) 2 Sri L.R. 220 | Orient Financial Services Corporation Ltd. v. Range Forest Officer, Ampara and Another, SC Appeal No. 120/2011 (SC Minutes 10.12.2013)
standard_of_review_applied: Balance of probability standard for assessing owner's precautions under Forest Ordinance.

judges: K. PRIYANTHA FERNANDO, J. | WICKUM A. KALUARACHCHI, J.
offence_sections: Section 140 of the Penal Code, Section 296 read with Section 146 of the Penal Code, and Section 296 read with Section 32 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The deceased was stabbed by the appellant while being held by the 5th accused. The assailants took the injured deceased in a three-wheeler, which later crashed after family members jumped in front. The deceased was pronounced dead at the hospital. Key evidence includes eyewitness testimony and medical evidence.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 296 read with Section 32 of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the appellant for murder under section 296 read with section 32 of the Penal Code. The court found the eyewitness testimony credible and sentenced the appellant to death.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant challenged the conviction on grounds including prejudice from adding an alias name, discrepancy between eyewitness and medical evidence, failure of eyewitness to name appellant initially, and contradictions in prosecution evidence.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The learned trial Judge erred by allowing the prosecution to amend and add the alias name of the 2nd appellant during the trial as it causes a severe prejudice to the appellant. | The learned trial Judge failed to consider whether the evidence of the so-called eye witnesses to the incident tallies with the medical evidence. | The learned High Court Judge failed and neglected to give adequate consideration to the effect that the alleged eye witness had not named the appellant as the assailant at first given opportunity, which created a serious doubt on the prosecution case. | The learned High Court Judge failed and neglected to evaluate, inter se contradictions which cast a serious doubt on the prosecution case.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the eyewitness testimony consistent and credible, corroborated by medical evidence. The court noted that minor discrepancies do not undermine the overall reliability of the witnesses.
probability_assessment_by_court: Court found evidence sufficient to establish guilt beyond reasonable doubt, considering both direct and circumstantial evidence.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty. No defence witnesses were called for the appellant. The court found the prosecution evidence credible.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal dismissed all grounds of appeal. It held that amending the indictment to add the alias caused no prejudice, as the appellant had opportunity to cross-examine witnesses. The medical evidence corroborated the eyewitness testimony, and minor discrepancies were not material. The court deferred to the trial judge's assessment of witness credibility and found sufficient evidence for conviction.
coa_sentence_type: Death
brief_judgment_file_summary: The appellant was convicted of murder by the High Court of Colombo and sentenced to death. He appealed on grounds including procedural error in amending the indictment, inconsistencies between eyewitness and medical evidence, and contradictions in prosecution evidence. The Court of Appeal found no merit in the appeals, affirmed the eyewitness testimony as credible, and upheld the conviction and sentence. The appeal was dismissed.
defence_counsel: Shanaka Ranasinghe, PC with Anushika Ranasinghe
hc_analysis_summary: High Court convicted the appellant based on credible eyewitness testimony and medical evidence. Court of Appeal found no errors in the HC's analysis and upheld the decision.
precedents_cited_list: State of Uttar Pradesh V. M.K Anthony [1984] SCJ 236/ [1985] CRI. LJ. 493 | Fradd V. Brown & company Ltd. (20 N.L.R. Page 282) | Himachal Pradesh V. Thakuar Dass 1993 2 Cri 1694 | Motilal V. State of Madya Pradesh 1990 Cri LJ No. C 125 MP
standard_of_review_applied: Deference to trial judge's assessment of witness credibility and factual findings.

judges: K. PRIYANTHA FERNANDO, J. (P/CA) | WICKUM A. KALUARACHCHI, J.
offence_sections: Section 140 of the Penal Code, Section 296 read with Section 146 of the Penal Code, Section 296 read with Section 32 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The deceased was stabbed by the appellant while buying food for pigeons with others. The appellant and accomplices took the deceased in a three-wheeler, which crashed after family members intervened. The deceased died from injuries, and key evidence included eyewitness testimony and medical evidence.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 296 read with Section 32 of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the appellant of murder based on eyewitness testimony and medical evidence, and sentenced him to death.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant argued that the amendment to add his alias name was prejudicial, that eyewitness evidence conflicted with medical evidence, that the eyewitness did not identify him initially, and that there were contradictions in the prosecution case.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The learned trial Judge erred by allowing the prosecution to amend and add the alias name of the 2nd appellant during the trial as it causes a severe prejudice to the appellant. | The learned trial Judge failed to consider whether the evidence of the so-called eye witnesses to the incident tallies with the medical evidence. | The learned High Court Judge failed and neglected to give adequate consideration to the effect that the alleged eye witness had not named the appellant as the assailant at first given opportunity, which created a serious doubt on the prosecution case. | The learned High Court Judge failed and neglected to evaluate, inter se contradictions which cast a serious doubt on the prosecution case.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court found the eyewitness testimony consistent and credible, corroborated by medical evidence and the testimony of a co-accused. Minor discrepancies were not considered fatal, and the trial judge's assessment of witness demeanor was deferred to.
probability_assessment_by_court: The court found that the evidence proved the appellant's guilt beyond reasonable doubt, with direct and circumstantial evidence.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty. No alibi or defence witnesses were called; the defence relied on challenging prosecution evidence through cross-examination.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed each ground of appeal. It found no prejudice in the amendment to the indictment, medical evidence corroborated eyewitnesses, and witness credibility was upheld despite minor contradictions. The court cited precedents on appellate review and evidence evaluation, and affirmed the conviction and sentence.
coa_sentence_type: Death
brief_judgment_file_summary: The appellant was convicted of murder by the High Court and sentenced to death. He appealed on grounds including procedural error, inconsistency between eyewitness and medical evidence, identification issues, and contradictions. The Court of Appeal found no merit in the grounds, upheld the credibility of evidence, and affirmed the conviction and sentence.
defence_counsel: Shanaka Ranasinghe, PC with Anushika Ranasinghe
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted the appellant based on eyewitness and medical evidence. The Court of Appeal agreed with this analysis and found no errors in the High Court's reasoning.
precedents_cited_list: State of Uttar Pradesh V. M.K. Anthony [1984] SCJ 236/ [1985] CRI. LJ. 493 | Fradd V. Brown & company Ltd. (20 N.L.R. Page 282) | Himachal Pradesh V. Thakuar Dass 1993 2 Cri 1694 | Motilal V. State of Madya Pradesh 1990 Cri LJ No. C 125 MP
standard_of_review_applied: The court applied a standard of deference to the trial judge's factual findings, citing precedents on appellate restraint and the advantage of observing witness demeanor.

judges: K. Priyantha Fernando, J (P/CA) | Wickum A. Kaluarachchi, J
offence_sections: Section 54A(b) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance
brief_facts_summary: On 26 November 2007, police received information and stopped a three-wheeler. The first accused (appellant's sister) was found with two yellow covers containing heroin in her handbag. The appellant was the driver. From the locked cubbyhole of the three-wheeler, opened with keys from the appellant, police recovered a weighing scale with traces of heroin, four weights, and five similar yellow covers.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 54A(b) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the appellant for trafficking heroin and sentenced him to death. The Judge found the appellant had knowledge of the heroin being transported, based on the recovery of a weighing scale with traces of heroin and similar yellow covers from the locked cubbyhole of his three-wheeler.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant's counsel confined arguments to the issue of the appellant's knowledge of the offence. The main argument was that the appellant had no knowledge that his sister was carrying heroin in his three-wheeler, even if the prosecution version was accepted.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Lack of knowledge of the heroin being transported by the first accused in the appellant's three-wheeler
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal considered the unchallenged evidence of prosecution witnesses, including the police and Government Analyst. The defence failed to cross-examine on key points, leading to acceptance of the prosecution's facts.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court assessed that the only reasonable inference from the facts, especially the scale and similar bags in the locked cubbyhole, was that the appellant had knowledge, establishing guilt beyond reasonable doubt.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty. He made a dock statement offering a contradictory version about another woman 'Srimathi' and claimed heroin was introduced at the police station. The court found the defence versions contradictory and unreliable.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal held that the prosecution proved beyond reasonable doubt that the appellant had knowledge of the heroin being transported. It relied on the recovery of a weighing scale with heroin traces and similar yellow covers from the locked cubbyhole of the appellant's three-wheeler, to which only he had keys, as strong circumstantial evidence of knowledge. The court noted the defence's failure to cross-examine on material points and cited precedents on accepting unchallenged evidence. It affirmed the High Court's careful evaluation of evidence and found no reason to disturb the findings.
coa_sentence_type: Death
brief_judgment_file_summary: The appellant was convicted by the High Court of Colombo for trafficking 22.54 grams of heroin and sentenced to death. He appealed, arguing lack of knowledge that his sister was carrying the heroin in his three-wheeler. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal, finding that the recovery of a weighing scale with heroin traces and similar drug packaging from the locked cubbyhole of his vehicle, accessible only to him, proved his knowledge beyond reasonable doubt. The conviction and death sentence were affirmed.
defence_counsel: Shehan De Silva with Naveen Maha Arachchi
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court Judge carefully considered the evidence and found the appellant had knowledge of the heroin based on the scale and bags found in the locked cubbyhole. The Court of Appeal agreed with this analysis and found no error.
precedents_cited_list: Sarvan Singh v. State of Punjab (2002 AIR SC (iii) 3652) | Ratnayake Mudiyanselage Premachandra v. The Hon. Attorney General C.A. Case No. 79/2011, decided on 04.04.2017 | Himachal Pradesh v. Thakur Dass (1983) 2 Cri. L. J. 1694 at 1701 | Motilal v. State of Madhya Pradesh (1990) Criminal Law Journal NOC 125 MP | King Vs. Gunaratne 14 Ceylon Law Recorder 174 | Fradd Vs. Brown & Company 20 NLR 282 at 283 | State of Uttar Pradesh Vs. M. K. Anthony (1984) SCJ 236/(1985) CRI L.J. 493 at 498/499 | Oliver Dayananda Kalansuriya alias Raja Vs. Republic of Sri Lanka CA 28/2009 (13.02.2013) | Wickramasuriya V. Dedolina (1996) 2 Sri L.R. 95 | Alwis V. Piyasena Fernando (1993) 1 Sri L.R. 119 at 122 | V. Sivadasan & V. Pavadasan V. The Attorney General - CA 46/2008 decided on 13.07.2012
standard_of_review_applied: The appellate court will not lightly disturb the considered findings of a trial Judge on testimonial trustworthiness and evidence evaluation.
sentencing_principles_applied: The offence carries only life imprisonment or death sentence; the sentence imposed was lawful and correct in principle.

judges: N. Bandula Karunarathna J. | R. Gurusinghe J.
offence_sections: Sections 296, 364(1) (as amended by Act No.22 of 1995), and 317 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: Two masked persons entered a bungalow, injured two occupants, killed one, and took two women to a nearby tea estate where they were raped. The 2nd accused-appellant was convicted for murder, rape, and grievous hurt. Key evidence included eyewitness testimony and medical evidence.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Sections 296, 364(1) (as amended by Act No.22 of 1995), and 317 of the Penal Code
hc_sentence_type: Death sentence for murder, 20 years rigorous imprisonment and fine for rape, and compensation for victims
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the 2nd accused-appellant on counts 1, 3, 4, and 5 (murder, rape, and grievous hurt) and sentenced him to death for murder, 20 years rigorous imprisonment and fine for rape, and compensation for victims. The 1st accused was acquitted.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant argued that the conviction was based on uncorroborated and inconsistent evidence, mistaken identity, and that the trial judge failed to consider common intention and defence witness properly.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The Learned Trial Judge has convicted the Appellant for all charges relying on uncorroborated and inconsistent evidence. | The identity of the appellant has not been proved beyond reasonable doubt and the appellant was indicted on the mistaken identity. | There are no grounds to adopt the evidence of PW 5. | The Learned Trial Judge has failed to consider the law and legal principle relating to common intention. | The learned Trial Judge has failed to offer appropriate prominence and due consideration to the defence witness by established legal principles.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found the evidence of key witnesses (PW4 and PW5) inconsistent and uncorroborated. Medical evidence did not support PW5's version. Identification was doubtful due to poor lighting and lack of proper guidelines application.
probability_assessment_by_court: The COA found that the prosecution failed to prove the case beyond reasonable doubt due to inconsistencies, unreliable identification, and lack of corroboration.
defence_version_summary: The 2nd accused-appellant made a dock statement denying the allegations and called his mother to give alibi evidence that he was at home at the time of the incident. The prosecution did not challenge the alibi evidence. The trial judge did not give due consideration to the defence witness.
legal_errors_description: Failure to properly evaluate uncorroborated and inconsistent evidence; adopting evidence under section 33 without ensuring the witness could not be found; misapplication of common intention principles; failure to consider defence evidence.
procedural_defects_description: Adopting the evidence of PW5 under section 33 of the Evidence Ordinance without satisfying that the witness's presence cannot be ensured.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed the evidence and found that the identification of the appellant was not proven beyond reasonable doubt due to poor lighting and inconsistencies. The medical evidence did not corroborate the rape victim's testimony. The trial judge failed to apply the Turnbull guidelines for identification. The common intention was not established as the appellant refused to cut the victims. The defence alibi was not considered. The prosecution did not prove the case beyond reasonable doubt.
coa_sentence_type: Conviction and sentence quashed; accused acquitted and discharged from all charges
brief_judgment_file_summary: The 2nd accused-appellant was convicted by the High Court of Nuwara Eliya for murder, rape, and grievous hurt and sentenced to death. He appealed on grounds of uncorroborated evidence, mistaken identity, and failure to consider common intention and defence evidence. The Court of Appeal found the prosecution evidence inconsistent and identification doubtful, and acquitted the appellant.
defence_counsel: Saliya Pieris PC with Susil Wanigapura AAL and Chan Godakumura AAL for the 2nd accused-appellant
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted the appellant based on unreliable identification and uncorroborated evidence. The COA found that the High Court failed to properly evaluate the evidence, misapplied common intention, and did not consider the defence.
precedents_cited_list: Gurcharan Singh V. State of Haryana AIR 1972 S.0 2661 | Sunil and another V. The Attorney General 1986 (1) SLR 230 | King v. Asappu 50 NLR 324 | CA 10-11/2010- decided on 07.02.2014 | Wimalaratne Silva and Another vs. Attorney General - SLR - 103, Vol 1 of 2008 [2008] LKCA 6; (2008) 1 SLR 103 (11 November 2008) | R V Turnbull [1977] QB 224
standard_of_review_applied: Review of evidence and application of beyond reasonable doubt standard

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
location_of_offence: Kaldemulla area and Dewata Road Bridge
brief_facts_summary: The appellant was arrested on 5th August 2015 for possessing and trafficking 1.38 grams of heroin. Police received a tip-off, conducted a raid, and found her with a pink bag containing heroin. She claimed she was arrested later in the day while borrowing money from a friend, with no drugs found, and that drugs were planted. Key evidence includes police testimony and government analyst report.
hc_sentence_type: Rigorous Imprisonment 10 years on each count, concurrent, with fine on count one
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court found the appellant guilty based on prosecution evidence, deemed contradictions minor, and sentenced her to 10 years rigorous imprisonment on each count concurrently, with a fine of Rs. 100,000 on count one.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant appealed on grounds of contradictions in prosecution evidence, failure to prove chain of custody, and failure to properly evaluate the dock statement and defence witnesses. The second ground was later conceded.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: The learned High Court Judge had failed to consider vital contradictions in the evidence of the prosecution witnesses | The learned High Court Judge had come to a wrong finding that the prosecution had proved the chain of productions | The learned High Court Judge failed to evaluate the dock statement and had rejected the same by applying wrong principles of law and had failed to give valid reasons for rejecting the evidence of the defence witnesses
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found contradictions in prosecution witnesses' evidence regarding time and actions, which were not minor and created reasonable doubt. The defence evidence was not properly evaluated by the High Court.
probability_assessment_by_court: The Court of Appeal assessed that prosecution evidence was not probable due to contradictions and raised reasonable doubt, leading to acquittal.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded not guilty, gave a dock statement claiming she was arrested later with no drugs and drugs were planted, and called two defence witnesses. The High Court rejected the defence, but the Court of Appeal found it should have been considered.
legal_errors_description: The High Court failed to properly evaluate the dock statement and defence witnesses, applying wrong legal principles in rejecting them.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found significant contradictions in prosecution evidence regarding time and actions, which the High Court erroneously deemed minor. The Court of Appeal also held that the High Court misapplied law in evaluating the dock statement and defence witnesses, failing to consider evidence in totality. This created reasonable doubt, leading to the setting aside of the conviction and sentence.
coa_sentence_type: Acquitted, no sentence imposed
brief_judgment_file_summary: The appellant was convicted by the High Court of Panadura for possession and trafficking of heroin and sentenced to 10 years rigorous imprisonment and a fine. She appealed on grounds of contradictions in prosecution evidence and improper evaluation of defence. The Court of Appeal found prosecution evidence flawed and High Court legal errors, leading to acquittal and setting aside of conviction and sentence.
defence_counsel: Neranjan Jayasinghe
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court considered contradictions in prosecution evidence as minor and rejected the defence. The Court of Appeal found these were significant errors, and the High Court failed to properly assess evidence and apply law regarding the dock statement and defence witnesses.
precedents_cited_list: James Silva Vs. The Republic of Sri Lanka (1980) 2 SLR 167 | Queen Vs. Kularatne (1968) 71 NLR 529 | Don Samantha Jude Anthony Jayamaha Vs. The Attorney General, C.A. 303/2006 | Don Ranasuriya Arachchige Rohana Kithsiri Vs. The Attorney General CA 214/2008 | D.N. Panday Vs. State of Uttar Pradesh, AIR 1981, Supreme Court 911 | Martin Singho Vs. Queen 69 CLW 21
standard_of_review_applied: Review based on totality of evidence and reasonable doubt standard

judges: N. Bandula Karunarathna, J. | R. Gurusinghe, J.
offence_sections: Section 365 B (2) b of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: The accused-appellant was indicted for kissing/sucking the lips of a 15-year-old boy. He pleaded guilty to two indictments before trial. However, the victim's evidence-in-chief did not mention the appellant kissing or sucking his lips, and the Judicial Medical Officer history did not reveal such incident. No violence, threat, or physical injury was caused, and the victim did not complain.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 365 B (2) b of the Penal Code
hc_sentence_type: 15 years Rigorous Imprisonment per count, cumulative 30 years, with fine and compensation
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the appellant upon his guilty plea to both indictments and sentenced him to 15 years Rigorous Imprisonment per count with fines and compensation. The conviction was based solely on the plea without examining the evidence.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appeal argues that the conviction upon guilty plea should be set aside as the evidence does not support the charge. The appellant may have been confused when pleading guilty to two indictments arising from the same facts. The Court of Appeal considered whether to intervene to prevent miscarriage of justice.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Evidence does not establish the charge | Plea of guilty may have been made in confusion due to multiple indictments from same facts
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The victim (PW1) gave evidence-in-chief but was not cross-examined. His testimony did not mention the appellant kissing or sucking his lips, and the JMO history did not reveal the incident. The evidence failed to establish the charge.
probability_assessment_by_court: The court found that the evidence does not establish the charge, and if the trial had proceeded, conviction might not have occurred due to reasonable doubt.
defence_version_summary: The appellant pleaded guilty to the charges. No alibi or witnesses were called. The court considered that the plea might have been confused due to multiple indictments from the same facts.
legal_errors_description: High Court convicted the appellant upon guilty plea without considering that the evidence did not establish the charge, leading to miscarriage of justice.
procedural_defects_description: The appellant pleaded guilty to two indictments arising from same facts, which may have caused confusion, and the conviction was entered without proper assessment of evidence.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The COA reviewed the evidence and found that the victim's testimony did not establish the charge. Referring to Supreme Court precedents, the COA exercised its revisionary powers under Articles 138 and 145 of the Constitution to prevent miscarriage of justice. The court set aside the conviction and sentence because the evidence negated the charge, even though the appellant had pleaded guilty.
coa_sentence_type: Conviction and sentence set aside; appellant acquitted
brief_judgment_file_summary: The appellant was convicted in High Court for sexual abuse of a 15-year-old boy after pleading guilty. He appealed to the Court of Appeal, arguing that the evidence did not support the charge. The COA found that the victim's testimony failed to establish the offence, and using revisionary powers, set aside the conviction and sentence, acquitting the appellant.
defence_counsel: Duminda de Alwis
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted the appellant based on his guilty plea without examining the evidence. The COA found this led to miscarriage of justice as the evidence did not establish the offence.
precedents_cited_list: SC Appeal 32/2020 SC SPL LA No. 232/2017 Hattuwan Pedige Sugath Karunarathne v. Hon. Attorney General | Somawathie v. Madauvela (1983) 2 SLR 15 | Jennison v. Backer (1972 (1) All E.R. 1006) | Mariam Beebee v Seyed Mohamed 68NLR 36
standard_of_review_applied: Revisionary powers under Articles 138 and 145 of the Constitution to correct errors and prevent miscarriage of justice

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
brief_facts_summary: On 27-04-2014, a vehicle was caught transporting Jak timber logs without a permit. The driver and three others pleaded guilty. The vehicle owner, the appellant, argued he was unaware of the illegal use and had taken precautions. Evidence included testimonies from the owner and the person who hired the vehicle for legitimate purposes.
hc_judgment_summary: High Court dismissed the revision application, agreeing with the Magistrate that there were contradictions in evidence and no exceptional circumstances to intervene.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant argued that the Magistrate and High Court misdirected themselves on the evidence, incorrectly finding contradictions between testimonies where none existed.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Magistrate misdirected on evidence analysis | High Court erred in dismissing revision based on non-existent contradictions
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: COA analyzed testimonies of appellant and Nalaka Dharmasiri Bandara, found no material contradiction, and concluded that the owner took due precautions to prevent illegal use.
probability_assessment_by_court: Court applied balance of probability standard for confiscation inquiry.
defence_version_summary: Appellant claimed he was unaware of illegal activity, had given instructions to driver, and vehicle was hired for legitimate transport. Court found his evidence credible.
legal_errors_description: Magistrate and High Court misdirected on evidence analysis by finding contradictions where none existed.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: COA re-examined the evidence, found no contradiction between appellant and witness testimonies, applied balance of probability, cited precedents on confiscation inquiries, and determined that the owner took reasonable precautions, thus setting aside the confiscation order.
coa_sentence_type: Release of vehicle, confiscation order set aside
brief_judgment_file_summary: The appellant, owner of a vehicle used in illegal timber transport, appealed against the confiscation order. High Court dismissed his revision application. COA allowed the appeal, finding no material contradictions in evidence and that the owner took due precautions, thus setting aside the confiscation order and directing release of the vehicle.
defence_counsel: Duminda de Alwis with Charuni de Alwis
hc_analysis_summary: High Court agreed with Magistrate's finding of contradictions in evidence and dismissed revision. COA found this erroneous as no material contradictions existed.
precedents_cited_list: Miller Vs. Minister of Pensions (1947) 2 AER 372 | CA/PHC/108/2010 dated 26-08-2014
standard_of_review_applied: Balance of probability for confiscation inquiries

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: section 19(b) and 19(c) of the Bribery Act
brief_facts_summary: The appellant, a principal of Matale Vijaya College, solicited a bribe from a parent for school admission. A raid was organized by the Bribery Commission where the bribe was given through an intermediary. Key evidence includes witness testimonies and phone records. The appellant denied the charges.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: section 19(b) and 19(c) of the Bribery Act
hc_sentence_type: Rigorous Imprisonment 5 years on each count with fines, concurrent sentences
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the appellant on all four counts of bribery. She was sentenced to 5 years rigorous imprisonment on each count with fines, and an additional fine under section 26. Sentences were to run concurrently.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: Appellant argued time gap between solicitation and acceptance creates doubt, discrepancy in who solicited and accepted bribe, and inconsistencies in witness evidence regarding money denominations.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Time gap of 16 days between solicitation and acceptance creates reasonable doubt. | Solicitation was on PW-01 but acceptance was from his wife through an intermediary, creating doubt. | Discrepancy in amount solicited (Rs. 200,000) and accepted (Rs. 150,000), and inconsistencies in denominations.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: COA found evidence of PW-01 and PW-02 credible for solicitation but contradictory for acceptance. Phone records corroborated solicitation date. However, inconsistencies in raid participation cast doubt on acceptance.
probability_assessment_by_court: COA applied reasonable doubt standard, holding that suspicion alone cannot convict, and prosecution must prove case beyond reasonable doubt.
defence_version_summary: Appellant pleaded not guilty and made a dock statement denying all charges. She claimed she only discussed an NGO project and properly processed the admission. No alibi or witnesses were called. COA found her defence not credible for solicitation but created doubt for acceptance.
legal_errors_description: COA found that the prosecution failed to prove acceptance of bribe beyond reasonable doubt due to contradictory evidence.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: COA analyzed evidence separately for solicitation and acceptance. For solicitation, witness testimonies and phone records were found credible, confirming conviction. For acceptance, inconsistencies in witness accounts and raid procedures created reasonable doubt, leading to acquittal on those counts. COA applied precedents on burden of proof and suspended the imprisonment sentence considering no prior convictions and loss of government service benefits.
coa_sentence_type: One-year rigorous imprisonment on each of counts 1 and 2, with fines, suspended for five years.
brief_judgment_file_summary: The appellant, a school principal, was convicted by the High Court on four counts of bribery for soliciting and accepting a bribe for school admission. She appealed, arguing inconsistencies in evidence. The Court of Appeal partly allowed the appeal, upholding conviction for solicitation but acquitting for acceptance due to reasonable doubt. The sentence was reduced to suspended imprisonment with fines.
defence_counsel: Prasantha Lal De Alwis, P.C. with Mohan Sellapperuma and L.A.D. Samith Kalhara
hc_analysis_summary: HC convicted appellant on all counts based on witness testimonies. COA agreed for solicitation but found that for acceptance, HC overlooked contradictory evidence, leading to unsafe conviction.
precedents_cited_list: The Queen Vs. M.G. Sumanasena 66 NLR 350 | Karunadasa Vs. Officer-in-Charge, Motor Traffic Division, Police Station Nittambuwa (1887) 1 SLR 155 | Alim Vs. Wijesinghe (S.I. Police, Batticaloa) 38 CLW 95
standard_of_review_applied: Review based on whether prosecution proved case beyond reasonable doubt, evaluating evidence credibility.
sentencing_principles_applied: Principles of proportionality, rehabilitation, and considering personal circumstances such as no prior convictions and loss of government service benefits.
final_charge_after_appeal: Conviction on counts 1 and 2 (solicitation) only.

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
offence_sections: Section 296 read with Section 32 of the Penal Code
brief_facts_summary: On February 16, 1996, the deceased was forcibly taken from his cousin's house by a group including the 1st and 4th Appellants and assaulted in 'Palu Watta', suffering fatal injuries. Eyewitnesses identified the appellants but their testimonies contained contradictions. There was prior animosity between the appellants and the deceased.
hc_offence_of_conviction_sections: Section 296 read with Section 32 of the Penal Code
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court convicted the appellants based on prosecution evidence and sentenced them to death. The judge found the prosecution case proved beyond reasonable doubt.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellants appealed on grounds including failure to prove death, identification issues, contradictions in witness testimony, and lack of judicial evaluation. The Senior Deputy Solicitor General did not contest the appeal for the 2nd and 3rd appellants.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Failure of the prosecution to prove the death of the person named in the indictment. | Identification of the 1st Appellant was not done beyond reasonable grounds. | Failure of the learned Trial Judge to make a judicial evaluation of the credibility of the prosecution witness by analyzing contradictions marked by the defence. | No observation notes prepared by the police officers regarding the incident during the investigation. | Has the prosecution proved the case against 4th Appellant beyond reasonable grounds. | If the contradictions and commissions in the evidence of PW2 and PW3 were evaluated according to law would that have created a reasonable doubt about the presence of the 4th Appellant at the scene of crime. | If the evidence of Ranil Fernando cannot be considered against the 2nd and 3rd Appellants does that create a reasonable doubt as regards the 4th Appellant as well. | Can the discovery of a witness in consequence of a statement made by an accused be led under Section 27 of the Evidence Ordinance.
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found contradictions and omissions in the eyewitness testimonies, particularly PW2, which affected credibility and created reasonable doubt.
probability_assessment_by_court: The court assessed reasonable doubt based on contradictions and omissions in identification evidence.
defence_version_summary: The appellants pleaded not guilty, made dock statements denying the charge, and called no witnesses. The court found the prosecution evidence unreliable, leading to acquittal.
legal_errors_description: The High Court failed to properly consider contradictions and omissions in witness testimony affecting identification.
court_of_appeal_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal analyzed the identification evidence from PW2, PW3, and PW4, noting contradictions and omissions that raised reasonable doubt. The court cited precedents on identification evidence and held that the prosecution failed to prove the case beyond reasonable doubt against the 1st and 4th appellants. The conviction was set aside due to unreliable witness testimony.
coa_sentence_type: Acquitted
brief_judgment_file_summary: The appellants were convicted of murder by the High Court of Colombo and sentenced to death. They appealed on grounds including identification issues and contradictions in witness testimony. The Court of Appeal found the prosecution evidence unreliable due to contradictions and omissions, acquitting all appellants as the case was not proved beyond reasonable doubt.
defence_counsel: Moditha T.B. Ekanayake for the 1st Accused-Appellant. Neranjan Jayasinghe with Harshana Ananda and Dulshan Katugampola for the 2nd Accused-Appellant. Saliya Pieris, PC with Pasindu Thilakaratne for the 3rd Accused-Appellant. Anil Silva, PC with J.Kalupahana for the 4th Accused-Appellant.
hc_analysis_summary: The High Court convicted based on witness testimony, but the Court of Appeal found that the High Court failed to properly consider contradictions and omissions, leading to an unsafe conviction.
precedents_cited_list: Karunaratne Mudiyansege Madduma Bandara v. The Attorney General CA/190-192/11 decided on 15/03/2013 | Gorle S. Naidu v. State of A.P. [1997] Appeal (crl) 232-234 | R v. Turnbull [1977] QB 224 | AG v. Sandanam Pitchai Mary Theresa (2011) 2 Sri L.R. 292 | K. Padmathilaka alias Sergeant Elpitiya v. The Director General of Commission to Investigate Allegation of Bribery and Corruption [2010] BLR 67
standard_of_review_applied: The COA reviewed the evidence for reasonableness and applied the standard of proof beyond reasonable doubt.

judges: Sampath B. Abayakoon, J. | P. Kumararatnam, J.
brief_facts_summary: Four accused were charged for illegally transporting Jak timber logs. The driver pleaded guilty, and the vehicle was confiscated. The appellant, the registered owner, claimed he was unaware and had taken precautions. The key evidence includes testimony from the appellant and a witness who hired the vehicle.
hc_judgment_summary: The High Court agreed with the Magistrate's finding of contradiction in evidence and dismissed the revision application, stating no exceptional circumstances to intervene.
grounds_of_appeal_raw_text_summary: The appellant argued that the Magistrate and High Court misdirected on the evidence, that there was no material contradiction, and that he had taken due precautions and was unaware of the illegal activity.
grounds_of_appeal_structured_notes: Misdirection on evidence analysis | Failure to properly assess contradictions | Error in applying burden of proof
witness_evidence_analysis_summary: The Court of Appeal found that the Magistrate misanalyzed the evidence, and there was no material contradiction between the appellant and the witness. The prosecution did not materially challenge the evidence.
